Title: introduce-server-timebox-and-idempotent-cancel-fallbacks-for-streaming-compat

introduce-server-timebox-and-idempotent-cancel-fallbacks-for-streaming-compat

Context: production customers observed cases where long lived streaming sessions (tool calls + structured output) were left in indeterminate states after a client network disconnect or a client-initiated Cancel. Motivation: we need a predictable server-side safety net that bounds resource residency time, ensures tool-call idempotency when retries/resume occur, and provides a clear fallback path (trimmed response + final event) that OpenAI-compatible clients can rely on. This PR implements a server-side streaming timebox (configurable per-route) that gracefully converts oversized/inflight streams into a final 'timeboxed' terminal event, augments client-cancel handling to be idempotent across reconnect/resume windows, and plumbs a compact resume token that includes tool-call idempotency metadata. Summary of changes: 1) stream manager: add configurable timebox_ms and a deterministic finalization path that emits a structured terminal event ("__redwood_timeboxed__") with a compact summary; 2) openai adapter: interpret Cancel events as idempotent markers tied to resume tokens; retries within the resume window will deduplicate tool calls using a request-level id; 3) tooling: map function-call invocations to idempotency keys and persist minimal call metadata to the stream checkpoint to support safe resume; 4) API: extend the OpenAI-compat streaming spec with two optional fields in the final event (timeboxed=true, resume_hint) without breaking existing clients; 5) tests & docs: integration tests for flaky network simulated disconnects and release notes for the behavior and recommended operational knobs. Rollout plan: feature guarded behind a runtime flag and route-level config. Backwards compatibility: default behavior is unchanged unless a route opts-in. Checklist: [x] unit tests for stream finalizer [x] integration test that simulates disconnect + resume [x] docs page and compatibility notes [x] change log entry. Related: ENG-1023 (stream lifecycle SLO), SUP-4572 (customer incident replicant).
stream: add timebox lifecycle and finalizer logic (runtime)
compat: interpret cancel as idempotent marker with resume token (openai adapter)
stream: persist minimal tool-call idempotency metadata to checkpoints
api: add 'timeboxed' and 'resume_hint' flags to streaming final event schema
tests: integration tests for disconnect/resume/timebox behavior
docs: add streaming-lifecycle/timebox operational runbook
Ava Chen (2026-02-19): Nice approach. Two asks: 1) can we make the default timebox conservative (eg 30s) and 2) add metrics for timebox-triggered finalizations so SRE can track this?
Marcus Li (2026-02-19): Thanks Ava. Default is 30s in the flags; added metric 'stream.timebox_finalized' with labels route/model; will push change.
Diego Martinez (2026-02-20): Concern about persisting tool-call metadata on every request path. How big can the checkpoint grow? What retention semantics?
Marcus Li (2026-02-20): Checkpoints store only a 64-bit idempotency hash + 3-field small metadata (call name, timestamp, status). We GC per-checkpoint on successful terminalization. Size is bounded and measured in tests.
Priya Nair (2026-02-21): Integration test flaky on first run, failure in 'resume-after-disconnect' when the simulated retry arrives slightly after timebox expiry. Can we make the test deterministic?
Marcus Li (2026-02-21): Fixed by injecting a deterministic clock to the stream finalizer and making the resume window configurable for tests. Reran CI locally.
SRE Team (CI bot) (2026-02-24): One lint failure in openai_compat_stream.go for an unused variable — fixed in follow-up commit.
Ava Chen (2026-02-24): Approved after last fixes. Marking as ready to merge.
Server-side streaming timebox (route-configurable) that guarantees a graceful terminal event when streams exceed a configured residency time. Client Cancel events are now idempotent within a short resume window; resume tokens include minimal idempotency hints to avoid duplicated tool/function executions on reconnect. Default behavior unchanged unless enabled per-route.

Title: Fix streaming metering edge cases: ensure accurate per-stream token accounting

Fix streaming metering edge cases: ensure accurate per-stream token accounting

Summary:

We observed multiple customer reports and internal alerts where streaming calls (server-sent chunks / chunked HTTP and websockets) result in incorrect billed token counts. Errors fall into 3 buckets: (1) reconnects and resumed streams cause duplicated output accounting, (2) partial chunk flushes (e.g., early truncation + later finalization) lead to mismatched input/output attribution, (3) aborted streams produce invoiceable tokens with no corresponding completion record.

Goals:
- Ensure per-stream token accounting is deterministic and idempotent across reconnections and retries.
- Maintain compatibility with existing non-streaming metering pipeline.
- Add end-to-end tests and monitoring to prevent regressions.

Background & root cause hypothesis:
- The metering pipeline currently increments token counts on two different events: chunk_emitted (client-facing streaming chunk) and response_finalized (completion). When a client reconnects, the runtime replays pending chunks; both the replay and the original recorded chunks were persisted, yielding duplicate counts.
- Streaming proxies sometimes split logical tokens across frames; our token counter treats frames as independent events, so partial frames can be double-counted when reassembly occurs later.
- Aborted streams (network failure) emit chunk events but never reach the reconciliation job that marks them as non-billable or reconciled.

Proposed design (high level):
1) Introduce a server-assigned stream_session_id for every streaming session. This id is authoritative for metering and survives client reconnects when a resume is requested.
2) Attach per-chunk sequence_id and running_token_offset (both integers) to every chunk event emitted by the runtime. Metering service will only accept chunk events with monotonically increasing sequence_id per stream_session_id. Duplicates or replays with the same sequence_id are ignored.
3) Update event schema (old events remain readable): add stream_session_id:string, sequence_id:int, final_chunk:boolean, token_count:int, running_token_offset:int. Implement backward-compat handling for non-stream events (null session id).
4) Reconciliation rules: if a stream_session_id is abandoned (no final_chunk within X minutes), create a "timed-out" reconciliation record that credits back incomplete or uncertain tokens based on policy (e.g., only bill committed final tokens).
5) Add a short-lived in-memory cache (LRU per runtime node) of recent (stream_session_id, last_sequence_id) to quickly drop duplicate replays at the source and avoid persistent DB writes.
6) Billing ledger: make adjustments idempotent by recording operation_id for every increment so replays can be ignored. Operation_id = stream_session_id + sequence_id.

Trade-offs discussed:
- Option A (chosen): server-generated stream_session_id + sequence_id gives strong correctness and is straightforward to enforce at metering layer, but requires a small runtime schema change and minor protocol bump for streaming clients.
- Option B (rely on client idempotency tokens): avoids touching runtime but depends on diverse client implementations and is brittle for third-party SDKs.
- Option C (post-hoc heuristics in reconciliation): low runtime change but yields possible over/under-billing windows and complex refund processes.

2026-03-04 — Decision note: Use sequence_id + running_token_offset. Sequence_id guarantees monotonicity; running_token_offset allows safe reconciliation of split-frame tokens. We will ignore older events if sequence_id <= last_seen.
2026-03-05 — Engineering: Implemented event schema changes in metering service (branch: feat/stream-session-metering). Added DB migration to add OperationRecords with operation_id. Running unit tests locally.
2026-03-07 — QA: Added e2e test harness that simulates network flaps and resume semantics. Found one edge case where unordered delivery from proxy hit the metering service out-of-order — fixed by buffering until sequence_id gap is filled or timeout.
2026-03-09 — PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/11842 — metering: add stream_session_id and sequence_id enforcement. Includes unit tests and integration test harness. Requesting runtime review.

Title: Add streaming-chunk-boundary-metrics and ephemeral-cache-guilt-scorer

Add streaming-chunk-boundary-metrics and ephemeral-cache-guilt-scorer

Context: Streaming inference workloads have an additional source of latency variance and token-cost leakage at chunk boundaries (when client chunks are concatenated or re-streamed). Existing token-level telemetry aggregates over whole invocations and misses short-lived boundary effects that drive tail latency and double-counted KV cache churn. Motivation: provide operators and SREs a lightweight signal to separate steady-state token cost from boundary-induced overheads, and a heuristic 'ephemeral-cache guilt' score to identify noisy clients or prompt patterns that cause excessive cache churn. What this PR does: 1) Introduces a set of streaming-chunk-boundary metrics emitted from the streaming runtime: stream.chunk_boundary.count, stream.chunk_boundary.latency_ms_p50/p90/p99, stream.chunk_boundary.token_duplication_rate. 2) Adds ephemeral_cache.guilt_score as a composite metric (0..1) computed from short windowed KV miss rates, repeated prefix patterns, and intra-invocation re-fetch counts. 3) Exposes both signals to the observability pipeline with labels: tenant_id, model, route, stream_session_id, and boundary_type (client_split/server_split/retry). 4) Dashboard: new 'Streaming Chunk Health' Grafana panel group + a compact explainer panel that correlates guilt_score with per-route cost delta. 5) Alerts: a new low-noise alert rule that triggers when guilt_score > 0.6 for 5m and cost_delta > 2x baseline; alerts are auto-suppressed for sessions marked synthetic. 6) SDK telemetry: updates to the JS/TS SDK to tag streaming calls with chunk_id and to opt-in to boundary metrics via a boolean flag (off by default). Checklist: - [x] Runtime metric emission hooks implemented and tested with unit tests - [x] Guilt scorer proto and implementation with deterministic tests - [x] Added OpenTelemetry mapping and metric names to docs/config - [x] Grafana panels and dashboards committed as JSON - [x] Alerting rules added to repo and tested in staging - [x] SDK change behind feature flag; example added to quickstarts Rollout plan: feature gated in main branch but disabled by default. Will enable in staging for 48h with dashboard dashboards/streaming-health-staging.json, then progressively enable for 10% of production streaming sessions using server-side config. If guilt_score produces >5% false positives after 24h, rollout will be reverted. Testing: synthetic replay harness used to create chunk boundary cases (split at token offsets: 1, 16, 64) and validated metric stability and guardrails. Linear/Related: ENG-4321 (streaming SLO decomposition), ENG-4399 (kv-cache followups). Notes: This metric family is intentionally compact to avoid a cardinality explosion; boundary_type is a controlled enum. The guilt score is heuristic by design and is documented in docs/observability/streaming-guilt.md. Implementation details and rationale included in the PR description body below.
Added new streaming-chunk-boundary metrics and an ephemeral-cache guilt scorer. These metrics enable fine-grained SLO attribution for streaming workloads and a new signal to auto-mute noisy cache churn. No behavioral changes to public APIs.

Title: Fix throughput metric double-counting for streaming responses

Fix throughput metric double-counting for streaming responses

Problem: Dedicated throughput SLO reporting was overcounting tokens for streaming requests. We were incrementing `deployment_tokens_generated_total` per-stream chunk (delta tokens) and then incrementing again on stream completion using the final `usage.completion_tokens` value. For non-streaming, the completion-path increment is correct; for streaming, it results in ~2x token totals (shape/model dependent) and skews derived tokens/sec in the SLO evaluator + dashboards.

Customer/ops impact: This primarily affects Dedicated throughput SLO compliance tracking (tokens/sec floor) and internal saturation indicators. It also contributed to customer confusion when comparing Console throughput graphs vs request-level `usage` totals (see SUP-18510). Billing exports are not impacted (billing uses metering events, not the SLO throughput counters).

Fix: Make streaming accounting single-source-of-truth by only emitting token increments from the streaming path, and skipping the completion-path increment when `streaming=true`. Additionally, guard against duplicate “final chunk” emission by tracking `last_emitted_completion_tokens` on the stream session and only emitting positive deltas.

What changed: - `api-gateway`: adjust token accounting so the completion handler does not increment throughput counters for streaming requests; the counter is incremented only via the stream chunk emitter. - `telemetry`: add explicit `streaming` + `accounting_source` labels to aid debugging (chunk vs completion). - tests: add unit tests for streaming lifecycle (N chunks + final usage) asserting exact token totals; add regression test covering the previously failing scenario where both chunk deltas and final usage were emitted.

Rollout notes: This changes the magnitude of streaming throughput counters immediately on deploy (expected ~-50% for affected traffic). SRE/Obs have been pinged to annotate the Dedicated throughput SLO dashboard and ignore pre/post comparisons for 24h.

Follow-ups (not in this PR): 1) Backfill/annotation for SLO reports that span the deploy window (SRE to decide). 2) Consider moving all throughput SLO computations to request-level usage events once metering latency is acceptable.

Validation: - Replayed a production trace set in staging (mixed streaming/non-streaming) and confirmed `deployment_tokens_generated_total` matches sum(usage.completion_tokens) within expected variance from retries/cancels. - Verified SLO evaluator output for a known Dedicated deployment no longer shows >2x spikes during high streaming traffic.
Sean Gallagher (SRE): Can you confirm this won’t undercount if the client disconnects before the final usage payload? Author: Yes—stream chunks already carry deltas. If the stream ends early, we count what was actually emitted; the completion-path increment was previously attempting to “catch up” but was double-counting when the final usage did arrive.
Allison Grant (Observability): Please add a label so we can distinguish stream chunk vs completion in case we have to debug again. Author: Added `accounting_source={chunk|completion}` and ensured completion source is only used for non-streaming.
Sergio Costa (Obs): Dashboard query expects `deployment_tokens_generated_total` without extra labels; will this break it? Author: Counter name unchanged; new labels are additive with stable defaults. Queries aggregating by deployment_id remain valid.
Owen Phillips (Support Eng): SUP-18510 mentions a mismatch between Console and customer-side totals; are we aligning with `usage.completion_tokens`? Author: Yes. For streaming, the sum of chunk deltas equals the final usage total (modulo cancels). We now avoid adding the final total on top.

Title: rework-sse-timestamping-and-unambiguous-delimiter-handling

rework-sse-timestamping-and-unambiguous-delimiter-handling

Motivation: In long-lived SSE connections we continue to see glitches where a delimiter ("

") or event boundary can be interpreted inconsistently across proxies and our client reassembly, producing partial JSON objects or ordering anomalies when packetization aligns with UTF-8 multi-byte boundaries. This PR reworks how we mark and reassemble fragments to make consumer-side reassembly deterministic even when fragments arrive out of logical order or are split on codepoint boundaries.

What this changes: adds a compact per-fragment monotonic timestamp + seq-offset header emitted by the server runtime, applies a normalization pass that collapses ambiguous delimiter runs into a canonical marker before parsing, and hardens the stream parser to accept and reorder within a short, bounded window using timestamps rather than relying solely on arrival ordering. Also instruments a new set of observability metrics for fragment reorder, delimiter-normalization rate, and reassembly retries.

Checklist:
- [x] Reassembly algorithm with timestamp window and idempotent normalization implemented in runtime stream layer
- [x] Backwards-compatible framing header (optional; parser tolerates both old and new framing)
- [x] Unit tests covering UTF-8 split boundaries and proxy-induced chunk reordering
- [x] Integration test against nginx proxy emulation and node/ts client harness
- [x] Added metrics and dashboards for fragment reordering and normalization events
- [x] Release note entry prepared

Rollout plan: feature gated by runtime flag (sse.fragment_ts=on). Default enabled in canary and dedicated, monitor metrics for 72h, then flip global flag. If regressions observed, runtime will fall back to legacy framing for affected connections and emit a debug trace to support.

Backward compatibility: The framing header is optional and ignored by older clients. Normalization step is idempotent and only affects internal stream boundary resolution; it does not mutate payload content outside of delimiting sequences.

Related work: Builds on ENG-1209 (previous delimiter fixes) but differs by moving to timestamp/small-offset ordering rather than larger sequence windows. Linked Linear items: ENG-1347, ENG-1372. Support ticket SUP-8821 repro included in tests.

Stabilize SSE stream reassembly by introducing per-fragment monotonic timestamps and deterministic delimiter normalization. Addresses rare partial-JSON emission and out-of-order event delivery under heavy backpressure. No public API changes.
Connor Lee: Nice approach. Two questions: (1) how does this behave with replayed fragments from proxies that buffer and retransmit? (2) Do we need an escape if payload legitimately contains the delimiter sequence?
Asha Patel: For (1) we use a short monotonic window (300ms by default) and also detect replays by identical fragment payload+seq checksum; replayed fragments outside the window are treated as duplicates and dropped. For (2) delimiter normalization only runs on the stream framing layer before payload parsing and respects explicit "data:" event prefixes; we added tests for payloads with embedded delimiter-like sequences.
Maya Singh: Can you add a telemetry tag to connect fragment reorders back to connection id and upstream proxy?
Asha Patel: Added r.conn_id tag to fragment_reorder metric and a debug trace emitted when reorder_count > 3 in a minute.

Title: Hosted SSE reconnect policy and partial-chunk reconciliation

Hosted SSE reconnect policy and partial-chunk reconciliation

Multiple customers reported truncated or duplicated SSE streaming responses after intermittent TCP disconnects. Symptoms differ across clients: some observe steady partial-chunk duplication, others see missing tails of responses and then a sudden short backfill. This ticket centralizes the investigation and implements a server-side reconnect and chunk-reconciliation policy for hosted API streams so customer apps observe fewer partial outputs and are able to recover without manual retry hacks.
1) Use hosted API streaming endpoint with message-level sequence IDs enabled in header
2) Send a long streaming generation (>= 1024 tokens) with continuous SSE output
3) Inject a TCP disconnect at random token boundary (simulate flaky network)
4) Reconnect client immediately and resume stream using existing client resume token
5) Observe either duplicated chunks, truncated final tokens, or out-of-order chunks depending on timing and client backoff behavior
Race between server token emission and connection teardown + weak resume handshake semantics. Server sometimes assigns sequence numbers before KV cache commit and, on quick reconnects, will replay in-flight chunks or drop final partial buffer. Client resume token lacks definitive last-ack offset, so reconciliation relies on best-effort matching which fails in edge timings.
Add server-side durable stream-offset ack: persist last-committed token offset before emitting 'event: data' boundary
Introduce explicit resume-handshake: client includes last-seen-offset and server returns canonical next-offset; if mismatch, server emits backfill of missing tokens instead of blind replay
Change SSE buffering to flush safe-chunk boundaries only (avoid splitting multibyte tokens across events)
Add lightweight idempotency markers on each chunk (stream-uuid + sequence) to dedupe out-of-order replays
Compatibility mode: opt-in header for Dedicated/Private that keeps old behavior for on-prem customers during rollout
1) Implement durable offset ack and handshake in staging behind feature flag
2) Run regression tests and chaos network test suite (10k short disconnects simulated)
3) Canary deploy to 5% of hosted traffic with header opt-in for affected customers
4) Monitor dedupe rate, backfill frequency, and customer error reports for 72 hours
5) Gradual ramp to 100% with kill-switch and incremental metrics gating
Disable feature-flag and revert runtime routing to previous emitter. If partial rollbacks required, toggle canary masks per-region until effect is mitigated. Emergency revert PR ready: runtime/revert/ENG-24876. Notify affected customers when rollback occurs.
Unit tests for commit-before-emit ordering
Integration test: simulated reconnect with randomized offsets validates backfill/seq correctness
E2E with official JS and Python SDKs ensuring resume-handshake flows pass
Load test to validate no increase in median latency (<= +10ms target)
slo_stream_duplication_rate: query=sum(stream_events.duplicated) / sum(stream_events.emitted) by region
slo_stream_truncation_rate: query=count(stream_events.truncated) / count(stream_sessions)
customer_errors_query: logs("sse:protocol-mismatch OR sse:unexpected-truncation") | group_by(customer_id) | top(50)

No regression in 50th/95th token latency beyond +10ms from baseline
Clients (JS/Python) resume handshake passes integration tests for 1000 randomized reconnects
Customer-reported truncation incidents for affected customers drop to zero for 7 days

Trade-off: persisting offset before emit adds a small latency increase; we scoped to <= 10ms median to limit customer impact.

Title: Session watermark finality and rate-limit reconciliation for streaming metering

Session watermark finality and rate-limit reconciliation for streaming metering

Production streams occasionally produce final token charges that are later rolled back or duplicated when rate-limit backpressure and client reconnects interact with our provisional-crediting path. Root cause appears to be a mismatch between the session-level watermark (what we consider "finalized" for metering) and the rate-limiter's hold/release semantics for multiplexed connections. This causes customers to see transient overcharges followed by retroactive credits, which undermines trust and increases support load.
Open a long-lived multiplexed websocket session with 3 concurrent streams using the streaming API
Trigger a burst: send a large prompt that causes server-side batching and a short-lived rate-limit enforcement window
Simulate a network blip causing client reconnect that resumes the same session id and replays pending chunks
Observe token ledger entries: duplicate finalization events, provisional credits not reconciled until a delayed backfill task runs
High: affects billing accuracy for long-running streaming sessions under bursty traffic. Several enterprise customers reported unexpected credit adjustments and opened support tickets. Financial exposure is bounded but reputational impact is material.
Introduce a deterministic session-finality watermarking algorithm plus a rate-limit-aware checkpoint handshake so that token finalization only occurs when both: (a) the session watermark advances past the fragment, and (b) the rate-limiter has acknowledged the request as committed (or the session is explicitly tombstoned). Add a telemetry counter for provisional vs finalized credits and a short-term backfill job to reconcile existing drift.
Session_finalized_watermark metric accurately monotonically advances per-session; no final token entry is emitted for a fragment until watermark and rate-limiter commit signals are observed
Idempotency key semantics preserved across reconnects: replayed fragments do not create duplicate finalized charges
New dashboard shows provisional_credit_count and final_credit_count per session and alerts when provisional > final for > 5m
Backfill reconciler runs and reduces number of outstanding provisional credits for impacted sessions by >= 90% in staging
Automated e2e test that simulates reconnect+burst verifies no duplicate final charges
Use a lightweight vector-clock-like watermark per session: (last_committed_offset, last_seen_offset, tombstone_flag). This avoids cross-session global locks and keeps memory bounded.
Rate-limiter will emit a commit token (rate_commit_id) when a request is accepted from the queue; metering will join on rate_commit_id before emitting final ledger rows.
To avoid latency regressions we will allow provisional credits to be shown to the console immediately but mark them as provisional; finalization path must be idempotent and cheap (single conditional write with compare-and-swap on session watermark).
Backfill job will scan sessions with provisional credits older than 2 minutes and attempt deterministic reconciliation using delivery receipts and stored fragment hashes.
Add session_watermark data structure to session store and expose atomic CAS endpoint (ENG-403218-1)
Instrument rate-limiter to emit rate_commit_id on accept and wire into metering pipeline (ENG-403218-2)
Introduce provisional_credit flag on ledger rows and a background reconciler that attempts commit -> finalize transitions (ENG-403218-3)
Add e2e test harness that simulates multiplexed reconnects with replay and verifies final ledger state (ENG-403218-4)
Update console to surface provisional vs finalized credits and add an alert rule (ENG-403218-5)
Unit tests for watermark CAS semantics including concurrent increments and tombstone behavior
Integration tests: simulate client reconnects, replayed fragments, and rate-limiter-induced holds; assert no duplicate final ledger rows
Load test: verify no more than 2% latency regression on median request path with watermark checks enabled
Staging backfill run on snapshot of impacted sessions and verification against ground-truth from logs
Feature-flag the new finalization join; default false
Deploy watermark/CAS endpoint and rate-limiter commit emitter to canary cluster; run synthetic reconnect tests
Enable feature flag for 5% of streaming traffic with monitoring of provisional>final delta and error rates
If stable for 48h, ramp to 50% then 100% and schedule backfill run during a low-traffic window
Post-rollout: run reconciliation audits and communicate adjustments to billing/support as needed

Drive spec: https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/folders/0B_example/session-watermarking-spec.pdf
Dashboard (staging): https://dashboards.redwood.ai/d/streams/provisional-vs-final

Title: Tiered SLO definitions (Hosted vs Dedicated): SLIs, targets, exclusions, and reporting windows

Tiered SLO definitions (Hosted vs Dedicated): SLIs, targets, exclusions, and reporting windows

## Purpose
This page defines the canonical Service Level Indicators (SLIs) and Service Level Objectives (SLOs) for Redwood Inference’s customer-facing inference paths across **Hosted (shared)** and **Dedicated (reserved capacity)** tiers.

These definitions are the source of truth for:
- SLO dashboards and alerting (burn-rate)
- Error budget computation (rolling windows)
- Product/Sales alignment (SLO → SLA mapping)
- Incident thresholds tied to budget burn

> Note: Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) is out of scope for enforcement in this phase. We reference it only where definitions should remain compatible.

---

## Scope
### In-scope request paths
Measurement covers the full customer request path:
1) API Gateway (edge) request acceptance
2) Routing/control plane policy evaluation
3) Model serving request path (including queuing / batching)
4) Response emission (final response for non-streaming; stream events for streaming)

### In-scope endpoint classes
We group endpoints into three endpoint classes for tiered SLOs:
- **Chat/Completions (non-streaming)**: `POST /v1/chat/completions` and `POST /v1/completions` with `stream=false`
- **Chat/Completions (streaming)**: same endpoints with `stream=true`
- **Embeddings**: `POST /v1/embeddings`

Reranking and other specialized endpoints are tracked but not included in this SLO set (future doc).

---

## Tier and labeling rules (must be true for SLO accounting)
All SLI events MUST be tagged at ingress and preserved through routing/fallback:
- `deployment_tier`: `hosted` | `dedicated`
- `region`: Redwood region identifier (see below)
- `endpoint_class`: `chat_nonstream` | `chat_stream` | `embeddings`
- `route`: stable route identifier (low-cardinality)
- `model_family`: stable family identifier (low-cardinality; e.g., `llama3`, `qwen2`, `mistral`)

Dedicated requests additionally carry:
- `account_id` (restricted access in dashboards; do not use for global recording rules)

Reference: ADR-0142 (tier-aware tagging at ingress).

---

## Supported regions (for SLO reporting)
SLOs are computed and reported **per region** and **per tier**.

Regions in this rollout:
- `us-east-1`
- `us-west-2`
- `eu-west-1`

Rollups:
- **Regional SLO**: primary enforcement surface (alerts, error budgets)
- **Global rollup**: informational only for Hosted; Dedicated global rollups are used in exec reporting but do not replace regional enforcement

---

## Canonical SLIs
We track three primary SLI families:
1) Request success rate (availability / error-rate)
2) End-to-end latency (percentiles + good-event coverage)
3) Streaming reliability (disconnect/error events)

### 1) Request success rate (Availability SLI)
**Intent:** Measure the fraction of eligible requests that complete successfully from the customer’s perspective.

**SLI definition (event-based):**
- **Total events**: all *SLO-eligible* requests reaching the API gateway for the endpoint class and tier.
- **Good events**: requests that return a successful response status and are not classified as platform errors.

**What counts as “bad” (counts against availability):**
- Any **5xx** returned by gateway, routing, or serving (includes `502`, `503`, `504`)
- Any **platform-generated 4xx** that indicates platform failure or overload *when not attributable to customer configuration*, specifically:
  - `429` with reason `overload_shed` (see exclusions below for quota/rate-limits)
  - `408` if emitted by gateway due to upstream timeout (rare; generally maps to `504`)

**What counts as “good”:**
- `2xx` responses for non-streaming
- For streaming: an established stream that completes normally (see streaming SLI for additional failure accounting)

**Example formula (PromQL-style, illustrative):**
- `availability = good_requests / eligible_requests`
- `good_requests = sum(rate(rw_api_requests_total{eligible="true", outcome="success"}[window]))`
- `eligible_requests = sum(rate(rw_api_requests_total{eligible="true"}[window]))`

### 2) Latency SLIs (End-to-end)
We publish and alert on **p50/p95/p99** latency, and we compute an **event-based good-latency SLI** for error budgets.

**Latency measurement points:**
- Start: `gateway_request_received_timestamp`
- End (non-streaming): `gateway_response_completed_timestamp`
- End (streaming TTFT): first token/first SSE data event emitted to client

**Latency SLIs reported:**
- **Non-streaming latency**: `e2e_latency_ms`
- **Streaming time-to-first-token (TTFT)**: `ttft_ms`
- **Streaming inter-token gap**: `inter_token_gap_ms` (computed on stream events)

**SLO-eligible latency population (guardrails):**
To avoid a single pathological request dominating the percentile distribution, latency SLO eligibility applies only when:
- Request is SLO-eligible (see Exclusions)
- `input_tokens <= 8,192` (measured/estimated at ingress)
- `max_output_tokens <= 2,048` (declared parameter)
- For embeddings: `input_tokens <= 16,384`

Requests outside these limits are still served and measured, but excluded from latency SLO accounting (availability still applies unless otherwise excluded).

**Event-based good-latency SLI (for budgets):**
- `good_latency = count(latency_ms <= threshold_ms) / count(eligible_latency_requests)`

We still publish p50/p95/p99 as primary observability signals; the budget uses the threshold-based SLI to support burn-rate math and consistent policy.

### 3) Streaming reliability SLI
**Intent:** capture stream health beyond HTTP status codes (e.g., mid-stream disconnects).

**Definition:** For streaming requests that successfully establish a stream, we count a stream as **bad** if the stream terminates unexpectedly due to server-side or upstream failures.

**Bad stream outcomes (count against streaming reliability):**
- Server-side disconnect with `termination_reason in {upstream_reset, serving_crash, gateway_timeout, internal_error}`
- Stream error event emitted by server prior to completion

**Excluded (do NOT count against streaming reliability):**
- Client abort / client disconnect (explicitly detected)
- Customer-requested cancellation (SDK cancellation)

**Illustrative formula:**
- `stream_reliability = 1 - (bad_streams / established_streams)`

---

## Exclusions (canonical)
Exclusions apply to SLO calculations to avoid charging the platform for customer-caused or explicitly non-service-impact outcomes.

### Excluded from ALL SLIs (availability + latency + streaming)
- Invalid requests: `400` schema/validation errors
- Auth errors: `401`, `403`
- Not found / wrong path: `404`
- Explicit customer quota or plan enforcement:
  - `429` with reason `quota_exceeded`
  - `429` with reason `rate_limit_customer`
- Requests blocked due to customer safety settings/policies (customer-configured): `4xx` with `policy_origin=customer`

### Excluded from latency + streaming only (still count for availability unless noted)
- Client aborts / disconnects prior to completion (classified as `outcome=client_abort`)
- Customer-requested cancellations (SDK cancellation)

### NOT excluded (counts against platform)
- `429` with reason `overload_shed` (platform overload protection)
- Any `5xx` and gateway/serving timeouts
- Routing fallback that returns an error (fallback itself is not an exclusion)

---

## Retries, fallbacks, and deduplication rules
To keep accounting consistent and avoid “double charging” when retries occur:
- We compute SLIs on the **final attempt** when the SDK/gateway attaches a stable `request_id` and monotonic `attempt`.
- Default aggregation uses `request_id` deduplication where available; otherwise we use `attempt="final"` tagging from gateway.

Fallback/routing rules:
- If a request is served by a fallback model/region and succeeds, it is **good** for availability.
- Latency is attributed to the **customer-visible tier and region** at ingress (i.e., what the customer targeted), not the internal fallback destination.
- We annotate fallback usage separately (not part of SLO numerator/denominator), so we can correlate SLO risk with mitigation actions.

Reference: SLI specification for gateway/routing (observability standards page).

---

## Reporting windows and aggregation
### Standard windows
- **SLO compliance reporting:** rolling **28 days** (default), updated every 5 minutes
- **Error budget computation:** rolling **28 days** (matches SLO compliance)
- **Alerting (burn-rate):** multi-window alerting as defined in ADR-0143 (e.g., fast burn on 5m/1h and slow burn on 6h/3d)

### Aggregation levels
- SLOs are computed **per** (`deployment_tier`, `region`, `endpoint_class`).
- Dedicated dashboards additionally support per-`account_id` views with RBAC.

### Minimum traffic for latency percentiles
Latency percentiles are only considered stable when there is sufficient traffic:
- If fewer than **300 eligible requests** occur in a 30-minute period for a slice, we show percentiles but do not page on percentile-only anomalies. (Availability/stream reliability still applies.)

---

Title: Instrument canonical per-deployment throughput metrics (deployment_id/model/region) for Dedicated SLO

Instrument canonical per-deployment throughput metrics (deployment_id/model/region) for Dedicated SLO

Context / why
We are formalizing a Dedicated throughput SLO and need a single canonical throughput signal that is attributable to a specific Dedicated deployment. Today we have a mix of per-pod / per-cluster perf counters and some request logs, but nothing that can be used as a stable SLO input for: (a) per-customer reporting (deployment_id), (b) tier-aware dashboards, and (c) SLO burn-rate alerts. This ticket adds per-deployment throughput metrics with consistent token accounting semantics (esp. streaming) and the required labels.

Scope
- Emit canonical throughput “inputs” at the inference gateway / request path for all Dedicated deployments:
  - tokens counted (input + output) with explicit definitions
  - wall clock generation time used for throughput calculations
  - request counts by completion outcome
- All metrics MUST be tagged by:
  - deployment_id (Dedicated deployment identifier; required)
  - model (canonical model slug as used in routing/catalog)
  - region (Redwood region for the serving pool)
- Provide dashboard hooks (metric names/labels/query examples) for Observability to add panels.
- Add acceptance tests and backfill documentation for metric semantics so SRE can write the SLO definition without re-litigating token accounting.

Non-goals
- This ticket does not define the final SLO thresholds or tier entitlements (handled in PM-482 / SRE SLO doc).
- This ticket does not build the full dashboards (handled by Observability). We provide stable metric contracts + sample queries.
- This ticket does not change routing behavior, admission control, or capacity policies.

Proposed metric contract (canonical)
Naming (Prometheus-style; final names can be adjusted to fit existing conventions as long as semantics match):
1) redwood_inference_generation_tokens_total
   - Type: counter
   - Value: number of tokens generated for responses (output tokens only)
   - Labels: deployment_id, model, region, streaming=(true|false)
   - Notes:
     - For streaming, increment tokens as they are flushed to the client.
     - For non-streaming, increment at request completion.

2) redwood_inference_prompt_tokens_total
   - Type: counter
   - Value: number of prompt tokens processed (input tokens)
   - Labels: deployment_id, model, region
   - Notes:
     - Includes system + user messages and any tool/function call arguments included in the prompt.

3) redwood_inference_generation_time_seconds_total
   - Type: counter
   - Value: wall-clock time attributable to token generation (seconds)
   - Labels: deployment_id, model, region, streaming=(true|false)
   - Definition:
     - Start: first token generation begins (post-queue, post-admission, after request assigned to a worker)
     - End: last generated token produced (or cancellation/timeout)
     - Excludes: time spent waiting in the front-door queue / admission control queue (we need a separate queue-time metric for saturation debugging, but SLO throughput should not be polluted by queue policy)

4) redwood_inference_requests_total
   - Type: counter
   - Value: number of completion/chat requests
   - Labels: deployment_id, model, region, status=(success|client_canceled|server_error|timeout|rate_limited|invalid_request)

Derived throughput (used by dashboards/SLO tooling)
- Output throughput (tokens/sec):
  sum(rate(redwood_inference_generation_tokens_total[5m])) / sum(rate(redwood_inference_generation_time_seconds_total[5m]))
- Optional “total tokens/sec” (prompt+output) for capacity planning:
  (sum(rate(redwood_inference_prompt_tokens_total[5m])) + sum(rate(redwood_inference_generation_tokens_total[5m]))) / sum(rate(redwood_inference_generation_time_seconds_total[5m]))

Rationale / semantics notes
- We will compute throughput from counters (tokens + time) instead of directly emitting tokens/sec as a gauge to avoid per-instance aggregation artifacts.
- We separate generation time from queue time so that overload protection changes do not retroactively change throughput measurement.
- We keep streaming=(true|false) to debug differences, but the canonical SLO query should aggregate both unless SRE decides otherwise.

Cardinality / performance constraints
- deployment_id is high cardinality but bounded by Dedicated footprint and required for customer attribution.
- model and region are low-ish cardinality.
- Do NOT add request_id or customer_id labels.
- Ensure metrics are emitted once per request per component (avoid double-counting across gateway + worker).

Implementation plan
1) Instrumentation location
- Emit counters in the request lifecycle code path where we already have:
  - resolved deployment_id (Dedicated only)
  - resolved model slug (post-routing)
  - region (serving pool region)
  - token counts from tokenizer + runtime
- For streaming, tokens are often counted at both “generated” and “sent” layers. We must choose one canonical point.
  - Decision: count output tokens at the flush-to-client boundary to reflect what the customer receives and to align with billing token accounting.

2) Token accounting sources
- Prompt tokens: from request normalization/tokenization stage.
- Output tokens: from streaming chunk encoder / final response serialization (single source of truth).
- Generation time: measured around the model execution phase (post-admission). Use monotonic clock.

3) Dedicated vs Hosted behavior
- Emit metrics only when deployment_id is present (Dedicated deployments). No-op for hosted multi-tenant routes for now to keep cardinality manageable.
- If we later need hosted per-route metrics, we’ll do that in a separate ticket with sampling and different labels.

4) Dashboard hooks
- Provide a short “how to query” section to Sergio/Allison for Grafana panels:
  - throughput floor line
  - throughput observed (p50/p95 across 5m windows)
  - saturation supporting signals: queue time, admission rejects (if available)

Acceptance criteria
- Metrics are present in the metrics backend for a canary Dedicated deployment in us-east and eu-west.
- For a controlled load test (fixed prompt/response lengths), derived throughput matches expected within +/- 5% over a 10 minute window.
- Streaming and non-streaming requests produce the same total output token counts for identical prompts/max_tokens settings (no double-counting).
- Metrics include the labels deployment_id, model, region on every sample.
- SRE can write an SLO query that returns a single time series per deployment_id (after aggregation) without additional joins.
- Add automated tests:
  - Unit test: streaming path increments output tokens exactly once per token
  - Integration test: one request, validate counters increment (prompt tokens, output tokens, generation time, requests_total)

Test plan (details)
- Local: run gateway with a fake streaming responder emitting N chunks; assert generation_tokens_total increases by exactly N_tokens, not 2*N.
- Staging: run k6 load against a Dedicated canary (single model pinned) and compare:
  - sum(output tokens) from logs/billing events vs counter delta
  - generation_time_seconds_total monotonic increase and reasonable per-request averages
- Regression: add a golden test for a known streaming payload that previously caused token double-counting.

Operational notes
- These metrics will be used for customer-facing reporting in the Console and for alerting. Treat any semantic change as a breaking change requiring review from SRE + Observability.
- Add a short docstring block in code referencing the Dedicated throughput SLO initiative and where to find the SLO definition / ADR.

Links
- Initiative ticket: PM-482 Dedicated throughput SLO and tier definitions
- Related engineering work: ENG-19288 burn-rate alerts, ENG-19257 tier-aware admission control
- Expected PR: PR-19321 add deployment throughput metrics

Open questions
- Do we want to include caching/batching effects explicitly (e.g., cache_hit label)? Current proposal: no; too high cardinality and confusing for SLO.
- Do we need to split “generated tokens” vs “delivered tokens” for streaming disconnects? Current proposal: requests_total will capture client_canceled, but output tokens counted are only delivered tokens. Confirm with SRE if SLO should treat client cancels as excluded.

Requested reviewers
- Aisha Bello (SRE implementation)
- Sergio Costa (Observability dashboards)
- Nadia Rahman (metering/cost attribution)

Title: session-reassembler-and-fine-grained-latency-contributors-dashboard

session-reassembler-and-fine-grained-latency-contributors-dashboard

Motivation: debugging SLO regressions often requires stitching together fragments from frontend request IDs, gateway hops, router handoffs, and backend runtime spans. Current dashboards surface aggregate per-route latency and token cost but lack an easy way to answer: which execution stage contributed most to tail latency for a given session or user flow? This PR introduces a session reassembler that groups spans and logs into session-level traces, computes a latency contribution matrix per-stage, and surfaces the results in a new dashboard with drilldowns. Design: 1) Session reassembler: deterministic session keys are computed from request headers (x-session-id when present), fallback to hashed {client_ip,user_agent,first-7-chars-of-request_id} for best-effort reconstruction. The reassembler runs as a bounded streaming transformer in the tracing pipeline and emits enriched spans tagged with session_id and stage_ordinal. 2) Late-arrival span stitching: implement a 30s buffer window with eventual reconciliation to handle spans that arrive after initial aggregation. Reconciled sessions are exported as session_digests which include per-stage p50/p90/p99 latencies and token counts. 3) Latency contribution matrix: for each session_digest we compute a normalized contribution vector across stages (gateway, auth, preproc, router, runtime-queue, runtime-exec, postproc). Matrices are aggregated into reservoir sketches to keep cardinality bounded. 4) Dashboard and alerting: new dashboard panel "Session Latency Matrix" visualizes dominant contributors for recent sessions and supports filtering by customer, route, and model. Introduce an SLO smoothing policy that uses session-level p95 of contribution instead of raw endpoint p95 to reduce noisy alerts from noisy frontends. 5) Backwards compatibility and opt-in: the reassembler is behind a rollout flag in the observability config; default is disabled. Customers can opt-in per-tenant. Rollout plan: enable in staging for 48 hours, shadow in prod for 7 days, then enable for 10% of traffic with metric gates. Telemetry: we emit reassembler.metrics.{sessions_processed,stitch_reconciliations,session_digest_size} and tagging on traces with session.id and stage.rank. Rollout notes: this PR adds additional memory for the buffering stage; sizing guidance documented in observability/README. Security: session keys do not materialize raw client_ip in exported payloads unless tenant-level PII flag is set; by default keys are salted and one-way hashed. Related work: this complements ENG-1942 (sampling improvements) and OBS-73 (session-based alerting).
feat(observability): add session reassembler transformer and session_digest export; feat(tracing): late-arrival stitcher and reconciliation; perf(tracing): reservoir sketch for contribution matrices; ui(dashboards): session latency matrix and drilldowns; docs: rollout and sizing guidance; test: unit+integration for reassembler and reconciliation
Aidan Keller: Can you clarify the semantics of the fallback session key? Maya Chen: Fallback uses a salted hash of client_ip+user_agent+req_prefix; salted per-tenant and not reversible. Priya Nair: The 30s buffer seems small for some tenants with eventual log shipping; any plan? Maya Chen: We reconciled to make the window configurable and added a reconnect/reconciliation metric; default remains 30s to bound memory. Diego Ruiz: Reservoir sketches look good but please add a test for cardinality drift. Maya Chen: Added tests to integration suite and a benchmark in scripts/size_estimator. Priya Nair: Approve after CI pass. Aidan Keller: Left a small nit on the UI (color scale) — updated in follow-up commit. Diego Ruiz: Verified metrics emission and endorses merge.
Adds an opt-in session reassembler for reconstructing traces across hops, per-session latency contribution matrices, a new Session Latency Matrix dashboard with drilldowns, SLO smoothing policy using session-level contributions, and observability metrics for rollout and sizing. No breaking changes by default; opt-in per-tenant.
Sizing guidance added under docs/observability/README.md; may require observability team to coordinate with infra for buffer memory when enabling for high-cardinality tenants.

Title: Buffered SSE window coordinator and deterministic call serializer

Buffered SSE window coordinator and deterministic call serializer

Stabilize SSE streaming by introducing a packetizer/window coordinator and deterministic call serializer to prevent partial-JSON emissions and function-call reordering on reconnect/replay.
Background: customers saw rare but high-impact cases where SSE fragment coalescing and transport-level reordering produced truncated JSON frames or out-of-order tool/function call events during reconnects and HTTP/2 headroom shifts. This PR introduces a buffered packetizer + window coordinator inside the streaming stack plus a deterministic call serializer (call-seq) and idempotency token handshake so clients and the OpenAI-compat layer can reliably resume and preserve fncall ordering. Motivation: reduce broken/partial JSON emissions, minimize application-level compensating logic, and make reconnect/replay deterministic. Implementation summary: 1) packetizer: aggregates incoming runtime tokens into bounded windows (configurable via env/route param) and emits well-formed SSE events only at window boundaries or when explicit epoch markers appear; 2) window coordinator: assigns a monotonically increasing window_id + window_checksum and exposes an optional checkpoint token (sse-checkpoint) that clients may ACK — used only for resume heuristics; 3) deterministic call serializer: when an event contains a tool/function call, serializer attaches call_meta: {call_seq, call_idempotency_token}. Calls are emitted in strict call_seq order and the OpenAI-compat adapter preserves call_seq across model fallbacks; 4) reconnect/resume behavior: on reconnect with a checkpoint, server attempts a fast-resume by replaying buffered windows from the last ACKed checkpoint. If checkpoint mismatch, server falls back to re-stream-from-start + explicit resync hint. 5) compatibility shim: openai-compat now maps call_meta to OpenAI-style function_call sentinel plus an embedded __call_seq to avoid breaking older clients. Tests & metrics: added deterministic replay unit tests, end-to-end integration that fuzzes HTTP/2 coalescing, and a perf microbenchmark to ensure added buffering does not regress 99th percentile latency in common short-response workloads. Rollout: feature guarded by route flag streaming.packetizer.enabled (default off). Progressive rollout: beta to select tenants for 48 hours, then broader ramp if no regressions. Backwards compatibility: default behavior unchanged when feature is disabled. See changed files for implementation details.
Maya Chen (review): Can we make the default packet window conservative for now (e.g., 16KB or 50ms) to avoid latency regressions on short responses? Also please add metrics for dropped partial-json events.
Priya Desai (author): Updated default to 16KB / 50ms and added metrics sse.packetizer.window_bytes and sse.packetizer.window_duration_ms. Added test that asserts no regressions for sub-1KB responses.
Ethan Li (review): Lgtm overall. A few nits: rename call_seq to __call_seq for the OpenAI shim only; ensure we don't leak internal window_id into public headers. Also please add a safety timeout to avoid indefinitely buffering a stalled connection.
Priya Desai (author): Addressed all nits: OpenAI shim uses __call_seq; window_id now only appears in internal logs and checkpoint tokens (opaque). Added 2s safety flush timeout configurable by route.
Rohan Kapoor (approval): Verified deterministic replay tests locally and ran the http2 fuzz harness. Approving pending CI green.
Feature gated; must enable streaming.packetizer.enabled per-route before traffic. Observability: new metrics and logs added; dashboards updated under Redwood Console > Streaming > Packetizer.
1) set route flag "streaming.packetizer.enabled=true"
2) monitor sse.packetizer.window_bytes and sse.packetizer.buffered_windows metric
3) if partial JSON regressions occur, set streaming.packetizer.enabled=false and file ENG ticket.

Title: Runbook Writing and Telemetry Bootcamp Curriculum — Operator Training

Runbook Writing and Telemetry Bootcamp Curriculum — Operator Training

Summary

This page documents a repeatable, instructor-led bootcamp to train platform operators and engineers to write high-quality runbooks that are telemetry-driven, testable, and maintainable. The curriculum is designed for new operators, service owners, and incident responders who will author or own runbooks for platform services (prefix cache, allocator, tenant-slicing, model-variant router).

Audience

- Platform operators and SREs
- Service owners in eng-platform and eng-serving-runtime
- Oncall engineers who respond to latency/cost incidents

Learning objectives (measurable)

1. Produce a runbook that contains a clear escalation path, data-driven detection predicates, and an operator checklist.
2. Write two telemetry queries (one metric-based, one log-based) that reliably surface the condition the runbook describes.
3. Create a synthetic verification (unit) that validates the runbook’s detection predicates against a small replay dataset.
4. Implement a post-incident update cycle and link to the action in the runbook so it can be closed by the owner.

Curriculum overview (3-day instructor-led)

Day 0 — Prework (self-paced)
- Read: "Runbook authoring and maintenance guidelines" (required).
- Complete a short quiz on SLO definitions and common platform failure modes.
- Setup: access to Grafana/Tempo, Kibana, and a sandbox tenant. Confirm permissions with infra-oncall.

Day 1 — Foundations and detection
- Morning: Lecture (1.5 hr) — Runbook structure and the telemetry-first principle.
  - Sections: Summary, Impact, Detection (metric + log predicates), Immediate actions, Escalation, Rollback, Postmortem link.
  - Example services: kv-prefix-cache, dynamic-allocator, model-variant-router.
- Lab (2.5 hr): Write detection predicates for a synthetic latency spike:
  1) Metric predicate: p95 latency > 300ms for 5m AND error rate > 1% for 2m.
  2) Log predicate: queries that include "kv-cache:miss" and "eviction-reason=reshuffle" for >50 events in 10m.
- Homework: Author a first draft runbook for a provided scenario.

Day 2 — Triage, actions, and testability
- Morning: Workshop (2 hr) — Mapping telemetry to operator actions.
  - Instrumentation checklist: SLI names, tag conventions (region, tenant_id, model_variant), and minimum retention expectations (30 days for alerts, 90 days for postmortem traces).
  - Ownership patterns: primary, secondary, oncall-runbook-maintainer.
- Lab (3 hr): Implement a synthetic verification for the runbook detection predicates using the synthetic-replay harness.
  - Deliverable: three test cases (baseline, transient spike, persistent degradation).
- Evening: Peer review session — teams exchange runbooks and provide 3 actionable comments.

Day 3 — Escalation, de-escalation, and lifecycle
- Morning: Tabletop simulation (2 hr) — live incident with operator rotation. Measured outcomes: time to detection, time to mitigate, number of escalations, checklist completeness.
- Afternoon: Retrospective (1.5 hr) — calibrate SLOs and adjust detection thresholds.
- Closing: Runbook merge checklist and post-incident update procedure.

Assessment and certification

- Pass criteria: runbook accepted in repo (PR merged), synthetic verification green, and at least one successful tabletop participation.
- Certificate: "Telemetry-Driven Runbook Author (Redwood)" valid for 18 months. Re-certification: 2-hour refresher + one tabletop.

Delivery model and resourcing

- Instructor: Platform training lead (approx. 1 dedicated trainer per cohort of 12).
- Duration: 3 days (24 total hours including pre/post work).
- Environment: sandbox cluster with one copy of kv-prefix-cache and dynamic-allocator seeded with synthetic load.
- Tools: Grafana (dashboards pre-built), Loki/Kibana, Tempo (trace slices), synthetic-replay harness (repo: infra/synthetic-replay).

Runbook template (required fields)

1) Title (single line)
2) Summary (1–2 sentences) — short impact statement
3) Owner (primary, secondary) — team and pager alias
4) Impact and user-visible symptoms — list
5) Detection
   - Metric predicate (exact expression)
   - Log predicate (example query)
   - Trace pattern (optional)
6) Immediate mitigation steps (numbered)
7) Escalation path (names/roles and contact method)
8) Safe rollback / service-level de-escalation (how to revert changes)
9) Diagnostics checklist (commands, queries, dashboard links)
10) Post-incident required actions (TTR SLA for update: 7 days)
11) Verification tests (links to synthetic tests)
12) Related runbooks and runbook-ids

Required telemetry examples (copyable)

- Metric predicate (PromQL):
  sum(rate(request_duration_ms_bucket{job="kv-prefix-cache",le="0.3"}[5m])) by (region) / sum(rate(request_duration_ms_count{job="kv-prefix-cache"}[5m])) by (region) > 0.95
- Log predicate (Loki):
  {app="kv-prefix-cache",env="prod"} |= "kv-cache:miss" | json | tenant_id!="" | count_over_time(10m) > 50
- Trace predicate (Tempo/trace): search for spans with operation.name =~ "kv-prefix-cache.*evict" and duration > 100ms, aggregated by tenant_id.

Synthetic verification example (bash)

- Reproduce a persistent-degradation case with synthetic-replay:
  1) ./synthetic-replay --scenario=kv-cache-eviction-heavy --duration=15m --tenants=10
  2) Wait for PromQL predicate to evaluate true in the sandbox (check metrics-exporter).
  3) Run owner diagnostics script: tools/diagnostics/kv-cache-inspect.sh --tenant <id>

Tabletop scenarios (catalog)

- KV cache shard reshuffle during black-box warmup
- Region-specific allocator starvation (spot preemption cascade)
- Model-variant fallback thrash causing token-cost spikes
- Multi-tenant cold-cache cold-start causing onboarding failures

Retention and SLO guidance for runbooks

- Telemetry retention required for runbook validation: metrics 30d, logs 90d, traces 90d.
- Alert SLO: detection-to-acknowledge median <= 3m for SEV2, median <= 1m for SEV1 during business hours.
- Escalation target: oncall primary owns initial mitigation within 15m of alert for SEV1.

Merge checklist (PR to runbook repo)

1) Runbook filled using template and linked to service metadata (service ID, repo).
2) At least one synthetic verification included and green in CI.
3) Two reviewers from different teams approved (one operator, one service owner).
4) Dashboard links present and dashboards annotated with threshold panels.

Ownership and follow-up

- Course owner: Priya Kapoor (eng-platform training). Contact: priya@redwood.ai (internal).
- Curriculum reviewers: see metadata above.
- Quarterly review: curriculum and scenario catalog reviewed each quarter; runbook templates updated at least annually.

Appendix A — Example telemetry queries and dashboard panels

- Grafana panel: "kv-prefix-cache p95 by region"
  - PromQL: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_ms_bucket{job=\"kv-prefix-cache\"}[5m])) by (le, region))
- Alert rule: "kv-cache-p95-region-high"
  - Expression: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_ms_bucket{job=\"kv-prefix-cache\"}[5m])) by (le, region)) > 0.3
  - For: 5m, Labels: severity=SEV2, owner=kv-cache-team

- Example debug command (operator):
  - kubectl -n platform logs -l app=kv-prefix-cache --since=15m | jq -r '.message' | grep eviction

Related pages and templates

- Runbook authoring guidelines (required pre-read) — /confluence/eng-platform/how-tos/runbook-authoring-and-maintenance-guidelines-2025
- Synthetic-replay repository — infra/synthetic-replay (internal git)

Revision history

- 2025-09-10: Created by Priya Kapoor (initial curriculum draft).
- 2025-11-02: Added PromQL examples and tabletop scenarios (reviewers: Ethan, Marta).
- 2026-02-15: Adjusted assessment criteria and certification validity (finalized).

Title: 429/overload responses when burst cap reached on Dedicated (expected behavior + retry guidance request)

429/overload responses when burst cap reached on Dedicated (expected behavior + retry guidance request)

Customer (Northpeak Search) reports receiving intermittent HTTP 429 responses with message similar to "overload" during their nightly indexing job when they exceed their Dedicated baseline and attempt to use burst capacity.

They want confirmation whether 429s are expected when burst caps are reached, and what retry strategy Redwood recommends (backoff, max retries, respect Retry-After, etc.). They also asked whether there is a way to "queue" rather than fail requests.

Issue summary:
- Symptom: 429 responses when concurrency spikes above baseline during burst window
- Impact: Indexing job retries; overall job completion time increases by ~20–35 minutes depending on spike magnitude
- Environment: Dedicated cluster in prod us-east
- Workload pattern: Nightly batch indexing job (high, short-lived spikes); day-time traffic is stable

Customer-provided examples (redacted):
- Endpoint: POST /v1/chat/completions (stream=false)
- Approx QPS during spike: 2.5x–3.2x baseline for ~10–15 minutes
- Example response:
  - HTTP 429
  - Body: {"error":{"type":"overloaded","message":"Burst capacity denied: tenant cap reached"}}
  - Headers observed (some requests):
    - x-redwood-denial-reason: BURST_TENANT_CAP_REACHED
    - retry-after: 2

Requested outcome:
- Confirm expected behavior
- Provide recommended client retry/backpressure guidance
- If configuration is wrong/mis-set, advise what needs to change
2025-05-22 (Miguel Santos, Support) - Ticket created from customer email to CS.

2025-05-22 (Customer - Northpeak Search, via Miguel) - We enabled burst to cover indexing peaks. When we hit the peak window we get 429s that look like overload. Is this expected? We’re not sure if we’re doing something wrong or if we should be handling it like rate limits. We can add retries but want to avoid making things worse. Is there a recommended pattern? Also: can you queue instead of rejecting?

2025-05-22 (Miguel Santos, Support) - Acknowledged. Asked for:
- Approximate time window (UTC)
- Example request IDs
- Confirmation of region + model
- Whether they’re seeing x-redwood-denial-reason and retry-after headers

2025-05-22 (Customer) - Provided window 2025-05-22 02:10–02:25 UTC, us-east, llama-3.1-70b-instruct. Provided request IDs (redacted in Jira).

2025-05-22 (Peter Holtz, Routing SRE) - Pulled dashboards for tenant during the window.
Findings:
- Burst admission controller was returning denials with reason=BURST_TENANT_CAP_REACHED (not pool saturation).
- Pool saturation was moderate (global headroom remained); main limiter was tenant’s configured burst cap (max burst ratio + per-tenant GPU cap).
- No evidence of non-burst neighbor SLO degradation during this window; SLO gate did not trigger.

Notes:
- For this tenant, configured burst limit appears to be: baseline 16 GPUs, max burst ratio 1.5x => cap at 24 GPUs effective. Their spike requested equivalent of ~30–34 GPUs for ~6 minutes.
- Admission semantics (per ADR) are "immediate deny" for burst requests once cap reached; we return a 429 with a denial reason code and (when available) a small Retry-After hint.

2025-05-22 (Miguel Santos, Support) - Responded to customer (drafted below; awaiting internal sign-off from SRE):
1) Yes—429s are expected when you hit either (a) your tenant burst cap or (b) the regional burst pool guardrails.
2) The response should include x-redwood-denial-reason to distinguish tenant cap vs pool safety vs cooldown.
3) Recommended behavior is to treat this as backpressure: reduce concurrency and implement exponential backoff with jitter; respect Retry-After when present.
4) If you want "queue" semantics, the current GA behavior is immediate rejection (to protect fleet + neighbors). We can discuss alternative patterns (client-side queue) or adjusting caps.

2025-05-23 (Cole Summers, Quotas/Billing hooks) - Confirmed this is not a billing/quota 429. This is burst admission deny 429. Customer should not be double-charged for denied requests (no completion, no burst usage metered). Metering shows no anomalies for this window.

2025-05-23 (Peter Holtz, Routing SRE) - Additional guidance for retry:
- Use retry budget: cap retries (e.g., <= 3) and a max total retry time (e.g., 10–20s) for interactive traffic; batch jobs can tolerate longer but should still enforce backoff.
- Prefer concurrency control: token bucket / semaphore on client; aim to keep sustained concurrency at/below baseline and allow burst only for short spikes.
- If they continuously exceed burst cap for > N minutes, they should either (a) increase baseline reservation or (b) request a higher burst tier/cap (paid).

2025-05-23 (Miguel Santos, Support) - Sent final response to customer with: (1) confirmation expected behavior; (2) how to interpret denial codes; (3) concrete retry/backoff template; (4) offer to increase burst cap if contract supports.

2025-05-24 (Customer) - Confirmed they were running with a fixed concurrency of 3x baseline. They will add adaptive concurrency + respect Retry-After. Requested a quote for higher burst cap for indexing nights.

2025-05-24 (Miguel Santos, Support) - Routed commercial ask to CS/Sales; closing support ticket as behavior is expected and mitigations are clear.
Confirmed behavior is expected: when Dedicated burst cap is reached, Redwood returns 429 (overloaded) with a burst denial reason code (e.g., BURST_TENANT_CAP_REACHED) and sometimes Retry-After. No platform bug identified.

Provided customer guidance:
- Treat as backpressure, not a transient server error.
- Implement exponential backoff with jitter and honor Retry-After when present.
- Reduce client concurrency / add adaptive concurrency control during batch spikes.

Validated via dashboards that denials were due to tenant-level configured burst cap rather than regional pool saturation; no neighbor SLO regression observed.
CS/Sales to follow up with Northpeak Search on higher burst tier/cap for nightly indexing job (commercial change).
Support to reference the denial reason codes + retry guidance in the Dedicated burst onboarding checklist for future customers.
Optional: file docs feedback to ensure burst-denial 429 guidance is easy to find (link PR-928 / Dedicated burst docs).
