Title: Draft Spec: Policy Engine Extensions for Regional Failover Automation

Draft Spec: Policy Engine Extensions for Regional Failover Automation

Context / why this exists
- We’re upgrading regional failover automation as part of Reliability Program (Q1–Q2 2026). Today, routing policy evaluation has a few gaps:
  - Non-deterministic behavior in edge cases (e.g., multiple signals firing, partial signal availability, time-window ambiguity).
  - Hard to reason about priority across trigger signals (reachability, 5xx burn, tail latency burn, capacity exhaustion).
  - No first-class “hold-down” / dampening in evaluation; logic is split between policy rules and external controller.
  - No consistent mechanism to enforce safety constraints per tenant/tier (max flips, blast radius caps, required approval).

Goals
- Add policy engine primitives so failover decisioning is:
  - Deterministic and auditable (same inputs => same decision; explainability built-in).
  - Compatible with ADR-042 (signal priority + corroboration) and ADR-043 (rollback + anti-flap).
  - Safe by default (rate limits, required corroboration, blast radius constraints).
- Support both:
  - “Recommend” (dry-run) mode: compute candidate flips + evidence.
  - “Enforce” mode: same evaluation but returns executable actions.

Non-goals
- Replace the automation controller. The controller still orchestrates execution, approvals, and cross-system workflow.
- Re-architect signal ingestion. We consume normalized, time-bucketed signals from Region Health + SLO toolkit.
- Build customer-facing UI here.

Terminology
- Policy: configuration describing routing behavior for a route/service/model/tier.
- Region set: primary and fallback regions eligible for this route.
- Trigger signal: normalized boolean or scalar indicating regional impairment or risk.
- Decision: computed outcome (no-op, failover, partial shift, rollback, hold).
- Action: executable change (policy flip, weight adjustment, circuit breaker mode) emitted by controller.

Inputs / data model assumptions
- Policy engine receives inputs as a single evaluation payload, including:
  - route_id (e.g., hosted.chat.completions, dedicated.pool.<pool_id>)
  - tenant_id (optional for shared Hosted; required for Dedicated)
  - tenant_tier (free/pro/enterprise/dedicated)
  - current_routing_state (primary region, weights, last_flip_at)
  - signals (per region, per signal type):
    - reachability: ok|degraded|down + confidence + last_updated
    - errors_5xx_burn: burn_rate + window + confidence
    - tail_latency_burn: burn_rate + p95/p99 deltas + confidence
    - capacity_headroom: percent + “hard gate” boolean
    - control_plane_health (optional): ok|degraded|down
  - evaluation_time (UTC epoch + monotonic sequence)
  - constraints (policy-level + tenant-level): max_flips_per_hour, min_hold_down_seconds, require_approval, blast_radius_limit

Determinism requirements (core)
1) Stable ordering
- Evaluation must not depend on map iteration order.
- Rule matching must define explicit ordering: by priority, then by tie-breakers.

2) Stable time semantics
- All windowed signals must be anchored to evaluation_time and include:
  - effective_start, effective_end, and a “freshness” timestamp.
- Engine must treat stale signals consistently:
  - If authoritative signals are stale beyond threshold, decision = HOLD (do not fail over) unless reachability is explicitly DOWN with high confidence.

3) Single decision per evaluation
- For a given (route_id, tenant_id, evaluation_time), engine emits exactly one decision object, even if multiple actions are possible.
- Multi-step actions (e.g., drain -> shift weights -> finalize) must be represented as a sequence recommendation but still within a single decision record.

4) Explainability
- Decision must include:
  - decision_type (NO_OP | FAILOVER | PARTIAL_SHIFT | ROLLBACK | HOLD)
  - chosen_reason (canonical enum)
  - evidence: ordered list of signals used, with values, freshness, and thresholds.
  - rejected_candidates: (optional) top 1–3 alternatives and why they were not selected.

Proposed changes to policy engine
A) New predicates / functions
1) region_health(region, signal_type) -> {status, value, confidence, freshness_seconds}
- Wrapper that pulls normalized data from payload and enforces freshness calculations.

2) is_authoritative_reachability_down(region) -> bool
- True only if:
  - reachability.status == down
  - confidence >= configured_min_confidence (default 0.9)
  - freshness_seconds <= reachability_max_staleness (default 30s)

3) burn_rate_exceeded(region, metric, window, threshold) -> bool
- Works for errors_5xx_burn and tail_latency_burn.
- Window must be one of approved windows (e.g., 1m/5m/30m) to avoid configuration drift.

4) capacity_hard_gate(region) -> bool
- True if headroom below threshold AND capacity signal confidence is high.
- Intended to prevent shifting into an already overloaded region.

5) corroborated(primary_signal, secondary_signal) -> bool
- Enforces ADR-042 “required corroboration signals” when configured.
- Example: if tail latency burn triggers, require either 5xx burn OR reachability degraded/down OR control plane degraded.

6) hold_down_active(last_flip_at, min_hold_down_seconds) -> bool
- If true, policy engine returns HOLD unless reachability down is authoritative.

7) flip_budget_ok(tenant_id, route_id, max_flips_per_hour) -> bool
- Input includes a precomputed counter from controller/state store (policy engine does not store state).

8) blast_radius_ok(tenant_tier, requested_action) -> bool
- Enforces “can’t shift more than X% traffic for tier Y without approval”.
- For Hosted, blast radius is route-scoped; for Dedicated, pool-scoped.

B) Deterministic evaluation mode (required)
- Add an “evaluation_mode” field:
  - recommend: compute decision + evidence; do not mark as executable
  - enforce: compute decision; include explicit requested_action(s)
- Engine must produce identical decision_type and evidence in both modes (action packaging differs).

C) Signal hierarchy evaluation (ADR-042)
Priority order (proposed canonical order for v1):
1) Reachability DOWN (authoritative) => FAILOVER (unless no healthy fallback)
2) Errors (5xx) fast burn (high severity) => FAILOVER or PARTIAL_SHIFT depending on blast radius and capacity
3) Tail latency burn (p99/p95) => PARTIAL_SHIFT first; escalate to FAILOVER if corroborated and sustained
4) Capacity exhaustion / hard gate => HOLD + load shed (controller action), avoid shifting into constrained region
5) Control plane degradation => HOLD (do not flip rapidly; prevent oscillation)

Notes:
- “No healthy fallback” means every eligible fallback region fails capacity_hard_gate OR reachability is down OR stale beyond threshold.
- If no healthy fallback, decision should be HOLD and include “degrade_allowed=true” hint (controller can activate load shedding / retry-after).

D) Policy language / config schema additions
Add new fields (names tentative):
- failover:
  - enabled: boolean
  - eligible_regions: [us-east, eu-west, ...]
  - signal_requirements:
    - primary_trigger: enum
    - corroboration: [enum]
    - min_confidence: float
    - max_staleness_seconds: int
  - dampening:
    - min_hold_down_seconds: int
    - require_sustain_seconds: int (for non-reachability triggers)
  - safety:
    - require_approval: boolean (default true for prod initially)
    - max_flips_per_hour: int
    - max_traffic_shift_percent: int
    - rollback:
      - auto_rollback_enabled: boolean
      - rollback_after_seconds: int
      - rollback_require_healthy_primary_seconds: int

E) Output schema
Decision output (single object, JSON):
- decision_id (stable hash of route_id + tenant_id + evaluation_time + policy_version)
- policy_version
- evaluation_time
- decision_type
- chosen_reason
- target_state (string encoding; owned by controller)
- requested_actions (string encoding; empty in recommend mode)
- evidence (string encoding; ordered)
- annotations (string encoding; includes thresholds, staleness, hold-down state)

Note: In our implementation we’ll likely use structured objects, but for logging/audit we must generate a stable, versioned string representation.

Safety constraints (ADR-043 alignment)
- Anti-flap:
  - Enforce hold-down between flips for non-reachability triggers.
  - Any rollback decision must respect a separate rollback hold-down (avoid ping-pong between primary and fallback).
- Rate limiting:
  - flip_budget_ok must be true, else HOLD.
- Approval hooks:
  - If require_approval is true, decision_type can still be FAILOVER but requested_actions must be empty and “approval_required=true” annotation set.
- Tenant/tier gates:
  - Enterprise/Dedicated can be configured with stricter “do not cross data residency boundary” constraint (policy engine should surface “constraint_violation:data_residency” rather than attempt partial shifts).

Edge cases and expected behavior
1) Partial outage in primary region
- Reachability degraded (not down), 5xx burn elevated, capacity OK in fallback.
- Expected: PARTIAL_SHIFT (e.g., shift 25–50% depending on max_traffic_shift_percent) if corroborated. If sustained and escalates to reachability down or error burn becomes severe => FAILOVER.

2) Signal missing / ingestion delayed
- Any authoritative signal is stale beyond max_staleness_seconds.
- Expected: HOLD. Evidence must explicitly call out staleness and which signal blocked action.

3) Fallback region constrained
- Primary is failing (5xx burn), fallback capacity_hard_gate true.
- Expected: HOLD + annotate “fallback_unhealthy_due_to_capacity”. Controller should invoke load shedding and retry-after rather than shifting load.

4) Control plane degraded
- Control plane health degraded; data plane signals ambiguous.
- Expected: HOLD unless reachability down is authoritative. (Avoid flipping policies when control plane is suspect.)

5) Multi-fallback selection
- If multiple eligible fallback regions are healthy, selection tie-breakers:
  1) policy-specified order
  2) lowest latency probe (if available in inputs)
  3) highest capacity headroom
  4) stable sort by region name

Testing plan (draft)
Unit tests
- Determinism:
  - Same payload with randomized key order => same decision_id, decision_type, evidence ordering.
- Staleness gating:
  - Stale error burn + fresh reachability OK => HOLD.
- Priority:
  - Reachability DOWN overrides hold-down.
  - 5xx burn overrides latency burn when both exceed thresholds.

Integration tests
- Replay recorded signal snapshots from staging incidents + controlled game day traces.
- Validate output is compatible with controller dry-run UX (must contain reasons + evidence).

Performance considerations
- Evaluation must be cheap; do not add per-eval remote calls.
- Evidence strings must be bounded in size. Cap rejected_candidates and evidence list.

Operational / observability hooks
- Emit a single log line per decision with:
  - decision_id, route_id, tenant_id (hashed in shared Hosted contexts), decision_type, chosen_reason
  - key thresholds and freshness
- Export metrics:
  - policy_engine_decisions_total{decision_type, chosen_reason, tier}
  - policy_engine_hold_reasons_total{reason}
  - policy_engine_eval_latency_ms

Open questions
- Exact shape of “target_state” string: should it be a controller-owned serialization of desired weights, or should the policy engine output high-level intent only?
- Do we want PARTIAL_SHIFT as a first-class decision type (recommended), or represent it as FAILOVER with weight < 100%?
- How strict should corroboration be for tail latency burn? (ADR-042 indicates corroboration required; we need the exact default set.)
- Where should data residency constraints live?
  - Option A: policy engine validates “region set allowed” and blocks action.
  - Option B: upstream policy compilation prevents invalid eligible_regions.

Near-term next steps
- Align with Miles/Ravi on canonical signal enum + reason enum.
- Draft schema PR for policy config additions (behind feature flag).
- Implement deterministic ordering + evidence output in policy engine.
- Wire to dry-run mode (ENG-2415) so the controller can display “recommended action + confidence + evidence” on game day.

Appendix: candidate enums (WIP)
chosen_reason
- REACHABILITY_DOWN
- ERROR_BURN_FAST
- LATENCY_BURN_SUSTAINED
- CAPACITY_HARD_GATE
- SIGNALS_STALE
- HOLD_DOWN_ACTIVE
- FLIP_BUDGET_EXCEEDED
- CONSTRAINT_VIOLATION_DATA_RESIDENCY
- NO_HEALTHY_FALLBACK

signal_type
- REACHABILITY
- ERRORS_5XX_BURN
- TAIL_LATENCY_BURN
- CAPACITY_HEADROOM
- CONTROL_PLANE_HEALTH

Title: Signal weighting and fallback notes for routing policy

Signal weighting and fallback notes for routing policy

Context / intent:
Quick working doc to capture an alternate approach to the smart routing decision path that focuses on signal weighting (attenuation, staleness, confidence bands) and explicit fallback transitions. Goal is to synthesize a lightweight policy primitive we can prototype in the control plane and test with traffic experiments in us-west/us-east/eu-west.

High-level problem statement:
- We have multiple signals to decide where to route inference requests: P99 latency (measured per-host and per-region), per-token cost (model variant + region egress/cost profile), and reliability (error rate / thundering/health).
- Signals arrive at different cadences and have different noise characteristics. Naive scoring/lexicographic policies lead to oscillation or excessive failovers under transient noise.
- Need a repeatable decision graph that: normalizes signals, discounts stale data, produces a unified score, and exposes an explicit fallback transition plan.

Design constraints and non-goals:
- Must be incrementally deployable: start as a feature-flagged policy in the control plane routing agent.
- Low CPU/latency cost in the hot path: score eval should be O(1) per candidate region/model.
- Non-goal: we are NOT building a full RL optimizer here; this is a deterministic policy that is easily reasoned about and tested.

Signal model and normalization:
1) Signals and raw ranges:
   - latency_ms (p50/p95/p99 available). Raw range observed historically: ~5ms (local) to 800ms (cross-region overload).
   - unit_cost_usd (per-token estimate based on model variant + region multiplier). Range: $0.00001/token to $0.01/token depending on model/quant/seq len heuristics.
   - reliability_score (1.0 = perfect, 0.0 = down). Derived from smoothed error rate: reliability = max(0, 1 - ema_error_rate).

2) Normalization approach:
   - Each raw signal is mapped to a 0..1 utility band where 1.0 is best for routing preference. Use monotonic transforms: latency -> latency_utility = clamp(1 - (latency_ms - Lmin)/(Lmax - Lmin), 0,1)
   - Lmin = 5ms, Lmax = policy-configurable (default 500ms). For p99 use more aggressive Lmax.
   - cost -> cost_utility = clamp(1 - (unit_cost - Cmin)/(Cmax - Cmin), 0,1). Defaults: Cmin = 0, Cmax = 0.005 USD/token for global ranking; keep configurable per-customer.
   - reliability_utility = reliability_score (already 0..1).

3) Staleness and confidence bands:
   - Attach a staleness factor s in [0,1] where s = exp(-(now - last_sample)/tau). Tau default 30s for latency, 5m for cost, 60s for reliability.
   - For each utility u, compute weighted_u = u * s * confidence_multiplier.
   - confidence_multiplier is derived from sample count and variability. For latency: conf = 1 / (1 + CV) where CV = stddev/mean. Clamp conf to [0.5,1.0] to avoid extreme punishments for noisy signals.

Score mixing and attenuation primitives:
- The mixing function is a weighted geometric mean to prefer balanced candidates and penalize any weak signal more strongly than arithmetic mean would:
   score = exp(wl*log(weighted_latency_utility + eps) + wc*log(weighted_cost_utility + eps) + wr*log(weighted_reliability_utility + eps))
- Weights (wl, wc, wr) are policy-configurable and can vary by route class (interactive low-latency vs batch low-cost). Default weights: wl=0.5, wc=0.25, wr=0.25 for interactive. For background batch jobs shift to wc=0.6.
- eps = 1e-6 to avoid log(0).

Attenuation / hysteresis to avoid flip-flopping:
- Use an exponential moving baseline per candidate: baseline_score[t] = alpha * score[t] + (1 - alpha) * baseline_score[t-1].
- Transition thresholds: only allow route switch if new_candidate_score > current_baseline_score + delta. Delta defaults: 0.08 for single-request path, smaller for canary/B2B routes where safety matters.
- Cooldown window (per-request-key): once switched for a given customer-token pair, pin for N seconds (default 10s) unless severe degradation triggers emergency fallback.

Fallback taxonomy (explicit):
1) Soft fallback: route to cheaper variant in same region when score_delta < -0.15 but reliability still > 0.9. This preserves low-latency while saving cost.
2) Hard fallback: route to replicated region with higher score if reliability < 0.7 or p99 > threshold.
3) Emergency degrade: if all candidates in preferred region have reliability < 0.5, fall back to local cached responses or minimal model. Emit audit event and open an incident trend.

Decision tree (textual) - top-level:
- Input: request(route_class, customer_tier, seq_len_hint, max_latency_slo)
- Candidates = variant x region list (filtered by compliance/region allowlist)
- For each candidate compute: normalized utilities, staleness, confidence -> score
- Sort by score desc -> top_k (k=3)
- Evaluate current_binding (if exists)
   - if current_binding in top_k and score_delta < delta: keep binding
   - else consider switch path: check cooldown + canary rules
- If top candidate reliability < reliability_hard_threshold -> consult fallback taxonomy and pick fallback
- If no candidate passes emergency gating -> route to degraded path and escalate

Example pseudo-config snippet (control-plane friendly):
- policy: "signal-weighted-multiplexer:v1"
- weights: {interactive: [0.5,0.25,0.25], background: [0.2,0.7,0.1]}
- normalization: {latency: {Lmax: 500, Lmin: 5}, cost: {Cmax: 0.005}}
- staleness_taus: {latency:30s, cost:300s, reliability:60s}
- transition: {delta: 0.08, cooldown: 10s, baseline_alpha: 0.35}
- fallbacks: {soft: {score_gap:-0.15}, hard: {reliability:0.7}, emergency: {reliability:0.5}}

Operational notes / metrics to capture in initial experiment:
- per-request routing decision latency added (target <1ms median, <3ms p95).
- fraction of switches per-minute per-customer (goal <0.5/min)
- re-route churn (daily unique customer-route changes)
- correlation matrix: score vs observed p99 latency after routing (lagged)
- fallback invocation rate and reasons (staleness vs reliability vs cost)

Testing and rollout plan (quick):
- Phase 0: unit tests + deterministic sim harness (feed synthetic bursts, sustained overload, oscillation).
- Phase 1: shadow routing on 5% of interactive traffic (us-west) and collect metrics + false-positive switch histogram.
- Phase 2: 10% canary with forced soft-fallback enabled; compare unit_cost and latency change.
- Phase 3: full rollout with gradually tightened thresholds and a rollback runbook.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to integrate model-specific cold-start cost for embeddings-heavy calls? (affects cost_utility)
- Should customer tier (paid vs free) directly bias weights or be applied as a multiplier on baseline_score? (proposal: tier multiplier after scoring, not in core weights)
- Add a simple policy language for expressing per-route overrides (e.g., per-route Lmax, cost caps).
- Need an offline harness that replays historical routing telemetry to simulate long-term cost impact.

Notes / references:
- See PLAT-321 for initial telemetry schema and metric names.
- Slack: #platform-routing has the early design thread (link pinned).
- Related: need to reconcile with the traffic governor work (ops/traffic-governor) so both users of the control plane share the same capacity signals.

Action items (short):
- [Aisha] implement scoring prototype in routing agent (PR stub assigned).
- [Lena] add sim harness and 3 synthetic scenarios (oscillation, slow drift, sudden region outage).
- [Omar] wire the telemetry metrics and dashboard skeleton in Grafana (metrics names in PLAT-321).
- [Priya] draft canary runbook and rollback steps for Phase 1.

Rough sketch of a decision-tree ascii (for whiteboard):
   START -> filter candidates by compliance -> compute scores -> sort -> top_k
      |
      +- if top.score < emergency_threshold -> EMERGENCY_DEGRADE
      +- else if current_binding in top_k and not significant_improvement -> KEEP
      +- else if cooldown_active -> KEEP
      +- else if top.reliability < hard_fallback_reliability -> HARD_FALLBACK
      +- else SWITCH_TO_TOP (emit audit)

Endnotes: This doc is intentionally pragmatic and makes conservative choices (thresholds, clamp ranges) so we can tune after real traffic. Focus next on implementing sim harness and short experiment in us-west dev region.

-- Aisha

Title: Tradeoff decision walkthrough: latency vs cost vs reliability

Tradeoff decision walkthrough: latency vs cost vs reliability

Purpose
------
Notes and a worked-through decision-tree sketch for smart routing policies that balance latency, unit cost, and reliability across multi-region deployments and fallback tiers. This is an operational-first draft designed to be concise and actionable for platform and runtime teams; it intentionally focuses on concrete decision points, observable signals, and simple resolvable rules rather than an exhaustive math-heavy model.

High-level problem statement
--------------------------
We need a compact routing policy system that:
- routes incoming inference requests to an endpoint (hosted/dedicated/private variant in region)
- respects per-customer latency SLOs, price targets, and reliability requirements
- supports fast fallback and graceful degradation when capacity or health changes

Constraints and assumptions
---------------------------
- Each candidate endpoint advertises: p95 latency (ms), available qps, estimated per-token cost multiplier, region tag, and reliability score (0-1).
- Control plane receives near-real-time metrics (1s--10s granularity) and can update routing weights/policies every 30s by default.
- Customers can pin latency or cost as primary objective; default is latency-first with soft cost budget.
- Fallback tiers: primary (low-latency variants), secondary (quantized or cheaper variants), tertiary (cross-region fallbacks).

Signals to use
--------------
- Observed p50/p95/p99 tail latency to the requester population.
- Queueing depth / active requests per endpoint (backpressure signal).
- Error rate 5xx / timeouts (3s threshold for marking as degraded).
- Effective unit cost estimate (in $/k token relative multiplier).
- Model-quality deltas (optional signal from eval probes) — used for soft gating.

Decision tree (operational steps, top-down)
-----------------------------------------
1) Quick health gate (fast pre-check, sub-second in control plane):
   - If endpoint.error_rate > 1% or endpoint.timeout_rate > 0.5% -> mark endpoint as degraded for routing and skip to step 3 for fallback.

2) Latency-first branch (customer SLO = latency):
   - If endpoint.p95 <= customer.latency_target AND endpoint.qps_available >= request.qps_need -> route to endpoint (good).
   - Else if endpoint.p95 slightly above target (<= target*1.2) AND endpoint.queue_depth low -> apply local smoothing: reduce batch sizes or prefer hot-cache routes; still route with conservative weight.
   - Else escalate to candidate selection: evaluate other primary-tier endpoints in same region; prefer those with p95 <= target and cost multiplier within budget.

3) Cost-first branch (customer SLO = cost/minimize price):
   - If primary endpoints all exceed cost_budget by >10% and secondary cheaper variant available with p95 <= 2x latency_target -> route to cheaper variant with notice flag (headers) so caller can apply degraded path handling.
   - If secondary variant quality signal falls below threshold -> move to cross-region cheaper candidate or apply rate-limiting at ingress.

4) Reliability-driven branch (customer SLO = availability/high reliability):
   - If available_primary_endpoints_count >= required_replicas -> prefer multi-region fanout with hedged calls (send to N endpoints and use first response).
   - If replicas low and error spike detected -> cut non-essential traffic (best-effort or lower-tier customers) using token bucket shaped throttles; route enterprise traffic to reserved capacity.

5) Fallback prioritization and cooldowns:
   - Fallback order: same-region primary variants -> same-region cheaper quantized -> cross-region primary -> cross-region cheaper.
   - Each fallback activation has an exponential cooldown (e.g., 30s, 60s, 120s) to avoid thrash.
   - Maintain a small circuit-breaker counter per endpoint (error streaks, slow-start after recovery).

Example policy snippets (pseudo-DSL)
----------------------------------
policy "customer-default" {
  prefer: latency
  latency_target_ms: 120
  cost_budget_multiplier: 1.0
  fallback_tiers: [primary, quantized, cross_region_primary]
  hedging: false
}

heuristic score(endpoint E, request R) = w_l * latency_score + w_c * cost_score + w_r * reliability_score
where latency_score = clamp(1 - (E.p95 / R.latency_target_ms), -1, 1)
cost_score = clamp(1 - ((E.cost_multiplier - R.cost_budget) / R.cost_budget), -1, 1)
reliability_score = E.reliability - 0.5  // center around 0

Weights are derived from customer preference: latency-first -> w_l=0.6, w_c=0.25, w_r=0.15. Cost-first flips the weights.

Operational playbook (short)
---------------------------
- Normal: control plane scores candidates every 30s, picks top N weighted endpoints and exposes a primary route.
- Degraded: on degradation signals, immediately mark endpoint as degraded and remove from candidate pool; run fallback selection and notify SRE/owner channel.
- Recovery: require 3 consecutive healthy measurement windows before restoring primary weight.
- Experiment: A/B rollouts use a traffic shadow for quality-sensitive changes (no production effect) and require eval probes for quality and latency.

Simulation plan (quick)
---------------------
- Synthetic load generator that can vary qps, seq length, and error injections.
- Sweep across: (latency_target, cost_budget, error_rate) to measure regret: additional latency or cost compared to ideal oracle.
- Track churn: how often endpoints flip state with different cooldowns. Tune cooldowns to keep flips < 2/hour per endpoint.

Open questions / TODOs
---------------------
- How to assimilate model-quality probe signals into routing without revealing model internals? (prob: use blind scalar quality metric).
- Should we support per-request hedging with partial-response merging? risk: duplicate cost and cache incoherence.
- Define APIs for customers to declare hard/soft constraints (hard SLOs should override cost).
- UX: what do we surface in Console for customers to understand fallback behavior and incurred extra cost?

Appendix: quick failure-mode examples
-----------------------------------
- Slow tail (p99 spikes): mark degraded only if p99>target*2 and p95 also worsening; otherwise apply smoothing.
- Capacity collapse: if available_qps drops sharply -> immediately shift lower-priority traf to tertiary routes and emit alert.
- Cross-region penalty: consider geo penalty (add 20ms per cross-region hop) when scoring far-region endpoints.

Endnotes
--------
This doc is intentionally pragmatic and iterative. Next step: convert the decision tree into a compact state machine for the control plane and add unit tests against the simulation harness.

Title: Failover trigger brainstorm (regional automation upgrade)

Failover trigger brainstorm (regional automation upgrade)

Context
- Project: Regional Failover Automation Upgrade (Reliability Program).
- This doc is a working brainstorm of candidate triggers/signals, dampening strategies, edge cases, and “do not fail over” scenarios.
- Goal: faster + safer detection, fewer false positives, avoid cascading overload.

Assumptions / constraints (as of 2025-12)
- Hosted API + Dedicated have different tolerances:
  - Hosted API: prefer fast detection and broader automated shifts, but must protect downstream capacity (no thundering herd).
  - Dedicated: prefer strict safety gates, per-tenant controls, and explicit operator visibility (sometimes approval required).
- We will have: region health aggregator (RHS), deterministic policy evaluation (policy engine), failover controller with dry-run + audit events.
- We need to support: partial regional impairment (not total black hole), and dependency-specific failures (e.g., network path to gateway vs GPU pool health).

Definitions (rough)
- “Region impairment”: condition where the region cannot reliably serve request class X within SLO for a meaningful fraction of traffic.
- “Trigger”: computed boolean (or scored state) that can cause routing policy flip or load shedding.
- “Corroboration”: second (independent) signal required before escalation.
- “Hold-down”: minimum time we keep a decision in place to prevent oscillation.

Principles / decision heuristics
- Prefer authoritative, hard-to-fake, hard-to-spike signals for primary triggers.
- Bias to “degrade locally” before “fail over globally” when uncertainty is high.
- If control-plane / policy engine health is uncertain, default to safe static routing rather than aggressive automation.
- Every trigger should have:
  - clear measurement window
  - scope (region, az, pool, route/model)
  - required corroboration (if any)
  - action type (drain, shed, flip) and max rate
  - rollback criteria and hysteresis

Candidate trigger signals (brainstorm)

A) Reachability / black-hole signals (authoritative)
1) Cross-region synthetic probes fail (HTTP + TLS + DNS resolution)
- What: perf-canary probes from multiple vantage points (other regions + external POPs) cannot reach {gateway}/healthz or /v1/chat minimal request.
- Why: strongest indicator of “can’t get there from here”, catches provider network events.
- Notes:
  - Must separate “our gateway dead” vs “our health endpoint dead”.
  - Use multiple vantage points + quorum (e.g., 3-of-5).
  - Distinguish external vs internal reachability.
- Suggested trigger:
  - Critical: 2+ independent vantage groups failing for >= 60s.
  - Action: immediate block routing to region for affected routes (or shift traffic weight to 0 for Hosted).
- Corroboration: optional if probe system is healthy + consistent.

2) Anycast/DNS steering anomalies
- What: observed DNS answers inconsistent or increased NXDOMAIN/servfail for region-specific endpoints.
- Risk: DNS data can be noisy; clients cache; TTL variations.
- Use as corroboration, not primary.

B) Error-rate / availability burn signals (strong, but can be tenant/path specific)
3) 5xx / gateway error burn (regional)
- What: error budget burn-rate for request success (2xx/3xx) vs 5xx/timeouts.
- Implementation idea: multi-window burn (fast + slow) per SLO toolkit.
- Suggested trigger:
  - Page/alert: 14x burn over 5m and 2x over 1h.
  - Failover candidate: sustained 5xx >= threshold for >= 2m AND corroborated by reachability OR latency OR capacity.
- Edge: avoid triggering on single bad deploy; add deployment annotation / canary awareness.

4) Upstream dependency error signatures
- Examples: auth/token validation, billing/quota service, model registry, KMS/HSM.
- If a dependency is global (shared) then failover doesn’t help.
- Need dependency-aware classification:
  - If dependency is regionalized: failover may help.
  - If dependency is global: trigger should shift to “degrade features / shed / hold” not “route away”.

C) Latency / tail burn signals (useful for partial impairment)
5) Tail latency burn (p95/p99) on key routes
- What: p95/p99 latency for gateway and end-to-end completion.
- Notes:
  - For streaming: separate “time-to-first-token” (TTFT) from overall completion.
  - Token-generation slowness can be capacity/queue vs network.
- Suggested trigger:
  - “Degrade” action first (shed low-priority, reduce max tokens, increase backpressure)
  - Failover only with corroboration (e.g., reachability OK but latency burn + capacity exhaustion = candidate).

6) Queueing indicators (proxy for backpressure)
- What: request queue depth, waiting time, batcher queue, router backlog.
- Danger: high cardinality + noisy; can be local hot-shard.
- Might be used as an input to RHS health score rather than direct trigger.

D) Capacity / saturation signals (gates; sometimes trigger for partial shifts)
7) Fleet headroom below safe threshold
- What: GPU pool utilization + “admit capacity” vs current demand. Include autoscaling lag.
- We should treat this mostly as:
  - a gate (don’t fail over into a region that can’t take traffic)
  - a reason for “controlled partial failover” (shift only a subset / tiers)
- Suggested threshold (placeholder): if projected headroom < X% for next 10 minutes, do not shift more traffic in.
- Needed: clear forecasting method; otherwise this signal will flap.

8) Admission control / shed-rate elevated
- What: gateway is actively returning retry-after / overloaded for >Y% of requests.
- Action: if local region is shedding and peer region has headroom, shift a portion.
- Corroboration: must confirm it’s not just one tenant or one model.

E) Network path quality (between components)
9) Control plane to data plane reachability degraded
- Example: routing can’t push policy updates into region; or region health can’t be read.
- This is tricky: automation may become blind.
- Default: if controller can’t confirm state, prefer “freeze” rather than “flip” unless reachability indicates hard outage.

10) Inter-region connectivity problems
- Example: us-east to eu-west packet loss; would hurt cross-region failover if we rely on control plane links.
- Need to know which communications are required during failover (policy write path, drain commands).

F) “Meta” signals about signal quality
11) Observability pipeline unhealthy
- If metrics ingestion is down in region, latency/error signals may lie.
- Rule: never fail over solely based on missing metrics. Missing metrics can raise “uncertainty” and require reachability corroboration.

12) Health aggregator staleness
- RHS data older than TTL => treat as unknown.
- Unknown should not be interpreted as unhealthy unless corroborated.

Trigger hierarchy (draft preference order; aligns with ADR-042 direction)
- Reachability/black-hole > 5xx burn > tail latency burn > capacity exhaustion.
- But: capacity is a hard gate for destination region (do not overwhelm).
- Additional note: some signals represent “cause”, others “symptom”. Prefer direct cause signals for primary decisions.

Dampening / anti-flap strategies (brainstorm)

1) Multi-window burn + quorum
- For burn-based triggers: require both fast window (e.g., 5m) and slow window (e.g., 30-60m) above threshold.
- For reachability: require multiple vantage points and stable failure for N seconds.

2) Corroboration requirements
- Examples:
  - If 5xx burn triggers: require either reachability failure OR tail latency burn OR elevated shed-rate.
  - If latency burn triggers: require 5xx OR capacity OR queueing signal.
  - If capacity triggers: require shed-rate OR rising tail latency.

3) Hysteresis thresholds
- Use different thresholds for entering unhealthy vs exiting unhealthy.
- Example: enter unhealthy at p99 > 2.0s for 2m; exit unhealthy when p99 < 1.2s for 10m.

4) Hold-down timers
- After a failover action, hold for a minimum period (e.g., 10-20m) unless hard evidence of recovery OR destination overload.
- Separate “policy hold-down” from “probe cooldown”.

5) Rate limits on policy flips
- Max flips per {tenant, route, region-pair} per hour.
- Global cap for overall automation actions to avoid broad churn during noisy events.

6) Scoped actions before global actions
- Prefer progressive escalation:
  - (a) shed low-priority tiers / apply retry-after
  - (b) reduce max tokens / disable non-critical features (if applicable)
  - (c) shift a small % of traffic (canary) with verification
  - (d) shift majority traffic

7) Outlier filtering
- Ignore single-tenant spikes (guardrails: require impact across >= N tenants or >= X% of traffic).
- For Dedicated, only act on signals scoped to that dedicated pool/tenant.

8) Deployment-awareness
- If a new release is in progress, treat some increases as suspect; still need protection but may prefer rollback of deploy vs region failover.
- Add “recent deploy in region” as a tag in audit output.

Edge cases / partial outages we must handle

1) Partial impairment: gateway ok, model execution degraded
- Symptoms: TTFT ok but throughput slow; p99 generation latency increases; 200s but slow.
- Risk: customers see “timeouts” client-side; server metrics may show 200.
- Proposed: include end-to-end latency + client-perceived timeout rate where possible.

2) Partial impairment: one model family impacted
- Example: only large model pool is saturated; small models fine.
- Routing should shift only impacted routes/models, not entire region.

3) AZ-level impairment inside a region
- If we can drain/evacuate within region, do that before cross-region failover.
- Need az-scoped signals (at least capacity + error + reachability by pool/az).

4) Control plane degraded but data plane healthy
- Automation may not be able to flip policies.
- Rule of thumb:
  - If data plane healthy: avoid flips, freeze state.
  - If data plane unhealthy AND control plane unhealthy: pre-authorize static fallback policy that can be activated via minimal path.

5) Metrics lying / missing
- If metrics ingestion dies in the region, error/latency may read as “zero” or “unknown”.
- Never interpret missing as good.
- Need explicit “signal_quality” dimension in RHS output.

6) Client retry storms during failover
- When we shift traffic, clients may retry aggressively (esp. streaming reconnect).
- Must coordinate with gateway circuit breakers + standardized retry-after.
- A trigger should consider “retry amplification risk” (if possible) before shifting 100%.

7) Multi-region event (both regions impaired)
- If both primary and secondary are unhealthy, failover will just move the problem.
- Need “no safe destination” state.
- Actions: shed, reduce load, protect dedicated, communicate.

8) Data residency / compliance boundaries
- Some enterprise tiers cannot be routed cross-border.
- Any automated decision must check policy constraints:
  - allowed_regions for tenant
  - allowed_failover_targets by tier
- This creates “do not fail over” even when region is unhealthy (see below).

“Do not fail over” scenarios (explicit list)

1) Single-tenant / single-route failures
- If impact < X% traffic and concentrated to one tenant, do not do regional failover.
- Action: isolate tenant, contact support/CS, investigate their traffic pattern.

2) Global dependency outage
- If auth/billing/global control plane is down, failover won’t help.
- Action: degrade gracefully, communicate, fix dependency.

3) Destination region lacks headroom
- If secondary region would exceed safe utilization or is already shedding, do not shift large traffic.
- Action: partial shift only (if any), otherwise shed/queue.

4) Uncertain signals / low confidence
- If primary signal comes from one source that might be broken (e.g., single probe cluster), do not fail over.
- Require corroboration.

5) Known bad config / policy engine mis-evaluation
- If we suspect policy engine bug or config drift, failover could worsen.
- Action: freeze automation; operator-driven decision with explicit review.

6) Planned maintenance or controlled test without customer notification (prod)
- If it’s a game day, we should use safe blast radius and ensure comms; but the main point: don’t trigger automation that expands blast radius beyond what was approved.

7) Cross-region network impairment (between clients and target)
- If the issue is a network path affecting client->target region, failover may increase latency/errors.
- Need probe coverage from client-like vantage points.

Candidate actions (what automation can do)
- Block region for route/model/tier (set weight to 0) (Hosted).
- Shift percentage (progressive rollout): 5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% if signals improve.
- Enable stricter circuit breakers and retry-after in region.
- Trigger Dedicated drain workflow (tenant-by-tenant, with explicit gate).
- Annotate incident timeline + dashboards with “automation decision” events.

Suggested output of dry-run mode (acceptance baseline)
- For each candidate action: recommended action, scope, confidence, evidence.
- Evidence should list:
  - top triggering signals (with values)
  - corroboration signals
  - destination capacity check result
  - constraints check (data residency / tier / allowlist)
  - dampening status (timers, hysteresis)
- Must include “why not” for suppressed triggers.

Open questions (to resolve in ADR / implementation)
- Thresholds:
  - What are default burn thresholds for Hosted vs Dedicated? (and can they be tuned per tier?)
  - Minimum duration for reachability failures before action?
- Scope model:
  - Do we trigger by region, by pool, by route/model, or some combination by default?
  - How do we represent “partial region unhealthy” to routing?
- Corroboration:
  - Which signal pairs are considered independent enough?
  - Do we require corroboration always, or only for some triggers?
- Recovery/rollback:
  - How do we confirm recovery without flapping? (probe + service metrics?)
  - What is rollback authority in prod when automation is enabled?
- Observability:
  - What is the minimal dashboard panel set for on-call to validate triggers quickly?
  - Which labels are acceptable (cardinality constraints)?

TODOs / next steps
- Align this brainstorm with ADR-042 signal priority and ADR-043 rollback semantics.
- Convert candidate triggers into a first-pass “trigger catalog” table (signal, window, threshold, corroboration, action).
- Identify 2-3 scenarios for Game Day #1:
  - Hard black-hole us-east
  - Partial impairment: elevated 5xx at gateway only
  - Capacity exhaustion in eu-west while failing over
- Decide initial safety defaults:
  - conservative thresholds + required approval hooks in prod
  - strict per-tenant caps for Dedicated

Notes from hallway chats (unstructured)
- Victor A: probes need to run from at least 2 cloud providers / networks if possible; otherwise provider-wide event could blind us.
- Vanessa O: capacity forecasting must include autoscaling lag + warm-up time; otherwise we’ll oscillate on headroom.
- Allison G: avoid high-cardinality labels like tenant_id in alerting; use tier + route + region; deep-dive via logs/traces.

Title: Routing Prioritization Slate: latency / cost / reliability tradeoffs

Routing Prioritization Slate: latency / cost / reliability tradeoffs

Purpose and scope:
This is an iterative notebook-style design doc for a smart routing policy that balances three competing axes: latency (user-facing P95/P99), cost (per-token and per-request), and reliability (error / timeout rates, regional availability). Target audience: platform engineers, SRE, and product owners for Dedicated/Hosted routing.

High-level goals:
- Ensure latency-critical traffic stays within strict SLO bands with graceful degradation paths.
- Reduce average unit cost where it does not materially affect perceived quality.
- Maintain reliability during region failures or capacity pressure through deterministic fallback sequences.
- Keep control-plane policy evaluation cheap and auditable.

Non-goals (for this phase):
- Full ML-based routing (that’s a later phase)
- Per-customer custom models beyond tiered priorities

Design primitives and signals (input to the policy engine):
- request_metadata: {region_hint, customer_tier, route_priority_tag}  -- lightweight and present on every request
- real_time_region_stats: {p95_latency_ms, p99_latency_ms, error_rate, available_capacity_pct, estimated_cost_per_token_usd} -- aggregated windowed signals (30s / 5m)
- model_variant_catalog: {latency_profile, cost_profile, reliability_profile, compatible_regions}
- customer_constraints: {min_region_set, max_cost_px, require_private} (looked up from control plane)

Scoring model (simple, explainable):
We normalize three axes into 0..1 where 0 is best and 1 is worst for that axis. Then compute a weighted linear score:
score = w_lat * latency_norm + w_cost * cost_norm + w_rel * reliability_norm
- latency_norm = clamp((observed_p95 - target_p95) / target_p95, -1, 3) scaled into 0..1
- cost_norm = scaled cost per token normalized against baseline model
- reliability_norm = recent_error_rate (0..1) mapped so higher error → higher penalty
Recommended initial weights (tunable per route):
- latency-critical routes: w_lat=0.6, w_cost=0.2, w_rel=0.2
- cost-sensitive routes: w_lat=0.2, w_cost=0.6, w_rel=0.2
- reliability-first routes: w_lat=0.2, w_cost=0.1, w_rel=0.7

Decision bands (policy layers):
1) Hard constraints (pre-filter): if request.customer_constraints forbids a region/model -> remove from candidate list.
2) Priority buckets: keep explicit route_priority_tag mapping (p0, p1, p2) -> determines default weight sets and emergency thresholds.
3) Soft score evaluation across candidate region+model pairs -> pick lowest score.
4) Capacity-aware check: if chosen candidate has available_capacity_pct < threshold (per-priority) then either: 
   - try next-best candidate, or
   - if none, trigger fast fallback (see below).

Example decision tree (textual):
- If region_hint matches and region healthy -> prefer local region if score below emergency_threshold.
- Else compute scores for all compatible candidates.
- If best_score < soft_threshold -> route to best candidate.
- Else if best_score between soft_threshold and emergency_threshold -> route to next best that meets capacity; and schedule a short-lived retry to best candidate if metrics improve in 5s.
- Else (best_score >= emergency_threshold) -> apply emergency fallback: route to high-reliability variant (quantized or smaller model) in a stable region, and mark request for quality-labeling for downstream regressions.

Fallback sequencing and examples:
- Normal fallback: same-region model_variant downgrade (e.g., 8-bit quantized) -> cross-region best latency-compatible -> cross-region cheap variant -> queued retry to primary.
- During region outage: immediate switch to cross-region stable pool with explicit rate limiting + circuit breaker per-customer.
- For corporate customers with private deployments: prefer their managed regions; if unavailable, consult customer contract: either fail-open to Redwood-hosted with consent flag OR reject with explicit error to caller.

Control plane responsibilities:
- Central policy store: JSON/YAML policy objects per route with weight sets, thresholds, and prioritized fallback lists. These must be versioned and immutable after rollout, with a canary flag.
- Real-time aggregator: produces region-level metrics, model-level metrics, and per-route aggregates. Exposes a small query API (REST / gRPC) for runtime routing agents.
- Runtime agents (stateless): receive a request, fetch cached policy snapshot, query aggregator for latest signals, compute candidate score, and route. Agents should not call central DB synchronously per-request (cache TTL 2s).
- Rollouts: policy changes roll out via canary percentiles by customer_tier. Automatic rollback triggers: increased p99 latency by >15% in canary cohort, or increased error_rate by absolute 0.5 percentage points.

Observability and telemetry (required metrics):
- Per-route: request_rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, success_rate, mean_cost_per_request, fallback_rate, rollback_count.
- Per-candidate: queue_depth, in_flight, capacity_pct, measured_cost_per_token.
- Control-plane: policy_eval_time_ms (should <1ms median), policy_cache_hit_rate, policy_rollout_progress.

SLOs and alerts (initial):
- Route-level SLO: p95 latency < X ms (depends on route), error_rate < 1% (for p0).
- Alert: fallback_rate > 5% sustained for 10m -> page platform oncall.
- Alert: policy_eval_time_99 > 50ms -> investigate control-plane scaling.

Implementation notes / proto pseudo-code:
--------------------------------------
function choose_route(request):
  candidates = filter_catalog(request, customer_constraints)
  if candidates.empty: return error("No candidate")
  signals = aggregator.get_snapshot()  // lightweight map of region->stats
  evaluated = []
  for c in candidates:
    s = compute_score(c, signals, request.priority)
    if c.capacity_pct < capacity_threshold_for(request.priority):
      s += capacity_penalty
    evaluated.append((c, s))
  sort evaluated by s asc
  best = evaluated[0]
  if best.score < soft_threshold: return route(best)
  if best.score < emergency_threshold:
    for next in evaluated[1:3]:
      if next.capacity_pct >= soft_capacity: return route(next)
    return route(best)  // last resort
  // emergency
  return route(select_emergency_variant(evaluated))
Tuning and experiments (short-term roadmap):

- Week 2: add capacity-aware penalties and per-priority thresholds.
- Week 3: A/B test on 10% of p1, monitor p95 and cost delta.
- Week 4: expand canary to 50% and run resilience tests (region failover drills).

Open questions / tradeoffs (items to resolve):
- Should scoring include token-length sensitivity? (long completions amplify cost) -> probably yes, add a length multiplier to cost_norm.
- How much smoothing on metrics to avoid flip-flopping (5s vs 30s windows)? Current thought: 30s for latency, 5m for capacity estimates.
- Rate-limiter interactions: do we pre-check quota before routing or after? Pre-check avoids wasted capacity but adds latency.
- Should we expose routing decision traces to customers? (useful for debugging but leaks infra detail).

Title: Autonomous routing backoff & tier-fallback policy for region and model variants

Autonomous routing backoff & tier-fallback policy for region and model variants

Implement an autonomous backoff and fallback policy that protects customer SLAs by automatically routing traffic away from strained capacity (region or tier) and selecting fallback model variants. This ticket defines thresholds (429s, timeouts, error-rate), circuit-breaker state transitions, and the rules for selecting fallback models (smaller/quantized or regional replicas). The policy must be per-customer and per-route configurable, support canary rollouts, and include observability hooks and traces for debugging decisions.
- Use sliding-window aggregation (60s window, 10s step) to balance sensitivity vs noise.
- Two-tier triggers: soft (early mitigation) and hard (guaranteed fallover). Soft-fallback reduces upstream impact while preserving primary preference.
- Circuit breaker states: CLOSED -> SOFT-OPEN -> OPEN -> HALF-OPEN -> CLOSED. SOFT-OPEN routes a configurable fraction to fallback while continuing monitoring.
- For fallback model selection prefer same-architecture quantized variants when available to limit quality regressions; fall back to regional replica only when model variant is unavailable or quality delta is unacceptable.
- Prioritize routing to Dedicated capacity for customers with reserved capacity before spilling to hosted fallbacks.
- Keep policy decisions tenant-scoped to avoid noisy-neighbor cross-customer effects.
1) Introduce an RT-based monitoring agent that computes sliding-window metrics per (route, region, model, tier) including p95 latency, 429 rate, 5xx rate, and GPU queue length.
2) Implement a policy engine with three modes: observe-only, soft-fallback, hard-open.
3) Soft-fallback: route 10% of traffic to fallback model when transient degradation meets soft thresholds.
4) Hard-open (circuit open): stop routing to primary after sustained threshold violation, route to fallback pool or alternative region.
5) Add hysteresis and cooldown: exponential backoff windows and minimum open duration to avoid oscillation.
6) Expose config via routing policy API and Console UI.
7) Add feature flags to enable canary (percent-based) and simulate mode for A/B testing.
Policy engine supports SOFT-OPEN and OPEN transitions with configurable thresholds.
Per-tenant and per-route overrides available and honored by the routing layer.
Canary rollout mechanism implemented (percent-based) and simulation mode available.
Dashboards show decision traces and key metrics; alert runbook updated.
Automated tests cover threshold edge-cases and state transitions; no regression on baseline latency for non-canary traffic.
Unit tests for state machine transitions, integration tests for policy-enforced routing, chaos tests simulating 429 spikes and region network partitions, and synthetic load tests to verify cooldown behavior. Run canary on internal orgs and two beta customers for 72 hours with intensive monitoring for quality drift.
1) Feature gated and off by default. 2) Enable simulation mode for 10% traffic for 48h. 3) Canary: 5% of production traffic for internal orgs, monitor 24h. 4) Expand to 20% and enable soft-fallback for selected customers. 5) After stable metrics for 7 days, enable for all tenants with default conservative thresholds.
