Title: Benchmark artifacts and pinning policy for hardware-specific model variants

Benchmark artifacts and pinning policy for hardware-specific model variants

Define an operational workflow and artifact format for publishing hardware-specific performance profiles (A100/H100/L40S/MI300 variants) as part of model onboarding, and formalize a version pinning policy that ties runtime serving configs to validated profile artifacts. This ticket consolidates benchmarking outputs, establishes canonical artifact metadata, and prescribes a pinning/rollout pattern for hosted/dedicated/private deployments.
Canonical performance profile JSON/YAML schema documented and committed to /docs/perf-profiles
Automated benchmark job produces profile artifacts for A100/H100/L40S/MI300 and uploads to artifact store with digest and metadata
Runtime can consume profile artifact by URI and apply kernel-selection/quantization hints without manual mapping
Pinning policy documented: model version + profile digest => immutable runtime config; rollback and fallback behavior specified
E2E test covering a sample model (gpt-large-open) verifies serving behavior matches published profile within 10% latency and throughput variance
Design profile artifact schema (fields: model_id, model_version, hw_sku, seq_distribution, tokens/sec@batch, latency_p50/p95, memory_peak, kernel_hints, quantization_profile, benchmark_commit_id, created_at)
Extend benchmarking harness to annotate runs with kernel/engine flags and environment (CUDA driver, cuDNN, ROCm, kernel versions)
Create CI job that runs subset benchmarks on representative instance pool (A100, H100, L40S, MI300) and stores artifacts in S3 with signed URIs
Implement runtime change to fetch artifact on model registration and cache by digest; expose API to pin/unpin artifacts per model-version
Write docs and migration guide for PMs/SEs on how to request new profiles or override defaults
Add E2E regression test in infra-ci that asserts serving metrics within documented tolerances
Profile drift: hardware driver or microcode updates could invalidate published profiles; need scheduled re-benchmarking
Artifact proliferation: one profile per model-version-per-sku-per-quantization may grow large; retention policy required
Pinning rigidity: overly strict pinning could prevent quick rollouts of runtime patches; must provide safe auto-fallbacks
Cross-sku compatibility: fallback from H100->A100 may produce unacceptable latency/cost; must document compatibility matrix
Related previous tickets: ENG-9921 has per-device profile exploration; use its measurement heuristics but change artifact format to be explicit about kernel hints
We recommend profile artifacts be content-addressable (sha256) and immutable once published. Runtime fetch should record artifact_digest in model metadata for auditability.
For Private deployments (VPC/on-prem) provide an offline profile bundle export/import flow (signed bundle) so customers can pin without outbound access.
Quantization profiles should refer to named quantization schemes (e.g., q4f16-8b, q8_0) rather than raw bit widths to keep mapping stable across toolchains.

Title: Adaptive compile matrix for sharded expert + grouped-attention models

Adaptive compile matrix for sharded expert + grouped-attention models

Goal: Produce an adaptive compile matrix and publishing workflow that ensures sharded MoE and grouped-attention (GQA) models receive deterministic, validated kernel selections and compilation tuning that meet performance SLOs across GPU families. This ticket covers: compile-key design, per-model manifest fields for pinning, CI/validation harness changes, rollout playbook (canary + rollback), and docs for model on-boarders in Research/Applied ML and Solutions Engineering.
Compile matrix format documented and added to model manifest schema (fields: kernel_variant, compile_flags_hash, hw_tags, seq_len_profile)
Automated compile cache keys produced deterministically for sharded-MoE and GQA variants
Validation harness produces P50/P95 latency and tokens/sec baseline for every profile and flags a >8% perf regression
Profile publishing pipeline writes immutable artifacts to runtime-artifacts bucket and creates a release entry with semantic version
Rollout policy supports canary (0.5-5% traffic), automatic health checks, and immediate rollback to previous pinned profile
Onboard checklist is usable by model-owners: QC tests, memory safety checks, and a required review by Applied ML
Background: MoE and GQA introduce nonuniform compute patterns (expert routing stalls, grouped matmuls) which require different kernel tilings and KV cache layouts. Implementation notes: 1) Extend compile-key to include shard topology (expert_shards:x), routing strategy, and group_size to avoid cross-model cache collisions. 2) Add a small ABI header to kernel artifacts that encodes expected tensor layout and prefetch plan so runtime can assert compatibility at load-time. 3) Compile flags: use tiling=auto, split-kv-cache=true for large seqs, fused_gqa_matmul=true where group_size>1. 4) Fallbacks: when optimized kernel fails on a given GPU, fall back to a verified scalar kernel and mark the profile health degraded. 5) Quantization: record quantization profile id in manifest and ensure compile path includes dequant ops if needed. 6) Cache: include model version, profile hash, and GPU kernel version in cache key to prevent phantom cache reuse. 7) Publishing: artifacts go to s3://runtime-artifacts/compile-profiles/<model>/<profile_hash>.tar.gz with metadata JSON alongside. 8) Pinning: model manifest gets fields pinned_compile_profile and pinned_profile_timestamp; pinning is immutable except via a controlled rollout PR.
Unit: compile-key canonicalization tests covering combinations of shard topologies, group sizes, and seq lengths
Integration: nightly compile of representative MoE/GQA models across cuda-12.1 and cuda-12.3 kernels with artifact upload to staging bucket
Perf regression: run eval harness using real prompt set (10k queries) and assert P95 latency delta <8% vs baseline
Smoke: canary rollout to a small dedicated pool and continuous health checks for 24h before wider rollout
Chaos: simulate a kernel load failure and verify automatic fallback and audit log entries
Stage 0: publish profile to staging bucket and run full CI (compile + perf + mem safety)
Stage 1: canary rollout to 1% of traffic on runtime-dedicated-canary pool for 6 hours, automated P50/P95 checks
Stage 2: expand to 10% for 24 hours if health OK, run additional throughput tests
Stage 3: full rollout to pinned pool and mark profile release as GA; create rollback snapshot of previous profile
Rollback triggers: >8% P95 regression, memory OOMs, increased error rate >1% absolute

Title: Heuristic Composer — personal scratchlog

Heuristic Composer — personal scratchlog

High-level idea (one-liner): lightweight in-console "heuristic composer" that lets product engineers assemble small, auditable inference policies (cost/latency gates, safety filters, scoring transforms) and apply them per-route or per-customer without code deploys.

Why: ops/PD are constantly tweaking ad-hoc rules in code or lambda layers. We need an authorable policy layer that is simple (no heavy rule engine), composable, and observable. This can reduce incidents where a change to routing or fallback logic requires infra rollout. It also democratizes quick experiments (A/B a cheap gating heuristic vs full model switch).

Core constraints:
- Must be tiny DSL or JSON config (no Java-like rules). Prefer declarative named predicates + actions.
- Runtime must evaluate per-request within 500us extra p99 over baseline on Hosted API for small policies.
- Policies versioned, diffable, and rollouts support: local canary, target subset of customers, fallback policy on eval error.
- Safety first: composition must be monotonic (no accidental bypass).
- Auditing: who changed, why (free-text notes), and link to tickets.

Example sketch of DSL (pseudo-YAML):
  name: cheap-fallback-for-chat
  match: route == \"chat.generate\" and customer_tier != \"enterprise\"
  predicates:
    - token_estimate > 1200
    - latency_window.mean_60s > 150ms
  actions:
    - set_model: mode: \"fallback\" model_hint: \"gptj-6b-q4\"
    - set_max_tokens: 256
  safety:
    - require_response_quality_min: 0.65
  rollout:
    - percent: 20
    - cohorts: [beta_customers, new_signups]

User stories (prioritized):
- As an infra engineer, I can author a policy that forces a cheap model when token_estimate exceeds threshold to control cost.
- As an SRE, I can attach latency-based triggers that route to a regional fallback model when p99 latency exceeds SLO.
- As a product manager, I can A/B a quality gate that runs a small reranker and measure downstream retention impact.
- As compliance, I can add a redact-and-mask action that post-processes outputs for flagged customers.

Acceptance criteria (MVP):
- UI: simple editor that validates DSL and previews effective action order.
- Runtime: policy evaluation added to request pipeline with feature-flag gating, p50 overhead < 150us, p99 < 600us for a 3-predicate policy.
- Audit logs created for policy-trigger events (policy_id, version, eval_result, decision).
- Can target policies by route, customer, and tag.
- Rollout controls: percent rollout and kill switch.

Telemetry and metrics to track:
- policy_evals_total, policy_triggers_total, policy_eval_latency_ms (p50/p95/p99), cost_delta_estimated_per_hour for affected routes, rollback_rate (auto/manual), downstream_quality_delta (eval harness).

Safety and failure modes (notes):
- Bad predicate might route all traffic to cheap model -> need hard upper/lower bounds or a circuit-breaker that stops policies that increase error rate above threshold.
- Complexity drift: if DSL becomes Turing-complete people will abuse it. Limit to boolean predicates + simple numeric transforms + named actions.
- Cross-policy conflicts: define deterministic priority (explicit weight + creation timestamp fallback). Prefer explicit ordering in UI.

Implementation sketch:
- Authoring UX: editor with live validation + preview on sampled traffic. Save creates versioned artifact stored in config DB (Postgres) and S3 for diffs.
- Runtime: lightweight evaluator in request path written in Go; compile policy to an op-code array for speed. Caching of compiled policies by route+customer_cohort.
- Safety net: automated canary where policy is first run in "observe" mode for N hours, produce telemetry but do not enforce action unless explicitly promoted.
- Integrations: Redwood Console (policy panels), Rollouts (reuse existing rollout infra), Optimize (recommend simple policies based on cost/latency signals).

Experiments to run before MVP:
- Microbenchmark: evaluate overhead of 3 predicate policy running on baseline CPU core (with and without compiled form).
- Simulated traffic: replay production traces and run policy in observe-mode to estimate trigger rates and cost impact.
- UX test: 3 PDs create policies from templates and attempt common tasks (cost cap, latency fallback, redaction). Time-to-complete task + mistakes recorded.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How expressive should predicates be? Allow regex on prompts? Allow embedding similarity predicates? (maybe keep advanced predicates as "pluggable" actions).
- Storage & rollback semantics: soft-rollback vs immutable versions. Need simple promote/rollback flow.
- RBAC: who can author vs who can promote to enforce rollout.
- How to represent stochastic actions (e.g., sample N% of requests for model shadowing)?

Next steps (my immediate checklist):
- Draft initial confluence page with above sketch + UX mockups (Devon to help).
- Run microbenchmark by 2025-11-08 (Ravi volunteering to implement Go evaluator prototype).
- Create GH PR prototype for config artifact schema (RFC PR numbering above).
- Schedule 30-min sync with console team to validate editor constraints.

Notes to self: keep the DSL minimal. Avoid reinventing feature flags. Focus MVP on 3 action types (set_model, set_max_tokens, redact) and 3 predicate types (numeric compare, tag match, windowed metric). Make the observe-first workflow the default so we build trust.

Random brainstormed names: PolicyPad, Composer, Runbook Rules, Hermes (or too mythological?), Heuristix (bad pun). I like "PolicyPad" for the UX and "heuristic-composer" for infra.

End of scratchlog. This is intentionally rough — capture quick ideas and next steps.

Title: Schema Tug-of-War: constrained-decoder experiments and recovery playbook

Schema Tug-of-War: constrained-decoder experiments and recovery playbook

Purpose: quantify and catalog trade-offs when enforcing strict JSON/schema constraints against unconstrained model decoding, and produce a recovery playbook for streaming + tool-calling scenarios. We call this the 'Tug-of-War' suite because it intentionally stresses competing objectives: schema strictness (zero false positives) vs model fluency and latency. Goals: 1) create reproducible stimuli that provoke schema violations in both full and partial streams, 2) measure impact of constrained decoding knobs (sampling temperature, logit penalties, lexicon masks, token-level backoff) on schema pass rate and latency/throughput, 3) validate repair and fallback strategies (repair-by-edit, toolcall re-run, model-variant fallback, short-prefix caching + re-decode), and 4) produce a lightweight runbook for rollout and automated gating in Console.
A reproducible test harness (Docker + CI job) that runs the Tug-of-War corpus across at least 3 model families and reports schema pass rate, latency P50/P95, and throughput
Experiment matrix with clear knobs and expected outcomes defined (temperature, top_p, constrained-decoder mode, lexicon mask types)
At least 3 recovery strategies implemented and compared with end-to-end measurements on streaming & interleaved toolcall sequences
Runbook with automatic gating thresholds for Console rollouts and a recommended default decoder configuration for hosted vs Dedicated tiers
2026-02-18 Sofia Martinez: Created ticket and initial hypothesis doc. Uploaded test corpus (tug_of_war_v1.json) to Drive. Link in links section.
2026-02-22 Liam Chen: Prototype constrained-decoder harness (python) checked in on feature/eng/eng-683219-harness. Initial pass shows schema pass rate up from 68% -> 92% at cost of +12% latency.

Title: Constrained decoder: backoff & graceful-degradation test matrix for streamed tool calls

Constrained decoder: backoff & graceful-degradation test matrix for streamed tool calls

Scope: Build an automated test harness and manual playbook that validates schema adherence when structured outputs are produced in streaming responses and during tool/function calls. This ticket covers constrained-decoder modes (strict/soft), a backoff/graceful-degradation strategy for partial or malformed outputs, and end-to-end compatibility checks across runtime-2.3 variants.

Goals:
- Verify JSON/object schema validity across streaming chunk boundaries and toolcall boundaries.
- Exercise constrained-decoding settings (hard reject, soft-correct, n-best rewrites) and measure trade-offs (validity vs latency).
- Implement + validate a backoff heuristic that emits best-effort structured payloads when strict enforcement fails, and confirm this keeps apps resilient.
- Add mutation-based fuzz and golden prompt sets to catch drift and edge cases.

Test matrix (high level):
- Modes: strict-constrained, soft-constrained, no-constraint baseline.
- Input classes: short single-turn, long prompt with prefix caching, streaming long outputs, nested tool-calls (function return objects), truncated token budget scenarios.
- Failure modes: partial JSON chunks, interleaved toolcall text, invalid types for required fields, extra unknown fields, KV-cache-induced token shifts.
- Load profiles: local dev harness (single worker), CI smoke (10 concurrent sessions), stress (100 concurrent sessions using dedicated-sim harness).

Acceptance criteria:
- Under CI smoke, schema-validity for strict-constrained >= 99.5% on golden prompts.
- Backoff path triggers < 0.5% on golden prompts and provides a documented fallback object with an explicit "fallback_reason" field.
- Latency overhead from constrained decoding (strict mode) <= 5% p50 relative to baseline unless validity gain > 30%.
- Streaming reassembly verifier must reconstruct chunked payloads and detect malformed boundaries with > 99% sensitivity.

Automation & artifacts:
- Add new harness 'hybrid-structured-verifier' in test infra repo: github.com/redwood-inference/test-infra/pulls/237 (WIP).
- Confluence plan + playbook: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/ENG/Structured+Output+Backoff+Playbook.
- Dashboard: create dashboard tile runtime-2.3 -> structured-output -> validity-rate on Grafana (placeholder link).

Risks & mitigations:
- Risk: strict enforcement may regress user latency-sensitive workloads. Mitigation: add soft mode and per-route toggles; measure per-route in staging.
- Risk: fuzzing may produce nondeterministic flaky tests. Mitigation: seed corpus + snapshot golden responses.

Implementation notes:
- We'll reuse streaming reassembly logic from ENG-14266 and the fallback semantics described in ENG-45120.
- Backoff algorithm: attempt 2 automated repairs (trim trailing comma, try simple type-coercion for numeric strings), then emit best-effort JSON with fallback_reason and truncated=true if still invalid.
- Tests will assert both the runtime log lines and the returned payload shape.

Next steps:
1) Deliver initial harness and golden prompts (owner: Arjun Patel) by 2026-02-24.
2) Add CI job and run on nightly stress by 2026-03-05.
3) Iterate on backoff heuristics based on results and ship runbook to ENGOncall by 2026-03-15.

Title: Partial-stream JSON-mode recovery and tolerant constrained-decoder tests

Partial-stream JSON-mode recovery and tolerant constrained-decoder tests

Goal: Expand the structured-output test harness to validate recovery semantics when streaming JSON-mode payloads are fragmented or partially malformed, and to verify a new 'tolerant constrained-decoder' mode that attempts best-effort reconstruction of fields without silently dropping required keys.

Background: We currently have strict JSON-mode enforcement tests and constrained-decoding suites, but most tests assume whole-response delivery. In production streaming (server-sent tokens / chunked responses) we observe edge cases where network truncation, interleaved tool-calls, or streaming artifacts produce: truncated JSON, trailing commas, or partial arrays across chunks. Consumers using older compatibility layers (v1 clients) expect either a full rejection or a workable fallback object; newer clients (v2) prefer a deterministic error token + structured partial payload.

Scope: Build automated tests and fixtures that simulate realistic streaming fragmentation patterns and evaluate two runtime behaviours: 1) strict-reject: current behavior that fails schema validation and emits an error; 2) tolerant-reconstruct: new experimental constrained-decoder option that applies a deterministic reconstruction policy (prefix completion, array padding with sentinel, required-key placeholders) and emits a schema-adherence score in diagnostic metadata.

Acceptance criteria:
- Add 24 unique test cases covering: chunk boundary splits inside strings, arrays split across chunks, KV-cache-inserted tokens mid-json, tool-call delimiters within object bodies, and trailing stream truncation.
- Each test exercises both strict-reject and tolerant-reconstruct modes and records: validation result, reconstructed payload (if any), diagnostics trace, and time-to-validate.
- Diagnostics format matches console and API trace expectations (trace_id linkable to QA dashboard).
- Tests run in CI (integration) without flaky failures >1% across 50 runs.
- Add compatibility verification that v1 client deserializers get a defined fallback object when tolerant-reconstruct is enabled (documented behavior).

Test plan summary:
1) Fixtures: generate tokenized streams from canonical model outputs, then synthesize fragmentation by injecting chunk boundaries at deterministic offsets and randomized offsets. Save fixtures in test-fixtures/streaming/partial-*.jsonl (link: https://drive.redwood.com/drive/streaming-fixtures/partial-stream-fixtures).
2) Harness: extend structured-output-test-runner to support streaming input and to toggle decoder modes via test config flags.
3) Metrics: add assertions for schema errors count, reconstruction accuracy (field-level F1), and diagnostic payload presence. Wire metrics to QA dashboard (https://dash.redwood.com/d/struct-out/stream-frag).
4) Backcompat tests: run baseline v1 client deserialization (JavaScript/Go) against reconstructed outputs and confirm client-visible shape.

Non-goals:
- This ticket does not implement production rollout of tolerant-reconstruct; it only tests and specifies behavior. Rollout/feature-flag will be separate (ENG-43012).
- No UI changes to Console are included here; console integration tracked in PM-518.

Outcomes and risk mitigation:
- If tolerant-reconstruct shows acceptable reconstruction accuracy and low false-positives, we will propose adding it behind a runtime flag for canary testing.
- To avoid silent data corruption, reconstructed payloads MUST include a diagnostics.topology field with reconstruction hints; tests assert presence.

Title: Strict JSON parser: recovery heuristics and compatibility experiment

Strict JSON parser: recovery heuristics and compatibility experiment

Goal: validate a strict JSON enforcement path that can 1) fail fast for schema violations, 2) gracefully recover partial streaming output without violating callers' contracts, and 3) emit telemetry that lets ops tune fallback policies. This ticket scopes an experimental testbed and a set of blackbox/whitebox tests to evaluate trade-offs between deterministic constrained decoders and probabilistic recovery heuristics when the model emits malformed or out-of-schema JSON during streaming and tool/function-calling scenarios.

Scope: build a harness that runs across three axes: (A) streaming partial output with injected token-level corruption, (B) tool-calling interleaved with JSON fragments, and (C) decoder fallbacks (strict reject, best-effort patch, allow-safe-keyword-rewrite). Measure: schema_violation_rate, fallback_latency_ms, recovered_tokens_ratio, and end-to-end client-visible error modes.

Non-goals: full product rollout or console UX changes. This is an infra/engine experiment focused on test coverage and metrics to inform a later rollout plan.
1) Harness runs deterministically in CI and produces reproducible metrics for schema_violation_rate and fallback_latency_ms.
2) For seeded corruption workloads, at least one recovery heuristic must reduce customer-visible error rate by >=25% vs strict reject with <50ms median decode penalty.
3) Telemetry fields (repair_hint, schema_failure_reason, recovered_tokens_ratio) are populated for all fallback events.
4) No regression in tail memory usage for typical KV cache sizes (<=2MB).
Complete fleet fuzz sweep (infra ticket created), finish long-tail telemetry dashboards, produce runbook with rollback triggers and recommended defaults for canary deployments, and present findings at next weekly Runtime sync. Estimate additional 2 cycles to finalize heuristics and product integration.

Title: backend-priority-and-tokenizer-fallbacks-for-structured-decoding

backend-priority-and-tokenizer-fallbacks-for-structured-decoding

Motivation: In production usage we keep seeing structured-output constraints fail intermittently when token boundaries split grammar terminals or regex anchors during streaming. This results in either malformed JSON outputs or function-calling payloads that fail decoding downstream. Goal: Add a prioritized backend selector and a tokenizer-aware fallback that preserves streaming compatibility and function/tool-calling hooks while improving CFG and regex constraint robustness. Summary of changes: 1) new runtime config `backend_priority` to prefer CFG or regex, with a third 'tokenizer-fallback' option that triggers byte/utf8-aware escapes when a constraint stalls mid-token; 2) selector implementation that probes backends in priority order and collects deterministic prefixes to allow safe streaming emission; 3) tokenizer-edge heuristics that detect partial multi-byte tokens and insert safe escape sequences or delay emission until token-complete to avoid breaking grammar anchors; 4) mapping layer updates to OpenAI-compat streaming envelopes so partial choices and function_call chunks remain consistent with existing clients; 5) tests and e2e corpus for cases combining nested CFGs and overlapping regex constraints. Config and API compatibility: default behavior unchanged (CFG preferred) unless `backend_priority` is overridden in the model profile or request-level `decoding.backend_priority`. Runtime exposes a non-breaking feature flag `enable_tokenizer_fallback` to roll out gradually. Performance and correctness: microbenchmarks show a 2-4% median latency increase on constrained workloads when tokenizer fallback triggers, but a 6-12x reduction in malformed structured outputs for the test corpus. Rollout plan: behind feature flag -> internal canary (Dedicated) -> staged release to hosted with telemetry -> enable by default after 2 weeks of canary. See linked linear tasks for follow-ups and metrics. Checklist: [x] backend selector implementation, [x] tokenizer heuristics, [x] OpenAI-compat mapping, [x] unit and integration tests, [x] docs update, [x] CI green. Title: Decoder Watchdog: constrained-decoder chaos harness & schema metering

Decoder Watchdog: constrained-decoder chaos harness & schema metering

Goal: Build an engineering-level test harness (Decoder Watchdog) that simulates partial/garbled streaming outputs, interleaved tool/function calls, and constrained-decoder failure modes to validate our JSON mode enforcement and schema adherence across models and runtimes.

Scope:
- A reproducible simulator that can inject: truncated token sequences, mid-stream token noise, toolcall markers inserted out-of-band, and KV-cache evictions to surface decoder divergence.
- A schema-metering layer that scores each output on: syntactic JSON validity, schema field coverage, type adherence, and ambiguity heuristics (fields present but null/untyped).
- Canary tests to compare behavior between: (a) stock decoding, (b) constrained-decoder enforcement, and (c) deterministic backoff + structured-repair heuristics.

Why now: Recent regressions in streaming schema compliance (partial emissions during tool calls) have caused degraded downstream parsing and higher error rates in Console rollups. This harness will let us quantify regressions, evaluate fallback strategies, and gate rollout for runtime-1.20.

Title: Constraint Synchronizer: decode sentinels & oscillation regression tests

Constraint Synchronizer: decode sentinels & oscillation regression tests

Add a focused regression test suite that verifies recovery and deterministic behavior when the decoder oscillates between schema-compliant and non-compliant outputs in streaming + tool-calling scenarios. This ticket builds a harness that injects failures and tool-call interleavings, asserts telemetry events (sentinel triggers, decode backoffs), and validates downstream structured-output consumers (function callers, SDK parsers) see either a valid JSON payload or a clearly signaled graceful-degradation path.
We have sporadic customer reports and internal CI flakiness where a streamed response begins emitting a valid JSON payload, then an in-flight tool call or a partial token error causes the model to emit additional tokens that break the schema. Existing suites cover many constrained-decoder paths but don't capture the specific 'oscillation' where the model flips compliance state mid-stream and then recovers or falls back. This causes downstream function-call handlers to either crash or silently drop important fields. The goal is to make these behaviors deterministic and observable in CI.
1) Implement a deterministic stream replayer that can inject: token drops, duplicate tokens, delayed tool-call sentinel chunks, and kernel-level backpressure events. 2) Create scenario matrix combining: short/long sequences, nested JSON objects, required vs optional fields, and function/tool call boundaries. 3) For each scenario assert: a) final output is schema-compliant OR b) a well-formed fallback marker is emitted ("__REDWOOD_JSON_FALLBACK") and partial structured data saved to a stable telemetry path. 4) Add flaky-tolerance thresholds: CI must fail only if >3% of runs deviate from expected recovery behavior across 50 runs. 5) Wire events to console rollup dashboard and alert rules for regressions.
- Deterministic harness committed and runnable via ./tools/so-harness/run.sh - Matrix of >=12 scenarios implemented covering streaming+tool-call boundaries - CI job added that runs harness 20x per PR and reports pass rate; failing PRs when the pass rate < 97% - Telemetry emits events: schema_violation_detected, sentinel_fired, constrained_decoder_backoff, fallback_emitted - Runbook created describing mitigation steps and temporary fallback config toggles - Tests validate that SDK-level parser never throws unhandled exceptions when fallback marker is present

Title: Output orchestration: edge case behaviors, streaming reconciliation, and retry SLA acceptance

Output orchestration: edge case behaviors, streaming reconciliation, and retry SLA acceptance

This ticket captures acceptance criteria and scope clarifications for the structured-output orchestration flow when the model emits partial/streamed payloads and/or invokes external tools/functions. Focus areas: schema reconciliation after partial streams, deterministic final payload composition, idempotent tool-calls under retry/backpressure, and clear error-mode semantics for clients and the Console. This is a scope refinement from the original PRD: we are adding an explicit reconnect/resume checkpoint format, telemetry gates for canary rollouts, and a permissive-by-default schema mode with opt-in strict enforcement for enterprise customers.
AC-1: Final-object determinism — When a request is streamed in N fragments (N>=1) and the client disconnects mid-stream, the system must provide a single, deterministic reconstituted JSON object after server-side resume/replay. Determinism verified by stable ordered field composition (sort-by-key and canonicalization) across 10k randomized fragment orders.
AC-2: Checkpointed resume protocol — Streaming fragments must include optional 64-bit monotonic checkpoint IDs. Resume must accept a checkpoint token and deliver the remaining fragments without duplicating side-effecting tool calls. Test: simulate disconnect at fragment 3 of 7 and resume via token; final reconstituted object must equal the original uninterrupted result.
AC-3: Tool-call idempotency and replay semantics — Any emitted tool/function call that is potentially side-effecting must include an idempotency key. On retry, the gateway will dedupe calls using the idempotency key and return consistent tool results. Required behavior for three failure classes: transient network, gateway timeout, and duplicate-invocation prevention. Test: three retry loops with injected transient failures must show a single effective tool execution in backend logs.
AC-4: Schema modes — Provide two schema-validation modes: permissive (default) and strict (enterprise opt-in). Permissive mode accepts extra fields and returns a warnings array in the final metadata object; strict mode rejects deviations and returns a typed validation error with code SO:SCHEMA_STRICT. Acceptance includes migration doc and example clients for both modes.
AC-5: Fragment-level backpressure and 95th latency SLO — For streaming requests with fragments <=512B, inter-fragment latency 95p must be <300ms in hosted regions; Dedicated pools must match or improve on that. Telemetry must include per-request fragment count, reconstituted size, and resume count.
AC-6: Error classification contract — Map runtime failure modes to client-visible categories: transient(retryable), degradable(partial output with warning), and terminal(failure with rollback instructions). Document clear retry headers and suggested client backoff windows. Unit tests must cover each mapping with example payloads.
AC-7: Partial-output reconciliation policy — If an unrecoverable terminal error occurs after a side-effecting tool call, the system must provide a remediation flag and an audit trace linking the tool invocation ID to the request ID. This trace must be visible in Console request details.
AC-8: Canary checklist and telemetry gates — Before full rollout, a canary must run for 72 hours with the following gates: <=0.02% increase in malformed-final-object rate, <1% of requests requiring manual reconciliation, and per-customer error surfacing below threshold. Metrics must be available on the Console dashboard and saturate alerts for regressions.
AC-9: E2E example suites — Provide three canonical e2e suites: (a) simple strict-schema scenario, (b) high-fragment stream with resume, (c) tool-invoke with induced duplicate-retries. Each suite must be runnable against hosted/Dedicated/Private and have expected outputs checked into the repo.
AC-10: Observability and provenance — All final objects must record provenance metadata (model_version, runtime_variant, checkpoint_ids, tool_invocation_ids) and a compact integrity hash. Console must surface these fields in request detail and in exportable logs.
AC-11: Security & PII handling — If strict schema opt-in requests contain PII fields, template data-masking rules must be applied before storage. Compliance tests and threat model signoff required prior to release for Private deployments.
TP-1: Unit tests for canonicalizer — validate stable key ordering, dedupe logic, and hash equivalence across 1000 randomized permutations.
TP-2: Integration: inject client disconnect at varying fragment boundaries (1..N) and assert resume token replay yields identical final object.
TP-3: Load test: 10k concurrent streaming sessions, mean fragments per session 6; validate 95p inter-fragment latency and reassembly success rate >= 99.95%.
TP-4: Tool-call replay test against a mock idempotent gateway that records invocation IDs; assert single-effect-per-id across 5 retry waves.
TP-5: Canary run plan: 72h, 5% traffic divert, telemetry dashboard with automatic rollback if malformed-final-object delta > 0.02%.
TP-6: Security test: PII masking rules executed on strict and permissive payloads; verify no unmasked PII stored in logs during tests.
RC-1: If malformed-final-object rate increases by >0.02% relative to baseline during canary.
RC-2: If tool-call dedupe fails and duplicate side-effects observed in backend more than once per 50k requests.
RC-3: If resume-token misuse causes data-exposure or incorrect reassembly on >0.01% of requests.
RC-4: Security signoff not obtained for Private deployments.

Title: Contract evolution and compatibility guarantees for streamed tool invocations

Contract evolution and compatibility guarantees for streamed tool invocations

Summary:
This ticket defines acceptance criteria, rollout strategy and test plan for evolving the structured-output contract used in streaming responses when the model emits tool/function call envelopes. The goal is to guarantee backward and forward compatibility guarantees across schema versions, define clear fallback behaviors and observable signals, and provide a failure injection harness to validate real-world degradations before release.

Goals (what success looks like):
1) Clear semantics for schema versioning used in streaming envelopes (v1, v2).
2) Deterministic fallback rules when a consumer sees an unknown field or partial object mid-stream.
3) Tool-call idempotency and retry semantics when tool invocations span stream boundaries or are interrupted.
4) Integration tests and a synthetic failure harness that can inject: message truncation, out-of-order chunks, schema-mismatch fields, and partial JSON fragments.
5) Observability and alerting: latency and error-rate SLIs tied to schema failures, tool-call mismatch counts, and fallback prevalence.

Non-goals:
- Redesign of the entire tool-calling API surface (we accept incremental schema extension only).
- Changes to model prompting strategies or model outputs beyond envelope rules.

Stakeholders:
- Product: Aisha Khatri (owner), Evan Morris (assignee)
- Eng: Runtime (kernel & batching) ENG-1842, API/SDK ENG-2710
- Design: consult for UX of error messages in Console
- Security/Compliance: sign-off if new audit fields are introduced

Acceptance criteria (must be satisfied for Done):
A. Schema versioning and negotiation:
  A1) Streaming envelopes must include a top-level "schema_version" string in the first chunk. If missing, consumer treats as v1.
  A2) The runtime must accept v1 and v2 envelopes concurrently and route to the appropriate parser without error.
  A3) Adding a new optional top-level field (e.g., "trace_id") must be backward-compatible: older consumers ignore unknown optional fields and continue parsing.

B. Partial object and chunk boundaries:
  B1) If a JSON object for a tool call is split across chunks, consumers must reconstruct using a streaming JSON decoder.
  B2) If stream is closed before object completion, the runtime should emit a structured "incomplete_object" diagnostic with the following fields: {"schema_version", "last_seq_id", "incomplete_fields"}. (Diagnostic format documented in Confluence link.)
  B3) Consumers must be able to request server-side rehydration (replay last N tokens) within 30s for transient truncation cases; API to expose replay is in ENG-2710.

C. Unknown fields and forward compatibility:
  C1) Consumers encountering unknown required fields must surface a metric and fallback to a pre-configured error mode (see D).
  C2) Unknown optional fields must be ignored; if the runtime sees >0.1% unknown-optional frequency across production traffic, an alert triggers to Platform SRE.

D. Error modes and fallback behaviors (deterministic):
  D1) FAIL_FAST: default for premium customers; if required field missing or incompatible type => terminate stream with structured error and HTTP 400 wrapper.
  D2) BEST_EFFORT: default for public hosted; on required-field mismatch attempt schema relaxation: drop unknown fields and emit structured warning chunk, continue stream.
  D3) REPLAY_AND_RETRY: for tool calls that were not confirmed (no tool response ack), runtime should enqueue a single transparent retry to the same tool endpoint with idempotency token; retries should happen only if the original invocation outcome is unknown.
  D4) All modes must record an event to the Audit log with: request_id, schema_version, fallback_mode, and decision_reason.

E. Tool-call semantics and idempotency:
  E1) Tool calls must carry a per-invocation "call_id" GUID generated by the runtime at emission start.
  E2) If the stream closes before the tool returns, the call_id is considered "in-flight" and eligible for REPLAY_AND_RETRY once within the configured retry window (default 60s).
  E3) Tool endpoints must accept an "idempotency_key" header and return a canonical status code when a duplicate call_id is received (ENFORCEMENT work in ENG-1842).

F. Streaming diagnostics and observable signals:
  F1) New metrics: schema_mismatch_rate, incomplete_object_rate, toolcall_unacked_rate, fallback_mode_rate (per-mode).
  F2) Dashboards must show top offending routes and model variants.
  F3) Alert thresholds: schema_mismatch_rate > 0.2% for 5m => P1 alert; incomplete_object_rate > 0.05% => P2 warning.

G. Testing and validation:
  G1) Unit tests for parser variants (v1/v2) with >95% coverage for streaming decoder edge cases.
  G2) Integration tests that simulate chunk loss, reordering, and truncation using the synthetic failure harness. Harness runs as part of CI nightly.
  G3) Canary rollout with 5% traffic on internal staging for 48h with synthetic failure injection enabled; promote only when error metrics are flat.
  G4) End-to-end QA checklist: run golden prompt set (100 prompts) against new schema with expected tool-call matches; allowable regression <0.5% in matching accuracy.

H. Docs and SDKs:
  H1) API docs updated with schema_version negotiation and fallback_mode query param.
  H2) JS and Python SDKs expose streaming parser primitives and a helper to surface structured diagnostics to user code.

I. Rollout and rollback plan:
  I1) Feature flag gating at runtime per-customer and per-route.
  I2) Canary 5% -> 25% -> 100% over 3 days if metrics stable.
  I3) Immediate rollback criteria: schema_mismatch_rate spike > 5x baseline or unacked toolcall increase > 10x.

J. Security & compliance:
  J1) Any new audit fields must be optional and redacted in logs unless acct opt-in. Security must sign-off pre-merge.

Implementation notes and engineering constraints:
- Streaming JSON decoder improvements are tracked in ENG-1842. We must ensure memory safety for reassembly buffers (max per-request buffer 2MB).
- Kernel-level batching must not reorder chunks of a single stream; tests must validate sequence IDs are monotonic.

Progress updates and decisions (chronological):

- 2026-02-18: Engineering raised concern about rehydration API; agreed to limit replay window to 30s to bound state. (ENG-2710 assigned)

- 2026-03-04: Security requested opt-in for verbose audit fields; decision: make audit fields optional and encrypted (KMS).
- 2026-03-10: Draft of synthetic failure harness uploaded; CI integration step scheduled.

QA test cases (examples):
1) v1 envelope, complete object in single chunk => pass, no diagnostics.
2) v2 envelope, optional unknown field present => pass, record unknown-optional metric.
3) v2 envelope, required field missing mid-stream => BEST_EFFORT continues with warning; FAIL_FAST terminates (test both).
4) Chunk truncation before object end and stream closed => produce incomplete_object diagnostic and allow replay request to recover.
5) Duplicate call_id sent to tool endpoint => ensure idempotency header used and tool returns canonical duplicate response; runtime maps to unacked vs succeeded correctly.

Open questions (to resolve before In Progress):
- Default fallback mode per customer tier: confirm mapping for free/public, paid, and enterprise.
- Exact audit redaction policy and storage retention for incomplete_object diagnostics.
- SDK ergonomics for streaming parser (sync vs async API surface).

Title: Structured output error-mode matrix and E2E verification

Structured output error-mode matrix and E2E verification

PRD-fragment: Define unambiguous acceptance criteria, verification tests, and operational telemetry for structured outputs with streaming and function/tool calling. Focus is on enumerating error modes (schema mismatch, truncated stream, tool failure, partial object emission, duplicate/tool reentry), mapping each to deterministic platform behavior and fallbacks, and specifying E2E tests that validate behavior across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
AC-1: Error-mode matrix documented and approved by PM+Eng+Design. Each mode lists expected platform actions, HTTP/stream status codes, and whether payload is persisted for replay.
AC-2: For 'schema-mismatch' during streaming, system emits a typed FRAME with status=validation_error, includes byte_offset, and closes the stream with canonical error envelope unless a soft-fallback policy is configured.
AC-3: For 'truncated_stream' (partial object at EOF), runtime must persist last checkpoint token in call metadata and surface a resumable_token in final envelope when model indicates continuation possible.
AC-4: For 'tool_failure' during function call, API returns structured tool_error frame containing tool_id, failure_class (retryable|non-retryable), and suggested mitigation (fallback_model|noop|retry-after).
AC-5: For 'partial_object' emissions (object fields streamed across frames), the client-visible API must never expose an object until object-level commit frame is emitted; intermediate frames are trace-only and accessible via debug-level trace logs only.
AC-6: Idempotency: repeated function-calls with identical idempotency_key must result in at-most-once tool invocation; platform records invocation_id and surface invocation_id in telemetry and final envelope.
AC-7: Streaming fallback policy: when latency SLO at edge is violated mid-stream, runtime triggers a 'fast-fallback' to a smaller model and emits a fallback_frame that explains reduction (model_id, reason, estimated_quality_impact).
AC-8: Observability: each acceptance test must produce telemetry events (emission_phase, frame_status, schema_validation, tool_outcome) with sample rate >= 100% in internal staging and >= 1% in canary production, and those keys must be visible in the Console exploratory view.
AC-9: Security: structured frames may include sensitive metadata only when KMS is enabled for the tenant; tests must validate that private deployments without KMS do not leak plaintext secrets in frames.
AC-10: Backwards compatibility: existing non-streaming clients continue to receive final JSON envelopes unchanged for calls with stream=false.
SM-1: Schema validation errors in production < 0.05% of structured-output calls within 30 days of rollout
SM-2: Resumable stream recovery success rate >= 98% in staging under injected 5% truncated_stream fault injection
SM-3: Tool duplicate-invocation incidents = 0 for calls with idempotency_key set across 30 days
SM-4: Mean time to detect (MTTD) frame-level validation errors < 5 minutes after rollout via Console alerts
Unit: schema validator tests for positive and negative examples (strict & permissive modes).
Integration: function-calling harness that simulates tool latency, transient errors, and explicit non-retryable failures. Validate tool_error frames and idempotency_id recording.
E2E-canary: Deploy to a single region on hosted with 2% traffic. Run canary suite that includes: TC-001 truncated_fragment_resume, TC-002 partial_object_commit_order, TC-003 fallback_model_switch_midstream, TC-004 idempotent_tool_duplicate_suppression.
Fault-injection: Inject 'truncated_stream' and 'tool_timeout' at runtime and assert recovery behavior according to error-mode matrix. Use chaos-monkey job that runs daily against staging for 72h.
Interoperability: Validate non-streaming SDKs (Python/JS/Go) receive consistent final envelopes when stream=false; streaming SDKs must support incremental on_commit callbacks and resume APIs.
Security tests: Run static scans and dynamic tests to ensure frames containing secrets are encrypted when KMS enabled; run privacy audit on stored checkpoints.
TC-001: truncated_fragment_resume - Start a streaming structured response, force EOF while last object missing closing field. Expect resumable_token in final envelope and successful resume that completes object when resumed with token.
TC-002: partial_object_commit_order - Emit object fields out-of-order across frames, ensure no object is exposed before commit frame and final object matches canonical schema on commit.
TC-003: tool_nonretryable - Function call returns non-retryable error. Expect tool_error frame with failure_class=non-retryable, no auto-retry, and consumer-visible final_envelope with error_code and mitigation hint.
TC-004: fast_fallback_midstream - Inject increased model latency to breach SLO after stream start. Expect fallback_frame with fallback_model and quality_impact estimate, and stream continues under fallback model.
TC-005: duplicate_tool_invoke - Replay same idempotency_key twice from client. Ensure platform invokes tool at most once and returns same invocation_id in both responses.
Phase 0 (dev): library-level validators enabled, local harness passes.
Phase 1 (staging): Enable full telemetry and fault-injection. Run 72h chaos tests.
Phase 2 (canary): Deploy to hosted region us-west-2 at 2% traffic, enable schema-strict for 50% of canary traffic and permissive for the rest, monitor Console dashboards and rollback on threshold breach.
Phase 3 (gradual): Ramp to 25% -> 60% -> 100% over 7 days with monitoring gates at each step. Dedicated customers will be contacted 10 business days before final switch; Private installs will receive an opt-in upgrade bundle.
Tradeoff A: strict schema validation reduces downstream parsing errors but increases false positives for heuristically-correct model outputs. Mitigation: support tenant-level permissive mode for first 30 days.
Tradeoff B: storing resumable checkpoints increases reliability but raises storage costs and retention questions. Mitigation: default 7-day TTL and opt-in longer retention for enterprise customers.
Tradeoff C: fallback to smaller model reduces latency but may degrade output quality. Mitigation: expose quality_impact estimate and allow caller policy to opt-out.

Title: Streaming session salvage: mid-request repair, deduplication, and capacity-aware backpressure tuning

Streaming session salvage: mid-request repair, deduplication, and capacity-aware backpressure tuning

Summary: A capacity surge on 2026-03-09 caused a cluster-wide degradation in streaming responses: intermittent disconnects, partial/duplicated tokens delivered to clients, and degraded resume behavior for long-lived sessions. This ticket tracks post-incident remediation work focused on (1) on-path mid-request repair and deduplication, (2) more conservative/explicit backpressure hysteresis tied to capacity headroom, and (3) telemetry/runbook improvements for faster incident detection and safe rollouts. The goal is to eliminate user-visible partial tokens and improve successful resume rates to >99.9% under 2x baseline load spikes.
2026-03-09: Incident declared at 11:42 UTC after Grafana alarm: streaming_session_complete_rate dropped 42% and token_gap_count increased. Initial mitigation: rerouted traffic to lower-utilized regions and increased short-term capacity via burst pool; enabled temporary connection keepalive extension to reduce socket churn. (on-call: Liam Chen)
2026-03-09: Emergency hotfix deployed to disable aggressive client-side chunk coalescing that caused partial-token delivery during backpressure; this reduced partial-token reports by ~60% within 30 minutes. Deployed as Canary to 5% then 50% then 100% traffic. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/6142
2026-03-10: Root cause analysis preliminary: a combination of (a) transient capacity saturation causing queue reordering and partial write buffers, (b) KV cache eviction mismatch during resume handshake, and (c) backpressure hysteresis thresholds that rapidly flipped between 'accept' and 'throttle' states. Repro harness created and failcases captured in staging. Related incidents: ENG-21450 backlog analysis and ENG-27801 surge thresholds work.
2026-03-11: Design review with PM and Reliability: agreed on three tracks (repair & dedupe, backpressure policy, telemetry & runbook). Prioritized by customer-impact and implementation risk. Action items created and owners assigned.

Title: Queueing impact analysis for multi-class arrival harness

Queueing impact analysis for multi-class arrival harness

Build and run a focused load-testing harness that isolates queueing effects under mixed-priority traffic. The goal is to quantify how continuous batching and request queue dynamics interact with multi-class arrivals (foreground low-latency vs. background high-throughput) and to produce stable metrics for tokens/sec, p95/p99 latencies, and regression detection thresholds. Deliverables: 1) reproducible harness (LoadForge) with configurable arrival distributions and priority preemption; 2) dashboards with control-chart based regression alerts; 3) a gang of experiments across model sizes, KV cache warm states, and batching window settings; 4) recommendations for autoscaler and routing policies that minimize tail regressions while preserving token throughput.

Title: Synchronized client retry window causing burst reconnections and high tail latency for streaming requests

Synchronized client retry window causing burst reconnections and high tail latency for streaming requests

Issue summary:
Customer reports a sudden increase in end-to-end inference latency and frequent streaming disconnects for long responses starting 2026-03-10T17:00Z. Symptoms are most pronounced for streaming chat sessions; non-streamed short responses show minor impact.

Impact:
- ~15% of customer streaming requests hit >5s tail latency, up from baseline ~200ms.
- Customer-visible streaming stalls and reconnects causing bad UX for real-time transcription product.
- Impacts 2 of the customer's Dedicated GPU pools in us-east.

Environment:
- Customer using Redwood SDK v2.4.1 (node) with default retry/backoff config.
- Dedicated cluster: dedicated-prod-us-east-2 (rwid-13b-v2 pinned).

Initial hypothesis:
Client SDKs with near-identical backoff defaults lost jitter (observed after SDK minor rollout) and therefore retried in lockstep when transient 429/503 responses occurred, causing a spike of simultaneous new connections and requests that overloaded NAT/proxy and produced head-of-line queuing at the API gateway. This produced apparent latency regressions and streaming stalls rather than a sustained higher error rate.

Additional context:
- Customer has a large fleet of ephemeral workers (autoscaling pods) that cycle frequently; many workers had identical SDK config and similar clock drift due to container start patterns during a deployment window.
- No scheduled Redwood platform maintenance at the time; our metrics show a short spike in 5xx/429 from 17:11–17:20Z concurrent with retry surge.

1) Deploy a fleet of clients using SDK v2.4.1 with default backoff settings.
2) Induce transient 429 responses by throttling a backend model pool (short circuit or simulate reduced capacity).
3) Observe client retry attempts aligning within a narrow window (few hundred ms) and resulting in a large simultaneous connection attempt count to the API gateway.
4) Observe streaming sessions stall or disconnect as server begins queueing and timing out.

- API gateway NewRelic: spike in connection attempts and 503s 2026-03-10T17:11:34Z -> 17:19:58Z.
- Support trace id sample: trace-20260310-5f3b (attached).
- Customer-side logs: repeated RetryAttempt events showing identical backoff timestamps across many pods.
- OS counters on infra NAT: short-term ephemeral port exhaustion and large TIME_WAIT count.

- Investigated request-level traces: high correlation between first observed 429s and a large cluster of retries ~200-600ms later.
- SDK release notes: v2.4.0 changed jitter implementation to a lightweight jitter that accidentally behaves like fixed offset when clients start nearly-synchronously.
- Wire-level capture from customer cluster shows burst of SYNs to api.redwood.prod around 17:12Z.
- Gateway logs show queue depth increased and per-route tokenization threads saturated for ~8 minutes.
- No model inference code regressions found; serving runtime CPUs and GPUs remained within normal utilization once requests were accepted — the problem is ingress queuing and connection storming.
- Reproduced locally by starting 500 clients with identical clocks and forcing initial 429s; when jitter set to zero, retries synced and queueing/p95 latency rose sharply.

Immediate mitigation (applied 2026-03-10):
- Recommended customer patch: downgrade SDK to 2.3.8 or apply SDK config override to enable full jitter (backoff_jitter=full), max_retries=3, connection_pool.max = 8. Customer applied overrides and tail latency returned toward baseline within 10 minutes.
- Edge-side temporary throttle change: API gateway accepted soft rate smoothing for the customer's tenant for 15 minutes to let clients recover.

Permanent fix (in progress):
- SDK PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/pull/4193 enforces full jitter by default and adds randomized start-up jitter for new client processes. Targeted release v2.5.0.
- Add a platform alert that detects synchronized retry patterns (high cross-client retry correlation) and raises a preemptive incident to trigger auto-smoothing.
- Update Dedicated onboarding docs to call out default retry/jitter and recommend connection pool sizing for large fleets.

- Engineering: roll v2.5.0 SDK default to full jitter and add startup jitter (owner: Marcus Liu, ETA 2026-03-20).
- SRE: add alert and dashboard for retry-correlation and ephemeral port pressure (owner: Priya Menon, ETA 2026-03-18).
- Support: update runbook to include immediate customer-side overrides and exact recommended config snippets (owner: Aisha Patel, ETA 2026-03-14).

Support (Aisha Patel) 2026-03-10T17:45Z: Created ticket after NimbleVoice support rep reported streaming stalls. Collected traces and requested customer logs and SDK config.
Customer (NimbleVoice - Jenna Ortiz) 2026-03-10T18:02Z: Confirmed SDK version v2.4.1 and provided deployment manifest. Noted brief autoscaler event at ~17:05Z which increased new pod churn.
SRE (Priya Menon) 2026-03-10T18:20Z: Observed gateway queue depth and SYN bursts. Suggested temporary tenant smoothing and asked customer to reduce max_connections per pod as a workaround.
Engineering (Marcus Liu) 2026-03-11T09:12Z: Found the jitter change in v2.4.0 that can degenerate into fixed offset under near-synchronous start. Drafted PR to restore full jitter by default and add startup jitter. Assigned to SDK team for expedited release.
Customer (Jenna Ortiz) 2026-03-11T13:30Z: Applied recommended SDK config overrides and reported meaningful improvement; tail p95 reduced to ~300ms within 10 minutes of change.
Support (Aisha Patel) 2026-03-12T08:02Z: Follow-up: confirmed monitoring shows no recurrence and customer satisfied with workaround. Will track SDK release and SRE alerting as open action items.

Title: Intermittent evening 5xx surge from streaming fanout + keepalive mismatch causing upstream worker preemptions

Intermittent evening 5xx surge from streaming fanout + keepalive mismatch causing upstream worker preemptions

Issue summary:
- Customer BlueArc reports elevated 5xx rate (502/503) on streaming routes during evening business hours. Errors began ~2026-03-13 18:05 UTC and show repeated short spikes (1–3 minutes) with increased tail-latency for streaming sessions.

Impact:
- Multiple long-lived streaming client sessions observed disconnecting and failing to resume. Customer reports degraded UX for interactive analytics feature; estimated 12% of streaming calls in the hour experienced errors.

Timeline / Observed pattern:
- 2026-03-13 18:02 UTC: first error cluster; apigw error rate to this tenant increased to 5xx ~18%.
- 18:05–18:12 UTC: short oscillations of 5xx with concurrent rise in upstream preempt events and runtime worker restarts.
- 18:20 UTC: transient decrease, then another cluster at 19:10 UTC with similar pattern.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool serving BlueArc (tenant id: ta-9043) in us-east-1, running model variants redwood/gptx-7b and redwood/gptx-13b-int8.
- Streaming route: /v1/stream/chat (http2). TLS termination at edge, keepalive proxied through streaming-proxy.

Steps to reproduce (customer reproduction):
1) Establish 40 long-lived streaming sessions that send alternating short user messages (~100 tokens) and occasional large prompts (~2500 tokens).
2) Let sessions idle with periodic keepalive pings from the SDK (interval ~25s).
3) Observe intermittent 502/503 responses and session resets after several minutes.

Observed artifacts / logs:
- apigw logs show HTTP/2 RST_STREAM followed by 502 responses from the proxy.
- streaming-proxy metrics show a short surge in concurrent streams per worker followed by worker preempt and SIGTERM -> restart.
- runtime logs: NVML preempt events and 'worker: preempted due to scheduler pressure' entries; no explicit OOMs.
- TLS logs: occasional TLS renegotiation (client-initiated) at time of spikes; keepalive intervals for some clients drifted to 0–2s in traces (SDK bug suspected).

Initial triage notes:
- Pattern suggests amplification: large prompt fanout (long generation) ties up worker threads while many short heartbeats/keepalives increase scheduling overhead at proxy, causing accept/handshake queuing and eventual worker preempt.
- TLS renegotiation coincident with stream spikes appears to increase CPU overhead on proxy and apigw.

Immediate customer-facing message we sent:
- "We're investigating elevated streaming errors impacting some long-lived sessions. Engineering is triaging runtime preemption and proxy scheduling; we'll follow up within the hour with mitigation steps and ETA."
2026-03-13 18:25 - Support (Aisha): Collected initial logs from BlueArc tenant and escalated to SRE. Noted concurrent keepalive storm patterns in proxy metrics.
2026-03-13 18:40 - SRE (Marco): Attached flamegraph of streaming-proxy CPU during spike; saw frequent context switches and a rising accept queue. Hypothesis: short keepalive intervals from SDK + TLS renegotiation amplifies per-connection CPU.
2026-03-13 19:05 - Eng (Liang Chen): Runtime reports worker preempt events when per-worker concurrent streams exceed ~48. No NVML OOMs, but scheduler marks GPU as busy and signals preempt to reclaim cycles for other tasks.
2026-03-13 19:30 - Support (Aisha): Informed customer of temporary mitigation (client-side keepalive increase) and asked for replication script. Customer provided reproduction harness that generates 40 streams with intermittent large prompts.
2026-03-13 20:10 - SRE (Marco): Deployed a temporary apigw config change to increase accept queue depth for the affected route by 2x and turned on more aggressive connection backpressure in streaming-proxy. Observed reduction in 5xx rate for subsequent spike window.
2026-03-14 09:12 - Eng (Liang Chen): Opening follow-up task to add telemetry: per-tenant streaming concurrency gauge and TLS renegotiation counter to correlate with preempt events. Assigned to runtime team backlog.
2026-03-14 11:00 - Support (Aisha): Customer confirmed seeing fewer disconnects overnight after applying keepalive workaround and after our temporary edge config change. Asking to keep ticket open while eng implements durable fix.
Detailed traces show two contributing factors: 1) client SDK bug causing aggressive keepalive behavior (25s configured but observed bursts of 0-2s) leading to high syscall rates at proxy; 2) large prompt fanout holds GPU kernels open for long real-time durations, which reduces worker availability and triggers scheduler preempt signals. Combined, these create a short-lived amplification loop where proxy CPU and runtime scheduler interact and produce 5xx spikes. Correlated metrics: streaming_proxy.cpu_ns, apigw.accept_queue_depth, runtime.worker_preempt_count. No memory OOMs observed. Next steps identified: durable proxy backpressure improvements, runtime scheduler rate-limits per-tenant long-running generation, and customer SDK patch to fix keepalive jitter.
1) Customer: Increase client-side keepalive interval to >=60s and disable client-initiated TLS renegotiation in SDK (patch available in customer SDK v2.3.1). 2) Platform: Applied temporary apigw accept-queue increase and enabled streaming-proxy backpressure—monitoring for regressions. 3) Avoid concurrent large prompt fanout across many long-lived streams until fixes rolled out.
- Engineering to implement per-tenant streaming concurrency telemetry and a soft cap to avoid worker preempt cascade (tracked in runtime backlog).
- Runtime to add a graceful preempt backoff to avoid immediate SIGTERM on scheduler pressure.
- SDK team to publish recommended keepalive defaults and patch to avoid renegotiation.
- Support to coordinate customer validation and keep ticket open until fix rolled out and validated (aim target: 2026-03-20).

Title: Streaming responses reset mid-generation in prod us-east (Acme AI) — connection resets / truncated streams

2) Observe that the stream ends early (no final "[DONE]" / missing end-of-stream event).

Title: Interleaved streaming fallback and tenant priority reshuffle triggered elevated 5xx error rate

Interleaved streaming fallback and tenant priority reshuffle triggered elevated 5xx error rate

Issue summary: Starting 2026-03-12 09:10 UTC we observed a sudden, sustained rise in 5xx responses for a single dedicated-tenant (BrightDocs) originating from streaming endpoints and elevated retry traffic from the API gateway. Impact: Customer-facing streaming sessions saw ~20-30% failure rate (502/503) for 45 minutes; non-streaming requests experienced increased latency and occasional 504s. Environment: prod | us-east | dedicated pool brd-east-1.

Observed behavior appears correlated with a tenant priority weight change (internal autoscaler action) followed by streaming failovers that caused the runtime to enter a cyclical fallback and connection churn loop. This amplified retries at the API gateway and led to upstream runtime process restarts under memory pressure.

Steps to reproduce (investigation runbook):
1) On a dedicated tenant with mixed streaming & short-polling traffic, change route weight to shift 30% of traffic to a lower-cost replica pool.
2) Initiate a sustained mix of long-lived streaming sessions (20 concurrent, ~1-2 tokens/sec) and bursts of short generation requests.
3) Observe increased keepalive resets from proxy -> runtime and kernel-level OOMs inside a subset of runtime workers after warmup prefetches.

Logs / key signals:
- apigw metrics: 5xx rate jump from baseline 0.5% to 22% at 09:10 UTC.
- gateway logs (excerpt): "upstream_reset: connection_reset by peer during streaming write" repeated across multiple upstreams.
- runtime logs (excerpt): "worker[12] kvcache_lock_wait=468ms prefetch_queue=full panic: runtime: memory allocation failed" then subsequent graceful restarts.
- autoscaler events: "priority-shift: apply-weight-adjust brd-east-1: 0.7->0.4 at 09:09:42 UTC"

Initial impact mitigation performed:
- Rolled back weight change (09:18 UTC).
- Temporarily increased runtime pool size by adding two warmed replicas (09:22 UTC).
- Enabled stricter streaming concurrency per-tenant throttle to limit new streaming sessions (09:25 UTC).

Current status: error rate dropping but residual elevated retries persist for some long-lived streams. Customer still experiencing sporadic streaming failures when connections are resumed after prefetch invalidation.

Suggested next steps:
- SRE run heap/profile capture on affected runtime workers to identify fragmentation or leak pattern during prefetch + streaming mix.
- Add a temporary circuit-breaker at apigw for repeated streaming reconnects from same tenant to prevent retry amplification.
- Update autoscaler policy to avoid immediate weight reshuffles during high streaming concurrency; gate weight changes behind a warmup window.
- Add a targeted regression test to reproduce streaming+prefetch interplay in staging.

References: linked runbook and dashboards provided below.
2026-03-12 09:30 UTC - Maya Chen (Support): Customer reports ~25% of streaming sessions failing. Escalated to SRE. Included initial request IDs and timestamps in private field.
2026-03-12 09:40 UTC - Luis Ortega (SRE): Observed autoscaler weight shift at 09:09:42. Kicking off worker heap capture on brd-runtime-3. Tentatively suspect kv-cache prefetch thrash causing memory pressure.
2026-03-12 09:55 UTC - Customer (BrightDocs - Alex Rivera): We saw clients reconnecting frequently; some clients hit retry backoff and eventually succeed. Requesting ETA on mitigation.
2026-03-12 10:05 UTC - Luis Ortega (SRE): Rolled back weight change (09:18 UTC) and added two warmed replicas (09:22 UTC). Applying per-tenant streaming throttle at 09:25 UTC. Monitoring for stabilization.
2026-03-12 11:00 UTC - Maya Chen (Support): Customer confirms error rate decreasing to ~3% but still reporting occasional 502s on resumed sessions. Offering post-incident analysis call at 14:00 UTC.
2026-03-13 08:40 UTC - Dev (Anika Patel): Retrieved heap profile and found elevated fragmentation in arena allocation; opening PR to add guardrails around prefetch concurrency. See PR in linked_github_prs.

Hypothesis: Rapid priority-weight reshuffle triggered prefetch cancellations and concurrent KV cache invalidations in a subset of runtime workers. Long-lived streaming sessions hold partial KV state and when prefetches are retried across replaced workers they create memory pressure and connection resets; API gateway retries amplify the churn. Evidence: correlated autoscaler event timestamp, repeated 'kvcache_lock_wait' traces, and worker OOM traces. Next diagnostic step: attach pmap and full jemalloc stats during replay and run a focused staging test that replays the exact mix of long-lived streams and short bursts while applying a weight change.
Mitigation applied: weight rollback, added warmed replicas, per-tenant streaming throttle, and apigw circuit-breaker for reconnect storms. Root cause under investigation: prefetch + streaming interaction causing memory fragmentation and process restarts. Follow-up actions: deploy fix to guard prefetch concurrency (PR referenced), update autoscaler rollout gating to include streaming warmup window, and create regression test in e2e suite. Customer scheduled for post-incident review on 2026-03-15.

Title: Edge proxy retry loop causes SSE stream freeze during long chat sessions

Edge proxy retry loop causes SSE stream freeze during long chat sessions

Issue summary: Customer reports repeated streaming chat sessions (SSE) that begin normally but freeze mid-generation after ~30-120s. The client observes no final event and connection remains open; eventually client-side times out. This appears correlated with bursts of 502/504 responses from an edge proxy in front of Redwood’s API and aggressive automatic retries by that proxy.

Impact: Several paid customers on Dedicated capacity experienced degraded UX for long multi-turn chats. Affected customers reported multiple sessions where partial output is delivered then stalls; some sessions recovered after forcing a client reconnect, others required server-side fix. No data exfiltration suspected.

Why this ticket: Customer asked for root cause, mitigation, and permanent fix. Ticket captures investigation and resolution plan.
Partial streaming output for long chats, client-visible stalls, increased support load. Customer reported ~12 impacted sessions across two accounts in the last 48h.
prod | dedicated | us-east (edge-proxy-3) and eu-west (edge-proxy-7)
1) Use a dedicated customer account with reserved capacity and open a long multi-turn SSE chat (>1k tokens).
2) Trigger a response that takes >30s to stream (complex prompt + external tool calls simulated),
3) During streaming, cause transient edge-proxy resource pressure (simulate burst of concurrent requests or apply artificial 502s),
4) Observe that SSE stream delivers some chunks then pauses indefinitely; client stays connected and no final event is emitted.
2026-03-09T14:22:11Z request_id=abc123 worker_id=w-42 proxy=edge-proxy-3 502 upstream_reset

2026-03-09T14:22:11Z request_id=abc123 retried by proxy (X-Retry: 1) -> new connection request_id=abc123-1, server accepted but stream eventually unblocks on worker but client sees no final chunk
2026-03-09T14:22:35Z serving-runtime: kv-cache-lock wait 240ms prior to emit chunk seq=12
2026-03-09T14:22:58Z connection remaining open, no further chunks; client-side heartbeat OK until client timeout at 2026-03-09T14:24:10Z
Initial hypothesis: serving runtime kernel swap or kv-cache eviction causing mid-stream stall. Logs show short cache waits but not long enough to explain full freeze.
Observed correlation: edge-proxy returned 502 for the original upstream connection then attempted an automatic retry. Proxy attaches X-Retry header and opens a new downstream connection with same request semantics.
Race condition found: server-side streaming handler expects a single long-lived connection per request_id. When a proxy retry opens a second connection carrying same idempotency markers, the server forks a second handler for the same logical stream but continues to keep the first stream in a semi-finalized state. Streaming chunks are interleaved; client receives first handler's output then stalls because jittered backpressure and connection pinning hold remaining tokens in the other handler.

Title: Hosted API streaming: stream rehydration failure postmortem (2026-08-07)

Hosted API streaming: stream rehydration failure postmortem (2026-08-07)

On 2026-08-07 at ~15:12 UTC we observed a sudden, sustained increase in hosted API streaming TTFB and partial session stalls for ~37 minutes. A subset of streaming sessions failed to successfully rehydrate KV cache after edge reconnects, which inflated per-request compute and caused head-of-line stalls in the streaming multiplexer. This manifested as p95/p99 TTFB spikes, client reconnect churn, and ~14% elevation in 5xx for streaming routes. User-facing responses were delayed (median streaming initial bytes +420ms) and some long-lived streams timed out. The incident is classified P0 due to customer impact and the hit to SLAs.
- Duration: ~37 minutes (15:12 - 15:49 UTC)
- Affected surface: streaming endpoints on hosted API in us-west-2 and eu-west-1 (traffic routed through edge nodes with reconnect churn)
- Customer-visible: increased time-to-first-byte and intermittent stream freezes; short-lived elevated 5xx (14% relative increase vs baseline)
- Estimated requests impacted: ~62k streaming connections experienced degraded performance; ~1.6k sessions hit stream timeout errors
- Business impact: several high-throughput customers reported user-visible slowdowns; internal SLAs for streaming p99 latency breached during window
Signal: automated streaming TTFB alert (p99 > 1.0s) fired at 15:14 UTC. Oncall received PagerDuty alert and Slack #sre-streaming channel filled with early telemetry. Customers also filed support tickets starting 15:18 UTC. Initial dashboards showed a correlated spike in edge reconnect rate and KV cache miss rate for rehydrations.
- 15:12 UTC: first anomalous rise seen in streaming TTFB metrics (automated detection threshold approaching)
- 15:14 UTC: p99 TTFB alert fires; oncall page triggered
- 15:15-15:20 UTC: engineers collect traces and flame graphs; identify elevated rehydration miss rate for reconnecting sessions
- 15:22 UTC: short-lived mitigation: increase rehydration RPC timeout and enable conservative fallback to uncached execution path for streams showing rehydration failures (manual config change)
- 15:28 UTC: partial reduction in head-of-line stalls but p99 TTFB still elevated; further mitigation: throttle concurrent rehydration attempts per-edge-host to 8
- 15:34 UTC: metrics show progressive decline in p99 TTFB and reconnect churn
- 15:49 UTC: system returns to baseline; monitoring confirms stability for 1 hour
- 16:55 UTC: post-incident analysis meeting begins (warroom)
- 2026-08-10: final report published
A sequence of contributing factors led to production-visible degradation: 
1) A recent change to the edge streaming reconnect path (deployed 2026-07-29) added parallelized rehydration attempts for speed, but under reconnect storms this allowed many simultaneous cache rehydration RPCs to the KV service from the same edge host.
2) The KV service had an under-provisioned connection limit per-front-end and an internal throttling heuristic that began rejecting/queuing rehydration requests under burst. The edge clients did not back off quickly, causing long RPC latencies.
3) The streaming multiplexer holds serialized write/flush ordering for a connection; when one rehydration RPC blocks, it effectively stalls other streams multiplexed over the same worker thread, causing head-of-line blocking and elevated TTFB.
4) Monitoring thresholds for rehydration miss rate were present but not routed to an automated circuit breaker; there was no automatic fallback to a safe slower path when RPC latencies exceeded the rehydration timeout.
- Increased rehydration RPC timeout to avoid tight failure loops (15:22 UTC)
- Enabled uncached fallback route for streams that failed rehydration to avoid infinite stalls (15:22-15:25 UTC)
- Rate-limited concurrent rehydration attempts per edge host to 8 (15:28 UTC)
- Rotated a small pool of KV frontends to shift traffic while capacity adjustments completed (15:30 UTC)
- Notified customer success and engineering stakeholders and opened JIRA ticket for follow-up (JIRA-INC-4312)
- Increase per-KV-front connection caps during burst windows (config change scheduled)
- Add a conservative exponential backoff in edge rehydration logic to reduce thundering herd behavior
- Add an automated circuit to detect sustained rehydration RPC latency and force fallback to uncached execution to protect multiplexers
- Expand runbook checklist for streaming reconnect storms (quick steps for rate-limiting rehydration and rotating KV frontends)
- Rework rehydration architecture: move from synchronous per-stream rehydration to probabilistic prewarming and shared prefix cache to reduce N x M RPCs during reconnect storms (RFC due 2026-09-01)
- Implement per-edge adaptive concurrency controller that reacts to KV backend latencies
- Improve throttling and autoscale behavior on KV frontends to better absorb reconnect bursts
- Add synthetic chaos tests that simulate mass reconnects + KV backend latency to validate protections before deploy
- New alert: rehydration RPC latency p95 > 250ms AND rehydration miss rate > 5% in a 3m window -> page eng-sre and trigger automated fallback
- Dashboard panels for rehydration concurrency by edge-host and per-region KV rejection rate
- Instrument streaming multiplexer stall metrics (blocked-time percent) and add p95/p99 to SLO smoke checks
- Added section: "Reconnect storm triage" with ordered steps: 1) confirm rehydration miss-rate and source edge hosts; 2) apply per-edge rehydration concurrency limit; 3) enable uncached fallback; 4) rotate KV frontends; 5) notify CS customers and execs if >10% baseline impact.
- Included quick CLI commands and exact feature flags to flip for immediate mitigation
- Provided playbook snippets for increasing KV frontend capacity on cloud provider (permission notes included)
- Why did the KV backend throttling heuristic not emit a high-priority alert? (investigate alert coverage)
- Consider whether deployment 2026-07-29 should have had a targeted canary that simulates reconnect jitter
