Title: Adaptive tiling + prefetch profiling diary

Adaptive tiling + prefetch profiling diary

Purpose and high-level summary:

This working diary collects experiments and hypotheses for an adaptive tiling + prefetch policy aimed at improving attention kernel stability across mixed sequence-length workloads. Goal: reduce p95/p99 token latency spikes during microbursts while preserving TFLOPS efficiency and end-to-end throughput. We prototype three levers: tile_size (work granularity), prefetch_w (lookahead KV pages/prefetch slots), and fused-op fallbacks (enable/disable fused attention+softmax fusion). This doc is intentionally conversational — notes to self and team — and records commands, oddball artifacts, and concrete next experiments.

Context and why this matters:
- Production traces show intermittent 3–5x token latency spikes when a mix of short (16–64) and long (512–2048) requests run concurrently on the same GPU slab.
- Existing policy selects FlashAttention when sequence length > 128 and falls back to paged-flash for >1024; fused-paths are autopicked when batch shapes align. We suspect tiling boundaries and prefetch windowing cause bank conflicts and late kernel fallback that manifest as jitter.

Environment and test harness:
- Hardware: H100 (80GB) and A100-40GB nodes used. Experiments labeled H100/A100 accordingly.
- Models: Llama2-13B (fp16), a trimmed decoder-only attention stack (custom bench harness) to isolate attention kernel paths.
- Workloads: synthetic mixes to emulate production — ratio short:long = 70:30 and a bimodal 50:50. Seqs used: [16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048].
- Tools: nsys for timeline + kernel occupancy, perf / nvprof for SM occupancy + instr throughput, nvtx markers around scheduler dispatch. Custom microbench runner: bench/attention_microbench.py (see linked PR).
- Metrics captured: per-token latency (p50/p90/p95/p99), tokens/sec, kernel occupancy, L2/DRAM bandwidth, memory copy times for KV pages, kernel selection frequency.

Quick experiment matrix (subset):
- A: base (flashattention enabled, fusedops on, tile=auto, prefetch_w=2)
- B: tile=64, prefetch_w=2, fusedops on
- C: tile=128, prefetch_w=1, fusedops on
- D: tile=128, prefetch_w=3, fusedops on
- E: tile=128, prefetch_w=2, fusedops off (force paged)
- F: adaptive_tile (runtime picks tile based on seq and active_batch), prefetch_w=2, fusedops on

Notes on real runs and surprising patterns:
1) H100 base (A) with mixed 70:30 workload: p95 token latency = 15.2ms, p99 = 37.9ms, throughput 68k tokens/s. Telemetry shows kernel handoffs mid-sequence when long sequences arrive; nvtx indicates a 0.6–1.2ms delay between dispatch and kernel start for some fused kernels.

2) Changing to tile=64 (B) shrunk p95 slightly (14.1ms) but increased p99 (42.3ms). Interpretation: smaller tiles reduce per-kernel work (avoids long blocking), but increases kernel-launch overheads and scheduling pressure for fusedops.

3) tile=128 + prefetch_w=1 (C) gave best p99 stability for long sequences but lowered average TFLOPS (~4% drop) on A100 due to less overlap of prefetch and compute. p95 improved to 13.6ms and p99 dropped to 28.4ms on H100.

4) Increasing prefetch_w to 3 (D) bumped throughput but reintroduced p99 spikes for mixed bursts — likely because larger prefetching causes more DRAM reads up-front and increases L2 eviction churn when many small requests interleave with large ones. On A100 we saw DRAM burst windows aligned with spike windows in token latency.

5) Forcing fusedops off (E) reduced kernel start jitter but increased per-token latency overall (p50 up ~8%), consistent with fused path being more efficient when it runs smoothly. The fused kernels seem fragile under bursty interleaving, but essential for peak efficiency.

6) Adaptive tile heuristic (F) where runtime selects 64 for seq<=64, 128 for 65<=seq<=512, and 256 for >512: gave the best balance in mixed workloads — p95 close to C, p99 30.1ms (slightly higher than C but more stable in 50:50 bimodal tests).

Telemetry deep-dive and kernel traces:
- NVTX traces show that in many p99 events the fused attention kernel is queued for an unusually long time (0.8–2ms) after nvtx-dispatch. This correlates with scheduler contention when many small-tile kernels occupy the launch queues.
- nsys occupancy shows SM utilization dips right before p99 spikes — indicating kernel preemption or long-running memory-copy ops (prefetch) that steal bandwidth.
- Kernel-level counters: bank-conflict counters are elevated for tile sizes that are not 128-aligned with the model head-dim (in our Llama2 build head_dim=128). This suggests stride/tiling alignment matters for bank-friendliness.

Hypotheses generated from observations:
H1: Tile sizes that are not a multiple of the attention head stride (head_dim or warp tile) cause increased bank conflicts and cache-line thrashing, especially on A100.
H2: Larger prefetch windows improve throughput for homogeneous long workloads but cause L2 churn when short requests interleave, leading to p99 spikes.
H3: Fused kernels are highly efficient but sensitive to launch-time latency; small kernel fragments (tile=64) create too many small fused launches, increasing launch/dynamic-scheduler pressure.
H4: Runtime kernel selection jitter arises because kernel-choice decisions happen late (during scheduler dispatch) and sometimes switch from fused->paged mid-request if memory pressure spikes. This fallback is expensive.

Quick experiments to validate hypotheses (planned/prioritized):
- Validate H1: run microbench with head_dim mismatch toy model (set head_dim to 96, 128, 160) and sweep tile sizes. Record bank-conflict counters.
- Validate H2: synthetic interleave where long requests prefetch but then are paused (simulate preemption). Measure L2 eviction rates.
- Validate H3: instrument fused kernel launch path to aggregate number of launches per request and queue-depth; test coalescing launches where possible.
- Validate H4: add telemetry to record kernel-choice timestamp (decision_time) vs dispatch_time to quantify late fallbacks.

Immediate tactical mitigations (dev-change ideas):
1) Tile alignment policy: prefer tile sizes that are multiples/divisors of head_dim to reduce bank conflicts. Add a small alignment table in runtime.
2) Prefetch backpressure: throttle prefetch when queue_depth>threshold or when many short requests recently arrived (sliding window).
3) Fused coalescing: aggregate adjacent small tiles into single fused launches when they belong to same request to lower launch pressure.
4) Faster fallback path: pre-compile paged-fusion kernels to reduce fallback latency.

Commands and snippets used (notes to reproduce quickly):
- Run bench: python bench/attention_microbench.py --model llama13b --device h100 --mix 70-30 --tile auto --prefetch 2 --fused yes --log perf/logs/runA
- NVTX profiling: nv-nsight-cu-profiler collect -o runA.nsys --capture-range=nvtx -- python bench/attention_microbench.py ...
- Kernel counters: sudo nsys profile --sample=none --trace=cuda --stats=true ... then use nsys cupti-exporter to extract bank_conflict counters.

Raw snippets (observed numbers, H100):
- A (base): p50 6.2ms, p95 15.2ms, p99 37.9ms, tokens/s 68k
- B (tile64): p50 6.7ms, p95 14.1ms, p99 42.3ms, tokens/s 66k
- C (tile128,pref1): p50 5.9ms, p95 13.6ms, p99 28.4ms, tokens/s 65k
- D (tile128,pref3): p50 5.8ms, p95 13.8ms, p99 35.6ms, tokens/s 71k
- E (no fused): p50 7.0ms, p95 18.9ms, p99 45.1ms, tokens/s 58k
- F (adaptive): p50 6.1ms, p95 13.9ms, p99 30.1ms, tokens/s 67k

Production traces correlation attempt:
- Pulled 20 hours of traces where customers experienced tails — bins of 5-minute windows show p99 spikes correlate with sudden influx of many small requests from a few customers (spammy bursts). Also correlated with scheduled rebalancing jobs that cause background paged memory compaction on some nodes.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How much does OS-level PCIe scheduling (host CPU) vs GPU SM contention contribute? We need host-level traces and to correlate with cgroups/CPU steal.
- Are there cross-tenant effects from simultaneous memory pressure (shared slab) that cause late kernel fallbacks? Need to test in fully isolated dedicated capacity to see difference.
- Can we implement a cheap runtime predictor that says "prefer fused if expected runtime > X ms" to avoid many small fused launches?

Decisions and proposed next steps (short horizon):
- Short-term (this sprint): implement tile alignment table and a metric gated prefetch throttle (PR in linked_artifacts). Add kernel-decision telemetry timestamps to quantify H4.
- Mid-term (2–4 sprints): prototype fused-launch coalescer to reduce small-launch pressure and evaluate stability.
- Long-term: explore a tiny ML predictor (linear model) inside runtime that picks tile/prefetch/fused flags per-request using recent short-term workload features. Evaluate cost of prediction vs benefit.

Todo (action items):
- [ ] Diego: instrument kernel-choice timestamp and add to logs (deadline 2026-02-24).
- [ ] Priya: run head_dim mismatch matrix on A100 and produce bank-conflict heatmap (deadline 2026-02-28).
- [ ] Ethan: isolate test in dedicated capacity and rerun mixed workload to see cross-tenant effects (deadline 2026-03-03).
- [ ] Maya: draft RFC for tile-alignment policy and prefetch backpressure heuristic (due 2026-03-07).

Notes-to-self and loose thoughts:
- There's a sweet spot between too many small fused launches and switching to paged kernels — optimizations should bias towards keeping the fused path healthy since it wins at steady-state but avoid sending it into pathological launch patterns.
- Consider exposing an observable metric in Console: "fused_launch_rate" and "prefetch_eviction_rate" to help customers debug tail latency regressions tied to workload mix.
- Small change experiment: on a couple of test nodes, pin the scheduler to prefer fused kernels by delaying non-fused kernel launches by 100–200us and see if that stabilizes tails (risky but informative).

Appendix: links to traces and artifacts
- nsys timeline files: gs://redwood-profiling/2026-02/tiling-prefetch/runA.nsys (internal)
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/874 (adaptive tile machinery)
- Jira task: INF-4819 (tiling-prefetch investigation)

End of diary entry. This is a working doc; expect updates as experiments complete.

Title: Intermittent 403s for impersonated admin calls after projected service-account token rotation in private deployment

Intermittent 403s for impersonated admin calls after projected service-account token rotation in private deployment

Issue summary: Customer reports intermittent 403 Forbidden responses when the Redwood control plane attempts to perform admin-level operations using impersonation (service-account token exchange) after projected token rotation on their private deployment. Impact: Admin console actions (user role changes, policy updates) and automated role-sync jobs fail intermittently for a subset of users, causing delayed user provisioning and blocked audit uploads. Environment: Private deployment (VPC) for Acme Health; Redwood control plane communicates with customer-managed auth-service that projects Kubernetes service account tokens into a sidecar volume. Problem first seen after IdP and K8s token lifetime changes on 2026-03-09.
1) Customer rotates projected service-account token TTL from 6h -> 15m on their cluster (k8s projected token).
2) Initiate admin action from Console that requires admin impersonation (e.g., add role binding via Console UI or run role-sync job).
3) Observe request path: Console -> Redwood control plane -> private auth-proxy -> exchange projected token for impersonation token -> call admin API -> sometimes 403 returned.
4) Reproduce attempts show that retrying the same operation immediately sometimes succeeds (race window).
auth-proxy: 2026-03-09T14:02:12Z WARN token-exchange: token exp (iat/exp mismatch) detected for svcacct:acme-admin projected: token_k8s_mount_abc123
control-plane: 2026-03-09T14:02:12Z ERROR impersonation: upstream 403 from auth backend (reason=invalid_audience) request_id=rp-3f9a
console: 2026-03-09T14:02:13Z INFO retrying impersonation attempt (attempt=2) -> success
kubelet: 2026-03-09T14:02:11Z INFO token reviewer validated token with bound_sa=acme-admin ttl_remaining_seconds=120
Initial hypothesis: projected token rotation shortened TTL introduces a race where the control plane reads a just-rotated token from the sidecar volume while the IdP/token reviewer has not yet accepted the new token binding, causing audience or jti mismatches.
Observed pattern: failures cluster around rotation window and affect only admin-impersonation flows that use token-exchange. Non-impersonated API calls from standard service tokens unaffected.
Reproduced internally by simulating projected token TTL=15m on staging private cluster. Saw deterministic 403s when token was read within 30s after rotation event.
Auth backend returns 403 with subcode 'invalid_audience' or 'jti_mismatch' in logs for failed exchanges. Token reviewer logs show transient validation failures for new tokens until cache refresh.
Related to previous tickets SUP-84721 (service-account impersonation rotation failure) but this case differs: failure is caused by short projected TTL + local filesystem propagation delay + token-reviewer cache TTL (customer-side).
Ava Thompson (Support): Customer reports ~15% of admin actions failing since they changed projected token TTL. They've paused rotation and failures rate dropped.
Marcus Li (SRE): Investigating token exchange path and caching in auth-proxy. Added increased logging and a request_id trace to isolate timing. Suspect race between kube projected token refresh and token-reviewer cache TTL on the IdP side.
Priya Natarajan (Customer Success): Noted customer cannot extend projected TTL due to security policy. Customer requests guidance for a config-based mitigation in Redwood while they revisit policy.
James Parker (Acme Health, Customer): We see failures mostly during our nightly key rotation window. Can Redwood add a small retry/backoff or validate token freshness before exchange?
Marcus Li (SRE): Proposed mitigation: 1) add short deterministic retry (3 attempts with 200ms jitter) on 403 with subcodes 'invalid_audience'/'jti_mismatch' during impersonation exchange, 2) optionally verify token 'iat' and wait up to 1s if token age < 5s before attempting exchange. Will validate with staging. Filing follow-up internal task to implement guarded retry.
Ava Thompson (Support): Scheduled call with customer 2026-03-13 to validate staging patch. Tracking SLA milestones.
Investigating - temporary mitigation recommended (pause aggressive projected TTL reduction). Patch under test: guarded retry on impersonation token-exchange and 1s token-stabilization wait when token iat is very recent.
2026-03-12: Implemented guarded retry in auth-proxy branch and validated on staging with projected TTL=15m; observed failure rate drop to ~0.5% from 15%.
2026-03-12: Coordinated with customer to re-run their rotation in staging; recommended final rollout with feature flag off-by-default for private deployments in case of policy constraints.
Follow-up: engineering task INT-1189 created to add configurable token-stabilization delay and document guidance for projected token TTLs in private deployments.

Title: Emission Stability and Tool-Orchestration: Soft-Fail & Streaming Acceptance

Emission Stability and Tool-Orchestration: Soft-Fail & Streaming Acceptance

PRD-style acceptance and behavioral specification for: (A) deterministic structured output envelopes during streaming, (B) robust tool/function-orchestration semantics when downstream tool calls fail or time out (soft-fail modes), and (C) observable signal set for debugging degraded emissions. This ticket captures requirements, tradeoffs, and concrete acceptance tests for engineering to implement and QA to validate.
Teams integrating function-calls and streaming structured output have encountered brittle failure modes: partial JSON emissions, stuck streams when a tool times out, and unclear signals in telemetry for root-cause. Previous specs focused on schema handshakes but did not fully specify soft-fail policies (when to continue vs abort), how to surface partial-but-valid objects, or required observability for production troubleshooting.
1) Define deterministic envelope semantics so consumers can parse incrementally and resume/reconcile partial objects. 2) Specify soft-fail modes for tool invocation: best-effort, fallback-only, and abort. 3) Establish acceptance tests for streaming + tool failures that exercise backpressure, resumability, and idempotent retries. 4) Define telemetry and SLI/alert thresholds to detect degraded emission reliability.
- Streaming text and structured frames emitted from Redwood API. - Function/tool invocation lifecycle (invoke, success, failure, retry). - Soft-fail policies and configuration. - Acceptance criteria and end-to-end test matrix (simulated tool latencies/failures).
- Changes to client SDKs beyond minimal parsing guidance. - New RPC transport protocols. - Billing/quotas changes related to retries (handled by a separate billing review).
- Strict abort-on-tool-failure yields highest data correctness but reduces availability; soft-fail increases availability at the cost of accuracy. We recommend defaulting to best-effort-with-degraded-indicators for hosted API and offering strict-abort configuration for enterprise Dedicated/Private deployments. - Emitting placeholder fields vs removing the field: placeholder maintains schema shape for parsers but may surface misleading data. We prefer placeholder objects with explicit 'soft_fail' enum and provenance metadata.
AC-1: Incremental Envelope Parsing: Streaming responses are emitted as ordered 'frames' where each frame is a top-level JSON object stringified and newline-delimited. Consumers can reconstruct the final object by concatenating frames and applying frame-level 'commit' markers. In tests, a slow client that disconnects and reconnects using resume token can re-sync and reconstruct a consistent object state.
AC-2: Soft-Fail Modes: System exposes three modes: 'abort' (default for strict endpoints), 'best_effort' (continue emitting remaining structured fields, include 'soft_fail' markers), and 'degraded_fallback' (switch to cheaper model or cached result then emit). Implementation must allow per-route configuration. Acceptance tests must validate each mode against simulated downstream tool failures.
AC-3: Partial-Object Validity: When a tool call fails and mode is 'best_effort', the emitted structured object must remain JSON-parseable at frame boundaries and include an explicit 'provenance' map with keys: source_variant, tool_status, tool_error_code, soft_fail=true. Test harness validates JSON validity after each frame and final reconciliation produces a documented 'incomplete' state.
AC-4: Function-Invocation Idempotency & Retry Signals: Tool gateway must return idempotency token on initial invocation. Retries (automatic or client-initiated) must attach token to avoid duplicate side-effects. Acceptance tests include simulated at-least-once delivery and assert idempotent behavior for a provided sample tool (mock webhook that records invocations).
AC-5: Timeouts & Backpressure Behavior: When a tool exceeds configured timeout: - in 'abort' mode, the stream emits an error envelope and closes (status=closed, code=TOOL_TIMEOUT). - in 'best_effort', emit soft-fail metadata and continue. System must not indefinitely block other concurrent streams; load tests will simulate N=500 concurrent streams with 10% slow tool responses and verify 99th percentile latency SLOs remain within target with degraded outputs accounted for.
AC-6: Observability Signals: For every streaming emission that includes a soft-fail, the following telemetry events must be emitted: tool_invocation.start, tool_invocation.end (status), stream.frame.commit, stream.soft_fail.marker, stream.resume.attempt (if consumer reconnects). Each event includes trace_id and frame_offset. Acceptance: Kibana dashboards show these events for a 1-hour test run and an alert rule triggers when soft_fail_rate > 0.5% over 5 minutes for production routes.
AC-7: Compatibility with Existing Schema Negotiation: Handshake must include 'preferred_envelope' and 'resume_token' semantics. Acceptance tests exercise older clients by verifying graceful degradation: if preferred_envelope is unsupported, server falls back to newline-delimited JSON frames and includes a compatibility header explaining the downgrade.
AC-8: Test Harness & E2E Test Cases: Provide automated tests that simulate network partitions, tool errors (500, 429, 504), tool latency spikes, and partial stream consumption. Tests must assert that consumers receive either a valid final object or a documented incomplete object with soft_fail metadata in all tested modes.
AC-9: Docs & Examples: Console docs must include examples for parsing frames, handling soft_fail metadata, configuring per-route mode, and troubleshooting guide with representative log queries. Acceptance: docs reviewed and approved by Developer Experience and Design reviewers and linked in PR.
AC-10: Security & Compliance: When soft-fail includes tool error payloads, sensitive fields must be redacted per PII policy. Acceptance: static analysis and a sample audit record confirm PII redaction for tool error messages containing email/SSN-like patterns.
TC-1: Best-effort tool timeout: Start streaming generation that triggers a tool lookup that sleeps for 8s (config timeout 2s). Mode=best_effort. Expect frames including 'tool_status':'timeout' and 'soft_fail':"true"; final object parseable. Verify telemetry events emitted.
TC-2: Abort mode on rate-limit: Simulate tool returning 429. Mode=abort. Expect error envelope and stream close with code TOOL_RATE_LIMIT. Verify client-observed close code and server-side logs reference idempotency token.
TC-3: Resume after disconnect: Consumer reads first N frames then disconnects. Server persists resume_token. Consumer reconnects with token and receives frames from last commit point through final. Assert final object equivalent to continuous stream.
TC-4: Fallback variant switch: Mode=degraded_fallback. Downstream model returns non-responsive. Server emits warning frame, switches to cached summary variant, emits final object with 'source_variant':'cached-summary' and 'tool_error_code' annotated. Verify SLO accounting attributes.
TC-5: Idempotent webhook verification: Mock tool endpoint records invocations. Trigger multiple retries with the same idempotency token. Verify single recorded invocation and correct response to client of 'duplicate-suppressed' marker.
Minimum telemetry must include trace_id, route, model_variant, frame_offset, resume_token, tool_invocation.id, tool_status, tool_error_code, latency_ms. Dashboards: streaming-frame-latency, soft-fail-rate, tool-timeout-trend. Alerts: soft_fail_rate>0.5% over 5m, resume_failure_rate>0.1% over 15m.
Implementation must include a clear config surface (route-level parameter 'tool_failure_policy' with enum values) and safe defaults for public API. Provide migration notes for existing routes currently using legacy streaming format.
2025-02-12 - Diego Ramirez: Added engineering constraints and initial implementation notes; runtime will add resume_token persistence to shard metadata store.
2025-02-18 - Priya Desai (Design): Reviewed placeholder UX for incomplete objects; approved 'soft_fail' inline marker but asked for explicit CTA in Console docs to avoid developer confusion.
2025-02-24 - Rafael Kim (SRE): Requested load test profiles for 500 concurrent streams; noted need to measure KV-cache impact for resumed streams.
2025-03-01 - Aisha Patel: Updated acceptance matrix to include PII redaction requirement following security review kickoff.
2025-03-03 - Diego Ramirez: Implementation branch opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtimes/pull/8123. Ready for review; QA harness in CI added under ci/e2e/streaming-softfail.
2025-03-03 - QA Lead (Elena Novak): Scheduled test window 2025-03-06 to run full E2E matrix against staging with flaky network injection.

Title: P0 multiplex scheduler queueing surge retrospective

P0 multiplex scheduler queueing surge retrospective

On 2028-11-21 at ~03:14 UTC Redwood experienced a P0 outage affecting hosted API streaming sessions. A sudden, high-cardinality surge from a single large customer triggered an interaction between the multiplexing scheduler and the session KV cache that resulted in head-of-line queueing, streaming fragmentation, and an elevated 5xx rate for roughly 14 minutes. The incident caused degraded tail latency and partial failure of streaming responses for ~12% of requests from impacted shards.
- Duration: 03:14 UTC to 03:28 UTC (mitigations started 03:18, full recovery by 03:28).
- Affected surface: hosted API streaming endpoints in us-west and us-east regions, ~7% of total streaming requests globally during the window (peak concurrency ~18k multiplexed sessions on affected hosts).
- Symptoms: visible client disconnects and stream reconnections, increased streaming fragmentation (chunks split across reconnects), 5xx increase from baseline 0.03% to 2.4% at peak, p95 latency from 240ms -> 3.2s for streaming handshake and first chunk.
2028-11-21 03:13 UTC - Gradual rise in multiplexed session attempts from a large customer (background load test)
2028-11-21 03:14 UTC - Alerts: streaming error rate alert fires; on-call paged
2028-11-21 03:15 UTC - Engineers confirm elevated 5xx and reconnects; initial hypothesis: network flaps or edge TLS
2028-11-21 03:16 UTC - Dashboard shows heavy queue depth on multiplex scheduler worker process; KV cache miss latency also increases
2028-11-21 03:17 UTC - Attempted mitigation: increase per-worker multiplex slot limit via dynamic config (rolled to 10% of hosts) — no immediate improvement
2028-11-21 03:18 UTC - Applied targeted routing: move new streams to cold pool (reduced new session acceptance) — visible reduction in new errors
2028-11-21 03:22 UTC - Identified root cause signal: scheduler backpressure + synchronous KV cache locking causing head-of-line blocking
2028-11-21 03:24 UTC - Hotfix: disable strict slot coalescing in scheduler and enable optimistic session de-duplication; 5xx trend declines
2028-11-21 03:28 UTC - Error rate returns to baseline, metrics stabilize; incident declared mitigated

A combination of factors created a tight failure mode: (1) A sudden burst of highly concurrent streaming session requests that targeted the same set of multiplexing worker shards; (2) the scheduler's aggressive coalescing optimization attempted to pack many logical streams into limited multiplex slots and performed synchronous session-key checks against the central KV cache; (3) KV cache lock contention and elevated RPC latency caused scheduler goroutines to block, which produced head-of-line blocking on the multiplex connection causing streaming fragments to be delayed and client timeouts to surface as 5xx. Secondary contributor: the autoscaler decision window reacted poorly to the rapid burst and performed partial scale-down/scale-up cycles (thrash) that amplified the instability for ~90s.
Detection: standard error-rate and streaming fragmentation alerts triggered. First human response within 2 minutes. Initial triage focused on network/edge because reconnects matched previous TLS-rehandshake incidents, but metric correlation (multiplex queue depth, KV cache RPC latency) quickly shifted root-cause hypothesis.
Response: on-call SREs throttled new session routing to cold pool, toggled scheduler coalescing config, and applied optimistic de-duplication to avoid sync KV lookups. Runtime engineers deployed a lightweight fix to change the KV session lookup from a blocking lock to a lock-free fast-path for hot keys. These combined mitigations removed the blocking pressure and allowed hosts to drain queued streams.
Communications: status page updated at 03:20 UTC. Customer success notified high-volume customers by 03:30 UTC with mitigation summary.
- Throttled onboarding of new streaming sessions to cold pool (re-route rule)
- Disabled strict slot coalescing in multiplex scheduler (config toggle)
- Enabled optimistic session de-duplication to avoid synchronous KV checks
- Increased autoscaler cooldown to 180s and temporarily suspended aggressive scale-down policies for affected worker pools
- Rolled a runtime patch that exposes a lock-free KV fast-path for session canonicalization
- (Priority P0) Replace synchronous KV session-lock path with a fully lock-free session canonicalizer across all regions (ENG-runtime, owner: Ravi Patel) — target: 2 sprints
- Harden scheduler coalescing heuristics: add request-distribution awareness and hot-key detection to avoid packing high-cardinality bursts onto single shards (ENG-runtime, owner: Jon Chen) — target: 3 sprints
- Autoscaler tuning: implement burst-aware adapters and a fast-path for forced emergency scale-up to avoid thrash (ENG-platform, owner: Marta Kline) — target: 4 sprints
- Add synthetic tests that emulate high-cardinality multiplex bursts and verify no head-of-line blocking (SRE + QA, owner: Ewa Nowak) — target: next on-call rotation
- Create runbook entries for rapid detection of KV lock contention and recommended temporary mitigations (on-call SRE playbook) — target: 1 week
- Create dashboard tile that surfaces per-worker multiplex queue depth, KV lock hold times, and per-key hotness (owner: Ravi)
- Land the lock-free session canonicalizer PR and measure tail latencies in canary cluster (owner: Ravi)
- Update alerting: add an aggregate metric combining queue_depth * kv_rpc_latency to triage faster (owner: Jon)
- Run tabletop exercise simulating similar burst from a single tenant and validate runbook effectiveness (owner: Ewa)
- Document customer communication template for rapid incident updates specific to streaming fragmentation (owner: CS lead)
- The initial triage tunnelled on edge/TLS due to symptom similarity; ensure future triage checks include multiplex queue depth and KV latency as first-class signals for streaming issues.
- Config toggles (coalescing, optimistic dedupe) worked well as short-term mitigations but underline need for safer defaults.
- Autoscaler behavior needs a burst-mode policy to avoid taking actions in response to transient telemetry spikes.
- Action items are prioritized; agree to bi-weekly progress check-ins until all P0 items completed.
- Consider customer-facing postmortem for the largest impacted tenant if requested by CS.
If you see similar symptoms:
1) Check multiplex_worker_queue_depth and kv_cache_rpc_p50/p95 immediately.
2) If queue_depth > threshold AND kv_rpc_p95 > 200ms: toggle scheduler.coalesce=false and enable optimistic_session_dedupe.
3) Route new streams to cold-pool for 10 minutes and notify platform to hold aggressive scale-down.
4) Escalate to runtime owner (Ravi) and autoscaler owner (Marta) if no improvement in 2 minutes.
Include these steps in the runbook and pin to the streaming alert runbook.
Metrics snapshot at peak:
- concurrent_streams_on_affected_hosts: ~18,400
- streaming_5xx_rate_peak: 2.4%
- multiplex_scheduler_queue_depth_p95: 6.2
- kv_cache_rpc_p95: 480ms
- autoscaler_scale_ops_during_window: 3 (one scale-down then two scale-ups)
Related links: runtime PR #1143 (lock-free key path), Linear RED-5482, Grafana dashboard link: grafana/redwood/streaming-multiplex-5482

Title: Keepalive ping storm — playbook draft

Keepalive ping storm — playbook draft

Between 2029-06-14T00:22 and 2029-06-14T01:05 UTC we experienced a significant degradation of hosted API streaming and short-generation latencies caused by an influx of client keepalive pings from a misbehaving SDK cohort. Symptoms included p95/p99 latency increases, a burst of 502/504s at the edge, and an elevated rate of streaming fragment reassembly failures. The burst affected ~18% of streaming sessions in US-west and produced service errors for several high-traffic customers.
~18% of active streaming sessions experienced mid-request disconnects or fragmented responses; non-streaming short generations saw p95 latency increase from 120ms to 550ms for ~10 minutes. No data loss was detected in user payloads. Several customers reported degraded UX; a small set triggered automated retries that amplified load on acceptor queues.
Alert: ephemeral-acceptor-queue-depth > 80% for multiple edge pods (alert rule: sre.edge.acceptor.queue.depth.high). Additional signal from streaming-fragment-errors metric and a spike in edge TCP resets. Oncall page had an automated alert at 2029-06-14T00:24 UTC.
2029-06-14T00:22 UTC - First acceptor-queue-depth alert triggered
2029-06-14T00:23 UTC - Streaming fragment error rate rises above baseline
2029-06-14T00:25 UTC - Pager notified SRE primary (Devon)
2029-06-14T00:28 UTC - Triage: surge of tiny keepalive frames observed from a small set of client IPs / SDK-version header 'ri-sdk/3.2.1'
2029-06-14T00:31 UTC - Mitigation: emergency ingress rate-limit rule deployed on edge ingress layer to aggregate/quotas small keepalive frames
2029-06-14T00:36 UTC - Immediate improvement in acceptor-queue depth, p95 latency begins returning toward normal
2029-06-14T00:45 UTC - Hotfix to streaming muxer deployed to coalesce adjacent keepalive frames (edge repo PR merged)
1) Deploy temporary ingress rate-limit that treats keepalive/keep-alive frame pattern as lower-priority and caps per-connection keepalive rate to 1/sec. 2) Hotpatch streaming muxer to coalesce contiguous keepalive frames and avoid scheduling a separate acceptor task per keepalive. 3) Throttle retries from downstream retry middleware via short-circuit on known SDK version header.
A rolling client SDK release (ri-sdk/3.2.1) introduced a regression in its keepalive logic causing certain clients to emit keepalive PINGS at an aggressive cadence (10–20x intended). This interacted poorly with the edge acceptor design: each keepalive created a tiny work item that bypassed batching and caused acceptor-thread thrash and small-window TCP churn. Amplifying factors: automated client retries and a lack of aggregation for sub-10-byte frames at the ingress layer.
Add server-side keepalive aggregation at the edge ingress so sub-64-byte keepalives are combined for a single acceptor enqueue operation
Introduce an SDK compatibility gate: detect ri-sdk/3.2.x and apply conservative per-connection heuristics until clients are upgraded
Update SLAs and telemetry: add dedicated metric for keepalive-influence on acceptor queue and on streaming reassembly errors
Customer communication play: automated warning to customers using ri-sdk/3.2.1 with recommended upgrade to 3.2.3
Improve retry middleware to be idempotent-aware and rate-limited to avoid amplifying short-duration spikes
EDGE-482: Implement sub-64B frame coalescing in ingress (owner: Rajat, due: 2029-06-28)
EDGE-483: Build dashboard for 'keepalive-throughput' and add SLO guardrails (owner: Sofia, due: 2029-06-21)
SDK-297: Release 3.2.3 with corrected keepalive backoff and instrumented telemetry (owner: SDK team, due: 2029-06-20)
SRE-211: Add canary ingress rule that limits low-cost frames by default (owner: Devon, due: 2029-06-30)
COMM-14: Email template to impacted customers and proactive advisories (owner: Liam, due: 2029-06-18)
Step 0: Acknowledge pager and post short summary to #sre-incidents with incident id
Step 1: Check acceptor queue panels and streaming-fragment-errors; capture current node list and p95/p99 latencies
Step 2: Identify top source IPs/SDK headers causing spike (query edge logs: frames < 64B grouped by user-agent and ip)
Step 3: If spike source is small cohort with SDK header, deploy temporary ingress rate-limit rule targeting that header and IP CIDRs
Step 4: Deploy streaming muxer coalescing hotpatch if available; otherwise enable ingress aggregation and remove at steady state
Step 5: Monitor metrics for 15 minutes; if no improvement, escalate to platform infra and product for customer communications
Step 6: After stabilization, run a post-incident data pull for affected customers and estimate customer impact window
When paging, prioritize connection-level signals over aggregate token metrics for this class of incidents. Keep an eye on tiny-frame histograms and the 'acceptor-enqueue-per-second' metric which climbs sharply during a ping storm. Final postmortem will include customer impact matrix and retrospective on SDK release processes.

Title: Typed stream failure modes and operator playbook for deferred tool handoffs

Typed stream failure modes and operator playbook for deferred tool handoffs

Purpose: define unambiguous acceptance criteria for streamed structured outputs that trigger deferred tool/function calls, enumerate failure classes for partial emits, and provide an operator playbook for safe recovery and customer-facing remediation. This ticket captures the PM-level requirements and acceptance criteria. Engineering will implement protocol changes (frame markers, commit points, idempotency tokens) and telemetry hooks; Design/DevEx may supply sample SDK helpers for clients to resume or reconcile partial state.
Motivation: production incidents in Q4 2025 and Jan 2026 showed two recurring failure patterns: (1) partial JSON-like fragments emitted before a tool call failed and could not be reconciled by downstream systems, and (2) ambiguous tool-invoke retries caused duplicate side effects. Existing docs cover schema evolution and progressive envelopes, but operators lacked a concise runbook tying failure class to immediate mitigation and customer communication. This PRD consolidates acceptance criteria, telemetry, and operator steps to reduce MTTR and avoid unsafe retries.
In scope: definition of failure modes for typed streaming frames, acceptance criteria for idempotent tool-handshake semantics, required telemetry/events, operator runbook steps, test cases, and rollout guidance. Out of scope: changes to persistence layer or long-term retention of tool invocation logs (handled by ENG-22111) and per-customer consent flows for resending actions.
Schema: Every top-level streamed frame must include a frame_version, frame_id (UUID), emit_type (partial|commit|abort), and optional tool_handshake object with tool_id and idempotency_token. All new fields must be backward-compatible with v1 clients.
Partial vs Commit semantics: A 'partial' emit can be followed by zero or more 'partial' frames and must be followed by either a 'commit' frame (finalization) or an 'abort' frame within 30s for real-time routes; if neither arrive within configured timeout, runtime must emit a 'emit.timed_out' event and mark the stream state as 'stalled'.
Tool handshake: When the runtime signals a deferred tool invocation, it must emit 'tool.invoke.start' with tool_id and idempotency_token and only deliver 'tool.invoke.complete' once external tool confirms success. If the tool returns a transient error, the runtime must follow exponential backoff and not emit duplicate 'commit' frames without explicitly incrementing retry_count in telemetry.
Idempotency: Tool backends must be invoked with an idempotency_token that is stable for the logical operation; acceptance tests must prove that replaying the same token results in at-most-once side effects for repairable and terminal error classifications.
Error classification: The runtime must classify errors into 'transient' (retryable), 'repairable' (requires operator or client intervention to rehydrate state), and 'terminal' (must abort stream). Tests must show deterministic classification for a representative set of external tool HTTP 4xx/5xx and network timeouts.
Observability: For every stream, the runtime must emit events: emit.partial, emit.commit, emit.abort, emit.timed_out, tool.invoke.start, tool.invoke.retry, tool.invoke.complete, tool.invoke.failed. These must include frame_id, session_id, route, model, and latency_ms. Acceptance requires dashboards and an alert rule that fires on >0.5% stalled streams in a 5m window for production routes.
Client SDK behavior: SDKs should expose a resume() helper that accepts the last-seen frame_id and idempotency_token and reconcilers must be able to request a reflection endpoint to obtain final commit/abort status; acceptance requires a sample integration test confirming resume() recovers deterministic final state in 3 simulated failure scenarios.
Streaming backward compatibility: v1 clients (no frame metadata) must continue to receive full responses for non-streamed routes. Feature flag must gate v2 frames on new routes until canary passes.
Security: idempotency_token must be treated as a secret with limited lifetime; logs must not contain raw tokens beyond ephemeral debug traces. Acceptance requires code paths that redact tokens in standard logs and keep token visibility to 'debug' only behind a flag.
Performance: Added frame metadata must not increase median latency by more than 3% on real-time routes under typical load (measured at 95th percentile over a 1h synthetic workload).
Automated: unit tests for encoder/decoder to assert frame envelope correctness; integration tests that simulate (A) tool success, (B) transient tool failures with automatic retry, (C) repairable error that requires operator resume, (D) network partition and stream timeout. Each must validate emitted telemetry events and final output reconciliation. Manual: run canary with 5% traffic for 48h against a synthetic consumer that validates idempotency and duplicate side-effect detection. Post-canary soak test for 7 days on dedicated capacity. Test artifacts: JSON test vectors and a GitHub Actions workflow under /ci/streaming-v2.
Rollout should use feature flag 'streaming_v2_frames' with staged gate: dev -> staging (smoke) -> canary (5%) -> canary (25%) -> global. During canary, enable verbose telemetry for 1h windows then revert to sampling. If stalled_stream alert triggers >3x baseline during canary, auto-roll back. Coordinate with Customer Success for any customers on Dedicated to opt-in. Communicate to SDK teams two weeks prior to enablement.
Required metrics/events: metric.emit_partial_count, metric.emit_commit_count, metric.emit_abort_count, metric.emit_timed_out_count, metric.tool_invoke_start_count, metric.tool_invoke_retry_count, metric.tool_invoke_success_count, metric.tool_invoke_failure_count. Traces must include frame_id, parent_request_id, route, model, worker_id, and timings for tool roundtrip. Logs must include structured reason codes for failures (e.g., TOOL_HTTP_502, TOOL_TIMEOUT, FRAME_PARSE_ERROR).
Detection: Alert 'stalled_stream' surfaces for a route. Use Observability dashboard 'Streaming v2 — Stalled Streams' to identify affected session_ids and frame_ids.
Quick triage: Check tool.invoke.* event rates. If tool.invoke.retry_count is increasing and tool_invoke_success_count remains zero, mark incident as TOOL_BACKEND_DEGRADED and escalate to Backend Tooling owner.
Customer mitigation: If >10% of a single customer's streams are stalled, toggle feature flag off for that customer and initiate graceful aborts for active sessions. Notify CS with template message and recommended remediation steps.
Repair flow: For repairable errors, run reconcilier script with last_committed_frame_id and idempotency_token to replay safely; if unknown state, use reflect endpoint to fetch authoritative state and instruct client SDK to resume with resume(frame_id).
Abort/rollback: For terminal errors or repeated retries beyond threshold, emit an automated abort frame on behalf of the model with reason code and surface user-facing error consistent with platform error schema.
Post-incident: Collect sample stream traces and attach to incident ticket; run RCA to update classification heuristics and tests. If caused by ambiguous idempotency token generation, schedule follow-up to rotate token provenance and update SDKs.
Communication: Use templated public and private messages. For high-severity events affecting SLAs, include timeline, customer impact, and remediation steps within 2 hours.
Escalation: If operator cannot determine safe repair within 30 minutes for high-impact customer, escalate to on-call Engineering runtime owner and Product manager.
Decision logs: prefer explicit commit/abort frames over inferring end-of-stream from idle gaps to avoid duplicate-tool-invokes. We will allocate an opt-in canary in dedicated clusters first. SDK resume helpers will be implemented in TypeScript and Python; other languages can reuse REST reflection endpoint. Consider future work: cryptographically signed commit frames for cross-service trust.
Validate every emitted telemetry event includes frame_id and session_id
Run at-most-once side-effect experiment for idempotency tokens
Ensure logs redact idempotency_token in non-debug levels
Smoke test client SDK resume() flow with simulated commit/abort races
Verify alert thresholds and dashboard tiles appear in staging

Title: Tenant action card and root cause teardown - streaming degradation

Tenant action card and root cause teardown - streaming degradation

Summary: We identified and mitigated intermittent high-latency and 5xx errors affecting streaming generation and long-lived sessions for a subset of tenants in us-west-2 and eu-west-1. Engineering applied a staged mitigation (traffic reroute + scaled safe-priority pool) at 2029-10-12T15:40Z. Service availability is recovering; customers may still see occasional truncated streams for up to 2 hours while backfills complete.
What happened: On 2029-10-12 we saw a sudden increase in failed streaming sessions and truncated outputs for multi-tenant streaming endpoints. Impact: roughly 6% of streaming requests across two regions experienced either early termination or 5xx responses for ~70 minutes, affecting customers using low-latency streaming and long-context generation. Root cause short: a rare interaction between the autoscaling threshold and KV-cache eviction logic that caused rapid eviction storms under a specific token-distribution pattern; this in turn triggered backpressure cascades in the serving runtime leading to request timeouts and failed stream finalization.
2029-10-12T14:22Z - First anomaly detected: elevated 5xx and stream truncation rate observed in monitoring. 2029-10-12T14:28Z - SRE on-call paged; initial triage points to increased retry traffic and resource contention on the streaming actors. 2029-10-12T14:45Z - Engineering identified correlation between a high-rate of short-prefix requests and cache eviction spikes in the affected pools. 2029-10-12T15:02Z - Canary reroute to safe-priority pool started; partial improvement observed. 2029-10-12T15:40Z - Full staged mitigation: traffic steadily rerouted, autoscaling threshold tuned, and KV-cache eviction soft-threshold increased. 2029-10-12T16:10Z - Errors decreased to baseline; streaming truncation rare but still under observation while background cache warms. 2029-10-12T17:30Z - Close monitoring window; customers notified of full remediation plan and timelines for permanent fix.
Two factors combined to cause the outage: 1) Autoscaling policy used an aggressive CPU-based scale-up step that was triggered by retry bursts; scale events caused short-lived actor churn during which in-memory KV caches were rebalanced. 2) A recently-introduced heuristic in the KV-cache eviction logic treated many very-short-prefix requests as low-reuse keys, evicting shared prefix entries too aggressively. Under the observed traffic pattern this produced an eviction storm where many concurrent requests missed cache, increasing token compute and creating backpressure that cascaded into stream termination and 5xx on dependent workers.
Immediate mitigations applied: - Rerouted streaming traffic to a 'safe-priority' pool with conservative autoscaling and sticky cache affinity. - Increased KV-cache soft-threshold to reduce eviction frequency during transient bursts. - Temporarily disabled the new low-reuse heuristic while we validate a corrected algorithm. Near-term engineering actions: - Roll out a targeted fix to the cache heuristic (PR merged, staging tests green). - Add a fast-path cache-warm before routing long-lived streaming sessions. - Update autoscaling policy to consider queue-length and KV-cache health signals, not just CPU. Long-term: - Add chaos tests covering eviction-churn + autoscale interactions. - Post-deploy: coordinated tenant-facing test window and full SLA credit assessment for affected customers.
What tenants can do now (concise action card): 1) If you operate long-lived streaming sessions, prefer sticky-session routing (set sessionAffinity=true in route config) to avoid cache re-warm on reconnects. 2) For workloads with many short-prefix queries (search-like patterns), batch low-latency calls or use a small prefix cache client-side to reduce calls that pressure shared KV cache. 3) If you see truncated streams, retry with exponential backoff up to 3 attempts; our SDKs will include a recommended helper in the next patch. 4) For high-criticality latency SLAs, consider temporarily enabling dedicated pools (Redwood Dedicated) for absolute isolation. Example quick check (curl): curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/health/stream -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" --data '{"test": "stream"}'  If you hit non-2xx responses, open a priority support ticket and include request ids from your client logs (x-rw-request-id header).
Q: Will I be billed for failed or truncated responses? A: Billing follows our published usage policy; failed requests that did not produce tokens are not billed. If you were materially impacted we will propose SLA credits as part of the post-incident review. Q: How do you guarantee this won't repeat? A: We implemented short-term mitigations and have a staged rollout of the cache heuristic fix plus autoscaling policy changes. We will extend testing and observability to detect eviction storms earlier. Q: Can we get a dedicated postmortem for our tenant? A: Yes — contact your customer success manager and we will schedule a tenant-specific review including request logs and remediation timelines.
Primary contact: Elena Park (Customer Success Lead) — elena.park@redwood.ai. SRE escalation: Marcus Liu — marcus.liu@redwood.ai. Open a priority support case: https://support.redwood.ai/cases/new and include a brief description + example request ids. For real-time updates: status.redwood.ai (incident RI-4823).
We recognize the impact of degraded streaming behavior on production applications and apologize for the disruption. Engineers are prioritizing a permanent fix and added observability gaps discovered during the event. We will follow up with a final postmortem and SLA credit proposal within 7 business days.

2026-03-13 09:42 - SRE (Diego Morales): Observed correlation between long tail of http2 window updates/ACKs and apigw queuing. CPU on runtime pods increased shortly before resets. Posting Grafana links in #support: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/streaming/handshake-latency?from=now-1h

Title: Postmortem: Streaming stalls during peak traffic (2026-01-12)

Postmortem: Streaming stalls during peak traffic (2026-01-12)

## Summary
On 2026-01-12, streaming responses intermittently stalled for a subset of chat completion requests. Affected clients observed streams that paused mid-response for 10–45 seconds, then resumed or timed out. The incident correlated with a traffic surge and increased concurrent connections on the edge streaming gateway.

## Customer impact
- Duration: 41 minutes (peak impact window)
- Symptoms: stalled Server-Sent Events (SSE) streams; elevated client timeouts
- Scope: ~9% of streaming requests in us-east-1

## Detection
- Alert: "stream-gateway open connections" exceeded threshold
- Secondary signals: increased 499/504 rates at the edge; elevated p95 time-to-first-token

## Timeline (UTC)
- 16:02: First alerts triggered (p95 TTFT + edge 5xx)
- 16:07: On-call confirms stalled streams in synthetic checks
- 16:15: Mitigation: reduce max concurrent streams per gateway pod; scale gateway
- 16:29: Runtime team rolls back a connection reuse optimization
- 16:43: Metrics return to baseline

## Root cause
A recently enabled connection reuse optimization increased head-of-line blocking within the streaming gateway under high concurrency. Combined with an overly permissive keepalive and a missing backpressure guard, the gateway accumulated slow clients and delayed flushes to the network.

## Contributing factors
- SRE alerting did not include a direct SLO for "stream stall duration"
- The runtime canary did not cover high-concurrency streaming workloads
- Gateway autoscaling policy used CPU only; connection count was the real driver

## What went well
- Synthetic streaming checks helped confirm impact quickly
- Scaling the gateway immediately reduced new stalls

## What didn’t go well
- Rollback decision took longer than expected due to unclear ownership between gateway vs runtime
- Lack of a dedicated runbook step for diagnosing SSE buffering

## Follow-up action items
(Each item counts toward the owning team’s total.)
1. Add an SLO/alert for "stream stall duration" derived from periodic flush timestamps. Owner team: SRE. Priority: P0.
2. Add connection-count based autoscaling to stream-gateway (HPA on open_conns). Owner team: SRE. Priority: P1.
3. Implement explicit backpressure guard in stream-gateway to drop/slow overly slow consumers. Owner team: Serving Runtime. Priority: P0.
4. Add load-test scenario for 20k concurrent streaming connections to perf-canary suite. Owner team: Serving Runtime. Priority: P1.
5. Update runbook: "Streaming issues" to include tcpdump/flush tracing steps and known failure modes. Owner team: SRE. Priority: P1.
6. Document gateway/runtime responsibility boundaries and escalation path. Owner team: Platform. Priority: P2.

## Lessons learned
Streaming incidents are often connection-management incidents. We need first-class metrics for stream health (stall duration, flush frequency) and scaling signals tied to open connections.

Streaming chat requests time out at 120s for Pinecone Labs (eu-west)

Impact: Affects long-running customer support agent flows; 'partial answers' and retries increasing cost.

Environment: Dedicated cluster behind ALB (eu-west).

Naomi Feldman (CSM): Customer says 'streaming starts then pauses for 2+ minutes when tool call runs' -> ALB closes.
Hiro Tanaka (Platform): Confirmed ALB idle_timeout=120s on their dedicated ingress. Current behavior: during tool execution we don't emit stream chunks.

Elliot Price (Runtime): Longer-term: add optional heartbeat event 'event: ping' every 15s when generation is blocked on tool. Tracking in internal issue INT-812.
Resolution: Customer updated ALB idle timeout to 300s; confirmed no more mid-stream disconnects. Ticket closed.

Title: Metering rounding delta between embedding and chat aggregation causing small invoice variance

Metering rounding delta between embedding and chat aggregation causing small invoice variance

Issue summary: Customer BrightCall reports a small but recurring variance (0.3-1.2 USD) on their monthly invoice where the line item labeled 'inference: embeddings' plus 'inference: chat' summed by the customer does not match the invoice total we generated. Impact: Small financial variance for accounting reconciliation; customer requests explanation and closing of the gap to prevent repeated disputes. Observed vs expected: BrightCall's internal aggregation of per-endpoint usage (embeddings + chat sessions) yields a different token total after rounding/aggregation than Redwood's billed total. Timeframe: discrepancies observed on invoices dated 2026-02-28 and 2026-03-01 (billing window 2026-02-01 to 2026-02-28).
1) Customer exported per-endpoint hourly usage (CSV) for the period 2026-02-01 to 2026-02-28 from their dashboard. 2) They summed token counts for rwd-embed-1 and rwd-chat-3b, then applied published per-unit rates. 3) Compared that local total to the invoice line items and found a delta of $0.36 (Feb invoice) and $0.89 (Mar preliminary). 4) Customer confirmed no subaccount cross-posting and single billing org.
2026-02-28T23:58:12Z usage-postback: org=brightcall endpoint=embed token_count=12345.4 postback_id=pbk_8f3c; 2026-02-28T23:58:13Z usage-postback: org=brightcall endpoint=chat token_count=9876.6 postback_id=pbk_8f3d; aggregator: hourly_bucket us-east 2026-02-28T23:00 -> total_tokens=22222.0 computed_billed_units=22222 rounding_strategy=ceil
Initial hypothesis: rounding strategy differences between raw postbacks (fractional tokens from streaming) and the billing aggregation (per-hour bucket rounding or per-request rounding). Query run against usage DB shows we store fractional token counts at ingestion but billing pipeline applies 'ceil' at per-hour per-endpoint bucket for dedicated customers in us-east to preserve revenue guardrails. Found two consumer postbacks with identical request IDs that were retried within 2s window and de-duplicated at ingestion, but rounding applied before de-dupe in one legacy path. Related: linked SUP-30192 flagged a similar hourly-window split affecting reserved hours. Next steps: patch billing transform to apply rounding consistently at final aggregation stage and create backfill for affected hours. Low-impact work-around offered: apply manual adjustment credit on current invoice while patch is scheduled.

SparkBarrel Systems

Primary pain: observed high tail latency (200-900ms/token) and several timeouts for multi-turn chat sessions. Customer reports "bursty slowdowns" during midday traffic and poorer performance for EU customers. They think it's 'our API' but likely region mismatch + some long prompts.

Title: airgap: add Ubuntu 22.04 slim runtime bundle, modular vendor indexer, and registry-sync TF updates

airgap: add Ubuntu 22.04 slim runtime bundle, modular vendor indexer, and registry-sync TF updates

Motivation: Customers deploying Redwood Private in stricter regulated environments requested a smaller Ubuntu-based runtime bundle (22.04) optimized for constrained air-gapped environments and an improved, modular vendor indexer that supports incremental delta snapshots. This PR introduces a slim Ubuntu 22.04 runtime bundle profile, refactors the offline image index format to be modular (index shards + manifest), and updates the Terraform registry-replication module to optionally use the new index format for faster syncs and reduced bandwidth.

Summary of changes: added ubuntu-22.04-slim runtime bundle (compressed tar.gz, stripped docs, minimal kernel modules), implemented index-shard format v1 for the airgap indexer (index-manifest.json + shard-<n>.json), added dedupe layer to offline image packaging, updated Helm chart to expose registry-proxy.enabled and mirror.oci settings, extended the installer "airgap-apply" flow to accept --index-shard flag and to perform atomic apply using snapshot fencing. Terraform: added optional parameter "use_index_shards" and optimized S3 upload concurrency for large delta snapshots. Rollback/upgrade: introduced preflight checks and a new rollback hook that validates bundle signature before applying a rollback.

How to test locally: follow docs/airgap/ubuntu-22.04/README.md (included). Example: ./bin/airgap-tool build --profile ubuntu-22.04-slim --index-shard-size 200MB && ./bin/airgap-tool pack --output /tmp/airgap-slim.tar.gz. Deploy to a k3s lab cluster with registry-mirror enabled and run ./scripts/e2e/airgap-sync.sh. CI includes an airgap-registry-indexer-e2e job that exercises shard creation and registry replication.

Upgrade notes: upgrade path is backwards compatible. Default behaviour remains the monolithic index unless --use-index_shards=true is set. For customers using the Dedicated registry replication Terraform module, enabling shards can reduce peak bandwidth but requires the newer airgap-tool >= 0.28.0. Please follow the migration checklist in docs/airgap/migration.md.

Checklist: - [x] Add ubuntu-22.04-slim bundle recipe and packaging pipeline - [x] Implement index-shard manifest and shard creation tools - [x] Helm changes for registry-proxy and mirror settings - [x] Terraform module parameter and docs - [x] E2E test for shard-based replication - [x] Package signing and verification step added

Related work: builds on prior airgap improvements (see SUP-1337 and ENG-6120) and complements the offline delta snapshot work in ENG-5830.

Notes: kept the new index format intentionally simple (manifest + shards) so on-prem mirrored registries can stream shards sequentially and resume. The packaging script also deduplicates blobs across bundles which reduced typical bundle size by ~12% in our benchmark sample.

Title: reduce auth ceremony: add credential-hydrator + stream-shuttle adapters (py/ts/go)

reduce auth ceremony: add credential-hydrator + stream-shuttle adapters (py/ts/go)

Background: Teams repeatedly reimplement credential prefetch/refresh and stream-resume glue in each SDK resulting in duplicated logic and subtle bugs during token swaps. Goal: provide a small, consistent primitive (Credential Hydrator) that centralizes TTL-aware prefetch/refresh and an orthogonal Stream Shuttle adapter to standardize minimal stream envelope metadata and pause/resume semantics across Py/TS/Go. Summary of changes: added a new auth primitive (Credential Hydrator) with a small public API: hydrate(ctx, key, ttl_hint) -> hydrated_token; added optional local prewarm caches and jittered refresh tasks; introduced Stream Shuttle (shuttle.{wrap,unwrap,checkpoint,resume}) which attaches a tiny typed header to stream frames to allow SDKs to implement pause/resume without changing user iteration patterns; implemented adapters in sdks/python, sdks/typescript, and sdks/go and wired into the existing session factories; added guided migration docs and examples; bump SDK versions. Why this design: hydrator centralizes token lifecycle (reduces double-refresh races), allows servers to prefer warmed delegated credentials, and provides observability hooks; shuttle is intentionally minimal to avoid coupling with transport layers while enabling safe resume points for long-running generators. Checklist: - Implement core hydrator + tests; - Implement shuttle and adapters for Py/TS/Go; - Add e2e scenario that simulates token rotation mid-stream; - Update examples and docs; - Add feature-flag gating and a migration guide; - Version bumps and changelogs. Testing and CI: unit test coverage added for hydrator jitter logic and shuttle checkpoint/restore; integration test scenario simulates token rotation during a streaming generation with resumable checkpoints; CI initially hit a flaky integ test (stream-resume-on-token-swap) which was retried and passed; load sanity run on dedicated infra shows no regressions in median latency. Rollout plan: feature disabled by default. Gradually enable for SDK beta channels over two weeks, monitor auth-error rates and stream-resume failure alerts; if stable, enable opt-in by default in next minor release and document best practices for hydrate TTL hints. Migration notes: existing SDK users are unaffected until they opt into the hydrator/shuttle APIs. For teams that already build custom refresh loops we provide a compatibility shim that maps older callbacks to the new hydrator interface. Docs: new doc page docs/sdk-auth-hydrator.md with examples in py/ts/go and a short troubleshooting appendix. Complexity: added a small background refresh scheduler per SDK instance; we limited default concurrency and added metrics so ops teams can tune it. Performance: measured small memory increase (~1.6MB per SDK client) and reduced surge of token-refresh calls by ~58% in synthetic rotation tests. Future work: instrument hydrator telemetry into Console, expose server-side hints for prewarming delegated credentials, and explore server-driven checkpoints for stream-shuttle. Related: ENG-4532 tracks further ergonomics and telemetry; SUP-1987 is the customer case that motivated resilient mid-stream token rotation handling.

Title: Fallback replay — command log and breadcrumbs

Fallback replay — command log and breadcrumbs

Notes to self: quick replay checklist and command history for the multi-region fallback incident on 2026-02-11. Intended as a reproducible scratchpad to run later in staging and to hand off to oncall for follow-up.

Summary / what happened
- Around 2026-02-11T21:06Z we saw a spike of route_ejections + regional fallbacks originating from EU-west (az-eu-3).
- Clients observed elevated latency and ~2.7% 5xxs for about 18 minutes; smart-routing triggered fallback to compatible model variant in us-central for some traffic.
- Automatic rollback to primary region was slow; suspect policy hysteresis + bad kvcache priming.

Observations gathered (metrics + quick reads)
- Route ejection metric: route_policy.eject_count[route=chat-text,region=eu-west] increased from 0 to 106 over 6m.
- Error class in traces: "handshake_timeout" + "kv_cache_miss" mixed with failed tcp handshakes.
- Token lat p50 jumped 30ms -> 220ms for routed requests to fallback target.
- Tracing showed request ids that crossed regional boundary had missing kv_cache headers (x-kv-prefix absent).

Immediate commands I ran (copy/paste friendly)
# grab recent traces for region slice (3x sources)
kubectl -n prod logs deploy/route-proxy --since=25m | rg "region=eu-west" -B3 -A4 | sed -n '1,500p' > /tmp/eu-west-traces-20260211.log

# sample telemetry query (metrics backend)
curl -s "https://metrics.internal/api/query?metric=route_policy.eject_count&from=2026-02-11T20:50Z&to=2026-02-11T21:30Z&tag=route:chat-text" | jq . > /tmp/eject-count.json

# fetch routing table at time of incident (config-db)
redis-cli -h conf-db.prod.internal HGETALL "routes:chat-text:2026-02-11T21:00Z" > /tmp/route-config-snapshot.txt

# check last rollout for model variant used as fallback
gh pr view 842 --json title,body,commits > /tmp/pr-842-summary.txt

# repro request to emulate region failure by forcing route header (staging)
curl -v -H "X-Client-Region: eu-west" -H "X-Force-Route: chat-text" -H "Authorization: Bearer $STAGING_KEY" \
  "https://staging.api.redwood.ai/v1/generate" -d '{"prompt":"hi","max_tokens":10}' --write-out "\\nHTTP_CODE:%{http_code}\\n" --connect-timeout 6 --max-time 10 > /tmp/repro-response-1.txt 2>&1

Observed snippet (from repro-response-1.txt):
> * Connection timed out after 6001 milliseconds
> HTTP_CODE:000
> curl: (28) Operation timed out after 6002 milliseconds with 0 out of 0 bytes received

Hypotheses (ranked)
1) Prefix/KV cache warming mismatch: some routed requests lost the x-kv-prefix header and hit cold model instances in fallback region -> cold start latency cascades and then triggers ejection policy.
2) Network egress flakiness between eu-west and internal infra (TCP handshake timeouts) causing route-proxy to mark backend unhealthy and initiate fallback.
3) Fallback policy threshold combined with slow retries (3 retries x 5s) exaggerated the outage window.
4) Load/queueing: sudden burst caused queue growth; autoscaler in dedicated pools didn't scale fast enough for fallback targets.

Error snippets pulled from logs
[route-proxy] 2026-02-11T21:07:12Z ERROR route-eject route=chat-text region=eu-west reason=handshake_timeout details="tcp handshake failed to 10.12.45.9:443 after 5000ms" trace_id=tr-0a1b2c
[kv-sync] 2026-02-11T21:07:14Z WARN kv-cache miss prefix=absent route=chat-text instance=fallback-us-3
[router] 2026-02-11T21:09:01Z INFO fallback-invoked route=chat-text target_variant=chat-small-v2 reason=policy_eject

Replay / repro plan (staging, controlled)
- Goal: reproduce route_eject behavior deterministically and capture full packet traces + spans.
- Steps:
  1) deploy a config with short eject thresholds in staging (eject_error_rate>1% over 30s) so we can trigger without broad impact. -> config name: test-eject-short
  2) instrument a small load generator to send 200 qps with X-Client-Region: eu-west header for 10 minutes.
  3) simultaneously introduce intermittent packet loss to fallback target (tc qdisc netem 100ms delay 10% loss) on staging fallback nodes.
  4) run the same curl repro above to observe curl timeout behavior.

Commands to set up simulated network flakiness (staging nodes)
# SSH into fallback node (staging-fb-3)
ssh core@staging-fb-3
sudo tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 100ms loss 10% 25%
# when done:
sudo tc qdisc del dev eth0 root netem

Load generator (minimal)
# quick golang wrk-style loop (run from bastion)
for i in {1..200}; do 
  curl -s -o /dev/null -H "X-Client-Region: eu-west" -H "X-Force-Route: chat-text" -H "Authorization: Bearer $STAGING_KEY" \
    "https://staging.api.redwood.ai/v1/generate" &
  sleep 0.005
done

Trace capture tips
- Start tcpdump on both sides to capture SYN retransmits and timestamps: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/fb-syns.pcap 'tcp port 443 and (tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0)'
- Increase sampling rate in tracing (temporarily) for route-proxy: setenv TRACE_SAMPLING=0.8 in deployment config and rollout.

Quick bash 'replay' script prototype (staging)
cat > /tmp/replay-failover.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
STAGING_KEY=REDACTED
for i in $(seq 1 60); do
  curl -s -H "X-Client-Region: eu-west" -H "X-Force-Route: chat-text" -H "Authorization: Bearer $STAGING_KEY" \
    "https://staging.api.redwood.ai/v1/generate" -d '{"prompt":"ping","max_tokens":6}' --max-time 8 -o /tmp/p.$i.json &
  sleep 0.1
done
wait
EOF
chmod +x /tmp/replay-failover.sh

Notes about traces and correlation
- Capture request ids (x-request-id) from route-proxy logs and align with trace ids. Some traces from the incident had missing kv-pref tags which correlate with the kv-cache miss warnings.
- Pay attention to rollout metadata: if fallback target was a different model family (eg chat-small-v2 vs chat-base) we will see tokenization differences and potentially token-level latency variance.

What to check post-replay (artifacts to gather)
- pcap files from both sides /tmp/fb-syns.pcap
- route-proxy logs with trace ids (time window)
- redis conf-db snapshot used for routing keys
- metrics snapshot: route_policy.eject_count, token_latency_p50/p95, instance_cpu, queue_length
- sample payloads and responses to check for missing x-kv-prefix header

Short-term mitigations to propose (if reproduced)
- Reduce eject hysteresis or increase sensitivity window to prevent mass-ejection cascades (only as a temporary experiment).
- Add aggressive KV prefetching for recently-failed routes to avoid cold-start hits on fallback targets.
- Add a temporary network health proxy to detect cross-region TCP anomalies and mark them for manual review instead of automatic full-eject.

Open questions / TODOs
- Did the routing config use 'regional-preference=soft' or 'hard'? need to confirm from conf-db snapshot.
- Which commit introduced the fallback variant change 2026-02-10? correlate with GH PR 842.
- Should we add a "grace window" for kv-pref absence before ejecting? (hypothesis: 30s)

Hand-off checklist (for next oncall)

- Attach route-proxy logs + trace ids to JIRA CON-4281 and ping Priya for model-family context.
- If reproduced, propose rollout of prefetched-kv experiment to prod-canary group.

End of scratchpad. Will refine after staging replay.

-- Aisha

Title: Cross-region SLO drift & traffic-shaping retrospective

Cross-region SLO drift & traffic-shaping retrospective

Summary: On 2026-03-09 between 22:14 UTC and 23:02 UTC we observed a cross-region degradation that caused a sustained SLO miss for the hosted text-generation API. Symptoms included elevated p99 latency (baseline ~320ms -> peak ~1.1s), a spike in 5xx error rate (~0.05% -> 2.6%), and customer-visible increased tail latency across EU and NA regions. The root of the event was a combination of a recent autoscaler config change, a traffic-shaping rollback in the control-plane route weights, and a circuit-breaker threshold that was too permissive, which delayed failover protective actions. This ticket is the postmortem and consolidated follow-up actions.
2026-03-09T22:14Z: Pager triggered by SRE for elevated error rate on /v1/generate in eu-west-1
2026-03-09T22:18Z: Incident commander confirmed p99 latency > 800ms and 5xx > 1%; traffic shifted from eu-west-1 to us-west-2 by smart-routing policy
2026-03-09T22:22Z: We observed queued requests and backpressure on the runtime pods in us-west-2; autoscaler had delayed scale-up due to recent change (minPool=3 -> 1 for short spikes)
2026-03-09T22:30Z: Circuit breaker for runtime instances did not trip until 22:37Z due to threshold misconfiguration (tripping at 10% error rate instead of 0.5%)
2026-03-09T22:38Z: Manual override set to reduce route weight to us-west-2 and re-enable EU-only traffic; emergency scale-up of dedicated pool initiated
2026-03-09T22:50Z: Traffic stabilizes but p99 remained elevated due to cached KV saturation; we enabled prefix-KV eviction and adjusted batch sizes

Approximately 4.3% of requests in EU and 2.1% in NA experienced >1s tail latency. Customer impact: several high-volume customers reported increased latency; no data loss or confidentiality concerns. Estimated revenue-impact window: 48 minutes; small subset of production traffic rerouted and saw degraded quality-of-service.
Multiple contributing changes aligned: (1) autoscaler configuration change deployed 2026-03-07 reduced min pool size to reduce cost; under cross-region failover this produced insufficient spare capacity for burst; (2) control-plane rollback of a traffic-weighting adjustment caused excess routing to a partially loaded region; (3) circuit-breaker parameterization was set conservatively high by a recent tuning PR (trips at 10% errors) delaying protective shedding; and (4) runtime KV cache experienced fragmentation under uneven load causing longer KV lookups and increased tail latencies. The immediate trigger was the traffic-weighting rollback + inadequate autoscaler floor which caused queueing and resource exhaustion in the target region.
