Title: Tenant-aware cross-region surge fallback and escalation procedure

Tenant-aware cross-region surge fallback and escalation procedure

Purpose: Create a tenant-aware runbook and escalation procedure to mitigate cross-region outages and large traffic surges that affect hosted and dedicated customers differently. Scope covers detection, automated and operator-driven traffic shifting, tenant-specific fallbacks, customer communications, and post-incident analysis. Excludes on-prem private installs beyond coordination notes (Private teams notified but manual actions required).
We observed multiple past incidents where region-level network or infra degradation caused asymmetric impact: hosted customers were routed via fallback regions but suffered higher latencies; dedicated tenants pinned to specific GPU pools experienced hard failures due to region-level control-plane flaps. Existing playbooks are region failover centric and do not encode tenant affinity, quotas, or dedicated tenant isolation needs. This ticket standardizes a tenant-aware approach that: 1) prioritizes SLA-backed dedicated tenants for capacity in fallback regions, 2) avoids cache-warmup storms by throttled warmup, and 3) communicates clear status and remediation steps to impacted customers and internal stakeholders.
Detection:
- Alert triggers: region-error-rate > 5% for 5m OR p95 latency spike > 2x baseline for 3m.
- On-call confirms via dashboards: /dashboards/region-health (link below).
Triage:
- Identify affected customer types: hosted vs dedicated vs private using query: SELECT tenant_id,type,region,active_routes FROM tenant_metadata WHERE region = :region.
- If >10 dedicated tenants in region failing, set severity S1 and notify Escalation Channel (#incidents-critical).
Immediate mitigation (automated):
- Activate emergency routing policy (routing-profile: emergency-shift) which moves new traffic to healthy regions respecting tenant routing prefs and capacity tags.
- For hosted traffic, enable model-variant fallback to cheaper variant (model:v1.2-compat -> model:v1.0-compat) to preserve availability.
Operator-driven mitigation (manual):
- For dedicated tenants pinned to region, begin tenant-aware drain: set tenant-routing to 'prefer-fallback' for tenants with SLA tier enterprise. Use api: POST /admin/tenants/:id/reroute body {action: "prefer-fallback"}.
- Throttle rehydrate: use KV-cache prefetch window of 30s staggered across tenants to avoid concurrent KV cache storm.
- Scale up dedicated GPU pools in fallback region if quota available (runbook note: contact sales/ops for reserved expand approvals).
Validation:
- Confirm successful route switch for sample tenants with curl to /health?tenant=:id and verify latency p95 < target and error rate < baseline.
- Watch for increased costs and token rate anomalies; tag incident with cost-alert if projected > 20% over baseline.
Internal:
- Post initial incident summary to #incidents-critical and tag SRE, Platform, Oncall Eng manager, and CSMs. Include affected regions, affected tenant count estimate, mitigation actions, and ETA for next update.
- Create incident GitHub issue (template: incident-runtime) linking this Linear ticket.
Customer comms:
- For Dedicated enterprise tenants: CSM to open priority 1 communication indicating degraded region and planned failover. Provide per-tenant timeline and whether manual acceptance is required.
- For Hosted customers: status page update (status.redwood.ai) with affected region and recommended mitigations; follow with targeted email to customers with traffic anomalies observed (list generated by query in runbook).
- Use standardized template (link in Links) and include contact for escalation: oncall+incidents@redwood.ai.
Rollback automated routing if: region-error-rate < 0.5% for 10m AND p95 latency returns within 1.2x baseline for 10m.
- Rollback must be staged: first return hosteds with canary 5% -> 20% -> 100% across 10m windows.
- For dedicated tenants, do not auto-move back; require tenant coordinator to approve and schedule tenant drain windows to repopulate original region.
- Record Rollback decision and approver in incident issue.
Region error rate: sum(errors) / sum(requests) by region over 5m.
P95 latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by region.
Affected tenants list: SELECT tenant_id, tier, region, last_30m_errors FROM tenant_incidents WHERE region = ':region' ORDER BY last_30m_errors DESC LIMIT 250.
KV cache warmup rate: rate(kv_cache_prefetch_events[1m]) by region.
Escalation thresholds are set as Grafana alerts: region_error_rate_high, p95_latency_regional_spike, dedicated_pool_degradation.
Post-incident tasks:
- Collect timeline (SRE + oncall) and publish within 48h.
- Run tenant-impact spreadsheet and send to Sales/CS for customer notifications and compensation considerations.
- Action items: policy engine: add tenant-weighted routing (eng PR); autoscaler: add soft-quota for dedicated pool burst; console: surface per-tenant failover history.
- Owner assignments: timeline doc owner = Diego Alvarez; customer impact spreadsheet owner = Priya Nair; follow-up tasks tracked as sub-issues.
- Schedule blameless postmortem meeting within 7 calendar days.
Dashboards: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/region-health
Incident template: https://confluence.redwood.ai/incidents/runtime-incident-template
Customer comms templates: https://docs.redwood.ai/comm-templates/failover
Related PRs: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1824 (tenant routing prototype)
PagerDuty run: https://pd.redwood.ai/incidents/ (incident number to be added on fire)

Title: Postmortem: Regional failover overload causing API SLO misses and emergency load-shedding

Postmortem: Regional failover overload causing API SLO misses and emergency load-shedding

Summary: On 2026-03-09 22:35 UTC a large-scale multi-region event impacted our primary EU region (eu-west-1) routing layer. Automated regional failover moved substantial traffic to NA clusters. Circuit breaker thresholds on several Dedicated pools were conservative and not updated for the increased prefix cache/memory footprint, causing a cascade of slow requests, SLO misses on 99th percentile latency for text-generation endpoints, and emergency load-shedding that impacted ~12% of active customer requests for ~46 minutes. This ticket documents timeline, root cause analysis, mitigations applied, and follow-up action items.
2026-03-09 22:32 UTC — EU control-plane spike detected by synthetic probes (1.5x error rate).
2026-03-09 22:35 UTC — Automated routing policy engaged: failover EU -> NA as per multi-region policy. Traffic shift peaked at 22:38 UTC.
2026-03-09 22:40 UTC — NA Dedicated pools reached higher-than-expected memory/KV cache pressure; autoscaler queued scale-ups but new nodes did not register fast enough.
2026-03-09 22:46 UTC — Circuit breaker mTLS health checks tripped for two Dedicated pools due to increased tail latency; fallback invoked to hosted pools.
2026-03-09 22:50 UTC — Load-shedding activated by emergency policy to preserve cluster health; customers experienced 429/503 responses.
2026-03-09 23:20 UTC — Manual intervention: adjusted circuit breaker thresholds, scaled sharding, temporarily increased burst capacity, and reverted routing for critical customers.
2026-03-09 23:22 UTC — Error rate and latency back within SLO window for most traffic; full recovery at 23:28 UTC.
SLO affected: text-generation latency (99th) target 600ms — observed spike to 2.9s during incident
Customer error rate: 12% of active requests received 429/503 during peak
Duration: ~46 minutes of elevated errors/latency; full recovery by 23:28 UTC
Revenue impact: estimated 0.08% of daily revenue (billing reconciliation in progress)
Confluence of events: (1) upstream multi-region routing decision routed high tail-traffic to NA due to eu-west-1 control-plane instability; (2) circuit breaker and health-check thresholds for Dedicated pools were tuned for steady-state, not for rapid cross-region failover bursts; (3) KV cache memory growth and larger-than-expected request fanout per request increased per-instance memory pressure causing slower kernel scheduling and delayed node registration during autoscale; (4) emergency load-shedding policy used a conservative cutoff that prioritized cluster stability but lacked customer-tier-aware exemptions for first-party and high-priority customers.
Incident was detected by synthetic latency probes and on-call alerts from the routing SLO dashboard. Pager fired for SRE rotation at 22:36 UTC. However, dashboards lacked a combined metric showing cross-region traffic shift + per-pool cache pressure which delayed root cause narrowing by ~6 minutes.
Applied mitigations in order: (A) Increased Dedicated circuit breaker thresholds and extended health-check grace period to allow nodes to come up during scale events; (B) Manually triggered scale-up of NA pools and increased burst capacity quota; (C) Adjusted routing policy to preserve a small percentage of traffic in EU for rate-limiting variance testing; (D) Applied customer-tier exemptions to load-shedding to avoid 429s for enterprise customers; (E) After stabilization, reverted temporary threshold changes and scheduled controlled rollout of new thresholds.
Design trade-off: current failover policy assumes downstream pools can absorb 2x baseline; real workload had 3.7x effective load due to increased KV cache misses and request multiplication. Consider adding an adaptive throttling window to the failover decision.
Engineering feedback: circuit breakers must be workload-aware not static; introduce per-model and per-customer budgeted headroom metrics.
Product input: customers expect predictable SLAs during region failover; need safer defaults or staged failover with proportional traffic shifts.
Operations: on-call runbooks lacked a single playbook for multi-region failover with Dedicated pools — created new combined runbook.

A2: Update circuit breaker configs to be model- and pool-aware; add automated simulation tests (owner: Mei Rodriguez, due: 2026-03-31)
A3: Add combined metric panel (cross-region traffic shift + per-pool KV cache pressure) and set synthetic alerts (owner: SRE Team, due: 2026-03-24)
A4: Revise load-shedding policy to include customer-tier exemptions and softer degradation modes (owner: Priya Nair, due: 2026-03-28)
A5: Increase autoscaler registration timeout and add health-check backoff jitter to prevent thundering during scale-up (owner: Marco Silva, due: 2026-03-22)
A6: Run tabletop exercise for multi-region failover with oncall and platform teams (owner: Aisha Kapoor, due: 2026-04-05)
A7: Post-release audit: verify PR runtime-1.20 includes KB for circuit-breaker tuning (owner: Release Engineering, due: 2026-04-01)
A8: Customer communication: send incident summary to impacted customers + offer SLA credit where applicable (owner: Customer Success, due: 2026-03-16)

Title: Mitigate variant misclassification causing cross-region reroute spirals

Mitigate variant misclassification causing cross-region reroute spirals

On 2026-03-09 a capacity-triggered fallback path interacted with a stale policy cache and an inconsistent variant compatibility map, causing a decaying oscillation where requests were rerouted across regions and to incompatible model variants. This produced elevated latencies (p95 +350ms), a spike in 5xxs for affected routes (~3.8% absolute increase), and visible user-facing slowdowns for multiple high-traffic tenants during a 42-minute window. Root cause: a race between policy rollout TTL refresh and variant-tag reconciliation that allowed an old mapping to be used as the canonical fallback target.
Add a synchronous variant-compatibility check in the routing decision path: verify model architecture + quantization schema before accepting a fallback target
Implement an epoched policy header (route_policy_epoch) that rejects stale policy cache entries older than N seconds to prevent silent acceptance
Deploy a short-circuit circuit-breaker that detects rapid bidirectional reroutes between two regions and forces a holdout to break oscillation
Enhance fallback telemetry: emit policy_version, variant_checksum, origin_region, chosen_region, and decision_reason for every fallback event to tracing and metrics
Add an automated CI regression that replays the incident repro (capacity drop + staggered policy refresh) against the smart-routing simulator
Create an integration test that validates fallback correctness across quantized variants (int8 vs fp16) to prevent incompatible mapping
Update the oncall runbook with explicit rollback steps for variant map changes and add a playbook section for oscillation detection and mitigation
Backfill 30 days of fallback decision logs to S3 for root-cause analysis and to support forensics requests
Schedule a cross-team design review (Runtime, Routing, Console) to validate rollout plan and telemetry schema before changes land
Perform a midnight canary rollout with throttled traffic and enhanced observability before global release

Title: Cross-region graded-degradation cascade: postmortem, runbook updates, and hardening plan

Cross-region graded-degradation cascade: postmortem, runbook updates, and hardening plan

During a capacity transient in us-west we observed a cascade of graded-degradation decisions that caused simultaneous circuit-breaker closures in secondary regions, amplified backpressure, and a sustained SLO drift for 37 minutes. This ticket documents the timeline, root causes, contributing factors, and an actionable hardening plan including runbook/alert changes and follow-up engineering work.
Duration: ~37 minutes (2026-03-09 14:12–14:49 UTC). Affected services: text-generation API (gen.v1) and chat endpoints; ~18% of customer requests experienced p95 latency > 3s and several high-throughput customers saw transient error rates up to 6%. External-facing SLO (p95 latency < 400ms) was breached for 37 minutes causing degraded user experience for customer cohort on Dedicated and Hosted plans.
2026-03-09 14:10 UTC: Rapid traffic spike in us-west observed on internal dashboard (traffic +2.6x baseline).
2026-03-09 14:12 UTC: Headroom in primary US region exhausted; smart-routing began failover to secondary regions (eu-west and ap-south) per policy.
2026-03-09 14:13–14:18 UTC: Secondary-region nodes received bursted fan-out; autoscaling attempted to satisfy throughput but instance spin-up lagged.
2026-03-09 14:18 UTC: Local circuit-breaker thresholds on eu-west tripped around the same time due to conservative hysteresis; control-plane rolled out graded-degradation measures (reduced token budgets and aggressive shedding).
2026-03-09 14:20 UTC: Multiple regions applied similar shedding simultaneously; priority queue starvation occurred for medium-priority requests leading to queue head-of-line blocking and KV-cache cold misses.
2026-03-09 14:25 UTC: Observability shows queue lengths and retry storms; error budget alarms fired but alert thresholds were missed by on-call routing rules for cascading failures.
2026-03-09 14:32 UTC: Emergency mitigation (manual lowering of circuit thresholds in eu-west, temporary routing to warm standby region) enacted by infra on-call.
2026-03-09 14:49 UTC: Traffic normalized and automated recovery resumed; gradual restoration to standard routing by 15:10 UTC.
Postmortem analysis window: 2026-03-10 to 2026-03-14.
Primary cause was synchronous, overly-conservative circuit-breaker hysteresis and identical shedding policies applied across regions without accounting for warm-up state and autoscale lag. This created a positive feedback loop: failover -> burst -> CB trips -> more failover -> queue amplification. Additionally, KV cache cold starts amplified latency for failover traffic and our detection thresholds didn't escalate to 'cascade' mode quickly enough.
Identical CB hysteresis and shedding thresholds in all regions (no differential for warm vs warmed regions)
Routing policy lacks staggered failover or jitter to avoid synchronized load jumps
Autoscaler warm-up time underestimated for the model instance type; scaling actions returned capacity too slowly
Priority queue algorithm allowed medium-priority traffic to preempt headrooms, causing starvation for critical requests
KV cache eviction policy results in cold-start latency spikes during mass failover
Alerting thresholds were tuned for single-region incidents and did not provide an early 'multi-region cascade' pager path
Detection: Control-plane metrics (queue depth and p95 latency) showed degradation but multi-region cascade signature (simultaneous CB closures) was not instrumented. Response: On-call infra manually adjusted routing weights and lowered CB sensitivity in secondary regions, and enabled a warm-standby routing override. Time to initial mitigation: ~20 minutes. Time to full recovery: ~37 minutes. Post-incident we performed traffic replay tests to reproduce the failure mode in staging.
Introduce temporary guardrail: increase stagger window for automated failover by 30s to prevent immediate synchronized fan-out (Config change rolled 2026-03-11)
Lower circuit-breaker sensitivity for warmed regions to prevent premature tripping (hotfix applied 2026-03-12)
Enable KV-prefetch on failover path to reduce cold-start hits (feature flag enabled 2026-03-12)
Add an emergency runbook step to enable warm-standby routing and manual weight adjustments (runbook patch PR #1289)
Add immediate alerting rule for 'simultaneous-CB-trip' pattern to page SREs (alert rule added 2026-03-13)
Whitelisting of high-priority customer flows from medium-priority shedding during cascade events (policy change 2026-03-13)
Implement region-aware CB profiles: separate hysteresis and backoff for warm vs cold regions (design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/resilience/cb-profiles)
Upgrade autoscaler predictive model to include traffic burst forecasts and instance warm-up windows (timeline: Q2 2026)
Introduce probabilistic failover jitter and staged fan-out to reduce simultaneous capacity shifts (design/RFC created)
Rework priority-queue algorithm to enforce SLA qps guarantees and prevent head-of-line blocking under failover load
KV cache pre-warming strategies for failover traffic plus adaptive eviction tuned by failover likelihood
Formalize a 'multi-region cascade' alerting and on-call playbook with dedicated escalation path

Title: Region traffic redistribution and customer escalation playbook for cross-region model degradations

Region traffic redistribution and customer escalation playbook for cross-region model degradations

Purpose: Define an operator-friendly runbook and customer escalation template for situations where one or more regions show sustained model degradation or routing anomalies. Scope covers Hosted API and Dedicated capacity; notes for Private/VPC customers include an assisted-playbook section. This ticket captures playbook steps, communication templates, automated routing knobs, and the short-term fixes (hotpatch candidates) that can be applied during incidents.
Detect: Monitor region-level SLO delta (p50/p95 latency, 5m error rate) and model token drop-off. Trigger threshold: p95 latency > 2x baseline OR error rate increase > 1.5% sustained for 3 minutes.
Triage: On alert, open incident channel (#inc-rr-<region>) and notify oncall. Attach tenant impact query and top 10 tenants by traffic in last 10 minutes.
Scope determination: Run tenant-influence query to determine if degradation is tenant-localized or region-wide. Label incident as 'tenant-local' or 'region-broad'.
Immediate mitigations (low-risk): enable per-tenant soft-throttle for noisy tenants; switch affected tenants to a warm model variant (lower memory/throughput footprint) if they accept degraded latency/quality.
Traffic redistribution: If region-wide and Dedicated pools are impacted, progressively shift traffic in 5% increments using 'soft-shift' route policy to neighboring healthy region with compatible model family. Validate KV cache hit-rate after each step and monitor tail latency.
KV cache resync: If KV cache desync suspected, trigger targeted cache flush for impacted replicas only and allow rebuild from prefix caching. Avoid global cache flush except as last resort.
Circuit controls: Toggle tenant circuit breaker thresholds to drain background batches and prevent head-of-queue stalls. For Dedicated, temporarily reduce max-concurrent-requests per GPU to protect latency SLOs.
Fallbacks: If shifting fails due to model compatibility, fallback to cross-graded quantized variant (documented in model catalog) and notify PM/ML for quality acceptance.
Customer communications: Use the escalation template to notify affected customers within 30 minutes (see attachments). Provide ETA windows for mitigation, and a post-incident summary timeframe.
Hotfix rollout: If a service-level configuration change is validated in staging, prepare a canary in the least critical region and observe for 15 minutes before global rollout. Link PR and release notes in incident channel.
Post-incident: Run automated validation (synthetic prompts and customer prompt-samples if available) against recovered region and mark incident stable only after 2 hours of sustained SLOs. Start postmortem within 72 hours.
Private/VPC customers: For on-prem or VPC customers, coordinate with customer SRE and provide the 'assisted-playbook' checklist; offer remote debugging session and a signed temporary support access token if authorized.
If traffic shift creates regressions: revert routing policy in reverse increments (5% back every 2 minutes) and restore original region weighting.
If cache flush increased errors: rehydrate from persisted snapshots and roll back to pre-flush KV snapshot. If unavailable, open an engineer-owned ticket to rebuild and notify customers.
If a hotfix causes regressions in canary: abort rollout, revert to previous binary, and create a rollback PR with root-cause notes.
Create incident channel and pin runbook
List top affected tenants and notify account managers
Apply soft-throttle to noisy tenants as needed
Execute progressive soft-shift with monitoring gates
Validate KV cache and model compatibility at each step
Prepare customer update and postmortem docket
Avoid global model swaps unless all routing fallbacks are exhausted; model compatibility mismatches are a common cause of shifted-traffic failures.
Prefer soft-throttle over immediate tenant eviction to preserve request ordering for conversational workloads.
When shifting traffic across regions, prioritize regions with identical quantization/kernel profiles to minimize cold-start degradation.
Dedicated customers with reserved pools may require contract-aware communication; consult Customer Success before automatic reroutes if SLA forbids cross-region serving.

Title: Aftershock: failover oscillation and aggressive shedding during cross-region surge

Aftershock: failover oscillation and aggressive shedding during cross-region surge

Summary: A high-traffic event on 2026-02-27 triggered a partial regional failover that exposed a configuration mismatch between circuit-breaker hysteresis and load-shedding thresholds across regions. Traffic oscillated between primary and secondary regions, causing p99 latency and success-rate SLO misses for a 22-minute window. The incident required an emergency rollback of a circuit-breaker hysteresis change, temporary relaxation of shedding policies, and a coordinated cache-warmup campaign to stabilise tail latency.

2026-02-27T14:05Z - Automated regional failover policy started redirecting 30% of new sessions to eu-west-1 as latency crossed the soft-SLO threshold.
2026-02-27T14:07Z - eu-west-1 circuit breakers, configured with more aggressive open thresholds in the recent rollout, began tripping and shedding according to the new profile.
2026-02-27T14:10Z - Observed traffic oscillation: as eu-west-1 shed, traffic remapped back to us-west-2, pushing us-west-2 over higher tail latencies leading to further failover attempts.
2026-02-27T14:25Z - Root-cause narrowing: mismatched hysteresis and lack of KV-cache priming in the receiving region amplified tail latency. Incident commander ordered temporary rollback of hysteresis change (PR #4102) and set shedding thresholds to conservative defaults.
2026-02-27T14:45Z - Cache-warmup job ramped for critical prefixes; traffic smoothing rules applied to routing to stop rapid oscillation.
2026-02-27T15:05Z - Metrics returned within SLO targets; emergency mitigation transitioned to follow-up action plan.
2026-02-27T15:25Z - Incident declared resolved for customer-facing impact; post-incident analysis kicked off.

Approximately 22 minutes of customer-visible SLO degradation across two regions. Measured impact: p99 latency increased from 520ms to 1.9s, availability (success_rate) dropped from 99.93% to 98.1% for affected routes. Estimated customer requests impacted: ~7.4k RPS aggregated over the incident window. No data leakage or security incident.
A rollout of a circuit-breaker hysteresis tuning (PR #4102) changed the open/close timers and allowed more aggressive opening in eu-west-1. That change was not coupled with coordinated load-shedding and routing policy adjustments nor with a cache-warmup step. When traffic was partially diverted during failover, eu-west-1's unprimed KV caches and aggressive breaker opened repeatedly, shedding load. The routing control plane immediately sent traffic back to us-west-2, creating an oscillation loop that amplified tail latency and triggered further failovers. Lack of cross-region simulation and missing automated canary gating for control-plane config changes allowed the configuration mismatch to reach production.
Short-term: rollback of PR #4102, revert eu-west-1 breaker hysteresis to previous values, reduce shedding aggressiveness to default thresholds, and enable temporary traffic smoothing (5s ramp windows). Initiated targeted cache priming for high-volume prefixes and increased short-term autoscaling allowances in eu-west-1. Long-term: multi-region canary for control-plane config changes, add hysteresis and shedding coupling checks to CI, improve runbooks for coordinated rollouts, and extend observability for cross-region hysteresis metrics.

Title: regional-routing-signal-attenuation-playbook

regional-routing-signal-attenuation-playbook

Goal and scope: This doc captures a practical checklist and decision logic for handling region-level signal attenuation (high error rates / partial network degradation) that impacts routing, DNS TTLs, and egress paths. It focuses on: 1) safely shifting traffic between regions with minimum cache thrash and client disruption; 2) coordination points with networking and platform teams; 3) quick mitigations (soft redirects, weighted routing) and hard cutovers; 4) rollback and verification criteria.

When to use this playbook: Use when we observe region-level SLO degradation for >5 minutes with request error rate or tail latency impacting >10% of requests and originating consistently from a specific region/cluster. Also applies to third-party egress outages (cloud interconnect, CDN) that cause routing anomalies.

Quick triage checklist (first 10 minutes):
- Confirm alerts: aggregate from Datadog and tracer spikes. Note the region tag (e.g., us-west-2-eu-west-1).
- Verify scope: query request counts and error breakdown by AZ and by edge POP. Command: curl to internal metrics API or check dashboards: /dashboards/slo/region-latency.
- Check KV cache hit rate delta for the region. Large cache-miss spikes mean replays if we shift too aggressively.
- Look at LB health checks and node drain state. If control plane shows node drain, coordinate with release-engineering.

Immediate mitigations (safe order):
1) Apply local circuit breaker: reduce concurrency or reject bulkhead-y endpoints for the affected region to reduce cascading failures. This buys time without shifting traffic globally.
2) Reduce DNS TTL for affected record(s) to 60s if currently >300s. Note: only do this if origin DNS provider supports sub-minute updates and ops has confidence in clients honoring TTLs.
3) Switch to weighted routing with conservative weights (e.g., shift 10-20% at a time) rather than an all-at-once DNS swap. Use traffic controller to adjust weights: update route-policy region-weight us-west-2 => 70%, us-east-1 => 30%.
4) Enable prefix/KV cache pre-seed on target region(s) before large weight increases. This is critical for models with large KV caches; failure to pre-seed causes token storm and increased latency. Steps: run cache-preseed job id cache-preseed-<timestamp> against target pools and confirm hit rate >80%.
5) If DNS fallback is needed for legacy clients, update low-priority A records and add HTTP 301 fallback headers for clients that respect origin responses.

Hard failover (when to execute):
- Execute full failover when error rate in primary region exceeds 50% of requests and degradation persists >15 minutes OR when customer SLA / legal/regulatory constraints require immediate isolation.
- Before hard failover: notify ExecOps, CS, and partner teams via #sre-incident and create incident bridge. Post ETA and rollback plan in the incident channel.
- Hard failover steps: incrementally move weights in 20% steps every 2 minutes while monitoring 95th/99th latencies and downstream queue lengths. If any metric regresses >15% relative to baseline after a step, pause and evaluate.

DNS specifics and pitfalls: 
- Avoid very short TTLs for long-lived clients (SDKs) — this causes constant re-resolution and spikes. Prefer weighted routing + CDN reconfiguration over TTL oscillation where possible.
- If using provider-side traffic steering (Cloud DNS geoproximity), validate how the provider interprets POPs vs. client IP. Misinterpretation can send mobile traffic to far-away regions.
- When updating DNS records: record changes with the provider transaction ID and monitor DNS propagation via global dig checks and DNSViz if necessary.

KV cache considerations:
- Cache warming: pre-seed frequently used prefixes and model KV for the target region. Use the pre-seed tool with a dry-run to estimate prewarming time.
- Cache eviction risk: if target region does not have sufficient RAM/GPUs, we will see high truncation and evictions causing latency spikes; check node memory pressure metrics before scaling traffic.

Coordination matrix (who to notify and when):
- Immediate: #sre-incident, platform-oncall, networking-oncall.
- 10-minute update: release-eng, model-ops, product-ops.
- 30-minute update: growth/CS for customer-visible incidents.
- Legal/compliance: only if customer data plane is affected or region isolation is driven by legal/regulatory reasons.

Validation and post-shift checks:
- Verify user-facing error rate returns to baseline for 10 consecutive minutes.
- Validate KV cache hit ratio in new region >= 75% within 10 minutes.
- Confirm model output quality checks (sample inference requests) against golden prompt set.
- Confirm logs and traces are present and route attributes include region tags.

Rollback criteria:
- If error rate or p95/p99 latency worsens by >15% after a weighting step, revert to previous weighting and re-evaluate.
- If cache hit ratio is <50% after 15 minutes despite pre-seed, rollback.
- If third-party egress shows repeated BGP flaps or packet loss >3% between our regions, restore original routing and escalate to networking provider.

Common gotchas and lessons learned from recent incidents:
- Too-fast DNS TTL changes caused SDK clients to hammer origin causing transient capacity depletion. Lesson: prefer weighted routing where you can adjust at the controller level.
- Not prewarming KV caused token storms and downstream throttles when traffic moved. Always run preseed; make it an automated step in the weight-change pipeline.
- Bumping weights without checking regional quotas led to capacity exhaustion in the target region. Precheck GPU/instance quotas before shifting traffic.

Action items (post-incident):
- Automate pre-seed job trigger in the routing service for any >10% weight move. Owner: Omar Singh. Due: 2026-03-15.
- Add synthetic golden prompt checks to the canary gating flow. Owner: Ellen Park. Due: 2026-03-22.
- Document DNS provider-specific caveats for geoproximity in confluence page CONFLUENCE-REGION-FLOW-23. Owner: Rajiv Menon. Due: 2026-03-10.

Open questions: 
- Do SDKs respect TTLs in all major client versions? We need a telemetry sweep across versions and platforms.
- Can the traffic controller perform automatic staged shifts based on observed SLO delta, or do we require manual ratcheting?

Incident reference example (short timeline):
- 10:04: Alert: us-west-2 latency spike (p99 > 3s).
- 10:08: Triage confirms region-level cache miss spike and increased 504s.
- 10:12: Circuit breakers applied to non-critical endpoints and DNS TTL lowered to 60s for affected A records.
- 10:20: Pre-seed started for us-east-1, weight shift started 10% -> monitor.
- 10:40: Reached 80% traffic in us-east-1; KV hit ratio recovered; incident declared mitigated.

References and artifacts: see linked_artifacts for PR and tickets. Also check internal dashboard: /dashboards/sre/region-failover. Slack thread: #sre-incident-thread-xyz.

Notes to self / quick reminders: keep communications simple and timestamped, record route-policy deltas in the incident ticket, and always capture the provider transaction IDs for DNS and cloud routing changes.

This is a living doc — feedback welcome. If you run through this playbook during an incident, paste the run timestamps and any overrides into the incident ticket for postmortem analysis.

Title: Consolidate routing drain detection and harden fallback resilience after multi-region misroutings

Consolidate routing drain detection and harden fallback resilience after multi-region misroutings

Postmortem and follow-ups for a Feb 12th incident where automated region drains + routing cache TTL mismatch caused large-scale misroutes and cascading fallback to underprovisioned model variants. This ticket captures the incident timeline, root cause analysis, immediate mitigations, and long-term remediation work we completed/triaged.
On 2026-02-12 03:14 UTC, customers in EU-West began seeing elevated latencies and 5xx errors. The control plane initiated an automated drain for a GPU cluster due to underlying hardware ECC warnings. A combination of stale routing cache entries and a mis-ordered drain handshake caused large swaths of traffic to be redirected to a low-cost fallback variant (quantized-8) which exceeded its capacity and triggered cascading fallbacks to smaller variants and rate-limit enforcement. The outage lasted ~42 minutes for impacted tenants and caused reduced throughput and higher tail latency for a subset of PLG customers.
2026-02-12 03:12 UTC: Hardware ECC alert on eu-west-a pool.
2026-02-12 03:13 UTC: Control plane issues drain: drain-job(v=4392) created and broadcast.
2026-02-12 03:14 UTC: Edge routing cache still had routes to drained nodes (TTL 300s).
2026-02-12 03:15 UTC: Smart router receives partial drain ack; due to race, routing policy fallback mapping prefers quantized-8 variant (capacity hint low) for some routes.
2026-02-12 03:18 UTC: Quantized-8 variant saturates; autoscaler does not trigger immediately because variant is marked non-scalable.
2026-02-12 03:20 UTC: Router cascades to even smaller variant and applies emergency rate limits. Error rates spike; customers report 5xx and degraded responses.
2026-02-12 03:54 UTC: Hotfix rolled: router logic patched to consult drain authoritative list and drain-proof routing table; traffic shifted to healthy eu-west-b region and rollback of rate limits.
2026-02-12 04:00 UTC: All routes stabilized; full traffic regeneration complete by 04:15 UTC. Post-incident monitoring continued for 24h.
Three contributing issues combined: (1) routing cache TTL (300s) allowed stale bindings to persist after control plane drain announcements; (2) drain workflow handshake was not atomic—partial ack states led the router to mis-evaluate node health; (3) fallback variant mapping included a 'non-scalable' flag for quantized-8 which prevented autoscale and made that variant a single point of saturation. A recent config change to reduce cache churn increased TTL but this was not coordinated with drain semantics.
~1,200 active customers temporarily experienced increased tail latency and intermittent 5xx; platform-wide token throughput reduced by ~18% for ~42 minutes. No customer data loss. Several enterprise tenants hit error budgets and filed incident support tickets.
Immediate steps taken during incident: (1) applied hotfix to routing service to prefer authoritative drain list over cached entries; (2) temporarily removed 'non-scalable' tag from quantized-8 variant to enable autoscaling; (3) increased emergency capacity in eu-west-b and diverted traffic; (4) rolled back recent TTL increase for routing cache; (5) reopened affected rate limit windows and lifted emergency throttles.
Completed and planned remediation items: short-term (done): change routing decision order to check drain authoritative set, revert cache TTL change, enable autoscale on fallback variants, and add immediate alerting for fallback saturation. Medium-term (in progress): implement atomic drain handshake, add read-through cache invalidation on drain events, and add simulation tests for drain+cache interactions. Long-term (backlog): policy engine rewrite to provide capacity-aware fallback selection and canary deployments for fallback variant config changes.

ENG-8633: Add read-through invalidation hook to routing cache when drain job is accepted (estimate 5)
ENG-8634: Add autoscale opt-in for all fallback variants and default min-instances to 2 (estimate 3)
ENG-8635: Create e2e chaos test for region drain + routing cache TTL interactions (estimate 5)
DOC-472: Update runbook: 'region-drain' section with new verification steps and rollback commands (owner: SRE)
OBS-189: Dashboard tile: 'fallback saturation' with per-variant queue depth and autoscale events (owner: Observability)
PM-501: Policy review to avoid non-scalable fallback as first-choice (owner: Product)
On-call debrief session scheduled: 2026-02-16 16:00 UTC (owner: Diego Martinez)
Key lesson: cross-system configuration changes (cache TTL vs drain semantics) require coordinated rollout and test coverage. We underestimated the risk of tagging fallback variants as non-scalable — cost optimization cannot come at availability expense. The immediate fix prioritized deterministic routing behavior (authoritative drain list) and restoring autoscaling resiliency for fallbacks. Follow-ups will harden both the control-plane protocol and the policy engine.
Several follow-ups already created and assigned (ENG-8632..ENG-8635). SRE completed the runbook update and Observability has a dashboard PR in review. Expected closure of all remediation work by runtime-1.20 quarterly patch.

Title: Surgical traffic remediation and staged rollback playbook for mixed-hosted/dedicated cross-region routing incidents

Surgical traffic remediation and staged rollback playbook for mixed-hosted/dedicated cross-region routing incidents

Summary: Create a prescriptive, low-risk runbook and playbook for repairing misrouted traffic and KV-cache divergence that can occur during cross-region traffic shifts involving mixed Hosted + Dedicated customers. This ticket focuses on: tenant-aware surgical remediation, staged rollback commands, validation checks, safe fallbacks to compatible model variants, and coordinated customer communication. Scope includes Hosted API, Dedicated pools, and coordination instructions for Private/VPC customers when operator action is needed. Excludes lower-severity non-tenant-isolating issues.
1) Runbook tested end-to-end in staging with simulated tenant traffic and at least two fault modes (regional network partition, autoscaler misplacement). 2) Clear command snippets for tenant pinning, partial region drain, and staged rollback validated by SRE run. 3) Communication templates approved by support & AMs. 4) Telemetry queries for correctness and SLA impact added to dashboards. 5) Postmortem checklist ready and linked.
Step 0 - Triage: Confirm incident type with oncall: Is this a cross-region routing anomaly affecting layer-7 routing or a backend KV-consistency issue in replicas? Capture symptoms: elevated 5xx, increased tail latency, per-tenant error spikes, KV-miss ratio. Note affected tenants and dedicated pools.
Step 1 - Freeze automation: Immediately disable autoscale-based migrations and any scheduled traffic rebalances for the affected regions via infra flags (infra-toggle:regional-rebalance=false). Record toggles in incident log.
Step 2 - Tenant pinning (if tenant-specific degradation): For each affected tenant, apply a routing pin to healthy region via routing-api: POST /v1/tenants/{tenant}/pin with body {region: 'us-west-2', mode: 'sticky', ttl: 3600}. Use dedicated routing key for Dedicated customers. Document commands used and TTL values.
Step 3 - Surgical traffic siphon: Gradually mirror 5-10% of affected tenant requests to candidate region for validation while leaving primary routing intact (traffic-siphon window = 10m). Monitor error and latency delta. If delta < SLO threshold, increase to 25%, then 50%.
Step 4 - KV cache reconciliation: If KV-desync suspected, run KV-snapshot on primary then apply incremental patch to standby: run tooling kv-sync --src-region=us-east-1 --dst-region=us-west-2 --tenants=tenant-list --max-ops=5000. If snapshot latency impacts runtime, run in background with lower op rate and enable read-repair heuristics.
Step 5 - Canary model variant fallback: If model variant incompatibility or latency spike traced to a specific quantization profile, switch only the pinned tenants to a lower-latency variant using model-router: /v1/routes/update with filters {tenants:[...], variant: 'quant-8b'}. Avoid global variant switches.
Step 6 - Progressive region drain: For a region-level failover, perform staged draining: 1) mark region read-only for new dedicated allocations; 2) shift new session establishment to standby region; 3) after 15m, divert 50% of new and 25% of in-progress completions; 4) full traffic cutover after stability window.
Step 7 - Customer comms and AM coordination: Immediately notify affected customers via template (see communication_templates). For Dedicated customers include estimated remediation ETA and whether a live migration is required. For Private customers, provide operator actions and a timeboxed maintenance window.
Step 8 - Validation and rollback gate: Maintain verification checks for 30m after each major step. If any check fails (per-tenant error rate > 2x baseline or USL latency breach), trigger rollback_commands for the last change and escalate to SE oncall.
Step 9 - Post-incident follow-up: Run postmortem checklist, record root cause hypothesis, corrective actions (code/infra/ops), and schedule a DR drill for the new runbook within next cycle.
Step 10 - Automate safe-guards: Create a follow-up ticket to add guardrails: automatic read-only during KV-syncs, tenant-level circuit-breaker thresholds, and telemetry alerts for unusual cross-region request ratios.
API health: 200/5xx ratio back to baseline for affected tenants across 3 consecutive 5-minute windows.
Latency: P95 and P99 for pinned tenants within SLO (P95 < 120ms hosted, < 200ms dedicated) over a 10-minute window.
KV correctness: sample key compare between regions % mismatch < 0.01% after sync.
Model output stability: fuzz-similarity score for mirrored requests > 0.9 compared to baseline.
No new customer tickets created in 60 minutes for the same issue after remediation steps.
Dashboard: Traffic routing ratio to regions shows expected shift and no unexpected spikes in other regions.
Smoke testing: Run synthetic prompt set for top 10 affected tenants, verify completion and structured output validity.
Routing rollback: POST /v1/routes/rollback with body {operation_id: <last-op>, force: true}
Tenant unpin: POST /v1/tenants/{tenant}/unpin to restore normal routing TTL expiry.
KV revert: kv-sync --reverse --src-region=<standby> --dst-region=<primary> --max-ops=2000 (only for emergency revert under SRE approval).
Model variant rollback: model-router: /v1/variants/set with filters {tenants:[...], variant: 'stable-previous'}
Autoscale re-enable: infra-toggle:regional-rebalance=true after confirmation from infra lead.

Title: Few-shot ordering perturbation chronicle

Few-shot ordering perturbation chronicle

Purpose: quick-running personal notebook to catalog how exemplar ordering (and small perturbations) affects model outputs for classification-style few-shot prompts. Want a compact decision matrix for when to randomize, when to anchor, and quick heuristics for shipping template defaults.

Motivation / hypotheses (short):
- H1: For conceptually homogeneous exemplars (same phrasing style + label balance), ordering has small effect; for mixed style examples, order triggers style transfer and label bias.
- H2: Placing a high-quality canonical exemplar first reduces hallucination for long-tail classes (acts as anchor).
- H3: Interleaving positive/negative examples stabilizes calibration vs grouped positives/negatives.

Quick experimental plan (mini runs):
- Model: open-llama-13B-quant (dev cluster), temperature 0.0/0.3/0.7, max_new_tokens 120.
- Task: product-categorization (6 labels) and sentiment-subcategory (fine-grained).
- Prompt template: short instruction + N exemplars + query. Keep instruction constant.
- Variables: ordering strategy (canonical-first, canonical-last, random-seed-1..5, grouped-by-label, interleaved), exemplar style (formal/colloquial), exemplar length (short/long), shot count (3/5/7).

Run log summary (high-level results):
- 3-shot runs: most sensitive to ordering (up to 18% absolute delta on F1 across orders).
- 5-shot runs: variance reduced but still present (5–9% delta).
- Anchoring (canonical-first): consistently improved long-tail recall by ~6% vs grouped-last.
- Randomized ensemble (avg of 5 different orderings): lower variance and slightly better macro F1; cost x5 tokens though.

Representative failure cases observed:
1) Label drift when first exemplar is long-winded and mentions unrelated tokens (model latches to spurious signal). Example: first exemplar contains brand name "Xylo" and then many tokens -> query with different brand is mis-labeled.
2) Style bleed: mixing colloquial and formal exemplars caused output tone mismatch with prompts; sometimes model answers in the style of the most recent exemplar.
3) Boundary confusion: when exemplars contain overlapping attributes (A+B vs A only) grouped together, model tends to under-predict the combined class if all combined examples are contiguous.

Micro-protocols (for reproducible small tests):
- Save seeds and exact ordering list (file: ordering-seeds.csv) with columns: seed, ordering-list, shot-count, exemplar-ids.
- Keep instruction and system message identical. If testing system-message effects, run separate sweep.

Heuristics distilled (for productizing prompt defaults):
- Default to canonical-first for 3-shot templates when there is a known representative example (short, precise).
- For multi-style training data, either (a) cluster exemplars by style and pick one exemplar from each cluster to interleave, or (b) normalize style (rewrite exemplars) before shipping.
- For label imbalance, ensure anchor exemplar for low-frequency label appears earlier in the list.
- If deterministic output is required, prefer 5-shot + interleaving + temperature 0.0.
- If exploring calibration, run 3 random-order ensemble (cheap middle-ground) instead of single ordering.

Concrete prompt template (working version):
- System: "You are a helpful classifier. Read examples and assign the single best label from the set: [A,B,C,D,E,F]. Reply with only the label name."
- Instruction: "Below are examples. Match the examples' pattern and label the query."
- Exemplars: (shot-1 canonical-short), (shot-2 alternate-short), (shot-3 contrast-long).
- Query: "Product: <title> -- Description: <desc>"

Examples (short):
EX1 (canonical-first): 
Q: Product: "SoothePro Heat Pad" -- Description: "12\" x 8\" reusable heat pad for muscle pain. Includes washable cover."
A: Health

EX2 (alt): ...
EX3 (contrast): ...

Quick notes on evaluation metrics used:
- Primary: macro F1 (because we care about rare labels).
- Secondary: per-label precision/recall, confusion matrix, calibration (confidence vs accuracy).
- For ensembling orderings: track both mean prediction and majority-vote; prefer majority-vote if label probabilities are noisy.

Open questions / things to try next:
- How does ordering interact with instruction phrasing? (short directive vs narrative examples).
- Can we synthesize a compact "meta-exemplar" combining features of multiple exemplars to act as a stronger anchor?
- Measure runtime/latency tradeoff on Redwood Dedicated (is random-ensemble viable under latency SLOs?).
- Explore learned exemplar selection: small scorer model picks 3 exemplars per query at runtime — does ordering still matter after selection?

Quick TODOs (personal):
- [ ] push small experiment scripts + seed logs to GHPR referenced above (assigned to me).
- [ ] draft a short one-pager for product on default shipping heuristics (1 page, include "canonical-first").
- [ ] run a small test on 30k-prod-sample with interleaved vs grouped exemplars and record costs.

Notes to self (random observations):
- Saw odd repeated-label tendency when exemplars used bullet lists vs inline sentences — formatting matters.
- For some queries, simply changing the spacing/newline between exemplars changed label output (probably tokenization/context parsing edge).
- Keep an eye on quantized models — some order sensitivity seems amplified at 4-bit quantization.

End of notebook entry. Will iterate and convert to a more formal playbook if patterns hold over larger datasets.

-- Asha

Title: Tiered Eval Fidelity Contract and Shadow Mesh Playbook

Tiered Eval Fidelity Contract and Shadow Mesh Playbook

Summary
-------
This playbook defines a standardized, tiered fidelity contract for evaluation (Tiered Eval Fidelity Contract — TEFC) and prescribes the operational pattern we call the "Shadow Mesh" for validating model changes across Dedicated/Private/Hosted deployments. It provides concrete acceptance gates, telemetry requirements, and deterministic fallback behaviors for quantized and KV-cache-sensitive deployments.

Why this exists
----------------
- Reduce costly rollbacks by enforcing graded trust across fidelity bands (smoke -> nominal -> fidelity -> canary).
- Make quantized rollout decisions reproducible and auditable.
- Provide a lightweight mesh for cross-environment shadowing that preserves privacy budgets and cost constraints.

Scope
-----
Applies to: model promotions for text generation and chat endpoints (all sequence lengths), quantized artifacts (Q4/INT8/FP16), and any candidate that will be routed under Redwood’s smart routing policies. Not intended for multi-modal binary-only models (see separate multimodal playbook).

Terminology
-----------
- Fidelity Band: A named level of eval fidelity with SLOs and required checks.
- Shadow Mesh: cluster of shadow runners that mirror live traffic under controlled sampling and resource limits.
- Eval Contract: machine-readable manifest (YAML) defining probes, thresholds, and fallback policy for a promotion.

Fidelity Bands and Acceptance Criteria
-------------------------------------
Each model candidate must declare a TEFC manifest (example below). The platform enforces band-specific checks:

1) SMOKE (fast sanity)
   - Purpose: detect catastrophic regressions before longer runs.
   - Requirements: 500 synthetic probes (representative slices), >=99% pass on hard-blocking sentinels (safety & PII), latency p95 < 3x baseline.
   - Allowed deviations: None on safety sentinels.

2) NOMINAL (basic functional)
   - Purpose: baseline functional equivalence for common slices.
   - Requirements: 10k probes spread across top-20 slices, mean coherence delta <= 0.03 on primary metrics, token-cost delta <= +10%.
   - Allowed deviations: up to 2% of non-critical slices may regress if justified and triaged.

3) FIDELITY (quality-first)
   - Purpose: capture nuanced regressions across rare slices and long-context behavior.
   - Requirements: 100k probes including long-context multi-turn sequences, multi-seed aggregation with variance budgeting, embedding drift <= 0.02, function-call fidelity measured on heldout contract.
   - Allowed deviations: requires peer review and an annotated remediation plan for any failing slice.

4) CANARY (production shadow)
   - Purpose: final production verification with live traffic in Shadow Mesh.
   - Requirements: 24–72 hour Shadow Mesh run with sampled traffic (default 1% but configurable by tenant), SLOs: latency p95 <= 1.5x baseline, error-rate delta <= 0.1% absolute, quality SLA (Fidelity band metrics) met on 99% of critical slices.

TEFC Manifest (example)
-----------------------
YAML manifest attached to every model promotion. Required fields: model_id, baseline_model, fidelity_profile, probe_sets (ids), shadow_sampling, quant_profiles (if applicable), fallback_policy_id. Example: 

---
model_id: redwood-mosaic-v2-q8n
baseline_model: redwood-mosaic-v2-fp16
fidelity_profile: fidelity
probe_sets: [longcontext_multi_turn_v3, top20_slices_2026Q1]
shadow_sampling: 0.01
quant_profiles: [q8n-standard, q8n-latency-hedge]
fallback_policy_id: fallback-policy-quant-01
---

Shadow Mesh Architecture and Controls
------------------------------------
- Shadow runners are isolated containers that receive replicated requests (request shim) with sensitive payload redaction and synthetic identity mapping.
- Mesh supervisor (service: eval-mesh-orchestrator) coordinates rollout phasing, telemetry collection, and automatic escalation.
- Resource limits: default mesh pool per model = 10% of baseline capacity, capped at absolute 100 vCPU-equivalents and 32GB GPU VRAM. These limits are enforced to avoid production interference.
- Privacy gating: PII-sensitive requests are dropped from the mesh by the PII-filter service using deterministic rules (see PII-filter spec link).

Telemetry and Required Signals
------------------------------
All TEFC runs must emit the following signal set to the telemetry pipeline:
- probe_id, slice_id, seed_id (for multi-seed runs)
- latency_ms (p50,p95,p99)
- token_count_in/out, token_cost_estimate
- top-k logits entropy and mean confidence
- embedding_cosine_to_baseline (for embedding stability)
- sentinel_safety_violations (boolean + violation_class)
- kv_cache_hit_rate (per-request)
- quant_fallback_triggered (boolean)

For canaries: distributed tracing (trace_id) and request sampling traces must be produced at 100% for flagged errors and 0.1% otherwise.

Onboarding Checklist (Model Owners)
----------------------------------
1) Create TEFC manifest and attach probe_sets.
2) Run SMOKE locally and upload results to eval-store.
3) Schedule NOMINAL run via eval-orchestrator (estimated cost and runtime shown in UI).
4) If NOMINAL passes, run FIDELITY; tag all failing slices and assign mitigations.
5) Request CANARY start and configure shadow_sampling.
6) Monitor mesh dashboard and run final acceptance sign-off via the model promotion UI.

Operational Play: Rollout and Rollback
-------------------------------------
1) Promotion begins in SMOKE. If any hard sentinel fails, immediate stop and block with auto-notification to owner.
2) NOMINAL/FIDELITY runs produce a triage report (auto-generated): top regressions, suggested fixes (quant profile swap, prompt rewrite, increased KV cache bucket).
3) CANARY begins: mesh supervisor incrementally ramps sampling from 0.1% to configured sampling over 6 hours while verifying telemetry gates every 30 minutes.
4) Automatic rollback triggers (immediate circuit-break): any safety sentinel violation, latency p95 > 2x baseline for 3 consecutive windows, or quant_fallback_triggered rate > 5% in a 15-min window.
5) Manual rollback: owner or SRE can trigger immediate rollback via the Console with justification. The rollback record is stored in audit logs (policy: retain 1 year).

Quantization Handoff and Fallback Patterns
-----------------------------------------
- Quant profiles must be enumerated in the TEFC manifest with explicit hedges: (e.g., q8n-latency-hedge -> fallback q4n-stability).
- Fallback behaviors: runtime will attempt up to N retries (default 2) with progressively higher-fidelity variants before falling back to baseline FP16.
- Quant-quality delta budgets are enforced: e.g., coherence_delta_budget <= 0.04 per-slice. Exceeding budget requires approval from Applied ML.

Regression Triage Workflow
-------------------------
- When a failed slice is detected, the triage ticket is auto-created with: slice_id, example inputs, baseline and candidate responses, token-delta, and recommended remediation.
- Triage levels: L0 (auto), L1 (owner-only), L2 (cross-team review), L3 (exec escalation).
- Time-to-first-action targets: L0 = 15m, L1 = 4h, L2 = 24h.
- For quant-related regressions, attach quant-profile artifacts and run the quant-replay harness (CLI example below).

CLI: running a local TEFC smoke test
------------------------------------
# assumes redwood-cli installed and AUTH_TOKEN set
redwood-cli eval run --manifest ./tefc.yaml --mode smoke --upload-results 

# replay a failure slice in quant harness
redwood-cli quant replay --artifact s3://quant-artifacts/q8n-latency-hedge.tar.gz --slice-id slice_98765 --seeds 5 --out results/

Metrics Dashboard (required widgets)
-----------------------------------
- Band-pass heatmap: per-slice pass/fail for each fidelity band (SMOKE/NOMINAL/FIDELITY/CANARY).
- Token-economy delta: cost and token count deltas against baseline.
- Safety sentinel trend: violations per 1k requests.
- Quant-fallback events: rate and correlated latencies.
- KV cache occupancy and hit-rate by tenant.

Ownership and Escalation
------------------------
- Model owner: primary responsible for manifest, probe selection, and remediation.
- Applied ML team: enforcement of fidelity contracts and review of FIDELITY-level regressions.
- SRE: Shadow Mesh operation, resource limits, and automated rollbacks.
- Security/Privacy: PII-filter rule updates and approvals for shadowing policies.

Related pages
-------------
- eval-harness/eval-mesh-orchestrator-ref (internal link)
- quantization-profiles/quant-fallback-quality-sla (internal link)
- regression-triage/automated-regression-bisect-tooling

Appendix: Example triage report (snippet)
----------------------------------------
| field | value |
|---|---:|
| slice_id | rare-nested-references-41 |
| baseline_resp_coherence | 0.86 |
| candidate_resp_coherence | 0.71 |
| token_delta | +18% |
| kv_cache_hit_rate | 42% |
| suggested_action | switch quant profile to q8n-stability; add 2 exemplars to longcontext probe; re-run FIDELITY |

Notes and caveats
------------------
- TEFC is intentionally prescriptive for higher-risk models; lightweight services may opt into a relaxed contract with approval.
- Cost: FIDELITY band runs are expensive — budget owners must approve before scheduling (UI enforces billing gates).

Owners and contacts
-------------------
- Document owner: Aisha Patel (Applied ML)
- Mesh lead: Michael Cheng (Eng Platform)
- SRE contact: Priya Rao

Change log
----------
2026-01-12: Initial draft
2026-02-02: Added quant-fallback budget rules and automated rollback thresholds

Title: Shadow Deployment Evaluation Playbook for Private & Dedicated Environments

Shadow Deployment Evaluation Playbook for Private & Dedicated Environments

Overview:

This playbook defines the standard process and acceptance criteria for "shadow" (non-traffic, mirrored) evaluation deployments of new model builds and quantized model variants in Redwood Private and Dedicated environments. Shadow deployment is intended to provide realistic, safety-aware, and cost-conscious validation without exposing production traffic to unvetted model behavior.

Goals:
- Detect functional regressions and quality drift early when promoting model builds to Dedicated or Private customer pools.
- Verify quantization/3rd-party compilation impacts under representative workload shapes.
- Validate operational metrics (latency p50/p95, memory pressure, KV cache hit distribution) in the target deployment topology.
- Produce deterministic promotion signals for canary/fallback policies in the Redwood Console.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to: model promotions intended for Dedicated pools and Private (VPC/on-prem) installs that will be pinned or exposed to customer traffic.
- Not intended for hosted-only experimentation (use hosted eval harness).

Key definitions:
- Shadow deployment: A deployment that receives a copy of production-like requests (via sampling or replay) but does not return responses to end users.
- Evaluation cohort: A configured set of prompts, demographic slices, and synthetic adversarial cases used during the shadow period.
- Quantization variant: Any model build with reduced precision or kernel-level compilation differences (int8, bfloat16, fq4) intended to lower unit costs.

Prerequisites:
1. Model build has passed unit and integration tests and a baseline acceptance in the central eval harness (see related eval-harness matrix).
2. Target Dedicated/Private environment is provisioned with matching runtime version and kernel profiles.
3. Baseline production telemetry snapshot captured (last 7 days) for comparison.
4. Owner, SRE, and customer (if applicable) sign-off on shadow window and data collection.

Evaluation inputs (test sets & strategies):
- Live-sampled traffic (1-5% of production routed to shadow) OR replayed request traces from the last 72 hours.
- Seeded prompt set: 500 in-distribution prompts representative of heavy-usage features (summarization, instruction-following, extraction).
- Robustness seed: 200 adversarial/noise prompts (typo/obfuscation, ambiguous instructions).
- Long-context stress: 100 prompts with >8k token context to exercise KV cache and attention kernels.
- Safety vectors: 250 safety-sensitive prompts focusing on policy and hallucination triggers.
- Quant-sensitivity partition: the above seed sets with token lengths and shot counts sampled to match expected CTA distributions.

Evaluation metrics and thresholds (promotion-oriented):
- Quality: semantic-similarity-based regression <= 5% drop relative to baseline on the seed test set (metric: pairwise BLEU/ROUGE + embedding cosine > 0.88 for key tasks).
- Safety: no new high-risk safety failures (severity >= 4) introduced; critical safety count must be zero.
- Latency: p50 delta <= +10ms, p95 delta <= +40ms relative to baseline.
- Memory: peak GPU memory <= baseline + 5% for Dedicated; for Private, must meet node capacity headroom >= 10%.
- KV cache behavior: cache hit-rate change <= 3 percentage points; cold-start token overhead <= 12%.
- Regression triage score: composite (quality, safety, perf) must be green for automated promotion. See scoring formula below.

Composite regression triage score (used to decide automated gating):
- Quality (50%), Safety (30%), Latency & Memory combined (20%).
- Score mapping: Green >= 90, Yellow 70-90 (manual review), Red < 70 (reject).

Shadow deployment configuration example (table as plain text):
- runtime_version: 2.14.0
- model_variant: my-model-v3-quant-fq4
- routing_mode: mirror (no user-facing responses)
- traffic_sample: 0.02  # 2% of production requests
- replay_window: 72h
- eval_window: 48h
- data_retention_for_debug: 30d
- telemetry_enabled: true (tokens, delta-logs, raw-outputs hashed)

Procedure (step-by-step):
1) Preparation (Day -3 to -1)
   - a) Create shadow deployment config in Redwood Console with owner, SLOs, and telemetry toggles.
   - b) Register evaluation cohort (IDs for seed prompt sets, adversarial cases, long-context suite).
   - c) Capture production baseline metrics snapshot (p50/p95 latencies, token cost per request, KV cache distribution).
   - d) Notify SRE and customer success of shadow start time and debug contact.
2) Launch & warm-up (Day 0)
   - a) Start shadow at 0.1% traffic-sample using mirror routing for 2 hours to validate no impact on production.
   - b) Validate telemetry ingestion (token-level breakdowns, kernel selection tags, memory traces).
   - c) Escalate and rollback if initial memory or latency anomalies exceed thresholds (see rollback criteria).
3) Full shadow evaluation (Day 0–2)
   - a) Ramp to target sampling rate (e.g., 2%).
   - b) Run scheduled seeded tests (nightly regression suite) and continuous adversarial stream.
   - c) Run quant-sensitivity comparisons: run paired inference for float vs quant variant on matched requests to compute per-request delta metrics.
4) Analysis (Day 2–3)
   - a) Produce evaluation report summarizing quality, safety, perf, and regression triage score.
   - b) If Yellow, schedule manual triage with ML owner, SRE, and Safety SME; for Red, block promotion and open a regression ticket.
5) Promotion decision (Day 3+)
   - a) If Green, proceed to canary traffic rollout as defined in the canary promotion playbook.
   - b) If manual remediation required, iterate on model or runtime config and re-run shadow.

Rollback criteria (immediate or automated):
- Any critical safety failure (severity >= 4) observed in the shadow outputs.
- Sustained p95 latency exceeding baseline + 100ms for >10 minutes.
- GPU memory OOM or >95% sustained memory utilization for >5 minutes.
- KV cache churn leading to cold-start amplification >25% over baseline.

Triage and debugging playbook (on Yellow/Red):
- Ownership: ML owner to lead quality triage; SRE to lead perf/memory; Safety SME to lead policy incidents.
- Minimum artifact set to open triage ticket: failing request IDs, model build hash, runtime kernel tags, quant config, and raw model output (hashed + redacted as needed).
- Standard steps: reproduce failure with isolated replay; narrow to minimal prompt; compare float vs quantized outputs; run profiler to capture kernel-level hot paths.

Privacy and telemetry controls:
- Shadow deployments must respect PII/data retention policies. Raw outputs used for triage must be hashed or redacted before storage.
- Data collected during shadow is governed by the customer-specific confidentiality flag; for Private installs, default to restricted unless customer explicitly permits debug artifact sharing.

Operational knobs and recommendations:
- Use continuous batching profiles tuned for the target pool to avoid spurious latency regressions when sampling traffic.
- Prefer paired inference (float vs candidate) for a statistically robust delta rather than absolute thresholds alone.
- When validating quantized builds, include both microbench kernels and end-to-end user-level prompts in the same shadow window.

Example commands and snippets:
- Create a shadow route (CLI pseudo):
```
redwood route create --env prod-dedicated-eu --model my-model:v3-quant --route-type mirror --sample-rate 0.02 --telemetry on --eval-cohort seedy-2026-01
```
- Run paired inference comparator (local):
```python
# comparator.py (simplified)
from redwood_eval import InferenceClient
client_float = InferenceClient(model='my-model:v3')
client_quant = InferenceClient(model='my-model:v3-quant')
for prompt in prompts:
    a = client_float.generate(prompt)
    b = client_quant.generate(prompt)
    print(prompt.id, embedding_similarity(a,b), latency_delta(a,b))
```

Acceptance report template (deliverable):
- Summary (one-paragraph)
- Baseline vs candidate comparison (table of metrics)
- Regression triage score and breakdown
- Safety findings (counts + examples)
- Perf findings (latency histogram, memory timeline)
- Recommendation: Promote / Remediate / Block (with owners and ETA)

Ownership and SLAs:
- ML owner: create shadow config, interpret quality signals, own remediation.
- SRE owner: validate runtime compatibility, address perf regressions, own rollback.
- Safety/Policy: review any flagged safety cases within 24 hours.
- SLA for shadow evaluations: evaluations should finish and a report be produced within 72 hours of shadow launch for standard promotions.

References and related artifacts:
- Eval harness promotion matrix (internal link)
- Model certification checklist (internal link)
- Canary promotion playbook (internal link)

Appendix: quick checklist (copyable)
- [ ] Register evaluation cohort
- [ ] Capture baseline telemetry
- [ ] Create shadow route with mirror routing
- [ ] Run warm-up and validate telemetry
- [ ] Ramp to target sampling and run seed/adversarial sets
- [ ] Run paired float-vs-quant comparisons
- [ ] Produce acceptance report
