Title: span-timeline-playbook-grooming-notes

span-timeline-playbook-grooming-notes

Purpose and scope:
This is a portable playbook-style doc for planning the span timeline (waterfall) surface in the Console trace viewer. Focus: practical interaction patterns for exploring long requests, span grouping, quick filters, and debug-friendly annotations. Intended audience: product, frontend, SRE, and UX who will ship the first iteration (MVP) for Q1 roadmap.

High-level goals (why):
- Help engineers quickly pinpoint latency hotspots in multi-model requests (KV cache misses, routing fallbacks, model switch latencies).
- Make it cheap to triage production incidents without switching to raw logs (link out when needed).
- Provide a compact summary view plus progressively revealed detail (progressive disclosure).

Constraints and assumptions:
- Must work for traces up to 10kms (long traces) and 200 spans without freezing the UI.
- First pass will support server-side timestamps + durations; no distributed tracing correlation yet (future).
- Prefers purely client-side rendering with virtualization for rows.

MVP surface (what to build):
1) Compact timeline (collapsed spans by default):
   - Row per span group (service.action) with count and aggregated duration range (p50/p95).
   - Tap/expand to animate open slot into full span rows beneath.
   - Visual cue for long-tail spans: thin red overlay on portion > threshold.

2) Span detail flyout:
   - Header: span name, service, duration, start offset, tags (key/value), request id.
   - Tabs: Metadata (headers/attrs), Logs (linked), Events (KV/cache hits), Raw JSON (copy).
   - Quick actions: "Copy timing", "Open in logs", "Create ticket" (prefill fields).

3) Filters & quick probes bar (persistent top strip):
   - Text search over span names + attributes (syntax: name:token, tag:key=value).
   - Prebuilt quick filters: long > 500ms, error spans, model-fallback, cache-miss.
   - Toggle: group-by-service / group-by-operation / show-only-errors.

4) Time-slice scrubber and zoom controls:
   - Mini-waterfall overview (Sparkline) with a brush to zoom time ranges.
   - Keyboard shortcuts: shift + drag to select, +/- to zoom, space to play animation.

Interaction notes and micro-flows:
- Expand flow: click on row -> row animates open -> fetch per-span details (lazy) -> arrow to first child span -> keyboard focus goes into expanded region.
- Inspect-range: user highlights a time window in the scrubber -> timeline reflows showing only spans intersecting window; counts of hidden spans shown as collapsed badge.
- Multi-select: shift+click selects multiple spans -> aggregate action bar appears with suggested next steps (trace compare, export, make ticket).

Wireframe description (ASCII sketch for devs):
[Header bar: trace id | duration | region | download]
[Quick probes bar: (search) | [long>500ms] [errors] [cache-miss] [group:service]]
[Mini-sparkline scrubber]\\n--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
| Row 1: auth-service.login (grouped) | #####-----   120ms p95    | [v]        |
| (expanded) child spans:           | [span bars with offsets and red warning]             |
| Row 2: routing (service)          | --###------- 40ms p95     | [v]        |
| Row 3: model-serving (group)      | -----####--- 420ms p95    | [!]        |
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[Footer: selected span details / copy buttons / open link to logs]

Accessibility and performance notes:
- All interactive elements must be keyboard focusable; aria labels for span durations e.g., 'span x duration 220ms start 1.3s'.
- Use row virtualization and canvas-based mini-waterfall rendering to reduce DOM counts.
- Defer heavy JSON formatting until user opens Raw JSON tab.

Open questions / discussion items (to resolve in grooming):
- How do we represent concurrent spans that overlap heavily? (Option A: stacked lanes per service, Option B: layered single lane with translucency). Decision needed by next sync.
- Should group-by default to service or operation? Metric: fewer clicks for common debug path.
- What threshold values for quick filters are product-configurable vs hard-coded?

Backlog & acceptance criteria (scoped for first 2 sprints):
- RW-2241: Timeline base rendering + virtualization
  - AC: Load traces with up to 200 spans, initial render < 300ms, maintaining 60fps scroll.
- RW-2242: Expand/collapse row groups with lazy span fetch
  - AC: Expanding a group fetches child spans and reveals them; keyboard focus lands on first child.
- RW-2243: Span detail flyout with tabs and logs link
  - AC: Flyout opens within 200ms, logs link is present and opens new tab to logs view with query prefilled.
- RW-2244: Quick probes & filters bar
  - AC: Text search supports name: and tag: syntax; presets shown and toggles update timeline live.

Implementation notes for engineers:
- API: propose trace GET /v1/traces/{id}?level=grouped|full&time_window=start,end. Grouped returns aggregation metadata for each group.
- Client: use react-virtualized for rows, canvas for sparkline. Avoid full JSON parse until flyout open.
- Metrics to capture: render_time_ms, expand_latency_ms, filter_apply_ms, avg_spans_loaded_per_trace.

UX validation plan:
- 3 quick guerrilla usability sessions with internal engineers (15 minutes each) to validate expand/collapse mental model.
- One incident-runbook test: have SRE resolve a seeded slow-model-fallback case using only Console trace viewer; record time to resolution.

Notes to self (brain dump):
- Consider a small 'annotation' feature where engineers can pin a comment to a span (private to org) — high value for knowledge transfer.
- Might want to show model version pins in the span bar for model-serving spans.
- If we support RL fallback, mark those spans with a distinct icon so they stand out in grouped view.

Next steps & owners:
- Design: Elena to produce high-fidelity mocks for stacked-vs-layered overlap options by 2025-11-20.
- Frontend: Raj to spike canvas-based sparkline and virtualization; report perf numbers by 2025-11-28.
- Backend: Samir to draft grouped trace API and example payload by 2025-12-02.
- Product: Maya to host grooming session w/ SRE on 2025-11-12 to decide default grouping and quick-filter thresholds.

Revision log:
- 2025-11-04 Maya created initial playbook.
- 2025-11-12 updated with SRE notes from grooming (meeting minutes linked in Confluence).
- 2026-02-20 added acceptance criteria and ticket IDs for sprint planning.

Unresolved: finalize overlapping span visualization; put on agenda for 2026-02-28 design sync.

Title: Trace Inspector: interactive spans timeline, correlation filters, and request breadcrumbs

Trace Inspector: interactive spans timeline, correlation filters, and request breadcrumbs

Design and prototype a Trace Inspector view in Redwood Console to enable engineers and SREs to drill into individual inference requests. The inspector surfaces an interactive span timeline, span waterfall, correlation IDs, request breadcrumbs, and powerful filters (model, region, host, response time, error codes). The goal is to make it fast to identify latency hotspots, correlate model fallback events, and trace requests across routing, batching, and cache layers.
Provide a compact, high-density timeline that shows spans inline with request metadata
Enable fast filtering by correlation ID, model variant, region, and SLO breach status
Support timeline zoom and span grouping for long-running requests and batched work
Expose useful request context (token counts, KV cache hits, chosen kernel, GPU host) without leaving the view
Integrate with existing Console traces and logs so users can pivot between a trace and its request-level details
Primary timeline is horizontal waterfall with collapsible span rows; spans color-coded by subsystem (routing, batcher, runtime, network)
Request header includes copyable correlation ID and a direct link to the raw span JSON and logs
Filters implemented as persistent chips above timeline; selected filters persist in URL for shareability
Details panel slides in from the right showing request payload meta, model info, cost estimate, and token deltas
Accessibility: timeline uses patterns compatible with screen readers (ARIA: role=list + labels) and keyboard-first zoom/navigation
Heavy timeline rendering for large traces could hurt Console performance; we propose incremental rendering and culling after X spans
Exposing too much raw telemetry may overwhelm non-engineer users — we provide a compact and an expanded details mode
Relying on backend-enriched spans requires backend instrumentation (timestamps, parent IDs, resource tags); until that lands some fields will show 'unavailable'
URL-shareable filters require stable filter keys from backend and careful encoding to avoid long query strings
Clickable correlation ID copies to clipboard and opens raw trace in new tab
Filters apply within 300ms for typical 50-span traces in stage environment
Timeline shows span start/end with millisecond precision and preserves parent/child relationships
Details panel surfaces model name, model variant, quantization profile, KV cache hit count, and estimated token cost
UX passes accessibility keyboard navigation checklist and has contrast ratios >= 4.5:1 for timeline colors

2025-02-14 - Eng sync (Rafael + Deepa): backend will emit span.resource and span.attributes for GPU host and kernel selection; ENG-2491 will add correlation headers to request logs
2025-02-15 - Design critique: reduce visual noise by collapsing zero-duration spans into grouped markers with a hover tooltip
2025-02-16 - Accessibility review (Noah): keyboard focus order needs to jump from timeline to details panel; ARIA labels added to span types
Finalize Figma with responsive variants for narrow Console panes (expected by 2025-02-20)
Coordinate with ENG-2491 to add minimal span fields to stage traces (target 2025-02-21)
Build a lightweight client-side renderer prototype to validate render performance with 1k span traces
Create acceptance test plan and example traces that simulate batcher contention and model fallback
2025-02-11 - Maya Chen: Initial concept completed. Focused on surfacing model and cache signals that matter for inference debugging.
2025-02-13 - Rafael Ortiz: Added notes on required backend tags; will open ENG tickets for missing telemetry.
2025-02-17 - Lina Park: Small UI tweak request — show 'SLO at risk' badge inline with spans that exceed configured latency thresholds.
2025-02-18 - Deepa Singh: Reviewed prototype. Approve to hand off to frontend; please include mock fixtures for span attributes (kernel, batch_id, kv_hit).

Title: Request Journey Explorer: timeline-first trace inspector and correlation drilldown

Request Journey Explorer: timeline-first trace inspector and correlation drilldown

Build a timeline-centric trace inspector inside Redwood Console that lets engineers inspect a single request’s journey end-to-end: spans, timeline, token-level events, correlation IDs, and lightweight cost attribution. This ticket captures the design prototype, review notes, trade-offs, and handoff artifacts for a tracing drilldown view optimized for LLM inference workloads.
As an SRE, I want to paste a correlation ID and jump to the full request timeline so I can debug latency spikes quickly.
As an ML engineer, I want to see per-span token counts and estimated cost so I can identify expensive model calls.
As a product engineer, I want to compare traces between rollout variants to see cost/latency regressions after a model switch.
As an on-call engineer, I want a compact summary row (p50/p95/total-cost) and a link to raw request JSON and logs for fast incident response.
Make trace data digestible with a timeline-first UI rather than a long flat span list.
Surface correlation IDs, request metadata, and model/route tags prominently.
Support quick filtering (route, model, region, customer id, trace id) and timeline zooming to inspect token-level events.
Keep the UI performant for traces with hundreds of spans via virtualization and lazy loading.
Provide actionable links: raw request JSON, linked logs/Grafana panel, GitHub PR (rollout) and ability to save a trace permalink.
Primary canvas: horizontal timeline with rows representing services/components (ingest, router, runtime, kernel, model). Spans drawn as bars with color by component and width = duration.
Left rail: summary card with trace id, route, model, total latency, token counts (input/added/output), estimated cost, and action buttons (Copy ID, Open logs, Open raw request, Save permalink).
Span panel: clicking a span expands a right-side detail pane showing span annotations, start/end times, parent/child links, host/pod, and a small flamechart for internal operations (batching, kv-cache hit/miss, quantization cost).
Correlation waterfall: collapsible view that groups spans by correlation_id prefix so related asynchronous work (background caching, fallback model calls) is visible inline.
Comparison mode: select two traces to overlay timelines or show synchronized timelines to compare latency and token distribution across rollout variants.
PM (Ava Morgan): prioritise copy-to-clipboard for correlation IDs and ensure per-trace permalink supports RBAC-aware access.
Engineering (Liam Chen): prefer server-side pagination for span lists and an API that can return span aggregates to avoid fetching entire traces by default.
Security (Priya Nambiar): verify that raw request JSON view redacts customer PII by default and respects data residency flags.
Design review: reduce visual noise by hiding low-duration spans under an aggregated marker; allow 'expand all' for deep debugging.
Tracing API needs endpoints: GET /traces/{id}?expand=timeline, GET /traces?correlation_id=..., and GET /traces/{id}/compare/{id2}.
Backend should compute per-span estimated cost (token_count * model_unit_cost) and supply a pre-aggregated cost-per-span metric to avoid client-side heavy compute.
Frontend must virtualize span rows and implement canvas/WebGL rendering for large traces to keep 60fps when zooming.
Privacy: raw payloads must be gated behind permission checks and redact keys flagged by KMS/audit config.
Search by correlation ID works from global console header and opens the trace inspector with the correct trace highlighted.
Timeline shows per-span duration, parent-child relationships, and span metadata (component, host, model tag).
Span detail pane shows token counts, estimated cost (USD), and links to raw request JSON and linked logs.
UI remains responsive with traces up to 500 spans (virtualization/lazy load verified in perf tests).
Permalink to trace preserves applied filters and respects RBAC (unauthorized users cannot open the raw request view).
Design handoff: prepare final Figma spec with component states, responsive behavior, and tokens (due 2025-03-05).
Engineering kickoff: sync with runtime and backend teams to finalize trace API contract (meeting 2025-03-07).
Security review: submit payload-redaction checklist to Security for approval (owner: Priya Nambiar).
Prototype user testing: schedule 3 sessions with SRE and ML Eng to validate filters and cost-attribution UX (target: Cycle 2025-W11).

Confluence PRD: https://company.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/CONSOLE/pages/Tracing+Request+Journey+PRD
Design Tokens & Components: https://company.design/system/console/traces
GitHub PR (initial sketches): https://github.com/redwood-inference/console/pull/1824
Grafana dashboard example: https://grafana.redwood.local/d/trace/console-traces?var-route=all

Title: Debug Traceboard — consolidated failed request explorer

Debug Traceboard — consolidated failed request explorer

Design a single, discoverable 'Debug Traceboard' in Redwood Console that surfaces failed requests, retries, error taxonomy, and request payload inspection in a lightweight, developer-friendly UI. This board should help engineers and SREs quickly triage production failures, understand retry behavior, and map errors to rollout/config changes or model variants. The goal is to reduce mean-time-to-diagnosis for transient and systemic errors while keeping data-access controls and PII redaction in mind.
A browseable Traceboard view accessible from Console -> Observability -> Errors
Ability to filter and group failed requests by time range, route, model, region, and release tag
Compact timeline view that shows initial failure and subsequent retries with expandable lanes
Payload inspector that shows request inputs and model responses with redaction toggle and 'safe sample' masking
Error taxonomy badges (e.g., network, model-runtime, decoding, rate-limit, auth) with count breakdowns
Quick actions: open incident ticket template, link to related logs, deep-link to Dedicated pool or Private deployment
Keyboard navigation for list and timeline expansions
Design handoff artifacts (Figma + specs) and a prioritized engineering tickets list
Surface Traceboard as a top-level page under Observability rather than a modal to allow persistent filters and deep-linking
Use a two-column layout: left for list & taxonomy filters, right for timeline + payload inspector, to keep inspection context visible
Represent retries as connected timeline nodes to make retry cascades visually traceable
Implement a read-only 'replay preview' for requests (no execution) that shows tokenized diffs and model variant used
Default payload view will redact detected PII; user can toggle 'show masked' if they have console data access
Prioritize performance: timeline should stream sample rows and lazy-load payloads to avoid blocking the console
Full request replay vs read-only preview: we chose preview to avoid accidental re-execution and security surface area
Side panel inspector vs persistent right column: persistent column increases surface area but keeps context when navigating failures
Detailed per-token diffs add developer value but increase render complexity; implemented as collapsed sections behind a toggle
PM (Rajiv): prefer a pill for release tags to correlate incidents to rollouts — add affordance to correlate by rollout ID
Eng (Maya): backend needs compact API that returns minimal payloads and a separate endpoint to fetch full request body; ensure lazy loading behavior
Security (Omar): require explicit consent + audit log for unredacting PII; surface role-based control in the inspector
Design (Nina): confirm color usage for error taxonomy meets contrast and is accessible to color-blind users
SRE (Tom): include a 'retry chain heatmap' export for offline analysis and incident reports
What degree of sampling is acceptable for high-volume routes before we start aggregating failures?
How will Dedicated / Private environments expose request payloads — will there be additional redaction rules?
Should the Traceboard be writable for on-console annotations (comments) vs linking to external incident systems?
Incorporate feedback and update hi-fi prototype (due 2025-02-24)
Coordinate with backend to define two endpoints: trace-summary and trace-detail (specs by 2025-02-28)
Run 3 unmoderated usability sessions with platform engineers and SREs (goal: 6 participants)
Accessibility audit and color-blindness pass
Create engineering tickets for: filters, timeline rendering, payload inspector, RBAC redaction toggles
This design intentionally scopes out active request replay in the first iteration to reduce risk.
We will track Mean Time To Diagnose (MTTD) and time-to-ticket-creation as primary KPIs for the next quarter.
Prototype includes keyboard shortcuts: 'j/k' to move rows, 'enter' to expand, 'r' to open retry heatmap
Confluence: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENG/pages/Traceboard+Design+Notes
GitHub PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/console/pull/4187
Design tokens: https://github.com/redwood-inference/design-system/tree/main/tokens/errors

Title: Deep-linkable Span Inspector and Compact Trace Lens

Deep-linkable Span Inspector and Compact Trace Lens

Problem: Operators frequently need to jump from high-level request dashboards into a focused trace view that is shareable and actionable. Current trace detail screens are heavyweight, not linkable at span-level, and are slow to scan for experiments (rollouts) or cost-impacting behaviors. Goal: design a compact "Compact Trace Lens" allowing fast identification of key spans, deep-linking to a specific span/correlation-id, and lightweight inline actions for troubleshooting and rollout diagnostics. This ticket covers the design prototype, interaction states, and handoff notes for engineering and PM review.
A clickable permalink exists for request-level and span-level deep links and preserves filter context (time range, environment, rollout variant)
Compact Trace Lens renders a condensed span list (max 15 rows) with sparkline latency and error badges and expands to full timeline on demand
Sticky timeline scrubber persists while scrolling spans and highlights active KV cache hits and SLO waterline
Inline quick-actions available on spans: Capture Snapshot, Open Logs, Mark as Suspect, Link to Rollout Variant
Prototype vetted by PM, Eng, and SRE; design sign-off recorded and engineering tickets created for front-end and backend work
Permalink resolves in < 2s for traces with up to 500 spans (backend requirement noted in dependencies)
Show 'correlation group' chips at the top to let users collapse all spans with the same correlation id across services
Use a condensed row layout with token-level heatmap on hover for heavy spans to save vertical space
Affinity to Rollouts: annotate spans generated by experimental variants and surface a 'variant delta' ribbon showing latency delta vs baseline
Expose filter bar with typed suggestions (service:, span:, correlation-id:, variant:) and support immediate-link copy
Performance tradeoff: initial render should stream first 50 spans and progressively hydrate remaining rows to avoid jank
Privacy: redact sensitive metadata by default; allow 'show sensitive fields' toggle requiring extra permission
Noah Patel (PM): prefer maintaining current deep-link param names for backwards compatibility; add rolloutVariant param
Samir Khan (Eng): backend must add trace-level indexing by correlation-id; suggested ENG-3024 to implement fast lookup
Priya Mehta (SRE): sticky scrubber ok, but ensure memory overhead for streaming is bounded; propose streaming + windowing approach
Mina Park (Design): request to explore a denser color palette for heatmap to aid color-blind users
Ship deep-linking using existing query params trace_id + span_id + context (time_range, env, variant)
Start with read-only quick-actions; implement actionable retries in a follow-up (security review required)
Compact Lens will be the default collapsed view in Console traces with a 'Expand to Full Trace' CTA
Create ENG tickets for backend index endpoints (ENG-3024) and streaming API changes (ENG-2987)
Design to provide high-fidelity assets and accessibility spec by 2026-03-18
PM to confirm rollout-variant telemetry schema with Product Analytics
SRE to profile memory overhead on a 10k-span trace sample and report findings
This design intentionally avoids cluttering the primary trace view; the Compact Lens is targeted at engineers performing rapid triage and platform owners verifying rollout effects. Front-end should support server-side pagination and client-side windowing. Follow security guidelines for permalink generation to avoid leaking tokens in URLs.

Title: Rollout Orchestrator: Signal Aggregation & Trace Bridge for Variant Health

Rollout Orchestrator: Signal Aggregation & Trace Bridge for Variant Health

Goal: Build a console-first Rollout Orchestrator feature set that aggregates signal streams (latency, error rate, token cost, semantic drift) across variants and ties them to traces and per-route telemetry. Deliver a single-pane Variant Health view with a Trace Bridge that can surface sampled traces linked to rollout deltas and allow operators to pivot between A/B, canary, and shadow traffic comparisons.

Background: Customers currently use separate dashboards and traces to investigate rollout regressions. This creates a slow feedback loop during canary and A/B experiments. The Orchestrator will combine time-aligned aggregated metrics, divergence summaries, and trace snippets so operators can make faster rollout decisions and optionally trigger auto-rollback.

Scope: Console UI components and backend telemetry aggregation pipeline only. Not in scope: changes to serving runtime scheduling or new model variants. Scope details:
- Aggregation: rollup token-level cost, p95/p50 latency, top-3 error fingerprints, and semantic divergence score per-variant and per-route.
- Trace Bridge: follow a request from aggregate metric spike to N sampled traces (client request -> route -> model variant) and show KV-cache hit/miss annotations and batch size.
- Diff Views: side-by-side delta visualization for any two variants or time windows; supports A/B splits and shadow vs live.
- Auto-rollback integration: pluggable policy rules (thresholds, evaluation windows, cooldown). When enabled, Orchestrator emits a decision event to the deployment service.

Acceptance criteria:
1) Console shows Variant Health for a selected route within 5s of selection and renders diff overlays for two variants.
2) Trace Bridge returns 3 sample traces correlated with the metric spike and annotates per-step metadata.
3) Aggregated metrics align with existing per-route dashboards within a 3% margin on p95 and error rate.
4) Auto-rollback rules can be created in the UI and successfully fire a dry-run decision against staging deployment without mutating production.

Key trade-offs and decisions we debated:
- Sampling vs full tracing: initial launch will use adaptive sampling to bound storage and latency; plan to tune sampling weight for rollout traffic.
- Aggregation window: 1m buckets provide fast feedback but increase noise; default to 1m with 5m smoothing option.
- Diff visualization: lightweight statistical summary vs full distribution plotting; we will ship summary + small sparkline and add full distributions in follow-ups.

Telemetry and metrics to track post-launch:
- Time-to-insight: median time from alert to a trace being surfaced.
- Precision of rollback triggers: percent of dry-run rollbacks that would have prevented a degraded SLO.
- Console latency: 95th percentile time to render Variant Health UI.

Notes for engineering: backend requires a rolling-join between metric aggregates and sampled trace index keyed by route+variant+time. Keep join window configurable. Provide an API for the console to request aligned metrics and traces.

1) Variant Health UI renders for selected route with two-variant diff in <5s; 2) Trace Bridge returns 3 representative traces annotated with KV/cache/batch info; 3) Aggregated metrics match per-route dashboards within 3%; 4) Auto-rollback dry-run can be executed from UI without changing production deployments.
2026-02-22 - Priya K.: Kickoff meeting with Eng and Design. Agreed to MVP scope: aggregation, trace bridge, simple diffs, auto-rollback dry-run only.
2026-02-26 - Ethan M.: Spike complete. Prototype shows adaptive sampling plus a small index for sampled traces. Backend needs a high-cardinality join strategy; proposing pre-aggregated keys at route+variant+bucket.
2026-03-02 - Lina Torres (Design): Initial mockups uploaded to Figma. Emphasis on quick signal triage: heatbar for error spikes, and a stacked cost/latency view.
2026-03-05 - Security review request filed (ENG-9102). Security flagged data retention of traces; recommend 30d retention for rollout traces by default and 90d for enterprise plan.
2026-03-08 - Infra note from Marcus O.: We should cap trace fetch to 250KB payloads for console requests to keep UI fast. Backend will return a short summary if traces exceed budget with a link to raw trace archive.
2026-03-10 - Priya K.: Scope locked for Cycle 2026-W09. Moving to implementation. Design and backend tasks split into tickets and assigned to ENG-8841, ENG-8842, ENG-8849.

Title: Trace Needle: rapid search & correlation flow for request traces

Trace Needle: rapid search & correlation flow for request traces

Design a focused, search-first trace exploration flow (nicknamed 'Trace Needle') that helps engineers find the single request or span of interest inside long traces and quickly see correlated metadata (logs, customer id, headers, downstream spans). This is intended as a complementary, fast-path alternative to the full trace waterfall UI for investigation workflows.
Current console trace views are waterfall-first and optimized for visual correlation and timeline analysis. Support tickets and user interviews show people frequently need a quick way to 'needle' into a trace with a correlation id, error signature, or short regex and jump to the exact moments, with supporting context (logs, sampling info, routing policy). We must preserve existing deep-dive capabilities while offering a faster investigative entrypoint.
Engineers spend too long scanning long waterfalls to locate the span(s) that match a correlation ID, error pattern, or API path; we need a fast, memory-efficient search + focused timeline view that surfaces relevant spans and surrounding context.
- Reduce time-to-first-insight for trace investigations by 50% for median cases.
- Surface the correlation ID and propagated headers prominently.
- Allow fast pivoting from search result to full waterfall or request replay.
- Keep the feature performant on traces >500 spans and in browser-limited environments.
Flow summary:
1) Top-level Query Bar: free-text + structured tokens (correlation_id:, service:, status:, latency>, path:, regex:). Autosuggest based on recent queries.
2) Result Needle List: compact list of matching spans across the trace with inline key metadata (timestamp, duration, service, status code, snippet of message). Each row shows a small sparkline of local timeline.
3) Focused Timeline Pane: selecting a needle opens a centered timeline that zooms to the span with ± configurable context (default 500ms before/after). Keyframes (child spans crossing service boundaries) are highlighted.
4) Sidecar: pinned context panel with raw headers, log lines with links to log viewer, request payload, and links to relevant APM traces or deployment metadata.
5) Quick Actions: open full waterfall (preserves zoom), create incident note with snapshot, deep-link share, and open in Request Replay studio.
6) Filters/Facets bar: one-click chips (error, slow, sampled, un-sampled, model-serving) and time bucketing to refine results.
7) Accessibility: keyboard-first operations (press / to focus search, j/k to navigate results, enter to open sidecar).
Decisions so far:
- Use compact row list rather than full waterfall for initial results to improve scan-speed and memory usage.
- Color palette reuses existing service color tokens; error statuses get a saturated accent to surface quickly.
- Timeline uses continuous scale with an overlay to show selected span context; we will lazy-render waveform/sparklines to avoid jank on large traces.

Title: trace-compare-facet-workflows-brainstorm

trace-compare-facet-workflows-brainstorm

Purpose and context:
- Quick exploratory doc capturing different interaction models for comparing traces, expressing trace filters as a small facet-driven language, and lightweight wireframe sketches for the console. Not a final spec; meant for grooming with SRE and UI engineering.

Background/problem:
- Users frequently need to understand differences between two or more requests: why one had a 120ms tail latency vs another 40ms, or why tokens spiked for a particular route. Current trace viewer shows a single waterfall; comparing across traces requires mental mapping and repeated toggling.
- Goal: make 'compare' a first-class operation with minimal context switch, preserve span alignment, and enable ad-hoc filtering/aggregation via a compact facet language.

High-level success criteria:
- Reduce time-to-insight for trace comparison by 40% (measured in user task tests).
- Allow engineers to create and persist filter facets for common debugging queries.
- Keep UI performant when showing 2-4 traces side-by-side or an aggregated timeline.

User stories / examples:
1) As an SRE I want to pin two traces (A and B) and see aligned span timelines so I can spot which stage added the extra latency.
2) As a backend engineer I want to apply a facet filter "db.duration>50ms" and have matching spans highlighted across selected traces.
3) As a platform engineer I want to open a comparison between a sample of 10 traces and a baseline average to detect regressions in span counts.
4) As a PM I want to save a compare-view as a named investigation and attach notes for later review.

Interaction model options (sketches + tradeoffs):
A) Side-by-side synchronized waterfalls (primary candidate)
  - Layout: vertical split, N columns (default 2), each column shows standard waterfall with spans, metadata header, and ability to expand/collapse spans.
  - Synchronization: vertical alignment by trace timeline using percent or absolute timestamps. Hover on span in any column highlights matching spans (by operation name) in other columns and draws a light connector line.
  - Pros: Familiar, direct comparison, easy to inspect span internals.
  - Cons: Screen real estate heavy; may be cramped for deep traces.

B) Unified stacked timeline with per-trace lanes
  - Layout: single waterfall where each trace is a lane; lanes are stacked vertically with a shared time axis.
  - Sync: spans align to the global time axis. Option to normalize start times to zero for relative comparison.
  - Pros: Easier to scan timing differences across many traces, compact.
  - Cons: Harder to see nested spans relationships when lane widths are small.

C) Diff overlay mode (dense)
  - Layout: baseline trace drawn in light gray; compared trace overlays in color, with delta markers and annotations for spans that diverge (duration delta>threshold).
  - Pros: Highlights deltas directly.
  - Cons: Visual clutter for many differences; accessibility concerns.

Quick ASCII wireframe (Side-by-side candidate):
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| Header: trace compare — [Traces: 2] [Save view] [Export CSV] |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| Left pane (controls)  | Column A (Trace A) | Column B (Trace B) |
| - Search / facets      | Header: trace id, route | Header: trace id, route |
| - Saved queries        | Waterfall (spans)      | Waterfall (spans)      |
| - Time alignment toggle| Span inspector panel (collapsible) for selected span  |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
Notes on interactions:
- Pinning: right-click on any trace in the main listing -> Pin to compare. Allow multi-select checkboxes and `Compare` button.
- Drag-to-reorder columns.
- Hover connectors: small bezier lines drawn between matched operations; there should be a toggle to disable connectors for performance.
- Keyboard flow: 'c' to open compare modal, arrow keys to move focus between lanes, 'p' to pin a span.

Facet language design (compact, human-readable):
- Intention: keep filters accessible to non-SREs while expressive enough for typical queries. Use a small DSL with field comparisons and logical ops.
- Examples: 
  - route = "/v1/generate" and db.duration > 50ms
  - span.op contains "kv.get"
  - status != OK
  - token_count >= 1024
- UI: provide a chips-based input where each facet can be created via autocomplete (field operator value), and a text-mode toggle shows the equivalent DSL string. Saved facets are reusable.

Highlighting and matching heuristics:
- Primary matching key: span.operation (op name).
- Secondary heuristics: span.tags.service, span.tags.db.statement fingerprint, and approximate duration bucket (fast/normal/slow).
- Allow manual mapping: user may mark span X in trace A as 'equivalent to' span Y in trace B to force connectors if automatic matching fails. Record mapping as a one-off annotation for the compare session.

Performance considerations:
- Lazy-render spans outside viewport; virtualization per column.
- Limit default compare to 2 traces; allow up to 4 with a warning and automatic summarization.
- Provide aggregated mode: compute per-operation mean/std and show small sparkline instead of full waterfall when many traces selected.

Backlog grooming (tasks, rough estimates, owners):
- UX: Finalize wireframes for side-by-side and stacked timeline (3d) — Rina (3d)
- Infra: API endpoints for bulk trace fetch + pre-aligned timeline payload (5d) — Jasper (5d)
- Backend: facet query engine extension (support range queries and duration units) — Tom (4d)
- Frontend: compare modal, column layout, connectors (8d) — EngConsoleTeam (8d)
- QA: Perf tests, accessibility checks (3d) — QA Team (3d)
- Docs: short how-to + save-view UX doc (1d) — Product Docs (1d)

Open questions / discussion items:
- Matching strategy: should we prefer span.operation equality or hash of (operation, service, parent.op)? Tradeoffs: strict matches miss renamed operations; fuzzy matches risk false positives.
- Saved compare views: should they capture raw trace ids or query that regenerates traces? Storing queries is more resilient.
- Export format: CSV with per-span diffs vs a JSON bundle.
- Access controls for compare: should compare sessions respect the same access controls as individual traces? (Probably yes)

Title: Decentralized tail-tracing and heatmap views for route/model/region

Decentralized tail-tracing and heatmap views for route/model/region

Problem: Our current latency dashboards provide aggregate quantiles but lack a lightweight, decentralized way to inspect tail events in context. Engineers need to quickly pivot from a p99 spike to example request traces, token/sec patterns, and sequence-length-conditioned heatmaps per route/model/region without overloading telemetry storage.

Goal: Add a distributed tail-tracing pipeline and per-route/model/region heatmap panels that surface representative tail requests, token/sec rhythm, and p95/p99 surfaces. The system should: (1) sample and store compact tail traces and key metrics at the edge, (2) emit heatmap rollups (sequence length vs. tokens/sec vs. latency) to the telemetry stream, and (3) power alerting/regression detectors that combine rolling-basis p95/p99 drift scoring with example trace links for root-cause triage.

Why this matters: On-call and SRE operate by bouncing between dashboards and PRs; having contextual, lightweight trace artifacts tied to heatmap clusters significantly reduces mean-time-to-detect and mean-time-to-fix for model-serving regressions introduced by kernel changes, batching policy changes, or quantization flips.

Scope:
- Instrumentation: add edge-side compact tail trace emitter, with configurable sampling rate and sequence-length bucketing.
- Aggregation: heatmap rollups emitted as pre-aggregated tiles (sequenceLenBucket, tokensPerSecBucket, latencyQuantileBucket) to the quantile telemetry topic.
- Storage: short-lived example trace store (14 days) with index by route/model/region and trace fingerprint.
- UI: Console panels: 1) heatmap explorer with brush-selection to list example traces, 2) tail-trace viewer (compact token-level timeline + KV cache hit markers + batching window boundaries), 3) regression timeline combining p95/p99 drift score and sample traces.
- Regression detection: implement drift detector using EWMA of p95/p99 per-slice + outlier scoring; when a slice's drift score crosses threshold, file a regression watcher and attach top-3 tail traces.
Edge emitter can be configured per-region and per-route with sampling_rate and sequence_len_buckets
Heatmap rollups appear in telemetry topic with keys: route, model_version, region, seq_bucket, tps_bucket, latency_quantile
Console shows interactive heatmap; brushing results in list of 10 representative tail traces with links to the trace viewer
Trace viewer displays token-level timeline, batching windows, and KV cache hit/miss markers for sampled traces
Automated drift detector raises regression watcher PR when p95/p99 drift score & sample size thresholds are met
End-to-end benchmark: synthetic harness can reproduce a seeded p99 regression and the system surfaces it with <15 minutes latency
Edge emitter: lightweight protobuf payload (~1.2KB avg) with compressed token offsets and event timestamps. Use existing edge sidecar pipeline; add config flag emit_tail_traces=true
Sampling strategy: stratified by route*model*sequence_len_bucket to avoid small-slice starvation; default sampling_rate=0.002 for high-volume routes, 0.02 for low-volume routes
Heatmap bucketing: sequence_len: 0-128/129-512/513-2048/2049+, tokens/sec buckets exponential (0-20,20-50,50-200,200+), latency quantiles stored as p50/p90/p95/p99 per tile
Rollup emission: tile size 5m -> aggregator emits to quantile-tiles topic. Use existing telemetry producer lib and ensure backpressure safeguards (circuit breaker per-producer)

Telemetry cost considerations: shrink trace payloads and limit default sampling to control storage cost; provide admin toggles for raising sample rates for debug windows

Title: Operator-friendly trace labeling and dashboard storyboard

Operator-friendly trace labeling and dashboard storyboard

Purpose:
This is a working doc to propose a compact, operator-friendly trace labeling schema and an associated dashboard storyboard focused on fast tail-latency and output-quality investigations. Goal is to reduce cognitive load for oncall operators (SE/SSMs) while preserving the signal needed by engineers.

Context / Why this feels necessary:
- Observability signal is huge and noisy for LLM inference (multi-hop calls, KV cache, routing, model variants).
- Oncall folks want a small set of actionable labels and a single-screen triage flow.
- Existing trace payloads are rich but inconsistent across services; that makes manual triage slow.

Design principles (constraints):
- Keep trace labels small (<= 10 operator-visible tags) and stable across rollouts.
- Labels should be generated at request entry point (edge/router) and enriched downstream, but never required to reconstruct a trace.
- Dashboard should support 3-minute triage: identification, grouping, and first-fix or rollback decision.
- Avoid heavy-cardinality tags (no freeform feature flags on primary ops path).

Proposed operator-visible trace label set (short names, semantics):
- request_source: {api | console | internal-batch}  -- where the request originated
- model_variant: {gptx-small | gptx-medium-q8 | redwood-rlhf-1}  -- canonical model id used for serving (string-limited)
- routing_path: {primary | fallback | cached}  -- high-level routing decision, prefer small set
- kv_cache: {warm | cold | miss}  -- indicates prefix/KV cache status at inference start
- latency_bucket: {p0: <50ms | p1: 50-150ms | p2: 150-500ms | p3: >500ms}  -- precomputed ordinal for dashboards
- token_count: integer-as-string (e.g. "312")  -- prompt+context tokens; kept as low-cardinality buckets where useful
- ops_stage: {ingress | compile | kv-lookup | infer | postproc}  -- primary stage where span latency concentrated
- user_intent: {chat | qa | summarize | embed}  -- best-effort hint from SDK/edge
- cost_estimate_cents: integer-as-string (small values ok) -- provided for spike-attribution heuristics
- operator_flag: {true | false}  -- for manual annotation (see runbook)

Labeling rules & heuristics:
- request_source and user_intent should be set by the SDK/edge using a small enum. If missing, default to "api" and "chat".
- latency_bucket is computed at response time from total request latency. Use p2/p3 thresholds configurable by region.
- token_count should be binned into small buckets on ingest (0-64, 65-256, 257-1024, 1025+).
- model_variant should be normalized via the model-catalog mapping service to avoid sticky vendor names.
- Avoid attaching experimental feature flags to primary trace tags; instead add them to an orthogonal debug context that is sampled at low rate.

Dashboard storyboard (single-screen operator flow):
Top strip (context):
- small breadcrumbs: region, cluster, retention window selector (15m/1h/24h)
- quick-filters: severity (p2/p3), request_source, model_variant

Main left: prioritized incident table (compact rows):
- key cols: time, latency_bucket, model_variant, kv_cache, request_source, token_bucket, sample_trace_link
- row actions: open trace, mark operator_flag, create Jira, escalate to eng
- table should surface an inline spark of per-row timeline (compact sparkline for last 60s latency)

Main center: focused trace/summary panel:
- high-level summary: total latency, top span and duration, kv cache status, routing_path, cost_estimate
- span waterfall simplified: show only ops_stage spans with percent of total (ingress, compile, kv-lookup, infer, postproc). Click-to-expand for full spans.
- automated hypothesis suggestions (see heuristics below) — small bullet list like "kv cold-start likely" or "model fallback used".

Right rail: quick investigation tools:
- Top correlated signals list (token_count high, model_variant = fallback, recent config rollout id)
- Small histogram: latency_bucket distribution for last 30 minutes with model_variant split
- Synthetic probe toggle: run single probe against model_variant from same region (rate-limited)

Footer: operator actions checklist (one-click macros):
- Re-run with debug headers (links to prefilled curl snippet)
- Mark as known-issue / create retrospective ticket template
- Trigger model-variant rollback (developer permission required)

Automated hypothesis heuristics (to generate the 1-3 bullets in trace summary):
- if routing_path == fallback AND kv_cache == miss => "fallback + cold cache: consider routing/eviction"
- if ops_stage == compile AND compile_time > 200ms => "JIT/compile regression: check build tag"
- if model_variant changed in last 10m for many requests => "recent rollout spike: consider rollback"
- if token_count bucket = 1025+ AND latency_bucket = p3 => "long prompt suspected"

Runbook: tail-latency quick triage (3-min flow):
1) Open dashboard, apply p3 filter, group by model_variant.
2) Pick top row; read summary. If hypothesis suggests cache or fallback, go to step 3; else if compile time flagged, notify infra-compile-oncall.
3) Click "re-run with debug headers"; compare latency with synthetic probe. If probe is fast, suspect client-side or request shape.
4) If multiple traces show same config rollout id, escalate and open Jira with template.
5) If single-tenant or high-cost spike, apply temporary rate cap on tenant via admin console.

Quick investigation snippets (for operators):
- curl for sample re-run (pre-filled with debug headers):
  curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -H "x-rw-debug: replay" -d '{"input":"<prompt>","max_tokens":32}'
- SQL (telemetry) to find recent p3 events for a model_variant:
  SELECT timestamp, latency_ms, token_bucket, kv_cache, config_rollout FROM telemetry.requests WHERE model_variant = 'redwood-rlhf-1' AND latency_bucket = 'p3' AND timestamp > now() - interval '30 minutes' ORDER BY latency_ms DESC LIMIT 250;

Open questions / TODOs:
- Do we standardize the token_count bins globally or per-model? (tradeoff: accuracy vs cardinality)
- Is cost_estimate something we can compute in the edge reliably? small prelim work needed with pricing service.
- Explore a "compact debug context" that can carry experimental flags but be sampled at 0.1% to avoid cardinality explosion.

Implementation notes (engineering):
- Add label enrichment at ingress service (edge/router). Use a lightweight protobuf for the operator-visible labels to avoid JSON bloat.
- Store operator-visible labels as top-level attributes in trace ingestion path; full debug context goes to a separate low-QPS archive.
- Dashboard widgets should use precomputed latency_bucket to keep queries cheap.

Appendix: example traces (operator-view flattened):
- Example A: {time: "2026-03-10T09:12:05Z", request_source: "api", model_variant: "gptx-medium-q8", routing_path: "primary", kv_cache: "warm", latency_bucket: "p1", token_count: "257-1024", ops_stage: "infer"} => likely normal; check token size.
- Example B: {time: "2026-03-10T09:14:11Z", request_source: "console", model_variant: "redwood-rlhf-1", routing_path: "fallback", kv_cache: "miss", latency_bucket: "p3", token_count: "65-256", ops_stage: "kv-lookup"} => probable eviction/fallback event.

Notes to self / meeting agenda for next sync:
- demo of one-screen flow (15m)
- decide token binning (20m)
- prototype trace enrichment at ingress in staging (owner: Liam)

Slack refs: #obs-ops, #infra-tracing

Title: Customer disputes status page accuracy during us-east degradation (status showed Operational while streaming requests failed)

Customer disputes status page accuracy during us-east degradation (status showed Operational while streaming requests failed)

Customer (Lattice Financial) reports that during the 2025-11-07 us-east degradation they experienced elevated errors and streaming disconnects, but our public status page showed "Operational" for the relevant timeframe. Customer is requesting (a) confirmation that Redwood recognizes the outage and (b) clarification on why the status page did not reflect the impact.

Issue summary:
- Customer observed: intermittent 5xx/stream resets on streaming chat completions in us-east; elevated end-user error rates.
- Redwood status page observed by customer: "All Systems Operational" (no component marked degraded/outage until after their peak impact window).
- Customer concern: status page is too coarse (global/hosted API only) and/or incorrectly classified impact (streaming vs non-streaming, per-region impact not reflected).

Impact (customer-reported):
- Duration: ~20–30 minutes (approx 16:05–16:35 UTC per customer); residual retries for another ~10 minutes.
- Symptoms: SSE stream dropped mid-response; some requests returned 502/504; retries succeeded.
- Affected endpoints: /v1/chat/completions (stream=true).

What we need to do:
1) Validate the timeframe and whether our internal incident timeline matches customer evidence.
2) Provide a customer-facing explanation for the status page mismatch without disclosing sensitive capacity/customer-specific details.
3) Capture action items feeding into the status page transparency upgrades project (component taxonomy + signal mapping + comms process).

Customer-provided artifacts (summarized):
- Request IDs: LF-7b2c1e, LF-7b2c33, LF-7b2c8a (sample)
- Error codes: 502/504; stream disconnect without final event.
- Region: us-east only (customer also has low-volume eu-west traffic not impacted).

Internal notes:
- Internal incident opened: INC-2025-1107-USE1-STREAMING (SRE).
- Public status page components at time were too coarse (Hosted API global), and our automated classifier did not mark the correct component/region promptly.
- Known gap tracked by SRE: inability to represent "Streaming (us-east)" separately from "Hosted API"; led to delayed and ambiguous external comms.

Requested outcome for closure:
- Provide written acknowledgement + corrected timeline to customer.
- Share our planned improvements: new component granularity (product surface + region), standard comms templates, and faster time-to-first-update goals.
- Confirm whether any post-incident summary will be published and when.

Title: P1 Incident Postmortem: Streaming responses intermittently hang

P1 Incident Postmortem: Streaming responses intermittently hang

## Summary
On 2026-02-03, some customers reported that streaming chat completions would start normally and then stop producing tokens. Requests remained open until client-side timeouts. The incident impacted hosted API streaming routes for ~27 minutes.

## Severity
P1

## Customer impact
- ~3.1% of streaming requests in us-east experienced a stall > 30s.
- Non-streaming requests were not affected.

## Timeline (UTC)
- 18:06: Incident starts (increased reports, elevated open connections).
- 18:11: On-call acknowledges; partial mitigation by lowering max concurrent streams per pod.
- 18:20: Hotfix: disable experimental backpressure setting in the stream proxy.
- 18:33: Metrics return to baseline.

## Root cause
A recent runtime upgrade changed the stream chunk flush behavior, which interacted badly with the gateway's backpressure configuration. Under specific token burst patterns, the stream proxy would stop forwarding chunks while keeping the connection open.

## Detection
Detected via customer reports and a delayed spike in "open_streams". No direct alert on "stalled_stream_ratio" existed.

## Follow-up action items (count these)
1) Add a runtime-side watchdog that forces a stream flush when no tokens are emitted for 2s. Owning team: Eng Serving Runtime.
2) Fix stream proxy backpressure handling to never block flush on the response writer. Owning team: Eng Serving Runtime.
3) Add a gateway default for max buffered bytes per stream and document it in the gateway config reference. Owning team: Eng Platform.
4) Create an alert on stalled stream ratio (stalled > 10s) per region and per model. Owning team: Eng SRE.

## References
- Related dashboard: Console > Streaming health > us-east
- Change that introduced regression: runtime release 2026.02.01

Title: Midday throughput lull in dedicated pool during short-stream bursts causing autoscaler lag and per-tenant GPU scarcity

Midday throughput lull in dedicated pool during short-stream bursts causing autoscaler lag and per-tenant GPU scarcity

Issue summary:
Customer NovusChat reports repeated mid-day throughput lulls in their Dedicated pool (prod-us-west) that coincide with a high volume of short-lived streaming requests. The symptom is a sudden P99 and P95 throughput drop for routes pinned to dedicated capacity, lasting 3–8 minutes before partial recovery.

Impact:
- Intermittent user-facing latency increases for NovusChat users (p99 latency up 4x).
- Background request queueing observed; some requests hit client-side timeouts.
- Business impact: degraded chat responsiveness during peak local hours.

Environment:
- Dedicated cluster: prod-us-west (reserved capacity for NovusChat).
- Customer tier: Dedicated/enterprise.
- Models: redwood/open-compat-13b and openlm/turbo-8k.
- Autoscaler config: min_replicas=4, max_replicas=24, scale_window=120s, short_stream_heuristic_enabled=true.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Send 300-600 concurrent short streaming sessions (1–3s per stream, frequent restarts) distributed across 20 tenants on the same dedicated pool.
2) Observe scheduler allocations and autoscaler decisions via the Console.
3) See throughput collapse on pinned routes and elevated request queueing.

Observed metrics & artifacts:
- GPU allocation saturation spikes on a subset of hosts (nvlink contention + high PCIe IO).
- Autoscaler shows delayed pod spin-up: mean time-to-ready increased from 35s -> 90s during events.
- KV cache eviction rate increases sharply; cache miss ratio climbs from 2% -> 18% within event window.
- Per-tenant slot utilization shows uneven hot-spotting: a small number of tenants consume many small slots, causing slot fragmentation.
- Monitoring screenshots and Prometheus query outputs attached in PR above.

Logs (selected):
- scheduler: "failed to place due to slot_fragmentation threshold exceeded"
- autoscaler: "scale_up blocked by placement_safety_check until rebalancer finishes"

Title: Regional egress flap caused routing fallback to remote region resulting in streaming hangs and elevated p95 latencies

Regional egress flap caused routing fallback to remote region resulting in streaming hangs and elevated p95 latencies

Issue summary:
A subset of NexaChat production traffic originating in us-west started experiencing increased p50/p95 latencies and frequent streaming WebSocket stalls around 2026-03-10 02:10 UTC. Customers reported generation streams freezing for 5-30s and occasional final response timeouts.

Impact:
- NexaChat customers (10+ apps) observed degraded streaming UX and token timeouts.
- Elevated token cost due to retrying behaviors.
- Triage flagged as P1 / Sev1 because dedicated capacity customer had SLA expectations.

Environment:
- Redwood prod (hosted) serving cluster: rw-infer-us-west-a (primary), rw-infer-eu-west-b (fallback)
- Affected regions: us-west (primary), failover to eu-west for some requests
- Affected models: rw-bert-13b, rw-chat-3b (customer pinned to latest stable)

Steps to reproduce / Observed behavior:
1) Start a streaming chat session from a NexaChat instance in us-west region.
2) Observe initial tokens stream correctly then stall after ~8-12s on ~1 in 6 requests.
3) Server-side logs show long tail on final chunk and occasional 504/502 from edge proxy.

Logs / metrics snippets (sanitized):
- edge-proxy[us-west] 2026-03-10T02:12:14Z: upstream_error=502, conn_id=42a1f
- serving-runtime: token_delay_ms p95 rose from 120ms -> 1.8s between 02:08-02:18 UTC
- nat-gateway-us-west-4: CPU 95pct, conntrack near max (7.9M/8M) around 02:09 UTC
- control-plane routing: observed traffic shift 14% -> eu-west for customer prefix at 02:10 UTC

Preliminary investigation notes:
- Correlation between NAT gateway saturation (conntrack exhaustion) and a subset of requests being routed to eu-west fallback cluster. The fallback increased RTT and exposed streaming timeouts.
- BGP/peering telemetry from provider shows a short withdrawal from primary egress peer for a /24 used by our us-west egress IPs at 02:08-02:11 UTC. Upstream provider logs show flapping.
- Edge proxy retries sometimes re-open connections to eu-west resulting in higher latency and TLS renegotiation overhead; streaming backpressure leads to client perceived stalls.

Workaround applied:
- Temporarily applied a per-customer routing override to pin NexaChat traffic to remaining healthy us-west egress IPs while we scale NAT and work with provider. This reduced stalls for the customer.

Next steps / action items:
- SRE: Increase conntrack table size and provision additional NAT capacity in us-west (in-progress).
- Network: Open escalation with upstream transit provider for BGP flap root cause and request monitored mitigation.
- Runtime: Add health gating on fallback routing so streaming sessions are less likely to be migrated mid-session.
- CS: Notify NexaChat of mitigation and provide timeline for permanent fix.

Related incident: INC-20260310-71

Title: MerchantEdge: session parity loss causing long-tail 5xxs and streaming fallback loop — post-incident follow-up

MerchantEdge: session parity loss causing long-tail 5xxs and streaming fallback loop — post-incident follow-up

Issue summary: Between 2026-03-10 03:10–03:45 UTC, MerchantEdge experienced elevated 5xx rates and repeated streaming disconnects. Customers reported truncated responses and repeated retry-triggered fallback requests that amplified load. The initial symptom was a rising tail latency on streaming sessions, then a cascade of 502/504 and a client-observed fallback loop.
2026-03-10 03:08 UTC: MerchantEdge support contact via #support-merchantedge.
2026-03-10 03:12 UTC: SRE triage declared incident and began traffic routing to secondary region.
2026-03-10 03:20 UTC: Observed increased error rate on streaming-proxy and smart-routing logs indicating session-state mismatch.
2026-03-10 03:27 UTC: Canary rollback of kernel-selection PR and temporary disablement of enhanced KV-cache routing applied for affected hosts.
2026-03-10 03:36 UTC: Error rate returned to baseline; streaming sessions stabilized.
2026-03-10 04:00 UTC: Declared major incident mitigated.
2026-03-12 10:00 UTC: Post-incident review and follow-up actions documented.
1) Create a long-running streaming session with stateful tool-calls and a sequence of >512 token prefixes.
2) Route requests through smart-routing policy 'latency-prefer' with prefix-KV caching enabled.
3) Trigger concurrent reconnections from the client (simulated network jitter).
4) Observe eventual 502s from streaming-proxy when session token IDs misalign and fallback routing issues cause duplicate inflight requests.
Excerpt from streaming-proxy logs (prod-us-east):
[2026-03-10T03:18:11Z] WARN session-mismatch session_id=ab12... expected_seq=112 current_seq=95
[2026-03-10T03:18:12Z] ERROR router fallback-loop request_id=ff23... target=quantized-host-07 502 Bad Gateway
[2026-03-10T03:18:13Z] ERROR serving-runtime kvcache-miss inconsistent-kv-length model=redwood-instruct-v1.2
Related dashboard: https://dashboards.redwood.internal/metrics/INC-91234-streaming-errors
Hypotheses tested: 1) Kernel-selection PR introduced a perf path that changed sequence-number assignment for quantized kernels under certain batch sizes. 2) Smart-routing's prefix-aware KV-cache returned an out-of-sync KV snapshot when sessions reattached to a different host. Evidence: repeated 'session-mismatch' WARNs and 'inconsistent-kv-length' errors in serving-runtime logs. Confirmed by correlating request IDs across proxy and runtime logs and replaying with client jitter in staging. Linked instrumentation traces: https://traces.redwood.internal/trace/INC-91234. Root cause narrowed to race between session-resume handler and KV-cache population code when a session migrated between hosts during enhanced kernel path selection.
Race condition in session-resume + KV-cache population interacting with an in-flight kernel-selection change. Under transient client reconnects, sessions could resume with stale sequence metadata, causing serving-runtime to reject requests (5xx) and triggering fallback routing that multiplied inflight attempts.
Immediate mitigation: rolled back kernel-selection change on canary and then full cluster (2026-03-10 03:27–03:33 UTC); disabled prefix-aware KV-cache routing temporarily for affected host pool; blocked smart-routing policy 'latency-prefer' from selecting quantized-hosts during customer sessions. Long-term fix: apply synchronization to session-resume handler, add validation and retry on KV-cache mismatch, and add unit/integration tests for session migration + jitter. Deployed hotfix branch serving-runtime@pr-2193-fix on 2026-03-11 and scheduled full rollout during low-traffic window 2026-03-14 02:00 UTC.

Title: Concurrent streaming requests trigger cascading 5xx amplification due to throttle/starvation

Concurrent streaming requests trigger cascading 5xx amplification due to throttle/starvation

Issue summary:
Customer (NovaDocs Inc.) reported a sharp increase in 5xx errors observed from streaming endpoints during a morning processing window. Errors began at ~09:12 UTC and continued in waves correlated with spikes of concurrent long-lived streaming sessions.

Impact:
- Customer streaming sessions experience dropped responses (5xx) and reconnect loops for ~12 minutes.
- Production latency increased for other tenants in same us-east pool by ~150ms.
- Customer reported degraded UX: failed transcripts and duplicate partial outputs.

Observed behavior:
- API Gateway returned 502/503 on ~18% of streaming handshake attempts during the window.
- Downstream serving-runtime processes showed fast crash/restart cycles (OOM-adjacent) and elevated KV cache eviction rates.

Context and recent changes:
- No customer-driven model rollouts in the 24h preceding the incident.
- Autoscaler pushed up replicas before the spike but observed thrashing afterwards.
- We had a scheduler change deployed to prod 48h prior that adjusted priority scheduling thresholds for streaming paths.

1) Customer opens ~120 concurrent streaming sessions to the /v1/stream endpoint with long-lived streams (~60s+).
2) Each stream sends a prefix-heavy prompt that taps into KV cache hot keys (repeated context patterns).
3) Gateway session proxies enter backpressure and apply priority scheduling that moves streaming requests to a low-bandwidth queue.
4) Serving-runtime processes start evicting KV cache segments, memory climbs and some processes restart, producing 502/503 to upstream proxy.

[2026-03-10T09:12:15.234Z] apigw - WARN - conn 172.18.x.y reached retry threshold - returning 502
[2026-03-10T09:12:16.110Z] runtime-rc-3 - ERROR - eviction: kv_cache_evictions=1243, mem_used=15.8GB, free=1.2GB
[2026-03-10T09:12:16.115Z] runtime-rc-3 - FATAL - oom-adj triggered, child-exit code=137
[2026-03-10T09:12:18.519Z] apigw - WARN - streaming proxy returned 503 - upstream restart
[2026-03-10T09:12:20.002Z] autoscaler - INFO - scale_in prevented due to recent crashloop assessment

Initial triage by Support (Aisha): correlated customer error spikes with gateway metrics and runtime crashloops. SRE (Priya) captured heap and eviction metrics; found elevated kv-cache churn and model kv misses.
Hypothesis 1: KV-cache hotkey eviction under high concurrency caused memory pressure on a subset of runtime replicas leading to OOM-adj process exits and 5xx responses.
Hypothesis 2: New priority-scheduling thresholds deprioritized streaming handshakes, amplifying connection backlog at the gateway which in turn caused upstream request timeouts and increased retries.
Evidence: eviction rate charts (consecutive spikes), gateway backlog metrics, and restart logs match the timeline.
Counter-evidence: a few runtime replicas reported stable memory prior to restarts; further profiling required on per-process allocator fragmentation.

Support (Aisha): Reached out to customer at 09:35 UTC for extra request traces.
Customer (NovaDocs SRE, Mark Liang): Provided a client-side capture; confirms 120 concurrent sessions during processing window. Requests included repeated contextual tokens.
SRE (Priya Menon): Collected heap dumps and started request-level tracing on suspect hosts. Noted large allocator fragmentation in one process.
Runtime Eng (Diego Ramos): Reproduced eviction pattern in staging using a high-concurrency prefix workload. Confirmed that priority scheduling pushes streaming handshakes behind heavy short RPCs under current thresholds.
Support (Aisha): Notified customer of temporary mitigation steps at 10:04 UTC.

A combination of KV-cache hotkey-induced eviction and a recent scheduler change that aggressively deprioritized streaming handshakes. Under heavy concurrent long-lived streams, a subset of runtime replicas experienced memory fragmentation leading to OOM-adj restarts; the gateway backlog and retried handshakes amplified 5xx rates across the pool.
Applied immediate mitigations at 10:05 UTC: 1) Increased concurrency cap for NovaDocs tenant to limit parallel long-lived streams. 2) Temporarily relaxed priority-scheduling thresholds for streaming paths to avoid handshake starvation. 3) Pinned customer to a warm runtime variant with larger KV cache to stabilize memory usage.
Customer applied client-side exponential backoff to reconnect attempts to reduce retry storms.
Short-term: Stabilized at 10:18 UTC after mitigation steps; error rate returned to baseline within ~20 minutes.
Long-term: Engineering change to be implemented: allocator/fragmentation fix in runtime and adaptive KV eviction policy to avoid whole-key thrashing. Scheduler change: refine priority thresholds and add handshake-preserving fast-path.
Follow-up RFC and rollout scheduled.

- OPS-1308: Adaptive KV eviction policy and instrumentation (owner: Priya Menon) - target: 2026-03-22
- ENG-2473: Scheduler priority fast-path for streaming handshakes (owner: Liam O'Connor) - target: 2026-03-19
- Postmortem to be published on Confluence under incident page (owner: Aisha Patel) - target: 2026-03-14

Title: Enterprise partner notice — limited inference glitch summary

Enterprise partner notice — limited inference glitch summary

Brief partner-facing summary of a localized inference degradation on 2029-04-17 affecting hosted inference in EU-west and US-east regions. Focused on enterprise partners with dedicated traffic routing where we observed intermittent model fallbacks and elevated p95 latency for streaming sessions. This doc contains a short statuspage-ready message, a customer-facing postmortem summary, concrete mitigation steps already applied, recommended customer actions (if any), and our remediation/compensation offer for enterprise contracts.

Our engineers applied targeted routing fixes and autoscaler threshold adjustments; customer-visible errors have declined and most sessions restored by 2029-04-18 01:30 UTC. We’ve prepared a concise postmortem and a short set of action items below. We will follow up with a formal SLA remediation proposal. — Aisha (Customer Success)
What happened: a coordination bug between the smart-routing layer and autoscaler caused KV-cache warmups to be delayed for long-lived streaming sessions. After autoscaler-triggered placement changes, requests were temporarily routed to a compatible but higher-latency model variant (quantized v2 fallback) while the KV cache was rehydrated, which increased p95/p99 latency and led to some truncated streams. When did it start: 2029-04-17 22:10 UTC. When did core mitigation occur: 2029-04-18 00:45 UTC (targeted routing policy rollback and autoscaler configuration change). Impact: 0.6% of total requests across the affected regions experienced p95 latency > 2s for durations up to ~45 minutes; streaming truncations observed in ~0.08% of sessions. Root cause: race between routing decisions and instance lifecycle signals during scale events, leading to missed early KV pre-warm for streaming sessions. Why it matters: customers with long-lived streaming sessions or strict latency SLOs saw transient degradations and higher error rates for structured streaming outputs.
- Identified the routing->autoscaler coordination gap via trace correlation and request sampling.
- Rolled back the experimental placement policy for affected regions to a proven stable policy (2029-04-18 00:47 UTC).
- Increased KV cache rewarm priority for streaming sessions and disabled the aggressive preemption path causing cache eviction.
- Deployed a hotfix to the autoscaler to emit clearer lifecycle events and to pause routing changes until KV prewarm confirmation is received.
- Notified customers and opened support tickets for impacted tenants.
Outcome: error rates reduced to baseline and streaming stability restored by 2029-04-18 01:30 UTC.
- Ship a coordinated handshake between routing controller and instance lifecycle that requires KV-ready acknowledgment before routing switch. (PR merged: runtime/pull/5123).
- Add canary and synthetic streaming probes for every region that validate KV warm state before redirecting live traffic.
- Update autoscaler thresholds and introduce a short cooldown window for streaming-heavy instances to avoid repeated placement churn.
- Introduce telemetry alerting on model-variant fallbacks to trigger early paging for SRE/Product.
- Plan: full rollout of handshake + probes by 2029-05-10 behind a gradual canary (10% -> 50% -> 100%).
- For partners using longest-lived streaming sessions, we recommend enabling the tenant-level 'pin-primary-node' option temporarily (instructions linked).
- Ensure client-side retry/backoff for streaming resumptions (best-practice snippet provided on the KB).
- If you experienced truncated structured outputs, please reply to this thread with the request IDs; we will prioritize log retrieval and reprocessing if possible.

We propose the following for impacted enterprise partners:
