Title: Sustained 5xx elevation from asymmetric upstream restart and HTTP/2 stream-slot starvation during mixed embed/chat burst

Sustained 5xx elevation from asymmetric upstream restart and HTTP/2 stream-slot starvation during mixed embed/chat burst

Issue summary: Customers started seeing a sustained elevation in 5xx responses for streaming and short-chat requests beginning 2026-03-12 10:50 UTC. Errors primarily reported as 502/503 from the API gateway with 'upstream reset' and 'stream slot unavailable' symptoms.

Impact: NovaDocs (dedicated tenant) observed 30-45% error rate on streaming chat routes for ~2 hours, causing real user failures and increased retry traffic. Other tenants on the same pool experienced degraded tail latency.

Environment: prod/us-east, Dedicated GPU pool (reserved), hybrid streaming+embedding workload (mix ratio ~60/40).

Steps to reproduce:
1) Start a burst of concurrent streaming chat sessions (50-80 concurrent streams) mixed with medium-size embedding uploads (batch size ~128).
2) Observe API gateway returning intermittent 502/503 and aborts within 30s.
3) Checking runtime shows frequent short-lived restarts on a subset of replicas and many HTTP/2 streams stuck in HALF-CLOSED_LOCAL state.

Observed logs/snippets:
- apigw: "upstream reset before response completed" / "502 upstream connection reset"
- runtime: "runtime: panic at kv_prefetch.go:482" followed by fast restart and subsequent "http2: stream slot unavailable" warnings
- autoscaler: flurry of scale-up/scale-down events within 10m window (oscillation)

Customer notes: NovaDocs reported that failures aligned with a product campaign spike and asked for priority remediation and mitigation while we investigate.

Urgency: Customer-facing impact for a paying dedicated tenant during business hours. Escalated to SRE oncall.
2026-03-12 11:05 - NovaDocs (CS contact): 'We're seeing 50% of chat requests fail with 502s since ~10:50 UTC. Can you route us to another pool? This is blocking our customers.'
2026-03-12 11:12 - Support (Aisha Khan): Acknowledged. We're investigating and will provide mitigation steps within 15 minutes. Asked for tenant id and example request IDs.
2026-03-12 11:28 - SRE (Jonah Park): Early telemetry shows a localized restart pattern on 3/12 runtime replicas and HTTP/2 stream slot exhaustion. Temporarily routed NovaDocs to a warmed fallback pool and disabled hedged retries for their tenant. Error rate dropped to ~8% after routing change.
2026-03-12 12:10 - Support (Aisha Khan): Customer confirmed partial recovery after routing. They still see intermittent 503s on long-lived streams.
2026-03-12 13:40 - SRE (Jonah Park): Collected core dumps and runtime logs from affected replicas. Uploaded artifacts to internal S3: s3://redwood-incident/SUP-277338/ and created trace links. Hypothesis added to investigation notes.
2026-03-13 09:15 - Engineering (Priya Desai): Reproduced stream-slot leak locally with a mixed workload harness. Found a race in prefetch cancellation that prevented HTTP/2 stream closure on restart. Draft patch PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2314
2026-03-14 08:30 - SRE (Jonah Park): Patch approved for canary rollout. Plan: deploy patch to 10% of pool, monitor stream slot metrics and 5xx rate for 30m before wider rollout.
Timeline of actions and findings:
- 10:50 UTC: Error elevation begins correlated with NovaDocs campaign spike.
- 11:00 UTC: API gateway shows high upstream reset rates and increased connection re-establishments.
- 11:12 UTC: SRE observed three runtime replicas restarting repeatedly; their restart cadence aligned with prefetch worker failures in logs.
- 11:30 UTC: Evidence of HTTP/2 stream slot saturation: large number of HALF-CLOSED_LOCAL streams around affected replicas, preventing new stream allocation.
- 11:40 UTC: Autoscaler reacted to perceived capacity shortage then backfilled; rapid scale events amplified the issue via transient cold starts.
Hypotheses considered:
H1: Runtime prefetch cancellation race causes panic and restart, leaving half-closed streams -> downstream apigw 502s (most likely).
H2: Autoscaler cooldown misconfiguration causing oscillation that amplifies transient restarts (contributor).
H3: Client retry amplification (hedged retries) increased concurrent open streams (contributor).
Evidence: core dumps show prefetch goroutine stack consistent with known race. Canary reproduction confirms leak under mixed streaming+embed load.
Temporary mitigations applied:
- Rerouted NovaDocs to warmed fallback pool which significantly reduced 5xx rate.
- Disabled hedged retries at the tenant-level for NovaDocs.
- Increased HTTP/2 max-concurrent-streams soft limit on the gateway for the pool to reduce immediate rejections.
Next steps: roll out runtime patch to fix prefetch cancellation, adjust autoscaler cooldowns to prevent oscillation, update hedged retry defaults and add tenant-level backoffs.
Monitoring: dashboards updated (grafana link: https://grafana.redwood/s/incident/SUP-277338), alert thresholds lowered for stream-slot utilization.
Workaround implemented: NovaDocs routed to fallback pool and hedged retries disabled for the tenant; HTTP/2 soft limit temporarily increased.
Permanent fix: merged runtime patch to properly cancel prefetch and ensure stream closure (PR merged 2026-03-13). Canary rollout completed 2026-03-14 09:10 UTC with success (5xx down to baseline).
Follow-up actions assigned:
- Adjust autoscaler cooldown and add jitter to reduce oscillation (owner: infra-autoscale team).
- Add automated acceptance test in the mixed-workload harness to detect stream-slot leaks (owner: runtime QA).
- Update runbook with steps for tenant routing during asymmetric restarts and document hedged retry opt-outs for large embedding/chat mixes.
Customer communication: NovaDocs informed of mitigation and planned fixes. They requested postmortem and we agreed to provide within 3 business days.

Title: Intermittent request timeouts for EU customers caused by cross-region routing to us-east during peering flap

Intermittent request timeouts for EU customers caused by cross-region routing to us-east during peering flap

Issue summary: Since 2026-03-12 10:40 UTC we have received multiple reports from EU customers (notably Inkwell Analytics) of high tail latency and request timeouts for text-generation and streaming responses. Impact: A subset of requests from eu-west were being routed to us-east (round-trip +120ms) causing queueing in serving runtime and SDK-level timeouts for streaming sessions. Environment: prod (eu-west); affected customers primarily enterprise tier. Timeline: 10:35 - spike begins; 10:40 - first customer report; 10:52 - alerting hit p1 threshold; 11:05 - mitigation pinned region routing; 11:20 - partial recovery for pinned routes; 12:00 - continued investigation. Observed behavior: large fraction of streaming sessions fail with: SDK error: "read timeout after 120s" and gateway 504s when backend token generation exceeded 110s. Cross-region latency correlated with a peering degradation reported by cloud provider in eu-west peering fabric. This ticket captures support engagement, investigation notes, and mitigation steps.
1) From an eu-west client, send a streaming chat request to /v1/chat/stream with rw-chat-3.0 and typical prompt (~800 tokens).
2) Observe SDK stream open then long silence; client eventually receives timeout at 120s or sees partial tokens then disconnect.
3) Check request routing headers X-Region-Routed-To and X-Routing-Policy in logs; observed value: us-east for affected requests.
4) Correlate with smart-router decisions in routing logs and with api-gateway connection traces to confirm cross-region proxied connections.
2026-03-12T10:42:11Z gateway[req-9a3d]: routed request region=eu-west -> target=us-east (route_policy=latency_fallback) ttl=30s
2026-03-12T10:42:13Z smart-router[decision]: evaluated peers: eu-edge-12 healthy=false last_check=00:20:07; selected us-edge-3 score=0.72
2026-03-12T10:44:55Z runtime[serve-42]: token-gen start id=req-9a3d latency_probe=0.0
2026-03-12T10:46:37Z runtime[serve-42]: token-gen long-tail: rpc to us-east backend RTT=128ms queue-wait=88s -> 504 threshold exceeded
2026-03-12T11:02:10Z sdk-client[inkwell]: stream disconnected with error: read timeout after 120s
Initial hypothesis: smart-router fallback to us-east due to transient eu-west peering health check failures (cloud provider reported BGP flaps).
Checked smart-router health checks: multiple eu-west edge peers marked unhealthy simultaneously; health-check interval set to 15s, but TTL for peer negative caching was 30s leading to over-eager failover.
Observed mismatch: routing rollout (PR #187) changed the fallback scoring weights last week and reduced locality bias; combination of health-check flaps and lower locality weight caused bulk reroute.
Metric correlation: spike in cross-region egress and RPC SLO violations coincident with peering event logged by provider (see provider status page).
Reproducibility: can reproduce by forcing eu-edge peers to 'unhealthy' in staging smart-router and observing routing to us-east and increased RTTs; confirms routing decision path.

2026-03-12 11:10 UTC - Inkwell support: "Partial recovery observed after 11:05 but still seeing increased latency for some requests. Please advise on mitigation and ETA for root cause fix."
At 11:05 UTC ops pinned routing policy for enterprise customers in eu-west to prefer in-region endpoints and increased health-check sensitivity to avoid blackholing on brief flaps. Added temporary rate-limit exemptions for affected customer to reduce retry storms.
Temporary: pinned eu-west routes for enterprise customers and rolled back upstream routing weight change (PR #187) that reduced locality bias. Permanent: schedule change to health-check negative caching TTL and add continuous test that simulates peering flaps to validate routing behavior. Follow-up task created to harden smart-router scoring algorithm (INT-412).
Customers recovered to baseline by 11:25 UTC after pinning. Post-incident, we will deploy: 1) revert routing weight change in production (done 2026-03-12 11:45 UTC), 2) lower negative-cache TTL to 5s for edge peer health, 3) add canary that simulates transient peer failure. Schedule code rollback verification for routing PR #187 in staging (owner: infra-team).
Create automated integration test for peering flaps in CI (owner: SRE).
Contact cloud provider to request postmortem for the eu-west peering anomaly and retain their timeline (owner: Partnerships).
Communicate summary and RCA draft to Inkwell and impacted customers (owner: CS - Nora Vega).

Title: Intermittent streaming timeouts due to stale POP affinity cache causing 'hot-potato' inter-region routing

Intermittent streaming timeouts due to stale POP affinity cache causing 'hot-potato' inter-region routing

Issue summary: Since 2026-03-10 02:00 UTC NordicFin (enterprise) reported elevated p95/p99 inference latency and intermittent streaming cancellations for chat endpoints. Impact: Customer observed client-side 504s and stalled streaming chunks; tail latency increased from baseline p99 ~800ms to >6s for some requests. Scope: Reported for customers with EU POP affinity but observed traces showing sudden handoffs to US POPs during request lifetime. Environment: prod eu-west. Steps to reproduce: 1) Use customer's API key and call /v1/chat with streaming=true from eu-west; 2) Issue a long multi-turn prompt (~600 tokens); 3) Observe first chunks arrive then long pause (3-10s) before resume or cancellation. Observed behavior: - Traces show initial connection to eu-west-edge-03, after 1-2 tokens traffic is forwarded to us-east-edge-01 (TTL ~20s) - TCP connection is reused at proxy layer without full reconnect leading to head-of-line blocking on the forwarding path - Kernel tcp retransmit counters spike on proxy host. Logs: "proxy=eu-west-edge-03 forward=us-east-edge-01 route_cache=stale pop_affinity_cache_age=128s conn_reuse=1". Metrics: - p50 unchanged, p95 up 300-900ms, p99 up to 6-8s for affected time windows - 504s correlated with abrupt route handover windows - Flow logs (vpc-flow) show small bursts of inter-region egress during incidents. Initial hypothesis: A stale POP-affinity cache in the regional proxy layer persisted past a routing failover; the proxy tries to preserve connections by reusing upstream sockets, forwarding to a remote POP resulting in extra RTT and occasional packet loss leading to stalls/timeouts. Investigation notes: - SRE captured tcpdump of a reproduced case and saw FIN/ACKs from upstream followed by retransmit backlog - Edge proxy config shows cache TTL misaligned with global route-change TTL (edge TTL = 120s, control-plane route TTL = 30s) - Early mitigation: rolled back cache TTL change on eu-west-edge fleet and enabled strict upstream reconfirmation for active streaming sessions (hotfix rolled at 2026-03-11 05:30 UTC). Current state: Hotfix reduced incidents but not fully resolved; working on a coordinated control-plane cache invalidation mechanism and test coverage for streaming handoff. Next steps: 1) Implement cache invalidation push (infra) and force refresh for all eu-west-edge (sprint P0) 2) Add E2E test that simulates route flapping during active streaming 3) Monitor for 72 hours and coordinate with NordicFin CS to validate. Runbooks/links: incident runbook: https://confluence.redwood.ai/incidents/INC-2026-03-10-27, grafana traces: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/streaming/latency-overview?orgId=1&var-region=eu-west

Title: Scheduled evidence exports and dashboard delivery for compliance (PDF/CSV + residency-aware delivery)

Scheduled evidence exports and dashboard delivery for compliance (PDF/CSV + residency-aware delivery)

Summary: Build first-class automated compliance reporting that can produce scheduled PDF and CSV evidence bundles and deliver them to residency-appropriate endpoints (S3 in region, secure FTP, or email with encrypted attachments). This feature surfaces on the Compliance dashboard and supports tenant-level retention settings, per-tenant data residency constraints, and audit traceability (signed export hashes and delivery receipts).

Why: Customers in regulated industries require regular, human-readable evidence of data handling and retention policies for audits. Currently they manually stitch logs, retention snapshots, and console screenshots. A native scheduled export + delivery system reduces manual effort, lowers time-to-evidence, and helps close renewal conversations with enterprise customers requiring demonstrable residency and retention controls.

Scope (MVP):
- UI in Console Compliance section to configure scheduled exports (daily/weekly/monthly), format (PDF summary, CSV raw data), recipient endpoint (regional S3 bucket, SFTP, secure email), and retention snapshot window.
- Export content templates: Audit summary (PDF), Raw records (CSV) with optional PII redaction rules, Retention snapshot (CSV) showing per-tenant retention policy enforcement over the period.
- Residency-aware delivery: exports for EU customers stored/delivered from EU region only; US customers from US region only.
- Evidence bundles must include a generated SHA-256 manifest and a signed delivery receipt logged to the audit trail.
- Scheduled job runner with retry/backoff, alerting to customer and Redwood support when delivery fails repeatedly.

Out of scope (MVP): ad-hoc one-off exports via API (will be follow-up), export of full request/response token streams (privacy review required), native long-term archival service (customers can deliver to their own buckets).
Console UI: Users can create a scheduled export policy with cadence, format (PDF/CSV), recipients, and regional constraint; saved policy persists and is editable.
Export generation: System can generate a PDF audit summary and compressed CSV payload for a sample EU tenant and US tenant within the configured cadence.
Residency enforcement: For an EU tenant configured with EU-only delivery, generated files are stored and delivered only from EU-hosted infrastructure (test proof: file metadata shows eu-west-1 storage and delivery endpoint).
Integrity evidence: Each export bundle includes a SHA-256 manifest and a signed delivery receipt recorded in the tenant audit log with timestamps and delivery status.
Delivery channels: Exports can be delivered to S3 (region-specific), SFTP, and as encrypted email attachments using customer-provided public key; failures trigger an alert to the support queue and an automated retry policy (3 attempts with exponential backoff).
Retention snapshot: CSV shows applied retention rules and the list of records deleted or marked for deletion during the snapshot window for the tenant; matches system retention enforcement logs.
Performance: Generating and packaging an export for a 30M token tenant should complete within 20 minutes in Dedicated environment (benchmarked during engineering spike).
Week 1: Finalize API schema for ExportPolicy and ExportRun; finalize PDF/CSV templates with Design.
Week 2: Build scheduled job runner service and residency-aware storage plumbing; implement S3/SFTP/email delivery adapters.
Week 3: Produce audit manifest signing and delivery receipt flow; integrate with audit log and support alerting.
Week 4: Console UI for policy creation/editing, QA, security review, and limited alpha with 3 pilot customers.
Rollout: Alpha -> Beta (2 customers) -> general availability in console-2026.04; Dedicated customers will receive region-specific config knobs in a patch release.
Residency enforcement complexity: ensuring exports are generated and egressed only from approved regions requires infra changes and legal verification.
PII leakage: CSV exports may unintentionally include sensitive tokens; must enforce redaction/pseudonymization policies and require customer acceptance for high-sensitivity exports.
Delivery failures: customers expect SLA for evidence delivery; need clear retry/backoff and escalation procedures to prevent missed audits.
Cost and performance: generating PDFs for very large tenants could impact runtime capacity; may require limiting historical window or parallelizing export generation.
Design decision: PDF should use a templating engine (HTML-to-PDF) to allow branding and readable audit summaries; engineering prefers wkhtmltopdf or headless Chromium but flagged for infra cost review.
Tradeoff: Including raw token-level data in CSV increases sensitivity and storage; MVP will include pseudonymization toggles and a customer opt-in for token-level exports.
Compliance nuance: Some customers require that the signing key for delivery receipts be customer-managed; plan to add KMS/HSM integration in follow-up (Private deployments first).
Related docs: Confluence spec - https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/COMPLIANCE/Scheduled+Exports (draft), Security review checklist PR - https://github.com/redwood-inference/security/pull/214

Title: Saga router fallback matrix & async orchestration notes

Saga router fallback matrix & async orchestration notes

Context and intent:

This is a working note to consolidate an operationally practical approach for control-plane async workflows across regions. The focus: how the router (control-plane request router + policy engine) should pick paths, when to fall back to lower tiers, how to coordinate distributed sagas across regions, and pragmatic idempotency/retry semantics that avoid thrash and double-side effects.

Goals:
- Provide a concise decision matrix for routing + fallback behavior (fast path -> degraded path -> queueing -> fallback responses).
- Standardize retry and idempotency token semantics for control-plane commands (e.g., model deploy, scale, pin/version changes).
- Surface tradeoffs for orchestrator vs choreography in multi-region sagas and recommend a hybrid pattern.
- List actionable TODOs, instrumentation hooks, and a small message-format sketch.

High-level assumptions:
- Control-plane operations are mostly eventually consistent and can be long-running (>30s to minutes).
- We run active-active regions; control-plane metadata is replicated with asynchronous replication and causal ordering guarantees from the metadata service.
- Workers processing commands are region-local by default (for data locality and IAM), but can failover to other regions if explicitly routed.
- We need predictable retry/backoff to avoid thundering herd on downstream infra (KMS, infra APIs, cloud provider quotas).

Router / policy engine responsibilities (summary):
- Evaluate request.priority, request.tenant_tier, region_affinity, SLA (sync/async), and idempotency metadata.
- Deterministically decide: execute-in-region, enqueue-in-region, proxy-to-dedicated-control-plane (dedicated capacity), or return a deferred-accept (202 + job-id).
- Apply per-tenant fallback policy: e.g., for enterprise tier, prefer synchronous success with cross-region failover; for free-tier, prefer queueing and eventual completion.

Routing + fallback matrix (textual):
Columns: request_tier | synchronous_capable? | preferred_execution | fallback_sequence
- enterprise | yes | execute-in-region-primary -> failover-to-region-secondary -> proxy-to-dedicated -> enqueue -> alert + 500 if impossible
- standard | partial | execute-in-region (with relaxed timeouts) -> enqueue-in-region -> return 202 + polling-hints
- free | no | enqueue-low-priority -> best-effort-execute-in-batch -> return 202 + long-poll suggestion

Notes on 'enqueue' vs 'proxy-to-dedicated':
- enqueue-in-region: create a durable work-item in the region-local queue (SQS / PubSub / Kafka). Preserves region locality and respects quotas.
- proxy-to-dedicated: if tenant has Dedicated capacity, route to that control-plane; expect lower latency and stronger SLOs. This uses different auth path and tracking.

Queue topology options (pros/cons):
1) Per-tenant queue (single-tenant queues)
   - Pros: easy tenant isolation, per-tenant retries, assertion of order.
   - Cons: heavy if many tenants; ops overhead.
2) Per-region shared queue with tenant sharding key
   - Pros: fewer queues to manage, cheaper.
   - Cons: requires worker-level tenant-id isolation and backpressure mechanisms.
3) Global queue with region-aware worker assignment
   - Pros: centralized scheduling, easier global rate-limits.
   - Cons: cross-region latency; requires strong anti-duplication.

Recommendation: Use per-region shared queue with strong tenant sharding key and rate-limit headers; create ephemeral per-tenant FIFO lanes for mission-critical tenants (enterprise).

Retry semantics and idempotency:
- All control-plane commands must accept an idempotency_key (UUID v4 or user-supplied stable token).
- System idempotency window: configurable per command type; default 24 hours for deploy-like commands, 7 days for long-running lifecycle operations.
- Retry policy (default): immediate fast retry 1x, exponential backoff starting at 500ms, max 6 attempts, then escalate to queueing/fallback. For network errors -> retry. For 409/optimistic-conflict -> do not retry automatically, return to caller with conflict info unless caller opts for retry.
- Workers must persist attempt_count and last_error in the work-item metadata. On worker crash, when work-item becomes available again, broker should apply jittered visibility timeout and increase backoff.

Idempotency storage and garbage collection:
- Store idempotency entries in the control-plane metadata DB with keys: (tenant_id, command_type, idempotency_key) -> {result_ref, created_at, status, result_shard}.
- GC policy: keep for idempotency_window + 1 day. For very high QPS tenants, use a bounded LRU cache with persistence to avoid replay storms.

Saga coordination patterns (orchestrator vs choreography):
- Choreography (event-driven): Each service emits events for its local state change; compensating actions are owned by the emitting service. Low coupling, easy to scale, but hard to reason globally and to observe for long sagas across regions.
- Orchestration (central orchestrator): Central saga coordinator drives steps and keeps state. Easier to reason (single source of truth for saga), easier rollback/compensation coordination, but becomes a central dependency and scaling point.

Hybrid recommendation (pragmatic): Use an orchestrator for multi-step tenant-facing control-plane flows (e.g., create-dedicated-cluster, attach-key, commit-policy) and choreography for intra-region post-processing tasks (metrics cleanup, audit logs). Orchestrator runs in the region of origin and persists saga state in the metadata service with replication metadata; orchestrator can spawn local choreographer events for each step.

Multi-region considerations for sagas:
- Region-of-origin anchor: the request defines an origin region that is the primary orchestrator. If origin region is degraded, we can failover orchestrator to a standby in another region, but only after acquiring a durable lease to avoid split-brain.
- Lease semantics: Use short (e.g., 30s) leader leases with renewals and transaction logs. On failover, candidate region must verify last-committed step idempotently before resume.
- Cross-region I/O: avoid synchronous cross-region calls in hot paths. Prefer eventual propagation via event streams. If synchronous cross-region is required, put a strict timeout and fallback path (enqueue or compensation).

Failure modes and example handling:
1) Worker processes step but fails to ack due to crash -> broker visibility timeout expires, step redelivered -> worker must detect prior completion via idempotency_key/result_ref.
2) Network partition: metadata writes may be delayed; orchestrator should write 'pending' step record and publish step-event locally; workers should be tolerant to missing global metadata when possible; use causal id fields in messages.
3) Double-commit risk during failover -> require last-committed-step id check and idempotent apply operations on resources (cloud API often allows idempotent create with client token).

Instrumentation & observability hooks (must-have):
- Saga trace id on every log/event. Correlate across regions.
- Per-step timing and retry counts exposed on dashboards.
- Work-item visibility timeline (queued -> dequeued -> processing -> retry -> done/failed).
- Alerting rules: step retry_count > threshold in last X minutes; queue growth rate > N per minute; replication lag > Y ms

Message format sketch (JSON text):
{
  \"job_id\": \"uuid\",
  \"tenant_id\": \"t-123\",
  \"origin_region\": \"us-west1\",
  \"command\": \"apply-model-pin\",
  \"idempotency_key\": \"client-supplied-or-generated\",
  \"payload\": { /* small canonical payload */ },
  \"attempts\": 0,
  \"created_at\": \"2026-02-15T14:22:00Z\"
}

(Keep payload small; put large artifacts in blob store and reference by URL + signed token.)

Open questions / tradeoffs we still need to decide:
- Should the router return a 202 with polling hints by default for long-running control-plane ops, or try to keep callers connected with streaming updates? (Implications for API surface.)
- GC window defaults: will 24h idempotency be sufficient for enterprise flows that can take days? Offer per-tenant override?
- Exactly which operations are allowed to cross-region synchronously under strong consistency? (KMS transactions are tricky.)

Immediate action items (next steps):
- (Priya) Draft a small RFC enumerating the router decision matrix and API changes for idempotency_key acceptance (due: 2026-02-28).
- (Ethan) Prototype per-region shared queue with tenant sharding and test backpressure behavior under 2x production traffic (due: 2026-03-14).
- (Samir) Add saga trace ids to existing control-plane logs and add dashboard: "saga step latency" (beta) (due: 2026-03-07).

Notes to self / rough todos on UX:
- Provide a lightweight client helper that auto-generates idempotency_key and retries with our policy. Expose environment variable hooks for tests to disable retries.
- Add clear API docs for which endpoints are synchronous vs asynchronous and provide sample polling code.

References and related tickets: JIRA-PLAT-483, PR #214 on serving-runtime, confluence:platform-sagas-v2.

Unresolved TODOs in this doc:
- finalize the lease duration and exact failover handshake protocol (open: Samir to propose).
- decide GC policy for idempotency per tenant tier.

End of note.

-- Priya (draft)

Title: Control Plane Operational Boundaries Heatmap

Control Plane Operational Boundaries Heatmap

Purpose and context:

This is a working heatmap-style sketch to surface current operational boundaries in the control plane: who owns what during normal ops and during multi-region failover. Goal is to call out ambiguous gaps and create a short list of follow-ups (owner assignments, runbook updates, API contracts). Not a canonical doc — an annotated work-in-progress for the platform-engineering and serving-runtime teams.

Assumptions and constraints (short):
- Single control-plane control path (API gateway -> orchestrator -> runtime adapters).
- We support 3 regions (us-west, eu-west, ap-southeast) with regional control-plane replicas and a global config plane.
- Traffic routing is policy-driven: latency-first, then cost, then compliance (region-locked).
- Runtime adapters are the thin bridge to GPU pools and on-prem agents.

High-level ownership summary (heatmap commentary):
- API Gateway (ingest): primary owner = platform-api team. Responsibilities: authentication, rate limiting, coarse routing decisions, quota enforcement, request enrichment. SLA: <100ms control-plane p99 for routing decision. Region fallback: platform-api config points to regional orchestrators; in loss-of-region, global gateway switches to nearest fallback pool.
- Orchestration Layer (request-to-runtime mapping, rollouts): primary owner = orchestration-service team. Responsibilities: model versioning, canary rollouts, route affinity, autoscale hints, batching policies. SLA: transactional durability and consistent rollout state across regions.
- Runtime Adapters (serving proxies): primary owner = serving-runtime team. Responsibilities: translate orchestration directives to runtime-specific calls (CUDA-optimized pools, on-prem RPC), manage KV cache metadata, surface local capacity. SLA: <50ms adapter handshake for pooled requests, best-effort KV cache sync.
- Routing Governance / Policy Engine: primary owner = platform-engineering (routing-gov subteam). Responsibilities: policy language, policy validation, policy audit logs, safety gates for fallback.
- SRE/Infra (ops): primary owner = infra-sre. Responsibilities: infra health, cross-region replication, infra failover, monitoring/alerting for control plane.

Operational boundary matrix (text table):
Service | Owner | Primary responsibilities | Decision boundary | Typical ops handoff
API Gateway | platform-api | auth, ingress, coarse routing | chooses region/orch config based on policy | handoff to orchestration via RPC (orchestration endpoint v2)
Orchestrator | orchestration-service | model routing, version pins, rollout rules | final route decision (which adapter pool) | handoff to runtime adapter with rollout metadata and batching hints
Runtime Adapter | serving-runtime | queueing, batching, KV cache, runtime calls | enforces local capacity and throttles | returns run metrics and fallback signals
Policy Engine | routing-gov | policy eval, validation, audit | rejects unsafe routing changes | notifies orchestration and platform-api on violations
SRE/Infra | infra-sre | infra failover, region replication | triggers region-level failover | notifies all owners, runs global incident runbook

Key decision boundaries to clarify (open questions):
1) Where is the canonical source-of-truth for route-to-adapter mappings?
   - current state: orchestrator maintains mapping but policy engine can inject overrides. Leads to potential race condition during rollout.
   - proposed: orchestrator remains source-of-truth; policy engine issues signed overrides that orchestrator applies with a reconciliation window (TBD).

2) How do we represent multi-region fallbacks in the API contract?
   - suggestion: add an explicit "fallback_chain" field in orchestration responses listing region adapters ordered by policy priority. This makes failover deterministic for adapters.

3) KV cache consistency vs latency: who owns reconciliation?
   - tradeoff: serving-runtime prefers local fast cache with eventual consistency. Orchestrator needs strong-ish invariants for prefix cache invalidation during model switch.
   - interim: add a lightweight invalidation message bus (owner: serving-runtime + infra-sre) with documented TTL semantics.

4) Rollouts across regions: canaries vs global sync?
   - current experiments: region-scoped canaries for low blast radius. Global rollouts often lag and produce inconsistency in inference quality metrics.
   - proposal: add rollout epoch metadata and a global acceptance gate managed by orchestration + product-eval.

Runbook and incident boundaries (short bullets):
- API ingress failures: platform-api owns mitigation (rate-limits, revert gateway config). Escalate to infra-sre on region degradation.
- Orchestrator inconsistencies (mismatched route assignments): orchestration-service owns reconciliation; if >5% mismatches cross-region, open sev3 and rollback last policy change.
- Adapter capacity exhaustion: serving-runtime implements emergency fallback to pre-defined model shards in another region; infra-sre handles cross-region route reweighting.
- Policy violation alerts: routing-gov triages; if unsafe changes detected auto-revert and notify on-call for platform-engineering.

Small proposal list (next steps):
- Draft an API change for orchestration response to include "fallback_chain" + rollout_epoch (owner: orchestration-service). Link: PLAT-4321.
- Prototype signed override flow from policy engine to orchestrator (owner: routing-gov + platform-api). Add TTL and audit log entry.
- Create simple invalidation bus for KV cache with at-most-once invalidation messages (owner: serving-runtime + infra-sre).
- Update incident runbooks to define clear threshold for cross-region inconsistency (owner: infra-sre).

Notes / references / bookmarks:
- Related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/control-plane/pull/198 (orchestration epoch prototype)
- Jira: PLAT-4321 (fallback_chain RFC), PLAT-4502 (KV invalidation proposal)
- Slack thread: #platform-routing – thread id: t0239-heatmap-draft

Open questions for the group meeting (TODOs):
- Acceptable reconciliation window between policy override issuance and orchestrator apply? (Suggested: 60s)
- How do we test cross-region rollout acceptance in CI without incurring expensive GPU runs? (Idea: synthetic traffic + small local model)
- Define exact schema for fallback_chain and rollout_epoch (owner: orchestration-service + api).

Appendix: quick sketch of fallback_chain sample (text only)
- fallback_chain: ["us-west-adapter-v3", "eu-west-adapter-v2", "ap-southeast-proxy"]
- rollout_epoch: "2026-02-14T18:32:00Z"
- policy_signature: "sig:v1:abcd1234"

This doc is intentionally lightweight — keep comments inline in the file, mark sections that need concrete RFC work. Proposed reviewers: Diego Ramos, Priya Patel, Connor Lee, and infra-sre on-call.

End of draft.

Title: Orchestration Routing and On-call Ownership — Whiteboard Sketch

Orchestration Routing and On-call Ownership — Whiteboard Sketch

Purpose:
Quick capture of a whiteboard session about who "owns" which slices of the control plane surface, how routing decisions get made across regions, and the on-call/hand-off expectations for outages or capacity events. This is intentionally informal — aim is to drive a clearer ownership table and a small set of routing/rollback rules we can bake into runbooks and the orchestrator policies.

Top-level constraints and assumptions:
- Single control-plane codebase with region-aware config. We do not want per-region forks of the orchestration logic.
- Gateways (edge) are stateless proxies; orchestration owns policy decisions and fallback.
- Runtime adapters (k8s adapters, on-prem agents, bare-metal connectors) are the boundary where infra-specific concerns live.
- SLOs: 99.95% API availability for hosted API routes; dedicated/private have higher isolation but same latency budgets.

Glossary (quick):
- API Gateway: public ingress (global LB + edge fleet) that authenticates, rate-limits, and forwards to orchestrator.
- Orchestrator: control plane service that decides routing targets, applies rollout policies, performs canaries, triggers fallbacks.
- Runtime Adapter: per-platform adapter that knows how to talk to a runtime (GKE pool, Dedicated GPU pool, Private on-prem agent).
- Fallback Tier: ordered list of compatible model variants/regions to route to when primary target unavailable.

Current pain points mentioned during session:
- Ambiguous ownership on cross-region fallback decisions — who sets the ordered fallback list?
- On-call playbooks contain both Gateway and Orchestrator steps; runbooks often duplicate checks and cause confusion.
- Runtime adapter errors surface as 502s with little semantic mapping (is it capacity, auth, or serialization?).
- Rollbacks currently manual for multi-region rollouts. Need a policy for automated fallback vs automated rollback.

Proposed ownership boundaries (working draft):
- API Gateway (edge routing, auth, basic validation): eng-platform-networking. Responsibilities: TLS, WAF, rate-limits, LB health filtering. On-call: network rotation (pager-level 1 for external connectivity issues).
- Orchestrator (policy, routing decisions, rollouts, canary gating): platform-engineering core. Responsibilities: routing graph, rollout engine, global fallback policy, canary metrics. On-call: platform-engineering primary; responsible for functional failures (incorrect fallbacks, rollout misbehavior).
- Runtime Adapters (k8s-adapter, dedicated-adapter, private-agent): infra-adapters team. Responsibilities: translation to runtime APIs, resource gating, adapter-level health, deployment hooks. On-call: infra-adapters for adapter-level failures; platform-engineering for client-facing regressions if adapter causes incorrect routing.
- Observability & Tracing: observability team (tooling/infra). Responsibilities: ensure traces propagate from gateway->orchestrator->adapter->runtime, token-level cost metrics, slow path alerts. On-call: support for query-level alert escalations.

Routing policy sketch (priority and decision points):
1) Local preference: prefer same-region runtime unless capacity/health issues detected.
2) Model variant compatibility: use semantic compatibility table (quantized ok? kv-cache homogeneous?) maintained by model-onboarding.
3) Tiered fallback: primary -> regional fallback pool -> cross-region compatible pool -> lower-cost batch-tier (with explicit latency degradation).
4) Safety thresholds: if error rate spikes > X% for 2m during canary, either throttle traffic back to previous stable or auto-fallback to next tier depending on traffic volume and SLO exposure.
5) Cost-aware routing: only used when requested (per-customer policy) or if automatic-cost-optimizations enabled and within error bounds.

Example operational flows (short):
- Primary runtime becomes unhealthy: adapter pushes health=false -> orchestrator receives health event -> orchestrator marks node pool unhealthy and recomputes routing graph -> traffic routed to regional fallback pool -> gateway updates LB target weights via control-plane API.
- Canary fails metric gate: orchestrator marks canary as failed -> rollout halted + traffic rolled back to previous model version -> operator receives alert with runbook link.

Ownership matrix (text table):
- API Gateway: eng-platform-networking; pager: net-rot; runbook: /runbooks/gateway-basic.md
- Orchestrator policy engine: platform-engineering; pager: platform-rot; runbook: /runbooks/orchestrator-fallback.md
- k8s runtime-adapter: infra-adapters; pager: adapters-rot; runbook: /runbooks/adapter-k8s.md
- Dedicated GPU adapter: infra-adapters; pager: adapters-rot
- Private on-prem agent: infra-adapters + solutions-eng (escalation path)

Escalation and hand-off rules (practical):
- If gateway shows global connectivity issues (packet loss to multiple regions), network on-call owns until outage localized. If orchestrator logic is suspected (incorrect failover ordering, cascading fallbacks), platform-engineering on-call owns.
- Adapter errors that are recoverable within 5 minutes should remain with adapter on-call. If adapter causes customer-facing SLO breach > 5 minutes, escalate to platform-engineering lead and open an incident.
- Cross-team handoff checklist (for incidents):
  - Timestamped decision log (who changed routing, why)
  - Snapshot of routing graph and weights (automatically collected by orchestrator)
  - Link to last deploys (gateway/orchestrator/adapters)
  - Triage notes and initial mitigation steps attempted

Sensible defaults for runbooks (to be turned into runnable scripts):
- Gather: trace id, request token id, route, model id, target runtime id
- Quick checks: adapter health, adapter logs (last 5m), orchestrator policy log for route decision, LB health for target nodes
- Next steps: if adapter shows OOMs or capacity, scale pool -> if scaling fails, failover to next tier; if orchestrator misrouted, rollback to prior policy version.

Observability additions proposed in this doc:
- Add explicit "fallback.reason" tag on traces when orchestrator triggers a fallback so we can query root cause across many requests.
- Adapter-level semantic error codes (CAPACITY, AUTH, SERIALIZATION, DEPLOYMENT) returned upstream to orchestrator and surfaced in 5xx metrics with labels.
- Per-customer routing policy audit log (who changed fallback order, when) for audit/compliance in Dedicated/Private.

Open questions (we did not resolve on board):
- Who authoritatively manages the region-fallback ordered list? (Options: model-onboarding, orchestrator policies, or customer overrides maintained in orchestration config).
- Auto-rollbacks: when should they be allowed vs only manual? What is the risk appetite?
- Is cost-aware routing enabled by default for small customers? (Probably not; opt-in via quota/toggles).
- How do we surface adapter semantic errors without leaking internal hostnames or sensitive identifiers in logs for Private deployments?

Immediate action items (owners):
- Platform-engineering: draft a short RFC for "fallback ownership" and a concrete schema for fallback lists (due 2025-03-07) — owner: Maya R. Singh.
- Infra-adapters: standardize semantic error codes and add a shim that maps internal adapter errors to the semantic codes (due 2025-03-14) — owner: Ibrahim Al-Kazemi.
- Observability: add fallback.reason tag and a dashboard for fallback frequency by model/region (POC by 2025-03-21) — owner: Lena Gómez.
- eng-platform-networking: confirm runbook split between gateway vs orchestrator (mini-review meeting 2025-02-28) — owner: Ethan Park.

Notes-to-self / scribbles: 
- Keep the orchestrator policy small and declarative: fallback lists + gating rules + cost overrides. Complex heuristics (ML-based routing) can be a later layer that consumes the same schema.
- Avoid allowing per-customer arbitrary cross-region overrides without SRE approval for Dedicated/Private.

Links referenced during the session:
- sketch: whiteboard photo: GDrive link (mock) -> https://drive.google.com/mock/whiteboard/board-238
- previous routing atlas (read for context) -> confluence:control-plane-routing-atlas
- incident playbook template -> /runbooks/incident-playbook-template.md

End of sketch.

(Will convert to a short RFC once consensus on fallback ownership emerges.)

Title: Control Plane Responsibility Atlas

Control Plane Responsibility Atlas

Purpose:
This doc is a concise, operational-first map of control plane responsibilities and ownership for API gateway, orchestration, and runtime adapters across multi-region deployments. Goal: reduce ambiguity during incidents and design reviews by making handoffs explicit (who owns what, and where routing/decision logic lives).

Scope and non-goals:
- In scope: control plane components that make routing, rollout, and runtime selection decisions (API gateway, smart router, policy engine, orchestration service, runtime adapters, model-catalog interface, multi-region coordinator).
- Out of scope: compute-side runtime implementation details (exact kernel implementations, per-GPU scheduling internals), client SDKs, and billing pipelines (these have separate owners but are linked).

High-level principles:
1) Single source of truth: control-plane config (routes, policies, model pins, rollouts) is stored in the Control Configstore (see linked Confluence page) and is the authoritative input for all region controllers.
2) Fail open with constraints: in a partial-control-plane outage, replicas should prefer degraded but safe behavior (route to compatible model-variant with stricter rate limits) rather than drop traffic.
3) Locality-first routing with regional fallbacks: prefer same-region runtime; fall back to cross-region only when policy permits and latency budget allows.
4) Ownership by responsibility, not by hostname: teams own behaviors (e.g., rate-limiting policy decisions) across tiers rather than single endpoints.

Service ownership roster (component -> primary responsibility -> owner):
- API Gateway: authentication, authorization, edge rate-limits, per-tenant quotas enforcement, initial request validation, request tagging (route/tenant/trace). Owner: eng-platform-gateway.
- Smart Router (control-plane routing engine): route selection (model variant, region, capacity tier), capacity-aware placement decisions, fallback chain evaluation. Owner: eng-platform-routing.
- Policy Engine: evaluation of fine-grained routing rules (SLAs, customer-specified pins, allowlists), feature flag gating for rollout behavior. Owner: eng-platform-engineering (policy subteam).
- Orchestration Service (control-plane lifecycle): deploys model slices to runtime adapters, rollout strategies (canary/A-B/gradual), autoscale commands (desired replica counts). Owner: eng-orchestration.
- Runtime Adapters (region-level): translate routing decisions into runtime-specific actions (start/stop containers, allocate GPU pools, apply quantization profile). Owner: eng-serving-runtime.
- Model Catalog API: version metadata, compatible runtime variant metadata (quantization, memory profile), deprecation signals. Owner: eng-models (applied-ml).
- KV/Prefix Cache Manager (control-plane coord): global cache invalidation policy, mapping of cached prefixes to runtime owners, cache warming recommendations. Owner: eng-serving-runtime (cache team).
- Telemetry & Tracing Pipeline (control-plane sidecar): ingest control-plane and route-level metrics, expose per-route latency/cost breakdowns. Owner: eng-observability.
- Audit & Compliance Store: immutable action logs for pin/rollout/route changes, access controls, retention policy. Owner: security-and-compliance.
- Multi-region Coordinator: config propagation, leader election for region mastership, conflict resolution rules for concurrent updates. Owner: eng-platform-engineering (multi-region subteam).

Routing policy primitives (what lives where):
- Route selection logic: Smart Router (control-plane) evaluates list of compatible runtime variants then scores by latency, cost, and affinity.
- Affinity rules: stored as part of tenant config in Control Configstore; enforced by Smart Router (region affinity), API Gateway (sticky session hints).
- Fallback chains: policy engine defines ordered fallbacks (same-variant different region, cheaper quantized variant, lower-priority dedicated pool). Fallback execution is orchestrated by Smart Router.
- Capacity-aware routing: runtime adapters publish capacity tokens; Smart Router uses soft and hard limits to avoid overcommit.

Multi-region behaviours and invariants:
- Control Configstore is multi-master read/write with CRDT-based last-writer-wins for non-critical routing hints; critical ops (rollout toggles, SLA changes) use single-leader write with optimistic locking.
- Propagation window target: 30s for config changes to reach all active region controllers under normal conditions; alerts if >2min.
- Leader election: Multi-region Coordinator elects a region master for cross-region global operations (e.g., global canary that needs synchronous cutover).
- Region failover: Smart Router prefers local runtimes; if regional outage detected, route to next-best region but only after passing latency and data residency checks.

API Gateway specific responsibilities:
- Edge auth + tenant identification (api keys/jwt verification).
- Quick-reject decisions for invalid requests before hitting routing pipeline.
- Rate-limit enforcement windows (burst vs sustained); owner must maintain default policies and tenant override API.
- Request enrichment (add trace headers, tenant metadata) before forwarding to Smart Router.

Orchestration responsibilities (lifecycle & rollouts):
- Model deploy lifecycle: validate model artifact against catalog (compatibility matrix), stage to canary region, monitor quality signals (eval hooks), promote or rollback.
- Autoscaling signals: accept telemetry-derived signals from runtime adapters and apply binning rules; preserve capacity buffers for SLA-bound tenants.
- Canary semantics: default canary size=1% of traffic for hosted API, configurable per-tenant.

Runtime adapter invariants and contracts:
- Runtime adapter exposes: health endpoint, capacity tokens, supported-variant list, KV cache ownership hints, telemetry endpoint.
- Any change to adapter API is a breaking change and requires a deprecation window and coordinated rollout.
- Adapter is responsible for ensuring model pinning (if requested) holds until orchestration confirms migration.

SLOs, Alerts, and Escalation:
- Control Plane availability SLO: 99.95% regional, 99.9% global for critical path (authentication + routing).
- Route latency budget: control-plane decision time < 50ms P95 under normal load; alert at >150ms P95.
- Canary health alerts: automatic rollback on model-quality regressions (>3x baseline error rate within 1h).
- Pager paths: eng-platform-routing -> eng-orchestration -> eng-serving-runtime depending on signal type. Ownership handbook (oncall rotations) lives in eng-platform engineering handbook.

Change process and governance:
- Any routing-policy change requires: design doc PR, staging test run (multi-region if global), and a rollout playbook entry.
- Minor config changes (rate limits, thresholds) can be submitted via change API with automatic audit log entry; major behavioral changes require a design review and cross-team signoff.
- Emergency quickfixes must be documented post-mortem and traced to a Jira ticket.

Open questions / action items:
- Decide exact semantics for cross-region data residency enforcement (legal vs latency tradeoffs). Owner: security-and-compliance + eng-platform-engineering.
- Finalize the format for capacity token exchange between adapters and Smart Router (binary vs JSON push). Owner: eng-serving-runtime. Action: prototype by 2025-03-01.
- Define default canary thresholds for Dedicated vs Hosted customers (business input needed). Owner: product-hosted-api + customer-success.

Next steps:
- Ship a short ‘ownership cheatsheet’ derived from this doc to oncall Slack and embed in runbooks. (Owner: Maya Chen, due 2025-02-20)
- Add missing telemetry gauges for propagation window and per-route fallback counts (Owner: eng-observability, due 2025-03-10).

Notes and references:
- See linked Confluence page for diagrams and sequence flows.
- Related tickets: PLAT-482 (multi-region coordinator design), PLAT-501 (smart router capacity API).

Document history:
- 2024-11-05 created (initial mapping)
- 2025-01-12 added multi-region coordinator details
- 2025-02-10 review updates and added action items

If you're reviewing: call out any missing owner or ambiguous handoff. This is intended to be operationally prescriptive — if a team can't accept an item, mark it as RACI-Disagree and propose a remap.

Title: Regional leadership fallback matrix and runbook

Regional leadership fallback matrix and runbook

Purpose:
This note is a compact operational decision aid for control-plane topology across multiple regions. It compares active-active vs active-passive leadership models, enumerates failure modes and routing policies, and provides a short runnable checklist for DR drills and on-call actors. Goal is pragmatic: give SREs and platform owners a single-page reference for runbook actions and trade-offs when we change topology or handle incidents.

Context assumptions (our stack):
- Control plane is stateless microservices fronting stateful backends (metadata DB, cluster allocations).
- Data plane (inference traffic) is region-local; control plane coordinates routing, rollouts, and config.
- Customers can be pinned to regions but we also support global fallbacks.
- We want to minimize user-visible consistency issues while keeping failover predictable and cost-efficient.

High-level tradeoffs (short):
- Active-Active:
  - Pros: lower failover time (no promotion), better utilization, less cold warm-up for control APIs.
  - Cons: stronger requirement for cross-region consensus or async reconciliation, increased risk of split-brain decisions without robust arbitration, more complexity in leader-compatible writes.
- Active-Passive (regional primary + global standby):
  - Pros: simpler correctness model for writes, deterministic ownership, easier to reason about role transitions.
  - Cons: capacity waste in passive regions unless warmed, longer promotion time, potential increased latency during metropolitan failover if routing chokes.

Leader election primitives we considered:
- Strong consensus (raft across regions): correct but high tail latency for writes, sensitive to network partitions. OK for small number of control shards, not good for global-scale fast API responses.
- Lease-based leader per region (short TTL, renewables): low-latency local decisions, needs robust clock skew handling and careful lease expiry logic to avoid double-leaders.
- Arbiter-based vote (third-party region or cloud service): useful to break ties during partitioning; operationally expensive.

Decision matrix (operational view) - choose one row per control surface (routing, rollout control, billing, audits):
- Routing decisions:
  - Model: Active-Active with region-local write + causal tagging for routing table updates.
  - Rationale: routing must be low-latency; eventual convergence acceptable if we provide TTL-based cache invalidation.
  - Failure mode mitigations: short-lived caches, convergence monitors, automatic reconciliation jobs.
- Route ownership for customer pinning (customer-tenant config):
  - Model: Active-Passive with single-region authority (primary) and read-replicas elsewhere.
  - Rationale: avoids split-brain for placement decisions; customer expectation for pinned locality.
  - Failover behavior: promote standby on region loss, announce via routing-control plane, set temporary traffic-steering rules.
- Rollout control (canary, A/B):
  - Model: Active-Active with global coordinator but per-region enforcement.
  - Rationale: rollouts need to be observable and can tolerate slight divergence; global policy plus local enforcer keeps latency down.

Operational states and quick actions (runbook style):
1) Region partial outage (API errors 5xx increasing, host flapping):
   - Step 1: throttle new leader elections by increasing lease TTL to avoid churn (patch config via config service).
   - Step 2: mark region as degraded in routing-control and start spilling 10-30% traffic to neighbor regions per policy.
   - Step 3: run healthcheck job for control-plane DB connectivity; if DB degraded, escalate to DB on-call.
2) Total region outage (BGP/major cloud-zone down):
   - Step 1: immediate traffic steering: enable emergency fallback policy (pre-canned in console).
   - Step 2: promote standby leaders for authority-limited surfaces (billing and tenant ownership) using promotion script that performs prechecks (replication lag under threshold, snapshot present).
   - Step 3: bake soft-read-only mode for auditing surfaces if replication not caught up.
3) Split-brain detection and reconciliation:
   - Detection signals: conflicting writes for same tenant, diverging allocation hashes, or lease double-grants.
   - Mitigation: pause cross-region writes, enable reconciliation worker with deterministic merge rules, notify owners and create incident.

Routing policy notes (for SRE and product):
- Prefer policy-based routing (weights + priorities) rather than hard cutovers. We keep 0/10/50/100% ramp profiles with automated rollback on errors.
- Use region-awareness in SDKs: prefer local region endpoints, but SDK should accept a fallback list (region, fallback-region, global).
- Cache invalidation: routing caches should be short (30s by default) and honor per-tenant override TTLs for heavy customers.

Telemetry and SLOs to monitor topology health:
- Leader churn rate (per-minute elections) - alert if > 3 in 5m for a shard.
- Cross-region reconciliation queue length and processing delay.
- Percent traffic hitting fallback routes by region (SLO: <0.5% sustained).

Title: Routing boundary design notes — hosted / dedicated / private (sketch)

Routing boundary design notes — hosted / dedicated / private (sketch)

Purpose:
Quick working notes to capture practical differences and trade-offs for tenant routing and isolation across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private modes. Goal is to bake a set of routing policy primitives we can reuse across control-plane designs and to highlight operational constraints for multi-region failover and data residency.

High-level summary (one-liner):
- Hosted: centralized control plane + global edge routing; logical tenant isolation, multi-tenant runtime pools, best-effort regional affinity, automatic fallbacks to cheaper model variants.
- Dedicated: per-customer reserved pools (soft network isolation), control plane still central for orchestration but routing table includes strong affinity to dedicated capacity; limited cross-tenant fallbacks.
- Private: customer-managed control plane (or private control-plane instances), network isolation by VPC/air-gap, explicit routing boundaries, no automatic cross-tenant fallback unless customer opts in.

Core routing primitives we should standardize:
- RouteKey: tenant_id + model_family + region_hint (string) — primary key for lookup in control-plane route table.
- Policy sets: {latency_slo, cost_tier, region_pref, isolation_level, fallback_strategy}.
- Route targets: {hosted_pool://pool-id, dedicated_cluster://customer-id, private_endpoint://customer-vpc}.
- Fallback chains: ordered list of route targets with a policy for token-level vs request-level fallback.

Isolation boundaries by mode (notes):
- Hosted:
  - Isolation: logical (namespaces + macroscopically shared GPUs). Tenant data in-flight is separated; persistent KV and caches are logically namespaced but share physical caches.
  - Network: public egress via cloud provider; no customer VPC.
  - Control plane: fully managed, global. Routing decisions made at edge control-plane and cached at edge proxies.
  - Trade-offs: easiest for automatic load balancing and global fallbacks; weakest for regulatory isolation.

- Dedicated:
  - Isolation: soft physical isolation — dedicated GPU pools guaranteed to a customer, but management plane still touches multiple dedicated pools.
  - Network: can be placed in tenant VPC or shared VPC with restricted subnets.
  - Control plane: central, but has stronger affinity pins and metadata mapping to dedicated capacity. Control plane can issue per-tenant routing that prefers dedicated clusters.
  - Trade-offs: predictable throughput, still allow controlled fallback to hosted pools (if tenant allows) or to read-only replica for lower-cost long-tail queries.

- Private:
  - Isolation: strong tenant control. Two sub-modes: (1) Redwood-managed private control-plane in customer VPC, or (2) customer-hosted control-plane (air-gapped).
  - Network: customer-managed networking, egress restrictions, possible HSM/KMS in-customer.
  - Control plane: local (per-customer) or federated; routing is owned by customer policy. Redwood's orchestrator only receives telemetry and metadata if configured.
  - Trade-offs: strongest compliance posture, but removes many automated global routing benefits and increases operational complexity for cross-region DR.

Practical routing examples and behavior:
- Tenant A (hosted, US primary) request arrives to edge in us-west: edge lookup by RouteKey picks hosted_pool://pool-23 (us-west). If pool is saturated, fallback_strategy is: try regional hosted_pool://pool-24 (us-east) with cross-region penalty header for caller. Automatic fallback to dedicated clusters not allowed unless tenant has "allow-dedicated-fallback" flag.

- Tenant B (dedicated, EU): control-plane maps tenant to dedicated_cluster://eu-ded-17. Edge will route to nearest gateway that has a healthy connection to eu-ded-17. If eu-ded-17 is unhealthy and tenant allows hosted overflow, control-plane may add hosted_pool://eu-overflow-4 to fallback chain but mark responses with "overflow=true" in trace.

- Tenant C (private, on-prem): RouteKey resolves to private_endpoint://vpc-12-local. Edge proxies in public cloud should not receive tenant data; routing happens via customer VPN/Direct Connect. No automatic routing fallback outside customer network unless explicit peering is configured.

Cache and KV semantics across modes:
- Hosted: shared prefix cache with tenant prefixing. Cache evictions are global; sensitive tenants can opt-out.
- Dedicated: optional per-customer cache instances colocated with the dedicated pool (preferred).
- Private: cache decisions entirely under customer control; Redwood provides optional caching component deployable inside the customer's network.

Control plane design implications:
- Centralized control plane makes policy rollouts and global routing adjustments easy (good for hosted + dedicated mixed fleets).
- For Private we need a federated model: control-plane operator (Redwood) publishes policy primitives, customer control plane consumes and decides local routing. Two-way reconciliation model and signed manifests.
- Critical: certificates and key distribution for route signing; use short-lived certs and rotate via KMS integrations.

Multi-region considerations and failure modes:
- Primary goals: preserve latency SLOs, respect data residency, and avoid cascading failures when a single region is disrupted.
- Region affinity: prefer same-region routing where available; penalty scoring function for cross-region picks (latency + egress cost + regulatory flags).
- Failover patterns per mode:
  - Hosted: automatic edge failover to next available region (configurable priority list).
  - Dedicated: failover to partner dedicated clusters if configured; otherwise optional hosted overflow.
  - Private: failover limited to customer-managed endpoints. Cross-region DR requires customer-run replication and routing rules.

Operational hooks and observability:
- Must emit per-request routing decision metadata: route_key, selected_target, fallback_history, policy_version, decision_timestamp.
- Tracing: correlate edge trace -> control-plane decision id -> runtime instance.
- Cost accounting: mark requests routed to hosted overflow separately for billing.

Unresolved questions / TODOs (working list):
- Policy granularity: do we allow per-route token-level fallback (mid-generation fallback) vs only per-request? Implications for model-state safety. (Action: PLAT-842 to prototype)
- Cache isolation SLAs: what eviction boundaries do compliance customers require? (Ping Legal and Security)
- Private control-plane UX: design signed manifests + reconciliation interval defaults (30s vs 5m). Security review required.
- Network egress accounting and cross-region costs: how to surface to customers when we overflow into other regions?

Title: routing-policy-escalation-matrix-and-simulation-notes

routing-policy-escalation-matrix-and-simulation-notes

Purpose and scope:
This note captures an operational runbook embedded in architecture guidance for our control-plane routing policies across regions. Intended readers: platform engineers, SREs, and on-call rotations who own routing policy distribution, state reconciliation, and multi-region failover behavior.

High-level problem statement:
When control-plane state diverges from dataplane policy (reason: partition, slow propagation, or buggy rollout), we see transient or sustained blackholes, route flapping, and customer-requested fallbacks. This doc ties routing policy design decisions to practical incident scenarios and prescribes an escalation matrix, deterministic remediation steps, and game-day simulation checklists.

Key primitives and assumptions:
- Control plane pushes policy bundles (route maps, priority lists, model-variant routing) to region controllers via gRPC multiplexed streams.
- Each region maintains a local policy cache and an applied-version ledger (applied_version, last_applied_ts).
- Heartbeat and compacted snapshot checkpoints every 30s; deltas streamed thereafter.
- Immutable model variants are referenced by digest; compatible fallbacks are encoded in the policy meta.
- Operators may trigger manual overrides via Console or CLI; overrides write to an override namespace that has precedence.

Metrics and SLOs to watch during incidents:
- policy_apply_latency_p50/p95/p99 (controlplane->region)
- policy_apply_error_rate (per-region)
- route_reject_rate (client-facing 5xx mapped to routing)
- KV_cache_divergence_count (differences between expected ledger and dataplane snapshot)
- request_fallback_rate (percentage routed to fallback model/region)
- inter_region_controlplane_rtt

Incident types and triggered alerts (examples):
1) Stale policy ledger in region (alert: KV_cache_divergence_count > 0 for > 120s)
   Observable symptoms: unchanged applied_version while controlplane shows newer version; customers in region see elevated 5xx or model regression.
   Immediate impact: incorrect routing, inability to access newly-rolled models or targeted throttles.

2) Partial control-plane partition (alert: inter_region_controlplane_rtt increased AND policy_apply_error_rate spike)
   Symptoms: some regions apply changes slowly, others fast; routing inconsistency across regions; occasional split-brain override conflicts.

3) Policy regression from a rollout (alert: route_reject_rate spike coincident with deploy tag)
   Symptoms: sudden route drop for a subset of customer tokens; increased fallback to default model.

4) Oscillating DNS/edge routing causing flapping (alert: client connection count oscillations + route change events)
   Symptoms: client reconns, timeouts, cache thrash.

Escalation matrix (decision tree text):
- Tier 0 (on-call platform engineer): verify alerts, gather metrics, check applied_version, check console overrides. If KV_cache_divergence_count > 0, run local reconciliation step (Step A). If simple rollout regression and can rollback via Console within 2 minutes, perform rollback.
- Tier 1 (senior platform eng): if Step A fails or partition detected, escalate to Tier 1. Tier 1 reviews control-plane cluster health, ETCD/consensus state, and network ACLs. If consensus unhealthy, initiate leader re-election or promote standby cluster.
- Tier 2 (platform lead + SRE): if manual fixes cause customer impact > 15 minutes or repeated flaps, open incident bridge, notify affected PMs/CS, and prepare cross-region traffic migration plan.

Concrete runbook steps (flat deterministic commands and checks):
Step A: Fast reconciliation for stale applied_version
- 1) Run: ./scripts/controlplane/check_applied_versions.sh --region <region> 
- 2) Check leader log: kubectl -n controlplane logs deploy/controlplane-leader -c applier --since=10m | grep "apply_error"
- 3) If applier process shows OOM or crashloop: kubectl rollout restart deploy/controlplane-applier -n controlplane --timeout=5m
- 4) If restart does not clear divergence in 90s, run: ./scripts/controlplane/force_snapshot_push.sh --region <region> --target-version <controlplane_version_digest>
- 5) Post-check: curl -sS http://<region-controller>/metrics | grep applied_version ; expect >= controlplane_version_digest

Step B: Partitioned control plane (partial region visibility)
- 1) Confirm network ACLs: gcloud compute firewall-rules list --filter="name~'cp-.*'" or aws ec2 describe-network-acls --region <region>
- 2) Validate etcd consensus: kubectl exec -n controlplane etcd-0 -- etcdctl endpoint status --cluster
- 3) If 2/3 etcd members unhealthy: add resource pressure action: scale controlplane statefulset replicas from N to N+1 in a region with low load (kubectl scale sts controlplane --replicas=<n+1>)
- 4) If metrics show heartbeat re-established, run Step A reconciliation.

Step C: Rollout regression rollback
- 1) Identify deploy tag from CI: check linked_artifacts or ci pipeline: https://ci.redwood.internal/pipelines/
- 2) If deployment < 15 minutes ago and rollback window open: Console -> Rollouts -> Select policy bundle -> Rollback to previous stable version.
- 3) If Console is unresponsive, use CLI: rwectl policy rollback --bundle <previous_digest> --regions <affected_regions> --force
- 4) Monitor route_reject_rate and route_success_rate for 10 minutes.

Step D: Cross-region traffic migration (hard mitigation)
- Preconditions: Tier 2 approval, run during maintenance window or after stakeholder notification.
- 1) Whitelist customers: construct migration list via query against tenant routing map.
- 2) Apply migration policy with gradual weight shift: rwectl traffic shift --from-region <bad> --to-region <good> --tenants-file migration-list.csv --rate 5%/min
- 3) Observe latency and success percent; roll back migration if per-tenant p50 latency increases > 50ms or error rate > 2x baseline.

Safety and invariants (to avoid cascading failures):
- Never apply a global "force override" across all regions unless Tier 2 approves.
- Prefer increasing fallback rate to a cached stable model over forcing a new policy bundle when propagation is uncertain.
- All force_snapshot_push and rollback actions must be logged to incident channel and annotated in the policy audit log.

Escalation channel templates (Slack snippets):
- When escalating to Tier 1: "@platform-tier1 seeing policy_apply_error_rate=12% and KV_cache_divergence_count=3 in us-west-2. Current applied_version=sha:abcd, controlplane target=sha:ef01. Running Step A (reconciliation). Joining bridge: <bridge link>"
- When moving to cross-region migration: "INCIDENT PRIORITY P1: initiating controlled traffic migration from us-west-2 -> us-east-1 for affected tenants. Tier 2 approval granted by @lead. Link to migration tracker: <sheet link>"

Game-day simulation checklist (run quarterly):
- 1) Simulate a policy bundle regression: deploy canary policy to a single region and assert correct rollback cadence and alerts.
- 2) Simulate control-plane partition by blocking gRPC between one region controller pair for 120s and validate reconciliation behaves per Step B.
- 3) Run chaos experiment for instance restarts of applier pods during high apply load. Confirm time-to-recover < 180s.
- 4) Validate cross-region migration script on staging with synthetic tenants and confirm no data leak in audit logs.

Open questions and action items:
- Q1: Should rollback be automated for specific class of policy regressions? Action: experiment in staging with limited automation and revertibility (owner: Marco Chen, due: 2025-01-15).
- Q2: Improve observability of ledger deltas: ship per-delta diff logs to centralized bigquery + a dashboard (owner: Sofia Ramirez, due: 2025-03-01).

Appendix A: Quick commands reference
- check versions: ./scripts/controlplane/check_applied_versions.sh --region <r>
- force snapshot: ./scripts/controlplane/force_snapshot_push.sh --region <r> --target-version <v>
- list control plane pods: kubectl get pods -n controlplane -o wide
- tail applier logs: kubectl -n controlplane logs deploy/controlplane-applier -c applier -f

Appendix B: Contact matrix
- Platform Tier 0: rotation@redwood-inference.com (primary: Asha Patel)
- Platform Tier 1: leads@redwood-inference.com (primary: Marco Chen)
- Product/CS notify list: product-alerts@redwood.com
