It privileges explicit commands and decision boundaries (e.g., thresholds for KV_cache_divergence_count and allowed rollback windows) to reduce ambiguity during on-call.

Title: Control plane orchestration roles — decision log and ownership rationale

Control plane orchestration roles — decision log and ownership rationale

Purpose and scope:
This note captures the rationale and concise ownership map for the control plane components that make routing decisions in multi-region deployments. Focus is on three logical layers: API gateway (ingress/edge), orchestration (control plane decisioning, policies, rollouts), and runtime adapters (region-local adapters that translate control-plane intent into runtime actions).

Intended audience: platform engineers, runtime owners, SRE, and product stakeholders who are designing or integrating routing and fallback policies across regions.

Summary of decision statements (short):
- API Gateway: owns public ingress, auth, TLS termination, and coarse-grained region affinity. Must be simple and stable; not responsible for model-level rollout decisions.
- Orchestration layer (control plane): owns routing policies, model variant catalog, rollout logic (canary/A-B), global fallback rules, and quota accounting for cross-region policies.
- Runtime adapters: own the local execution surface, health signaling, local autoscaling triggers, and applying runtime-specific optimizations (quantization profile selection, kernel hints).

Why we split responsibilities this way (rationale):
- Separation of concerns reduces blast radius: edge can remain minimal and reliable; complex policy logic lives in orchestrator where we can version and audit it.
- Local runtimes must be able to act autonomously under degraded control-plane connectivity; that capability is essential for meeting regional SLOs.
- Centralized catalog + decentralized execution enables quick rollouts and consistent observability across environments (hosted/dedicated/private).

Concise ASCII ownership map (logical):

[Client] -> [API Gateway (edge)] -> [Orchestrator (control plane)] -> [Region Adapter] -> [Serving Runtime]

Responsibilities by component (detailed):
- API Gateway (Edge):
  - Tasks: TLS, auth, rate limit, client-facing metrics, coarse region routing (latency-based or geo-preference), initial header enrichment (x-region-hint), basic request shaping (max tokens override per plan).
  - NOT owned: model-level rollback, token-level billing reconciliation, runtime autoscaling knobs.
  - Owners: eng-platform-edge + eng-sre.

- Orchestration / Control Plane:
  - Tasks: policy store (routing policy DSL), model catalog and compatibility matrix, rollout engine (staged canary, weighted split), fallback policy engine (per-tenant, global), decision history (audit), quota/shaping coordination across regions, rollout-safety checks (quality/regression gating).
  - Exposes: decision API (sync) and async notification stream for adapters; audit log; simulated dry-run endpoints for product and SE to test changes.
  - Owners: eng-platform-orchestration (primary), eng-applied-ml (policy inputs), product for rollout definitions.

- Runtime Adapters (per-region):
  - Tasks: receive decisions, translate into runtime config (instance-to-model mapping, queue priorities), local health checks and metrics emission, autonomous fallback behavior if control plane unreachable, enforce local resource limits and pre-configured cache policies.
  - Runtime adapters must be lightweight and idempotent when replaying commands.
  - Owners: eng-serving-runtime (adapter code), local infra teams for region-specific infra.

Edge cases and failure modes we explicitly designed for:
1) Control plane unreachable (partial outage): adapters use last-known policy + pre-configured safety defaults. This includes max per-customer rate caps and sticky default model variant mapping.
2) Region isolation (network partition): API Gateway should be able to route to alternate region using orchestrator fallback hints; orchestration fallback may be disabled by tenant if they require strict data residency.
3) Upscale event where a region exhausts capacity: orchestrator signals burst policy to adapters and API Gateway can triage requests to lower-cost or higher-latency regions depending on tenant fallback policy.

Routing policy primitives (DSL sketch):
- match { tenant, model_family, request_latency, model_quality } -> action { region_preference: [pdx, iad, lon], variant_weight: {v1: 80, v2: 20}, fallback: {redirect, queue, reject}, ttl: 120s }
Notes: TTL on decisions allows adapters to cache for short windows; orchestration can push immediate invalidations when safety gates trip.

Decision log (chronological, condensed):
- 2025-03-11 — Initial proposal: single control plane with region-aware routing. Problems: too many edge responsibilities; risk of cold-starts on failover. (author: Marcus Chen)
- 2025-04-02 — Variant: push routing decisions entirely to edge. Rejected because it made edge too complex and slowed rollout velocity. (review: eng-sre, eng-platform)
- 2025-05-17 — Adopted hybrid: edge handles coarse routing and authorizations; orchestrator owns model-level rollouts & policy DSL. Approved with experimental canary in iad. (owner: Elena Torres)
- 2025-08-09 — Added requirement: adapters must operate independently for up to 15 minutes without control plane connectivity. Rationale: meet 99th percentile SLO during control-plane upgrades. (owner: Priya Nair)
- 2025-11-21 — Introduced tenant-level opt-out flag for cross-region fallback (compliance-driven). Requires explicit sign-off and opt-in for fallback otherwise. (owner: Alyssa Grant)

Operational runbook highlights (short):
- Deploying policy changes: use dry-run mode for 30 minutes against synthetic traffic; check quality metrics in console before enabling rollout.
- Emergency rollback: orchestrator exposes a kill-switch that sets all weighted policies to 100% stable variant and propagates invalidation to adapters. API Gateway will start blocking new model pulls for a short TTL to stop rollout.
- Observability: every routing decision gets a decision_id returned to the client and logged; correlates with token-level billing for cost analysis.

Multi-region considerations (practical guidance):
- Regional model pinning: for compliance, allow tenants to pin to specific regions; orchestrator must enforce pinning at policy-evaluation time.
- Geographic latency steering: edge should choose a preferred region by latency probe; orchestration can override for capacity reasons.
- Data egress: orchestrator must annotate decision with egress_cost_estimate and data_residency_tags. Billing tags should be emitted by adapters.

Open questions / trade-offs (to resolve):
- Should orchestration maintain soft-state placement suggestions (where to spin new runtime capacity) or should that be left to infra/autoscaler? Proposal: orchestrator emits placement hints but not direct autoscaling commands.
- How large should the TTL be on cached decisions? Current default 120s — tradeoff between responsiveness and control-plane load.
- Authentication model for decision API: mTLS + short-lived tokens vs signed JWTs. Prefer mTLS for adapters but need onboarding UX.

Action items and owners (next steps):
- (Elena) Draft API schema for decision API (v0) and publish by 2026-03-01.
- (Marcus) Implement dry-run harness that feeds synthetic traffic into orchestrator and adapters by 2026-03-15.
- (Priya) Define adapter autonomy spec (timeouts, retries, default fallbacks) and land as RFC by 2026-02-28.
- (Alyssa) Update compliance checklist to cover tenant opt-out lifecycle and auditing by 2026-03-10.

Title: Multi-region routing & control-plane failover playbook (working notes)

Multi-region routing & control-plane failover playbook (working notes)

Purpose:
This is a working architecture + runbook hybrid covering expected failure modes for the control plane and request routing across multiple regions. Goal is to provide an operational checklist and decision tree engineers can follow during incidents, and to capture architecture rationale for future automation.

Scope:
- Global control-plane components: API gateway, control-plane API servers, config store (etcd), leader-election, routing-policy service, heartbeats.
- Regional components: regional routers (ingress), model-serving clusters, edge proxies, health-check aggregators.
- Traffic routing policies: latency-based, cost-tiered, customer-pin, capacity-aware.

High-level assumptions:
- Each region runs a local routing agent that receives global policy and reports capacity metrics to the control plane every 10s.
- Control-plane state is stored in a quorum-backed etcd cluster spanning two primary and one arbiter (eventual plan to move to three full voting members).
- Failover uses: primary->secondary region; fallbacks to lower-cost model variants if capacity constrained.

Key metrics to watch (dashboards):
- Control-plane API error rate (5m/1m)
- etcd leader term changes / election count
- Routing-policy delta apply latency (time between policy publish and agents ack)
- Regional healthscore (avg latency p50/p95, token throughput, memory/CPU on serving nodes)
- Unroutable requests (%) and fallback-activation rate

Incident scenarios + runbook steps:
1) Control-plane API errors (500s) across regions
- Triage: check control-plane pods in primary region: kubectl -n controlplane get pods -o wide; check restart counts.
- Check etcd health: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=$ENDPOINT endpoint health; if unhealthy, check logs for tombstones / disk pressure.
- If leader flapping: capture leader history (etcdctl endpoint status) and increase logging.
- Short mitigation: scale control-plane API replicas (kubectl scale deployment/controlplane-api --replicas=5) if resource saturation.
- If etcd quorum lost and cannot be recovered: follow emergency restore (see Confluence-ETCD-DR) - caution: data loss risk. Consider redirecting routing agents to a standby read-only control-plane (see below).
- Communication: post summary to #platform-ops with runbook steps taken, time, and link to incident channel.

2) Routing policy publish delay / agents not acking
- Check policy-service logs and the outgoing queue. Run: curl -s http://policy-service:8080/queue | jq .pending
- If queue growth is due to slow downstream (network / proxy), confirm network ACLs and NAT gateway metrics.
- Short mitigation: enable policy diff mode: publish minimal override (critical-fallback) to force immediate agent fallback to safe-policy. Command: /scripts/publish-fallback.sh --policy-id critical-fallback
- If a specific region not acking: SSH to regional agent leader, run agent diag: /opt/router/diag.sh --status. Look for time skew, TLS handshake errors.

3) Region-wide network partition (region R loses connectivity to control plane)
- Detect: regional agent stops reporting; control-plane dashboard shows drop in heartbeats.
- Runbook: automatic behavior should have regional routers enter 'graceful autonomous mode' serving pinned customers allowed in local cache for up to 20 minutes. Confirm autonomous mode active: GET /agents/$REGION/state -> returns autonomous: true.
- Manual: if autonomous mode not triggered, force switch by publishing local policy: POST /policy/localize --region=$R --ttl=20m.
- If region cannot reach other regions for failover, ensure can serve pinned customers by routing to local smaller instances. Notify CS teams for impacted customers.

4) Cross-region routing loop / mis-route (policy bug)
- Symptoms: requests bounce between regions or zig-zag, p50 latency spikes across multiple regions.
- Triage: capture request traces (trace-id) and inspect routing decisions in trace. Use /traces/lookup?trace_id=... to get path.
- Mitigation: immediately apply emergency circuit-breaker policy to stop cross-region routing: /policy/enact --id circuit-breaker-global --action block-cross-region=true.
- Rollback: identify policy commit that caused loop (policy-service accepts last-commit id). Use git history of policy-repo to revert and re-publish safe commit.

5) Capacity shortage in a primary region (headroom exhausted)
- Auto-behavior: routing engine should shift new requests to secondary region based on capacity scoring. Verify by checking routing decisions stream.
- If automatic shifting isn't happening: check scoring service (score-service logs), confirm capacity signals reported by regional agents. If missing, manual override: update routing weight for region X -> reduce to 0.4 (POST /routing/weights).
- Consider applying model-variant fallback to smaller quantized model for non-enterprise customers: POST /model-routing/fallback --percent=30 --variants=[q4_0,q8_0].

Standby control-plane / read-only fallback mode (short description):
- We maintain a warm standby control-plane in secondary region with config sync of last-known-good policy every minute. In DR events, we promote standby to read-only mode for agents to continue reading policy without writes. Promotion steps: 1) verify standby etcd has consistent snapshot, 2) flip DNS to standby endpoints in global gw ttl (script: scripts/promote-standby.sh), 3) disable writes in console (feature flag).

Title: Control Plane: operator scenarios and routing decisions

Control Plane: operator scenarios and routing decisions

Purpose and scope

Quick / messy operator-focused notes to capture ownership edges between API gateway, orchestrator, and runtime adapters when we need to make fast routing decisions across regions and capacity tiers. This is a working doc (notes, scenarios, operator actions, and TODOs) — intended for platform on-call and platform-ownership syncs.

Audience
- Platform engineers (on-call)
- SREs who escalate to platform
- Product/platform PMs who make rollout decisions

High-level problem statement
We expose a unified Redwood API surface but traffic may traverse multiple control-plane components: ingress/API gateway -> orchestration service (route decision + rollout rules) -> runtime adapters (model routing, quantization variant selection, regional endpoints). During partial failures, capacity constraints, or multi-region cutovers we must coordinate fast decisions with clear ownership. Operational ambiguity causes: 1) conflicting fallbacks, 2) double-counted quotas, 3) silent latency regressions. This doc enumerates operator scenarios and recommends clear actions and owners.

Service responsibilities (short operator cheat-sheet)
- API Gateway (team: eng-gateway):
  - Accepts/validates client requests, enforces auth/quotas at the route level, applies global rate-limits.
  - Fast-fail for malformed or obviously rate-limited requests.
  - Emits ingress-level latency metrics and request traces.
  - Owner for TLS, ingress scaling, WAF rules.

- Orchestrator (team: eng-orchestration):
  - Decision point: given request metadata, selects target model variant, region, and adapter pool.
  - Responsible for rollout policies (canary %, A/B), fallback policy table (region fallback, model-family fallback).
  - Enforces routing constraints (tier-based routing, geo restrictions).
  - Owner for policy config, rollout state, and feature flags.

- Runtime Adapters (team: eng-serving-runtime):
  - Translate orchestration decisions into adapter-specific invocation (batching, quantized binary selection), maintain health status for adapter pools.
  - Implement per-pool throttles and backpressure signals to orchestrator.
  - Owner for adapter health, kernel/quantization compatibility, and pool capacity reports.

- Cache Service (team: eng-storage-cache):
  - Prefix/KV caching for repeated prompts. Acts as optional short-circuit for low-latency responses.
  - Owner for cache eviction policies and metrics.

- Quota & Billing (team: eng-platform-ops):
  - Enforces tenant quotas after gateway acceptance, reconciles usage with billing, emits billing metrics.

Common ambiguity zones (where operators need clear guidance)
1) Fallback ownership: if orchestrator routes to fallback region because adapter pool signals degraded, who marks the request for billing in the fallback region? Answer: Quota & Billing uses the final invoke record produced by runtime adapters. Gateway still records ingress counters.
2) Double-fallback: gateway-level DNS failover + orchestrator fallback becomes a double-hop. Operator action: disable gateway DNS failover if orchestrator-managed cross-region fallback is enabled for the route.
3) Cache vs Adapter consistency: stale cache hits may serve older model outputs (version mismatch). Owner: cache service must validate model-version header with orchestrator during cache set; runtime adapters must insert model-version header on successful execution.

Operator scenarios and playbook (step-by-step)
Scenario A: Single-region adapter pool overload (high latency, 503s)\- Detection: adapter pool health shows increased tail latency and 5xx; orchestrator marks pool degraded, orchestrator metrics show increased queue depth. Alert: ORCH-HighLatency-Pool.\- Immediate operator actions:\ 1) Confirm degradation in runtime-adapter dashboard (owner: eng-serving-runtime).\ 2) Orchestrator should automatically reroute to secondary variant or region per policy (if enabled). If automatic reroute did not happen, operator triggers manual policy flip in orchestrator (owner: eng-orchestration).\ 3) If reroute elevated latency for some tenants, gate via rollout % (orchestrator).\ 4) Notify gateway team if ingress rate needs to be temporarily rate-limited or traffic shaped (owner: eng-gateway).\- Post-incident follow-up:\ 1) Root cause (resource exhaustion, bad kernel, network blips).\ 2) Add a protective rollout rule: auto-throttle when queue depth > X.

Scenario B: Regional cloud outage (us-east-1) with live Dedicated customers pinned to region\- Detection: broad service degradation, region metrics down, health probes failing.\- Immediate operator actions:\ 1) Assess customer pinning/constraints via orchestrator UI (owner: eng-orchestration + customer success).\ 2) If customer is pinned and cannot be moved, escalate to sales/CS and SREs for mitigation; raise incident call.\ 3) For unpinned traffic: orchestrator should reroute to next-best region per cost/latency tradeoff. If orchestrator policy disallows cross-region fallback for specific workloads (compliance), mark those requests as impacted and route to degraded response path.\ 4) Gateway DNS failover must be checked: if DNS cutover already in place, coordinate rollback with gateway owners to avoid routing loops.\- Post-incident:\ 1) Review pinned-customer policy and disaster-playbook for pinned capacity (customer-failover contracts).

Scenario C: Orchestrator policy bug causes routing loops (orchestrator->adapter->orchestrator retry)\- Detection: amplified traffic spikes, repeated traces showing same request id hitting orchestrator multiple times. Alert: ORCH-Routing-Loop.\- Immediate operator actions:\ 1) Quarantine the offending policy in orchestrator (owner: eng-orchestration).\ 2) Pause retries at gateway-level if possible (owner: eng-gateway).\ 3) Scale down orchestrator evaluation workers if loops cause control-plane CPU exhaustion.\ 4) Check runtime adapters for idempotency and request dedupe.\- Post-incident: add automatic loop detection (trace cycles > 2) and circuit-breaker in orchestrator.

Decision matrix: who does what in 90s, 10min, 60min windows\- 90s:\  - API Gateway: emit ingress metrics, fast-fail traffic waves, apply emergency rate-limits.\  - Runtime Adapters: update health flags to orchestrator.\  - Orchestrator: evaluate automatic fallback and execute if policy exists.\- 10min:\  - Platform on-call (primary): decide manual reroutes and brief stakeholders.\  - Gateway: temporarily reduce global rate for noisy tenants.\  - Serving runtime: triage kernel/adapter failures and consider draining pool.\- 60min:\  - Cross-team incident call, customer notifications, escalate to product & sales for pinned customers.\  - Config changes (rollout policy adjustments) applied with small percentages first.

Routing policy examples (pseudocode)
- Geo-first failover policy:\  if region.available and latency < 200ms then route(region) else route(nearest_region_with_capacity)
- Cost-aware fallback:\  prefer cheaper variant if latency delta < 50ms and predicted token cost reduces by >10%
- Compliance-lock:\  if tenant.requires_data_residency then restrict(route) to tenant.region_pools

Operational invariants (must hold)
1) Orchestrator is the single source-of-truth for routing decisions. If gateway has a conflicting routing behavior it must be explicitly labeled and justified.
2) Runtime adapters must always report final invoke metadata (region, adapter-id, model-version, tokens) for billing reconciliation.
3) No silent double-billing: billing uses adapter final records, but gateway counters are used for rate-limits only.

Observability checklist for on-call\- Dashboards: ingress-qps, ingress-5xx, orchestrator-decision-latency, adapter-pool-tail-latency, adapter-5xx-rate, cache-hit-rate.\- Traces: end-to-end trace correlated by request id; ensure orchestrator decision span is present and annotated with policy id.\- Alerts: ORCH-Decision-Latency, ADAPTER-Pool-Health, GATEWAY-Rate-Limit-Surge, CACHE-Thundering-Herd.

Runbook excerpts (fast commands)\- Force a policy rollback in orchestrator (console link): ORCH console -> policies -> rollback to previous stable -> apply with 5% ramp. (owner: eng-orchestration)\- Remove gateway DNS failover: gateway console -> route -> toggle DNS-failover=false -> confirm with prod-dns. (owner: eng-gateway)\- Quarantine adapter pool: runtime console -> pool -> mark unhealthy -> drain -> notify. (owner: eng-serving-runtime)

Open questions / TODOs\- TODO: Add policy schema v2 to make fallbacks declarative and composable (work item: JIRA-PLAT-1501).\- Question: Should orchestrator own tenant-level sticky-routing (session affinity) or should that live at the gateway? Proposal: orchestrator owns affinity for model-version stickiness; gateway can implement short-lived sticky sessions for connection-affinity.\- TODO: Add a canonical field in trace that indicates final billing region (to remove ambiguity).\- TODO: Write e2e chaos test that simulates adapter pool flapping + orchestrator rollback and validate no customer traffic is double-counted.

Post-incident action items (owners)
- Add auto-circuit-breaker for routing loops (owner: Priya / eng-orchestration) – due 2025-02-15\- Add model-version header enforcement for cache entries (owner: Marco / eng-storage-cache) – due 2025-02-28\- Policy schema draft v2 (owner: Aaron / eng-platform) – due 2025-03-10

Notes and references
- Keep this doc intentionally practical — aim to capture the immediate operational decisions rather than architecture-only diagrams.
- For the canonical architecture and past ownership maps, see Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/PLAT/Control+Plane+Topology\- Related PRs: https://github.com/redwood-inference/control-plane/pull/789

Changelog\- 2025-01-10: created (initial scenarios and actions)\- 2025-02-02: added decision matrix, runbook commands, and open TODOs

End of doc

Title: Control plane ownership & regional routing sketch

Control plane ownership & regional routing sketch

Purpose
---
Working sketch to clarify service boundaries, who owns which control-plane responsibilities, and the routing rules that span regions and tiers. Intended audience: platform-engineering, serving-runtime, SRE, and product infra. Not final; collection of constraints, proposals, and open questions.

Scope and non-goals
---
- Scope: API gateway surface, orchestration layer (control-plane), region-aware routing policy, runtime adapter responsibilities (GPU pools, quantized variants, fallback logic).
- Non-goal: implementation details of kernel selection in runtime nodes (that's serving-runtime). This doc instead defines the contracts and ownership for higher-level decisions.

High-level desiderata
---
- Predictable latency SLAs per customer tier (hosted vs dedicated).
- Deterministic fallback: an app should not see unexplained model/region jumps.
- Cost-aware routing: prefer cheaper compatible variants when within quality delta.
- Clear ownership so on-call rotations have crisp escalation paths.

Component-level ownership (summary)
---
- Edge API Gateway (ingest, auth, rate-limits, initial routing decisions): owned by platform-edge (oncall: platform-edge). Responsible for request classification, enforcing quotas, and selecting initial route policy.
- Control-plane Orchestrator (route policy execution, rollout orchestration, canary/A-B rules): owned by platform-orchestration (oncall: platform-orchestration). Exposes an evaluation API for gateway to call (lightweight, <10ms target).
- Runtime Adapter Layer (adapter per runtime family: NVIDIA RTX, A100, CPU-quantized, on-prem HSM clusters): owned by serving-runtime (oncall: serving-runtime). Responsible for compatibility checks, health signals, and spin-up/teardown of instances.
- Regional Routing Service (region affinity, compliance constraints, regional capacity accounting): owned by platform-regional (oncall: platform-regional). Provides authoritative region availability and fault-domain mapping.
- Policy Store & Audit (policy JSON, rollouts history, audit trails): owned by platform-control-data (oncall: platform-control-data).

Routing decision flow (at a glance)
---
1) Gateway receives request, authenticates, attaches token metadata (customer tier, dataset tags, prompt length distribution hint).
2) Gateway queries local policy cache -> if stale beyond 15s call Orchestrator / Regional Routing Service for authoritative decision.
3) Orchestrator computes candidate routes (ordered preference list) using: region affinity, tier SLAs, cost tier, runtime compatibility.
4) Gateway attempts candidate 1; if runtime adapter responds with capacity or incompatible error, gateway retries candidate 2, etc., with exponential backoff and strict timeout budget.
5) Successful route is recorded to Policy Store for telemetry.

Routing policy primitives (proposed)
---
- region_preference: list (e.g., [us-west-2, us-east-1])
- min_latency_ms: soft threshold per tier
- acceptable_quality_delta: e.g., 2% relative scoring drop allowed for cheaper variants
- runtime_compat_tags: required features (kv_cache, quantized_int8, half_precision)
- failover_strategy: immediate, delayed, sticky (sticky preferred for session-based chat)
- capacity_reserve: boolean for dedicated customers

Adapter compatibility & fallback rules (notes)
---
- Adapter should expose a /capabilities endpoint: comma-separated tags and a numeric "compat_score" per model family.
- Orchestrator must be able to prefer adapters with same model family and quantization (preferred) and only fall back to variants with documented quality delta.
- For on-prem/private deployments, runtime adapters may advertise 'no-fallback' to prevent cross-tenant leakage; orchestrator must respect.

Multi-region considerations
---
- Region affinity: prefer same-region serving where available to minimize latency; otherwise, honor compliance tag (e.g., data-residency: eu-only).
- Cross-region fallbacks must include a controlled TTL for session data rehydration (e.g., KV-caches may be invalidated).
- Cost-aware cross-region routing: if remote region cost > 2x, only allow fallback for high-priority requests or after local timeout threshold.
- Global outage behavior: define a "degraded read-mode" where inference requests can be routed to smaller/cheaper backends with explicit header X-Inference-Degraded: true so downstream apps can surface "degraded" UX.

Operational contracts (SLO/SLA)
---
- Orchestrator API: 99.9% availability; median 95th pct <= 10ms for policy lookup in-region; cross-region lookups <= 30ms.
- Gateway-to-adapter handshake: 99.95% success within configured time budget; failover retries bounded to avoid cascading requests.
- Incident path: platform-edge -> platform-orchestration -> serving-runtime -> platform-regional (primary escalation).

Telemetry & observability (what to record)
---
- Per-request chosen-route, candidate list, latencies per step, adapter capability snapshots, cost_estimate, and quality_delta if fallback used.
- Rollout events: who changed policy, diff, and rollout id.
- Cross-region fallback frequency by tenant (to surface mis-sized regional capacity or policy misconfig).

Open questions / decisions to make
---
- Should the gateway perform the first compatibility filter (cheap) or always consult orchestrator for policy truth? Tradeoff: latency vs central reasoning. Proposal: gateway local cache + soft-filter, orchestrator authoritative.
- How granular are the capability tags? Model family + quantization + runtime feature list or free-form? Proposal: a fixed set of tags with a versioned schema (v1 tags).
- Sticky session semantics: per-customer vs per-conversation. Need product input. (see PLAT-REQ-56)
- Backpressure: if adapter signals overload, do we queue or immediate failover? Suggest immediate failover with telemetry to avoid cascading queues.

Short-term action items (next 2 sprints)
---
- (INF-3120) Define capability tag schema v0.1 — owner: serving-runtime (Marco).
- (INF-3121) Implement gateway policy cache with 15s TTL and fallback path — owner: platform-edge (Priya).
- (INF-3122) Sketch orchestrator API contract and perf targets — owner: platform-orchestration (Aisha).
- Add canary test that intentionally triggers cross-region fallback to measure UX and telemetry end-to-end.

Appendix: example policy fragment (human readable)
---
- customer_tier: dedicated
- region_preference: [ eu-west-1, eu-central-1 ]
- acceptable_quality_delta: 0.01
- failover_strategy: sticky
- runtime_compat_tags: [ "kv-cache", "fp16", "quant-int8-optional" ]

Notes / references / threads
---
- Slack: #platform-routing thread id: slack.com/archives/C01234567/p1700000000000000
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/987
- Related confluence: Control Plane Vision (linked above)

Title: Stabilize embedding metric behavior across SDK versions and server-side adapters

Stabilize embedding metric behavior across SDK versions and server-side adapters

Problem summary:
Customers rely on both cosine and dot-product semantics for embedding similarity across SDK versions and community clients. Recent changes to internal normalization (automatic L2 normalization for some model families) and a server-side metric adapter introduced subtle behavioral differences: identical vector pairs sometimes changed score by >1e-3, and downstream reranking precision at top-5 changed for a small portion of queries.

Scope and goals:
1) Define and enforce a stable, explicit contract for how Redwood computes embedding similarity (cosine vs dot) at the API surface across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
2) Implement a compatibility layer so older SDKs/clients that assumed pre-change behavior continue to get deterministic scores unless they opt in to new semantics.
3) Repair and harden server-side normalization logic so it is numerically stable, perf-conscious, and documented.
4) Add telemetry, tests, and a gradual rollout plan to measure impact on quality and latency.

Why this matters now:
- Reranking customers are sensitive to small score shifts (precision@k regressions can break UIs).
- Private deployments need a deterministic rule they can pin to for audits.
- Inconsistent semantics across SDKs creates support overhead and migration churn.

Non-goals:
- Changing default model embeddings or retraining models.
- Rewriting customer reranker logic; we will offer migration guidance instead.
Define public API contract describing difference between 'metric=cosine' and 'metric=dot' and the treatment of input norms
Server returns identical scores (within 1e-8 relative) for a defined compatibility mode compared to pre-change baseline for a representative test corpus
New normalization path reduces per-request CPU overhead by <=5% at p95 for embedding-only endpoints compared to prior implementation, or document trade-offs if slightly slower
Telemetry shows no statistically significant regression in precision@5 and precision@10 on the production reranker testset after gradual rollout (95% CI), or we can successfully rollback
Public SDK changelog and migration guide published and linked from API docs
Audit current code paths that perform normalization: runtime embedding pipeline, Local adapter, and compatibility shim
Design deterministic compatibility mode API flag: e.g., 'metric=cosine&norm_mode=preserve' and spec for parameter precedence
Implement server-side normalization utility with stable algorithms (Kahan-like reduction where needed) and explicit epsilon handling for zero norms
Add end-to-end unit tests and numeric regression tests against archived baseline vectors (small corpus from reranker suite)
Add telemetry: record metric used, input norms distribution, pre/post-normalization checksum, and per-request score delta buckets
Create SDK patches for JS and Python exposing metric and norm_mode flags and adding integration tests
Run canary rollout on 5% of traffic with automatic rollback thresholds for precision@5 and latency
Prepare and publish migration guide and release notes; coordinate with Support and Solutions teams

These double-normalize in some flows. Drafting safe single-source-of-truth for normalization.

Title: Embed Gatekeeper: Canary + Per-tenant Version Pinning and Rollback Playbook

Embed Gatekeeper: Canary + Per-tenant Version Pinning and Rollback Playbook

Goal: Add a robust 'Embed Gatekeeper' flow for onboarding new embedding model versions that enforces quality, latency, and cost constraints while enabling per-tenant version pinning and fast rollback. This work spans: automated canary evaluation, drift and quality thresholds, quantization compatibility checks, end-to-end latency budgets for the reranking endpoint, cost delta estimation, and an operator-facing rollback/playbook. The ticket covers design, infra changes, telemetry, tests, and runbook docs.
1) New model can be deployed to production with an automated canary that runs synthetic and sampled traffic checks. 2) Canary emits pass/fail signals for quality (embedding cosine drift vs baseline), P50/P95 latency, and token-cost delta. 3) Per-tenant pinning API allows admins to pin tenants to a specific model version (create/read/delete). 4) Operator UI shows canary health with drilldowns and a single-click rollback that routes traffic back to previous version. 5) Rollback completes within configured SLA (90s) and has a verified no-loss path for in-flight requests. 6) Telemetry feeds available in the Console (cost/latency/quality).
Phase 1: Canary infra (2 weeks) - implement lightweight canary runner that replays sampled requests through candidate model; integrate with existing inference gateway; add metrics export (cosine_drift, rerank_ndcg_sampled, p50_latency, p95_latency, cost_per_request). Phase 2: Tenant pinning and routing (1.5 weeks) - persist per-tenant model pins in Config DB, extend router to honor pin, add API + Console controls. Phase 3: Rollback and runbook (1 week) - implement single-click rollback, ensure KV cache warm-path fallback, create operator playbook and safety checks. Phase 4: QA and perf validation (1 week) - run stress tests for embedding throughput, validate batching impact, and verify quantized variant compatibility. Phase 5: Launch and monitoring (ongoing) - dashboarding, alerts, and post-launch sample audits.
1) Internal canary: enable on 5% of internal test traffic for 48h. 2) External beta: allow opt-in for 3 pilot customers via tenant pin API; monitor for 7 days. 3) Gradual ramp: 0% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% across non-pin customers with automated gate checks at each step. 4) Full deprecation window: when sunsetting older version, notify pinned tenants and provide migration guidance; refuse automatic swap until pin removed or tenant approves. 5) Emergency rollback: authorized operators can trigger immediate rollback; system performs health-checks and warms primary KV cache before switching.

- Include fuzzed queries with heavy sequence length and long doc contexts. - Verify quantized 8-bit and float16 variants under same canary harness. - Ensure KV cache warm path correctness when switching versions (prefix collisions). - Validate per-tenant pinned routing under high-concurrency (5000 RPS) and observe tail latencies.

Title: Predictable-quality hosted endpoints — evaluation-gated PRD and canary launch checklist

Predictable-quality hosted endpoints — evaluation-gated PRD and canary launch checklist

Goal: Ship a minimal, unified hosted endpoint suite (text-generation/chat, embeddings, rerank) that guarantees predictable output quality using an evaluation-gated rollout. This PRD captures measured acceptance gates (quality and infra), operational runbook items, and a staged canary plan tied to automated evals so we can safely replace legacy endpoints without regressing customer-facing behavior.
Functional: Single hosted endpoint surface supports chat/completions/embeddings/rerank with consistent routing and documented request/response contracts for each mode.
Quality: For each workload (chat, completion, embeddings, rerank) we define a reference eval suite and require no more than 2% relative degradation vs the current GA baseline on key metrics (BLEU/ROUGE-style proxies for gen, cosine-sim recall@1 for embeddings, rerank@N for rerank).
Latency: P95 token-latency for generation endpoints <= 350ms on standard lane; embeddings P95 <= 120ms for 768-dim vectors; overall request P99 error rate < 0.5% across canary slices.
Reliability: Canary run must show zero severity-1 incidents and demonstrate healthy autoscaling actions for Dedicated-like loads (burst to 2x for 15 minutes).
Safety: Default safety filters are enabled and pass the safety smoke tests defined in safety-evals (no allowed unsafe outputs across a 500-item prompt set).
Observability: Console dashboards expose token-level cost, per-model latency histograms, live eval-score deltas, and per-customer fallback counts — all with retention appropriate for oncall postmortems.
Rollback criteria: Any observed eval metric regression exceeding thresholds, or production error spike > 2x baseline sustained for >= 10 minutes, triggers immediate automated rollback to previous model variant and an incident bridge.
Security & Compliance: SSO auth flows, tenant-isolation headers, and KMS key usage are validated in a security checklist and security review flagged as complete prior to GA.
Docs & SDKs: Public API reference, examples for migration from legacy endpoints, and SDK patches (python/js) merged and published before staged canary begins.
Pre-canary: Run offline evals against recorded production traffic sample (30M tokens) and a held-out rating set; pass quality gates for 3 consecutive daily runs.
Canary-0 (internal): 0% external traffic — internal customer teams and Redwood integration tests for 48 hours.
Canary-1 (seeded): 0.5% traffic for 24 hours to seeded customers (opt-in list); continuous eval scoring every 15 minutes; automated rollback on gate failure.
Canary-2 (broader): 5% traffic for 48 hours across regions with traffic shaping (latency-sensitive slice + cost-sensitive slice); monitor per-slice metrics and manual review at 24h.
Canary-3 (ramp): 25% traffic for 72 hours with throttled burst windows and A/B quality probes; require engineering sign-off to proceed to GA.
GA: Full rollout after 7 days of stable canary with no regression and completed post-mortem review for any minor issues observed.
Unify routing: chose a single endpoint surface (mode parameter) rather than multiple distinct endpoints to reduce SDK churn; agreed to keep explicit content-type fields in the request body.
Default caching: ephemeral KV caching enabled at 60s by default with per-tenant override — trade-off accepted between freshness and cost reduction for repetitive prompts.
Model variants: will surface two primary model profiles (high-quality, low-latency) instead of an open catalog at GA to simplify eval coverage and rollout gating.
Quantization: postpone wide quantization options at GA; allow internal beta for select tenants to avoid divergent behavior at launch.
Pricing alignment: Should the GA pricing change when routing customers to the new unified surface (cost-per-token vs per-endpoint)? Finance + GTM decision needed.
Determinism: Do we guarantee deterministic seeds for completions when user supplies seed param? This affects caching and eval reproducibility.
Embeddings naming: Do we keep legacy embedding model names for compatibility or issue new v2 names? Existing customers may rely on names in stored vectors.
Migration window: How long do we accept legacy endpoint traffic and what is the deprecation notice period? Product + Support to define.

Title: Cohort-based embedding onboarding scheduler with safety gates

Cohort-based embedding onboarding scheduler with safety gates

Context: We onboard new open-source and fine-tuned embedding models frequently. Previous monolithic canaries expose high risk (either regressions in quality or hidden latency/cost regressions). Goal: build an automated, cohort-based scheduler that groups tenants by workload characteristics and stages traffic through gated steps with automatic rollback triggers. Scope: - Cohort classifier service that assigns tenants to cohorts based on query distribution (avg tokens, query type), dataset cardinality, and historical NN recall profiles. - Scheduler that stages traffic: dry-run -> small cohort -> broaden cohorts by similarity -> global swap. - Safety gates: quality thresholds (p@10 delta, MRR delta), latency SLOs (p99), embedding distribution drift metrics, and cost delta cap. - Observability and alerting: dashboards and automated pager thresholds. - APIs for manual overrides and emergency rollbacks. Acceptance criteria: 1) Scheduler can orchestrate a model swap for 50 tenants end-to-end without human intervention in test cluster. 2) No cohort sees p@10 drop > 2% or MRR drop > 0.03 for the first two broadening steps. 3) End-to-end p99 latency increase <= 10ms across cohorts. 4) Rollforward and rollback actions recorded in audit logs and visible in Console rollout timeline. Out of scope: per-tenant custom model selection UI (follow-up ticket).
E2E run for 50 test tenants completes without manual steps
No cohort experiences p@10 regression > 2% during step expansion
p99 latency increase <= 10ms across cohorts
Automatic rollback executes within 3 minutes of threshold breach
Audit logs contain cohort assignments and decision reason codes
1) Dry-run: collect embeddings for new model and compute offline quality metrics (precision@10, MRR) vs baseline for a sample set. 2) Cohort A (low-risk small tenants): 1% traffic, 30m observation. 3) Cohort B (similar query distribution): ramp to 10% over 2h if metrics within gate. 4) Cohort C (large customers with stable distributions): staged 5% increments with strict SLI checks. 5) Global cutover when all cohorts pass. Each stage has rollback triggers: quality delta, avg cosine drift, norm shift, e2e latency, and cost-per-embed delta.
Primary: precision@10, MRR@10, recall@K (K=10), nearest-neighbor recall at 1/10/50, cosine similarity distribution shift (KL divergence on binned cosines), embedding norm distribution, inference p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens-per-embed cost, error rate for the embeddings endpoint. Secondary: downstream reranking click-through signal (when available), semantic search success rate from KPI tests.
p@10 drop > 2% absolute for any cohort over 30 minutes
MRR drop > 0.03 absolute
cosine similarity distribution KL divergence > 0.08 from baseline
p99 embedding latency increase > 15ms
cost per 1k embeds delta > +20%
endpoint error spike > 0.5%

Title: Canary probes and watermarking for embed+rerank quality

Canary probes and watermarking for embed+rerank quality

Design and implement a lightweight canary probing harness and watermark-based drift detectors to catch embedding + reranker quality regressions caused by config or model changes. The harness must run automatically when model variants, quantization profiles, or reranker hyperparameters are modified, and produce an actionable scorecard (recall/precision deltas, per-query regressions, drift metrics) before changes are rolled out. Goal: catch quality regressions earlier than full shadow-eval runs and avoid human-in-the-loop delays.
Provide automated pre-rollout gating with < 24h feedback, reduce post-deploy embedding/reranker regressions by 60% vs baseline, and generate scorecards that map to rollout decisions (accept, require manual review, block).
Canary harness triggers on model/config change events in CI and Console change API
Generates a scorecard with baseline vs candidate: recall@1/5/10, precision@k, average MRR, and per-query delta list
Implements a watermarking metric for embedding population shift (cosine distribution drift + Wasserstein on pairwise similarities)
Automated decision rules: PASS (delta within thresholds), REVIEW (outliers present but no global fail), FAIL (stat sig degradation or drift > threshold)
Integrates with evals dashboard and sends alerts to #infra-evals when FAIL
End-to-end run completes within budgeted compute (<= 2 GPU-hours per full canary run for 100k probe queries)
Probing dataset: curated synthetic + customer-like queries (10k-100k) sampled by workload buckets (short / long / multi-turn / domain-specific)
Two-tier evaluation: lightweight canary (fast, lower sample) vs bulk shadow-eval (deep, scheduled)
Use stratified sampling to preserve distribution of sequence lengths and token budgets so batching behavior stays representative
Scorecard components: aggregate metrics, cohort breakouts, per-query top-N difference heatmap, embedding drift summaries
Drift detection: compare cosine similarity histograms (candidate vs baseline) and compute Wasserstein distance; also compute embedding centroid shift and a tail-regression indicator for top-k nearest neighbor changes
Significance testing: bootstrap confidence intervals for recall/precision deltas and Holm–Bonferroni correction when evaluating multiple cohorts
Trade-offs: heavier statistical tests increase run time; we bias canary for precision on false-positive reduction (avoid blocking safe changes) while surfacing risky regressions for manual review

Title: P99 smoothing: hybrid microbatch scheduler + kernel autotuner for embedding endpoint

Goal: reduce P99 to <=250ms without increasing average latency or unit cost by more than 10%. Approach is a combined scheduler and kernel tuning initiative: implement a hybrid microbatch scheduler that uses per-request tail-sampling heuristics to group latency-critical small requests into opportunistic microbatches, and add an online kernel-parameter autotuner that selects kernel launch / workspace sizes based on recent sequence-length and KV-cache hit patterns.

Title: Tenant fairness burn-rate policy and quantized-variant rollout checklist

Tenant fairness burn-rate policy and quantized-variant rollout checklist

PRD excerpt and scope: Define a tenant-fair error-budget burn-rate policy and a stepwise rollout checklist for serving quantized model variants. This ticket captures requirements, acceptance criteria, and rollout gates for progressive activation of int8/4-bit variants across hosted and dedicated deployments. It clarifies scope (hosted API + Dedicated; excludes Private on-prem air-gapped installs for this phase), surface-level telemetry requirements, and the minimal dashboard/alerting that must exist before canary starts. Also lists trade-offs between cost savings and potential tail-latency regressions and defines rollback expectations.
SLO definitions: p50/p95/p99 latency envelopes per workload class (interactive chat, embeddings, batch) published to the console; target p99 <= 800ms for chat on dedicated capacity under nominal load.
Availability: 99.95% monthly for hosted model endpoints and 99.9% for dedicated pools while quantized variant is in canary. Any drop below 99.8% triggers immediate canary pause.
Error budget policy: monthly error budget defined per tenant weight. A tenant-level burn-rate calculator must be available and tested; automated soft-throttles applied when tenant burn rate > 2x baseline for > 10 minutes.
Tenant fairness: rollout must include weighted traffic steering so that no single tenant exceeds 3x their historical token rate during canary sampling windows.
Canary gating: prometheus alerts must be in place for p99 latency increase > 20% absolute or error rate increase > 0.5% (absolute) compared to baseline; two consecutive 5-minute buckets trigger rollback flag.
Quality guards: end-to-end regen-eval on 1k seeded prompts showing no regression in BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-similarity beyond defined thresholds (documented in Confluence) before broad rollout.
Observability: dashboards for per-tenant burn, p50/p95/p99, successful tokens/sec, and model variant distribution exist and are linked in the PRD.
Operational playbook: runbook page created with steps for pausing rollout, resharding traffic, and emergency revert with contact on-call rotation.
Canary duration and ramp: initial canary window 1 hour at 1% sample traffic (weighted across 5 tenants), progressive ramps to 10% over 48h if no alerts; must pass automated checks at each step.
Release checklist: GitHub PR for runtime kernels approved, quantized model artifact checksum verified, canary infra terraform reviewed and merged before activation.
Scope clarification: Private (air-gapped) deployments will require a separate validation matrix; excluded to reduce compliance burden for initial rollout.
Trade-offs: Aggressive quantization gives 30-45% cost reduction on token compute but risks tail-latency regressions on long sequences. We prefer conservative initial ramps for chat workloads.
Data retention/telemetry: store per-tenant latency histograms for 30 days to enable post-mortem correlation with quantization toggles.
Design ask: Console team to add a 'variant view' toggle so operators can see model variant distribution across regions and tenants during canary.
Security: KMS rotation for quantized artifacts is required; coordinate with Security for approval before canary launch.

Title: Hostname suffix truncation during imaging causes Intune device object merge and check-in flapping

Hostname suffix truncation during imaging causes Intune device object merge and check-in flapping

Issue summary: Devices imaged with the new OEM task sequence (ts-2026-03) are being assigned hostnames that get truncated by a legacy hostname-sanitize script to 15 characters. When the corporate DNS suffix is later appended by the join script the resulting FQDN collides with an existing device name in Intune/Azure AD. Intune merges device objects in some cases when the primary DNS/hostname matches, causing device check-in to alternate between two device objects (flapping) and blocking configuration profiles/policy assignment.

Impact: Multiple newly imaged seats in prod-us-west and APAC are failing to receive critical configuration profiles; desktop management and endpoint security policies not applied. Affected users report intermittent policy loss and inability to access mapped network printers. No data loss reported, but this blocks autopilot/dedicated device rollouts and delays repairs.

Observed behavior: Hostnames generated by ts-2026-03 look correct during imaging (example: rw-infer-nyc-emb-20260312), but after the legacy sanitize step the local .computername gets truncated to 15 chars (rw-infer-nyc-eb). When domain join/appending-suffix runs we end up with rw-infer-nyc-eb.corp.redwood.com which matches an existing old device object (previously registered) and Azure AD/Intune merges or links to the older object. This creates two Azure device IDs with the same physical machine reporting intermittently and both show check-ins.

Expected behavior: Hostname sanitization should preserve uniqueness used by TS naming templates or the join process should ensure a stable, unique device identifier is used for Intune registration (preferably HW hash/autopilot entry), avoiding collisions with legacy objects.
1) Use imaging task sequence ts-2026-03 that runs hostname template: rw-infer-<region>-<team>-<shortdate>.
2) Run legacy hostname sanitize script (hostname-sanitize.sh) which truncates to first 15 characters for legacy NetBIOS compatibility.
3) Complete OOBE and domain join which appends corporate suffix.
4) Observe Intune portal: device appears to merge with an existing device object which has matching shortname; check-in timestamps alternate between two device IDs.
5) Reproducible on repro VM/hardware with imported autopilot hardware hash for same model.

Notes: Repro only after the sanitize step is executed; skipping sanitize prevents the merge.

Intune MDM enrollment: EnrollmentID=9f2b3c... status=success (deviceId: d-0a1b2c)
Intune device sync: 2026-03-12T09:45:02Z - DeviceObjectMerge detected - matched on NetBIOSName 'RW-INFER-NYC-EB' with existing object id e-5d6f7g

SCCM client log (clientid.log): 2026-03-12T09:47:30Z - Client registered new GUID; policy request failed: 0x87d00324 (no policy assigned)

Initial hypothesis: hostname truncate to 15 chars causes name collisions with older device records created prior to autopilot rollouts. Verified by imaging a test unit and checking AAD device list - old device (decommissioned) reused same shortname.
What we tried:
- Re-imaging and excluding sanitize script -> new device registers cleanly (no merge).
- Created synthetic long hostnames and observed Azure registers new device id consistently.

Title: rate-engine-weighted-priority-starvation-during-bulk-tenant-migration

rate-engine-weighted-priority-starvation-during-bulk-tenant-migration

During a scheduled bulk tenant migration (shard rebalance) we observed a subset of tenants enter long-lived soft-throttles despite no change in their request patterns. Early investigation shows the rate engine's weighted-priority allocator temporarily computed near-zero effective allocations for affected tenant keys, causing sustained enforcement until a manual intervention (rollback) completed. This ticket tracks root cause analysis, remediation, and test coverage to prevent recurrence.
Provision two shards with existing tenant set A (1k tenants) and target shard B.
Trigger bulk tenant migration using shard-rebalancer with parallel move batch size 200.
Run synthetic steady-state traffic generator (1 QPS per tenant key) against all tenants during migration.
Observe enforcement metrics and per-tenant effective_allocation metric in console dashboard for duration of migration.
Verify that affected tenants see sustained 429s while others remain within quota.
2025-09-18T03:14:22Z [allocator] compute_normalized_weights(total_priority=1200, changed_count=198)
2025-09-18T03:14:22Z [allocator] tenant_key=org_42:key_873 priority=1 raw_weight=0.0000 effective_allocation=0
2025-09-18T03:14:22Z [enforcer] enforce_result key=org_42:key_873 allow=false reason=effective_allocation=0.0
2025-09-18T03:17:05Z [rebalance] lease_transfer finished batch=3/5 duration=2.8s
2025-09-18T03:18:01Z [metrics] per_tenant_allocation_p50=0.0002 per_tenant_allocation_min=0.0
A normalization/rounding bug in the weighted-priority allocator combined with an unprotected fast-path for allocation recomputation during high-volume tenant move batches. When many priorities change simultaneously, the normalization used 32-bit float math and an integer-floor step that produced zero effective allocation for low-priority tenants. Additionally, a race between lease-update handler and allocation snapshotting allowed stale totals to be used, amplifying the effect.
Immediate mitigation applied: restricted parallel tenant move batch_size to 25 via feature flag in shard-rebalancer and rolled back in-flight large migrations. Ops configured temporary alert to detect any tenant with effective_allocation==0 for >1m and auto-pause migration for that tenant group.
Patch allocator: switch normalization to 64-bit double, apply conservative min_allocation clamp (epsilon) to avoid zeroing small weights.

Title: Intermittent region-affinity flip causing bursty cross-region inference and timeouts for Chronos Health

Intermittent region-affinity flip causing bursty cross-region inference and timeouts for Chronos Health

Issue summary: Chronos Health reported sudden elevated p95/p99 latency and a spike in streaming request timeouts beginning at 2026-03-10 09:40 UTC. The customer's traffic, normally pinned to us-west for low-latency inference, experienced intermittent routing to eu-west for a subset of requests, producing cold KV-cache misses and high tail latency. Impact: Several production endpoints used by Chronos' clinician-facing workflow saw ~15% request failures (stream disconnects / 504s) and 3x p99 for generation calls over a ~40 minute window.
Customer-facing production inference degraded for Chronos Health: increased 504s and stream disconnects, user-visible timeouts in the care app during 09:40-10:20 UTC. Estimated 12k requests impacted, some time-sensitive workflows delayed.

1) Send sustained generation requests from a Chronos Health customer account with region affinity set to us-west (via account-routing tag).
2) Observe p50/p95/p99 for streaming and non-streaming endpoints over 5-10 minute windows.
3) Correlate request trace ids with smart-routing logs to detect unexpected eu-west handoffs.

Initial hypothesis: BGP/peering issue causing traffic to egress via eu-west. Rejected after routing plane BGP checks showed stable adverts.
Observed correlation between a spike in 'affinity-lookup-miss' events and region flips. TTL for account routing metadata had expired earlier than expected due to a bug in cache-refresh logic (recent release 2026-03-09 02:12 UTC).
Root cause candidate: a regression in account-routing cache refresh where a backoff timer could cause immediate TTL expiration for accounts with infrequent updates, producing transient fallback to default geo-detect which resolved to eu-west for some requests.
KV/cache impact: Customers pinned to us-west rely on local prefix caches; cross-region handoff caused cold KV lookups and model weights not warm on the eu-west pool, increasing initialization and token latency.
Scope: Only accounts whose routing metadata refresh interval aligned with the backoff edge observed the flip. Not a universal platform outage but high-impact for affected customers.
Correlated items: linked incident INT-4021 flagged a suspicious cache refresh change in the routing service, and PR #1894 updated retry/backoff behavior three days ago.

Title: Healthcheck throttle + runaway backoff causing elevated 5xx and runtime restarts during tenant fairness reshard

Healthcheck throttle + runaway backoff causing elevated 5xx and runtime restarts during tenant fairness reshard

Issue summary:
Customer (NimbleHealth, dedicated tenant) reported an abrupt increase in 5xx responses and elevated latency starting ~2026-03-13T09:10Z. Errors are predominantly 502/504 from the API gateway and a subset of upstream serving runtime processes reporting OOM/kernel-fallback restarts. Impact: multiple production endpoints degraded (chat generation and embeddings).

Impact:
- Customer reports ~15% request failure rate for the affected routes over a 30m window.
- Real-time product features degraded for end users; increased retry traffic observed.

Environment:
- Prod cluster: us-east, tenant: nimblehealth-dedicated-pool-7
- Affected routes: /v1/chat/completions, /v1/embeddings/batch
- Autoscaler: horizontal with warm pools; healthcheck policy: aggressive (3s interval, 2 failures to mark unhealthy)

Steps to reproduce / observed pattern:
1) Send steady traffic for chat route at 120 rps with sporadic embedding spikes.
2) After a spike, API gateway returns 502/504 for ~1-3 minutes, then partial recovery followed by repeated micro-waves.
3) Runtime logs show repeated healthcheck failures, followed by exponential backoff from the healthcheck scheduler and aggressive scaling decisions (ephemeral worker churn).

Observed logs (examples):
- apigw: "upstream response timeout (deadline exceeded)" and "502: upstream connection refused"
- runtime: "kvcache lock timeout", "watchdog: runtime restart due to OOM", "kernel fallback triggered for attention kernel"

Expected behavior:
- Failures should be isolated and graceful fallback to compatible variants should avoid impact to success rate.

Notes:
- Customer attached a timeline and request IDs in their initial support email. See Confluence page for full attachments.
2026-03-13 09:20 - Maya Patel (Support): Acknowledged customer, collecting logs and escalating to SRE. Notified oncall.
2026-03-13 09:33 - Carlos Rivera (SRE): Observed same 5xx spike on apigw metrics dashboard. Marked as P1 and pulled autoscaler and healthcheck dashboards. Adding hypothesis: healthcheck flapping + backoff amplification.
2026-03-13 09:45 - Customer (NimbleHealth): Provided request IDs 20260313-9a7 and 20260313-9b3, confirmed degraded UX for chat previews. Asked for ETA on mitigation.
2026-03-13 10:05 - SRE: Temporarily increased healthcheck interval to 10s for nimblehealth-dedicated-pool-7 to reduce flapping; placed warm pool freeze to prevent aggressive churn. Early telemetry shows drop in 5xx rate to ~6%.
2026-03-13 12:15 - Eng (runtime): Found evidence of kernel fallback events coincident with prefetch-heavy embedding jobs. Pushed a collector to throttle prefetch concurrency on the tenant as a temporary control.
2026-03-14 08:12 - Support (Maya): Customer confirmed partial recovery overnight but still occasional 502s during embedding spikes. Working with Engagement to schedule follow-up postmortem.
2026-03-14 11:00 - Carlos Rivera (SRE): Escalated to runtime team for deeper kernel fallback and nvml reset correlation. Assigned follow-up task INT-400102 to track runtime patch rollout.
Timeline and metrics:
- 09:08-09:20Z: Embedding bulk upload from tenant A caused prefetch ramp; kvcache latencies increased from 2ms to 120ms.
- 09:10-09:50Z: API gateway 5xx rate peaked at 18% for affected routes.
- Grafana links: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/ingress/api-gateway-error-rate?orgId=1&from=1610&to=1630; https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/runtime/kv-latency?var-tenant=nimblehealth

Hypotheses considered:
1) Healthcheck sensitivity + transient kvcache lockups caused multiple worker reboots; the scheduler backed off healthchecks and then overscaled on perceived unhealthy workers, which increased cold-start and prefetched work leading to more kvcache contention.
2) A kernel fallback path for a specific attention kernel exits to a slower implementation under mixed quantization; this increased per-request latency and collided with aggressive healthchecks.
3) Network-level transient (short-lived) packet loss between API gateway and runtime proxies amplified retries and triggered upstream connection resets.

Evidence collected:
- Runtime process logs show repeated "kernel fallback" messages around 09:12Z followed by GC pressure logs and then "watchdog restart" entries.
- NVML driver logs show a single GPU reset on node ip-10-1-23-45 at 09:14Z.
- Healthcheck logs show repeated fast-fails (2 failures within 6s) before the scheduler increased backoff.

Actions during investigation:
- Increased healthcheck interval for affected pool (mitigative).
- Throttled tenant prefetch concurrency as a stopgap.
- Temporarily pinned a model variant to a known-good kernel profile for nimblehealth routes.

Open questions:
- Is the kernel fallback deterministic for specific model quantization and sequence length? Runtime team to reproduce in staging.
- Does our healthcheck backoff algorithm need to factor in ongoing kernel fallback latencies to avoid misclassifying slow but healthy nodes?
Mitigation applied (temporary/short-term):
- Raised healthcheck interval from 3s -> 10s for nimblehealth-dedicated-pool-7 at 2026-03-13T10:02Z to reduce flapping.
- Throttled prefetch concurrency for tenant to limit kvcache lock contention.
- Pinned model variant to kernel profile v2.1 for chat routes for the affected tenant to avoid fallback path.

Permanent/next-step actions (post-incident):
- INT-400102: runtime team to roll a targeted fix that avoids kernel fallback in the v2.1 path and improves quantization fallback performance.
- ENG-OPS-237: update healthcheck backoff algorithm to consider median request latency signals before marking unhealthy.
- Runbook update: add a section for "healthcheck-flap + prefetch amplification" with recommended mitigations (freeze warm pool, increase HC interval, throttle prefetch).
- Schedule postmortem with NimbleHealth for 2026-03-16; include customer-facing summary and SLA credit evaluation.

Customer communication:
- 2026-03-13 11:30: Sent initial mitigation note explaining temporary healthcheck and throttle changes and ETA for a runtime investigation.
- 2026-03-14 09:00: Sent follow-up acknowledging partial recovery and committing to a postmortem.

Status: Monitoring. Permanent fixes tracked in INT-400102 and ENG-OPS-237.

Title: Edge priority fanout amplification causing intermittent 5xx and streaming drops during tenant concurrency ramp

Edge priority fanout amplification causing intermittent 5xx and streaming drops during tenant concurrency ramp

Issue summary: During a tenant concurrency ramp for customer NimbusHealth (dedicated), we observed sustained, intermittent 5xx responses and streaming session drops starting at ~2026-03-13T22:05UTC. The pattern correlated with an edge priority change combined with an automated keystore rotation window. Impact: Multiple production clients reported degraded streaming sessions (short responses, aborted streams) and increased 5xx rate (~8% error-rate for affected tenant traffic) for ~55 minutes. Environment: prod - us-east; affected tenant on Dedicated pool A; traffic spike originated from a scheduled data migration at the customer's side that produced bursty concurrent short requests. Observed behavior: API-Gateway accept queue grew rapidly; hedged/mirrored requests amplified fanout to multiple runtime pools; a transient TLS handshake slowdown during keystore rotation increased handshake latency and caused upstream connection stalls; runtime threadpool utilization went to 95% and a subset of runtime proxies returned 502/503 on request hedged paths. There were frequent short-lived stream disconnects instead of graceful cancelation. This ticket tracks the immediate incident and follow-ups.
1) Simulate a high-concurrency ramp from a single tenant with many short streaming requests (concurrency > 1200 per shard)
2) Trigger a keystore rotation (TLS session rehandshake) on the edge proxies during the ramp window
3) Observe accept queue growth in API-Gateway, hedged request fanout increased across serving runtime pools, and rising 502/503 rates for short-streamed sessions
apigw.accept_queue.size: 15000 -> observed growth at 2026-03-13T22:07:11Z
edge.tls.handshake_95th: baseline 18ms -> peaked 470ms during rotation 2026-03-13T22:06-22:12Z
runtime.threadpool.util: 68% -> 95% on pool-c and pool-d at 22:08:30Z
runtime.proxy: upstream reset (RST) on hedged-variant, 502 returned to client (count=1428 in 10m)
Support (Aisha): Customer NimbusHealth opened a support channel. They reported multiple aborted live-transcription sessions. Asked for immediate mitigation and whether a rollback is possible.
SRE (Marco): Initial triage shows accept queue blowup and concurrent TLS latency spike coincident with keystore rotation. Throttled new tenant connections as temporary mitigation.
Customer (NimbusHealth - ops): Confirmed they started a migration job at 22:03 UTC which drastically increased small streaming sessions. Asked whether Redwood can roll back any recent edge change.
SRE (Marco): No recent edge code change deployed around incident time; priority-scheduler tweak was deployed earlier in the day (PR linked). Working hypothesis: scheduler change + keystore rotation + tenant burst caused fanout amplification.
Support (Aisha): Sent customer workaround: reduce client concurrency and enable client-side exponential backoff for short streams; we also recommended pinning to a lower concurrency route (temporary).
Eng (Priya, priority-scheduler): Added logs to track fanout multiplier and hedging counts. Will instrument a circuit to limit simultaneous hedged copies per tenant.
00:15 - Correlated timeline: Tenant ramp started 22:03, keystore rotation at 22:05-22:12, error-rate spike 22:06-23:00.
00:30 - Edge metrics show hedged/mirrored request multiplier increased from 1.1x -> 2.6x for affected tenant during high queuing conditions.
00:45 - Keystore rotation led to many edge proxies performing TLS rehandshakes simultaneously; this pushed handshake latencies above the hedging timeout window and caused retried/duplicated hedged requests to be sent upstream.
01:10 - Runtime thread pools were saturated because hedged requests massively increased total inflight token generation work for short-lived sessions (KV cache warmups amplified CPU usage).
01:30 - No evidence of persistent OOMs; runtime recovered after the tenant ramp subsided and keystore rotation completed. Some proxies did perform transient restarts tied to connection resets.
02:00 - Related PR #8241 changed priority-scheduler behavior to be more aggressive in hedging under perceived latency; combined with the keystore rotation this produced the observable amplification.
Suggested root cause: Interaction between aggressive hedging logic in priority-scheduler and simultaneous TLS rehandshake/backpressure from keystore rotation, triggered by an unusually high short-stream concurrency spike from a single tenant.
1) Short-term: Applied tenant-level connection throttle for NimbusHealth to cap concurrency to 600 across affected shards at 22:20 UTC.
2) Disabled hedged request escalation for tenant-level traffic at edge to prevent multi-variant fanout (rolled at 22:35 UTC).
3) Coordinated with infra to stagger keystore rotations and avoid broad simultaneous rehandshake windows (ad hoc scheduling immediate).
4) Customer instructed to pause migration job while throttles in place; customer confirmed decreased error-rate after throttles.
5) Instrumentation: Added metric to track hedged copy count per tenant and per-route (hotfix merged).
Status: Partial mitigation in place; customer traffic stable with throttles and hedging disabled for affected tenant. Monitoring shows 5xx rate returned to baseline ~30 minutes after throttles.
Next steps (short term): Roll a conservative hedging cap to production-wide policy to limit copies per tenant (ENG- prioritize).
Next steps (mid term): Update keystore rotation orchestration to perform rolling rotations staggered by edge-proxy-subset to avoid clusterwide TLS rehandshake spikes.
Longer term: Rework priority-scheduler hedging logic to factor in accept-queue depth and per-tenant fanout cost (RFC in progress, linked PR and confluence page).
Post-incident: Schedule a brief postmortem with NimbusHealth and internal stakeholders; create runbook entry for tenant-induced burst scenarios and keystore rotation overlap.
Follow-up tickets: INT-2203 (priority-scheduler hedging cap), SUP-421999 (customer-facing postmortem and billing check for retry amplification).

Title: Adaptive batching config swap caused tail-latency cascade; request for safe unwind and verification

Issue summary: Customer observed increased 95th/99th token latency and sporadic streaming disconnects immediately after we enabled an adaptive batching experiment for their tenant (coalesce_small_reqs=true, adaptive_grouping=aggressive) and a matched experimental quant profile (q8_dyn_prefetch). Title: AegisPharm private deployment: multipath failover amplified requests, ordered-stream reassembly failures, and billing exposure

AegisPharm private deployment: multipath failover amplified requests, ordered-stream reassembly failures, and billing exposure

Issue summary:
During a scheduled nightly batch from AegisPharm (private deployment, eu-west), the Redwood private control plane entered a multipath failover loop causing amplified request fanout, repeated retries, and ordered-stream reassembly failures for streaming completions. Symptoms started at ~2026-03-10T01:12Z and lasted for ~90 minutes.

Impact:
- Customer observed duplicate completions and truncated streaming transcripts across ~18% of requests for the 90-minute window.
- Significant token accounting discrepancies led to a billing exposure (estimated 2.4x token inflation for affected requests).
- Several model variants in the customer's pinned rollout experienced high tail latency and intermittent 5xx errors.
- Business impact: AegisPharm paused nightly ingestion jobs and opened an escalation call.

Environment:
- Deployment: Redwood Private (customer-managed control plane)
- Region: eu-west-1
- Cluster: aegispharm-prod-cluster-3 (dedicated GPU pool)
- Canary config: pinned redwood-quant-4bit behind routing policy with multipath failover enabled

1. Customer ran concurrent batch job (fanout to 4k concurrent sub-requests) against the private endpoint with streaming enabled.
2. During transient scheduler pressure, router invoked multipath failover to secondary replicas.
3. Failover logic retried requests while upstream still delivered partial streams, causing duplicates and out-of-order stream segments.
4. Client resumed and reassembled streams but hit reassembly logic edge cases that truncated transcripts.

Title: Dynamic burst throttle rewrite and customer escalation runflow

Dynamic burst throttle rewrite and customer escalation runflow

Summary: Multiple enterprise customers experienced sudden denied bursts and unexplained reserved-pool shortfalls during interleaved surge windows. Investigation shows the autoscaler admission controller can oversuppress burst admission when heterogeneous GPU clouds and KV-cache churn coincide. This ticket captures the rewrite of the burst throttle logic to a composite, telemetry-driven admission policy, the short-term emergency hotfix to restore fair burst admission, and the customer escalation/runflow to communicate mitigations and RCA timeline.

Repro: Load generator replay of Customer-A traffic shape (90th percentile short spikes + baseline QPS) on a mixed GPU fleet reproduces denied burst events after sustained KV cache evictions. Root causes include: 1) headroom estimator double-counting preemptible capacity in multi-az scenarios; 2) admission window aligning with KV cache eviction causing transient memory pressure and slot eviction; 3) weight normalization bug that amplifies large-tenant throttling under credit scarcity.

Impact: Affected customers see increased tail latency and 429/503s for short-lived spikes. Revenue and SLA risk for Dedicated tenants flagged as high.

Mitigation (temporary): apply soft-headroom bump (+15%) for VIP tenants, introduce a 30s "slot preemption grace" to prevent immediate eviction during KV churn, and enable hosted-fallback routing for critical routes. These were rolled to canary region us-west-2 at 2026-03-13 21:00 UTC and reduced customer 429s by ~72% on the canary.

Planned fix (longer-term): Replace the single-threshold admission heuristic with a composite policy that considers predicted short-burst probability, KV-cache pressure metric, and available burst-credit ledger. Add gated canary rollout with per-tenant assert checks and a synthetic-eval suite. Enhance telemetry: per-tenant headroom time-series, admission decision traces, and a burst-decision histograms dashboard.
