Title: Control Plane Operational Boundaries Heatmap

Control Plane Operational Boundaries Heatmap

Purpose and context:

This is a working heatmap-style sketch to surface current operational boundaries in the control plane: who owns what during normal ops and during multi-region failover. Goal is to call out ambiguous gaps and create a short list of follow-ups (owner assignments, runbook updates, API contracts). Not a canonical doc — an annotated work-in-progress for the platform-engineering and serving-runtime teams.

Assumptions and constraints (short):
- Single control-plane control path (API gateway -> orchestrator -> runtime adapters).
- We support 3 regions (us-west, eu-west, ap-southeast) with regional control-plane replicas and a global config plane.
- Traffic routing is policy-driven: latency-first, then cost, then compliance (region-locked).
- Runtime adapters are the thin bridge to GPU pools and on-prem agents.

High-level ownership summary (heatmap commentary):
- API Gateway (ingest): primary owner = platform-api team. Responsibilities: authentication, rate limiting, coarse routing decisions, quota enforcement, request enrichment. SLA: <100ms control-plane p99 for routing decision. Region fallback: platform-api config points to regional orchestrators; in loss-of-region, global gateway switches to nearest fallback pool.
- Orchestration Layer (request-to-runtime mapping, rollouts): primary owner = orchestration-service team. Responsibilities: model versioning, canary rollouts, route affinity, autoscale hints, batching policies. SLA: transactional durability and consistent rollout state across regions.
- Runtime Adapters (serving proxies): primary owner = serving-runtime team. Responsibilities: translate orchestration directives to runtime-specific calls (CUDA-optimized pools, on-prem RPC), manage KV cache metadata, surface local capacity. SLA: <50ms adapter handshake for pooled requests, best-effort KV cache sync.
- Routing Governance / Policy Engine: primary owner = platform-engineering (routing-gov subteam). Responsibilities: policy language, policy validation, policy audit logs, safety gates for fallback.
- SRE/Infra (ops): primary owner = infra-sre. Responsibilities: infra health, cross-region replication, infra failover, monitoring/alerting for control plane.

Operational boundary matrix (text table):
Service | Owner | Primary responsibilities | Decision boundary | Typical ops handoff
API Gateway | platform-api | auth, ingress, coarse routing | chooses region/orch config based on policy | handoff to orchestration via RPC (orchestration endpoint v2)
Orchestrator | orchestration-service | model routing, version pins, rollout rules | final route decision (which adapter pool) | handoff to runtime adapter with rollout metadata and batching hints
Runtime Adapter | serving-runtime | queueing, batching, KV cache, runtime calls | enforces local capacity and throttles | returns run metrics and fallback signals
Policy Engine | routing-gov | policy eval, validation, audit | rejects unsafe routing changes | notifies orchestration and platform-api on violations
SRE/Infra | infra-sre | infra failover, region replication | triggers region-level failover | notifies all owners, runs global incident runbook

Key decision boundaries to clarify (open questions):
1) Where is the canonical source-of-truth for route-to-adapter mappings?
   - current state: orchestrator maintains mapping but policy engine can inject overrides. Leads to potential race condition during rollout.
   - proposed: orchestrator remains source-of-truth; policy engine issues signed overrides that orchestrator applies with a reconciliation window (TBD).

2) How do we represent multi-region fallbacks in the API contract?
   - suggestion: add an explicit "fallback_chain" field in orchestration responses listing region adapters ordered by policy priority. This makes failover deterministic for adapters.

3) KV cache consistency vs latency: who owns reconciliation?
   - tradeoff: serving-runtime prefers local fast cache with eventual consistency. Orchestrator needs strong-ish invariants for prefix cache invalidation during model switch.
   - interim: add a lightweight invalidation message bus (owner: serving-runtime + infra-sre) with documented TTL semantics.

4) Rollouts across regions: canaries vs global sync?
   - current experiments: region-scoped canaries for low blast radius. Global rollouts often lag and produce inconsistency in inference quality metrics.
   - proposal: add rollout epoch metadata and a global acceptance gate managed by orchestration + product-eval.

Runbook and incident boundaries (short bullets):
- API ingress failures: platform-api owns mitigation (rate-limits, revert gateway config). Escalate to infra-sre on region degradation.
- Orchestrator inconsistencies (mismatched route assignments): orchestration-service owns reconciliation; if >5% mismatches cross-region, open sev3 and rollback last policy change.
- Adapter capacity exhaustion: serving-runtime implements emergency fallback to pre-defined model shards in another region; infra-sre handles cross-region route reweighting.
- Policy violation alerts: routing-gov triages; if unsafe changes detected auto-revert and notify on-call for platform-engineering.

Small proposal list (next steps):
- Draft an API change for orchestration response to include "fallback_chain" + rollout_epoch (owner: orchestration-service). Link: PLAT-4321.
- Prototype signed override flow from policy engine to orchestrator (owner: routing-gov + platform-api). Add TTL and audit log entry.
- Create simple invalidation bus for KV cache with at-most-once invalidation messages (owner: serving-runtime + infra-sre).
- Update incident runbooks to define clear threshold for cross-region inconsistency (owner: infra-sre).

Notes / references / bookmarks:
- Related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/control-plane/pull/198 (orchestration epoch prototype)
- Jira: PLAT-4321 (fallback_chain RFC), PLAT-4502 (KV invalidation proposal)
- Slack thread: #platform-routing – thread id: t0239-heatmap-draft

Open questions for the group meeting (TODOs):
- Acceptable reconciliation window between policy override issuance and orchestrator apply? (Suggested: 60s)
- How do we test cross-region rollout acceptance in CI without incurring expensive GPU runs? (Idea: synthetic traffic + small local model)
- Define exact schema for fallback_chain and rollout_epoch (owner: orchestration-service + api).

- fallback_chain: ["us-west-adapter-v3", "eu-west-adapter-v2", "ap-southeast-proxy"]
- rollout_epoch: "2026-02-14T18:32:00Z"

Title: Introduce "safelock" fast-path gating + precision toggle and KV-eviction safety for runtime

Introduce "safelock" fast-path gating + precision toggle and KV-eviction safety for runtime

Context and motivation:
This PR addresses a recurring class of incidents where aggressive fast-path kernel selection and lower-precision execution (fp16 / int8) produced rare but hard-to-detect correctness deviations for edge prompts. At the same time, customers expect throughput and lower cost. We need a runtime mechanism that lets us enable high-performance paths without risking silent correctness regressions in production.

What this PR does (summary):
- Adds a 'safelock' gating layer in the kernel selection path. The safelock prevents switching to a fast path unless a set of runtime validators pass (numerical consistency, kv-cache integrity checks, and recent success window).
- Introduces a precision toggle API (per-model, per-deployment) with three modes: strict (fp32 only), balanced (fp16 with strict validators), aggressive (fp16/int8 allowed once warmed).
- Adds a lightweight runtime validator harness: stochastic correctness probes run as background requests against canary inputs to compute divergence metrics (token-level mismatch rate, logit-delta distribution). Validators are cheap and attach metadata to requests that triggered path selection failures.
- Changes KV cache eviction policy to be conservative when cache-warmness is below threshold; combined with safelock it avoids invalidating cached KV frames that fast kernels rely on.
- Integrates safelock signals with the continuous-batching scheduler: until a deployment's validators reach a success threshold, scheduler prefers conservative batching and disables cross-model micro-batching that can expose interleaving bugs.
- Adds observability hooks: metrics (safelock.blocked_count, validator.mismatch_rate, precision.switch_count, kv.eviction_suppressed) and a dashboard stub.
- Adds a feature flag runtime.enable_safelock (default true for new deploys) and model config fields precision_mode and validator_policy.

Design notes and rationale:
- The safelock is intentionally conservative: it is designed to minimize customer-visible regressions at the cost of initial throughput until a model warms. We prefer false negatives (staying on slow path) over false positives (silent incorrect outputs).
- Validators are probabilistic and run only on a small fraction of traffic (configurable). We do not rely on end-user prompts alone; the system feeds a small canary corpus that includes known edge cases and adversarial tokens used in previous incidents.
- KV-cache eviction suppression is implemented as an additional guard in the eviction worker: if cache_warmness < 0.7 and safelock.enabled, eviction respects a soft TTL and only evicts when memory pressure exceeds a higher threshold. This prevents state churn that invalidates prefix caching assumptions used by some kernels.

Commits (high-level):
- feat(runtime): add safelock kernel gating and validator harness (A. Kumar)
- feat(config): model precision_mode and validator_policy proto + defaulting (A. Kumar)
- fix(kv): conservative eviction path and warmness estimator (R. Patel)
- perf(scheduler): integrate safelock signal into batching decisioning (L. O'Connor)
- test: end-to-end validator integration tests and canary job (E. Tan)
- docs: runtime safelock/precision-mode doc, migration notes (doc team)

Files touched (high-level):
- runtime/kernel_selector.cpp/h (safelock implementation, gating checks)
- runtime/precision_policy.proto (new model-level config)
- runtime/validator/ (background probe harness, small canary corpus)
- serving/scheduler/continuous_batcher.cpp (respect safelock signals)
- serving/kvcache/eviction_worker.cpp (suppressed eviction path)
- metrics/registry (new metrics added)
- tests/e2e/validators_integration_test.cc (new suite)
- docs/runtime/safelock.md (operator-facing guide and flags)

Small illustrative snippet included in the patch (non-executable):
"""
if (safelock.enabled() && !validators.passed_recently(dep)) {
  // force fallback to conservative kernel + fp32 path
  selectKernel = KernelSelector::conservative(model, seq_len);
} else {
  selectKernel = KernelSelector::fastpath(model, seq_len, precision_mode);
}
"""

Benchmarks / numbers:
- Baseline (main, before PR) on rtx-a100-80gb, long-tail tests: median latency 48ms, p99 180ms, throughput 2200 tok/s.
- With safelock enabled (default config) immediately after deploy: median latency +6% (51ms), throughput -8% (2024 tok/s) while validators warm.
- After 30m of live traffic and validator success: median latency +1% (48.5ms), throughput -2% (2160 tok/s).
- Aggressive mode (opt-in, warm): throughput +12% over baseline; we see a measurable cost win.
- We ran a correctness sweep against our regression corpus (n=1200 prompts) showing token-level mismatch reduced to <0.02% for balanced mode; in aggressive mode mismatch rises to ~0.6% on the corpus (expected, opt-in).

Testing and CI:
- Added unit + integration tests for validator harness and eviction behavior.
- Added synthetic stochastic tests that simulate rare floating-point edgecases.
- CI: initial pipeline had one flaky test (eviction_worker race) failing on Linux-asan; fixed in second commit. Final CI: all checks passed (build, unit, integration, perf-smoke).

Review discussion (highlights):
- Marco: "I like the safelock abstraction; can we ensure the validator corpus is editable by SREs without code changes?"
- Aisha: "Yes — validators read a canary file from /etc/redwood/validators/corpus.json and we added operator docs. SRE can update via configmap for k8s deploys."
- Eve: "Concerned about metric cardinality when we annotate every request with validator metadata."
- Aisha: "We emit aggregated counters and histograms; only a small sampling logs request-level debug traces behind a flag."
- Liam: "Scheduler changes look sane. Need additional canary rollout plan for enterprise customers with strict SLAs."
- Aisha: "Added rollout doc and an opt-out label on deployment config; default for existing deployments is unchanged (safe-mode learned)."

Edge cases / known tradeoffs:
- There is an initial throughput hit until validators warm. We mitigate by sampling only a small portion of traffic for validators and allowing manual warm-up (canary traffic injection).
- Aggressive precision_mode is opt-in; customers should enable only after verifying on internal test prompts. We include a CLI tool for running the validator corpus locally against a deployment.
- The KV eviction suppression increases memory use under some failure modes; we documented emergency knobs and introduced an automatic disable threshold if memory pressure remains high for 10s.

Migration / operator guidance:
- New deploys: safelock enabled by default. Operators can set runtime.enable_safelock=false to revert (not recommended).
- To opt into aggressive precision: update model config: precision_mode=aggressive and monitor validator.mismatch_rate.
- Dashboards: added a starter Grafana dashboard (docs link) and alerts for validator.mismatch_rate > 0.1% and safelock.blocked_count being unexpectedly high.

Backward compatibility:
- All config fields default to conservative behavior; no breaking changes. Models without precision_mode set continue to use fp32 until they pass validators.

Post-merge actions / follow-ups (linear):
- ENG-4983: add automated warmup job to inject synthetic canary traffic during deploy windows (follow-up).
- ENG-5122: add per-customer precision analytics and billing impact report.

Merge outcome:
- Final status: merged via squash. Branch merged to main after approvals from Marco, Eve, and Liam. CI green at merge.

If you want to test locally: run tools/runtime_cli --run-validators --config test/configs/precision_local.yaml against a dev deployment; run scripts/kv_warmup.sh to pre-fill the kvcache with the canary prefix set.

Thanks to Rohan Patel for eviction work, and the QA team for extended regression runs.

Patch size: moderate; favors safety and observability over aggressive micro-optimizations up front.

Added a runtime 'safelock' gating mechanism to avoid correctness regressions when enabling fast-path kernels and lower-precision execution. New precision toggle with runtime validators. KV-cache eviction made conservative under uncertain cache-warmness. Backwards-compatible; opt-in via config.

Title: Low-precision execution guidelines: INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ kernel constraints & KV cache interplay

Low-precision execution guidelines: INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ kernel constraints & KV cache interplay

Purpose:
This doc captures pragmatic constraints and recommendations for implementing a unified low-precision execution path across INT8, FP8, GPTQ, and AWQ payloads inside the serving runtime. Focus is on kernel compatibility, scheduling/capacity implications, and how KV cache formats and cache hits interact with quantized execution.

Status and audience:
- Draft for runtime/kernel engineers and applied-ML folks onboarding model variants.
- Not a final spec — intended as a working checklist and set of constraints to feed PRDs and kernel implementations.

Executive summary (short):
- We must treat quantized models as first-class variants but avoid fragmentation in the runtime: prefer a small set of kernel entry patterns that cover INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ with graceful fallbacks.
- Key constraints: alignment/padding rules, accumulation precision, fused op assumptions (attention/query/key/value layout), and KV cache serialized format with versioned metadata for scale factors.
- Where hardware cannot support a fused low-precision kernel, runtime should transparently fall back to mixed-precision (FP16 accumulators or FP32 where necessary) while preserving latency SLOs as a priority.

1) Kernel constraints and invariants
- Block sizes and alignment:
  - All low-precision GEMM kernels must accept inputs padded to 32-byte alignment for CUDA and to the SIMD width for CPU AVX variants.
  - Prefer blocking at 128x128 or 256x64 tile shapes for GPU kernels; ensure INT8/AWQ packing doesn't change the tile granularity expected by the scheduler.
  - FP8 path kernels should be tolerant to variable exponent bias encoding (E4M3 vs E5M2) via metadata flags; avoid hard-coded exponent assumptions.

- Accumulation precision:
  - INT8 and AWQ kernels must accumulate into at least FP16 (prefer FP32 where budget allows for critical layers like classifier head and output projection).
  - GPTQ-path kernels (weight-only quantized) can keep activations in FP16 -> accumulate in FP32 if quality regressions observed in critical benchmarks.

- Quantization metadata (per-layer):
  - Every quantized weight tensor must carry: quant_type (INT8/GPTQ/AWQ/FP8), scale(s) (per-channel or per-block), zero_point if used, block-size if grouped quantization, and a bitfield for kernel compatibility flags.
  - Use a compact header prepended to artifact blobs stored in model cache; header versioning required to support future packing changes.

- De/quantization points and fused ops:
  - Minimize explicit dequantize->compute->requantize hops. Where possible implement fused kernels (dequantize + matmul + activation + requantize) for INT8 and AWQ to reduce DRAM traffic and preserve latency.
  - Attention kernels should accept packed QKV layouts for quantized weights; if packed format not available, runtime must unpack to an internal fused format before KV cache insertion.

2) Scheduling and capacity behavior
- Scheduling unit and batching
  - Scheduler should treat quantized models as compatible with mixed-precision routes but prefer quantized-capable executors when available.
  - Prefetch/prepare step: ensure quantization metadata is available before scheduling; if metadata incompatible, route to fallback node early to avoid wasted scheduling attempts.
  - Continuous batching: quantized paths reduce compute but may be more memory-bound—batcher heuristics must be aware of reduced per-token compute and adjust batch sizes upward until memory SLOs are hit.

- Fallback policies and graceful degradation
  - When a quantized kernel fails compatibility checks (alignment, unsupported exponents, missing scale), fallback to FP16/FP32 kernel on same node if capacity allows; otherwise route to a non-quantized node.
  - Record telemetry events for each fallback: reason code, layer name, model version, node type, and latency delta.

3) KV cache format and interactions
- Cache layout for quantized activations:
  - Store KV cache in a format that includes a "storage_format" field: one of [FP16, INT8_PACKED, AWQ_PACKED, FP8_PACKED]. Each entry must include per-tensor scale metadata or a reference to the model's quant metadata.
  - If cached keys/values were produced by a fused low-precision attention kernel, they should remain in that packed format to avoid expensive de/quantize on cache hit.
  - Cache lookup must compare model version + quant header version + executor compatibility bitfield; mismatch triggers cache invalidation or on-the-fly reformat.

- On-the-fly reformatting costs
  - Reformatting from packed INT8/AWQ to FP16 is expensive; measure and cap the runtime reformatting budget per request (configurable, default 5ms). If budget exceeded, fall back to node-level dequantization route (higher latency but predictable).

- Prefix sharing and KV reuse
  - To maximize cache hits across routes, adopt canonical packed format per model served (decided at model load). Conversions at load time are acceptable; avoid per-request canonicalization.

4) Model artifact packaging and on-disk layout
- Packaging requirements:
  - When saving quantized model artifacts, include a machine-readable manifest.json with: quantization_scheme, per-layer scale shapes, kernel_compat_flags, preferred_kernel_tile_sizes, cache_storage_format_recommended.

Title: Precision path interoperability constraints and KV-cache notes

Precision path interoperability constraints and KV-cache notes

Status: draft; purpose: capture kernel-level constraints and runtime scheduling interactions for the low-precision execution paths (INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ) and how the KV-cache and batching layer must adapt.

Summary
This doc records concrete constraints and compatibility rules we've discovered while prototyping mixed-precision execution paths. It focuses on the intersection of three components: (1) kernel contracts and layout requirements for different quant formats, (2) the scheduler/batcher behavior that must be aware of precision constraints to maintain latency and throughput SLOs, and (3) KV-cache semantics when keys/values are produced/consumed by quantized kernels or when evict/fill paths cross precision boundaries.

Goals
- Enumerate kernel ABI expectations for INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ kernels that the runtime must enforce.
- Define scheduling rules and fallback routes when matching kernels are unavailable.
- Specify KV-cache invariants and migration/fallback strategies if cached KV blocks are from a different precision than the requested model variant.
- Produce a small test matrix and microbenchmarks to validate trade-offs (accuracy, latency, memory).

Kernel constraints (high level)
1) Weight memory layout and alignment
   - INT8/GPTQ/AWQ kernels assume tightly packed int8 weight tiles in row-major order with 32B alignment for vectorized loads.
   - FP8 kernels expect 16-bit-aligned buffers with an 8-byte header per weight tensor describing scale/zero-point metadata when using per-block quantization.
   - Runtime must expose a canonical layout converter for on-the-fly reformatting if model artifact uses a different convention. Avoid conversion in hot path unless cached formatted weights are available.

2) Per-channel vs per-tensor scales
   - GPTQ/AWQ often use per-channel scales for matmul outputs. Kernels will expose whether they accept per-channel scale arrays or only per-tensor.
   - ABI: kernel descriptor must include scale_ptr (nullable) + scale_stride to support both. Null implies per-tensor only.

3) Accumulator precision and reduction semantics
   - INT8 and AWQ kernels rely on int32 accumulators then requantize; FP8 kernels often use float32 accumulation on CUDA/ROCm with later casting.
   - For identical numerical results across paths, define reduction order and rounding behavior in descriptor (reduce_left_to_right bool; rounding_mode enum).

4) KV cache production/consumption contract
   - KV tensors produced by quantized transformer attention kernels may be in compressed/quantized format. The cache store needs two modes: raw_format (same layout as kernel output) and canonical_fp16/float32 representation.
   - Cache writes: kernel should indicate produced_precision field (one of: int8, awq, gptq, fp8, fp16, float32) plus format_id string.
   - Cache reads: scheduler must prefer raw_format hits when requested precision == produced_precision. If mismatch, runtime must either (a) convert on read (costly), (b) re-compute using unquantized fallback model, or (c) route to compatible kernel that accepts the stored format.

Scheduling & batching implications
1) Precision-aware queueing
   - Each worker/gpu queue maintains sub-queues by precision family. This prevents enqueuing an INT8-only kernel on a GPU instance set up for FP8 fast paths.
   - Policy: for tight latency SLOs, prefer same-precision batching even if batch utilization is slightly lower. For throughput-first contracts, allow cross-precision coalescing only when kernels share identical memory layouts and accumulator types.

2) Dynamic fallback & rollout paths
   - If a cluster lacks INT8/GPTQ optimized kernels for a model version, fallback options in order: (a) INT8->FP16 compatible kernel (if supports dequantized weights), (b) FP8 kernel (if supports mapping), (c) software dequantization then FP16 matmul. Documented fallback chain must be encoded in model manifest.

3) Cost of on-the-fly layout conversion
   - Measured conversion tax: reformatting a 2GB weight shard from GPTQ format to INT8 tiled format is O(N) and may take tens of ms on CPU/host; unacceptable on hot-path. Action: preformat weights during model load; keep a single canonical hot-format in device memory. Eviction policy must prefer keeping hot-format for currently scheduled precision.

KV-cache specific rules and invariants
1) Cache key for format-awareness
   - Cache key = (model_id, model_version, precision_tag, format_id, seq_position_block). precision_tag must be included. This enables safe reuse only when precision matches.

2) Migration strategies
   - Transparent conversion: when storage is canonical FP16 but request wants INT8 kernels, we can quantize cached FP16 KVs into INT8 on read and write a backfilled int8 representation if space allows. Prioritize conversion for recent hot-blocks.
   - Recompute-on-miss: if conversion cost > threshold and model allows partial recompute, prefer computing KVs for new precision instead of converting. Threshold tunable per-customer SLA.

3) Eviction & fragmentation
   - Mixed-precision caches lead to fragmentation. Recommended allocator: segregated pools per precision, with an LRU within each pool and a global swapping policy using age-and-frequency heuristics.

Compatibility matrix (proposal)
- Row = produced_precision; Column = requested_kernel_precision; cells: allowed/convert/recompute.
- Example rows: produced=int8, requested=int8 -> allowed; produced=int8, requested=fp16 -> convert on read (fast dequant); produced=gptq, requested=int8 -> convert only if same tile alignment; else recompute.

Tests and microbenchmarks
- Simple microbench suite: generate KV tensors for standard Llama-2 13B layers under each quant scheme, measure: write latency, read+convert latency, hit-rate impact for prefixes of 16/64/128 tokens, and accuracy delta after conversion.
- Stress test: mixed-precision traffic simulator hitting scheduling logic with configurable ratios (INT8:FP8:FP16 = 70:20:10) to validate queue isolation and throughput.

Open questions / TODOs
- Tile descriptors: finalize compact header format for weight tiles that supports both AWQ and GPTQ metadata without doubling header size. (Owner: Rina)
- Hardware offload: can newer Ampere/Blackwell kernels perform FP8 accumulation with int8-like memory layout? If yes, we can unify some code paths. (Action: Ethan to benchmark)
- Runtime API: extend model manifest schema to include fallback_chain and supported_format_ids. Need PR to schema repo. (ENG-1198)

Next steps
1) Add canonical layout converter to runtime/lib/format_conversion; mark hot-format caches pinned during model load.
2) Implement precision_tag in KV-cache key and change eviction policy to segregated pools.
3) Create microbench harness and run across target hardware (A100, H100, RTX) to populate conversion cost table.
4) Draft runtime spec PR describing kernel descriptor fields (produced_precision, format_id, scale_ptr, accumulator_type, rounding_mode).

Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally a pragmatic, implementation-first draft. I expect API names to change. Focus feedback on invariants (cache key must include precision) and scheduling policy trade-offs for latency SLOs.

References & links
- Draft PR with kernel descriptor prototype: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/842
- Ticket tracking mixed-precision cache behaviour: ENG-1198

Title: Introduce precision-aware fast-path gating and safe-mode fallbacks for runtime kernels

Introduce precision-aware fast-path gating and safe-mode fallbacks for runtime kernels

Motivation and summary: We observed rare correctness regressions in production when the runtime selected aggressive high-throughput kernels (mixed-precision, fused attention variants) under tail-case sequence patterns. These regressions correlate with two factors: (1) precision toggles (bfloat16/int8 paths) where numerical drift can cross threshold checks, and (2) scheduling-induced KV cache aliases when continuous batching mixes sequences with different policy hints. This PR implements a multi-pronged runtime mitigation: (A) fast-path gating that evaluates a cheap oracle before selecting an aggressive kernel, (B) per-request precision policy toggles with fallback coherence, and (C) a global 'safe-mode' that enforces conservative kernel selection for deployments that prioritize determinism over peak throughput. The changes are designed to be conservative by default and configurable per-deployment.

What this PR changes (high-level): - fast-path gating: a lightweight verification that runs at kernel-selection time; checks include sequence-length alignment, head-dim divisibility, kv-cache layout compatibility, and a floating-point stability heuristic. Gate returns ALLOW or DENY for fast kernels. When denied, runtime picks a conservative compatibility kernel. - precision toggles: requests may specify a preferred precision (fp32, bf16, int8) in the runtime flags. When an aggressive precision is selected, we attach a precision-stamp to the request and ensure that batched operations only group compatible stamps or demote to a conservative execution path. - safe-mode: a deployment/runtime flag that forces deterministic kernels (no fused/approximated kernels), disables some heuristics that risk nondeterminism (e.g. async kernel chaining), and enables stricter KV cache verification. Intended for regulated customers or incident mitigation. - KV cache invariants: added explicit verification hooks when moving KV shards between devices or reusing cached prefixes; these checks are lightweight by default but can be promoted to strict checks in safe-mode. - scheduling changes: continuous-batching scheduler now respects precision-stamps and fast-path gate outcomes when forming batches; the scheduler will split or reorder to preserve correctness rather than blindly maximizing batch size. - tests and benchmarks: added unit tests reproducing prior regression patterns and a micro-benchmark to measure fast-path gate overhead.

Description/notes for reviewers (single-line style): This is a behavioral change to kernel selection — default experience should be unchanged unless a customer enables precision overrides or safe-mode. The fast-path gate is intentionally cheap (single-digit microseconds for common inputs) and caches decisions per model/sequence-profile. The PR contains both the gate logic and the policy integration points (runtime flags, scheduler hooks). Please focus review on correctness of the KV cache invariants, scheduler batch-paths, and the interaction between precision-stamps and continuous batching.

Checklist: - [x] Implement fast-path gate and integrate with kernel selector - [x] Add per-request precision-stamp plumbing (API flag + internal propagation) - [x] Modify scheduler to respect stamps and gate results - [x] Add KV cache verification hooks and safe-mode toggle - [x] Unit tests reproducing regression patterns - [x] Micro-benchmark and perf numbers in bench/notes - [x] Docs: docs/safe_mode.md and runtime-config.md - [x] Add migration note for Dedicated/Private deployments

Commits summary: ["a8f3c4e: runtime: add fast_path_gate interface and basic heuristics", "f4b1e27: scheduler: honor precision_stamp when batching", "c2d9a14: runtime: attach precision_stamp to request context", "7b01d88: kvcache: add light invariant verifier + strict mode", "9d3e7b5: flags: add --runtime-safe-mode and precision policy options", "2f5a33c: tests: add kv-cache-regression and precision-batch tests", "bb9f2b0: bench: continuous batching micro-bench + docs"]

Files changed (high-level): ["src/runtime/fast_path_gate.h", "src/runtime/fast_path_gate.cpp", "src/runtime/precision_policy.h", "src/runtime/precision_policy.cpp", "src/runtime/scheduler.cpp", "src/runtime/scheduler.h", "src/runtime/kv_cache_invariants.cpp", "src/runtime/kv_cache_invariants.h", "src/flags/runtime_flags.cpp", "tests/kv_cache_regression_test.cc", "tests/precision_batching_test.cc", "tools/bench/continuous_batching_bench.py", "docs/safe_mode.md", "docs/runtime-config.md"]

Small snippet (illustrative, not full diff): `if (fast_path_gate.allow(model, profile, req.precision_stamp)) { kernel = select_aggressive_kernel(...); } else { kernel = select_conservative_kernel(...); }`

Review conversation highlights: - Aarti: "Can you explain the gate cache invalidation strategy? I'm worried a long-lived cache could mask model upgrades." — Noah: "Gate caches are keyed by (model_id, model_checksum, profile_hash); we invalidate when model checksum changes. Added explicit invalidation in model-upgrade path (src/runtime/model_manager.cpp)." - Diego: "Scheduler change looks correct but we need to ensure we don't regress p50 latency for small requests." — Noah: "Bench numbers added; p50 unchanged, p95 improved by 4% in scenarios with mixed precision. Gate overhead is ~3us per decision and is amortized by cached results for common profiles." - Lena: "KV invariant verifier might be too expensive in strict mode; any way to sample?" — Noah: "Yes, we expose sample_rate and a strict boolean. Default strict=false; safe-mode forces strict=true. Documented in runtime-config.md." - Diego (post-approval): "Please add an opt-out flag for Dedicated customers who rely on the old aggressive kernel selection." — Noah: "Added --runtime-fastpath-opt-out and documented in Dedicated migration notes."

CI summary: - linux-build: pass - unit-tests: pass (one flaky test initially; re-run succeeded) - integration-tests: pass - bench-smoke: pass - lint: pass

Perf notes: - Continuous batching micro-bench shows fast-path gate adds 2-6% CPU overhead on tight loops but enables use of high-throughput kernels for 60% of steady workloads, resulting in net token/sec improvements of 8-12% on our RPU cluster for mixed-precision-enabled models. - In safe-mode, throughput is reduced (~18% on average) but p99 latency variance improves and numerical determinism is preserved.

Backward compatibility / migration: Default runtime behavior unchanged. New flags: --runtime-safe-mode (bool), --precision-preference (string), --runtime-fastpath-opt-out (bool). Dedicated/Private operators should review migration notes; safe-mode intended as an incident mitigation toggle.

Testing and validation: Added regression tests that reproduce previously observed KV aliasing read errors and precision-bound drift failures. Manual run against a staging fleet (redwood-staging) for 48h; no regressions observed. Bench harness included and results under tools/bench/README.md.

Follow-ups (future work): - Extend gate to consider dynamic temperature and response-length distributions - Add telemetry events for gate-deny reasons to improve ops diagnostics - Explore hardware-specific micro-optimizations for safe deterministic kernels

Merge details: Squash-merged into main after approvals from Aarti and Diego. Changelog and release notes updated by release-manager bot.

Title: Quant profile sensitivity: batching & long-burst (FP8/INT8) latency-accuracy study

Quant profile sensitivity: batching & long-burst (FP8/INT8) latency-accuracy study

Long-burst sensitivity study to understand how FP8 and INT8 quantization profiles interact with batching and very long context workloads. Goal: produce a set of calibrated quant profiles and an automated validation harness that measures throughput, p50/p95/p99 latency, tail latency stability, and quality regressions against FP32 baseline for context lengths 2048, 8192, and 32768 tokens across batch sizes [1,4,8,16]. The study will drive profile recommendations for runtime-1.22 and inform autoscaling/rollout policies for Dedicated.
Previous runs (ENG-61234, ENG-54678) covered short to medium contexts; field requests have reported sporadic tail-latency spikes in long-context generation and occasional quality drift after aggressive FP8 packing. This ticket centralizes experiments and the calibration workflow to: (1) ensure KV cache handling doesn't amplify quantization error; (2) measure batching-induced latency amplification for long KV sequences; (3) identify calibration knobs that recover accuracy with minimal throughput loss.
1) Properly tuned calibration (per-layer activation clipping + per-channel scales) will recover >98% of FP32 quality (measured by log-prob difference on eval set) while improving throughput 1.6-2.5x in INT8 and 2.2-3.5x in FP8.
2) Large batch sizes (>8) with long-contexts increase tail latency superlinearly due to KV-cache transfer costs; smart micro-batching or partial kv-scheduling will recover p99 without losing more than 10% throughput.

2. INT8 profile - generate per-layer calibration using representative traces; run same grid and record metrics.
3. FP8 profile - test dynamic FP8 exponent range settings and per-channel vs per-tensor scales; run grid.
4. Micro-batching - evaluate split-batch and partial-KV strategies to reduce peak memory transfer and tail latency.
5. KV warmup - instrument warmup sequences and measure p99 behavior pre/post warmup.
6. Robustness - run noisy inputs and repeated microburst patterns to measure jitter and stability over 24 hours.

Title: Tightrope: precision-variant benchmarks and degradation modes

Tightrope: precision-variant benchmarks and degradation modes

Purpose
This is a field-facing, pragmatic snapshot of cross-precision behavior when serving mid-size to large decoder models under realistic traffic shapes. The intent: identify repeatable modes where INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ choices improve unit-cost without silently degrading instruction-following or increasing tail latency.

Executive summary (short)
- We ran a set of throughput/latency/quality tests across four precision families (native FP16 baseline, FP8 emulation, INT8 symmetric, two GPTQ/AWQ variants) on two representative models: Llama-2-13B-instruct and Redstone-7B (internal).
- Primary findings: FP8 gives the biggest p50 token speedup (1.35x vs FP16) with modest instruction-quality drop (~3% on instruction-F1). INT8 can hit 1.6x token throughput but shows a non-linear quality cliff on longer prompts (>512 tokens) for one kernel flavor we used. GPTQ/AWQ variants give intermediate throughput with more predictable quality but expose kernel-specific tail-latency amplification under multiworkload contention.
- Real-world implication: prefer FP8 for interactive use where tail-latency SLO is tight and prompt lengths are short-to-medium; use GPTQ/AWQ or mixed-precision routing for long-context or safety-critical workloads.

Setup and methodology (concise)
- Hardware: 1x A100-80GB (hosted test cluster node type H1) and 1x H100-80GB (H2) for cross-arch comparison. Kernel stack: two vendors — internal optimized matmul scheduler (v3) and vendor-gemm (nvx-11).
- Models: Llama-2-13B-instruct (hf: llm/llama2-13b) and Redstone-7B (internal eval build). All weights exported and converted to target formats using the same tokenizers and config.
- Precision variants tested: FP16 baseline, FP8 (e4m3 emulation path), INT8 (symmetric 8-bit with per-channel scale), GPTQ-4-bit (k-lasso variant), AWQ-4/8 hybrid.
- Workloads: three synthetic traffic shapes
  - Interactive: 1–4 token incremental user messages (latency-sensitive)
  - Assistant: 200 instruction prompts (avg len 120 tokens) for instruction-following quality
  - Long-context: 1k-token context retrieval + 400-token response (memory-heavy)
- Metrics collected: p50/p90/p95 latency per-response, tokens/sec throughput, GPU util, CPU overhead, prompt-cost (tokens*compute ms), and quality metrics: instruction-F1 (binary answer match), BERTScore (avg), semantic-similarity (embedding cosine), and a simple hallucination count (manual spot-check on 200 responses).

Representative results (high-level numbers)
- Llama-2-13B-instruct (H100, matmul v3):
  - FP16 baseline: p50=110ms, p95=235ms, throughput=750 tokens/s, instr-F1=0.88, BERTScore=0.914
  - FP8 (e4m3 emul): p50=82ms, p95=205ms, throughput=1015 tokens/s (+35%), instr-F1=0.85 (-3.4%), BERTScore=0.906
  - INT8 (symmetric): p50=72ms, p95=310ms, throughput=1200 tokens/s (+60%), instr-F1=0.78 (-11.4%), BERTScore=0.892
  - GPTQ-4-bit: p50=96ms, p95=260ms, throughput=860 tokens/s, instr-F1=0.86 (-2.3%), BERTScore=0.908
  - AWQ hybrid: p50=88ms, p95=245ms, throughput=920 tokens/s, instr-F1=0.87 (-1.1%), BERTScore=0.911
- Long-context variant (same model) showed much larger INT8 degradation: instruction-F1 fell to 0.66 and p95 inflated to 520ms on INT8 kernel sample — indicates instability when KV-cache and tiled kernels interact.

Observations and plausible causes
1) INT8 tail-latency amplification
   - Pattern: excellent median speed, but wide p95/p99 on multiworkload stress tests. Kernel traces show repeated slowdowns when tile reorder + dispatcher contention happens (matmul fallback paths and kernel retries). Suspect numeric overflow/patching and code-path fallback causing extra GPU kernel launches.
2) FP8 is the best median improvement for interactive paths
   - FP8's quant noise is small for short prompts and classification-like completions. Emulation path overhead is visible on A100 but smaller on H100 where custom FP8 ops existed.
3) GPTQ/AWQ preserve quality with moderate cost
   - These schemes minimize instruction regressions; AWQ hybrid in our run was the best quality/latency compromise for sensitive workloads.
4) Kernel-dependent behavior dominates cross-precision comparisons
   - Same quant format on two different matmul kernels produced different tail-behavior. Thorough kernel profiling (microsecond traces) is necessary before fleet-wide rollout.

Reproducibility notes
- Script: perf/tightrope/run-suite.sh (internal repo). Seeded workloads and a pinned tokenizer hash included in linked_artifacts.
- Deterministic measurement windows: each datapoint is median of 5 runs, outlier discard using IQR-based filter. Multiworkload mixes used poisson arrival modeling with burst ratio 3:1.

Quick triage checklist (for engineers)
- If p95 >> p50 on INT8, collect: per-kernel launch counts, kernel-retry logs, GPU stream serialization traces, and dispatcher occupancy heatmaps.
- Confirm per-channel scaling was computed on same calibration set. Mismatched calibration across layers can create long-context drift.
- Try mixed-precision per-layer: keep first/last attention blocks at FP16, quant rest to INT8.
- For immediate mitigation on production: use FP8 for interactive routes and route long-context or “sensitive” API keys to GPTQ/AWQ variants.

Actionable next steps (prioritized)
1) Short (1–2 sprints): Add kernel-level microtrace collector to the smoke harness; add automatic detection of tail amplification patterns.
2) Mid (1 month): Run a cross-matrix sweep of matrix shapes to map which layer shapes trigger INT8 fallback in matmul v3.
3) Mid (1 month): Implement mixed-precision routing rules in the model router (per-route policy) so we can A/B FP8 vs GPTQ without model duplication costs.
4) Longer (quarter): Integrate a per-inference ‘precision predictor’ that chooses quantization on the fly based on context length, recent tail signals, and cost-SLO constraints.

Open questions
- How much of the INT8 long-context failure is due to calibration data mismatch vs kernel tiling interference? Need a controlled experiment isolating those two.
- Can block-sparse-friendly kernels reduce INT8 tail path cost? Vendor collaboration required.
- For FP8, what is the long-term drift under on-the-fly fine-tuning (few-shot adaptation)? Early signs positive but not tested.

Appendix: quick logs and example failure transcript (trimmed)
- Example failure: INT8 run with 1k context: model produced incoherent slot-references on turn 4; manual check grouped 22/200 outputs flagged on hallucination check. Kernel log excerpt: repeated kernel fallback on tile_i=43 causing repeated synchronization stalls.

Contact/owners for followups
- Primary: Aisha Patel (eng-serving-runtime)
- Kernel traces and harness: Ravi Menon
- Eval metrics and quality checks: Xiao Chen

Notes: this is a living note intended to capture reproducible, field-observed tradeoffs. If you copy experiments, add your kernel and arch tags (nvx-11/matmul-v3/A100/H100) to the run name so we can aggregate across clusters.

Title: low-precision-path-allocator-and-kernel-hookups

low-precision-path-allocator-and-kernel-hookups

Motivation: Continued work to reduce per-token cost and tail latency for low-precision inference. Prior PRs added isolated INT8/FP8 kernels and dequant fusion primitives; this change weaves those pieces into the serving runtime with a small, deterministic allocator and dispatch layer that routes requests to the best low-precision execution path based on model variant, sequence-length distribution, KV-cache state, and batching profile. The goal is pragmatic: improve throughput and p99 latency for production workloads while preserving correctness and fast fallback to FP16/FP32 when numerical risk is detected.

Summary of changes (single-shot): adds a LowPrecisionPathAllocator that makes per-request routing decisions, wires kernel dispatch tables for INT8 and FP8 fused-dequant paths, introduces lightweight per-worker hints to the continuous-batching scheduler to avoid head-of-line blocking when long sequences and small batches mix, and optimizes KV cache hot-path bookkeeping to reduce CPU overhead on cache-miss heavy workloads. Also includes microbench harness changes and canary rollout config for safe production enablement.

Why this is different: previous PRs provided kernels and fusion infra in isolation; this PR focuses on connecting those kernels into runtime scheduling and KV-cache-aware routing so that benefits are realized in end-to-end serving. It emphasizes deterministic allocation (no global locks), low-overhead decision logic, and explicit fallback rules when stability checks fail.

Behavioral details and invariants: allocator decisions are per-request at enqueue time and are stable for the request lifetime; dequant fusion is only selected when the model variant metadata marks weights as stable for fusion and dynamic range checks pass for the first token; KV cache uses an additional small per-request bitmap to avoid expensive lookups for fully warmed prefixes. Fallback to FP16 is immediate and logged when a numerical anomaly (NaN/Inf or outlier token likelihood shift exceeding a threshold) is detected.

Benchmark highlights (internal perf harness, 8xA100 p4d-like profile, mixed sequence lengths): INT8 fused-dequant path: +12% throughput, p99 latency -18% on chat-like traffic compared to baseline FP16 runtime; FP8 path: +8% throughput, p99 -10% for short-sequence-only workloads; KV cache bookkeeping optimization reduces CPU-side cache-miss accounting overhead by ~25% in high-concurrency tests. End-to-end cost projection (model-dependent) shows unit token cost reduction up to 20% in aggressive INT8 mode under production batching distributions. Full benchmark run artifacts attached to the PR.

Compatibility and safety: feature gated behind runtime flag low_precision.path_enabled and staged via canary config (release/ops/rollouts). No model format changes required. Contains extensive checks that prevent low-precision selection for models listed in a denylist or when model metadata lacks quant-stability hints.

Testing: unit tests for allocator heuristics, kernel routing, and fallback; integration tests with the continuous-batching scheduler and KV cache; regression tests exercising numerical stability thresholds. CI includes microbench regression checks on the perf lab.

How to exercise locally: run tools/perf/harness --profile=canary-int8 --model=gpt-medium --seq-distribution=chat-mix; the harness supports toggling low_precision.path_enabled. See docs/perf/low_precision_readme.md for experiment configuration and metrics artifacts.

References: related Linear ticket ENG-2145, earlier kernel PRs that added fused-dequant primitives and FP8 kernels.

Release strategy: deploy to a 5% canary for 48h with end-to-end latency/cost monitors and automatic rollback if p99 regresses beyond the configured SLO delta.

- [x] kernel hookups and fused-dequant path enabled behind flag
- [x] KV cache bookkeeping optimization implemented

Title: On-demand Precision Modes — PRD sketch

On-demand Precision Modes — PRD sketch

Problem statement:
- Customers want finer control over per-request quality/cost tradeoffs without creating separate model endpoints or complex routing rules.
- Current options (pin to model variant, use quantization globally, or change model entirely) are heavy-weight and cause churn for devs.
- Need a lightweight surface for app teams to express when they need higher fidelity vs when they want to conserve tokens/costs.

Idea (one-liner):
Provide an "on-demand precision" parameter that applications can set per-request (and set policy-level defaults) to trade off latency/cost vs output fidelity. Backed by: model config profiles, dynamic quantization hints, and runtime fast-fallbacks.

Goals / success metrics (90d):
- Developer adoption: 10 internal integrations + 3 external beta customers.
- Cost delta: average cost-per-request reduction of 18% for customers using economy mode on non-critical flows.
- Quality regressions: <1% of eval prompt sets flagged as regression when using mode-based routing.
- Latency SLOs maintained for balanced/eco modes within 10% of baseline.

Mode concepts (examples):
- economy: aggressive batching, 8-bit quantized kernels, prefix cache eviction for long contexts; best-effort coherency.
- balanced: default runtime (current production kernels/quant), moderate batching, preserve KV cache for session.
- fidelity: run higher-precision kernels, disable some batching optimizations, optional slow-path reranking when applicable.
- smart: heuristic that promotes a request to fidelity if flags (e.g., long-form generation, code, eval-set match) or user tier indicates higher quality.

API surface (rough):
- request param: precision: "economy" | "balanced" | "fidelity" | "smart"
- optional hints: fidelity_budget_tokens (int), require_rerank (bool), preferred_model_family (string)
- route policy: default_precision: string, scaling_rules (e.g., promote to "fidelity" for specific endpoints or user segments)

Console UX sketch:
- Per-route toggle for default precision + histogram of cost delta and quality regressions
- Traffic split UI: show how much traffic went to each precision mode and simulated monthly spend impact
- Quick A/B: enable experiment to route 10% of traffic to fidelity for N days with automatic eval hooks

User stories:
- As a product engineer, I want to set "economy" for low-value chatbot replies so we cut token costs without creating a different endpoint.
- As an ML engineer, I want to run a fidelity-only canary on new model weights to surface regressions before global rollout.
- As a platform engineer, I want to apply a policy that forces internal QA traffic to always use fidelity so our tests are stable.

Acceptance criteria (MVP):
- API: precision field accepted and honored by serving runtime for supported models (documented list).
- Console: per-route default_precision toggle, mode traffic breakdown.
- Metrics: cost and latency per-mode, and a quality-sampling pipeline that runs a small eval set across modes daily.

Backend approach (high level):
- Map precision -> runtime configuration bundle (model_variant, quant_level, kernel_flags, batching_hint).
- Runtime switches: light-weight fast path vs slow path; ensure KV cache compatibility between modes where possible to prevent large session degradation.
- Telemetry: tag traces with precision mode, model_variant, and any fast-fallback triggers.

Risks & open questions:
- Cache compatibility: if fidelity preserves KV cache and economy evicts aggressively, resuming session with a different mode might cause incoherent responses. Need eviction/restore heuristics.
- Observable regressions: how many eval prompts to run to detect a regression confidently per-customer? Cost of that eval.
- SLA semantics: will fidelity mode change SLA tiers (longer tails)? Need to document and surface to customers.
- Billing model: per-token pricing vs per-mode multiplier? Simpler to start with usage-based tokens + transparency table.

Experiment plan (first 6 weeks):
1) Internal pilot: implement precision param and two bundles (economy, balanced) on a single low-risk model (opensourced family). Route internal docs-bot traffic to economy and measure metrics (2 weeks).
2) Eval harness: run daily micro-eval comparing economy/balanced on 1k prompts (2 weeks).
3) External beta: invite 3 customers (SaaS chatbot, internal docs, code assistant) to opt in with console controls; collect feedback + telemetry (2 weeks).

Implementation tasks (rough backlog):
- runtime: precision flag parsing, config bundle wiring, kernel/quant switches (ENG-CORE)
- console: route-level control, traffic visualization (ENG-CONSOLE)
- telemetry: per-mode metrics, eval-runner integration (ENG-OBS)
- product: docs, developer quickstart, migration notes

Notes / brainstorming fragments (TODOs):
- Consider "micro-slots": ability to apply precision only to a subset of tokens (start/continue) — probably post-MVP.
- Investigate model families that tolerate aggressive quantization vs those that don't; maintain model-compat list.
- Add opt-in automatic promotion: if user message contains specific markups (e.g., <!--quality-->), route to fidelity.

References / links to tickets: INF-6732 (pilot), RFC:precision-modes-v1 (design), INF-6789 (eval harness infra).

Questions for next sync:
- Legal/contract: do we need to reflect precision options in enterprise contracts? (Evan to check)
- Billing: prefer multiplier or raw token accounting for clarity? (Finance + Sales input)
- UX: what are acceptable defaults for new accounts? (Growth/product)

Bottom line:
- This gives customers a simple, flexible lever to tune unit economics without model sprawl. Start small (economy + balanced), iterate with telemetry and a tight eval loop, and expand to policy-level controls and smart heuristics once stable.

Title: Precision runtime boundary matrix and fallback heuristics

Precision runtime boundary matrix and fallback heuristics

Purpose:
This doc captures a compact, pragmatic set of constraints and heuristics for the runtime to safely operate mixed-precision quantized models (INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ) and provide coherent KV-cache behavior plus graceful fallbacks. Goal is to minimize tail latency and correctness regressions while enabling opportunistic low-precision kernels.

Scope and motivation:
- Applies to the serving runtime's kernel selection layer, the request scheduler, and the KV cache coherency layer.
- Focuses on: (1) binary compatibility boundaries between kernel implementations, (2) scheduling heuristics that pick precision variants under capacity/latency targets, and (3) rules for maintaining KV cache correctness when switching precision/format between requests.
- This is intentionally pragmatic (not a full math proof); it trades strict generality for low-risk operational rules we can ship quickly.

Assumptions:
- Models are exported with explicit quant metadata: bitwidth, quant scheme (symmetric/asymmetric), per-channel vs per-tensor, and quantization backend tag (GPTQ/AWQ/other).
- Kernels expose a capability descriptor (supported bitwidths, supported layouts, required preprocessing) to the runtime at startup/load time.
- KV cache stored entries are tagged with canonical format + model-version id. Cache entries are immutable once created (append-only).

Key principles:
1) Safety first: avoid silent correctness regressions. If compatibility is uncertain, prefer higher precision.
2) Locality: prefer kernel choices that reuse warmed memory and data layouts to reduce jitter.
3) Explainability: runtime decision logging should include rationale (why we chose kernel X for request Y).

Compatibility matrix (human readable):
- Native-match: request precision == model export precision == kernel precision => safe to use kernel and reuse KV cache entries without conversion.
- Upcast-safe: runtime can run a lower-bit model (e.g., INT8 weights) in higher precision execution (FP16/FP32) by upcasting; safe for correctness but costs cycles. Allowed when latency SLO slack > threshold.
- Downcast-risky: executing a higher-precision model in lower-precision kernel (e.g., FP16 model on INT8 kernel) is disallowed unless model was annotated explicitly as "downcast-validated" by model onboarding process.
- Format-mismatch: GPTQ/AWQ compressed formats are only compatible with kernels explicitly built for that compression. No implicit conversion.

Concrete kernel capability labels (to be emitted by kernel modules):
- allow_upcast_execution: boolean (true => we can run input tensors in a higher-precision path)
- supports_int8, supports_fp8, supports_gptq, supports_awq: booleans
- layout_tag: e.g., kv64x4, kv_stride, etc. (string)
- supports_mixed_kv: boolean (whether kernel can load KV from different bitwidths with internal conversion)

Example runtime rules derived from matrix:
- If kernel.supports_{format} == true AND model.export_format == format => select kernel, reuse KV entries tagged with same model-version and format.
- If model.export_format == int8 and kernel.supports_fp16 and allow_upcast_execution && SLO_has_slack => upcast-run on fp16 kernel (do not reuse int8 KV cache; create new fp16 cache entries).
- If request.precision_hint == "use_low_cost" then prefer int8/AWQ kernels but only if model export is int8/AWQ or model is downcast-validated.

KV cache coherence rules:
- Cache entries carry metadata: model_version_id, quant_format_tag, sequence_start_token_id, layout_tag, creation_timestamp.
- Read semantics: A request can only reuse cache entries with identical model_version_id and quant_format_tag unless the selected kernel advertises supports_mixed_kv==true.
- Conversion forbidden at read path: runtime will not implicitly convert KV entries across quant formats on the hot path. Conversion can be performed offline or via a background task when promoting a model to a new runtime format.
- Cache warmup strategy: when we upcast-run (e.g., int8 model on fp16 kernel), we create a parallel KV namespace for the upcasted runtime to avoid invalidating the cold int8 cache. This prevents cross-talk and keeps eviction policies simple.

Fallback heuristics and scheduler interaction:
- Goal: keep p95 latency under configured SLO while minimizing cost (prefers low-precision kernels when safe).
- Inputs to scheduler decision per request: model_version, request_sequence_length, cold_cache (boolean), client_priority, precision_hint, current_queue_depth, measured_tail_latency for last N requests.
- Decision scoring function (simple additive heuristic):
  score(kernel_candidate) = base_latency_estimate(kernel_candidate, seq_len) - cost_saving_factor * cost_per_token_delta + penalty_if_cold_cache(kernel_candidate) + safety_penalty_if_incompatible
- Safety penalty is very large if kernel_candidate would require unsupported downcast or format conversion. Safety penalty for "mixed-kv but not supported" = +inf (disallow).
- Cold-cache penalty: if candidate requires assembling a fresh KV cache due to format mismatch, add explicit cold_warmup_penalty proportional to expected startup tokens until steady-state.

Fallback chain example (ranking):
1) exact-format, warmed-kv kernel (preferred)
2) exact-format, cold-kv kernel (acceptable if slack)
3) upcast kernel with fresh kv namespace (allowed if slack)
4) higher-precision remote fallback (route to other capacity tier) if local nodes overloaded
5) reject / queue for later if no safe kernel and SLA requires it (rare)

Runtime logging and observability:
- Every kernel selection decision must emit: selected_kernel, reason_code (e.g., "format_match_warm_kv", "upcast_due_to_slack"), fallback_chain_considered (list), decision_score_breakdown. These fields feed into Console traces and cost dashboards.

Testing and validation matrix (minimal viable tests):
- Unit tests for kernel capability descriptors (correct parsing and fallback behavior).
- Integration test: INT8-export model served on INT8 kernel -> ensure cache reuse and numerically expected outputs within tolerance.
- Upcast test: INT8-export model served on FP16 kernel -> results must match baseline within configured divergence threshold; measure p95/p99 delta.
- Rejection test: FP16-export model should NOT be served on INT8 kernel unless downcast-validated flag present.
- KV-coherence test: interleaved requests switching between kernels must not observe cross-format cache contamination.

Operational rollout plan (staged):
- Phase 0 (internal canary): enable decision logging, but disallow automatic upcast; operators can flip an experiment flag per node to allow upcast.
- Phase 1 (dogfood): allow upcast for low-priority traffic, enable parallel KV namespace creation, collect metrics.
- Phase 2 (gradual): enable for more traffic when delta metrics are within thresholds; run background task to compact caches for promoted formats.

Open issues / TODOs:
- How to represent per-channel scale metadata compactly in KV entries so kernels with different quant schemes can co-exist with fewer conversions. (Ravi to prototype compact header format)
- Cost accounting for parallel KV namespaces: need to surface to billing (should attribute to model-version + promotion tag). (Finance sync required, JIRA: RINF-3621)
- Explore safe fast-path for mixed-kv kernels (if supports_mixed_kv == true) — microbenchmarks needed to quantify conversion overhead.
- Confirm semantics for dynamic quantization adapters that may change quant metadata between in-flight versions.

Notes to implementers (practical tips):
- Keep kernel descriptors small and immutable after module load to simplify scheduler caching.
- Avoid blocking the fast path for format checks: use bitmask flags and pre-computed compatibility table per model instance.
- When creating parallel KV namespace, name it deterministic: <model_version_id>::<runtime_format_tag>::<node_id> to make cache debugging easier.

Appendix: minimal pseudocode for decision path
- see below (informal):

function choose_kernel(request, model):
  candidates = list_kernels_that_load(model)
  for kernel in candidates:
    if kernel.format == model.format and kernel.warmed_kv_exists(request.sequence_prefix):
      return kernel, "format_match_warm_kv"
  // evaluate scores
  scored = []
  for kernel in candidates:
    if kernel.requires_downcast and not model.downcast_validated:
      continue
    score = estimate_latency(kernel, request.seq_len)
    if kernel.format != model.format:
      if kernel.supports_mixed_kv:
        score += cold_warmup_penalty
      else if kernel.allow_upcast_execution and kernel.precision > model.precision:
        score += upcast_cost_penalty
      else:
        score = INF
    scored.append((kernel, score))
  return argmin(scored)

Contact and ownership:
- Primary: Aisha K. Moreno (eng-serving-runtime)
- Secondary: Daniel Park (kernel team)

References and related docs:
- GH PR: runtime kernel descriptor schema (linked above)
- Serving runtime: quant kernel safety matrix (older draft, in folder)

End of doc.

Unpolished notes / brainstorm (scratch):
- Might be useful to have a lightweight "compatibility digest" per model that precomputes an ordered list of preferred kernels based on historical latencies. That would let scheduler just pick first available.
- Consider sampling a small percentage of upcasted requests to route to exact-format kernel in parallel to detect silent deviance (shadow testing).
- If compression formats (GPTQ/AWQ) start exposing metadata that permits in-kernel partial decoding of KV entries, we can relax the mixed-kv restriction, but only after careful benching.

TODO: create GH issue to add logging fields to Console; add unit tests matrix to CI.

Title: heterogeneous-quant-fallback-coordinator-and-kv-prefetch-adapter

heterogeneous-quant-fallback-coordinator-and-kv-prefetch-adapter

Motivation: On mixed-precision fleets we observe sporadic tail-latency spikes when the serving runtime switches between INT8 and FP8 kernels under pressure. Root causes include coarse-grained fallback logic (per-device) and KV-cache prefetches that assume a single precision for the entire microbatch. This PR introduces two cooperating components: (1) a HeterogeneousQuantFallbackCoordinator that reasons about per-request and per-layer precision compatibility and orchestrates graceful handoffs between quantized kernels (INT8/FP8) and the full-precision path; and (2) a KVPrefetchAdapter that annotates KV prefetch windows with precision hints and aligns cache warming to the coordinator's decisions.

What this PR does (high level):
- Adds a coordinator service inside the runtime scheduler that keeps lightweight, epoched precision-maps for active model versions and routes requests to the most compatible kernel path while minimizing kernel switch overhead.
- KVPrefetchAdapter propagates precision hints into the KV cache warming pipeline so that prefetched KV entries use the quantization layout expected by the chosen kernel or include a small inline dequantization token when mixed precision is unavoidable.
- Introduces a small lock-free per-GPU staging structure used by the coordinator to avoid global scheduler locks during precision transitions.
- Adds metrics and tracing hooks (precision.route, precision.transition_ms, kv.prefetch_mode) so we can observe fallback frequency and prefetch mismatches.
- Includes unit tests and microbenchmarks (CPU/CUDA) and a perf harness to reproduce the tail-latency scenarios.

Design notes and tradeoffs:
- The coordinator chooses per-request precision by combining: request-level hints (from model config or client headers), per-layer compatibility scoring (fast heuristics computed from kernel profiles), and recent observed quantization success rate. This avoids gratuitous fallbacks for requests that can run entirely in INT8.
- We did not implement model-rewrite to stitch different precision layers into a single fused kernel (out of scope for this PR). Instead we focus on runtime orchestration and cheap data-path transforms.
- The KVPrefetchAdapter supports three modes: exact-layout (prefetch using kernel's preferred layout), dequant-inline (prefetch with small dequant tokens appended), and universal (store in a neutral layout and convert on load). The adapter selects mode based on memory pressure and observed conversion cost.

Testing and results summary:
- microbench/perf/hetero_quant_bench reports: average latency unchanged, P99 improved by ~12% on a mixed INT8/FP8 workload compared to naive device-level fallback, and token throughput improved ~6% under 75% quantizable workload.
- CI runs: linux-build: pass; cuda-tests: initially flaky (race in coordinator startup), fixed and re-run: pass; lint: pass; benchmarks: included baseline.

Backwards compatibility: Coordinator integrates behind an opt-in runtime flag (--hetero-quant-fallback=on). Default behavior is unchanged unless the flag is enabled. KV adapter is gated behind a config flag and defaults to universal mode for older deployments.

Follow-ups:
- Expand kernel-side fast-paths to accept pre-converted KV layouts to further reduce dequant overhead.
- Add a sampling-based evaluator to surface which layers would most benefit from static model rewrites.

References: Linear ENG-7421 for the incident ticket and ENG-7523 for the follow-up performance work; SUP-1982 captured customer repro traces.
Ethan Morales (2026-02-22): Can you explain how the epoched precision-map avoids stale decisions when models are rolled out quickly? Suggest adding a TTL and metrics for decision staleness.
Priya Shah (2026-02-22): Added TTL and a precision.map.stale counter, and documented the tradeoffs (PR updated).
Wei Zhang (2026-02-24): I saw a small memory regression in the bench run. Is the staging buffer size configurable? We should bound it based on GPUs and model context length.
Priya Shah (2026-02-24): Made the staging buffer tunable via runtime config and added a safeguard to cap entries per-GPU. Bench results re-run and mem regression resolved.
Lucas Carter (2026-02-26): CI showed a sporadic crash on coordinator init under heavy concurrency. Looks like a startup race with the epoch counter. Please harden initialization and add a test that spawns many concurrent routers.
Priya Shah (2026-02-27): Fixed the race (commit g9d2a44), added the concurrent init test; CI green after rerun.
Introduce opt-in heterogeneous quantization fallback coordinator and KV prefetch adapter to reduce tail latencies on mixed-precision fleets; enable via --hetero-quant-fallback flag.

elaine: Heads up - POC with OrbitPay in 25m. Customer copied key from UI but every /v1/embeddings call returns 403: {"error":{"message":"permission denied: tenant mismatch","code":403}}. They say the dashboard shows key attached to "orbitpay-main" :weary:

samir: that "tenant mismatch" string usually means the key is bound to a different org/tenant than the request header (Redwood-Org) or their SDK is sending a different env. Quick asks: can you get a sanitized header dump and key id/account id?

presales-bot: Tip: Keys created via the sales console can be bound to a staging tenant by default. Docs: https://docs.redwood.ai/auth#key-bindings :information_source:

elaine: customer paste (sanitized):
```
curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/embeddings 
 -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_orbit_42" 
 -H "Content-Type: application/json" 
 -d '{"model":"redwood-text-embed","input":"hello"}'
```
No Redwood-Org or X-Project headers. Dashboard says key bound to org `orbitpay-main`. They also have an internal wrapper that sets REDWOOD_ORG=orbitpay-prod (note the different suffix).

meera: env mismatch is very common. If their SDK picks up REDWOOD_ORG=orbitpay-prod and the key is bound to orbitpay-main you'll hit that 403. Easiest fix: ask them to set explicit header `Redwood-Org: orbitpay-main` in the demo.

elaine: security won't rotate keys. They asked if we can make the key accept orbitpay-prod requests for the demo (no code change).

ops: we can add a temporary tenant alias mapping server-side for that account. Requires approval and audit. How long do they need it?

samir: also ask them to try this debug curl to confirm it's header related: 
```
curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/embeddings 
 -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_orbit_42" 
 -H "Redwood-Org: orbitpay-main" 
 -H "Content-Type: application/json" 
 -d '{"model":"redwood-text-embed","input":"status"}'
```
If 200 -> header fix. If still 403 we need x-rw-request-id.

elaine: they tried header curl and got 403 still. Response included `x-rw-request-id: rq_abc123` and body: `{"error":{"message":"permission denied: action not permitted: embeddings.create","code":403}}`.

meera: that suggests the key policy doesn't allow embeddings.create. Keys can be scoped to actions (e.g., embeddings-only, generate-only). We'll need to inspect policy server-side. Please send key id (not secret) + account id.

elaine: account `acct_77122`, key id `key_orbit_42`. Customer insists no policy changes without legal sign-off. Can we do a temporary action grant for demo?

ops: temporary action grants are possible but must be approved by SecOps and logged. We can grant embeddings.create for up to 30 minutes. Also can bump RPS to 20 for the demo window if they saw rate limits earlier.

presales-bot: Checklist: [x] collect key id/account, [x] try explicit Redwood-Org header, [x] collect x-rw-request-id, [ ] request temporary action grant, [ ] log audit entry, [ ] optional RPS bump. Docs: https://docs.redwood.ai/troubleshooting#auth-403

meera: one more debug step: ask customer to call a different endpoint allowed by limited keys (e.g., /v1/usage or /v1/ping) that often returns 200 even for restricted keys. If that succeeds, it's definitely action-based.

elaine: they ran `curl https://api.redwood.ai/v1/ping -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_orbit_42"` and got 200. So it's action-limited.

ops: I'll draft the SecOps exception: "Temporary grant embeddings.create for key key_orbit_42 on acct_77122 for 30m for live sales demo; approver ops; audit required." Approving RPS bump to 20. @audit-bot please record.

audit-bot: Audit entry created: "TEMP-PERM-GRANT acct_77122 key_orbit_42 embeddings.create expire_in=30m approver=ops reason='live sales demo'"

meera: once we flip the permission please have them retry and paste the x-rw-request-id if it still fails. Also suggest they correct their REDWOOD_ORG env to avoid future issues.

elaine: thanks team. I'll update the customer: temporary grant + RPS bump live in 5m, please retry then and paste `x-rw-request-id` if any failure. Will report back. :thumbsup:

Title: Model assurance scorecards: messaging & sales scripts

Model assurance scorecards: messaging & sales scripts

TL;DR: Draft messaging framework and sample sales scripts for a new Model Assurance Scorecard we want to surface in the Model Catalog. The scorecard communicates model quality, runtime compatibility, and expected unit economics to engineering buyers. Goal: give SEs and AE motion-friendly language to close decisions faster and reduce the back-and-forth on model evaluation requests.

Context and problem statement:
- Buying teams are overwhelmed by open model variability: accuracy on narrow tasks, hallucination rates, latency/cost tradeoffs and unknown operational quirks.
- Existing ‘verified profiles’ in the catalog are too checklist-y for technical buyers — they want quickly consumable, comparable signals tied to runtime outcomes (latency, cost, stability).
- Sales and SEs spend cycles running bespoke evals for every customer. We need a repeatable articulation that reduces custom eval asks and accelerates trust.

Proposed artifact: Model Assurance Scorecard (MAS)
- One-card summary per catalog model combining: Quality signal, Safety/hallucination band, Runtime compatibility badges, Economics band, Prompts/drift-sensitivity note.
- Score elements (short labels we’ll surface in UI and in one-pagers):
  - Quality delta (Qd): concise numeric: model vs baseline on reference eval set (e.g., +3.2% vs base open model)
  - Hallucination band (H): qualitative: Low | Moderate | High (with short examples)
  - Runtime compatibility (R): badges: "cpu-friendly", "gpu-optimized", "kv-cache-ready", "quantization-safe" (indicates validated paths in Redwood runtime)
  - Cost band (C): expected per-token relative band (S/M/L) and a representative p99 latency at 512 tokens
