Title: Unexpected fallback to degraded variant during staged graceful rollout despite model pin and prewarm success

Unexpected fallback to degraded variant during staged graceful rollout despite model pin and prewarm success

Issue summary: Customer reported that during a scheduled staged rollout (graceful promote) of h-gpt-7b-quantized-v2 the tenant traffic unexpectedly diverted to the degraded fallback variant for ~6 minutes despite the tenant being explicitly pinned to the new version and prewarm checks returning healthy.

Impact: Horizon Analytics (dedicated) observed elevated error rates and lower-quality completions for a subset of sessions affecting two production cohorts. Business impact: several active inference pipelines returned degraded outputs, increasing latency and manual retries. Estimated affected requests: ~4.2k during window.

Environment: production (us-west-2), dedicated capacity pool ID: ded-pool-05, orchestrator release tag: v2026.03.10-canary, edge-proxy version: 1.18.2.

Observed behaviour: explicit model pin for tenant T-98765 was present in control plane; the serving runtime reported KV-cache warmed; prewarm probes returned 200/OK. Despite that, routing logs show a switch to fallback variant serving-degraded-1 for requests that previously had pinned affinity. Edge retry traces show a short spike of 503 from a single host at 15:21:12 UTC then a cohort-wide redirect to degraded variant until the orchestrator snapshot reconciliation corrected routing at 15:27:42 UTC.

Expected behaviour: with explicit tenant pin and successful prewarm, traffic should remain pinned to h-gpt-7b-quantized-v2 for the session until explicit unpin or TTL expiry; fallback to degraded variant should only occur if the primary variant is unreachable or healthcheck fails across a quorum of hosts.

1) Schedule a staged canary promote for a dedicated pool with a small initial weight and tenant pin set for a test tenant.
2) Ensure prewarm completes and servicing runtime reports warmed KVCACHE.
3) Induce a transient single-host 503 from a healthcheck probe (simulated) on one node in the pool around the time of weight increase.
4) Observe routing decisions and edge logs for tenant-bound requests.

Note: We reproduced locally in a staging replica by simulating probe latency + single-host 500s and saw candidate fallback in the orchestrator under certain snapshot-merge timings.
- Edge log excerpt: [2026-03-12T15:21:12.203Z] edge-proxy-23: tenant=T-98765 requestId=64a8... -> upstream=primary-07 status=503 error=connection-reset
- Orchestrator event: [2026-03-12T15:21:13Z] snapshot-apply: merge_id=sn-9215 stage=prewarm_success target=h-gpt-7b-quantized-v2 pinned_tenants=[T-98765]
- Routing decision trace: [2026-03-12T15:21:14Z] route-eval tenant=T-98765 -> chosen_variant="serving-degraded-1" reason="fallback-path-elected"
- Control plane log: [2026-03-12T15:27:42Z] reconcilier: snapshot-consensus achieved, pinned_affinity reconciled for tenants: [T-98765]
- Customer supplied transcript: "responses started returning short generic completions at 15:21:30 UTC"

Customer reported in support email: "We pinned our tenant to the new model and saw it warm successfully, but at 15:21 requests started returning low-quality completions and some 5xx accompanied by our monitoring alerts. We need to know why the system ignored the pin and how to prevent recurrence."
Support (Maria): Received customer alert at 15:34 UTC. Opened ticket and escalated to SRE. Assigned Ian for triage.
SRE (Ian): Initial triage shows single host 503 around 15:21; orchestrator snapshot merge log indicates a concurrent snapshot replace. Suspect race between snapshot replace and in-flight pin commit.
Customer (Horizon): We did not change our client-side token or session parameters. We need confirmation that pinned sessions won't divert during canary promotions.
Eng (Priya, Orchestrator): Looked at PR history: PR #1549 modified snapshot apply ordering to reduce wait on prewarm. There is a path where in-flight snapshot replace can update routing epoch before pinned-commit acknowledgement reaches edge caches.
SRE (Ian): Applied a temporary mitigation: increased pin TTL and launched a targeted reconcile job to force reassertion of pin affinity for affected tenants. Customer reporting restored fidelity at 15:28 UTC.
Support (Maria): Notified customer of mitigation and asked if they observed resumed normal behaviour. Customer confirmed outputs normalized at 15:28 and requested root cause analysis.
Eng (Priya): Propose follow-up: add atomicity to snapshot commit that includes pinned-affinity writes, or hold snapshot epoch advancement until pinned-commit ack from edge caches. Filed ENG follow-up task.
SRE (Ian): Will deploy temporary config to delay ephemeral snapshot promotion in the dedicated pool until we have a pin-consensus metric above threshold.
Support (Maria): Will keep ticket open until postmortem and code fix are scheduled and customer accepts resolution plan.
Hypotheses considered: (1) pin commit reached control plane but edge cache TTL/stale entries caused edge-to-orchestrator mismatch, (2) orchestrator advanced routing epoch before pin-affinity persisted in snapshot leading to fallback election, (3) single-host health flapping triggered fallback policy that didn't respect explicit pin in certain race windows.

Title: Tenant edge header rewrite causes pin to be claimed during canary prewarm, producing mixed model responses

Tenant edge header rewrite causes pin to be claimed during canary prewarm, producing mixed model responses

Issue summary: During a staged canary prewarm for model redwood/llama-3b-v1, several tenants observed mixed responses where requests that should have stayed on the pinned variant returned outputs from the canary variant. Impact: Customer reported regression in inference outputs (semantic differences) and elevated token consumption for pinned sessions. This affects a dedicated customer in prod (Acme Health) and is causing customer-facing errors for health-reporting microservices that rely on deterministic outputs. Environment: production (us-east-1) dedicated capacity pool for Acme Health. Canary rollout initiated 2026-03-12 02:00 UTC; prewarm traffic started 02:05 UTC. Steps to reproduce: 1) Customer pins route to redwood/llama-3b-v1 via dashboard or route header. 2) Initiate staged canary promotion to redwood/llama-3b-quantized-v1 with prewarm mirror enabled. 3) Simulate tenant traffic with X-Tenant-ID and X-Prefer-Model headers set; note that customer has a CDN that rewrites headers (X-Tenant-ID -> X-Tenant). 4) Observe that sessions previously pinned to v1 begin receiving canary responses intermittently. Logs / traces: - Edge ingress logs show header mutation: "X-Tenant-ID: 84231" rewritten to "X-Tenant: 84231" for ~15% of requests during prewarm window. - Orchestrator audit shows "claim_session" events for tenant 84231 at 02:06:12 from prewarm worker (prewarm-worker-7). - Routing mesh traces show a pin-update event followed by immediate request routing to the canary variant. - Observability dashboard: token rate spike for tenant 84231 between 02:05-02:10 UTC; request latency stable. Initial hypothesis: The prewarm worker performs an opportunistic claim operation to populate KV cache and prewarm model shards. Because the edge header rewrite changed the tenant header name, the orchestrator treated mutated requests as a different session identifier and the claim logic exercised a higher-precedence path that overwrote the existing pin for tenant sessions (claim precedence > explicit pin). Race condition between prewarm claim and pinned-session lease refresh resulted in transient ownership change and mixed responses.

Issue summary:
Customer (DataMill Analytics, dedicated tenant) reports intermittent high p95 latency for inference calls from EU-based traffic. Tenant is pinned to eu-west pool but we are seeing a subset of requests routed via ap-southeast-1 which increases p95 from ~180ms to ~850ms.

Impact:

- Errors are not increased; primary impact is latency and customer SLA concern.

Environment:
- Tenant: datamill-prod (dedicated gpu pool)
- Region: eu-west primary pin configured via tenant routing policy (strict_pin: false by default)
- Time window: first observed 2026-03-09 18:20 UTC, reproducible intermittently through 2026-03-10

Steps to reproduce:
1. Send batched generation requests for model redwood-1-large pinned to tenant datamill-prod from EU IPs.
2. Observe latency distribution in Console -> Per-route latency (p50/p95/p99).
3. Correlate request IDs that show p95 > 500ms with router decision logs.

Observed logs / snippets:
- Example request IDs (observed high p95): rqd_20260309_7a1b, rqd_20260310_10c3
- Router decision trace (extracted): route.decide(tenant=datamill-prod, geo=eu) -> selected_edge=eu-west-3 primary, fallback_path=[ap-southeast-1] -> chosen=edge=ap-southeast-1 due to available_capacity_low=true at timestamp 2026-03-10T09:12:18Z
- Network traceroute excerpt from selected host: 10 hops, transit via sfo -> ap-southeast-1 (unexpected)

Initial hypothesis:
1) Autoscaler or capacity scoring occasionally marks eu-west pool as low-capacity causing smart-router to choose apac pool as low-cost fallback, even when tenant pinned.
2) Sticky pin TTL or route-staleness in our control-plane allows short-lived multipath routing for dedicated tenants when strict_pin is not set.
3) Mis-evaluation of latency/cost scoring metric in smart-routing that underweights geo-penalty in edge cases.

- Confirmed: tenant routing policy shows pin to eu-west but strict_pin=false; that means fallback to compatible variants is allowed by policy.
- Checked autoscaler metrics for eu-west pool around timestamps: GPU utilization spiked to 92% for 30s windows; however capacity autoscaler added nodes but with a 45s startup delay. During that window routing score favoured ap-southeast-1.

- Found related deployment PR that adjusted pin bonus to be dynamic: https://github.com/redwood/inference/pull/3412 (author: infra/team). The change was merged 2026-03-08 and rolled out 2026-03-09.

- Improve autoscaler warm-up smoothing to avoid transient low_capacity signals.
- Follow up with customer on SLA credits and permanent config options (allowing them to opt into strict_pin or dedicated hard-residency).

Title: Tenant routed to secondary variant despite explicit model pin during orchestrator retry surge

Tenant routed to secondary variant despite explicit model pin during orchestrator retry surge

Issue summary: One enterprise customer observed tenant traffic being routed to a secondary (fallback) variant even though their project had an explicit model version pin. Impact: customer-facing production traffic experienced degraded model behavior and increased cost due to falling back to a larger, higher-cost variant. This started during a rolling canary of a separate release when orchestrator retry activity spiked.
1) Create a tenant-level model pin to redwood/rlhf-3b-v2 with strict affinity; 2) Initiate a rolling canary that toggles health checks for a different model in the same region to induce orchestrator retries; 3) Observe routing decisions in the control plane and edge traces for a burst window; 4) Repeat with increased orchestrator retry rate and note whether pinned affinity holds.
During a control-plane retry surge the tenant's session affinity was dropped and requests were routed to the secondary variant for ~8 minutes. Edge traces show the pin still present in the tenant metadata but the orchestrator returned a fallback routing decision. Requests received mixed variant outputs and embeddings were inconsistent with pinned model behavior.
Tenant-level explicit pins should be honored across transient orchestrator retries; traffic must remain bound to pinned model unless an explicit unpin or capacity-driven fallback policy is triggered by SLOs.

Title: Audit log retention and access

Audit log retention and access

# Scope
This page defines how long Redwood retains audit logs and who can access them. Audit logs cover security-relevant events across Hosted API, Dedicated, and Redwood-managed control plane components that support Private deployments.

# Retention
- Hosted API: 365 days retention for audit logs.
- Dedicated: 365 days retention for audit logs.
- Private: 365 days retention for Redwood control-plane audit logs (actions taken in Redwood-managed components).
- Customer-owned Private audit logs: customer-configured; Redwood does not set or enforce retention for customer-side logging systems.

# Access controls
- Audit logs are accessible only to Security and SRE on a need-to-know basis via the Audit Explorer tool.
- Access is governed by least-privilege RBAC and requires SSO + MFA.
- Any export of audit logs for a customer request must be approved by Security and tracked via a support ticket.

# Customer requests
- Standard turnaround: 5 business days for audit log exports (unless contractually obligated otherwise).
- Deletion: audit logs are not deleted early except where required by law or contract; exceptions require Legal + Security approval and are documented in a support ticket.

Title: consolidate-sampled-context-anchors-and-cost-delta-annotations

consolidate-sampled-context-anchors-and-cost-delta-annotations

Motivation: Long-tail requests and multi-turn sessions make it hard to correlate expensive tokens with the actual prompt context. Alert noise for cost spikes often stems from superficially similar traces that differ in a few context tokens. This PR introduces two complementary observability primitives: (1) sampled context anchors — compact, privacy-safe snapshots attached to selected traces that let engineers inspect a representative prefix without storing full payloads; and (2) cost-delta annotations — span-level annotations that capture the incremental token cost relative to a baseline (baseline = first N tokens of the session or pinned model variant), enabling per-span cost-attribution and easy identification of regression candidates.

What this change does (high level):
- Adds a lightweight sampled-context store and recorder in the runtime that writes encrypted, k-anonymized anchors for 1% of long-tail sessions (configurable). Anchors include token fingerprints, anonymized prompt length buckets, and hashed prompt-context tags for grouping (no raw PII/token content stored).
- Adds cost-delta annotations into the tracing pipeline: each model-stage span now carries cost.delta and cost.baseline fields (numeric micro-units). These are added as span attributes and surfaced to OTEL and internal trace indexer.
- Dashboard updates: new dashboard panels on Console -> Observability that show per-route cost-delta distribution, anchor-cluster heatmap (session groups), and annotated trace + anchor join views.
- Alert tuning: new alerting rule that groups alerts by anchor-hash first and surfaces a single grouped alert for clusters of similar high-cost traces (reduces noisy duplicates). Added docs and runbook snippets for triage.

Implementation notes and constraints:
- Context anchors are generated at the runtime layer (redwood/service/runtime) before caching/quantization to avoid skew. Anchors emit a deterministic anchor-hash derived from a salted rolling-hash; the salt is customer-scoped to avoid cross-tenant correlation.
- Cost delta math: cost.delta = observed_token_cost - baseline_token_cost, baseline_token_cost is computed using a rolling median of the first 32 tokens for the route/model combo and periodically recomputed by a background aggregator.
- Privacy compliance: anchors are truncated and tokenized into fingerprint sketches; feature flags and customer-level opt-out is supported.
- Performance: profiling showed a 0.2% median p99 added latency on typical requests in our stage perf lab; batching and non-blocking flush paths mitigate the tail impact.

Title: introduce-chain-aware-span-grouper-and-stream-cost-adapter

introduce-chain-aware-span-grouper-and-stream-cost-adapter

Add chain-aware span grouping for streamed responses and a lightweight stream-cost adapter to approximate per-token cost on partial/chunked responses. Improves trace readability and enables token-cost breakdowns for long streaming sessions.
Motivation: Streaming responses and multi-turn chains produce lots of small spans and partial tokens, which makes trace graphs noisy and costs hard to attribute. Customers running chat-heavy workloads asked for clearer trace grouping and approximate per-token costing for streamed chunks so ops can debug and attribute spend without having to rehydrate full sessions. This PR introduces two complementary pieces: 1) a chain-aware span grouper in the tracing pipeline that coalesces consecutive spans belonging to the same logical chain/session into a single rollup span with aggregated metrics and deterministic keys; and 2) a Stream Cost Adapter that consumes chunked/partial token events and emits ephemeral cost-attribution metrics with conservative heuristics (prefix-fractioning + model-profile weights) so dashboards can show near-real-time token-costs for streaming responses. Checklist: - [x] Implement span grouper and config flags - [x] Add stream-cost adapter with pluggable model weight table - [x] Expose metrics: stream_tokens_total, stream_token_cost_estimate, chain_span_length, chain_span_error_rate - [x] Wire OTEL span attributes for chain_id, chain_role, chunk_index - [x] Add unit and integration tests for grouping heuristics - [x] Console dashboard: chain stream-cost view + example alert rules - [x] Backfill migration script: noop safe default - [x] Docs: observability streaming guide Summary of changes: Commits: - a9f3b9c: initial implementation of chain-aware span grouper (core logic + unit tests) - b4d1e2f: add stream cost adapter, model weight table, and conservative heuristics - c2d4a88: metrics export hooks and Prometheus labels for chain_id/model - d9f7b1a: add console dashboard JSON and alert example - e1b7f04: tests and CI fixes + docs updates Files changed (high level): - tracing/span_grouper.py: core grouping algorithm and deterministic key derivation - tracing/tests/test_span_grouper.py: unit tests that exercise boundary conditions - observability/stream_cost_adapter.py: adapter that converts partial chunk events into token-cost estimates - metrics/exporters/prometheus_chain_exporter.py: export hooks with chain labels - console/dashboards/chain_stream_cost.json: dashboard definition + example widgets - docs/observability/streaming-traces.md: how it works, tuning knobs, and migration notes - infra/ci/test_observability.sh: new test harness for integration run - examples/streaming/README.md: quickstart and expected traces Review/Conversation: - Diego Alvarez (reviewer): "Nice approach. Two requests: (1) make the group key stable across retries so we can join traces in storage, (2) add a note about accuracy bounds for the stream cost heuristic." - Author (Maya): "Added deterministic nonce derivation so group keys are stable when upstream request_id is present; otherwise we derive from session fingerprint. Also added a short accuracy section to docs listing our conservative +/-10–25% bound depending on model/quantization." - Priya Nandakumar (reviewer): "CI caught a flaky integration test on bursty streams — tracing pipeline was dropping some chunks under high concurrency." - Author (Maya): "Fixed: increased internal buffer window and added backpressure metrics. Re-ran integration; green locally." - Samir Patel (final approver): "Approach looks sound; leaving a couple of nit comments on logging verbosity." CI Summary: - unit tests: pass - lint: pass - integration (observability suite): initial run failed (trace_buffer_overflow flaky) -> buffer window increased and test retried -> pass - e2e smoke: pass Note on accuracy and safety: The Stream Cost Adapter is intentionally conservative: it attributes fractional token counts for partial chunks and multiplies by model-weight factors from the model profile table. We label these metrics with attribute cost_estimate=approximate and provide a confidence tag (high/medium/low) so alerting can ignore low-confidence metrics. Default behavior is opt-in via observability.enable_stream_cost_adapter=false to avoid surprising billing spikes for customers who rely on exact billing. Configuration and tuning: - observability.span_grouper.enabled (bool, default true) - observability.span_grouper.max_merge_window_ms (int, default 300) - observability.stream_cost_adapter.enabled (bool, default false) - observability.stream_cost_adapter.model_weight_table (config map) - observability.stream_cost_adapter.confidence_threshold (float, default 0.6) Backwards compatibility and migration: - Grouping is additive at the tracing ingest layer; original fine-grained spans are still stored for 7 days controlled by observability.span_grouper.keep_fine_spans_days (default 7) so users can revert. - Stream cost adapter metrics are namespaced with stream_ prefix and do not feed billing pipelines unless an explicit opt-in flag is set. Rollout plan: - Canary on a small subset of hosted region (10% of streaming traffic) for 48 hours - Monitor chain_span_length, stream_token_cost_estimate, trace_error_rate - If no regressions (latency or spike in metric cardinality) after 48h, increase to 50% and run full canary window - GA after two successful canaries and customer docs updated Observability dashboards and alerts added: - New dashboard: "Chain Stream Cost (Canary)" with per-model cost estimates and chain latency histograms - New alert: "StreamCost: high-unattributed-variance" (fires when estimate variance > 40% for 10m) - New alert: "TraceGrouping: buffer-saturation" (fires on buffer occupancy > 85%) Known limitations and follow-ups: - Edge cases where upstream partial retransmits can double-count chunks; follow-up ticket ENG-3310 to add idempotency tags - Model-profile table is conservative and needs periodic calibration; follow-up ENG-3312 to add automated calibration job - Large cardinality risk: chain_id labels increase high-cardinality metrics; we implemented a capped cardinality rollup and will monitor; follow-up ENG-3313 to add reservoir sampling for low-traffic chains Merge: Squash-merged to main after reviewers approved and CI green. Notes: small telemetry spike observed during canary but within expectations. Docs, tests and dashboard JSONs included so console team can iterate.

Title: Introduce invocation cost-phasing tags and priority-reranker for trace surfaces

Introduce invocation cost-phasing tags and priority-reranker for trace surfaces

Background: Investigations into high-cost invocations frequently require operators to stitch together multiple spans that contribute to token billing. This PR introduces deterministic "cost_phase" span tags written at token emission boundaries and a configurable priority-reranker in the ingestion path so high-impact spans are surfaced in compact traces and dashboards. What: 1) Runtime emits telemetry.cost_phase = prebill|billable|postbill for kernel, batching, kv, io spans when a token emission boundary or billing checkpoint occurs. 2) A priority-reranker computes a lightweight cost impact score (tokens_emitted * token_weight + kernel_ms * kernel_weight + kv_miss * kv_weight + wait_ms * wait_weight) and reorders the compact trace digest and the UI summary. 3) New observability assets: Cost Phasing overview dashboard (heatmap: prebill -> billable delta, per-route slope panel) and an alert rule "Per-route billable-slope" that uses the slope of billable tokens with a configurable window and backoff to reduce alert churn. Engineering notes: implementation in src/serving/telemetry/cost_phasing.go and telemetry/ingest/priority_ranker.go; feature gated by TELEMETRY_PRIORITY_RERANK (off by default). Tests include unit coverage for tag emission and score calc, an integration replaybench validating top-3 span recall in compact traces, and a canary against beta tenants. Rollout: gated default-off; staged to internal, then opt-in beta tenants; documented migration behavior (missing tags fall back to default ordering). Related work: ENG-2833 PM-1101; incident SUP-4502 raised need for better span surfacing.

Added: cost_phase span tags (prebill, billable, postbill) and a priority-reranker to surface cost-impact spans; Dashboard: Cost Phasing overview with heatmap and per-route slope; Alert: Per-route billable-slope with configurable window and cooldown. Title: Sampled token-span tracing and aggregation pipeline for token-level cost attribution

Sampled token-span tracing and aggregation pipeline for token-level cost attribution

Add a low-overhead, sampled tracing pipeline that emits token-level spans and aggregates them into rollups for cost and latency attribution. Title: Introduce contextual span weighting and token-cost conductor for observability

Introduce contextual span weighting and token-cost conductor for observability

Motivation: Long-tail latency and cost spikes often correlate with specific invocation phases and prompt shapes which are under-sampled by uniform trace capture. This PR implements a lightweight contextual span weighting algorithm to bias sampling toward spans with high phase-contribution and a coordinating token-cost conductor service that ties sampler budgets, token-cost estimates, and alert thresholds into a single runtime control plane. The result is higher-fidelity telemetry for the parts of the invocation lifecycle that drive cost and latency without increasing overall sampling volume. Design and changes: 1) span_weighting module implements a per-invocation phase scorer that consumes phased timing buckets and prompt-shape hashes to produce a dynamic weight for each span. 2) token_cost_conductor service exposes a gRPC control endpoint and REST read-only surface to allocate per-route sampling budgets, reconcile token-cost estimates with billing data, and emit sampling directives to downstream collectors. 3) telemetry samplers (prefetch and fallback samplers) were updated to honor span weights and conductor directives. 4) dashboards: new "Conductor Cost Rhythm" and "Phase Heatmap Detail" panels added to the observability space with linked drilldowns. 5) alerts: added adaptive alerting rule that scales alert thresholds by conductor-provided cost multipliers to reduce alert noise during known high-cost prompts. 6) docs and runbook: new runbook section describes how to tune conductor budgets, interpret phase-weighted traces, and rollback. Rollout plan: feature gated behind runtime flag observability.phase_weighting and conductor.enabled. Default rollout: internal canary in us-west for 48 hours, followed by staged rollout to all regions over one week. Observability validation: unit tests for span weighting and conductor reconciliation, integration test that simulates prompt-shape distribution and validates sampler directives, and a synthetic replay that shows 38% more high-impact spans sampled at equal budget. Backwards compatibility: collectors ignore conductor directives if the conductor is unreachable; sampling falls back to local defaults. Related work and tracking: links to linear tasks ENG-4217 and OBS-88 for tuning and alert adjustments.
Adds phase-aware span weighting, a token-cost conductor service, new dashboard panels, and an observability runbook entry.

Title: Per-subtoken latency decomposition and adaptive cache-credit model

Per-subtoken latency decomposition and adaptive cache-credit model

Instrument per-subtoken timings across the serving runtime to decompose observed latency into model compute, KV cache lookup, kernel scheduling, and transport. Build an adaptive cache-credit model that apportions marginal cost and latency to individual subtokens when cache hits/misses change the token-level cost. The signals must feed both the billing export and latency/error dashboards in Console. Design constraints: keep tracing overhead minimal (<1% p95 latency increase for typical workloads), avoid increasing ingestion volume materially for free-tier tenants, and maintain backward compatibility with existing token traces.

Cache-hit delta metric computed and joined to token traces in the ingestion pipeline

Title: Cost Baseline Archaeology: establish workload econ baselines and lineage for batching/caching/quantization

Cost Baseline Archaeology: establish workload econ baselines and lineage for batching/caching/quantization

Why: We lack consistent, workload-specific cost baselines that tie concrete serving knobs (batch size, prefix/KV cache TTL, quant profile) to downstream unit economics and user-observed latency. This makes rollouts risky and A/B experiments noisy. Goal: build a repeatable baseline archaeology process that reconstructs per-route and per-customer econ baselines, clearly attributes cost changes to specific knobs, and produces lineage artifacts usable by Console, Autoscaler, and Release controls. Scope: - ingest historical traces (token length distributions, latency P99, model variant, batch distributions) - generate per-route baseline reports (cost/token, cost/request, latency SLO risk) - surface change lineage for each optimization applied (who flipped what, when, observed delta) - integrate baseline artifacts into rollout gating and the Optimize recommendations engine
1) Baseline generator produces stable per-route baseline reports for top-200 routes by volume; 2) Each baseline includes token-econ, latency SLO risk score, and recommended safe knob ranges; 3) Changes to knobs are recorded with lineage metadata and viewable in Console; 4) Two pilot rollouts (one batching, one quantization) use baselines to automatically select safe config and show >=8% net token-cost reduction without exceeding latency SLOs for the pilot cohort.

Title: token-span-attribution-and-adaptive-alert-smoothing

token-span-attribution-and-adaptive-alert-smoothing

Motivation:
We currently surface token-level cost and latency aggregations but lack a clear way to attribute SLO impact to specific token spans (e.g. model prompt prefix vs generated tail) and we get frequent alert flapping on percentile SLOs when low-volume, high-cost tails show up. This PR introduces two complementary capabilities: 1) span-level token attribution traces and rollups keyed by token position buckets (prefix/mid/suffix) and cache-affinity (kv-hit vs kv-miss); and 2) an adaptive alert-smoothing layer that reduces noise for route-level token-cost SLOs using a decayed-reservoir quantile estimator that weights tokens by cost and recency.

What this changes (high level):
- Runtime telemetry: emit token-level spans with attributes: token_index, span_bucket (prefix|mid|suffix), kv_affinity (hit|miss), token_cost_units. These are synthesized as aggregated metrics and lightweight trace annotations to avoid high-cardinality explosion.
- Metrics rollups: new Prometheus/OpenMetrics series and Cortex rollup pipeline config to produce: rwd_token_span_cost_sum, rwd_token_span_cost_count, rwd_token_span_latency_p75/p95/p99 per route and per span_bucket.
- Sampling strategy: a token-aware reservoir sampler in the tracing pipeline that biases retention probability proportionally to token_cost_units and recent latency anomalies to preserve informative tails.
- Alerting: SLO rules updated to reference the smoothed quantiles produced by the adaptive estimator; alerting notifications include the top contributing span_bucket breakdown and a compact token-cost histogram snapshot.
- Console: observability UI adds a per-route Token Span panel with heatmap, selectable span_bucket filters, and a toggle to show raw vs smoothed SLO curves for a chosen time window.
- Docs/Quickstart: example notebook showing how to interpret span attribution and how to tune smoothing window for a given workload.

Implementation notes:
- The runtime emits a compact token-span protobuf (rwd.trace.TokenSpan) and a new lightweight counter for kv-affinity to keep cardinality low; the code path in serving/runtime/telemetry is hardened to avoid sync disk writes.
- Reservoir estimator implemented as a fixed-memory sketch using a weighted priority queue and exponential decay; state is materialized at the rollup tier and also emitted as a derivative metric so alert rules can reference it directly without additional query-time compute overhead.
- Backwards compatibility: when normalized flags are off the system falls back to previous token aggregation metrics (no name changes to legacy meters).

Title: Percentile-aware cost attribution and tapered span sampling for bursty token distributions

Percentile-aware cost attribution and tapered span sampling for bursty token distributions

Motivation: long-tail bursts (e.g., chat sessions and batch spikes) cause noisy p99 token-cost signals and poor alert precision. This PR introduces percentile-aware token cost attribution (per-route+model cardinality) plus a tapered reservoir span-sampling algorithm to preserve long-tail traces during bursts without exploding storage or noise. Changes summary: 1) New aggregated metrics: redwood.token_cost.p{50,90,95,99} (labels: tenant, route, model, quantization_profile) implemented as Prom-compatible histogram rollups and lightweight approximate percentiles for real-time panels. 2) Attribution pipeline: per-request token attribution uses a per-span token counter and an aggregation step that attributes cost to route/model buckets and emits delta metrics at flush. This avoids double-counting across KV cache hits and model-fallback cascades. 3) Tapered reservoir sampling: a new sampler replaces uniform reservoir in edge collectors. The sampler ramps sampling weight down as per-tenant burstiness increases, keeping a fixed memory envelope while preferentially retaining older or high-cost traces. Configuration knobs exposed via runtime flags and Redwood Console: target_sample_budget, taper_half_life_seconds, cost_priority_bias. 4) Alerts and dashboards: revamped SLO dashboard with percentile ribbons, a p99-cost-trend alert rule that uses week-over-week percentile deltas and a minimum-volume guard to reduce noise. Added an examples dashboard template for large-tenant cost debugging (pre-aggregated query panels and query snippets). 5) Migration and rollout plan: the feature is gated behind feature flag observability.percentile_cost and ramps by tenant tier (dev->staging->enterprise) with a canary that forwards both old and new metrics for 48 hours. Backwards compatibility: legacy token_cost.{avg,sum} metrics still emitted for 90 days; dashboards default to new percentiles but include toggles. Implementation notes: changes touch collectors, ingestion pipeline, metric exporter and Console UI; introduced a small C++ sampler component compiled into the collector binary and a Go sidecar for attribution flush coordination. Performance: local perf harness shows 6% CPU on collectors at 10k rps with 1% memory overhead; ingestion tail-latency unchanged within measurement noise. Why different: previous PRs added token timing, mikro-rollups, or span sampling variants; this one focuses on accurate percentile-aware cost attribution combined with an adaptive sampling strategy that keeps representative long-tail traces under bursty loads. Rollback: feature flag off or toggle sample_budget=0 reverts to baseline. Requested follow-ups: automated regression tests for attribution correctness, a migration playbook for enterprise customers with large historical dashboards, and a monitoring smoke test to validate percentiles match historical aggregates within tolerance.
Omar: We need a safety valve for sampler memory under pathological multi-tenant bursts; can we add a hard cap? Author: added max_memory_bytes and a fallback LRU when budget exceeded.
Priya: Attribution correctness question — how do we handle model fallbacks that generate extra tokens? Author: attribution tags each fallback span with origin_model and an attribution_deduct flag; flush step dedupes tokens by request id and origin to avoid double-counting.
Jonas: CI noticed a flaky test in attributor_test.go on macOS runners. Author: adjusted test timing and added a retry harness; test now stable in our CI matrix.
SRE (comment): recommend an alert to detect sudden divergence between legacy sum-based cost and new percentile aggregates. Author: added alert 'token_cost_percentile_divergence' with 15m window and RTV guard.
Security: confirm no PII flows into percentiles. Author: confirmed attribution tags are keys-only and all request identity is hashed and truncated before export.
Added percentile-aware token cost metrics (p50/p90/p95/p99), tapered reservoir sampling for bursty workloads, UI dashboard template for percentile cost debugging, and new alert rules to reduce noisy p99 alerts. Feature gated and phased rollout.
Enable observability.percentile_cost for staging and run the canary for 48h. Verify token_cost_percentile_divergence alert is silent or acknowledged. If issues, flip flag off to revert to legacy metrics.

Title: adaptive-peer-fanout-and-kvcache-prefetch-for-tensor-parallel-overlap

adaptive-peer-fanout-and-kvcache-prefetch-for-tensor-parallel-overlap

Motivation: In high-concurrency tensor-parallel workloads we observed tail latency caused by excessive NCCL peer fanout and uncoordinated KV-cache prefetches that saturate NVLink and host PCIe at the same time as collective launches. This PR introduces two complementary runtime optimizations: an adaptive peer-fanout policy that bounds and staggers NCCL fanout under high heap/PCI pressure, and a prioritized KV-cache prefetcher that favors high-probability shards and coalesces prefetch work with compute bursts.

Summary of changes: 1) peer_fanout_scheduler: new heuristic that computes a per-node fanout cap based on active outstanding sends, measured bandwidth utilization, and a per-model locality score. The scheduler will now stagger fanout windows (micro-windows of 200-500us) to avoid synchronous starts across replicas. 2) prefetch_prioritizer: lightweight scoring model (LRU + token-prob offset + recent access frequency) to rank KV shard prefetches. Prefetch requests are bucketed into priority queues and can be throttled by the peer_fanout_scheduler when comm pressure is detected. 3) compute_comm_coalescer: small scheduler change that groups prefetch + immediate small allreduce opportunities into the same launch batch to reduce kernel launch overhead and improve overlap. 4) contiguous_chunk_selector: kernel selection tweak to prefer contiguous-chunk memcpy kernels for the typical TP layout observed in our internal 8xA100 experiments; this reduces host-side scatter costs and improves PCIe utilization. 5) tests and docs: new microbenchmarks and integration tests under tests/, and a short perf doc with recommended knobs.

Commits (high-level): - Add adaptive fanout scheduler and tests - Implement KV-cache prefetch prioritizer and integrate with scheduler - Add coalescer and kernel selector heuristic - Microbenchmarks and CI fixes - Docs and perf notes

Files changed (high-level): - runtime/tensor_parallel/peer_fanout_scheduler.*: core heuristic and control loops (~360 loc) - runtime/kv_cache/prefetch_prioritizer.*: scoring + queueing subsystem (~210 loc) - runtime/scheduler/compute_comm_coalescer.*: small scheduler glue (~80 loc) - runtime/kernel_selector/contiguous_chunk_selector.*: policy rules (~40 loc) - tests/*: new benchmarks and integration tests (~122 loc total)

Benchmarks: - 8xA100 (NVLink) 100-token seq_batched inference workload: throughput +14% median, +12-18% steady-state; p99 token latency reduced by 22% under load when multiple clients concurrently send small batches. - 4xA40 (PCIe) multi-client noisy workload: observed 9-11% throughput gains and fewer NCCL retries/timeouts in synthetic saturation tests. - End-to-end REDWOOD internal bench harness scripts included under tests/ with sample configs.

Backwards compatibility: no API or config semantics changed. New runtime knobs (opt-in via runtime config): peer_fanout.max_concurrent, prefetch.priority_threshold, coalescer.enabled. Default values chosen conservatively to be safe for current production fleets.

Testing and CI: - Unit tests for scheduling logic and prioritizer: pass - Integration tests in CI run against a lightweight mocked NCCL environment - Perf CI: bench_peer_fanout.py run on nightly perf nodes (results attached in docs/)

Review thread (high-level): - Diego: "Can the fanout cap be derived from real-time bandwidth stats instead of outstanding sends?" Author: "We sample bandwidth via the new comm_meter; fallback to outstanding sends if sample unavailable. Bandwidth-based cap added in 2nd commit." - Evelyn: "Tight coupling between prefetch prioritizer and scheduler may complicate future work." Author: "We added an explicit scheduler adapter interface so other prefetch policies can be plugged in without touching scheduler core." - Sanjay (SRE): "Are there failure modes where prefetch throttling starves model KV loads?" Author: "Prefetch is always best-effort and we added a hard emergency bypass when an access misses and the model is critical; tests added to validate bypass."

CI history: - Initial CI: lint + unit tests failed (missing include + flake) - Author push: fix includes and add mock stubs - CI flake: integration timing test flaky on macOS runners, we mark as platform-specific and skip on macOS - Final CI: all checks passed.

Merge rationale: empirically reduces tail latency and NCCL contention for our TP workloads, conservative defaults, opt-in knobs available.

Rollout plan: staged rollout to Dedicated clusters in canary pool, then gradual increase to remaining fleets over two weeks with perf monitoring dashboards added (redwood-console: TP/Prefetch/Fanout).

Checklist: - [x] Design doc and perf notes - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Benchmarks and scripts - [x] Backwards compatible defaults - [x] Reviewer approvals (Evelyn, Diego, Sanjay)

Related: ENG-1742 (perf investigation), ENG-1829 (kv-cache stability incident). Misc notes: removed an earlier attempt that increased NCCL stream count (regressed throughput on PCIe-only nodes). The contiguous-chunk kernel preference is gated behind a runtime flag to avoid regressions for custom model layouts. This PR is intentionally conservative: small changes with measurable wins and safe fallbacks.

Title: openai-compat: adaptive tool aliasing and choice-priority resolver

openai-compat: adaptive tool aliasing and choice-priority resolver

Context: We're seeing subtle differences in tool selection when downstream systems expect tool aliases (e.g., 'weather' vs 'weather_v2') and when model-produced tool_choice signals arrive as ranked lists or soft-probabilities. This PR introduces an adaptive aliasing layer plus a priority-resolver that normalizes tool_choice semantics across streaming and non-streaming paths.
Adds a canonical alias map, selection weighting resolver, and streaming-safe tool-choice handling to the OpenAI compatibility adapter. Preserves backwards compatibility while enabling deterministic fallbacks and tunable preference weights for enterprise tool routing.
Operators previously had to maintain brittle 1:1 name mappings in the application layer. With multiple model variants and function name drift, misrouted tool invocations caused retries and incorrect outputs. This change centralizes alias resolution and introduces a priority resolver that consumes: 1) explicit tool_choice entries, 2) streaming partial tool hints, and 3) operator-provided preference weights to produce a single canonical tool invocation decision.
- alias_map: YAML-backed mapping supporting exact, prefix, and regex aliases with optional deprecation metadata.
- priority_resolver: scoring pipeline that combines operator weight, model confidence (soft or hard), and recent invocation success metrics.
- streaming_adapter: incremental aggregation of partial tool_choice fragments to avoid premature invocations while maintaining low latency.
- compatibility_mode: feature flag to toggle strict legacy 1:1 resolution for customers that rely on old semantics.
- New optional parameter in /v1/compat/dispatch: 'alias_profile' (string) and 'choice_resolution' (enum: strict|adaptive|legacy).
- SDK: redwood-sdk-python adds DispatchOptions.alias_profile and .choice_resolution with docs and example.
- Admin: YAML schema for alias_map under /config/openai/aliases.yaml.
Note: Default remains legacy-compatible but uses adaptive resolution for new accounts.
1) feature gated behind 'openai_adaptive_aliasing' runtime flag; 2) start with internal canary (10% traffic) for 48h; 3) enable for PLG accounts opted-in; 4) full rollout after two weeks if no regressions.
Traffic routing includes automatic fallback to the previous resolver when invocation error rate increases above 2x baseline.
Operators can supply an alias_profile to map existing tooling names. A migration tool (scripts/migrate_aliases.py) is included to convert customer-provided CSVs into the YAML alias_map format. Backwards compatibility tests included for customers with strict mappings.

Tomás Alvarez (approver): Verified canary metrics: no change in 95th p50 latency, error rate decreased for aliases with multiple names. Approving.

Title: Audit log retention and access

Audit log retention and access

# Scope
This page defines how long Redwood retains audit logs and who can access them. Audit logs cover security-relevant events across Hosted API, Dedicated, and Redwood-managed control plane components that support Private deployments.

# Retention
- Hosted API: 365 days retention for audit logs.
- Dedicated: 365 days retention for audit logs.
- Private: 365 days retention for Redwood control-plane audit logs (actions taken in Redwood-managed components).
- Customer-owned Private audit logs: customer-configured; Redwood does not set or enforce retention for customer-side logging systems.

# Access controls
- Audit logs are accessible only to Security and SRE on a need-to-know basis via the Audit Explorer tool.
- Access is governed by least-privilege RBAC and requires SSO + MFA.
- Any export of audit logs for a customer request must be approved by Security and tracked via a support ticket.

# Customer requests
- Standard turnaround: 5 business days for audit log exports (unless contractually obligated otherwise).
- Deletion: audit logs are not deleted early except where required by law or contract; exceptions require Legal + Security approval and are documented in a support ticket.

Title: Customer data + logs retention policy (Hosted, Dedicated, Private)

Customer data + logs retention policy (Hosted, Dedicated, Private)

# Purpose
This page defines the default retention and deletion timeframes for customer data and operational logs across Redwood Inference products (Hosted API, Dedicated, and Private).

# Definitions (quick)
- Customer content: prompts, files, and model outputs (request/response payloads).
- Operational logs: API gateway logs, runtime logs, error logs, and request metadata (e.g., request id, status code, latency).
- Debug payload logging: optional feature that stores limited request/response payloads for troubleshooting.
- Audit logs: security-relevant actions (e.g., login, key creation, RBAC changes).

# Default retention windows
## Hosted API (Redwood-managed)
- Customer content (prompts/outputs): Not stored persistently by default.
- Debug payload logging (if explicitly enabled for an org): 7 days retention.
- Operational request logs (metadata, not payloads): 14 days retention.
- Tracing spans linked to request ids (no payloads): 14 days retention.

## Dedicated (Redwood-managed, isolated capacity)
- Customer content (prompts/outputs): Not stored persistently by default.
- Debug payload logging (if enabled): 7 days retention.
- Operational request logs (metadata, not payloads): 14 days retention by default.
- Enterprise retention add-on (contracted): Operational request logs can be extended to 30 days (requires Security approval and support runbook change).

## Private (VPC / on-prem)
- Customer content + operational logs: Retention is customer-configurable because storage is customer-managed.
- Private default installer values (if customer does not change settings): 30 days for operational logs in the in-cluster log store.
- Redwood control-plane access logs (when Redwood engineers access the private control plane for support): 90 days retention in Redwood systems.

# Deletion requests
- If a customer submits a deletion request for stored data within Redwood-managed systems (e.g., debug payload logs), Redwood will complete deletion within 30 days of verification of the request.

# Notes and guardrails
- Debug payload logging must be explicitly enabled and is intended for time-bounded troubleshooting.
- Any change to retention windows for Redwood-managed systems requires Security + SRE review and an update to the customer-facing Security FAQ.

Title: Data retention and deletion (Security FAQ excerpt)

Data retention and deletion (Security FAQ excerpt)

# Q: Do you store customer prompts and model outputs?
A: By default, Redwood does not persistently store prompts and model outputs for Hosted API or Dedicated.

# Q: Do you retain request logs? For how long?
A: Yes. For Hosted API and Dedicated, Redwood retains operational request logs (request metadata such as request id, timestamps, status codes, and latency) for 14 days by default.

# Q: Do you log full request/response payloads?
A: Only if a customer explicitly enables debug payload logging for time-bounded troubleshooting. When enabled, the retention period is 7 days by default.

# Q: What is the retention period for audit logs?
A: Redwood retains audit logs for 12 months (365 days).

# Q: How does retention work for Private deployments?
A: For Private (VPC/on-prem), the customer controls retention for customer content and operational logs in their environment. Redwood’s control-plane audit and access logs are retained for 365 days (audit) and 90 days (access logs) in Redwood systems.

# Q: How long does deletion take?
A: For Redwood-managed systems, validated deletion requests are completed within 30 days.

Title: Log lifecycle tiering and schema evolution guidelines

Log lifecycle tiering and schema evolution guidelines

Purpose and scope:
This doc captures operational guidance for the full lifecycle of Redwood audit logs: from hot ingestion through indexing and tiered storage to long-term cold retention and eventual deletion. It focuses on practical rules for tiering, schema evolution (v2+), automated backfills, and known failure modes in the indexing/export pipelines (SIEM, warehousing). The goal is to consolidate engineering and security requirements so ops, SRE, and compliance teams have a single reference for retention decisions and remediation steps.

Key terms (quick):
- Hot store: low-latency indexed store used for immediate search/alerts (OpenSearch cluster).
- Warm store: compressed, queryable indices (fewer replicas, slower nodes).
- Cold/Archive: object store (S3) with lifecycle rules (Glacier/Archive) for compliance retention windows.
- Evidence bundle: tamper-evident copy of logs for legal hold with signed hashes and KMS-wrapped keys.
- Schema version: audit_log_v1, audit_log_v2, etc. Each version must be backward-compatible or have explicit migration plan.

Retention policy summary (compliance-driven):
- 90 days: hot search in OpenSearch (full index, instant queries).
- 1 year: warm indices in OpenSearch (replicas reduced, ILM rollover to warm).
- 7 years: cold archive in S3 (encrypted), accessible via controlled rehydration procedures for legal/eDiscovery.
- Legal hold: suspend deletion and create evidence bundle; retain checksum provenance.
Notes: retention durations are policy-driven; above are defaults for most customers but tenant-level overrides may exist.

Indexing strategy and ILM (OpenSearch/Elasticsearch):
- Use daily indices with rollover when index size > 50GB or age > 1d for high-volume tenants, otherwise use 7d windows.
- ILM phases: hot -> warm -> cold -> delete. Configure separate policies per tenant group (hosted vs dedicated vs private).
- Mapping: use explicit mappings for known fields (timestamp, tenant_id, user_id_hash, event_type, resource, action, outcome, request_id, rbac_version). Avoid dynamic mapping for top-level fields to prevent mapping explosion.
- Aliases: maintain read/write alias (audit-logs-write) that points to current hot index; search alias per retention window for queries.
- Shard sizing: target shards ~30–50GB post-compression. Use shard allocation awareness across AZs.

Schema evolution (v2 guidance):
- Version field: every log must include "schema_version" (e.g., "audit_log_v2").
- Additive changes only by default: new optional fields OK. Removal or renaming requires a migration window and backfill plan.
- Compatibility matrix: maintain a matrix in Confluence mapping which consumers (SIEM exports, internal alerting, data warehouse transforms) can read which versions.
- Transform functions: implement canonicalizers in the pipeline that can upgrade older messages to latest shape before indexing/exports. Canonicalizers are small, idempotent mapping steps in the ingestion stream.
- Example: v1 had "user_id" (plaintext). v2 has "user_id_hash" and a "pii_redaction" enum. The transformer must compute user_id_hash for v1 entries and set pii_redaction accordingly.

Ingestion pipeline (high-level):
- Sources -> Fluentd/Vector -> Kafka (topic: audit-raw) -> Stream processors (Flink/Spark Streaming) apply transforms -> audit-enriched topic -> Indexer (bulk writes to OpenSearch) AND archive-writer (S3 parquet).
- S3 archive is the canonical durable copy and source of truth for backfills and evidence bundles. Keep raw and enriched copies for 30 days to allow reprocessing.

Backfill and reindex patterns:
- Use S3 as the canonical input for backfills. Backfill pipeline (Airflow DAG): read parquet partitions, apply canonicalizer, write to temporary index, atomically swap alias.
- For schema changes that require reindex: run a staged backfill in a lower-cost cluster (reindex cluster), validate counts and diffs, then cut alias to new indices.
- Idempotency: all backfill jobs must be idempotent. Use deterministic document IDs (sha256(tenant + request_id + event_timestamp)) to avoid duplicates.

Failure modes and runbook (common):
1) Indexer bulk write failures (429/timeout)
   - Symptom: high bulk request rejections, growing lag in Kafka consumer lag, slow downstream alerts.
   - Immediate action: throttle the indexer (reduce batch size), add backpressure on consumer, switch to emergency warm nodes if available.
   - Long-term: increase index write capacity or reduce indexing QPS via sampling.

2) Schema mismatch causing mapping exceptions
   - Symptom: bulk writes failing with mapping errors referencing unexpected field type changes.
   - Immediate action: pause writes to affected index alias, create a new temporary index with relaxed mapping (use runtime fields or text) and resume writes to alias pointing to temp index. Notify owners.
   - Follow-up: run backfill/canonicalizer to normalize data types and reindex into correct mapping.

3) Kafka topic retention misconfigured -> data loss
   - Symptom: consumer seeks beyond earliest offset when attempting backfill; expected partitions missing old messages.
   - Immediate action: check S3 archives for canonical data; reconstruct topic using archived parquet for reprocessing.
   - Preventive: monitor head/tail offsets and set alerts when retention < 2x expected backfill window.

4) SIEM export failed batch or malformed payloads
   - Symptom: SIEM vendor rejects API with 4xx/5xx or partial acceptance.
   - Immediate action: pause export DAG, inspect error payloads, run sanitizer over archive for the period and retry with smaller batches.
   - Permanent fix: tighten schema validation before export and add contract tests (end-to-end) in CI.

Evidence bundles and legal hold
- When legal hold is requested: snapshot S3 partitions for requested time range into an evidence-bucket with immutable object lock enabled and versioning. Generate SHA256 manifest and sign manifest with KMS key. Store manifest pointer in audit metadata and notify Legal + Compliance.
- Do not delete or transition objects under an active evidence lock. Update deletion pipeline to check legal_hold index before any TTL action.

PII & redaction rules
- Redact at ingestion when possible. Fields flagged as PII must be replaced with one-way hash (salted tenant-specific) and set pii_redaction status. Raw plaintext containing PII must not remain in hot indices beyond 7 days unless explicitly required for an investigation with approved justification.
- Keys for hashing must be rotated per policy. Maintain rotation metadata so re-hashable material can be reprocessed only when permitted.

Monitoring and alerts
- SLOs: consumer lag < 15m for high-priority tenants, indexing error rate < 0.1%, archive write success 100% for each daily partition.
- Alerts: ILM phase failures, index growth anomaly, S3 lifecycle errors, rehydration job failures. Use runbook links in alert messages.

Operational playbook snippets (copy-paste safe):
- Delete-safe check before index delete:
  1) query legal_hold index for tenant/date range
  2) check evidence snapshot existence in evidence-bucket
  3) if any positive, abort deletion and escalate
- Rehydrate and search archived partition:
  1) kick off rehydrate job (S3 -> warm Parquet) via Airflow; attach canonicalizer
  2) write to temp index with alias audit-restore-<ticketid>
  3) notify requestor with temp query endpoint and TTL (default 72h)

Operational checklist before a major schema change: 
- Lock: small freeze on production schema writes (announce 48h)
- Create migration branch and canonicalizer code
- Run schema compatibility tests against last 90 days of archived data
- Schedule rolling backfill window (non-peak hours) and canary subset (1% tenants)
- Run integrity audits (counts, checksum diffs) and runbook signoff from Compliance

Open questions / TODOs:
- Decide final retention window for dedicated customers with contractual overrides (legal needs a per-customer override flag).
- Define exact rotation cadence for hashing salts and where rotation metadata is stored (wallet or KMS tags).
- Formalize SLA for evidence bundle creation (target: 48 hours after legal hold request).

Appendix: minimal audit log example (recommended canonical shape v2)
- timestamp: 2025-01-01T12:34:56Z
- tenant_id: t-abc123
- schema_version: audit_log_v2
- event_type: permission.update
- resource: repos/my-model/config
- action: update
- actor_id_hash: sha256:xxxxx
- request_id: r-20250101-abcdef
- outcome: success
- rbac_version: v2
- pii_redaction: hashed
- meta: {"client_ip_truncated": "10.0.0.x"}  <-- note: meta must be small and typed

Contact and ownership:
- Primary: Aisha Patel (security infra)
- Backup: Marco Rivera (SRE)
- Compliance review owner: Evelyn Zhang

Title: evidence-ttl-slo-and-grace-periods-for-audit-events

evidence-ttl-slo-and-grace-periods-for-audit-events

Purpose
This doc captures operational guidance and pragmatic decisions for audit event retention (TTL) and SLOs across our stores (hot index, warm index, blob storage, SIEM export). It is an ops-focused cookbook: how we enforce retention, how we react to pipeline failures, and how RBAC v2 and evidence automation affect retention decisions.

High-level principles
- Preserve forensic integrity: events required for investigations or legal holds must not be dropped by automated TTLs.
- Cost-aware tiering: move older, low-access events to cheaper storage while keeping rehydration paths.
- Observable and reversible: retention actions must be logged, audited, and reversible when under legal hold.
- Minimize data divergence: SIEM exports should be as close to the source as practical; handle eventual consistency explicitly.

Retention tiers (recommended)
1) Hot index (0–90 days): full fidelity, sub-second query SLO for internal audits. Primary store for product+security SLOs.
2) Warm index (91–365 days): compressed index, no real-time ingestion guarantee; queries are slower (seconds).
3) Cold blob (1–7 years): gzipped/parquet blobs in object storage, indexed by minimal metadata (id, timestamp, event_type, tenant). Rehydrate to warm/hot on demand.
4) Archive/long-term (7+ years): legal-hold only (cold mirror, write-once). Access requires approved runbook and audit trail.

TTL and grace periods
- Default TTL per tenant: 365 days.
- Shorter TTLS may be applied to non-sensitive subsystems (eg analytics-only event streams): 90 days.
- Grace period on deletion: 72 hours between scheduled deletion job and irrevocable wipe to allow emergency holds.
- Legal hold overrides: when a hold is placed, disable scheduled expiry for all matching artifacts. Holds must be immutable (recorded with actor, timestamp, reason).

Enforcement mechanics
- Deletion jobs run nightly per shard/tenant. Stages: mark-for-deletion -> audit-log-entry -> soft-delete (move to quarantine bucket) -> final-delete after grace.
- Soft-delete is required to support fast recovery (restore from quarantine within 7 days).
- Final-delete is performed via lifecycle policy with a separate audit entry signed by system identity.
- For indices, we use index lifecycle policies to roll indices and shrink shards before snapshot + delete. For small tenants we group multiple tenants per index with tenant-tags.

SIEM export behavior and guarantees
- Export semantics: best-effort at-at-least-once delivery to SIEM sink. We cannot guarantee strict ordering during large backfills or replays.
- Retention mapping: events exported to SIEM must be preserved in vendor for a minimum of 90 days (contractual). If client requests longer SIEM retention, we flag via metadata and adjust export policy.
- Drift handling: if the SIEM sink confirms loss, we attempt re-export from cold blob within 30 days if available. After 30 days, rehydration is possible but may be missing intermediate state (eg KV caches).

RBAC v2 implications
- RBAC v2 introduces tenant-scoped deletion privileges. Only 'data-retention-admin' role can place/unplace legal holds and initiate final-delete.
- Deletion job service account must have a narrow ephemeral elevation path recorded in the audit log (who escalated, why, TTL).
- Access to rehydrate/archive artifacts is gated by 'forensics-read' and 'forensics-restore' roles; any restore action emits an evidence access event.

Backfill and reindex strategies
- Backfill triggers: schema changes, index optimization, SIEM re-exports, or corruption repair.
- Preferred path: reindex from cold blob snapshots to a staging cluster, run validation (checksum + sample queries), then swap aliases to avoid double-writing.
- For small reindexes (< 50M events) prefer live reindex; for larger sets use offline staging to avoid production impact.
- Throttling: use adaptive concurrency based on current CPU latency metrics; default = 10% of cluster capacity.

Failure modes and response checklist
1) Missed SIEM exports (partial)
   - Detect: export-lag alert > 2 hours or high retry rate.
   - Mitigation: escalate to on-call, run targeted re-export job for missing tenant/time-range, increase ephemeral throughput for export pipeline.
   - Postmortem action: capture root cause, add invariant check (sink ack vs internal checkpoint).
2) Index corruption or shard failure
   - Detect: index_health != green, checksum mismatch.
   - Mitigation: failover to replica, restore from snapshot of warm/cold tier if replica unavailable.
   - If snapshot older than required, initiate rehydrate from blob store and rebuild index.
3) Deletion job accidentally runs on wrong tenant
   - Detect: spike in deletion audit events, owner alert.
   - Mitigation: pause deletion pipeline immediately, mark impacted artifacts as quarantined, escalate legal/team leads. Attempt restore from quarantine (soft-delete buffer).
   - Postmortem: add dry-run validation step and tenant-safe-guard checkbox for next runs.
4) Legal hold misapplied or not cleared
   - Detect: investigators flag missing events or hold inventory mismatch.
   - Mitigation: if hold missing, search for soft-deleted artifacts and rehydrate; if wrongly applied, require approval to lift with two approvers.

Monitoring and SLOs
- Metrics to emit: retention_age_distribution, soft_delete_count, final_delete_count, quarantine_restores, siem_export_lag, rehydrate_success_rate, legal_hold_count.
- Key SLOs: 99.9% scheduled-deletions executed within 24h window; SIEM export lag < 5 minutes for hosted-tier, < 1 hour for dedicated-tier; rehydrate success rate > 95% for requests within 30 days.

Operational playbook snippets
- Emergency restore (short path): 1) Suspend deletion pipeline, 2) Search quarantine by tenant + timeframe, 3) Restore artifacts to warm index staging, 4) Run validation queries, 5) Promote to alias, 6) Record restore action in audit.
- SIEM reconciliation run: compare export checkpoints vs SIEM ack list, report missing segments, re-export missing ranges in time-sliced batches, mark completed in reconciliation ticket.

Cost and capacity notes
- Estimate: 1B events/year ~ 10 TB hot, 50 TB warm, 200 TB cold compressed. Adjust by event size and sampling rates.
- Encourage teams to reduce noise events (debug-level telemetry) and annotate events with retention-class tags to avoid storing high-cardinality ephemeral traces in hot tier.

Open questions and follow-ups
- Should the default tenant TTL be lowered to 180 days for non-security tenants to reduce cost? (tradeoff: reduces rehydrate window)
- How do we surface legal hold duration and approval metadata in the Console? Need product/console ticket.
- RBAC v2: define the exact permission set for the deletion job service account (SEC-1123).

Notes to self / TODOs
- Add sample queries for retention_age_distribution to shared dashboards.
- Draft compliance-ready phraseology for customer-facing retention policy doc.
- Schedule dry-run of deletion job in staging next quarter with failsafe canary.

References
- Confluence SEC-AUD-RET-2024 (policy draft)
- JIRA SEC-1123 (RBAC v2 deletion-perm work)
- infra repo: github.com/redwood/infra/audit-archives (scripts, snapshots)

End of notes.
