Title: Ceres Platform Security

Ceres Platform Security

Priority: high — banking division, regulated data. Short notes / call snippets and audit checklist.
Deliver final VPC audit checklist and SIEM export POC by 2026-03-05
legal sign-off on KMS import policy
clarify retention for debug logs
2026-02-20: On-site security review w/ infra + legal. request: full SIEM export and sample log schema.
2026-02-08: Technical deep-dive (Fireflies ff_20260208_01_ceres_sec_review). Covered KMS import vs. external key policy.
2026-01-28: Demo of Private (VPC) with routing/fallback. SE presented autoscaling and canary rollout options.
2026-01-15: Initial discovery call; shared security questionnaire and SOC2 attestation copy (drive doc link).
(customer asks) Must export structured logs to their SIEM (Splunk/Elastic/Datadog) with both real-time streaming and S3 archival. Preferred transport: syslog over TLS (syslog-ng) or HTTPS JSON-lines endpoint. Logs must include request and response metadata but be configurable to redact PII and full prompt text for production. Support for HEC (Splunk) and Elastic Beats preferred.
Customer requested JSON schema; suggested fields below. They want field-level definitions and examples for ingestion mappings. Fields: timestamp, iso8601; request_id; customer_account_id; user_id (nullable); client_ip (anonymize option); route_name; model_name; model_version; prompt_hash (sha256); prompt_redaction_level; response_status (200/4xx/5xx); token_count_input; token_count_output; latency_ms; cache_hit (true/false); kv_cache_event (evict/load); kms_key_id (if envelope encryption used); encryption_context; audit_action (generate, retrieve, delete); sampling_rate (for full prompt capture); redaction_version; host_instance_id; region; deployment_type (private/dedicated).
Default: hot logs (30 days) in SIEM, warm (90 days) in managed S3, cold archive (7 years) on customer-managed storage for regulatory needs. Customer requires immutable retention option and WORM support for specific accounts. Need to confirm SLA for log delivery and replays. Legal wants 7 years for transaction-related prompts, but product recommends redaction + hash-only for long-term retention.
Separate admin/audit channel required: identity of operator actions (deploy model, change routing, key rotation), with SAML assertion UID and IP, stored separately from request logs and retained 3-5 years. Must include before/after snapshots for config changes. Support for pushing to cloud-native audit pipelines (CloudWatch/Stackdriver) or customer SIEM via secure connector.
- Need a POC exporter: support Splunk HEC token + HTTPS ingestion, Elastic index template, Datadog logs ingestion.
- Backpressure and retry semantics critical: prefer at-least-once with dedupe id (request_id) vs exactly-once impossibility.
- Recommended delivery: streaming + periodic batch flush to S3 for compliance archives.
- Encryption in transit (TLS1.2+) and at rest (SSE-KMS) for S3 archives.
- Provide sample ingestion pipeline config for their SOC team.

Title: Quickstart Templates: Provider Abstraction and Model Pinning

Quickstart Templates: Provider Abstraction and Model Pinning

## Summary
This page defines how Redwood quickstart templates (Python + TypeScript) must:
1) abstract LLM providers to minimize lock-in and enable local/enterprise routing, and
2) pin models and versions safely so template apps are reproducible, rollout-friendly, and supportable.

The guidance applies to RAG and agent templates (including tool calling + structured output). It also covers when and how we support Redwood’s OpenAI-compatible surface.

---

## Goals
- **Reproducibility:** A template scaffold created today should behave the same tomorrow (within documented bounds).
- **Rollout safety:** Provide a straightforward way to do canaries / A/B tests and controlled upgrades.
- **Provider flexibility:** Allow swapping providers (Redwood hosted, Redwood Dedicated/Private endpoints, OpenAI-compatible) with minimal code changes.
- **Supportability:** Make it easy for Support/SRE to identify the exact model + version used, and to correlate issues with traffic and telemetry.

## Non-goals
- Full multi-provider feature parity. We support a minimum common set of capabilities used in templates.
- Dynamic provider selection “per request” by default. Templates may support it, but safe defaults prefer a single configured provider.

---

## Key definitions
- **Model alias:** A human-friendly name used in docs/README (e.g., `rw:general-chat`). Aliases are *not* stable identifiers.
- **Pinned model identifier:** A stable provider-specific identifier used for production runs (e.g., `rw://chat/redwood-verified/llama-3.1-70b-instruct@2025-02-10`).
- **Template default model:** The model configured out-of-the-box for first success. It must be pinned.
- **Compatibility profile:** A small set of constraints the template expects (tool calling/JSON mode, streaming behavior, max context, etc.).

---

## Provider abstraction: required interface
All templates must implement a thin provider abstraction so the rest of the app depends on **capabilities**, not vendor SDKs.

### Required capabilities (v1)
Templates must assume these features exist; provider adapters must emulate/guard accordingly:
- Chat/completions (streaming and non-streaming)
- Tool calling (function/tool schema submission + tool result return)
- Structured output (either native JSON mode or validated parsing)
- Timeouts + retries (with streaming-aware behavior)
- Request metadata hooks for observability (request id, trace context, template telemetry tags)

### Recommended interface shape (language-agnostic)
- `generate()` for non-streamed responses
- `stream()` for streamed responses
- `supports(capability)` for gating optional features
- Adapter must return:
  - `text` (final assistant message)
  - `tool_calls` (if present)
  - `raw`/`provider_response` (optional; must be redacted before logging)
  - `usage` (tokens in/out where available)
  - `request_id` (Redwood request id or provider equivalent)

### Provider selection: config-driven
Provider selection must be driven by configuration (env/config file), not by code edits.

---

## Supported providers in templates (v1)
Templates may ship multiple adapters, but must include:
1) **Redwood native adapter (preferred):** Uses Redwood SDKs and Redwood endpoints.
2) **OpenAI-compatible adapter (optional but recommended):** Works with Redwood’s OpenAI-compatible endpoint when enabled, and can also work with OpenAI-style providers if the user supplies keys/URLs.

Important: “OpenAI-compatible” refers to request/response *shape*. It does not guarantee identical semantics (error codes, streaming chunking, tool-call edge cases). Templates must be resilient and document differences.

---

## Model pinning: policy and rationale
### Why pinning is mandatory in templates
- Reduces “it worked yesterday” failures when default models are updated.
- Enables meaningful perf/cost baselines for docs and dashboards.
- Makes support triage tractable (model regressions vs app bugs).

### What must be pinned
For template defaults, pin:
- **Model name/family** AND
- **Serving profile/version** (or equivalent) AND
- **Tokenizer/context assumptions** when relevant (documented)

### What must not be pinned (by default)
- Region and capacity tier are typically **not pinned** in templates; these are deployment/environment concerns.
- Provider-specific “experimental” flags should be avoided unless explicitly documented.

---

## Configuration: required env vars and precedence
Templates must expose the following config knobs (names are normative for templates; internal code may map to provider-specific fields).

### Precedence order
1) CLI flags (if present)
2) Environment variables
3) `config.(yaml|toml|json)` (optional)
4) Template defaults (checked into repo)

### Required environment variables
| Variable | Required | Example | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|
| `RW_PROVIDER` | Yes | `redwood` \/ `openai_compat` | Selects adapter. Default should be `redwood`. |
| `RW_API_KEY` | Depends | `rw_live_...` | Required for `redwood` and for Redwood OpenAI-compat if it requires auth. Must never be logged. |
| `RW_BASE_URL` | No | `https://api.redwoodinference.com` | Used for hosted; for Dedicated/Private this may be a tenant/VPC URL. |
| `RW_MODEL` | Yes | `rw://chat/redwood-verified/llama-3.1-70b-instruct@2025-02-10` | Must be pinned by default. |
| `RW_MODEL_FALLBACKS` | No | `rw://...@2025-01-20,rw://...@2024-12-15` | Optional, comma-separated. Used for graceful degradation. |
| `RW_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS` | Yes | `512` | Safe default; templates must cap output. |
| `RW_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS` | Yes | `30000` | Must be streaming-aware (see safe defaults). |
| `RW_RETRY_MAX_ATTEMPTS` | Yes | `3` | Retries must be bounded and jittered. |
| `RW_TEMPLATE_TELEMETRY` | No | `off` \/ `on` | Must default to `off` if it injects non-standard headers (proxy safety). |
| `RW_OPENAI_COMPAT_BASE_URL` | No | `https://api.redwoodinference.com/v1` | Used when `RW_PROVIDER=openai_compat`. |
| `RW_OPENAI_COMPAT_MODEL` | No | `gpt-4o-mini` or `rw:...` | For OpenAI-compat adapter only; if unset, map from `RW_MODEL` when possible. |

Notes:
- If `RW_PROVIDER=redwood`, use `RW_MODEL`.
- If `RW_PROVIDER=openai_compat`, templates must support either `RW_OPENAI_COMPAT_MODEL` or an automatic mapping from `RW_MODEL` (see mapping section).

---

## Redwood model identifiers: recommended format
Templates should treat Redwood pinned models as opaque strings, but docs should encourage a consistent format:
- `rw://<api_surface>/<catalog>/<model>@<version>`

Examples:
- `rw://chat/redwood-verified/llama-3.1-70b-instruct@2025-02-10`
- `rw://embeddings/redwood-verified/bge-large-en@2025-01-05`

If Redwood model IDs evolve, templates should only need mapping changes inside the Redwood adapter.

---

## Mapping pinned models to OpenAI-compatible mode
When using Redwood’s OpenAI-compatible endpoint, the adapter will still send a `model` string. There are two allowed strategies:

### Strategy A (preferred): Explicit compat model
User sets:
- `RW_PROVIDER=openai_compat`
- `RW_OPENAI_COMPAT_MODEL=<string>`

Pros: transparent; avoids surprises.

### Strategy B: Deterministic mapping (best-effort)
Template maps `RW_MODEL` to a compat model string using a small maintained mapping table.

Rules:
- Mapping must be explicit, version-controlled, and documented.
- If mapping fails, error message must recommend setting `RW_OPENAI_COMPAT_MODEL`.

Example error:
- "Unable to map RW_MODEL `rw://chat/...@2025-02-10` to OpenAI-compat model string. Set `RW_OPENAI_COMPAT_MODEL` explicitly or switch to `RW_PROVIDER=redwood`."

---

## Rollout-safe pinning patterns
### 1) Pin by default; upgrade intentionally
- Template scaffold writes the pinned default into `.env.example` (or config) at init time.
- README must include an “Upgrade model” section with a controlled flow.

### 2) Support controlled upgrades via "candidate" configuration
Templates must provide a simple way to test a new model without replacing the stable pin.

Recommended pattern:
- `RW_MODEL` remains stable.
- Introduce `RW_MODEL_CANDIDATE` for canary routes or manual testing.

Example routing approach:
- `/chat` uses `RW_MODEL`
- `/chat/canary` uses `RW_MODEL_CANDIDATE`

Or (advanced) percentage-based selection:
- `RW_CANARY_PERCENT=5` for 5% traffic (must be off by default)

### 3) Add fallbacks for graceful degradation (optional)
If configured, the adapter may retry with a fallback model on capacity errors or model-specific failures.

Rules for fallback usage:
- **Only** trigger on safe-to-fallback classes (e.g., capacity / 503 / certain gateway errors).
- Do **not** fallback on prompt/tool schema validation errors.
- Emit an explicit metric/log field when fallback occurs.

---

## Logging and observability requirements (model + provider)
Templates must record provider/model info in **low-cardinality** attributes.

### Required log fields
- `provider` (e.g., `redwood`, `openai_compat`)
- `model` (pinned string; avoid per-request dynamic values)
- `model_version` (if available separately)
- `redwood_request_id` (if present)
- `template_version` (from scaffold stamp)

### Required trace attributes (minimum)
- `rw.provider`
- `rw.model`
- `rw.template_version`
- `rw.request_id` (when available)

### Cardinality guardrails
- Never attach raw prompts, tool arguments, or retrieved chunks as span attributes.
- Do not attach user ids or emails as attributes. Use a hashed stable id if absolutely necessary and approved by Security.

---

## Error handling expectations across providers
Provider adapters must normalize errors into a small set of template error types so the rest of the app doesn’t become provider-specific.

### Normalized error categories
- `AuthError` (401/403)
- `QuotaError` (429)
- `TimeoutError`
- `NetworkError`
- `ProviderError` (5xx)
- `ModelCapabilityError` (tool calling not supported, structured output unsupported)
- `UserInputError` (invalid tool schema, invalid JSON output when strict mode is enabled)

Adapters must attach:
- `http_status` (if known)
- `retryable` (boolean)
- `provider_request_id` and/or `redwood_request_id`

---

## Dedicated and Private deployments: special considerations
Templates must work when the Redwood endpoint is:
- Hosted multi-tenant (default)
- Dedicated capacity URL
- Private/VPC or on-prem URL

Guidance:
- Always allow overriding the base URL (`RW_BASE_URL` or compat base URL).
- Do not assume public internet egress; document how to run with a local OTel collector.
- TLS/cert handling: do not encourage disabling TLS verification. If Private requires custom certs, document proper trust store configuration.

---

## Recommended README sections (must exist in template repos)
- **Model configuration**
  - How to change models
  - What "pinned" means and why
- **Provider selection**
  - `redwood` vs `openai_compat`
  - When to choose each
- **Upgrade guide**
  - Steps to test candidate model
  - How to roll forward / roll back
- **Troubleshooting**
  - Capability mismatch (tool calling/structured output)
  - Common 401/429/timeout cases
  - Proxy issues with optional telemetry headers

---

## Code patterns (reference)

### Python: adapter selection (illustrative)
- Keep adapter selection in one module (e.g., `providers/__init__.py`).
- Validate config at startup; fail fast with actionable errors.

Example (pseudo-code):
- Read `RW_PROVIDER`
- If `redwood`: initialize Redwood client with `RW_API_KEY`, `RW_BASE_URL`, and `RW_MODEL`
- If `openai_compat`: initialize OpenAI client with `RW_OPENAI_COMPAT_BASE_URL`, key, and model
- Expose unified `llm.generate()` and `llm.stream()`

### TypeScript: adapter selection (illustrative)
- Use a small interface + two implementations.
- Avoid leaking provider-specific response types to route handlers.

---

## Testing and CI requirements
Template repos must include at least:
- A unit test that asserts the default model is pinned (contains `@<version>` or matches the current pinning regex).
- An integration smoke test for:
  - streaming success path
  - tool calling roundtrip
  - capability gating (clear error if unsupported)

For OpenAI-compat:
- Include a minimal test that initializes the compat client and performs a simple request (can be nightly or behind a CI flag to avoid flakiness).

---

## Security and privacy notes
- API keys must be read from env and never written to disk by the CLI.
- Do not log:
  - `Authorization` headers
  - raw prompts
  - retrieved documents/chunks
  - tool arguments/results (unless explicitly redacted and size-limited)
- Telemetry tagging for adoption metrics must be **opt-in** when it uses non-standard headers to reduce proxy breakage.

---

## Ownership and change process
- **Owner:** DevEx (templates) – Monica Patel
- **API/model policy:** Hosted API PM – Nikhil Sharma / Henry Cho
- **Observability conventions:** Allison Grant
- **Security review:** Marcus Lin

Changes to:
- env var names,
- pinning rules,
- supported providers,
- compat mapping behavior

…must be reviewed by DevEx + Hosted API PM + Observability. Breaking changes require a template version bump and explicit upgrade notes.

---

## Appendix: example configuration snippets

### Example `.env.example` (Redwood native)
RW_PROVIDER=redwood
RW_BASE_URL=https://api.redwoodinference.com
RW_API_KEY=YOUR_KEY_HERE
RW_MODEL=rw://chat/redwood-verified/llama-3.1-70b-instruct@2025-02-10
RW_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS=512
RW_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS=30000
RW_RETRY_MAX_ATTEMPTS=3
RW_TEMPLATE_TELEMETRY=off

### Example `.env.example` (OpenAI-compatible)
RW_PROVIDER=openai_compat
RW_OPENAI_COMPAT_BASE_URL=https://api.redwoodinference.com/v1
RW_API_KEY=YOUR_KEY_HERE
RW_OPENAI_COMPAT_MODEL=rw-chat-default
RW_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS=512
RW_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS=30000
RW_RETRY_MAX_ATTEMPTS=3
RW_TEMPLATE_TELEMETRY=off

Title: Intermittent region-affinity flip causing bursty cross-region inference and timeouts for Chronos Health

Intermittent region-affinity flip causing bursty cross-region inference and timeouts for Chronos Health

Issue summary: Chronos Health reported sudden elevated p95/p99 latency and a spike in streaming request timeouts beginning at 2026-03-10 09:40 UTC. The customer's traffic, normally pinned to us-west for low-latency inference, experienced intermittent routing to eu-west for a subset of requests, producing cold KV-cache misses and high tail latency. Impact: Several production endpoints used by Chronos' clinician-facing workflow saw ~15% request failures (stream disconnects / 504s) and 3x p99 for generation calls over a ~40 minute window.
Customer-facing production inference degraded for Chronos Health: increased 504s and stream disconnects, user-visible timeouts in the care app during 09:40-10:20 UTC. Estimated 12k requests impacted, some time-sensitive workflows delayed.
prod | us-west (customer region affinity expected)
smart-routing
serving-runtime
api-gateway
cache
1) Send sustained generation requests from a Chronos Health customer account with region affinity set to us-west (via account-routing tag).
2) Observe p50/p95/p99 for streaming and non-streaming endpoints over 5-10 minute windows.
3) Correlate request trace ids with smart-routing logs to detect unexpected eu-west handoffs.

2026-03-10T09:40:13Z serving-runtime: kv-cache: miss model=redwood-2-small session=abc123 host=eu-node-12 latency_ms=75
2026-03-10T09:40:14Z api-gateway: stream: client=chronos-app conn_id=xyz987 error=upstream_stream_reset code=504
09:35-09:40 UTC: p95=240ms p99=480ms error_rate=0.6%
09:40-09:55 UTC: p95=780ms p99=2.4s error_rate=12%
09:55-10:10 UTC: p95=260ms p99=510ms error_rate=1.2%
Initial hypothesis: BGP/peering issue causing traffic to egress via eu-west. Rejected after routing plane BGP checks showed stable adverts.
Observed correlation between a spike in 'affinity-lookup-miss' events and region flips. TTL for account routing metadata had expired earlier than expected due to a bug in cache-refresh logic (recent release 2026-03-09 02:12 UTC).
Root cause candidate: a regression in account-routing cache refresh where a backoff timer could cause immediate TTL expiration for accounts with infrequent updates, producing transient fallback to default geo-detect which resolved to eu-west for some requests.
KV/cache impact: Customers pinned to us-west rely on local prefix caches; cross-region handoff caused cold KV lookups and model weights not warm on the eu-west pool, increasing initialization and token latency.
Scope: Only accounts whose routing metadata refresh interval aligned with the backoff edge observed the flip. Not a universal platform outage but high-impact for affected customers.
Correlated items: linked incident INT-4021 flagged a suspicious cache refresh change in the routing service, and PR #1894 updated retry/backoff behavior three days ago.

2026-03-11 09:00 UTC - SRE (Liam O'Connor): Added extended logging around affinity TTL expiry to capture edge-case behavior. Created INT-4098 to add unit tests for cache-backoff scenarios.

Workaround applied: customer-side header 'x-region-pin: us-west' recommended and supported for Chronos Health. Immediate fix: rolled back the cache refresh regression in routing-service to reinstate prior TTL behavior. Long-term: SRE and Product to ship a config flag to strictly honor account pins and add unit/regression tests for cache backoff logic. Follow-up action items logged in INT-4098. Customer verified reduced error rates and restored latency to baseline post-rollback.
1) Deploy canary for 'strictly-enforce-region-pin' feature to enterprise accounts on 2026-03-18.
2) Add automated synthetic checks that simulate TTL edge cases to alert on affinity-lookup-miss spikes.
3) Complete unit tests for cache backoff in INT-4098 and link PRs to this ticket.

Title: Peregrine CrossLingo Search

Peregrine CrossLingo Search

Summary: Global KM/insights provider building a cross-lingual enterprise search product for consulting + client-facing knowledge. Heavy emphasis on embeddings + reranking pipeline. Wants predictable unit economics at scale and per-language tuning.

Key points from discovery/demo: compact, choppy CRM notes style.
- Use-case: RAG for internal knowledge + client deliverables; public website search pilot for multi-site e-commerce clients.
- Languages: EN, FR, DE, ES, PT-BR, JA, ZH-CN, AR — need per-language recall/precision guarantees.
- Scale: Plan initial index ~50M docs (PDFs, transcripts), long-term 500M+; estimated 10B+ embeddings. Concerned about storage + nearest-neighbor cost.
- Latency targets: p50 < 120ms, p95 < 350ms for retrieval+rerank in EU/NA; JA/ZH budget for slightly higher tail (~450ms).
- Cost target: blending embeddings + cross-encoder rerank, aim $0.002 - $0.01 per query (average), willing to trade cost for quality on enterprise routes.
- Model preference: open models (multilingual dense encoders), but will accept Redwood-hosted fine-tuned reranker (cross-encoder) if private deployment approved.
- Routing: regional routing required; fallback to lower-cost model family when Dedicated capacity constrained.
- Security: EU data residency + KMS keys, SSO via SAML, audit logs retention 5+ years for regulatory clients.

Quotes: "Need per-language recall reports — not just global metrics; FR and PT are business-critical for LATAM/EU markets." — Head of Search (M. Dupont)

POC asks: 2M doc pilot with 10k eval queries across languages; per-language relevance labels (client will provide ~5k labeled pairs initially). Want Redwood SE to run indexing and measure throughput, vector store cost, and reranker latency on Dedicated GPUs.

Concern/Notes: tokenizer/normalization differences (CJK vs. whitespace), need to evaluate per-language candidate counts (k retrieval) and reranker re-ranking span budgets. Interested in Redwood Optimize suggestions for quantization vs quality tradeoffs.

Sales ask: present Dedicated vs Private TCO for 12/24 month commits, show fallback routing policy demo, include SLA on p99 tail for EU region.

Stubs: Drive deck link above, security FAQ shared; started a Jira RDW-2381 for KMS questions.

Title: Crossglot Bridgeworks

Crossglot Bridgeworks

Background: Crossglot Bridgeworks builds enterprise cross-lingual search for regulated verticals (legal, pharma). Primary differentiator is language-coverage & per-language tuning.

Summary from discovery:
- Customer has multi-tenant search product used by EU legal firms. Index size currently ~3M docs, expecting 10M+ in 12 months.
- Working languages: EN, FR, ES, DE, AR, RU, JA. Priority: FR/ES/AR for recall improvements.

Title: Chat session initial output starvation after ephemeral router flush during model/runtime hot-swap

Chat session initial output starvation after ephemeral router flush during model/runtime hot-swap

Issue summary:
Customer (AcmeDocs, enterprise) reports a sharp increase in time-to-first-token (TTFB) for chat completions immediately after a scheduled model binary swap combined with a runtime upgrade and an automated router ephemeral-flush during a canary rollout. Impact: multiple customer sessions observed first-token delays of 5–12s, plus intermittent 504 on long-tail requests, affecting SLAs for interactive product features.

Impact:
- Elevated TTFB for chat completions across a subset of connections (est. ~12% of sessions during the window).
- Affected product flows: interactive Q&A, live document summarization.
- Customer-facing errors: increased 504/502 rate on long requests; user-visible stalls.

Environment:
- Prod (us-east) serving cluster running runtime v2.4.0-rc + router v1.9.
- Autoscaler policy: aggressive scale-down idle-time 30s, ephemeral router flush enabled for canary swap.
- Model pinned: redwood-llama2-13b-v1 -> hot-swap to rw-compat-variant-13b-q4 during rollout.

Steps to reproduce (observed):
1) Triggered canary model swap and runtime bundle rollout at 2026-03-10T08:02Z.
2) Router performed ephemeral flush (per rollout script) to drain sessions during handoff.
3) Within 30–90s many incoming chat sessions attached to new serving nodes experienced long pre-stream stalls before first token emission.
4) Some sessions escalated to 504s when cumulative stall > 15s.

Observed behavior:
- Initial handshake completes (HTTP 200 / websocket open), but first token emission delayed 5–12s.
- Logs show repeated KV cache miss storms and synchronous cache-pop churn on the new nodes.
- Router metrics show increased connection affinity rebinds and short-lived route churn at the exact timeframe of the ephemeral flush.

Expected behavior:
- First token emitted within baseline TTFB distribution (<= 300–600ms for warm sessions).
- Router flush should not cause KV-miss amplification or stall serving runtime tokenization/priming.

Relevant logs and snippets:
- Router trace (2026-03-10T08:02:15Z): "ephemeral_flush: drain_start canary_id=rw-compat-variant-13b-q4"
- Serving runtime (2026-03-10T08:02:22Z): "kv_cache: miss_shard=27 storm_detected=1 concurrent_pop=48"
- API gateway: "request_id=abc123 first_token_delay=8123ms status=200"
- Autoscaler: "node_termination: scale_down triggered by idle_timeout=30s at 2026-03-10T08:01:58Z"

Hypothesis so far:
- The ephemeral router flush caused a wave of new connections to be rebalanced to nodes that had cold KV caches after the hot-swap.
- Aggressive scale-down and immediate model runtime load led to concurrent cache population (kv miss storm), blocking the serving runtime critical path for first-token emission.
- Runtime v2.4.0-rc introduced a synchronous cache-pop path for some KV shards which amplified blocking under concurrent population.

Immediate mitigations applied:
- Temporarily disabled ephemeral router flush for the remaining canary rollout window (rolled to sticky routing) at 2026-03-10T09:05Z.
- Increased autoscaler idle timeout to 5m to reduce node churn during rollouts.
- Pinned AcmeDocs traffic to the older model variant for a rolling 2-hour window while we investigate.

Next steps / action items:
- Eng: instrument and add non-blocking async KV population in runtime (PR submitted, see related PRs).
- SRE: add rollout guard that staggers router drains and enforces grace period before accepting new traffic to freshly-warmed nodes.
- Support: confirm customer impact window and monitor for regression after changes; coordinate communication.

Notes: this ticket will remain open until runtime patch and rollout-safe guards are in place and AcmeDocs confirms baseline TTFB recovery.

Title: Cinnamon Brook Solutions

Cinnamon Brook Solutions

Lead background:

Primary ask: latency is too high for core chat flows. CEO said: "users notice pauses on reply, drop-off on mobile". Goal: reduce perceived reply time to <400ms p50 for single-turn suggestions.

Observed details (from support/SE):
- Default requests currently hitting eu-west region; product audience ~75% NA.
- Typical request shape: 1 system + 4 user messages with context; prompt ~900–1400 tokens; max_tokens set to 512.
- Measured p50 ~650ms in NA (via client-side timing), p95 spikes 1.8–2.4s; EU deployments show consistent 800ms+ p50 depending on route.
- Throughput low: ~5–12 reqs/sec during peaks, cost-sensitive.

Recommendations already discussed (to be validated in POC):
- Region change: route requests from NA users to us-east region for lower RTT (customer agreed to test).
- Prompt guidance: move long, static context into server-side retrieval + cache embeddings; send only recent turns + retrieved doc snippets. Target prompt <= 600 tokens.
- Adjust max_tokens & stop sequences to avoid over-generation; reduce default max_tokens to 128 for quick replies.
- Enable streaming in the client to improve perceived latency for longer responses.
- Client timeouts: set HTTP connect timeout 2s, total request timeout 10s; abort and backoff for retries (avoid cascading retries).
- Use token caching for repeated system prompts and KB snippets.

POC scope:
- 1 engineer to implement region header override + streaming demo
- 1-week telemetry: compare p50/p95 before vs after region + short prompt changes
- Success criteria: p50 below 400ms for NA traffic and no more than 15% p95 > 1s; same or lower token cost per session.

Quotes / snippets from calls:
- "If we can shave 200–300ms consistently the engagement metric improves" (Head of Product).
- "We tried increasing client-side polling but it made retries worse" (platform eng).

Title: Route budget manifest & SDK sketch

Route budget manifest & SDK sketch

Notes to self - high-level goal:
Make it trivial for developers to declare per-route or per-interaction token budgets (soft + hard) with fallbacks, and expose a small SDK + YAML manifest so infra can enforce and telemetry can attribute costs.

Why:
- Customers keep asking for predictable budgets per feature (chat, summarize, search) so they can guarantee latency/cost SLAs for paid tiers.
- We already have routing, batching, and session-crediting; missing piece is a developer-facing manifest + runtime enforcement that maps nicely to billing and autoscaling hints.

Design goals (non-exhaustive):
- Declarative: devs write a short manifest (route name -> budget profile).
- Pluggable: SDK can be used server-side or in serverless handlers; manifest can live in repo or in Console.
- Signal-preserving: budgets should optionally trigger graceful degradations (shorter responses, lower-fidelity model), not just hard rejects.
- Telemetry first: every request annotated with budget-id, intended budget, actual tokens consumed, fallback path.
- Experiment-friendly: enable A/B of budget profiles with rollout flags.

Persona / user stories:
- As a backend engineer, I want to attach a 120-token soft budget and 400-token hard budget to /api/v1/compose so that front-end product tiers don’t blow past quotas.
- As a growth PM, I want to try a cheaper budget for new users (+ fallback to higher-fidelity model on error) so we can measure retention impact.
- As SRE, I want the runtime to emit per-budget queue latency percentiles so capacity planning can map to budget usage.

Budget semantics (proposal):
- soft_budget: target tokens for good UX. Hitting soft_budget -> signal to runtime to prefer concise responses or lower-cost model variant (policy).
- hard_budget: absolute max tokens allowed before abort or switch to a stubbed response.
- penalty_window: timeframe to accumulate tokens (per-request vs per-session options).
- priority: numeric priority for scheduling when capacity constrained.
- fallback_chain: ordered list of fallback actions (truncate, switch-model:model-small-q4, respond-with-summary, return-429-with-prescription).

Rough manifest (YAML-first) example:
---
budgets:
  compose_api:
    routes: ["/api/v1/compose", "compose:mutation"]
    soft_budget: 120
    hard_budget: 400
    penalty_window: request
    priority: 50
    fallback_chain:
      - type: truncate
      - type: switch_model
        model: redwood-small-q4_8bit
      - type: refuse
        code: 429
        message: "response budget exceeded: consider upgrading"

SDK sketch (JS pseudocode):
// server handler
import { Budget } from '@redwood/inference-sdk';
const profile = Budget.load('compose_api'); // from repo manifest or console
app.post('/api/v1/compose', async (req, res) => {
  const ctx = Budget.startRequest(profile, { userId: req.user?.id });
  try {
    const resp = await RedwoodApi.generate({ prompt: req.body.prompt, ctx });
    await ctx.recordConsumption(resp.tokens);
    res.json(resp.output);
  } catch (err) {
    const decision = await ctx.onError(err); // might trigger fallback_chain actions
    // surface graceful message, log telemetry
    res.status(decision.code || 500).send(decision.message || 'internal');
  }
});

Runtime enforcement notes:
- Enforcement should be local to the serving node to avoid roundtrips. Node caches manifest + fallback policy.
- For streaming, if soft_budget exceeded mid-stream, runtime should switch model or append a trailer advising truncation.
- We must not drop tokens silently — consumer-visible reason codes are important for debugging.

Telemetry and metrics to emit:
- budget_id, route_name, request_id, user_tier
- intended_soft_budget, intended_hard_budget, tokens_requested_estimate, tokens_consumed
- fallback_taken (enum), latency_p95_by_budget, queue_time_ms
- per-budget burn-rate: tokens/sec aggregated 1m/5m intervals

Acceptance criteria (MVP):
- Developer can declare a manifest and attach to a route (repo or Console).
- Runtime enforces soft and hard budgets for request-scoped budgets.
- SDK provides startRequest/recordConsumption simple surface.
- Console shows per-budget token consumption and a sample of fallback events.
- E2E test for streaming switch model on soft_budget exceed.

Experiment matrix / early hypotheses:
- H1: 10% reduction in median cost per request for routes with soft budgets and switch-to-small fallback, with <5% drop in task success on PRD tasks.
- H2: Showing explicit "budget exceeded" UX increases upgrade conversion vs silent truncation.

Edge cases & open questions:
- How to handle multi-tool/function calling where token consumption is outside of the model runtime? (record custom counters?)
- Session-scoped budgets vs request-scoped: session makes sense for chat but needs rolling-window semantics + decay.
- Interaction with autoscaling: can budget profiles emit autoscale hints (expected tokens/sec) to Dedicated scheduler? Probably yes, sketch separate field "autoscale_hint" with qps and tokens/sec.
- Security: manifest ownership and who can edit in Console; need audit logs.

Prototype plan (2-week sprint):
1) Implement manifest parser and local cache in runtime (edge: 2 days).
2) Add soft/hard enforcement hook and fallback runner (3 days).
3) Build tiny JS SDK (start/record/complete) and sample repo integration (3 days).
4) Wire minimal Console row for per-budget consumption (2 days).
5) Smoke tests and streaming switch-case e2e (2 days).

Next steps / TODOs:
- Sync with infra on model-switch latency and whether switching model mid-request is feasible for streaming paths. (ask: infra/serving-runtime)
- Confirm telemetry schema and sample event size impact. (ask: observability)
- Mock UX copy for "budget exceeded" flows and see legal & support implications. (ask: PM & CS)
- Write a short experiment proposal and include guardrails for user-visible degradations.

Random ideas to jot down:
- Offer a Console toggle to auto-generate budget suggestions from 7-day token percentiles for a route.
- Provide a "budget simulator" in Console to replay a week's traffic and predict fallback counts and cost savings.
- Allow the manifest to reference eval prompt-sets so we can simulate quality impact when switching to cheap models.

Quick sketch of a budget event payload (for telemetry):
{
  "budget_id": "compose_api",
  "route": "/api/v1/compose",
  "user_id": "u-123",
  "soft_budget": 120,
  "hard_budget": 400,
  "tokens_consumed": 225,
  "fallback": "switch_model:redwood-small-q4_8bit",
  "timestamp": "2025-03-02T14:18:00Z"
}

Signing off — this is rough, want to iterate with Mira on SDK ergonomics and with SRE on metrics.

Title: Add probabilistic prompt-cascade detector and CI soft-blocker

Add probabilistic prompt-cascade detector and CI soft-blocker

Motivation: Intermittent multi-turn regressions have surfaced where small prompt edits cascade down generation chains and amplify hallucination rates across prompt-sets. This PR introduces a probabilistic "prompt-cascade detector" that flags PRs where a proposed prompt change is likely to produce cascading failures across related prompts. The detector is intended as a 'soft-block' CI hook: it fails PR checks with a descriptive report but does not auto-revert. The goal is to give reviewers and engineers early, prioritized signal for high-risk prompt edits without creating a hard gate that blocks rapid iteration. What this PR does: 1) Adds a new detector module that computes a cascade-risk score using a lightweight Bayesian model combining: semantic drift (embedding cosine shift between baseline and candidate prompts), structural sensitivity (token-level delta and prompt-template branching factor), and cross-example amplification (a small simulated replay that measures disagreement amplification across a sampled cohort). 2) Integrates the detector as a CI plugin (ci/hooks/prompt_cascade_check.py) that runs in PR checks and emits a score + recommended actions. 3) Adds a dashboard-friendly JSON report format and an automated issue suggestion when score > high threshold (creates text to prefill a Linear issue). 4) Adds unit and integration tests and a short docs page outlining thresholds and how reviewers should interpret the signal. Non-goals: This is not a replacement for full regression evals or human review; the model is calibrated to minimize false positives and surface high-confidence cascade patterns. Score interpretation: - score < 0.15: low risk, pass quietly. - 0.15 <= score < 0.45: caution, report added to PR checks. - score >= 0.45: high-risk, CI soft-block — check cannot be merged without explaining mitigation in PR description, but maintainers can override. Implementation notes: The core detector is in src/eval_harness/detectors/prompt_cascade.py and exposes a single function `compute_cascade_score(candidate_prompt, baseline_prompts, sampling_config)` that returns a numeric probability and a short explanation list. The CI hook wraps that and calls a small 10-sample simulated replay using mocked model responses via our existing eval-mock harness to keep runtime under 30s in CI. Config: A new config block in eval-config/ci_hooks.yml allows teams to tune thresholds per repo. Backwards compatibility: Existing CI only sees a new optional check; default behavior is opt-in per repo via config. Privacy: All in-PR prompt text remains in PR context; no external telemetry is sent by default. Checklist: - [x] Detector implementation - [x] CI hook integration - [x] Unit tests and integration smoke - [x] Docs and threshold guidance - [x] Linear auto-suggest template Included artifacts: short JSON report schema, example Linear text, and guidance in docs/ci/prompt-cascade.md. Risks and mitigation: We tuned the Bayesian prior conservatively to limit noisy soft-blocks; added an allowlist for known benign prompt scaffolding patterns. Future work: tie the detector to the eval-harness historical registry to perform per-prompt historical variance priors and surface more actionable diffs. See also ENG-4721 for follow-up metrics telemetry and ENG-4789 for per-team thresholding.

Title: Inline comment signal map — personal review heuristics

Inline comment signal map — personal review heuristics

Objective:
- Capture lightweight heuristics for interpreting inline review comments quickly (what needs immediate action vs. follow-up vs. FYI).
- Produce a small, reproducible signal map I can use while triaging a review queue and to seed a bot later.

Context / why this matters:
- I spend ~20–30% of review time deciding whether a comment is blocking, optional, or noisy.
- Small contractors + rotating on-call reviewers contribute inconsistent phrasing; having a heuristic speeds the triage loop and reduces ping fatigue.

Signal categories (ranked for triage):
1) BLOCKER (must fix before merge) — immediate action
   - Keywords: "regression", "breaks", "security", "wrong result", "data loss", "racy", "undefined behavior"
   - Examples: "This change causes request timeouts", "Will break existing saved workflows"
   - Signals: references to a test, CI failure, or specific user-visible bug id improve confidence
   - Action: mark PR as blocked, add reviewer assignment, require fix commit or explicit waiver from owner

2) CORRECTNESS / LOGIC — high priority but may be fix-in-place or follow-up depending on scope
   - Keywords: "off-by-one", "edge case", "null handling", "tokenization mismatch"
   - Examples: "What happens if model output is empty?", "This math is inverted for negative scores"
   - Action: ask for a small repro or unit test; if trivial, request patch; if deep, request an issue + label "follow-up: correctness"

3) SECURITY / PRIVACY — treated as BLOCKER for private deployments
   - Keywords: "secrets", "plaintext", "k-anon", "PII", "leak"
   - Examples: "Exposes S3 key in logs", "serializes user PII to metrics"
   - Action: immediate stop and escalate to security team for Private deployments; put hold on merge until sign-off

4) STYLE / CONSISTENCY — low priority, often optional
   - Keywords: "nit", "style", "nit:", "format"
   - Examples: "nit: rename this var", "nit: use fold-left"
   - Action: optional small follow-up commit; prefer to batch these into a cleanup PR unless they reduce clarity

5) PERFORMANCE / COST — medium priority depending on SLOs
   - Keywords: "hot loop", "allocations", "hotpath", "cache miss", "batching"
   - Examples: "This allocs per token", "I think we can use KV cache here"
   - Action: if storage/latency/cost impact likely > 5% or in a hotpath, treat as high and require benchmarks or canary; otherwise tag "perf: investigate"

6) USABILITY / DOCS / API contract — actionable but often post-merge
   - Keywords: "docs", "signature", "error message", "API"
   - Examples: "error message not actionable for integrators"
   - Action: create issue for docs updates; if the change affects user-visible contract, require patch before merge
n
Heuristic scoring (quick mental model):
- +3 severity: blocker/security with CI/test evidence
- +2 severity: correctness, performance with evidence/benchmark
- +1 severity: usability/docs increases cognitive load or ambiguous error strings
- -1 severity: nit/style
- If score >= 3 -> block/require; 1–2 -> require explicit owner comment/plan; <=0 -> optional

Quick checklist when I open a PR:
- Read title + description: does it include a user story or bug id?
- Scan CI: failing tests -> immediate stop
- Search for inline "TODO" or "XXX" in changed files
- Grep for secrets/keys (small script below)
- Prioritize comments using signal categories above

Small scripts / tools I use (notes to self):
- secret grep: (simple) grep -E "(AKIA|AIza|-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY|ssh-rsa)" -n || add heuristics for base64-like blobs
- quick perf check: run a microbenchmark of changed function vs main branch using `pytest -k perf --bench` (we need to standardize this)
- comment classifier prototype: `review-signal.py --pr 4217` (local prototype that uses keyword weights above)

Patterns I see & suggested team conventions:
- "nit:" prefix is 80% harmless; prefer reviewers use the prefix so bots can auto-classify
- Always include an expected outcome in a correctness comment (e.g., "I expect X to be non-null because Y"); fewer follow-ups if comment asks for a repro
- For private deployments, tag security-related comments with "security:" explicitly
- Use labels on PRs: perf/will-change-user-experience/docs/blocker to make triage visible

Automation ideas (MVP):
- Small bot that tags comments by keyword weight and posts a summary comment: "Signals: 1 blocker, 2 correctness, 3 nit"
- Auto-add checklist when PR description contains "WIP"/"RFC" to prevent accidental merge
- Suggest checklist template: Regression test? Bench results? Docs? Changelog?

Open questions / unresolved tradeoffs (note to follow up):
- How conservative should the bot be? (Blocking false positives are costly; missing regressions are costly too)
- Do we allow style nits to be auto-fixed via CI (prettier/gofmt) or do we insist on human commit?
- For performance comments without a benchmark, do we require a microbenchmark before blocking? Who writes it?

Title: Cinnamon Brook Solutions

Cinnamon Brook Solutions

Lead background:
- SMB, B2B helpdesk SaaS (customer-facing chat + agent-assist). Mobile web widget + agent desktop.
- Onboarded via self-serve; small engineering team (2 backend + 1 frontend) experimenting with chat completion.

Primary ask: latency is too high for core chat flows. CEO said: "users notice pauses on reply, drop-off on mobile". Goal: reduce perceived reply time to <400ms p50 for single-turn suggestions.

Observed details (from support/SE):
- Default requests currently hitting eu-west region; product audience ~75% NA.
- Typical request shape: 1 system + 4 user messages with context; prompt ~900–1400 tokens; max_tokens set to 512.
- Measured p50 ~650ms in NA (via client-side timing), p95 spikes 1.8–2.4s; EU deployments show consistent 800ms+ p50 depending on route.
- Throughput low: ~5–12 reqs/sec during peaks, cost-sensitive.

Recommendations already discussed (to be validated in POC):
- Region change: route requests from NA users to us-east region for lower RTT (customer agreed to test).
- Prompt guidance: move long, static context into server-side retrieval + cache embeddings; send only recent turns + retrieved doc snippets. Target prompt <= 600 tokens.
- Adjust max_tokens & stop sequences to avoid over-generation; reduce default max_tokens to 128 for quick replies.
- Enable streaming in the client to improve perceived latency for longer responses.
- Client timeouts: set HTTP connect timeout 2s, total request timeout 10s; abort and backoff for retries (avoid cascading retries).
- Use token caching for repeated system prompts and KB snippets.

POC scope:
- 1 engineer to implement region header override + streaming demo
- 1-week telemetry: compare p50/p95 before vs after region + short prompt changes
- Success criteria: p50 below 400ms for NA traffic and no more than 15% p95 > 1s; same or lower token cost per session.

Quotes / snippets from calls:
- "If we can shave 200–300ms consistently the engagement metric improves" (Head of Product).
- "We tried increasing client-side polling but it made retries worse" (platform eng).

Open items / risks:
- Procurement asks for SOC2 reference before committing to monthly pricing (we provided security doc link).
- Engineering bandwidth limited; need example diff/snippet to drop-in streaming + region header.
- They use a 3rd-party routing proxy (cloudflare worker) that may mask client IPs; SE recommended server-side routing by user region.

Title: aggregate artifact origins into release index for private-installer

aggregate artifact origins into release index for private-installer

Add cross-repo artifact origin aggregation to release index used by private-installer; includes pipeline changes, index schema extension, signature/verification cross-checks, and docs for operator consumption.
Context and motivation: Private-installer releases consume artifacts produced by multiple build pipelines (core runtime, helm charts, terraform modules, third-party vendor artifacts). Existing release index entries pointed to single build blobs but lost origin metadata (repo/build-job/container image digest). This PR extends the release index generation to aggregate origin provenance across repos/pipelines so operators can inspect where each artifact came from and verify chain-of-custody at install time.

What this PR does: - Adds an `origins` aggregate block to the release index JSON that lists source repository, pipeline job id, build commit, and optional SBOM/cosign references per artifact. - Modifies the private-installer indexer job to query multiple artifact registries and cross-reference artifact digests to upstream build metadata (via the new origin-mapper service). - Adds origin-mapper microservice (lightweight Go lambda) that merges build metadata across internal buildkite/jenkins/job-run APIs and returns a normalized origin statement for an artifact digest. - Updates CI/CD pipelines: new step in release pipeline to call origin-mapper and attach signed origin blobs to TUF/manifest staging area. - Enhances verification: indexer validates cosign signatures on origin blobs (if present) and records signature verification result in the index. - Adds operator docs and an index API example in private-installer docs for auditors to query artifact origins during upgrades/rollbacks.

Checklist (implemented): - [x] Extend release index schema (index-schema/v2) with `origins` field and verification metadata - [x] Origin-mapper service implementation and unit tests - [x] Release pipeline changes (buildkite/jenkins) to emit origin blobs - [x] Indexer changes in private-installer repo to consume origin blobs - [x] Add integration test that replays multi-repo build metadata into staging index - [x] Docs: private-installer operator guide section on origin queries - [x] Security review: minimal privileges for origin-mapper to query job metadata APIs

Commits (high-level): - feat(indexer): add origin mapping hooks and schema v2 metadata - feat(origin-mapper): initial service with buildkite and jenkins adapters - ci(release): add origin-stage and sign-origin steps, upload to staging TUF area - docs(installer): add operator guide and example queries - test(integration): multi-repo origin aggregation smoke test - fix(ci): tolerate missing SBOM references for third-party mirrored artifacts

Files/areas changed (high-level): - private-installer/cmd/indexer: indexer changed to call origin-mapper and persist origins into index JSON - private-installer/internal/index/schema_v2.go: new schema and JSON marshaling changes - tools/origin-mapper/: new Go service and adapters for buildkite/jenkins - infra/ci/pipelines/release.yml: added origin-stage, sign-origin and upload steps - docs/private-installer/origins.md: operator documentation and API examples - charts/private-installer/values.yaml: small annotation for chart provenance - scripts/dev/replay-origins.sh: local dev helper to simulate upstream metadata

Review conversation (summary): - Lina: "Nice; can we guarantee origin-mapper rate limits won't blow up during a large release?" Author: "Origin-mapper queues queries and caches job metadata for 24h; added circuit-breaker and bulk query path. See origin-mapper/README for eviction rules." - Ethan: "Add tests for mirrored artifacts where upstream job metadata is absent." Author: "Added integration test that marks missing upstream metadata and attaches best-effort origin assertion with source:mirror and mirror-ref." - Zoe: "Signature verification path looks good, but require operator flag to enforce failed verification as hard-fail for critical releases." Author: "Added CLI flag `--enforce-origin-verification` to indexer and documented recommended usage in docs." - Security review (internal): "Ensure origin-mapper tokens scoped read-only and short lived." Author: "Confirmed; CI injects ephemeral tokens, and service uses read-only tokens with minimal TTL. Details in infra/ci/README-security.md."

CI summary: - Initial run: integration tests failed due to missing adapter for legacy Jenkins job API (fixed in second commit). - Second run: unit + integration + lint passed. - E2E staging run: origin blobs uploaded and cosign verification passed for signed artifacts; unsigned third-party artifacts recorded with `verified:false`. Final ci_status: pass.

Edge cases and limitations: - For artifacts mirrored from external vendors we may not retrieve upstream build job metadata; index will include `source: mirror` and a pointer to mirror provenance where available. - This PR does not change TUF signing policy; origin blobs themselves are uploaded to staging and signed with cosign in the release pipeline. TUF package signing remains the authoritative release signature. - Performance: origin-mapper adds an extra ~200-400ms per artifact during index generation in current staging; indexer runs concurrently and batching mitigates impact in typical releases.

Migration and rollout plan: - Index schema v2 is backward-compatible: indexer writes `schema_version: 2` and tooling falls back to v1 when v2 entry not present. - Rollout: release pipeline will emit v2 indexes to a staging bucket for two release cycles; operator tooling supports reading v1 and v2. - Post-merge action: update release-runbooks and notify SRE and compliance teams to start auditing origin queries on next private-installer release.

Merge outcome: Approved by Lina and Zoe after two rounds of review and tests; merged via squash on 2025-11-12.

Notes for future work: - Consider adding signed SBOM references into origin blobs for deeper attestation. - Explore offloading origin metadata to a dedicated provenance catalog service with search capabilities.

Title: add reproducible-build manifest + hashchain indexer for private-installer releases

add reproducible-build manifest + hashchain indexer for private-installer releases

Introduce a reproducible-build manifest and a signed hashchain indexer for Private Installer releases. Motivation: customers running Private (VPC and on-prem) need strong, verifiable release provenance that supports deterministic rebuilds, incremental delta fetches, and atomic rollbacks. This PR implements: 1) a reproducible-build manifest format (repro-manifest.json) emitted by our build pipelines that records build inputs, pinned toolchain versions, build environment nonce, and a canonical content-addressed artifact list; 2) a hashchain indexer that consumes build manifests and produces a signed, append-only index (index-hashchain.jsonl) where each entry contains the prior entry hash to enable tamper-evident release timelines; 3) dual-signing support in the release pipeline (cosign + GPG) for both individual artifacts (helm charts, installer tarballs, terraform modules) and the produced index; 4) a small installer-side verifier library (bash + Go shim) that validates hashchain continuity and signature coverage before applying upgrades or rollbacks; 5) CI/build changes to emit deterministic archive ordering and stamp SBOM entries so 'repro-manifest.json' can be validated by third parties. The description below documents integration points, rollback story, and operator commands for verification.
Add reproducible-build manifests and a tamper-evident hashchain indexer for Private Installer releases. Releases now include dual signatures (cosign + GPG) and a small verifier shipped with the installer to validate release continuity and signatures. Backwards compatible: existing installers will ignore the index if not present.
Verify a release index: curl -sS https://releases.redwood.ai/private/index-hashchain.jsonl | jq -r 'last' > entry.json && ./installer/verifier/verifier.sh entry.json
Rebuild deterministically: ./ci/release/indexer/rebuild --manifest repro-manifest.json --out ./repro-rebuild.tgz
Perform a safe rollback: ./installer/verifier/verifier.sh --rollback-to <entry-hash> --apply

Title: ci: add provenance bundles + staged release manifest pipeline for private-installer

ci: add provenance bundles + staged release manifest pipeline for private-installer

Motivation: For Private deployments we need cryptographically verifiable release bundles (artifacts, SBOMs, attestations) and a deterministic, staged manifest that operators can consume for air-gapped or VPC installs. This PR wires a CI pipeline that builds release artifacts for the private-installer chart and associated Terraform modules, produces SLSA-style provenance attestations, signs artifacts with cosign (KMS-backed keys), uploads signed bundles to a staging bucket, and emits a chained release manifest that references digested artifacts and attestation records.

- Artifact builders: added scripts/packaging/build_private_bundle.sh that produces tar.gz bundles containing Helm chart, rendered kustomize overlays, module zip, and SBOM JSON.
- Signing: integrates cosign via k8s-secrets-backed KMS path (uses ephemeral signing key rotation step for CI). Cosign signatures and bundle attestations are uploaded alongside artifacts.

- Upgrade/rollback tooling: adds tools/release/rollback-helper.sh which can validate manifests and perform an automated rollback plan for in-cluster private deployments (uses chart and module digests to revert).

- [x] Generate SBOMs (Syft) and attach to bundle

Title: Automate attestation + notarization for private-installer Helm/Terraform releases

Automate attestation + notarization for private-installer Helm/Terraform releases

Motivation:
We need reproducible, auditable release artifacts for Private deployments (VPC/on-prem installer). This PR wires up automated attestation and notarization into the existing release pipelines so that Helm charts, Terraform modules, and the on-prem installer tarballs are (1) reproducibly built, (2) cryptographically attested for build provenance, and (3) notarized with a timestamped signature stored alongside release manifests.

What this changes (summary):
- Adds a CI pipeline that produces deterministic build artifacts, generates SBOMs, and emits in-toto attestations for: Helm chart bundle, terraform modules, and the private-installer tarball.
- Integrates a notarization step that signs artifacts using a hardware-backed key (KMS/HSM integration stubbed for e2e; sees scripts/notarize.sh).
- Enhances release manifest generator to include provenance links (attestation uri, sbom uri, signature digest) and to publish a compact release-manifest.json to the releases bucket.
- Updates Helm chart metadata (Chart.yaml) with immutable digest fields and chart provenance annotations consumed by the installer.
- Terraform module releases now include a module_manifest.json with module version, provider pinning, and attestation reference.
- Adds a rollback-safe release marker: when a bad release is detected we can toggle 'active_release' in the manifest which the installer reads for safe rollback.

Design notes and tradeoffs:
- We use in-toto attestations (simple layout) instead of full SLSA pipeline enforcement for now to reduce blast radius and unblock ops. Future work will add stricter SLSA levels.
- Notarization uses an HSM-backed signing flow where the key material is kept in KMS. For CI we use a test key; the pipeline includes a gate to require a production KMS binding for production releases.
- Deterministic builds: we pin builder images and canonicalize timestamps when generating tarballs and charts to minimize non-determinism. This increases build complexity but is necessary for reproducible provenance.

- installer/helm/private-installer/Chart.yaml (add provenance annotations)
- installer/helm/private-installer/values.schema.json (validation for manifest-driven upgrades)
- installer/ci/release/provenance-pipeline.yaml (new)
- build/pipelines/attest-notarize.yaml (new)

- terraform/modules/private-network/module_manifest.json (generated)
- terraform/modules/registry/Makefile (release step integration)
- installer/release/release-manifest-generator.go (adds provenance fields)
- docs/private-deploy/release-provenance.md (docs)

Testing and validation:

- CI integration job runs attestation pipeline with test key and verifies signature and SBOM content.

Title: Signed Plugin Runtime and Verified Container Exhibit

Signed Plugin Runtime and Verified Container Exhibit

Purpose and scope:
This exhibit defines minimum security, supply-chain, and operational requirements for third-party or customer-supplied inference runtime plugins, containers, or binary artifacts that are installed into Redwood-managed runtime environments (hosted, dedicated, or private). The goal is to provide a repeatable verification and acceptance process that minimizes risk from untrusted code running in production inference paths, supports air-gapped deployments, and provides evidence for audits.

Applicability:
Applies to any vendor, partner, or customer-supplied container images, OCI bundles, or signed runtime plugins that will be executed by Redwood Inference on behalf of customers or within Redwood-managed infrastructure. Where a separate agreement governs supply of artifacts, this exhibit is incorporated by reference into the procurement or onboarding agreement.

Definitions (selected):
- "Artifact": a container image, OCI artifact, plugin binary, or packaged runtime component intended for execution.
- "Supplier": provider of the Artifact (vendor, partner, or customer).
- "Verifier": Redwood security team or its authorized third-party tool that performs acceptance checks described below.
- "Provenance Metadata": SBOM, signatures, build logs, and any attestations that demonstrate where and how the Artifact was produced.

Minimum deliverables from Supplier prior to deployment:
1) Signed release artifact(s): all container images or plugin binaries must be cryptographically signed using an industry-standard signing scheme (e.g., cosign/Rekor Rekor transparency / sigstore) and the signature must be accompanied by a signing certificate chain or key identifier. Keys must be subject to Supplier key management policies (see Key management).

2) SBOM: A full Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) in SPDX 2.2 or CycloneDX v1.4 format listing component packages, versions, build time, and source locations. SBOM must include hashes for each component.

3) Reproducible build manifest: instructions and a minimal build script and inputs sufficient for Redwood or an authorized third party to reproduce the build environment that generated the Artifact. If full reproducibility is not achievable due to proprietary components, Supplier must provide an attestation describing the gap and additional compensating controls.

4) Build logs and provenance: machine-readable build logs (timestamped), CI identifiers, and links to the source commit/PR (or internal source identifier for closed-source components).

5) Vulnerability baseline: supplier-provided scan report from a recognized scanner (e.g., Trivy, Clair) produced within 72 hours prior to delivery. Reports must include CVE identifiers and fix status.

6) Runtime Attestation script: an automated test harness that Redwood can execute in a sandbox that validates the plugin's runtime behavior (see Acceptance tests).

Key management and signing requirements:
- Private signing keys used by Supplier for release signing must be managed in a hardened KMS or HSM OR following NIST SP 800-57/800-131A equivalent controls. If keys are maintained in CI, the Supplier must provide CI key access controls, rotation cadence, and a compromise response plan.
- Supplier must publish a signing key rotation policy and provide prior notice to Redwood at least 30 days for key rotations for production artifacts (unless emergency rotation is required).
- If sigstore/cosign is used, Supplier should publish a Rekor log entry for each signed release. Redwood will validate signatures against Rekor transparency logs where available.

Container provenance and runtime guarantees:
- Immutable tags: production artifacts must be immutable (content-addressable digest references) rather than mutable tags. Redwood will only accept artifacts referenced by digest (sha256:...).
- Minimal privilege runtime: Supplier must document recommended runtime security context, non-root user guidance, required filesystem mounts, and network egress expectations. Artifacts should be designed for least-privilege execution.

Air-gapped and private deployment considerations:
- Offline attestation: for air-gapped deployments, Supplier must deliver an offline verification bundle that includes the SBOM, signed digest, signed build artifact, and a set of signed attestations. Redwood will provide a verifier container that can be executed in-customer air-gapped environments; Supplier must ensure compatibility and sign the verification results.
- Transferable evidence: Supplier must include portable logs (gzipped) of build and signing steps and a signed manifest allowing rooftop verification without Internet access.

Acceptance and verification checks (Verifier responsibilities):
Redwood will validate the Artifact using the following checks prior to any production rollout:
1) Signature verification: verify cryptographic signature and certificate trust chain or Rekor entry.
2) SBOM conformance: ensure SBOM format valid and components match contents of the image; component hashes verified.
3) Vulnerability assessment: run automated scanners and reconcile Supplier-provided vulnerability report with live scanning results. If critical or high vulnerabilities exist without a documented mitigation plan, the Artifact is rejected.
4) Reproducibility sanity checks: attempt to reproduce build metadata or run deterministic checks against provided build logs.
5) Acceptance tests: execute Supplier-provided runtime attestation scripts in a sandboxed environment (see Acceptance tests section). All acceptance tests with non-deterministic outputs must be run multiple times to identify flaky behavior.
6) Resource and performance checks: validate resource limits, memory/cpu/access patterns to ensure no denial-of-service behavior in multi-tenant hosts.

Acceptance tests (Supplier obligations):
- Supplier must provide an automated test harness with:
  - A deterministic smoke test that validates the primary runtime API surface (e.g., loading model, initialization, a small inference call with a known seed).
  - A stability test that runs a short sequence of requests for 10 minutes under bounded concurrency and records memory/CPU metrics to detect leaks.
  - Failure mode tests that intentionally provide malformed inputs to verify safe failure paths.
- Test harness output must be machine-readable (JSON) and include timestamps, return codes, and resource metrics.

Patch, update, and emergency rollback procedures:
- Update cadence: Supplier must describe patch frequency and SLAs for security fixes. For critical/vulnerable components, Supplier must provide hotfixes within 72 hours of CVE disclosure or cooperate in mitigation/segmentation plans.
- Rolling updates: Supplier's artifacts must support graceful upgrade/rollback by digest reference. Redwood will apply canary deployments and requires that Supplier artifacts are backwards compatible for at least one minor release window (or provide a compatibility matrix).
- Emergency rollback: Supplier must provide a known-good digest for rollback and a signed statement that the rollback artifact remains supported.

Auditability, logging, and evidence retention:
- Evidence retention: Supplier must retain build logs, signing events, SBOMs, and vulnerability reports for at least 3 years and provide records on request in a machine-readable format.
- Audit access: on reasonable request and subject to agreed scopes, Supplier must provide Redwood or Redwood-appointed auditors access to build systems or redacted logs sufficient to validate provenance claims. For highly restricted environments, mutually-agreed redaction rules can be applied.

Incident handling and disclosure:
- Compromise notification: Supplier must notify Redwood within 24 hours of detecting a suspected compromise of build or signing infrastructure and provide remediation steps and timelines.
- For exploitation of an Artifact running in Redwood infrastructure that results in data exposure or service degradation, Supplier and Redwood will coordinate incident response per the primary agreement's incident response annex.

Liability and remedial obligations (summary):
- Supplier represents that Artifacts do not intentionally include backdoors, exfiltration code, or undisclosed remote administration functionality.
- If Supplier-provided Artifact causes a security incident attributable to Supplier negligence (e.g., weak signing keys, known unpatched critical CVE), Supplier will bear remediation costs as described in the master agreement (or liability schedule).

Operational notes and recommendations (best practice):
- Prefer reproducible builds and public transparency logs.
- Use content-addressable artifact references (digests) in all production manifests.
- Maintain an SBOM lifecycle: update SBOMs for each patch and include delta files when feasible.
- Automate verifier runs in CI to detect issues earlier in the onboarding flow.

Appendix A: Example verification flow (high level)
1) Supplier uploads signed artifact and SBOM to onboarding bucket and files a ticket (SEC-xxx).
2) Redwood verifier pulls artifact by digest, verifies signature against Rekor (or provided certificate), parses SBOM, and runs a vulnerability scan.
3) Verifier executes acceptance tests in isolated sandbox.
4) If all checks pass, artifact is marked as "accepted" for staging. Canary rollout is scheduled per deployment policy.
5) If checks fail, Redwood provides Supplier a reproducible failure package and expected remediation items.

Appendix B: Template checklist (to be attached to onboarding ticket)
- [ ] Artifact digest provided (sha256:...).
- [ ] Signature present and Rekor entry (if used).
- [ ] SBOM attached (SPDX/CycloneDX).
- [ ] Vulnerability report attached (<=72h).
- [ ] Reproducible build manifest provided.
- [ ] Runtime attestation harness attached (JSON output).
- [ ] Compatibility matrix for rollback and forward compatibility.

Acknowledgements and governance:
This exhibit was drafted by Redwood Inference security-and-compliance in coordination with product and engineering (serving runtime). It is intended as an operational exhibit and can be tightened into contract language for enterprise procurement. For questions or suggested edits, contact the owner in the document metadata.

End of exhibit.

Title: Add SBOM pointer + sha256 to offline bundle manifest and verify offline

Add SBOM pointer + sha256 to offline bundle manifest and verify offline

Context: Air-gapped customers are asking for a verifiable SBOM as part of the offline bundle so they can do internal intake (security scanning / procurement) without relying on external links. We already sign the manifest and verify artifact hashes; this PR extends the manifest to reference the SBOM artifact(s) and verifies the SBOM file hash offline during preflight. Summary of changes: (1) Manifest schema: adds an optional `sbom` entry with fields for `uri` (relative path in bundle or file:// URI), `sha256` (hex), and `format` (e.g., spdx-json, cyclonedx-json). The SBOM entry is included in the signed manifest payload, so tampering is detected via signature verification and also via explicit hash verification. (2) Bundle layout convention: recommends placing SBOMs under `sbom/` in the bundle root (e.g., `sbom/redwood-private-<version>.spdx.json`). The manifest stores the relative path (preferred) or file:// URI for non-standard layouts. We explicitly do NOT support fetching SBOMs over the network during install; if the manifest uses http(s) and `--air-gapped` is enabled, preflight fails with an actionable error. (3) Installer preflight: adds a verification step `verifySbom()` executed after manifest signature verification and before chart/image checks. Behavior: if `sbom` is present, the installer resolves the SBOM file path, computes sha256, compares to manifest, and fails closed on mismatch; if the SBOM file is missing, it fails in air-gapped mode and warns (non-fatal) in connected mode (to preserve forward-compat while we migrate internal bundle builders). If `sbom` is not present, preflight proceeds with a single warning line noting SBOM verification was skipped. (4) Tests: adds unit tests for schema parse + canonicalization (sbom fields included), and preflight verification tests covering: missing sbom file, mismatched hash, and a valid SBOM hash. Adds a regression test to ensure we never attempt network access in air-gapped mode even if a URI is mistakenly set to https://. (5) UX: introduces specific error codes/messages used by Support: `BUNDLE_SBOM_NOT_FOUND`, `BUNDLE_SBOM_HASH_MISMATCH`, `BUNDLE_SBOM_URI_UNSUPPORTED_OFFLINE`. Includes remediation tips (verify transfer integrity, re-extract bundle, confirm you have the correct SBOM file that matches the bundle build id). Implementation notes: The manifest remains canonicalized via our existing stable JSON encoder; the new `sbom` fields are treated as normal keys and appear deterministically. We intentionally kept this additive (no schema version bump) to avoid bricking older bundles; older installer versions will ignore the new fields, but this installer will verify them when present. Follow-ups (out of scope here): (a) make SBOM presence required for GA bundles (gated in release tooling), (b) allow multiple SBOMs (per-component) if compliance asks; current schema supports a single top-level SBOM pointer which is sufficient for pilot customers. Security considerations: This reduces supply-chain risk for offline deployments by ensuring the SBOM itself is integrity-protected and tied to the exact bundle contents. It also prevents a class of “swap SBOM during transfer” issues that came up during customer security reviews. Related: ENG-4821 (manifest schema/canonicalization), ENG-4823 (installer verification), ENG-4829 (audit events for verification outcomes; this PR does not add new audit events beyond existing preflight result logging).
- Offline bundle manifest can now include SBOM metadata (path/URI + sha256). - Installer preflight verifies SBOM hash offline when present; fails closed on mismatch/missing file in offline mode.
Marcus Lin (Security) requested we fail closed on SBOM hash mismatch and ensure no network fetch occurs in air-gapped mode, even if a URI is provided. Author updated the resolver to reject http(s) URIs when `--air-gapped` is true and added a regression test that asserts no outbound attempts. Kevin Osei asked whether the SBOM hash verification result would be visible in support bundles/audit logs; Jordan noted this PR only adds preflight errors and warnings and referenced ENG-4829/PR-25011 for wiring bundle metadata into support bundles. Ethan Park requested clearer messaging for the “SBOM missing in connected mode” case to avoid confusing customers; author adjusted the warning to include next steps (rebuild bundle / contact support) and added the exact path that was attempted. Connor O'Brien asked about schema compatibility with older installers and release tooling; author confirmed the field is optional and that release tooling can start populating it immediately without needing a manifest version bump, and added a small note to docs/offline-bundles.md.

Title: provenance-aggregator-seeding-and-rollback-safepoints

provenance-aggregator-seeding-and-rollback-safepoints

Motivation: Customers running Private (VPC/on-prem) deployments require deterministic rollback points and strong provenance for release artifacts. This PR implements a lightweight provenance aggregator that seeds release manifests with artifact attestations and creates 'rollback safepoints' that the private-installer can use to perform deterministic upgrades and rollbacks. It also adds a validation stage in the CI pipeline that verifies cosign signatures, KMS-backed key rotation metadata, and TUF-compatible provenance blobs before a release is promoted.

What changed: single continuous description string below lists key components committed in this PR — provenance-aggregator service (small Go utility), CI pipeline steps for seeding attestations, helm chart templating knobs to consume safepoints, terraform module updates for installer state bucket lifecycle, and a migration that backfills safepoint metadata for the last two released delta bundles. Included conservative opt-in behavior: private customers must enable 'provenanceSeed=true' in their installer config to activate runtime usage.

Design notes: the aggregator collects cosign attestations emitted by the build pipeline and normalizes them into a compact JSON provenance envelope (artifact_sha, cosign_sig_refs, attestation_payload_refs, build_id, timestamp, signed_by_key_id). These envelopes are uploaded to the installer state bucket under /provenance/{release_tag}/envelopes/*. A small 'safepoint-manifest' is derived that pins a set of artifact SHAs and a signed manifest index (cosigned by the release signing key) that the upgrade/rollback controller can atomically download and validate at runtime. The approach avoids migrating the full SBOM into the installer and keeps per-release provenance lightweight while preserving verifiability.

Migration and safety: added a migration job (CI triggered) that backfills provenance envelopes for the past two release windows. The installer now refuses to apply a rollback across a non-safepoint boundary unless an operator passes --unsafe-allow-migration and acknowledges the audit checklist.

Security and key rotation: integrates with existing KMS binding for cosign key references. A new small helper script records key rotation events as provenance metadata so the controller can reject manifests signed by keys that have been revoked.

CI changes: added two new steps to the release workflow: 1) provenance-seed: aggregates artefacts from the build bucket, verifies cosign signatures and uploads envelopes; 2) safepoint-validate: verifies the new safepoint-manifest cosign signature and runs a TUF-style provenance validator against the envelope set. Both steps run in the private-installer pipeline and are gated behind a feature flag in CI for staged rollout.

Backward compatibility: opt-in by default. Helm chart provides values.provenance.enabled (default false). Terraform module adds an optional state_bucket_prefix variable; existing installs are unaffected unless they opt in.

Testing: unit tests for the aggregator, integration test in the release pipeline that seeds a synthetic release and ensures the installer controller accepts the safepoint-manifest and can simulate an atomic rollback. CI records included test flakiness info and two reruns of flaky network-bound tests.

Merge: squash-merged after approvals and a green CI run with final re-run of safepoint-validate.
