Title: Introduce supply-chain KMS attestor and RBAC tamper-guarding hook

Introduce supply-chain KMS attestor and RBAC tamper-guarding hook

Problem: Recent compliance reviews highlighted a gap in our supply-chain integrity story: operators and installer tooling could not cryptographically assert that deployable artifacts (helm charts, installer bundles) were provisioned with a customer-scoped KMS key provenance. This limits our ability to produce non-repudiable audit records for Private installations and on-prem flows.

Goals: 1) Add an attestor service that validates a signed provenance blob against configured KMS providers and emits a tamper-evidence header used by RBACv2 decisioning. 2) Integrate a lightweight RBAC hook (tamper-guard) that rejects operator-scoped role grants when provenance checks fail. 3) Provide an operator-facing runbook and CI guards to validate the attestation flow.

What this PR does: Adds a new internal attestor component (pkg/attestor) which consumes artifact metadata, verifies KMS-wrapped signatures across our supported KMS adapters (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault), and returns a signed assertion with a canonicalized audit fingerprint. Introduces an RBAC enforcement hook (pkg/rbac/tamperguard.go) that consults the attestor via gRPC and attaches a tamper-evidence claim into the authorization pipeline. Installer/helm changes wire the attestor sidecar into Private and Dedicated installers with a default disabled flag. Includes e2e CI job and a new compliance runbook that documents expected signals in the audit logs.

Title: Batching vs Residency: Latency and Cost Tradeoffs - Foxden Logistics discovery

Batching vs Residency: Latency and Cost Tradeoffs - Foxden Logistics discovery

Discovery focused on cost/unit economics for a pilot across hosted vs dedicated vs private. Major themes: batching and cache impact on per-token cost, residency/data controls, latency SLOs for customer facing features, pilot budget constraints and benchmarking plan. Customer worried about peak latency during 99th pct and how batching affects user-perceived latency. Security/CISO asked for SOC2, KMS, and VPC integration details. Agreed next steps for pilot pricing and benchmark run.
1) Current stack and constraints 2) Target throughput/latency 3) Unit cost levers (batching, KV cache, quantization) 4) Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs 5) Compliance/residency needs 6) Pilot scope and success metrics
[00:00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate the time. Quick intros?
[00:00:08] Priya (Foxden): Hi I'm Priya, head of ML at Foxden, we run parcel ETA models and want to add LLM-based routing assistant and a post-delivery summarizer.
[00:00:15] Marcus (Foxden Product): Marcus, product, thinking about customer-facing chat summarization.
[00:00:19] Ethan (Foxden Infra): Ethan, infra lead. Mainly here for cost, networking questions.
[00:00:23] Samira (Foxden CISO): Samira, security. I'll be skimming compliance items.
[00:00:26] Darius (Redwood SE): Darius, SE, I'll cover perf and batching specifics.
[00:00:30] Maya: Great. High level — you're evaluating hosted, dedicated, or private deployment for inference. Today we want to understand your traffic shape and budget constraints so we can recommend a pilot.
[00:00:45] Priya: Exactly. Our baseline traffic for the routing assistant is about 150k requests/day with an average prompt+response length in the 350-800 token range. Peaks up to 400 reqs/sec during morning windows. Budget is tight — we'd like to keep unit cost under something that scales.
[00:01:04] Darius: Okay so two levers: model choice and runtime settings. Batching and KV caching are the main cost reducers. But batching increases effective latency unless we tune thresholds and continuous batching.
[00:01:18] Ethan: When you say KV caching, you mean prefix/key-value cache for repeated context, right? We've got a lot of repeated context for the same delivery routes.
[00:01:25] Darius: Yep, KV cache — sorry sometimes docs say KV cash in speech — essentially the model's key-value attention cache we can persist across short sessions to avoid recomputing tokens. For your use-case there's a high reuse fraction so it's a big win.
[00:01:38] Priya: Quantitatively, what's the percent saving we should expect? Even a sketch is fine.
[00:01:43] Darius: Ballpark: with good prefix reuse and cache hit rates 60-80%, you can see 30-60% per-token cost reduction. With batching alone, depending on seq lengths, another 20-40% on GPU-backed serving. Combined, maybe 50-70% lower than naive single-token-per-request runs. But that depends on tail latency tolerances.
[00:02:02] Marcus: Tail latency — our SLO is 450ms p95 for interactive features. If batching raises p95 above that users will notice.
[00:02:09] Maya: Right. So tradeoff is latency vs cost. Hosted mode gives you immediate access to batching and caching suggestions and we can tune continuous batching to keep p95 under your SLO. Dedicated reduces noisy neighbor risk and predictable throughput, and Private gives you residency and VPC controls but has higher ops overhead.
[00:02:27] Samira: On Private — we need to know encryption in transit and at rest, KMS integrations (HSM), and audit logs. Is SOC2 in scope for hosted?
[00:02:35] Maya: Yes, hosted Redwood has SOC2 Type II. We integrate with common KMS providers — we have a managed option and also support customer-managed keys for private. Audit logs and per-token tracing are available in the Console.
[00:02:46] Samira: Good. Also want SAML SSO, RBAC, and retention controls. We cannot keep any PII beyond 30 days for this workload.
[00:02:54] Olga (Redwood SE): We can set up retention policies and redaction pipelines for logs; or configure no-persist modes in private deployments. SAML is supported for the console and RBAC can be scoped to teams.
[00:03:06] Ethan: Back to cost — you mentioned continuous batching. How do you avoid batch-wait latency for single, low-volume requests?
[00:03:13] Darius: We use a latency-aware batching policy — small time windows and adaptive thresholds. For interactive single users we keep batch latency under ~40ms by setting max-wait timers and prioritizing small batches. For background bulk ops we allow larger batch windows to maximize throughput.
[00:03:28] Priya: If we go dedicated, is there a predictable per-token price? Or do we still pay unit costs?
[00:03:34] Maya: Dedicated is committed capacity — effectively a monthly reservation. You'll pay for the capacity slot and then there's a per-token usage layer for burst or overage depending on the contract. For pilots we often provision a small dedicated pool to validate throughput then scale.
[00:03:50] Marcus: Our budget for pilot is about $12k for 4 weeks. We need to understand if that's enough for a credible test with your medium-sized model.
[00:03:58] Darius: With $12k and your traffic profile, a hosted pilot using batching+KV cache can simulate production-like costs. If you need strict residency or to measure noise-free latency, a short dedicated run for a week would consume a chunk of that. We'll model both.
[00:04:13] Priya: Can you run a bench for both hosted and dedicated with our token distribution?
[00:04:17] Darius: Yes — we ask you to provide token-length histogram and request-rate timeline. We'll run a perf job measuring p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and cost-per-1k-tokens with different batch sizes and cache configs.
[00:04:29] Ethan: How do fallbacks and multi-model routing work? If we prefer a light model at the tail to reduce cost, can Redwood route automatically?
[00:04:36] Maya: Yes — Smart routing will send requests to preferred model variants by policy. You can do latency-first for low token sequences and cost-first for async jobs. We also support automatic fallback to smaller models when dedicated capacity is saturated.
[00:04:47] Samira: A question on auditability — does per-token tracing expose prompt content in logs? We need to ensure PII isn't leaked to logs.
[00:04:54] Olga: Logs can be redacted or suppressed; we offer metadata-only traces and token-level cost accounting without storing user prompt text. For SOC2 we can provide details in the security packet.
[00:05:06] Priya: A bit concerned about the percieved complexity. If batching and cache configs are fiddly, who's responsible for tuning?
[00:05:12] Darius: Redwood Optimize provides recommendations automatically based on observed traffic. For pilots our SE will help tune thresholds and batching. Over time, the system learns and recommends quantization or model variants.
[00:05:24] Marcus: About quantization — do you support int8 or more aggressive Q4 variants? Any quality regressions we should expect?
[00:05:29] Darius: We support several quantization profiles. Q4 or int8 can dramatically reduce memory and cost with small quality impacts — depends on your task. We'll run evals on your prompt sets to measure regressions; we surface the delta in the Console.
[00:05:41] Ethan: Networking — if we go Private in our VPC, do we need to open outbound egress to Redwood, or is it a peering setup?
[00:05:47] Maya: Private can be either VPC peering or onsite on-prem package. For VPC we do peering and customer-managed networking — no broad egress to the public internet required — we support strict ACLs and private endpoints.
[00:06:00] Samira: Does private require an on-call ops team from our side?
[00:06:04] Maya: We have options — fully managed Private where Redwood runs the control plane with minimal hands-on required, or self-managed on-prem which will need your ops. For regulated workloads we often do a hybrid where we manage the runtime but keys and audit logs stay with the customer.
[00:06:18] Priya: Ok what's the success criteria for the pilot? What should we measure?
[00:06:21] Darius: Agree on: 1) p95 < 450ms for interactive flows 2) per-token effective cost under X (we'll propose) 3) cache hit rate > 60% for route context 4) minimal quality delta for quantized model < 2-3% on your evaluation prompts.
[00:06:38] Marcus: For pricing, will you give a per-token hosted rate and an equivalent effective per-token for dedicated?
[00:06:44] Maya: Yes — we'll send two modeled price sheets: hosted per-token tiers, and a dedicated reservation example that amortizes hardware and gives effective per-token based on your projected throughput. We'll include a sensitivity table for different batch and cache assumptions.
[00:06:57] Priya: Any gotchas on billing granularity? Do you round tokens or do subtokens matter?
[00:07:02] Maya: We bill per token with internal tokenization. We publish tokenization details and sample reconstructions; for costs we show tokens per request averaged over the sample traces you send.
[00:07:12] Ethan: One more — what's the quickest way to prove it without blowing the pilot budget?
[00:07:16] Darius: Start with hosted with caching enabled and simulated peak load tests. That gets you real p95/p99 numbers fast. If the tail looks noisy, do a short dedicated slice for peak windows.
[00:07:27] Samira: Security packet and SOC2 please.
[00:07:30] Maya: We'll attach the security packet in the follow up.
[00:07:33] Priya: Great. Also can you include an example of cache hit vs miss cost delta?
[00:07:36] Darius: Yes will include a worked example based on your token histogram.
[00:07:40] Maya: Quick recap: Redwood to send pilot pricing, sample perf configs; SE to run bench after customer shares token histogram and hourly traffic; Customer to share compliance list and retention constraints. Any other items?
[00:07:53] Marcus: No, that's it.
[00:07:55] Samira: I'll add the compliance doc to the shared folder.
[00:07:58] Maya: Perfect — thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the pricing and schedule.
[00:08:02] END
Transcript contains minor transcription artifacts (KV cash, SAM l). Discussed concrete pilot constraints: $12k budget, 4-week pilot, target p95 450ms. Agreed data sharing needed: token histogram, traffic timeline, compliance list.

Title: Adaptive link-rate smoothing and NCCL pacing for heterogeneous interconnects

Adaptive link-rate smoothing and NCCL pacing for heterogeneous interconnects

Background: On clusters with heterogeneous interconnects (mixed NVLink/NIC link speeds and asymmetrical topologies) we observed recurring NCCL stalls and bandwidth oscillation under TP workloads. This manifested as throughput variance across microbatches and elevated p99 tail latency for short-running inference requests. Motivation: previous fixes focused on static stream priorities or rigid batching heuristics which either underutilize good links or exacerbate stalls on slow links. This PR implements an adaptive link-rate smoothing layer and NCCL pacing integration to harmonize collective launches with per-peer link conditions and the runtime scheduler. Key changes and approach: 1) Link-rate estimator: continuous lightweight probe that measures effective per-peer bandwidth and short-term variability; estimator lives in scheduler/peer-rate-estimator and exports a smoothed rate with decay/window parameters tuned for inference workloads. 2) NCCL pacing adaptor: introduces optional pacing tokens in the comm adapter to space collective launches when peer variability is high; pacing is conservative by default and disabled for uniformly fast topologies. 3) Slack windows & micro-shear prevention: scheduler now computes a small slack window for kernel dispatch to absorb jittered arrival times from peers and aligns kernel launches with KV-cache prefetch completion when available. 4) KV cache alignment hook: prefetch manager negotiates a preferred alignment point with the scheduler for batched requests so comm-heavy windows avoid blocking on cache population. 5) Telemetry & guardrails: new metrics (peer_effective_bw, nccl_pacing_suppressed, pacing_tokens_issued) and a dynamic safety threshold that disables pacing if aggregate throughput would drop. Performance: in lab runs (8-node, mixed NVLink + EDR InfiniBand topology) typical large-TP workloads gained 12-18% sustained throughput and p99 latency improved by ~25% for short requests; NCCL stall events as recorded by tracers dropped ~60%. Testing and validation: - microbench suite: tp_collectives_bench extended with hetero-link scenarios - end-to-end canary: perf-canary harness with 10% traffic for 48h - unit + integration: scheduler, comm adapter, kv prefetch mocks - stress: ramp tests up to 200 concurrent sessions Rollout plan: canary 10% on dedicated clusters for 48h -> 50% -> global. Operator flags: pacing enabled=false by default for existing clusters; enabled=true for targeted clusters requires no code rollback. Risk and mitigation: conservative defaults, auto-disable if pacing causes throughput regression, and manual opt-out available via runtime flags. Related work: this complements prior comm scheduling efforts (see ENG-6123 family) and is intended to pair with future topology-aware kernel selectors. Notes: preserves existing public API surface; only runtime internals and ops docs are updated.
Ethan Wu: Can you explain how the probe traffic avoids perturbing production workloads? We should bound probe sample size.
Author (Priya): Probe uses a low-rate in-band estimator with adaptive throttling; added explicit bound and backoff to avoid congestion (see peer_rate_estimator.cc).
Marisol Ortega: Approve with one nit: prefer metric name 'peer_effective_bw_bytes' for clarity.

Dmitri Petrov: Requested change: make pacing opt-out dynamic via operator API (not just startup flag).
Author (Priya): Added runtime flag and operator endpoint; documented behaviour and rollout safety checks.
Introduce adaptive NCCL pacing and link-rate smoothing to reduce comm stalls on heterogeneous interconnects; opt-in via runtime flag. Improves throughput and tail latency on mixed-topology TP clusters.

Title: ValeHealth on-prem implementation capture

ValeHealth on-prem implementation capture

Call notes (2024-09-17) — discovery with ValeHealth (CTO: Aaron Li, SecOps: Maya Singh, Arch: Dan Ochoa)

- Context: ValeHealth is a mid-sized digital health provider planning to run conversational triage + discharge-summary generation inside their data center (air-gapped option discussed). They must not send PHI outside their network. Primary asks: private control plane with VPC peering to their corp network, KMS/HSM integration for key material, audit logs for every inference, and 12 month retention for audit records.

- Key constraints called out by customer:
  - PHI: full PHI scope, must meet SOC2 + HIPAA controls.
  - Network: strict egress rules; anything that talks to hosted control plane needs explicit allow list.
  - Hardware: they will provision 2x A100 80GB per zone initially, plan to add 4x after pilot.
  - Throughput target: 12 concurrent triage sessions, average 40 tokens/response, target p95 token latency per token <= 90ms (end-to-end p95 for a 200-token response <= 18s) — customer expects interactive feel.
  - Burst behavior: expect spikes morning 8–10AM and post-op 3–5PM.

- Functional reqs (high level):
  1) On-prem Redwood Private with local model hosting and local KV/prefix caching.
  2) VPC-only control plane connectivity (can run in their VPC or peered) — no public IPs on inference nodes.
  3) KMS or HSM integration: must support AWS CloudHSM or on-prem Thales via KMIP.
  4) Audit logs: immutable tamper-evident logs for each request (user id, route, token counts, prompt hash).
  5) Structured outputs: discharge summary templates + JSON schema enforcement + function-calling hooks.
  6) Streaming WebSocket support for triage chat UI.
  7) Canary deploys and fast rollback; cannot have model drift affecting PHI fidelity.

- Non-functional / ops notes:
  - Warmup: with A100s expect ~20–40s cold start for large Llama-family models to reach peak throughput. Need pre-warm policy for scheduled windows.
  - Batch sizing: small batch sizes to preserve latency SLO; recommend continuous batching with low-latency cutoff (15ms).
  - KV cache: prefix caching will significantly cut token generation for repetitive triage prompts; plan to instrument cache hit rate in pilot.
  - Quantization: they want FP16 or 4-bit quant for cost; warn: 4-bit may slightly degrade token-level probabilities -> risks for hallucination in medical text. We should plan eval prompts + acceptance criteria.
  - Telemetry: customer wants token-level cost/latency breakdown exported to Splunk (on-prem) every 1 minute.

- Gotchas / open technical risks:
  - Network egress policy: Control plane components that check for model updates may require egress. Customer requires whitelisting; need to enumerate IPs and acceptable update cadence. Offline update flow (airgap) must be documented.
  - HSM cert exchange: support for KMIP versions and cert rotation timeline — Ops needs runbook for emergency rotation.
  - Model licensing: some open models require attribution; legal to confirm whether ValeHealth agrees to the model license and distribution in-country.
  - Tokenization mismatch: current front-end uses older tokenizer library; we need to validate prompt/encoding parity to avoid token count surprises and cost overruns.
  - Long output trimming: discharge summaries sometimes exceed 1,000 tokens; need to support streaming + progressive flush to UI and chunked audit records.

- Example acceptance tests ValeHealth suggested (rough):
  1) PHI redaction test: send synthetic PHI and ensure logs do not contain raw PHI in plaintext except authorized fields.
  2) Latency test: 200-token generation p50 < 2s, p95 < 18s under steady load of 12 concurrent sessions.
  3) Regression test: standard eval suite of 150 prompts for hallucination / clinical accuracy; failure rate < 3% vs baseline model.

- Quick numbers back-of-envelope (for sizing discussion):
  - If we run Llama-3-classic-70B FP16 on A100-80: single GPU peak concurrency for low-latency ~6–8 simultaneous single-stream sessions (depends on context length). With 2 GPUs expect ~12–16 sessions — matches their initial 12 target.
  - If they quantize to 4-bit, can increase concurrency ~1.5x but verify regressions.

- Prompts / eval plan notes to self:
  - Set up a small eval harness with their sample chart notes (deidentified) + golden summaries from clinicians. Use rouge/med-sa metrics and human spot checks.
  - Create prompt templates that force structured JSON output with explicit "extractionConfidence" fields so UI can flag low-confidence sections for clinician review.

- Compliance & legal items to loop in:
  - Legal: confirm data residency policies and model license acceptability.
  - Security: run threat model for Private control plane; provide pen-test window.
  - Privacy: document data retention and deletion for audit logs (they asked 12 months but want ability to purge per request).

- Action items / next steps (owners + dates):
  - Priya: Draft on-prem architecture sketch & airgap flow; include IP whitelist and update cadence -> due 2024-09-23.
  - Jordan: Prep rough cost/throughput matrix comparing FP16 vs 4-bit and likely concurrency -> due 2024-09-25.
  - Evan: Prototype tokenizer parity check using ValeHealth frontend sample prompts; report tokenization deltas -> due 2024-09-26.
  - Rita: Open legal thread with licensing & PHI handling questions; sync with Legal -> create ticket VALE-124 by 2024-09-20.
  - Schedule: Book follow-up workshop for pilot scoping (architect deep-dive + security) w/ ValeHealth and infra ops -> target week of 2024-09-30.

- Meeting artifacts to attach to pilot folder (TODO):
  - Synthetic PHI test vectors (anonymized)
  - Clinician gold-summaries (deid) for eval harness
  - Network diagrams and firewall rules template for their infra team

- Notes to self (raw):
  - Keep canary window small, ensure rollback by model tag (do not rely on in-place weights swap without versioned checkpoints).
  - Need a short (1–2 slide) cheat sheet on expected latency/cold-start behavior for sales to set expectations.
  - Consider offering a Managed Updates opt-in where we push vetted model/security updates on a monthly cadence to reduce their ops burden.

- Questions to raise in next call:
  1) Can ValeHealth provide a stable internal registry (S3 or Artifactory) for model artifacts and container images?
  2) Which exact HSM vendors do they have on-prem? (Thales, AWS CloudHSM, Gemalto?)
  3) Do they expect encryption-in-use (SGX/Confidential VMs) beyond KMS-at-rest?

End of raw capture.

-- Priya (notes kept informal, will formalize into pilot scoping doc after internal sync)

Title: Cross-functional Activation & Access Provisioning: New-hire Handoff and Role Readiness

Cross-functional Activation & Access Provisioning: New-hire Handoff and Role Readiness

Overview

Purpose: This page documents a standardized, cross-functional process for activating new hires, provisioning the accounts and tooling they need on Day 0/Day 1, validating role readiness, and handing off ownership between People Ops, IT/Cloud, Security, and the hiring manager. The goal is to reduce time-to-productivity, eliminate repeated requests for access, and ensure compliance with least-privilege principles.

Scope
- Applies to all full-time employees, long-term contractors (>90 days), and principal external contributors.
- Excludes short-term contractors (<90 days) who follow the contractor onboarding checklist.
- Covers identity, cloud and infra accounts, developer tooling, Slack/Zoom, internal dashboards, and hardware provisioning.

Key Principles
- Least privilege: provide only what is necessary for the role/team and escalate access via documented approvals.
- Single source of truth: People Ops must open a single activation ticket that drives downstream provisioning workflows.
- Role readiness gate: hiring manager signs off on access and tooling after a checklist validation.
- Auditability: every activation has an audit trail (Okta request ID, ticket ID, approvers).

Roles and Responsibilities
- People Ops (Owner): collects hire data, opens activation ticket, schedules orientation, confirms equipment shipping.
- Hiring Manager (Owner): completes role readiness checklist, approves elevated access, assigns buddy.
- IT/Cloud (Executor): provisions hardware, cloud accounts (GCP/AWS), repository access, VPN.
- Security (Reviewer): reviews and approves IAM roles above baseline (see Access Baseline table).
- Employee/Buddy (Assignee): completes verification tasks and confirms access.

Activation Workflow (High level)
1. Offer accepted -> People Ops creates Activation Ticket in ServiceDesk with tag activation-step-1 and populates the Activation Form (fields below).
2. People Ops triggers automated provisioning via Okta SCIM and the infra provisioning automation (CI job: infra-provision/new-hire).
3. IT/Cloud provisions hardware and cloud accounts; Security reviews any non-standard role requests.
4. Hiring Manager completes Role Readiness Checklist and signs off within 72 hours.
5. People Ops closes activation ticket after Manager signoff and employee confirmation.

Activation Form (minimum fields to include in ticket)
- candidate_name
- start_date
- office_or_remote
- role_title
- manager_name
- team_name
- required_tools (comma-separated list e.g. repo,db,analytics)
- access_exceptions (yes/no; if yes, justification)
- equipment_needed (laptop, dock, monitors)

Day 0/Day 1 Access Matrix (table)
| Category | Baseline access (Day 0) | Role-elevated (Manager request) | Provisioning owner | SLA |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Corporate identity | Okta account, SSO to Google Workspace | N/A | People Ops (Okta) | 4 hours before start |
| Communication | Slack, Miro, Zoom | Admin channels by request | People Ops | 24 hours |
| Code repos | Read access to team GitHub org | Write on repo or team-admin | IT/DevPlatform | 24-48 hours |
| Cloud console | Billing console view (read) via group | Project-editor or custom role (approved) | IT/Cloud + Security | 48 hours (security approval adds 24h) |
| Internal dashboards | Read access to dashboards.team | Product/admin as needed | Data Platform | 48 hours |
| CI/CD | No access until training | Pipeline trigger rights after training | DevOps | 72 hours |

Role Readiness & Signoff Checklist (hiring manager to complete)
1. Verified identity and Okta login (employee)
2. Slack and Zoom access confirmed
3. Development environment booted and repo cloned
4. Test commit pushed to non-prod branch (if dev role)
5. Access to relevant dashboards and tickets granted
6. Hardware receipt confirmed and VPN tested (if remote)
7. Buddy assigned and first-week plan scheduled

Manager signs: [Manager name] [Date]

Non-standard Access Requests (escalation steps)
- If manager requests access beyond baseline, they must include: justification, duration (if temporary), and list of resources.
- Security will triage within 24 hours and either approve, request mitigating controls, or deny.
- Approved temporary elevated roles must include an expiration date and owner for removal.

Automation and Templates
- Okta activation: SCIM provisioning template located at /infra/okta/scim-new-hire.yaml (automation ID: okta-scim-newhire).
- infra-provision/new-hire CI job accepts a JSON payload with fields: candidate_name, team_slug, start_date, role_template. Example:

Title: BrambleBox Content Labs

BrambleBox Content Labs

Lead source: inbound marketing signup (content marketing template generator).
Point of contact: Eliza Moreno (Head of Product) - eliza@bramblebox.co — technical but cost-constrained.
Why Redwood: fast time-to-market for hosted API, transparent per-token billing, suggestion for caching/batching to reduce unit costs.
Summary of need:
- High-volume short-copy workloads: email subject lines, 10-variant landing headers, social posts (mostly <120 tokens).
- Expected monthly volume: rough estimate 30M-60M generation tokens during Q3 ramp.
- Latency target: 100-300ms p50 for single-shot prompts (interactive UI).
- Cost target: want to keep average per-output cost under $0.0016 across variants.
- Model preference: open-weights or Redwood-curated small/medium models; willing to test quantized variants.
Deployment intent: Hosted API self-serve initially; may evaluate Dedicated only if unit economics require reserved capacity.
Security/compliance: basic SOC2 and audit logging required for vendor selection; SSO not blocking for now.
Conversation highlights (bullets, shorthand):
- 2026-02-11: Intro demo w/ Jordan + Eliza (FF id ff-20260211-bramblebox-demo). Product fit confirmed for short-copy templating.
- 2026-02-14: Email follow-up sent with pricing ranges + quickstart (Gmail thread/Gm-20260214-01).
- 2026-02-18: Eliza asked for concrete batching examples and expected savings for 10-variant outputs. "If batching saves 30% on token cost, that's a game-changer"
- 2026-02-20: Internal cost-model note from SE: run sample using hosted_api with 2 model variants (small, medium quantized) to compare latency/cost.
- 2026-02-22: Sync call to agree on benchmark data points; client to provide representative prompt set (sent).
Technical notes and asks:
- Primarily short outputs; prefix caching might help for template scaffolds. KV cache less relevant (no long conversations).
- Want to understand streaming vs non-streaming trade-offs for UX and cost.
- Interested in automatic batching configuration: want recommendations for batch size and timeout given 50 RPS bursty traffic.
- Question on model fallback: can Redwood route to cheaper variant automatically when quota hit? client likes policy-based routing idea.
Next steps (explicit):
- Provide 14-day trial API keys + 50M free tokens for benchmark.
- SE (Maya) to run 3-scenario benchmark (small, quantized-medium, medium) and return per-token cost and latency percentiles.
- Deliver short doc with recommended batching/timeouts + example SDK snippet for concurrent batch sends.
- Sales to send short T&Cs and expected ARR bands for SMB tier.
Open issues / blockers (short):
- Token cost still primary blocker until benchmark; need clear projected monthly bill for 30-60M tokens.
- Want assurance on per-route rate limits and throttling behavior for multi-tenant customers.
- No SSO yet; not blocking but will be needed if larger pilots proceed.
Notes tone: choppy/actionable. client is pragmatic, focused on unit economics.
Potential: high-volume low-ticket ARR — likely start as self-serve, convert to paying SMB within 1-2 months if cost target met.
"If we can get predictable costs and decent latency, we'll push this into our editor and onboard users next quarter." — Eliza M.

Title: Capacity triage, forensic telemetry, and scaling rollback plan for Dedicated pools

Capacity triage, forensic telemetry, and scaling rollback plan for Dedicated pools

Summary: On 2026-03-13 we observed a repeatable capacity shortfall affecting a subset of Dedicated pools serving latency-sensitive routes. Customers saw throttled throughput and elevated tail latency; autoscaler failed to replenish headroom for ~18 minutes in the worst-impacted pools. This ticket consolidates the live triage notes, proposed short-term rollback/containment, forensic telemetry plan, and the longer-term resilience actions we will track in the postmortem.
2026-03-13T09:24Z - Alert: Dedicated pool headroom below 10% for pool: eu-west-2-dedicated-4. Alert surfaced from capacity-monitoring rule 'dedicated.headroom.low'.
2026-03-13T09:27Z - Autoscale controller reported repeated scale-up errors: 'quota_exceeded' and 'dealbreaker: kernel selection mismatch'.
2026-03-13T09:30Z - On-call rotation (SRE) started containment runbook; temporarily increased burst capacity for affected customers using reserve tokens.
2026-03-13T09:42Z - Manual rollback: rolled back runtime build runtime-1.21.7 -> runtime-1.21.4 on two affected zones; autoscaler recovered and headroom returned to >30% by 09:50Z.
2026-03-13T10:10Z - Stabilization: routing policy enabled temporary throttle for non-SLA routes; observability dashboards show token-level latency returned to baseline over next 20 minutes.
Enabled reserve headroom policy for top-10 impacted accounts (temporary config override).
Rolled back recent runtime image (runtime-1.21.7 -> runtime-1.21.4) in impacted zones to unblock autoscaler flow.
Applied emergency routing fallback to cheaper model variants for bursty routes to reduce token pressure.
1) Kernel selection path regression in runtime-1.21.7 causes per-GPU resource skew, triggering quota_exceeded errors when autoscaler attempts to instantiate new replicas.
2) A change to continuous-batching thresholds increased effective active sequences per GPU, reducing headroom at typical request concurrency patterns.
3) Metric drift in our headroom estimator (recent change to the moving-window) caused delayed detection and inappropriate scale decisions.
Collect per-GPU allocation traces and kernel selection logs from 2026-03-13T09:00Z - 2026-03-13T11:00Z (ENG: telemetry team tag).
Extract autoscaler event stream and reconcile with cloud provider API responses (quota/limit codes) for failed scale attempts.
Replay representative traffic against runtime-1.21.7 in a staging cluster with identical batch/concurrency settings to reproduce the quota_exceeded condition.
Generate a timeline correlating model variant routing changes, batching metric changes, and headroom estimator outputs to identify the first causal deviation.
headroom_percent (per-pool, per-zone)
autoscaler_success_rate and autoscaler_latency
per-GPU active_sequence_count and kernel_selection_path
per-route token throughput and 99th/99.9th latency
cloud provider quota error codes and rate of quota errors
PRI: Add verbose kernel-selection logs behind a trace flag in runtime (OWNER: Priya Kapoor, ETA: 3d).
SRE: Backfill detailed autoscaler event history and annotate failures with cloud API responses (OWNER: Miguel Alvarez, ETA: 2d).
Telemetry: Add a short-lived high-cardinality view for per-GPU allocation and batch size (OWNER: Linh Tran, ETA: 4d).
Engineering: Create a canary gating step in the rollout pipeline that runs the autoscaler smoke test during image promotion (OWNER: Marcus Chen, ETA: 5d).
Product: Notify impacted customers with a clear timeline and remediation steps; coordinate credits if SLA breached (OWNER: Elena Rossi, ETA: 1d).
Runtime: Add conservative fallback to skip kernel path X if kernel-selector returns an unsupported combo (OWNER: Runtime Team, ETA: 2w).
Console: Surface 'headroom risk' indicator on Dedicated pool dashboard and per-route cost/latency tradeoff selector (OWNER: Diego Park, ETA: 3w).
When autoscaler failures spike above threshold and headroom < 15% for >5m, perform targeted runtime rollback to last-known-good image for impacted zones (manual approval required).
Ensure rollout pipeline supports immediate artifact promotion rollback within 10 minutes and provides automated verification hooks for autoscale smoke-tests.
Document a quick CLI operation to re-enable reserve headroom policy for a customer group until a permanent fix lands.
Increasing reserve headroom reduces available capacity for new customers and can increase unit costs — will need to throttle non-SLA routes while reserve is active.
Adding verbose kernel-selection logs increases telemetry volume and storage costs; flagging behind trace prevents sustained cost growth but complicates reproductions later.
Faster rollbacks increase churn and risk of oscillation if root cause persists; we must implement autoscale smoke-tests to reduce false rollbacks.
Post incident summary to #incident-redwood with initial findings and mitigation within 24h (OWNER: Priya Kapoor).
Draft customer-facing timeline and next steps, share with account-sds for impacted large customers (OWNER: Elena Rossi).
Schedule a cross-functional postmortem meeting in 72h with SRE, Runtime, Telemetry, and Product.

Title: AZ affinity misallocation causing reserved pool under-provision and customer burst failures

AZ affinity misallocation causing reserved pool under-provision and customer burst failures

Summary: Multiple enterprise customers observed repeated burst failures and silent token drops during regional peak windows. Root cause traced to a recent autoscaler change that over-applied AZ affinity multipliers when computing usable headroom for reserved pools. One AZ per region was effectively starved of headroom despite global capacity being available, preventing burst routing and causing customer-facing throttles. Impact included sustained error rates for Dedicated tenants, degraded SLAs, and escalations from two large customers.

Scope: Affects Dedicated reserved pools under the new topology-aware allocation mode when tenant affinity + private-agent-nodes flags are set. Observed in eu-west-1 and us-east-1 clusters. Estimated 7% of Dedicated capacity windows saw degraded performance during the incident window.

Hypothesis: An arithmetic regression multiplied the AZ headroom penalty twice when computing per-tenant reservation weights. This produced artificially low per-AZ allocations and prevented the normal cross-AZ fallback logic from engaging because affinity checks erroneously marked pools as "ineligible" rather than "low headroom."
1) Provision a Dedicated tenant with AZ affinity enabled and private-agent-nodes=true
2) Simulate burst traffic pattern with 20-30x baseline RPS spike for 3 minutes
3) Observe reserved-pool allocator logs: per-AZ headroom reported negative for the affinity AZ while overall region headroom is positive
4) Submit requests and check that routing fails to fallback to compatible pools due to ineligibility flag
Autoscaler headroom metric (autoscaler.headroom.per_az) frequently reported -5%..-30% for one AZ while region headroom remained >= 40%
Spike in reserved-pool-declared-ineligible events correlated with customer 5xx rates
KV cache hot-shard persisted in starved AZ leading to coldstarts when fallback should have been used
Deployment times: regression introduced in runtime-2.4.0 -> runtime-2.4.1 path

A logic regression in topology-aware allocator: when both tenant AZ affinity and private-agent-nodes were true, an AZ penalty multiplier was applied twice due to merging two code paths (affinity_penalty * private_node_penalty) without normalizing for the shared dimension. This caused the allocator to mark pools as ineligible rather than low-headroom, preventing fallback and cross-AZ routing. Additionally, there were no unit/e2e tests covering the combined flag interaction, so the regression escaped CI.
Patch: Adjust allocation math to apply a single normalized AZ penalty and add guard checks that convert negative headroom into 'low_headroom' state instead of 'ineligible'

Title: Sporadic cold-start cascade from backfill + burst-replenish race causing reserved-pool depletion

Sporadic cold-start cascade from backfill + burst-replenish race causing reserved-pool depletion

Several customers experienced simultaneous 5xx errors and sustained latency spikes during an overnight maintenance window. Root cause appears to be an interaction between the backfill service (which replenishes tenant burst credits) and the autoscaler’s warmup preheat logic: many tenants were scheduled to replenish at the same time, triggering simultaneous warmup tasks that caused allocator saturation, rapid reserved-pool headroom consumption, and then emergency shedding. This ticket tracks the incident, immediate mitigations applied, the short-term patch, and longer-term resilience work.
- 503 errors and request timeouts for 18 minutes across multiple tenants in EU-west-1 and us-east-1
- Token-level latency up to 3x baseline during warmup cascade
- Reserved pool headroom dropped to 6% triggering burst gating and customer-facing denials
- Console alerts: burst_replenish_rate spike, allocator_queue_length spike, pool_headroom low
Affected ~12 enterprise tenants (billing tier: Dedicated) during high overnight throughput. Customer-reported incidents from two accounts (AcmeHealth, AtlasForms). Estimated revenue risk for window: medium-high. SLA alerts triggered for latency and error-rate. Engineering pager fired twice.
1) Create 200 small tenants with burst credits nearly depleted.
2) Schedule backfill service to top up credits at the same timestamp (simulate a cron alignment).
3) Observe allocator warmup tasks spawn concurrently; monitor reserved-pool headroom and allocator queue.
4) If allocator saturates, API starts returning 503s after headroom threshold crossed.
Note: we reproduced locally by simulating warmup handlers and a mocked allocator service under a 4 GPU reserved pool.
- Throttled backfill service to add jitter and a randomized stagger window (+30s-5m)
- Enabled emergency headroom holdback: reserve 20% of reserved pool capacity for safety during replenishment windows
- Routed critical VIP tenants to hosted fallback model in different AZ for 40 minutes
- Opened support threads with affected customers with status updates
Apply a patch to backfill controller to implement exponential backoff + coordinated jitter and a concurrency cap per AZ. Modify allocator admission to honor a per-tenant warmup token bucket so warmups are rate-limited. Patch PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/autoscaler/pull/1125
1) Redesign backfill scheduling: use distributed lease + stagger policy and add tenant-priority decay.
2) Extend autoscaler to include warmup orchestration with fairness (fairshare warmup queue), preheat pacing, and per-tenant burst throttles.
3) Add predictive headroom predictor that simulates bulk replenishment events.
4) Run canary in eu-west-1 for 72 hours before global rollout.
1) Merge short-term patches to release branch autoscaler-2.8.1 (hotfix).
2) Canary deploy to non-production then to EU-west-1 dedicated pools with feature flag backfill_jitter=true.
3) Monitor pool_headroom, allocator_queue_length, and customer 5xx; if stable 72h, enable globally.
4) Schedule long-term refactor in Q2 cycle with product sign-off.

Title: Headroom estimation cascade + customer escalation (reserved pools & burst limits)

Headroom estimation cascade + customer escalation (reserved pools & burst limits)

Summary: During a weekday traffic surge (US morning peak) multiple dedicated reserved pools underreported available headroom which triggered conservative scale-down and prevented timely burst replenishment. Customer tenants experienced elevated 429s and 2–20s tail latencies for burst traffic while fallback routing amplified load on cold pools. Support tickets called out 'burst capacity not available' for multiple tenants — pattern consistent with reserved-pool accounting rather than model-serving errors.
Immediate: Raised soft headroom floor from 5% to 15% for impacted AZs to prevent premature scale-down; enabled emergency bypass to allow burst credits to be consumed even if allocator headroom was negative. Race condition in cross-AZ leader snapshot merge where pending warmup reservations were dropped when a leader changed. Secondary factor: insufficient observability—no metric exposed for 'pending_warmup_slots' across leader boundaries, which delayed diagnosis.

Title: Postmortem: asymmetric failover cascade during regional autoscale and circuit breaker misconfiguration

Postmortem: asymmetric failover cascade during regional autoscale and circuit breaker misconfiguration

Summary: On 2026-02-14 18:12 UTC a traffic surge from a partner integration exposed an asymmetric configuration between regions that caused a cascade of failovers and unexpected load shedding. The control plane routing pushed traffic to the secondary region (eu-west-1) while circuit breaker thresholds and per-region concurrency limits there were misaligned with the primary (us-east-1), resulting in prolonged SLO misses and increased 99th-percentile tail latency for generation endpoints. This ticket captures the timeline, root causes, mitigations, and concrete action items.
What happened: A partner integration generated a characterized burst of long-sequence generation requests starting 2026-02-14 18:09 UTC. Primary region autoscaling lagged on a small subset of cells; smart routing attempted failover to eu-west-1. Because the CB and concurrency profiles in eu-west-1 were tuned lower and had asymmetric retry/backoff behavior, the region entered partial overload and started shedding load aggressively. That shedding fed back into the control plane routing heuristics which attempted repeated failovers, amplifying the surge. Impact: hosted inference generation SLO (p99 latency target 1500ms) was missed for 28 minutes; ~11% of requests experienced 500/503 or tail latency >5s. Immediate mitigations restored normal traffic after 26 minutes and full SLO recovery after 42 minutes.
Asymmetric circuit breaker defaults: eu-west-1 had a lower open threshold and longer cooldown compared to us-east-1 due to an old regional tuning change that was never propagated.
Per-region concurrency mismatch: deployment profiles and cell capacity metadata drift allowed eu-west-1 to accept more concurrent long-sequence allocations than the autoscaler anticipated, exhausting memory and increasing GC pauses.
Routing hysteresis bug: the smart routing policy retried failover rapidly without accounting for region recent failure counts, causing flip-flopping and amplification.
KV cache cold-start penalty: the secondary region did not have warmed KV caches for many active model prefixes causing amplified per-request compute and elevated tail latency.
Insufficient runbook coverage: the on-call runbook lacked a clear playbook for simultaneous autoscale lag + failover oscillation, leading to manual mitigation delays.
2026-02-14 18:09 UTC - Large burst of long-sequence generation requests detected (partner integration traffic spike).
2026-02-14 18:12 UTC - Primary cells in us-east-1 observed elevated p99; autoscaler reacted but new pods not fully provisioned yet. Control plane routed ~30% of traffic to eu-west-1 per failover policy.
2026-02-14 18:15 UTC - eu-west-1 CBs tripped due to lower thresholds; region began shedding and returning 503s for a subset of routes. On-call paged.
2026-02-14 18:22 UTC - Routing oscillation observed: repeated failover attempts between regions increased tail latency globally.
2026-02-14 18:35 UTC - Emergency mitigation: engineers applied temporary routing quiesce to stop cross-region failovers and increased eu-west-1 concurrency caps. Immediate error rate dropped.

Title: INC-2025-0303 Postmortem: Dedicated autoscaler lag + quota ceiling caused sustained throttling

INC-2025-0303 Postmortem: Dedicated autoscaler lag + quota ceiling caused sustained throttling

# Summary
On 2025-03-03, a set of Dedicated customers saw elevated 429 throttling and increased queueing latency for ~62 minutes. The dedicated autoscaler attempted to add GPU nodes but hit a cloud quota ceiling, while the fallback routing policy was configured to prefer in-region capacity.

**Incident ID:** INC-2025-0303
**Customer impact:** Dedicated tier (subset), primarily eu-west
**Owning engineering team:** Eng SRE

# What happened
A scheduled load test by a customer coincided with a new prompt pattern increasing average output length. The autoscaler hit scale limits and then failed to provision due to quota. The system kept retrying, causing prolonged throttling.

# Timeline (UTC)
- 2025-03-03 09:12: Alert: dedicated-throttle-rate > 2%
- 09:17: Eng SRE on-call engaged
- 09:24: Identified provisioning failures due to quota ceiling
- 09:29: Mitigation: temporarily enabled cross-region burst for dedicated pool
- 10:14: Quota increased; scale-out succeeds

# Root cause
**Primary:** Provisioning blocked by GPU quota ceiling; autoscaler did not fast-fail to fallback behavior.
**Contributing factors:**
- Quota monitoring was not tied to paging
- Dedicated fallback policy prioritized in-region too strongly during scale events

# Corrective actions
1. Add quota ceiling alerts with paging for dedicated pools (owner: Eng SRE)
2. Update dedicated fallback policy to allow burst after 5 minutes of provisioning failure (owner: Eng Platform)
3. Add playbook: customer load test notifications routed to capacity planning (owner: Customer Success)

Title: Parametric eval harness for detecting config-change blindspots

Parametric eval harness for detecting config-change blindspots

Background: Recent incidents surfaced quality regressions after config and model variant rollouts where existing smoke evals missed narrow but severe quality cliffs. Postmortems call out two recurring gaps: (1) our eval suites validate a single nominal config per route, and (2) we lack a lightweight, parameter-sweep runner that can probe low-probability config combinations (e.g., long-prefix KV + aggressive batching + q4f quantization).

Goal: Build a parametric evaluation harness and assertion library that can run fast, targeted sweeps across a configurable matrix of runtime/model parameters (kv_ttl, batch_size, qconfig, kernel_variant, max_seq, temperature) and surface regression deltas with artifactized repro cases and minimal-resource execution. This harness should be usable by postmortem owners, CI gates for config rollouts, and scheduled scavenger jobs that look for quality cliffs in production-like slices.

Scope (MVP):
- Parametric runner service that accepts a small YAML matrix and executes a suite of evals in parallel with early-fail signal aggregation.
- An assertion DSL (JSON/YAML) with common metrics (exact match, logprob delta, canonicalized BLEU/F1, hallucination flags) and a way to declare per-route tolerances.
- Auto-capture of minimal repro (input + model/config snapshot + seed) and upload to the eval artifacts bucket with a short permalink.
- Dashboardable output: per-cell metric diffs, heatmap export, and suggested triage label.
- Lightweight CI integration: a pre-deploy job that runs a small sweep (3x3 matrix) for config changes and fails the rollout when assertions trip with high confidence.

Out of scope (for this ticket): full integration with the canonical eval oracle library, long-running golden-corpus backfills, and UI polish in Console. Those will be follow-ups.

Acceptance criteria:
- Harness can run a 12-cell matrix (3 params x 4 values) on staging within 45 minutes using burst pool.
- For a seeded synthetic regression (created as part of this ticket) the harness surfaces a metric regression >= 5% on the targeted slice and produces a reproducible artifact link.
- CI job template exists and is documented; at least one config PR uses the template and demonstrates a blocked rollout when assertions fail.
- Library of 6 assertion templates checked into repo (exact-match, top-k token shift, mean logprob delta, response-length-regression, hallucination-count, structured-field-mismatch).

Approach / Implementation plan:
1) Design: (Samir + Aisha) finalize the param space schema and assertion DSL. Draft in Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/EVAL/Parametric+Eval+DSL (link is working draft).
2) Prototype runner: lightweight Python service that schedules eval jobs to the existing eval-worker pool, supports concurrency limits, and uploads artifacts to gs://redwood-eval-artifacts/parametric/ENG-49127.
3) Assertion library: implement metric hooks using existing eval metrics code but with wrapper that tolerates numeric jitter and reports CI-friendly pass/fail.
4) Minimal repro capture: enforce deterministic seeding, collect model config + runtime flags, store a 1-2MB JSON repro artifact with link in the harness results.
5) CI integration: add GitHub Action workflow template .github/workflows/parametric-sanity.yml that invokes a 3x3 sweep against a staging model.
6) Dashboard: emit a compact JSON summary that Console’s infra can ingest; provide temporary Kibana dashboard link for triage.

Tradeoffs / discussion points:
- Running larger matrices increases coverage but also cost; default will favor targeted slices defined by incident owners.
- We will intentionally keep the assertion DSL small to start (no programmatic transforms) to encourage FRs instead of complexity.
- For deterministic repro we may need temporary snapshotting of model weights or model hash; for now we'll capture model artifact id and runtime flags.

Risks and mitigations:
- False positives from noisy metrics: mitigate with confidence intervals and repeated sampling.
- CI latency: default CI template uses small sample sizes; full sweeps reserved for scheduled runs.
- Access control for artifact links: store artifacts in private bucket with short-lived signed URLs for triage links.

Deliverables:
- repo: infra/evals/parametric-harness (prototype + CI template)
- Confluence design doc + examples: link above
- Demo PR that blocks a sample config rollout in staging and attaches a repro artifact
- One-pager for on-call/postmortem runbook on using the harness for incident follow-ups

Notes: This ticket aims to reduce the time-to-repro and increase coverage for edge config combos without turning on combinatorial sweeps in production by default. The harness should be easy to extend by PM/Eng incident owners to codify 'slices we care about'.

Title: KVCache: Sanitizer Shelving & Evictor Probe

KVCache: Sanitizer Shelving & Evictor Probe

Summary: During a production capacity event on 2025-01-15 we observed a sustained memory growth in the KV/prefix cache leading to degraded throughput and cascading evictions. Initial mitigation restored service but the post-incident analysis revealed a class of entries that could be 'poisoned' by a combination of concurrent prefetch and eviction race, causing live references to be retained incorrectly and preventing slab reclaim. This ticket captures the follow-ups: a quarantine ("sanitizer shelving") mechanism for suspect cache entries, a synthetic 'evictor probe' harness to reproduce and stress eviction under controlled conditions, telemetry additions to detect poisoning early, and a phased rollout plan for the fixes.
2025-01-15 02:18 UTC – First alerts: node p-05 reported memory growth + elevated eviction rate; autoscale initiated
2025-01-15 02:32 UTC – Emergency mitigation: reduced prefetch tunables and introduced short-term eviction-throttle; memory stabilized
2025-01-15 05:00 UTC – Incident declared resolved; team started forensics on heap profiles and cache histograms
2025-01-16 to 2025-01-21 – Reproduction attempts in staging exposed a deterministic window: concurrent prefetch + async compact + eviction = live pointer retention for ~1-2 minutes
2025-01-22 – Root cause hypothesis validated in local harness: a race allowed a retired slab pointer to be re-referenced before tombstone cleanup
2025-01-24 – Initial PR with conservative sanitizer shelving landed behind feature flag (non-default) for canary testing
A race between prefetch insertion, async compaction, and eviction created a window where a cache entry could be re-inserted while its previous slab metadata was being compacted. The writepath did not atomically transition the entry to a quarantined state, so stale pointers could survive and be referenced by in-flight requests. Over time, these phantom references prevented memory reclamation and amplified eviction churn.
Short-term: reduce prefetch concurrency and enable eviction-throttle during high mem-pressure (rolled out 2025-01-15)
Medium-term: ship sanitizer shelving to quarantine suspect entries when a conflicting transition is detected (this ticket)
Long-term: redesign compact/writepath to use epoch-based reclamation and remove asymmetric state transitions
ENG-A1: Finish sanitizer shelving implementation behind feature-flag; ensure quarantined entries are scanned and either healed or fast-evicted. Owner: Tomás Rivera. Due: 2025-02-07.
ENG-A2: Build the evictor-probe harness (deterministic eviction/reinsertion simulator) and add to nightly e2e; include presets that match production traffic shape. Owner: Priya Anand. Due: 2025-02-10.
ENG-A3: Add targeted telemetry: tombstone counts, quarantine hits, re-insert-after-compact rate, and histogram of 'time-to-reclaim' per-concurrent-writer. Owner: E2 Observability team (James Liu). Due: 2025-02-01.
ENG-A4: Create an automated test that fuzzes prefetch+compact+evict under different slab sizes; surface regression in CI gating. Owner: QA Automation (Marisol Vega). Due: 2025-02-12.
ENG-A5: Run a staged canary in Dedicated us-west-2 with feature-flag enabled at 5% traffic, monitor quarantine/telemetry signals for 72h, then expand. Owner: SRE (Liam O'Connor). Due: 2025-02-20.
ENG-A6: Postmortem doc update and KB article for on-call runbooks describing how to detect and temporarily mitigate poisoning scenarios. Owner: Incident Lead (Aisha Kapoor). Due: 2025-02-05.
Decision: implement sanitizer shelving as a minimally invasive quarantine that delays reclamation for a short TTL and forces a secondary validation pass; chosen because it reduces blast radius and is reversible.
Trade-off: shelving increases short-term memory by design but prevents long-lived phantom references; TTL default tuned to 90s to match observed window.
Rollback plan: feature-flag + telemetry gates; if quarantine_hit_rate > 0.5% of cache ops with reclaim_time growth > 2x in canary we will revert flag and iterate.
Coordination: schedule a cross-team sync (runtime, obs, QA, SRE) on 2025-02-03 to finalize canary checklist and SLA targets for rollout.
Follow-up research: evaluate epoch-based reclamation (RCU-like) in Q2 as a permanent fix; prototype to be tracked under project kvcache-epoch-reclaim.

Title: Urgent: Conversation stream slowdown — customer impact & next steps

Urgent: Conversation stream slowdown — customer impact & next steps

Subject: Realtime chat responses slowing across user sessions

Hi Stephanie,

We're seeing a significant slowdown on the streaming/chat endpoint for interactive sessions across multiple users since ~07:40 PDT. Messages are still delivered, but tokens arrive in big bursts (20–30s gaps) making the UI stutter badly. Impact: 60% of active sessions show degraded UX, and one of our voice agents dropped mid-conversation.

- first_token_delay: 2200ms
- token_emission_pattern: [fast, fast, gap 23s, fast]

Ishaan Rao

NovusTech

Hi Ishaan — thanks for flagging this and for the trace. We see the pattern in our telemetry (intermittent token-emission gaps on a subset of edge shards). We're treating this as high priority.

Short-term mitigations you can test now (low friction, non-code):
- Fall back to the non-streaming /generate endpoint for mission-critical flows (reduces UX fidelity, restores predictable latency).
- Reduce max_tokens_per_call by 30% for long-context sessions to reduce KV-cache growth.
- If you can, set a client-side streaming timeout of 10s and auto-retry once; this avoids long blackouts and keeps sessions responsive.

We'll apply a temporary server-side pacing fix (see temporary-config.patch attached) to limit KV cache growth on affected shards — this should reduce burst gaps within ~60–90 minutes. Monica, Ben: can you own the patch rollout + customer verification?

Ishaan — I'll keep you updated at 9:30 and then hourly until resolved.

Best,
Stephanie Nguyen
Director, Customer Success | Redwood Inference

> Ishaan — thanks for flagging this and for the trace. We see the pattern in our telemetry...

Laura — ops runbook: we suspect KV-cache growth from large-context interactive sessions is causing occasional GC/eviction pressure on westus-edge-3 (affects ~12% of live streaming capacity). Plan:

Hi all — update from ops after the rollout and verification: 
- Root cause: a memory-pressure cascade on westus-edge-3 triggered by long-context streams combined with a recent model change that increased per-token KV size. When KV exceeded a threshold some shards entered a backpressure state that deferred token emission until a background eviction cycle, producing 15–30s gaps.

- Customer impact window: 2025-04-11T07:39:58Z to 2025-04-11T10:05:00Z (approx).

- Infra/Runtime (Laura): push permanent guarding for KV growth and add a telemetry alarm (done: SR-11032).
- Product (Monica/Stephanie): share recommended client-side config (max_tokens, streaming-timeout) by 2025-04-13.
- Account (Ben): propose a goodwill credit; coordinate with customer finance.

Ishaan — we sincerely apologize for the disruption. We'll set up a 30-min follow-up tomorrow to walk through the postmortem and the recommended config changes; please let us know a window that works.

Thanks for your patience.
Laura Bennett
Site Reliability Manager, Redwood Inference

Title: Chat streaming truncated after transient pipeline reset for dedicated customer

Chat streaming truncated after transient pipeline reset for dedicated customer

Issue summary: Customer reports that SSE/WebSocket streaming responses abruptly truncate mid-sentence following short transient errors in the serving pipeline (worker restart / routing flip). Impact: customer chat sessions for multiple users end with partial output (last token(s) missing), leading to degraded UX and automated retry loops on their side. Environment: LexiVoice dedicated cluster in us-west-2, running dedicated pool rp-lexivoice-usw2 on redwood-rlhf-13b pinned version v2026-02-28. Observed intermittently starting 2026-03-10 18:12 UTC and reproducible for customer under bursty input patterns (20-30 concurrent long-form chats).
1) Use LexiVoice account credentials to send a streaming chat request to /v1/chat with stream=true and model=redwood-rlhf-13b (pinned).
2) Send a long prompt that triggers ~800-1200 token response (typical LexiVoice assistant reply),
3) Simulate burst concurrency: 20 simultaneous streaming requests from distinct client sockets,
4) While streams are in-flight, trigger a light worker restart or cause a routing update (in test: toggle an autoscaler event or redeploy a serving worker).
5) Observe that a subset (~5-12%) of client streams terminate with a final socket close before end-of-stream token; no explicit 5xx returned to client.
Streaming socket closes without final chunk and without explicit error payload. Client receives partial text and then a TCP FIN/WS close. On platform side, logs show a short-lived pipeline reset (worker SIGTERM and graceful restart) correlated with router reassignments. No 5xx spike on public API layer, but internal worker logs show 'inflight-request-evicted' and 'kv-cache-miss -> eviction' in proximity.
Streaming responses should continue to completion or, if interrupted, return a clear error frame (HTTP 5xx or SSE event) and ensure client can resume or receive a final summary chunk. Model fallback or worker restart should trigger graceful draining of in-flight streams rather than silent truncation.

2026-03-10T18:12:23Z worker[w-771]: SIGTERM received, beginning graceful shutdown, inflight=7
2026-03-10T18:12:24Z worker[w-771]: kv-cache eviction triggered for model redwood-rlhf-13b shard=2
2026-03-10T18:12:24Z worker[w-772]: accepted request id=aa3f..., start-forwarding-kv-cache-mismatch
2026-03-10T18:12:24Z worker[w-771]: inflight-request-evicted id=aa3f..., closed-connection-without-error
2026-03-10T18:12:24Z api-gateway[gw-9]: downstream connection closed by peer for client c-984 (status unknown)
Initial triage: patterns point to graceful shutdown window not fully draining SSE/WS streams when a worker is restarted under load; router reassigns requests mid-generation rather than waiting for completion.
Hypothesis A: draining timeout on worker is too short under long-response workloads leading to abrupt close before remote worker can finish sending final chunks.
Hypothesis B: KV cache miss when reassigning a long-running request causes partial output to be lost when the new worker cannot reconstruct the current generation state quickly, leading to immediate connection termination.
Temporary reproduction in staging: forced SIGTERM with 5s drain results in ~40% of streams truncating; increasing drain to 30s eliminated truncation in staging tests but increased tail latency and backpressure on autoscaler.
Observation: api-gateway does not always surface a 502/503 to client when downstream closes mid-stream; need to verify gateway stream-forwarding behavior on abrupt downstream close.

2) Adjust worker graceful-drain default to 20s for dedicated pools with long-response heuristics while we evaluate tail effects.
3) Modify api-gateway to translate downstream abrupt closes to explicit 5xx frames for streaming clients to make failure visible to customers.

Title: Elevated first-token latency and intermittent 504s on short chat prompts after runtime/compile swap

Elevated first-token latency and intermittent 504s on short chat prompts after runtime/compile swap

Customer QuillDocs reports that after last night's runtime/compile backend swap (runtime v2.11 + new kernel selector), short chat prompts that previously returned token(s) within ~80-120ms are now seeing time-to-first-token (TTFB) spikes to 600-1500ms and occasional request 504s. Problem started immediately after the rollout window (2026-03-10 23:30 UTC). Impact: partial degradation for enterprise traffic on dedicated pools in us-west-2; some requests time out. Business impact: affects document assistant features (autosuggest) where perceived latency directly impacts UX. Support ticket opened by customer at 2026-03-11 02:04 UTC.
1) Use customer API key scoped to QuillDocs dedicated pool in us-west-2
2) Send a series of short chat prompts (e.g., 'Summarize this: <10 words>') with streaming enabled and low max_tokens (<=16), 100 concurrent small requests
3) Observe initial bytes delivered and any 504s or long TTFB on a sample of requests
4) Compare same workload against staging pool (runtime v2.10) to confirm regression

Hypothesis 1: Kernel selector in runtime v2.11 misclassifies short prompts and selects a quantized kernel path that has a heavy first-call initialization cost (~700-1000ms) even when KV cache is empty.
Hypothesis 2: Router connection scheduling now prefers a 'connect-to-warm' policy that queues requests while kernel init occurs, raising conn_wait_ms and surface 504s when overall queueing exceeds upstream timeout.
Action taken: enabled detailed kernel-selection logging on 3 nodes (usw2-serving-42/43/44) and gathered p50/p95/p99 TTFB per kernel variant for 2 hours starting 2026-03-11T03:00Z.
Finding: quant-opt-3 kernel shows median first-token 880ms and subsequent tokens ~60ms. legacy-opt kernel shows median first-token 120ms. Quant kernel used in ~37% of observed short prompts post-rollout; pre-rollout quant usage was <5% for same customer workload.
Finding: conn_wait_ms for requests that hit the quant-opt-3 kernel correlated strongly (rho=0.82) with elevated TTFB and 504s. Router CPU remained below threshold; queueing originates from per-node kernel init serializing first calls.
Temporary mitigation test: forcing kernel selection to legacy-opt for sample traffic returned TTFB to baseline (p95 160ms) with 0 observed 504s in 15-minute test window.
Next steps: runtime eng to add a short-circuit to prefer 'warm' kernel variants for predicted short prompts, or perform lazy pre-warm of quant kernels during rollout. Also adjust router upstream timeout and backoff for dedicated pools as stop-gap.

Mitigation in progress. Engineering created PR to change selector fallback heuristics and add an async kernel pre-warm hook (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/8761). Temporary customer workaround provided: pin to legacy kernel profile via model config or route small prompt traffic through a canary pool running v2.10. SRE adjusted router conn upstream timeout from 1.5s to 2.5s for QuillDocs dedicated pool to reduce observed 504s while fix lands. Follow-up: post-fix we will run 24h performance validation and coordinate a maintenance window for safe rollout.

Title: Multiplexed SSE client experiences prolonged idle spike then silent disconnect during long multi-turn chat

Multiplexed SSE client experiences prolonged idle spike then silent disconnect during long multi-turn chat

Issue summary:
Customer reports that long multi-turn chat sessions over SSE multiplexed connections intermittently go silent for ~25-40s mid-generation and then the client receives a 504 or connection reset. This affects sessions that use connection multiplexing (multiple user conversations over a single persistent connection) and often occurs after an earlier token-at-a-time progress period.

Impact:
- Affected customer: Veridian Analytics (dedicated tier) sees production users' chat sessions aborting mid-response 3-12 times per hour for heavy sessions.
- User visible: long pauses mid-generation followed by connection error or truncated final token.
- Business impact: product feature degradation for ~200 active users during peak window; P1.

Timeline (UTC):
- 2026-03-10 09:12: first support report received from Veridian via in-app ticket
- 2026-03-10 09:20: Support reproduced on a staging multiplexed client and opened incident
- 2026-03-10 10:00: SRE collected tcpdump + proxy metrics; observed windowing/backpressure behavior on streaming-proxy
- 2026-03-10 11:30: temporary mitigation deployed (shorter keepalive, disabled conn reuse for warm workers)

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):

Title: Intermittent p99 latency / 504s for repeat-chat prompts due to per-shard KV TTL desync and cache refill storms

Intermittent p99 latency / 504s for repeat-chat prompts due to per-shard KV TTL desync and cache refill storms

Issue summary:

Customers observed intermittent high p99 token latency and occasional 504 / streaming timeouts when sending repeated chat prompts that reuse a short prefix. The problem started at ~2026-03-10T09:20Z for LexiChat (dedicated pool in us-east) and correlated with spikes in backend KV fetch volume and backend RPC retry errors.

Impact:
- LexiChat: multiple users reported stalled streaming responses and 504s during repeat prompts; visible in their app as long delays between the first and subsequent tokens (p99 > 5s).
- Other dedicated customers in us-east experienced elevated p99s but fewer 504s.

Environment:
- prod/us-east dedicated serving pool (shared backend kv-store)
- affected model: redwood-chat-13b for LexiChat routes

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Create a chat session and send an initial prompt to warm a prefix (e.g., "Summarize the following chat ...").
2) Send 12–20 short follow-up prompts that reuse the same prefix/context within ~2 minutes.
3) Observe streaming token arrival: first prompt completes quickly; subsequent prompts sometimes stall for multiple seconds or return 504 after timeout.

Observed logs / telemetry:
- Serving runtime traces show a burst of KV prefix read RPCs per request when stall occurs (miss rate for prefix cache jumps from ~2% baseline to ~45% during incidents).
- kv-store TCP errors (ECONNRESET) and elevated RPC retry counters in the same window.
- Streaming sessions show prolonged backpressure inside the serving worker while waiting on KV fetch completion; worker-level queue length climbs and triggers request-level timeouts.
- No immediate correlation to model GPU exhaustion or scheduler throttling.

Investigation notes:
- Initial hypothesis: prefix cache eviction (thrashing) causing cold KV reads.
- Deeper trace: per-shard TTL values for prefix entries were inconsistent after a config push on 2026-03-09 that updated TTL algorithm thresholds. Some shards had shorter effective TTLs due to an off-by-one unit conversion between config bundles and runtime readers.
- Resulting behavior: when a shard's TTL expired slightly earlier, many simultaneous requests for the same hot prefix caused a cache refill stampede. The refill path performs a small but blocking CP-heavy KV aggregation call that can take ~30–300ms; when many such calls occur concurrently it exacerbates latencies and increases the probability of RPC retries to the kv-store, leading to backpressure and timeouts in the streaming pipeline.
- The cache-warmer background job that normally smooths refills had been disabled in the affected pool (flagged as part of an earlier experiment) which magnified the effect.
- Repro on staging: reproduced by artificially desyncing TTL between two replica groups and disabling warmers; observed same p99 spike and streaming stalls.

Temporary mitigations applied:
- Re-enabled cache-warmer flag on LexiChat's dedicated pool (rollout completed 2026-03-10T12:00Z).
- Increased per-prefix soft TTL floor on the affected shards to prevent micro-evictions (applied as emergency config 2026-03-10T12:30Z).
- Added a per-prefix in-flight request coalescing gate in front of the KV refill path to ensure only one refill RPC per prefix per short window (hotfix PR referenced below).

Customer-facing workaround provided:
- Advised LexiChat to add a lightweight client-side micro-batching of repeat prompts (delay 50–100ms) to avoid synchronously hammering the same prefix while we roll fixes.

Longer-term fixes and follow-ups:
- Root cause fix merged to ensure consistent TTL encoding across config bundles and runtime readers (PR github.com/redwood/re-runtime/pull/487).
- Permanent gating + smarter jitter for cache-warmers to avoid coordinated refills (PR github.com/redwood/re-runtime/pull/492).
- Improve observability: add a serving-runtime metric for per-prefix refill concurrency and a sentinel alert for refill storms.
- Runbook update: add steps to quickly re-enable warmers and apply TTL-floor if refill storm detected.

Resolution notes (in-flight):
- Immediate mitigations reduced incidents for LexiChat; we observed the prefix cache miss rate fall back to baseline within ~45 minutes of the emergency changes.
- SRE and runtime teams are scheduling the TTL encoding fix and the coalescing logic for early-week production deploy (target: 2026-03-14).

Observed pattern: failures co-occur with high kv_cache_size and increased eviction rates; finalizer component shows GC/serialization pauses correlated with stalled streaming.
Repro locally: synthetic workload with 35 messages and max_tokens=12k reproduces ~60-90s stall on redwood-v2-large when using default kernel swap path.
Profiling: blocking syscall in kv-serialization routine while writing >2.5MB KV frames to temp storage; scheduler backlog increases and timeouts follow.
Grafana panels: contended finalizer threads (thread_cpu>85%), scheduler queue depth spike, p99 latency for token emission increases sharply.
Temporary mitigation verified: trimming history to reduce KV size avoids the stall; switching to model variant with smaller key/value footprint also avoids issue.
Related to recent runtime change: PR #3412 introduced a lazy-serialization optimization but has a path that falls back to blocking serialization for large KV blobs — likely trigger for these workloads.
Customer-specific: NovaHealth uses long structured system prompts + document snippets which inflate tokenized history size beyond typical chat loads.
Blocking KV serialization path that performs synchronous writes for large KV blobs (triggered by very deep conversation history and high max_tokens), causing finalizer threads to stall and scheduler backlog to grow, resulting in request timeouts and streaming disconnects.
Implemented a hotfix that avoids blocking serialization on the streaming emission path: large KV blobs are now asynchronously checkpointed and finalizer is prioritized for active streaming requests. Hotfix rolled to affected us-west-2 Dedicated pool at 2026-03-12 03:20 UTC. Monitoring shows error rate dropped to baseline.
1) Trim conversation history (remove older assistant turns) or summarize earlier context before sending.
2) Reduce max_tokens to <= 4096 for large-history sessions.
3) Temporarily pin to a model variant with smaller KV footprint.
4) Set prefer_fast_path=true to favor low-latency execution if available.
Postmortem write-up and root-cause doc scheduled for 2026-03-15 (owner: Marco).
Backport async-serialization fix to stable branch and release to Dedicated clusters next week (owner: runtime team).
Add telemetry alert for kv_cache_size > 3GB + finalizer_queue_depth > 50 to catch regressions early.
Customer follow-up: schedule a sync with NovaHealth to review long-term guidance for handling deep-history workflows and offer migration assistance.

Title: introduce conditional-privilege seeding controller with coordinated-rollback workflow

introduce conditional-privilege seeding controller with coordinated-rollback workflow

Motivation: Private installs must seed tenant RBAC and secrets without leaving elevated privileges if the install fails. This PR adds a controller that applies transient privileges only when preflight checks and plan fingerprints match, and a coordinated rollback path to revoke those privileges and clean up partial resources on failure. Scope includes: a new controller that manages seed lifecycle for tenant CRs, Helm changes to render conditional rolebindings and a pre-seed hook, a Terraform module that emits a deterministic plan fingerprint consumed by the controller, preflight KMS/HSM and network checks, and an orchestrated rollback handler that is idempotent and annotated on the Tenant CR for operator follow-up. Design highlights: principle-of-least-privilege transient ServiceAccounts with TTL annotations and ownerRefs for GC; plan fingerprint validation to prevent drift-based secret injection; exponential backoff and requeue on GC races; observability via events, metrics (tenant_seed_success_total, tenant_seed_rollback_total) and structured logs; feature gated behind installer flag enable_conditional_seed to preserve backward compatibility. Testing: unit tests for controller transitions and sanitizer behavior; integration e2e in CI using KinD + mocked KMS to validate acceptance and failure paths; e2e asserts rollback revokes rolebindings within expected window and annotates the Tenant CR with failure_step and failure_reason. Migration and operator guidance: operators should enable feature in maintenance windows, run terraform plan with the tenant bootstrap module to collect tenant_plan_fingerprint and store it as a TenancyPlan custom resource; docs/privileged-seeding.md includes runbooks and recovery steps. Security notes: logs sanitized to avoid exposing full KMS ARNs, grant windows default to 5 minutes TTL, and a follow-up is tracked to add HSM-backed signing for fingerprints (SUP-1984).
Diego Martinez (reviewer): Can we avoid listing raw KMS keys in logs? Please sanitize any key identifiers in logs and ensure we only emit key IDs, not full ARNs.
Ava Lin (author): Good catch — sanitized logs and added a unit test asserting the sanitizer behavior (commit d4e5b6f).
Priya Shah (reviewer): The terraform module outputs need clear names; otherwise automation will misbind. Suggest renaming output 'plan_fingerprint' to 'tenant_plan_fingerprint'.
Ava Lin (author): Renamed outputs and adjusted controller to read tenant_plan_fingerprint (commit c3f4a0d).
Liam O'Connor (reviewer): E2E was flaky on first runs due to race in garbage collection; add a small backoff and requeue in controller delete path.
Ava Lin (author): Added exponential backoff and requeue logic; CI e2e stabilized after change (commit a1c9b4c).
Security team (comment): design approved with follow-up to support HSM-backed signing for plan fingerprints (tracked SUP-1984).
Diego Martinez (approval): LGTM after CI green — merging once two approvals and smoke pass.
Add conditional-privilege tenant seeding controller with coordinated atomic rollback. Feature gated behind enable_conditional_seed. Includes terraform module fingerprinting, preflight KMS checks, and improved RBAC hygiene for private installs.
