Title: Template Contrapositives Workbench

Template Contrapositives Workbench

Goal:
Experiment with "contrapositive" training examples and template variants to surface brittle instruction-following behavior and produce guarded templates that reduce silent failures. The idea: instead of only providing positive few-shots (how to do X), explicitly include inverted or wrong examples (how NOT to do X) and add scaffolding prompts that steer the model away from high-risk misinterpretations.

Background / motivation:
- Observed classes of failure in downstream apps where a short instruction is ambiguous and the model confidently returns undesired content (hallucinated facts, policy violations, misformatting).
- Regular few-shot sets improve style/format but do not consistently reduce semantic misinterpretation.
- Hypothesis: providing 1–2 contrapositive exemplars (deliberate bad outputs + short rationale why they are bad) will increase model calibration around the instruction boundaries and reduce brittle generalization.

Quick glossary (informal):
- Contrapositive exemplar: an example pair (instruction -> intentionally bad/incorrect output) annotated with a one-line critique and a corrected output.
- Template smoothing: small natural language scaffolds inserted pre/post-instruction to reduce abrupt generalization leaps.
- Failure probe: a short test input designed to reveal overconfident incorrect behavior.

Design constraints / rules for examples:
- Keep contrapositive exemplars obviously wrong but plausible-sounding (so the model can't treat them as noise).
- Keep critique brief: 6–12 tokens, explicit ("Incorrect because...").
- Follow with a corrected exemplar immediately after to anchor the desired behavior.
- Limit few-shot context to 4 examples total to preserve tokens; try 2 normal + 1 contrapositive + 1 correction ordering.

Micro-experiment matrix (to run on hosted API):
1) Baseline: 0-shot instruction only
2) Std few-shot: 2 positive exemplars
3) Contrapositive: 2 positive + 1 contrapositive + 1 correction (ordering varied)
4) Smoothing: contrapositive set + short scaffold preface ("Do not repeat the mistake in the examples below.")
5) Negative-control: 2 positive + 1 contrapositive but no correction (to test harm vs. benefit)

Sample few-shot set (working draft) — use for classification / short answer tasks:
---
Instruction: "Summarize the email below in 2 sentences for a senior manager."
Example A (good):
Email: "Q2 numbers beat forecast; need headcount next quarter; see attached table."
Summary: "Q2 exceeded forecast. Request for additional headcount next quarter; details in attached table."

Example B (good):
Email: "Customer reports recurrent API timeout when payload > 10k; repro steps attached."
Summary: "Customer sees timeouts on large payloads; repro steps attached for investigation."

Example C (contrapositive):
Email: "We had a minor display issue on Tuesday; fixed by front-end patch."
Summary: "The product is totally broken and unusable."
Why it's bad: "Overstates severity; misrepresents fix state."
Corrected (immediately after):
Summary: "Display issue observed Tuesday; front-end patch deployed to resolve the problem."
---
Notes: ordering matters — correction should immediately follow contrapositive so the model learns the contrast.

Failure probes (starter list):
- Under-specified numeric boundaries ("Filter users with high churn") where model invents threshold.
- Policy edge: ask for content transformation that skirts moderation (paraphrase a borderline prompt).
- Role confusion: short role labels that could be misinterpreted ("As a legal advisor, say X").

Observed heuristics so far (scratch observations):
- When contrapositive example uses strong negation words ("totally broken"), the model tends to adopt the polarity if correction is absent.
- Short critiques ("Incorrect: overclaims") are more effective than long rationales — keep them terse.
- Putting contrapositive at start vs middle: start makes the model overly cautious; middle achieves better calibration in preliminary runs.

Edge-case safety checks:
- Ensure contrapositive examples do not themselves include disallowed content (e.g., violent or hateful phrasing) — craft sanitised faux-errors.
- Check for adversarial amplification: contrapositive should never be the longest example.

Logging / evaluation plan:
- Run 200 probes per experimental condition across 6 probe types.
- Metrics: semantic accuracy (human-labeled), overclaim rate (model asserts facts not in input), style/length compliance, calibration (model confidence if available), token cost delta.
- Tag runs in Datadog / metrics backend with experiment key: cf:contrap-workbench-2025-07

Implementation notes (quick ops checklist):
- Use hosted-api small-medium model first (cheaper) before scaling to higher-capacity variants.
- Warm-up cache by running 20 benign prompts to stabilize latency.
- Save few-shot templates as templating JSON entries in repo: templating/fewshots/contrap_v1.json (PR reference above).

Open questions / TODOs (short list):
- How many contrapositive examples are optimal before diminishing returns? (1 vs 2)
- Does the approach transfer to multi-turn dialog (yes/no?) — need to test with conversation context preserved.
- Should critiques be free text or a constrained label set ("overclaim", "format error", "tone mismatch") for better model understanding?
- Test on long-form generation tasks (summaries > 200 tokens) — do contrapositives still help?

Next actions (this week):
- Ethan: wire up batch experiment harness and add probes from the 'policy-edge' folder (INFR-4213).
- Maya: craft 10 sanitized contrapositive exemplars for each probe type and add to repo.
- Me (Sofia): run initial 800-query sweep and collect manual labels for 120 samples.

Random notes to self:
- Try variant where critique is encoded as a short tag after the example — "[bad:overclaim]" — might be easier for models to latch onto.
- Consider combining with temperature scheduling: contrapositive+low-temp might reduce hallucination more than either alone.
- If we see regression on style, fall back to A/B rollback logic in console (canary).

Appendix: short list of sample contrapositive templates to copy/paste when building few-shot sets:
- "Incorrect: exaggerates findings; should not change numeric claims."
- "Incorrect: changes the requested format (must be 3 bullets)."
- "Incorrect: introduces unsupported assumptions about the customer."
- "Incorrect: translates but alters sentiment (should be neutral)."

End of draft. Notes deliberately terse; this is a working notebook. Will iterate after first run and record concrete numbers.

Title: Prompt resilience sandbox — personal journal

Prompt resilience sandbox — personal journal

Purpose
---
Working personal notes for iterating on a small prompt-library focused on robustness/resilience across: few-shot ordering, negative exemplars, instruction bleed, and numeric constraint handling. Want compact templates I can drop into quick E2E eval harness. Not a polished doc — notes, failures, small reproducible examples, TODOs.

High-level goals
- Build a tiny set (~20) of reusable few-shot blocks (templates + 2–5 exemplars each) that are resilient to: short context, repeated calls, and adversarial user edits.
- Capture common brittle patterns and produce short mitigation recipes (1–3 line prompt fixes).
- Track quick experiments and quick wins to fold into the shared prompt-library.

Quick experiment log (most recent first)
1) Shot order sensitivity — summary
   - Task: convert product bullet to plain-English micro-copy (concise, active voice).
   - 4-shot set: (ex1 helpful -> ex2 neutral -> ex3 negative -> ex4 helpful). Model (gpt-style dev VM): heavy reliance on last exemplar: when last exemplar is negative, model produced neutral tone even when instruction asked for "concise, active".
   - Mitigation: add explicit header before exemplars: "EXEMPLARS (do not override instruction):" + add trailing directive after exemplars: "Now apply the instruction above exactly." Small fix reduced regressions from 42% -> 8% in quick run.

2) Numeric constraints failure case
   - Task: produce 3-5 word summary of a sentence, strict token limit.
   - Observed: model often returns 6–7 words (exceeding limit) when exemplars include variable-length outputs.
   - Hypothesis: model learns content pattern but not enforced cardinality.
   - Workarounds tried: (a) explicit template with "Return EXACTLY N words:" (b) post-filtering (reject responses that violate) (c) zero-shot with formatting tokens (<n>) — (a) + post-filtering best.

3) Negative exemplar usage (counterexamples)
   - Tried: include 1 negative exemplar to show what NOT to do.
   - Outcome: helpful for some models to reduce style drift, but increases risk of instruction bleed: model sometimes paraphrases the negative example as an allowed variant.
   - Rule of thumb: if using negative exemplars, add a short explanation line after each: "(bad: repeats brand name, avoid)" and then a final anchor: "Do not emulate bad samples above."

4) Adversarial user edits (session state)
   - Scenario: user edits original instruction mid-conversation and app resends old few-shot context. Model sometimes mixes old and new instructions.
   - Quick fix: send a one-line confirmation prompt before heavy ops: "Confirming final instruction: <user instruction>. If correct, continue; if not, wait." Not ideal but reduces silent mis-execution in prod.

Example templates (copy-pasteable)
- TEMPLATE A: microcopy-refactor (concise + active)
  Instruction: "Rewrite the following product bullet in 1-2 short sentences, concise, active voice, friendly but professional."
  EXEMPLARS:
    1) IN: "Allows admins to change settings across many users"
       OUT: "Admins can update settings for multiple users in one step."
    2) IN: "Sync data nightly between services for consistency"
       OUT: "Automatically sync services nightly to keep data consistent."
  HEADER: "EXEMPLARS (do not override instruction)"
  FOOTER: "Apply the instruction above exactly. Output only the rewritten text."

- TEMPLATE B: extract-action-items (from meeting notes)
  Instruction: "Read the notes and return a bulleted list of action items. Each item should include owner (if present), a one-line task, and a due-date if mentioned."
  EXEMPLARS: two short pairs showing free-form notes -> structured bullets.
  NOTES: explicit keys (Owner:, Task:, Due:) improved parsability.

Failure modes observed (catalog)
- Instruction bleed: exemplars accidentally override instruction (most common).
- Ambiguous prompts: unconstrained adjectives produce hallucinated facts.
- Repetition loops with few-shot sets containing a repeated pattern — model copies repetition.
- Overfitting to numeric details in exemplars (e.g., "3-step" -> insists on 3 even when impractical).

Micro-mitigation recipes (1–3 lines each)
- Stop instruction bleed: put instruction both before and after exemplars; add a header explicitly saying exemplars are examples only.
- Reduce hallucination for small factual tasks: include a final guard: "If unsure, respond with 'unknown' or ask for clarification."
- Avoid forced numeric rigidity: use "aim for approximately N" when flexibility needed.

Mini test harness notes (how I run quick checks)
- Local run: toy VM with model X (dev), set temperature=0.2, top_p=0.9, max_tokens tuned per task.
- Evaluate: 50 quick examples from backlog (hand-curated) and compute pass/fail on strict and fuzzy metrics.
- Logging: save input, prompt context, model output, and a short failure tag (e.g., "overlimit", "style-mismatch", "hallucination").

Ad-hoc few-shot bank (ideas to implement)
- "Tone drift anchors": 3 exemplars, last is explicit rejection of drift.
- "Numeric guardrails": small block that enforces count constraints using both instruction + post-check snippet.
- "Neg exemplar + annotation": show bad example and short parenthetical explanation.

Open TODOs
- Standardize header/footer language across templates (pick 2 variants).
- Convert top 10 mitigation recipes into automated pre-prompt transforms in prompt-harness.
- Add a small 'sanity-checker' that runs a regex-based post-filter on strict outputs (counts, date formats, required keys).

Quick personal observations
- Small changes in wording ("Do not" vs "Avoid") have outsized effects on some model families — document soon.
- Negative examples are powerful but require explicit meta-commentary or they backfire.

Random ideas to explore later
- Use chained micro-prompts: first contact model to produce constraints, then a second call that generates output while strictly referencing produced constraints as a 'schema'. Might help enforce cardinality.
- Explore mixing distilled exemplars (shortened versions) vs full examples to reduce transfer of incidental details.

End of notes for now. Will push a cleaned set of 6 templates next sprint and add them to prompt-lab PR referenced above.

Title: Cueforge prompt assemblage & micro-failure catalog

Cueforge prompt assemblage & micro-failure catalog

Purpose:
Quick personal lab for composing tiny few-shot sets, hunting brittle cases, and assembling small template patterns we can share with SEs. Not polished; mostly heuristics + failing examples to seed evals.

Notes / Principles (working):
- Keep exemplars tight: 2–6 shots depending on task complexity. More shots -> higher context cost and more brittleness.
- Anchor style before content: start with a 1-line role + desired verbosity then examples.
- Explicit negative examples can reduce hallucination but can confuse models if mixed with positives.
- Prefer contrastive pairs (good vs bad) for preference tuning tests.
- Always include an instruction to "explain step" for debugging outputs (not for production).

Current experiment buckets:
1) Micro-template families
  - Role+format anchor: "You are a concise assistant. Answer in 2–3 bullets."
  - Chain anchor: "First rewrite user query in 1 sentence, then answer."
  - Submit/response framing: "User query => Goal => Constraints => Final answer" (helps long-context consistency)

2) Few-shot order sensitivity tests
  - Hypothesis: mixing examples by difficulty increases variance. Test: easy->hard vs hard->easy vs random.
  - Metric: BLEU/ROUGE not great; use token-level divergence + discrete error counts (factual mismatch).

3) Failure-mode catalog (micro cases)
  - Tokenization boundary drift: prompts that end with punctuation + emoji cause truncated instruction parsing on smaller tokenizers. Example: "Summarize: Who did X? 🤔" produced truncated output in model-v2-7b-q4 on seq>512.
  - Conflicting directives: positive+negative examples cause role flip. Example: one exemplar says "always be brief" and another says "detail tradeoffs" -> model averages and produces inconsistent length.
  - Repetition amplification: multi-shot with near-duplicate exemplars causes identical repeated sentences. Fix attempt: dedupe exemplars and add a randomness seed instruction.
  - Hallucinated sources: asking for citations without exemplar guidance -> model invents sources. Use exemplar with "source: none if unknown".
  - Token budget bleed: including long context a la conversation history pushes out few-shots; tradeoff analysis needed.

Concrete prompt prototypes (mini):
A) Role+Example skeleton (2-shot)
Instruction:
"You are a terse assistant. For each user instruction, provide: 1) 1-sentence summary, 2) 2 bullet actionable steps, 3) single-line confidence (low/med/high). Keep total <= 70 words."
Shots:
- Input: "How do I reverse a linked list in Python?"
  Output:
  "Summary: Reverse singly-linked list using iterative pointers."
  "Steps: 1) Prev=None; cur=head; 2) Loop: nxt=cur.next; cur.next=prev; prev=cur; cur=nxt; Return prev."
  "Confidence: high"
- Input: "How to write unit tests for an API?"
  Output: ... (short)

Fail case noticed: when I add a 3rd shot with an example that mixes frameworks (pytest vs unittest) model picks pluralized guidance mixing both. So keep domain homogenous.

B) Contrastive negative example pattern (for hallucination)
Instruction:
"Given a question, answer succinctly. If you do not know, explicitly respond 'I don't have reliable info'."
Shots: one good, one bad (hallucinates). Then production test set to measure false-positive rates.

Evaluation heuristics:
- Syntactic: exact-match for templated replies (dates, phone numbers), token overlap for short answers.
- Semantic: human-label spot check on a ~200 sample subset per variant. Use pairwise A/B with 25% overlap to estimate inter-rater variance.
- Cost: average tokens consumed per coherent answer; prioritize tokens/accuracy frontier.

Open experiments / TODOs:
- [ ] Run shot-order sweep on 7b-q8 and 13b-int8 to compare sensitivity. Setup: 500 samples of triage Qs from support dataset. (See JIRA AI-3425)
- [ ] Add negative exemplar template & run hallucination test on 1k retrieval prompts.
- [ ] Build a small script to auto-dedupe near-duplicate exemplars using trigram Jaccard.
- [ ] Try prefix-caching exclusion: move exemplars to external cache token to see latency + consistency tradeoff. (Platform ticket GH PR linked above).

Quick micro-debugging checklist (when thing goes weird):
- Are exemplars semantically consistent? (check domain, style)
- Did I accidentally include a contradictory instruction in system line?
- Is temperature set too high for deterministic tasks? (0.0–0.2 recommended)
- Is model variant quantized? (q4/q8 sometimes shift behavior)

Notes to self (short snippets):
- "try explicit 'do not invent' sentence in every exemplar" => reduces hallucination for factoid Qs but increases 'I don't know' frequency.
- "swap shot order every 50 iters during eval" => reduces overfitting to deterministic order.
- Slack thread: #prompt-engineering has earlier examples from Nadia re: citation anchoring (link above).

Examples to preserve for reproducibility (copy into eval harness):
- small set: 50 support triage prompts (anonymized) + 3-shot variant A/B/C
- failing case: boundary emoji example + long input (seq len ~640)

End notes: this is a scratchpad. When something stabilizes, move canonical templates to shared_drives/product/hosted-api/prompt-library. For now, keep iterations messy.

Revision log:
- 2025-10-03 initial sketch
- 2025-11-15 added failure modes and concrete prototypes
- 2026-01-18 updated TODOs and linked GH/JIRA

Title: fewshot-failures-playground

fewshot-failures-playground

Purpose: quick, personal scratchpad for enumerating few-shot prompt templates that surface failure modes (hallucination, instruction drift, token waste). Not a polished playbook — working notes to iterate on tests and small evals.

Main goals:
- Capture compact, portable few-shot templates that we can A/B vs zero-shot and chain-of-thought for targeted failure classes.
- Record examples that reliably trigger specific bad behaviors so QA can reproduce.
- Track heuristics for mitigation (explicit constraints, token budgets, stop sequences, reply framing).

High-level experiments to run (short checklist):
- [ ] Hallucination stress: factual Q->answer prompts with model asked to 'confirm source' and forced to say "I don't know" when unsure. Compare top-1 hallucination rate at temp=0.0/0.2/0.6.
- [ ] Instruction drift: 3-shot instruction-following templates where one example mixes subtle off-task phrasing; measure drift fraction.
- [ ] Token efficiency: few-shot vs compressed-system-message + 1-shot; measure avg tokens per useful token and latency impact.
- [ ] Stop-sequence robustness: multi-part answers where naive stop tokens cause truncation.

Canonical quick templates (raw, minimal):
1) Factual-check few-shot (goal: elicit conservative "I don't know" where appropriate)
Prompt: "You are an assistant that must only answer when confident. If uncertain, reply exactly: 'I don't know'. Examples:
Q: Who invented the transistor?
A: John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley.
Q: When was Kubernetes first released?
A: 2014-06-07 (first public release).
Q: What is the capital of Noveria?
A: I don't know.
Q: {USER_QUESTION}
A:"
Notes: works fairly well on verifiable facts. Failure mode: model paraphrases 'I don't know' into hedged claims. Test for paraphrase detection.

2) Instruction-anchor few-shot (goal: reduce drift)
Template: 3 examples where assistant strictly repeats the requested output format, followed by a maliciously phrased request that tries to change format. Ex:
Example 1 input + expected format -> output.
Example 2 input + expected format -> output.
Example 3 input + expected format -> output.
User: (tries to request extra commentary)
Assistant: (should return only the expected format)
Notes: measure fraction of responses violating explicit format. Add an explicit post-amble: 'Do not add commentary.' If model still adds, consider adding a final guard-shot: 'Assistant must reply with [FORMAT] or EXACT TOKEN: <END>'.

3) Token-compression few-shot (goal: explore compressed exemplar encoding)
Idea: replace full exemplars with compressed key-value pairs separated by pipes. Compare performance vs full exemplars for style transfer tasks.
Example compressed: "E1|Q: summarize->S: short,neutral; E2|Q: translate->T: es"
User: Q: {long input}
Assistant: S: "
Notes: evaluate with BLEU/ROUGE for fidelity and measure bytes. Failure case: compressed exemplars can lose nuance and increase hallucination.

Failure cases observed (short log):
- Hallucination despite 'I don't know' examples: model invents confident-sounding sources or gives partial facts + fabrications. Observed on model-x-small at temp 0.2.
- Format bleed: when user includes extraneous examples in prompt, the assistant sometimes concatenates them into final answer.
- Stop token truncation: multi-step outputs with inline codeblocks get cut if stop seq matches a fence.
- Overfitting to exemplars: when few-shot examples use very specific vocabulary, model mirrors vocabulary and misses synonyms.

Quick mitigations tried (notes):
- Add explicit 'If you are uncertain, stop' as last shot -> reduces hallucination but increases 'I don't know' false positives.
- Use negative examples (show incorrect answer labeled WRONG) -> helps reduce a specific mistaken pattern but makes style inconsistent.
- Append validator function prompt: 'Now check your answer for unsupported claims. If any claim lacks a verification path, replace with I don't know.' Works sometimes but doubles token cost.

Metric ideas for each experiment (mini eval harness):
- Hallucination rate: percent of answers containing verifiably false claims (use small ground truth set).
- Format adherence: whether the response matches a strict regex.
- Token efficiency: tokens out / tokens in useful.
- Precision at top-k facts (for extraction tasks).

Mini reproduction cases (copy-paste ready)
Case A: 'Who founded Redwood Labs and when?' (ambiguous/made-up org) -> expected: I don't know.
Case B: 'Summarize this paragraph in 10 words or fewer' with an example that asks for 7 words -> check strict length enforcement.
Case C: 'Translate the phrase but include a literal bracketed note [DO NOT TRANSLATE]' -> tests bracket handling and guard tokens.

Open questions / TODOs for follow-ups:
- How often does compressed exemplar encoding generalize across styles? run 100-sample sweep.
- Is there an efficient validator prompt pattern that scales (low token overhead) for hosted API flows? (ticket INF-2173)
- Can we autobuild negative examples from previous hallucinations? (screencap pipeline + small finetune)

Scratch ideas for guard rails in product:
- Quick toggle: 'Conservative mode' that activates final validator and forces explicit uncertainty tokens. Tradeoff: throughput and cost.
- Auto-stop heuristics: detect codeblocks and set safer stop tokens.

Notes-to-self: add a short README for QA with reproduction steps. Tag examples with 'regression-id' when a new hallucination is filed. Keep this doc minimal and mobile-friendly for quick edits during pairing sessions.

References / context links:
- Linear: INF-2173 (few-shot regression)
- GitHub PR: prompts/pull/142 experimental harness for compressed exemplars
- Slack: #prompt-sherpas thread 2026-01-12 (contains a few failing examples)

End of scratchpad.

Title: Prompt Combinator — Personal Lab Notes

Prompt Combinator — Personal Lab Notes

Purpose:
- Quick personal workspace to try combinatorial prompt assembly patterns (mixing templates + small exemplar sets + control tokens).
- Goal: find compact building blocks that generalize across instruction families (summarization, extraction, rewrite).

High-level hypothesis:
- A small library of orthogonal micro-templates + 2–3 exemplar micro-shots can cover 60–80% of common downstream prompt needs, with fewer brittle failure modes compared to long monolithic templates.
- Failures concentrate when: ambiguous role framing + adversarial content + long-tail edge semantics (dates, units, nested lists).

Quick constraints:
- Keep prefix <= 140 tokens where possible (prod token budget).
- Favor explicit output schema when downstream pipeline expects JSON.
- Try both direct-instruction and chain-of-thought disabled runs.

Experiment matrix (sketch):
- Template variants: directive-only / directive+context / role+directive / role+example
- Exemplar styles: positive-only, contrastive (good/bad), noisy-realistic
- Model variants: rwd-1-3b, rwd-1-13b-quant, open-llama-7b (ish)
- Eval axes: fidelity, hallucination, token-cost, latency (measured in console)

Micro-templates (building blocks) — shorthand: T1..T6
- T1: ROLE + TASK ("You are a concise editor. Rewrite the following to be clearer:")
- T2: TASK + OUTPUT-SCHEMA ("Return json with keys: summary, bullets")
- T3: CONTROL + EXAMPLES ("If unsure, write 'INSUFFICIENT' for the field")
- T4: CONTEXT-ANCHOR ("Source: <news snippet>. Focus on who/what/when")
- T5: TEMPERATURE-SAFE ("Avoid speculation; only use explicit facts from input")
- T6: FORMAT-ONLY ("Return a single JSON object, no explanation")

Few-shot micro-shots (2–3 per set) — style A/B
- Good: {input: "...", output: "..."} (concise)
- Bad: {input: "...", output: "hallucinated or verbose answer"}
- Contrastive: show one good + one bad to nudge away from common failure mode

Selected assembled prompt examples (real quick runs recorded):
1) Assembly A: T1 + T6 + 2x good shots
Prompt:
"You are a concise editor. Rewrite the following to be clearer:

Example 1 input: 'The CEO said tomorrow is shipping'
Example 1 output: 'The CEO said the product will ship tomorrow.'

Example 2 input: 'They will release next quarter maybe Q3'
Example 2 output: 'The company expects a release in Q3.'

Now rewrite:
{{user_input}}

Return a single JSON object: {"summary":..., "bullets": [...] }"
- Observed: fewer format violations; occasional truncation for long inputs. rwd-1-13b-quant produced tighter token usage.

2) Assembly B: T2 + T3 + 1 good + 1 bad shot (contrastive)
- Prompt emphasizes 'If unsure write INSUFFICIENT'
- Observed: reduced hallucination on entity extraction when the input lacked explicit dates. But models sometimes still guessed relative dates from tense.

Failure cases (notes / reproduction steps):
- Date normalization drift:
  - Pattern: input: 'late spring' then expected ISO or clear fail; model sometimes returned 'May 20' (invented).
  - Reproduce: use T2 + contrastive few-shot with examples that show explicit mapping -> still leaks.
  - Mitigation ideas: stronger negative exemplars (show 'INSUFFICIENT' for ambiguous phrases), or include explicit deny rule 'Do not invent numeric dates'.

- Nested list flattening tear-down:
  - Pattern: long bulleted notes -> expected structured list; model collapses or interleaves items.
  - Reproduce: give 7+ bullets and ask to return numbered JSON list. rwd-1-3b fails earlier than 13b.
  - Quick workaround: add 'Preserve ordering. If >5 items, return array of arrays grouped by topic.' (hacky but helps).

- Contrived adversarial pruning:
  - Pattern: input contains deliberate tokens that look like JSON; model returns input instead of transformed output.
  - Fix: pre-sanitize input or wrap input marker: "<<SOURCE>>...<<ENDSOURCE>>" before giving tasks.

Logging / metrics snippets (notes to self):
- Need to capture: prompt-version id, model, tokens_in, tokens_out, latency_ms, fail_reason tag.
- Console trace shows many 'format_violation' cases where model responds with extra commentary.
- TODO: add a quick post-checker function that diffs response against expected schema and automatically re-asks with "strict format only" fallback once.

Open questions / experiments to try next:
- How few examples are 'enough' when examples are micro (1–2 lines each)? Quick A/B suggests 2 shots gives most gains; test 0/1/2/4 methodically across 200 samples.
- Try contrastive few-shot where bad shot is synthetically generated by truncation rather than hallucination — does that teach the model to avoid brevity errors?
- Role drift: long-running convo context causes role to fade. Try injecting role reminder every N tokens or preceding each user turn with short role token.
- Quantized model behavior: run same assembly against quant vs fp models and log false-positive hallucination rate.

Random micro-examples (copy/paste for quick runs):
- Example input A:
"CompanyX announced integration with PlatformY in late spring. They hinted at more details"
Prompt (T1+T2+T5+T6): rewrite -> JSON with keys 'summary' and 'date_normalized' (date or INSUFFICIENT)
- Example input B (edge):
"Payment scheduled: within 2-6 weeks (likely end of Q2?)" -> test whether model picks interval or picks a concrete date.

Session notes:
- 2026-02-18 run (rwd-1-13b-quant): contrastive set reduced hallucination from 18% -> 9% on sample of 120 news blurbs. Still leaking numerics in 4% of cases.
- 2026-02-28: small improvement by adding explicit 'deny rules' line. Side-effect: verbosity sometimes increased; need T6 staple to enforce single JSON object.

Action items (short):
- [ ] Build small harness: take 500 in-domain docs, run permutations (T1-T6 combos), output per-case metrics (fidelity/hallucination/format_violation). (LIN-4237)
- [ ] Implement auto-fallback post-checker and re-prompt with T6 enforced. (GH:inference/prompt-combinator#89)
- [ ] Curate 10 negative exemplars for each common failure class (dates, lists, nested JSON-like inputs).
- [ ] Share distilled patterns with Solutions Eng for customer playbook draft (one-pager).

Notes to self / heuristics that worked:
- Contrastive = Good + Bad is stronger than 2x Good in many cases for format adherence.
- Always combine FORMAT-ONLY token (T6) with a small penalty: if model includes explanation, auto-strip and re-run with 'STRICT MODE'.
- When in doubt, add explicit 'Do not invent numbers/dates/percentages'.

Riff ideas (for later):
- Minimal control token protocol: [ROLE=editor][STRICT=1][SCHEMA=json:summary,bullets] — try to see if models learn bracketed tokens faster than English instructions.
- Mini-grammar layer: small regex-based post-checker + 1-shot repair prompt to patch common string formatting issues.

Scratch log (one-liners):
- 2026-02-16: seed tests -> a few-shot pair reduced halluc vs baseline but increased token usage by ~12%
- 2026-03-01: tried bracketed control tokens; ambiguous improvement. Need more runs.

Title: micro-prompt-lab-notes

micro-prompt-lab-notes

Micro prompt lab - scratchpad (notes to self, rough templates, failure modes)

Goal: assemble 8-12 compact prompt templates that can be used as building blocks in the prompt library. Focus on modularity (context + instruction + examples + format guardrail). Capture common failure modes and quick mitigations.

Notes / heuristics (personal):
- prefer explicit output schema instead of vague instructions when downstream parsing matters.
- use 2-shot instead of 0-shot when the task is ambiguous; 1-shot can be noisy for style.
- ask model to "think step-by-step" only when chain-of-thought is allowed; otherwise use "brief reasoning" to avoid verbosity.

Template A — concise instruction + schema
INSTRUCTION: "Summarize the following customer message in 2 sentences and extract the top intent as one word. Output JSON with keys: summary, intent"
EXAMPLE 1: {"summary": "Customer can't login after password reset; error page 502", "intent": "login_issue"}
EXAMPLE 2: {"summary": "Wants invoice copy for March; provides order #1234", "intent": "billing_request"}
EDGE CASES: long threaded messages -> truncate to last 3 turns; multi-intent messages -> label primary intent and add secondary_intents array (optional).

Template B — transformation (CSV->JSON table)
INSTRUCTION: "Convert the CSV below into a JSON array of objects. Keep numeric fields as numbers and dates in ISO format."
FEW-SHOT: include 1 tricky row with missing cell to show null handling.
FAILURE MODES: model returns CSV again or mixes delimiters. Mitigation: add an explicit "ONLY RETURN JSON" guard and include final token check for leading '['.

Experiment matrix (quick)
- axis1: shots = [0,1,2]
- axis2: instruction_length = [short, medium, long] (short: 1 line; long: explicit constraints)
- axis3: schema_enforcement = [none, example, format_guard

- failure triage: gather last 20 parse failures, categorize into: (a) trailing commentary after JSON, (b) wrong types, (c) omitted keys, (d) hallucinated keys.

Example few-shot set — meeting notes normalization (3-shot)
PROMPT: "Normalize meeting notes into sections: decisions, action_items, owners. Output as YAML list of blocks."
SHOT1: raw note -> normalized YAML (shows mapping owners->email)
SHOT2: raw note with ambiguous owner -> normalized with owner: null (shows how to handle)
SHOT3: long note with nested decisions -> normalized with nested list

Failure patterns seen (personal):
- hallucinated owners (invents names) — mitigation: include explicit instruction: "If owner not present, write null; do not invent".
- format drift where model adds commentary lines before YAML block — mitigation: "ONLY RETURN YAML CONTENT, no explanation".
- truncation mid-JSON -> mitigation: limit context tokens + request short outputs + use streaming to catch partials.

Title: Microprompt Constraint Corridor — Sketches & Failure Modes

Microprompt Constraint Corridor — Sketches & Failure Modes

Purpose: quick experimentation hub for compact prompts that must operate inside tight token/format constraints (mobile endpoints, short preview UIs, trimmed KV cache).

High-level idea: treat the model's instruction as a narrow corridor: small explicit constraints + 2–3 high-signal examples + a minimal rubric. Aim for output < 60 tokens typical, predictable structure, low hallucination.

Why "constraint corridor"?
- Corridor = explicit bounds for style, length, and factuality checks.
- Microprompt = under ~40–80 tokens of instruction + examples.

Notes-to-self / heuristics observed:
- Always include an explicit final-line format marker (e.g., "OUTPUT: JSON with keys label,text") when we need structure. Without it, models drift in short outputs.
- Examples are more efficient when they change only one axis (tone or factuality) per example. Too many edits across examples increases confusion.
- For very short instruction budgets, anchor with a "do not invent" token: e.g., "If unsure, write 'UNKNOWN'." This reduces hallucinated specifics in ~60% of trials.
- Temperature = 0.0/0.2 for deterministic short outputs on hosted infra. Good tradeoff.

Microprompt templates (compact) — experimental bank
1) Summarize-for-preview (goal: 30–60 tokens)
PROMPT:
"Summarize the following paragraph in 1 short sentence for a mobile preview. If no clear central idea, output 'NO SUMMARY'.
TEXT:
<<input>>
OUTPUT: one sentence, max 30 words."

2) Intent-classifier (3-label, fewshot)
PROMPT:
"Classify user intent as: ask-product, report-bug, ask-billing. Reply only the label. If ambiguous, reply 'unclear'.
EXAMPLES:
'My app crashes when I tap save.' -> report-bug
'I need to change my billing address.' -> ask-billing
'I want to add search to the sidebar.' -> ask-product
INPUT:
<<input>>
LABEL:"

3) Micro-reeval for facts
PROMPT:
"Given the statement, respond TRUE / FALSE / UNKNOWN. If FALSE, give one short correction (<=12 words). If UNKNOWN, give 'UNKNOWN'.
S: <<input>>
REPLY:"

Few-shot set (compact) — testing trio for intent-classifier
- Example A: 'How do I reset my password?' -> ask-product
- Example B: 'Charge appeared twice on my card.' -> ask-billing
- Example C: 'Save button freezes on iOS 17' -> report-bug

Failure cases observed
- Instruction dilution: when examples plus constraints exceed ~80 tokens, the model tends to copy wording from examples rather than generalize.
- Overfitting to examples: too-specific examples cause label leakage; create synthetic variety instead.
- Implicit context bleed: when earlier messages in convo mention examplar nouns, microprompt ends up mirroring those nouns. Reset context or inject 'ignore prior messages' line.
- Abbreviations cause misclassification e.g., 'cc'd' -> interpreted as billing-related in some runs. Add a short normalization step in prompt if possible.

Experimental runs summary (quick):
- Intent-classifier, small prompt (template 2), T=0.0, 500 eval items: accuracy ~88%, unknown rate 4%, hallucinated label 0.8%.
- Same prompt with examples longer/descriptive: accuracy dropped to 81% (more confusions).
- Micro-reeval factual check: adding 'If unsure, reply UNKNOWN' cut false-positives by ~45%.

Edge-case notes and oddities
- Sometimes the model returns a short sentence but with a trailing commentary like '(see above)'. For microprompts, append 'do not add commentary' explicitly; still see occasional slips.
- Newer model variants (opt-quantized) show less hallucination but more truncation; adjust 'max_new_tokens' up by 6 when using strict format.

Quick experiments to run next
- A/B: 3 vs 1 example for intent-classifier with matched lexical diversity, measure precision for rare labels.
- Test 'UNKNOWN' vs explicit null token '<NULL>' vs 'I-DONT-KNOW' to see which reduces hallucination best across multilingual inputs.
- Try inserting a single-line normalization prestep: 'Replace abbreviations: cc'd -> copied to, w/ -> with' and measure effect on classifier accuracy.
- Run microprompt tests on private deployment (gpu-reserved) with kv-cache disabled to simulate cold-start prefixes.

Implementation notes for Redwood integrations
- Keep microprompt as a snippet object in prompt-library with fields: instructions, examples (list), format_marker. This doc is just the scratch idea; the library schema will be fleshed in product area.
- Consider a small runtime safety check: if output length > X tokens when format requires Y, auto-truncate and tag 'TRUNCATED'.

Random scraps / brainstorm
- Could use a 'corridor badge' system for prompts to indicate strictness levels: corridor-1 (very strict, deterministic), corridor-2 (flexible), corridor-3 (creative).
- For UI previews, try two-line outputs: L1 = one-sentence summary, L2 = 8-word context tag.

References / TODO: link runs to GH/CONFLUENCE ids above. Add more evals, synthetic datasets, and then move polished templates into shared prompt library.

Unresolved questions
- How low can we go on examples before accuracy collapses for multi-label tasks? (need controlled ablation)
- Are there measurable differences between tokens used for 'do not invent' phrasing across languages?

Signed,
Asha (scratch notes)

Title: Prompt Parkour — roundtrip transforms & failure probes

Prompt Parkour — roundtrip transforms & failure probes

Purpose:
Quick personal lab: exercise a "roundtrip" evaluation pattern for prompt templates. The goal is to surface brittle failure modes that don't show up in single-run accuracy checks: instruction drift, exemplar misbinding, tokenization splits, and implicit-constraint erosion over transforms.

High-level idea:
1) Start from a human-readable template (T0).
2) Produce a model output (O1) given T0 + input X.
3) Derive a canonicalized prompt T1 from O1 (automatic simplification/paraphrase).
4) Re-run model on X with T1 -> O2.
5) Compare O2 to O1 and the intended target. Repeat with a few-shot wrapper, different temperatures, and small perturbations.

Why roundtrip?
- Single-pass evaluation misses subtle instruction content that is implicit in examples.
- If T1 fails to reconstruct the important constraints, we find that the template relies on fragile linguistic cues.
- Helps spot when exemplars encode facts that the instruction text doesn't capture.

Experiment matrix (quick):
- Models: vicuna-13b, mixtral-8x, galactica-lite (local), redwood-test-7b (dev).
- Temp: 0.0, 0.3, 0.7
- top_p: 0.95
- max_tokens: 128
- Few-shot sizes: 0, 2, 5 examples (hand-picked + shuffled)
- Perturbations: swap order of examples, anonymize labels, inject odd punctuation, break exemplar context with "---" separator.
- Metrics: fidelity (BLEU-ish), constraint-violation count (manual), hallucination flag (manual), exemplar-binding errors (count).

Base template (T0) — simple instruction: 
"You are an assistant that summarizes product feedback into a bulleted list of issues and suggested action items. Output only bullets. Keep each bullet <= 20 words. If the input is empty, respond with 'No feedback.'"

Few-shot wrapper (F0):

Example 1:
Input: "App crashes when tapping export"
Output:
- Crash: export flow fails when large PNGs attached
- Action: add guardrail and async upload, add telemetry

Example 2:
Input: "Confusing onboarding steps"
Output:
- UX: first-run gets too many modals
- Action: collapse into single flow, add progressive hints

Then: Prompt = F0 + "Input: {{user_text}}" + T0

Roundtrip procedure notes:
- Canonicalization function used: auto-paraphrase with temperature=0.2; heuristics remove hedging phrases, normalize bullets to "- " prefixed lines.
- For each run, save T0, O1, T1 (paraphrase of O1), O2. Also save token counts and the first 64 tokens of each output.

Observed failure patterns (examples):
1) Exemplar misbinding: when examples use labels like "Crash:" and "UX:" the model sometimes applies label semantics to new inputs even when instruction forbids labels. Roundtrip shows label leakage — T1 may not contain "Crash:" token but O2 still inserts it.
2) Quantifier loss: constraints like "<= 20 words" get dropped during paraphrase step. O2 frequently violates word budget.
3) Punctuation fragility: injecting a trailing ellipsis in examples causes the model to switch to paragraph outputs.
4) Tokenization-edge hallucination: in one seed, a model split "onboarding" into subword pieces and inferred "on board" in the generated summary, changing meaning.
5) Separator overfitting: when we add "---" between examples the model treats the final example as higher weight; re-ordering changes behavior unpredictably.

Concrete run vignette (short):
X: "Export button fails on 2.1.3 when files > 4MB"
T0 run -> O1:
- Crash: export fails on large files >4MB
- Action: add chunked uploads and retry
(Complies with 20-word rule)
T1 (canonicalized from O1) -> "Summarize the issue and suggest an action. Use two bullets. Keep each under 20 words."
O2 (from T1) ->
- Export failure for files over 4MB
- Add retry and chunked uploads to prevent failure
Result: O2 is close but loses numeric precision (drops the version context), and in other cases the 'Action' line became a recommendation instead of an actionable TODO.

Failure classification heuristics (todo):
- Leaked label: O2 contains label tokens not present in T1 (flag)
- Constraint-drop: measured length > 20 words
- Semantic drift: cosine(O1, O2) < 0.75 (embedding check)
- Example-binding mismatch: counts where the action maps to wrong entity (manual label)

Quick prompt variations to test (new seeds):
A) Make constraints explicit as a separate "CONSTRAINTS:" block rather than inline in prose.
B) Replace exemplar labels with natural-language commentary instead of shorthand labels.
C) Use a normalization step that preserves numeric tokens and units (special rule).
D) Add a short rubric at the end: "If uncertain, ask for clarifying question instead of guessing."

Small test template (to paste into harness):
"SYSTEM: You are a concise summarizer.
CONSTRAINTS: Output only bullets. Each bullet <= 20 words.
EXAMPLES:
[ex1]
[ex2]
INPUT: {{text}}
OUTPUT:"

Quick results notes (running logs):
- Mixtral-8x @ temp 0.0: best fidelity to O1 but more brittle ordering of bullets.
- vicuna-13b @ temp 0.3: more creative actions, sometimes adds unnecessary steps.
- redwood-test-7b: token budget respected when constraints block is present, drops numbers when paraphrase step used.

Next steps / TODO:
- Expand sample set to 40 inputs spanning: numerical details, multi-issue reports, empty input, sarcastic feedback.
- Implement automatic numeric-preserve rule for canonicalizer.
- Add an explicit "LABELS ARE FOR EXAMPLES ONLY" line in prompt and run A/B.
- Log per-token costs and store examples where constraint-drop occurs.
- Share rough findings with Omar and Ruth; propose a small PR to harness with the constraints-block experiment.

Notes to self:
- Keep this doc intentionally light and messy — it's a scratchpad. Capture a few failing seeds and the example that caused them.
- Save interesting example outputs to /tmp/prompt-parkour-samples (for now).

Useful search keywords for follow-up: roundtrip prompting, exemplar leakage, constraint erosion, prompt canonicalization, few-shot overfitting, tokenization drift.

End of file.

Title: Heuristic Scribe: Aperture Notes on Prompt Templates & Failures

Heuristic Scribe: Aperture Notes on Prompt Templates & Failures

Purpose:
Quick personal record of promising prompt templates, small few-shot banks, and recurring failure modes I've seen while iterating on the assistant templates. Not a final spec — this is an exploratory scratchpad for heuristics I want to lock into the prompt-registry later.

High-level goals (what I want from templates):
- determinism for structured outputs (avoid freeform when schema expected)
- graceful fallback for out-of-scope queries
- economy: minimal tokens with high fidelity
- robustness across model variants (Llama-like, Mistral, open weights)

Quick notes / instincts:
- explicit negative examples often help with hallucination more than extra positive exemplars. Sketchy but true in 3/5 cases.
- role-priming + short instruction tends to beat long justification paragraphs for few-shot generalization in low-context budgets.
- keep a tiny calibration step (1–2 lines) when switching models or quantization levels to reduce tone drift.

Minimal few-shot template (fast, low-token):
--INSTRUCTION--
You are an assistant that answers concisely and uses bullets for steps. If the question is out of scope, reply: "I don’t have that info. Here’s how you can find it:" and give 2 pointers.

Example 1:
Q: How do I rotate an S3 key?
A: 1) Identify service principals 2) Create new key 3) Swap usages 4) Revoke old key.

Example 2:
Q: What is TTL in Redis?
A: TTL is time-to-live. Use EXPIRE to set, TTL to read. If expired, key removed.
--END--

Variants to try:
- add a single negative exemplar: show a hallucinated answer and then the corrected short answer.
- force an output schema: prefix with "OUTPUT AS JSON: {"answer": string, "sources": [string]"}". Test truncation behavior.

Medium template (for structured tasks + examples):
Role: "Policy assistant. Cite policy section IDs or say "none". Keep reasoning under 40 tokens."
Few-shot set (3 items): each example shows question, brief reasoning, output with section id.

Observed failure modes (notes + rough frequency):
- style drift (30%): voice changes across long dialog — likely due to hidden system/context switches. Fix: reassert role every 6–8 turns or add short reminder at top of each system message.
- hallucinated citations (45%): model invents section numbers or fake URLs. Fixes to try: negative exemplars, explicit "If you cannot verify, say unknown" anchor, or require numeric confidence token.
- verbosity bleed (20%): assistant ignores concision instruction when user asks follow-ups. Try: token budget hint ("Answer in max 80 tokens").
- token-bloat in few-shot sets (non-linear cost): keep exemplars as distilled Q/A pairs — remove commentary.
- schema corruption on truncation (15%): when outputting JSON schema the model sometimes emits partial JSON. Fix: add closing sentinel string e.g., "<END>" and post-parse with safe fallbacks.

Failure-case mini-catalog (for prompt-registry tests):
1) Instruction ignoring when examples use different phrasing. Test: swap example phrasing to match edge-case user phrasing.
2) Overfitting to examples: model copies example phrasing verbatim rather than adapting. Test: paraphrase examples to encourage abstraction.
3) Repetition loops: model repeats last bullet twice when list framing ambiguous. Test: add "Do not repeat items" explicit rule.

Lightweight experiment matrix (priority):
- E1 (high): Compare negative-exemplar vs extra positive exemplar on hallucination rate across 3 models, 200 queries each. Metric: hallucination rate via gold-labeled answers.
- E2 (med): Schema + end-sentinel vs schema-only: measure JSON parse success and partial outputs.
- E3 (low): Short role re-assertion every N turns: N={3,6,9} — measure tone drift.

Measured heuristics to record (for each run):
- model, quantization, sequence length distribution, exemplar token count, hallucination rate, JSON-parse success %, average response tokens.

Small prototype few-shot bank (draft examples) — aim for 3 exemplars that cover typical variants:
1) Definitional question (short ask)
Q: What is OAuth?
A: OAuth is an authorization framework to allow apps delegated access. 2–3 lines. Sources: RFC6749.
2) Procedural short (steps)
Q: How to rotate a DB password with minimal downtime?
A: 1) Create new creds, 2) stage rotation with read-only, 3) swap, 4) revoke. Add one fallback pointer.
3) Out-of-scope case (should refuse and give pointers)
Q: Provide personal data for user X.
A: "I can’t help with personal data retrieval. Here’s how to request it formally: [link to privacy request form]"

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Add automatic post-checker that marks answers with "confidence-low" tag when model used heuristics to fill gaps.
- Push E1 to CI and add an entry in prompt-registry with experiment metadata (link to PR above).
- Draft a short explainer for Solutions Eng on how to pick exemplars (keep it <1 page).

Unresolved questions (brain dump):
- Is one negative example always better than two positives for hallucination? My hunch: depends on task ambiguity. Need controlled test.
- How much does exemplar paraphrasing increase generalization vs cold few-shot? Anecdotal but not measured.

Quick references I want to keep handy:
- Confluence: Prompt Guidelines (linked above)
- JIRA-3421: prompt-registry schema changes
- PR 87: initial negative-exemplar implementation

Last quick thought: aim to make the prompt-registry support a compact attribute set for each template: {role_hint, exemplar_count, negative_examples_allowed, output_schema, end_sentinel}. If we standardize that, we can automate fail-safe transforms (insert sentinel, wrap schema, add short refusal exemplar) before sending to model.

-- end of aperture notes --

(These are rough; keep this file as source-of-truth for small experiments before I formalize.)

Title: Signal Sculpting Kitchen: prompt tinkering and failure notes

Signal Sculpting Kitchen: prompt tinkering and failure notes

Purpose

Short scratchpad for an experimental prompt playbook I ran over a few days. Trying to surface brittle modes and a small set of compact, deployable few-shot templates that are cheap (token-wise) and robust across style shifts. This is messy — notes-to-self style.

Quick context
- Model target: opensource-repro-13B (quantized run on dev cluster) and hosted/fast-16k for cross-check; prefer conservative temperature schedule.
- Workload: multi-turn customer-support summarization + extraction for short answers (1-3 slots) and optional explanatory justification text.
- Constraint: keep few-shot examples under 120 tokens total so per-request budget stays low.

Overall approach: "signal sculpting"
- Think of the prompt as a small hammer: shape a small, clear objective (slot list + required style) then add 1-2 exemplars that contrast the failure case.
- Use explicit negative exemplar rather than implicit instruction when model tends to hallucinate (show instead of tell).
- Anneal temperature across shots: lower temperature for the final instruction, slightly higher in exemplars to surface variety.

Experiments run (short notes)
1) Condensed slot template + contrast negative shot
- Prompt pattern: header -> slot list -> positive ex -> negative ex -> user query -> expected format line.
- Result: large reduction in extra hallucinated fields. Negative ex where the answer is "N/A" for a missing slot helps the model avoid inventing content.
- Failure: when user phrasing is indirect (implied dates), model sometimes copies partial context into slot and marks as present. Need clearer missing-value rules.

2) Progressive exemplar annealing (temp schedule)
- Setup: provide two exemplars; exemplar 1 generated at temp=0.6, exemplar 2 at temp=0.4, final instruction executed at temp=0.1 via inline system tag suggestion. (We simulate by wording: "Use terse deterministic style like example 2.")\- Result: more concise outputs, fewer style drift errors. However this is fragile with long context chains.

3) Role-swap robustness test (assistant asked to be "analyst" vs "agent")
- Found: small wording changes in role line produce major variance. When prompt included an explicit "do not ask follow-ups" line model sometimes dropped critical clarifying behavior. Need A/B on allowing one clarifying question vs strict no-clarify.

Compact few-shot templates (cheap)
- Template A: 2-shot extraction + missing-value rule (approx 90 tokens)
  HEADER: "Extract: [name, date, issue, resolution] — return JSON only. If unknown, use null. Keep explanations to 1 sentence max."
  EX1 (pos): "Input: 'Order 4432 — customer said item arrived broken on 2024-09-05 — replaced' -> {name: null, date: '2024-09-05', issue: 'broken item', resolution: 'replaced'}"
  EX2 (neg): "Input: 'No date provided, customer vague' -> {name: 'Jane D', date: null, issue: 'customer vague', resolution: null}"
  INSTR: "Now extract from: <USER_INPUT>"
- Notes: using explicit JSON keys reduces token churn when downstream parsing expects keys. Keep key order consistent.

- Template B: slot + justification (short) (approx 110 tokens)
  HEADER: "Answer with two items: 1) JSON with keys [slot1..], 2) Single-sentence justification labeled 'why'. Do not include extra text."
  EX (one shot): show positive extraction with a single-sentence why that cites phrase location.
  INSTR: "Extract and justify for: <USER_INPUT>"
- Notes: justification increases tokens but catches hallucinations in QA. Use only on heavy-risk flows.

Observed failure cases (catalog)
- Implicit context bleed: model picks up tokens from earlier conversation turns and attributes them to current slots (especially person names). Mitigation: anchor prompt with 'Context after this line is no longer relevant.' but performance mixed.
- Over-eager short answers: model returns a default phrase like 'no issue' when uncertain. Fix: negative exemplar where unknown->null and small penalty via phrasing 'do not guess'.
- Role ambiguity: 'agent' triggers step-by-step action bias; 'analyst' triggers summarization bias. For mixed flows pick 'analyst (do not take actions)'.
- Multi-meaning dates: '3/4' ambiguous locale. Use explicit expectation: 'dates in ISO (YYYY-MM-DD) when you can' and show conversion example.
- List ordering inconsistency: model sometimes reorders keys. Enforce stable key order by example and by final format line 'keys must appear in this order: ...'.

Edge-case seeds I want to test next
- Very short context + sarcasm: user says 'yeah great, thanks' meaning complaint — model shouldn't mark 'positive'. Add sarcasm negative ex.
- Token budget ablation: run same template with only 1 exemplar to see token tradeoffs vs accuracy drop.
- Cold-start few-shot: neutralizing system messages vs explicit in-prompt instructions; which is stickier across model restarts?

Quick runbook suggestions (for moving to shared recipes)
- Export Template A with: exemplar compression (remove prose, keep only essential tokens), fixed key order, explicit missing-value policy.
- Add an optional 'safety fallback' route: if extraction fails confidence threshold -> return minimal 'needs human' JSON with flag.
- Track failure rates by issue type in the Console (sparse events spotlight) and add one regression alert for sudden jump in 'invented_person' events.

Questions for the team
- Jordan: can we add a 'dont_invent' model hook that biases logits away from names unless a token substring match exists in context? (technical feasibility?)
- Priya: if we enable 'justification' as a premium opt-in route, what is our token pricing guidance for customers?

Next steps (my TODOs)
- Run ablation: Template A with 0,1,2 exemplars across opensource-repro-13B / hosted-16k. Log invented_field rate.
- Draft a trimmed shared recipe (<=100 tokens) to add to the prompt-recipes repo and link to Confluence index.
- Prototype 'missing-value example' negative shot variants (explicit 'N/A' vs null vs 'unknown') and compare parse stability.

Notes to self
- Keep this doc intentionally rough — snapshot of experiments. Move cleaned recipe to /prompt-recipes once one stable exemplar set verified.
- Avoid copying language from other scratchpads; this is meant to be compact and mechanistic.

---
End of scratchpad

Title: nomad-prompt-contrivance-notes

nomad-prompt-contrivance-notes

Purpose / position: quick personal sandbox for trying compact few-shot sets that are tolerant to slot-swaps and token-budget drift. Not a canonical repo file — ephemeral thinking. Aim is to capture a small set of high-signal prompt micro-patterns and the weird failure modes that show up under cascade prompting + temperature jitter.

Top-level questions I want answers to:
- How resilient is a 3-shot exemplar set when we permute order and swap one exemplar with a paraphrase? (practical tolerance)
- Which instruction anchors reduce hallucination on named-entity transformations? (anchor wording vs. exemplar overload)
- Can concise scaffolding + a single counterexample avoid repetition in multi-turn generation?

Quick notes / heuristics observed so far:
- Anchor phrasing matters more when the task requires strict format (CSV, JSON) than when it's freeform. Use explicit markers like "Output exactly as JSON" rather than softer verbs.
- Mix of positive and negative exemplars helps on tasks with common model biases (e.g., overattribution). But negative examples must be minimal — too many and model flips to adversarial mode.
- Short prefix context (<= 60 tokens) + 2 exemplars beats long single exemplar for throughput-limited endpoints in most cases.

Experiment sketches (run ids TBD):
1) Slot-swap tolerance (baseline: 3-shot anchored)
- Instr: "Rewrite the sentence to formal tone. Preserve named entities exactly."
- Ex1: informal -> formal (short)
- Ex2: informal -> formal (contains quoted name)
- Ex3: paraphrase transform that changes punctuation only
- Variants: shuffle order; replace Ex2 with a paraphrase generated by model at temp 0.8; drop Ex3.
- Metrics: exact match on preserved entity tokens, BLEU-ish for tone, perplexity delta.
- Quick observation: when Ex2 replaced with paraphrase generated at high temp, entity preservation drops ~7% but tone consistency still ok. Implication: exemplar provenance matters.

2) Named-entity transformation with anchor vs exemplars
- Task: map product names to canonical IDs from a small table provided in prompt. Output: lines of "product_id, canonical_name".
- Anchor A: "Use the table below and output exactly two columns separated by comma."
- Anchor B: "Refer to the mapping table; if unsure, output UNSURE."
- 4 exemplar rows vs 0 exemplars.
- Failure case noted: with Anchor B + no exemplars, model often invents IDs instead of UNSURE. Anchor A combined with one exemplar reduced invented IDs by ~60%.

3) Counterexample scaffolding for repetition control
- Problem: multi-sentence instructions produce repetitive lists.
- Approach: include one counterexample showing repetition and explicit correction. Example snippet in prompt: "BAD: A, A, A -> GOOD: A, B, C"
- Result: tends to produce less repetition even at temp 0.9. Works best when counterexample is directly adjacent to instruction, not buried behind examples.

Micro prompt bank (draft templates)
- micro/json-strict: "You are a conversion engine. Input: <text>. Output: a single-line JSON object with keys 'source' and 'converted'. Do not add commentary."
- micro/dirichlet-shot: "Given these 3 examples, infer the transformation rule. Output the rule as a short sentence, then apply it to the input."
- micro/negexample-anchor: "Here is an incorrect output followed by the corrected output. Use that correction style."

Representative few-shot set (for format enforcement)
---EXAMPLES---
Input: "buy 3 apples, deliver to 5th st."
Output: {"action":"purchase","qty":3,"dest":"5th st."}

Input: "send invoice to Acme Co, acct #219"
Output: {"action":"invoice","company":"Acme Co","account":219}
---END---

Failure modes to catalog (ongoing):
- Hallucinated fields: model invents 'priority' tokens when no exemplar shows them. Often occurs when anchor uses terms like 'important' in instruction.
- Overfitting to exemplar surface: exact punctuation in examples leads to brittle outputs when input punctuation deviates. Workaround: vary punctuation across exemplars.
- Counterexample overshoot: model flips tone and becomes overly corrective (adds explanations) — use explicit "Do not add commentary" anchor.
- Temporal drift: paraphrase exemplars generated at different times (or using different model checkpoints) yield inconsistent behaviors in production A/B tests. Recommendation: re-generate exemplars from the same checkpoint used in production.

Small checklist before promoting a few-shot set to repo:
- [ ] Re-run with exemplar permutation (3 orders)
- [ ] Test with exemplar paraphrase from higher temperature
- [ ] Validate token budget under production truncation (check prefix token counts)
- [ ] Run 100-sample QA for hallucination / invented fields
- [ ] Add one negative exemplar if hallucination > 5%

Open hypotheses to test (short):
- H1: A single explicit 'format enforcement' sentinel token (e.g., "<<JSON>>") reduces hallucination more than a full example. Quick A/B planned.
- H2: Mixing one synthetic exemplar (model-generated) with two human-written exemplars increases robustness vs. all-human set.

Notes-to-self / next steps:
- Schedule small run with C1 (anchor sentinel) vs baseline this week. Attach run ids here when available.
- Clean up the best-performing micro templates into prompt-kit under experimental/nomad. Create PR linking to JIRA-ENG-9876.
- Ask Riley to try slot-swap tolerance test using Dedicated infra to confirm latency vs token budget tradeoffs.

Slack crumbs / links: debugging thread: slack://channel/dev-prompt-lab/thread/16234; related PR: github.com/redwood-inference/prompt-kit/pull/234

Random brain dump (incomplete):
- Might be useful to try an "anti-anchor" technique: ask model to list what it "won't do" before generating (think of negative instructions first). Could reduce silent hallucination.
- Consider adding short provenance tag in output for production ("_exemplar_used: X") for easier regression triage.

-- Evan

Title: Customer Network Safety KPIs and Compact Audit Hypotheses

Customer Network Safety KPIs and Compact Audit Hypotheses

TL;DR: Draft a compact, operationally-actionable set of safety KPIs and audit hypotheses for customer-managed networking (VPC / on-prem) that balances forensic fidelity with storage/query cost. Propose a lightweight audit envelope ("evidence capsule") format, sampling rules for change events, operator UX hooks for rapid rollback, and measurable SLAs for approval gates. Prioritize: (1) forensic triage speed, (2) probability of having sufficient evidence for rollbacks/PD, (3) customer privacy and minimal egress, (4) bounded storage cost per customer.

Context / problem statement:
- Private deployments mean many networking changes occur outside Redwood's infra (customer-controlled firewalls, peering, NAT changes, operator scripts). When incidents happen we have limited visibility and must rely on compact telemetry and customer-provided artifacts.
- Existing PRD drafts focus on exhaustive attestation ledgers and long retention; customers push back on data egress, retention, and legal complexity. We need a middle path: deterministic, small audit payloads that enable triage and automated rollback without full packet-level telemetry.

Goals (what success looks like):
- KPI-1: Mean time to triage (MTT) for network-change incidents <= 25 minutes for incidents where evidence capsule exists.
- KPI-2: Probability that a random critical change (as defined by our risk model) has a usable evidence capsule >= 85% at GA.
- KPI-3: Average storage per tenant for audit envelope <= 5 MB/day (configurable by tier).
- KPI-4: Approval gate latency 95th percentile <= 300ms for automated pre-checks; human approval median <= 4 minutes when reviewers alerted.
- KPI-5: Rollback fidelity (ability to restore a previous known-good config without customer intervention) >= 70% for operator-initiated rollbacks where capsule exists.

Key concepts and proposed artifacts:
1) Evidence capsule (compact audit envelope):
   - Purpose: single-file, cryptographically-signed bundle capturing minimal data needed to reason about a change and perform a rollback or reconstruct intent.
   - Suggested fields (compact): version, change_id, actor_id (pseudonymized/hashed if required), timestamp, change_type (route/table/peering/firewall/nat), delta (compact diff), pre_state_digest (hash of prior config), optional snapshot pointer (if customer allows full snapshot), operator-comment (free text), approval_proof (signed approval token), sampling_flag, schema_version.
   - Size budget: aim for < 50KB per typical change when snapshot omitted.
   - Storage/retention: default 90 days for evidence capsule metadata + 7 days for attached snapshots (tiered).

2) Sampling and heuristics:
   - Always-capture events: creation/destruction of peering, route table replacements, public egress rule openings, operator-initiated mass changes (> N rules), and any change that matches risk rules.
   - Probabilistic sampling: small config tweaks (single rule edits) sampled at 10% by default. Sample rate configurable by customer or by Redwood policy.
   - Adaptive sampling: ramp up sampling (to 100%) if system detects repeated failures from same actor or an increase in error surface.
   - Rationale: reduces storage; keeps high signal for high-risk changes.

3) Approval gates and pre-checks:
   - Preflight static checks run in Redwood control-plane (local simulation against recent capsule digest): conflict detection, route blackhole detection, egress leak heuristics, overlapping CIDR warnings, permit/deny precedence anomalies. Preflight should fail-fast and return clear human-friendly hints.
   - Automated approvals allowed for low-risk changes with past successful rollout history; otherwise require 1 human approver. Use canary windows and auto-revert triggers.
   - Approval SLAs and alerting: allow teams to set their own approval windows and escalation paths; Redwood sends structured evidence capsule with notification to approvers (Slack/email webhook).

4) Operator UX for incident response:
   - Search-first UI: query by change_id, actor_id, time window, CIDR, or impacted subnet. Capsules indexed by digest and tags.
   - One-click rollback: reconstruct delta from capsule and offer a "revert candidate" that can be applied with optional dry-run. Show expected impact and confidence score.
   - Forensic timeline: visualize sequence of capsules and system metrics around the change (CPU, connection drops, application error spikes if telemetry provided).

5) Privacy and minimal egress model:
   - Capsule fields default to pseudonymized actor_id; full identity resolved only with customer opt-in or during joint incident review.
   - Snapshots and richer telemetry require explicit customer consent and per-capsule authorization.

6) Compact data model and query patterns:
   - Use columnar store for capsule metadata and object store for capsule payloads. Keep payloads compressed (brotli) and index top-level fields for fast retrieval.
   - Query patterns to optimize: change_id lookup, actor/time range, impacted-subnet search (precompute inverted index), risk-score filtering.

Rollout proposal (phased):
- Phase 0 (experiment): implement capsule v0 collector + local dry-run preflight. Test with 3 pilot customers (SaaS, fintech, health) focusing on capture and rollback UX.
- Phase 1 (beta): sampling controls + adaptive sampling + basic UI for search/rollback. Retention: 30-day metadata.
- Phase 2 (GA): full approval integration, configurable retention tiers, SLA-backed approval latency, integration with KMS for capsule signing.

Operational and cost considerations:
- Storage budget caps per tenant with tiered pricing; alert when approaching cap and provide auto-archive option.
- For high-volume tenants, prefer sampling + on-demand full-snapshot request.
- Encryption and signing: use customer-managed KMS when available; otherwise Redwood-managed keys with strict access controls and audit logging.

Open questions / tradeoffs (needs decisions quickly):
- Q1: Default sampling rates by change_type (we propose 100% for peering/egress open, 10% for single-rule edits). Product decision needed.
- Q2: Legal/retention constraints for regulated verticals — default 90 days may be insufficient (health/finance); should we offer longer as part of enterprise package?
- Q3: Should actor_id hashing be reversible by Redwood for root-cause analysis, or require customer-provided resolution keys?
- Q4: Snapshot pull vs push model: who initiates when a deeper snapshot is needed during triage? Push increases egress risk.

Monitoring & success measurement (launch metrics):
- Adoption: % of pilot tenants enabling capsules within first 60 days. Target >= 60% for pilots.
- Effectiveness: fraction of incidents where capsule enabled automated or semi-automated rollback. Target >= 50% in pilot.
- Cost: average daily storage per tenant and query latency P95 for lookup by change_id (target < 200ms).

Next steps / immediate TODOs:
- [Product] Lock sampling defaults and retention tiers (decision by 2025-02-10).
- [Eng] Prototype capsule schema and brotli compression pipeline; expose sample API for partners (pr: github.com/redwood-inference/private-deploy/pull/47).
- [SE] Recruit 3 pilot customers and draft pilot runbook (owners: Diego Morales, Maya Singh).
- [Legal] Quick review of retention/transfer requirements for US/EU healthcare customers.

Notes to reviewers: this is intentionally compact — the goal is operational parity (fast triage + rollback) without exhaustive data exfiltration. Looking for feedback on sampling defaults, retention policy, and whether the capsule model meets typical SRE workflows.

Relevant links and references:
- internal pilot notes: CONF-PrivateNet-SAFETY-42
- pilot Jira: JIRA-PDP-9123
- proto schema: https://github.com/redwood-inference/private-deploy/blob/feature/audit-envelope/schema/capsule_v0.md

Unresolved checklist (for doc maturity):
- [ ] Finalize capsule JSON schema and size budget test (bench with real customer data).
- [ ] Build preflight rule set and test against historical incident corpus.
- [ ] Wire approval notifications to on-call rotation and Slack escalation.
- [ ] Document legal opt-in language for snapshot collection and retention exceptions.

End of doc.

Title: Evidence-driven offer evaluation and onboarding trigger playbook

Evidence-driven offer evaluation and onboarding trigger playbook

Summary:
This playbook defines a measurable, evidence-driven process for offer evaluation and the automated triggering of role-specific onboarding pathways at Redwood Inference. It replaces ad-hoc offer decisions and fragmented onboarding handoffs with a single decision matrix, a negotiation and risk log, and concrete onboarding triggers tied to role risk, compliance needs, and ramp objectives.

Who this is for:
- Hiring managers
- Recruiters and Talent Acquisition
- HR Business Partners (HRBPs)
- People Ops specialists who build onboarding curricula
- Legal and Finance for offer approvals

Goals and principles:
- Make offer decisions transparent and auditable using a standardized scorecard.
- Reduce time-to-offer while preserving quality of decision-making (target: 48-hour typical offer SLA from verbal approval).
- Trigger onboarding pathways automatically based on objective signals (role, clearance, vendor status, critical deliverables).
- Record negotiation outcomes and commitments centrally for manager and HR ownership.

Key owners and roles:
- Recruiter: manage candidate communications, prepare initial offer package, populate scorecard.
- Hiring Manager: complete technical/cultural evaluation, set ramp objectives, confirm L4/L5+ approvals.
- HRBP: ensure compliance with compensation bands and local labor law; finalize benefits language.
- Finance: sign-off on salary above band midpoint + 15% (approval threshold).
- Legal: review for contractor/consultant engagements and NDAs.

Offer evaluation process (step-by-step):
1) Populate Offer Scorecard (required before verbal offer)
   - Responsible: Recruiter + Hiring Manager
   - Required fields: role level, base salary proposed, equity award, bonus eligibility, reason for hire, candidate score (0–5) across: technical fit, problem-solving, role-specific skills, team fit, ramp risk.
   - Attach: interview scorecards, reference-check notes, and compensation benchmarking snapshot.

2) Automated Decision Matrix applies
   - If candidate_score >= 4.0 AND proposed_comp <= band_midpoint + 10% -> auto-approve (Recruiter/HRBP finalize).
   - If candidate_score between 3.0–4.0 OR proposed_comp between band_midpoint + 10% and +25% -> HRBP + Hiring Manager sign-off required.
   - If candidate_score < 3.0 OR proposed_comp > band_midpoint + 25% OR offer contains atypical clauses -> Finance + Legal review and exec sponsor.

3) Negotiation and Risk Log (template)
   - Fields to capture: candidate_request (text), impact_on_budget (Y/N), manager_commitments (Y/N), date, negotiator name, final decision.
   - All negotiated deviations from the standard package must be recorded and stored in the candidate dossier.

4) Offer SLA targets
   - Verbal offer: within 48 hours of decision to hire.
   - Written offer (signed by HRBP/Legal): within 72 hours of verbal acceptance.
   - Exception path: roles requiring external contractor conversion, export control, or security clearance: review window up to 10 business days.

Offer Scorecard (required fields — flat table representation)
- candidate_name | role | level | technical_score (0-5) | problem_solving (0-5) | team_fit (0-5) | ramp_risk (low/med/high) | aggregate_score (0-5) | proposed_comp_pct_vs_band_mid | approvals_required

Decision and approval thresholds (examples)
- Aggregate score >= 4.0 and comp <= +10% => Recruiter + HRBP sign.
- Aggregate score 3.0–3.9 or comp +10%–+25% => Hiring Manager + HRBP required.
- Aggregate score < 3.0 or comp > +25% => Finance + Legal + Exec sponsor.

Onboarding trigger taxonomy
This section maps objective signals in the scorecard and offer to an onboarding pathway. Triggers are evaluated automatically by the People Ops intake system when the candidate signs the offer.
- Role risk triggers (immediately escalate): access to PII/PHI, admin network access, SOC2 high-impact role. => Trigger: Restricted onboarding pathway (security clearance checklist, 1:1 with Security engineer before first day).
- Compliance triggers: EEA employment, contractor vs. employee conversion, background check flags. => Trigger: Extended HR/Legal onboarding (pre-hire paperwork, local labor compliance steps).
- Ramp-critical triggers: role with measurable Q1 deliverables or cross-team dependencies. => Trigger: accelerated immersion track (prestart reading list, assigned buddy, condensed 30-day objectives).
- Remote/new-country triggers: candidate located outside primary region or requiring relocation. => Trigger: remote-localization packet and payroll/accounting enrollment steps.

Onboarding pathways (short descriptions)
- Core Standard Onboarding: baseline 90-day plan with security training, benefits enrollment, manager 30/60/90 goals and weekly 1:1 cadence.
- Restricted Onboarding: additional security orientation, expedited IAM provisioning, elevated audit logging for first 30 days.
- Accelerated Immersion: preboarding reading checklist, assigned project with narrow scope, daily standups first 2 weeks, weekly deliverable reviews.
- Compliance-Extended: staged paperwork, legal sign-offs, delayed access to production until checks complete.

Manager checklist (first 30/60/90 — condensed)
- Day 0–7: complete role-specific equipment and access; schedule 30/60/90 goal alignment; introduce to buddy; assign first-week small deliverable.
- Day 8–30: weekly check-ins; confirm completion of security and compliance training; evaluate initial pass/fail on deliverable; adjust ramp plan.
- Day 31–90: bi-weekly checkpoints; evaluate against three core KPIs defined at offer; formal 90-day calibration with HRBP.

Metrics and reporting:
- Offer conversion rate (verbal -> signed) target: >= 85%.
- Time-to-offer median: <= 4 days.
- Offer approval exceptions: logged and reviewed monthly; target fewer than 5% of hires.
- Onboarding pathway accuracy: measure after 90 days if assigned pathway matched actual risk/need; target >= 90% correct routing.

Escalation and exceptions:
- Use the Hiring Exception queue for unusual packages. Exception requests must include business justification, alternate candidates considered, and an ROI statement.
- Exceptions older than 7 days without approval auto-escalate to People Ops Director.

Templates and artifacts (examples to copy into ATS or People Ops system):
1) Negotiation log CSV header: date, negotiator, field_changed, candidate_request, decision, cost_delta_to_budget, manager_comment
2) Offer email snippet: "We are excited to extend the role of <ROLE> at Redwood Inference. Your base salary will be <AMOUNT>, equity <DETAILS>, and benefits <LINK>. Please review the attached offer and return a signed copy by <DATE>."
3) 30/60/90 Goals template: three objectives per period, success criteria, owner, and measurement method.

Related playbooks and references:
- Structured hiring committee protocol (link in related_pages).
- Manager 30/60/90 templates (People Ops templates library).

Revision history and governance:
- This playbook is maintained by People Ops (owner: Nina R. Shah).
- Review cycle: annually or after any significant comp band or legal change.
- Change approvals: HRBP + Head of People for policy changes; People Ops Director for process changes.

Appendix: example offer approval email subject
- Subject: "Approval Request: Offer for <Candidate Name> — Role <Role> — Level <L#> — Compensation uplift <+X%>"

End of document.
