Title: people-ops

people-ops

dave (Eng Manager): Quick question from a manager: we promoted someone during a hiring freeze and want to increase comp beyond band max. Is that allowed?
cecilia (People Ops): Hiring freeze doesn't automatically block promotions, but increases above band max are exceptional. You need manager + director sign-off and a compensation justification packet.
sasha (Compensation): Correct. Submit /forms/comp-change-request and pick 'Exception: Above band'. Provide 3 evidence bullets tied to the leveling rubric and any peer comps. Committee will evaluate tradeoffs (parity, compression).
harper (HRBP): Also include employee impact notes (retention risk, flight risk) and confirmation that this isn't part of wide-scale band rework.
dave (Eng Manager): If committee approves, can we do retro pay? employee started receiving lower comp for 2 pay cycles already.
mike (Payroll): We can do retro pay as a one-off if approval is before payroll cutoff (10th). If after cutoff it'll post on next payroll. Retro amounts are taxed per payroll rules.
sasha (Compensation): One nuance: if this pushes someone past the band max by a lot, Compensation might propose an alternate like a phased raise or spot retention bonus to avoid long-term compression. We'll document options in the decision.
cecilia (People Ops): Managers, checklist to speed this: 1) /forms/comp-change-request -> 'Exception' 2) attach rubric examples, peer comps, and director sign-off 3) state requested effective date 4) cc Finance if >$25k ARR impact.
dave (Eng Manager): What about equity? can we top-up equity instead of base to avoid pushing them above band?
sasha (Compensation): Equity top-ups are possible but require Total Rewards approval and may wait for the next grant cycle. If timing is urgent, committee sometimes approves a one-time cash + future equity plan.
cecilia (People Ops): Final note: exceptions create precedent. If you're uncertain, ping me or @sasha with a short summary before submitting the form and we'll do a quick pre-check.
dave (Eng Manager): Thanks, will DM the summary now.
cecilia (People Ops): thx! I'll log a playbook example after this case is closed.

Title: people-ops

people-ops

Jamal (Hiring Manager): Hey folks — candidate for Senior Infra Eng is asking for $185k base which is above our Seattle pay tier for this role. They also need to start 2 weeks earlier than our proposed window. Can we do a market adjustment + expedite approval so we don't lose them?
Priya (People Ops): Thanks Jamal. Can you paste the complete proposed offer (base, equity, sign-on, relocation if any) and the reason we should approve an exception? Also flag if candidate has a competing offer.
Jamal (Hiring Manager): Sure — they have an offer from a startup at $190k but no RSUs. Our proposed:
```
base: $185000
RSU: 10k over 4 yrs
sign-on: $7k (one-time)
start_date: 2026-04-06 (need to move from 2026-04-20)
location: Seattle (remote-first)
reason: rare infra infra background + immediate ramp needed for major customer P0
```
Carlos (Comp & Ben): Ok. Seattle pay tier for Senior Infra is $150–165k base typically. Market adj to $185k is material. Need short justification memo for comp committee: business justification, candidate scarcity, external comp evidence (e.g., offer), and confirmation that total comp stays within approved band+budget after adjustments. Title: offer-negotiation-and-evidence-based-comp-guidance-2026

offer-negotiation-and-evidence-based-comp-guidance-2026

Summary:
This guide explains Redwood's recommended approach for offer conversations, manager negotiation cadence, and the evidence required to approve exceptions to published compensation bands. It is written for hiring managers and people-ops partners who are operating within our PLG-led hiring funnel and need to close offers quickly while preserving internal equity and auditability.

Scope and intent:
- Applies to all full-time and long-term contractor offer decisions made by hiring managers in North America and Europe.
- Does NOT supplant legal review for international tax/immigration clauses, nor special enterprise-customer sign-on incentives (refer to Finance & Legal).
- Purpose: accelerate decision-making, reduce offer cycles, and create auditable compensation decisions with clear business justification.

Key principles (short):
1) Evidence-first: Every offer above midpoint of band requires at least two documented data points (market comp data, internal benchmark, or demonstrable business impact).
2) Manager accountability: Hiring manager owns initial offer strategy; people-ops owns approval and audit.
3) Speed with guardrails: 48-hour SLA on approvals for standard offers; 72–96 hours for comp-exceptions.

Pre-offer checklist (Manager):
1. Confirm role band and level using Compensation Bands doc.
2. Document candidate target in ATS with: current comp, target comp, sign-on needs, relocation, and preferred start date.
3. Capture 2 supporting evidence artifacts (select at least two):
   - Market benchmark snapshot (Radford, levels.fyi, external recruiter comps)
   - Internal comparator evidence (names of 1–2 recent hires at same band + hire dates and onsite summaries)
   - Unique candidate outcome evidence (e.g., published patents, shipped feature with metrics, prior revenue/ARR linked to role)
4. Early people-ops sync: Drop a 30-minute slot in People-ops intake channel with docs attached.

Offer structure recommendations (standard template):
- Base salary (annual)
- Target bonus / variable comp (if applicable)
- Equity grant: grant size, expected vesting schedule, refresh eligibility note
- Sign-on bonus (one-time): amount and payment timing
- Relocation or work-authorization support (if applicable)
- Start date and probation period highlights

Manager negotiation script (concise, for live or email):
- Positive open: "We're excited about your skills — we think you'll add X to our team in the first 90 days."
- Offer summary: "The proposed package is..." (list components succinctly).
- If counter: "We evaluated market data and internal precedents. Here are two reasons we landed here..."
- If candidate requests more: "I hear that. To request an adjustment, I'll need one or more of these: 1) competing offer docs; 2) evidence of materially different responsibilities; 3) a short summary of business impact the candidate will drive. I'll get back within 72 hours."

Escalation & approval workflow (people-ops + manager):
1. Standard offer (within band midpoint or below): Manager issues offer; people-ops notified via ATS for audit. Approval SLA: 48 hours.
2. Near-band top (between midpoint and top): Manager must attach evidence checklist and people-ops signs off. Approval SLA: 48–72 hours.
3. Above-band/top or outlier total comp (>15% above top of band or large equity deviation): People-ops requires executive compensation sign-off (Head of People or Finance), written justification with evidence, and a calibrated review meeting. Approval SLA: 72–96 hours.
4. Special cases (counteroffers, relocation packages above guideline, or candidate-requested guaranteed bonuses): Legal and Finance routing required; expect longer lead time.

Required evidence matrix (for exceptions):
- Exception type: External competitive offer 
  - Required evidence: full competing offer document (redacted as needed), recruiter confirmation, and market benchmark 
- Exception type: Role scope misalignment with band 
  - Required evidence: updated job packet, peer comparator list, and hiring manager written justification (150–300 words)
- Exception type: Critical hire for product or revenue impact 
  - Required evidence: product/CS/BD owner email with measurable OKR/impact and a 30/60/90 plan

Audit & recordkeeping:
- People-ops will attach the compensation decision record to the ATS candidate record and the central comp-exceptions spreadsheet (retained 7 years).
- All approvals must be captured as a signed email thread or approval in the HRIS approval flow.
- Redacted evidence may be saved for future calibration sessions.

Manager templates (copy/paste):
- Offer email subject: "Redwood | Offer: [Role] — [Candidate Name]"
- Offer email body (short):
  "Hi [Candidate],

  We're excited to offer you the [Role] on the [Team]. Below is the summary of your offer: 
  - Base: $[base]
  - Bonus target: [X%] of base
  - Equity: [grant, vesting]
  - Sign-on: $[amount] (if applicable)

  This is a formal offer contingent on standard background checks. Please let me know if you'd like to discuss. We request a decision by [date].

  Best,
  [Hiring Manager]"

People-ops intake form (fields to copy into ATS notes):
- Candidate name, role, band, proposed comp, candidate current comp, additional ask amount, evidence links (market/internal/comparators), business-impact note, manager name, proposed start date, hiring manager ETA for response.

Common negotiation scenarios and recommended responses:
1. Candidate asks for higher equity because of anticipated future value: Explain our refresh cadence and grant philosophy; offer a targeted performance-linked milestone for a mid-year review if appropriate.
2. Competing cash offer materially higher: Request proof of offer; evaluate whether this hire is mission-critical and whether an exception is warranted.
3. Senior hire asking for above-band salary for retention from current employer: Validate retention risk and document the business impact. Consider limited sign-on tied to 6–12 month retention clause.

Operating metrics and SLAs to monitor (people-ops):
- Time from verbal acceptance to written offer: target <24 hours for standard offers.
- Approval SLA adherence: 95% within stated SLAs.
- Offer acceptance rate by band and role: tracked monthly; escalate negative trends to Head of Talent.

Training and calibration cadence for managers:
- Quarterly 45-minute calibration sessions run by People-ops covering 10 recent offers (redacted) with comparative evidence.
- Annual comp-band refresh workshops with Finance to update midpoint/top guidelines.

Appendix A — Example justification snippet (150 words):
"Candidate X commanded a lead engineering position at a competitor where they led delivery of a low-latency feature that improved retention by 8% and enabled $3M incremental ARR. We have two internal comparators hired in the last 12 months at the same level whose profiles and responsibilities align closely; market benchmarking from two vendors supports a proposal 12% above midpoint. Given the role is critical to Q3 roadmap delivery and the quantified business impact, we request an above-band base with a conditional 6-month performance review for a staged equity refresh."

Appendix B — Legal & regional considerations:
- EU hires: Include gross-to-net guidance specific to country. Work with Finance on tax gross-up only if pre-approved.
- Relocation and immigration: Offer contingencies must be explicit; coordinate with Ops and Legal for timelines.

Questions, exceptions, or requests for a calibration review should be directed to people-ops@example.redwood.com.

Document ownership and revision history:
- Owner: People-ops (Comp & Offer Operations)
- Next scheduled review: 2027-01-15
- Revision notes: 2026-03-02 — published initial People-ops approved version.

Title: Synchronous Incident Orchestra: Playbook, Bridge Operator Guide, and Status Lexicon

Synchronous Incident Orchestra: Playbook, Bridge Operator Guide, and Status Lexicon

Summary:
This document defines Redwood's Synchronous Incident Orchestra (SIO) pattern: a prescriptive, low-latency operational model for coordinating cross-functional responders during high-severity incidents. It includes: the Bridge Operator role checklist, a concise signal/status lexicon for internal and customer updates, micro-runbooks for three frequent incident classes (kv-cache storm, GPU throttling/backpressure, model-quality regression), an evidence collection template, an on-call rotation heuristic, and a reusable customer status template set.

Purpose and scope:
- Purpose: reduce cognitive load during live incidents by standardizing who does what, how we speak internally and externally, and what evidence we collect for postmortem.
- Scope: applies to incidents that trigger a PagerDuty P2/P1 and/or affect Redwood-hosted inference availability, latency SLOs, or model quality affecting customer SLAs. Does not replace service-specific runbooks; it supplements them with orchestration guidance.

Key principles (two-line reminders):
1) Single conductor: the Bridge Operator centralizes messaging, run loop cadence, and decision capture. Do not have multiple people simultaneously authoring customer-facing statuses.
2) Fast evidence, slow narrative: capture telemetry and timelines aggressively; craft the narrative after stabilization.
3) Tiered customer signal: internal severity -> public status -> targeted customer notice (only if impacted).

Roles and responsibilities:
- Bridge Operator (primary): open and operate the incident bridge, own public status cadence, coordinate canary rollbacks/fallbacks, ensure evidence collection. Recommended rotation: on-call SRE or most senior engineer available for first 90 minutes.
- Service Owner(s): subject-matter expert for the failing service (runtime, routing, kv-cache, model infra). Responsible for triage and runbook execution.
- Customer Liaison (CS): drafts targeted customer notices, triggers legal/enterprise comms if necessary.
- Incident Commander (if declared): focuses on high-level decisions (escalate to execs, pause rollouts).
- Observability Lead: owns metric dashboards, traces, SLO delta calculations.

Bridge Operator checklist (first 10 minutes):
1. Acknowledge the page and declare bridge with YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC timestamp.
2. Create incident ticket in tracking system: priority, short summary, affected services, initial hypothesis. Example (curl):
   curl -X POST https://incidents.company/api/v1/tickets -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' -d '{"summary":"P1: Inference latency spike - us-west-2","priority":"P1","service":"runtime-routing"}'
3. Post short internal Slack channel message (incident-bridge-<id>): one-line impact and link to ticket and status page. Use STATUS LEXICON (below).
4. Assign roles: service owner, observability, customer liaison, and a scribe.
5. Run immediate health checks: service pod counts, 95th/99th latency, error rate, GPU metrics (util, memory errors), KV cache miss rate. Paste outputs to bridge.
6. Decide containment action (throttle, fallback model, regional routing) and execute safe mitigation.

Signal & status lexicon (single-line canonical phrases) for rapid messages:
- INTERNAL: degrading / partial-degradation / outage / performance-regression / quality-regression.
- PUBLIC (status page short form):
  - Operational: no customer impact.
  - Partial degradation: some requests slower or erroring; workaround available.
  - Service outage: customers unable to use endpoint(s).
  - Quality anomaly: model outputs inconsistent with baseline (may not affect availability).
- CUSTOMER NOTICE templates are below (Targeted Notice = TN).

Escalation thresholds (SLO-driven):
- Severity P1 (outage): >= 10% of global requests failing or >99th latency exceed SLO by 200% for >5 minutes.
- Severity P2 (partial degradation): 2–10% customer requests impacted, or 99th latency >150% of SLO for >10 minutes.
- Severity P3: localized/regional noise or single-customer degradation.

Micro-runbooks (quick playbooks intended for Bridge Operator & Service Owner):
1) KV-Cache Storm (symptoms: sudden spike in backend calls, miss_rate >= 20%, tail latency jump)
   - Immediate checks: cache eviction logs, Redis/etcd CPU, network saturations.
   - Quick mitigations (in order):
     a) Enable read-through bypass: route hot prefixes to model runtime with an enforced rate limit.
     b) Scale caching tier (vertical or horizontal) if autoscaler healthy.
     c) Re-enable prefix KVC previews (rolling restart with mem profiling).
   - Rollback criteria: if miss_rate < 5% and tail latency returns within SLO in 15m.
   - Evidence to collect: cache metrics (hit/miss), trace samples showing cache lookup latency, example request ids.

2) GPU Throttle / Backpressure (symptoms: queue buildup, 'cuda OOM' logs, degraded throughput)
   - Immediate checks: node GPU memory, per-process GPU utilization, scheduler queue lengths, host-level I/O.
   - Quick mitigations:
     a) Shift non-critical traffic to lower-priority pool or degraded model variant.
     b) Enable admission control: cap max tokens or per-request concurrency for affected routes.
     c) If hardware fault suspected, cordon node and trigger replacement; if capacity issue, enable burst capacity from Dedicated.
   - Safety note: do not kill model processes without capturing minidumps/traces.
   - Evidence: GPU dmesg, pod logs (OOM traces), scheduler events, admission control metrics.

3) Model Quality Regression (symptoms: increased human-reported failures, eval metric drift, regression alerts)
   - Immediate checks: recent deployments, model rollouts, prompt set failures, eval harness baseline diffs.
   - Quick mitigations:
     a) Rollback to pinned model version or enable deterministic model variant.
     b) Fallback to safety-output filter or apply conservative decoding params.
     c) If rollback infeasible, throttle usage for customers with strict QA.
   - Evidence: prompt/eval set diffs, example model responses, deployment diffs, config changes.

Incident run loop template (recommended cadence):
- T+0m: Bridge open, 10-min triage, containment decision.
- T+10m: Status check, mitigation in-progress, post first public status if customer-impacting.
- T+30m: Stabilization checkpoint; if not stabilized, escalate to Incident Commander.
- T+60m: Decision point: continue mitigations vs. rollbacks vs. declare extended outage and notify execs.
- Recovery: run stabilization 30/60/120 minute updates; after stable for 60 minutes, prepare recovery notice.

Customer status templates (canonical fragments to reduce back-and-forth):
- Short public update (for status page):
  "[HH:MM UTC] Partial degradation: API latency elevated in US-WEST. We have identified increased cache miss rates as a contributing factor and are routing traffic to a fallback path. Engineers are investigating; customers may see higher latency for up to 60 minutes."

- Targeted customer notice (for impacted enterprise customers):
  Subject: [Incident #ID] Brief service impact affecting inference latency
  Body:
  Hi <CustomerName>,
  We observed elevated inference latency impacting <routes>. Our engineers are applying a traffic fallback to reduce error rates while we stabilize the cache layer. Estimated time to full recovery: ~1 hour. We will send updates every 30 minutes or when there is material change.
  - Impact: increased latency, potential timeouts
  - Mitigation in-progress: routing to fallback model, temporarily reducing per-request concurrency
  - Point of contact: <Customer Liaison> (link)

- Recovery notice:
  "[HH:MM UTC] Service recovery: latency back within SLOs. Root cause analysis in progress; postmortem to follow within 72 hours."

Postmortem & evidence checklist (requirements for a publishable RFC-style postmortem):
1) Incident summary (impact, duration, severity).
2) Timeline (minute-granular, who did what). Use the timeline shorthand: [HH:MM] <actor> - <action>.
3) Root cause analysis (1–2 paragraphs) and contributing factors.
4) Evidence artifacts linked: dashboards (direct URLs), logs (selected tsv/csv of error lines), traces (span ids), heapdumps/minidumps, ticket ids.
5) Corrective actions (owner and due date) and preventative actions (monitoring, runbook changes).
6) Customer impact and communication copies.

On-call rotation heuristic (policy, not rigid):
- Principle: minimize cognitive burden for mid-night responders while ensuring senior coverage in business hours.
- Pattern: 7-day primary rotation with a 3-day overlap 'senior-on-call' shadow for high-severity windows (08:00-20:00 local).
- Handovers: automated slack post with recent escalations (last 24h), active incidents, and outstanding action items. Handover must include ticket links and the last three status messages.

Game day (practice) recipe (2–3 hour lab):
- Objectives: validate SIO cadence, test bridge operator handoff, evaluate customer notice creation speed, and measure mean-time-to-first-mitigation (target <15m).
- Participants: 1 Bridge Operator, 2 SREs, 2 Service Owners, 1 Customer Liaison, 1 Observability lead.
- Scenario examples: simulated kv-cache evictions during peak load; model variant rollback during canary.
- Success criteria: attendees complete run loop, evidence artifacts captured, and postmortem written as a learning doc within 48h.

Runbook governance & maintenance:
- Every micro-runbook must be reviewed quarterly by the owning team and validated during at least one game day per year.
- Bridge Operator playbook to be updated after every P1 with a corrective-action that changes language or procedure.

Appendix A — Status page message lexicon (short forms for automated publish):
- OP: operational
- PD: partial_degradation
- OUT: outage
- QRG: quality_regression

Appendix B — Quick evidence command snippets:
- Dump recent 1k logs for service runtime: kubectl -n runtime logs --tail=1000 -l app=runtime > /tmp/runtime-logs-$(date +%s).log
- Capture 99/95 latency: prometheus query: rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{service="runtime"}[5m]) -> export as CSV via /api/v1/query_range

Appendix C — Minimal postmortem template (copy/paste):
Title: [Incident #ID] <one-line summary>
Severity: P1/P2
Start: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC
End: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC
Impact: <short list>
Timeline:
- [HH:MM] Bridge Operator - opened bridge and created ticket #ID
- [HH:MM] Service Owner - executed mitigation Y
Root cause:
Contributing factors:
Corrective actions:
Preventative actions:
Evidence links:
Customer communications:
Owner(s):
Reviewers:

Related pages and references:
- eng-sre/incidence-metrics (dashboards)
- eng-serving-runtime/kv-cache-architecture
- eng-private-deployments/rollback-guides

Contact & escalation directory:
- PagerDuty: prod-oncall@srv.rdwd.co
- Slack bridge channel: #bridge-<incident-id> (created per incident)
- SRE lead: Diego Alvarez (diego@redwood.com)
- Oncall policy steward: Priya Nair (pri@redwood.com)

Document maintenance log:
- 2025-11-15: created (Maya Chen)
- 2026-03-02: updated signal lexicon and added GPU throttle section (Maya Chen)

End of document.

Title: Perf Suite Profiling Playbook (Q1 2026 Baseline)

Perf Suite Profiling Playbook (Q1 2026 Baseline)

## Purpose
This playbook describes how to reproduce a perf-suite result and capture the artifacts needed to attribute changes (runtime, scheduler, kernels, environment). It is intended for:
- Investigating perf-canary regressions (PR-level, nightly, or release-branch).
- Explaining deltas between baseline runs (Q1 2026 “golden” anchor) and candidate changes.
- Producing consistent traces/logs that can be shared across Runtime, Kernels, and SRE.

This page focuses on *how to profile* (traces, kernel timelines, scheduler logs) rather than *what workloads to run*. For workload definitions and required metrics, see the baseline plan and representative suite pages.

---

## What “good” looks like (minimum artifact set)
For any investigated run, attach or link the following artifacts (even if you also have dashboards):
1) Run manifest JSON (per ADR-0172) with *all* environment capture enabled.
2) Results JSON/CSV (p50/p95/p99 TTFT, TPOT, throughput, plus variance statistics if available).
3) Scheduler log bundle:
   - Queue wait time distribution
   - Batch assembly time distribution
   - Batch size histogram
   - Load-shed/drop counters (if any)
   - Correlation IDs / request IDs for trace alignment
4) Kernel selection debug dump (sampled) with fallback reasons (if any).
5) Nsight Systems (nsys) trace for at least one representative interval.
6) Optional but recommended: Nsight Compute (ncu) capture for the top 1–3 kernels (only when kernel-level regression is suspected).

---

## Measurement boundaries (so traces match reported metrics)
To avoid “apples to oranges,” ensure the profiling run uses the same boundaries as the perf suite metrics:
- **TTFT (Time To First Token)**: measured at the server boundary: request admitted → first token emitted to server streaming layer. Excludes client read/parse time.
- **TPOT (Time Per Output Token)**: measured at the server boundary for decode tokens only. Excludes prefill; excludes client overhead.
- **Throughput**: server-side tokens/sec or requests/sec depending on endpoint mode.

If you must deviate (e.g., reproducing a customer report with client-side timings), label the run explicitly as “client-inclusive” and do not compare to baseline dashboards without adjustment.

---

## Preconditions / Setup checklist
### A. Confirm you are targeting the same baseline anchor
Before profiling, confirm the baseline anchor for comparison:
- Runtime git SHA / tag (baseline)
- Benchmark harness version
- Model revision (weights + tokenizer)
- Scheduler profile and kernel-selection ruleset
- Region and GPU SKU

If you are unsure which build is the Q1 baseline anchor, check the baseline freeze thread and the baseline run tracker.

### B. Reduce variance (required for attribution)
These steps are required for “baseline-comparable” profiling runs:
1) Use a dedicated benchmarking node (no co-tenancy).
2) Lock GPU application clocks where permitted by fleet policy.
3) Pin CPU governor to performance.
4) Ensure consistent container image and driver/CUDA versions.
5) Run standardized warmup (see below).

If any variance-reduction step cannot be applied, mark the run as “non-baseline-comparable” in the run label and expect higher noise.

### C. Warmup standard (required)
Warmup reduces first-run variance from model load, JIT/compilation caches, allocator behavior, and KV cache initialization.
- Warmup duration: 3–5 minutes per (model, GPU, workload mode)
- Warmup workload: same request shape as the measured workload, but with lower concurrency
- Discard warmup metrics; only analyze traces taken after warmup completes

---

## Run labeling and naming conventions
Consistent naming is required so engineers can drill down from dashboard → manifest → traces.

### Run ID format
Use the following run_id format (single line, no spaces):
`perfq1_2026/<workload>/<model>/<region>/<gpu>/<runtime_sha>/<harness_ver>/<timestamp_utc>/<run_variant>`

Examples:
- `perfq1_2026/chat_streaming/llama3_1_70b/us-east/h100/7c3a91f/v1.8.2/2026-02-03T21-14-08Z/cold_cache`
- `perfq1_2026/long_prefill/qwen2_5_72b/eu-west/a100/7c3a91f/v1.8.2/2026-02-03T23-40-51Z/warm_cache`

### Required run_variant tags
Include at least these tags as part of the run_variant suffix:
- `cold_cache` or `warm_cache` (we report both; do not mix)
- `baseline_comparable` or `non_baseline_comparable`

Optional tags (use when relevant):
- `kernel_pin_<name>` (if pinning a kernel)
- `scheduler_override_<name>` (if changing scheduler knobs)
- `client_inclusive` (only if using client-side TTFT)

---

## Step-by-step: reproduce a perf suite run with profiling enabled
> The exact CLI flags may vary by harness version; the intent is to capture the same artifact set. If a flag below doesn’t exist in your harness build, file an issue in benchmark-lab and note it in the run summary.

### 1) Create (or locate) the canonical manifest
1. Start from the manifest used by the baseline run (from dashboards or the run tracker).
2. Copy it and increment `manifest_version` only if required by schema changes.
3. Verify these fields are present and accurate:
   - Model identifier + revision
   - Hardware: GPU SKU, GPU count, MIG settings (if any)
   - Region/zone
   - Runtime build SHA + build type
   - Driver/CUDA/Triton versions
   - Scheduler profile name + knobs
   - Kernel selection ruleset version
   - Workload seed and distribution parameters
   - Cache mode (cold/warm)

**Output:** `run_manifest.json`

### 2) Ensure environment capture is on
Enable full environment capture in the harness:
- GPU info (nvidia-smi dump)
- Driver/CUDA versions
- Container image digest
- Host kernel version
- CPU model, NUMA topology summary
- Power/clock settings (if available)

**Sanity check:** ensure the manifest “env” section is populated before you proceed. Missing env capture is a common reason runs can’t be compared later.

### 3) Run standardized warmup
Run warmup using the same workload generator but with reduced concurrency.
- Confirm warmup completes without errors (no OOM, no load-shed unless expected).
- Confirm steady-state GPU utilization.

**Output:** warmup logs (attach if investigating stability issues).

### 4) Run the measured workload and collect scheduler + kernel dumps
Run the measured workload with:
- Scheduler instrumentation enabled (queue wait, batch assembly time, batch size distributions).
- Kernel selection debug dump enabled (sampled is fine; 1–5% sampling is typical).

**Outputs:**
- `results.json` (metrics)
- `scheduler_metrics.jsonl` or equivalent
- `kernel_selection_dump.jsonl`

### 5) Capture an Nsight Systems (nsys) trace (required for attribution)
Capture nsys for a representative steady-state window. Recommendations:
- Trace window: 30–90 seconds during steady state.
- Capture CUDA + NVTX ranges.
- Minimize trace overhead: avoid tracing the full run unless necessary.

Operational guidance:
- If you control the runtime build, ensure key phases emit NVTX ranges:
  - request admitted
  - queue wait
  - batch assembly
  - prefill
  - decode
  - stream flush
- If ranges are missing, still capture the trace; file an issue for missing NVTX markers.

**Output:** `trace.nsys-rep` (or equivalent).

### 6) Optional: Nsight Compute (ncu) for kernel regressions
Use ncu only when:
- A regression correlates with a kernel selection change, or
- nsys shows kernel time dominated by one/few kernels, or
- Kernel-level variance is suspected (e.g., new fused attention path).

Guidelines:
- Profile a single process and short window to keep overhead manageable.
- Focus on top kernels by time; avoid broad “collect everything” profiles.

**Output:** `kernel_profile.ncu-rep` (or equivalent).

### 7) Upload artifacts and link them in the run summary
For every run you investigate, create a short run summary (Confluence comment, Slack triage thread, or ticket) that includes:
- run_id
- manifest link
- results link
- trace links
- “what changed” hypothesis
- whether the run is baseline-comparable

---

## Artifact checklist and where to find them
Attach links (preferred) rather than pasting raw files into Confluence.

Required artifacts:
- Run manifest: `run_manifest.json`
- Results: `results.json` (or results CSV exported by harness)
- Scheduler logs: `scheduler_metrics.jsonl`
- Kernel selection dump: `kernel_selection_dump.jsonl`
- Nsight Systems trace: `trace.nsys-rep`

Recommended context:
- Full runtime logs for the measured window (with correlation IDs)
- GPU clock/thermal readings during the run
- Harness configuration file used to launch

---

## How to align traces with reported metrics
When investigating TTFT p99 or TPOT p99 changes, align the following:
1) Pick a set of request IDs from the tail (p99 cohort) in the results export.
2) Locate those request IDs in scheduler logs:
   - Identify whether tail comes from queue wait, batch assembly, prefill, decode, or stream flush.
3) In the nsys trace, confirm:
   - GPU busy/idle patterns during the tail interval
   - Kernel timeline changes (different kernels, different durations)
   - CPU-side stalls that correlate with queue wait or dispatch
4) Cross-check kernel selection dump:
   - Ensure the expected kernel regime is selected for the sequence length bins
   - Investigate fallback reasons (often the root cause of step-function regressions)

Common interpretations:
- **Higher TTFT p99 with stable throughput:** often queueing/backpressure or batch-assembly changes.
- **Higher TPOT with stable TTFT:** often decode kernel changes, KV cache behavior, or reduced overlap.
- **Lower throughput with higher TTFT:** often saturation, contention, or poor batching efficiency.

---

## Common failure modes and quick triage
### 1) Trace shows client bottleneck (not server)
Symptoms:
- Server-side metrics look stable, but external client TTFT inflates.
Actions:
- Confirm you’re using server-boundary TTFT.
- Ensure streaming pacing is server-driven in the harness (avoid client read throttling).

### 2) Variance too high to attribute
Symptoms:
- Repeated runs differ by more than the regression threshold; p99 swings without code changes.
Actions:
- Verify clock locking and isolation.
- Increase sample size.
- Ensure warmup was performed.
- Check for node-level noise: thermal throttling, background jobs, noisy neighbor.

### 3) Kernel fallback
Symptoms:
- Step-function slowdown at particular sequence lengths.
Actions:
- Inspect kernel selection dump for fallback reasons.
- Compare to the kernel selection matrix for expected regimes.
- Consider pinning the baseline kernel temporarily for diagnosis; label run_variant accordingly.

### 4) Scheduler overload / load-shed
Symptoms:
- Elevated drop counters, timeouts, or long queue wait.
Actions:
- Confirm concurrency targets match workload spec.
- Validate backpressure thresholds (baseline vs overridden).
- Use scheduler metrics to determine whether overload is admission control vs batch assembly.

---

## When to open a ticket vs continue debugging
Open a Linear issue (or escalate to perf triage) when any of the following are true:
- Regression is reproducible in baseline-comparable conditions.
- Kernel selection changed unexpectedly vs matrix.
- Scheduler metrics show a clear regime shift (queue wait, batch size collapse) not explained by workload.
- Trace indicates a new stall in a known critical path (prefill/decode overlap, KV cache operations).

Include in the ticket:
- run_id(s)
- baseline comparison run_id(s)
- links to manifest/results/traces
- suspected component owner (scheduler/kernels/runtime infra)

---

## Owner / Questions
Primary owners:
- Benchmark harness & methodology: Rina Kobayashi, Claire Dubois
- Scheduler instrumentation: Sofia Ivanova
- Kernel selection & kernel timelines: Hiro Tanaka
- SRE benchmarking fleet stability: Sean Gallagher

If you encounter missing instrumentation (NVTX ranges absent, logs not emitted, schema fields missing), file an issue against the appropriate repo and link it in the run summary so the next investigation is faster.

Title: Responder rotation synthesis and deferred postmortem protocol

Responder rotation synthesis and deferred postmortem protocol

Overview:

This playbook describes Redwood's responder rotation synthesis process and a lightweight Deferred Postmortem (DPM) protocol for incidents that meet defined criteria. It combines on-call scheduling practices, a structured bridge handoff procedure, and customer-facing messaging templates designed for speed and clarity. The goal is to reduce cognitive load during high-impact events and to ensure timely learning when full postmortems are not immediately practical.

Scope:
- Applies to: SRE, Serving Runtime, Platform, and Incident Response stakeholders.
- Excludes: low-priority alerts that resolve without human intervention (see 'Auto-resolved alerts' below).

Definitions:
- Responder rotation synthesis: periodic review and rebalancing of on-call shifts, handoffs, and escalation ladders to maintain equitable load and coverage.
- Deferred Postmortem (DPM): a time-boxed post-incident review that defers non-critical analysis until stakeholders are available, while still capturing root evidence and action items immediately.

Key principles:
1) Fast stabilization first: prioritize containment and customer impact minimization.
2) Minimal friction handoffs: standardized bridge transfer reduces repeated context overhead.
3) Continuous learning: short DPMs for low-severity incidents; full postmortems for Sev1/Sev2.
4) Equity in rotations: no responder assigned >36 hours continuous duty without relief.

On-call rotation design (synthesis process):
1. Quarterly synthesis review (owner: SRE lead):
   - Pull the last quarter's on-call logs and pager counts.
   - Calculate median and 95th percentile pager counts per responder.
   - Identify top-10% busiest windows and common root causes.
2. Rebalance rules:
   - Move noisy services to a dedicated micro-rotation if they account for >25% of pages.
   - Limit night-weekend primary duty to volunteers in the rotation unless emergency staffing required.
3. Local fairness check (monthly):
   - Team leads run a 15-minute review in the first week of each month to confirm schedule fairness and swap if needed.

Rotation constraints (config):
| Constraint | Value | Rationale |
|---|---:|---|
| Max continuous on-call | 36h | Prevent fatigue and degraded decision-making |
| Minimum handoff overlap | 15m | Time to summarize bridge state and outstanding actions |
| Max weekly duty | 56h | Prevent single-responder overload across teams |
| Handoff notes retention | 90d | Auditability and incident reconstruction |

Bridge handoff procedure (step-by-step):
1) Pre-handoff checklist (outgoing):
   - Summarize incident timeline, current hypotheses, mitigation steps in progress, and customer impact.
   - Confirm runbook page(s) in Bridge tab are current and link to traces/log queries.
2) Live handoff (over bridge):
   - 5–15 minute verbal summary; ensure incoming acknowledges critical mitigations.
   - If unresolved customer-impacting work remains, assign an owner and ETA.
3) Post-handoff (incoming):
   - Record a 1-line status in the incident timeline and attach a minimum evidence set (logs, traces, alert IDs).

Incident lifecycle and DPM decision matrix:
- If incident is Sev1 or multi-tenant Sev2 -> full postmortem required within 72 hours of remediation.
- If incident meets ALL of the following, use DPM: single-tenant, <30 minutes customer-visible impact, known cause, effective mitigation applied at resolution.
- Otherwise triage for full postmortem.

Deferred Postmortem (DPM) protocol (when to use and how):
Purpose: capture essential facts and actions quickly when resource constraints or ongoing high operational tempo would make a full postmortem impractical in 72 hours.
DPM steps (owner: incident lead):
1) Within 8 hours of incident resolution: populate DPM template with
   - 1-line summary, impact window (start/end), services affected, severity, and customer impact.
   - Evidence snapshot (link to logs, runbook used, mitigation commands).
2) Create action items with clear owners and SLAs (default: 14-day action SLA).
3) Flag DPM for follow-up in the next synthesis meeting.
4) If DPM reveals systemic risk or unresolved unknowns, escalate to full postmortem.

DPM template (minimum fields):
- Title (1 line)
- Date/time window
- Affected services and teams (comma-separated)
- Immediate mitigations executed
- Evidence links (logs, traces, alert IDs)
- Action items (owner | due date | description)
- Decision to close DPM or escalate (yes/no)

Escalation and timeline expectations:
- Immediate: severity declaration and customer status update within 30 minutes of detection for Sev1/Sev2.
- Short window: initial triage and bridge stand-up within 60 minutes.
- DPM creation: within 8 hours.
- Full postmortem: published within 72 hours for Sev1/Sev2.

Customer communications templates (for bridge operator use):
- Initial status (first 30m):
  "We have identified an issue affecting [feature/service]. Our team has engaged and is investigating. We will provide an update within 30 minutes."

- Follow-up status (post-triage):
  "Update: The issue is caused by [brief cause]. Mitigations underway include [actions]. Current impact: [scope]. Next update scheduled at [time/ETA]."

- Resolution notice:
  "Resolved: The issue affecting [service] has been mitigated at [time]. Root cause and next steps will be published in a follow-up note or postmortem."

- SLA-credit preliminary message (if applicable):
  "We are assessing impact against our SLA commitments. If you are eligible, we will follow up with credit details once our postmortem is complete."

Game day design and schedule (90-minute template):
- Goal: validate handoff, DPM creation, and customer comms speed.
- Attendees: 1 bridge operator, 2 responders, 1 product EM, 1 customer success observer.
- Timeline:
  00:00 — Inject alert and distribute pager
  00:05 — Bridge up and first customer status sent
  00:20 — Handoff simulation between responders
  00:45 — DPM skeleton completed and action items assigned
  01:05 — Demo of status page update flow and mock SLA notice
  01:20 — 15-minute retro and lessons logged

Runbook snippets (examples):
- Quick KV-cache eviction (serving-runtime):
  "# Commands
  kubectl exec -n runtime svc/cache-operator -- cache evict --pattern=*
  # Verify: tail logs for 200 responses to health endpoint for 5m"

- Throttle mitigation (traffic spike):
  "1) Move non-critical traffic to burst_throttle=true route.
   2) Increase instance headroom by policy 'scale-now' for model-serving service.
   3) Notify customers via status page if >5% error rate persists after 5m."

Ownership and metrics (who owns what):
- On-call synthesis owner: SRE manager (quarterly cadence).
- DPM governance: Incident review council (product + SRE rep)
- Bridge operator: maintains status templates and runbook links.
- Metrics to track: mean time to ack (MTTA), mean time to remediate (MTTR), percentage of incidents resolved with DPM, action-item closure rate within 14 days.

Audit and retention:
- DPMs and postmortems retained for 2 years in the incident archive.
- Handoff notes retained for 90 days.

Related pages and references:
- Link: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-evidence-collection-standard (internal)
- Link: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/kv-cache-eviction (internal)

Appendix: triage decision quick chart:
- High latency + multi-tenant -> Sev1 -> full postmortem
- Short outage <30m + single-tenant + known fix -> DPM
- Repeated flapping events -> escalate to hypothesis-driven postmortem

Revision history:
- 2026-01-12 — created by Priya Shah
- 2026-02-02 — added DPM SLA guidance (review: Miguel Alvarez)
- 2026-03-01 — formalized rotation constraints and game day template (review: Sara Kim)

Title: Response playbook: voice-call prep & follow-up (scratch)

Response playbook: voice-call prep & follow-up (scratch)

Purpose:
- Quick single-sheet prep for an ad-hoc voice call with a paying customer (Acme Analytics) experiencing model-serving latency spikes during batch scoring. Keep this focused: get to containment, assign owners, and confirm next steps.

Call objective (15–25 min):
- Verify customer impact and SLAs affected (latency > 2s p95 on /v1/generate for batch-run).
- Confirm containment steps we can run during the call (fallback model, throttling, disable heavy reranking).
- Assign immediate owners and timeboxed actions.
- Agree on communication cadence and internal follow-up.

Pre-call quick checks (5 min, do these before dialing in):
- Ticket: CS-4873 – read last customer message.
- Logs: tail last 200 lines from model-serving pod (kubectl -n redwood logs -f deploy/model-serve --tail=200).
- Metrics: open Grafana panel - model-serving latency (p50/p95/p99), queue depth, GPU utilization for the last 30m.
- Recent deploys: check last rolling deploy (git tag + CI pipeline ID) and note if any model or infra change in last 2 hrs.
- Known mitigations: fallback to quantized-variant v1-q, enable prefix-cache (if safe), or increase autoscale target for dedicated pool.

Attendees / suggested roles (modify as needed):
- Jasper Reed (you) — call lead / notes / customer comms.
- Maya Patel — runtime engineer (attempts live mitigation).
- Rowan Li — SRE (infrastructure-level throttle / scale).
- CS AE (Acme contact) — customer readout.
- Optional: Eng on-call for model (if deploy-level rollback likely).

Suggested call agenda (time-boxed):
1) 0:00–02:00 Introductions / objective (Jasper)
2) 02:00–06:00 Customer describes observed behaviour & business impact (AE)
3) 06:00–12:00 Rapid diagnostics review (Maya/Rowan) — metrics, recent deploys, errors
4) 12:00–18:00 Containment proposal & quick actions (choose 1 or 2):
   - Switch route to fallback model variant (v1-q quantized) — expected cost/latency tradeoffs
   - Apply request-level throttling (limit concurrency per API key) for batch jobs
   - Temporarily disable heavy reranking step in pipeline
5) 18:00–22:00 Assign owners / ETA on actions (who will execute and check-in times)
6) 22:00–25:00 Customer comms & wrap-up: next update time, escalation path

Live troubleshooting checklist (ordered, practical commands):
- Confirm impact windows on Grafana -> note timestamps for scope.
- kubectl -n infra get hpa, pods, nodes -> check scaling issues.
- kubectl -n redwood exec -it svc/model-proxy -- curl -s -D - -o /dev/null "http://localhost:8080/health"
- tail logs for error patterns: connection resets, OOMs, long GC pauses.
- If model variant rollback chosen: route-switch command (internal): rtr switch --route acme-prod --model v1-q --confirm
- If throttling chosen: apply policy via console -> RateLimit: key=acme-prod, concurrency=2, burst=4

Containment decision guide (quick heuristics):
- If p95 latency > 2s and GPU utilization < 60% -> likely model-level compute inefficiency or hot KV cache misses: try quantized fallback or restart serving workers.
- If queue depth spikes and autoscaler not reacting -> scale config / HPA issue: escalate to SRE; temporarily throttle incoming requests.
- If recent commit touched tokenizer or attention fusion -> rollback to previous release and test on canary.

Customer message templates (copy-paste and adapt)
- Opening (0–2 min): "Thanks for taking this call. We see the latency spike you reported and our priority is containment while we investigate root cause. We will propose a short set of actions and agree an immediate plan. ETA for first corrective action: 15 minutes."
- After action applied: "We've switched you to a lower-latency fallback variant and are monitoring. We expect latency improvement; will confirm within 10 minutes and follow with a root-cause update."

Roles / RACI quick map (for this call):
- Responsible: Maya (runtime mitigation), Rowan (infra scaling), Jasper (external comms + notes)
- Accountable: CS AE (customer sign-off on mitigation), Jasper (ensuring follow-ups happen)
- Consulted: Eng on-call (deploy/rollback decisions)
- Informed: Product PM (if model variant changes affect feature behavior)

Immediate post-call actions (0–24h):
- Within 15m: confirm containment result + post to slack #cust-acme-ops (Jasper)
- Within 60m: collect logs, snapshots, and add to CS-4873 (Maya) -> attach Grafana snapshots and kubectl dumps (pods/nodes).
- Within 3h: if rollback executed, run regression smoke tests on canary and report results (Eng on-call)
- Within 6h: prepare short incident email to customer summarizing root cause hypothesis and next steps (Jasper + AE)
- By EOD: internal postmortem outline (template) created in Confluence with action owners (Rowan)

Longer-term follow-ups (48–72h):
- Confirm permanent config changes (autoscale tuning, model-variant defaults) and schedule a controlled deploy window (Product + Infra).
- Run load replay using synthetic batch from Acme traces in staging and report delta.
- Add a synthetic alert (p95 > 1.5s) to avoid regression.

Notes-to-self / heuristics learned (for future calls):
- Keep the call to 25 minutes max. Rapid containment then offline RCA works better for engineering productivity.
- Have the route-switch command pre-authorized for this customer in the console — saves precious minutes.
- Standardize the 3 containment options and keep the cost/latency tradeoffs documented in one slide.

Scratch log (live notes) -- fill during call: 
- 14:02: customer reports spike started 13:47, affected batch jobs only, interactive calls ok.
- 14:05: Grafana p95 = 3.7s, GPU util = 42%, queue depth = 120 (baseline 15).
- 14:08: last deploy 13:40 (model code + tokenizer) -> potential suspect.
- 14:12: applied throttling (concurrency->2) -> queue depth dropped to 40, p95 -> 2.1s.
- 14:18: switched to v1-q fallback -> p95 -> 1.0s; customer confirms improvement.

Post-call artifacts to attach to ticket CS-4873:
- Grafana snapshots (before/after), kubectl pod dumps, routing change command audit logs, timestamps of customer confirmations.

Open questions / things to validate after the call:
- Why did autoscaler not increase worker count? (HPA metrics, cloud provider throttles?)
- Is the tokenizer commit causally linked to latency? Run unit perf tests.
- Are there cache-warmup steps we can do on deploy to avoid cold-start penalties for large prefix loads?

Personal checklist before closing ticket:
- [ ] Draft and send customer follow-up email (template above).
- [ ] Add regression test to nightly suite covering this scenario.
- [ ] Confirm alert threshold changed and document in runbook.
- [ ] Schedule retrospective sync with PM/infra next week.

End-of-doc note: this is a lightweight, portable pad for phone/Zoom calls. Keep it short, copy the bits you need into a formal incident report after we have evidence.

Title: Postmortem-to-QBR Translation and Customer Readout Playbook

Postmortem-to-QBR Translation and Customer Readout Playbook

Purpose:
This playbook defines a repeatable process for turning internal incident postmortem findings into a concise, customer-facing QBR (Quarterly Business Review) narrative and readout. The goal is to:
- Surface root causes and mitigations in a way that maps to customer SLAs/SLOs and business impact.
- Provide a clear, action-oriented plan customers can review and sign off on.
- Standardize the rhythm and artifacts for CS-led incident readouts so engineering, SRE, and account teams stay aligned.

When to use this playbook:
1) Any incident that triggered a postmortem with customer-visible impact (latency SLO breach, model-quality regression, outage affecting >1% of tenant traffic, billing anomalies tied to runaway token usage).
2) Major configuration or migration failures that change expected behaviour for a customer.
3) Recurring or high-severity issues flagged by the Customer Success or Enterprise Support teams.

Scope and audience:
- Primary audience: Customer Success Manager (CSM), Account Executive (AE), Engineering Lead on the incident, and the affected customer’s technical stakeholders.
- Secondary audience: SRE, Product PM, and Support.

High-level process overview:
1) Postmortem author finalizes root-cause analysis and mitigation items.
2) CS partner maps technical findings to customer-facing metrics and prepares readout slide deck.
3) Joint internal rehearsal with engineering and CS to agree on messaging and acceptance criteria.
4) Customer readout meeting and follow-up commit list.
5) Tracking through to closure; reflect changes in the next QBR.

Roles and responsibilities (quick reference):
- Postmortem Author (Engineering): Produce final postmortem doc, timeline of events, RCA, impact window, and proposed technical mitigations.
- SRE/Oncall Lead: Confirm artifact accuracy (metrics, graphs, SLO timelines) and sign off on planned mitigations and rollbacks.
- CSM (Owner of Readout): Draft customer narrative, schedule readout, lead the meeting, and maintain follow-up tracker.
- AE: Coordinate customer commercial expectations and any contractual communications.
- Product PM: Provide roadmap context for long-term fixes and prioritization.

Minimum artifact checklist (required before scheduling a customer readout):
- Final internal postmortem (link) with clear RCA and timeline.
- Impact table (customers, tenant IDs, affected routes/endpoints, time windows).
- SLO/SLA graph(s) showing deviation and recovery (PNG/SVG).
- Action items table with owners, due dates, and verification steps.
- Customer-facing 6-slide deck (template below).

6-slide customer readout deck template (concise):
1) Title slide: incident name, customer, date, presenters.
2) Executive summary: one-sentence outcome, one-sentence customer impact, and current status.
3) What happened: brief timeline and root cause (non-technical summary first, technical appendix as follow-up).
4) Impact on your service: mapped to the customer’s SLOs/usage and any financial impact or credits.
5) Actions we took and next steps: short-term mitigations and planned long-term fixes with target dates.
6) Ask of the customer and close: verification plan, acceptance criteria, and scheduled follow-up checkpoint.

Translating technical findings into QBR metrics (mapping guide):
- Latency spike -> translate to: percentage of requests > 2x SLO, P95 and P99 delta vs baseline, affected endpoints, and customer business flows impacted (e.g., search, generation).
- Model-quality regression -> translate to: evaluation testset delta (accuracy/score), customer-facing examples (before/after), percentage of calls classified as ‘regression’ by monitoring rules, and remediation confidence level.
- Partial availability / degraded throughput -> translate to: minutes of reduced capacity, number of failed/queued requests, and effective availability percentage for the customer during the window.
- Cost anomaly -> translate to: additional token spend, specific prompt patterns, tenant configuration that caused increase, and recommended guardrails.

Customer readout runbook (step-by-step):
1) Internal sign-off (T-72h): postmortem author and SRE sign the artifacts. CSM schedules the readout with customer and internal stakeholders.
2) Draft deck (T-48h): CSM drafts slides using the 6-slide template; include appendices with graphs and raw query samples.
3) Rehearsal (T-24h): 30–45 minute dry run with engineering and AE to align on answers to likely questions (root cause, regression probability, rollback options, ETA for fix).
4) Readout meeting: 30–45 minutes max. Suggested agenda: 5m exec summary, 10m technical but non-dense timeline, 10m actions and verification plan, 10m Q&A + next steps. Keep the readout focused on outcomes and customer verification.
5) Post-readout (within 48h): CSM publishes the slide deck and the public-friendly incident summary to the customer. Create/update a follow-up tracker in the customer’s onboarding board.
6) Checkpoint (T+14 days): Verify short-term mitigations; engineering provides status update and evidence (metrics, synthetic runs).
7) QBR inclusion (next scheduled QBR): One slide summarizing the incident, impact, mitigations completed, and remaining open items with owners.

Acceptance criteria for customer sign-off (examples):
- Short-term mitigation validated by both engineering (SRE) and customer via agreed synthetic test (pass criteria: <X% error over 24h; configurable per customer).
- Long-term fix scheduled into product/infra backlog with a committed target quarter and owner assigned.
- Any commercial remediation (credits, SLA adjustments) agreed and captured in the renewal/billing system.

Templates and language guidance (do/don’t):
- Do: Use plain language first, then technical appendix. Lead with the impact to the customer and what we have done about it.
- Do: Provide concrete verification (metrics, test names, runbook checks).
- Don’t: Overuse internal jargon in the customer-facing slides. Avoid speculative language (e.g., 'probably', 'might').
- Don’t: Dump raw logs into the readout — include curated examples in the appendix instead.

Example translation (short):
Internal postmortem finding: "KV cache eviction race under heavy prefix fanout caused N+1 model loads between 11:12–11:41 UTC, increasing P99 latency from 420ms to 1.8s for /v1/stream."
Customer QBR translation: "Between 11:12–11:41 UTC we observed a cache coordination issue that temporarily increased tail latency for streaming responses used by your search feature. Approximately 3.2% of requests served hit the degraded window, resulting in elevated P99 (1.8s vs normal 0.42s). We deployed config changes (KV cache backoff and faster rehydration) and are monitoring; a long-term fix (improved cache coordination and bakeoff) is scheduled for the next release. A synthetic test is in place and will be shared for customer verification."

Communication templates (short):
- Readout invite subject: "Readout: [Incident name] — impact summary and next steps"
- Readout invite body: "Hi <Customer>, we’d like to schedule a 30-minute readout to review the incident on <date>. We will cover impact, immediate mitigations, and proposed next steps. Please invite any technical stakeholders who should sign off on the verification plan."
- Post-readout email subject: "Follow-up: [Incident name] — artifacts and verification plan"

Tracking and verification fields (example table - store in customer board):
- item_id | short_description | owner | due_date | verification_method | status
- PM-101 | KV cache fix scheduled | Eng-Cache | 2026-12-15 | E2E synthetic v2 pass | open
- CS-202 | Customer synthetic verification | CSM-Jane | 2026-11-30 | Shared test run and screenshot | in_progress

Escalation and sensitivity notes:
- If the incident has regulatory or data-exposure implications, escalate to Security and Legal immediately and adjust customer messaging to ‘restricted’ confidentiality.
- For incidents with contractual SLA impacts, involve Finance and Sales leaders before the readout to pre-clear commercial remediation options.

Metrics and artifacts to attach to the readout (required):
- Tenant-level availability and latency time series (P50/P95/P99).
- Synthetic test results before/after mitigation.
- Short curated log snippets and query samples (appendix).
- Postmortem link and the public-friendly incident summary.

Follow-up governance and closure criteria:
- All action items must have owners and dates and be tracked in the customer’s board.
- CSM verifies short-term mitigations within 14 days and marks the checklist items green when verified.
- Long-term fixes are tracked quarterly; any slip requires notification in the next scheduled QBR.

Related playbooks and templates:
- QBR slide templates (internal asset link)
- Incident postmortem template (eng-sre)
- Customer synthetic validation guide (integration-guides)

Appendix: Example Q&A prep (anticipated questions and suggested answers):
Q: "How likely is recurrence?"
A: "We have applied a short-term mitigation that reduces the known attack surface and put a synthetic monitor in place. Probability is low in the short term; the long-term fix will remove the root cause and is scheduled for Q1. We will provide a confidence update after the T+14 validation."

Q: "Will my usage bill be affected?"
A: "We have evaluated the token spend impact for the incident window and will surface any credit recommendation if the customer experienced material additional cost. Commercial remediation requires AE and Finance approval and will be captured in the follow-up tracker."

Document ownership and updates:
Owner: Customer Success (CSM guild).
Update cadence: Review after every readout that includes technical incidents; refresh template quarterly or when guidance changes.

End of playbook.

Title: Containment Checklists and Post-Incident Learning Path

Containment Checklists and Post-Incident Learning Path

Actionable containment checklists for common Redwood incident classes plus a structured post-incident learning path and governance checklist. This page is the single-source reference for first-responder actions, communications cadence, and how to convert incidents into prioritized engineering work and measurable improvements.
On-call engineers, SREs, incident commanders, product and CS leads responsible for customer communications, and owners of production services.
This document provides concise, role-oriented containment checklists (what to do in the first 30/60/120 minutes), a severity classification table tied to SLO impact, a template cadence for internal and external communications, and the Post-Incident Learning Path that turns incidents into tracked improvements. Use these checklists immediately when an incident is suspected; escalate to the Incident Commander (IC) when a checklist does not restore service within the first containment window.
Severity | Customer Impact | Typical SLO Signal | Target Response Window
--------|----------------|-------------------|------------------------
P0 (Sev-0) | Complete service outage for a region or global failure (API returns 5xx or timeouts) | >=20% error rate or >3x latency SLO breach | Page IC and begin containment within 5 minutes
P1 (Sev-1) | Major feature degraded for many customers (model generation timeouts, heavy token backlogs) | 5-20% error or 2-3x latency SLO breach | Acknowledge and begin containment within 15 minutes
P2 (Sev-2) | Partial degradation or single-region/tenant impact; mitigations available | Degraded tail latency or increased token cost by >25% | Begin investigation within 1 hour
P3 (Sev-3) | Minor, non-customer-impacting anomalies or alerts with no clear customer effect | Metric deviation without SLA breach | Triage in next on-call shift

SLO references: API latency p50/p95 targets are defined per service in /confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets; use those thresholds when classifying severity.
CONTAINMENT CHECKLIST - FIRST 30 MINUTES (P0/P1)
1) Triage and establish the channel
   - Confirm error signature (5xx, auth failure, model OOM, network error). Use metrics: api_gateway.errors_total, runtime.oom_events, queue.depth.
   - Create incident channel: #incident-<service>-<region>-<sequential-id>. Add IC, on-call, product owner, CS lead.
2) Stabilize customer impact
   - Apply immediate traffic policy: route traffic to fallback model variant or healthy region (smart routing runbook).
   - If load-induced: enable request shedding for non-critical endpoints (X-Delay header or token-budget enforcement).
   - If model OOMs: scale up worker JVM/GPU memory profile OR switch to lower-memory quantized variant.
3) Short-term mitigation commands (examples)
   - kubectl rollout pause deployment/<service> -n production
   - curl -X POST https://control-plane/api/v1/route-redirection -d '{"from":"us-east-1","to":"us-west-2","policy":"read-only"}'
   - redis-cli FT.SEARCH incident_cache "*" --truncate 0  (check backlog)
4) Validate customer-facing recovery
   - Confirm 200 responses for health-check endpoint /_health and a drop in 5xxs for 5 consecutive minutes.

CONTAINMENT CHECKLIST - FIRST 2 HOURS (P0/P1)
1) Deep triage and metrics correlation
   - Correlate traces (jaeger) with error spikes; search for recent deploys or config changes.
   - Check autoscaling and GPU utilization dashboards (Grafana panels: inference/gpu_util_pct, inference/queue_depth).
2) Revert or patch
   - If recent deploy suspected: revert to prior stable tag and monitor.
   - If configuration error: apply hotfix via config-management and restart routing proxies.
3) Communicate
   - IC posts an initial incident summary within 30 minutes. Use the INTERNAL UPDATE template below.
4) Escalation criteria
   - If service still degraded after 2 hours, prepare cross-team war room and notify exec on-call.

CONTAINMENT CHECKLIST - MODEL QUALITY REGRESSION (P1/P2)
1) Quick isolation
   - Pull recent model variant rollout logs and compare eval metrics for the latest prompts.
   - Temporarily pin traffic to previous model version in the catalog.
2) For generation hallucination spikes
   - Adjust decoding parameters (temperature=0.2, top_k=40) via the dynamic policy service.
   - Apply prompt-anchoring guardrails (prefix template) if available.
3) Monitor and rollback
   - Watch quality evaluation dashboard (prompt-evals/regressions) and customer tickets for improvement.

SECURITY-TYPE INCIDENT (DATA/ACCESS) - FIRST STEPS
1) Preserve evidence
   - Do NOT restart affected hosts. Snapshot volumes and capture process lists.
2) Notify Security@Redwood and follow the Security Incident Response runbook.
3) If data exfiltration suspected: rotate affected keys and revoke sessions.

RUNBOOK INVOCATION
1) Who may run: on-call engineer, IC, SRE lead.
2) Invocation steps: create incident channel + set incident channel topic to severity, short summary, and link to this runbook.
3) Tagging convention: add label 'active-incident' and include 'ic:<name>' in the channel topic.

COMMON COMMANDS & SNIPPETS- Check API error rate:
  curl -s 'https://metrics.internal/api/query?expr=rate(api_gateway_errors_total[5m])' | jq
- Re-route traffic (control plane):
  rwctl route set --service inference --from us-east-1 --to us-west-2 --policy emergency-fallback
- Pin model version via catalog API:
  curl -X PATCH https://catalog.internal/models/my-model/traffic -d '{"pin_version":"v20260110-rc"}' -H 'Content-Type: application/json'

NOTES ON TOOLING
- Use the Incident Manager UI only for ticketing and follow-up action items; real-time coordination should occur in the chat channel for speed.
- All critical commands must be run by at least two team members when the incident is classified P0/P1 (safety check).
POST-INCIDENT LEARNING PATH (objectives -> outputs -> timelines)
1) Immediate (within 24 hours)
   - Incident log: IC compiles a timeline with timestamps and key actions.
   - Action item creation: convert immediate fixes into tracked JIRA tasks and tag with 'incident:<id>'.
2) Postmortem (within 3 business days)
   - Draft a blameless postmortem covering: summary, timeline, impact, root cause analysis, action items, and risk assessment.
   - Required reviewers: IC, service owner, SRE lead, product manager, and customer success rep.
3) Learning artifacts (within 10 business days)
   - Runbook updates: add missing steps or clarify ambiguous commands.
   - Create a short internal HowItWasFixed note for knowledge-sharing (1-2 page).
   - Schedule a 60-minute 'learning sync' in the owning team to review changes and proposed experiments.
4) Closure and measurement (30 days)
   - Verify action items: owners must post progress updates and link evidence (tests, dashboards).
   - Measure regression risk: run synthetic tests and compare to pre-incident baselines; mark postmortem as closed only when regression risk is mitigated or accepted.

POSTMORTEM TEMPLATE (short)- Title, Incident ID, Date, Severity, Summary (1-2 sentences)- Impact (customers affected, minutes of downtime)- Timeline (concise chronology)- Root cause hypothesis and evidence- Actions (owner, due date, verification steps)- Signal improvements (what metrics will show success)- Link to runbook changes and testing artifacts

SYNTHETIC TESTING STRATEGY
- Objective: detect regressions to latency, throughput, and quality before customers are affected.
- Tests to run: per-region health probes, end-to-end generation sampling (10 prompts x 1000 calls/day), cold-start latency sweep, KV-cache hit-rate tests.
- Frequency: lightweight probes every 1 minute; heavier E2E suite every 6 hours; full-day smoke every Sunday.

GAME DAY SCHEDULING & BLUEPRINT
- Quarterly tabletop exercise: 2-hour session, 1 IC per simulated incident, cross-team observers.
- Annual full-scale simulation: 4-hour live exercise with customer comms mock, status page fake incidents, and exec on-call observer.
- Post-game-day outputs: After-action report, runbook updates, and mandatory learning session for participants.

INTERNAL UPDATE (first 30 minutes)
- Subject: [INCIDENT] <service> - <short impact> - <region>
- Body: 1) Current status (what we see), 2) Actions taken, 3) Next steps, 4) Owner / IC, 5) Estimated time to next update.

CUSTOMER STATUS PAGE TEMPLATE (initial)
- Title: Service disruption affecting <service> in <region>
- Summary: We are investigating increased errors and latency affecting API requests in <region>. No data loss is suspected at this time.
- Current status: Investigating
- Impact: Customers may experience failed requests or elevated latency.
- Next update: <ETA or timeframe>
- Contact: support@redwood.ai (for affected customers request priority support)

CUSTOMER UPDATE (30-90 minutes)
- Clear summary of what changed and what customers should expect. If workaround exists, provide concrete steps (e.g., set region header to us-west-2). Avoid technical internal-only jargon.

EXECUTIVE ESCALATION NOTE
- 1-line impact, estimated revenue/customer SLA risk, critical path to recovery, ask (resources/approvals).
GOVERNANCE CHECKS
- Owners: Each runbook must have a named owner and a backup. Owners are responsible for quarterly verification.
- Review cadence: Quarterly review for critical runbooks (P0/P1), annual for lower severity. Document results in the runbook header.
- Test coverage: Every runbook must include at least one synthetic test or game-day scenario that verifies the primary containment steps.
- Decommissioning: Mark runbooks 'deprecated' and archive them with a linked rationale when services are retired.

ROLES & RESPONSIBILITIES (quick)
- Incident Commander (IC): control channel, decide severity, own external comms.
- On-call engineer: execute containment steps, run commands, feed timeline.
- SRE lead: cross-team coordination and postmortem signoff.
- Product/CS rep: customer-facing updates and ticket prioritization.

APPENDIX A: QUICK CHECKLIST CARD (copy into chat when incident starts)
- Create channel and set topic
- Confirm error signature & severity
- Apply emergency routing/fallback
- Validate recovery (health endpoint & 5xx reduction)
- Post initial internal update

APPENDIX B: QUICK STATUS PAGE JSON (example){
  "incident_id": "INC-20260218-001",
  "service": "inference-api",
  "region": "us-east-1",
  "status": "investigating",
  "next_update": "2026-02-18T15:30:00Z"
}

APPENDIX C: SAMPLE JIRA LABELS
- incident-2026, severity-p0, area-runtime, owner-sre, hotfix-required

Containment is the priority for the first 2 hours; learning and prevention are the long-term goals. Use this page as the canonical checklist for first responders and follow the Post-Incident Learning Path to ensure incidents produce durable improvements. If you identify gaps in these procedures, open an action item and tag it 'runbook:review' so it will be triaged in the next runbook governance cycle.

Title: Warroom ops checklist + after-action (solo runbook)

Warroom ops checklist + after-action (solo runbook)

Purpose / intent:
- Quick personal runbook for kicking off and running a customer escalation war-room when I am the primary responder (solo or with a small core). Not an org playbook — this is my scratchpad for the first 90–180 minutes and post-mortem framing.

Before dial-in (first 5–10m):
- Confirm scope: affected customer(s) + perceived impact (latency spike vs errors vs data leak risk).
- Grab customer details: account owner, contract SLA, current P0 contact (CS AE or AM). Note: ask for any live customer-facing comms copy to review.
- Start a private war-room Slack channel: #warroom-<cust-short>-<date> (example: #warroom-acme-20260305). Add SRE, CS, PM, Eng oncall.
- Create short incident thread in channel with TL;DR and triage updates. Pin one message with links (Jira, Confluence, runbook).

Initial triage checklist (0–15m):
- Validate alert: error logs, recent deploys, infra changes (check rollout dashboard + k8s events).
- Quick health checks: model-serving pods, GPU utilization, KV cache hit rates, active batching queue length. Commands I run first:
  - kubectl get pods -n serving | grep <model-service>
  - dashboards: serving/runtime/latency, serving/runtime/errors, infra/gpu-usage
- Check routing/fallback rules: is traffic being diverted to fallback model? If yes, note RTT differences.
- If customer-facing: ask CS to confirm whether they will pause traffic or inform users.

Roles I call out on the call:
- War-room lead: me (Ethan) — coordinates updates and blockers.
- SRE/serving-runtime lead: Maya Chen — root cause and mitigation.
- CS lead: Rowan Patel — customer comms and expectations.
- Infra oncall (if GPU infra suspected): assign from pager duty.

Immediate mitigation (if applicable):
- Quick rollbacks: only if there was a deploy in last 30–60 min AND rollback is low-risk. Open PR/rollback request in Slack and note PR id.
- Route traffic to backup model variant or degrade to lower concurrency to keep latency under SLA.
- Enable temporary rate limits or circuit-breakers for noisy clients.
- If KV cache suspected: flush selectively (document the key prefix), monitor for cold-start penalty.

Communication cadence and templates:
- 00:05: initial status update — "Investigating, impact X, core team assembled, next update in 15m."
- 00:20: update with findings and mitigation plan.
- After mitigation: note time of mitigation, who executed it, metrics showing improvement.
- Use short, factual sentences. Avoid speculation in customer-facing messages.

Logging decisions and evidence (my habit):
- Take short timestamps (UTC): when alert fired, when I joined, when mitigation attempted, when metrics improved.
- Save key query results to the channel: e.g., /saved-logs incident-7621/latency-15m.log
- Attach screenshots of dashboards if helpful.

Action items template (post-call):
- Owner: short name — Action: description — Due: YYYY-MM-DD — Priority: P0/P1 — Notes
  - Ethan — collect timeline and CLI command outputs; prepare initial RCA draft — Due: 2026-03-13 — P0
  - Maya — deep dive into serving-runtime memory spike, attach flamegraphs — Due: 2026-03-15 — P0
  - Rowan — customer comms follow-up and confirm whether credits/compensation required — Due: 2026-03-14 — P1
  - Infra oncall — validate kernel/driver updates on GPU hosts, report host-level anomalies — Due: 2026-03-13 — P1

Post-incident: quick AAR (within 72h)
- Short one-page: what happened, root cause hypothesis, immediate mitigations, and permanent fixes. Keep it <= 1 page for execs.
- Add a checklist of changes to platform guardrails (e.g., automated rollback, improved alert thresholds, synthetic tests).
- Mark any customer action (credits, postmortem readout) and owner.

Notes to self (things I forget under stress):
- If rolling back, always confirm migration of KV caches and schema compatibility first.
- Don’t run cluster-wide evictions as first mitigation — it creates noisy side effects.
- When asking for logs, specify time window and correlation id pattern (X-Trace, request id).

Evidence snippets from today (copied into warroom channel):
- 2026-03-05T14:07Z alert: latency p95 jumped from 220ms -> 2.1s for model x-3; errors increased by 3.4%
- Recent deploy: serving-runtime@f2d6a3 (2026-03-05T13:58Z) — rollback initiated at 14:18Z (rolled back to f2c1b8)
- Post-rollback: p95 returned to 270ms over 10 minutes; errors trending down but not back to baseline.

Unresolved / follow-ups to capture in RCA:
- Why did KV cache miss rate spike after rollback? (Maya investigating warmup behavior)
- Were any regional routing rules mistakenly applied during the rollout? (check routing audit logs)
- Need a replayable synthetic test that exercises long tail batches for model x family.

Quick reference snippets (commands / links):
- k8s pods: kubectl get pods -n serving -l app=model-x -o wide
- recent deploy: gh pr list --state merged --author deploy-bot --search "model-x"
- logs (by req id): logsrv query --start 2026-03-05T13:50Z --end 2026-03-05T14:30Z --filter "req_id=abcd-1234"

Checklist before closing war-room (my signoff):
- Customer informed with timeline and next steps (Rowan confirms)
- Metrics stable for >= 30 minutes (latency/errors)
- Action items captured with owners and due dates in JIRA/Linear
- Short exec note prepared (1 paragraph) and shared with oncall manager

Personal reflection: keep this lightweight and adaptable. When solo, prioritize containment + clear comms over deep dives. Once stabilized, handoff to RCA owners and schedule a follow-up that includes engineering + CS + product.

End of note.

Title: Rapid Reassurance Playbook — weekend-mode comms scratch

Rapid Reassurance Playbook — weekend-mode comms scratch

Purpose:
Quick personal scratchpad for crafting short-form internal comms during a weekend/after-hours service disruption. This is NOT the formal ops runbook — think: what to say fast, where to post, who to ping, and a tiny Q&A crib for leadership and product PMs that will inevitably ask for a timeline.

Audience:
- Primary: SRE oncall, who needs one-line slack + status templates
- Secondary: Eng leads and PMs who will be copied on comms and want a short blurb
- Tertiary: Execs (very short summary + impact)

TL;DR (what to hit in first 10 minutes):
1) Confirm scope & impact: which regions/customers affected (if unknown, say: under investigation, targeted customers being triaged).
2) Post short initial Slack in #sre-oncall and #platform-incidents with link to incident stub.
3) Create/hand off status page entry (minimal: title, impact, eta placeholder).
4) Notify CS/Support lead (DM + brief) so they can prepare customer-facing replies.

Initial Slack template (post in #sre-oncall and #platform-incidents):
- SUBJECT: [URGENT] Serving latency spike — investigating
- BODY: Hey all — seeing elevated inference latencies in prod (primary: us-west1, maybe eu-west). Error rates up ~4x on model-route /v1/generate for the last 8m. Oncall investigating; creating incident OPS-1729. Will update in 15 mins. If you see customer reports, DM me.

Status page minimal entry (status.redwood.ai):
- Title: Elevated inference latency for hosted API
- Impact: Intermittent increased latency and 5xxs for text generation routes affecting a subset of customers in US-WEST and EU-WEST
- Started: 2026-03-12T02:18Z
- Update: Investigating — updates every 30 minutes
- Contact: support@redwood.ai (for customers)

Short exec blurb (for CEO/GM):
- One-liner: We’re experiencing intermittent elevated latencies on hosted text generation in two regions; root cause under investigation; mitigation work in progress.
- Current impact: ~2–6% of requests degraded, spike correlates to a rollout of a new batching config on dedicated hosts (hypothesis).
- Next step: rollback config on canaries, validate, and widen if stable. ETA for next update: 30m.

All-hands talking points (if asked to repeat):
- We have an active incident; SRE + Serving runtime leads are on it. Our priority is to keep customer-facing latency and 5xxs minimized and restore normal traffic patterns.
- We have fallbacks in place (model routing to compatible variants) and are evaluating traffic-steering to reduce load on affected pools.
- No data loss reported, all user data paths intact.

Rapid Q&A crib (expected questions & short answers):
Q: Is this customer impacting?
A: Yes — some customers may see slower responses and occasional errors; we’re prioritizing the highest-volume tenants and payment-related routes.

Q: Do we have a rollback plan?
A: Yes — the immediate rollback candidate is the recent batching/queue config pushed to canaries. If canary rollback reverses the spike, we’ll proceed to affected pools.

Q: How long until normal?
A: Early estimate 1–3 hours depending on rollback validation or routing changes. Will update every 30 minutes.

Monitoring & quick checks (what I run first):
