Title: Rapid customer feedback loop and status drivers — SRE comms playbook

Rapid customer feedback loop and status drivers — SRE comms playbook

Working draft: lightweight SRE runbook focusing on incident communications that close the loop with customers (status page + targeted customer outreach) and internal war-room checklist emphasizing time-to-first-update, impact estimation, and triage ownership.
Purpose:
This doc is a short, practical playbook for incident communications with a focus on reducing customer uncertainty and surfacing actionable feedback to product/rv teams. The idea is to prioritize timely, honest updates and an operational feedback loop so post-incident analysis is informed by customer signal (not just metrics).

Audience:
- SRE on-call and bridge owner
- Product manager / owner of the affected service
- Support/CS leads for impacted accounts
- Comms/Legal as needed for high severity or regulated customers

Design goals (why different):
1) Fast cadence: first public update within 15 minutes for Sev1/2, 30 minutes for Sev3 if customer-visible.
2) Tiered messaging: use the same source-of-truth text but customize customer outreach by segment (free, paid, enterprise).
3) Feedback capture: include an embedded short feedback ask (checkbox + free text) in enterprise follow-ups to collect whether the incident caused data loss, business impact, or downstream outages.
4) Actionable artefacts: each update must include "next action" and "owner" fields so follow-ups are assigned.

Definitions/Severity & expectations:
- Sev 1 (critical): service unavailable or major functional loss for multiple customers. First public update: 15 min. Hourly updates until recovery or stable mitigation.
- Sev 2 (major): degraded latency/throughput causing user-facing errors for a segment. First public update: 15 min. Updates every 2 hours.
- Sev 3 (minor): single-customer issue or non-critical regression. First public update: 30–60 min if customer-visible.

Timeboxes and responsibilities (quick):
- T+0–5m: Pager fires, primary oncall joins (bridge) and posts short "investigating" signal on Slack #sre-incident and triage.
- T+5–15m: Bridge owner determines severity, impact estimate, and owner for customer comms. Prepare first status page message (template below).
- T+15–60m: Publish public update, notify CS for enterprise customers and open dedicated Slack threads/Zoom for top customers.
- T+60m+: Repeat updates per severity cadence, track actions in JIRA ticket, escalate to PM/Eng director if not progressing.

Status page templates (concise; use minimum friction):
- Initial (published publicly)
  Title: [Incident {incident_id}] Degraded {service_name} – Investigating
  Body: We are aware of and investigating reports that {service_name} is experiencing {short-symptom}. Our engineers are actively investigating. Impact: {estimate_customers_or_percent}. Next update: {ETA or time window}. Incident owner: {owner_name}.
  Visibility: public (all), tag: {severity}.

- Update (progress)
  Title: [Incident {incident_id}] Update – {service_name} – {brief-status}
  Body: Summary of actions taken since last update (bullets), current impact (improved/worse, remaining percent or flow), next steps (what we will do next), ETA if known, contact for enterprise customers.

- Resolved
  Title: [Incident {incident_id}] Resolved – {service_name}
  Body: Root cause (short), mitigation applied, customer impact summary (duration, who affected), follow-up/next steps (postmortem schedule, link), owner.

Customer email / targeted outreach templates (short + variations):
- Enterprise proactive notification (first outreach)
  Subject: Incident {incident_id}: {service_name} degraded – we are investigating
  Body: Hi {customer_contact},
  We’re currently investigating an issue affecting {service_name}. Impact we see: {impact_description: e.g., failed API calls for some requests}. We recognize this may affect your workflows. Our engineers are working on a fix; next update by {ETA}. If this causes immediate business impact for you, please reply with "URGENT" and we’ll prioritize a dedicated update/bridge.
  Sent by: SRE oncall ({oncall_name}) and CS lead ({cs_name})

- Enterprise follow-up (after mitigation)
  Subject: Incident {incident_id} – mitigation complete and next steps
  Body: Hi {customer_contact},
  We have mitigated the issue affecting {service_name}. Summary: {one-line root cause + mitigation}. Impact window: {start_time} to {end_time}. Did this cause data loss or downstream failures? [Yes/No] (please reply). We’re scheduling a post-incident review and will follow up with a write-up and any customer-specific remediation items.

- Public shorter notice (for large customer-base)
  For general customers, use status page and a short tweet-style update: "We’re investigating {service_name} issues; follow status.redwood.ai/{incident_id} for updates." Avoid jargon, link to status page.

Internal war-room checklist (stripdown, usable as pinned paste in bridge):
- Before publishing anything: confirm severity and scope (metric + at least 2 customer reports or synthetic fail).
- Establish bridge roles (ops lead, comms lead, PM owner, SRE tracer, CS liaison, oncall backup).
- Metrics to watch: 95th/99th latency, error rate by region, queue length, GPU utilization, retry/backoff patterns.
- Immediate mitigations (do first): traffic redirect, scale up shards, fail open to a safe degraded mode, toggle feature flags.
- Communication steps: draft status page initial -> post -> notify CS -> create customer follow-ups list (spreadsheet) -> send targeted emails to top-10 impacted customers.
- Track actions in JIRA: create incident-{incident_id} with labels [committed-fix, rollback, customer-followup]. Assign owners & ETA.
- Post-resolution: schedule follow-up meeting within 72 hours and assign postmortem writer.

Customer impact estimator (quick heuristic):
- Small: < 5 customers or less than 0.5% of requests affected.
- Medium: 5–50 customers or 0.5–5% of requests.
- Large: >50 customers or >5% requests.
Use estimator to decide whether to escalate to CS lead/Exec comms.

Feedback loop and outcomes capture (unique part):
- Immediately after resolution: CS sends a 2-question survey to enterprise contacts (impact severity + business effect). Add answers as comments in the incident ticket.
- During postmortem: product/rv team reviews customer feedback and tags any follow-up code changes as customer-driven.
- Scorecard metric: Time between first public update and first customer response; target < 48h for enterprise customers.

Templates for short Slack comms (bridge to #sre-incident):
- Investigating: "[INVESTIGATING] {incident_id} {service_name} – symptoms: {short}. Bridge: {link}. Owner: {owner}."
- Update: "[UPDATE] {incident_id} - {brief} - impact: {estimate} - next: {next_step}"
- Resolved: "[RESOLVED] {incident_id} - summary: {one-line}. Postmortem on {date}."

Post-incident follow-ups (actionable closure):
- Postmortem should include root cause, timeline, impact (metric + customer list), corrective actions, and a specific owner for each action with ETA.
- CS outreach summary: add the list of customers contacted and any replies to the incident JIRA.
- Long-term detection: create an alert or synthetic that would have caught this earlier; include alert runbook if applicable.

Open questions / to iterate on:
- Should we auto-open a dedicated Zoom/phone bridge for any enterprise customer reply of "URGENT"? (current practice: manual)
- How to structure an automated feedback form for enterprise customers that plugs into JIRA without manual copying?
- Which customer segments get SMS vs email vs Slack pings? (needs GTM input)

Notes / references:
- Related: CONFLUENCE-INC-COMMS-2024 (archived templates)
- Internal Slack: #sre-incident, #cs-enterprise-alerts

Usage guidance: keep updates short, authoritative, and consistent across channels. The aim is to reduce repeated customer outreach and place friction on internal decision making: every update must move the incident forward or assign a clear owner.

Draft history: created 2025-01-09 by Taylor Chen. Iterations: 2025-01-21 (added feedback loop), 2025-02-12 (refined timeboxes).

[Incident {incident_id}] {severity_label}: {service_name} – {short_status}
Impact: {estimate_customers_or_percent}.
What we know: {one-line}.
What we're doing: {one-line mitigation}.
Next update: {time_or_eta}.
Owner: {owner_name}
Subject: Incident {incident_id}: {service_name} status

Hi {customer_contact},

We wanted to let you know we're investigating an issue affecting {service_name}. Impact: {brief_impact}. We're on it and will update by {eta}. If you're seeing production blockers, reply with URGENT and include your customer id: {customer_id}.

SRE oncall: {oncall_name}
CS contact: {cs_name}

Thanks for your patience,
The Redwood Inference Team
1) Confirm severity and metrics thresholds.
2) Claim bridge and assign roles.
3) Publish initial status page message (15m for Sev1/2).
4) Notify CS + compile impacted-customer spreadsheet.
5) Post short Slack notice to #sre-incident and #cs-enterprise-alerts.
6) Apply immediate mitigations and document steps in ticket.
7) Maintain updates cadence until stable.
8) After mitigation, publish resolved message and notify enterprise customers.
9) Schedule postmortem and collect customer feedback.
10) Close with action items assigned and timelines.
Use this for oncall training. CS should customize enterprise emails with account context (SLA references, contract numbers). Legal should review any message that mentions data loss.

Title: Oncall throttle tuning experiments and mitigation notes

Oncall throttle tuning experiments and mitigation notes

Context and purpose:

This doc captures a set of on-call observations and a small experiment backlog related to throttle/quotas behavior during bursts and small-scale abuse patterns. It grew out of a late-night incident (11/2025 burst) where a multi-tenant customer had a sudden amplification of short-lived refresh calls that evaded per-client burst controls and caused noisy downstream KPIs (queue growth and KV cache churn). Use this as an informal runbook + experiment log — not final policy.

Executive summary (TL;DR):
- Symptom: short-lived client bursts (~100 req/min for 2–3 minutes) that did not trip existing token-bucket per-key limit, but caused high request churn and increased tail latency for other customers.
- Root causes suspected: (1) client implemented aggressive SDK-level retries with jitter and low backoff, (2) caching TTL for token metadata shorter than expected causing repeated auth lookups, (3) current limiter config had large burst allowance for new token_id hash buckets.
- Immediate mitigation used: flip emergency global reservoir limiter to 500 rps, deploy soft-429 policy for best-effort customers, and add temporary WAF rule to drop known noisy IP / ASN ranges while we triaged.
- Outcome: tail latency returned to acceptable SLOs within ~7 minutes; cost impact estimated ~2.8% increased egress and 1.3% increase in GPU token processing for that window.

Oncall timeline (abridged):
- 2025-11-12 02:11 UTC: Datadog alert - endpoints/runtime/requests p99 latency > 2.5s for 5m.
- 02:14 UTC: Initial triage: traffic spike from small set of tokens (~120 tokens) with lots of fresh connection churn.
- 02:20 UTC: Enabled global reservoir = 500 rps, set soft 429 for non-SLA tiers.
- 02:25 UTC: Added WAF drop rule for IP ranges seen in spike.
- 02:33 UTC: Latency p99 back to normal. Monitoring for re-occurrence.

Immediate runbook checklist (what we did) — put in order for a responder:
1) Identify scope: query bigquery for token_id counts and source IPs for the 10m window around alert. Query below.
2) If spike is small set of customers -> contact CS/AE and consider key revocation or temporary quota-multiplier reduction.
3) Toggle emergency limiter: POST /api/admin/limiter/global {"rps":500} (ops-only).
4) Apply soft-429 for best-effort routes: config flag ops.rate_limits.soft_429=true.
5) WAF: create ip-set sized rule (drop) for ASN/IPs used by the burst; labelled ephemeral.
6) After stabilization, revert WAF rule within 24–48h if no recurrence; track for false positives.

Datadog / BQ debugging snippets (copy/paste):
- Datadog: APM service:runtime | facet:token_id | avg:trace.duration{env:prod} by {token_id} - sort by p95 desc.
- BigQuery: sample for counts per token_id
  SELECT token_id, COUNT(1) AS req_count, COUNT(DISTINCT remote_ip) AS ips, MIN(timestamp) AS t0, MAX(timestamp) AS t1
  FROM `redwood-prod.telemetry.requests`
  WHERE timestamp BETWEEN TIMESTAMP_SUB(TIMESTAMP("2025-11-12 02:10:00"), INTERVAL 5 MINUTE) AND TIMESTAMP_ADD(TIMESTAMP("2025-11-12 02:10:00"), INTERVAL 15 MINUTE)
  GROUP BY token_id
  ORDER BY req_count DESC
  LIMIT 100;

Observed telemetry patterns worth noting:
- High short-burst spikes often accompany high distinct remote_ip counts for a single token (suggests client-side horizontal fanout or CDN misconfig).
- KV cache miss rate spiked = additional auth calls and header parsing overhead.
- Existing per-token bucket with large initial burst (burst_capacity=200) allowed these short attacks to pass.

Experiment backlog (prioritized):
1) Fuzzy rate limiter: implement a secondary heuristic layer that detects "burst shape" vs long-lived client traffic. Heuristics: rapid p95 inter-arrival drops, high distinct IP ratio per token, short-lived high qps. Action: prototype in staging with counters at proxy. Success metric: reduce tail latency regressions in replay test by 70%.
2) Adaptive burst decay: instead of static burst_capacity, use an exponential decay per bucket that reduces allowed burst after initial high usage for the next N minutes. Config knobs per-tier. Action: design PR and run chaos tests.
3) Global reservoir probation: introduce a probation window for new token_ids to prevent unlimited initial burst. For token age < 5m, cap rps to 10. Need to watch new customer onboarding UX.
4) Auth TTL alignment: increase token metadata cache TTL from 30s -> 120s for low-risk routes to reduce KV churn, and add proactive refresh jitter in SDK.
5) WAF integration test: create synthetic traffic that imitates refresh-loop to validate WAF drop rules don't block non-malicious CDNs.

Playbook for different scenarios (draft):
- If small-number-of-tokens spike (<500 tokens) and high ips per token: prioritize key revocation and 429s.
- If large distributed spike (>5000 tokens): assume broader attack, escalate to security, enable reservoir limiter at regional edge and coordinate with CDN partner.
- If internal SDK misbehave (we identify SDK version): coordinate with devex to push patch and ship advisory.

Commands and quick toggles (ops-only):
- Emergency limiter API: curl -XPOST https://admin.redwood/api/limiters/global -d '{"rps":500}' -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPS_TOKEN"
- Soft 429 flag: gcloud secrets versions access latest --secret=ops-flags | jq '.rate_limits.soft_429=true' | gcloud secrets versions add --data-file=- --secret=ops-flags
- Revoke key: POST /api/admin/keys/revoke {"token_id":"<id>"} - track in INC ticket.

Metrics to capture for the incident postmortem:
- p50/p90/p99 latency pre/during/post window for runtime service and routing service.
- Token churn (new token_id count per minute) and KV cache miss rate.
- GPU token-processing token/sec and cost delta during incident.
- WAF hits/hits blocked and false positive rate.

Follow-ups and owner assignments (short):
- Priya: write lightweight KB article for CS on when to request emergency key revocation. Due 2025-12-01.
- Marcus: prototype fuzzy-limiter POC in staging and create perf tests. Due 2025-12-15.
- Lena: run WAF integration tests and document false-positive cases. Due 2025-12-10.
- Runtime team PR required: change default burst_capacity behavior for new buckets (see linked PR).

Open questions / discussion items:
- How will probation rules affect new customer bootstrap flows? Need PM input.
- Should SDKs ship backoff defaults that vary by route (e.g., management vs inference)?
- What's acceptable latency tradeoff for aggressive soft-429 on best-effort tiers vs revenue impact?

Notes to self / heuristics we found useful:
- Look at distinct ips per token first — it's cheap and often diagnostic.
- Prefer soft-429 and reservoir limiter over immediate key revocation unless abuse is confirmed.
- Label any ephemeral WAF rule with incident id and auto-expire metadata to avoid creeping blocks.

Appendix: sample incident tag and short log excerpt

- sample log: "2025-11-12T02:13:22Z pid=23111 token_id=tok_7gH3 ip=34.201.12.44 path=/v1/generate status=200 time_ms=1200"

End of notes. This file is intentionally informal — use it as a starting point for a formal postmortem or runbook consolidation.

Title: Quick actions & templates for API fallout

Quick actions & templates for API fallout

Purpose: quick, copy-paste action items and short templates to shave minutes off common API incidents (client timeouts, 429s/rate-limits, degraded streaming chunks, elevated 5xx/error rates). This is intentionally terse — use as a pocket-runbook during PagerDuty rotations.

How to use: pick the section that best matches symptoms, run the immediate actions in order, then move to investigation checklist. If you hit an obvious fix (eg. scale up or toggle fallback) note it in the incident channel and mark Status=stabilized.

-----
Immediate triage summary (0–10 minutes)
- Who: grab primary oncall + owner from the most recent deploy (check deploy metadata).
- Channel: create incident channel #incident-api-<short-id> and invite eng-sre, infra, product-owner.
- PagerDuty: acknowledge and set severity (S1/S2) per impact matrix below.
- Short status post: "Observing increased API errors/timeouts affecting X% of requests, interventions: investigating. Triage checklist running."

Severity impact matrix (quick):
- S1: >20% of production requests failing or all customer-facing routes returning 5xx / hard timeouts for multiple customers -> Full incident.
- S2: 5–20% of requests affected or a single critical customer severely impacted -> Scoped incident.
- S3: <5% or non-critical background jobs -> Monitor + Investigate.

-----
Templates for immediate actions by symptom (copy/paste form)
A) Client timeouts (requests hitting server-level deadline or network idle)
1) Confirm: tail logs for 500/timeout patterns: kubectl -n redwood logs -l app=api-gateway --since=10m | grep -E "context deadline|timeout|504"
2) Check pod resource pressure: kubectl top pods -n inference | sort -k3 -nr | head -n 10
3) Check upstream engine latency (model pool): curl -s http://engine-metrics.internal/latency | jq '.p95'
4) Temporary mitigation: deploy a short-lived route-level timeout increase (config route X: timeout 60s -> 90s) OR enable "fast-fallback" path to smaller model variant. Command: curl -X POST $ADMIN_API/routes/X/config -d '{"timeout_s":90}'
5) If CPU or mem saturated: scale horizontally: kubectl scale deployment api-gateway --replicas=$((current+2))
6) If network congestion suspected: toggle region fallback to nearest healthy region: /admin/fallback/enable?region=us-west-2
7) Post in channel: action taken, metrics links, owner.

B) 429s / Rate-limited responses
1) Confirm client-facing 429s via logs: kubectl -n inference logs -l route=<route> --since=5m | grep "HTTP/1.1\" 429"
2) Check quota/rl configuration: curl -s $ADMIN_API/quotas/route/<route>
3) Short mitigations:
   - Increase per-route token/quota temporarily (admin UI or API).
   - Enable burst override policy: POST $ADMIN_API/policies/override -d '{"route":"<route>","burst":true,"duration_s":600}'
   - Apply client-side backpressure guidance: send immediate advisory to clients in channel with recommended retry-after header use.
4) Long-term note: add missing client-retrofit tickets if clients are retrying aggressively.

C) Degraded streaming (chunks delayed / truncated)
1) Confirm: check streaming worker logs and connection resets: kubectl logs -l component=stream-worker --since=5m | grep -E "reset|closed|chunk"
2) Check connection counts and per-connection memory: curl -s http://streaming-metrics/conn | jq '.active'
3) Short mitigations:
   - Flip to chunked fallback: admin toggle stream_chunked=true for route (keeps progress but reduces memory pressure).
   - Reduce max_concurrent_streams on fronting proxies to keep latency stable.
   - If NVMe-backed cache is hit rate-limited, temporarily increase KV cache size for prefix caching.
4) If streaming workers OOM: rollout to previous revision or scale worker pool by +30% until root cause identified.

D) Elevated error rate (5xx surge)
1) Confirm scope: sample errors by code: curl -s $METRICS_API/errors?since=10m | head -n 50
2) Identify correlated changes: recent deploys (git tag), infra changes, config rollouts in last 30m: curl -s $ADMIN_API/audit?since=30m
3) Short mitigations:
   - Automatic rollback of last deploy if error spike aligns with new revision. Command: /admin/rollout/rollback?service=api-gateway&to=previous
   - Activate circuit breaker: set route-level failure threshold to 50% for 10m and divert to safe-path.
   - Enable model-variant degrade: switch calls to quantized/cheaper variant to reduce failure surface.
4) If third-party dependency causing errors, switch to cached/replicated fallback path (serve last-good response template) and notify partner.

-----
Investigation checklist (10–60 minutes)
- Confirm scope: percentage errors by route, region, customer (get from dashboards).
- Correlate latency/throughput: p50/p95/p99 for downstream model pools and database/kv.
- Recent code/config changes: review last 2 deploys and feature flags.
- Resource saturation: CPU/GPU/Memory/I/O across API and engine nodes.
- SLO hit calculation: compute projected burn for next 24h.
- Are retries/backpressure loops causing amplified traffic? Use sampling to inspect client retry headers.
- Check autoscaler logs and decisions (scale-up throttles, cooldowns).
- Confirm that fallback policies are reachable (no ACL or network blocking).

Quick commands (reference):
- kubectl get pods -n inference -o wide
- kubectl describe pod <pod> -n inference
- kubectl logs -n inference <pod> -c api --tail=200
- curl -s $METRICS_API/summary | jq .
- tail -n 200 /var/log/redwood/api-gateway.log | grep -i error

-----
Escalation and comms templates
- Short incident status update: "T+15m: Elevated 5xx across /v1/generate affecting ~12% of requests. Temporary mitigations applied: scaled api-gateway +2 replicas and enabled model-variant fallback for high-latency routes. Investigating deploys and engine latency."
- Executive summary (for +2 hours): one paragraph with impact, customers affected, mitigation, next steps, ETA for fix.
- Customer-facing message (if needed): "We're currently experiencing higher-than-normal error rates affecting some API requests. We're actively mitigating and expect restoration within X hours. We will follow up with a root cause once confirmed."

-----
Post-incident capture (use this template in the incident channel)
- Title: concise incident name
- Start: ISO timestamp
- Impact: S1/S2/S3 + short bullets (routes/customers)
- Actions taken: ordered list with timestamps
- Root cause hypothesis: initial and final (update after RCA)
- Rollback/patch: links to PRs or config changes
- Engineering owner: name + pager duty reference
- Follow-ups: tickets created, owners, due dates
- Retro notes: what went well, what failed, automation opportunities

-----
Tactical notes / gotchas observed in past incidents (short list)
- Aggressive client retries can amplify a small transient into full-blown overload. If you see many quick retries, implement client advisory + server-side short-circuit.
- Increasing timeouts without addressing root cause can mask failure and worsen resource contention. Prefer capacity or fallback first.
- Streaming truncation often correlates with upstream model GC or KV evictions; look for sudden LRU evictions on caches.
- 429s sometimes caused by a single noisy API key — use per-api-key dashboards to identify and throttle.

-----
Open items to convert into engineering tickets
- Add a route-level "safe-mode" toggle to automatically enable fallback when p95 engine latency > 3s for 5m.
- Make per-client retry headers visible in logs and trace spans.
- Add a lightweight health endpoint for streaming workers that includes active connection count and memory pressure.

-----
Appendix: quick checklist to paste into an incident channel
- [ ] Channel created: #incident-<id>
- [ ] Pager acknowledged
- [ ] Primary owner assigned
- [ ] Short status posted
- [ ] Immediate mitigation applied (scale/rollback/fallback)
- [ ] Errors reduced (observe metrics)
- [ ] RCA ticket created

If you used a mitigation that will impact cost (scale/replicas, increased cache), call out in the postmortem and notify finance/ops leads.

Notes-to-self: keep this doc intentionally terse; longer form runbooks for each subsystem live in confluence link above. If you add a new quick-action, add it as a bullet under the relevant symptom and ping the SRE guild for review.

Title: Enterprise Contract Governance and Billing Acceptance Playbook

Enterprise Contract Governance and Billing Acceptance Playbook

Summary:
This playbook defines the cross-functional governance steps and minimum acceptance criteria required to move an executed enterprise contract into production billing and revenue recognition. It aligns Legal, Finance, Sales, Procurement and Engineering (Billing/Platform) on a single, auditable path from contract signature to billing enablement. The goal is to eliminate handoff ambiguity, reduce time-to-bill, and ensure revenue recognition controls (SOX-friendly) are satisfied.

Scope:
- Applies to all enterprise customer contracts and amendments that will be invoiced via Redwood billing systems (hosted API subscriptions, Dedicated commitments, customer private deployments add-ons).
- Covers commercial terms ingestion, contract metadata standards, billing acceptance checks, revrec triggers, procurement handoffs for CAPEX/OPEX requests, and exception handling.
- Excludes routine self-serve subscriptions that are covered by standard billing automation.

Owners and stakeholders:
- Document owner: Finance (Sofia Morales)
- Legal owner: ContractOps (Liam Chen)
- Billing/Platform: Revenue Engineering (Marcus Lee)
- Sales/Account: Account Executive / Sales Operations (named AE)
- Procurement: Procurement Ops (Priya Nair)

Key definitions:
- Billing Enablement: The point at which the Billing Service (revrec-api) is configured to issue invoices for the customer and usage is billable.
- RevRec Trigger Event: The specific contractual milestone that starts revenue recognition (e.g., service delivery, shipment, SaaS activation date, or pro-rated subscription start).
- Contract Canonical Record (CCR): Single source of truth record in ContractOps (contract-id) that contains required contract metadata.

Minimum contract metadata (Contract Canonical Record)
The following fields MUST be captured in the CCR before billing enablement. Missing fields are a gating issue. Each field maps to the internal Billing Service and RevRec pipeline.

| Field name | Required | Example | Notes |
|------------|----------|---------|-------|
| contract_id | yes | CT-2026-1345 | UUID generated by ContractOps upon countersignature |
| customer_id | yes | cust_0a1b2c | Redwood customer PK |
| billing_entity | yes | Redwood Inc (US) | Legal entity responsible for invoicing |
| currency | yes | USD | 3-letter ISO |
| sku_list | yes | hosted-api-monthly,dedicated-reserve | Comma-separated SKUs mapped to pricebook |
| contract_start | yes | 2026-03-15 | date (YYYY-MM-DD) |
| billing_start | yes | 2026-03-15 | date - when invoices begin |
| revrec_trigger | yes | SaaS_activation | enum: SaaS_activation, Shipment, Milestone |
| payment_terms | yes | Net 30 | used by AR and dunning |
| auto_renew | no | true | boolean |
| termination_fee | no | 50000 | currency amount |

Minimum billing acceptance checks (pre-boarding checklist)
1) Contract record completeness: CCR fields present and validated.
2) Pricebook mapping: All SKUs in contract have mapped pricebook entries in Pricebook Service (pricebook-v2).
3) Entity & tax: Billing entity and tax configuration verified; VAT/Tax ID validated for non-US customers.
4) Payment instrument: Payment method on file (if required by Sales) or AR onboarding complete for invoiced customers.
5) Start/End dates and proration rules: Confirm billing_start, contract_start, and any trial or grace periods.
6) RevRec alignment: Revrec_trigger confirmed by Finance with revrec policy (see "Revenue Recognition Routing" below).
7) System access: Billing Service (revrec-api), ContractOps, and Customer Portal accounts verified for the AE and Billing Onboarding owner.
8) Compliance flags: Check confidentiality/data residency flags; if restricted, follow Private Deployment billing route.

Step-by-step: Contract to Billing Enablement (recommended sequence)
1. Sales executes contract and uploads final countersigned PDF to ContractOps. (owner: AE)
2. ContractOps creates CCR and populates required metadata; runs automated validation rules. (owner: ContractOps)
3. Legal reviews and approves any non-standard clauses; signs off in ContractOps (owner: Legal).
4. Finance performs pricing review and confirms SKU mappings & revrec_trigger. (owner: Finance Revenue Ops)
5. Procurement (if customer requires purchase order or if Redwood needs to raise PO for third-party procurement) completes procurement handoffs. (owner: Procurement)
6. Billing/Platform receives CCR and performs system-side mapping to pricebook-v2 and sets up billing_entity. (owner: Revenue Engineering)
7. Billing acceptance checklist executed. If all checks pass, Billing Service flagged as ENABLED for customer. (owner: Revenue Engineering)
8. First invoice scheduled per payment_terms and billing_start. (owner: AR)

Sample CCR payload (YAML example)
```yaml
contract_id: CT-2026-1345
customer_id: cust_0a1b2c
billing_entity: "Redwood Inference, Inc"
currency: USD
sku_list:
  - hosted-api-monthly: 1
  - dedicated-reserve: 2
contract_start: 2026-03-15
billing_start: 2026-03-15
revrec_trigger: SaaS_activation
payment_terms: Net 30
auto_renew: true
```

Revenue recognition routing (high level)
- SaaS_activation: Recognize revenue over the service period from billing_start to contract_end on a straight-line basis unless a milestone schedule exists.
- Shipment/delivery: Recognize when goods are delivered and customer acceptance criteria are met.
- Milestone: Recognize upon objective milestones; Finance must record milestone schedule and linkage in RevRec ledger.

Examples of gating and approval thresholds
- Any contract with total contract value (TCV) >= $1,000,000 requires Director of Finance approval for revrec_trigger and billing_start.
- Any non-standard payment_terms (e.g., Net 90) require Legal + Finance sign-off.
- Contracts with revenue deferral > 12 months require VP Finance review.

Procurement & CAPEX handoff (when applicable)
- If the customer's contract requires Redwood to procure specific hardware or dedicated capacity on the customer's behalf, Procurement must produce a Purchase Order (PO) and SOW. The PO number must be noted in CCR.purchase_order.
- For on-prem/private deployments, infrastructure installation acceptance is a separate milestone; Billing Enablement for the managed services portion may be staged only after installation acceptance.

Escalation and exception handling
- If CCR validation fails, ContractOps creates a "Contract Block" and assigns a remediation ticket to the AE and ContractOps. Block reasons are recorded in the CCR (e.g., pricebook_missing, tax_mismatch, missing_payment_instrument).
- If billing_enablement is delayed > 10 business days after countersignature, an escalation to Director, Revenue Ops is triggered automatically.
- For disputes about revrec_trigger or revenue timing, raise a "RevRec Dispute" in the RevRec Issue Tracker (link: /revrec-issues) with Finance, Legal, and Revenue Engineering copied.

Audit & controls
- Every change to CCR must be auditable. ContractOps maintains an immutable activity log with user, timestamp, and change reason.
- Monthly sampling: Finance will sample 10% of newly enabled accounts each month to confirm contract to system mapping and revrec treatment. Findings must be remediated within the same quarter.

Operational playbook: common scenarios
A) Amendment that increases TCV but does not change billing_start
1. AE uploads amendment PDF and selects "amendment" in ContractOps.
2. ContractOps validates delta SKU mappings and TCV.
3. Finance confirms pricing and determines whether a change in revrec schedule is required.
4. Billing Service applies delta invoices starting on the agreed date.

B) Customer requests delayed billing start (retroactive activation)
- Requires written approval from Director, Revenue Ops and update to CCR with justification. Retroactive billing cannot be more than 90 days prior to approval date without VP Finance approval.

C) Early termination with termination fee
- ContractOps records termination_fee in CCR. AR will issue final invoice for outstanding amounts plus termination fee in the next invoice cycle. Finance will evaluate revrec implications and reverse deferred revenue where applicable.

Metrics and SLA targets for billing enablement
- Target time from countersignature to billing-enabled: 5 business days (SLA).
- Escalation threshold: >10 business days -> Director, Revenue Ops notified.
- Billing error rate (post-enable invoices requiring correction): <0.5% of invoices in a 30-day rolling window.

Related tools and services
- ContractOps: Contract canonicalization and activity log (owner: Legal)
- Pricebook-v2: Central pricebook service mapping SKUs to catalog prices (owner: Product Finance)
- Revrec-api / Billing Service: Invoice orchestration, taxation, and AR handoffs (owner: Revenue Engineering)
- ProcureFlow: Procurement tracking & POs (owner: Procurement)

Change log
- 2025-10-12: Initial published version (Sofia Morales).
- 2026-02-28: Clarified revrec_trigger enum and added procurement CAPEX handoff (reviewers: Liam Chen, Priya Nair).

Appendix: Quick remediation checklist for common CCR failures
- pricebook_missing: Request Pricebook-v2 mapping; temporary charge hold until mapping complete.
- tax_mismatch: Engage TaxOps for VAT/TIN verification; hold invoices until resolved.
- missing_payment_instrument: AE to collect payment details or AR to confirm invoicing cadence.

Contact points
- Revenue Ops (revops@redwood.com)
- ContractOps (contractops@redwood.com)
- Revenue Engineering (reveng@redwood.com)
- Procurement (procurement@redwood.com)

End of document.

Title: Improve errors for missing/invalid API key to reduce onboarding drop-off

Improve errors for missing/invalid API key to reduce onboarding drop-off

Context: During the Lifecycle Growth Experiments sprint we saw a non-trivial % of first-session failures caused by users attempting a first request without an API key, with the TS SDK surfacing a generic 401/403 or a low-signal fetch error. This PR adds clearer, action-oriented errors for missing/empty keys and invalid/unauthorized keys, including guidance that matches our current onboarding flow (create API key in Console, set env var, retry). What changed: (1) Validate apiKey at client construction time (and before first request) with a dedicated RedwoodAuthError, (2) map 401/403 responses to a RedwoodAuthError with a short remediation message + docs/console links, (3) improve default error text for "Bearer undefined" / empty string cases, (4) update README quickstart snippet to show recommended env var usage, and (5) add unit tests for key edge cases (undefined, empty string, whitespace, revoked key, malformed header). Notes: We intentionally do not log the API key and we avoid echoing request headers in error strings. This is meant to reduce early onboarding frustration and improve activation rate by making the "next best action" explicit. Related: PM-659 onboarding email/console CTA alignment; ENG-10492 activation funnel instrumentation (this reduces noise from accidental auth failures).
Marissa Cole (review): The message is much better. Can we make sure the guidance points to the Console path users actually see during onboarding ("API Keys" under Settings) and not an internal URL? Also please keep the copy short enough for in-console surfaced errors (some users paste errors into support).
Dylan Brooks (author): Good call. Updated links to /console/settings/api-keys and shortened the remediation text to 2 sentences + one docs link. Also ensured the error message is stable and doesn’t include request headers.
Nadia Rahman (review): Please double-check that we don’t accidentally emit a new error type that breaks downstream users catching by name/message. Do we expose a stable code property? Suggest adding error.code = "AUTH_MISSING_API_KEY" / "AUTH_INVALID_API_KEY". Also confirm we don’t include the apiKey value anywhere (even truncated).
Dylan Brooks (author): Added `code` field on RedwoodAuthError with `AUTH_MISSING_API_KEY` and `AUTH_INVALID_API_KEY`. Also added a regression test asserting the message does not contain `Authorization` or `Bearer`.
Nikhil Sharma (review): Love the onboarding alignment. One more suggestion: mention the env var name we recommend in docs. People copy/paste snippets. Also for 403 vs 401, the remediation is the same but the phrasing should avoid implying their key is "wrong" if it’s a permissions issue.
Dylan Brooks (author): Updated copy to say "API key is missing or not authorized" for 401/403, and the README snippet now shows `REDWOOD_API_KEY`. Split messages: missing key is explicit; unauthorized suggests checking key + org/project selection in Console.
Marissa Cole (approval): Approved after link/copy changes.
Nadia Rahman (approval): Approved with code field + no-secret assertions.
Nikhil Sharma (approval): Approved.
TypeScript SDK now provides actionable errors when API keys are missing/empty or unauthorized (401/403), with stable error codes and updated quickstart guidance.

Title: Neon-orchestrated attention: hybrid Flash + kernel tiler with lazy-KV streaming

Neon-orchestrated attention: hybrid Flash + kernel tiler with lazy-KV streaming

Summary: Introduces a neon-orchestrated hybrid attention path that combines a lightweight FlashAttention-style fast path with a tiled microkernel fallback. The patch adds a tiler that decides at runtime between (1) the optimized Flash micro-path for dense short sequences and (2) a new neon-prefetch tiled kernel for long contexts and odd sequence-lengths. Additionally this PR implements a lazy-KV streaming integration: instead of allocating/evicting large KV pages eagerly, the runtime streams KV slabs on demand and performs background prefetch with priority hints from the batcher. Motivation: our production traces show two dominant sources of per-token latency and cost: kernel selection overhead for mixed-length workloads and expensive full-KV swaps on long-context workloads. The hybrid path reduces kernel dispatch overhead and keeps the fast Flash path density benefits while the tiler maintains throughput on longer sequences. Design notes: - Kernel Tiler: a lightweight heuristic that computes tile sizes based on seq_len, k/v cache hits, and device utilization. Tiler exposes hints to the scheduler (tile_size, prefetch_priority, use_flash_path). - Flash micro-path: minimal changes to the existing Flash bridge to support neon-friendly memory layout and allow partial-row processing for non-4x head dims. - Neon tiled kernel: a new microkernel optimized for moderate tile sizes (32..256) with streaming prefetch and FP16 accumulation; includes an in-kernel rotary index remap to avoid extra memory passes. - Lazy-KV streaming: KV is broken into logically contiguous slabs. When a request needs a slab not present, we schedule an async prefetch and continue with partial KV (best-effort) to maintain tail latency. Background prefetching uses LRU+priority hints from the tiler. - Scheduler integration: continuous-batcher emits per-request hints (hot_token_prefix, expected_future_tokens) so the runtime favors coalescing requests that share KV slabs. - Fallback semantics: graceful fallback to the tiled kernel if flash_path fails or when the tiler estimates minimal benefit. Implementation touches: serving/runtime/tiler/* (core tiler & heuristics), serving/runtime/kvcache/streamer.* (lazy slab manager + prefetch worker), serving/runtime/kernels/neon_tiled_attn.* (new kernel), serving/runtime/kernels/flash_bridge adjustments, tests/perf/bench_attn_tiler.py, docs/attn_tiler.md. Testing & benchmarks: - Microbenchmarks across sequence lengths 8..16384, heads 8..64, model dims 1024..6144. - Canary on dedicated pools (pool-attn-4g). Results (canary): p50 latency -6%, p95 latency -12% on mixed-length workloads (avg seq ~512), throughput +18% on long-context workloads, token-cost -9% (due to fewer KV churns). Rollout plan: canary to 5% dedicated capacity for 48h, monitor tail latency, KV cache miss rate, memory OOMs. If no regressions, gradual increase over 7 days. Migration notes: no API changes. Config flags: runtime.tiler.enabled (default: true), kvcache.lazy_streaming (default: false) — kvcache.lazy_streaming off by default during initial rollout. Checklist: - [x] Design doc (ENG-1842) - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Perf harness runs - [x] Canary plan - [x] Docs update - [x] Security review (no new surface) Known limitations: streaming introduces additional background IO which can increase memory churn under extreme concurrency; tiler heuristics are intentionally conservative and will be tuned as we gather telemetry. Backwards compatibility: existing model pins and rollouts remain unaffected.
Maya Singh: Nice approach. Can you add a short unit test that simulates partial-KV availability so we exercise the partial-forward path?
Evan Chen: Added a test in tests/unit/partial_kv_sim.cc and a perf harness scenario to the bench suite. Also added metrics 'kvcache.partial_forward_count'
Liam O'Rourke: Two nits: (1) rename prefetch_priority -> slab_priority (2) add a short comment on why rotary remap is in-kernel. Otherwise LGTM.
Evan Chen: Renamed per request and expanded the kernel comment to explain avoiding extra memcpy during remap.
Ravi Iyer: Observability: add an exported trace span around tiler decisions and the async prefetch edge. Please ensure spans include tile_size and slab_id.
Evan Chen: Added spans and unit tests for trace fields. Verified with local Jaeger that spans are emitted.
Maya Singh: Approving after CI pass.
Liam O'Rourke: Approved. Good microbench wins are convincing.
Introduce neon-orchestrated hybrid attention tiler and lazy-KV streaming: reduces p95 latency on mixed workloads and improves throughput for long-context models. Config flags introduced: runtime.tiler.enabled, kvcache.lazy_streaming. Backwards-compatible.

Title: attention-memory-slice-powercurve-profiling

attention-memory-slice-powercurve-profiling

Purpose / TL;DR:
- Explore a memory-slicing approach (split attention into smaller memory-resident tiles) to avoid OOMs and reduce GC/peak-memory pressure for long sequences while keeping latency acceptable.
- Compare three attention execution strategies: FlashAttention2 (monolithic kernel), Paged-attention (paged KV + tiling), and Fused-ops (attention fused with layernorm/ffn microkernels).
- Produce power/latency curves across sequence lengths (64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 1536, 2048) and batch sizes (1,2,4) on A100-80GB and H100-80GB.

Context / why this matters:
- We keep seeing customer apps hit OOM or sudden latency spikes when sequence length distribution has a heavy tail (some requests at 2k tokens).
- FlashAttention is great for short-medium seq (<=1024) but sometimes fails gracefully for long sequences under reserved pools because of memory fragmentation and transient spikes.
- Paged approaches can trade off extra copies/indirections for lower peak resident memory and better steady-state throughput.
- Fused ops reduce kernel launch overhead for small tokens but show weird tail-latency regressions when combined with dynamic KV cache usage.

Hardware/Environment:
- Nodes: 4x A100-SXM4-80GB (driver 535.54), CUDA 12.2, PyTorch 2.2 with Triton 2.0, kernel build from branch: gpu/attention-profiling-v3.
- Also ran subset on H100 (driver 535.54, CUDA 12.2) to check SM/warp sched differences.
- Docker image: redwood/serving-bench:2024-11-01 (includes perf tooling).
- Profiler tools used: nvprof-like metrics via Nsight Systems (nsys), nvtx markers + cupy/cuda event timers, and torch.profiler aggregated traces.

Models tested:
- small: 7B (bfloat16, no quant) mimic Llama-7B spec
- med: 13B (int8/4bit experiments disabled for baseline)
- microbench framework: synthetic transformer block that isolates single attention call with configurable seq_len, head_count, head_dim.

Experiment design notes (rough):
- For each (seq_len, batch, model) do: 20 warmup iterations + 200 measured iterations; record mean latency, p50/p90/p99, GPU Memory high-water mark, CUDA kernel timeline.
- Two modes: cold-start (no KV cache), streaming (incremental tokens appended where KV cache grows) to capture repeated kernel launches on growing cache.
- Evaluate two scheduling policies: continuous-batching (we pack up to N tokens across requests) and single-request scheduling (no cross-request batching) to measure worst-case tail.

Memory-slicing idea (short):
- Split Q/K/V compute into S slices along sequence dimension so each slice fits comfortably in device memory budget. Compute attention for slice pairs and accumulate outputs.
- Benefits: lower instantaneous peak allocation; can prevent OOM and reduce GC from allocations collateral.
- Cost: more kernel launches, extra temporary buffers for partial accumulations, slightly higher total compute due to boundary handling.

Key experiment runs (summarized):
- Test matrix: seq = [256,512,1024,1536,2048], batch=1, head_dim=128, heads=16.
- R1 FlashAttention baseline (no memory slicing).
- R2 Paged-attention (page size tuned: 256 tokens/page).
- R3 Memory-slice (slice sizes tried: 128, 256, 512).
- R4 Fused-ops attention (attention fused w/ residual+ln microkernel).

Observed notes (raw):
- seq<=512: FlashAttention wins in latency and p99. Kernel durations dominated by a single big attention kernel (flash_cuda_attention) with high SM utilization (~85%). Small number of kernel launches (<=6) per forward.
- seq in [1024,1536]: Flash shows steadily rising peak memory; occasional slowdown due to CUDA out-of-memory retries in our reserved environment. Paged-attention shows flatter memory curve; latency slightly higher but p99 more stable.
- seq=2048: Flash baseline often hits OOM in tight memory environment; paged-attn and memory-slice both complete. Memory-slice with slice=512 achieves ~1.15x latency vs paged but uses 25% less peak memory.
- Fused-ops: for seq<=256 fused wins (fewer kernel launches). For seq>=1024 fused regresses—profiling shows lots of small kernels with low occupancy (~25–30%) and high scheduler overhead.

Representative numbers (batch=1, 7B, A100):
- seq 512: Flash: mean 21.4ms, p99 34.0ms, mem 28.5GB. Paged: mean 26.1ms, p99 36.7ms, mem 20.1GB. Slice(256): mean 24.7ms, p99 35.9ms, mem 18.9GB.
- seq 1024: Flash: mean 46.0ms, p99 88.2ms, mem 41.2GB (OOM attempts in 2/10 runs). Paged: mean 55.6ms, p99 62.3ms, mem 30.2GB. Slice(512): mean 51.2ms, p99 59.8ms, mem 29.4GB.
- seq 2048: Flash: OOM. Paged: mean 138.5ms, p99 182.2ms, mem 58.3GB. Slice(512): mean 126.8ms, p99 149.1ms, mem 43.7GB.

Profiling excerpts (nsys / nvtx observations):
- FlashAttention kernel: large single kernel, high SM efficiency, long duration. But when memory pressure increases we saw device-to-host fallback allocations in allocator trace (~2–3ms stalls) which correlate to p99 spikes.
- Paged-attn timeline: series of repeated small kernels performing page loads + attention on each page. Host->device page transfer (pinned memcpy) overlapped well with compute for large pages, leading to steady throughput.
- Memory-slice: increased number of kernel launches ~ (num_slices * base_kernels). Slice boundary accumulation produces small extra kernel for reduction. Slicing improved allocator behavior (less fragmentation events in allocator traces).
- Fused-ops: observed numerous tiny kernels converting layout + fused-ops; SM occupancy low and many back-to-back launches causing CPU driver overhead.

Hypotheses / interpretation:
1) Peak memory is the primary failure mode for Flash on longer sequences; avoiding big monolithic allocations (via paging or slicing) makes system more stable in shared reserved environments.
2) Paged approach has slightly higher per-token overhead but offers best p99 stability in production-like multi-tenant settings.
3) Memory-slice is a good compromise: lower peak than Flash and lower latency than Paged in our tests if slice size is tuned.
4) Fused-ops need rework: fusion should aim to reduce kernel count while preserving occupancy—current implementation over-fuses into many micro-kernels. Consider multi-stage fusion with larger tiles.

Actionable follow-ups / TODOs:
- [ ] Run same matrix on H100 and report relative delta; early H100 runs show 10–15% lower kernel latency but similar memory dynamics. (assigned: Tom)
- [ ] Add simulated multi-tenant load (concurrent small + large requests) to measure allocator fragmentation and evictions. (assigned: Priya)
- [ ] Try hybrid: paged-attn for KV storage + memory-sliced compute in each page; aims to combine best of both worlds. Implement prototype in branch hybrid/paged-slice. (assigned: Marco)
- [ ] Investigate allocator behavior: reproduce with environment variable MALLOC_TRIM_THRESHOLD-like tuning for CUDA caching allocator; capture allocator debug logs. (assigned: Aisha)
- [ ] Measure power/energy per token (wall time * average power draw) to quantify cost tradeoffs — add nvidia-smi polling in bench harness.

Notes on tuning knobs tried:
- page_size: values 128/256/512 tested; 256 had best overlap of memcpy+compute on A100.
- slice_size: 128 gives lowest peak memory but too many kernel launches; 512 reduces launches but peak memory increases; 256 appears sweet spot for 7B configs.
- prefetching: prefetch next page overlapped with current compute reduced p99 by ~8% for paged-attn.
- cudaGraph: attempted capture for Flash; graph capture reduced CPU overhead for repeated calls but didn't help with allocator fragmentation.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How do these results change with int8/4-bit quantized models where attention math has smaller memory footprint but different kernel characteristics?
- Can we expose slice/page sizing as an adaptive policy at runtime (based on free memory + sequence length) without user intervention?
- For long streaming sessions (many steps) does paged approach yield better amortized throughput over time? Need longer-run experiments (1k+ steps).

Title: Attention kernels exploration notes

Attention kernels exploration notes

Purpose:
Quick running notes + experiment log for attention-kernel profiling work. Goal is to collect reproducible microbenchmarks across FlashAttention, paged attention, and our fused-attention kernels to understand latency tail, memory behavior, and where batching/kv-cache pressure causes regressions. This is a working doc — messy, checkpoints + TODOs included.

Background / motivation:
- Customers push long context (8k-64k tokens), pinned on Dedicated and Private. Our current serving runtime supports multiple attention implementations; runtime picks based on model config and sequence length heuristics.
- Recent customer reports: apparent latency regressions at 2k+ tokens for some models when running with bursty small-batch traffic and enabled KV cache. Hypothesis: interaction between prefix KV-cache reuse, paged attention memory recomputation, and degraded kernel scheduling.

What I profiled so far (high-level):
- Kernels: FlashAttention v2 (cuBLAS/soft-fused), our paged-attention path, fused-attention (single-kernel matmul+softmax+mm), and baseline naive attention (GEMM + custom softmax).
- Tools: Nsight Systems for end-to-end traces, Nsight Compute for per-kernel metrics, pprof for host stacks, cupy/cuda events for micro timings. Also used Triton microbench harness for kernel-level comparisons.
- Workloads: GPT-like decoder-only with 16-heads, head_dim=64, model widths tested: 1.5B and 13B analogs. Sequence lengths: 128, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192. Batch sizes: 1, 4, 8. KV-cache warm and cold scenarios.

Quick experimental commands (repro):
- Launch harness: python benchmarks/attn_harness.py --kernel flash --model 13b --seq 4096 --batch 1 --kv-warm --reps 200 --device 0
- Nsight capture: nsys profile --output=nsys_attn_flash_4k --trace=cuda,osrt --sample=none --capture-range=cudaProfilerApi python ...
- Nsight compute: ncu --target-processes all --set full --launch-skip 1 --launch-count 50 --import-source-only nsys_attn_flash_4k.qdrep

Findings (raw):
1) FlashAttention (v2)
- Fast for short to medium (<=2048) seqs for single-token generation: kernel throughput excellent, low SM utilization variance.
- For 4k+ seqs, observed increased L2 traffic and repeated device-to-host driver syncs from our runtime when swapping paged KV blocks. Nsight shows repeated small memcpy/host-sync events (~0.3-1ms each) in between attention calls when KV-cache eviction policy triggers.
- Tail latency: 95th/99th percentiles increase sharply when batch>1 under bursty arrival (interleaved requests). Hypothesis: flash kernels block on streaming of KV pages into GPU memory because they expect contiguous key/value tensors.

2) Paged attention path (our in-house paging)
- Designed to split KV into chunks and stream. Works well when streaming bandwidth saturated and kernel compute is the bottleneck.
- But when kernel compute is fast (FlashAttention), paging overhead dominates. Paging code introduces additional cudaMemcpyAsync calls plus host-thread coordination to manage page readiness — these appear in nsight as CPU stalls and driver work.
- Memory fragmentation: after multiple model loads/unloads (Dedicated heavy multiplexing test), we saw allocation retries that pushed latency to tens of ms. Need to add explicit allocator diagnostics.

3) Fused ops kernel (prototype fused softmax+matmul)
- Single-kernel fusion reduces device synchronization and eliminates materializing large intermediate softmax tensors.
- For long sequences with warm KV-cache (no paging), fused kernel beats FlashAttention by ~10-25% in end-to-end kernel time for 13B-equivalent config.
- However, code path currently not compatible with paged streaming; fusion assumes contiguous KV tensors. Extending fusion to streaming is non-trivial and would require tile-level accumulation and atomic adds or multi-pass reductions.

Micro metrics summary (example numbers, 13B, batch=1):
- seq=1024: Flash attention kernel time ~12.4 ms, fused ~10.9 ms, paged overall ~16.7 ms (paging overhead included).
- seq=4096: Flash ~74 ms, fused ~63 ms, paged ~95 ms (paging dominating).
- KV warm vs cold: cold (first access) adds ~6-12 ms due to page fetches depending on page size (2-16MB).

What I instrumented beyond kernel times:
- PCIe transfer sizes and frequency (from nsys) — critical to understand page size vs transfer overhead. We need to move to larger page granularity if the model architecture and latency SLOs allow.
- L2 cache hit/miss rates (ncu) — FlashAttention uses tiled shared memory patterns; as seq length grows, L2 misses rise and memory-bound behavior appears.
- SM occupancy and stall reasons — warp stalls primarily due to memory dependency for long seqs.

Open hypotheses / questions:
- Is our paging policy too eager? We currently prefetch next N pages where N=2. For some traces this causes unnecessary traffic; maybe adapt prefetch based on measured inter-request gap or request priority.
- Can we implement a low-latency path for single-request KV hits that bypasses page manager and pins contiguous KV when it fits?
- How much of the tail is caused by host-side coordination and not kernel execution? Nsight shows host threads blocking on a mutex in page manager during high concurrency. We should replace with lock-free ring/queues.

Short-term actionable items:
- Add telemetry gates in runtime to emit per-request page fetch count and total memcpy bytes. (owner: Hana)
- Implement a 1st-pass fused kernel compatible with tiled streaming (research approach: accumulate partial attention results per tile on-device and finalize with a small kernel). (owner: Ravi)
- Increase default page size for Dedicated GPUs in the config to 8MB for models >6B and measure impact. (owner: Leo)
- Add stress test that runs mixed seq-length workload with bursty arrivals to reproduce tail. (owner: Maya)

Longer-term ideas:
- Evaluate RDMA direct transfer (for Private on-prem) to reduce host-mediated page fetch costs.
- Work with FlashAttention upstream to expose a streaming-friendly API or hooks where we can feed non-contiguous KV as a list of segments (rather than contiguous buffer).
- Consider kernel-level page-aware attention: the kernel iterates pages internally and uses per-page shared memory staging to avoid host syncs. This is advanced but could pay off for 8k+ seqs.

Experiment logs (selected):
- 2025-02-20: baseline flash vs fused, seq 4096, batch1. nsys capture attached to PR 487. Observed fused 15% faster end-to-end.
- 2025-02-24: added nsight compute counters for L2 hit rate: for seq>=4096 L2 hit drops from 72% to 41% on A100.
- 2025-02-28: stress with batch=4, interarrival jitter 10-200ms — observed mutex contention in page manager; 95th increased by 3.6x.

Notes for reproducing locally (dev laptop/GPU):
- Make sure driver >= 525.x and CUDA 12.1 (some flash kernels expect sm_80). Set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES accordingly.
- Use dataset with repeated short prefixes to simulate warm-KV and interleave cold requests to exercise paging.

Risks and tradeoffs:
- Larger page sizes reduce frequency of host-device transfers but increase GPU memory pressure and may reduce batch parallelism. Need automated guardrails in scheduler: only allow large pages when free memory > threshold.
- Aggressive fusion reduces flexibility: harder to support multiple attention variants and fallback model-compatibility; need thorough validation.

Appendix / TODOs (short):
- [ ] Add page-manager lock-free queue prototype (owner: Hana).
- [ ] Run dedicated 24hr stress with mixed TTL models to surface fragmentation (owner: SRE).
- [ ] Add per-request tracing id to correlate nsight traces with runtime logs (owner: Leo).
- [ ] Evaluate whether changing memory allocator (jemalloc vs default cuda malloc) affects fragmentation (owner: infra).

Questions for next sync:
- Can Product/Support share customer traces where latency tails started appearing? Need real traffic shape to prioritize.
- Is it OK to change default page size on Dedicated for new model images? Ops approval needed.

References / links (tickets & PRs):
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/487 (nsys captures + fused kernel prototype)
- Ticket: JIRA-INVEST-112 (attention kernel investigation)
- Internal note: confluence/Serving Runtime Kernel Notes v2

Final quick take:
- FlashAttention is great for contiguous KV workloads and short-medium sequences. Paging overhead and host-coordination are where we lose ground for long sequences. Fused kernels show promise but we need to design streaming-friendly fusion and reduce host-side blocking. Next week: prototyping lock-free page manager + run A/B with increased page size to quantify tradeoffs.

Title: Fused-attn paged-cache cont-batch eval diffs and onboarding notes

Fused-attn paged-cache cont-batch eval diffs and onboarding notes

Purpose:
This note collects observations from the model-onboarding evaluation for the 2025-07 runtime change that replaced the older attention microkernel with a fused attention path, enabled a paged-cache style KV eviction/management, and turned on continuous request-level batching by default for small-sequence workloads. Goal is to summarize behavioral diffs (latency, quality, cost), surface concrete regression cases from our prompt sets, hypothesize root causes, and propose immediate mitigations for Dedicated/Demo clusters while we iterate on kernel fixes.

Background and context:
- Candidate runtime change: fused-attention kernels (vectorized fused-qkv), paged-cache (segmented KV pages with LRU-driven pinning), continuous-batching (auto-aggregate small requests within 8ms window).
- Baseline: release v2025-06 with legacy attention kernels, simple KV ring cache, and batching only via explicit batch endpoints.
- Models in scope: gpt-xl-open-2024 (causal), redwood-chat-7b (chat), and two small encoder-only rerankers used by onboarding prompts.
- Evaluation harness: replay of production-simulated traffic (6 prompt sets: long-context summarization, short chat replies, instruction-following, code-gen microbench, reranking, safety probes). Each prompt set contains 500 samples; sampling deterministic seeds for n=3 runs. Metrics collected: p50/p95 latency, throughput (tokens/s), GPU utilization, token cost estimate, token-LL, perplexity proxy, task accuracy (where applicable), and hallucination/TOX flags from safety evals.

High-level results summary (aggregated):
- Latency: p50 improved modestly (-8% median), p95 worsened for long-context prompts (+18% in gpt-xl long summaries). Short-chat p95 improved (-10%).
- Throughput: overall tokens/s up +12% for mixed workloads due to fused kernels, but degraded -7% for long sequence tails because paged-cache evictions caused KV reload stalls.
- Cost: estimated token GPU cost down ~9% for small/medium requests; up ~6% for long-context heavy workloads.
- Quality: end-task accuracy stable for instruction following and reranking (+/-1%), but two notable regressions in summarization ROUGE-L (-4.2 pts on average) and an increase in low-confidence tokens (token-LL shifted by -0.24 for long-contexts).
- Safety: no new systemic toxicity triggers, but one prompt in the safety probe diverged to a more assertive hallucinated fact after kernel change (see example below).

Detailed diffs by prompt set:
1) Long-context summarization (500 samples)
- Baseline p95: 1.82s -> Candidate p95: 2.15s (delta +18%), p50: 0.92s -> 0.86s (-6%).
- ROUGE-L: baseline 38.2 -> candidate 34.0 (delta -4.2).
- Token-LL mean: baseline -1.42 -> candidate -1.66 (worse).
- Observations: paged-cache introduced page-thrashing when sequences exceed page-size (page size configured at 4k tokens). Models keep flushing and reloading KV pages for long recurrences leading to stalls and context-truncation-like behavior visible in tokens with repeated context references.
- Regression case story: sample prompt id 327 had repeated entity references and anaphora; candidate output omitted earlier context references leading to factual mismatch. Example (sanitized):
  - Prompt excerpt: 'In the Q4 board notes we discussed roadmap X, then in the follow-up... summarize the actions tied to roadmap X and link to the earlier decision rationale.'
  - Baseline summary included 3 decision bullets referencing prior rationale.
  - Candidate summary collapsed the rationale into an ambiguous paragraph and missed two actions.
  - Hypothesis: KV page eviction happened mid-attention, causing partial KV state loss for older tokens.

2) Short-chat (lightweight interactive requests, 500 samples)
- p95 improved: baseline 220ms -> candidate 198ms (-10%).
- Throughput improved: +18% tokens/s.
- Reply quality: statistically stable; small latency improvement leads to fewer timeouts in UI tests.
- Notes: continuous-batching gives clear benefit here; fused-attn lowers kernel overhead on short sequences.

3) Instruction-following tasks (complex multi-step instructions)
- Accuracy within noise (+0.9%).
- One failure mode: a step-ordering hallucination persisted in candidate where baseline was correct for 7/500 samples. Root cause unclear — may be tied to subtle numerical differences in attention weights with fused kernels.

4) Code-gen microbench (short code completions)
- Token-level perplexity unchanged; wallclock latency p50 slightly lower.
- Candidate produced one instance of incorrect variable scoping in a 3-line snippet (sample id 198). On repro, divergence occurs deterministically; candidate weights produce different token-prob scoring near end-of-file.

5) Reranking (encoder-based)
- NDCG@10 stable (+0.3%).
- Throughput improved on batch endpoints. No regressions.

6) Safety probes (adversarial prompts)
- One sample (id 412) changed from safe neutral answer to an assertive but hallucinated citation. Investigating attention trace shows missing KV entries at citation token positions.

Micro-observations from traces and logs:
- Attention weight marginals differ in fused-attn by small epsilon (avg L1 diff ~3.1e-3) but concentrated on long-range tokens. This amplifies in long contexts where small weight shifts drop token contributions below the page keep threshold, triggering eviction.
- Paged-cache metrics: average page reloads per request increased from 0.12 -> 1.8 for sequences > 6k tokens. Eviction policy currently evicts lowest-ranked page when free pages < 2.
- Continuous-batching side-effect: it groups short requests into sporadic micro-batches; when a long request arrives in the same cycle, resource contention leads to temporary KV bandwidth spikes and page fetching delays.

Hypotheses and root cause theory:
- Primary: interplay between fused-attn numeric differences and paged-cache keep policy causing long-range KV entries to be evicted prematurely; quality regressions come from missing past token context in attention sums.
- Secondary: continuous-batching increases bursty memory I/O for KV pages, leaking latency to p95 for long-contexts.

Immediate mitigations (short-term, can be toggled):
- For Dedicated customers and demo infra, revert continuous-batching to opt-in for deployments handling >4k average context length. Flag: runtime.contbatch.enabled=false.
- Increase page pin threshold: keep top 25% pages pinned when sequence length > 3k. Config: pagedkv.pin_fraction=0.25_dynamic.
- Add conservative numeric fallback in fused-attn: if long-range attention marginals drop >1e-2 compared to baseline, temporarily fall back to legacy attention for that request. (PR exists: see linked PR).

Planned experiments (next 2 weeks):
- Ablation: run fused-attn + no-paged-cache to isolate numeric vs cache policy effects.
- Kernel numeric tuning: reduce quantization of intermediate accumulation to match legacy fp accumulation pattern; measure attention marginals.
- Continuous-batching window sweep: 2ms, 5ms, 8ms, 12ms with mixed traffic replay to measure p95 delta.
- Page-size sweep: 2k, 4k, 8k tokens.

Action items and owners:
- Asha: coordinate toggle rollout for contbatch on Dedicated (action by 2025-07-22).
- Diego: run fused-attn + no-paged-cache ablation and post results in this doc (2025-07-24).
- Priya: add end-to-end trace hooks to surface per-request page reloads to the Console trace UI (2025-07-27).
- Elliot: prototype numeric fallback patch and bench on internal perf cluster (2025-07-26).

Notes to reviewers / open questions:
- Is the paged-cache eviction threshold policy acceptable for model types with long-range dependencies (some instruction-following cases)? Consider a model-type-aware default.
- Should continuous-batching be opt-in per-route rather than per-runtime? Ops/console implications.
- Need to decide on customer communication: do we roll back globally or gate by cluster type?

Appendix: short reproducible repro (sanitized)
- Model: gpt-xl-open-2024 (weights hash: abc1234-x)
- Baseline runtime: v2025-06 (legacy-attn on)
- Candidate runtime: v2025-07-fused (fused-attn + paged-kv + contbatch)
- Repro command: replay harness with prompt-set 'long-summary-v2' sample id 327 (seed 42), compare outputs and attention page logs.

If you want raw diffs (token-wise) or the evaluation artifacts, ask and I will attach the CSVs and the trace flamegraphs in the Confluence page linked above.

- 2025-07-15: added microtrace insights (Diego)
- 2025-07-20: updated mitigations and action owners after follow-up benches (Asha)

Title: Nanopause context-switch penalty — exploratory logs

Nanopause context-switch penalty — exploratory logs

Quick personal runbook and raw logs for measuring short-request context-switch overhead on multi-tenant GPU hosts. Goal: quantify per-request latency penalty when the runtime repeatedly preempts and restores KV cache / CUDA contexts for a mix of short (50–150 tokens) and long (800–2048 tokens) requests.
- Observed a consistent extra 6–18 ms p50 penalty per short request when preceded by a long request that caused an eviction of model context on A100 40GB host with two tenants.
- Penalty scales with cold KV cache size and quantization mode: FP16 had ~12–18ms extra, int8->int8-quantized path had ~6–9ms extra (likely because we pre-compile/int8 kernels and warm-up less heavy). 
- Batch size and request coalescing reduced penalty (single-request streams suffer most). Setting a short 5ms batching window eliminated ~60% of penalty in synthetic mix.
- Host: n1-standard-like node with A100 40GB (Prod-sim cluster, isolated test pool)
- CUDA driver: 520.61
- Runtime build: serving-runtime@main (commit 5d3f7a2), with dynamic KV-cache eviction toggles enabled
- Model: llama-2-13b-instruct (fp16 / int8 variants)
- Quantization path: bitsandbytes int8-enabled multi-kernel
- Client harness: locust-derived harness (single-threaded client agents) + lightweight generator that alternates short/long
- Traffic pattern: Zipf-ish intermittent: 80% short, 20% long but long requests are bursty (clustered)
A) Baseline: continuous short requests (50–80 tokens), warm cache
B) Long-only: continuous long requests (1024 tokens), warm cache
C) Alternating: 8 short -> 1 long repeated (emulates periodic large instructions)
D) Clustered long: 1 long every 30s with short stream otherwise
E) Batch window 5ms vs 20ms comparison on alternating pattern
- Worker: python harness/runner.py --pattern alternating --short 60 --long 1024 --qps 120 --clients 40
- Runtime flags: --kv-eviction-threshold=0.85 --context-persist=true --coalesce-window-ms=5/20
- Measurement: in-server tracing (token emit timestamps) + client-side end-to-end
- Scenario A (Baseline short-only, warm): p50=18, p95=34, p99=58, qps=850 sustained
- Scenario B (Long-only): p50=380, p95=610, p99=980, qps=22 (long CPU/GPU dominated)
- Scenario C (Alternating, coalesce-window=5ms): short requests (immediately following a long) p50=36 (+18 over A), p95=64, p99=112; short requests not following a long p50=20
- Scenario D (Clustered long, coalesce=5ms): short requests p50=30 (+12 over A), p95=58, p99=98
- Scenario E (Alternating, coalesce-window=20ms): short following long p50=24 (+6 over A), p95=46, p99=82
- Penalty is dominated by two factors: (1) KV cache miss / re-population cost (copying KV tensors back into GPU memory / warming the causal cache) and (2) CUDA context re-bind and possible kernel reinitialization if memory layout differs after an eviction.
- Int8 path shows smaller per-request penalty; hypothesis: int8 kernels have smaller workspace and faster restore times, plus lower memory pressure reduces eviction.
- Coalescing helps because it amortizes the restore across multiple short requests (one restore for the batch). Short coalesce window (5–20ms) is a practical knob.

- Provide a routing policy where very long requests are sent to a separate tenancy pool (Dedicated) or have higher eviction grace.
