Title: Adaptive prefetch and fusion field notes

Adaptive prefetch and fusion field notes

Context:
These are field notes from a short spike exploring adaptive prefetch heuristics and the runtime cost of kernel fusion for attention paths. Goal: reduce 95th/99th tail without regressing average throughput for mixed-length workloads (small chat turns + occasional >2k seqs). Work happened on a small fleet of A10/RTX8000 test nodes; traces collected with tracebench and custom hoplog hooks.

Summary / TL;DR: 
- FlashAttention (FA) gives best steady-state throughput on long sequences when kernels stay warm and memory is contiguous.
- Paged attention (PA) helps memory-constrained workloads by limiting activation residency, but introduces latency jitter from page-in costs and kernel switch overhead.
- Fused-ops kernel (FO) reduces kernel launch overheads at small batch sizes, but increases register pressure causing occasional long-tail stalls on >1024 sequence lengths.
- Adaptive prefetch (AP) that biases KV cache retention for recent prefixes + opportunistic prefetch on expected continuation points (based on prompt length distribution) reduced 95th latency by ~18% in our mixed workload trace without reducing throughput.

Hypotheses we tested: 
1) Prefetching entire KV on short-turns wastes bandwidth; partial prefix prefetch based on token probability distribution can save memory bandwidth.
2) Kernel fusion avoids CPU/GPU synchronization for small-batch chat queries, but fused kernels can become memory-bound earlier, losing benefits for long seqs.
3) Switching from FA to PA mid-request (hybrid) is high-overhead due to kernel-state translation (KV layout conversion) unless we maintain an intermediate fast-convert format.

Experiment matrix (short):
- Variables: kernel_type in {FlashAttention, PagedAttention, FusedOps}, prefetch_strategy in {none, full_kv, adaptive_partial}, batch_shapes = [single_small(1x64), burst_small(8x64), mixed_streams(uniform 1-2048)]
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency (ms) for token step, GPU util, SM occupancy, memory copy time, kernel-launch time, KV-conversion time (if any), end-to-end tokens/sec.

Representative commands used: 
- tracebench run --config spike-mixed-2025.json --collect=hoplog,devtools
- nvprof equivalent traces collected with NSYS (limited sampling due to perf impact)
- instrumented: serving-runtime/component/kv_cache metrics (hit_rate, evictions, prefetch_ops)

Key raw observations (spot samples):
- Mixed_streams + FA + no prefetch:
  p50 token latency: 12ms, p95: 78ms, p99: 210ms, tokens/sec: 4.2k
  Notes: large p99 from cold-activation page-ins on >1024 seqs.
- Mixed_streams + FA + adaptive_partial_prefetch:
  p50: 11.6ms, p95: 64ms, p99: 162ms, tokens/sec: 4.15k
  Notes: smaller gains on p50, larger tail improvement due to avoiding full KV copy on many short queries.
- Mixed_streams + PagedAttention + adaptive_partial_prefetch:
  p50: 13ms, p95: 69ms, p99: 170ms, tokens/sec: 3.9k
  Notes: throughput drop but tail similar to FA+adaptive. Page-in spikes still present for >2k sequences.
- Mixed_streams + FusedOps + no prefetch (small-batch burst workload):
  p50: 9.8ms, p95: 46ms, p99: 112ms, tokens/sec: 4.6k
  Notes: excellent small-batch latency; however observed occasional 400-800ms stalls correlated with register/spill cycles in sm_8x kernels for >1k seqs.

Profiling notes: 
- Kernel-launch time contribution is significant for single-token small-batch queries. FusedOp reduces the number of kernel launches by ~40% in our microbench harness.
- Memory copies (device<->device and device<->host) were 2x higher in full-KV prefetch; adaptive_partial kept copies closer to working set.
- KV-layout conversion (FA <-> PA) cost ranges 1.2ms - 18ms depending on sequence length and whether we do a streaming converter vs naive copy. This explains why hybrid switching mid-request is expensive.
- Page-in cost spikes: when paged-attention triggers page fault paths, observed up to 120ms stall for single request (rare but catastrophic for SLAs).

Adaptive prefetch heuristic we prototyped: 
- Maintain per-route rolling histogram of observed continuation lengths and LRU rank of keys.
- If predicted remaining tokens <= 64, prefetch only recent 2-4 KV blocks (partial). If predicted > 512, prefetch full KV incrementally (in background) and pin first pages.
- Backoff policy: if GPU mem pressure > threshold or prefetch queue backlog grows, reduce prefetch aggressiveness for low-priority requests.
- Implementation notes: prefetch implemented as async CUDA memcpy streams with priority (low for background). Ensured we cancel outstanding prefetches on early termination to avoid wasted bandwidth.

Tradeoffs / open questions: 
- How to pick the predictor? We used an exponential moving average on route-level continuation lengths and also fed small LLM that predicted continuation length from prompt context; latter is promising but adds model-in-loop cost.
- Is the complexity worth it? For PLG routes with many tiny chat steps, AP reduces SLO breaches. For compute-heavy long-form routes, AP adds no value and adds complexity. Maybe per-customer or per-route config.
- Conversion format: should we introduce a canonical KV representation that both FA and PA can reference to reduce switch costs? That would require a short-lived jitted converter or memory layout that both kernels accept.
- FusedOps stability: can we reduce spill by splitting fused kernels by sequence length bands or adding dynamic shared-memory tuning?

Actions and TODOs: 
- (A) Add lightweight route-level continuation predictor metrics to Console for a week-long A/B. Owner: Arjun. Timeline: 2 weeks.
- (B) Prototype intermediate KV layout that supports zero-copy view for FA/PA kernel variants. Owner: Maya. Timeline: 3 sprints.
- (C) Implement prefetch backpressure telemetry (queue sizes, mem pressure). Owner: Lena. Timeline: 1 sprint.
- (D) Run long-duration soak with mixed_streams workload for 72 hours with AP on/off to quantify SLO impact. Owner: Diego. Timeline: next week.

Notes for future benchmarks: 
- Add a 'conversion time' column to bench harness and log format to capture FA<->PA translation cost explicitly.
- Introduce synthetic spike workload that simulates burst of long context generation to measure page-in event frequency.
- For fused ops, collect register pressure counters and L2 miss counters to pinpoint spill triggers.

Appendix: quick checklist of reproducibility steps
- Checkout: git@github.com:redwood-inference/serving-runtime.git spike/adaptive-prefetch
- Build: bazel build //runtime:bench_driver --config=dev-nsight
- Run harness: ./bazel-bin/runtime/bench_driver --scenario mixed_streams --profile hoplog --out /tmp/bench/mixed_ap
- Collect traces: nsys profile --output /tmp/nsys/mixed_ap --trace=cuda,osrt -- ./bazel-bin/runtime/bench_driver --scenario mixed_streams

Random notes / gotchas observed during spike: 
- Some GPUs (older Ampere variants) show better behavior under PA because their memory subsystem tolerates scattered accesses better. Not uniform across fleet.
- Prefetch cancellation races: need to deconflict with eviction path; previously saw double-free-like metrics when prefetch and eviction collided.
- Small-batch fused kernels are great for PLG but complicate rollouts because A/B testing kernel variants causes noisy client-side performance signals unless routed properly.

Questions for review: 
- Prioritize (B) canonical KV layout vs (A) predictor telemetry? Which yields bigger ops win faster?
- Acceptable operational complexity for per-route prefetch? Should default be off for enterprise until stable?

End of notes.

Title: Admission surface optimizer and attention-prefetch policy for continuous batching

Admission surface optimizer and attention-prefetch policy for continuous batching

Background:
Redwood's continuous batching stack achieves good average throughput but customers report occasional tail-latency spikes during sustained mixed workloads (short/long tokens, variety of models). Many of our existing tickets improve batching heuristics or kernel matching independently; this ticket packages two tightly-coupled runtime changes: (1) an adaptive admission-surface optimizer that reshapes how prefill requests are admitted to the prefill queue based on instantaneous kernel-fit utility and tail risk, and (2) an attention-prefetch policy that proactively warms attention KV caches and selects kernel variants earlier in the prefill -> decode handoff to avoid decode-time stalls.

Goals:
- Reduce 95th/99th token latency for mixed short+long streams by 20–35% without lowering average throughput by more than 5%.
- Avoid any regression on 50th/75th latency and throughput SLOs.
- Provide observability hooks (per-request kernel choice, prefetch decision, reason code) for post-rollout regression detection.

Success metrics:
- 95th token latency reduction >= 20% on benchmark mix (70% short, 30% long).
- 99th latency reduction >= 15% on same benchmark.
- No >5% throughput drop on steady-state synthetic load.
- New trace fields available in Console for 100% of production requests after rollout.

Proposed design (high level):
1) Admission surface optimizer (ASO):
   - Compute a lightweight per-request "kernel-fit utility" score at admission using: model profile, sequence-length estimate, cached KV hit probability, and current kernel queue occupancy.
   - Use an admission policy that accepts requests to prefill slots that maximizes expected throughput while bounding expected tail-latency risk via a sliding-window quantile estimator.
   - The optimizer runs on the serving node's admission layer and assigns a reason code (e.g., accepted-fast-path, delayed-prefill, rejected-burst-backpressure) stored in request metadata.

2) Attention-prefetch policy (APP):
   - On prefill acceptance, make an early decision whether to prefetch KV blocks and select kernel variant (FP16 / Q4 / int8-ish) needed for decode.
   - Prefetch uses an LRU-weighted prefetch queue prioritized by predicted reuse (prefix similarity and session affinity) and by kernel candidate warm score.
   - Kernel variant selection is optimistic: for ambiguous cases select the lower-latency compatible variant; attach fallback plan to decode path in case mismatch discovered (transparent model fallback with metrics emitted).

Trade-offs and rationale:
- Prefetch increases GPU memory pressure; mitigation: conservative prefetch budget per-GPU and prefetch eviction by reuse score.
- Early kernel selection risks mismatch when downstream decode needs higher-precision; mitigation: always provide a fast fallback path and measure fallback rate (target <1%).
- Optimizer complexity vs benefit: keep kernel-fit utility computation O(1) and cache recent estimates to avoid admission CPU spikes.
Load test with mixed short/long whitebox traffic shows >=20% 95th latency improvement and <=5% throughput regression compared to baseline.
All production traces include admission_reason, kernel_variant_choice, and prefetch_decision fields.
Per-tenant prefetch budget enforcement enabled and can be toggled via console feature flag.
Fallback rate <1% on representative workloads or documented mitigation plan if higher.
1) Implement lightweight kernel-fit utility and incorporate into admission path (ENG sandbox branch).
2) Add prefetch queue with per-GPU budget and reuse-weighting, wire into prefill acceptance path.
3) Implement optimistic kernel-variant selection with attached fallback plan and telemetry emission.
4) Integrate per-tenant quota checks and console flag for prefetch budgets.
5) Run 72h A/B private cluster run, collect 50th/95th/99th token latencies, throughput, GPU memory metrics.
6) Rollout canary (10% traffic) -> 50% -> 100% with automated rollback if 95th latency increases or fallback rate >2%.

2026-01-27 — Prototype admission scoring landed in sandbox branch: github.com/redwood/runtime/pulls/432. Early microbench: 12% 95th improvement but prefetch memory pressure high on 4-GPU node.
2026-02-05 — Design review feedback from runtime-ops: add explicit per-tenant prefetch budgets and quota checks (will reuse Dedicated quota primitives).

Title: Prefetch-Priming Tension: Lab Brief

Prefetch-Priming Tension: Lab Brief

Summary:
This note captures a small lab we ran to quantify the tradeoffs between:
 - opportunistic prefetch (background KV/context prefetch before request arrives)
 - session priming (client-driven warm prompts / short primer executed at request time)
Goal: produce quick, reproducible heuristics for product recommendations when to enable prefetch vs require priming for a given session profile.

High-level takeaway (draft):
 - Prefetch reduces median tail (p50/p90) for high-burst workloads with predictable next-turn distributions, but increases steady-state cost ~3–12% depending on cache hit assumptions.
 - Priming (on-request) reduces cold-first-token latency more aggressively for low-concurrency, high-latency-sensitive apps but adds per-request token overhead that inflates cost linearly with request rate.
 - Hybrid: short predictive prefetch + lightweight priming gives best p99 where session continuity is uncertain.

Experiment setup (short):
 - Model variant: open-llm-small-14b-quant (mix of float16 + int8 KV paths)
 - Hardware: 4xA100 equivalent (server pool emulation)
 - Workloads: three synthetic mixes derived from production traces (trimmed):
    * chat-burst (80% short turns [10–40 tokens], bursts of 200 qps for 30s)
    * steady-stream (steady 25 qps, turns 80–200 tokens)
    * sparse-long (5 qps, long turns 500–1200 tokens)
 - Prefetch configs: none (baseline), aggressive (prefetch full last-K KV for top-5 predicted intents), conservative (prefetch only first-block KV)
 - Priming configs: none, micro-prime (10 token primer), full-prime (50 token primer)
 - Measurements: p50/p90/p99 first-token and full-response latency, tokens generated, additional KV read count (proxy for IO cost), dollars/1k queries (cost)

Representative results (condensed, median across 5 runs):

ASCII table: latency in ms, cost = dollars per 1k queries (approx)

Notes on numbers:
 - cost_1k includes baseline compute + token cost (very rough, normalized to internal price tiers). Prefetch cost assumes charged KV reads and occupied memory prefetch amortization.
 - extra_tokens indicates tokens sent as primers or side-effects (prefetch counts as additional reads not tokens but normalized here as equivalent token-cost for quick comparison).
 - sparse-long micro-prime shows huge token inflation because primers were full-document style for long context marking — this is expected and demonstrates priming is expensive when turn-length >> primer length.

Micro-observations and hypotheses:
 - Prefetch pays off when: prediction-accuracy > ~35% for next-turn prefix and when cold-cache penalty (first-token p99 uplift) > ~30–40ms.
 - Priming pays when request rate is low (so per-request token overhead is tolerable) and when the primer meaningfully reduces decode steps (e.g., summarization where primer includes task framing).
 - Hybrid is advantageous for chat-burst: small predictive prefetch reduces the probability we need a heavy priming step; micro-prime can be kept small to capture intent drift.
 - Prefetch-aggressive spikes cost disproportionately for steady workloads because it materializes a lot of KV memory writes that are amortized poorly across low churn sessions.

Operational notes for productization:
 - UI toggle surface: add 3 knobs: prefetch_mode (off/cons/agg), prime_template (off/micro/full), hybrid_hint (auto/manual).
 - Safety: prefetch must respect data residency + tenant isolation — prefetching cross-tenant contexts must be disabled.
 - Telemetry: instrument prefetch_predicted_intent, prefetch_hit, primer_tokens, additional_kv_reads. Add SLO budget counters for prefetch budget consumption.
 - Cost reporting: expose a prefetch KPIs line item in Console (estimated delta $/month for enabling aggressive prefetch by tenant).

 - (Marco) Validate prefetch prediction accuracy against live intent model (we used a simple Markov predictor in lab).
 - (SRE) Confirm KV read accounting assumptions in billing: do we charge per prefetch read or amortize to session?
 - Product: build small A/B in sandbox to validate hybrid for a customer that mirrors chat-burst (recommendation: 2 week run, target sample 100k sessions).

Unresolved / raw thoughts:
 - Can we do a TTL-aware prefetch that decays aggressive prefetch for low-activity sessions? Would reduce steady-state waste.
 - Consider cheap client-side micro-prime (local short primer before roundtrip) to avoid server token charge — privacy implications to assess.

Title: staged attention pipeline: tiled flash kernel + async KV spill + fused rotary microkernel

staged attention pipeline: tiled flash kernel + async KV spill + fused rotary microkernel

Motivation: tails on long-context workloads (8k-32k tokens) show two dominant costs: attention kernel memory pressure and blocking KV management during cache overflow. This PR introduces a staged attention pipeline that (1) tiles attention into multi-stage ops to keep compute on fast paths for common sequence shapes, (2) provides an async KV spill path to host memory for oversized contexts to avoid blocking the inference thread, and (3) ships a small fused rotary/rope microkernel that reduces per-token assembly overhead for rotary embeddings. What changed: - New CU kernel: runtime/attn/staged_flash_kernel.cu implementing tiled Flash-like attention with stage boundaries (qk tile, softmax tile, out tile) and explicit small-size microkernels for rotary application. - Scheduler: runtime/scheduler/hetero_batcher.cpp adds heterogeneous batch splitting so long sequences are split into staged sub-requests and routed to the tiled kernel; includes continuous-batching hooks to merge short requests while preserving latency SLOs. - KV cache: runtime/kv/async_spill.cpp and kv/host_serialization.h implement an async spill-to-host path with lock-free handoff to an IO worker thread and LRU hinting to avoid noisy eviction. - API surface: minor flags to the model config (staged_attention: on/off, kv_spill_threshold) and runtime feature gates. - Tests/benchmarks: tests/attn/perf_long_context.py, benchmarks/long_context/* and microbenchmarks for the rotary microkernel. - Docs: docs/perf/attn_staging.md describing operation and tuning knobs. Key design notes: - The tiled kernel is optimized for sequence lengths where max(seq_len) > 1024; it falls back to the existing fused Flash path for small sequences to avoid regressions. - Async KV spill is bounded: we surface per-request mem usage and backpressure; when the host queue is saturated requests fall back to a best-effort KV truncation policy. - The rotary microkernel was implemented as an in-register fused op to avoid an extra memory pass; it targets float16/AMP paths and has guardrails for fp32. Checklist: - [x] Unit tests for tiled kernel correctness (small matrices) - [x] Integration tests with scheduler split/merge logic - [x] End-to-end perf harness runs on p4d and g5 instances - [x] Backwards compatibility: feature gated and off by default for existing models - [x] Docs and release notes added Risks and mitigations: - Memory regression on some models: mitigated by staged_attention=false toggle and automatic fallback on OOM. - Race in KV spill handoff: leveraged lock-free queue and added deterministic reproduction test. - Accuracy drift due to tiling numeric order: validated against reference single-kernel attention on representative prompt sets and added tolerance checks. Rollout plan: deploy to canary fleet with staged_attention enabled for a small percentage of traffic, collect latency and quality regressions, then graduate to general availability depending on metrics in ENG-4821. Notes: this is intentionally conservative in kernel fusion (we only fuse rotary+apply in the microkernel) to make future integration with advanced Flash variants simpler.
Ethan Cole: This looks promising, can you add a fast-path switch so we don't hit extra register pressure for <512 sequences?
Priya Nair: Added a short-seq fast-path to route back to existing fused kernel if max_seq < 512; updated config and tests.
Jordan Kim: KV spill path needs a hard cap to avoid OOM storms on host memory. Suggest exposing kv_spill_threshold and queue_depth limits.
Priya Nair: Exposed kv_spill_threshold and host_spill_queue_depth; added saturation behavior and metrics; added e2e test that asserts backpressure behavior.
María Alvarez: Benchmarks show 18% token/sec win on 16k context for decoder-only models but 2% regression on short seqs—acceptable if gated.
Priya Nair: Confirmed short-seq regression is eliminated by short-seq fast-path; added canary rollout plan to release notes.
- Introduce staged attention pipeline: tiled flash kernel + rotary microkernel + async KV spill (feature gated).
- Default: disabled. Opt-in via model config (staged_attention=true).
- Improvements: significant throughput gains for long-context workloads (8k-32k).
- Notes: monitor kv_spill_host_queue_depth metrics when enabling.

Title: Long-context recall + latency regression notes

Long-context recall + latency regression notes

Purpose:

Quick working notes on a regression we started seeing in recall/latency when serving long-context retrieval chains under load. This doc captures the experimental matrix, a compact prompt set used for automated regressions, preliminary results, and hypotheses about attention-sink / truncation interactions. Intended as a stability-first triage doc for the model onboarding pipeline (esp. v1.x model variants + quantized builds).

Background / motivation:
- Over the past two weeks we observed a repeatable uptick in p95 generation latency and a drop in recall@5 for a subset of workloads when traffic includes heavy retrieval + chain-of-thought prompts and contexts >32k tokens.
- Customer impact note: a mid-market search-product (internal pilot) saw more frequent fallback to smaller-model variants and a spike in unit costs.

Goals for this eval:
1) Reproduce regressions across 3 context buckets (8k, 32k, 128k) with deterministic prompt sets.
2) Measure truncation behavior (where in the context the model drops tokens) and correlate with recall degradation.
3) Exercise attention-sink patterns via synthesized adversarial distractors to see if retrieval hits are being overwritten or diluted in KV cache.
4) Produce a short actionable set of mitigations (runtime routing, prefix-preservation heuristics, cache warming) to test in Dedicated.

Test matrix (high level):
- Models: model-x-1.2 (fp16), model-x-1.2-q4 (4-bit), model-y-2.0 (fp16) as a sanity comparator.
- Context lengths: 8k, 32k, 128k.
- Retrieval patterns: single-hit (1 relevant doc + 9 distractors), chain-hit (3 incremental retrievals concatenated, each with 10 distractors), adversarial-sink (100 distractors with high token overlap to increase attention churn).
- Load profiles: single-shot (no concurrency), burst-concurrency (100 concurrent requests with batching window tuned), steady-stream (RPS=50).
- Metrics captured: recall@1/5/10, exact-match needle retrieval rate, p50/p95 latency (generation + retrieval join), truncation-start-token-index (where truncation began when > context limit), token-loss-rate (fraction of tokens in ground-truth passage missing from model output), repeat-rate (n-gram repetition), perplexity-on-passage (where computable).

Prompt set (short examples used in harness):
- System: "You are a precise assistant. Use the provided context to answer concisely. If information is not in the context, say 'NOT_IN_CONTEXT'."
- User (QA): "Given the documents below, what is the answer to: [QUESTION]? Provide the single-sentence answer and the document id(s) that support your answer."
- Chain-of-thought probe (synth): "Walk through the steps you used to find the answer within the context, then give the final answer."

Example prompt instance (literal):
--CONTEXT START--
[DOC_3270] The company acquired Zephyr Labs in 2019. Timeline: 2019 acquisition details...
[DOC_1842] unrelated paragraph about weather and policy.
... (many distractors)
--CONTEXT END--
Question: "When did the company acquire Zephyr Labs?"
Expected: "2019 [DOC_3270]"

Preliminary observations (raw, noisy):
- 8k: stable recall@5 ~0.86 across builds; p95 latency acceptable. No obvious truncation.
- 32k: small drop in recall@5 to ~0.74 on model-x-1.2-q4 under burst load; truncation events rare but when they occurred, it was typically suffix-truncation (model output lacked early-doc evidence).
- 128k: recall collapse to ~0.48 for adversarial-sink, with p95 latency spiking 2.8x. Truncation behavior inconsistent: some runs show internal KV eviction (partial answer present earlier in generated tokens then disappears mid-generation), others show final outputs missing supporting doc ids.
- FP16 model-y-2.0 is more robust on recall for 128k but with higher baseline p95 latency. Quantized variant shows susceptibility to attention sink at lower concurrency.

Hypotheses (rank-ordered):
1) Attention sink / KV eviction: long contexts + high-distractor-token overlap cause the runtime to evict or overwrite cached KV entries for earlier retrieval hits, which results in reduced recall even though retrieval returned the correct doc IDs.
2) Truncation alignment: our assembly logic for retrieval chains concatenates newest retrievals at the tail; when sequence length > model max, runtime currently keeps last tokens and drops earlier ones (suffix-preserve). This interacts poorly with our evaluation prompts that expect earlier doc evidence to be preserved.
3) Quantization sensitivity: q4 path has different kernel selection causing more attention head instability under heavy sequence-length variance, amplifying the sink effect.

Investigation plan / experiments to run next (short list):
- Instrument KV metrics in serving runtime to capture per-request KV eviction events and sequence indexes (trace correlation id). Add a flag to log first-hit-token-index and last-hit-token-index.
- Run the same adversarial-sink workload with alternative assembly ordering (prefix-preserve: keep earliest hits) and compare recall/latency trade-offs.
- Warm the KV cache: pre-prime the runtime with the needle documents before test to see if pre-warming mitigates eviction.
- Re-run q4 quantized workloads with kernel fallback to fp16 for attention kernels to isolate quantization vs runtime scheduling effects.
- Add a synthetic low-entropy distractor variant (repeating filler tokens) to separate token-overlap vs token-count effects.

Quick notes / things I scribbled during runs:
- Diego: saw a trace where model generated correct doc mention then a 300-token gap then hallucinated alternate doc id. Attaching trace id in linked artifacts.
- Linnea: suggested we try interleaving retrievals (round-robin) rather than concatenation; worth a micro-experiment.
- Ravi: recommended measuring internal attention norm variance across tokens — we do not currently surface this metric at scale.

Actionable mitigations to prototype (if hypotheses hold):
- Prefix-preserve assembly option in runtime with configurable headroom (reserve X tokens for early retrieval hits).
- Truncated-output guardrail: detect if supporting doc id is missing from final output and automatically retry with a narrower retrieval set or alternate routing.
- KV-cache LRU tuning by request class (prioritize retrieval hits vs distractors).
- Quantization kernel gating: detect heavy long-context traffic and route to fp16 variants for critical customers.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How much model-vs-runtime contribution is there? (we need runs with a deterministic runtime but swapped model binaries; conversely deterministic model but swapped runtime config).
- Can we create a lightweight synthetic metric that predicts attention-sink before p95 latency rises (for use in circuit-breakers)?
- Is there a meaningful difference between suffix-preserve vs prefix-preserve for real-world customer prompts? Our Canary data is mixed.

Next steps (owners and rough ETA):
- Add KV eviction logging + trace correlation (owner: Ravi) — ETA 1 week for prototype logs in staging.
- Run prefix-preserve assembly micro-experiment (owner: Linnea) — ETA 3 days.
- Kernel-gating q4 -> fp16 toggles for one model (owner: Diego) — ETA 10 days including perf sweep.
- Summarize results and recommend runtime config for Dedicated canaries (owner: Amina) — ETA 2 weeks after above experiments.

Notes to self: keep prompt set small and deterministic; save random seeds for retrieval shuffling. Add a short section to the consolidated onboarding eval template about assembly-ordering and truncation expectations so this doesn't regress again.

Raw captures / useful artifacts location: see linked_artifacts above. Will attach the run logs and the CSV of metric time series to the Jira ticket MLINF-4823.

-- end --

Title: Interaction flow capture and action backlog - Feb 2026

Interaction flow capture and action backlog - Feb 2026

Purpose and scope:
Quick capture from 6 moderated usability sessions (cust pilot + internal beta) focused on model route creation, rollout settings, and runtime troubleshooting flows. This is a working synthesis — capture of friction points, concrete micro-interactions that confuse users, and a prioritized list of small-to-medium fixes we can push in the next 2 sprints.

Method:
- Tasks given: create new route (from model catalog), pin model version, configure canary rollout (10% -> 50%), set a fallback model, and inspect a slow request trace.
- Participants: 4 platform engineers (mid-market customers), 2 product leads (internal beta). Sessions remote, screen shared, think-aloud.
- Prototype used: Figma prototype v2.1 (link above).

Top-level themes (raw):
1) Surface-level discoverability: users expected to find "rollout" controls on the route detail page; many looked in settings and then left flow to search docs. Confusion around where canary % is applied (per-route vs per-model).
2) Microcopy mismatch: labels like "bias threshold" and "fallback priority" are overloaded. Several users interpreted "fallback" as an automated model ranking rather than a static configured model.
3) Implicit state: users were unsure when changes were staged vs live. The CTA language ("Apply" vs "Save draft" vs "Deploy") created uncertainty about whether traffic would switch immediately.
4) Troubleshooting surface: request traces are dense; users want a quick header that shows "likely cause" (e.g., KV cache miss, long decode) and a suggested next action ("retry with shorter prompt", "route to smaller model").

Representative quotes (verbatim):
- "I thought deploy meant 'push to prod' — why is this still in the drafts area?"
- "Where is the canary percentage? I would expect a slider on the route page."
- "The trace shows numbers but I don't know what's good or bad here."

Context: Multiple SDKs exposed slightly different streaming iterator ergonomics and credential refresh hooks which made cross-language examples and platform integrations brittle. This PR introduces a lightweight SessionDecorator abstraction and a small set of shared semantics (ResumeToken v2 + telemetry markers) to harmonize behavior across Python/TypeScript/Go. Goal: make stream consumers simpler to implement, provide a single place for automatic credential rotation and graceful resume, and add telemetry points to measure reauth/backpressure heuristics.

- Introduce ResumeToken v2 semantics: small stable opaque token returned at stream checkpoints; safe to persist short-term for fast reconnection.
- Unify async iterator ergonomics: all SDKs now offer .stream() returning an async/pullable iterator with a single .resume(resume_token) helper. This removes previously divergent push/pull naming.

Title: introduce-stream-checkpointing-and-retry-presets-across-py-ts-go

Motivation: Provide a small, consistent ergonomics improvement across Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs that makes long-lived streaming sessions more resilient and easier to integrate with application-level checkpointing. This PR introduces a lightweight stream checkpointing API (checkpoint/restore points for pull/push streams) plus a curated set of Retry Presets (backoff profiles) that teams can opt into. The goal is parity across SDKs for the most common production patterns (resuming partially-read streams and applying well-tested backoff profiles) without forcing teams to adopt a monolithic session manager.

Summary of changes: added StreamCheckpoint API to each SDK (py: StreamCheckpoint class + helper methods, ts: StreamCheckpoint interface + resume helpers, go: streamcheckpoint package + examples); introduced RetryPreset enum/config with three profiles (fast, balanced, conservative) implemented in each SDK and wired into existing retry machinery; bumped SDK package versions (py 3.1.0 -> 3.2.0, ts 2.7.0 -> 2.8.0, go 1.9.0 -> 1.10.0) and updated changelogs.

Compatibility notes: default behaviors are unchanged unless the new APIs are used. RetryPresets are additive wrappers around existing retry config - existing users using custom backoff or the old retry config will not be affected. StreamCheckpoint is opt-in: callers must explicitly create a checkpoint handle and pass it when rehydrating a consumer.

Integration smoke tests validate a resume after simulated network interruption and ensure token reauth is preserved across resume when session is sticky. Example flow: start stream, persist checkpoint token/id, on reconnect instantiate consumer with restore_from(checkpoint). For teams who rely on session affinity, this integrates with the existing session lease logic and does not change lease semantics.

Title: credential-dampener-stream-checkpoint-and-retry-floor

credential-dampener-stream-checkpoint-and-retry-floor

Motivation: Multiple customers reported intermittent token churn + bursty retry storms when streaming clients reauth concurrently. This PR introduces a lightweight 'credential dampener' in the Go SDK runtime and a small set of ergonomics and parity fixes aligned with the TypeScript and Python SDK teams: 1) credential dampener: coalesces rapid credential refreshes for concurrent consumers and exposes a small backoff jitter window to reduce synchronized reauth. 2) stream checkpoint tokens: allow streaming consumers to persist small opaque checkpoint tokens for resumability across transient reconnects. 3) retry-floor policy: new default retry profile adds a minimum backoff floor and caps immediate fast-retries to avoid token-thrashing loops. 4) ergonomics: clearer client ctor options (CredentialStrategy, StreamResumeHook) and improved docstrings. 5) cross-SDK parity: bump and document canonical retry profile names ("retry-floor" / "retry-standard"), and coordinate version bumps with py/ts (see linked Linear tasks). Implementation notes: credential dampener is an in-process, per-client optional component that keeps an LRU of recent refresh requests and returns a shared pending refresh promise when thresholds are hit. Stream checkpoint is intentionally opaque (byte blob) to avoid coupling with server internals; SDK only stores/returns the token to the user on graceful shutdown/resume hooks. The retry-floor profile is conservative (min backoff 250ms, multiplicative 1.6). This PR introduces a lightweight, in-process "credential-attendant" abstraction and a small compact-iterable shim to harmonize streaming ergonomics across Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs. Goals: (1) provide a single, well-documented credential lifecycle primitive that supports proactive refresh, lease handoff, and fallthrough chain; (2) surface a compact async/pull iterable that reduces ceremony for callers using streaming responses and makes parity easier across languages; (3) ship non-breaking, opt-in defaults and bump SDK versions to include adapters. Title: sdk: consolidate auth, retry logic and streaming parity across Python/TS/Go

Motivation: multiple SDKs (Python, TypeScript, Go) had diverging behaviors around authentication refresh, transient retry semantics, and the streaming API surface. This caused user confusion and intermittent production regressions when teams switched SDKs or upgraded individual client libs.

This PR unifies three areas: auth token refresh middleware, retry/backoff semantics for 429/5xxs, and streaming helper ergonomics (client- and server-facing helpers). The goal is parity for common primitives and ergonomics improvements without changing server-side contracts.

Summary of changes: 
- Introduced a shared auth adapter behavior (same refresh triggers and single-flight refresh) implemented in each SDK idiomatically.
- Standardized retry policy: idempotency map + jittered exponential backoff with capped attempts and configurable per-client override. 429s use a longer initial backoff and honor Retry-After when present.
- Streaming: added unified client helpers (Python async iterator, TS async generator, Go channel helper) that surface an identical framing behavior and consistent early-close semantics.
- Ergonomics: better default timeouts, simpler initialization interface (Auth + Retry optional struct/object), and improved error classes/messages for transient vs terminal errors.
- Docs and CHANGELOG entries for each SDK and small example apps demonstrating streaming with reconnect versus fail-fast semantics.

Title: introduce resumable checkpoint streaming protocol and ergonomic SDK helpers across py/ts/go

introduce resumable checkpoint streaming protocol and ergonomic SDK helpers across py/ts/go

Motivation: Production streaming workloads occasionally need to resume long-lived streams after transient disconnects without replaying the entire conversation. This PR implements a lightweight resumable/checkpoint hinting protocol (session-checkpoint v0.1) and exposes ergonomic helpers in all three SDKs so product teams can opt-in with minimal code changes. Summary of changes: 1) Protocol: introduce an optional 'X-Session-Checkpoint' header and resumable token semantics returned on streaming completion (response metadata). Server will emit stable checkpoint tokens that encode minimal KV cursor + prefix hash; clients can pass checkpoint token on a new stream to resume from that point where supported. 2) SDK surface: Python: add AsyncResumeableStream and helper resume_from_checkpoint(checkpoint: str) on StreamingClient; TypeScript: augment createStream({ resumeToken?: string }) and add generator helper stream.resumeWith(token); Go: introduce ReaderWithCheckpoint and streaming.ResumeFrom(token string) convenience wrapper. 3) Retries/backoff: align retry windows when resuming so clients don't double-retry content; introduce 'jitter_scale' in retry presets and expose opt-in PWM (progress-weighted multiplier) so resumption retries favor shorter windows for resumption flows. 4) Ergonomics/parity: ensure all three SDKs provide an idiomatic way to accept a checkpoint token and return one on normal completion or explicit checkpoint() call. 5) Docs & examples: cross-SDK quickstarts and a migration guide. Commits (high level): - Add protocol docs + OpenAPI extension for X-Session-Checkpoint header - Implement server side checkpoint generator and validation (small shim) - Add Python AsyncResumeableStream + unit tests - Add TS generator helpers + typed resumeToken types + e2e test - Add Go ReaderWithCheckpoint and examples + integration test - Add retry presets and jitter_scale implementation for client-side resume flow - Update changelogs and quickstart examples - Add CI job to run tri-sdk resume e2e matrix Changed files (high level): server/api/streaming_spec.yaml, server/handlers/checkpoint.go, sdk/python/redwood/streaming.py, sdk/python/tests/test_resume.py, sdk/typescript/src/stream.ts, sdk/typescript/tests/resume.spec.ts, sdk/go/stream_resume.go, docs/guides/resumable_streams.md, examples/multi-sdk/resume_quickstart.md, changelogs/py-0.19.0.md, changelogs/ts-1.30.0.md, changelogs/go-1.9.0.md. Testing notes: added targeted unit tests in each SDK and a small end-to-end CI matrix that spins a local handler-sim (lightweight checkpoint mock) and validates resume semantics under network jitter. CI initially failed on a flaky TS e2e due to an intermittent timing assumption; fixed by switching to a polling-based resume readiness probe and re-ran. Backwards compatibility: The transport change is opt-in — servers only emit X-Session-Checkpoint when checkpointing enabled; old clients ignore unknown headers. Clients that want resume must explicitly opt-in via the new helper surfaces. Rollout: feature-flagged on server side; SDK helpers are behind minor versions and documented. Migration: minimal — example included for each SDK. Usage examples (short): Python: stream = client.stream(...); cp = stream.checkpoint(); resumed = client.resume_from_checkpoint(cp) TypeScript: const stream = client.createStream(); const cp = await stream.checkpoint(); await client.createStream({resumeToken: cp}) Go: r := sdk.NewResumeReader(...); token := r.Checkpoint(); resumed, _ := sdk.ResumeFrom(token) Security notes: checkpoint tokens are opaque signed blobs (HMAC) - servers validate; no user data returned in token. Title: Adaptive link-rate smoothing and NCCL pacing for heterogeneous interconnects

Adaptive link-rate smoothing and NCCL pacing for heterogeneous interconnects

Background: On clusters with heterogeneous interconnects (mixed NVLink/NIC link speeds and asymmetrical topologies) we observed recurring NCCL stalls and bandwidth oscillation under TP workloads. This manifested as throughput variance across microbatches and elevated p99 tail latency for short-running inference requests. Motivation: previous fixes focused on static stream priorities or rigid batching heuristics which either underutilize good links or exacerbate stalls on slow links. This PR implements an adaptive link-rate smoothing layer and NCCL pacing integration to harmonize collective launches with per-peer link conditions and the runtime scheduler. Key changes and approach: 1) Link-rate estimator: continuous lightweight probe that measures effective per-peer bandwidth and short-term variability; estimator lives in scheduler/peer-rate-estimator and exports a smoothed rate with decay/window parameters tuned for inference workloads. 2) NCCL pacing adaptor: introduces optional pacing tokens in the comm adapter to space collective launches when peer variability is high; pacing is conservative by default and disabled for uniformly fast topologies. 3) Slack windows & micro-shear prevention: scheduler now computes a small slack window for kernel dispatch to absorb jittered arrival times from peers and aligns kernel launches with KV-cache prefetch completion when available. 4) KV cache alignment hook: prefetch manager negotiates a preferred alignment point with the scheduler for batched requests so comm-heavy windows avoid blocking on cache population. 5) Telemetry & guardrails: new metrics (peer_effective_bw, nccl_pacing_suppressed, pacing_tokens_issued) and a dynamic safety threshold that disables pacing if aggregate throughput would drop. Performance: in lab runs (8-node, mixed NVLink + EDR InfiniBand topology) typical large-TP workloads gained 12-18% sustained throughput and p99 latency improved by ~25% for short requests; NCCL stall events as recorded by tracers dropped ~60%. Testing and validation: - microbench suite: tp_collectives_bench extended with hetero-link scenarios - end-to-end canary: perf-canary harness with 10% traffic for 48h - unit + integration: scheduler, comm adapter, kv prefetch mocks - stress: ramp tests up to 200 concurrent sessions Rollout plan: canary 10% on dedicated clusters for 48h -> 50% -> global. Operator flags: pacing enabled=false by default for existing clusters; enabled=true for targeted clusters requires no code rollback. Risk and mitigation: conservative defaults, auto-disable if pacing causes throughput regression, and manual opt-out available via runtime flags. Related work: this complements prior comm scheduling efforts (see ENG-6123 family) and is intended to pair with future topology-aware kernel selectors. Notes: preserves existing public API surface; only runtime internals and ops docs are updated.

Title: Cinder Labs — session tear causing token reordering, retry amplification, streaming truncations and billing spike

Cinder Labs — session tear causing token reordering, retry amplification, streaming truncations and billing spike

Issue summary:

During a peak traffic window on 2026-03-09 17:22 UTC, Cinder Labs began seeing partial/stale streaming responses, token reordering for long chat sessions (>4096 tokens), and a surge in client retries that amplified upstream throughput. This led to increased 5xx rates from serving nodes, transient throttles from the API gateway, and an unexpected billing delta for the customer.

Impact:
- Multiple customer endpoints experienced truncated streams and out-of-order token sequences (~1200 user sessions affected).
- Observed 5xx rate peaked at 6.3% for the customer’s traffic window.
- Billing spike estimated at +42% for the affected 2-hour window due to retry amplification.
- Customer escalated to enterprise support and requested immediate mitigation, crediting and a post-incident review.

Environment:
- Production (us-east-1) serving cl-13b-v1-quant behind api-gateway v2.13.
- Dedicated routing policy: enterprise-reserved-us-east.

Steps to reproduce (internal):
1. Create a multi-turn chat session pinned to cl-13b-v1-quant with >4096 token context and stream responses.
2. Induce a partial runtime eviction (simulate KV cache evictions / kernel reselect) while continuing to stream.
3. Observe token gaps and client-side automatic retries causing multiple inflight requests for the same session.

Observed behavior:
- When a serving shard dropped the KV prefix during a background compaction, subsequent token continuation resumed from an earlier cache state and produced overlapping token sequences.
- Client SDKs retried idempotently but without session-affinity checks, creating duplicate in-flight completions.
- API gateway detected elevated error rates and began conservative throttling; some requests received 429s while others returned 5xx from the runtime.

Initial mitigation and timeline:
- 17:28 UTC: Support opened escalation and notified SRE and Serving Runtime teams.
- 17:35 UTC: Temporary routing policy change to route Cinder Labs traffic to a healthy pre-warmed pool (bypassed recently-updated autoscaler rules).
- 17:42 UTC: Disabled aggressive client-side retry guidance sent to Cinder Labs; asked temporary SDK toggle to backoff.
- 18:10 UTC: Rolling kernel-selection rollback (PR linked) deployed for us-east pool which stopped KV prefix evictions during active streaming.
- 19:00 UTC: Error rates returned to baseline; streaming behavior normalized.

Timeline and findings:
- 2026-03-09 17:22 UTC: first elevated 5xx and streaming truncations for Cinder Labs observed (api-gateway metrics + their telemetry).
- Root cause hypothesis: interaction between a recent kernel-selection tweak (PR 4821) and aggressive KV compaction led to transient state loss for long-lived sessions.
- Evidence: heap/kvcache flush logs on serving nodes show compaction events coincident with affected session IDs.
- Replay of workload on staging reproduced token reordering when compaction was force-triggered during active streaming.
- Throttle amplification: client SDK retry logic started new requests that did not enforce session-affinity, creating fanout and repeated token generation for the same logical conversation.
- Billing delta analysis: aggregated request counts for Cinder Labs during the window were 2.4x baseline; cost-weighted tokens increased proportionally.
- Contrib factors: recent autoscaler tuning reduced pre-warmed buffer by 20% in us-east pool, increasing likelihood that compaction/eviction occurred under pressure.

Support (Maya Chen) — 2026-03-09 17:30 UTC: Customer reported truncated streams and repeated partial messages. Opened incident and paged SRE.
SRE (Arjun Patel) — 2026-03-09 17:38 UTC: Identified KV compaction entries correlated with session IDs. Temporarily rerouted traffic to healthy pool.
Customer (Elena Ruiz, Cinder Labs) — 2026-03-09 17:45 UTC: Confirmed temporary improvement after reroute; requested timeline and credit for billing spike.
Eng (Tomasz Novak) — 2026-03-09 18:05 UTC: Rolled back kernel-selection change (PR 4821) in us-east as mitigation; monitoring for regressions.
Billing (Priya Shah) — 2026-03-10 09:12 UTC: Preliminary credit calculation prepared; recommended 50% credit for the affected window pending final audit.
Support (Maya Chen) — 2026-03-11 11:02 UTC: Sent post-incident summary and next steps to Cinder Labs; scheduled follow-up review on 2026-03-12.
Customer (Elena Ruiz) — 2026-03-11 15:40 UTC: Appreciated rapid response; requested concrete SDK guidance to avoid amplification in future.
Root cause: interaction between a kernel-selection optimization and KV compaction behavior on serving nodes caused transient session state loss for long chat contexts, leading to token reordering. Secondary amplification: client SDK retries without enforced session-affinity produced duplicate inflight completions and a billing spike.

Fixes applied:
- Rolled back kernel-selection tweak in us-east (PR 4821) and deployed a guarded kernel rollout that disables compaction during active streams.
- Temporary routing to pre-warmed pool restored stability during the rollout.
- Issued a targeted billing credit to Cinder Labs (50% of the two-hour delta) and submitted final audit for adjustment.

Status: Mitigation deployed, monitoring in place, customer credited; incident closed after validation period.

Add a compaction-safe flag to the runtime that prevents KV prefix eviction during active streams (owner: Eng/Serving Runtime) — ETA 2026-03-25

Title: CumulusMart — intermittent streaming fragment interleaving due to routing oscillation (post-incident escalation)

CumulusMart — intermittent streaming fragment interleaving due to routing oscillation (post-incident escalation)

Issue summary:
Customer CumulusMart reported intermittent streaming responses that showed interleaved fragments and partial duplicate transcripts for multi-part chat completions. Symptoms began 2026-03-10 01:20 UTC and recurred on subsequent traffic spikes. Impact: several customer-facing sessions returned mixed transcripts (segments from two separate handler instances), resulting in corrupted messages and increased token billing for duplicate partial outputs.

Impact:
- Affected ~12% of CumulusMart's streamed completions during the incident window (peak 01:20–03:50 UTC).
- Some sessions exhibited fragment interleaving (parts from two different responses merged out-of-order).
- Elevated token usage contributed to a billing delta (temporary credit issued — see Resolution).

Environment:
- Dedicated pool: cumulus-dedicated-us-east (reserved capacity).
- Models used: redwood-8k-v1 primary, redwood-quant-4bit-v1 as fallback.
- Traffic routed through api-gateway cluster rgw-3 and routing control-plane region us-east-ctrl.

Steps to reproduce (observed in customer traffic):
1) Start a multi-turn streaming chat against their pinned model (redwood-8k-v1).
2) During a reservoir spike (>180 rps), routing control-plane health-checks flagged a subset of model hosts as degraded and initiated fallback to redwood-quant-4bit-v1.
3) Requests for long-context sessions got partially served by host A (old KV state) then re-routed mid-stream to host B (different KV prefix), producing interleaved chunks and duplicate partial completions.

Observed behavior / logs:
- api-gateway logs show rapid route flips for a subset of session IDs: route-change events within single request lifetime. (logs: s3://redwood-logs/prod/us-east/rgw-3/2026-03-10/stream-flip-*.gz)
- Serving runtime traces show mismatched KV-cache-version headers (kv-v: 17 vs kv-v: 18) across stream fragments for the same session id.
- Control plane health-checks returned transient 503s to router with increased flapping between 01:18–01:36 UTC.
- Linked incident on status page INC-20260310-03 (routing failover automation triggered).

Immediate mitigation applied:
- Support enabled sticky routing for affected customer (sticky until session end) at 01:40 UTC to prevent mid-stream handoff.
- Disabled cross-variant automatic fallback for sessions with active KV cache > 1k tokens.
- Opened emergency SRE rotation and paused a pending routing rollout.

Customer impact and communication:
- Customer sent urgent escalation via account channel at 01:30 UTC. Support acknowledged at 01:34 UTC and provided mitigation timeline.
- Customer-facing SLO degradation: brief stream corruption and billing exposure. Credits offered and accepted (details in Resolution).

Next actions (follow-up):
- Short-term: add KV-cache-version propagation to routing handshake to avoid cross-variant mismatches.
- Medium-term: add atomic route handoff that drains active KV namespaces before switching host for sticky sessions.
- Postmortem: full RCA and retro, update runbook for routing rollout safety checks.

Title: Multi-signal autoscaler evaluation and outcomes (signal fusion)

Multi-signal autoscaler evaluation and outcomes (signal fusion)

This sheet captures a 3-week evaluation of a multi-signal autoscaling policy that fuses utilization, queue depth, tail-latency, and predicted arrival-rate signals into a probabilistic scale decision. Goal: reduce cold starts and SLO breaches while limiting steady-state waste compared to our baseline min/max hysteresis autoscaler.
Validate that signal fusion + small stochastic smoothing can reduce 99th pct latency SLO violations and cold-start counts by >=30% with <=8% steady-state GPU idle increase across EU and us-west fleets.
Combining orthogonal signals (util + qlen + tail-latency + arrival forecast) with a weighted voting ensemble and short randomized backoff will trigger earlier scale-ups for transient spikes and delay scale-downs for recovering workloads, improving SLOs with modest cost impact.
Three policy variants (Fusion-A, Fusion-B, Fusion-C) vs Baseline. Each ran for 72h in parallel on dedicated shadow capacity slices per region (eu-west-1 and us-west-2). Traffic replay used production traces sampled from May 2026 (weekday peak + weekend). Key knobs: voting threshold, signal weights, random backoff distribution, min_pool per shard, prewarm buffer. Autoscaler operated at shard granularity (by model-size bin + region).
Signals: GPU_util (15s avg), queue_depth (1s sample), tail_latency_p95/p99 (sliding 60s), arrival_rate_forecast (10s EWMA), cold_start_rate (per-model counter). Example weights tested: {util:0.25, qlen:0.35, tail:0.25, arrival:0.15} and alternative skewed profiles. Fusion decision computes weighted score then compares to scale thresholds; separate logic for scale-up vs scale-down with asymmetric hysteresis.
Baseline: min/max + hysteresis (existing). Fusion-A: equalized weights, deterministic threshold, 30s cooldown. Fusion-B: qlen-heavy weights, randomized backoff ~Uniform(5s,20s) on scale-down. Fusion-C: forecast-amplified (arrival weight doubled), prewarm small ephemeral GPUs for predicted spikes. All Fusion variants respect per-shard min_pool and region capacity caps.
eu-west-1: 160 GPUs reserved for experiment (A100/80G mix), us-west-2: 200 GPUs (80G + 40G mixture). Shards: small (7B models) mapped to 1 GPU nodes, large (70B+) mapped to 4-GPU nodes. Prewarm buffer sizes: 2%/4% of region fleet for Fusion-C. Spot-backed auxiliary pool used in us-west-2 only for burst recovery (cold-start risk mitigation).
1) PLG chat (burst traffic from feature launch), 2) nightly batch embedding jobs (steady high-throughput), 3) unpredictable conference demo spikes (short, high QPS), 4) mixed steady + bursts from multiple customers (multi-tenant stress). Each workload run used 24–72 hour windows with throughput multipliers to stress tails.
Per-shard score S = sum(w_i * normalized(signal_i)). Scale-up if S > U_threshold OR qlen > q_thresh. Scale-down if S < D_threshold AND no tail-latency excursions in last 90s. Randomized delay applied to scale-down to avoid synchronized drains. Separate emergency scale-out path: if p99 tail-latency > 1.5x SLO AND arrival_rate spike > 2x forecast, open emergency burst pool (spot) if available.
p50/p95/p99 latency, cold_start_count, scale_up_events, scale_down_events, time_to_add_capacity (s), steady_state_gpu_idle_pct, added_gpus_hours, cost_delta_estimate ($), SLO_breach_minutes, emergency_burst_usage_hours
- Fusion-B reduced p99 SLO-breach minutes by 41% vs Baseline in eu-west-1 during weekday peak windows. - Cold starts fell 38% (Fusion-C best) due to prewarm + forecast path. - Steady-state idle increased 6.2% on average (Fusion-A) and 9.1% for Fusion-C; cost modeling shows Fusion-C cost +7% gross but net cost per successful request improved due to fewer retries. - Randomized backoff cut oscillatory scale-churn by ~52% across both regions. - Emergency burst pool used twice in us-west-2; spot init latency contributed 22s median additional time but prevented extended p99 spikes.

Fusion-A | 78 | 56 | 6.2% | 8.1 | +3.2%
Fusion-B | 71 | 48 | 5.8% | 6.4 | +2.7%
Fusion-C | 69 | 32 | 9.1% | 7.9 | +7.0%
Simple model: delta_cost = steady_idle_delta * region_hourly_gpu_cost * hours + ephemeral_spot_costs + prewarm_delta. Using EU cost assumptions, Fusion-B projected +2.4% monthly cost for customer-facing fleets, offset by ~12% fewer SLO-related retries/mitigations (engineering ops labor + incident cost).
- One 45-minute window in eu-west-1 where Fusion-A repeatedly failed to scale due to metric probe gap (monitoring pipeline delay). Root cause: transient metrics ingestion lag from a new exporter version. - Nightly embedding job patterns created long tails that arrival-forecast underestimated; Fusion-C prewarm helped but arrival model needs longer horizon for batch windows.
1) Ship conservative rollout of Fusion-B to 10% of production shards for two weeks; monitor p99 and cold-starts. 2) Harden metrics ingestion: add fallback and local aggregator to reduce probe gaps. 3) Improve arrival_rate_forecast model to incorporate 10m horizon for batch windows. 4) Add a per-customer sensitivity flag to avoid prewarm for low-value tenants (cost control). 5) Run cost analysis including incident-reduction savings for finance review.
This sheet intentionally mixes numeric summaries and observational notes for quick handoff. Keep Fusion-C as an engineering playbook for high-SLO tenants but default rollout should be Fusion-B. Watch for correlated scale-downs triggered at 03:00 UTC after DST transitions — possible clock drift in exporter. Create ticket to schedule follow-up A/B with longer-run traces.

Title: Sporadic inference stalls during high-concurrency bursts on dedicated reservation

Sporadic inference stalls during high-concurrency bursts on dedicated reservation

Issue summary: Customers on a dedicated reservation (Datawave Inc) reported intermittent inference stalls and 30-60s request timeouts during short, high-concurrency bursts on prod/us-west. The behavior started 2026-03-13 ~09:20 UTC and recurred in bursts across the morning. Impact: Client-facing features experienced elevated P95/P99 latency and ~12% user-facing errors during spikes (timeouts and 504s). Business impact: degraded UX for live features (search/rerank) for Datawave enterprise tier.

Environment: Dedicated reservation; prod region us-west; running serving-runtime v2.7.1; autoscaler config: min=2, target=5, max=8; tenant pinned to a set of GPU nodes with mixed A100-s and A10-s. Typical requests are short (avg tokens per request ~18) but concurrency bursts reach 300-600 simultaneous inflight.

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Simulate burst: 500 concurrent short requests (10-30 tokens) from single tenant for 30s.
2) Observe queue length at routing layer climb; tail-latency jumps at worker side.
3) A subset of requests (5-12%) enter prolonged stall (20-60s) before timing out.

Logs / metrics (selected excerpts):
- Scheduler queue backlog spike: routing-queue-length > 450 at 2026-03-13T09:21:12Z
- GPU utilization per-node: 40-70% but compute stalls observed (nvml stall counters incrementing)
- Serving runtime trace: many requests stuck in "acquire-kv-cache" / "gpu-lock" for 18-52s
- Autoscaler event: no scaling event until 90s after burst began (scale-up latency observed)
- Per-node error: occasional CUDA driver retries logged on A10 nodes (driver-retry=1..3)

Observed hypothesis: Short-token heavy bursts create many inflight requests that are small but frequent, producing scheduling pressure and head-of-line blocking on GPU resources. Autoscaler min/target settings plus conservative scale-up cooldown permit a transient undersupply of fully-ready GPUs; meanwhile background maintenance/batch workloads (on the same pool) intermittently contend for PCIe / MPS resources causing stalls rather than steady high utilization. This looks like a noisy-neighbor + slow autoscale ramp scenario rather than full GPU saturation.

Immediate impact: Elevated client latency and request timeouts for Datawave.

Requested customer action: None required immediately; support applied mitigations (see Workaround).

For follow-up: perform node-level forensic capture across affected window, review autoscaler cooldown settings and admission control thresholds for short-request workloads, consider tenant placement changes or burst-only buffer capacity.
1) From a client in prod/us-west, issue a 30s burst of 300-600 concurrent requests (10-30 tokens each) to the customer's pinned deployment. 2) Observe routing queue and per-node inflight counters. 3) Note that after ~10-20s queue lengths increase and a subset of requests stall for 20-60s before timeout.
- SRE (Tomas Novak) captured full nvml/gpu metrics and observed driver-retry spikes on A10 nodes.
- Support repro (Lina Gomez) was able to recreate higher queueing with synthetic load; stalls correlate with periods where the autoscaler has not yet provisioned additional nodes.
- Admission control tests show that limiting inflight per-tenant to 200 reduces stalls but increases upstream client throttling.
- There are intermittent background batch jobs scheduled on the same physical host group (found via scheduler logs) — not fully isolated.
- Hypothesis refined: a combination of head-of-line queueing, slow autoscaler reaction, and occasional noisy batch interference producing PCIe contention / driver retry leading to request stalls.
- No evidence of model-level deadlocks; KV cache behavior shows long wait times while holding locks for many small requests.

Applied by Support (2026-03-13 11:05 UTC):
- Temporarily raised autoscaler target and max for this reservation (target=7, max=10) to add headroom; nodes provisioned and reduced stalls after ~120s.
- Temporarily set admission control to 250 inflight per-tenant to limit head-of-line blocking.
- Isolated scheduled background batch jobs from the affected GPU node group for the next 48 hours.
Effect: immediate reduction in stalls and timeouts, P95 latency improved toward baseline within 3 minutes of node readiness.

Mitigation applied: autoscaler headroom increased and noisy batch jobs isolated. Engineering to follow up with a targeted fix: tune autoscaler cooldown/scale-up aggressiveness for short-burst workloads, add a per-tenant lightweight admission controller that preferentially throttles low-value concurrent requests, and update placement policy to avoid colocating batch workloads on dedicated reservations. Next steps tracked in INT-4011 and a follow-up runbook will be created. Status: monitoring; customer notified and reporting improved metrics.

Title: Rapid Rescue: Seller Sprint for Escalations and Recovery (v0.3)

Rapid Rescue: Seller Sprint for Escalations and Recovery (v0.3)

Overview
---
Purpose: Quick, actionable playdeck for sellers + SEs to triage, stabilize, and convert deals at risk due to latency/cost/regulatory objections. Focus: 20-minute call readiness, 60-minute tech follow-up plan, and handoff checklist to Solutions Engineering.
Audience: Field sellers, Solutions Engineers, AE + CSM for midmarket & enterprise deals.
Tone: tactical scripts, checklists, data points, and escalation paths — intentionally pragmatic.

Slide 1 — TL;DR (for quick prep)
- When to use: customer flags >2x expected latency, token cost shock, or network/data residency concerns during POC.
- Immediate goals: 1) calm the customer; 2) show measurable mitigation; 3) create a short timeline to remediate or provide a fallback.
- Key hooks to convert risk into value: Reserved capacity trial, Private deployment pilot, fast-fallback policy.

Slide 2 — Quick battle metrics to memorize (seller friendly)
- Typical hosted latencies: 50–250ms (short completions) / 300–1200ms (chat with history) — cite internal perf bench (Q4 2025).
- Cost ballpark: 1M tokens ~ $X hosted vs ~Y on Dedicated (show approximate multipliers). (Use real-time calc in demo)
- Conversion triggers: sustained load >500 qps or >$10k/mo spend -> Reserved discussion; compliance/regulatory -> Private.
Speaker note: don't waffle on numbers — use: "our telemetry shows X for this workload; we can run a tailored microbenchmark in 48h."

Slide 3 — 20-minute call script (starter)
1) Open: acknowledgement + empathy: "I hear this feels worse than expected — we'll get a reproducible plan."
2) Quick repro ask (under 3 min): "Can you share one request example, average sequence length, and whether embeddings/rerank used?"
3) Reassurance + immediate mitigation: "We can switch routing to Dedicated fallback or enable prefix-caching; both are reversible and low risk."
4) Next steps: "We will run a focused perf test and return with a remediation plan within 48 hours."

Slide 4 — Repro checklist for SE (what to capture in 20 mins)
- Exact request JSON / prompt + sample tokens
- Model name + pinned version (if any)
- Sequence length distribution (p90, median)
- Concurrent QPS during issue
- Whether streaming/stop tokens used
- Any policy/region constraints (data residency, IP allowlist)
- Business impact: features blocked, user-visible errors, cost delta

Slide 5 — Short technical mitigations (fast wins)
- Route to near-term Dedicated pool (if customer has reserved or trial) -> immediate latency stabilization.
- Enable prefix/KV caching on repeated prompts (saves up to 60–80% tokens for similar queries).
- Aggressive sequence truncation + summarization before model call.
- Lower precision / quantized model variant to reduce GPU memory pressure (trade quality).
- Fallback model with identical API surface + lower compute (automate in routing policy).
Notes for SE: list model variants and expected qualitative impact; include sample routing config snippet in Confluence page INF-RESCUE-2026.

Slide 6 — Cost comparison mini-math (talk track + numbers to show)
- Example workload: 200k monthly requests, avg 800 tokens/request -> 160M tokens/month.
- Hosted estimate: $A per 1M tokens -> monthly cost = calc (replace A during call).
- Dedicated reserved estimate: committed baseline + lower per-token unit -> show scenarios: 3mo trial vs 12mo commit.
- Upsell moment: show break-even month for reserved at current telemetry.

Slide 7 — Regulatory/Private pilot framing (sales hook)
- If customer raises data residency or auditability: propose 4-week Private pilot (VPC) -> collect logs/audit + KMS integration.
- Checklist for Private readiness: infra contacts, IP allowlist, compliance reviewers, dev/test dataset availability.
- Value props: audit logs, no-egress to public internet, optional on-prem packaging.

Slide 8 — Objection playbook (short scripts)
1) "Too expensive" -> "Let's run a focused token reduction + caching experiment for 2 weeks; if it doesn't reduce costs by >=X%, we'll propose a Dedicated pricing model with a cost guarantee."
2) "Latency spikes" -> "We can run canary routing and guarantee a 7-day SLA on the fallback pool while we root cause."
3) "We can't share telemetry" -> "We can do a collab session where you share sanitized traces; if needed, provide an on-site SE session under NDA or do a Private pilot."

Slide 9 — Demo checklist (to run live)
- Pre-call: create demo tenant with identical model variant and synthetic traffic that mirrors their average tokens and QPS.
- Show: baseline latency, enable prefix cache, re-run synthetic traffic, show delta.
- Show fallback policy in console: change routing to Dedicated/Lower-cost model and switch back.
- Capture screenshots and attach to the follow-up email.

Slide 10 — Escalation matrix (who to ping, when)
- T+0–24h: AE + field SE to own customer comms.
- T+24–48h: Eng on-call for Serving Runtime (pager: eng-sre on-call) if root cause looks infra-related.
- T+48–72h: Solutions Eng + Applied ML for model/quantization changes.
- Internal shortcut: if customer expresses churn risk in next 30 days, escalate to GTM leadership (cc: Head of Sales).
Contact hints: use Slack #field-rescue for synchronous patches; include JIRA GTMSUP-3421 in all updates.

Slide 11 — Quick email templates (copy/paste)
- Immediate follow-up after 20-min call: "Thanks — recap + agreed 48h action plan" (short bullets + attachments).
- After mitigation test: "Results + recommendation" (show numbers, next formal offer: Dedicated trial / Private pilot).
- Renewal/commit ask template: "Given our test showed X% latency reduction and Y% token reduction, can we commit to a 3-month reserved trial?"

Slide 12 — Risk to convert: timing & procurement tips
- Procurement note: reserved contracts need 3–4 week lead for procurement + finance signatures at midmarket.
- Sticky conversion levers: pilot success metrics (latency p95, cost per 1k tokens, availability), and short SLA bump for Dedicated trials.
- Ask for commitment: include a conditional clause to convert trial credits to reserved capacity if metrics met.

Slide 13 — Companion artifacts (where to find the deep links)
- Confluence: INF-RESCUE-2026 (playbook + routing examples)
- Demo tenant: demo/rapid-rescue/region-us-west (ask infra to provision)
- JIRA: GTMSUP-3421 (customer: AcmeCorp placeholder)
- Field kit: /go-to-market/field-kits/rescue-checklist.csv (attach screenshots)

Slide 14 — Postmortem template (capture in CONFLUENCE)
- Summary: one-line problem statement.
- Timeline: events T0..Tn.
- Root cause hypothesis + evidence.
- Mitigations applied and impact numbers.
- Action owners + deadlines.
- Customer sentiment + next steps for success plan.

Slide 15 — Open questions & product asks (send to Product/Applied ML)
- Auto-telemetry sampler that masks PII but preserves perf distributions.
- One-click private pilot provisioning (reduce infra lead time from weeks to days).
- Routing-dashboard: show live cost delta if you switch to fallback model.
- Request: prioritize JIRA INF-3810 (canary auto-fallback heatmap).

Appendix: quick rebut bullets vs common competitors
- Competitor A: lower latency at cost of model precision -> reply: "We offer routing + quantization profiles so you can tune per-route quality guarantees."
- Competitor B: promises on-prem but long lead time -> reply: "Private pilot template reduces time to first audit by provisioning standard artifacts up front."

Title: SLO Sentinel: Prefetch Routing and Graded Circuit Breakers for Multi-Region Requests

SLO Sentinel: Prefetch Routing and Graded Circuit Breakers for Multi-Region Requests

Problem: We see recurring SLO drift during regional capacity pressure and cold-KV-cache misses. Current geo-steering only reroutes after failures or gross latency spikes; this causes user-facing p99 regressions and noisy fallback loops. Goal: introduce an SLO-driven controller (SLO Sentinel) that (1) predicts imminent latency risk, (2) prefetches/warms KV cache and minimal model state in candidate regions, and (3) enforces graded circuit breakers and capacity-aware steering to avoid cascading failures while preserving high-priority traffic.

Design summary:
- SLO Sentinel: a central controller that ingests region-level telemetry (p50/p95/p99, CPU/GPU utilization, queue depth, capacity tokens) and computes a risk score per region using an EWMA trend + short-term derivative.
- Prefetch routing: when a region's risk score exceeds a warmup threshold, the controller triggers targeted prefetch ops to warm KV caches and small model kernels in the target region (prefetch budget controlled per-customer and globally). Prefetch uses an async lightweight path and applies only to routes with high recent locality.
- Graded circuit breakers (three bands):
  * Green (OK): normal steering by latency-weighted preference.
  * Yellow (degraded): soft-shed non-critical routes (batch jobs, non-PLG traffic) and divert new requests to nearby healthy regions; keep existing sessions sticky for a grace window.
  * Red (severe): open circuit for non-essential traffic; enforce strict geo-pin relax + route to fallback model variant (quantized/smaller) for critical sessions.
- Capacity-aware steering: instead of naive ejection, each request consumes a token from per-region capacity escrow. The routing decision is token-aware: prefer regions with headroom. A background allocator replenishes tokens based on autoscaler signals and a hysteresis window.

Key thresholds and SLOs (proposed):
- Interactive SLO: p95 < 120ms, p99 < 400ms global for hosted tier.
- Yellow trigger: region p99 > 350ms for 30s OR 70% GPU queue depth sustained for 60s.
- Red trigger: region p99 > 700ms for 15s OR >90% capacity tokens consumed.
- Prefetch budget: limit to 5% of traffic-equivalent warmups per region per minute; configurable per-customer.

Telemetry and metrics to add:
- region_risk_score (EWMA + derivative), prefetch_count, prefetch_success_rate, circuit_level{green,yellow,red}, capacity_tokens_total/consumed, headroom_estimate, route_latency_{p50,p95,p99} by route/model/region.

Rollout plan:
1) Implement controller and minimal hooks in runtime (prefetch API + token escrow) behind feature flag.
2) Internal canary: enable for infra test tenant in us-west-2 only (1% of prod traffic). Monitor SLOs, prefetch cost, and false positive warmups for 1 week.
3) Gradually expand to non-critical customers globally (10% traffic), then to all hosted API with opt-out.
4) For Dedicated customers, expose circuit-level controls and prefetch budgets as config in Console.

Trade-offs and risks:
- Prefetching reduces p99 but increases bandwidth and GPU cycles; cost must be guarded with budgets and per-customer limits.
- Over-eager prefetching could amplify thrash; we mitigate with derivative-based risk scoring and cooldowns.
- Token escrow adds complexity to routing; failure modes include token desync — plan includes reconciliation and fail-open paths.

Open implementation tasks:
- Add prefetch endpoints to runtime and a lightweight prewarm DAG (ENG tasks).
- Implement SLO Sentinel controller and scoring library.
- Telemetry: Grafana panels and alerts for circuit transitions and prefetch anomalies.
- Console UI: expose per-customer prefetch budget and circuit-level overrides.

Acceptance criteria:
- No regression on baseline SLOs in control regions.
- p99 improvement >=15% in simulated partial-capacity events in canary.
- Prefetch cost < 10% incremental infra cost in canary.
- Clear dashboards and alerts; on-call runbook updated.
