Title: Zone-aware tiered failover strategy notes

Zone-aware tiered failover strategy notes

Purpose
This note captures a variant approach to multi-region traffic steering: a zone-aware, tiered failover strategy that combines local edge decisions, soft-ejection tiers, and capacity-aware routing signals from the control plane. The goal is to provide predictable SLO behavior under region-level degradations while minimizing cross-region egress costs and preserving session locality for long-lived chats.

Motivation and constraints
- We need a steering model that behaves well for both bursty short requests (stateless text generation) and sticky long sessions (chat with KV cache).
- Cross-region egress is expensive and adds latency; avoid broad blast radiuses of failover when only a subset of AZs or racks are unhealthy.
- Some customers pin region preference for compliance; failover must respect per-customer policy tiers.
- Operators want clear, low-risk actions: soft-ejects, capacity throttles, and explicit cold-failover only when needed.

High-level approach
1) Local Edge First: edge proxies (region ingress) should make the first steering decision using recent probes + cached control plane policy. The edge attempts regional-serving paths first and performs minimal hedging.

2) Tiered Ejection Model: three escalating tiers applied per logical region or zone:
   - Tier 1: Smart-soft-eject (30s–5m). Redirect small fraction of traffic off the primary AZ/region using weighted sampling; used for transient latency spikes.
   - Tier 2: Capacity-aware reroute (5m–30m). When sustained high queuing or GPU pressure observed, reroute non-sticky requests to secondary region(s) while preserving sticky sessions locally.
   - Tier 3: Cold failover (30m+). Full region ejection and client rebinds to alternate region; used for confirmed region outage or sustained control plane consensus that region is unhealthy.

3) Customer Preference and Compliance: policy layers applied in control plane specify per-tenant region preference and allowlist for failover targets. Edge enforces these as absolute constraints (no automatic cross-region unless explicit allowlist).

Control plane signals and APIs
- DesiredState (DS): authoritative per-route steering policy (weights, allowed regions, tier thresholds). Small, frequently updated blob pushed to region control-plane caches.
- ObservedState (OS): aggregated telemetry from region agents (latency histograms, GPU util, queue lengths, probe status). OS drives automated recommendations but is not a hard override.
- EdgePolicyCache: each ingress node keeps a locally reconciled policy = f(DS, OS, local probes, tenant overrides).

API sketches (informal)
- GET /policy/v1/tenant/{id}/route -> returns DesiredState with failover tiers and allowedRegions
- POST /telemetry/v1/region/{r}/observed -> time-windowed aggregates (p50,p95,p99 latencies, cpu/gpu%, queueDepth)
- PATCH /policy/v1/route/{r}/override -> operator trigger for manual ejection

Local probing model
- Probes are two-tiered: fast syn-probes to control-plane endpoints (1s TTL) and slow end-to-end synthetic requests that exercise full inference path (60s TTL).
- Probe scoring uses exponential decay windows (short: 60s, medium: 10m, long: 1h). Edge computes a single health score H in [0,1]. Thresholds map to tiers: H>0.8 healthy; 0.5–0.8 soft-eject; 0.2–0.5 capacity reroute; <0.2 cold failover candidate.

Hedging and sampling strategy
- For Tier 1 soft-eject we apply probabilistic sampling: 1–10% initial traffic, ramping up if probes remain degraded. Ramp controlled by a token-bucket per-route at the edge to avoid sudden traffic spikes to secondary region.
- Sticky sessions: identify via tenant/session cookie and pin to primary as long as KV cache exists and H above sticky threshold (0.3). For sticky requests above threshold, we allow limited failover only if explicit operator override exists.

Capacity-aware prioritization
- Control plane publishes a region-capacity-index (RCI) per model family: estimated concurrent tokens served for 50ms p50 tail. Edge multiplies RCI by allocated weight to compute soft-capacity limits.
- When queueDepth > soft-capacity*0.9 and OS shows rising GPU util, edge triggers Tier 2 reroute for best-effort routes. Critical routes (by tag) are exempt unless operator escalates.

Cost and latency tradeoffs
- Default policy biases locality: prefer same-region at cost delta <= 50ms. For latency-sensitive customers, a per-route SLA can override to prefer lower latency even if cross-region egress cost doubles; such SLAs are recorded in DS.
- During Tier 2, route-level cost budgets are decremented and reported to billing/alerts to avoid runaway egress charges.

Consistency and control-plane reconciliation
- Edges reconcile DS every 30s and accept DS with last-write time. For transient control-plane partitioning, local probes are authoritative for 2 minutes to avoid oscillation.
- A simple vector clock appended to DS ensures we can detect stale policies and avoid applying superseded manual ejections.

Observability and debugging primitives
- Per-request steering trace headers: x-steering-reason, x-policy-version, x-probe-score, x-rc-index. These are surfaced in Console logs and sample traces to SRE.
- Rollup dashboards: region health heatmap, per-tenant failover events, cross-region egress costing by hour.
- Postmortem tags: when a route escalates to Tier 3, automatically open a 'steering-eject' issue with attached telemetry snapshot.

Operational playbook (short)
- Detection (automated): when probe H drops below 0.5 for >120s, Tier 1 soft-eject starts at 2% sample. Notify SRE and tenant owners.
- Evaluate: after 10m if H still <0.5 and GPU util >85%, escalate to Tier 2 for non-sticky routes. Notify finance if cost threshold exceeded.
- Escalate: Tier 3 requires >=30m sustained degraded H and cross-region quorum from control plane (2 of 3 region agents). Manual override permitted.

Failure modes and mitigations
- Control plane partitioning: rely on local probes for short windows and limit policy TTL to avoid stale global ejections.
- Oscillation between regions: use hysteresis by requiring both time and delta magnitude before adjusting weights (min-change = 5% weight, min-duration = 60s).
- Over-ejection causing overload in secondaries: use token-bucket ramp + capacity feedback loop to throttle incoming reroutes.

Example lightweight policy YAML (for human readers)
route: /v1/generate
models: [redwood-3b-fp16, redwood-3b-qt8]
preferred_regions:
  - us-west1
  - us-central1
allow_failover: true
failover_tiers:
  soft_eject:
    probe_threshold: 0.8
    initial_sample: 0.02
    max_sample: 0.2
    ramp_seconds: 180
  capacity_reroute:
    probe_threshold: 0.5
    exclude_sticky: true
  cold_failover:
    probe_threshold: 0.2
    min_duration_minutes: 30

Open questions and next steps
- How to generalize RCI across model families with mixed precision/quantization? Need a benchmark-based translator (tokens/sec -> RCI).
- Tenant communication: what is reasonable default notification SLA for soft-eject events? 15m? 30m?
- Can we prototype an edge-side simulation harness to validate hysteresis parameters before rollout? (recommended)

Summary
This note proposes a conservative, zone-aware multi-tier approach that leans on local edge decision-making combined with control-plane policy for constraints and telemetry aggregation. The emphasis is on minimizing cross-region churn, preserving sticky session locality, and providing clear operational levers (soft-eject, capacity reroute, cold failover). Next steps: prototype edge policy cache reconciliation, implement probe scoring in edge binary, and run a chaos experiment simulating partial region pressure to tune tier thresholds.

Title: Queue Fallback Orchestration and Soft Throttling for Multi-Region Stability

Queue Fallback Orchestration and Soft Throttling for Multi-Region Stability

Problem: During regional overload or downstream degradation we currently either outright reject requests or apply blunt global caps that harm high-priority customers. We need a finer-grained, multi-region aware mechanism that gracefully reduces resource consumption while preserving latency SLOs for critical traffic and avoiding global cascading failures.

Goal: Implement a queue orchestration layer that coordinates per-region ephemeral queues, performs soft throttling (delay + lightweight degradations) and orchestrates controlled failover to remote regions or cheaper model variants when necessary. The system should be policy-driven, observable, and reversible by runbook or automated SLO triggers.
Canary deploy in eu-west-1 handling 10% of traffic: soft-throttle paths exercised with no more than 5% increase in p50 and preserving p99 latency SLO for tier-1 tenants
Grace levels implemented: DELAY (client-visible short delay), TRUNCATE (return partial/summary output), REDIRECT (route to secondary region/model), REJECT (final fallback)
Per-route policy config UI + API in console and feature-flag toggle for experiments
Dashboards show queue occupancy, average soft-throttle delay, degrade-mode hit-rate, and error-budget burn per-region
Automated rollback if error rate increases >200% above baseline or if 10m sustained p99 breach
Design trade-offs: prefer temporary, reversible soft degradations over immediate hard rejects to maintain developer UX and avoid automated client retries that amplify load.
We will avoid tenant-wide hard caps. Instead use dynamic per-route prioritization with a simple priority mapping (tier-1,tier-2,tier-3) supplied by auth token metadata.
Soft throttling actions ordered by cost-impact: 1) small randomized delay (50-500ms), 2) compress/summary output, 3) shorten max_tokens, 4) route to cheaper quantized model / secondary region.
Latency SLOs targeted: p50 < 120ms, p95 < 400ms, p99 < 900ms for tier-1 within region; soft-throttle should preserve these for tier-1 under mild overload.
Will implement a policy evaluator library in runtime that is lightweight and suitable for hot path execution; policies stored in control plane with aggressive caching.
Circuit-breaker integration: the orchestrator will watch regional health and decide to escalate degradations or initiate cross-region reroute when capacity fallbacks occur.
Avoiding cascading failure: introduce backoff windows and minimum dwell time before lowering degradation level to prevent flip-flop.
Security: no customer data modification in degrade modes; summaries must be deterministic and respect PII redaction policies. Security review not required for core orchestration (operator controls only).

Title: Seamless Region Fallback Controller with Graceful Traffic Drain and Model-variant Circuit Breakers

Seamless Region Fallback Controller with Graceful Traffic Drain and Model-variant Circuit Breakers

Goal: Implement a region-fallback controller that coordinates warm-standby readiness, performs graceful traffic drain from a failing region, and automatically falls back to compatible model variants with circuit-breaker semantics.

Scope: controller + runtime hooks + health gate definitions + rollout strategy. Not in scope: UI console changes (follow-up ticket) and billing changes.

Design highlights:
- Health gates: define multi-tier readiness checks (node-level kube probe, model-process liveness, KV-cache primer, synthetic latency/quality probe) that must pass before a region accepts production traffic.
- Warm-standby orchestration: maintain minimal pool in standby regions with GPU memory reserved for pinned models; use a priming flow that pre-populates KV caches for common prefixes tied to customer routes.
- Graceful drain: on region degraded signal, run a prioritized drain where VIP/routing layer shifts new requests to fallback targets while in-flight requests continue until token-limit or timeout. Implement back-pressure so downstream dedicated pools are not overwhelmed.
- Tier routing and circuit breakers: if primary model variant is unavailable, automatically route to a semantically-compatible variant (smaller quantized or different architecture) only when QoS metrics for that variant are within configured thresholds; otherwise escalate to deny/queue policy. Circuit breaker opens on sustained error rate or latency breach and closes progressively with canary checks.
- Metrics and SLOs: controller exposes per-region gates and model-variant health metrics to Grafana dashboards plus alerting rules for SRE and on-call.

Non-functional constraints: must add no more than 1.5ms mean added latency on request path in steady-state; controller decisions must be auditable and reversible; all changes follow rollout canary and feature-flagging patterns.

- Draft architecture doc: https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/folders/1A2b3c-fallback-controller

Title: Regional affinity, hysteresis, and probabilistic failover — design notes

Regional affinity, hysteresis, and probabilistic failover — design notes

Summary:

These notes capture a proposed design for multi-region traffic steering that prioritizes regional affinity for lower latency and data locality while avoiding global synchronized failovers and flip-flop during transient outages. The approach combines:

- preference-weighted routing (GeoDNS / control-plane weights)
- Anycast for coarse-grained region selection where applicable
- edge-local health + capacity signals
- hysteresis windows and a probabilistic failover mechanism to smooth transitions
- capacity-aware admission control to avoid overloading healthy regions during spillover

Goals:
- Preserve regional affinity for the majority of sessions to minimize p95 latency and cross-region egress.
- Fail fast for unhealthy regions but avoid global traffic avalanches if a single region reports transient issues.
- Support predictable canary and incremental rollouts across regions.
- Integrate with our control plane (config push + xDS-style) and metrics pipelines.

Constraints / assumptions:
- We operate in 6 active regions with regional Dedicated pools (us-west1, us-east1, eu-west1, ap-southeast1, etc.).
- Data-plane agents publish local health/capacity to the control plane every 5s.
- DNS is managed by a multi-provider stack supporting GeoDNS and EDNS-client-subnet annotations; Anycast is used for some low-latency endpoints.
- Some customers require strict regional residency (cannot cross region) — those requests must be honored prior to preference logic.

High-level design decisions:

1) Control-plane vs DNS vs Anycast responsibilities
- Use Anycast + local LB for first-hop connection locality where low-ttl DNS is not acceptable (e.g., streaming websocket endpoints). Anycast gives quick routing to closest POP.
- Use GeoDNS for long-lived HTTP clients where we can leverage small TTLs and preference weights. GeoDNS will be the canonical place for region preference weights, but it is a read-only reflection of decisions made in the control plane.
- The control plane computes region weights per route based on: regional latency SLOs, capacity headroom, recent error rates, customer residency flags, and business-tier preferences.

2) Affinity model
- Default: soft affinity for 90% of new requests — try to route to the preferred region. If the preferred region lacks headroom, route to the next-preferred region.
- Strong affinity (session stickiness) when a session_id or conversation_id is present: prefer the same region for the life of the session unless region becomes unhealthy for > hysteresis window.
- Affinity enforcement is token-aware. Route decisions use a consistent-hash on session_id + bucketed weights to keep distribution stable.

3) Hysteresis & stabilization
- For any region state change (healthy -> degraded or vice-versa) we apply a stabilization window to prevent flip-flop:
  - degrade_threshold: sustained error rate above 3% or p95 latency > 2x baseline for 30s -> mark degraded (soft).
  - unhealthy_threshold: sustained error rate above 7% or p95 latency > 3x baseline for 90s -> mark unhealthy (hard).
  - recovery_threshold: metrics under degrade_threshold for 120s -> mark healthy.
- During a degrade->healthy transition we use a ramp-up profile (25% -> 50% -> 100%) over 5 minutes to rehydrate traffic.

4) Probabilistic failover to avoid traffic avalanches
- When spilling traffic from region A to other regions, we do not immediately move 100% of the failing region’s traffic. Instead we use weighted probabilistic spillover:
  - Compute candidate destinations (B, C, …) with available capacity.
  - For each new request destined for A, if A is degraded/unhealthy, draw a random number r in [0,1]. If r < p_spill(A), route to backup region according to weight distribution; else attempt A.
  - p_spill starts small (0.05) when degrade first detected and grows exponentially toward 0.9 over a configured ramp (e.g., 5 minutes) if error signals persist.
- Rationale: randomized routing prevents synchronized retries from overwhelming a single backup region and spreads load probabilistically across multiple healthy regions.

5) Capacity-aware admission and per-region headroom
- Control plane maintains per-region capacity estimate (tokens/sec and active sessions). Backups must be chosen such that (current_load + expected_spill) <= safe_capacity (e.g., 75% of provisioned).
- If all candidates lack headroom, circuit-break to a lower-cost fallback model or return a controlled degraded response (503 with Retry-After and hint). For customers with strict residency, return 451 / policy error.

6) Data-plane implementation notes
- Each edge POP runs a local steering agent that:
  - pulls control-plane routing profiles (weights, ttl, thresholds) via authenticated gRPC stream.
  - exposes local health metrics aggregated from local workers.
  - runs routing decision logic locally for sub-10ms decision latency.
- Agents must be stateless regarding global decisions; they only persist short-lived session-affinity caches (LRU, TTL=24h).
- For anycast endpoints, we only permit intra-region rebalancing: if POP health degrades, BGP withdraw + control-plane weight updates used. Anycast cannot easily guarantee per-customer residency — for residency contracts we disable Anycast and use GeoDNS+sticky config.

7) DNS TTL and caching strategy
- GeoDNS records: TTL 20s for high-change routes (canary or unstable), 60s for normal preference routes, 300s for locked enterprise-only records.
- Publish DNS hints that indicate region preferences (EDNS options) for recursive resolvers; when possible, use short TTLs combined with control-plane push to edge agents to make data-plane authoritative.

8) Canary and rollout support
- Rollouts are modeled as incremental changes to region weights with explicit ramp schedules encoded in the control plane.
- Canary example: route 5% new sessions to eu-west1 for 10 minutes, monitor p95 and error rate. If metrics OK, increment to 20%, etc. Canary is enforced via probabilistic assignment at the edge agent.

9) Observability & alarms
- Key signals: regional p50/p95 latency, error_rate (4xx/5xx), CPU/GPU utilization by model, active sessions, queue depth, token throughput.
- Derived signals: regional_headroom_pct, spill_rate, routing_entropy (to detect hotspots), cross-region_egress_bytes.
- Alerts:
  - P1: region_unhealthy (unhealthy_threshold exceeded) -> page on-call SRE + ops.
  - P2: spill_rate sustained > 5% for 10m -> Slack channel and duty engineer.
  - P3: routing_entropy drops suddenly -> investigate possible misconfiguration or traffic storm.

10) Operational playbook (simplified)
- Automatic: control plane detects unhealthy region -> begins probabilistic spill over -> edge agents apply rate checks and route.
- Engineer flow: verify metrics, if targeted fix available (e.g., scaling) then prefer scaling; otherwise manually adjust weights.
- Emergency: if region is fully down, escalate to manual DNS/Anycast withdraw, then route via baseline global pool.
- Recovery: once metrics stabilize, ramp down p_spill and reintroduce traffic according to ramp-up profile.

11) Failure modes and mitigations
- Synchronized client retries: mitigate with jittered retry guidance in SDKs; probabilistic routing reduces correlated retries.
- DNS resolver caching longer than TTL: use control-plane hints, and for critical customers use IP pinning/enterprise overrides.
- Capacity estimation drift: conservative headroom defaults and periodic calibration tests (synthetic traffic).

12) Testing plan
- Chaos tests: region failure (simulate partial network partition), rapid flapping, heavy burst that forces spillover. Run against staging with scaled-down realistic traffic for 6 regions.
- Load tests: ramp global QPS and validate headroom calculations and backpressure.
- Canary paths: opt-in internal customers to validate behaviour before wider rollout.

Open questions / next steps:
- How do we differentiate spill policies for streaming websocket sessions vs short HTTP calls? (Proposed: prefer local Anycast for websockets; fallback via sticky session proxy if re-route required.)
- Integration with pricing tier: should premium customers be prioritized for spill targets? (Tie to contractual SLOs and SLA-engineered weights.)
- Policy UI on Console: expose per-customer residency enforcement and manual override knobs for SRE.

Action items:
- (Daniel) Prototype probabilistic spill algorithm in redwood-routing (PR referenced above) — 2 weeks.
- (Leila) Add synthetic calibration job for regional headroom metrics — 1 week.
- (Marco) Draft console UI wireframe for residency toggles and manual weight override — 2 weeks.
- (Priya) Create chaos test plan and schedule first run in staging — 2 weeks.

References:
- Confluence: PLAT-MULTI-REGION-ARCH-122
- Jira: PLAT-2401
- GitHub PR: repo/redwood-routing/pull/387

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally conservative on immediate traffic movement and emphasizes smoothing. Looking for feedback on thresholds, p_spill ramp shape (linear vs exponential), and whether to centralize probabilistic decision in control plane vs local agent.

End of doc.

Title: Capacity-aware steering and gradual failover playbook

Capacity-aware steering and gradual failover playbook

Purpose:
This note captures a pragmatic design and operational playbook for steering user traffic across regions with awareness of regional capacity, warm-standby pre-warming, and a gradual failover path designed to avoid sudden overload and to minimize user-visible degradation. It is intended to inform the control-plane implementation and ops runbooks (DNS/Anycast/Traffic Manager).

Assumptions and constraints:
- We have multiple regions (us-west, us-east, eu-west, ap-southeast) with different GPU capacity profiles and variable spare capacity.
- Data residency controls may require sticky-region routing for some tenants; these are handled as policy constraints upstream of steering logic.
- Runtime supports model variants and autoscaling but cold-start penalties make sudden traffic spikes risky.
- DNS TTLs are finite (e.g., 30s–60s) and many clients respect caching leading to delayed convergence.
- Anycast is available from edge POPs for fast routing but regional affinity is required for some workloads.

High-level goals:
- Prefer local/low-latency regions when capacity allows.
- Avoid saturating a single region; steer based on spare capacity and historical load patterns.
- Provide a controlled failover path that ramps traffic to backups gradually (percentage-based ramping) rather than immediate cutover.
- Pre-warm (reserve) capacity for likely failover targets when downstream health degrades beyond thresholds.
- Make routing decisions explainable and auditable: record reasons for weights/decisions.

Key concepts and vocabulary:
- Spare Capacity Ratio (SCR): (available_slots / max_slots) measured per model-class and region.
- Effective Weight: base_weight * min(1, SCR / SCR_target) — reduces weight when region is constrained.
- Warm Pool: reserved fraction of instances kept ready to absorb ramped traffic for X minutes.
- Gradual Failover: a timed sequence of weight shifts (e.g., 10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100%) with each step gated by health/latency metrics.

Control plane responsibilities:
- Compute per-region steering weights at configurable cadence (default 15s).
- Ingest telemetry: p95 latency, queue backlog, GPU utilization, model inference errors, and synthesis of SCR per model-class.
- Maintain policy layer for tenant-level constraints (region locks, allowed-fallbacks).
- Orchestrate warm-pool commands to Dedicated/Private clusters (API call to autoscaler).
- Emit signed decisions to data plane (DNS entries, Anycast policy, proxy config) with decision metadata and TTL hints.

Data plane options and tradeoffs:
1) GeoDNS (region-pref weighted answers):
   - Pros: fine-grained weight control by region, cheap, integrates with DNS-based geographic affinity.
   - Cons: DNS caching delays, clients that ignore all answers, can't steer in-flight TCP connections.

2) Anycast + regional origin selection (edge directs to closest origin then edge-to-region steering):
   - Pros: fast path for new connections, better when client IP geography is inconsistent with desired region.
   - Cons: requires edge to be smart and trust control-plane signals; complexity increases.

3) Application-layer routing (redirects, signed routing headers, or proxy-level routing):
   - Pros: greatest control and immediate reaction; can respect tenant constraints and sticky session semantics.
   - Cons: adds hop and latency; higher ops complexity.

Hybrid recommendation: use GeoDNS as primary long-lived weight distribution, with Anycast edge ensuring low-latency ingress. The edge uses control-plane weight updates to bias region selection for sessions started at that edge. Application-layer steering is used for tenant-level overrides and emergency traffic siphons.

Capacity-aware weighting algorithm (sketch):
1) For each model-class M and region R compute SCR_R = available_capacity_R_M / provisioned_capacity_R_M.
2) Compute base_weight_R from latency preference map (local regions higher).
3) Apply capacity dampening: weight_R = base_weight_R * sigmoid((SCR_R - target_scr) / smoothing).
4) Normalize weights across allowed regions.
5) If any region SCR < critical_threshold then trigger warm-pool activation in top-N candidate fallback regions.

Warm-pool semantics:
- Target: bring reserve_nodes = ceil(requested_qps / qps_per_node * warm_margin) online within warm_window (default 3–5 minutes).
- Billing/cost: track warm-pool minutes separately and expose to cost dashboards; operator must be able to opt-out for cost-sensitive tenants.
- Health gating: increase steering weight to a warm-pool region only after health checks (control-plane probe and model-level readiness) pass for two successive intervals.

Gradual failover sequence (example):
Trigger condition: primary_region p95_latency > 2x SLO for 3 consecutive evaluation intervals or SCR < 0.15.
1) Step 0 (detection): Record event, annotate decision intent (why). Keep primary traffic at 100% for up to detection_cooldown (30s) while issuing warm-pool calls.
2) Step 1 (initial shift): Shift 10% of new session traffic away to fallback regions according to capacity-aware weights. Monitor error rate and p95. Wait 45–60s.
3) Gate: if error rate increase < 2x and p95 doesn't degrade in fallback, proceed. Otherwise rollback to Step 0 and try alternate fallback region.
4) Step 2 (ramp): Move to 30% over next 60–90s. Continue monitoring.
5) Step 3 (aggressive): Move to 60% if metrics continue to meet acceptance.
6) Step 4 (full cutover): If primary is still degraded, advance to 100% failover.
Notes: session affinity — for stateful sessions we drain existing sessions gradually (TTL-based or via token-level routing) to avoid mid-session disruption.

Health and gating signals (control-plane uses):
- p95 inference latency, error-rate, queue_length_growth_rate, GPU OOM/eviction events, model warmup status.
- Synthetic probes per region/model that exercise the same model path as traffic.
- Cross-region delta checks to detect global incidents (e.g., network partitions causing artificial low-latency reports).

Operational considerations and edge cases:
- DNS TTL tuning: For hosts expected to failover quickly, use low TTL (30s) but accept increased DNS overhead. For stable endpoints use 60–120s.
- Cold-start spikes: detect amplification loops where failover increases cold-starts causing higher latency and more failover. Mitigate by limiting ramp rate and using warm pools.
- Partial POP outage: Anycast decisions should degrade to region preference rather than all-to-one collapse. Edge-level fallback config must be conservative.
- Cost vs reliability: expose a tenant-level option in the control plane (reliability_priority: high/medium/cost_saver) that affects warm-pool and multi-region preference.

Testing and validation plan:
- Chaos tests: introduce a simulated regional capacity drop (reduce available_slots) and validate gradual failover timeline and absence of overload in fallback regions.
- Load replay: replay production traffic shape against staging multi-region infra to validate SCR signals and steering stability.
- DNS convergence drills: measure client-side failover times under different TTLs by instrumenting synthetic clients globally.
- Runbook dry-runs: operators execute manual failover using the playbook to ensure control-plane commands behave as expected.

Telemetry and observability requirements:
- Per-decision audit log: decision_id, timestamp, inputs (SCRs, base_weights, policy flags), output weights, operator override flag.
- Dashboards: per-region capacity, weight history, ramp events, warm-pool status, and incidents correlated with decision_id.
- Alerting: composite alerts that fire when ramps exceed configured thresholds or when warm-pool activation fails.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How many pre-warmed minutes are acceptable from a finance perspective for enterprise tenants? Need input from finance for default budget guardrails.
- Should we implement a secondary failover strategy that prefers model-quantized variants in backup regions to reduce resource needs? (pros/cons: reduced quality vs cost).
- Integration with Tenant routing policies: what is the canonical API for specifying region locks and allowed fallback sets? Proposal: tenant policy object with allowed_regions list + reliability_priority enum.

Appendix: simple pseudo-config examples (control-plane friendly)
- Tenant policy example: {
  "tenant_id": "acme-prod",
  "allowed_regions": ["us-west","us-east"],
  "reliability_priority": "high",
  "sticky_sessions": true
}
- Steering decision record (flat view): {
  "decision_id": "dec-20250310-0410",
  "model": "text-gen-v2",
  "input_weights": "{us-west:0.6, us-east:0.4}",
  "scrs": "{us-west:0.2, us-east:0.45}",
  "output_weights": "{us-west:0.35, us-east:0.65}",
  "reason": "us-west SCR below target, warmed us-east pool"
}

Conclusion:
A capacity-aware, gradual failover mechanism reduces blast radius during region degradations and prevents overload of fallback regions. The control plane must tightly integrate telemetry, autoscaling (warm pools), and weight computation while providing clear audit trails for decisions. Next steps: prototype the weight function in the steering service, add warm-pool orchestration endpoints in autoscaler API, and run the chaos/validation plan against staging.

Title: Adaptive backpressure and prioritized admission control for multi-region failover

Adaptive backpressure and prioritized admission control for multi-region failover

Problem: During cross-region outages we observe sudden traffic surges that exceed local capacity. Current shedding is binary and global: whole model variants are dropped or global rate limits trigger, which causes severe user-visible failures for high-priority tenants and long tail requests. We need a region-aware, priority-sensitive backpressure system that applies graceful degradation at multiple levels (request admission, per-tenant soft caps, response-quality degradation) and coordinates with circuit breakers to avoid cascading failures.
A region-aware admission controller is implemented that enforces prioritized lanes (system, SLA, best-effort) and can demote or delay best-effort traffic under contention
Per-tenant soft caps are configurable via Console and enforced by admission control with metrics exposed (rejection_rate, queued_ms, demotion_count)
A graceful degradation policy exists that can switch routes from full-generation -> reduced-token -> metadata-only modes dynamically and independently per tenant/route
Circuit-breaker integration: when downstream model latency/error thresholds are crossed, controller triggers demotion of low-priority lanes and opens a short circuit for non-essential paths
Canary rollout in two regions with traffic shaping and automated rollback if SLO regressions exceed thresholds
Dashboard shows per-region lane utilization, dropped_requests_by_reason, and per-tenant SLOs; alerts fire on >1% high-priority rejection over 5m or >10% latency p99 regression
Use lane-based admission rather than single global token queue to allow targeted shedding and visibility
Admission controller runs as a sidecar in edge proxies and as a centralized control-plane policy for cross-region decisions
Demotion strategy: prefer reducing compute (reduced-token) before outright rejecting for tenants with medium SLAs; best-effort tenants can be rejected earlier
Circuit-breaker thresholds are conservative to avoid flip-flopping: 3s p95 latency or 10% error rate sustained over 30s triggers demotion
Backpressure signal uses token-based budget accounting (remaining_compute_budget) per route/tenant to prevent head-of-line blocking
Configuration exposed via Console + API with default safe profiles to avoid accidental total denial of service for new tenants

Title: Proactive congestion-island detection and sticky-region guardrails

Proactive congestion-island detection and sticky-region guardrails

Summary: During a progressive traffic surge on 2026-03-09 we observed cross-region failover amplification that caused an SLO miss for request p99 latency and error rate for hosted inference customers. Secondary regions entered a congestion mode that persisted despite circuit-breaker trips; routing replays and probe jitter amplified load to warm caches and overloaded GPUS. This ticket captures the postmortem analysis and prescribes mitigations and follow-ups to prevent recurrence.
2026-03-09 09:12 UTC - Automated health checks detected increased tail latency in region-eu-west-1.
2026-03-09 09:18 UTC - Smart routing triggered failover policy to reroute ~18% of traffic to region-us-west-2 (secondary).
2026-03-09 09:21 UTC - Circuit breakers in us-west-2 tripped and then rapidly reset due to short hysteresis config; controllers replayed queued requests.
2026-03-09 09:26 UTC - Observed progressive KV cache cold misses and repeated replays; GPU utilization saturated and request queues began to grow.
2026-03-09 09:40 UTC - On-call rotated, emergency mitigation (partial traffic pause to a warm standby) executed at 09:47 UTC.
2026-03-09 10:30 UTC - Traffic rebalanced with stricter admission control; SLOs recovered by 11:15 UTC but p99 latency remained degraded for the remainder of the day for some customers.
- SLOs: p99 generation latency for hosted API exceeded SLO by ~220ms for 45 minutes; error rate increased from 0.15% to 1.9%.
- Affected customers: multiple production customers experienced elevated tail latency and intermittent 5xx errors; several support tickets opened.
- Operational pain: manual interventions required to rebalance traffic and warm caches, leading to longer mitigation time than expected.
Aggressive failover policy without region-congestion damping: policy moved significant traffic quickly without detecting capacity headroom in target region.
Insufficient circuit-breaker hysteresis and rapid reset logic: short reset window led to oscillation and replay amplification instead of sustained shedding.
Admission control thresholds and queue high-water marks were tuned for steady-state rather than surge conditions; queues allowed long backpressure tail leading to GPU saturation.
Probes and health checks were noisy during failover and triggered repeated cache-warming requests (probe replay amplification).
Lack of a congestion-island detector that can identify localized overload and quarantine it from global routing decisions.
Executed emergency partial pause of non-critical routed traffic to us-west-2 to limit incoming load (09:47 UTC).
Manually increased circuit-breaker hysteresis to prevent rapid reset (temporary change in control plane).
Applied conservative admission control at the ingress (lower concurrency per model) to buy time for cache warmup.
Opened high-priority support thread with affected customers and provided visibility and ETA for stabilization.

Title: Client-proximity SLO-driven egress heuristics

Client-proximity SLO-driven egress heuristics

Purpose
This note captures a candidate approach for steering outbound inference traffic to the closest healthy region while respecting per-customer latency SLOs, capacity constraints, and graceful degradation under cross-region failure scenarios. The focus is on combining active probing, short-term backpressure signals, and SLO-driven weighting to drive GeoDNS/Anycast decisions via the control plane.

Context and goals
- Problem: As traffic grows, naive geography-based routing (by country/region) causes hotspots when regional pools saturate. We need an automated mechanism to prefer proximity but fall back quickly and predictably without oscillation.
- Goals:
  1) Honor customer-configured p50/p95 latency SLOs where possible
  2) Prefer region-proximal nodes for latency/cost reasons
  3) Avoid cascading failovers when one region degrades
  4) Provide explainability / observability for steering decisions
  5) Work with both GeoDNS and Anycast fronting models

High-level design
1) SLO-aware scoring: each (client-subnet -> region) candidate is scored periodically using a composite metric: score = w_lat * normalized_latency + w_load * normalized_capacity + w_probe * probe_health + w_cost * cost_factor. We convert score to a weight in the control plane.

2) Active probes and short-term smoothing:
  - Every egress region exposes a lightweight probe endpoint for each service version (probe path returns version, qps, and a small checksum).
  - Probe frequency: per-region per-pop once every 10s for hotspots, 60s otherwise.
  - Smoothing: maintain an exponential moving average (EMA) on latency and error rate with alpha=0.25 to avoid reacting to single spikes.

3) Backpressure propagation:
  - Backend pools export a soft-capacity signal (available_tokens) computed from headroom (target_rps - current_rps) and queue length.
  - When available_tokens < threshold, region enters backpressure mode and emits a "soft-failsafe" flag to the control plane via the egress controller API.
  - The control plane converts backpressure into a weight penalty multiplier (e.g., x0.2) that reduces DNS weights / Anycast preference.

4) GeoDNS vs Anycast differences:
  - GeoDNS: control plane writes weighted DNS records with per-region weights (0-1000). TTL strategy: default 30s for high-change clients, 120s otherwise. On backpressure, we immediately reduce weight and lower TTL to 10s for affected prefixes to accelerate migration.
  - Anycast: operate via BGP prepends + local preference adjustments where supported. The controller updates local-preference and, when immediate failover needed, uses withdraws for extreme situations. A/B testing of prepends must be conservative: only 1-2 AS prepends per change window to limit churn.

5) Client-proximity SLO targeting:
  - Each customer can set a latency SLO profile (e.g., p50 60ms, p95 250ms). The scoring function penalizes regions that cause higher tail latency for that customer’s traffic (learned from recent requests). Customers without explicit SLOs use platform defaults.

6) Oscillation controls and hysteresis:
  - Minimum hold: once weight for a region changes by >30%, hold for 60s before further reductions (unless region offline).
  - Recovery ramp: when a region recovers, weights ramp up in 3 steps (10%, 40%, 100%) every 30s to allow gradual reflow and prevent thrashing.
  - Cooldown windows per client-subnet and per-region to avoid oscillation between two proximate regions.

Control plane API (example interactions)
- POST /egress/weights/update
  payload: {"client_prefix":"203.0.113.0/24","region_weights":[{"region":"us-west1","weight":700},{"region":"us-east1","weight":300}],"reason":"p95>threshold || backpressure"}
- GET /egress/probe-status?region=us-west1 returns last_probe_ts, ema_latency_ms, error_rate, available_tokens

Metrics to push to telemetry
- per-client-prefix: selected_region, selection_reason (proximity/slo/failover), weight_vector
- per-region: ema_latency_p50/p95, available_tokens, probe_ok_ratio, recent_weight_changes
- global: reroute_rate (changes/sec), DNS_updates/sec, Anycast_prepends/sec

Failure modes and mitigations
- Probe flapping: require 2 consecutive failing probes before marking region degraded for routing (but allow single failing probe to influence weights slightly).
- DNS propagation delay: mitigate with short TTLs in high-impact scenarios and explicit HTTP redirection post-DNS if needed for sticky clients.
- BGP instability: Anycast path changes should be rate-limited and gated by canary ASNs to avoid global instability.

Testing and rollout plan
1) Lab: synthetic client-subnet simulation with controllable latency and queueing. Validate scoring and ramp behaviors.
2) Canary: opt-in customer prefixes (<=1% global) get new steering. Monitor reroute_rate and tail latency impact for 48h.
3) Gradual rollout: 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100% with rollback gates (reroute_rate spike, p95 regressions).

Operational runbooks (short pointers)
- If region shows sustained p95 degrade and available_tokens low: trigger emergency weight drain to 0 over 30s and lower DNS TTLs to 5s for affected prefixes.
- If anycast withdraw loop observed: toggle to GeoDNS fallback for affected prefixes and open incident for BGP investigation.

Open questions / follow-ups
- How to reconcile client source IP geolocation inaccuracies (mobile/proxy traffic)? Consider integrating edge geolocation + client-declared region header for verified enterprise customers.
- Should we expose a per-customer knob for "latency-first" vs "cost-first" steering? (important for enterprise pricing tiers)
- Explore ML-based weight prediction using recent probe + telemetry to preemptively reroute before SLA breaches.

Action items
- [Evelyn] prototype probe agent and API by sprint end (PLAT-4812)
- [Diego] implement TTL/weight control endpoints in egress-controller (GH #234)
- [Priya] draft dashboards showing per-prefix selection_reason and reroute_rate

Notes on uniqueness
This approach emphasizes customer SLOs and soft backpressure signals rather than hard regional cutover rules. It blends short-term reactive signals (probes/backpressure) with SLO-aware preference to preserve latency and reduce costly overprovisioning.

Title: probabilistic-regional-shard-routing-proposal

probabilistic-regional-shard-routing-proposal

Purpose:

This note proposes a probabilistic regional shard routing strategy that blends GeoDNS, Anycast, and a lightweight control plane for gradual regional preference and automatic failover. The goal is to reduce tail-latency variance and avoid brittle binary cutovers during region degradation, while keeping the control-plane responsibilities small and the client behavior simple.

High-level idea:

- Each customer/client is assigned a small routing state: an ordered list of preferred regions with associated weights and a local stickiness token (TTL).
- Clients prefer the first region but probabilistically failover to secondary regions according to weights when probing/requests show degradation.
- A central control plane maintains region health signals and periodically nudges client weights by publishing short-lived signed configuration snapshots (control-plane deltas).
- Anycast is used for initial ingress where possible; GeoDNS provides coarse-grained region hints and a failback path for clients that don't accept signed snapshots.

Why this differs from existing approaches:

- Not purely failover-first (binary). Instead of switching all clients to a backup region, traffic is spread according to probability to avoid overwhelming a second region.
- Clients make decentralized decisions based on local metrics (p95 latency, error-rate, probe windows) combined with control-plane guidance — reduces control-plane pressure and allows graceful, organic load redistribution.

Core components:

1) Client routing agent (lightweight SDK behavior)
- Maintains a small state: preferences = [(region, weight, last_update_ts)], stickiness_token, local_probe_history.
- On each request, picks region R with probability proportional to weight and an exponential backoff adjusted by observed recent latency and error rate for R.
- Probing: if chosen R latency exceeds threshold, client increments a local penalty score and will reduce probability for R for N seconds unless control-plane snapshot counters this.
- Telemetry upload: periodic small beacons (aggregate: counts, p50/p95/p99, errors) to control-plane telemetry endpoint.

2) Lightweight control plane (egress-steering service)
- Aggregates telemetry with coarse granularity (per-region per-customer per-minute).
- Runs a smoothing and anomaly detection pass to detect region-wide systemic issues vs localized noise.
- Publishes signed snapshot files on a CDN with short TTL (e.g., 30s - 2m). Snapshots carry region weights and optional instructions (e.g., "degradation_detected: true, reduce_weight(region-x, 0.1)").
- Exposes a small API for clients to fetch latest snapshot and for operators to set manual overrides/canary policies.

3) Ingress layer (Anycast + GeoDNS)
- Anycast provides a low-latency default path, terminating closer to client. Use regional Anycast rings with region tags.
- GeoDNS resolves client to a local-edge resolver that typically lands in preferred region; DNS TTL is medium (60-120s) to allow bounce-back but avoid thrash.
- If client lacks SDK support (e.g., third-party integrations), GeoDNS + short TTL acts as a coarse fallback.

4) Back-pressure shaping on the serving side
- Each region enforces capacity-based admission and per-tenant throttles. Accepting probabilistic overflow requires regions to expose current headroom via real-time endpoints consumed by control plane.

Control-plane APIs (sketch):

- GET /snapshots/latest?tenant=xxx -> returns signed snapshot JSON with generation id, published_at, and per-region weights
- POST /telemetry/beacon {tenant, region, window_ts, p50, p95, errors, requests} -> 202 accepted
- GET /region-headroom -> internal call to retrieve coarse headroom numbers

Snapshot format (human-readable sketch):

{
  "generation": "g-20250220-12",
  "valid_until": "2025-02-20T17:02:00Z",
  "prefs": [
    {"region": "us-west-2", "weight": 0.75},
    {"region": "us-east-1", "weight": 0.2},
    {"region": "eu-west-1", "weight": 0.05}  
  ],
  "meta": {"note": "auto-adjusted after 3m p95 spike in us-west-2"}
}

Client pseudocode (simplified):

- on_startup: fetch snapshot -> set local_prefs
- for each request:
    pick region R ~ categorical(local_prefs.weights adjusted by local penalties)
    send request to endpoint for R (via Anycast/Azure edge or DNS)
    record latency/error into local window
    if window shows degradation increment penalty[R] and optionally trigger immediate re-fetch of snapshot
    every T seconds post aggregate telemetry beacon

Pros and trade-offs:

Pros:
- Smooth redistribution: probabilistic decisions avoid complete traffic storms to secondaries.
- Rapid local adaptation: clients respond to immediate QoE degradations faster than full control plane rollouts.
- Small control-plane role: publishes hints rather than orchestrating every client.
- Compatibility: falls back to GeoDNS/Anycast for clients without SDKs.

Trade-offs / Risks:
- Client complexity increases (needs to implement weight logic + telemetry).
- Harder to reason globally: emergent behavior potential where many clients reduce weight simultaneously causing oscillations. Mitigation: control plane smoothing and randomized jitter in client re-check intervals.
- Telemetry volume: need aggregation and rate limiting. Use sampling and coarse time windows (1m).
- Security/trust: snapshots must be signed to avoid tampering; clients must validate signatures.

Failure modes and mitigations:

1) Oscillation between two regions
- Mitigate by hysteresis: clients keep local penalty that decays slowly and control plane enforces minimum weight floors for short periods. Use randomized backoff windows per-client.

2) Snapshot delivery failure (clients offline or CDN issue)
- Default to last-known snapshot. GeoDNS TTL acts as safety net. If snapshot expired, clients reduce chosen weights progressively to long-tail fallback distribution across all healthy regions.

3) Uncoordinated mass migration to single region
- Control plane publishes explicit soft-limits per-region (max fraction per-tenant). Clients must respect max_fraction by capping sampling. Server-side admission enforces hard caps.

Experiments and rollout plan:

Phase 0: Simulation (2-4 weeks)
- Build an agent-based sim with realistic client populations (mix of SDK-enabled and plain-DNS clients).
- Inject region degradations and measure surge magnitude in next-best region. Tune weight adjustment and decay parameters.

Phase 1: Canary SDK clients (internal + alpha customers, 2-3 weeks)
- Enable probabilistic routing in SDK behind a feature flag. Collect telemetry and review emergent behavior.

Phase 2: GeoDNS + Snapshot pilot for limited tenants (4 weeks)
- Publish snapshots but keep conservative weights. Confirm CDN snapshot delivery, signature verification, and client handling.

Phase 3: Wider gradual release (ongoing)
- Expand tenant cohort. Enable operator overrides and automated smoothing thresholds in control plane.

Operational visibility required:

- Real-time per-region headroom dashboard (requests/sec, p95, spare-capacity)
- Snapshot publication history and signing audit log
- Client-aggregate telemetry (per-tenant per-region) with coarse retention (30d)
- Anomaly alerts: e.g., >20% clients change primary within 3m or region headroom dropping below 10%

Open questions / TODOs:

- What minimum SDK footprint is acceptable for our customers? Keep as a tiny client-side library or require server-side proxy?
- How to onboard legacy clients that do not upload telemetry? (Probable answer: heavier reliance on GeoDNS + longer TTLs.)
- Exact smoothing algorithm at control plane: moving median vs EWMA vs robust-trim outlier rejection. Need experiments.
- Policy UI for SREs/product to set max_region_fraction per-tenant and emergency evacuation controls.

Notes/References:

- This approach is inspired by congestion-aware multipath scheduling literature (probabilistic multipath) and CDN origin-shift strategies.
- Related internal docs: regional ejection heuristics, headroom API design (see linked_artifacts).

Appendix: Example client config (for SDK integrators)

client_config:
  snapshot_url: https://snapshots.redwood.internal/tenants/{tenant_id}/latest.json
  snapshot_fetch_interval_seconds: 45
  local_penalty_decay_seconds: 120
  min_weight_floor: 0.05
  max_region_fraction: 0.8  # server-side enforced ideally
  telemetry_window_seconds: 60
  telemetry_endpoint: https://telemetry.redwood.internal/beacon

Closing:

This proposal aims to create a resilient, low-control-plane-overhead routing fabric that avoids hard cutovers and spreads risk probabilistically during incidents. Next steps: simulate, decide on client SDK minimal API, and prototype snapshot publication/signing.

-- Ava M.

Title: Graded latency triage and capacity-quota router

Graded latency triage and capacity-quota router

Design and implement a graded multi-region request router that combines latency-based routing, soft geo-pinning, and capacity-aware quotas to protect SLOs during regional degradation. Goal is to allow controlled, proportional load shedding and fast failover while minimizing cross-region latency impact and preserving priority user traffic.
We have seen two classes of incidents in the last 6 months: transient region-level latency spikes that cause global SLO drops, and slow capacity drain where oversubscription in a region causes high tail latency for new requests. Current routing is too binary (pin or failover) which either overwhelms remote regions or causes unnecessary global degradation. We need a middle ground that enforces per-region admission budgets, uses graded latency cost to steer requests, and includes per-region circuit breakers that trigger proportional shedding rather than hard ejection.
Introduce a scoring router that computes a composite score per candidate region: score = latency_penalty + geo_preference_bonus - capacity_backoff. Latency_penalty is derived from 95th/99th ms moving-window compared to SLO; geo_preference_bonus encodes soft pin (stickiness) tiers by customer/route; capacity_backoff is proportional to regional token consumption versus reserved quota. The router will allocate each request to the highest-scoring region subject to per-region admission credits. When a region's circuit breaker trips, it moves from normal -> degraded -> shed modes, each increasing capacity_backoff and enabling partial shedding via token-budget rationing. Also add a fast-soft-failover path that sends a small hedged probe to next-best region for high-priority traffic while remaining mindful of cost. Implement throttles at the admission controller to enforce budgeted shedding and preserve token-level accounting for cost and billing consistency.
Router selects locally-preferred region for >= 90% of requests under steady-state with no capacity pressure
When one region experiences 2x 99th latency increase, global SLO (99th latency) recovers to within 10% of baseline within 90s using graded shedding and failover
Token shedding is proportional: at region overload, requests from P3/P4 labels are shed first with at least 70% reduction in their accepted throughput while P0/P1 remain >= 95% acceptance
Circuit breaker transition time and hysteresis prevent flapping (no more than 2 transitions per minute under noisy signals)
No significant increase (>5%) in average cost per successful token at steady-state after rollout
End-to-end automated test coverage for policy calculation and admission enforcement (unit + integration)

Prototype router scoring module and unit tests — Jonas
Implement per-region admission controller with token budgets — backend team
Add circuit breaker state machine (normal,degraded,shed) and hysteresis — reliability team
Create integration harness to simulate multi-region latency and capacity scenarios — SRE
Add observability: per-region score, admission decisions, tokens_shed, and SLO attainment metrics
Run canary in west-europe with select customers and collect 2 weeks of telemetry
Iterate thresholds and rollout globally
Unit tests for scoring math (edge cases: zero capacity, extreme latency)
Integration test: three-region simulator driving 99th latency spikes and verifying routed fractions
Chaos test: abrupt region loss and partial capacity drain to validate soft-shed behavior
Load test: ensure admission controller scales to 10k qps in dedicated mode
Cost regression test: compare per-token cost across baseline and graded routing under typical workloads
Phase 0: off-by-default in staging, run synthetic scenarios
Phase 1: enable for internal infra routes in canary region (west-europe) with metric guardrails
Phase 2: enable for 10% of traffic for non-critical routes in production for 48h, analyze
Phase 3: expand to 50% with tuned quotas and hedging disabled for low-tier traffic
Phase 4: full rollout with SRE on-call and rollback playbook

Unexpected shedding: tokens_shed spikes > 3x baseline
Risk: Overly aggressive shedding might impact paid customers. Mitigation: priority-aware admission and explicit whitelist for enterprise customers
Risk: Cross-region failover could increase egress cost and latency. Mitigation: include cost penalty in scoring and tune hedging probability for P0/P1 only
Risk: Flapping circuit breakers. Mitigation: add exponential backoff and minimum stable interval before re-enable
Risk: Edge cases where capacity metrics lag telemetry. Mitigation: use short-term moving averages with conservative smoothing and safety caps

Title: Tenant Quick-Glance micro-strip for Private Clusters

Tenant Quick-Glance micro-strip for Private Clusters

Goal: Design a compact, horizontally stacked 'Quick-Glance' strip that appears at the top of a Tenant or Cluster page in the Private Console. The strip should give engineers and SREs a single-row summary of the most actionable signals: SLA exposure (latency/error risk), upgrade exposure (pending/failed nodes), recent networking anomalies (egress spikes, flaky peers), cost delta (24h), and one-click mitigations (roll back, throttle, open incident playbook).

Why: Private deployments demand concise situational awareness for tenants that are often managed by platform teams. Current Private Console pages require drilling into multiple dashboards to understand whether an upgrade or network event requires immediate action. This micro-strip aims to reduce decision-to-action time and lower cognitive load during incidents.

Scope: initial design will target desktop and compressed tablet widths; mobile will be a follow-up. The strip must be keyboard-navigable and meet WCAG contrast requirements. It should be implemented as a reusable UI component (design token-ready) that product and engineering can place on Tenant, Cluster, and Upgrade pages.
- Use a fixed-height horizontal strip, max 56px, with five modular cards.
- Priority ordering: SLA exposure, upgrade exposure, network anomalies, recent errors, cost delta.
- Each module shows an icon, 1-line metric, and a micro-action (ellipsis or single CTA).
- Color semantics consistent with console palette: amber for warning, red for critical, blue for info, gray for healthy. Avoid saturated reds on non-critical surfaces.
- Telemetry hooks: quick_glance.view, quick_glance.click.module, quick_glance.action.invoke with module and tenant tags.
- Accessibility: modules must have aria-labels describing current state and action; ensure 4.5:1 text contrast for primary metrics.
- Performance: lazy-load detailed hover cards and only poll underlying signals at a 10s cadence when the tenant page is in focus.
Component implemented as a single strip with five modules on Tenant and Cluster pages
Each module exposes the telemetry events and label keys documented in the spec
Micro-actions (roll back, open incident playbook, view traces) open the correct modal or route
UX tests: 5 SREs can interpret strip state and select correct mitigation in < 90s in a simulated incident
Accessibility: keyboard focus order logical, screen reader announces state and action, color contrast verified

Backend: expose aggregated quick-glance endpoint (ENG-2301) - owner: Priya; minimal shape: {state,module_metric,action_link}
SRE: run tabletop with patch cluster to validate micro-action rollbacks - owner: Lina
PM: prepare rollout plan and feature flag gating (canary) - Clara
PM feedback (Clara J): 'Love the single-row approach. Add an explicit 'confidence' small-dot for probabilistic signals (eg. predicted SLA breach). Please surface the time-range for the cost delta.'

Engineering feedback (Omar): 'Backend needs a lightweight aggregated endpoint to avoid multiple calls; prefer server-side aggregation every 10s. Also prefer module configs to be feature-flag driven.'

Design follow-up (Aisha): 'Iterate hover card to include quick links to traces and the last 3 deploys. Reduce icon weight for low-contrast environments.'

Title: Developer Shield: SDK Chaos & Recovery Lab

Developer Shield: SDK Chaos & Recovery Lab

Summary:
This lab is a hands-on developer-ready guide for intentionally breaking SDK integrations, observing telemetry "golden traces", and validating recovery strategies against Redwood inference endpoints. The goal is to provide a repeatable workshop that SDK authors, platform engineers, and support oncall can run in ~90 minutes to verify resilience SLA behaviors and canonical fixes.

Goals:
- Create deterministic fault patterns targeting SDK -> runtime interactions (timeouts, partial responses, truncated streams).
- Validate observability: traces, spans, logs, and token-level cost telemetry for each failure mode.
- Exercise client-side fallbacks (retry jitter, streaming resume, local cache) and server-side graceful degradation (model variant fallback, rate-aware routing).
- Produce documented artifacts: golden-trace examples, regression tests, and a triage checklist for support.

Prerequisites:
1) Developer machine with Python 3.10+ and Node.js 18+.
2) Access to a Redwood dev tenant (api key with dev-level quota).
3) Local test harness repo cloned: git@github.com:redwood-inference/sdk-chaos-lab.git (or use the starter scaffold below).
4) Docker (for running a local network proxy/fault injector) and curl.

Quickstart scaffold (clone + bootstrap):
1. git clone git@github.com:redwood-inference/sdk-chaos-lab.git && cd sdk-chaos-lab
2. cp .env.example .env && edit REDWOOD_API_KEY and REDWOOD_BASE_URL if needed
3. make deps  # installs node_modules and pip env
4. ./scripts/start-proxy.sh  # starts the fault-injection proxy on localhost:8080

High-level lab exercises (90 minutes):
1) Golden-trace capture (15–20m)
   - Objective: record a baseline successful call for the workload (embed -> retrieve -> generate).
   - Steps: run scripts/capture_trace.py --scenario baseline --output traces/golden_baseline.json
   - Expected output: spans for http.request, sdk.deserialize, runtime.kv_cache_hit metrics.

2) Timeout and retry behavior (20m)
   - Fault: the proxy introduces a 1200ms delay for the first POST to /v1/generate.
   - Client expectations: Sane client-side timeout (default 1s) should trigger retry logic with exponential backoff; the SDK should not double-bill tokens when retrying.
   - Commands: ./scripts/inject_fault.sh --type delay --path /v1/generate --ms 1200 --once
   - Validation: run examples/python/stream_resume_test.py and assert: one logged retry, one successful response, token_cost metric unchanged compared to baseline.

3) Truncated stream and resume semantics (20m)
   - Fault: proxy truncates server-sent event stream mid-response.
   - Client behavior to validate: library should surface a resumable id/token and resume the stream without user-visible duplication.
   - Example (Node):
     const r = await Redwood.generateStreaming({ prompt, resume: true });
     // on 'truncated' event the client should call r.resume()

4) Partial model fallback (15m)
   - Fault: simulated out-of-capacity on preferred model (m-latest) causing 503 on cold start.
   - Desired platform reaction: automatic fallback to m-latest-quantized variant or regional replica within 200ms.
   - Validation: ensure request latency remains below 800ms and output quality regression < 2% on the golden prompt set. Use scripts/quality_check.sh --baseline traces/golden_baseline.json --target traces/fallback_run.json

5) Telemetry and cost guardrails (10m)
   - Validate that trace includes token_count, model_variant, quantization_profile, route_key, and billing_unit fields.
   - Confirm alert firing: a synthetic gauge (sdk.request.latency.p50) exceeding 1s triggers an alert in the sandbox paging channel.

SDK patterns and canonical code snippets
- Python retry wrapper (idempotent generation calls):

  import time
  import requests

  def call_with_retries(payload, max_attempts=3):
      backoff = 0.2
      attempt = 0
      while attempt < max_attempts:
          attempt += 1
          try:
              resp = requests.post(
                  "http://localhost:8080/v1/generate", json=payload, timeout=1.0
              )
              resp.raise_for_status()
              return resp.json()
          except requests.exceptions.Timeout:
              time.sleep(backoff)
              backoff *= 2
              continue
      raise RuntimeError("exhausted retries")

- Node streaming-resume pattern:

  const { RedwoodClient } = require('@redwood/sdk');
  const client = new RedwoodClient({ baseURL: process.env.REDWOOD_BASE_URL });

  async function streamingExample() {
    const stream = await client.generateStream({ model: 'm-latest', prompt: 'Hello' });
    stream.on('error', async (err) => {
      if (err.code === 'TRUNCATED') {
        await stream.resume(); // library handles token-prefix dedupe
      } else {
        throw err;
      }
    });
  }

Golden trace format and required fields (table):
- The lab standard for a golden trace is a JSON file with a top-level array of spans. Each span in the array must contain the following string fields:
  - trace_id
  - span_id
  - parent_id (nullable string allowed; include as empty string if none)
  - name (e.g., http.request, sdk.serialize, runtime.infer)
  - start_ts (ISO 8601)
  - end_ts (ISO 8601)
  - attributes (a flattened comma-separated key=value list including model_variant, token_count, route_key, billing_unit)

Example attributes string: "model_variant=m-latest,token_count=42,route_key=us-east-1,billing_unit=gen_token"

Triage checklist (support-friendly):
1) Reproduce the failure with the lab harness using the same API key and region.
2) Capture and attach the golden trace and failing trace.
3) Check telemetry for double-billing: token_cost spikes immediately after retries.
4) If truncated stream: confirm resume id exists in traces (span name runtime.stream.resume).
5) If fallback occurred: compare model_variant attributes between baseline and failing trace.
6) File a regression ticket including: failing_trace.json, command run, SDK version, and proxy logs.

Config matrix (copyable CSV row for quick reference):
"scenario,proxy_fault,client_timeout_ms,expected_behavior,primary_validation"
"baseline,none,1500,success,golden_trace match"
"delay-first-post,delay(1200ms),1000,retry-with-backoff,no double-billing"
"truncate-stream,truncate-after-3-chunks,2000,resume-able stream,resume span present"
"model-oom,503-on-cold-start,800,auto-fallback,latency<800ms"

Operational notes and ownership:
- Lab owner: eng-developer-experience (primary: Maya Chen).
- Oncall escalation: if the lab reproduces a production bug, open an incident in PagerDuty and tag "runtime-serving" and "sdk".
- Persist golden traces under s3://redwood-dev-golden-traces/sdk-chaos-lab/ with role-based ACLs.

Rollout and integration guidance (how teams should use this lab):
- SDK authors: integrate one golden-trace capture into CI for each major release (post-merge job). If a change causes a >5% regression vs the golden baseline, block the release.
- Platform: run the full lab in the dedicated staging cluster before deploying model-serving kernel changes or routing logic changes.
- Support: use the triage checklist when customers report truncated streams or unexpected token billing.

Artifacts to produce after running the lab:
- traces/golden_baseline.json (golden)
- traces/failure_mode_<name>.json (failing traces)
- coverage/regression_<sdk-version>.md (short summary)
- ticket templates/auto-fill for support with fields pre-populated from the harness run

References and related docs:
- eng-developer-experience/quickstarts-and-templates/sdk-resiliency-orchestrator-and-ops-playbook-2026
- eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-streaming-troubleshooting-2025
- security-and-compliance/incident-response-security/streaming-data-retention-policy

Appendix: common canonical fixes (short list)
- Ensure idempotency tokens are attached to generation requests; server will dedupe within 30s window.
- Surface resume IDs for streaming RPCs and persist a short-lived local buffer to permit dedupe.
- Add token-cost snapshot before and after retries in telemetry to detect billing anomalies.
- If model fallback is frequent, add a cold-start pre-warm task for high-SLA tenants and/or enable burst-capacity for the dedicated pool.

Contact:
- Maya Chen (owner, eng-developer-experience) - maya@redwood.ai
- Support escalation alias: support-oncall@redwood.ai
