Title: Perf Suite Profiling Playbook (Q1 2026 Baseline)

Perf Suite Profiling Playbook (Q1 2026 Baseline)

## Purpose
This playbook describes how to reproduce a perf-suite result and capture the artifacts needed to attribute changes (runtime, scheduler, kernels, environment). It is intended for:
- Investigating perf-canary regressions (PR-level, nightly, or release-branch).
- Explaining deltas between baseline runs (Q1 2026 “golden” anchor) and candidate changes.
- Producing consistent traces/logs that can be shared across Runtime, Kernels, and SRE.

This page focuses on *how to profile* (traces, kernel timelines, scheduler logs) rather than *what workloads to run*. For workload definitions and required metrics, see the baseline plan and representative suite pages.

---

## What “good” looks like (minimum artifact set)
For any investigated run, attach or link the following artifacts (even if you also have dashboards):
1) Run manifest JSON (per ADR-0172) with *all* environment capture enabled.
2) Results JSON/CSV (p50/p95/p99 TTFT, TPOT, throughput, plus variance statistics if available).
3) Scheduler log bundle:
   - Queue wait time distribution
   - Batch assembly time distribution
   - Batch size histogram
   - Load-shed/drop counters (if any)
   - Correlation IDs / request IDs for trace alignment
4) Kernel selection debug dump (sampled) with fallback reasons (if any).
5) Nsight Systems (nsys) trace for at least one representative interval.
6) Optional but recommended: Nsight Compute (ncu) capture for the top 1–3 kernels (only when kernel-level regression is suspected).

---

## Measurement boundaries (so traces match reported metrics)
To avoid “apples to oranges,” ensure the profiling run uses the same boundaries as the perf suite metrics:
- **TTFT (Time To First Token)**: measured at the server boundary: request admitted → first token emitted to server streaming layer. Excludes client read/parse time.
- **TPOT (Time Per Output Token)**: measured at the server boundary for decode tokens only. Excludes prefill; excludes client overhead.
- **Throughput**: server-side tokens/sec or requests/sec depending on endpoint mode.

If you must deviate (e.g., reproducing a customer report with client-side timings), label the run explicitly as “client-inclusive” and do not compare to baseline dashboards without adjustment.

---

## Preconditions / Setup checklist
### A. Confirm you are targeting the same baseline anchor
Before profiling, confirm the baseline anchor for comparison:
- Runtime git SHA / tag (baseline)
- Benchmark harness version
- Model revision (weights + tokenizer)
- Scheduler profile and kernel-selection ruleset
- Region and GPU SKU

If you are unsure which build is the Q1 baseline anchor, check the baseline freeze thread and the baseline run tracker.

### B. Reduce variance (required for attribution)
These steps are required for “baseline-comparable” profiling runs:
1) Use a dedicated benchmarking node (no co-tenancy).
2) Lock GPU application clocks where permitted by fleet policy.
3) Pin CPU governor to performance.
4) Ensure consistent container image and driver/CUDA versions.
5) Run standardized warmup (see below).

If any variance-reduction step cannot be applied, mark the run as “non-baseline-comparable” in the run label and expect higher noise.

### C. Warmup standard (required)
Warmup reduces first-run variance from model load, JIT/compilation caches, allocator behavior, and KV cache initialization.
- Warmup duration: 3–5 minutes per (model, GPU, workload mode)
- Warmup workload: same request shape as the measured workload, but with lower concurrency
- Discard warmup metrics; only analyze traces taken after warmup completes

---

## Run labeling and naming conventions
Consistent naming is required so engineers can drill down from dashboard → manifest → traces.

### Run ID format
Use the following run_id format (single line, no spaces):
`perfq1_2026/<workload>/<model>/<region>/<gpu>/<runtime_sha>/<harness_ver>/<timestamp_utc>/<run_variant>`

Examples:
- `perfq1_2026/chat_streaming/llama3_1_70b/us-east/h100/7c3a91f/v1.8.2/2026-02-03T21-14-08Z/cold_cache`
- `perfq1_2026/long_prefill/qwen2_5_72b/eu-west/a100/7c3a91f/v1.8.2/2026-02-03T23-40-51Z/warm_cache`

### Required run_variant tags
Include at least these tags as part of the run_variant suffix:
- `cold_cache` or `warm_cache` (we report both; do not mix)
- `baseline_comparable` or `non_baseline_comparable`

Optional tags (use when relevant):
- `kernel_pin_<name>` (if pinning a kernel)
- `scheduler_override_<name>` (if changing scheduler knobs)
- `client_inclusive` (only if using client-side TTFT)

---

## Step-by-step: reproduce a perf suite run with profiling enabled
> The exact CLI flags may vary by harness version; the intent is to capture the same artifact set. If a flag below doesn’t exist in your harness build, file an issue in benchmark-lab and note it in the run summary.

### 1) Create (or locate) the canonical manifest
1. Start from the manifest used by the baseline run (from dashboards or the run tracker).
2. Copy it and increment `manifest_version` only if required by schema changes.
3. Verify these fields are present and accurate:
   - Model identifier + revision
   - Hardware: GPU SKU, GPU count, MIG settings (if any)
   - Region/zone
   - Runtime build SHA + build type
   - Driver/CUDA/Triton versions
   - Scheduler profile name + knobs
   - Kernel selection ruleset version
   - Workload seed and distribution parameters
   - Cache mode (cold/warm)

**Output:** `run_manifest.json`

### 2) Ensure environment capture is on
Enable full environment capture in the harness:
- GPU info (nvidia-smi dump)
- Driver/CUDA versions
- Container image digest
- Host kernel version
- CPU model, NUMA topology summary
- Power/clock settings (if available)

**Sanity check:** ensure the manifest “env” section is populated before you proceed. Missing env capture is a common reason runs can’t be compared later.

### 3) Run standardized warmup
Run warmup using the same workload generator but with reduced concurrency.
- Confirm warmup completes without errors (no OOM, no load-shed unless expected).
- Confirm steady-state GPU utilization.

**Output:** warmup logs (attach if investigating stability issues).

### 4) Run the measured workload and collect scheduler + kernel dumps
Run the measured workload with:
- Scheduler instrumentation enabled (queue wait, batch assembly time, batch size distributions).
- Kernel selection debug dump enabled (sampled is fine; 1–5% sampling is typical).

**Outputs:**
- `results.json` (metrics)
- `scheduler_metrics.jsonl` or equivalent
- `kernel_selection_dump.jsonl`

### 5) Capture an Nsight Systems (nsys) trace (required for attribution)
Capture nsys for a representative steady-state window. Recommendations:
- Trace window: 30–90 seconds during steady state.
- Capture CUDA + NVTX ranges.
- Minimize trace overhead: avoid tracing the full run unless necessary.

Operational guidance:
- If you control the runtime build, ensure key phases emit NVTX ranges:
  - request admitted
  - queue wait
  - batch assembly
  - prefill
  - decode
  - stream flush
- If ranges are missing, still capture the trace; file an issue for missing NVTX markers.

**Output:** `trace.nsys-rep` (or equivalent).

### 6) Optional: Nsight Compute (ncu) for kernel regressions
Use ncu only when:
- A regression correlates with a kernel selection change, or
- nsys shows kernel time dominated by one/few kernels, or
- Kernel-level variance is suspected (e.g., new fused attention path).

Guidelines:
- Profile a single process and short window to keep overhead manageable.
- Focus on top kernels by time; avoid broad “collect everything” profiles.

**Output:** `kernel_profile.ncu-rep` (or equivalent).

### 7) Upload artifacts and link them in the run summary
For every run you investigate, create a short run summary (Confluence comment, Slack triage thread, or ticket) that includes:
- run_id
- manifest link
- results link
- trace links
- “what changed” hypothesis
- whether the run is baseline-comparable

---

## Artifact checklist and where to find them
Attach links (preferred) rather than pasting raw files into Confluence.

Required artifacts:
- Run manifest: `run_manifest.json`
- Results: `results.json` (or results CSV exported by harness)
- Scheduler logs: `scheduler_metrics.jsonl`
- Kernel selection dump: `kernel_selection_dump.jsonl`
- Nsight Systems trace: `trace.nsys-rep`

Recommended context:
- Full runtime logs for the measured window (with correlation IDs)
- GPU clock/thermal readings during the run
- Harness configuration file used to launch

---

## How to align traces with reported metrics
When investigating TTFT p99 or TPOT p99 changes, align the following:
1) Pick a set of request IDs from the tail (p99 cohort) in the results export.
2) Locate those request IDs in scheduler logs:
   - Identify whether tail comes from queue wait, batch assembly, prefill, decode, or stream flush.
3) In the nsys trace, confirm:
   - GPU busy/idle patterns during the tail interval
   - Kernel timeline changes (different kernels, different durations)
   - CPU-side stalls that correlate with queue wait or dispatch
4) Cross-check kernel selection dump:
   - Ensure the expected kernel regime is selected for the sequence length bins
   - Investigate fallback reasons (often the root cause of step-function regressions)

Common interpretations:
- **Higher TTFT p99 with stable throughput:** often queueing/backpressure or batch-assembly changes.
- **Higher TPOT with stable TTFT:** often decode kernel changes, KV cache behavior, or reduced overlap.
- **Lower throughput with higher TTFT:** often saturation, contention, or poor batching efficiency.

---

## Common failure modes and quick triage
### 1) Trace shows client bottleneck (not server)
Symptoms:
- Server-side metrics look stable, but external client TTFT inflates.
Actions:
- Confirm you’re using server-boundary TTFT.
- Ensure streaming pacing is server-driven in the harness (avoid client read throttling).

### 2) Variance too high to attribute
Symptoms:
- Repeated runs differ by more than the regression threshold; p99 swings without code changes.
Actions:
- Verify clock locking and isolation.
- Increase sample size.
- Ensure warmup was performed.
- Check for node-level noise: thermal throttling, background jobs, noisy neighbor.

### 3) Kernel fallback
Symptoms:
- Step-function slowdown at particular sequence lengths.
Actions:
- Inspect kernel selection dump for fallback reasons.
- Compare to the kernel selection matrix for expected regimes.
- Consider pinning the baseline kernel temporarily for diagnosis; label run_variant accordingly.

### 4) Scheduler overload / load-shed
Symptoms:
- Elevated drop counters, timeouts, or long queue wait.
Actions:
- Confirm concurrency targets match workload spec.
- Validate backpressure thresholds (baseline vs overridden).
- Use scheduler metrics to determine whether overload is admission control vs batch assembly.

---

## When to open a ticket vs continue debugging
Open a Linear issue (or escalate to perf triage) when any of the following are true:
- Regression is reproducible in baseline-comparable conditions.
- Kernel selection changed unexpectedly vs matrix.
- Scheduler metrics show a clear regime shift (queue wait, batch size collapse) not explained by workload.
- Trace indicates a new stall in a known critical path (prefill/decode overlap, KV cache operations).

Include in the ticket:
- run_id(s)
- baseline comparison run_id(s)
- links to manifest/results/traces
- suspected component owner (scheduler/kernels/runtime infra)

---

Primary owners:
- Benchmark harness & methodology: Rina Kobayashi, Claire Dubois
- Scheduler instrumentation: Sofia Ivanova
- Kernel selection & kernel timelines: Hiro Tanaka
- SRE benchmarking fleet stability: Sean Gallagher

If you encounter missing instrumentation (NVTX ranges absent, logs not emitted, schema fields missing), file an issue against the appropriate repo and link it in the run summary so the next investigation is faster.

Title: Trace Orchestra Conductor Profiling

Trace Orchestra Conductor Profiling

Objective:
Quick, reproducible exploration of the long-tail E2E latency behavior observed on the v2 serving runtime (public fleet). We want: 1) a compact per-stage decomposition for p50/p95/p99, 2) a small set of high-confidence hypotheses for root causes, and 3) actionable experiments to run in the next sprint.

Context / why now:
Over the last two weeks we've seen intermittent p99 spikes (clients reported 10x slower responses on small chat completions). Dashboard snapshots: overall generation p50=14ms, p95=64ms, p99=320ms. Spike pattern looks correlated with bursty multi-route traffic and a handful of long-seqlen traces. This doc gathers trace excerpts and preliminary attributions.

Methodology (how traces were selected):
- Sampled traces via the SLO-driven sampler (slo-sample window 100s, weight p99-biased).
- Focus set: 200 traces in the 250–600ms wall-clock bucket from the last 48h on region-us-west1, model-family: rw-base-13b (quantized).
- For each trace we stitch stage spans: (http-ingest -> tokenization -> request-queue -> batcher-wait -> kernel-exec(s) -> kv-lookup -> emit -> egress).
- Derived per-stage percentiles using per-trace summed durations.

High-level numbers (sample cohort, region=us-west1, model=rw-base-13b):
- End-to-end: p50=12ms, p95=72ms, p99=330ms
- Median per-stage breakdown (p95 cohort): tokenization 1.2ms (6%), request-queue 8.6ms (12%), batcher-wait 22.4ms (31%), kernel-exec 17.8ms (24%), kv-lookup 9.5ms (13%), emit+egress 3.2ms (4%)

Observation 1 — Batcher wait dominates many p99 traces:
- In ~62% of p99 traces the 'batcher-wait' stage alone accounts for >25% of wall time. We see groups of traces where batcher waits stack: backends receive many small requests that are not coalescing well (arrival jitter).
- Representative trace (timestamps are relative to request start):
  - 0.0ms http-ingest
  - 0.8ms tokenization 0.8ms
  - 2.1ms request-queue 1.3ms
  - 15.2ms batcher-wait 13.1ms
  - 36.0ms kernel-exec 20.8ms
  - 46.9ms kv-lookup 10.9ms
  - 52.1ms emit 5.2ms
  - 54.3ms egress 2.2ms
- Notes: batcher-wait spikes are often accompanied by small jittered arrivals from upstream clients (PLG bursts + multi-route fan-in).

Observation 2 — Kernel execution variance for longer sequences:
- Kernel-exec time scales with seqlen non-linearly; for sequences > 1k tokens p95 kernel-exec jumps significantly. In our p99 bucket some traces are misclassified (seqlen reported low in request metadata but stage snapshot shows extended kernel time) — suggests mismatch between client-declared seqlen and actual token emission pattern (clients using streaming with longer followups).
- Example: two traces with similar declared seqlen=64 but kernel-exec 18ms vs 120ms. The longer one had repeated small emits (backpressure + micro-batching).

Observation 3 — KV-cache misses amplify p99 tail:
- KV lookup stage shows bimodality. In ~25% of p99 traces kv-lookup latency >40ms, typically tied to cache miss + fallback to slower index (remote sharded store).
- When kv-lookup is slow, kernel-exec often waits for KV results due to dependency on cached keys for attention.

Observation 4 — Request-queue congestion during microbursts:
- A few traces show request-queue durations of 30–90ms, usually when regional ingress has brief saturation and requests wait behind a single noisy tenant with large footprint.

Correlation notes:
- Batcher-wait correlates with high small-request QPS spikes from PLG onboarding flows and with clients that set max_tokens low and do many short completions.
- KV misses correlate with particular model-variant builds deployed last week (build 2025.09.29; PR linked). We should test rollback.

Hypotheses (ranked by confidence):
1) Arrival jitter and small-RPS fan-in cause batcher not to coalesce efficiently -> longer batcher-wait -> p99 tail. (High confidence)
2) A regression in quantized kernel scheduling (PR #7890) increases kernel exec variance on some sequences -> p99 outliers. (Medium confidence)
3) KV cache sharding occasionally routes to a cold shard under sustained churn causing expensive misses -> adds 40–120ms to trace. (Medium confidence)
4) Egress slowdowns (network egress throttling) are rare and explain a tiny fraction of p99. (Low confidence)

Immediate experiments (next 7 days):
- Experiment A: Enable arrival-smoothing heuristic at the batcher (soft 4ms delay for small queuing class) on a canary subset (10% hostpool). Measure p95/p99 and overall latency impact. Owner: Riley. Linear: CONDUCT-212.
- Experiment B: Rollback kernel scheduling PR (7890) in a dedicated staging fleet and replay the long-seqlen traces. Owner: Marcus. GH PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/7890
- Experiment C: Add shard-hotness telemetry for KV store (emit per-shard miss-rate and 99-latency). Quick instrument and ship a 24h sample. Owner: Sofia. Jira: JIRA-RT-1023.

Instrumentation / data collection improvements:
- Capture per-batch composition metadata in traces (batch size, per-batch request ids) — currently unavailable in ~40% of traces which limits attribution.
- Add a small histogram for 'batcher-idle-wait' with microsecond buckets, export to traces.
- Surface a combined timeline view that overlays ingress QPS, per-host queue depth, and batcher wait; this will make microburst cause-and-effect explicit in dashboards.

Low-effort mitigations (if experiments delayed):
- Rate-limit noisy-tenant at ingress when per-tenant queue depth spikes. Quick mitigation with DDoS-like backpressure policy.
- Temporarily increase coalesce timeout for small requests on high-latency days (config flag).

Acceptance criteria for success:
- Experiment A: reduce batcher-wait contribution to p99 traces by >=30% and overall p99 end-to-end by >=20% for the canary pool without increasing p50 by more than 5%.
- Experiment B: reproduce kernel variance; if rollback reduces kernel-exec p99 by >=40%, prioritize revert.

Follow-ups / action items:
- [Riley] Kick off canary for arrival-smoothing (due 2025-10-07).
- [Marcus] Stage rollback tests and trace replay (due 2025-10-06).
- [Sofia] Ship shard hotness telemetry and 24h sample (due 2025-10-09).
- [Aisha] Prepare short triage write-up for oncall and schedule sync with SRE and serving runtime tomorrow.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Are there client SDK patterns causing repeated tiny completions? (Need SDK team to sample representative client traffic.)
- Is the quantized kernel variance limited to specific hardware (A100 vs H100) or system config? (Need cross-hardware trace comparison.)

Notes to self:
- Keep sample traces and provenance raw; do not redact in working doc. Some user-facing incidents were tied to the same trace signatures.
- If experiments show arrival-smoothing shifts latency to p50 for some paths, consider adaptive dynamic coalescing rather than fixed timeout.

Appendix — short trace snippet (raw span dump):
SPAN: req=abc123 | host=usw1-host-22 | model=rw-base-13b-q
  span.http-ingest start=0.000 end=0.900 dur=0.900
  span.tokenize start=0.900 end=1.600 dur=0.700
  span.req-queue start=1.600 end=3.800 dur=2.200
  span.batcher-wait start=3.800 end=26.200 dur=22.400
  span.kernel-exec start=26.200 end=45.950 dur=19.750
  span.kv-lookup start=45.950 end=56.100 dur=10.150
  span.emit start=56.100 end=59.500 dur=3.400
  span.egress start=59.500 end=60.300 dur=0.800

If helpful I can: 1) attach the raw trace bundle (200 traces) to CONDUCT-212, 2) run a targeted smoke on the canary pool, or 3) produce a short slide deck for oncall review.

Title: Service-mesh impact and networked-fidelity benchmarks

Service-mesh impact and networked-fidelity benchmarks

Overview

This document captures the rationale, experiment design, sample configurations, and runbook for benchmarking how different service-mesh and network topologies affect inference fidelity and operational SLOs. It is intended for engineers running distributed Redwood Private or Dedicated clusters where network pathing (sidecars, mTLS, mesh proxies, ingress controllers) may interact with runtime components (frontends, routers, model shards, kvcache, and tracing).

Why this matters

- Network pathing can add microsecond-to-millisecond tail latency that changes batching behaviour and kernel scheduling decisions.
- Proxies and sidecars may buffer, reorder, or aggregate requests which alters sequence arrival patterns and therefore KV cache hit rates and generation quality for stateful chat sessions.
- mTLS and service-mesh observability can introduce CPU overhead on nodes hosting lightweight services and affect co-located scheduler performance.

Scope

- Topologies: direct (no mesh), mesh sidecar (Envoy-like), ingress+mesh (gateway + sidecar), and cross-region overlay.
- Workloads: interactive chat (median tokens 40, tail 1024), streaming token-by-token generation, and bulk embeddings (batched).
- Hardware: A40/RTX/T4 pools and mixed GPU pools used in Dedicated clusters.
- Not covered: model-level quantization effects (handled in quantization-profiles).

Success criteria / SLOs

- Median generation latency (token emission) delta vs direct baseline <= 8% for interactive workloads.
- 95th percentile latency delta <= 20% for streaming workloads.
- KV cache hit-rate deviation <= 3 percentage points.
- Fidelity regressions: BLEU/ROUGE-like drops or hallucination-rate increases must be <= 1.5% absolute vs baseline for canary pass.

Experiment design

1) Controlled variables
   - Same model binary and runtime kernels across runs.
   - Fixed token budget and prompt corpus (prompt-sets-and-benchmarks corpus v2026-09).
   - Identical request surface (headers, chunking, streaming flags).

2) Independent variables
   - Network topology (direct, sidecar, ingress+sidecar, overlay).
   - TLS on/off (and session reuse policy).
   - Proxy concurrency and buffer sizes.
   - Placement variants: co-located sidecar on GPU node vs sidecar on separate infra node.

3) Metrics collected (minimum set)
   - Service-level: median, p95, p99 for request latency; queue length; dropped requests.
   - Runtime-level: per-kernel execution time, kernel scheduling latency, kv cache hit rate, batch size distribution.
   - Network-level: RTT distribution, sidecar CPU/memory, open connections, TLS handshake rate.
   - Fidelity: token-level log-prob deltas, output differences against golden responses, hallucination rate, semantic-similarity score.

Environment matrix (example)

| Test ID | Topology | TLS | Proxy CPU | Node placement | Notes |
|---------|----------|-----|----------:|----------------|-------|
| T01     | direct   | off | 0%       | none           | baseline |
| T02     | sidecar  | on  | 10%      | co-located     | typical small mesh sidecar CPU cgroup 10% |
| T03     | ingress+sidecar | on | 12%  | gateway on infra node | gateway does TLS termination + routing |
| T04     | overlay cross-region | on | 15% | mixed | simulates inter-region hops (~20-40ms) |

Benchmark harness and step-by-step procedure

1) Provisioning
   - Use the workload-sim tool (internal) to instantiate traffic replay. Example: 
     ./workload-sim --corpus=prompt-sets/chat-2026.json --qps=250 --shape=poisson --seed=202602 --streaming=true --out=run-T02

2) Deploy topology
   - Direct: disable sidecar injection and point frontend to runtime service.
   - Sidecar: enable mesh injection; apply sidecar resource limits using sidecar-cgroup.yaml (sample below).
   - Ingress+sidecar: install gateway config and route to mesh; enable TLS passthrough vs termination variants.

3) Run baseline and experiments
   - Run baseline (T01) for 60 minutes to warm caches and collect stable metrics.
   - For each topology, run 3 x 30-minute trials. Restart the runtime between each trial to reinitialize KV cache when testing cold-cache effects.

4) Data collection and verification
   - Export telemetry to the benchmarking S3 bucket with tags: topology, trial, seed, model-version.
   - Verify trace correlation IDs are preserved end-to-end. If trace sampling removes tail events, increase sampling to 100% for test windows.

Sample sidecar resource YAML (sidecar-cgroup.yaml)

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: sidecar-cgroup
data:
  CPU_LIMIT: "100m"
  CPU_REQUEST: "50m"
  BUF_SIZE: "65536"

Network measure snippets

- To measure RTT and handshake overhead: 
  time curl -w "RTT:\t%{time_connect}\tTLS: %{time_appconnect}\n" -o /dev/null -s https://runtime-host/api/gen

- To surface out-of-order or reordering statistics we use tcpdump + reorder-detector: 
  sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/run-T02.pcap &
  ./reorder-detector --pcap /tmp/run-T02.pcap --out /tmp/reorder-summary.json

Interpretation guide

- Small median deltas with large p99 deltas typically indicate buffering/queueing inside proxies or gateway resource saturation.
- A decreased KV cache hit rate with identical prompt distribution indicates request reordering or session affinity breakage: check sticky-session configuration and cookie/session-id propagation.
- Token-level log-prob deltas correlated with increased per-token latency usually point to batching changes (smaller effective batches) or kernel time-slicing; reconcile with batch-size histograms.

Example analysis queries

- Query: p99 latency by topology and kernel-version: 
  SELECT topology, kernel_version, percentile(latency_ms, 99) FROM inference_traces WHERE run_tag = 'T02' GROUP BY topology, kernel_version

- Query: kv cache hit rate drop traces and session-affinity mismatch: 
  SELECT session_id, kv_hit, request_ts FROM kv_cache_events WHERE run_tag='T03' ORDER BY request_ts DESC LIMIT 1000

Runbook: when networked topology causes production regressions

1) Detection: automated canary monitors should flag the fidelity alert (>=1% absolute drop in semantic-similarity) or SLO breach.
2) Immediate mitigation (0-15 minutes):
   - Reduce proxy buffer sizes and disable request aggregation on the gateway: set BUF_SIZE=16384 and reload gateway.
   - If sidecar CPU is saturated, enable automatic sidecar eviction policy for canary cohort.
3) Secondary actions (15-60 minutes):
   - Repoint traffic to the direct path (bypass mesh) for the affected cohort. Use routing policy: 
     curl -X POST https://controlplane/api/route-adjust -d '{"match":"account:1234","route":"direct"}'
   - If session-affinity is broken, rotate to sticky-session fallback using jwt-subject header as affinity key.
4) Post-incident analysis (>60 minutes):
   - Re-run the controlled experiments to reproduce and capture kernel-level traces. Document config deltas and upload to the benchmark bucket.

Ownership and contacts

- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime perf team (Ava Martínez).
- On-call contact: runtime-sre@redwood.ai.
- Escalation: Priya Rao (Runtime Platform), Oliver Singh (SRE).

What to log and attach to tickets

- Benchmark run tags and S3 path.
- Topology YAMLs and k8s manifests used.
- Pcap and reorder-summary if reordering suspected.
- Kernel trace slices (timestamps aligned with trace IDs).

Limitations and caveats

- This harness assumes uniform client-side TLS termination where applicable. Real client diversity (mobile vs server) can show different handshake and multiplexing behavior.
- Overlay cross-region tests must account for background internet noise; use VPC-peered emulation where possible.

Next steps and proposed improvements

- Add a synthetic jitter injector to emulate tail network spikes and observe scheduler response.
- Automate a compare-committee that runs fidelity checks in CI when gateway or sidecar versions are changed.
- Integrate result dashboards into the Redwood Console benchmarks view so product owners can see topology sensitivity when evaluating Dedicated/Private options.

Appendix: quick checklist for running a gated canary

1) Confirm model-version pinned and binary checksum matches baseline.
2) Run baseline T01 for 1 hour and archive metrics.
3) Run mesh topology trials (T02/T03) with same seed and warmup.
4) Run fidelity checks against golden corpus and send results to reviewers.
5) If failures observed, follow the runbook above and open a postmortem ticket with attachments.

End of document

Title: Stability Anchors and Load Sequencing Manifest

Stability Anchors and Load Sequencing Manifest

Purpose:
This document captures a practical, reproducible manifest for throughput benchmarking runs that focuses on: stability anchors (deterministic signals we expect to hold across runs), load sequencing (how we schedule and prime traffic), and hygiene steps for repeatability. Its intentionally operational: copyable commands, config snippets, and a short checklist you can follow before a run.

Motivation / problem statement:
- We repeatedly see run-to-run variance driven by thermal drift, kernel scheduling, KV-cache state, and loadgen randomness.
- Teams need a lightweight, copy/pasteable procedure that reduces tail variance and surfaces real regressions, not noise.
- This is not a formal acceptance test; its an engineering harness for comparative throughput experiments.

Key terms (how we use them here):
- Stability anchor: an observable metric or small step whose value should be invariant across experiments (e.g., single-request p95 on an idle instance, or a small priming sequence RTT).
- Priming/warmup: a sequence of requests sent prior to measuring that brings caches, kernels, and accelerator state to a steady operational point.
- Load sequencing: ordering of traffic phases (ramp, anchor probes, plateau, microbursts) planned to isolate effects.

Overall experiment template (high-level):
1) Environment reset and baseline capture (5-10m)
  - Node-level sanity (GPU temp, fan, clocks)
  - Capture idle latency anchor: 10 single-request probes at inter-arrival 2s
2) Controlled warmup (10-30m)
  - Stepwise increase in qps with prefix-seeded requests to populate KV cache
  - Include small constant-rate background traffic to simulate multi-tenant interference if required
3) Stability anchor probes (every 5 minutes)
  - 50 single-request probes at moderate concurrency (c=4) to ensure anchors stable
4) Measurement plateau (20m)
  - Target qps held using pacing shim; collect full telemetry
5) Microburst stress checks (3x short bursts)
  - 30s bursts at 2-3x plateau qps to exercise scheduler and batching heuristics
6) Cooldown observation (5m)
  - Ensure metrics return to baseline; capture final anchors and resource state

Load generator configuration examples (copyable):
- Minimal JSON profile snippet (used by our loadgen wrapper):

{
  "name": "plateau-anchors-1",
  "phases": [
    {"type": "idle-probe", "duration_s": 60, "arrival_distribution": "poisson", "rate": 0.5},
    {"type": "ramp", "duration_s": 600, "from_qps": 1, "to_qps": 200},
    {"type": "plateau", "duration_s": 1200, "qps": 200, "concurrency": 8},
    {"type": "microburst", "duration_s": 30, "qps": 600},
    {"type": "cooldown", "duration_s": 300, "qps": 0.5}
  ]
}

Notes on that profile: the "idle-probe" is the stability anchor probe. We use poisson arrivals for the ramp to reduce simultaneous burst artifacts.

Priming recipes (practical):
- Short model priming sequence (when KV cache matters): send 8 copies of the canonical prompt family used in production at c=2, spaced 100ms apart. Repeat the family 3x during ramp.
- Thermal priming: sustained 60% of target QPS for 10 minutes to allow GPU clocks to settle. If you see slow drift in latency after this period, increase thermal priming to 20 minutes.

Seed hygiene and RNG control:
- Ensure loadgen RNG seeds are fixed between comparative runs (we embed the seed in run metadata).
- When testing quantization or kernel changes, keep sample prompts identical and pinned to a sha’ed corpus. Store corpus in artifacts repo and reference the sha in run metadata.

Metrics to collect (minimum):
- Client-side: per-request latency percentiles (p50/p90/p95/p99), QPS, retries, http error codes, response sizes
- Server-side: per-token execution time, request queue length, batch size distribution, batch formation latency, GPU util, GPU power draw, GPU temperature, CPU steal, NIC rx/tx, disk I/O (rarely relevant but capture), kernel preemption events if available
- Platform: autoscaler decisions, node churn events, network egress/policy rejections

Stability anchors (recommended set):
1) Idle single-request p95 (10 probes) 
2) Small-prefix KV probe latency (50 probes)
3) Batch formation median at low qps (where batching should be minimal)
4) GPU clock and temp recorded at baseline

Decision thresholds for a run being valid:
- Idle single-request p95 must be within ±3% of previous run baseline OR we mark run invalid for comparative claims.
- Batch size distribution at plateau must not shift by >1 in median unless intentionally testing batching changes.
- Thermal drift: if GPU temperature rises by >8C during plateau relative to baseline run, tag as "thermal-variant" and annotate separately.

Failure modes and investigation hints:
- Symptom: plateau p99 spikes after 10 minutes.
  - Check for kernel eviction events, OS background jobs (cron, apt), thermal throttling.
  - Inspect batch formation traces: are large batches forming unpredictably? That points to arrival pattern changes.
- Symptom: lower throughput than expected with high GPU idle.
  - Check model fanout, model loading times, KV cache miss rates. Also verify that request shapes match model input sizes used during profiling.
- Symptom: reproducible but small regression (~4-6%):
  - Verify RNG seeds, corpus sha, env vars that affect CUDA kernels (e.g., CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING), compiler flags, and microcode/driver versions.

Run metadata and naming convention (important for dataset slicing):
- Use this format: "run/<model>-<variant>/plateau-<qps>-seed-<seed>/date-<YYYYMMDD>-tag-<short>"
- Example: run/gpt-mini/v1/plateau-200-seed-8421/date-20250109-tag-primeshield
- Always attach: commit sha for runtime, docker image tag, driver/kernel versions, exact loadgen profile file, and corpus sha

Quick commands (helpers):
- Start a baseline probe: 
  ./loadgenctl run --profile profiles/idle_probe.json --metadata "seed=8421,sha=abcd1234"
- Capture server-side telemetry (one-liner for the agent):
  ssh node-01 'sudo dstat -cdn 5 240 > /tmp/dstat.log & nvidia-smi --query-gpu=temperature.gpu,utilization.gpu,power.draw --format=csv -l 5 > /tmp/gpu.csv &'
- Aggregate artifacts:
  ./run-artifact-collector --run-dir /tmp/current-run --out s3://redwood-benchmarks/runs/$(date +%Y%m%d)-8421

Interpretation rubric (quick):
- If plateau p50 improves and p99 degrades -> likely variance/queuing differences or batching tail effects.
- If all percentiles shift uniformly -> likely deterministic perf change (kernel/quantization/compilation path).

Notes to self / unresolved questions (work in progress):
- We still need a compact automated test to assert "anchor stability" preconditionally before flagging run as valid. Prototype in PR 678 but not merged.
- Microburst phase duration and intensity need tuning per model family; current defaults are conservative.
- Consider adding a small network jitter emulator for runs that want to reproduce multi-region jitter.

Appendix: example minimal run manifest (YAML-ish plain text)

run_name: stability-anchor-20250109
runtime_sha: abcd1234
loadgen_profile: profiles/plateau-200.json
seed: 8421
plateau_qps: 200
plateau_duration_s: 1200
warmup_thermal_minutes: 10
corpus_sha: corpora/promptset/v1/sha:deadbeef
notes: "Baseline comparison vs 20250102 nominal run"

References and links:
- Related ticket: JIRA INFR-122 (benchmark instability investigations)
- Prototype harness PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/678
- Confluence: serving-runtime/benchmarking-notes (internal)

If you use this manifest: copy the profile, pin the artifacts, and paste the run name into the run tracker spreadsheet. If anchors fail, stop and investigate before claiming a regression.

-- aisha

Title: Span & Model-Call Tracing Cookbook for Tooling and Function Calls

Span & Model-Call Tracing Cookbook for Tooling and Function Calls

Purpose:
This is a pragmatic cookbook for instrumenting spans across model calls, tool/function invocation, and multi-model fanouts. The goal is to make traces useful for: (1) fast incident investigation, (2) cost attribution for tool usage, and (3) quality regression debugging when model outputs differ after rollouts.

Scope and motivation:
- Why: model->tool->model cycles and function/tool-calling are common in chat and structured output flows. Current traces often collapse these calls or lose context (arguments, prompt snippets, chosen tool). That makes it hard to: identify which tool call introduced latency, which model variant produced a divergent answer, or whether KV cache evictions happened mid-flow.
- Audience: instrumentation engineers, SREs doing incident debugging, solutions engineers validating customer flows.

High-level tracing rules (opinionated):
1) Preserve human-readable context but limit size. Include short prompt hashes and truncated prompt fingerprints (first 512 chars) only when sampling low.
2) Parent-child mapping: every tool/function call must be an explicit child span of the model inference span that initiated it. If a model fanout spawns N downstream model calls, create a fanout root span with a field fanout.count=N.
3) Idempotent identifiers: include request_id, session_id (if available), and prompt_id in every span to allow session-based reconstruction without deep trace joins.
4) Sampling policy: prefer low-sampled traces for full prompt payload; high-rate synthetic probes should use minimal span attributes to avoid storage blowup.

Recommended span schema (flat key/value attributes, keep to ~20 keys):
- span.name: short identifier (e.g., model.generate, tool.call, model.embedding)
- span.type: inference | tool | embedding | routing
- telemetry.request_id: global request id (uuid)
- telemetry.session_id: session or user id (if available)
- telemetry.prompt_id: internal prompt fingerprint
- model.name: e.g., redwood/vicuna-13b-q4
- model.variant: quantized | fp16 | int8
- model.seq_len: integer
- tool.name: e.g., code-exec, web-search, calc
- tool.latency_ms: reported from the tool (if measured separately)
- fanout.index: index within model fanout (0..N)
- fanout.count: total spawned
- kvcache.warm: true | false
- sample.rate: effective trace sampling rate (e.g., 0.01)
- error.code: internal error code
- error.message: brief
- cost.tokens_in / cost.tokens_out: numeric strings (for later aggregation)

Span examples (textual):
- Model root span: span.name=model.generate; type=inference; contains telemetry.request_id, model.name, model.variant, telemetry.prompt_id, kvcache.warm, sample.rate.
- Tool call child: span.name=tool.call; type=tool; parent= model.generate; contains tool.name, tool.latency_ms, fanout.index (if part of fanout), linked_artifact (e.g., external request id).
- Fanout root (when single user request fans out to multiple models or multiple prompt prefixes): span.name=model.fanout; fanout.count=N; child spans model.generate#0, model.generate#1 etc.

Sampling heuristics:
- Full payload traces (prompt text + tool args) at 0.1% of production traffic by default (configurable per route). Use stored prompt hash in high-sample traces only.
- For all errors/exceptions, force-sample full trace (100%).
- Canary traffic: sample at 5-10% for the first week after rollout to catch quality regressions.
- Synthetic probes: sample headers-only traces; keep body suppressed.

Dashboard and investigation notes (practical widgets):
- Tool latency heatmap: x axis = tool.name, y axis = 50/90/99 quantiles, filterable by model.variant and tenant. Intent: find tools causing downstream tail latency.
- Fanout cost scatter: show fanout.count vs tokens_out and cost per request. Useful to detect regression where rollout causes more downstream calls.
- Prompt-fingerprint drift panel: track frequency of top 50 prompt hashes over time; sudden changes can signal UX or prompt engineering issues.
- Trace-linked error explorer: counts by error.code with link to representative sampled trace; automatically expand to show tool calls and kvcache.warm flag.
- Session-replay shortcut: for a given session_id show sequence of spans + top-level logs (if available).

Operator playbook (quick steps during an incident):
1) Query trace by telemetry.request_id or session_id in the incident time window (start with a small window + high QPS routes).
2) If trace sample missing, use prompt_id and fanout.count to reconstruct via logs/dashboard panels (fanout scatter helps).
3) Inspect child spans for tool.latency_ms or error.code. Use tool-latency heatmap to see if this is single-tenant or global.
4) Check kvcache.warm on model spans; if multiple cold cache flags appear concurrently, suspect cache eviction/rolling restart.
5) For regressions in output quality, pull canary vs prod traces and compare model.variant and model.seq_len distribution.

Instrumenting common SDKs (notes for implementers):
- JS/TS SDK: attach telemetry.request_id to headers: x-rw-request-id. Ensure model.generate wraps outgoing tool calls to create child spans using the tracing client.
- Python: provide a contextmanager (rw_tracing.model_span(...)) that automatically sets parent spans for any tool.call calls done while active.
- Go: explicit SpanFactory with helpers for fanout indices to avoid name collisions in parallel goroutines.

Operational constraints and cost control:
- Cap span attribute size: any string longer than 2048 chars should be truncated or stored as a reference id.
- TTL: raw trace retention policy should be tiered: full traces 14 days, compact metadata 90 days, aggregates indefinite.
- Cardinality: avoid high-cardinality keys where possible (user email, raw prompt). Use hashed IDs with friendly aliases in sampled traces.

Open questions / TODOs (for follow-ups):
- Decide canonical field names for cost.* attributes and whether to include currency in trace (JIRA-OBS-889).
- Prototype a trace-enrichment service that can attach model eval metrics (per-prompt quality score) to sampled traces.
- Sampling configuration UI: knob suggestions and default per-route profiles.

Appendix: quick checklists
- From PR: instrumented endpoints must populate telemetry.request_id and telemetry.session_id (if available).
- From SRE: ensure synthetic probes have dedicated trace tags to exclude them from production SLO calculations.
- From product: tag rollout canary traces with deployment.id to make per-rollout comparisons easy.

References:
- see linked artifacts for trace spec and telemetry PR.

Notes to reviewers (informal):
- This is intentionally prescriptive; aim is to reduce investigation time. Feedback: is the recommended ~20-attribute budget realistic for our current SDKs?
- If you have sample trace JSONs from real incidents that exercise tool chains, attach them to JIRA-OBS-882.

Title: Trace Synthesis Workload Catalog and Regression Playlist

Trace Synthesis Workload Catalog and Regression Playlist

Purpose:
This is a working catalog of synthetic workload scenarios derived from production traces, plus a short regression "playlist" (priority order of microbench steps) for quickly reproducing perf regressions. The goal is to standardize inputs for kernel/scheduler/kv-cache experiments so bench runs are comparable across engineers and CI lanes.

Scope and motivation:
- We frequently see flaky perf changes due to small kernel changes, scheduler tweaks, or KV cache invalidation behavior. Having canonical synthesized traces that exercise specific micro-paths (short prefix reuse, long KV-eviction churn, dense attention vs sparse tokens, varied batch-deltas) reduces debugging time.
- This doc is intentionally pragmatic: scenarios are small, reproducible, and parameterizable. Not every scenario mirrors full-prod traffic; instead they isolate subsystems.

High-level harness architecture (notes):
- Core components: trace-synth engine (python), workload-driver (go), local-run harness (docker-compose for dev), CI lane (k8s job).
- Input format: sequence of request events (arrival_ts_ms, model, prompt_hash, key_prefix_id, seq_len, sampling_params). We keep the format CSV-like for ease of diffs.
- Outputs: per-request latency, per-token time breakdown (attention, kernel exec, scheduler-batch-wait, kv-lookup), kernel-call-counts, GPU occupancy summary (sampled), memory high-water marks.
- Observability hooks: spans injected into harness and translated to our tracing schema (trace_id -> span events) so microtrace replay can map to production traces.

Scenario catalog (each scenario is ~30-120s depending on scale):
1) Short-prefix reuse (S-PREFIX-1): many small requests (seq_len 32) with identical first-8 tokens across a 60s window to exercise prefix KV hits and prefix-merge fast path. Params: QPS 200, batch max 32, kv_cache_ttl=5m. Expected to show high KV hit rate and low per-token kernel exec.
2) Long-eviction churn (EVICT-LOOP-2): high variety prompts that force constant KV insert+evict cycles. Params: QPS 50, unique_prefixes_per_min 5000, kv_capacity small (simulated 4k entries), batch max 16. Useful for testing eviction heuristics and mem copies.
3) Heterogeneous-batches (HETER-3): mixed seq lengths (16/64/512) arriving in patterns to stress continuous batching and scheduler heuristics. Pattern: 70% short, 20% mid, 10% long. Evaluate batch packing penalties and kernel fallback costs.
4) Kernel-stress-quant (KERNEL-QUANT-4): synthetic tokens that force quantized kernels with different alignment (non-multiple-of-8 channels) to catch slow paths in low-precision kernels. Single GPU at QPS 30, repeat for various channel widths.
5) Cold-kv-warmup (COLD-WARM-5): start with empty cache and ramp QPS from 0 -> 300 over 3 minutes to measure warm-up spike and cache population latency.
6) Tooling-edge-cases (TOOLING-6): includes malformed requests, slight param variance, and frequent fallback model switches to ensure robust tracing and failover telemetry.

Metric definitions (what we measure):
- p50/p95/p99 request latency (ms) end-to-end
- per-token median kernel exec time (ms)
- scheduler-wait time breakdown (ms): time spent waiting for batch, serialization overhead, inter-op queue waits
- kv-hit-rate (by prefix length), kv-eviction-rate (% of insertions that trigger evict), kv-copy-bytes
- batch-utilization (avg batch size / max batch size)
- GPU occupancy: sampled SM utilization and mem bw (approx)
- regression score: a synthetic single-number combining 99th latency and kv-eviction spikes (used for alerting in CI)

Synthesis method (how traces are derived from prod traces):
- Step 1: extract anonymized sequence features from prod traces (prefix hashes, seq_len distribution, inter-arrival delta distribution per route).
- Step 2: cluster sessions by heavy hitters (top 100 prefixes) and tail patterns (long seq tail).
- Step 3: generate parametric workload descriptions (CSV). Add random jitter between inter-arrival times to avoid lockstep.
- Step 4: validate: run 3x short replay in sandbox and compare feature distributions to source traces (KL divergence thresholds).

Recent microbench runs (sample notes, dev runs on dev-gpu-4):
- 2026-02-25: Ran S-PREFIX-1 against kernel-merge-opt branch. Observed 7% p95 regression vs baseline. Per-span breakdown shows increased scheduler-batch-wait (median +6ms) despite lower kernel exec. Suspect change to packer logic introduced serialization that prevented opportunistic merging. Logged PR #842.
- 2026-02-28: EVICT-LOOP-2 run with kv-lru-fix reverted — eviction-rate dropped but memory copies increased 12% (copy bandwidth spike). Root cause: copying semantics moved to slow path in commit a1b2c (see PR).
- 2026-03-03: HETER-3 exposes degenerate batch composition where long-seq requests hold batch slots for 800ms and block short samples; temp mitigation: add short-request priority lane in scheduler (config flag: scheduler.short_priority=true) — reduced p99 by 18% in smoke runs.

Regression playlist (ordered reproduce steps):
A) Reproduce S-PREFIX-1 p95 regression locally: check out runtime@merge-opt-pr842, run harness with --scenario S-PREFIX-1 --seed 42 --collect-spans. Attach output to PR.
B) Run kernel micro-tests: run kernel bench binary with alignment patterns used by KERNEL-QUANT-4; assert no slow path triggered.
C) EVICT-LOOP-2 mem-profiling: run scenario under nvprof and capture memcpy histogram. If memcpy > baseline by 10%, block further rollouts.
D) HETER-3 scheduler trace: enable verbose scheduler tracing and produce flame graph; confirm whether long requests are occupying batching windows for >500ms.

Playbook & quick checklist (for oncall/dev):
- If CI flags regression score > threshold:
  - Run regression playlist A-D on the failing commit.
  - If reproduction successful, post short debug summary to #eng-serving-runtime and tag authors.
  - Create Jira with minimal repro steps + attached harness output.
- Oncall quick commands (devbox shortcuts):
  - ./harness/run.sh --scenario S-PREFIX-1 --ci-mode --upload-artifact 
  - tools/microbench/kernel_bench --pattern=odd-channels --iters=1000
  - python tools/kv_inspect.py --run=EVICT-LOOP-2 --output=evict.hist

Open questions / TODOs:
- Formalize thresholding rules for regression score and add to CI gating. (TODO: draft proposal, owner: Aisha)

Title: Trace context enrichment guidelines and metrics bridge

Trace context enrichment guidelines and metrics bridge

Purpose:
This is a compact working guide to standardize minimal trace context enrichment in the inference runtime and to define a small, stable mapping from trace attributes -> metric anchors -> dashboard widgets. The goal is: make production debugging fast, make SLI computation and alerting deterministic, and bound observability query cost.

Scope and constraints:
- Applies to serving-runtime and request-path spans for tokenized inference (hosted, dedicated, and private).
- Minimal set of attributes only: add where cheap to capture; prefer enums/ids to free text.
- Sampling & retention tradeoffs: traces must contain enough metadata to reconstruct root causes without exploding storage.
- This doc is a living checklist (draft) — we expect follow-up refinements after a small pilot.

Design decisions (summary):
1) Always capture a canonical request_id (UUID) on root span and propagate to child spans.
2) Keep tenant and route identifiers short (tenant_id, route_hash) rather than full tenant name.
3) Use discrete codified attributes for runtime state: model_variant, quantization_profile, kernel_path, gpu_type, fallback_tier.
4) Preserve cost-relevant attributes for post-hoc chargebacks: token_count, decode_batch_size, kv_cache_hit (bool), prefix_cache_hit_percent (0-100).
5) Tracing should enrich metrics (not replace them): each critical span will set a small set of attributes that are then rolled up into counter/hist aggregator labels.

Minimum trace attribute set (required on root span):
- request_id: string (uuid)
- timestamp_iso: string
- tenant_id: string (short)
- route_hash: string (short)
- model_variant: string (e.g., gptx-7b-q4)
- seq_len: integer (input_length + expected_output_length)
- token_count: integer (generated tokens)
- kv_cache_hit: boolean (true if prefix cache used)
- batching_key: string (if using batching routing)
- fallback_reason: string|null (e.g., overloaded, kernel-mismatch, cold-start)

Span naming & attributes (examples):
- span.name = "request.root" -> root attributes above
- span.name = "model.decode" -> attributes: model_variant, decode_batch_size (int), kernel_path, gpu_type, gpu_pstate
- span.name = "cache.kv_lookup" -> attributes: kv_cache_hit (bool), lookup_ms (float), keys_examined (int)
- span.name = "router.selection" -> attributes: route_hash, selected_pool, queued_ms
- span.name = "fallback.swap" -> attributes: fallback_from, fallback_to, fallback_reason

Mapping: trace attrs -> metric anchors (recommended label set):
We recommend a small canonical set of labels for high-cardinality-sensitive metrics. For any metric emitted from a span, attach at most these labels: tenant_id, model_variant, route_hash, kv_cache_hit. If the metric is cost-related (token or gpu), also attach seq_len_bucket and batch_size_bucket.

Suggested label buckets (to reduce cardinality):
- seq_len_bucket: small|medium|long (0-128,129-512,>512)
- batch_size_bucket: solo|micro|bulk (1, 2-8, >8)

Metric definitions (starter set):
- inference.request.count: counter by labels [tenant_id, model_variant, route_hash] -> increment on root completion
- inference.request.latency_ms: histogram (use quantiles for dashboard) by [model_variant, seq_len_bucket]
- model.decode.tokens_generated: counter by [model_variant, seq_len_bucket, kv_cache_hit] -> increment by token_count
- kv.lookup.latency_ms: histogram by [kv_cache_hit]
- fallback.swap.count: counter by [fallback_reason, model_variant]
- cost.estimated_gpu_ms: gauge computed at end of request by summing kernel execution durations; label by [model_variant, gpu_type]

Dashboard implications and panel recipes (cost-aware):
- Keep an always-on compact panel: request rate (1m), p50/p90 latency, token rate per second. Labels: model_variant. This is the operator quick-look.
- Cost panel (daily): estimated GPU-ms / tenant_id for last 24h (roll up by model_variant). Use aggregation windows to avoid heavy queries.
- Cold-cache detector: request latency delta between kv_cache_hit=true vs false, plotted by seq_len_bucket.
- Fallback heatmap: matrix with fallback_reason on Y, model_variant on X; cell shows count and p95 latency.
- Query cost guardrails: a dashboard that flags panels with >5s query runtime or >1M series scanned. Mark these as "heavy" with a per-panel cost note.

Tracing sampling & retention strategy (proposal):
1) Head-sample 5% of all traces for full retention (30d) for debugging.
2) Target-sample 100% of traces for root-sample-only (metadata + logs, no full span payload) for 7d.
3) Exception-sample 100%: any trace that triggers fallback_reason or high-latency p95 threshold captured in full regardless of head-sample.
4) On-demand capture: provide an API to temporarily raise sample rate for a tenant or route for investigation.

Instrumentation notes for runtime engineers (practical):
- Where to add attributes: in request ingress handler (tenant_id, route_hash, request_id), in router (selected_pool, queued_ms), in executor (kernel_path, gpu_type, decode_batch_size), in cache layer (kv_cache_hit, lookup_ms).
- Keep attribute values short and stable (avoid embedding user prompts, full model configs, or raw request bodies).
- Use code helpers to set enum-like attributes (e.g., TraceAttr.set("kv_cache_hit", TraceAttr.Bool.TRUE)) to ensure consistent naming.

Example trace annotation snippet (text):
-- root span attrs --
request_id: 5f2e1a6a-...
tenant_id: acct-42
route_hash: r234
model_variant: redwood-7b-q4
seq_len: 256
token_count: 38
kv_cache_hit: false
fallback_reason: null

Open questions and tradeoffs (for next sync):
- How to encode model version stability vs model_variant (we want both but model_version increases cardinality). Option: expose model_version only on sampled traces and use model_variant for metrics.
- Should prefix_cache_hit_percent be stored as integer label or a numeric gauge? Storing as a label increases cardinality but helps immediate filtering.
- Exact thresholds for seq_len_bucket and batch_size_bucket — need workload profiling to finalize.
- How to budget trace storage costs across hosted vs private customers — do we strip attributes automatically for private deployments?

Pilot plan (30d):
Week 0-1: implement root span attr set + router and cache spans; emit metric anchors.
Week 2: add model.decode attributes and cost. Roll out to 10% of traffic on staging.
Week 3: collect dashboards, run operator tabletop for cost queries and latency investigations.
Week 4: iterate on buckets and sampling; finalize instrumentation helpers and docs.

Checklist before wide rollout:
- [ ] SDK helpers for setting canonical attributes (Python/Go/Node).
- [ ] Dashboards for operator quick-look and cost guardrails created and validated.
- [ ] Sampling policy implemented in tracer and configurable via console.
- [ ] Performance test to ensure span annotations add <0.5% P99 latency overhead.

Quick notes to reviewers:
- This doc tries to balance debugging fidelity with cardinality and query cost. If you think we should capture any additional attribute for immediate investigative value (e.g., compile_kernels set), call it out but expect we'll sample it.
- If you are an infra owner and want to run the pilot for a particular pool or tenant, add a comment below with target date.

Action items (owners):
- Priya/Rao: finalize trace attr enum list and open the tracer PR (due 2024-12-05).
- Ethan Kim: prototype dashboard widgets and include query cost notes (due 2024-12-12).
- Lara Chen: run a storage-cost estimate for 1%, 5%, 20% full-trace sampling (due 2024-12-08).
- Samir Patel: validate SDK helpers on a demo client (due 2024-12-18).

Appendix: quick glossary
- metric anchor: the minimal set of labels we attach to metrics so they can be correlated back to traces without exploding cardinality.
- root-sample-only: capture minimal trace metadata and logs but omit verbose span payloads and large buffers.
- fallback_reason: small enum listing the cause for fallback logic (e.g., resource_pressure, model_unavailable, kernel_error, routing_timeout).

Notes-to-self and loose thoughts (raw):
- maybe add a "route_tier" label for premium vs free customers — helps cost-alloc but increases cardinality; maybe derive at aggregation time instead.
- if we can compute estimated GPU-ms cheaply from kernel timers, include it as a label for cost panels but keep raw timers in trace payload for in-depth digs.
- consider auto-trimming long attribute strings in private deployments to reduce PII risk.

-- end --

Title: Trace ensemble and quantile stitching scrapbook

Trace ensemble and quantile stitching scrapbook

Goal:
Short: build a repeatable, low-effort workflow to produce production-weighted p50/p95/p99 end-to-end latency profiles and per-stage contribution breakdowns from mixed samples (synthetic + sampled prod traces).

Why this doc exists (notes to self):
- We have many single-window trace audits but no compact, comparable report that stitches multiple sampling periods and synthetic runs into a single quantile-aware view.
- Need something that PMs and infra can read: big quantiles, what stage is the offender, and a prioritized mitigation list with expected tail impact.

Inputs we used for the first pass (source / sample details):
- Production sampled traces: 24h window (2025-01-07), trace sampling 1/1000 overall, increased to 1/100 for anomalous routes. Fields: trace_id, route, seq_len, model_variant, host_type, stage_times{tokenize, kv_lookup, batching_wait, model_fwd, postproc, egress}, cold_kv_flag, timestamp_ms
- Synthetic replay runs: 5 workloads (chat-short, chat-medium, completion-long, embeddings, rerank). Each replay ran for 30 minutes on a spare cluster to capture microburst behavior.
- Benchmarks: single-request microbenchmarks for model_fwd on GPU types A and B (median + tail from 100k in-process runs).

Instrumentation notes (gaps / gotchas):
- Batching_wait is reported as delta between 'batch_scheduled' and 'batch_started' in host-local time; some hosts have clock skew up to 5ms which inflates p50 slightly. We corrected by converting to monotonic deltas when possible.
- KV misses are flagged by cold_kv_flag but we only have presence, not miss_reason.
- Egress includes both encode time and network send; for dedicated hosts with local clients egress is <2ms, for hosted it can be 8–50ms depending on downlink.

Method: quantile stitching and per-stage attribution (high-level):
1) Partition traces into cohorts: route x model_variant x seq_len_bucket (0-64,65-256,>256) x host_type. This reduces confounding.
2) For each cohort, build empirical CDF of end-to-end latency and per-stage latencies.
3) To aggregate across cohorts with different traffic weight, compute traffic-weighted quantiles: sample N traces per cohort proportional to observed QPS (cap per cohort to avoid rare-cohort overdomination).
4) Compute p50/p95/p99 of end-to-end latency on the assembled sample.
5) Per-stage contribution to a given quantile: two complementary views:
   a) "Additive quantile attribution" (fast, approximate): compute per-stage median/95/99 and present stage share = stage_quantile / total_quantile. Useful for quick triage but can exceed 100% when stages overlap in tail.
   b) "Conditional slice decomposition" (more robust): for traces in the top X% (e.g., top 1% for p99), compute the distribution of stage times and report percent of traces where a stage >= 40% of trace. Also compute co-occurrence matrix for top-tier traces. This gives actionable signals (e.g., p99 dominated by batching_wait in 62% of top traces).
6) Cross-check with synthetic replays and kernel microbenchmarks to separate host-local model_fwd regressions from system-level batching/queueing effects.

Example results (first-pass numbers, approximate):
- Composite (traffic-weighted) latencies: p50 = 48ms, p95 = 215ms, p99 = 480ms
- Cohort examples (chat-medium, variant-v1, seqlen 65-256): p50=62ms p95=310ms p99=680ms

Per-stage quick-attribution (additive approx):
- Tokenize: p50=1ms p95=2ms p99=5ms (negligible)
- KV_lookup: p50=3ms p95=12ms p99=45ms (in p99 often cold misses)
- Batching_wait: p50=8ms p95=90ms p99=320ms (major tail contributor)
- Model_fwd: p50=28ms p95=70ms p99=90ms (tails grow with seqlen but not the dominant p99 for these cohorts)
- Postproc+egress: p50=4ms p95=18ms p99=30ms

Conditional slice decomposition (top 1% traces):
- 62% of top-1% traces have batching_wait >= 50% of total latency
- 21% of top-1% traces include cold_kv_flag == true and these traces have median extra +110ms
- Co-occurrence: when batching_wait high, model_fwd is rarely the largest fraction (only 14% of these cases) -> suggests queueing/scheduling vs model slowdown

Hypotheses generated from the above:
- Root cause for p99: rare large batching_delay spikes (scheduling jitter + contention for async worker slots) amplified by occasional cold KV misses.
- Model_fwd micro-regressions exist but contribute more to p95 than p99 in normal traffic mix.

Mitigation candidates (with rough impact estimate):
- Reduce max_batch_wait from 50ms -> 30ms for chat-medium routes: estimated p99 reduction ~30–45ms but increases p50 slightly for some throughput-critical bursts. (owner: Liam)
- Prewarm KV for hot prefixes during load spikes (heatmap-triggered prefetch): reduces cold_kv tail; estimated p99 improvement ~+80–120ms on affected cohort. (owner: Diego)
- Introduce a small prioritized fast-path queue for latency-sensitive routes to avoid head-of-line batching waits; prototype via adaptive queue knobs. Expected p99 wins for sensitive routes. (owner: Aisha)
- Investigate host scheduler jitter: instrument host-level worker wakeup histograms and kernel scheduling events during top traces. (owner: SRE)

Visualization recipe (for the dashboard / one-page slides):
- Top-left: composite CDF (log x-axis) p50/p95/p99 markers
- Top-right: stacked bar per-quantile showing additive-approx stage slices for p50/p95/p99
- Middle: cohort heatmap (rows=route, cols=quantiles) shading by p99 magnitude
- Bottom: conditional co-occurrence matrix for top-1% traces (percentages) + example trace timelines (3 exemplar traces annotated)

Open questions / follow-ups (in rough priority):
- How stable are the batching_wait spikes across days? Need rolling 7-day window sample comparison.
- Can we get richer KV diagnostics (miss reason, backend latency) without PII exposure? (product/security)
- Is there a correlation with autoscaling events / node churn? Add autoscaler event markers to traces.
- Validate synthetic replay representativeness for microburst shapes (saturday vs weekday differences).

Action items (short):
- [ ] Liam: change max_batch_wait on staged route and run 24h A/B (jira:SRV-3489)
- [ ] Diego: prototype prefix prewarm for top-100 hot prefixes during spike windows (PR: repo/cache-prefetch#6)
- [ ] SRE: add worker wakeup histogram to trace payload for a 48h window (link to infra ticket)
- [ ] Aisha: build dashboard mockup and attach 3 exemplar traces for review (confluence:trace-ensemble-dash)

Notes-to-self / style: keep the composite report conservative (use conditional decomposition for any claim of "dominant cause") and always show both additive and conditional views. Present expected impact ranges with uncertainties (low/med/high) and attach raw cohort counts so PMs understand sample sizes.

Appendix (quick reproducibility steps):
1) pull sampled traces: python tools/trace_export.py --start 2025-01-07 --end 2025-01-08 --routes chat-* --out traces.jsonl
2) run cohort assembler: python tools/cohort_assembler.py --in traces.jsonl --weight-by qps --cap 50k --out stitched_sample.jsonl
3) run quantile reporter: python tools/quantile_report.py --in stitched_sample.jsonl --cohorts meta.json --out report.yml
4) generate dashboard plot: tools/plot_maker --report report.yml --examples 3 --out report.pdf

If anything above looks off or someone wants raw numbers, ping and I will attach the trace slices and the synthetic run configs.

(end of draft)

Title: devex

devex

rachel: quick flag: our new Next.js LangChain + LlamaIndex starter is flaking in the eval suite. The embeddings batch sometimes returns results in a different order and once left out an item after a retry.
tony: ugh. which sample path & sdk?
rachel: samples/next-llama-langchain-starter, using @redwood/sdk@0.9.x (Node). Python consumers not affected.
vishal: any reproducible log snippet?
rachel: yep pasted small excerpt: 
```
payload ids: [u1,u2,u3,u4]
responses observed: [u1,u3,u2]
retry happened -> returned [u2]
final merged: [u1,u3,u2,u2]  // u4 missing, u2 duplicated
```
priya: looks like two problems: (1) the JS batch resolves as promises complete so ordering can shuffle, (2) retry merge appends duplicates instead of re-inserting at the original index.
tony: for evals we need deterministic output. Short-term: add a sample-side postprocess that maps by client id and then reorders. Longer-term: fix SDK.
priya: I pushed a tiny sample patch that normalizes results in api/embeds.ts and gated it behind SAMPLE_STABLE_EMBEDS=true in .env so we don't change runtime semantics for everyone. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/samples/pull/7001
devex-bot: preview deploy for pr/7001 created  status: pending
vishal: good. I'll file an SDK issue for parity and include a small repro payload that the eval harness can run.
tony: create issue and label sdk/parity/bug, please. Also include a unit that simulates an auth error mid-batch to exercise the retry merging logic.
vishal: opened https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/issues/1988  title: "Node SDK: batch embeddings may reorder and duplicate on partial retry"  labels: sdk,bug,parity
devex-bot: issue #1988 created by vishal  labels: sdk,bug,parity
priya: plan for SDK fix: allocate an array of placeholders sized to input, fill slots as responses arrive (by index) and ignore duplicate client ids on retry. Expose opt-in flag `preserveInputOrder=true` for now; if perf looks fine we can make it the default.
tony: please add microbenchmarks at 100 qps and 500 qps to quantify overhead. We need numbers for release notes.
rachel: sample PR is green locally but CI preview failed because the eval harness caught the mismatch (expected). So gating with env var protects release until SDK fix lands.
devex-bot: preview deploy for pr/7001 rolled back  reason: ci/tests:eval-harness failed
vishal: assign @tony to the SDK patch, @priya to add harness tests that assert: all ids present, no duplicates, and preserved order. I'll own the sample follow-up to remove the gate when the SDK fix merges.
priya: adding harness test: run with concurrency 8 and assert stable ordering across 20 iterations to catch flakiness. Also add a dedupe-by-id guard to avoid false positives while the SDK is in progress.
tonY: will draft an SDK PR that implements placeholder-array + id-based dedupe. I'll include a changelog note about preserving input order for batch endpoints and a migration snippet for anyone relying on unordered behavior.
rachel: also added a section in the Next.js starter README describing the repro steps and the temporary env workaround so community contributors don't keep opening duplicate issues.
devex-bot: linked issue #1988 in samples PR 7001  comment: "SDK issue tracked; remove workaround after SDK patch"
vishal: once SDK PR lands we should update the sample and add an integration test to prevent regression. Also update devex checklist: "assume JS batch may reorder unless preserveInputOrder=true".
priya: final note: watch out for key rotation/401 mid-batch because that triggers a retry that historically caused duplication. Added that as an item in issue #1988.
tonY: PR incoming this week, will ping eng-ml for review and include bench results.
rachel: thanks all — keeping the sample gate until SDK lands to keep eval CI stable.

Title: Hosted model rollout and fallback runbook

Hosted model rollout and fallback runbook

# Overview
This runbook describes the standard procedure to roll out a new model to the Hosted API catalog and configure safe fallback/rollback. It is written for Release Engineering, Platform, and on-call responders.

# Preconditions (must be true before rollout)
- Model intake ticket exists and is in `ready-for-rollout` status.
- Applied ML has provided eval gates pass results and a one-paragraph risk assessment.
- Serving Runtime has signed off the performance bar results for the default profile.
- Security has approved the third-party model risk review (or an exception is linked).

# Roles
- Rollout owner: Release Engineering
- Routing change owner: Platform
- On-call: Eng Oncall (runtime + platform)

# Required artifacts
- GitHub PR in `redwood-model-registry` adding the model and quant profiles
- Perf suite run IDs (default profile)
- Eval harness run links (Suites A + any tool-calling suite)
- Security risk review link + any restriction text that must appear in docs

# Step-by-step rollout procedure
## 1) Create the catalog entry (registry PR)
- Ensure the PR includes:
  - Model ID, version, tokenizer identifier
  - Allowed context lengths
  - Supported features (streaming, structured output, tool calling)
  - Quant profiles and default profile
  - Artifact hashes/provenance notes
- Merge only after required approvals are present.

## 2) Deploy behind feature flag (dark launch)
- Add a routing rule in `router-policy` with state `disabled` and scope `internal`.
- Deploy config to staging and run smoke tests:
  - `/v1/chat/completions` streaming
  - basic JSON schema output
  - max-context request (ensure clean error message on overflow)

## 3) Canary to production
- Enable routing for 0.5% of traffic on one region (us-east-1) for 3060 minutes.
- Monitor dashboards:
  - `hosted_inference_latency` (TTFT p95)
  - `hosted_inference_errors` (5xx, timeouts)
  - `gpu_oom_events`
  - `quality_regression_alerts` (if shadowing enabled)
- If error rate > 0.5% or TTFT p95 breaches the SLO for 10 minutes, abort canary and rollback (see section below).

## 4) Expand rollout
- Increase to 5% in us-east-1, then add eu-west-1, then ap-southeast-1 (if applicable).
- If the model is replacing a default/alias, keep the old model as the first fallback for at least 7 days.

## 5) GA and documentation
- When traffic reaches 100% for the intended routes, mark the Linear ticket as `shipped`.
- DevEx must publish docs updates with:
  - model ID, default settings, limitations, and restriction text (if any)

# Fallback and rollback
## Fallback policy (required)
Each new catalog model must specify:
- Primary: new model ID
- Fallback #1: previous stable model in same family
- Fallback #2: cross-family safe default (product-approved)

## Rollback triggers (examples)
- Sustained TTFT p95 regression > 20% vs baseline for 30 minutes
- Elevated 5xx > 0.5% for 10 minutes
- Confirmed quality regression on `p0` prompts post-launch

## Rollback steps
1. Disable routing rule for new model (set weight to 0)
2. Promote fallback #1 to 100%
3. Notify #incidents if customer-impacting; otherwise update #eng-releases
4. File post-incident ticket referencing dashboards and logs

# Post-launch (first 7 days)
- Keep canary/quality shadowing enabled where possible
- Watch for:
  - tokenizer edge cases (stop sequences, special tokens)
  - intermittent OOMs due to KV cache fragmentation
  - higher-than-expected safety blocks (policy tuning may be needed)

# Related pages
- Hosted API model intake
- Model launch evaluation gates
- Hosted model performance bar
- Third-party model risk review workflow
