Title: On-prem Cutover Readiness: Egress & Capacity Playbook - weekly sync

On-prem Cutover Readiness: Egress & Capacity Playbook - weekly sync

Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-09-30 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lila Novak (Redwood SE), Diego Ramos (Redwood), Marco Rivera (Aurelia CTO), Priya Singh (Aurelia NetOps), Ethan Cole (Aurelia SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
- Week 5 of on-prem pilot; focus on cutover readiness, egress routing, kernel upgrade and capacity shaping.
- Identified two main blockers: egress firewall rules & kernel compatibility test failures in one host.
- Agreed next steps: run soak test, share runbook, provide firewall rules, finalize rollback steps.

Topics: cutover readiness, egress NAT/allowlist, kernel upgrade 6.x, capacity/traffic shaping, fallback policies, soak tests

Action items (captured in metadata too)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samir (AE): okay, hi everyone, thanks for joining. good to see you. this is our weekly sync for the on-prem pilot, focused on cutover readiness. we have samir, lila, diego on redwood side. aurelia: marco, priya, ethan, thanks for making time.

[00:22] Marco (CTO): yeah thanks, morning for us. short timezone note, we're on a hard deadline for a staged cutover in two weeks so want to make sure blockers are surfaced.

[00:35] Lila (SE): quick agenda I have — egress readiness, kernel upgrade status, capacity shaping + soak plan, and then open issues. if that works for you we can dive in.

[00:48] Priya (NetOps): works. first item, priya here, egress. we tried to lock down the firewall allowlist but there are some internal groups that route via a proxy and we saw some TLS handshake fails when we hit the redwood private endpoints from our test lab. not sure if it's our proxy or the egress ip set.

[01:12] Samir: got it. can you paste the exact error / log snippet? sometimes the handshake looks like a cert chain timing out vs ip-level block.

[01:24] Priya: (typing sound) i've pasted a snippet in the chat — "tcp reset after 3s handshake timeout, peer cert not found" — and the source ip is from our transit proxy 10.88.4.23, which I believe isn't in your allowlist.

[01:40] Diego: hmm, our NAT egress pool for your VPC should include the proxy range. it's possible the mapping didn't include the transit subnet when we provisioned the private connectors. i can check that mapping now.

[02:00] Ethan (SRE): quick note — when we ran the preflight yesterday one of the nodes failed the kernel self-test after the inference kernel install, showing a page-fault under 95th percentile memmap op. we reverted that host but want a root cause.

[02:18] Lila: memory map page fault, interesting. do you have the kernel version? is that the 6.4 pre-release we pushed? sometimes the jemalloc path and the inference kernel's custom mmap path collide.

[02:32] Ethan: it's 6.4-rc1, yes. test host showed crash on first warmup batch for the redwood runtime, with logs mentioning unknown symbol for fast-attn.

[02:47] Samir: okay that aligns with a note we had — some early 6.4 kernels changed the module symbol resolution, causing our custom fast-attn kernel to fail to load, which causes fallback to slower op path and on some images to segfault. we pushed a patch to the kernel adaptor last week but haven't verified across images.

[03:06] Marco: so is that a blocker for cutover? our timeline is 14 days out, we need a firm yes/no.

[03:15] Lila: at present it's a risk. we have two mitigation paths: 1) pin hosts that will run the pilot to a known-good kernel (6.3.x) until we finish validation; or 2) apply the redwood kernel adaptor patch and run a quick validation across staging nodes. option 1 is faster rollback but means a temporary policy to avoid 6.4. option 2 is more future-proof but needs 24-72 hour validation window.

[03:41] Priya: pinned older kernel sounds easier for our ops team — less change. but we have a corporate policy to keep kernels updated monthly, so it would need an exception.

[03:54] Diego: i can prepare a short pre-check list for the kernel update that includes module load tests, fast-attn probe, and a small-batch inference run. that checklist will let you decide to approve the patch route.

[04:10] Samir: diego will own the checklist and the rollback steps. diego, can you give a timeline?

[04:18] Diego: yes — i can produce the checklist today and run the adaptor patch validation tomorrow on two staging nodes, that'll take about 6 hours of total run time but we need access and the same image set you plan to use.

[04:33] Marco: we'll provision two staging nodes with the same image and grant access. marco to coordinate with ethan to provide creds.

[04:42] Ethan: i'll do that after the call. next topic — capacity shaping. we measured steady token throughput on your sample workload and saw CPU steal and occasional queuing that increased p95 latency when batch size > 8.

[04:59] Lila: right, that's the batching threshold where our continuous-batching heuristic swings from sub-ms to burst mode. we can tune the target batch size and the max latency threshold. generally recommend target batch 6-8 for your LLM family, but if you need lower p95 we can drop to 4 and accept a higher cost per token.

[05:20] Priya: cost vs latency tradeoff — what do you estimate for our projected QPS? we gave a sample of 120 qps average overnight, peaks at 450 qps.

[05:33] Samir: with those numbers, on our Dedicated VMs for private you could expect X tokens/sec per GPU. (note: Samir points to a shared spreadsheet link) quick back-of-envelope: if we target batch size 6, you see 18% cost improvement vs batch 4 but p95 goes up ~20ms. if we reduce batch to 4 p95 improves by ~25ms but cost increases ~22%.

[05:59] Marco: send that table. the spreadsheet link in chat isn't accessible to me.

[06:06] Samir: will resend with org-level perms. link: https://redwood.app/sheets/pilot-aurelia-capacity (placeholder)

[06:15] Lila: also note prefix caching can help — your workload has many repeated system prompts so we could enable prefix/KV cache behavior to cut token compute by 10-15% at little latency cost. needs a small policy change on your side regarding cache TTL.

[06:33] Priya: TTL question — how long do cached prefixes live and is that compliant with our data retention? we can't keep unencrypted user data in cache longer than 48 hours per policy.

[06:46] Diego: our prefix cache stores KV only, not user-identifying metadata unless you opt in. we can set TTL at 12 hours for the pilot to be safe. encryption at rest is via customer KMS if you want.

[06:59] Priya: okay if KMS integration is enabled, 12 hour TTL is fine. please document that.

[07:06] Samir: noted — document in runbook. next — egress allowlist specifics, who has the list?

[07:14] Priya: i do. sending... (chat) list contains the corporate NAT ranges and transit proxies. i see in the snippet you have 3 public IP ranges, but ours uses a shared egress IP that goes through a floating NAT behind the proxy.

[07:31] Diego: that's probably the gap — our automation maps VPC subnets to egress ip pools but floating nat from your proxy might show as multiple ephemeral IPs. we can accept a CIDR block instead of single IPs if that helps.

[07:45] Priya: we can provide a /24, but security insists on narrow allowlists. i'll file a waiver but need to show proof-of-control.

[07:57] Marco: can redwood provide a signed cert or token that proves the endpoint identity so we can allow wildcard but limit to verified TLS endpoints?

[08:08] Lila: we have mTLS options and client-cert verification for private connectors. we can provide a cert bundle and an SNI-based validation. not a signed token per se but a cert chain that your proxy can validate.

[08:24] Ethan: good — how quickly can we get that cert shipped?

[08:29] Samir: we can generate a cert bundle after you confirm a CSR; timeline 24-48 hours. we'll attach the CSR template to the runbook.

[08:38] Priya: excellent. next: soak tests — we want a 3-hour latency soak in staging that mirrors peak. are there scripts we can run?

[08:46] Lila: yes, we have a harness that replayed your sample traces. i'll share the script and a docker container. it will drive the same distribution including ramp and peak. we need your staging creds and a window during off hours.

[09:01] Ethan: proposed window: 2026-10-07 02:00 - 05:00 UTC. works for our ops.

[09:10] Diego: we'll bring extra monitoring hooks during that test — token-level latency, queue depth, kernel module load traces and kernel dmesg. if we hit the earlier crash signature we'll auto-roll back that host.

[09:23] Marco: rollback behavior then — what exactly is the automatic rollback?

[09:27] Diego: if the host shows the mmap pagefault signature or segfault in inference runtime, our orchestration will cordon and drain the host, move incumbent tasks to other hosts, and if host doesn't recover under 20 minutes we mark it for reprovision. rollback playbook will be in runbook.

[09:46] Priya: question about tracing — can the logs be forwarded to our Splunk instance? we prefer central observability.

[09:54] Lila: yes, we can configure log forwarding via syslog/HTTP ingest; most customers forward to Splunk or S3. we'll add example config. note there is PII scrub option on logs.

[10:10] Samir: quick pause — does anyone have any other blockers we haven't covered?

[10:16] Marco: yes, licensing question — if we pin kernels to 6.3 for some hosts, does that change the pricing? we had a quoted price for mixed throughout.

[10:26] Samir: short answer: no immediate change. kernel pinning itself doesn't affect cost unless you require dedicated reserved capacity for older images. if you keep the same instance sizes and GPUs it's cost-neutral.

[10:36] Marco: okay good. next item — fallback routing and traffic shaping during cutover. how do we route traffic if the new egress path fails?

[10:45] Lila: we propose a staged fallback: primary -> regional fallback -> global fallback. primary is direct private connector, regional fallback routes to a non-private but dedicated path with IP ACLs, global fallback uses a lower-tier model variant we host in our public infra. global fallback degrades quality but keeps service online.

[11:05] Priya: for compliance we need explicit audit/tracing when we cross from private to public infra. do you log that event?

[11:12] Diego: yes every routing decision is logged with token counts and model id; those logs are forwarded and can be retained per your retention policy. we'll surface an event in console and send an alert.

[11:25] Ethan: one more item — the perf discrepancy we saw between nodes. one node shows 8-10% higher latency under same load. we suspect CPU frequency scaling or NUMA misconfig. any suggestions?

[11:36] Lila: check governor settings and ensure CPU turbo is enabled and cpufreq governor set to performance for inference hosts. also verify NIC interrupts and IRQ affinity — sometimes NICs are pinned wrong causing CPU steal.

[11:50] Marco: we'll run that ops checklist. marco to confirm.

[12:00] Samir: to recap, we have: diego creates kernel pre-check and rollback playbook; lila will share soak test harness and scripts; samir to update runbook with egress CSR template and pricing sheet; priya to share firewall rules; ethan to provision staging and run the soak. agreed?

[12:21] Priya: agreed. quick note on docs sharing — please use our secure share link.

[12:27] Samir: will do. i'm going to attach the runbook draft after this call.

[12:33] Marco: any risks we haven't discussed? performance regressions on quantization settings — we should ensure quality checks post-quant.

[12:42] Lila: yes let's add a quality regression eval: sample prompts and an automated rouge/bertscore probe for structural/regression detection. we'll add to runbook.

[12:55] Ethan: for the soak test I'd like to capture full kv-cache hit ratio and batch occupancy percentiles — can your harness emit those?

[13:05] Lila: yes, the harness can capture batch occupancy and kv hits. we'll add those metrics to the test output.

[13:14] Samir: final administrative — next sync same time next week? or do we want a pre-soak checkpoint?

[13:21] Marco: let's do a short pre-soak check on 2026-10-06 and a full post-soak review on 2026-10-08.

[13:30] Samir: noted. i'll send invites. thanks all.

[13:36] (call ends)

Title: Deployment safety checks and A/B cutover sync

Deployment safety checks and A/B cutover sync

Weekly POC sync focused on go-live safety: agreed on an A/B cutover with a canary ramp, defined metrics and rollback criteria, planned a staging dry-run, and assigned runbook and telemetry deliverables.
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-03
Start time: 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~54 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Daniel (Redwood SE), Lena (Redwood CSM), Priya (KiteWave), Ethan (KiteWave SRE), Marisol (KiteWave Product), Tom (KiteWave Infra)

[00:00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check — agenda is safety checks for deployment, confirm A/B cutover plan, monitoring knobs, and next steps. Sound good?
[00:00:12] Priya: Yep, that's what we want. We have the exec alignment for next week so this is the last POC sync before staging dry-run.
[00:00:25] Daniel: Cool. I'll run through current telemetry, recent perf numbers, and the proposed canary ramp with thresholds.
[00:00:33] Ethan: Before you start, real quick — we saw a spike in tail latency on Friday when prefix cache was cold, wanted to see if that's reproduced on Redwood dedicated or if it's our end.
[00:00:45] Daniel: Right, that was the KV cache warm-up issue — sometimes transcribed as K V cash — it's basically prefix and kv-cache fill. On Dedicated we see similar behavior if the prefix set is very diverse; our suggestion was a short pre-warm step in the runbook.
[00:01:02] Tom: Pre-warm how? Do we pre-send a sample of warmup prompts or run a synthetic batch?
[00:01:09] Daniel: Synthetic batch — we recommend a small set of representative prompts at low QPS for 10 minutes. We'll provide a script. That reduces p99 by about 40% in our test.
[00:01:22] Marisol: And that script lives in the runbook you mentioned?
[00:01:25] Sofia: Exactly. I'll share the runbook after the call. It's the cutover playbook plus rollback checklist.

[00:02:10] Daniel: Ok, I'll pull up the telemetry snapshot. Note — transcription may say Redwood API as 'Red wood a p i' — little audio artifact — but the metrics are: steady-state QPS 180, median latency 23 ms, p95 110 ms, p99 340 ms during the last 48 hours on the pilot. The spike Ethan mentioned aligns with a cache miss pattern.
[00:02:35] Ethan: The 340ms p99 is a concern for product folks; our internal SLO is 200ms p99. Is A/B able to route only a portion so we don't breach that across the whole fleet?
[00:02:49] Sofia: Yes — A/B routing allows you to send, say, 15% to the new variant and 85% to control. Canary ramp then increments at defined gates. We propose starting at 5%, hold 30 minutes, check metrics, then 20%, hold, etc.
[00:03:04] Priya: We had chatted internally about faster ramps — exec wants to see feature usage quickly. Can we do a faster ramp if metrics look stable?
[00:03:12] Daniel: You can, but you need automated guards. Our suggested gates: p50, p95, p99, error rate, and a quality proxy (we can use a rerank score or a small eval set). If any gate trips beyond threshold, automatic rollback to control.
[00:03:27] Marisol: What's the quality proxy you mentioned?
[00:03:30] Daniel: We recommend a lightweight regression test set — about 50 prompts representing your top intents — run every 5 minutes during canary. If the semantic similarity or confidence drops, that's a red flag. We'll include the harness in the gates.

[00:04:10] Tom: On infra — what's the recommended canary traffic percentage? Are we starting at 1%, 5%, 10%?
[00:04:15] Daniel: For model variant changes with potential latency differences, start at 5%. For config-only changes maybe 10%. For you, given the p99 concern, 5% is safer.
[00:04:25] Priya: Ok. How long do we hold at each step? 15 min, 30 min?
[00:04:29] Daniel: 30 minutes for initial hold — enough to see tail behavior — then double hold after 20% increments. We can make the timing conditional in the runbook.

[00:05:00] Priya: Alerts — we need to make sure our on-call doesn't get paged for noise. What thresholds should map to pages versus tickets?
[00:05:07] Sofia: (laugh) small typo earlier — but good question. We usually recommend paging for sustained p99 breaches > 2x SLO for 15 minutes or error rate above 0.5% for two consecutive windows. Non-urgent anomalies go to a ticket. We'll send a suggested mapping.
[00:05:25] Ethan: Can you give concrete numbers? Our SLO is 200ms p99 so paging threshold would be 400ms p99 sustained, correct?
[00:05:31] Daniel: Yes, that's a good starting point. Also page on request timeouts or elevated 5xxs above 0.5% for 10 minutes.

[00:06:25] Sofia: Criteria — we have automatic traffic switchback and manual failover option. Automatic rollback will default to the last known-good model variant and hold traffic at control. Manual rollback requires operator confirmation after which we re-run the pre-warm.
[00:06:45] Ethan: Who has permission to initiate rollback? We need RBAC in console so not anyone can flip traffic.
[00:06:52] Lena: Good point — we'll add RBAC steps in the runbook; by default only Ops and Platform leads have rollback rights.

[00:07:20] Daniel: On observability — we created a dashboard template in the Console: per-route p50/p95/p99, error rate, throughput, rerank quality proxy, and infra signals (GPU memory, queue length). We'll share the dashboard link.
[00:07:35] Priya: Please include a panel for model variant comparison so we can see control vs canary side-by-side.
[00:07:39] Daniel: Yes, side-by-side and delta panels. Also we'll wire a synthetic probe hitting the canary route every minute hitting your top-intent set.

[00:08:10] Tom: Regarding network and data residency — we need to ensure request logs are sent to our SIEM and that logs do not include PII. Are the audit logs persisted and filterable?
[00:08:20] Sofia: For Private and Dedicated we support routing logs to your SIEM and we can redact or hash PII fields; we'll share the security guide and our SOC 2 summary.
[00:08:33] Marisol: Can we keep verbose debug logs only in staging, not prod?
[00:08:36] Daniel: Yes, debug logging can be gated by a flag and exported only to staging buckets; prod will keep structured traces and metrics.

[00:09:05] Priya: One more on A/B: We want to run a feature A/B that surfaces a new prompt template and measure engagement and error uplift. Does Redwood support per-customer routing or only per-route?
[00:09:16] Sofia: You can do both. The routing layer supports cookie and header based weighting; we can pin by user id for long-running experiments.

[00:09:42] Ethan: For the dry-run on staging — what validation tests should we run? We want checklist items.
[00:09:49] Daniel: Suggested checklist: 1) Pre-warm KV cache synthetic; 2) Run 1 hour soak at 50% QPS; 3) Validate regression test set; 4) Confirm telemetry dashboards ingesting; 5) Verify rollback and RBAC; 6) Confirm SIEM log delivery. We'll put this in the runbook as discrete steps.

[00:10:20] Marisol: Time wise — we said dry-run on 2025-09-10 earlier, is that still good?
[00:10:24] Priya: Yes, team is ok with that but need runbook by 09-05.

[00:10:45] Sofia: On communications — during cutover you should notify product, ops, and support channels; we recommend a brief status bot in your #deployments slack channel and an incident channel standing by.
[00:10:58] Tom: We'll do that. Who will own the post-cutover smoke test?
[00:11:02] Ethan: Ops will own smoke test and then hand to Product for functional checks.

[00:11:25] Daniel: A small note on caching and batching to save cost during canary: enable adaptive batching but with max latency cap, Redwood Optimize suggested these settings — the idea is to trade micro-latency for fewer tokens charged. We'll surface recommended batch size and quantization profile in the runbook.
[00:11:48] Marisol: Quantization profile — does that change quality? We can't have user-visible regressions.
[00:11:52] Daniel: If you're using mild int8 quantization (our recommended profile for this model), quality diff is negligible on your eval set; we'll include eval deltas in the runbook.

[00:12:30] Priya: Anything else from Redwood before we close?
[00:12:34] Daniel: I'll summarize the proposed canary plan in bullets: start 5% canary -> hold 30m -> check p50/p95/p99/error/quality -> ramp to 20% -> hold 60m -> ramp to 50% -> full cutover if stable. Auto-rollback on guard fail.
[00:12:50] Sofia: And I'll attach the runbook + rollback checklist and the dry-run checklist. Also sending the dashboard link and a small script for pre-warm.
[00:13:10] Priya: Great. Quick question — what's the expected impact on cost during canary? We want a high-level estimate.
[00:13:18] Sofia: With 5% traffic routed to the canary, cost bump is near-linear for token usage — so roughly 5% plus overhead for parallelism/extra probes. We'll include an estimated delta in the runbook; Redwood Optimize recommendations can further reduce it.
[00:13:42] Ethan: For SLA — when we shift to Dedicated later, will SLA change?
[00:13:48] Sofia: Dedicated comes with committed capacity and SLA guarantees; we'll discuss contract language with sales and legal after the pilot. For now pilot is in hosted sandbox.
[00:14:20] Priya: One operational wrinkle — our legal wants a short note on log retention and deletion policy for PII.
[00:14:26] Sofia: We'll include the data retention addendum and options for log redaction.
[00:14:50] Marisol: Ok, let's recap.
[00:14:53] Sofia: Recap: 1) Sofia sends cutover runbook + rollback checklist (due 09-05); 2) Daniel sends telemetry/log exports and dashboard link (due 09-04); 3) KiteWave to confirm canary percentages and SLO owners (due 09-06); 4) Dry-run scheduled 09-10 staging; 5) Ethan runs kv-cache soak test and posts results (due 09-08).
[00:15:20] Priya: That matches our notes. Any blockers?
[00:15:24] Tom: RBAC change in console — need confirmation that only Ops can rollback. We'll need a short doc on how to set that up.
[00:15:31] Lena: We'll add RBAC steps to the runbook and a how-to doc.
[00:15:50] Sofia: OK. I'll open a shared drive folder and drop the runbook and scripts; Daniel will drop telemetry artifacts. We'll link the CRM deal with the dry-run milestone.
[00:16:05] Marisol: One last note — product would like a light A/B analytics snippet so we can compare engagement metrics across variants. Is that part of the dashboard?
[00:16:15] Daniel: Yes, we'll add engagement KPIs as part of the variant comparison panels.
[00:16:40] Sofia: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with materials and confirm dry-run time in the calendar.
[00:16:48] Priya: Thanks all.
[00:16:50] Ethan: Thanks.

[00:20:00] (Call continues with smaller technical clarifications and off-line sequencing; meeting ends at 14:54)

Post-call notes: runbook link placeholder: https://drive.redwood.example/runbooks/kitewave-cutover-2025-09-03 (will be finalized by 09-05). Dashboard placeholder: https://console.redwood.example/dashboards/kw-poc-canary

Date: 2026-01-20

[00:00] Maya: okay team, thanks for joining. quick agenda — rerun the soak results, pick an anchor model for pinning, and lock down emergency routes. anyone need to add?
[00:12] Sarah: no, that's good. i mostly want to know whether the p99 latency bump last night is model-related or infra. we saw a spike around 02:40 PST.

[00:34] Carlos: to add, the autoscaler didn't spin up fast enough because our bursting policy is conservative; we saw queueing.
[00:43] Maya: right, so two levers: infra (autoscale) and model profile (quantization / shorter context heuristics). today let's compare the two catalog candidates: v1.2-q4 (light quant) vs v1.3a (newer decoder, slightly higher token cost but better coherency).
[01:05] Priya: for product, coherence on the clinical-summary prompts is higher priority than raw cost. a hallucination on a discharge summary is worse than 20% extra token cost.
[01:18] Sarah: agreed. but we still need to hit 200ms median and keep p99 under 700ms if possible. what were we seeing in the soak?
[01:29] Jonah: soak numbers — median tokens/time was 180ms, p95 around 420, p99 spiked to 820 during that KV-miss window. with v1.3a pinned we see slightly better conditional coherence but p99 still hits 700-900 in cold-start tails. v1.2-q4 had p99 lower by ~80ms but produced shorter, sometimes choppier completions.
[01:58] Maya: so tradeoff is cost/latency vs quality. our recommendation previously was to pin v1.3a on staging and use soft fallback to v1.2-q4 if latency exceeds threshold for X minutes.
[02:12] Sarah: what's the exact trigger we should simulate? we want an automated escape hatch before customers observe failures.
[02:20] Jonah: proposal: if rolling p99 > 800ms for 5 minutes AND error rate > 0.5%, route new sessions to v1.2-q4 for 10 minutes, then evaluate. also make the alert noisy but human-confirm gating for production cutovers.
[02:37] Carlos: can that routing be regional? we saw tail latency concentrated in us-west-2 due to that maintenance window.

[03:16] Priya: hmm, could be a good middle ground — prewarm top 50 prefixes from last week for the soak and see how p99 moves.
[03:24] Jonah: yeah i'll script that for the soak.
[03:28] Maya: let's talk about quantization profiles — jonah, you had suggested two profiles: q4-lite and q8-mixed?
[03:35] Jonah: correct. q4-lite reduces memory and token cost but sometimes truncates semantic depth; q8-mixed keeps better quality at slightly higher cost. brighthealth's clinical needs likely need q8 on the decoders. we recommended v1.3a with q8 for production, but for emergency fallback we keep v1.2-q4.
[03:56] Sarah: ok. can you attach the benchmark spreadsheet after the call? we'll run it through our QA prompts.
[04:03] Maya: yes i'll share.

[04:32] Sarah: also SSO team asked about RBAC for the Redwood console — we need to make sure product folks can't accidentally flip pin policies.

Title: Scheduled atomic transfer sanity check and priority-shed procedure for active-passive DR drills

Scheduled atomic transfer sanity check and priority-shed procedure for active-passive DR drills

Objective: Run an orchestrated, repeatable active→passive transfer that validates backup/restore integrity, KV/prefix cache reconciliation, tokenstore quiesce, and progressive priority-based load-shedding. The goal is to prove an atomic transfer window for latency-sensitive tenants while exercising circuit-breaker and surge-shed choreography. This ticket owns the drill runbook, test harness automation, telemetry gates, and post-mortem template for scheduled rehearsals.
Pre-drill: notify stakeholders (SRE, platform, on-call, security, customer success) and post maintenance window in Status page
Snapshot: trigger consistent point-in-time KV snapshot and tokenstore export; compute checksums and fingerprint manifests
Quiesce: pause background compaction and non-critical scheduled jobs on active region; mark route as drain-ready
Traffic taper: apply staged weight reduction to active region with 90s holdpoints and synthetic traffic validation at each stage
Atomic cutover: flip router at regional control-plane to passive region while enabling canary routing to 5% of production traffic
KV reconcile: run prefix-hash compare between restored snapshot and live passive store; run incremental replayer for missing deltas
Circuit breaker probe: simulate high-latency backend call and confirm circuit opens/fails over to fallback tier
Priority shed: apply priority-based token bucket thresholds and sequentially shed non-critical routes (embeddings batch jobs, low-tier ML inference) while measuring latencies for P0 clients
Soak: keep passive region serving for 30 minutes under reduced load with synthetic and sampled production traces
Rollback or Promote: decision point based on acceptance criteria — either rollback traffic to original active region or promote passive to primary and run post-promote tasks
Post-drill: run integrity audit, publish telemetry summary, and capture lessons in post-mortem template
All KV snapshot checksums match within defined tolerances, or documented reconciliation steps executed successfully
SLOs for P0 routes remain within doubled latency budget during the atomic transfer window
Circuit breaker behaviour observed and confirmed (open, fallback, closed) according to the runbook tests
Priority-based load shedding reduces non-critical request volume by at least 70% without violating P0 availability targets
Automated runbook scripts finish without manual intervention for non-exception paths
Post-drill audit contains a reconciled timeline, binary pass/fail flags for each gating check, and next-action items
Compare per-route latency p95/p99 pre-cutover vs during-cutover
Tokenstore restore rate (items/sec) and time-to-first-successful-auth
KV snapshot byte-level checksum match and missing keys count
Error budget burn-rate for the hour surrounding the cutover
Circuit-breaker open-rate and fallback invocation count
Queue length / backlog for batch workers after shed begins
Immediate: abort promotion and flip router weights back to active region
Rehydrate: if passive had mutated data, run a replay/merge job using snapshot deltas collected during promotion
Circuit reset: clear in-flight circuit-breaker timers and allow controlled re-introduction of shed routes
Validate: re-run checksum and tokenstore sanity checks after rollback
Post-incident: capture root cause, adjust runbook step timing or thresholds, escalate if data divergence occurred
Add a scripted kv-snapshot + fingerprint generator to infra-scripts (PR linked)
Extend runbook CLI to accept --priority-shed-profile and --soak-duration flags
Create synthetic traffic manifests that mirror production route mix for 15m windows
Add an alert that gates promotion if checksum mismatch > 0
Risk: long replay time for KV deltas causing extended CT (cutover time). Mitigation: pre-warm incremental replayer and parallelize read streams
Risk: tokenstore restore latency prevents auth for clients. Mitigation: staged route lift with auth bypass for internal canaries and progressive traffic ramp
Risk: incorrect shed policy impacts paying customers. Mitigation: enforce canaryed priority rules and manual approval for full-shed escalation
Risk: cascading circuit-breaker opens after cutover. Mitigation: adaptive retry-backoff and service-level CB thresholds tuned in test harness
Timeline: minute-by-minute annotated events
Gates: each acceptance criterion with pass/fail and evidence links
Telemetry: snapshot of key metrics and diffs
Root cause analysis and contributing factors
Action items: owner, estimate, and due date
Keep the first rehearsal in a lower-traffic window and use a subset of customer-facing routes to reduce blast radius
Coordinate with Sales/CS for a small set of customers who may observe degraded performance during the drill
Document all manual overrides and keep them to a minimum — every manual step increases learning value

Title: probing-aware-fallback-throttle-and-slo-hysteresis-resolver

probing-aware-fallback-throttle-and-slo-hysteresis-resolver

Motivation: In production we observed rapid probe-triggered regional failovers during transient capacity spikes which caused oscillation and tenant impact. Existing SLO enforcement reacted on single probe failures and immediately escalated to full regional fallback. This PR introduces a probing-aware fallback throttle and an SLO hysteresis resolver to smooth decisions, reduce rejoin churn, and provide a short grace window for transient probe failures. Summary of changes: 1) probing-aware fallback throttle: add a probe-backoff state machine that delays promoting a probe failure into a regional failover until a configurable probe window and retry budget are exhausted; 2) SLO hysteresis resolver: compute an adjusted SLO breach score by applying temporal smoothing (EWMA) and tenant-weighted penalties so short blips do not flip circuits; 3) telemetry: emit new metrics (slo_hysteresis_score, probe_backoff_state, probe_backoff_count) and tracing hooks for decision paths; 4) config surface: runtime flags with safe per-region defaults and a feature flag to gate behavior; 5) tests and docs: unit tests for transitions, integration canary harness scenario, ops dashboard and runbook updates. Testing and validation: unit + integration harness covering probe flapping scenarios, local canary with synthetic probe noise showing 4x reduction in false failovers, load test with 10% of traffic showed latency SLOs maintained. Rollout plan: feature-flagged off by default; staged canary: 5% traffic for 48h, then 25% for 24h, then full rollout if metrics stable. Monitoring: new dashboard tile and alerts for slo_hysteresis_score > 0.8 for >10m and probe_backoff_state == "stalled" for >5m. Rollback plan: flip feature flag off; if immediate revert required, also reapply config snapshot from release. Related work: ENG-1842, incident SUP-4218. Impact: expected to reduce regional rejoin churn and unnecessary capacity shuffling at the cost of a small additional delay (configurable) before hard failover. Configuration defaults chosen conservatively for safety. Checklist: [x] unit tests added [x] integration scenario [x] telemetry and dashboards [x] docs/runbook updated [x] feature flag present [x] post-deploy verification steps documented.
Ethan Keller: This looks sensible, but we need to ensure the default probe window doesn't delay genuine failovers. Please add a unit test for a long tail probe failure scenario. | Priya Kapoor: Added a unit test that simulates a sustained 3-minute probe fail and verified that after the probe budget expires the failover path is taken immediately. | Marta Ivanov: Please surface metric tags for tenant_id and region on slo_hysteresis_score so paging is actionable. | Priya Kapoor: Updated metrics_registry and added tenant_id/region tags; dashboard queries updated. | Luis Chen: CI flaked on the integration harness once; can you make the test harness deterministic? | Priya Kapoor: Hardened harness by fixing timing race and added retry with backoff; CI passed on rerun.

Title: Streaming write-stall + TTL regression — hosted API outage postmortem (2026-04-25)

Streaming write-stall + TTL regression — hosted API outage postmortem (2026-04-25)

Summary:

On 2026-04-25 at ~02:12 UTC the hosted streaming API experienced a high-severity outage that manifested as 5xx errors for streaming sessions and extreme tail latency for non-streaming requests. Impact lasted ~43 minutes for customers on affected regions and degraded for another 90 minutes during mitigation rollouts. Root cause: an unintended change to a per-connection TTL/keepalive config combined with an edge buffer write-stall bug in the streaming proxy, which caused head-of-line stalls and backlog amplification under normal traffic spikes.

Impact:
- Scope: ~11% of streaming sessions experienced repeated 5xx (502/504) immediately; additional ~7% of non-streaming requests saw 95th+ latency spikes from 600ms -> 3.2s.
- Customers: 23 enterprise tenants saw visible error rates; a handful of PLG customers reported degraded developer experience. No data loss or model correctness issues were observed.
- Business: Incidents triggered PagerDuty P0 and on-call SREs initiated incident response. External status page was updated.

How it was detected:
- First alert: custom anomaly detector on streaming session error-rate crossed threshold at 02:13 UTC (SRE paging).
- Secondary signals: edge response-time dashboards and increased connection resets observed in edge logs.
- Pager: 02:14 UTC, SRE lead ack at 02:15 UTC.

Timeline (UTC):
- 02:12 — initial spike in streaming session errors; error rate rose from baseline 0.3% to 18% in 2 minutes.
- 02:13 — anomaly alert fires; on-call SRE starts investigation.
- 02:14 — correlating logs show write stall metrics on streaming proxy (high write queue depth).
- 02:18 — quick mitigation: rolling restart of streaming-proxy fleet in affected region, partial drop in errors but tail latency persisted.
- 02:25 — rollback of a recent edge-config change that adjusted connection TTL made at 01:55 UTC. Edge config rollback began.
- 02:35 — error rates fall to ~2%; tail latency trending down but not fully recovered.
- 02:55 — full rollback complete and additional throttling rules temporarily applied; streaming success rates returned to baseline.
- 03:00 — status page updated to reflect mitigation progress.
- 04:30 — follow-up remediation runs and validation; monitoring shows stable behavior. Incident declared mitigated at 04:35.

Root cause analysis (why):
- Primary bug: an existing bug in streaming-proxy write handling where a stalled TCP write (EAGAIN/later drain) could leave per-connection buffers frozen while the proxy's internal queue accounting incorrectly marked the connection as writable. This allowed the proxy to continue accepting streaming state and buffer memory without advancing network writes, producing head-of-line stalls.
- Trigger: a separately deployed edge config tweak at 01:55 UTC reduced keepalive/TTL for upstream connections from 90s -> 10s to aggressively free idle connectors for recent scaling changes. This increased connection churn during normal traffic bursts and surfaced the proxy write-stall bug.
- Amplification: the serving runtime's KV cache prefetch caused more concurrent active streaming sessions per process during a traffic spike at 02:10 UTC, compounding queue depth and memory pressure on streaming-proxy workers.

Contributing factors:
- A config change (edge TTL) was rolled without a targeted canary to measure streaming-specific impact.
- The proxy bug existed in the binary for ~3 months but was low-probability; normal workloads had not triggered it at scale.
- Alerts were configured for absolute error-rate thresholds but not for queue depth or write stall latency in the streaming-proxy.
- Rollback of edge-change required coordination across teams and took longer than expected because the change was bundled with other minor fixes.

Immediate remediation performed:
- 02:18 — rolling restart of streaming-proxy processes to clear stuck write buffers (short-term relief).
- 02:25 — rollback of edge TTL config to previous value (90s).
- 02:55 — deploy temporary traffic shaping: soft concurrency limit per upstream instance and reject-new-session policy for overloaded proxies.

Longer-term fixes and planned actions:
(Planned timeline + owner)
- Fix proxy write-stall bug in runtime and add explicit writeback checks (PR: runtime#657). Owner: Miguel Torres. ETA: 2026-05-03.
- Add unit+integration tests that simulate partial write backpressure and verify buffer accounting. Owner: Juno Kim. ETA: 2026-05-10.
- Update deployment practices: require streaming-sensitive canary (1% traffic for 30m) for edge/TCP-level TTL or connection lifecycle changes. Owner: Priya Raman (edge infra). ETA: 2026-05-01.
- Implement alerting for streaming-proxy write-queue depth and per-connection write latency (new SLI). Owner: Liam O'Connor. ETA: 2026-04-30.
- Run a chaos experiment to model connection churn under reduced TTLs to ensure proxy resilience. Owner: Evelyn Zhang. ETA: 2026-05-07.

Runbook and playbook changes (immediate edits):
- Add a new streaming runbook section: "Detect and mitigate write stalls" including commands for probing write queue depth, safe rolling restart procedure, and temp traffic shaping knobs. Owner: Ana Patel. Actioned: draft added to Confluence, see linked runbook.
- Add step that any edge-level connection/TTL changes must include a streaming-canary approval checkbox. Owner: Priya Raman.

Monitoring & alerts to add/modify:
- New alert: streaming-proxy.write_queue_depth > 500 for > 2m -> P1.
- New alert: streaming-proxy.per_conn_write_latency_p95 > 1s -> P1.
- Adjust anomaly detector to correlate streaming error-rate with write-queue depth before auto-scaling decisions.
- Dashboard: new streaming health panel with per-region metrics: conn churn, write queue depth, buffer memory, and per-second stream accepts.

Customer communication:
- At 02:20 UTC we published a short status page update.
- Post-incident public note to affected tenants drafted and queued for account team review. Owner: Customer Success (cc: Ana Patel). ETA for send: 2026-04-27.

Action items (owner — due):
- Miguel Torres — land runtime fix and coordinate canary release (2026-05-03).
- Juno Kim — add integration tests and run pre-merge CI scenarios (2026-05-10).
- Priya Raman — update edge deployment checklist + canary gating (2026-05-01).
- Liam O'Connor — implement monitoring alerts + dashboard (2026-04-30).
- Evelyn Zhang — run chaos/connection-churn experiment and share findings (2026-05-07).
- Ana Patel — finalize runbook writeup and schedule SRE runbook walk-through (2026-04-29).

Lessons learned / retrospective notes:
- Low-probability bugs can become high-impact when paired with seemingly innocuous config changes (keepalive/TTL tweaks).
- Edge-level changes touching connection lifecycle must be treated as high-risk for streaming customers; they require a streaming-aware canary path.
- Having more fine-grained streaming proxy SLIs (queue depth & per-conn write latency) would have accelerated detection and reduced MTTR.
- Rolling restarts are effective short-term mitigation but we need faster rollback paths for edge configs (decouple TTL change from unrelated cleanup fixes).

Appendix (commands and quick diagnostics):
- Check streaming proxy write queue depth: 
  - curl -s http://proxy-metrics/metrics | grep write_queue_depth | awk '{print $2}'
- Live tail to detect stuck writes: 
  - ssh proxy-node && sudo journalctl -u streaming-proxy -f | grep "write stall"
- Safe rolling restart (recommended): 
  - kubectl rollout restart deployment/streaming-proxy -n hosted-api --selector=region=<region> --max-unavailable=2

Document history:
- Drafted: 2026-04-25 by Ana Patel
- Updated with timeline & remediation 2026-04-26 by Miguel Torres
- Final review notes added 2026-04-27 by Priya Raman

If you have questions or need clarifications on any section ping #sre-incident or @ana.patel on Slack.

Title: Intermittent inference requests time out during long streaming completions; ALB header growth and chunked keepalive suspected

Intermittent inference requests time out during long streaming completions; ALB header growth and chunked keepalive suspected

Issue summary:
Customers (Lexicraft AI) report intermittent 504/502 timeouts and stalled streaming responses when completing long-running generation requests (~40-120s). Failures are not constant; many sessions complete normally but a subset terminate mid-stream with no application error.

Impact:
- Multiple production customers on dedicated clusters observing tail latency regressions and occasional stream termination.
- User-facing sessions show stalled TTFB followed by ALB-generated 504 or occasional 502 from API gateway.

Environment:
- Dedicated capacity cluster serving Lexicraft (us-east-1).
- Requests are proxied through ALB -> API Gateway (NLB path for some customers) -> edge mesh -> serving runtime.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Start a streaming chat completion with a long expected token count (prompt + continuation ~ 4k tokens).
2) Keep connection open and allow streaming tokens to be emitted for >60s.
3) Observe occasional stall around 30–90s then abrupt connection close with 504/502.

Observed behavior:
- ALB access logs show connection closed with "502/504" and "Target timed out" variants.
- Request headers include long tracing header (x-trace-cookie / x-client-trace) and rotating cookie header from customer app (~6k-12k header size observed intermittently).
- When headers are large and chunked keep-alive is used, TTFB rises before eventual ALB idle reset.

Expected behavior:
- Streaming requests should maintain open connection while tokens are produced; idle/reset behavior should trigger only after configured SLO timeout.

Relevant logs/traces:
- ALB logs (filtered by request_id): multiple entries showing target_response_time ~85–110s then 504.
- API gateway request logs: intermittent 502 returned with "upstream closed connection".
- Serving runtime logs: long-running KV warmups observed but no internal OOMs or worker crashes.
- Sample traces attached in comments below.
2026-03-10 - Initial triage by Support: Reproduced a stalled stream in staging by replaying customer headers; when we injected large Cookie+Trace headers (~9KB) the ALB session showed delayed ACKs followed by idle reset.
Checked ALB idle timeout (60s default) and internal proxy timeouts. Customer's client kept socket open but had large header churn as they rotate a session cookie every 15s; header growth correlated with stalls.
Observed proxy buffering behavior in API Gateway config: buffering enabled for endpoints which causes whole response to be accumulated before flush under some conditions, combined with HTTP/1.1 chunked transfers and keepalive reuse leading to edge-level TTFB regression.
No serving-runtime errors. Worker CPU and GPU utilization normal. KV-cache warmups coincide with first 1–2 seconds only and do not explain 60–120s stalls.
ALB access-log correlation: requests with larger "request_processing_time" and "target_response_time" consistently hit timeouts. Requests with smaller headers succeed.
Hypothesis: large rotating headers cause ALB or API gateway to alter connection framing (HPACK/H2 -> HTTP/1.1 translation) or trigger proxy buffering paths which increase internal buffering and push the response into an idle state longer than ALB idle timeout, resulting in ALB resetting the connection.
Cross-reference: see SUP-27384 and SUP-62177 for prior header/buffering related streaming incidents; those were resolved by disabling proxy buffering for streaming endpoints and tightening header size on the client side.
Captured tcpdump of streaming session: shows server sending chunks but some downstream proxy ACKs delayed; suggests middle-tier buffering or Nagle/keepalive interactions rather than server pause.
2026-03-10 10:12 - Avery Chen (Support): Customer reports ~3-8% of streaming sessions end with 504 during high-throughput bursts. They provided sample request IDs and full request headers; uploading to ticket.
2026-03-10 13:45 - Liam O'Neill (SRE): Reproduced similar behavior in a staging cluster by simulating cookie rotation and long traces. ALB logs show target_response_time ~95s before 504. Adding to investigation.
2026-03-11 09:22 - Support (Avery): Customer tried disabling client-side cookie rotation and reported immediate reduction in failures across a 24h window (confirming correlation). Customer requests a permanent fix on our side as they rely on rotating cookies for auth refresh.
2026-03-11 11:05 - SRE (Liam): Temporary mitigation deployed to customer route: increased ALB idle timeout to 120s for the affected target group and disabled proxy buffering on API Gateway stage for streaming endpoints. Monitoring for 24h.
2026-03-12 08:30 - Customer (Lexicraft support): After the mitigation deploy, they observed successful completion of previously failing sessions; will monitor and provide final confirmation tomorrow.
2026-03-12 12:10 - Eng (runtime lead, Priya Rao): Logged eventual follow-up: evaluate default API Gateway stage streaming config to ensure buffering is disabled by default for 'stream-completions' route and add header-size telemetry to detect risky sessions.
Temporary workaround (deployed 2026-03-11): Increased ALB idle timeout for Lexicraft's target group to 120s and disabled proxy buffering at API Gateway stage for streaming endpoints. Customer advised to reduce rotating cookie frequency as an interim measure.
Root cause (provisional): Combination of large, frequently rotating request headers and proxy buffering/HTTP translation at edge caused increased internal buffering and extended time between network-level ACKs; ALB idle timeout then reset connections producing 504s.
Permanent remediation plan:
- Short term: Push change to default streaming route config to disable proxy buffering and ensure chunked streaming is passed through without accumulation.
- Medium term: Add header-size guardrails and telemetry (alert when request headers >8KB) and publish recommended client header limits in developer docs.
- Engineering task: Assess whether API Gateway -> ALB translation config can be hardened to avoid triggering buffering when encountering large headers. Create tracking task INT-4572.
Follow-ups: Add automated test in benchmarking harness to replay large-header streaming sessions (PR referenced in related_github_prs). Update runbook with steps to increase ALB timeout and disable buffering for streaming endpoints.
Status: Mitigation in place; monitoring for 72h before moving ticket to Resolved. If no regressions, we will close with documentation + default config change.

Title: Intermittent 503s and long tail latency from gateway buffer oscillation + growing request headers for streaming sessions

Intermittent 503s and long tail latency from gateway buffer oscillation + growing request headers for streaming sessions

Issue summary:
Multiple customers (notably Lumina Health) reported intermittent 503 responses and long-tail (500ms–6s) latency on streaming completions when sessions carry large request metadata. Failures are concentrated on streaming endpoints during sustained KV cache warm-up and at times of high connection churn.

Impact:
- Several production streaming sessions from Lumina Health experienced mid-stream 503s and reconnects, degrading UX for real-time assistants.
- Error rate spike ~2.7% on /v1/streaming/completions for us-east between 2026-03-10T09:10 and 2026-03-10T11:45 UTC.

Environment:
- Hosted API (dedicated capacity) serving in us-east-1; Redwood gateway + AWS NLB in front for TLS termination; internal nginx sidecars and internal api-gateway cluster.

Observed behavior:
- Streaming sessions with repeated small requests and rotating metadata headers (trace IDs, customer-provided context headers) showed progressive header size growth in the downstream path.
- When aggregated header size exceeded proxy buffer thresholds, upstream proxy started buffering then hitting idle/write timeouts, causing mid-stream 503s and connection resets.
- TTFB and token emission delays correlated with periods of proxy flush/backpressure in the gateway logs.

Expected behavior:
- Streaming sessions should maintain steady low p95 latency and not experience mid-stream 5xx due to header/connection buffering.

Steps to reproduce (approx):
1) Start a long streaming completion session against /v1/streaming/completions with a client that rotates per-chunk metadata headers (simulates tracing middleware that appends a small header on each chunk).
2) Send a series of ~40 small messages over 90s; observe request/response headers growth at the gateway.
3) Monitor gateway/nginx proxy logs and stream for 503 or ECONNRESET events when header accumulation crosses ~16KB.

Title: Edge connection-hold flood from long-lived keepalive clients causing 5xx spike and runtime CPU pressure for dedicated tenant

Impact:

- Observed increased tail latency and client-visible stream disconnects.
- Customer reported degraded SLA and raised a high-priority support case.

Environment:
- Dedicated tenant: BeaconHealth Analytics, prod-us-east, routing through edge-proxy cluster ep-us-1
- API Gateway version: apigw-3.7.1
- Edge proxy: envoy-1.26-custom
- Serving runtime image: redwood-runtime:2026-03-05-prod

Observed symptoms / logs:
- Edge accept-queue length increased prior to error wave: accept_queue_depth ep-us-1 peaked at 11k connections.
- Large number of long-lived keepalive connections from a small set of client IPs (slow-client pattern) holding multipath HTTP/2 streams in half-open state.
- Runtime pods serving the tenant logged frequent "worker-saturated" and "kv-cache-rate-limit-ejection" messages followed by "watchdog-reset" on high CPU.
- API gateway returned 502/503 to callers when upstream runtime stopped responding to new requests.
- Netstat/metrics show high socket count with many connections in CLOSE_WAIT / HALF_OPEN for the tenant's routed IPs.

Hypothesis:
- A small subset of clients are performing connection-holding/keepalive behavior (similar to slowloris), preventing the edge from reusing sockets efficiently and causing accept-queue growth. This in turn amplifies head-of-line blocking and creates load on specific runtime workers (KV cache hot-sharding + continuous batching starvation), pushing CPU to saturation and triggering watchdog restarts leading to 5xx responses.

1) Route a burst of long-lived HTTP/2 keepalive connections from ~200 clients that hold idle streams while occasionally sending small requests.
2) Maintain these connections over several minutes while the normal traffic mix continues.
3) Observe accept queue growth at edge-proxy and elevated runtime CPU for tenant-scoped workers.
4) Confirm increase in 502/503 responses and streaming session disconnects for routes mapped to the tenant.
Initial triage performed by SRE shows concentrated socket-hold behavior from a small set of customer IPs. Edge metrics indicate accept-queue became the bottleneck before runtime CPU throttling. We reproduced a FIFO starvation pattern in a local simulation by holding HTTP/2 streams open while issuing infrequent requests; this caused per-worker batch queues to back up and CPU utilization to rise due to retry/spin loops.

We correlated the tenant's request logs with the IP ranges in the customer's environment; BeaconHealth confirmed a third-party data-collector update rolled out earlier that morning which altered clients to keep connections open for longer to reduce TLS handshakes. This change inadvertently increased connection concurrency.

Temporary mitigations trialed:
- Enabled per-tenant connection rate-limiter on the edge for a subset of routes (reduced connection growth by ~60%).
- Adjusted accept queue high-water mark alerting and increased ephemeral worker pool by +2 for the tenant's shard.

Title: Intermittent long-tail TTFB from HAProxy per-connection buffering + keepalive churn affecting streaming completions

Intermittent long-tail TTFB from HAProxy per-connection buffering + keepalive churn affecting streaming completions

Issue summary:
Customers have reported intermittent, long-tail increases in time-to-first-byte (TTFB) for streaming completions during peak traffic windows. The pattern is: initial bytes arrive quickly for most requests, but a subset of streaming sessions stall for 5–20s before the first chunk is delivered.

Impact:
- Several enterprise customers experienced degraded UX on long completions; a small percentage (~0.6% p95-p99) of streaming requests hit >5s TTFB.
- Errors are not always returned; many requests eventually succeed but at unacceptable latency for real-time apps.

Environment:
- Fronted by HAProxy 2.6 in the edge fleet (tcp/http mode), using connection reuse (keepalive) between client and frontend.
- Backend pool: dedicated serving-runtime instances pinned to the customer’s pool.
- Observed in prod (us-west-2) during peak morning traffic.

Steps to reproduce (intermittent):
1) Open streaming completion request with large per-request metadata (cookies and trace headers ~12–20KB).
2) Reuse the same TCP/HTTP connection for multiple simultaneous small streaming and non-streaming requests from the same client.
3) Observe that some streaming requests do not receive the first chunk until another connection activity triggers a flush or until internal buffer thresholds are reached.

Observed logs / metrics:
- HAProxy edge metrics show spikes in output-buffered-bytes for specific backend servers correlated with TTFB spikes.
- No 5xx spike in backends; backend latency (processing) remains stable.
- TCP stats show many reused client connections with >100 requests and intermittent write-blocks on frontend sockets.
- Sample haproxy log lines around incidents: "Mar 10 08:14:22 haproxy[2345]: Server srv/usw2-srv1 output buffer full, flushing delayed" (derived from edge debug).

Initial hypothesis:
- HAProxy per-connection output buffering + aggressive connection reuse (keepalive) is coalescing multiple backend responses or trace-heavy request headers into a per-connection buffer and delaying flushes to clients. For streaming responses this results in head-of-line delays until the buffer either fills or a flush event occurs.

Why unique / not earlier tickets:
- Earlier tickets focused on ALB/APIGW idle timeouts and HTTP/2 hpack growth. This incident implicates HAProxy's per-connection buffering behavior combined with keepalive reuse and unusually large request metadata as the root contributor to delayed-first-byte for streaming flows.

What we looked at:
- Correlated HAProxy metrics (bytes_out_buffered, conn_reuse_ratio) with p95/p99 TTFB and found strong temporal correlation.
- Captured socket-level traces showing frontend socket write blocked while HAProxy queued additional responses/headers.
- Verified backends return streaming chunks promptly (via internal trace), so problem is in the edge path.

Hypothesis refinement:
- Large request metadata leads to read-side buffering and increased internal memory pressure; combined with keepalive reuse, HAProxy accumulates bytes to optimize network writes. For streaming this optimization harms latency because HAProxy waits for larger chunks before flushing.

Tests run:
- Reproduced with synthetic client that: (a) sends streaming request with 16KB headers, (b) reuses connection for 40 mixed requests. Observed same TTFB stalls.
- Canary config changes applied to a small subset of edge nodes: (1) option http-server-close, (2) tune.bufsize=131072, (3) enable 'debug-flush-on-response' (internal flag) for experimental flush behavior.

Open questions:
- Does increasing bufsize mask the issue by allowing more coalescing before stall? Early signs show better p99 but more memory use.
- Are there traffic shaping knobs at client SDK level we should document (e.g., avoid extremely large per-request metadata, enable connection rotation)?

Workarounds applied:
- Canary edge nodes updated with 'option http-server-close' and tune.bufsize increased; this reduces connection reuse buffering and forces HAProxy to flush more eagerly for responses.
- Recommendation to LexiCorp: patch SDK to rotate connections every N requests (N=20) and reduce per-request metadata where possible.

- Implement targeted instrumentation to expose 'haproxy.output_buffered_bytes' at per-tenant granularity into Console dashboards and create an alert if > 64KB aggregated per connection.
- Long-term: evaluate switching streaming frontends to an HTX-enabled path with explicit flush triggers or migrate to a proxy mode that better supports chunked streaming semantics.

Status:
- Mitigation validated on canary, customer acknowledged improvement. Rolling to rest of fleet pending capacity validation. Monitoring until 2026-03-16, after which we will close if stable.

Steps to reproduce: 1) Start a long-running chat completion with multi-turn context and tracing baggage headers enabled. 2) Stream responses back to client for ~60-120s. 3) Observe intermittent periods where bytes stop flowing for ~30-90s and then connection resets with 504 or timeout. Observed behavior: interleaved TTFB spikes, streaming stalls with zero bytes for tens of seconds, followed by 504s. Logs/metrics: edge-proxy write buffer growth correlates with increasing per-request header sizes (baggage/trace metadata), envoy stats show upstream_bytes_buffered and downstream_write_failed. Expected behavior: steady streaming without stalls, within latency SLOs. Additional notes: problem appears bursty and correlated with sessions that rotate trace/authorization metadata frequently (client library re-attaches baggage headers every turn).

Confirmed correlation between requests where cumulative request headers >6KB and occurrences of downstream_write_blocked metric on envoy (edge) and sudden increase in upstream write retries.

Title: Intermittent TTFB regressions for streaming completions when API gateway connection reuse interacts with proxy buffering

Intermittent TTFB regressions for streaming completions when API gateway connection reuse interacts with proxy buffering

Issue summary: Customer reports intermittent increases in time-to-first-byte (TTFB) for streaming completions. The symptom is that some streaming requests return initial tokens after a 2-6s delay even though request enters the serving runtime quickly. Impact: customers see perceived latency spikes for interactive flows and partial timeouts when clients have strict idle time windows. Observed at scale across multiple backends in us-west and reproduceable in limited cases from internal synthetic tests.

Observed behavior:
- Requests accepted by API gateway and routed to serving cluster immediately (backend request logs show sub-200ms queuing).
- First chunk from serving runtime often delayed by multiple seconds before being flushed to client. Subsequent chunks stream normally after first flush.
- When we disable proxy buffering on edge (apigw/nginx) the TTFB returns to expected ~120-300ms range.

Why this is likely: preliminary triage indicates a protocol/conn-reuse mismatch between API gateway (proxy) keepalive behaviour and the serving runtime's chunking strategy. When proxy buffering is enabled and the proxy reuses a keepalive connection that previously saw a large header/tracing payload, it sometimes buffers until either (a) a buffer threshold is reached, or (b) the backend explicitly flushes by closing or hitting a chunk boundary we do not trigger. This causes the first-chunk delay but not subsequent tokens once the stream is warmed.
1) Use customer streaming API with small prompt (~80 tokens) against redwood/bison-2-7b in us-west.
2) Ensure client keeps a short idle timeout (2-5s) between request start and consuming first token.
3) Send 100 concurrent streaming requests over a reused keepalive connection from same client IP.
4) Observe distribution of TTFB; ~15-30% of requests exhibit 2-6s TTFB while others respond fast.
5) Toggle proxy_buffering off on the APIGW/nginx side and re-run; issue disappears in synthetic test.
6) Re-enable buffering and run with a clean TCP connection per request; TTFB regressions reduce substantially.
api-gateway access: 2026-03-09T18:52:12Z GET /v1/streams 200 upstream_latency=0.18s downstream_latency=2.64s conn_reuse=true
serving-runtime: 2026-03-09T18:52:12Z request_id=abc123 stage=generate first_token_emitted=2.3s kv_warmup=0.05s
load-balancer tcp: 2026-03-09T18:52:12Z conn_id=97 last_used=2026-03-09T18:50:12Z keepalive_ms=90000
edge-proxy (nginx) error: 2026-03-09T18:52:12Z buffered 1 bytes waiting for flush: proxy_buffering=on
2026-03-10 - Aisha Khan (Support): Customer NimbleDocs reported frequent user-facing stalls starting 2026-03-08 after a traffic spike. Provided initial logs and sample request/response headers.
2026-03-10 - Diego Martinez (SRE): Reproduced with internal loadtest. Noticed correlation with connection reuse and presence of large trace headers. Opening investigation with edge team.
2026-03-11 - Priya Rao (Edge Eng): Found nginx proxy_buffering and proxy_http_version differences when connection reused after large header set. Suggested testing disabling proxy_buffering as quick mitigation.
2026-03-11 - Customer (NimbleDocs): Verified turning off 'proxy_buffering' in their test environment eliminated stalls in 200/200 samples.
2026-03-12 - Diego Martinez (SRE): Rolled a config change to disable proxy_buffering for streaming routes in canary; monitoring telemetry for regressions.
2026-03-12 - Aisha Khan (Support): Notified customer about temporary mitigation and ETA for permanent fix.
Hypothesis 1: proxy_buffering combined with keepalive reuse causes proxy to wait for enough data or connection-close to flush first chunk. Evidence: disabling buffering returns normal TTFB.
Hypothesis 2: large tracing headers from upstream clients sometimes change buffer allocation path and push proxy into a different flush policy. Evidence: requests with >8KB combined headers show higher probability of stalls.
Telemetry: 95th percentile TTFB for streaming endpoints jumped from ~480ms to ~2.8s for a subset of connections with conn_reuse=true between 2026-03-08 and 2026-03-09.
Reproduced locally using nginx with proxy_buffering=on and proxy_http_version=1.1 vs off; behaviour matches customer reports.
Risk: disabling proxy_buffering increases upstream load and may expose backend to small write amplification; need to tune keepalive and buffer thresholds.
Follow-ups: add a low-risk canary for proxy_buffering=false on streaming routes, add metric for 'first_chunk_delay' to per-route dashboards, and audit header size distribution for customers.
Mitigation applied: disabled proxy_buffering for streaming routes in APIGW canary (rolled to 10% of edge hosts). Also aligned keepalive timeouts between APIGW (now 120s) and load balancer to avoid reuse windows that previously exposed the bug. Permanently: engineering will add an explicit backend flush hook for first-chunk emission and add a feature flag to prefer flush-on-first-chunk for streaming models. Customer notified and accepted workaround. Postmortem planned; estimated full rollout after performance validation.
1) Instrument first_chunk_delay metric and add alert at 1.5s for streaming endpoints
2) Implement explicit flush-on-first-chunk in serving-runtime (PR opened)
3) Run load test with proxy_buffering disabled at 50% edge capacity to measure upstream load impact
4) Communicate permanent fix ETA to NimbleDocs and update docs on streaming tuning

Title: JamBench observatory weekly log - Nov 30 2026

JamBench observatory weekly log - Nov 30 2026

JamBench observatory weekly sync — condensed notes

Date: 2026-11-30
Attendees: Emily Chen (owner), Raj Patel, Sofia Alvarez, Liam O'Neill, Priya Rao, Ashwin K. (SRE drop-in)
Duration: 45 minutes
Location: Zoom + perf-observatory channel

Goal: capture oddball throughput/latency signatures from last week's JamBench sampling, triage hypotheses, and assign follow-ups for targeted lab runs. This session focused on a new wildcard sampling artifact we observed on 11/27 that produced repeatable p95 jitter under mixed-short workloads.

1) TL;DR of discoveries
- New wildcard sample pattern: short-hot bursts (~30–90s) that reduce effective QPS by ~25% on a 4k context model variant when prefix-cache miss-rate spikes above 18%.
- Worst-impacted quantiles: p95 increased from 68ms -> 140ms; p99 tails show step-like jumps to ~420ms during burst window. p50 relatively stable.
- Reproducer: JamBench run id JB-20261127-wild-4 produced the signature on two different clusters (g4x2 and private-dedicated pool).
- Correlated signal: KV cache churn and small-batch kernel fallback events observed in runtime logs at the same timestamps.

2) Data & quick metrics (summarized)
- Baseline steady-state: 950 QPS sustained, p50=42ms, p95=68ms, p99=120ms.
- JamBench wildcard window: 720 QPS effective (control client issued same load), p50=45ms, p95=140ms, p99=420ms. CPU/GPU util: GPU memory pressure up by 8% during window, CPU-side scheduler loops increased 2x.
- KV cache stats: miss-rate jumped from 5% -> 18% concurrent with bursts; median KV latency jumped 1.8x.

3) Repro attempts and environment notes
- Repro on mainline (docker image: serving-runtime:2026-11-25) succeeded on two independent clusters. Repro runs used JamBench config: mixed-short-heavy.json (seq_len distribution 16/64/512).
- Repro without prefix caching disabled: no burst signature observed, which strengthens cache-churn hypothesis.
- Shadow run with disabled micro-batching heuristic (experimental flag --heuristic-v2=false) reduced p95 increase by ~40% but worsened throughput consistency; implies interaction between batching heuristics and cache state.

4) Hypotheses (ranked)
H1 (primary): prefix/KV cache temperature sweep causes more frequent cold hits; the runtime shifts to a slower kernel path for affected sequences causing latency tailing.
H2: batching heuristic oscillation under mixed sequence lengths leads to microbatch fragmentation and kernel fallback (esp. for quantized kernels) causing increased completion time for some requests.
H3: rare scheduler starvation from background maintenance tasks (checkpointing / eviction) aligns with burst windows. Lower confidence; observed in one cluster trace.

5) Quick instrumentation gaps to fill
- Need finer-grained KV cache telemetry per-pod: sample-size, eviction-rate per-second, origin sequence id tag.
- Add histogram of kernel selection frequency (fast/slow quant paths) keyed by sequence-length bucket.
- Correlate JamBench client-side timing (enqueue->ack) with pod-level L1/L2 cache miss counters if available.

6) Immediate actions and owners (short horizon, 1–7 days)
- Emily: schedule targeted JamBench sweep JB-20261201-ext to run 20 iterations across 3 clusters with explicit cache seeding/eviction toggles. (Due: 2026-12-01)
- Raj: add a short patch to runtime to emit kernel-selection events as lightweight logs (flag: --emit-kernel-events) and land PR. JIRA-RT-2127. (Due: 2026-12-02)
- Sofia: add per-pod KV cache eviction rate metric to Prometheus exporter and create dashboard panel in Console under serving-runtime/observatory. (Due: 2026-12-03)
- Liam: reproduce experiment with microbatching disabled/enabled and record end-to-end traces; store traces in S3 perf-buckets/jb-repros/. (Due: 2026-12-02)
- Priya: run a maintenance-task blackout window (disable eviction scripts) during one JamBench sweep to test H3. (Due: 2026-12-04)

7) Longer-term work (2–6 weeks)
- Engineering spike (owner: Raj): evaluate a TTL-backed KV cache policy vs current LRU to reduce temperature storms; prototype in a branch and run A/B tests against JamBench. (Estimate: 3 weeks)
- Product/Console (owner: Sofia): add a per-route 'cache-heat' warning that surfaces when miss-rate exceeds threshold for >60s to help SREs route traffic or increase cache allocations. (Estimate: 2 weeks)
- Perf team: expand JamBench sample space to include synthetic 'prefix-churn' traces that intentionally rotate a small set of prefixes at high QPS to exercise cache eviction boundaries.

8) Risks and mitigations discussed
- Risk: naive mitigation (increase cache sizes) could mask other issues (batching scheduling) and increase cost; prefer targeted experiments first.
- Mitigation: run canary changes on dedicated pool with controlled traffic; use fallback policy to hosted variants if regressions exceed thresholds.

9) Notes on cross-team coordination
- SRE may need to temporarily provision an extra dedicated pool for long-running JamBench sweeps to avoid impacting prod shadow runs. (Ashwin to confirm capacity)
- Solutions Eng: keep a short customer-facing note ready if we detect customer-affecting regressions; target hold until we have root cause and mitigation.

10) Open questions for next sync

- What is the threshold cache-miss-rate that reliably predicts burst onset? (need ROC-style analysis)

- Enable kernel logs: export SR_RUNTIME_FLAGS=\"--emit-kernel-events\" and restart pod set perf-lab-1

Next sync: Wednesday 2026-12-02 (15:00 PST) — focus on results from JB-20261201-ext and first kernel-events PR landing.

End of notes.

Title: Control Plane Operational Boundaries Heatmap

Control Plane Operational Boundaries Heatmap

Purpose and context:

This is a working heatmap-style sketch to surface current operational boundaries in the control plane: who owns what during normal ops and during multi-region failover. Goal is to call out ambiguous gaps and create a short list of follow-ups (owner assignments, runbook updates, API contracts). Not a canonical doc — an annotated work-in-progress for the platform-engineering and serving-runtime teams.

Assumptions and constraints (short):
- Single control-plane control path (API gateway -> orchestrator -> runtime adapters).
- We support 3 regions (us-west, eu-west, ap-southeast) with regional control-plane replicas and a global config plane.
- Traffic routing is policy-driven: latency-first, then cost, then compliance (region-locked).
- Runtime adapters are the thin bridge to GPU pools and on-prem agents.

High-level ownership summary (heatmap commentary):
- API Gateway (ingest): primary owner = platform-api team. Responsibilities: authentication, rate limiting, coarse routing decisions, quota enforcement, request enrichment. SLA: <100ms control-plane p99 for routing decision. Region fallback: platform-api config points to regional orchestrators; in loss-of-region, global gateway switches to nearest fallback pool.
- Orchestration Layer (request-to-runtime mapping, rollouts): primary owner = orchestration-service team. Responsibilities: model versioning, canary rollouts, route affinity, autoscale hints, batching policies. SLA: transactional durability and consistent rollout state across regions.
- Runtime Adapters (serving proxies): primary owner = serving-runtime team. Responsibilities: translate orchestration directives to runtime-specific calls (CUDA-optimized pools, on-prem RPC), manage KV cache metadata, surface local capacity. SLA: <50ms adapter handshake for pooled requests, best-effort KV cache sync.
- Routing Governance / Policy Engine: primary owner = platform-engineering (routing-gov subteam). Responsibilities: policy language, policy validation, policy audit logs, safety gates for fallback.
- SRE/Infra (ops): primary owner = infra-sre. Responsibilities: infra health, cross-region replication, infra failover, monitoring/alerting for control plane.

Operational boundary matrix (text table):
Service | Owner | Primary responsibilities | Decision boundary | Typical ops handoff
API Gateway | platform-api | auth, ingress, coarse routing | chooses region/orch config based on policy | handoff to orchestration via RPC (orchestration endpoint v2)
Orchestrator | orchestration-service | model routing, version pins, rollout rules | final route decision (which adapter pool) | handoff to runtime adapter with rollout metadata and batching hints
Runtime Adapter | serving-runtime | queueing, batching, KV cache, runtime calls | enforces local capacity and throttles | returns run metrics and fallback signals
Policy Engine | routing-gov | policy eval, validation, audit | rejects unsafe routing changes | notifies orchestration and platform-api on violations
SRE/Infra | infra-sre | infra failover, region replication | triggers region-level failover | notifies all owners, runs global incident runbook

Key decision boundaries to clarify (open questions):
1) Where is the canonical source-of-truth for route-to-adapter mappings?
   - current state: orchestrator maintains mapping but policy engine can inject overrides. Leads to potential race condition during rollout.
   - proposed: orchestrator remains source-of-truth; policy engine issues signed overrides that orchestrator applies with a reconciliation window (TBD).

2) How do we represent multi-region fallbacks in the API contract?
   - suggestion: add an explicit "fallback_chain" field in orchestration responses listing region adapters ordered by policy priority. This makes failover deterministic for adapters.

3) KV cache consistency vs latency: who owns reconciliation?
   - tradeoff: serving-runtime prefers local fast cache with eventual consistency. Orchestrator needs strong-ish invariants for prefix cache invalidation during model switch.
   - interim: add a lightweight invalidation message bus (owner: serving-runtime + infra-sre) with documented TTL semantics.

4) Rollouts across regions: canaries vs global sync?
   - current experiments: region-scoped canaries for low blast radius. Global rollouts often lag and produce inconsistency in inference quality metrics.
   - proposal: add rollout epoch metadata and a global acceptance gate managed by orchestration + product-eval.

Runbook and incident boundaries (short bullets):
- API ingress failures: platform-api owns mitigation (rate-limits, revert gateway config). Escalate to infra-sre on region degradation.
- Orchestrator inconsistencies (mismatched route assignments): orchestration-service owns reconciliation; if >5% mismatches cross-region, open sev3 and rollback last policy change.
- Adapter capacity exhaustion: serving-runtime implements emergency fallback to pre-defined model shards in another region; infra-sre handles cross-region route reweighting.
- Policy violation alerts: routing-gov triages; if unsafe changes detected auto-revert and notify on-call for platform-engineering.

Small proposal list (next steps):
- Draft an API change for orchestration response to include "fallback_chain" + rollout_epoch (owner: orchestration-service). Link: PLAT-4321.
- Prototype signed override flow from policy engine to orchestrator (owner: routing-gov + platform-api). Add TTL and audit log entry.
- Create simple invalidation bus for KV cache with at-most-once invalidation messages (owner: serving-runtime + infra-sre).
- Update incident runbooks to define clear threshold for cross-region inconsistency (owner: infra-sre).

Notes / references / bookmarks:
- Related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/control-plane/pull/198 (orchestration epoch prototype)
- Jira: PLAT-4321 (fallback_chain RFC), PLAT-4502 (KV invalidation proposal)
- Slack thread: #platform-routing – thread id: t0239-heatmap-draft

Open questions for the group meeting (TODOs):
- Acceptable reconciliation window between policy override issuance and orchestrator apply? (Suggested: 60s)
- How do we test cross-region rollout acceptance in CI without incurring expensive GPU runs? (Idea: synthetic traffic + small local model)
- Define exact schema for fallback_chain and rollout_epoch (owner: orchestration-service + api).

Appendix: quick sketch of fallback_chain sample (text only)
- fallback_chain: ["us-west-adapter-v3", "eu-west-adapter-v2", "ap-southeast-proxy"]
- rollout_epoch: "2026-02-14T18:32:00Z"
- policy_signature: "sig:v1:abcd1234"

This doc is intentionally lightweight — keep comments inline in the file, mark sections that need concrete RFC work. Proposed reviewers: Diego Ramos, Priya Patel, Connor Lee, and infra-sre on-call.

End of draft.
