Title: Graceful SSE resume and partial-output handling for Hosted API disconnects

Graceful SSE resume and partial-output handling for Hosted API disconnects

Multiple enterprise customers reported truncated/partial responses and abrupt SSE connections when using the hosted /v1/streams endpoints behind customer proxies and internal gateways. Symptoms observed: final tokens missing, last-event-id gaps, client-side reconnects that produce duplicate or inconsistent completions, and tokens not flushed to logs. This ticket defines the reproducible conditions, root cause hypotheses, chosen remediation, and rollout plan for a hosted-side fix that (1) makes SSE output atomic at event boundaries, (2) provides a resume token/last-event-id semantic for safe reconnects, and (3) introduces conservative server-side buffering/keepalive to avoid mid-stream truncation on common proxies. The goal is to reduce customer-facing truncation incidents by 95% and provide deterministic behavior for clients that retry after transient network failures.
1) Use curl to open an SSE stream to the hosted endpoint with a long-running generation (500+ tokens) and small chunk_size to force many events.
2) Introduce a TCP reset or simulate proxy idle timeout after ~3s of inactivity (Cloudflare/NGINX).
3) Observe that client receives an 'event: done' may be missing and last event payload ends mid-token.
4) Use Last-Event-ID header on reconnect and attempt to resume; currently server rejects or replays from start, causing duplicates or inconsistent final state.
Example curl: curl -N -H "Accept: text/event-stream" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/streams?model=open-rl.mini"
1) Our streaming runtime flush path sometimes emits partial frames when a write syscall encounters an EPIPE or early connection close; the output buffer is not checkpointed into a durable resume state.
2) We lacked a lightweight resume token per 'SSE chunk' boundary (not per-token) which means there is no safe, idempotent replay point.
3) Network intermediaries (proxies/gateways) that close idle TCP after a short window drop connections while backend is computing longer prefix tokens; our keepalive interval is too coarse for some environments.
4) Dedicated and Private deployments showed fewer reports because local networking often preserves connections; hosted customers behind corporate proxies are the main affected group.
5) Log/telemetry gaps: some token-level emission events are never flushed to persistent logs when the connection closes during syscall failures, making postmortem reconstruction hard.
High-level approach in three coordinated changes: 
A) Emission atomicity: change server-side SSE encoder to only emit events at token-boundary-safe frames. Introduce a small per-event buffer and ensure we mark the event boundary in an append-only resume log.
B) Resume token: attach a concise resume_id to each SSE event (base64 of stream_id + offset + crc8) and support Last-Event-ID on the endpoint to resume from resume_id. Resume semantics: replay from the last durable token boundary and mark the previous partial event as truncated if it didn't reach durability. 
C) Keepalive/flow: tighten server-side keepalive and introduce optional sub-second ping events for customers annotated as behind proxies. Expose new header X-Redwood-Resume-Support: true/false in handshake.
D) Fallback: when resume not available (older client), provide deterministic fallback: either deliver a final non-streaming consolidated completion or return explicit error code instructing client to retry non-streaming.
E) Telemetry: emit resume_id, final_status (complete|truncated|failed) and last_flushed_offset to logs/metrics for SLA tracking.
- Code changes: streaming runtime (golang) encoder + resume log writer; API gateway handler for Last-Event-ID parsing; runtime-safe resume recovery path to replay from durable offset.
- Resume token format: v1:{stream_id}:{flush_offset}:{crc8} base64-encoded to keep headers compact.
- Backward compatibility: if client does not send Last-Event-ID, server behaves as today but with better atomic flush to reduce truncation.
- Edge cases: function-calling streams will include resume markers but must ensure side-effect idempotency (see dependency ENG-4811). We will surface a new function-calling flag in the protocol to disallow resume when server-side actions already executed and not idempotent.
- Testing: unit tests for resume token encoding/decoding, integration tests simulating connection resets, and long-tail soak tests behind Envoy/NGINX proxies with varying idle timeouts.

1) Canary rollout to 5% of hosted traffic for read-only clients (non-enterprise) with metric hooks.
2) Second canary: enable resume handshake header for 10 targeted enterprise customers who reported incidents, collect logs for two days.
3) Gradual ramp to 50% then 100% if metrics pass.
4) Release will be labeled runtime-2.3.1-hotfix and coordinated with Customer Success for targeted customers.
5) For Dedicated/Private we will publish a backport suggestion (configuration toggles) and a migration note for on-prem kernel versions.
If we observe increase in duplicate outputs or a new class of truncation: revert to previous runtime image and toggle X-Redwood-Resume-Support off via config. Maintain emergency runbook to offer non-streaming export to affected customers while rollback completes.
Hotfix rollback latency target: <30 minutes for critical regressions.
- Unit tests for resume token correctness and crc mismatch.
- Integration: simulated proxy timeouts (Envoy with connection close at 5s, 10s), assert that clients either resume correctly or receive final consolidated completion.
- Chaos tests: random TCP RST injected at server output path during long-generation.
- Customer verification: coordinate with 3 customers to validate resume behavior in their environments.
- Automated e2e in staging with realistic token counts (100-1000 tokens) and both streaming and function-calling payloads.
New metrics to add: stream_resume_attempts, stream_resume_success_rate, stream_truncated_rate, last_flushed_offset_histogram, sse_keepalive_pings_sent.
Alerting: page on stream_truncated_rate > 0.5% for 10 minutes for enterprise-tier tenants.
Dashboards: per-tenant timeline of resume_id reuse and per-region truncation heatmap.
Logs: include resume_id and final_status in structured logs; add a debug mode to capture token diffs for truncated streams.

Title: Server checkpoint advisories and resumable window for SSE streams

Server checkpoint advisories and resumable window for SSE streams

Problem: Clients reconnecting to long-running SSE streams can either request a coarse resume token (drop-and-resume) or attempt fine-grained reassembly using opaque tokens. This leads to trade-offs: long-lived requests can replay large amounts of data, and proxies/load-balancers may rewrite connections which breaks some resume strategies. We need a pragmatic server-driven advisory mechanism that reduces wasted retransmit work, is robust to intermediate proxies, and preserves tool/function-call atomicity and structured output boundaries.

Proposal: Implement server checkpoint advisories and a resumable window. Servers will emit lightweight 'checkpoint' events periodically (configurable cadence) that include: sequence_id, last_complete_logical_offset, optional canonical-hash, and an advisory_ttl (ms). Clients may use the most recent checkpoint to request a resume at or after the checkpoint offset. Crucially:
- Checkpoints are advisory only; servers may still permit resume at earlier offsets but can prefer heuristics that avoid expensive rehydration.
- Checkpoints include semantic boundary markers so function/tool-call events are not cut mid-call.

Title: SSE snapshot resume indexing and correction procedure

SSE snapshot resume indexing and correction procedure

Multiple enterprise customers reported truncated or duplicated tokens after transient network disconnects when using the Hosted SSE streaming API. Symptoms included final partial sentences, duplicate fragments after resume, and occasional fragment reordering. This ticket defines a deterministic snapshot/resume indexing contract, short-term mitigations, and a correction service to repair affected transcripts and prevent recurrence.
1) Open a long-running streaming session (output > 1024 tokens or >45s) to the hosted SSE endpoint via Node or Python SDK.
2) Induce a transient network disconnect at the edge (TCP RST or proxy restart) during token emission.
3) Reconnect with current SDK resume heuristics (client offset + last_event_id).
4) Observe reconstructed transcript: missing token ranges, exact duplicate fragments, or fragments arriving out of order.
Observed on macOS Node SDK v3.1.2, Python SDK v2.8.1, and raw SSE clients behind edge proxies in us-west1.
A mismatch between ephemeral edge buffering/coalescing and server-side in-flight session state. Edge buffers sometimes asynchronously flush or replay fragments while the runtime's in-memory cursor advanced without a durable checkpoint. Resume heuristics that used optimistic client offsets and last_event markers are brittle across proxy coalescing and worker failover, causing missing tokens, duplicated fragments, and rare reordering. There was also no per-fragment checksum or authoritative durable session snapshot persisted outside process memory.
1) Tweak edge proxy config to reduce aggressive coalescing and enable a conservative graceful-drain before restart.
2) Ship SDK patch that computes per-fragment hashes and performs client-side deduplication and tolerant merges (drop exact duplicates, prefer lower fragment_seq on conflict).
3) Offer per-tenant emergency fallback to non-streaming endpoints for highly impacted customers for 24-72h during rollout.
4) Notify affected customers with an incident summary and expected timeline; provide rollback instructions for critical workloads.
1) Persist a canonical per-session snapshot index (snapshot_id + last_committed_sequence_number) to a durable kv with strong write semantics at periodic checkpoints (default every 256 tokens or 5s).
2) Add fragment metadata headers: (session_id, snapshot_id, fragment_seq, payload_length, sha256_fragment_hash) and validate on append.
3) Define deterministic resume handshake: client supplies last_seen_snapshot_id and last_seen_fragment_seq; server responds with an explicit open_resume_range or a continue token; remove implicit heuristics.
4) Build an async backfill and correction service that replays logs between snapshots to produce corrected transcripts and records corrections to an immutable corrections table exposed in Console and API.
5) Update SDKs to implement the new resume contract, checksum verification, and de-duplication logic.
6) Provide a compatibility gateway and migration path for older clients, and schedule an EOL for legacy heuristics after rollout.

Title: SSE interrupt detection and edge-proxy timeout mitigation for truncated streams

SSE interrupt detection and edge-proxy timeout mitigation for truncated streams

Summary: Multiple customers reported sudden SSE streaming truncations where the connection closed without a final event, producing partial outputs that could not be recovered by SDK resume logic. This ticket scopes a multi-pronged mitigation: detect proxy-induced mid-stream TLS/connection timeouts earlier, emit deterministic end-of-stream sentinel events when possible, add server-side per-request soft-checkpoints to allow reconstructions, and ship an urgent SDK compatibility patch.

Background: Over the past 3 weeks we saw five escalations from three enterprise tenants using the hosted API behind corporate edge proxies. They observed: final tokens missing, no 'done' event, and client-side SDKs failing to resume because session metadata was not persisted when the upstream connection was torn down by a 60s idle-timeout enforced by the customer's edge proxy. Existing SSE resume and idempotency markers assume graceful close or server-initiated sentinel.

Scope and goals:
- Implement server-side interrupt detection hook that classifies disconnect cause (client disconnect, upstream proxy timeout, server OOM, network flake).
- Emit an explicit EOF sentinel event when the runtime detects an upstream reset mid-stream and can safely compute finalizaton markers.
- Introduce a lightweight per-request soft-checkpoint persisted in our session store every 8s for long streams (> 3s total generation) to enable partial reconstruction on resume. Checkpoints are compact (KV of last token offset + checksum + model version + request signature).
- Add an SDK patch (hosted-js v3.1.2, hosted-go v0.9.5) to attempt a graceful polling fallback when resumed via checkpoint and to present user-friendly error codes and retry hints to customers.
- Ship telemetry: new metrics and logs to measure frequency of proxy timeouts and effectiveness of checkpoint-based resume.

Design decisions and trade-offs:
- Checkpoint cadence: 8s chosen as tradeoff between storage/IO and recovery granularity. 4s would increase S3/Redis churn; 15s risked larger lost output.
- Soft-checkpoints are non-authoritative: they are used only to provide a best-effort reconstruction and must not be considered full determinism guarantees. We will surface this in API docs and customer communications.
- We will not immediately change global socket idle timers; edge proxy behavior is customer-controlled. Instead we add detection and mitigation to make hosted API resilient.
- For privacy, checkpoints exclude prompt PII and only store hashes for prompt identifiers.

Implementation plan:
1) Server runtime: add DisconnectCause enum and hook into the network stack to detect TCP RST, TLS alert, and upstream 408/502 when proxied. (Owner: Marco)
2) Checkpointing: add a compact checkpoint writer that appends to per-session Redis hash with TTL 48h. Checkpoint content: token_offset:int, token_checksum:sha256, model_id, model_hash, request_signature. (Owner: Lin)
3) EOF sentinel: runtime emits event type 'stream.eof' with best-effort final_token_count when disconnect type is upstream-reset and no final token was emitted. (Owner: Marco)
4) SDKs: hosted-js and hosted-go add resume flow to read checkpoint and request reconstruction via /v1/streams/resume. Fallback polling introduces exponential backoff and user-visible hints. (Owner: Devrel + SDK team)
5) Telemetry: add metrics sse.disconnects.by_cause, sse.checkpointed_resumes, sse.reconstruction_success_rate. Add a Kibana dashboard and PagerDuty alert when proxy-timeout rate > 0.5% of streaming requests in an hour. (Owner: Observability)

Title: Hosted SSE: resume and partial-response repair after midstream failure

Hosted SSE: resume and partial-response repair after midstream failure

Summary: Several customers reported truncated or duplicated tokens when resuming Server-Sent Events (SSE) streams after transient network disconnects to the Hosted API. Users observed partial outputs (incomplete JSON blocks) and client-side reconstructions that produced invalid application states. This ticket tracks triage, mitigation, hotfix, and follow-ups to prevent recurrence.

Scope: Affects Hosted API streaming endpoints only (text and chat generation SSE). Dedicated and Private clusters showed related symptom reports in 2 customers routed through the hosted gateway; those are included in scope for coordinated mitigation.

Observed behavior: When a long-running generation stream was proxied through our edge/gateway layer and the client disconnected briefly, the resumed request occasionally returned: 1) duplicated tokens (repeat of last 1–3 tokens), 2) truncated JSON blocks that caused downstream JSON parsing failures, or 3) missing trailing tokens (partial output). Repro rate increased under high-concurrency bursts and when backend model shards changed under autoscaling.

Initial Triage Notes:
- Most incidents occurred when resume requests were routed to a different backend pod than the original stream.
- Resume tokens were generated from an in-memory ephemeral checkpoint at the gateway; this checkpoint could be stale under heavy concurrency and when the gateway restarted.
- Downstream buffering and SSE chunk boundary detection relied on newline-delimited chunk framing; when backpressure occurred, a chunk could be cut mid-record and the resume offset would point to the next logical token, leaving the client with partial JSON.

Root Cause Hypothesis (validated during RCA):
1) Resume token contained a gateway-local sequence id and offset that were not globally durable. When resume was forwarded to a different backend, the target used a compatible but non-identical offset interpretation, causing small overlaps or gaps.
2) The SSE framing logic trimmed chunks at the wire-level without attaching explicit offsets to chunk boundaries, making recovery dependent on best-effort reassembly.
3) Autoscale-induced model reloads caused minor changes to tokenization timing which surfaced as repeated tokens when the resume offset aligned near a tokenizer boundary.

Immediate Mitigation (hotfix deployed 2025-02-20):
- Gateways now persist a compact resume checkpoint to the central checkpoint store (Redis) for 120s so resume tokens reference a globally-consistent session id + offset.
- Server now emits an explicit "x-stream-offset" header every N SSE chunks (N=4) so clients and proxies have an authoritative checkpoint to reconcile on resume.
- Backfill logic added: on resume, server will replay up to 32 tokens prior to reported offset and deduplicate on a deterministic hash to avoid duplication for close-boundary resumes.

Testing and Canary:
- End-to-end canaries ran against production traffic replicas and synthetic high-concurrency workloads. Repro scenarios previously showing 12% failure rate for a particular customer dropped below 0.5% in canaries.
- Added unit tests for (a) resume token serialization/deserialization across gateway versions and (b) SSE chunk boundary recovery with partial-line inputs.

Customer Communication:
- Incident summaries sent to affected customers with mitigation steps and request for logs. Eng/Support shared a client-side advisory recommending a 3s backoff and deterministic resume attempt strategy until hotfix deployed.

Longer-term Actions:
- Replace in-memory-only checkpointing with durable per-session metadata persisted for the stream lifetime.
- Add a small stable identifier to tokenization outputs so small tokenizer timing differences do not produce ambiguous resume semantics.
- Console diagnostics: expose per-request last-ack-offset in Console trace view and add an alert for high resume mismatch rate per customer.

4) Observe resumed stream: some mid-stream fragments appear duplicated or the expected terminal fragment arrives earlier/later than its preceding fragment (order skew).

Title: Streaming race after auth token refresh causes interleaved paragraphs and missing closing punctuation

Streaming race after auth token refresh causes interleaved paragraphs and missing closing punctuation

Issue summary: Customer reports that long-running SSE streams intermittently return interleaved paragraph fragments and sometimes omit final punctuation after a short auth token rotation. Impact: QuantaDocs observed 3-7% of streaming responses missing closing punctuation or containing sentences where paragraphs are mixed (two paragraphs merged with parts out of order). This leads to downstream parsing failures for their document ingestion pipeline. Environment: Production, us-east-1, Dedicated tenancy with token rotation frequency: 5 minutes for short-lived session tokens. Steps to reproduce (observed by customer): 1) Start an SSE chat session to /v1/streams with a standard system+user prompt that elicits a multi-paragraph long-form answer (~300-500 tokens). 2) Allow the session to be open for >3 minutes. 3) Trigger an auth refresh (customer-side or via normal rotate) or wait for automatic token refresh to happen. 4) Client reconnects/resumes using the session id/last-event-id; sometimes receives interleaved fragments from two worker backends. Expected: Resume should stitch fragments in order and preserve terminal punctuation. Actual: On ~3-7% of attempts, the resumed stream contains chunks that interleave paragraph fragments (e.g., the end of paragraph 1 followed by the beginning of paragraph 3, then the remainder of paragraph 2), and in ~1% the closing punctuation for the final paragraph is missing. Additional notes: Customer uses an HTTP reverse proxy before the client which preserves Last-Event-ID header. They rely on the server-provided resume token in SSE body. They experimented with longer token TTL and saw reduced frequency.
Open SSE stream to /v1/streams with a prompt returning multi-paragraph output (~400 tokens)
Keep the connection idle for >3 minutes so token rotation will occur on client or server side
Allow auth-flow to issue a new short-lived token, then perform reconnect/resume using Last-Event-ID or resume token
Observe assembled stream for out-of-order paragraph fragments and missing final punctuation
Initial support triage: reproduced at low rate on staging when forcing short token TTL to 10s and performing reconnect during mid-generation.
Hypothesis 1: resume routing race — resume request can be routed to a different worker which begins producing the next sequence before the previous worker finishes sending its tail; mismatch in sequence ordering in assembly logic causes interleaving.
Hypothesis 2: token rotation causes a transient double-connection window where both workers consider themselves authoritative for the session; last-event-id hints diverge between workers.
Observed evidence: logs show overlapping seq numbers and two workers (worker-08 and worker-12) with partial_choice_ids pc_43 and pc_44 both sending segments within milliseconds of each other. Assembly reported "mismatch" and sequence array indicates out-of-order arrival: [202,203,201].
Edge-proxy behavior: proxy preserves Last-Event-ID header, but when cookie/token rotates, client may open a new TCP connection that LB routes to a different backend; LB sticky session TTL observed to be 30s so not always sticky across rotates.
Reproducer: integration test created that simulates rotation mid-stream and triggers reconnect; failing rate ~5/1000 on local agent with two simulated workers; increasing inter-worker arbitration (locking) reduced failure rate to zero in the test harness.
Potential regressions: recent change in resume orchestration (PR #2387) touched worker handoff and reduce-lock path for resume speed — may have opened a microwindow where two workers can both believe they should serve the resumed stream.

Title: Staged proxy window shift suppresses final paragraph on streaming resume for large HTML responses

Staged proxy window shift suppresses final paragraph on streaming resume for large HTML responses

Issue summary: Customer reports that when a long streaming response (HTML-encoded, ~2.5k chars) is interrupted and the client resumes via SSE, the final paragraph (usually the last ~120-300 chars) is missing from the assembled output. The problem appears only when the request path traverses two chained proxies (Corp CDN -> customer edge proxy) that perform HTTP/2->HTTP/1.1 conversion and have differing idle/keepalive settings.

Impact: Affects production users at BlueArc Health with private deployment. Missing concluding sentences in generated reports cause critical downstream ingestion failures (data validation rejects the document). Approximately 3–7% of resumed streams in this customer's traffic show the symptom during peak hours.

Environment: prod | us-east | private deployment behind corporate CDN + customer edge proxy.

1) Create a long HTML streaming request via SSE that produces a ~2.5k char response (we used a summarization prompt producing HTML lists and a closing paragraph).
2) Route traffic through staged proxies: our edge (envoy-based) -> customer CDN that performs h2->h1 conversion and buffers small chunks.
3) Trigger an interruption (network flake) mid-stream so client reconnects and performs resume.
4) Observe assembled stream at client; compare original vs resumed output.

Repro script used: curl --no-buffer -H 'Accept: text/event-stream' "https://api.redwood.example/sse?model=rw-gpt-8k&stream=true" then induce TCP RST on the middle proxy for 1–2s to force a resume.

When resume happens behind the chained proxies, the final paragraph is truncated entirely in some sessions. In other sessions the final paragraph arrives but the trailing metadata event ('event: end') is duplicated and the parser rejects the payload. Binary/special HTML entities like & and < are sometimes split across chunk boundaries and not reassembled correctly, producing corrupted final markup.
Logs show resume delta mismatches: worker logs report resume_offset 12478 but incoming bytes resume at 12452; edge-proxy logs show a buffered flush at the same time with a rewrite of chunk framing.

On resume, the assembled stream should contain the complete final paragraph and a single well-formed terminal metadata event. HTML entities should not be corrupted by chunk boundary manipulation. Resume offset calculations should map to logical token/byte offsets so no bytes are dropped.

[serving-runtime] 2026-03-10T08:17:21.452Z INFO request_id=abc123 resume_requested offset=12478
[edge-proxy] 2026-03-10T08:17:21.460Z DEBUG connection=conn-33 flush_buffer length=512 coalesce=true
[edge-proxy] 2026-03-10T08:17:21.461Z WARN rewriting: h2->h1 content-length injected=chunked
[worker-12] 2026-03-10T08:17:21.492Z ERROR reassembly: expected_end_offset=12603 actual_last_received=12579 keys mismatch
[client SDK] 2026-03-10T08:17:21.500Z INFO reconnect sequence=6 resume_token=tok-9 last_chunk_hash=0x7a1f

- Replicated in staging with a two-proxy chain that mirrors customer's timeout settings (customer edge: 60s idle, corp CDN: 15s idle).
- When corp CDN aggressively coalesces small keepalive frames and converts h2->h1, the byte boundaries we rely on for resume deltas shift by small amounts (tens to hundreds of bytes).
- Hypothesis: resume protocol currently assumes a stable mapping between server-side byte offsets and client-visible chunk boundaries. Chained proxies that rewrite HTTP framing break that assumption.
- Found one correlated pattern: sessions where corp CDN performed a buffered flush during the last heartbeat/keepalive before the connection drop had the highest failure rate.
- SDK behaviour: older JS SDK (v1.3.2) retries resume with chunk-based offsets; newer SDK includes an experimental header 'X-RW-Resume-Mode: token' which uses token-level checkpoints; still under test.
- Edge-proxy change in PR #5287 attempted to mark streaming responses as 'connection: keep-alive' and add a boundary marker for our runtime; initial tests reduce but do not eliminate the failure (still occurs when CDN rewrites content-length).

1) Use websocket streaming instead of SSE for affected clients (bypasses HTTP framing conversion at CDN).
2) Upgrade JS SDK to v1.4.0-beta which enables 'X-RW-Resume-Mode: token' to use token checkpoints rather than raw bytes.
3) Configure customer CDN to disable h2->h1 coalescing for streaming endpoints (if possible).

- Short term: update edge-proxy to emit a robust resume boundary marker (both content and a sideband 'resume-checkpoint' header) so downstream rewrites can preserve mapping. This is the change in PR #5287; needs further hardening to survive content-length injection.
- Medium term: extend resume protocol so server and client negotiate resume-mode: byte vs token vs sequence; prefer token-mode for multi-proxy topologies.
- Long term: add a validation handshake where the runtime returns a short suffix hash (SHA1) for the last N bytes before disconnect; on resume the client verifies hash and requests retransfer for any mismatch.

In Progress — edge-proxy PR #5287 deployed to staging and reduced failure rate from ~5% to ~0.7% in replicated tests. Next steps: iterate on handling of CDNs that inject content-length and run a controlled customer bypass test.

Title: Resume race after HA proxy failover produces truncated final choice and duplicated trailing fragments in SSE streams

Resume race after HA proxy failover produces truncated final choice and duplicated trailing fragments in SSE streams

Issue summary:
Customer BrightAssist reports that after an HA proxy failover in their environment, SSE streams used for chat completions resume but the final choice is truncated and the client receives duplicated trailing fragments. This causes the customer application to fail JSON parsing for structured responses and to show incomplete assistant messages.

Impact:
- Multiple production requests (15-30/min for a single customer pod) end with malformed final choices leading to downstream app exceptions.
- Customer reports increased error rate and user-visible truncations during a recent network maintenance window.

Environment:
- Dedicated customer deployment, hosted in us-east-1 on Redwood Dedicated.
- Fronted by customer's HAProxy cluster (two-tier: edge -> internal LB -> customer nodes).
- SDK: JS browser client using EventSource (SSE) with Last-Event-ID resume logic.
- Models: redwood/chat-deployment-v2.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1. Start a long-running chat generate request which streams 200-400 tokens.
2. Force a HAProxy edge failover (reload/restart) during token stream generation.
3. Client reconnects and passes Last-Event-ID to resume.
4. Observe final fragments: duplicate trailing fragments interleaved and the end event missing or the choice body truncated.

Observed behavior:
- Client receives duplicate chunks that contain trailing token fragments (e.g., ",\"metadata\":{...}" appears twice).
- A terminal 'event: end' is sometimes missing after resume, or arrives but with sequence offsets that cause the client to drop the final token batch.
- Some resumed streams contain a short garbled fragment appended to the previous choice, producing invalid JSON in structured outputs.

Expected behavior:
- After reconnect/resume the stream should continue without duplication or truncation; the final 'end' event should be delivered exactly once and the choice body should be intact.

Relevant logs (customer excerpts):
- "edge: connection reset by peer; replaying Last-Event-ID=6734"
- "internal-lb: 502 during upstream shutdown, resume requested with id=6734"
- A sample fragment sequence the customer saved (sanitized) shows duplicated trailing suffix lines with identical token offsets.

Workarounds tried by customer:
- Forcing full restart instead of resume avoids duplicated fragments but increases latency.
- Using long-polling instead of SSE avoids the issue but is not acceptable for UX.

Notes:
- Customer is on a paid dedicated contract and is impacted for multiple production users.

Support reproduced a variant of the issue in staging by simulating TCP connection close during SSE stream and replaying Last-Event-ID; observed truncated final chunk intermittently.
Hypothesis 1: HAProxy or intermediary is buffering and splitting SSE event boundaries; on failover re-inserted fragments cause the server/runtime to re-emit overlapping token ranges leading to duplicate trailing fragments.
Hypothesis 2: Last-Event-ID resume logic expects monotonic offset acknowledgement from client; proxy-induced reordering of small TCP fragments causes the resume offset to point to a byte boundary inside a multi-byte token, producing truncated JSON on reassembly.
Hypothesis 3: The serving-runtime may commit and stream a final 'end' event before all socket buffers are flushed; a mid-flight failover can cause a partial 'end' event emission that the resume path doesn't canonicalize (idempotency gap).
Collected traces: request IDs and event offsets from customer; shared a trace dump via secure link with SRE team (internal ticket attached).
Reproduced in our lab using HAProxy 2.6 config with 'option http-server-close' toggled; duplication frequency increased when proxy had response-buffering enabled.
SRE note: Node-level TCP FIN+RST timing correlates with missing 'end' events; suggests race between socket teardown and application flush path.

Title: Partial-result Checkpointing and Client Resume Contract

Partial-result Checkpointing and Client Resume Contract

Summary
-------
This document defines a cross-service contract and operational playbook for partial-result checkpointing and client-driven resume for streaming inference calls. It provides a deterministic HTTP/WebSocket/HTTP/2 streaming contract that enables clients to tolerate transient connection failures, resume long-running generation requests, and reconcile partial outputs without risking duplicate side-effects or quality regressions. The contract balances developer ergonomics, predictable economics, and production safety for Redwood’s hosted and dedicated offerings.

Scope
-----
Applies to API surfaces that provide: text generation streaming, structured output streaming (tables/records), long-running embeddings/rerank jobs with incremental progress, and any route that supports server-sent partial outputs (examples: /v1/generate.stream, /v1/chat.stream, /v1/rerank.stream).

This specifically covers:
- Wire-level semantics for checkpoints and resume tokens.
- Idempotency requirements and server-side deduplication semantics.
- Storage, retention, and encryption requirements for checkpoint artifacts.
- Operational SLOs and alerting thresholds.
- Client and server rollout and compatibility strategy.

Motivation
----------
We observe that long-running streams (interactive assistants, long-form generation, batched rerank) are sensitive to transient network glitches and HTTP connection limits, which cause poor user experience or expensive restarts. Implementing a lightweight checkpoint/resume mechanism: reduces perceived latency, lowers token cost by avoiding full re-generation, and improves reliability for customers on poor networks or intermediate proxies.

Goals (non-exhaustive)
- Allow clients to resume a previously-started stream from the last acknowledged checkpoint.
- Guarantee exactly-once external side-effect semantics for requests that produce side-effects (webhooks, downstream writes) via server-side gating.
- Keep checkpoint storage small and short-lived by checkpointing only the minimal resume state (KV cache ID, consumed token count, model variant id, deterministic RNG seed if applicable).
- Make the contract backward-compatible with clients that do not implement resume.

Contract: Wire semantics and payloads
----------------------------------
1) Checkpoint messages
- Servers MUST emit a stable checkpoint envelope at configurable intervals (default every 512 tokens or 10s, whichever comes first).
- Checkpoint envelope fields (JSON):
  - type: "checkpoint"
  - checkpoint_id: string (UUIDv4)
  - request_id: string (Redwood request id)
  - model_variant: string
  - token_offset: integer (number of tokens produced so far)
  - kv_cache_ref: string (opaque id for server-side cache)
  - truncated_output_hash: string (SHA256 of last emitted chunk to enable client reconciliation)
  - expires_at: ISO8601 timestamp (checkpoint TTL)
  - signature: string (HMAC-SHA256 of envelope using per-tenant key)

Example checkpoint envelope (server -> client):
{
  "type": "checkpoint",
  "checkpoint_id": "b8f3d8f8-3d2f-4d5a-9f2b-6a7c12c4e9bb",
  "request_id": "r-2026-00012345",
  "model_variant": "redwood-large-v2-quant",
  "token_offset": 1536,
  "kv_cache_ref": "cache://tenant-42/shard-17/ckpt-42",
  "truncated_output_hash": "sha256:abcd...",
  "expires_at": "2026-03-12T18:42:00Z",
  "signature": "sig:..."
}

2) Resume requests
- Client may initiate a resume by sending a ResumeRequest to the same endpoint (prefer HTTP/2 or WebSocket), passing the checkpoint_id and an optional client_ack_hash to indicate the last received chunk.
- ResumeRequest fields (JSON):
  - type: "resume_request"
  - checkpoint_id: string
  - client_ack_hash: string (optional)
  - client_id: string
  - request_metadata: map (opaque string kvs)
  - desired_resume_window: integer (tokens; server may honor subset)

Example ResumeRequest (client -> server):
{
  "type": "resume_request",
  "checkpoint_id": "b8f3d8f8-3d2f-4d5a-9f2b-6a7c12c4e9bb",
  "client_ack_hash": "sha256:abcd...",
  "client_id": "web-6d2a",
  "request_metadata": {"ui_session":"sess-123"},
  "desired_resume_window": 1024
}

3) Server resume response
- Server verifies signature and TTL. If valid, server responds with either:
  - resume_accepted: provides a new stream that resumes generation from token_offset, or
  - resume_denied: provides reason (expired, checkpoint-not-found, variant-mismatch) and optional best-effort fallback (restart token and cost estimate).
- Servers must not resume across incompatible model variants; resume across quantization variants is allowed only if deterministic equivalence is guaranteed (see model-compatibility ledger).

4) Idempotency and side-effect handling
- For requests that may trigger external side-effects, servers MUST not replay side-effects on resume. Implement one of two modes chosen per-route:
  - server-gated side-effects: the first successful finalization of the request generates an immutable side-effect token; clients must present this token when invoking any follow-up action.
  - client-ack-guarded mode: side-effects are only emitted after explicit client acknowledgement of final chunk.

5) Failure modes and reconciliation
- If the client’s client_ack_hash does not match the server’s truncated_output_hash, server SHOULD emit a ‘divergence’ event containing the minimal suffix the client is missing and a suggested merge strategy.

Operational requirements and configuration table
------------------------------------------------
| Key | Default | Unit | Description | Owner |
|-----|---------|------|-------------|-------|
| checkpoint.interval_tokens | 512 | tokens | Default token cadence for emitting checkpoints | inference-runtime |
| checkpoint.interval_seconds | 10 | seconds | Time-based cadence upper bound | inference-runtime |
| checkpoint.ttl_seconds | 86400 | seconds | Default checkpoint retention (24h) | storage-team |
| checkpoint.max_size_bytes | 16384 | bytes | Max size of serialized checkpoint metadata | storage-team |
| resume.auth_window_seconds | 300 | seconds | Time window after checkpoint creation where resume is allowed without re-authorization | identity |
| resume.p95_restart_latency | 150 | ms | SLO for resuming and starting token emission after a resume request | eng-sre |
| resume.max_parallel_resumes_per_tenant | 5 | count | Rate-limit per tenant to prevent abuse | quota-service |

Storage and encryption
- Checkpoints are stored in the checkpoint-store service (S3-compatible). All checkpoint metadata must be encrypted at rest with customer KMS, and signed with a per-tenant resume key. Checkpoint payloads must avoid storing user PII or full prompts unless configured by customer (private deployments).

SLOs and alerts
---------------
- Resume success rate (per-tenant) >= 99.5% over 24h.
- Resume p95 latency <= resume.p95_restart_latency (150ms default).
- Checkpoint persistence latency (write to checkpoint-store) p99 < 200ms.
- Alert if > 1% of resumed streams require full restart due to divergence in a 24h window.
- Alert on checkpoint-store error rate > 0.5% sustained for 5 minutes.

Observability and telemetry
-------------------------
- Emit events with standardized tags: checkpoint.emitted, checkpoint.persisted, resume.requested, resume.accepted, resume.denied, resume.divergence.
- Each event must include: request_id, checkpoint_id, tenant_id, model_variant, route, token_offset, and p99 latency metric dimensions.
- Trace spans: stream-gateway -> checkpoint-service -> inference-runtime -> checkpoint-store must be stitched with the same trace id for end-to-end debugging.

Rollout and compatibility
-------------------------
1) Backwards compatibility
- If an older client does not implement resume, server continues to emit checkpoints but ignores resume requests. The server must support default behavior of restarting from scratch with a clear restart-cost estimate.
2) Canary rollout steps (recommended):
  a) Implement server-side checkpoint emission behind a runtime flag (flag: checkpointing.enabled).
  b) Enable for internal tenants only and run synthetic failover tests for 72h.
  c) Gradually enable for 5% of external tenants, monitor resume success metrics and downstream cost delta.
  d) Increase to 25% then 100% if thresholds met.
3) Rollback plan: TTL reduction + immediate disable of checkpointing flag. Documented incident playbook in eng-platform/runbooks.

Testing and validation checklist
-------------------------------
- Unit tests for checkpoint envelope creation and signature verification.
- Integration tests: simulate connection interruption at token boundaries and mid-chunk; validate client resume produces the same final payload within tolerance threshold for structured outputs.
- Chaos tests: drop TCP connections, simulate transparent proxies, and ensure resume success > 99.5%.
- Cost regression: ensure average token cost delta after enabling resume < 3% (positive or negative).

Security considerations
----------------------
- Ensure checkpoint signatures use per-tenant HMAC keys stored in KMS. Rotate keys with zero-downtime using dual-signature validation during rotation window.
- Checkpoints must not expose raw secret keys, or PII unless explicitly enabled by customer and documented in private deployment configs.

Appendix: example CLI flows and cURL
-----------------------------------
Emit stream (client):
curl -N -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" -d '{"prompt":"Write a long analysis...","stream":true}' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate.stream

Resume flow (client):
# client reads checkpoint_id from last message and issues resume
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ 
  -d '{"type":"resume_request","checkpoint_id":"b8f3d8f8-3d2f-4d5a-9f2b-6a7c12c4e9bb","client_id":"web-6d2a","client_ack_hash":"sha256:abcd..."}' \ 
  https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate.resume

Operational owners and contact
----------------------------
- inference-runtime: @inference-runtime-team (primary implementer)
- checkpoint-store/storage-team: @storage-team (persistence, encryption)
- stream-gateway: @edge-team (protocol / rate-limiting)
- eng-sre: oncall for SLO violations and rollback.

Related reading
---------------
- Model variant compatibility ledger (model-serving-standards/variant-compatibility-ledger-and-stewardship-protocol-2026)
- Cost-aware streaming payload schema guideline
- Runbook: stream-resume-incident-playbook (eng-platform/runbooks/stream-resume-incident-playbook)

Revision history
----------------
- 2026-01-12: Initial draft by Maya Chen.
- 2026-02-05: Added SLO thresholds and storage encryption detail (reviewers: Rohit, Liam).
- 2026-03-05: Final edits and publication, clarified divergence reconciliation logic.

Title: Operator fallback experiment matrix and cost penalty catalog

Operator fallback experiment matrix and cost penalty catalog

Overview
========

This document captures a reproducible experiment matrix for operator-driven fallback strategies and an associated cost-penalty catalog used to evaluate trade-offs between SLO preservation and unit economics across regional surges. It is intended for platform operators, SREs, and product engineers running controlled degradation experiments or designing automatic fallback policies.

Why this exists
---------------
- Fallbacks are a major lever for preserving SLOs during capacity scarcity or model regressions, but they have measurable cost and quality impacts.
- Operators need a concise experiment plan with metrics, dashboard queries, and a cost penalty model to compare candidate strategies.
- This doc standardizes experiment telemetry, rollout/rollback steps, and decision criteria for productionizing fallbacks.

Goals and scope
---------------
- Goal: Provide a repeatable experiment matrix that yields quantitative comparisons of: latency SLO retention, token-cost delta, quality regressions (evaluations), and operator intervention effort.
- Scope: Multiregion inference surface (hosted + dedicated), model variant fallbacks (quantized, smaller model families), and routing degradations (regional drain, tenant throttling).
- Out of scope: Model training/data pipelines, legal/customer contract negotiation.

Definitions and abbreviations
---------------------------
- Fallback variant: Any alternative response path (e.g., model C => model B, or cached response) used when the primary path is unavailable or overloaded.
- Cost penalty: Unit cost increase or revenue impact metric associated with using a fallback (e.g., tokens * $/token diff, or additional infra cost).
- SLO preservation: Fraction of requests meeting 95th percentile latency target and error-rate SLO.

Experiment matrix (canonical)
---------------------------
Columns: experiment_id | description | fallback_type | trigger | primary-metric | cost-metric | quality-metric | run-length | owner

Example rows (use these as templates):
1) EXP-001 | Model-variant degrade (Llama-70B -> Llama-13B-int8) | model_variant | queue-depth > 100 OR p95 latency > 600ms | p95 latency, error-rate | token-cost-delta-per-hour | eval-regression@20 prompts | 2h | operator-team
2) EXP-002 | Regional drain to peer region (eu-west -> us-east) | regional-routing | region capacity throttle 80% | p99 tail latency cross-region | egress-cost-delta | user-visible-quality (latency jump) | 4h | platform-network
3) EXP-003 | Prefetch cache fallback (serve from prefix cache) | cache_prefetch | cold-start rate > 30 req/min | mean latency | compute-cost-savings | correctness mismatch ratio | 3h | runtime-team
4) EXP-004 | Token-budgeted throttling for low-priority tenants | quota_throttle | burst credits exhausted | 95th latency of high-priority | revenue-at-risk | customer-error-annotations | 6h | platform-ops

Telemetry and dashboarding recipe
--------------------------------
Create a dedicated experimental dashboard with following panels per experiment run:
- SLO heatmap: p50/p95/p99 latency over time (per region, per tenant priority). Query examples:
  - latency_p95{experiment_id="EXP-001"} (PromQL)
  - request_duration_bucket_sum by (le, region)
- Cost delta stream: rolling token-cost-per-minute and infra-cost-surge.
  - token_cost_rate{fallback_variant!=""}
- Quality regression signal: evaluation pass-rate across a held promptset (20-50 prompts) run every 15 minutes.
  - eval_pass_rate{promptset="fallback-20"}
- Operator interventions: number and duration of manual rollbacks, with links to runbook tickets.
  - operator_rollbacks_total{experiment_id="EXP-001"}
- Composite KPI panel: cost-penalty vs. SLO-preservation scatter plot for each variant.

Minimum instrumentation checklist
--------------------------------
1) Annotate requests with experiment_id and fallback_variant in trace metadata.
2) Emit fallback_reason counter in request pipeline.
3) Record per-request token accounting and model_version label.
4) Attach prompt-set id for synthetic eval traffic.
5) Ensure operator actions log into the incident system with experiment_id tag.

Cost penalty catalog (examples and formulae)
-------------------------------------------
Catalog rows: fallback_variant | per-token-diff | expected-throughput | hourly-cost-delta | rollback-cost-estimate | notes
Example entries:
- L70B -> L13B-int8 | +0.002 $/token (lower cost) | 2k tokens/s | -$14.4 / hour per 1000 rps | negligible | reduced quality on long-form completion
- cross-region-eu->us | +$0.05 / 1k tokens (egress) | 1k tokens/s | +$180 / hour at 1000 rps | potential SLA credits | watch cold-start p95
- cached_prefix_response | -$0.001 $/token (savings) | N/A | -$3.6 / hour per 1000 rps | risk of stale content | requires invalidation policy
- quota-throttle-low | revenue-at-risk estimate (see calc) | depends on tenant mix | - | revenue-impact = average-MRR-per-req * blocked-reqs | requires customer comms plan

Cost calculations (short formulas)
- token_cost_delta_hourly = sum_over_requests(token_count * (cost_primary - cost_fallback)) per hour
- egress_delta_hourly = egress_bytes * egress_rate
- revenue_at_risk = blocked_requests * avg_revenue_per_request
Include these calculations in the dashboard as derived timeseries.

Experiment run playbook (step-by-step)
-------------------------------------
1) Planning (2–4 days)
   a) Define hypotheses: e.g., "model-variant fallback preserves p95 latency with <5% quality regression and cost delta < $200/hr"
   b) Pick held promptset (20–50 prompts) and synthetic traffic profile matching customer mix.
   c) Create experiment_id, add telemetry tags and dashboard.
2) Preflight (1 day)
   a) Run synthetic traffic against fallback in staging and collect baseline metrics.
   b) Validate eval pass-rate and trace annotation.
   c) Pre-commit rollback playbook and test it in canary.
3) Execution (2–6 hours normally, up to 24 hours for long-run metrics)
   a) Apply experiment on a small cohort (1% of traffic or single region).
   b) Monitor SLO panels and operator intervention panel.
   c) Escalate to oncall if p99 > target * 2 or error-rate increases > 2x baseline.
4) Ramp or rollback (decision gates)
   a) If cost-savings or SLO-preservation meet hypothesis -> ramp to 10% then 50% using pre-defined step intervals.
   b) If quality regression > threshold or operator rollbacks > 1 -> rollback immediately, file incident.
5) Post-run analysis (within 48 hours)
   a) Populate experiment report template (see artifacts).
   b) Archive synthetic trace samples and evaluation results.

Rollback quick commands (examples)
--------------------------------
- Immediate global rollback: CLI helper
  - redwoodctl rollout cancel --experiment EXP-001 --force
- Regional undo (eu-west):
  - redwoodctl routing set-region-weight --region eu-west --weight 1.0 --experiment EXP-001
- Re-enable primary model:
  - redwoodctl model set-default --model redwood/llama-70b --variant baseline --experiment EXP-001
Include these command snippets in runbook templates and verify operator RBAC before using.

Decision criteria matrix (accept/ramp/abandon)
--------------------------------------------
- Accept: p95 latency maintained within 10% of baseline AND eval regression <= 3% AND hourly cost delta within budgeted threshold.
- Ramp: p95 within 20% and eval regression <= 7% with operator acceptance.
- Abandon: p95 > 20% degradation OR eval regression > 10% OR unexpected customer errors in the error-tracking system.
Document reasons in experiment report.

Artifacts to capture and store
----------------------------
- Experiment report (.md) with: hypothesis, traffic profile, duration, metrics before/after, cost calculations, operator notes.
- Trace bundle (link to S3) and synthetic eval outputs (json).
- Dashboard snapshot and Prometheus queries used.
- Postmortem if rollback occurred.

Operational responsibilities and ownership
----------------------------------------
- Owner: platform-ops (primary contact: oncall@platform) for run coordination.
- Instrumentation: runtime-team for trace and metric changes.
- Cost modeling: finance-eng liaison for hourly cost validation.
- Security review: security-team if any customer data is used in synthetic prompts.

Safety and customer communication
--------------------------------
- For tenant-facing throttles or degradations that materially impact customer SLAs, coordinate with Customer Success for banner messaging and QBR notes.
- For enterprise customers with Dedicated/Private deployments, require explicit sign-off per the customer SLAs before ramping.

Retrospective template (post-experiment)
--------------------------------------
1) Summary: one-paragraph outcome
2) Metrics: baseline vs. experiment (latency, error-rate, cost, eval pass-rate)
3) What went well
4) What failed / surprises
5) Action items (owner + due date)
6) Decision: accept/ramp/abandon

Appendices
----------
A. Sample PromQL snippets
- p95 latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="inference",experiment_id=~"EXP-.*"}[5m])) by (le, region))
- fallback rate: sum(rate(fallback_reason_total[1m])) by (fallback_variant)

B. Template experiment report checklist (copy into new experiment ticket)
- Experiment ID: 
- Owner: 
- Hypothesis: 
- Synthetic promptset id: 
- Baseline run links: 
- Dashboard link: 
- Rollback commands verified: Y/N
- Customer communication required: Y/N

C. Related runbooks and pages
- emergency-model-swap-and-token-surge-mitigation (runbook)
- platform-operator-handbook-degraded-kv-prefix-cache (operator runbook)

D. Change log
- 2025-11-12: Document created by Aisha Patel.
- 2025-12-08: Added cost-penalty formulas and cross-region egress example (review: Miguel Torres).
- 2026-01-18: Finalized decision criteria and PromQL snippets (review: Dana Li).

Contact and follow-up
--------------------
For questions or to schedule a live walk-through of the experiment templates, ping #platform-ops or email aisha.patel@redwood.ai.

unit-cost-sandbox-variant-scenarios

Sandbox spreadsheet used to evaluate alternative unit-cost assumptions across regions and model families for the Hosted API. Purpose: quick 'what-if' variants to surface high-leverage optimizations (caching, quantization mix, routing) and prioritize small experiments that change per-request economics by >5%.

- BaseTokenCost_per_1k: estimated infra cost per 1000 tokens served (includes GPU amortization + infra ops).
- QuantizedFactor: multiplier applied to base token cost to represent cheaper execution for quantized model variant (0.65 means 35% cheaper).
- KVCacheHitRate: fraction of tokens avoided via prefix/KV cache; assumed uniform token reduction on long contexts.
- EffectiveTokenCost_per_request = (BaseTokenCost_per_1k * QuantizedFactor * AvgTokensPerRequest / 1000) * (1 - KVCacheHitRate).
- PriceCharged_per_request: example list price applied in this sandbox (not final).
- Sensitivity_+10pct_GPU_cost: delta in margin per request if GPU-related component increases by 10%.
- Exchange rates and cloud egress costs modeled separately (not included in this sheet), but regional BaseTokenCost captures average historical impression of those elements.
- Run three small experiments within 6 weeks: (A) Enable quantized-default routing for small-model traffic in US/EU, (B) Deploy prefix-KV cache for top 200 user prompts, measure hit rate, (C) Add cross-region fallback policy for large-model requests to US-west when APAC quota is saturated.
- Owner assignments: A: Marcus Chen; B: Naomi Ruiz; C: Samir Kulkarni.
- Measurement plan: track EffectiveTokenCost_per_request, observed KVCacheHitRate, p50/p95 latency, request rejection rate, and net margin delta weekly.
- Decision thresholds: if margin improves by >5% without >10% p95 latency regression, roll change to prod; else iterate.
- Small-model quantization yields the largest low-effort wins (15–30% per-request cost reduction in our assumptions).
- Large-model routing and regional placement have outsized impact on margin due to higher AvgTokensPerRequest; small changes in GPU price or utilization produce large margin swings.
- Embeddings are low-cost per token but high-volume; caching repeated vectors and batching can reduce unit cost meaningfully.
- Recommendation: prioritize caching + quantization experiments before pricing changes or capacity commits.
- Caveat: latency SLOs may constrain batch sizes; measure real p95 impacts in canary traffic.
This file is intentionally a fast-moving sandbox (not canonical financial model). Use it to prioritize low-effort technical experiments that translate immediately into per-token savings. For reconciliation with official finance forecasts, we will export a reconciled slice after experiments complete and submit INF-1293 for accounting update.
Questions for reviewers: are regional surcharge assumptions for APAC appropriate? Should we include egress and KMS costs explicitly in next iteration?
Formatting: kept as CSV-style rows for easy copy/paste into Sheets. Numeric values are placeholders tied to current infra telemetry (Nov 2025) and should be refreshed monthly.
History: initial draft created 2025-11-02; major rework (added APAC scenarios + embedding rows) on 2026-03-10.

Title: Edge CAPEX & Ops algorithmic pricing sandbox

Edge CAPEX & Ops algorithmic pricing sandbox

Purpose:
This is a working sandbox (spreadsheet-style) for exploring hybrid CAPEX/OpEx pricing heuristics and bundle recommendations for private deployments (on-prem and VPC). The goal is to produce compact, actionable rules-of-thumb that an AE or solutions engineer can use to: (1) estimate first-order TCO for a customer, (2) recommend a licensing + support bundle mix, and (3) identify early upsell levers (dedicated vs burst, premium SLAs, managed-initial-deploy).

High-level approach / assumptions (living):
- Time horizon: 36 months by default; sensitivity runs at 24 and 60 months.
- Hardware amortization: default 36mo straight-line for purchased hardware; 36mo blended for leased GPUs with 8% effective lease carry.
- Utilization definition: average of peak batchable utilization (weighted tokens per second) with headroom planning +20% for safety.
- Software license: base perpetual or term license depending on customer preference; default pricing model = term annual license with % of monthly OpEx floor.
- Support tiers: Bronze (email, 48h), Silver (business hours, 24h), Gold (24/7, 4h), Platinum (SLA-backed, 1h + on-call).
- Quantization/acceleration discounts: assume token cost reduction 18%-40% depending on aggressiveness of quantization and model family (applied as negative OpEx).

Key levers included in the model (to iterate):
- HW: GPUs count, GPU type, PUE, density (nodes per rack), spare capacity reserve.
- Licensing: flat seat fee vs usage multiplier vs blended term license.
- Support: included hours, response SLA, remote-hands level.
- Managed services add-ons: initial deployment, patching, monitoring exports, 3rd-party KMS integration.
- Routing/fallback policy: ability to route to hosted tier reduces peak capacity requirement by X% at cost Y per token.

Quick heuristics produced so far (draft):
1) Small customers (<10 peak GPUs) - recommend VPC term license + Bronze support + optional managed on-boarding. Rationale: low capex sensitivity, faster time-to-value.
2) Mid customers (10-50 peak GPUs) - recommend hybrid bundle: 36mo partial-capex (customer buys 60% of baseline GPUs or leases) + Silver support. Add optional burst credit to hosted layer to cap capex and handle seasonal peaks.
3) Large customers (>50 peak GPUs) - recommend Dedicated private licensing (term + annual reserved commitment), Gold support, and offer hardware financing to smooth CAPEX. Include incentive: reserved throughput discount (8%-15%) vs pure on-demand.

Representative sensitivity outputs (see sheet rows):
- Break-even month (compared to fully-hosted at current list unit price) calculated with 36-month horizon and discount rate 7%
- Unit token cost (USD per 1e6 tokens) after amortization and support allocation
- Monthly effective spend by category: amortized capex, hw maintenance, electricity, license amort, support, managed services, hosted fallback credits

Open questions / modeling gaps to resolve:
- How to model colocation/space/network egress variability across regions (EMEA/APAC). Currently we use a single geography multiplier table; need finer granularity.
- Fleet heterogeneity: mixing A100 and H100 variants - how to fold into utilization and packing efficiency.
- Exchange rates and tax treatment for multi-year leases.
- Precise defintion of "peak GPUs" for burstable workloads - should we model percentiles (p50/p95/p99) instead of an absolute peak?

Immediate next steps (owners):
- Miguel: wire-up variant table for GPU unit prices and lease vs buy math (JIRA-5568).
- Priya: interview 3 recent mid-market customers to validate recommended Silver bundle and managed onboarding willingness (target by 2026-03-01).
- Jordan: prototype UI compact estimator (copy-ready) for AE quoting tool - MVP supporting 3 scenario presets and CSV export.

Notes to reviewer:
- This is intentionally messy - the purpose is to capture heuristics and counterexamples not yet formalized in the canonical pricing model. Please highlight any false assumptions and paste example customer profiles that contradict these heuristics.

Metrics we want surfaced in console for bundle decisions (for product/AE alignment):
- Effective USD per 1e6 tokens (amortized) per route (private / hosted)
- Breakeven months vs hosted baseline
- Monthly committed spend vs incremental managed fees (to flag value of managed services)
- Fraction of capacity hedged by hosted fallback (reduces capex need)

Reference formulas (exposed in sheet rows as plain text):
- amortized_capex_monthly = purchase_cost / amortization_months + maintenance_pct * purchase_cost / 12
- effective_token_cost = (monthly_amortized_capex + monthly_hw_ops + license_monthly + support_monthly + managed_monthly - hosted_credit) / estimated_monthly_tokens * 1e6
- break_even_months = cumulative_cost_private_vs_hosted crosses zero (discounting applied at 7% annual)

TODO / tidy before marking final:
- Convert this sheet into canonical product pricing inputs (Confluence page) with tidy presets for Small/Mid/Large.
- Add EMEA/APAC region multipliers per market.
- Validate quantization discount bands with Applied ML team (SRE and Runtime).

End of sandbox description.

Title: Million Token Cost Bridge — Regional Slab and Instance Mix

Million Token Cost Bridge — Regional Slab and Instance Mix

A compact spreadsheet-style model that maps GPU-instance cost and throughput into $/1M tokens by region and workload profile. Includes interactive vs batch profiles, preemptible adjustments, and simple sensitivity knobs for quantization and batching improvements.
This sheet is a decision-facing calculator to compare regional unit economics (USD per 1M tokens) across instance classes and workload profiles. It intentionally uses conservative throughput assumptions and exposes a few levers (batch size, quantization uplift, preemptible discount) to show where runway or routing policies buy the most savings.
Throughput expressed as GPU-hours required per 1M tokens (lower is better).
Interactive profile: seq_len=512, avg_out_tokens=128, batch=1, latency-optimized kernel paths.
Batch profile: seq_len=2048, avg_out_tokens=256, batch=16, sustained throughput kernels active.
Preemptible discount assumed = 30% of raw GPU-hour cost; we apply a reliability penalty (requeue / orchestration) of +0.05 USD per 1M tokens when using preemptible instances.
Quantization/optimizations: conservative savings set at 15% reduction in GPU-hours for recommended models (can be toggled).
GPU-hour list prices are indicative cloud-on-demand equivalents and include an ops markup where appropriate for reserved capacity comparators.

- reserved-hours (applied)
- model usage lines (chat/embedding)
- new line: private-egress: euro-amount 1320.00 (no detailed tag or cost center)

Title: PPK regional COGS snapshot and ops recommendations (working)

PPK regional COGS snapshot and ops recommendations (working)

Sheet: PPK regional COGS snapshot (working)

Purpose:
- Provide a compact per-model, per-region PPK (price-per-kilo-tokens) COGS breakdown and a short ops playbook for immediate wins. This is a working export for stakeholder review (eng/product/finance).

Legend / shorthand:
- PPK = price per 1,000 tokens (USD).
- COGS components: compute (GPU amortized), network egress, storage & KV cache amortized, infra overhead (monitoring, control plane), support allocation.
- Latency slices: p50 (low-latency tier), p90 (mid), p99 (tail-sensitive) — routing and batching behavior differ by slice.

ASSUMPTIONS (baseline scenario - Medium load):
- GPU hourly blended cost: us-west $2.75/hr, eu-north $3.10/hr, ap-sin $4.30/hr (includes infra margins).
- Effective tokens/sec per GPU (avg across request mix): small models 2000 tok/s, mid 800 tok/s, large 220 tok/s.
- Average token length per request: 60 tokens (prompt+response average).
- Bandwidth egress cost included only for non-cached responses: $0.0008 per 1k tokens in us-west, +15% eu, +40% ap.
- Cache hit reduces compute tokens by 35% on average (prefix+KV reuse).
- Overhead allocation: 8% of compute COGS.

TABLE (selected rows, numbers are illustrative):
Columns: model_family | region | model_size | p50_COGS_PPK | p90_COGS_PPK | p99_COGS_PPK | retail_price_PPK (current) | margin_p90 | notes
1) redwood-7b | us-west | 7B | $0.45 | $0.48 | $0.62 | $1.20 | 60% | high batching potential, cache-friendly
2) redwood-13b | us-west | 13B | $0.62 | $0.69 | $0.95 | $1.60 | 56% | modest cache gains, use quantized variant for low-cost tier
3) open-30b | eu-north | 30B | $1.40 | $1.60 | $2.25 | $3.00 | 47% | tail-heavy; reserve capacity recommended for predictability
4) llm-x70 | ap-sin | 70B | $3.10 | $3.55 | $5.10 | $6.00 | 43% | high egress in AP; consider regional remapping
5) reranker-lite | us-west | small | $0.08 | $0.09 | $0.12 | $0.20 | 55% | cheap, profitable - surface as default for ranking workloads

Scenario columns explanation:
- p50_COGS_PPK: assumes optimal batching and KV cache behavior for latency-sensitive p50 traffic.
- p90_COGS_PPK: realistic operating point with mixed batching and partial cache reuse. This is the primary cost baseline.
- p99_COGS_PPK: includes extra overheads from autoscaling churn, smaller effective batches, and fallbacks to higher-capacity variants.

Short formula notes (textual):
- compute_ppk ~= (gpu_hour_cost / tokens_per_hour) * 1000 * (1 + overhead_pct) * quant_factor
- tokens_per_hour = tokens_per_second * 3600 (tokens/sec is model dependent and workload-profile dependent)
- quant_factor = 0.8..1.2 depending on quantization and memory bandwidth (lower for 4-bit modes)
- effective_ppk_with_cache = compute_ppk * (1 - cache_reduction_pct) + egress_ppk + storage_amp_ppk

Observed sensitivities (from simulated microbench):
- 1) tokens/sec variance: small models: +/-20% across request mix drives PPK change of ~15%.
- 2) cache hit rate: +10pp hit rate => 6–9% PPK reduction on mid models, up to 18% on large models.
- 3) regional GPU price delta: AP (x1.55) => ~30–45% higher final PPK after egress and overhead.

Ops recommendations (quick win list):
- A: Route best-effort, non-latency traffic to cheaper region where legal/compliance allows (map by customer tenant tier). Threshold: use regional remap when expected p90_COGS difference > 20% and latency delta < 120ms.
- B: Introduce an automatic "quantized-fallback" variant for >13B models in hosted-api pricing: users hit highest latency  (p99) triggers fallback to quantized endpoint (saves ~25–35% PPK at cost of minor quality delta).
- C: Aggressive prefix KV caching pilot for chat workloads: rollout to top-20 customers with structured prompts; target +25–40pp hit rate uplift.
- D: Batching policy: raise batch window by +10ms for p90 traffic in dedicated pools where SLO allows; expected PPK drop ~8%.
- E: Reserved capacity trigger: move models with >5k QPS and >60% utilization in a region to Dedicated pricing path to reduce effective GPU blended cost by ~18% (contract permitting).

Pricing experiments to run (A/B candidates):
1) New PPK tier: "quantized-saver" at 0.85 * retail_price for qualifying models and with explicit quality caveat; measure churn and conversion.
2) Latency-tiered discounts: 5% discount for customers who opt-in to p90-only (no hard p50 SLA) across chosen endpoints.

Title: Intermittent EU->US routing: encryption/egress path and observed latency spikes

Intermittent EU->US routing: encryption/egress path and observed latency spikes

Issue summary:
Customer (BrightLedger) reports intermittent request routing from eu-west that terminates in us-east causing increased tail latency and unexpected egress charges. They are concerned whether cross-region traffic is encrypted end-to-end and whether routing is honoring data-residency pin for their account.

Impact:
- A subset (~0.5-1%) of production requests from eu-west are observed with 200-400ms additional token-latency and elevated egress bytes. Customer reports monthly invoices with higher-than-expected inter-region egress.
- Customer has Dedicated commitment and expects eu residency for inference traffic by pin configuration.

Environment:
- Customer account ID: BL-7732 (dedicated pool)
- Region primary: eu-west (customer pinned)
- Observed fallback region: us-east
- Model: redwood-open-7b and gptx-small (both pinned in account config)
- Time window: 2026-03-10 02:00 UTC -> 2026-03-11 23:00 UTC

Steps to reproduce (customer supplied):
1) Send standard generate calls pinned to account region eu-west with model redwood-open-7b.
2) Repeat over 48h.
3) Observe occasional latency spikes and in logs see routing entries indicating us-east egress.

Expected behavior:

Investigation notes so far:
- Support pulled routing traces from the smart-routing logs for BL-7732 for the time window and saw ~0.7% of requests routed to us-east. Trace hints show "capacity-fallback" and "kv-cache-miss" tags on those traces.
- Serving-runtime logs show short-lived host termination events in eu-west autoscaler at 2026-03-11T12:59Z correlating to a burst of 429s and subsequent routing adjustments.
