2025-02-18 14:10 PT — Sean Gallagher (Assignee, SRE): Confirmed symptom aligns with ordering: restore applying CRs before CRDs are present. In air-gapped mode, CRDs must come from the offline bundle (not fetched). Looping in Ethan Park for control-plane restore sequencing expectations.
2025-02-18 15:03 PT — Ethan Park (Control plane eng lead): Restore workflow currently assumes prerequisite operators/CRDs exist (cert-manager, external-secrets, and Redwood platform CRDs via helm install of control-plane chart). If customer ran restore on a completely fresh cluster without running the "bootstrap" step, CRDs will be missing. We should improve preflight to detect and provide a deterministic checklist, and optionally extract CRDs from bundle for install-first.
2025-02-18 16:22 PT — Fatima Noor (Support): Sent interim workaround to customer: install prerequisite CRDs first (from offline bundle) then re-run restore. Asked customer to confirm whether they can run helm from bundle and whether images are already loaded into their registry.

1) Verify CRDs missing:
   - `kubectl get crd | egrep '(cert-manager|external-secrets|platform.redwood.ai)' || true`
2) From the offline bundle, install prereq charts WITH CRDs enabled (do not use `--skip-crds`):
   - cert-manager: `helm upgrade --install cert-manager ./charts/cert-manager -n cert-manager --create-namespace --set installCRDs=true`
   - external-secrets: `helm upgrade --install external-secrets ./charts/external-secrets -n external-secrets --create-namespace`
3) Install Redwood control-plane chart to lay down Redwood CRDs before applying CR instances:
   - `helm upgrade --install redwood-control-plane ./charts/redwood-control-plane -n redwood-system --create-namespace`
4) Confirm CRDs exist:
   - `kubectl get crd | egrep '(cert-manager.io|external-secrets.io|platform.redwood.ai)'`
5) Re-run restore:
   - `redwood-private restore apply --from /mnt/backup/backup_2025-02-17T0312Z --continue-on-preflight=false`
6) Validation:
   - `kubectl -n redwood-system get pods`
   - run the post-restore health check in the runbook (control-plane API ready, tenant config present, routing policy objects present).

Restore failure was due to missing prerequisite CRDs (cert-manager, external-secrets, Redwood platform CRDs) on a fresh on-prem cluster, causing "no matches for kind" during manifest apply. Workaround: install prerequisite charts/CRDs from the offline bundle first, then re-run `restore apply`. Follow-ups filed to improve restore preflight and documentation to explicitly cover fresh-cluster ordering.
Install prerequisite CRDs/operators from the offline bundle (cert-manager with installCRDs=true, external-secrets, then Redwood control-plane chart to install Redwood CRDs) before running `redwood-private restore apply`. Title: Add `restore apply` workflow with preflight checks and post-restore validation report

Add `restore apply` workflow with preflight checks and post-restore validation report

Implements the end-to-end restore path for Redwood Private in the installer CLI. This adds a new `restore apply` command that: (1) performs strict preflight checks (cluster connectivity, namespace/CRD readiness, version compatibility, storage backend access, and integrity checks on the backup artifact), (2) restores control-plane state in a deterministic order (cluster prerequisites, control-plane chart values/config, DB restore, then service rollout), and (3) runs post-restore health checks and emits a validation report that Support/SRE can use for escalation. The goal is to make restores repeatable, safer to run under time pressure, and easier to debug when something goes wrong. Restore ordering is intentionally conservative to avoid the on-prem issues we saw in SUP-18477 (missing CRDs/incorrect bootstrap order). Security note: we do not restore secret material from backups; we restore secret references and validate that required KMS/external secret providers are reachable. The report includes sanitized environment details (versions, timestamps, artifact IDs), step-by-step results, and pointers to relevant logs. Usage examples: `private-installer restore apply --artifact s3://<bucket>/backups/<id> --namespace redwood-private --report /tmp/restore-report.json` and `private-installer restore apply --artifact ./backup.tgz.enc --offline --validate-only`.

Title: Fix streaming metering edge cases: ensure accurate per-stream token accounting

Fix streaming metering edge cases: ensure accurate per-stream token accounting

Summary:

We observed multiple customer reports and internal alerts where streaming calls (server-sent chunks / chunked HTTP and websockets) result in incorrect billed token counts. Errors fall into 3 buckets: (1) reconnects and resumed streams cause duplicated output accounting, (2) partial chunk flushes (e.g., early truncation + later finalization) lead to mismatched input/output attribution, (3) aborted streams produce invoiceable tokens with no corresponding completion record.

Goals:
- Ensure per-stream token accounting is deterministic and idempotent across reconnections and retries.
- Maintain compatibility with existing non-streaming metering pipeline.
- Add end-to-end tests and monitoring to prevent regressions.

Background & root cause hypothesis:
- The metering pipeline currently increments token counts on two different events: chunk_emitted (client-facing streaming chunk) and response_finalized (completion). When a client reconnects, the runtime replays pending chunks; both the replay and the original recorded chunks were persisted, yielding duplicate counts.
- Streaming proxies sometimes split logical tokens across frames; our token counter treats frames as independent events, so partial frames can be double-counted when reassembly occurs later.
- Aborted streams (network failure) emit chunk events but never reach the reconciliation job that marks them as non-billable or reconciled.

Proposed design (high level):
1) Introduce a server-assigned stream_session_id for every streaming session. This id is authoritative for metering and survives client reconnects when a resume is requested.
2) Attach per-chunk sequence_id and running_token_offset (both integers) to every chunk event emitted by the runtime. Metering service will only accept chunk events with monotonically increasing sequence_id per stream_session_id. Duplicates or replays with the same sequence_id are ignored.
3) Update event schema (old events remain readable): add stream_session_id:string, sequence_id:int, final_chunk:boolean, token_count:int, running_token_offset:int. Implement backward-compat handling for non-stream events (null session id).
4) Reconciliation rules: if a stream_session_id is abandoned (no final_chunk within X minutes), create a "timed-out" reconciliation record that credits back incomplete or uncertain tokens based on policy (e.g., only bill committed final tokens).
5) Add a short-lived in-memory cache (LRU per runtime node) of recent (stream_session_id, last_sequence_id) to quickly drop duplicate replays at the source and avoid persistent DB writes.
6) Billing ledger: make adjustments idempotent by recording operation_id for every increment so replays can be ignored. Operation_id = stream_session_id + sequence_id.

Trade-offs discussed:
- Option A (chosen): server-generated stream_session_id + sequence_id gives strong correctness and is straightforward to enforce at metering layer, but requires a small runtime schema change and minor protocol bump for streaming clients.
- Option B (rely on client idempotency tokens): avoids touching runtime but depends on diverse client implementations and is brittle for third-party SDKs.
- Option C (post-hoc heuristics in reconciliation): low runtime change but yields possible over/under-billing windows and complex refund processes.

2026-03-03 — Design sync with runtime: agreed to add server_assigned stream_session_id. Runtime owners flagged a minor protocol bump for websocket resume semantics (ETA for runtime change: 2 sprints).
2026-03-04 — Decision note: Use sequence_id + running_token_offset. Sequence_id guarantees monotonicity; running_token_offset allows safe reconciliation of split-frame tokens. We will ignore older events if sequence_id <= last_seen.

Title: Activation funnel dashboard discrepancy (EU-West drop + mismatch vs warehouse) after lifecycle growth instrumentation changes

Activation funnel dashboard discrepancy (EU-West drop + mismatch vs warehouse) after lifecycle growth instrumentation changes

Issue summary
- Growth/Marketing and Product flagged a sudden drop and cross-source mismatch in the activation funnel metrics (signup → API key created → first request) used for the Lifecycle Growth Experiments sprint.
- Primary symptom: EU-West conversion from signup → api_key_created appeared ~12–18% lower than US-East starting 2026-01-21 18:00 UTC, and overall “new signups” appeared higher than expected vs auth/user tables.
- Impact: Week 1–2 experiment readouts risked being invalid/noisy; we paused one planned expansion of the email A/B until numbers were reconciled.

Impact
- Affected dashboards: Activation Funnel (Observability Pack) + internal Looker view used by Growth.
- Impacted decisions: stop/go thresholds and lift calculations for onboarding email v2 and console nudge experiments.
- Customer impact: none direct (reporting/measurement issue only), but could cause us to make incorrect product/GT-M decisions.

Detection
- Reported via Slack #help thread ("events missing in one region") and follow-up in #eng-platform on 2026-01-22.
- Observability Pack funnel panel showed EU-West drop; Mei Lin noted mismatch vs daily new users in warehouse.

What changed recently
- PR-28431: added/standardized activation events for signup → api key → first request → first 100k tokens.
- PR-241: new dashboard panels + funnel query definitions.
- Console nudge framework shipped behind flags; additional event properties and cohort assignment introduced during the week.

Initial hypotheses
1) Ingestion lag or partial pipeline outage in EU-West.
2) Region routing misconfiguration (EU events landing in US dataset or vice versa).
3) Event validation rejecting records due to missing required properties (user_id, event_id) for EU only.
4) Duplicate event emission inflating baseline in one region, making EU look like it dropped.

Investigation notes (high level)
- Confirmed ingestion health: Kafka consumer lag normal; no sustained drop in raw event volume by region at the edge collectors.
- Cross-checked three sources for the same window (2026-01-21 00:00–2026-01-22 23:59 UTC):
  - Raw collector logs: stable event counts in eu-west.
  - Warehouse fact_events table: stable api_key_created events in eu-west.
  - Activation Funnel dashboard: apparent eu-west drop.
- Found the discrepancy was query-side + dedupe behavior:
  - The funnel panel’s Step 1 “signup” was keyed off signup_created events and deduped by (user_id, day), but the Step 1 event was being emitted twice for a subset of flows in US-East due to a console/auth edge case.
  - EU-West had fewer duplicates, so the “conversion rate” (step2/step1) looked artificially worse in EU-West when comparing regions.
  - Additionally, the dashboard query used a join that unintentionally filtered some EU users when event_time skew occurred near midnight UTC (session boundary + region bucket), amplifying the appearance of a regional issue.

Root cause
- Duplicate emission of signup_created/signup_completed for users who hit both (a) email verification completion and (b) immediate console onboarding flow that retriggered the signup event. This was more common in US-East due to traffic mix and a feature-flag exposure path.
- Dashboard query logic for Step 1 + Step 2 used inconsistent dedupe keys (Step 1 deduped by user_id/day; Step 2 deduped by event_id) and a region/date join condition that excluded a portion of EU events at boundary times.
- Net effect: inflated Step 1 counts in US-East and undercounted Step 2 in EU-West in the visualization layer, while the warehouse raw events were largely correct.

Resolution
- Engineering fix: PR-28521 shipped to stop duplicate signup event emission; verified by before/after comparison on a canary cohort and then full rollout.
- Analytics fix: updated Activation Funnel panel query to use consistent dedupe (event_id preferred, fallback to (user_id, event_name, request_id) for older records) and removed the join condition that filtered EU events at UTC boundaries.
- Backfill: no backfill required for canonical fact tables; dashboard now recomputes accurately from warehouse. Noted that historical conversion rates for 2026-01-19 to 2026-01-22 should be interpreted with caution; we annotated the dashboard.

Validation
- Post-fix checks (2026-01-26):
  - Regional conversion rates are within expected variance (eu-west no longer showing step-change).
  - New user counts align within ~1–2% between auth table and deduped signup events.
  - Funnel step drop-offs align with expected product behavior and match secondary metrics (API key creation table).

Follow-ups
- Add a data-quality alert: spike in duplicate rate for signup_created and api_key_created by region.
- Add unit tests/contract tests for event emission idempotency in console/auth flows.
- Document dedupe keys and “source of truth” definitions in the activation metrics notes + dashboard README.

Stakeholders
- Growth: Ben Carter (experiment owner), Tyler Benson (attribution)
- Product: Marissa Cole (console), Paula Mendes (telemetry/rollouts)
- Eng/Analytics: Logan Wright (assigned), Nadia Rahman, Mei Lin

References
- Slack: #help (tracking discrepancy), #eng-platform (taxonomy + dedupe)
- Related PRs: PR-28431, PR-28521, Observability Pack PR-241

Title: Fix duplicate signup event emission (skewing activation funnel)

Fix duplicate signup event emission (skewing activation funnel)

## Context
We’ve been seeing inflated counts at the top of the activation funnel (signup stage) since the lifecycle growth sprint instrumentation landed. This has been most visible in regions with higher auth callback latency and for users who refresh the console during the post-signup redirect.

Root cause: `signup_completed` was emitted from *two* places:
1) Auth callback handler (server) when we exchange the OAuth/session token
2) Console bootstrap (client) when `currentUser.isNew == true`

In the happy path these happen once each (still bad), but in the presence of retries/refresh, the client-side emission could occur multiple times, leading to 2–4 events per new user. This skewed the funnel conversion rate, especially when computing “% of signups completing first request within 7 days” with naive event counting.

## What changed
- Make the server-side emission the single source of truth for `signup_completed`.
- Remove client-side fallback emission and replace it with a debug-only log (behind an internal flag) to preserve troubleshooting signal without polluting analytics.
- Add idempotency guard on the server event publisher:
  - Dedupes `signup_completed` per `user_id` for a short window (30 minutes) using an event-key in Redis.
  - Also dedupes `activation_signup` alias to avoid re-introducing duplicates via legacy event name.
- Add a regression test for the callback handler to ensure repeated callbacks do not emit additional signup events.

## Why this is safe
- The event is informational/analytics-only (no product logic is gated on it).
- Server is already the canonical place where we know the signup is complete.
- Dedup window is short and keyed by user, so it won’t suppress legitimate re-signups (new user id) or later lifecycle events.

## Validation
### Before
- Sample (2026-01-27 UTC): ~1.82 `signup_completed` events per distinct `user_id` (p50=2, p95=3)
- Funnel dashboard showed occasional >100% “signup → api_key_created” conversion for small cohorts (clear sign of duplication)

### After (staging + prod canary)
- Staging load test (forced refresh + retry): 1.00 `signup_completed` events per distinct `user_id`
- Prod canary (5% of traffic for 3 hours): 1.01 events per distinct `user_id` (small remainder due to legacy clients still in flight)
- Funnel conversion rates returned to expected ranges and the signup stage volume dropped ~35% relative to distinct users (consistent with prior duplication rate)

## Rollout
- Ship as hotfix to `main`
- No migrations
- Dashboard owners: Sergio Costa / Allison Grant are aware; update their sanity-check query to use distinct users as a guardrail until the canary completes.

## Checklist
- [x] Confirmed no downstream systems require client-side emission
- [x] Added tests
- [x] Verified event schema unchanged (only emission sites)
- [x] Coordinated with Growth (Ben Carter) on expected dashboard deltas

Refs:
- INT-3310 (activation funnel discrepancy)
- Lifecycle growth sprint instrumentation (ENG-10492)
- Activation funnel dashboard work (ENG-10533)
Logan Wright (review): Can we confirm we’re not suppressing legitimate replays if a user opens two tabs during signup? Also, why 30 minutes for the dedupe window?
Nadia Rahman (author): Yes—two tabs will hit the same user_id and we *do* want one logical signup event. 30m is meant to cover retries/refreshes around auth callback + console bootstrap; we can tune shorter if you prefer. Also keyed by (event_name,user_id) only, so it won’t affect other funnel events.
Dylan Brooks (review): Removing the client emission makes sense. Any chance older console builds still rely on the client event for experiment cohort assignment?
Nadia Rahman (author): Cohort assignment is via feature flag service on signup timestamp + user id; not tied to this event. Confirmed with Ethan/Benji on ENG-10501 thread; this event is analytics-only.
Paula Mendes (review): Please add a note in the PR about the legacy alias event name (`activation_signup`) so we don’t get bitten again in SQL.
Nadia Rahman (author): Added to “What changed” + validation section; also dedupes both names. Good call.
Logan Wright (review): Test looks good. One suggestion: make the redis key include environment to avoid any weirdness in shared infra.

Title: ephemeral-boot-and-attestation-playbook-for-onprem-deploys-2026

ephemeral-boot-and-attestation-playbook-for-onprem-deploys-2026

Overview:

This playbook documents Redwood Inference's recommended operational procedures for building, delivering, and operating ephemeral-boot images for private (on-prem / VPC) deployments with measured boot attestation and secure live-patching. It focuses on reducing blast radius for field operators, minimizing sensitive image exposure, and enabling safe fast path upgrades for model runtime artifacts (weights, quantized kernels, KV cache formats) in environments where full air-gapped, FIPS, or HSM-backed requirements may apply.

Intended audience:
- Field engineers responsible for on-prem installs and upgrades
- SRE and platform engineers running Private control planes
- Security reviewers and compliance owners

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to private-deployments using Redwood Private or our operator-managed on-prem packages.
- Target platforms: x86_64 with UEFI secure boot support, select ARM deployments where measured boot telemetry is available.
- Assumes customer has a hardware root-of-trust (TPM 2.0) or equivalent and network connectivity for attestation channel (can be configured to use an offline cassette for fully air-gapped installs).

Goals:
1) Provide a reproducible ephemeral image pipeline where images are: minimal, signed, and have verifiable boot measurements.
2) Enable safe live-patching and model artifact swaps without full host reimaging whenever possible.
3) Define deterministic rollback and isolation steps to recover from failed updates.

Terminology:
- Ephemeral boot image: a read-only OS+runtime artifact that boots a compute node into a known state and mounts model artifacts remotely or from local immutable storage.
- Measured boot: a chain-of-trust measurement (UEFI/TPM PCRs) recorded during boot used for attestation.
- Attestation server: Redwood or customer-side service which verifies measurements against a trusted allowlist.

Prerequisites (checklist):
1) Hardware: TPM 2.0 present or HSM accessible; BIOS/UEFI firmware supports Secure Boot and measured boot PCRs.
2) Network: management plane access between node and attestation endpoint (or pre-seeded attestation cassette).
3) Software: image-builder (Packer/BuildStream), signatures toolchain (cosign or internal sigserver), kexec utility for fast kernel swaps.
4) Keys: signing keys stored in KMS/HSM; only public verification material distributed to operator consoles.

Ephemeral image build and pipeline (recommended flow):
1) Base build: Create minimal OS image with only necessary kernel modules, GPU drivers, container runtime, and Redwood runtime binaries. Remove SSH keys, admin credentials, and cloud agents.
2) Immutable runtime layer: package Redwood runtime and GPU optimizations as a read-only artifact. Validate with unit tests and perf smoke tests.
3) Model artifact packaging: store model binaries and quantized variants as separate, versioned blobs. Do NOT bake large model weights into ephemeral images unless required for air-gapped installs (see Air-gapped section).
4) Sign and attest: generate SBOM, compute image hash, sign image with HSM-backed key (cosign recommended), and produce a signed measurement manifest describing expected UEFI PCR values for the image.
5) Publish to registry/artifact store: push signed artifacts to customer-side registry (or Redwood storage for hybrid installs) and update the attestation allowlist.

Attestation modes:
- Online attestation: node boots, collects PCR values, and POSTs measurement manifest to attestation server. Server verifies signature and returns a short-lived attestation token used to unlock model blob decryption keys.
- Cassette (air-gapped) attestation: pre-compute measurement allowlist and provide cassette (signed token package) to operator to be imported during install. Tokens expire after specified window to enforce rotation.

Boot and runtime verification steps (operator commands):
1) Boot the ephemeral image with secure boot enabled. Check UEFI settings: 'SecureBoot: Enabled', 'BootOrder set to PXE/LOCAL'.
2) Verify measurement: curl -ksS --cert <operator-cert> https://attest.example.com/verify -d '{"node_id":"$(hostname)","pcr_values":"$(tpm2_pcrread)"}'
3) Confirm attestation token present: /opt/redwood/attestation/token.json (expires).
4) Pull model blobs using attestation token: redwoodctl fetch-model --token /opt/redwood/attestation/token.json --model-id m1234

Live-patching and kernel swap strategy (to avoid full reboot):
- When only runtime libraries, inference kernels or quantized weight shims need update, prefer kexec-based kernel+initramfs swaps together with overlayfs model blob updates. This reduces downtime and avoids re-attestation for unchanged PCR measurements if configured carefully.
- Constraints: kexec will change kernel measurement PCRs; include kexec-allowed hashes in attestation allowlist or use attestation server policy to accept approved kexec events.
- Steps for safe kexec-based update:
  1) Stage new kernel and initramfs on /var/lib/redwood/staged/
  2) Run integration smoke-tests against staged runtime in a containerized verifier.
  3) Mark node as "draining" in control-plane and migrate active requests.
  4) Trigger kexec: sudo /usr/sbin/kexec -l /var/lib/redwood/staged/vmlinuz --initrd=/var/lib/redwood/staged/initrd.img --command-line="$(cat /proc/cmdline) redwood.upgrade_token=<token>"
  5) On reboot, node will re-attest. Control-plane verifies token and unmarks node when model pull completes.

Rolling upgrade playbook (operator procedure):
1) Canary: select 2 nodes in each availability stripe. Apply ephemeral image and runtime changes, run full end-to-end eval against canary prompt set (latency, accuracy, throughput).
2) Gradual rollout: 10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100% with 30–60 minute observation windows and automated auto-rollback conditions.
3) Auto-rollback triggers:
  - 99th percentile tail latency increase > 30% vs baseline for 15 minutes
  - Token fetch failures > 2% of requests for 10 minutes
  - Model correctness regression: dropped generation score > configured threshold on regression prompts
4) Manual hold: SRE or release owner can pause rollout in console. Document reason and required remediation steps.

Rollback and failure isolation matrix:
- Failure type: Node boot fails (bootloop) -> Isolation: detach from LB, boot into recovery image, collect TPM/UEFI logs, escalate to firmware vendor if needed.
- Failure type: Model blob decryption fails -> Isolation: revoke attestation token, fallback to cold model variant with local copy, notify security.
- Failure type: kexec failure -> Isolation: auto-fallback to previous kernel via bootloader saved entry; if not present, instruct operator to recover via console and re-image from signed artifact.

Verification and acceptance tests (must pass on every upgrade):
1) Boot measurement validity check (scripted).
2) Attestation handshake round-trip within 5s average latency.
3) Model fetch with token success rate >= 99.9% in staged network.
4) E2E perf: p50 latency within +10% of baseline, p99 under SLA.
5) Regression check: prompt-set accuracy drop < configured threshold (default 1.5% relative).

Air-gapped/fully offline deployment guidance:
- Option A (preferred): pre-seed model blobs and signed attestation cassette. Provide local attestation server appliance that validates PCRs against precomputed allowlist.
- Option B (immutable images): bake model weight bundles into read-only image signed by HSM. Larger image size increases distribution time; ensure checksum verification and storage lifecycle policies.

Telemetry and observability recommendations (day-2):
- Collect boot measurement deltas, attestation result codes, token issuance latencies, model fetch success/failure, and kexec event logs.
- Tag telemetry by tenant_id, node_role, and orchestration_phase. Retention: default 90 days for operational events, 365 days for security-critical attestation events.

Runbook snippets (quick commands):
- Verify signed image: cosign verify --key kms://projects/prod/keys/onprem-signer <image-ref>
- Read TPM PCRs: tpm2_pcrread sha256:0,1,2,3
- Force node into recovery: redwoodctl node set-state --node-id n-12345 --state recovery --reason "boot failure"
- Rotate attestation cassette (air-gapped): redact and sign with operator key: redwoodctl cassette sign --cassette /tmp/cassette.json --key /opt/keys/operator.pem --expire 72h

Ownership and escalation:
- Build & Sign pipeline: Platform Security (owner).
- Field installs / day-2 ops: Private Deployments field-engineering team.
- Attestation server: Security + Infra (joint ownership).
- Escalation path: On-call field-eng -> On-call infra -> Security pager -> Firmware vendor.

Troubleshooting matrix (common symptoms):
- Symptom: Attestation token not granted. Checks: verify cosign signature of image, check TPM PCRs mismatch, inspect attestation server policy logs for mismatches.
- Symptom: Model fetch timeout. Checks: token TTL, network egress rules, registry reachability (tcp/443), token-scoped permissions.
- Symptom: Unexpected reboots after kexec. Checks: kernel command-line parity, signed initrd, bootloader preserved previous entry.

Related pages:
- Incident playbooks for private deploys (link internal)
- Container image signing & verification standards (link internal)
- Private deploy acceptance and smoke validation (link internal)

Appendix A — Minimal security checklist (table-style):
- Signed image present: YES
- SBOM attached: YES
- TPM present: YES / NO (action: do not proceed without TPM unless HSM path)
- Attestation path available: ONLINE / CASSETTE
- Recovery image available: YES

Appendix B — Example attestation policy (pseudo YAML):
policy_id: redwood-ephemeral-1
allowed_pcrs:
  - sha256: [<hash-kernel>, <hash-initrd>, <hash-os>]
kexec_policy: require_signed_kexec: true
trusted_keys: ["projects/prod/keys/onprem-signer"]

Change history:
- 2025-11-03: Created by Maya Chen (initial draft).
- 2025-12-15: Added kexec guidance and acceptance tests (reviewers: Diego Alvarez).
- 2026-02-14: Finalized air-gapped cassette workflow and escalation path (published).

Contact:
- Primary author: maya.chen@redwood.ai
- Field-eng on-call: field-eng-oncall@redwood.ai

End of playbook.

Title: Adaptive link-rate smoothing and NCCL pacing for heterogeneous interconnects

Adaptive link-rate smoothing and NCCL pacing for heterogeneous interconnects

Background: On clusters with heterogeneous interconnects (mixed NVLink/NIC link speeds and asymmetrical topologies) we observed recurring NCCL stalls and bandwidth oscillation under TP workloads. This manifested as throughput variance across microbatches and elevated p99 tail latency for short-running inference requests. Motivation: previous fixes focused on static stream priorities or rigid batching heuristics which either underutilize good links or exacerbate stalls on slow links. This PR implements an adaptive link-rate smoothing layer and NCCL pacing integration to harmonize collective launches with per-peer link conditions and the runtime scheduler. Key changes and approach: 1) Link-rate estimator: continuous lightweight probe that measures effective per-peer bandwidth and short-term variability; estimator lives in scheduler/peer-rate-estimator and exports a smoothed rate with decay/window parameters tuned for inference workloads. 2) NCCL pacing adaptor: introduces optional pacing tokens in the comm adapter to space collective launches when peer variability is high; pacing is conservative by default and disabled for uniformly fast topologies. 3) Slack windows & micro-shear prevention: scheduler now computes a small slack window for kernel dispatch to absorb jittered arrival times from peers and aligns kernel launches with KV-cache prefetch completion when available. 4) KV cache alignment hook: prefetch manager negotiates a preferred alignment point with the scheduler for batched requests so comm-heavy windows avoid blocking on cache population. 5) Telemetry & guardrails: new metrics (peer_effective_bw, nccl_pacing_suppressed, pacing_tokens_issued) and a dynamic safety threshold that disables pacing if aggregate throughput would drop. Performance: in lab runs (8-node, mixed NVLink + EDR InfiniBand topology) typical large-TP workloads gained 12-18% sustained throughput and p99 latency improved by ~25% for short requests; NCCL stall events as recorded by tracers dropped ~60%. Testing and validation: - microbench suite: tp_collectives_bench extended with hetero-link scenarios - end-to-end canary: perf-canary harness with 10% traffic for 48h - unit + integration: scheduler, comm adapter, kv prefetch mocks - stress: ramp tests up to 200 concurrent sessions Rollout plan: canary 10% on dedicated clusters for 48h -> 50% -> global. Operator flags: pacing enabled=false by default for existing clusters; enabled=true for targeted clusters requires no code rollback. Risk and mitigation: conservative defaults, auto-disable if pacing causes throughput regression, and manual opt-out available via runtime flags. Related work: this complements prior comm scheduling efforts (see ENG-6123 family) and is intended to pair with future topology-aware kernel selectors. Notes: preserves existing public API surface; only runtime internals and ops docs are updated.
Ethan Wu: Can you explain how the probe traffic avoids perturbing production workloads? We should bound probe sample size.
Author (Priya): Probe uses a low-rate in-band estimator with adaptive throttling; added explicit bound and backoff to avoid congestion (see peer_rate_estimator.cc).
Marisol Ortega: Approve with one nit: prefer metric name 'peer_effective_bw_bytes' for clarity.
Author (Priya): Renamed metric and updated dashboards.
Dmitri Petrov: Requested change: make pacing opt-out dynamic via operator API (not just startup flag).
Author (Priya): Added runtime flag and operator endpoint; documented behaviour and rollout safety checks.
Introduce adaptive NCCL pacing and link-rate smoothing to reduce comm stalls on heterogeneous interconnects; opt-in via runtime flag. Improves throughput and tail latency on mixed-topology TP clusters.
Default behavior unchanged; to enable: set runtime.pacing.enabled=true on staging cluster. Monitor metrics 'nccl_pacing_suppressed' and 'peer_effective_bw' during rollout.
Deploy canary config to 3 dedicated clusters, update perf dashboards, schedule follow-up to evaluate interactions with kernel-selector heuristics (ENG-7392).

Title: Billing question: Burst usage line item appears higher than expected for Dedicated tenant (reconciliation request)

Billing question: Burst usage line item appears higher than expected for Dedicated tenant (reconciliation request)

Issue Summary
Northpeak Search reached out with questions about the new “Dedicated Burst Usage” line item on their June invoice draft. They believe the burst charges for 2025-06-15 to 2025-06-18 are ~1.6–1.9x higher than expected based on their internal job schedule.

Customer Context
- Customer: Northpeak Search
- Product: Dedicated (Burst enabled)
- Region / hardware: us-east (H100 pool)
- Workload: periodic indexing jobs that intentionally burst for ~30–90 minutes, plus steady baseline serving.

Impact
Billing trust / customer confidence issue. No production outage, but customer requested we pause invoice approval until reconciliation is complete.

What the customer observed
- Invoice draft shows:
  - Dedicated Baseline (as expected)
  - Dedicated Burst Usage (higher than expected)
- Customer believes they ran 3 burst windows; our charges look closer to 5–6 windows.

Initial Hypotheses
1) Retries are being counted as additional burst usage (idempotency / double-counting bug).
2) Console “Burst Usage” view is lagging or using a different aggregation window than billing export.
3) Burst “cooldown / denial” behavior caused extra retries that increased token/GPU-sec usage (but should still be accurately metered).

Requested from customer (to reconcile)
- Approximate timestamps of indexing job bursts (start/end) and request IDs if available.
- Confirmation whether client is retrying on 429 / overload or admission-denied responses, and what retry policy/backoff is configured.

Internal Reconciliation Plan
1) Compare billing export (daily burst usage CSV) vs. Console usage charts for same tenant/time range.
2) Query metering pipeline for tenant_id + request_id aggregation; look for duplicate request_id entries.
3) Cross-check gateway logs for elevated retries and response codes during windows in question.
4) If discrepancy confirmed, coordinate credit/rebill with Finance (Rishi/Laura) and provide a customer-readable explanation.

Current Status
Confirmed discrepancy due to retry-path double-counting for burst metering under specific client retry behavior (see investigation notes). Fix merged and scheduled for backfill + billing adjustment.

Next Steps
- Apply metering fix (already merged) + run backfill job for affected dates.
- Provide reconciled burst usage report to customer with timestamps and methodology.
- Finance to issue invoice adjustment/credit memo as needed.

Owner(s)
- Support / CS: Miguel Santos
- Billing hooks: Cole Summers
- Metering pipeline: Nadia Rahman
- Finance: Rishi Malhotra (analysis), Laura Bennett (approval)

Attachments / Links
- PR: pr-24108-fix-billing-double-counting-on-burst-retries
- Burst usage report export job: pr-24091-add-burst-usage-report-export
- Packaging / metering definition: Dedicated burst option packaging doc
2025-06-19 (Miguel Santos): Customer flagged burst usage line item as higher than expected. They requested reconciliation before approving invoice. Looping in Cole (billing hooks) + Nadia (metering) + Rishi (FP&A).
2025-06-19 (Customer - Northpeak Search): We ran three indexing jobs that should have burst for about ~1 hour each. The invoice draft suggests almost double. Can you confirm what’s included in burst usage and whether retries can inflate it?
2025-06-19 (Cole Summers): Acknowledged. We meter burst usage as incremental usage above baseline capacity allocation (GPU-seconds and token accounting rolled up daily). Retries should not double-count if request IDs are consistent, but we’ll validate in the pipeline. Can you share your retry settings and whether you retry on 429/admission-denied?
2025-06-20 (Miguel Santos): Customer confirms client retries on 429 with exponential backoff; they also had a transient spike in 429s during one of the windows. They can’t easily provide request IDs but provided burst window timestamps: 06/15 ~09:10–10:05 PT, 06/17 ~08:55–09:40 PT, 06/18 ~09:05–10:00 PT.
2025-06-20 (Nadia Rahman): Checked metering aggregation for tenant. Seeing duplicated entries with same upstream correlation key but different internal attempt IDs. Looks consistent with double-counting on retry path when idempotency key not propagated to metering event. Escalating to Cole + Vikram for confirm in gateway->metering event payload.
2025-06-21 (Cole Summers): Confirmed bug: burst metering event increments on each retry attempt when idempotency_key is missing/empty, and the downstream de-dupe is keyed only on (tenant_id, request_id). In some retry cases, request_id changes per attempt (gateway regeneration). Fix in progress: use idempotency_key when present; otherwise derive a stable hash from upstream trace/correlation IDs with safeguards.
2025-06-21 (Rishi Malhotra): From finance side: OK to hold invoice finalization for Northpeak pending a reconciliation report + adjustment. Please provide estimated delta and a customer-facing explanation for approval.
2025-06-22 (Cole Summers): Fix merged: pr-24108-fix-billing-double-counting-on-burst-retries. Includes: (1) idempotency key propagation requirement from gateway, (2) de-dupe improvements, (3) reconciliation check that flags duplicate-attempt spikes. Next: run backfill for 06/15–06/18 and generate corrected usage report export.
2025-06-23 (Miguel Santos): Updated customer that we found a metering bug related to retry attempts and we’re running a backfill to correct the burst usage line item. ETA 24–48 hours for final reconciled numbers and invoice adjustment.
2025-06-24 (Nadia Rahman): Backfill completed for affected dates. Corrected burst usage reduced by 41% for 06/15 and 18% for 06/18; 06/17 unchanged. Exported corrected report to billing bucket and validated against Console usage (now consistent within normal aggregation variance).
2025-06-25 (Laura Bennett): Approved issuing a credit/adjustment for the delta and proceeding with corrected invoice. Please document in the ticket and attach the reconciled report summary for audit trail.
2025-06-26 (Miguel Santos): Sent customer reconciled burst usage summary (daily totals + explanation). Customer confirmed it matches their expectations and approved moving forward. Closing ticket as Resolved.
Root cause was double-counting burst metering on retry attempts when a stable idempotency key was not used; request_id changed per attempt and downstream de-dupe did not catch duplicates. Fix merged (pr-24108), backfill run for affected dates, and Finance approved invoice adjustment/credit for the corrected delta. Provided reconciled burst usage report to customer and clarified retry guidance to avoid unnecessary 429-triggered retries.
Follow-up actions: (1) Add automated detection alert for sudden duplicate-attempt ratio in burst metering events; (2) Update customer docs to recommend idempotency keys and retry-on-denial guidance; (3) Ensure Console and billing exports share the same aggregation window definitions; (4) Post a short note to #support with the symptom pattern and how to spot it quickly in dashboards.

Title: Fix billing double-counting on Dedicated burst retries (idempotency + reconciliation)

Fix billing double-counting on Dedicated burst retries (idempotency + reconciliation)

Problem: we are double-counting burst usage when the same customer request is retried (client retries, gateway retries after 5xx/timeout, and some 429 backoff paths). In beta, this showed up as duplicate burst usage line items for the same request window and was flagged in SUP-28488 and during reconciliation sampling. Root cause: the burst metering emitter currently treats each attempt as billable because we do not have a stable request-scoped idempotency key carried end-to-end into the metering aggregation stage; request_id/trace_id are not consistently preserved across retry code paths. Fix: introduce a request-scoped idempotency key that is generated at the gateway if missing, propagated to the data plane and metering emitter, and used to dedupe burst billable events before exporting to billing. Also add a reconciliation guard that detects duplicates that slip through (e.g., telemetry lag / partial outages) and blocks export with an alert. Details: 1) API/gateway: accept and forward X-Redwood-Idempotency-Key; if absent, generate a ULID per incoming request and reuse it across internal retry attempts. 2) Metering: include idempotency_key on burst usage events; dedupe in the burst_usage_aggregator on (tenant_id, region, hw_class, pool_id, idempotency_key) with a bounded TTL and hashed storage to avoid high-cardinality raw keys. 3) Billing export: export a deduped_usage_count and dropped_duplicate_attempts metric; add a hard reconciliation check that fails the export batch if duplicate keys exceed a small threshold (defaults to 0.01%) and pages on-call for billing pipeline. 4) Tests: add integration test for retry paths to ensure only one billable burst event per idempotency key; add unit tests for dedupe window behavior and hash collisions (expected negligible; we still include tenant/pool scoping). Rollout: behind feature flag billing.burst_idempotency_dedupe_enabled (default off). Plan is to enable in staging immediately, then 10% of Dedicated burst tenants in us-east for 24h, then ramp. Risk: incorrect dedupe could under-bill if keys are reused incorrectly; mitigated by scoping on tenant+pool and generating server-side keys when absent. Note: this PR does not change customer-visible request semantics; it only makes billing/metering idempotent across retries.
Cole Summers: Can you confirm we’re deduping at the right layer? If we dedupe at emission we might still get duplicates due to retries from different processes. Nadia Rahman: Agreed; dedupe is in the aggregator (central path before export), not at the emitter. Emitter always emits per-attempt but includes idempotency_key so we can attribute retries and track dropped duplicates. Ethan Park: Please make sure the header is documented and that control plane schema doesn’t accidentally treat it as a stable customer identifier. Also, what’s the validation story? Nadia Rahman: Updated OpenAPI to mark header as optional, max length 128, allowed charset [A-Za-z0-9-_]. Internally we hash it (xxh3_128) and store only the hash; raw header is not persisted. Rishi Malhotra: Reconciliation behavior: failing a batch blocks invoicing—what’s the expected frequency and who gets paged? Nadia Rahman: Threshold default 0.01% duplicates per batch; in normal behavior it should be 0. The job pages billing pipeline on-call (rotation includes me + Cole) and posts to #eng-platform with tenant and batch id. We also emit a metric so finance can spot anomalies before invoice close. Sean Gallagher: Any chance this creates noisy alerts during telemetry lag incidents? Nadia Rahman: The check uses a sliding window and ignores known-degraded states when metering ingestion lag > 2m (existing metering_lag gate). Added a runbook note and ensured we don’t flap by requiring 3 consecutive failing batches before paging. Cole Summers (requested changes): Please add an integration test that simulates 429 retry and ensure we don’t charge twice. Nadia Rahman: Added burst_retry_billing_idempotency_test covering 429 backoff and a synthetic gateway retry on 5xx. Cole Summers: Approved. Ethan Park: Approved. Sean Gallagher: Approved after runbook link added. Merge: Squash + merge.
Billing/metering: Burst usage is now idempotent across retries via request-scoped idempotency keys. Added reconciliation guardrails and metrics to detect duplicate charging attempts. No API behavior change; customers may optionally provide X-Redwood-Idempotency-Key, otherwise Redwood generates one.

Title: Dedicated Burst Capacity — Post-beta retro notes (SRE)

Dedicated Burst Capacity — Post-beta retro notes (SRE)

Doc goal
Capture what we learned from the Dedicated Burst Capacity beta (May 2025): what broke, which guardrails were too strict/too lax, what we changed during beta, and what must be completed before GA.

Retro logistics
- Date: 2025-05-28 (60 min)
- Facilitator: Rafael Mendes (SRE)
- Notetaker: Peter Holtz (Routing SRE)
- Beta window covered: 2025-05-06 to 2025-05-24
- Scope: burst pools (regional/hardware), admission controller, routing integration, SLO gates, dashboards/alerts, metering/billing hooks, supportability

Attendees (high signal contributors)
- SRE/Obs: Sean G., Rafael M., Peter H., Allison G., Sergio C.
- Infra/Fleet: Vanessa O., Keiko Y.
- Control plane/policy: Jordan L.
- Routing: Mina H.
- Billing/metering: Cole S., Nadia R.
- CS feedback: Rachel K.

What went well (keep)
1) Global safety cap + circuit breaker concept worked in practice
- We hit the cap once in staging and once “near miss” in prod beta; breaker prevented runaway neighbor impact.
- The playbook of “reduce caps -> drain queues -> disable burst for lowest tiers first” is operationally sound.

2) Denial reason codes improved triage materially
- Support/CS could distinguish “cap reached” vs “pool saturated” vs “cooldown” vs “telemetry stale”.
- Routing logs + reason codes made it clear where to look first.

3) Dashboards were mostly the right primitives
- Saturation, queue depth, admit/deny rates, and p95 deltas by tenant were enough to debug 80% of issues.
- SLO gate signal (non-burst tenant latency regression) is a good north star even if thresholds need tuning.

4) Rollout gating/feature flags prevented blast radius
- Per-region allow list + per-tenant enablement meant we could pause EU-West issues without impacting US-East.


What broke / painful incidents
A) Telemetry lag caused unfair denials + occasional starvation
- Symptom: a few tenants saw denial spikes while pool appeared underutilized; the “laggy” telemetry made the controller think they were still consuming burst tokens.
- Customer-visible effect: burst requests denied unexpectedly; some clients retried aggressively and amplified load.
- Root cause (likely): our admission controller relied on near-real-time usage signals; when signals were delayed, the smoothing window + token bucket refill behavior effectively penalized active tenants.
- Fix during beta: hotfix added smoothing + guard conditions + conservative fallback when telemetry freshness is below threshold.
- Ref: GitHub:redwood/pr-23944

B) EU-West burst admission timeouts (controller dependency chain)
- Symptom: admission calls intermittently timed out in eu-west under high request rate; routing fell back but increased gateway error rates briefly.
- Root cause: admission controller p99 latency spiked due to dependency (policy evaluation + fleet telemetry query) not being bounded; threadpool saturation.
- Mitigation: enable circuit breaker + temporarily tighten per-tenant caps + disable burst in eu-west allow list until patched.
- Ref: Jira:SUP-28579

C) Billing: burst usage double-counted on retry paths
- Symptom: customer asked why burst line item didn’t match dashboard usage; we found ~1.8–2.3% overcount in a specific retry pattern.
- Root cause: metering event emitted pre-idempotency; retried requests emitted duplicate usage increments.
- Fix: idempotency keys + reconciliation checks.
- Ref: GitHub:redwood/pr-24108, Jira:SUP-28488

D) Noisy neighbor scare (tail latency increase for a non-burst tenant)
- Symptom: p95/p99 latency increase for a non-burst tenant correlated with another tenant’s burst window.
- What we learned: even if pool isolation is “logical,” shared control-plane/routing and some shared fleet components can cause tail amplification under saturation.
- Mitigation used: reduced global cap + increased cooldown for bursting tenant + forced routing fallback for that tenant for 30 min.
- Ref: Jira:SUP-28455

E) Support confusion: 429s when burst cap reached (expected but poorly messaged)
- We returned 429/overload when both baseline+burst caps were reached; some customers expected queuing instead.
- For GA we need crisp guidance: recommended retry/backoff strategy and what will/won’t queue.
- Ref: Jira:SUP-28503


Guardrails that were too strict (beta feedback)
1) Cooldown windows were overly punitive for spiky-but-legit workloads
- Current behavior: once a tenant hits max burst ratio, cooldown kicks in even if they drop below quickly.
- Effect: denial bursts after short spikes; customers perceive “flaky burst.”
- Proposal: cooldown should be based on sustained saturation (e.g., N seconds over threshold) or make cooldown proportional to burst duration, not a flat window.

2) Max burst ratio default (x1.5) was too conservative for “weekly batch” customers
- Several beta tenants expected x2–x3 for short windows (10–30 min) and were willing to pay.
- But we must pair higher ratios with stronger fairness + fleet safety + SLO gates.

3) Admission determinism vs latency tradeoff
- We enforced determinism by evaluating multiple signals synchronously; in some cases this added controller latency and increased timeouts.
- Suggestion: determinism requirement should be: “same inputs => same decision” but inputs can be snapshot-based (cached) within a bounded TTL.


Guardrails that were too lax (or missing)
1) Retry amplification guard
- When customers got denials, some clients retried immediately with high concurrency.
- We need an explicit “retry-after” / backoff hint tied to denial reason codes, and optionally server-side throttling at gateway.

2) Alerting gaps for “telemetry freshness” and “admission controller dependency health”
- We lacked a strong, paging-quality indicator for telemetry freshness degradation (it showed in graphs but didn’t page until customers complained).
- Admission controller dependency p99 did not have an error-budget aligned alert.

3) Fairness under mixed priority tiers needs stronger anti-starvation proofs
- We introduced priority tiers late in beta; we didn’t run enough multi-tenant stress tests for gold/silver combos.
- Need explicit starvation bound (e.g., min guaranteed tokens) and test harness enforcement.

4) Config propagation / console staleness
- One customer ticket: burst limit updated but Console showed stale value for too long.
- Root cause likely caching/prop delay; not a safety issue but it undermines trust.
- Ref: Jira:SUP-28541


Key metrics from beta (rough, from dashboards)
- Total burst attempts: dominated by 2 tenants with scheduled batch jobs.
- Denial rate: ranged 0–18% by tenant depending on time-of-day; spikes correlated with telemetry lag and cooldown behavior.
- Admission controller p99: stable in us-east; spiky in eu-west (timeouts).
- Neighbor impact: one validated event (SUP-28455) where non-burst p99 regressed ~12–18% for ~20 minutes before mitigation.
- Billing reconciliation: identified retry double-counting bug; now fixed but we need ongoing automated checks.


What we changed during beta (already merged or in progress)
- Telemetry smoothing / prevent starvation under lag: GitHub:redwood/pr-23944
- Global circuit breaker for burst pools: GitHub:redwood/pr-23919
- SLO-based auto-gating (reduce/disable burst on non-burst regression): GitHub:redwood/pr-23988
- Billing idempotency + prevent double-counting: GitHub:redwood/pr-24108


GA readiness action items (must do)
P0 (blockers)
1) Telemetry freshness as a first-class signal
- Add metric + alert: “telemetry freshness seconds” by region/hardware + admission controller decision mode (fresh vs degraded).
- In degraded mode: enforce safer decisions (lower caps) + include explicit denial reason “TELEMETRY_STALE_DEGRADED_MODE”.
- Owner: Allison Grant + Logan Wright
- Target: by 2025-06-07

2) EU-West admission controller latency hardening
- Bound dependency calls with strict timeouts; add cached snapshots; add load shedding in controller.
- Define routing behavior when controller is slow: deterministic fallback decision + do not hammer controller.
- Owner: Jordan Lee + Mina Haddad
- Target: by 2025-06-10

3) Retry guidance + “Retry-After” semantics tied to reason codes
- Standardize: which denials are immediate (cap reached) vs transient (pool saturated) and include a backoff hint.
- Update docs + support macros.
- Owner: Peter Holtz + Kira Thompson
- Target: by 2025-06-12

4) Billing reconciliation automation
- Nightly job: compare metering export vs dashboard aggregates within tolerance; page billing on drift > X%.
- Owner: Nadia Rahman + Cole Summers
- Target: by 2025-06-12

P1 (strongly recommended for GA)
5) Cooldown redesign proposal
- Experiment with sustained-threshold cooldown vs proportional cooldown.
- Add simulation + real-world replay tests.
- Owner: Keiko Yamamoto
- Target: proposal by 2025-06-14; implement behind flag if time.

6) Neighbor impact circuit breaker thresholds
- Define concrete thresholds: p95 delta, tail amplification, and error rate deltas for non-burst tenants.
- Ensure breaker annotations show “why” and which tenant(s) triggered.
- Owner: Sean Gallagher
- Target: 2025-06-14

7) Priority tier fairness tests
- Extend multi-tenant integration tests to include tier mixes; assert starvation bounds.
- Owner: Jordan Lee
- Target: 2025-06-15

8) Console/config propagation SLO + fix
- Set expectation: config changes visible within N minutes; instrument end-to-end propagation time.
- Owner: Chloe Martin
- Target: 2025-06-15


Operational notes / runbook improvements
- Add a “first 5 minutes” checklist for burst-related pages:
  - Check global circuit breaker status
  - Check telemetry freshness + telemetry lag panels
  - Check admit/deny by reason code
  - Check pool saturation + queue depth
  - Check non-burst tenant latency deltas
  - Decide: tighten per-tenant cap vs disable region/hardware allow list
- Ensure runbook has a customer comms template (what happened, what we did, what to expect next).


Open questions (need decision)
1) Queue vs immediate denial for pool saturation
- Today we mostly deny quickly; some customers want queuing.
- SRE view: queuing can hide fleet pain and increase tail; if we add queueing it must be bounded with clear max wait + cancellation and must not break determinism.

2) How much “degraded mode” behavior is acceptable?
- If telemetry is stale, do we:
  a) deny all burst? (safe but may be overly strict)
  b) allow small burst with conservative cap? (better UX)
  c) continue as-is with risk? (not acceptable)
- Tentative: (b) with tight global caps + explicit surfaced state.

3) GA scope: region/hardware allow list
- Recommendation: GA in us-east H100 first; add eu-west after EU-West latency fix + game day rerun.


Appendix: customer support learnings (from tickets)
- SUP-28411 (unexpected denials): customers interpret “burst enabled” as “guaranteed extra capacity.” We must emphasize “best-effort within guardrails,” with clear reasons.
- SUP-28503 (429s): customers need explicit guidance on client-side backoff, concurrency control, and how to detect “you are at cap.”
- SUP-28488 (billing question): customers will audit the burst line item against their own job schedule; we need accurate exports + transparent calculation.

Title: Tenant reservation realignment and soft-burst attenuation orchestrator

Tenant reservation realignment and soft-burst attenuation orchestrator

After the 2026-02-27 dedicated-cluster capacity spike, several tenant workloads experienced sustained tail latency and evictions. This ticket implements a coordinated set of follow-up items: a reservation re-alignment pass using temporal smoothing heuristics, a soft-burst attenuation orchestrator to avoid runaway token buckets, and a noisy-tenant isolation mode that incurs minimal cold-starts. Goal: reduce eviction rate by 90% for impacted clusters, bring 95th percentile latency under SLA, and avoid customer-visible retries during rollout.
The event was caused by (1) abrupt changes in per-request token distributions from a small number of tenants leading to KV-cache churn and eviction cascades; (2) aggressive reservation decay logic that under-allocated capacity during the burst tail; (3) burst tokenbucket settings allowed long-duration high-throughput sequences that starved co-located tenants. The autoscaler also misinterpreted short-lived spikes as sustained demand because of insufficient temporal smoothing of allocation metrics.
2026-02-27 03:12 UTC: Traffic spike detected in cluster d-34; 3 tenants showed 10-20x increase in long-sequence requests.
2026-02-27 03:30 UTC: Eviction storm begins; several dedicated pods evicted leading to cascade and higher queue latency.
2026-02-27 04:05 UTC: Fallback to smaller model variants triggered; some endpoints returned degraded throughput.
2026-02-27 05:20 UTC: Incident declared; mitigation: rate-limited noisy tenants and temporary reservation bump for affected clusters.
2026-03-01 10:00 UTC: Postmortem draft published; initial action items triaged.
2026-03-05 09:00 UTC: ENG-209501 created to implement orchestration and permanent fixes.
2026-03-10 16:00 UTC: Spike-simulator PR reviewed and merged (see prs).
(A1) Implement reservation re-alignment service that re-evaluates tenant reservations every 10m using an EWMA of peak-quantiles (owner: Marcus Lee, estimate: 5).
(A2) Add temporal smoothing window to autoscaler to prevent reacting to sub-5m spikes; default window=15m configurable per pool (owner: Priya Desai, estimate: 3).
(A3) Introduce soft-burst attenuation: when a tenant exceeds 'burst-duration' threshold, reduce token-generation rate by 50% with exponential backoff instead of immediate hard throttle (owner: Marcus Lee, estimate: 5).
(A4) Noisy-tenant isolation mode: lightweight cgroup-like fencing that can be enabled per-tenant for 1h during investigation; fencing isolates KV-cache and metrics to prevent cross-tenant degradation (owner: Diego Ramirez, estimate: 8).
(A5) Create tenant synthetic workload tests and include them in the dedicated-cluster CI job to validate eviction surface under mixed workloads (owner: SRE team, estimate: 3).
(A6) Dashboard and alerting: add new alerts for (a) cross-tenant KV cache churn rate, (b) token-bucket saturation >80% for >5m, and (c) reservation decay delta >30% in 10m (owner: Observability, estimate: 2).
(A7) Run a staged rollout (canary 5% clusters, then 25%, then 100%) for the orchestration changes with rollback hooks and telemetries (owner: Release Eng, estimate: 2).
(A8) Post-release runbook update and customer communication template for 'transient capacity events' (owner: Customer Success, estimate: 1).
Eviction rate for previously impacted tenants drops >=90% over a 7-day window after rollout.
95th percentile tail latency for dedicated clusters returns to SLA baseline within 24 hours of canary promotion to 25%.
Canary rollout exposes no increase in P0 incidents; automatic rollback triggers successfully on threshold breach.
CI synthetic test covers at least three mixed-workload scenarios (long-sequence-heavy tenant + many short requests + KV-warmup pattern).
Trade-offs: soft-burst attenuation prefers graceful degradation over strict fairness; this reduces tail latency impact but allows noisy tenants to make progress with reduced rate.
Decision log: we rejected a hard-eviction-first strategy because it causes cascading cold-starts and customer-visible errors; chosen path emphasizes isolation + smoothing.
Review feedback: Security requested an audit of isolation mode interactions with KMS when fencing is active (assigned to Security team).
Follow ups: Evaluate whether per-tenant RV (reservation velocity) trend is a better signal than raw peak for autoscaler in a separate spike-analysis spike (see dependencies).

Title: Instrument GPU queueing and backpressure span propagation

Instrument GPU queueing and backpressure span propagation

Context: Customers have intermittent tail-latency incidents attributed to unseen GPU-side queueing and scheduler backpressure. Existing telemetry exposed per-invocation latency and kernel timings but lacked per-device queue depth, kernel wait-time histograms, and an end-to-end trace showing where scheduler backpressure cascades into request stalls. Motivation: provide deterministic signals for (1) detecting kernel saturation before request SLOs are violated, (2) surface backpressure spans across scheduler -> runtime -> GPU driver boundary, and (3) reduce alert noise by tuning thresholds using real queue metrics. Changes in this PR: added a Prometheus collector for per-GPU queue depth and producer/consumer rates; emit OTLP spans at scheduler enqueue/dequeue points with a backpressure.reason tag; propagate a lightweight backpressure_trace_id through KV cache and runtime worker handoff; add kernel_wait_time histogram and per-queue tail-percentile gauges; new Grafana dashboard panels (device queue depth heatmap, enqueue/dequeue rate timeseries, kernel wait waterfall) and an alerting rule that triggers when device queue depth > 90% for 30s AND kernel_wait_p95 > 200ms. Rollout plan: feature gated via telemetry.enable_gpu_queue_metrics (default: false) and staged rollout to dedicated infra then hosted canaries for 48h. Observability: dashboards and alerts added; playbook drafted (link: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-2301) for runbook steps and mitigation (scale-up, redistribute shards, apply per-tenant throttles). Testing: unit tests for collectors and propagator, e2e integration against a synthetic kernel-saturation bench, manual verification on a dedicated pool. Backwards compatibility: propagation uses optional header and degrades to no-op for older runtimes. Risk: low-risk telemetry addition; a potential perf impact from extra metrics is mitigated by sampling and batching in the collector. See changed_files for code pointers and short snippets. Merge: squash-merged after two approvals and CI green.
Marcus Diaz: Can we avoid emitting per-invocation tags that increase cardinality? Suggest adding a sampled backpressure.reason and restricting gpu_id label cardinality.
Ava Chen: Addressed — added sampling and coalesced gpu_id into device_group label for the collector. Updated tests to assert label cardinality remains bounded.
Priya Iyer: Nit: prefer histogram buckets aligned with kernel latencies observed in perf lab (5ms, 10ms, 25ms, 50ms, 100ms, 250ms, 500ms). Also asked for a clear rollback flag.
Ava Chen: Updated histogram buckets and added telemetry.enable_gpu_queue_metrics=false default and telemetry.force_disable_gpu_traces for emergency rollback.
Liam O'Connor: Verified e2e bench reproduces queueing; approved after CI fixed intermittent flaky test (fixed by increasing test timeout).
Instrumented GPU scheduling queue metrics and backpressure traces: new Prometheus collectors, OTLP spans at enqueue/dequeue, Grafana panels for queue depth and kernel wait times, and an alert rule to detect kernel saturation. Feature is gated and disabled by default.

reference.text:
Title: ADR-022: Public error contract for data residency policy violations

ADR-022: Public error contract for data residency policy violations

## Status
Published (effective for Hosted API and applicable Dedicated entrypoints).

## Summary
This ADR defines the **public-facing error contract** returned when a request is blocked by **Hosted data residency region pinning**. It standardizes:
- HTTP status code and response shape
- Stable machine-readable error codes
- Message templates and non-leaky guidance
- Request ID linkage for support correlation
- Streaming endpoint behavior
- SDK surface expectations (typed exception + fields)

This contract is used by:
- API Gateway enforcement (pre-routing)
- Smart Routing (as a defensive backstop; must not return divergent formats)
- SDKs (Python/TS/Go) mapping to a dedicated error type

## Context / Problem
We are introducing region pinning (allowed region set + primary region) for Hosted API. When a request would be processed outside the pinned region set (including via fallback), the platform must block the request deterministically and return a **clear and actionable** error.

Prior behavior in similar policy blocks has been inconsistent:
- Different endpoints returned different status codes (403/409/500)
- Streaming paths sometimes returned generic 500s after the connection was established
- Clients had difficulty correlating blocks with internal logs due to missing request IDs

We need a stable contract that:
1) is unambiguous for programmatic handling,
2) is consistent across streaming and non-streaming endpoints,
3) avoids exposing sensitive internal routing or infrastructure details,
4) provides enough context for customers to remediate without contacting support.

## Decision
### 1) HTTP status
For residency policy violations, the API MUST return:
- **HTTP 409 Conflict**

Rationale:
- The request is syntactically valid and authenticated, but conflicts with a configured policy state (residency constraints).
- 403 Forbidden conflates authorization vs. policy configuration and is commonly retried/handled incorrectly.
- 422 Unprocessable Entity is typically reserved for semantic payload validation; this is not a payload issue.

### 2) Canonical error envelope
All residency blocks MUST use the standard Redwood error envelope:

Response headers:
- `x-redwood-request-id: <req_...>` (always present)
- `content-type: application/json` (for non-streaming responses)

Response JSON body:
- top-level key: `error`
- `error.code` is stable and machine-readable
- `error.message` is human-readable and actionable
- `error.request_id` matches `x-redwood-request-id`
- `error.help_url` points to public documentation
- `error.details` provides bounded, non-sensitive diagnostic fields

### 3) Error codes
#### 3.1 Primary code (stable)
All residency blocks MUST set:
- `error.code = "residency_policy_violation"`

#### 3.2 Subcode (stable)
Additionally, the API MUST set:
- `error.subcode` to one of:
  - `"region_not_allowed"` (candidate region is outside allowed set)
  - `"primary_region_unavailable"` (primary region would have been used, but is unavailable and cross-region fallback is not allowed)
  - `"policy_misconfigured"` (invalid/empty allowed regions, invalid primary, or invalid precedence state that passed earlier validation)

Notes:
- `subcode` is intended for customer-side routing/UX and for stable metrics.
- Avoid adding endpoint-specific subcodes; keep this list short and documented.

### 4) Required fields
The following fields are REQUIRED in `error`:
- `message` (string)
- `code` (string)
- `subcode` (string)
- `request_id` (string)
- `help_url` (string)

The following fields are REQUIRED in `error.details`:
- `allowed_regions` (comma-separated string of region IDs; see “Region identifiers” below)
- `candidate_region` (string; the region the system would have selected without the block)
- `policy_scope` (string: `"org" | "project" | "api_key"`)

The following fields are OPTIONAL in `error.details`:
- `primary_region` (string)
- `policy_id` (opaque string identifier; safe to expose)

### 5) Region identifiers
Public region identifiers in error payloads MUST use the same region IDs customers see in Console and docs:
- `"us"`, `"eu"`, `"apac"` (tier-1)
- or more specific when the customer has configured it (e.g., `"eu-west"`), as documented.

Do not expose internal cloud region names or infrastructure locality identifiers in the public error payload.

### 6) Message templates
Messages MUST:
- State that the request was blocked by data residency policy
- Provide the allowed region(s)
- Provide a single remediation step (Console path and/or API setting)
- Avoid mentioning internal failover groups, capacity tiers, or provider-specific regions

Approved templates (gateway selects based on subcode):

**A) region_not_allowed**
"Request blocked by data residency policy. This project is restricted to regions: {allowed_regions}. This request would be processed in: {candidate_region}. Update your residency settings in the Redwood Console (Settings → Data residency) or use an API key for an allowed region. See: {help_url}."

**B) primary_region_unavailable**
"Request blocked by data residency policy. The primary region ({primary_region}) is temporarily unavailable and cross-region fallback is not permitted for this project. Retry later or contact support if this persists. See: {help_url}."

**C) policy_misconfigured**
"Request blocked by data residency policy due to a configuration error. Verify your allowed regions and primary region in the Redwood Console (Settings → Data residency). See: {help_url}."

### 7) Streaming endpoints behavior
Residency enforcement MUST occur **before any streaming bytes are written**.

For streaming endpoints (SSE / chunked responses):
- If the request is blocked, the server MUST return **HTTP 409** with the standard JSON error body (i.e., do not start the stream).

Non-compliant behavior (explicitly disallowed):
- returning HTTP 200 and then emitting an ad-hoc "error" SSE event
- returning a generic 500 mid-stream
- closing the connection without a structured error

### 8) Retry semantics
Clients/SDKs MUST treat `residency_policy_violation` as **non-retriable by default**.

Exception:
- `primary_region_unavailable` MAY be retried with backoff, but MUST NOT attempt cross-region reroute by default.

### 9) SDK surface requirements
SDKs MUST:
- Create a dedicated, typed exception (name by language):
  - Python: `ResidencyPolicyViolationError`
  - TypeScript: `ResidencyPolicyViolationError`
  - Go: `*ResidencyPolicyViolationError`
- Include fields/properties:
  - `code` (always `residency_policy_violation`)
  - `subcode`
  - `message`
  - `request_id`
  - `help_url`
  - `allowed_regions`
  - `candidate_region`
  - `primary_region` (optional)
  - `policy_scope`
  - `policy_id` (optional)
- Preserve the raw HTTP status (409) and headers for debugging.

SDKs SHOULD:
- Provide a short default suggestion in docs/examples: “Check Console → Settings → Data residency.”
- Avoid automatically switching endpoints/regions unless the customer explicitly opts in.

## Error payload examples
### Example 1: Region not allowed
HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict
x-redwood-request-id: req_01J3H7Y0Q3J2QF3B4A1Z9PZQ0N
content-type: application/json

{
  "error": {
    "message": "Request blocked by data residency policy. This project is restricted to regions: eu. This request would be processed in: us. Update your residency settings in the Redwood Console (Settings → Data residency) or use an API key for an allowed region. See: https://docs.redwoodinference.com/errors/residency-policy-violation.",
    "code": "residency_policy_violation",
    "subcode": "region_not_allowed",
    "request_id": "req_01J3H7Y0Q3J2QF3B4A1Z9PZQ0N",
    "help_url": "https://docs.redwoodinference.com/errors/residency-policy-violation",
    "details": {
      "allowed_regions": "eu",
      "candidate_region": "us",
      "primary_region": "eu",
      "policy_scope": "project",
      "policy_id": "pol_8f2b1f2e4f1a"
    }
  }
}

### Example 2: Primary region unavailable (no cross-region fallback)
HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict
x-redwood-request-id: req_01J3H82A4K0YB2G9D6Z7E0ZVQ9
content-type: application/json

{
  "error": {
    "message": "Request blocked by data residency policy. The primary region (eu) is temporarily unavailable and cross-region fallback is not permitted for this project. Retry later or contact support if this persists. See: https://docs.redwoodinference.com/errors/residency-policy-violation.",
    "code": "residency_policy_violation",
    "subcode": "primary_region_unavailable",
    "request_id": "req_01J3H82A4K0YB2G9D6Z7E0ZVQ9",
    "help_url": "https://docs.redwoodinference.com/errors/residency-policy-violation",
    "details": {
      "allowed_regions": "eu",
      "candidate_region": "us",
      "primary_region": "eu",
      "policy_scope": "org",
      "policy_id": "pol_ba31c7a9c102"
    }
  }
}

## Implementation notes (non-normative)
- Gateway is the enforcement source of truth for formatting. Downstream services may attach structured context for logs/metrics but MUST NOT craft customer-facing payloads.
- Routing may detect a violation as a backstop. If so, it must return the same envelope/fields (or forward a gateway-generated error).
- Ensure request ID generation happens early (before policy evaluation) so blocked requests are traceable.

## Security and privacy considerations
- Do not include prompts, completions, embeddings, or customer identifiers in the error payload.
- `policy_id` is safe to expose only as an opaque ID (no encoding of org/project identifiers).
- `candidate_region` must not reveal internal provider region codes.
- `help_url` must point to public docs that do not reveal internal architecture.

## Consequences
### Benefits
- Consistent customer experience across endpoints
- Deterministic handling for streaming clients (no mid-stream 500)
- Clear remediation reduces support load
- Strong correlation via request ID

### Trade-offs
- 409 may surprise some customers expecting 403; mitigated by docs and SDK typing.
- Includes a small amount of diagnostic region info (allowed/candidate). This is intentional and bounded.

## Rollout / Migration
1) Implement contract in gateway (feature-flagged).
2) Update SDKs to surface typed exception and fields.
3) Update public docs and error catalog entry for `residency_policy_violation`.
4) Add conformance tests:
   - non-streaming block returns 409 + envelope
   - streaming block returns 409 pre-stream
   - request_id header/body match
5) After rollout, treat deviations (500s, missing fields) as P1 bug for residency-enabled orgs.

## Open questions (resolved)
- Expose policy identifier? **Yes**, as `policy_id` (opaque), optional.
- Which status code? **409 Conflict**.
- Streaming semantics? **Block pre-stream; return normal JSON error**.

Title: gateway: return 409 + standardized error payload for residency policy violations

gateway: return 409 + standardized error payload for residency policy violations

Context
We’re introducing Hosted data residency enforcement (region pinning) across routing + gateway. The gateway must return a deterministic, consistent error when a request is blocked by residency policy (instead of falling back, timing out, or returning generic 500s in some streaming paths).

This PR implements the public error contract for residency violations:
- Returns HTTP 409 (Conflict) when residency policy blocks a request
- Standardized JSON error payload with stable `error.code`, `error.type`, and `help_url`
- Works consistently for both streaming and non-streaming endpoints
- Propagates `request_id` and `residency.decision_id` for support/debug (without exposing full policy content)
- Maps internal policy-engine outcomes to a small set of public-facing reason codes

Motivation / user impact
- Customers with EU-only pinning should get a clear, actionable error when their request would route outside allowed regions (or when they call the wrong regional base URL)
- SDKs can reliably detect this as a residency issue and surface guidance (instead of treating as retryable 5xx)
- Support gets deterministic identifiers to locate decision logs and troubleshoot quickly

Behavior
- Non-streaming: respond with 409 immediately
- Streaming: if policy block is known before starting the stream, the gateway responds with a normal 409 JSON error (no stream initiated). If a block is discovered after headers would have been sent (should be rare; mostly during phased rollout), we terminate the stream with a final SSE error event using the same error schema and include `request_id`.

Public error schema (example)
{
  "error": {
    "type": "invalid_request_error",
    "code": "data_residency_policy_violation",
    "message": "Request blocked by data residency policy: allowed regions are [eu-central-1]. Update your project’s residency settings or use an API base URL in an allowed region.",
    "param": null,
    "help_url": "https://docs.redwoodinference.com/errors#data_residency_policy_violation"
  },
  "request_id": "req_01H...",
  "residency": {
    "decision_id": "rdc_01H...",
    "selected_region": null,
    "allowed_regions": "eu-central-1",
    "reason": "target_region_not_allowed"
  }
}

Notes:
- `allowed_regions` is returned as a comma-separated string to keep the payload stable across languages/SDKs and to avoid accidental JSON shape drift.
- We do NOT return `policy_id` in the public response. We do return a `decision_id` which can be looked up in internal logs.
- `help_url` points to docs anchors; docs PR will add that section (tracked separately).

Implementation details
- Adds a dedicated `ResidencyViolationError` type in the gateway domain layer with a strict mapping from internal policy evaluator outcomes.
- Centralizes error serialization in `gateway/errors/public_errors.ts` to guarantee the same shape for REST + streaming adapters.
- Adds regression tests for:
  - /v1/chat/completions (json)
  - /v1/completions (json)
  - /v1/embeddings (json)
  - streaming chat SSE path (ensures no generic 500)
- Adds structured logging fields:
  - `residency.blocked=true`
  - `residency.reason`
  - `residency.decision_id`
  - `http.status=409`

Rollout
- Guarded by feature flag `residency_enforcement_error_contract_v1` (default ON in staging, OFF in prod until routing enforcement is enabled per-region).
- When flag is OFF, behavior is unchanged.

Refs
- Linear: ENG-4833, PM-1490
- Support: SUP-28577 (streaming endpoint returning generic 500)
- ADR: ADR-022 Error contract for residency violations (implemented here)

Checklist
- [x] Error payload matches ADR templates (code, type, help_url)
- [x] Streaming + non-streaming parity
- [x] Unit tests + integration tests
- [x] PII review: no prompt/content in error message
- [x] Added logs for oncall triage
- [ ] Docs link validation (follow-up in docs repo)

2) `allowed_regions` is being returned as an array in one handler and as a string in another. We should standardize.

Amara Diallo (author)
1) Yep, updated `error.type` to `invalid_request_error` everywhere and added a snapshot test.
2) Good catch — moved serialization into `public_errors.ts` and made `allowed_regions` a comma-separated string in all responses + SSE.

Marcus Lin (security) — 2025-02-22

Amara Diallo (author)
- Removed `policy_id` from the payload; `decision_id` is a random ULID generated server-side per request.

Amara Diallo (author)

Kaitlyn Nguyen (auth) — 2025-02-24

Amara Diallo (author)

Approvals
