Title: Load shedding: consistent Retry-After + correlation IDs; document client retry contract

Load shedding: consistent Retry-After + correlation IDs; document client retry contract

Context: During canary we saw overload responses missing Retry-After on some routes (notably chat completions + a subset of streaming paths), which caused clients to implement ad-hoc retry behavior and in one case a retry storm. This PR standardizes how we emit Retry-After and correlation IDs for overload/load-shedding responses, and adds a short internal "client retry contract" comment block to keep behavior stable across gateway/routing/runtime.

What changes: 1) Retry-After is now set for all overload-class responses emitted by the API gateway (admission control + breaker open + dependency brownout mapping) and for propagated overload errors from downstream services when they bubble back through the gateway. 2) Correlation ID plumbing is tightened: we prefer an existing inbound X-Request-ID (if present), otherwise generate a Redwood request id, and we always return it to clients in both X-Request-ID and X-Redwood-Correlation-ID for a deprecation window. 3) Centralizes overload response construction into a shared helper that sets headers + JSON payload consistently (status, error.code, error.message, retry guidance, request_id). 4) Adds a code comment (internal contract) that documents semantics: when clients should retry, how to treat 429 vs 503 overload, and that Retry-After is in seconds.

Notes/constraints: - Retry-After is emitted as an integer number of seconds (RFC-compliant); we do not emit HTTP-date format. - For streaming (SSE) requests, we only attempt overload rejection before the response is committed; once headers have been sent, we cannot reliably add Retry-After. This PR ensures the admission decision happens before initiating the stream in gateway. - We do not change error codes/status mappings here (see ADR-014); this PR only enforces header + correlation id consistency.

Testing: - Unit tests for overload response helper (header presence, seconds formatting, correlation id behavior). - Integration test covering /v1/chat/completions streaming: overload rejection happens before stream start and includes Retry-After + request id. - Regression test for SUP-2860 reproduction (route missing header).

Rollout: Safe for dark launch; header additions are backwards compatible (additive). Client-visible change is improved consistency (some clients previously saw no Retry-After).
Ethan Park (review): Can we confirm Retry-After is always seconds (not date) and consistent across 429/503? Also please ensure we don't accidentally set it on non-overload 5xx.

Christine Wong (author): Yep. Helper only used by overload paths (breaker open, admission shed, downstream mapped overload). Added a guard test to ensure generic 5xx errors do not set Retry-After.

Aisha Bello (review): Please add a metric for missing Retry-After as a canary safety check. We should be able to alert if this regresses.

Christine Wong (author): Added api_gateway.overload.retry_after_missing counter (dimensions: route_group, region, status) and wired it into logging when helper isn't used (should stay at 0). No tenant_id dimension.

Ibrahim Khan (review): For SDKs we key off X-Request-ID today. Returning both X-Request-ID and X-Redwood-Correlation-ID is fine, but we should document the precedence and avoid breaking existing clients.

Christine Wong (author): Updated request_id.ts to prefer inbound X-Request-ID and always echo it back; X-Redwood-Correlation-ID is additive for now. Added comment in helper about deprecation window.

Mina Haddad (review): On routing fallback, we sometimes return an overload from routing with a retryable code. Are we certain Retry-After is preserved when routing returns its own error payload?

Christine Wong (author): Gateway now overwrites/sets Retry-After on mapped overload regardless of downstream body, but preserves downstream error.code/message. Also ensures request_id is our canonical id.

Nikhil Sharma (review): Please keep the "client retry contract" short and explicit. We should avoid promising exact backoff durations.

Christine Wong (author): Tightened language: we only promise Retry-After is present and in seconds; clients should add jitter and cap retries. No guarantees on exact window beyond header value.
Hosted API: overload/load-shedding responses now consistently include Retry-After (seconds) and return a stable correlation ID header for easier client retry/backoff and support debugging.

Title: ADR-014: Hosted overload error taxonomy (customer-facing)

ADR-014: Hosted overload error taxonomy (customer-facing)

## Summary
This ADR defines the **customer-facing error taxonomy** for overload protection in the Redwood Hosted API, including:
- Stable **error codes** and their semantics
- HTTP **status mapping** (primarily 429 vs 503)
- Standard JSON **response payload shape** (additive and backwards compatible)
- **Retry-After** header semantics and client retry guidance

This taxonomy is used by the API Gateway admission layer, Smart Routing, and serving runtime admission points.

## Context / Problem
The Hosted API experiences bursty workloads. During saturation, failures have historically presented as ambiguous timeouts and generic 5xx errors, causing:
- Retry storms and further overload
- Confusing customer experience (unclear whether to retry, when, and how)
- Difficult incident triage due to inconsistent error signatures across services

We need **stable, explicit overload errors** so:
- The platform can shed load early and predictably
- Customers can implement safe retry/backoff
- Support/SRE can quickly classify and mitigate overload scenarios

## Goals
1. Provide a stable, documented set of **error codes** for overload and rate limiting.
2. Ensure errors are **machine-actionable** (retryable vs non-retryable, suggested delay).
3. Avoid client breakage: payload changes must be **JSON-compatible and additive**.
4. Standardize headers and IDs for correlation across gateway, routing, runtime, and support.

## Non-goals
- Redefining billing/credit quota semantics (usage/billing errors remain separate).
- Introducing new SDK API surface beyond parsing and exposing these fields.

## Decision
### 1) Error envelope (JSON payload shape)
All overload/rate limit responses from Hosted API MUST use the following top-level envelope:

- Top-level object contains **"error"**.
- Required fields inside `error` are `type`, `code`, `message`, `request_id`.
- Additional fields are additive and optional.

**Canonical schema (conceptual):**
- `error.type` (string): broad category; see below
- `error.code` (string): stable machine-readable code; see taxonomy table
- `error.message` (string): human-readable; safe to show in logs/UI
- `error.request_id` (string): Redwood request identifier (also returned via header)
- `error.correlation_id` (string, optional): consistent across internal hops where available
- `error.retryable` (boolean, optional): whether retry is recommended
- `error.retry_after_ms` (integer, optional): suggested wait time (mirrors Retry-After when possible)
- `error.param` (string, optional): request field most related to error (e.g., `model`)
- `error.region` (string, optional): region that handled the request (e.g., `us-east`)
- `error.details` (object, optional): reserved for future use; MUST remain bounded and non-sensitive

**Example (503 overload):**
```json
{
  "error": {
    "type": "overload_error",
    "code": "overload_circuit_open",
    "message": "Service is temporarily overloaded. Please retry after a short delay.",
    "request_id": "req_01JDR6P3Q9G2V2H2QY9X2S8A1B",
    "correlation_id": "corr_01JDR6P3R1K9J8YJ9A0ZQ4TQG2",
    "retryable": true,
    "retry_after_ms": 2000
  }
}
```

**Backwards compatibility note:** Some existing clients rely on the presence of `error.message` and may ignore unknown fields. We will keep the `error` envelope and `message` semantics consistent. New fields are additive.

### 2) Required headers
For all overload/rate limit errors:
- `Content-Type: application/json`
- `X-Request-ID: <req_...>` (MUST match `error.request_id`)
- `X-Redwood-Error-Code: <error.code>` (best-effort; for quick grep)

For retryable overload/rate limit errors:
- `Retry-After: <seconds>` (see section below)

Optional headers (best-effort, may be omitted to control cardinality / privacy):
- `X-Redwood-Region: <region>`
- `X-Redwood-Model: <model>`

### 3) Taxonomy: types, codes, and HTTP mapping
We standardize on a small set of stable codes. Internal components may have more granular reasons, but they MUST map into this public taxonomy.

#### 3.1 `error.type` values
- `overload_error`: capacity-related refusal or dependency brownout handling (generally HTTP 503)
- `rate_limit_error`: tenant- or route-scoped admission control limits (generally HTTP 429)

#### 3.2 Public error codes
| HTTP | error.type | error.code | When returned | Retry guidance |
|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 503 | overload_error | overload_circuit_open | A circuit breaker is open at the gateway/routing/runtime admission point due to sustained saturation or dependency brownout. | Retryable. Respect Retry-After; use exponential backoff + jitter. |
| 503 | overload_error | overload_shed | Request was intentionally load-shed due to real-time saturation signals (queue depth, token/sec saturation, memory pressure proxies, regional capacity). | Retryable. Respect Retry-After; avoid immediate fan-out retries. |
| 503 | overload_error | overload_queue_full | Runtime admission rejected because per-model/per-pool queue is at a hard cap to protect latency SLOs. | Retryable. Retry-After is usually short (e.g., 1–5s). |
| 503 | overload_error | overload_dependency_unavailable | A required downstream dependency is degraded/unavailable (e.g., routing policy service, authz, internal model registry) and continuing would amplify impact. | Retryable unless specified otherwise; Retry-After may be longer (e.g., 10–60s). |
| 429 | rate_limit_error | rate_limit_exceeded | Tenant/route/model rate limit exceeded (token bucket / QPS). | Retryable. Retry-After provided when possible; otherwise back off conservatively. |
| 429 | rate_limit_error | concurrency_limit_exceeded | Tenant concurrency cap exceeded (especially relevant for streaming requests). | Retryable. Retry-After typically short; also reduce parallelism. |

Notes:
- We intentionally map overload conditions to **503** (Service Unavailable) rather than 500 to communicate that the service is healthy enough to reject safely.
- We intentionally use **429** for tenant/route admission controls where a customer can often mitigate by reducing call rate/concurrency.

### 4) Retry-After semantics
#### 4.1 Format
- `Retry-After` MUST be an **integer number of seconds**.
- We do not emit HTTP-date format.

Examples:
- `Retry-After: 2`
- `Retry-After: 15`

#### 4.2 When Retry-After is required
- For `503` with codes: `overload_circuit_open`, `overload_shed`, `overload_queue_full`, `overload_dependency_unavailable` where `retryable=true`: **MUST** include `Retry-After`.
- For `429` with codes: `rate_limit_exceeded`, `concurrency_limit_exceeded`: **SHOULD** include `Retry-After`.

If we cannot safely recommend a retry window, omit `Retry-After` and set `error.retryable=false`.

#### 4.3 Relationship to payload
- When `Retry-After` is present, the payload SHOULD include `error.retry_after_ms` equal to the header value in milliseconds.
- When streaming has already begun and headers cannot be modified, include `error.retry_after_ms` in the terminal error event (see streaming section).

#### 4.4 Client retry contract (documented guidance)
Clients SHOULD:
1. Respect `Retry-After` when provided.
2. Apply exponential backoff with jitter for additional attempts.
3. Cap retries (e.g., 2–5 attempts) and avoid unbounded retry loops.
4. Reduce concurrency when receiving `concurrency_limit_exceeded`.
5. Prefer idempotent patterns on retry (see below).

### 5) Correlation and supportability
- `request_id` is required for every error response and is the primary support handle.
- `correlation_id` is optional but recommended when a request traverses multiple internal hops (gateway → routing → runtime). If present, it must be safe to share with customers.

### 6) Streaming behavior
For streaming responses (SSE / chunked):
- If overload is detected **before any bytes are sent**, return the normal HTTP error response (429/503) with headers.
- If overload is detected **after streaming has started**, emit a terminal SSE error event with the same JSON `error` envelope and then close the stream.

**Example (SSE terminal error event):**
```
event: error
data: {"error":{"type":"overload_error","code":"overload_shed","message":"Stream interrupted due to temporary overload. Please retry.","request_id":"req_...","retryable":true,"retry_after_ms":2000}}

```

### 7) Idempotency and safe retries
- For non-streaming write-like operations (where relevant), clients SHOULD use `Idempotency-Key` to prevent duplicate work when retrying after 429/503.
- For completion/generation requests, retries can produce different outputs even if idempotent at the HTTP level; this is expected. The goal is to avoid duplicate billing/work where applicable and to keep retries controlled.

## Alternatives considered
1. **Use generic 503 without codes**
   - Rejected: ambiguous, hard for clients and support; does not prevent retry storms.

2. **Use 500 for overload to count as “server error”**
   - Rejected: overload is not an unexpected crash; 503 communicates controlled shedding and allows explicit retry guidance.

3. **Expose internal granular reasons directly**
   - Rejected: would create stability burden and potentially leak sensitive capacity/dependency details. We instead map internal reasons to a stable public set.

## Consequences / Follow-ups
### Implementation requirements
- Gateway, routing, and runtime must map local refusal reasons to the public taxonomy above.
- SDKs must surface `error.code`, `error.type`, `request_id`, and parse `Retry-After`.
- Observability should key dashboards/alerts off `error.code` and HTTP status rather than ad-hoc strings.

### Documentation and support enablement
- Developer docs: add a section “Overload and retry guidance” with examples for each code.
- Support playbooks: include quick explanation of each code and what data to request from customers (request_id, timestamp, region/model if known).

### Compatibility guarantees
We commit to:
- Keep `error.code` values stable once published.
- Only add new codes with documentation and release notes.
- Only add new fields (no breaking schema changes) under the `error` object.

## Appendix A: Message templates (customer-facing)
These are suggested `error.message` strings; services may vary wording slightly but should preserve meaning.
- `overload_circuit_open`: “Service is temporarily overloaded. Please retry after a short delay.”
- `overload_shed`: “Request could not be served due to temporary capacity constraints. Please retry.”
- `overload_queue_full`: “Service is busy. Please retry shortly.”
- `overload_dependency_unavailable`: “A downstream dependency is temporarily unavailable. Please retry later.”
- `rate_limit_exceeded`: “Rate limit exceeded. Please retry after the indicated delay.”
- `concurrency_limit_exceeded`: “Too many concurrent requests. Please reduce parallel requests and retry.”

## Appendix B: Quick reference (copy/paste)
- Use **429** for rate/concurrency admission controls.
- Use **503** for overload/circuit breaker/load shedding.
- Always include `X-Request-ID` and `X-Redwood-Error-Code`.
- Include `Retry-After` whenever `retryable=true` and we can safely recommend a delay.

Title: Intermittent 429 bursts for multiplexed websocket chat causing degraded UX

Intermittent 429 bursts for multiplexed websocket chat causing degraded UX

Issue summary: NimbusHealth is seeing intermittent bursts of HTTP 429 responses returned to multiplexed websocket clients on the hosted API during peak business hours. Impact: Users in their clinical triage chat are experiencing message failures and UI retries, increasing perceived latency and leading to dropped conversations. Scope: Affects ~10 client connection pools from NimbusHealth (enterprise account) in us-east region; seen across redwood-chat-small and medium models. Expected: Multiplexed websocket connections should see smoothing by token-level and connection-level rate limits with transparent backpressure, not sudden 429 bursts. Observed: Spikes of 429s lasting 20-40s every ~15 minutes, correlating with bursty fan-out from a single internal service. Steps to reproduce: 1) Establish multiplexed websocket session using shared API key for multiple browser clients (as customer implemented). 2) Simulate parallel message bursts (20 simultaneous requests over the same websocket multiplex) with messages that produce ~80-200 tokens. 3) Observe intermittent 429 responses returned with X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0 and Retry-After headers. Logs: Attached sample gateway headers and rate-limiter trace (see comment #2). Customer note: This started after migration to a client-side multiplexer used to reduce websocket count. Customer requests guidance on configuration to avoid disruption without dramatically lowering throughput.
Initial hypothesis: shared API key + multiplexing causes client-level bucket exhaustion because token and concurrency limits are aggregated per-API key in current rate-limiter config. Evidence: Rate-limiter traces show single token bucket hit (bucket_id=acct-nimbushealth) with short refill cycles; connection-level counters spike to 100+ concurrent inflight requests. API gateway metrics indicate per-key bursts coincide with 429 timestamps. Alternate hypothesis: upstream quota-service mis-evaluating multiplexed connection headers; less likely given consistent bucket_id. Mitigation applied: temporarily increased per-key burst window for NimbusHealth from 200 to 500 tokens for 2 hours via emergency override (PR referenced). Next steps: implement per-connection bucketing (split by websocket connection-id) as a more robust fix and add an opt-in config for enterprises using multiplexers. Engineering owner: Liam O'Connor (rate-limiter). Related work: design doc draft in linked Confluence page.

Short-term: emergency per-key burst uplift applied for NimbusHealth while engineering builds a connection-scoped bucket model. Follow-up ticket INT-33377 created for infra work.

Title: Client Handoff + Triage Landing Pad — Prep & Actions

Client Handoff + Triage Landing Pad — Prep & Actions

Purpose / quick context:
- Short: Capture everything I need to run a first 60–90m war-room + clean handoff to SRE/PM/Engineering for critical client incident. This is a personal landing pad — not the official postmortem.

Immediate objectives for first 30 minutes:
- Stabilize communication: confirm channel (slack #client-<org>-incident) and phone bridge if requested.
- Pull latest state: incident JIRA (JIRA-5923), last deploys, error-rate graphs, recent rollouts.
- Decide initial response tier: Is this page-to-oncall? (yes if P1 production outage or data loss).

Key info to gather (fast):
- Who reported and when: inbound from CSM at 08:07 PST, escalated by customer SRE.
- Scope: affected endpoints (/api/v1/generate, /chat-stream), % of traffic impacted ~40% (from dashboards).
- Impact: generation failures and latency >10s for >5% of calls.
- Recent changes: canary deploy 2026-01-17 (model pin + kernel swap) — check commit abc123.

Stakeholders / contacts (order to ping):
- Customer success: Maya Li (primary), Jamal Ortiz (backup) — call first to confirm customer expectations.
- On-call SRE: Omar Patel — priority.
- Serving runtime lead: Priya Menon — technical lead for kernel/model swap rollbacks.
- PM (product): Lina Gomez — for customer comms / timelines.
- Legal/security: if data exposure suspected, loop in security@redwood.

Initial comms templates (copy/paste, personalize):
- To customer (short): "We’ve opened an incident and our on-call is actively investigating. Initial investigations show increased latency affecting ~40% of requests. We’ll provide an update within 30 minutes with next steps. — Rene/Redwood CS"
- Internal Triage post (slack): "INCIDENT: JIRA-5923 — Elevated error/latency on /api/v1/generate. On-call SRE @omar on it. First update in 30m. Key suspects: canary kernel swap (2026-01-17) or KV cache regression. Link to dash: <dashboard-url>"

Triage checklist (first 60 minutes) — check off as done:
- [ ] Confirm incident channel + email thread + phone bridge if requested
- [ ] Snapshot key dashboards (latency, errors, QPS) + time window 30m pre/post spike
- [ ] Collect recent deploys and rollouts (deploy tags, model versions, quantization changes)
- [ ] Ask on-call to run targeted smoke: curl /health, /api/v1/generate with short prompt
- [ ] Check KV cache hit rates and batching latency metrics
- [ ] Validate fallback routes (model-variant, region fallback) are healthy
- [ ] Decide whether to rollback canary or scale dedicated pool

Decision criteria (quick rules):
- Rollback canary if errors spike correlated with canary hosts and rate >5% and customer impact is P1.
- If latency only at tail and local to a region, consider routing around region before rollback.
- If model outputs corrupted (data integrity), escalate to security and consider immediate rollback & disable model.

Action items (assign during call) — populate owners & ETA here:
- Create incident timeline note (owner: Rene) — ETA 20m
- SRE: run kernel/host health checks + attach sample traces (owner: Omar) — ETA 15m
- Runtime lead: validate recent kernel selection & compare perf on canary hosts (owner: Priya) — ETA 30m
- CS: confirm customer tolerance window and preferred comm cadence (owner: Maya) — ETA 10m
- PM: draft customer update if rollback needed (owner: Lina) — ETA 25m

Communication cadence (first 3 hours):
- T+0: Incident opened + customer ack
- T+30: Short internal status update (what we know, next steps)
- T+60: Decision on rollback / mitigation + customer update if impacted
- Every 60m after until stable: status updates, then shift to postmortem planning

Handoff checklist (to SRE/eng for follow-through):
- [ ] Save concrete artifacts: logs, request IDs, sample latencies, core dumps if any
- [ ] Push any agreed rollback through release-engineering checklist (link: confluence://deploy/rollback-steps)
- [ ] Assign postmortem owner once stabilized (preferably non-oncall)

Notes to self / heuristics I've learned:
- Keep comms templated and short; customers want cadence more than details early on.
- Early rollbacks can reduce blast radius but sometimes mask root cause; prefer targeted routing if viable.
- Lean on canary host logs — kernel selection and quantized model ops are frequent culprits for tail latency.

Open questions to resolve in call:
- Is there any scheduled maintenance in infra for the affected region?
- Any customer-side config changes reported recently?
- Are we seeing correlated increase in KV cache misses across models?

After-action quick notes (post-call to fill in):
- What we did (timeline entries) — fill and attach artifacts
- Who was informed and when (customer + execs)
- Short list of follow-ups with owners and deadlines

Scratch area (things I might paste into the incident):
- "Investigations pointing to kernel swap on canary hosts; rolling back canary while preserving traffic to dedicated pool. Temporary mitigation: increase pool size + route 30% away from canary region."
- "Sample request IDs: req_44af, req_44b0, req_44d9 — added to JIRA as attachments."

-- end landing pad --

(If this turns into a long-running incident, migrate notes to shared confluence page and drop this file into customer folder for record.)

Title: Streaming event model conventions (canonical for SDK + docs examples)

Streaming event model conventions (canonical for SDK + docs examples)

## Purpose
This page defines the canonical *example-level* streaming event model used across Redwood docs, quickstarts, and SDK READMEs.

**Goals**
- Provide a single mental model for streaming across Python/TypeScript/Go.
- Make copy/paste examples robust to real-world issues (partial deltas, tool-call argument fragmentation, disconnects).
- Standardize naming and logging so support and Solutions Engineering can quickly interpret customer logs.

**Non-goals**
- This is not a product-level protocol redesign.
- This does not introduce new SDK APIs; it documents how examples should consume the events that already exist.

---

## Definitions
- **Stream**: A sequence of events emitted by the server for a single request.
- **Event**: A typed envelope with metadata plus a payload (delta/final/error).
- **Delta**: Partial data emitted incrementally (e.g., assistant text tokens, partial tool args).
- **Final**: A terminal representation for a logical unit (e.g., a completed message, completed tool call), or the end-of-stream marker.
- **Transcript**: The assembled conversation messages (user, assistant, tool, etc.) that the client maintains.

---

## Canonical event types (examples MUST use these names)
Examples must treat events as an envelope with at least: `type`, `request_id`, and a type-specific payload.

### Event type table
| Event type | When it appears | What examples do | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `response.started` | First event for a stream | Initialize per-request state, record start time | Always expected for healthy streams |
| `message.delta` | Assistant is producing text (or other message content) | Append delta to the current assistant message buffer | Deltas may be empty or may arrive in bursts |
| `tool_call.delta` | Model is emitting tool call(s) with partial arguments | Accumulate tool call args as raw text; do not parse until final | Partial args are expected; must handle fragmentation |
| `tool_call.final` | A tool call is complete (name + args complete) | Validate + parse arguments; enqueue tool execution | Parsing should happen here, not on delta |
| `message.final` | Assistant message is complete | Freeze the assistant message, add to transcript | May arrive with or without prior `message.delta` |
| `response.completed` | Normal end-of-stream | Emit final assembled result; stop loop | The only “success terminal” event |
| `response.error` | Non-retryable failure (request rejected, validation error, etc.) | Surface error, stop loop, log structured error details | May appear after `response.started` |
| `response.interrupted` | Stream ended prematurely (disconnect, timeout, cancellation) | Trigger retry policy (if applicable) or fail with guidance | Examples should distinguish this from `response.error` |

**Important:** SDKs may internally expose slightly different shapes, but examples and docs must map to these canonical types for explanation, comments, and logging.

---

## Envelope and required fields (for examples + logging)
Examples should assume the following fields are available (or can be derived).

### Required fields to log
- `type`: canonical event type string
- `request_id`: stable identifier for the request (used for support correlation)
- `event_id`: monotonically increasing per stream if provided; otherwise maintain a local counter
- `model`: the model identifier used for the request (when available)
- `created_at`: server timestamp if available; otherwise local receive time

### Optional (recommended) fields
- `attempt`: retry attempt number (client-side)
- `stream_id`: if the backend provides a stream-level id distinct from request id
- `usage`: token usage summaries (often only present on final/completed)
- `warnings`: server-provided warnings (e.g., degraded mode, fallback model)

---

## Message assembly rules (assistant text)
Examples MUST assemble assistant content in a predictable way.

### State model
Maintain these per-request variables:
- `current_assistant_text` (string builder)
- `current_tool_calls` (map keyed by `tool_call_id` to a tool-call accumulator)
- `transcript_messages` (list of messages to show in examples)

### Assembly algorithm
1) On `response.started`:
   - Reset all per-request accumulators.
   - Log: `stream_start` with `request_id`, `model`, `attempt=0`.

2) On `message.delta`:
   - Append `delta.text` to `current_assistant_text`.
   - Print streaming output in examples only if it improves clarity (see “Logging guidance”).

3) On `message.final`:
   - If `final.text` exists, set `current_assistant_text = final.text` (final wins over delta accumulation).
   - Append an assistant message to `transcript_messages`:
     - `role = "assistant"`
     - `content = current_assistant_text`
     - If tool calls exist, attach them as part of the assistant message context as appropriate for the SDK.
   - Clear `current_assistant_text` (so a subsequent assistant message starts fresh).

4) On `response.completed`:
   - Stop consumption.
   - Return the finalized transcript and any usage details.

### Final-wins rule
If both deltas and a final are present:
- **Always prefer the final** as the canonical message content.
- Deltas are for streaming UX and intermediate logging only.

### Handling “no delta” streams
Some models/configurations may produce only `message.final` without deltas. Examples must still work.

---

## Tool calling assembly rules (partial args + finalization)
Tool call arguments may be streamed as fragments; examples must handle **partial JSON** safely.

### Tool call accumulator
Track per `tool_call_id`:
- `name` (string, may arrive early or late)
- `args_text` (string builder of raw argument text)
- `is_final` (bool)

### Assembly algorithm
1) On `tool_call.delta`:
   - Identify `tool_call_id`.
   - If `name` is present, set it.
   - Append `delta.args_fragment` to `args_text`.
   - **Do not parse JSON here.**

2) On `tool_call.final`:
   - Mark the tool call `is_final=true`.
   - Parse `args_text` as JSON.
   - Validate against the tool’s argument schema (or minimal required fields if no schema is available in the snippet).
   - If parsing/validation fails:
     - Log `tool_args_invalid` (include `tool_call_id`, tool name, and a truncated args preview).
     - Follow the example’s documented fallback (see “Error handling and fallbacks”).

### Partial-arguments guidance (must be explicitly called out in examples)
- Partial tool args are normal; they may be split across many events.
- Never assume a delta ends on a JSON boundary.
- Never run a tool until `tool_call.final` is received.

### Parallel tool calls
When multiple tools are requested:
- Accumulate each tool call independently.
- On each `tool_call.final`, enqueue tool execution.
- Examples may run tools in parallel *only if the language supports it ergonomically*; otherwise run sequentially but preserve ordering in logs.

### Tool result messages
After a tool is executed, examples should add a tool-result message into the transcript before requesting the model to continue:
- `role = "tool"`
- `tool_call_id = <id>`
- `name = <tool name>` (if required by the SDK)
- `content = <string result>` (JSON-stringified if structured)

---

## Structured output / JSON schema notes (streaming-safe)
Structured output is frequently requested alongside streaming, but incremental JSON is fragile.

### Canonical guidance for examples
- If you need reliable JSON validation: **prefer non-streaming** for the structured-output request, or stream but only parse at `message.final`.
- If streaming UI is required: stream deltas to the console, but validate only once the final message is received.

### Minimal safe parsing approach (examples)
At `message.final`:
1) Extract the candidate JSON string.
2) Parse JSON with a strict parser.
3) Validate against the schema.
4) If invalid: apply the fallback (see below).

---

## Error events, interruption, and retry conventions
Examples must distinguish between **terminal errors** and **interruptions** that may be retried.

### `response.error` (non-retryable by default)
Typical causes:
- Request validation error (bad tool schema, invalid parameters)
- Authentication/authorization failure
- Model not available / unsupported features for that model

Example behavior:
- Stop the stream consumer.
- Raise/return a clear error.
- Log `request_failed` with:
  - `request_id`, `type=response.error`, `status_code` (if present), `error_code`, `message`.

### `response.interrupted` (retryable depending on cause)
Typical causes:
- Client network disconnect
- Idle timeout
- Server-side transient disconnect

Example behavior:
- Stop the stream consumer.
- If safe to retry, retry with backoff.

### Retry rules used in examples
Examples should implement a small, deterministic policy:
- Max attempts: **2 retries** (total attempts = 3)
- Backoff: exponential with jitter (e.g., 250ms, 500ms)
- Retry only if:
  - The request is idempotent for the given example, AND
  - The failure is an interruption/transient network error, AND
  - The tool side effects are safe (see below)

### Idempotency + side effects
If the example executes tools with side effects (e.g., “send_email”, “create_ticket”):
- The example MUST either:
  - Use an idempotency key passed into the tool, OR
  - Disable auto-retry after tool execution begins, OR
  - Use a “dry_run” tool variant in the example.

Recommended convention for examples:
- Before running any side-effecting tool, generate `idempotency_key = <request_id>:<tool_call_id>`.

---

## Logging guidance (examples and supportability)
Examples should print enough to be educational *without* dumping sensitive payloads by default.

### Required log points (canonical keys)
Examples (and golden tests) should log the following events in a consistent shape:
- `stream_start`: `{request_id, model, attempt}`
- `stream_event`: `{request_id, attempt, type, event_id}` (only when running in debug)
- `tool_call_started`: `{request_id, tool_call_id, tool_name}`
- `tool_call_finalized`: `{request_id, tool_call_id, tool_name, args_bytes}`
- `tool_result_ready`: `{request_id, tool_call_id, tool_name, result_bytes}`
- `stream_completed`: `{request_id, attempt, duration_ms}`
- `stream_interrupted`: `{request_id, attempt, reason}`
- `request_failed`: `{request_id, attempt, error_code, status_code}`

### Redaction rules
- Never log raw authorization headers or API keys.
- Tool arguments: log a **truncated preview** (e.g., first 200 chars) only in debug mode.
- Structured output: log validation failures with a short reason + pointer to schema, not the full payload.

### Debug toggles
Examples should accept an env var or flag:
- `REDWOOD_DEBUG_STREAM=1` enables per-event logs.

---

## Golden test / fixture conventions (cross-language parity)
When examples are backed by “golden transcript” fixtures, they must:
- Assert a stable sequence of canonical event types (not raw provider-specific fields).
- Verify the **final assembled assistant message** text and tool-call arguments after `tool_call.final`.
- Include at least one fixture with:
  - fragmented tool args across multiple `tool_call.delta` events
  - an interruption and a successful retry

Recommended fixture naming:
- `streaming_text_only.<lang>.jsonl`
- `streaming_tool_call_fragmented_args.<lang>.jsonl`
- `streaming_interrupted_then_retry.<lang>.jsonl`

---

## Example snippets: reference pseudocode
These are not copy/paste SDK code; they represent the required control flow.

### Streaming consumer loop (canonical)
1. `start = now()`
2. `attempt = 0`
3. `while attempt <= 2:`
   - create stream
   - for each event:
     - switch on `event.type`
     - apply assembly rules
     - on `response.completed`: return
     - on `response.error`: raise
     - on `response.interrupted`: break and retry
   - `attempt += 1`
   - sleep(backoff(attempt))
4. raise “stream interrupted after retries”

### Tool calling loop (canonical)
- Consume stream until you have one or more `tool_call.final`.
- Execute tools.
- Append tool-result messages.
- Send a follow-up request (may be streaming) to allow the model to incorporate tool results.

---

## FAQ / common pitfalls (what examples must proactively address)
**Pitfall: Tool-call args look truncated mid-stream.**
- Expected behavior: args are fragmented across deltas.
- Fix: accumulate raw args text; parse only at `tool_call.final`.

**Pitfall: JSON parsing fails during streaming.**
- Expected behavior: incremental JSON is often invalid until complete.
- Fix: parse only at `message.final`; validate; retry with a stricter instruction if needed.

**Pitfall: Customers retry and accidentally double-execute a tool.**
- Fix: idempotency keys or disable retries after side-effecting tool execution begins.

**Pitfall: Mixing provider-specific event names in docs.**
- Fix: always present the canonical event types on this page; add a brief mapping note elsewhere if needed.

---

## Change control
- Owner: DevEx (SDK parity)
- Any change to canonical event names must be reviewed by:
  - SDK parity tech lead (Ibrahim Khan)
  - API/SDK semantics reviewer (Brian Murphy)
  - Docs owner for Hosted API (Wei Chen)
- If a change impacts fixture formats, update all language fixtures in the same PR set.

Title: ADR: Example-Level Payload Shape for Streaming Tool Calls

ADR: Example-Level Payload Shape for Streaming Tool Calls

## Status
Published (applies to examples in docs, quickstarts, and SDK READMEs).

## Decision summary
For **developer-facing examples** that demonstrate *streaming tool calls*, Redwood will standardize on a **minimal, stable event envelope** and a **canonical tool-call object shape**:

- Streaming events shown in examples MUST include:
  - `event` (string)
  - `data` (object)
- Tool call identity MUST be represented as `tool_call_id` everywhere (stream deltas, final tool call, and tool-result messages).
- Tool call arguments MUST be treated as **an opaque string during streaming**:
  - partial updates: `arguments_delta` (string)
  - final: `arguments` (string)
  - parsing happens **only after** the tool call is complete.

This ADR intentionally defines the **example-level** payload shape (what we show and teach), not the full internal wire format.

## Context / problem
Across Python/TypeScript/Go and the docs site, streaming tool-calling examples diverged in:

- Field naming (`id` vs `tool_call_id`, `function.name` vs `name`).
- Whether arguments were shown as JSON objects vs strings.
- How partial arguments were represented during streaming.
- How parallel tool calls were assembled when deltas interleave.

These inconsistencies contributed to:

- Copy/paste failures and type mismatches (e.g., TS example failures).
- Confusion about “truncated” arguments mid-stream (SUP-18421): users attempted to parse JSON before the stream completed.
- Support load due to unclear guidance on delta assembly and tool-result linkage.

The refresh project requires a single mental model that is consistent across SDKs and documentation.

## Goals
1. Provide a simple, consistent model for assembling tool calls from streaming deltas.
2. Avoid encouraging fragile behavior (incremental JSON parsing, relying on internal fields).
3. Make examples resilient to model variability (argument emission timing, interleaving).
4. Keep parity with common industry patterns (OpenAI-style semantics) without claiming strict wire compatibility.

## Non-goals
- Redesigning Redwood’s underlying streaming protocol.
- Defining every field available in the raw streaming payload.

## Decision details
### 1) Canonical event names used in examples
Examples will use the following `event` names. SDKs may expose richer objects; examples should map to these concepts.

| Event | When it fires | Required fields in `data` | Notes |
|------|---------------|---------------------------|-------|
| `message.delta` | Assistant message text arrives incrementally | `message_id`, `content_delta` | `content_delta` is appended to a per-message buffer. |
| `message.done` | Assistant message is complete | `message_id`, `content` | Examples may omit if the SDK returns final content elsewhere; if present, it is authoritative. |
| `tool_call.delta` | Tool call arguments arrive incrementally | `tool_call_id`, `name` (optional), `arguments_delta` | Deltas may interleave across multiple tool calls. Do not parse JSON here. |
| `tool_call.done` | Tool call arguments are complete | `tool_call_id`, `name`, `arguments` | `arguments` is a complete JSON string (still validate before use). |
| `response.done` | No more events for the response | `response_id` (optional) | Marks end-of-stream for the example loop. |
| `error` | Stream fails or server returns an error | `code`, `message` | Examples should demonstrate a single retry policy or a clear abort. |

Rationale: dot-separated names are readable in logs, consistent across languages, and avoid leaking internal event taxonomies.

### 2) Canonical tool call object shape
Examples will represent a tool call as:

- `tool_call_id` (string): stable identifier for the call
- `name` (string): tool/function name
- `arguments_delta` (string): partial JSON text during streaming
- `arguments` (string): complete JSON text when done

**Arguments are always strings** in streaming examples.

Rationale: during streaming, the JSON is frequently incomplete and not parseable. Representing deltas as strings prevents users from writing broken “parse on every chunk” logic.

### 3) Tool-result messages MUST reference `tool_call_id`
When returning tool output back to the model, examples must send a tool-result message that includes the `tool_call_id`:

```json
{
  "role": "tool",
  "tool_call_id": "call_01HZZ...",
  "content": "{\"temperature_f\": 71, \"conditions\": \"clear\"}"
}
```

Rationale: a stable link is required for parallel tool calls and avoids ambiguity when multiple tools share the same name.

### 4) What examples should *not* show
To keep examples stable and avoid implying unsupported semantics, examples should not depend on:

- Internal IDs unrelated to tool execution (e.g., per-token counters, shard IDs).
- Incremental JSON parsing of arguments.
- Assuming tool call `name` arrives before `arguments_delta` (models differ).
- Assuming tool calls cannot interleave.

If the SDK exposes a richer native event type, examples may log it behind a debug flag, but the canonical logic should operate on the minimal fields above.

## Example transcript (canonical)
Below is the reference shape used in docs/quickstarts for streaming tool calls.

### Tool definitions (request)
```json
{
  "model": "redwood/sonoma-3",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is the weather in Seattle right now?"}],
  "tools": [
    {
      "type": "function",
      "function": {
        "name": "get_weather",
        "description": "Fetch current weather for a city.",
        "parameters": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": {
            "city": {"type": "string"},
            "units": {"type": "string", "enum": ["metric", "imperial"]}
          },
          "required": ["city"]
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

### Streaming events (response)
```json
{"event":"message.delta","data":{"message_id":"msg_1","content_delta":"Let me check that for you."}}
{"event":"tool_call.delta","data":{"tool_call_id":"call_1","name":"get_weather","arguments_delta":"{\"city\":\"Sea"}}
{"event":"tool_call.delta","data":{"tool_call_id":"call_1","arguments_delta":"ttle\",\"units\":\"imperial\""}}
{"event":"tool_call.delta","data":{"tool_call_id":"call_1","arguments_delta":"}"}}
{"event":"tool_call.done","data":{"tool_call_id":"call_1","name":"get_weather","arguments":"{\"city\":\"Seattle\",\"units\":\"imperial\"}"}}
{"event":"response.done","data":{"response_id":"resp_1"}}
```

Notes:
- `name` may be omitted on subsequent `tool_call.delta` events; examples must cache it if needed.
- The arguments are intentionally shown as JSON text, not a JSON object.

## Assembly rules (normative for examples)
Examples (across languages) must implement the following assembly rules:

1. Maintain a map keyed by `tool_call_id` with:
   - `name` (string, optional until first seen)
   - `arguments_buffer` (string)
2. On `tool_call.delta`:
   - Append `arguments_delta` to `arguments_buffer` for that `tool_call_id`.
   - Do not parse.
3. On `tool_call.done`:
   - Prefer `arguments` from the done event if provided.
   - Parse once (`JSON.parse` / `json.loads`) and validate against the tool schema.
4. If the stream ends without `tool_call.done`:
   - Treat as incomplete.
   - Either retry the request (if safe and idempotency is configured) or surface a clear error.

This directly addresses the “arguments truncated” support issue: arguments are expected to look incomplete mid-stream.

## Parallel tool calls
Examples must assume:

- Multiple tool calls may be active.
- Deltas may interleave across tool calls.

Canonical behavior:
- Use `tool_call_id` as the sole key.
- Never assume “the latest tool call” is the target of a delta.

## Compatibility guidance (docs copy)
Docs should include a short callout:

- “Streaming tool-call arguments are emitted as text deltas and may not be valid JSON until the tool call is complete. Always assemble and parse after `tool_call.done`.”

If a page discusses OpenAI-compatibility, it must clarify that:

- The Redwood examples use OpenAI-like semantics (tool definitions + tool result messages), but the raw streaming payload may contain additional fields and may not be byte-for-byte identical.

## Alternatives considered
1. **Expose the full raw streaming payload in examples**
   - Pros: transparent.
   - Cons: noisy, unstable, encourages reliance on non-contractual fields.

2. **Represent arguments as JSON objects in deltas**
   - Pros: “feels typed.”
   - Cons: not feasible when JSON is incomplete; encourages incremental parsing and fragile merge logic.

3. **Standardize on OpenAI’s exact streaming schema**
   - Pros: familiarity.
   - Cons: limits Redwood’s ability to evolve payloads; risks implying strict compatibility where edge cases differ.

We chose a minimal envelope that is stable, teachable, and implementation-agnostic.

## Consequences
### Positive
- Cross-language parity improves (shared mental model and fixtures).
- Examples become more robust to model variability and interleaving.
- Reduced support burden from premature JSON parsing and ID confusion.

### Negative / tradeoffs
- The example-level shape is a simplification; docs must avoid implying it is the full wire contract.
- SDKs may need small adapter helpers to map native stream types to the canonical fields used in examples.

## Rollout plan
- Apply this ADR to:
  - Docs code tabs (Python/TS/Go)
  - Quickstarts “agentic workflow” template
  - `redwood-examples` runnable samples
- Add golden transcript tests that validate:
  - `tool_call_id` stability
  - interleaving correctness
  - presence of `tool_call.done` before parsing

## Open questions
- Whether `message.done` should be mandatory in the example envelope for all SDKs (some SDKs provide final message out-of-band). For now it is optional, but `response.done` is required in transcript-style examples.

## Owner
API Standards / DevEx parity: Ibrahim Khan (tech lead) with review by Brian Murphy (API/SDK semantics).

Title: eng-platform

eng-platform

Ibrahim Khan: heads up on examples refresh — we keep getting tripped up by OpenAI-compat behavior differences for tool calling + streaming. we should add a doc callout + a small compat table so we stop implying "1:1".

Wei Chen: +1. I’m updating the streaming/tool pages and I’m not sure what to claim re: payload shape. what are the actual diffs we care about for examples?

Brian Murphy: main ones I’ve seen:
1) tool call object shape differs (naming + where args live)
2) streaming deltas for tool args arrive as partial string chunks in OpenAI-compat; Redwood native examples usually show assembled/typed args
3) finish_reason semantics differ around tool calls

Dana Lo: for TS SDK examples this matters a lot. our canonical pattern is `event.type` + `delta` assembly. OpenAI compat stream gives you `tool_calls[].function.arguments` as a string that grows over time.

Mateusz Zielinski: Go example loop also assumes we can buffer tool args and parse JSON at the end. If folks try to parse on every chunk they get errors.

Ibrahim Khan: yep. support has tickets about "args truncated" because they parse mid-stream. (SUP-18421)

Wei Chen: ok can we enumerate exact field diffs? I want something we can paste into docs + link from examples.

Brian Murphy: quick list from my notes (not exhaustive):
- Redwood native tool call message uses `tool_name` and `arguments` as an object (SDKs surface typed map/struct).
- OpenAI-compat uses `tool_calls: [{ id, type: "function", function: { name, arguments: "{...}" } }]`.
- During streaming on OpenAI-compat, `function.arguments` is emitted as string deltas; not valid JSON until the end.
- Some models emit whitespace/escaped newlines in arguments; consumers should treat as opaque string until final.

Dana Lo: also parallel tool calls:
- Redwood native: we show multiple tool calls as separate call events, and you can run tools in parallel.
- OpenAI-compat: multiple tool_calls can be present in one assistant message; the IDs matter for mapping results.

Sabrina James: re examples: should we *show* both shapes in docs? or just one canonical and a callout box for OpenAI-compat?

Elliot Price: docs direction: keep one canonical example per page (Redwood SDKs), add an "OpenAI-compat notes" callout + a compact table. if we show two full examples per language it’ll explode the page.

Nikhil Sharma: +1. messaging should be: "Redwood supports an OpenAI-compatible API surface for ease of migration, but streaming/tool calling payload details can differ." keep it factual, no FUD.

Wei Chen: can someone draft a compatibility table I can drop into PR? i’ll tweak formatting.

Ibrahim Khan: drafted below. please sanity check:

Ibrahim Khan: 
Compatibility notes (Streaming + tool calling)

| Concern | Redwood SDKs (canonical examples) | OpenAI-compat endpoint |
|---|---|---|
| Tool definition | `tools=[{ name, description, parameters(JSON Schema) }]` | `tools=[{ type:"function", function:{ name, description, parameters } }]` |
| Tool call shape | `{ tool_name, arguments: <object> }` (SDK returns map/struct) | `tool_calls[].function.arguments` is a JSON *string* |
| Streaming tool args | Deltas may be emitted as partial fragments; examples buffer then parse once complete | Arguments arrive as incremental string chunks; do not `JSON.parse` until message is complete |
| Parallel tool calls | Examples may show parallel invocation and then send tool results back in any order with IDs handled by SDK | Multiple tool calls may appear in a single assistant message; preserve `tool_call.id` and attach results to it |
| finish_reason | "tool_call" / "stop" depends on model; examples should rely on presence of tool call events | May return `finish_reason: "tool_calls"` (or `"stop"` after tool_results); don’t branch only on finish_reason |

Brian Murphy: looks good. tweak: the first row is slightly off — we accept the OpenAI shape on compat, but for Redwood SDK we still present `parameters` as JSON Schema either way. maybe call the difference "wrapper".

Dana Lo: + add note that in compat streaming, tool_call *name* may arrive before arguments; arguments can be empty string for a bit.

Mateusz Zielinski: +1 also mention that some providers send `arguments: ""` initially and then append. our Go consumer should treat empty as normal.

Wei Chen: got it. I’ll add a callout:
- "If you’re using the OpenAI-compatible endpoint or an OpenAI client: treat `function.arguments` as an opaque string during streaming; buffer and parse only after the tool call is complete."

Connor O'Brien: does this need a release note? it’s docs-only but changes phrasing around compat.

Elliot Price: no formal release note, but we should link to the compat doc from the refreshed examples pages. also add to "known pitfalls".

Redwood Deploy Bot: build redwood-openai-compat#881 passed on main (docs updates + compat notes). (automated)

Ibrahim Khan: nice. can we link that PR in the docs refresh PR so reviewers see the source of truth?

Wei Chen: will do. also adding a one-liner to examples READMEs: "These samples use Redwood SDKs (recommended). If using OpenAI-compat, see compatibility notes.".

Brian Murphy: last thing: don’t claim schema-constrained output works identically via compat. some clients call it "json mode". maybe a footnote: "structured output guarantees vary by model; validate and retry".

Nikhil Sharma: +1. keep it consistent with PM messaging thread (structured output terminology). don’t promise strict JSON at every delta.

Sabrina James: action items I captured:
- Wei: add callout + table to docs pages
- Ibrahim/Brian: final wording on finish_reason + parallel tool calls
- Dana/Mateusz: ensure language examples mention buffering tool args, avoid parsing mid-stream

Ibrahim Khan: sounds good. I’ll drop a short snippet we can reuse in all languages:
"When streaming tool calls, buffer partial argument fragments and parse JSON only once the tool call is complete. Partial chunks are not valid JSON."

Title: KV + prompt explorations: microbench and eval notes

KV + prompt explorations: microbench and eval notes

Quick overview:

This is a scratchpad for a two-day microbench on KV-cache behaviour + prompt permutations against the 7B open model we onboarded last week. Goal: surface surprising latency/throughput tradeoffs when using small-group quantization and when prefix caching is enabled for short-chat workloads. Not polished — notes to self + TODOs.

Environment:
- model: open-7b-a1 (float16 baseline)
- infra: local dev rig (A100-40GB) + dedicated dev node (T4 pooled) for repeatability tests
- serving runtime: local build at commit b3f9d2c (kernel selection tweak for rotary attention)
- quantization tool: qconfig-v2 (per-channel symmetric, group size paramizable)

What I ran (high level):
1) Baseline float16, no caching, batch_size 1, seq_len 64 -> token latency ~ 48ms (p99 82ms)
2) 4-bit per-channel (g=128), no caching, batch_size 1 -> token latency ~ 29ms (p99 54ms), small quality drop on long-range completion (>120 tokens)
3) 4-bit + KV-prefix cache enabled (cache warm) -> token latency down to ~12ms steady-state (p99 18ms), initial token for new convo still 28ms due to cache warm-up
4) 8-bit + KV cache -> similar latency to 4-bit in steady-state but slightly higher memory footprint; perplexity on eval set ~+0.6 relative to f16
5) Group-size sweep (g=64,128,256) showed min latency at g=128; g=64 increased kernel call overhead (slower), g=256 increased quantization error on feedforward weights

Prompt/Chat experiments (short-turn chat workload):
- Prompt pattern A: system + short user prompt (10 tokens) -> good candidate for prefix caching. Observed that caching only prefix tokens (system+static context) gave 1.8-2.2x speedup vs no-cache.
- Prompt pattern B: long dynamic user context (~120 tokens) -> caching had less impact because KV cache dominated by dynamic prefix; still saw ~1.2x benefit in repeated-turn chats where earlier turns reused tokens.
- Prompt variations: using a light instruction template ("You are a helpful assistant.") vs heavy context (document paste) changed token distribution and therefore batch efficiency. Heavy contexts amplify KV memory pressure.

Quality checks (quick):
- Rouge-like sketch on 200 eval prompts: 4-bit g=128 retained ~97% of f16 ROUGE-L for short answers (<40 tokens). Degradation grows for >100 tokens.
- Behavioral glitches: occasional repetition when mixing cached prefix with dynamic system messages — hypothesis: cache invalidation rule bug when system message changes mid-session. Filed Linear RED-345.

Oddities / gotchas noticed:
- On T4 pooled nodes, the p99 latency for 4-bit quant jumped ~10ms compared to A100 for same config. Seems tied to kernel parallelism (fewer warps) and increased kernel-launch overhead. Follow-up: compare kernel launches per token for each device.
- When enabling streaming + KV cache, observed slightly out-of-order token emission for long sequences on dev build b3f9d2c — might be a scheduling race between batch flusher and cache writer. Add tracing around StreamFlusher.
- Memory reporting in console sometimes undercounts KV memory by ~200MB. Suspect accounting vs reserved-alignment rounding.

Commands / quick reproducibility notes:
- baseline run: ./bench/run_microbench --model open-7b-a1 --dtype fp16 --batch 1 --seq 64 --commit b3f9d2c
- 4-bit test: ./bench/run_microbench --model open-7b-a1 --quant 4 --gsize 128 --cache on
- collect traces: ./tools/collect_trace.sh --run-id $RUN_ID --include stream,kv,alloc

Immediate TODOs (ordered):
- [ ] Reproduce cache invalidation bug (RED-345) with minimal script (today) and attach trace (Riley to help)
- [ ] Add kernel-launch counters to the microbench harness (compare A100 vs T4)
- [ ] Try hybrid 4+8-bit profile: attention layers 4-bit, FFN 8-bit (quick patch) — see if quality/latency sweet spot exists
- [ ] Clean up prompt templates used in eval set and push small eval harness to repo (PR candidate)
- [ ] Add a per-request KV-size metric to Console traces to help correlate p99s to per-request cache size

Notes to self / ideas:
- Maybe try a tiny LRU window for dynamic tokens: keep last 64 dynamic tokens in a hot buffer, move older parts to cold storage — could reduce cache pressure for long documents with small returns.
- Consider exposing group-size tuning suggestions in Optimize UI: scan workload seq_len distribution, recommend gsize 64/128/256.

References / links:
- Linear RED-231 (KV rollout plan): https://linear.app/RED-231/optimize-kv-cache-rollout
- Kernel PR that touched rotary kernels: github.com/redwood-inference/kernels/pull/442

End of scratchpad. Will iterate and move useful bits to a proper RFC once reproducible artifacts and traces are attached.

Title: Incident Classification Policy (incident_type + owner required)

Incident Classification Policy (incident_type + owner required)

## Purpose
This policy defines when and how incidents must be classified using the **Incident Taxonomy v1** (incident_type + subtype), who is responsible for setting/updating classification during an incident, how to handle “unknown” classifications, and the enforcement rules that prevent closing incidents without required fields.

Classification is required so we can:
- Route mitigation work to the correct owning team quickly.
- Track incident volume and impact by type/owner.
- Measure remediation SLA compliance by severity and customer tier.
- Reduce recurring incidents through clear accountability.

## Scope
This policy applies to all incidents created via incident-bot and tracked in our incident tooling, including:
- Customer-impacting incidents (Hosted API, Dedicated, Private).
- High-severity internal incidents that threaten reliability (even if impact is not yet confirmed).

This policy does **not** replace root-cause analysis; detailed causal analysis remains in postmortems.

## Definitions
- **incident_type / subtype:** Required taxonomy fields selected from the v1 taxonomy list.
- **Owner (primary):** The single team accountable for mitigation coordination and driving the fix plan for the incident’s primary type.
- **Severity:** Sev0–Sev3 as defined in the standard incident severity rubric.
- **Tier:** Hosted / Dedicated / Private (choose the tier primarily impacted; if multiple, use the highest commitment tier impacted and note the others).
- **IC:** Incident Commander.
- **Scribe:** Person responsible for timeline and artifacts.

## Policy summary (requirements)
1) **Every incident must have incident_type + subtype set**.
2) **Every incident must have a primary owner team set**.
3) For **Sev0/Sev1**, classification must be set early (see timing below) and revisited during the incident.
4) Incidents **cannot be closed** (resolved/closed state in incident-bot) without:
   - incident_type
   - subtype
   - primary owner
   - tier
   - (Sev0/Sev1) a postmortem link or placeholder follow-up ticket

## When classification is required
### Incidents requiring immediate classification
Classification is required for **all severities**, but with different time expectations:
- **Sev0 / Sev1:** classification required within **10 minutes** of incident declaration (or incident-bot creation time, whichever is earlier).
- **Sev2:** classification required within **30 minutes**.
- **Sev3:** classification required before marking the incident resolved.

### Incidents created from alerts (pre-incident)
If an alert creates an incident automatically (or an on-call opens one preemptively):
- Set a best-effort incident_type/subtype immediately.
- If impact is unconfirmed, use the closest likely type and add a note in the incident channel: “Impact unconfirmed; classification provisional.”

## Ownership and responsibility (who sets/updates classification)
### RACI (practical)
- **Incident Commander (IC)**
  - Accountable for ensuring classification is set and accurate.
  - May delegate the act of setting fields, but not the outcome.

- **Scribe (or delegated responder)**
  - Responsible for entering/updating incident_type/subtype and confirming the owner in incident-bot.
  - Responsible for documenting any uncertainty and when the classification will be revisited.

- **Primary owner on-call**
  - Consulted on correctness of type/subtype and assists with refining classification.
  - Responsible for ensuring follow-up fix ownership is correctly assigned once mitigation is underway.

- **SRE on-call / SRE Duty Manager**
  - Consulted for edge cases and multi-cause incidents.
  - Responsible for arbitration if ownership/classification is disputed.

## How to classify during a live incident
### Step-by-step procedure
1) **Pick the primary symptom category** using the decision tree in the taxonomy doc (e.g., availability/5xx, latency regression, streaming disconnects, routing/fallback misbehavior, capacity shortage, control plane outage, auth/RBAC, telemetry blind spot, private connectivity/config).
2) **Choose a subtype** that best matches current evidence.
3) **Confirm tier** (Hosted / Dedicated / Private). If multiple tiers are impacted, select the tier with highest operational commitment impacted and note others in the incident channel.
4) **Confirm primary owner** via the ownership mapping matrix (incident-bot should auto-resolve this once type/subtype is selected).
5) **Announce in the incident channel** (one-line):
   - “Classification: <type>/<subtype> | Owner: <team> | Tier: <tier> | Provisional: yes/no”

### Updating classification
Classification is expected to evolve as evidence improves.
- Update incident_type/subtype when new evidence indicates the initial choice is wrong.
- When changing classification, post a short note in the incident channel:
  - “Reclassified from <old> to <new> based on <signal/logs/customer reports>.”
- If reclassification changes the primary owner, the IC must ensure the new owner on-call is engaged immediately.

## Unknown / ambiguous classification policy
“Unknown” is allowed, but it is not a final state.

### When to use unknown
Use **incident_type = unknown** (and **subtype = unknown**) only when:
- There is active impact (or credible risk of impact), and
- Evidence is insufficient to choose among two or more top-level types without guessing.

### Requirements when using unknown
If set to unknown, you must:
- Assign **primary owner = SRE (Reliability)** temporarily.
- Post a note in the incident channel with:
  - what is known (symptoms, impacted endpoints/regions/tenants)
  - what is unknown (missing signals)
  - the next 1–3 steps to disambiguate
  - the time you will revisit classification

### Revisit cadence for unknown
- **Sev0/Sev1:** revisit at **T+30 min** and **T+60 min** from incident start.
- **Sev2:** revisit at **T+60 min**.
- If still unknown at the second checkpoint, IC must explicitly ask for SRE Duty Manager help to arbitrate and pick the least-wrong category for reporting/routing.

### Prohibited use of unknown
Do not use unknown to avoid choosing between teams or to delay paging.

## Multi-cause incidents (capacity + routing, etc.)
Many incidents involve multiple contributing factors. For v1 reporting consistency:
- Choose **one primary incident_type/subtype** based on the **initial customer-visible failure mode** (what customers experienced first / what drove the page).
- Capture additional systems in:
  - incident channel notes (“Contributing: <system/team>”) and
  - the postmortem “Contributing systems/factors” fields.

If there is a genuine split-brain scenario (two independently failing systems with separate mitigations), the IC may open a second incident and link them, but this should be rare.

## Enforcement in tooling
### Closure gating
Effective immediately for new incidents:
- incident-bot will block transitions to **Resolved/Closed** unless required fields are present:
  - incident_type
  - subtype
  - primary owner
  - tier
  - (Sev0/Sev1) postmortem link or placeholder ticket

### Owner resolution
- The primary owner is determined by a versioned mapping (type/subtype → owner team) maintained in the control plane.
- If incident-bot’s resolved owner appears wrong:
  1) confirm the selected subtype is correct
  2) check the ownership mapping matrix
  3) escalate to #eng-platform-oncall or SRE if the mapping is incorrect (file a tooling issue)

### Override policy
Overrides are permitted only when tooling is malfunctioning or during force majeure events:
- Only **SRE Duty Manager** (or delegated SRE incident tooling admin) may approve an override to close without required fields.
- Overrides must include a reason in the incident record.

## Audit and compliance
SRE will track and review:
- % of incidents classified within target time (by severity)
- % closed with required fields
- reclassification rate (signal for taxonomy ambiguity)
- unknown usage rate and time-to-resolution from unknown → final type

Repeat non-compliance will be addressed through on-call training and, if needed, escalation to engineering management.

## Examples
### Example 1: 5xx spike due to overload
- Symptom: elevated 5xx + saturation signals
- Classification: Availability/Overload (subtype per taxonomy)
- Owner: Fleet/Capacity or Serving Gateway (per mapping)
- Note: If routing is failing to shed load correctly, keep primary as overload if customers see errors first; note routing as contributing.

### Example 2: Latency regression during rollout
- Symptom: p95 latency step change after model version rollout
- Classification: Latency/rollout regression
- Owner: Serving Runtime (if runtime change) or Control Plane (if policy/config), per subtype mapping

### Example 3: Private deployment connectivity after upgrade
- Symptom: DNS/TLS handshake failures in customer VPC/on-prem
- Classification: Private connectivity/config
- Owner: Private Deployments / Networking (per subtype mapping)

## Where to find the allowed values
- Taxonomy definitions + decision tree: Incident Taxonomy v1 Definitions
- Owner mapping + remediation SLA matrix: Incident Ownership Mapping and Remediation SLA Matrix

## Change log
- 2026-02-05: Clarified unknown revisit cadence and temporary owner = SRE requirement; added explicit reclassification announcement guidance.
- 2026-01-10: Initial publish aligned to ADR-0142 and incident-bot enforcement rollout.
