Title: Remediation SLA timers + breach alerting (with pause/override policy)

Remediation SLA timers + breach alerting (with pause/override policy)

Problem
- We approved a remediation SLA matrix by severity/tier (Hosted/Dedicated/Private) and incident_type, but today we do not enforce it consistently.
- ICs often lose track of “when do we breach” for mitigation/fix targets, and escalation is ad-hoc.
- We need (1) a deterministic SLA clock, (2) a way to pause/override for force majeure/customer-caused incidents with auditability, and (3) alerting for impending breach and breach events.

Scope (this ticket)
1) Implement remediation SLA timers keyed by:
   - severity (Sev0/Sev1/Sev2/Sev3)
   - customer tier (Hosted/Dedicated/Private)
   - incident_type/subtype (from taxonomy v1)
   - “time-to-mitigate” (TTM) and “time-to-fix” (TTF) targets
2) Emit signals and alerts:
   - warning at T-30m and T-10m for Sev0/Sev1 mitigation target (TTM)
   - warning at T-60m for Sev0/Sev1 fix target (TTF) when applicable
   - breach alerts to Slack + paging rules per severity/tier
3) Document and implement pause/override policy:
   - allow pausing the SLA clock with explicit reason codes
   - require approval + audit trail
   - ensure overrides are visible in dashboards and postmortems

Non-goals
- Re-defining the SLA matrix (owned by SRE + Product via PM-912).
- Replacing postmortem RCA; this is purely timer logic + alerting + policy enforcement.
- Perfect automation for identifying customer-caused events; we will require explicit human attestation.

Proposed SLA clock rules (v1)
- Start: when incident is declared in incident-bot (timestamp incident.created_at) AND severity is set.
- If incident_type is unknown at creation time:
  - start a “classification grace period” timer (15 minutes for Sev0/Sev1; 60 minutes for Sev2/Sev3).
  - after grace, use incident_type = "unknown" (conservative/default SLA targets per tier/severity) until updated.
- Stop TTM (mitigation): when incident state transitions to "Mitigated" in incident-bot.
- Stop TTF (fix): when incident state transitions to "Resolved".
- Severity changes: recompute due times from original start time using the new severity, but record the change in an audit log. (Rationale: avoid gaming by downgrading/ upgrading late; timeline is still anchored to start.)

Pause/override policy (auditable)
- Supported pause reason codes (single-select):
  1) force_majeure_cloud_provider (e.g., region-wide cloud outage)
  2) force_majeure_internet_backbone (broad internet routing issues)
  3) customer_caused (bad client deploy, exceeded contracted load pattern, misconfiguration on Private)
  4) planned_maintenance_window (only if pre-announced and explicitly linked)
  5) other_requires_sre_approval
- Who can pause:
  - Incident Commander may request pause
  - Requires confirmation from SRE on-call (or SRE program lead delegate) for Sev0/Sev1; for Sev2/Sev3, IC can self-approve but must provide reason + link.
- Enforcement:
  - pause creates an immutable audit entry with actor, reason, timestamp, and freeform note (required)
  - total paused duration is capped at 6 hours without explicit SRE Director approval for Sev0/Sev1 (recorded as a second audit entry)
- Reporting:
  - dashboards must show: paused_duration, pause_count, and pause_reasons distribution.
  - postmortem template must include “SLA paused?” + reason.

Implementation plan
A) SLA evaluator library
- Use slo-toolkit evaluator (see PR: sources/github/slo-toolkit/pr-311-incident-sla-policy-evaluator.json).
- Config source of truth:
  - read SLA matrix (type/subtype + tier + severity => TTM/TTF) from control-plane versioned config (ENG-4825).
  - provide a safe default when taxonomy is unknown (kept deliberately strict for Hosted; aligned with Dedicated/Private commitments via PM-912).
- Provide deterministic outputs:
  - ttm_due_at, ttf_due_at
  - state: on_track | warning | breached
  - breach_type: mitigation | fix

B) Incident-bot integration
- Store SLA fields on the incident object:
  - ttm_due_at, ttf_due_at, sla_state
  - paused (bool), paused_reason, paused_total_seconds
  - audit log entries (append-only)
- Commands (Sev0–Sev3):
  - /incident sla status (prints due times, remaining time, pause state)
  - /incident sla pause --reason <code> --note <text> (with approval rules above)
  - /incident sla resume --note <text>
  - /incident sla override --ttm <duration> --ttf <duration> --reason <code> --note <text> (SRE approval required; for edge-case contracts)

C) Alerting
- Slack:
  - warnings => #incidents (threaded on incident channel if available)
  - breaches => #incidents + #eng-sre
- Paging:
  - Sev0 breach => page primary owner on-call + SRE on-call
  - Sev1 breach => page SRE on-call; notify primary owner channel
  - Sev2/S3 => Slack only
- Alert identity includes: incident_id, tier, severity, incident_type/subtype, primary_owner, ttm/ttf due times.

D) Observability + dashboards
- Emit metrics (low cardinality):
  - incidents_sla_breach_total{tier,severity,incident_type,breach_type}
  - incidents_sla_pause_total{tier,severity,pause_reason}
  - incidents_sla_warning_total{tier,severity,breach_type}
  - incidents_sla_due_seconds{tier,severity,breach_type} (gauge, sampled)
- Guardrails: incident_type is from the taxonomy allowlist only; unknown/unclassified collapses to "unknown".

Acceptance criteria
- For any new incident created in incident-bot with severity + tier:
  - SLA due times are computed and visible within 60 seconds.
  - warning messages fire at configured thresholds.
  - breach messages fire when due time is exceeded, including a link to the incident and the runbook.
- Pause/resume works and is audited:
  - cannot pause Sev0/Sev1 without SRE approval signal.
  - audit entries appear in incident timeline + exported to dashboards.
- SLA evaluation is deterministic across severity/type updates:
  - due times update predictably and are recorded.
- Dashboard can show breach rate by severity/tier/type, and excludes paused duration correctly.

Rollout
- Phase 1 (shadow): compute due times + emit metrics only (no paging), 1 week.
- Phase 2 (warn): enable Slack warnings + breaches, no paging, 1 week.
- Phase 3 (enforce): enable paging for Sev0/Sev1 breaches.
- Include a kill switch: sla_alerting_enabled and sla_paging_enabled in config.

Links
- Confluence SLA matrix: sources/confluence/eng-sre/reliability-initiatives/incident-ownership-mapping-and-remediation-sla-matrix.json
- Dashboard spec: sources/confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/incident-taxonomy-dashboards-spec.json
- Implementation PR (breach alerts): sources/github/redwood/pr-28635-add-remediation-sla-breaching-alert.json
- Evaluator library: sources/github/slo-toolkit/pr-311-incident-sla-policy-evaluator.json
- Incident-bot closure gating (related): sources/github/incident-bot/pr-839-enforce-postmortem-link-and-owner-before-close.json

Notes / open questions (resolved in updates below)
- What is the default SLA for incident_type="unknown"? (Resolved: conservative defaults aligned to severity/tier; see config notes in PR-28635.)
- How to handle customer-caused incidents? (Resolved: require explicit pause reason + note + SRE approval for Sev0/Sev1; audit & reporting.)
- Force majeure carve-outs? (Resolved: pause reason code + approval workflow; still track total time for transparency.)
2025-12-12 (Allison Grant): Please keep incident_type labels to allowlist only; unknown bucket is mandatory. Avoid subtype in metrics to keep cardinality stable.
2025-12-15 (Lauren Bishop): Dedicated commitments: we need clear language that “pause” is an internal mechanism; customer comms should still focus on mitigation ETA and next update time. Also ensure cloud-provider outage carve-out is possible but auditable.
2025-12-17 (Aisha Bello): Align warning thresholds with how we run incidents: T-30m and T-10m for mitigation on Sev0/1 makes sense; fix warnings should be less noisy (T-60m only).
2025-12-20 (Dylan Brooks): Implementing evaluator in slo-toolkit to keep logic centralized. incident-bot will call evaluator with {tier,severity,type,created_at,paused_segments}. Control plane will provide SLA matrix config + kill switches.
2026-01-03 (Rafael Mendes): Approval rule for pause: Sev0/1 require SRE on-call ack; Sev2/3 IC self-approve but reason+note required. Cap paused time at 6h for Sev0/1 without director approval to prevent abuse; record as audit entry.
2026-01-09 (Dev Patel): Support request: make the incident-bot message include whether SLA was paused and why, so CS can avoid accidentally promising contractual credits during customer-caused events.
2026-01-13 (Dylan Brooks): PR up with end-to-end breach alerting + pause/resume commands; added config flags sla_alerting_enabled and sla_paging_enabled. Shadow mode enabled by default. Requesting review from SRE + Observability.
2026-01-16 (Sergio Costa): Dashboard panels updated to include paused_duration and breach_rate. Confirmed metrics are allowlisted and sampling is in place for due_seconds gauge.
2026-01-18 (Rafael Mendes): Marking Done. Phase 1 (shadow) enabled in prod; paging remains off until after one-week validation. Follow-up task: add a playbook section explaining pause criteria + examples (tracked in docs PR).

Title: Incident Ownership Mapping + Remediation SLA Matrix (v1)

Incident Ownership Mapping + Remediation SLA Matrix (v1)

## Purpose
This page defines the **primary ownership mapping** for each incident type/subtype in the v1 taxonomy, plus **remediation SLAs** (time-to-mitigate and time-to-fix expectations) by **severity** and **customer tier** (Hosted / Dedicated / Private).

The intent is to:
- Make ownership **unambiguous** during live incidents (one accountable team per incident).
- Enable consistent paging/escalation and reporting by type/owner.
- Set realistic but improvement-driving remediation expectations.

**Applies to:** customer-impacting incidents and high-severity internal incidents that materially threaten reliability.

---

## Definitions (used throughout)
- **Primary owner:** the single team accountable for mitigation and driving the incident to resolution (may delegate tasks but retains accountability).
- **Secondary owner:** team likely needed for mitigation/fix; consulted early; may lead specific workstreams.
- **Consulted:** subject-matter experts who may be needed depending on symptoms.
- **Time-to-mitigate (TTM):** time from **incident declared** (Sev assigned) to a mitigation that restores service to within agreed SLO/SLA guardrails (or to “degraded but stable” per policy).
- **Time-to-fix (TTF):** time from **incident declared** to a durable fix (merged + deployed or config updated) that prevents recurrence of the same failure mode.

**Severity scale (v1):**
- **Sev0:** complete outage / widespread critical customer impact; no viable workaround.
- **Sev1:** major degradation (sustained 5xx/latency/streaming failures) affecting many customers or a top-tier Dedicated/Private tenant.
- **Sev2:** partial degradation or limited-scope impact; mitigations exist; some customers affected.
- **Sev3:** minor impact / near-miss / internal-only reliability risk.

---

## Escalation and paging rules (global)
1) **SRE is always paged for Sev0/Sev1** (IC + comms + coordination), regardless of incident type.
2) The **Primary owner on-call** is paged immediately once incident_type is set (or once the IC is confident on a likely type).
3) If incident_type is **Unknown/Unclassified** after 10 minutes:
   - IC pages **SRE + Platform Control Plane on-call** (default triage), then updates type as soon as evidence emerges.
4) **Multi-cause incidents:** pick a **single primary incident_type** based on the *first-order driver of customer impact* (see taxonomy decision tree). Record other drivers as **contributing systems** in the incident record/postmortem.
5) **Security triggers:** if auth failures look suspicious (credential stuffing, impossible travel, token anomalies) or audit findings require, **dual-track** with Security Ops (see security alignment page).
6) **Cloud provider / force majeure events:** still classify and mitigate, but SLA breach evaluation may be paused per the carve-outs section below.

**Escalation path (when primary owner cannot mitigate quickly):**
- **T+15 min (Sev0/1):** page secondary owner(s) if not already engaged.
- **T+30 min (Sev0/1):** page engineering manager (EM) for primary owner.
- **T+60 min (Sev0) / T+90 min (Sev1):** page director for primary owner; engage executive sponsor (SRE) if cross-org blockers persist.

---

## Ownership map (v1)
Notes:
- Team names align to current rotations and Slack channels.
- “Service boundary” indicates the system most likely to contain the change/fix.
- Owner mapping is implemented in control plane config (versioned + auditable) and consumed by incident-bot.

### Top-level incident types → ownership
| Incident type (v1) | Subtype (v1) | Primary owner (team) | Secondary owner(s) | Consulted | Primary service boundary | Primary Slack | Pager rotation |

| Private deployments | Customer config / upgrade regression | Private Deployments/Networking | Platform Control Plane | Support, SRE | private-agent, upgrade-controller | #eng-private-oncall | private-networking |

### Ownership notes for common disputed boundaries
**Overload vs routing:**
- If the *trigger* is lack of GPU capacity / saturation / provisioning lag → **Capacity/Fleet primary**.
- If the *trigger* is incorrect policy, routing loop, or wrong fallback execution even with healthy capacity → **Smart Routing primary**.
- If both present, choose the type that best explains the *first-order* customer impact and list the other as contributing.

**Streaming disconnects:**
- If disconnects correlate with gateway errors, websocket/SSE resets, or ingress churn → **Platform Control Plane primary**.
- If streams are established but stall mid-generation with runtime errors/oom/kv-cache thrash → **Serving Runtime primary**.

**Auth anomalies:**
- If it’s clearly a production bug (token validation library change, cert rotation mistake) → still classify under **Auth/RBAC**, but **Security Ops primary** unless Security explicitly delegates to Platform.

---

## Remediation SLA matrix (v1)
These are **internal remediation SLAs** used for operational discipline and reporting. Customer-facing SLA/credit terms remain governed by contracts and published policies.

### SLA philosophy by tier
- **Hosted:** optimize for fast mitigation; durable fixes follow normal change management unless Sev0/1.
- **Dedicated:** stronger expectation for mitigation + fix because customers have reserved capacity and explicit commitments.
- **Private:** mitigation may require customer participation; our SLA focuses on *our* response/mitigation within Redwood-managed components and clear handoffs.

### Default remediation SLAs by severity and tier
TTM and TTF are measured from the time the incident is declared with a severity.

| Severity | Hosted TTM | Hosted TTF | Dedicated TTM | Dedicated TTF | Private TTM | Private TTF |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Sev0 | 30 min | 72 hours | 20 min | 48 hours | 30 min | 5 business days |
| Sev1 | 60 min | 5 business days | 45 min | 3 business days | 60 min | 10 business days |
| Sev2 | 4 hours | 10 business days | 3 hours | 7 business days | 4 hours | 15 business days |
| Sev3 | 2 business days | 30 days | 2 business days | 21 days | 3 business days | 45 days |

**Interpretation notes:**
- **TTM** = “service restored” or “degraded but stable” per incident commander + SRE sign-off.
- **TTF** requires a tracked change (PR/config) and deployment (or customer-delivered upgrade for Private, if the fix is on their side; see carve-outs).
- If a durable fix requires a longer roadmap change, the TTF can be met by delivering a **risk-reducing fix** (guardrail, rollback, safer default) plus a committed follow-up milestone.

### Type-specific adjustments (overrides)
Some incident types have different practical fix timelines. Use these overrides when applicable.

| Incident type | Subtype | Override applies to | Dedicated/Hosted/Private | TTF override | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---:|---|
| Control plane | Config write failures | Sev0–Sev2 | All | 3 business days | Config integrity bugs typically require code + migration; prioritize hotfix lane. |
| Telemetry / observability | Metrics ingestion outage | Sev0–Sev2 | All | 7 business days | Durable fix often includes capacity + pipeline changes; ensure interim mitigations (sampling, backpressure) are in place. |
| Private deployments | Connectivity (DNS/TLS/VPN/peering) | Sev0–Sev2 | Private | 10 business days | May require customer networking changes; our obligation is fast triage + clear “next action owner”. |
| Capacity / fleet | Regional GPU shortage | Sev0–Sev2 | Hosted/Dedicated | 10 business days | Durable fix may be procurement/provider constrained; require documented mitigation plan + capacity forecast update. |

**Who approves overrides:** SRE on-call for live incidents; post-incident, SRE program lead (Rafael Mendes) for reporting consistency.

---

## SLA timer start/stop + breach handling
### When the clock starts
- SLA clocks start when the incident is **declared** with severity (Sev0–Sev3) in incident-bot.
- If the incident is initially declared as Sev2 and later upgraded to Sev0/1, the SLA clock for that severity starts at the **upgrade time** (we retain the original for audit).

### When the clock stops
- **TTM stops** when mitigation is in place and validated via dashboards/metrics (or customer confirmation where metrics are unavailable).
- **TTF stops** when the fix is deployed (or config change is rolled out) and a verification check is complete.

### Pausing timers (allowed but audited)
Timers may be paused only with an explicit reason recorded in incident-bot:
- **Cloud provider outage / region-wide event** that is the dominant cause.
- **Customer-caused incident** (e.g., invalid client behavior, misconfigured private networking) once confirmed.
- **Force majeure** events.

**Pauses require:** SRE approval (Sev0/1) and a post-incident note describing evidence.

### Breach escalation
- Any projected TTM breach for **Sev0/Sev1** triggers:
  - Immediate page to primary owner EM at **T-10 min** to breach.
  - Escalation to director at breach time if not already engaged.
- Any actual breach triggers:
  - A postmortem requirement (Sev0/Sev1 always; Sev2 if breach is customer-impacting).
  - A follow-up ticket tagged **reliability-sla-breach** with owner + due date.

---

## How to use this during an incident (operator checklist)
1) Declare incident + set severity.
2) Classify **incident_type/subtype** using the decision tree.
3) Confirm **Primary owner** from mapping (incident-bot will resolve after selection).
4) Page primary owner on-call; add secondary owners if the boundary is unclear.
5) Track TTM and TTF targets in the incident channel topic (incident-bot prints due times).
6) If classification changes, update incident_type and record the reason.

---

## Examples
### Example A: Dedicated tenant sees 429s during burst
- Symptoms: 429s + queue depth + GPU utilization pinned.
- Classification: **Capacity / fleet → Dedicated tenant saturation**.
- Primary owner: **Infrastructure/Fleet**.
- Secondary: **Support/CS** (customer comms + burst expectations).
- SLA (Dedicated Sev1 typical): **TTM 45 min, TTF 3 business days**.

### Example B: Global spike in streaming disconnects after gateway deploy
- Symptoms: websocket resets, elevated gateway errors, runtime healthy.
- Classification: **Streaming → Stream disconnect spike**.
- Primary owner: **Platform Control Plane**.
- SLA (Hosted Sev1 typical): **TTM 60 min, TTF 5 business days**.

### Example C: Auth failures with suspicious pattern
- Symptoms: token validation failures, anomalous IP patterns.
- Classification: **Auth / RBAC → Token issuance/validation failures**.
- Primary owner: **Security Ops** (dual-track security incident if warranted).

---

## Changelog
- **2026-02-12:** Clarified overload vs routing primary-owner rule; added TTF override for regional GPU shortage; added timer pause requirements.
- **2026-01-24:** Added Private connectivity subtype details and clarified customer handoff expectations.
- **2026-01-10:** Initial v1 published.

IronPeak Systems - Inference routing and p95 targets discovery

Intro + qualification -> deep dive on p95 latency targets and streaming token/sec expectations -> hosted vs dedicated vs private decision factors (latency, caching, KV cache behavior, quantization) -> benchmark ask and next steps. Customer needs p95<=250ms for short turn responses and predictable capacity for peak spikes. Action: run token/sec streaming bench & share security pack.
p95 latency targets
streaming vs batch tradeoffs
concurrency and token/sec benchmarks
hosted/dedicated/private decision factors
KV cache/prefix caching
security/compliance (SOC2, KMS)

[00:30] Liam Ortiz: great, thanks. quick clarifying Qs: what's your expected concurrency at peak and typical tokens/sec per session?
[00:38] Tom Reed: at peak we estimate 400 concurrent users hitting the model with about 30 requests/sec, average 90 tokens per request, but token bursts can go to 600-800 tokens for longer responses. our SLA demands p95 for the first 200 tokens ideally.
[00:50] Maya Chen: cool, that helps. do you currently host models yourselves or are you using a managed API?
[00:55] Rajiv Patel: currently hybrid—we run some lightweight models on prem for compliance and use public APIs for heavier workloads. but running larger models in-house has been painful. looking at redwood as a unified path that gives us both predictability and the option to move sensitive workloads privately.
[01:10] Liam Ortiz: got it. for p95 <250ms with streaming on ~100-200 tokens, two levers matter: model variant and serving mode (dedicated GPU pools vs hosted). also batching behavior and prefix/KV caching will change effective throughput.
[01:25] Sofia Gomez: we've found prefix reuse is huge; many conversations start with the same system prompt and user context, so any caching would help a lot. how mature is redwood's kv cache and prefix caching?
[01:34] Liam Ortiz: we have an automatic prefix caching layer in the runtime—it's not perfect in the transcript sorry—uh, the KV cache stores activations per session when appropriate. it reduces token compute for repeated prefixes. in dedicated deployments we can pin cache locality to GPUs to avoid cross-host hops. in hosted mode it's available but subject to eviction policies under heavy load.
[01:52] Tom Reed: eviction policies—what controls those? is it LRU, time-based, or by memory pressure?
[01:58] Liam Ortiz: mostly LRU plus memory-pressure heuristics, and you can set TTLs in Dedicated. in Private we can tune eviction aggressively to keep your working set resident.
[02:08] Rajiv Patel: latency wise, how do you get down to 200ms? we're worried about attention kernels and long contexts.
[02:14] Liam Ortiz: kernel selection + quantization profiles. for shorter tokens we pick optimized attention kernels and use int8/4 quantization where quality permits. also continuous batching can be tuned—if you enable micro-batching you trade a few ms for higher throughput. since you want p95 strict, we recommend Dedicated low-latency pool with small batch sizes and no micro-batching for customer-facing streaming.

[03:03] Rajiv Patel: hmm, to meet our 400 concurrent users at 30 rps, what's that translate to?
[03:08] Liam Ortiz: quick calc—if average req is 90 tokens and 400 concurrent with 30 rps, you'd need to model request concurrency differently. but roughly: tokens per second demand = 30 rps * 90 tokens = 2700 tokens/sec average. with a 7B at 1000 tokens/sec you'd need ~3 GPUs steady state, with headroom for burst maybe 5+ and autoscale. 13B at 300 tokens/sec would need ~9 GPUs steady state. this is simplified—real deployment tweaks (batching, cache) can reduce that need.
[03:36] Tom Reed: ok that math helps. can we run a redwood-provided token/sec benchmark with our prompt set? we want apples-to-apples.
[03:43] Maya Chen: absolutely. next step is Liam runs a tokenburst benchmark against a hosted sandbox and we run a dedicated bench if you want on-prem sim. we'll need your sample prompts and representative concurrency pattern.

[03:58] Rajiv Patel: security: we need SOC2, SSO (SAML/Okta), KMS for key management, and audit logs retained for 1 year. how does redwood support that across hosting modes?
[04:10] Liam Ortiz: hosted supports SOC2 and SAML; KMS for key encryption at rest is available via provider-managed keys, and audit logs are on by default with configurable retention. Dedicated and Private give you more control—Private lets you bring your own KMS/HSM and keep logs in your VPC. i'll flag that in the security pack.
[04:26] Tom Reed: good. what about multi-region failover? we need <500ms region-to-region failover for availability.
[04:33] Liam Ortiz: smart routing can route by policy and we have warm standby replicas. failover adds latency initially but we can route to fallback smaller models to keep responses online while warm-up happens.

Title: Persistent kernel SM phase separation - Nsight notes

Persistent kernel SM phase separation - Nsight notes

Goal:
- Understand why the persistent kernel we launched to amortize kernel-launch overhead shows phase-like SM behavior in Nsight captures: bursts of high SM activity followed by low utilization windows rather than steady utilization.
- Determine whether this is scheduling (grid/CTA placement), memory subsystem backpressure, or kernel-side idle (waiting on async copy / stream ordering).

Context / quick summary:
- This is a follow-up to microbatch experiments where average occupancy looked OK but tail latency increased under mixed-length sequences. We switched to a persistent-kernel prototype (single long-running kernel that services many requests via device-side queues) to reduce launch overhead.
- Observed: in long Nsight timelines (30s captures), SM active ratio oscillates at ~200-400ms periods: ~60-90% utilization windows then 5-15% windows.
- Hypothesis: either (A) persistent kernel stalls waiting on device-side queue pop when work is sparse, (B) memory system flushes / cache thrashing between batches (KV cache interference), or (C) stream/async-copy synchronization (host enqueues large memcpy bursts) creates interference across other concurrent kernels.

Test environment / reproducibility notes:
- HW: A100-40GB, driver 525.xx, CUDA 12.2. Nsight Systems capture 2026-03-08 v2026.1.
- Runtime: serving-runtime branch persistent-queue-proto (PR-738), compiled with -O3, sm_80 kernels, use cuGraph / CUDA graphs only for fallback path (not for persistent kernel).
- Workload: mixed prompt lengths: 32 tokens (50%); 512 tokens (30%); 1024 tokens (20%). Arrival: Poisson lambda tuned to target 1800 tokens/s aggregate.
- Capture flags: nsight --trace=cuda,nvtx --sampling-interval-ms=1 --kernel-chunk=1 --duration=30s. Additional ptx-level counters collected: global_load_stalled, inst_issued, sm_efficiency, l2_hit_rate (estimated).

Key observations from capture (high-level):
1) Timeline visualization:
   - Persistent kernel shows long-lived execution block (as expected). Inside the block, per-SM activity shows sharp phase shifts: clusters of CTAs with high IPC and memory throughput followed by quiet periods.
   - When the quiet periods hit, other short-lived helper kernels (host-triggered copy kernels + fallback kernels) spike. Those helper spikes align with tail windows.

2) Counters and metrics:
   - SM Efficiency during active windows: 78–92% (good). During quiet windows: 8–18%.
   - L2 traffic: sustained during active windows, drops during quiet. But per-SM global-load-stalled increases during quiet windows (weird).
   - Async copy streams: timeline shows bursts of cudaMemcpyAsync calls from host every ~250ms, which correspond to helper kernels launching to re-balance device-side queue memory buffers. Those memcpy bursts appear to preempt device memory bandwidth and temporarily pause persistent-kernel progress.

3) NVTX annotations:
   - Device-side queue handling (device_pop) marked; host-side refill marked. The quiet windows align with host refill windows where host does bulk cudaMemcpyAsync to update request buffers.

4) CUDA graph interactions:
   - Not used by persistent-kernel path in this run, but we ran a control run with CUDA graphs for fallback kernels. When fallback uses cudaGraphInstantiate/Launch, we still see the same phase effect, implying the root cause is not graph overhead but memory bandwidth/contention.

Micro-experiments run from the capture insights:
- Experiment A: reduce host bulk memcpy size by splitting refills into 8 smaller async copies spaced 10ms apart. Result: phase amplitude reduced, but quiet windows still present. Tail latency reduced ~12%.
- Experiment B: pin host-side refill thread to a dedicated CPU core, increase NIC/PCIe priority (where applicable). Result: minor improvement.
- Experiment C: throttle persistent kernel internal polling backoff (exponential backoff when queue empty). Result: reduces frequent low-amplitude oscillations but doesn't remove 250ms windowing.
- Experiment D: enforce cudaStreamSynchronize on helper copy streams (serializes refills). Result: removes synchronization jitter between helper kernels but increases average latency — bad tradeoff.

Interpretation / current working hypothesis:
- The persistent kernel itself is compute/latency efficient when it has work. The low-util windows are primarily caused by bursts of host-driven refills that saturate device copy engine (DMA/PCIe) and temporarily reduce available device memory bandwidth and scheduling headroom, which indirectly increases global_load_stalled for the persistent kernel and causes SMs to stall.
- There may be a contributing factor of device-side queue design: if queue empty condition triggers a host refill of large contiguous buffer, the persistent kernel sees a relatively long wait while host prepares the next batch. Splitting refills helps but doesn't fully fix because scheduling and PCIe flush semantics lead to periodic contention.

Immediate mitigations to prototype:
- Change refill strategy: switch from large bulk memcpy to ring-buffered small pages with double buffering (producer writes into a buffer already enqueued), aiming to avoid large PCIe bursts. (Low-risk, mid-effort).
- Tune persistent kernel polling: add adaptive sleep/backoff that correlates with observed refill cadence to avoid tight busy-wait during expected refill windows. (Low-effort).
- Move more of refill cost onto device: investigate RDMA or GPUDirect where possible, and explore batching host-to-device via pinned pages to reduce PCIe transactions. (Longer-term).
- Add NVTX + fine-grained counters around memory copy APIs to get better correlation in future captures.

Open questions / next steps:
- Are other concurrent workloads (multi-tenant) on the same device able to trigger similar phase shifts? We should run a multi-tenant synthetic to see cross-tenant interference.
- Confirm whether L2 eviction patterns change during refills; collect L2 tag counters next capture.
- Try using cudaMemcpyAsync with different stream priorities (high/low) to see if copy engine prioritization helps.
- Explore converting persistent kernel to be less memory-bound by prefetching KV cache entries before serving, so main loop has less PCIe/host visible stalls.

Quick checklist / action items (owners):
- Rafael: implement ring-buffered small-page refill prototype and run 60s Nsight capture (due 2026-03-18).
- Priya: add L2 and global_load_stalled detailed counters + NVTX around memcpy (due 2026-03-15).
- Evan: run multi-tenant interference test (two model contexts) and record tail latencies (due 2026-03-16).
- Me (Maya): update PR-738 with adaptive backoff heuristic and benchmark (due 2026-03-14).

Notes-to-self / random observations:
- Persistent kernels help a lot for short sequences — latency up to 25% improved — but the periodic stalls kill tail. The perf-win is still there but unpredictable.
- Consider a hybrid: persistent kernel + occasional short kernel launches to drain backlog if persistent enters idle for > X ms. Might reduce starvation.

References / related tickets:
- GH Issue: serving-runtime/issues/812 (linked above) — contains telemetry for earlier runs.
- Confluence draft: persistent-kernel-design (internal) — diagrams of queue layout.

Appendix (commands / capture shorthand):
- nsight capture: nsight-sys --output capture-0308.qdrep --capture-duration 30s --trace=cuda,nvtx --sampling-interval-ms=1 --metrics sm_efficiency,ipc,global_load_stalled,l2_hit_rate

reference.text:
Title: Quickstart Templates: KPI + telemetry requirements (events, tags, dashboards)

Quickstart Templates: KPI + telemetry requirements (events, tags, dashboards)

Goal
Define a minimal, privacy-safe telemetry spec for Quickstart Templates (RAG + agents) so we can measure adoption + activation ("time-to-first-success"), and so Console/Analytics can segment template-originated traffic.

This ticket produces:
1) Event + tag definitions (what we capture, where it’s emitted, cardinality rules)
2) Source-of-truth definitions for KPIs (especially TTFS)
3) Implementation guidance for SDK/templates + gateway allow-listing
4) Dashboard requirements for Console/Analytics

Context
DevEx is shipping language templates + a small CLI (init/doctor) and wants to measure:
- template adoption (created projects, active installs)
- activation (successful first run)
- retention (active installs after N days)
- support deflection (docs/troubleshooting effectiveness)

Constraints
- Must not leak prompts, user content, PII, or customer identifiers.
- Must avoid high-cardinality dimensions in metrics.
- Tagging must work behind restrictive corporate proxies; telemetry should be opt-in and degrade gracefully.

Non-goals
- Full product analytics instrumentation for all SDK usage.
- Any per-user tracking requiring customer consent flows.
- Capturing document contents, embeddings payloads, or tool outputs.

Proposed measurement model (high level)
We measure template success primarily via:
A) CLI/template-local events (init, doctor, deploy) -> sent to analytics via a lightweight endpoint (opt-in)
B) API request tagging (template tags on inference calls) -> server-side derived KPIs (first successful completion)
C) OTel spans/metrics (for operational visibility) -> not used as the primary source for product KPIs

KPI definitions (v1)
1) Activation rate: % of installs that reach a first successful completion within 60 minutes of init
- numerator: installs with a "first_success" within window
- denominator: installs with init

2) Time-to-first-success (TTFS)
TTFS is computed per install_id as:
- start: template_init timestamp (CLI) OR first tagged API request timestamp (fallback if CLI telemetry disabled)
- end: first API response that meets "success" criteria
- report median / p75 / p90 by template_name + language

Success criteria (for the API-derived end event):
- HTTP 2xx from inference endpoint
- streamed responses must complete normally (no client disconnect before final chunk) OR non-streaming returns a complete response
- response has > 0 output tokens
- not classified as a retry-exhausted/network failure

3) Template retention (D7)
% of installs that have >= 1 tagged successful completion on day 7 (UTC) after init

4) Support deflection proxy metric
Reduction in template-related tickets per 100 active installs (requires Support tagging alignment; tracked separately)

Telemetry: required tags (used for segmentation)
These are the only tags we intend to use for KPI dashboards.

Tag keys (stable):
- rw.template.name: e.g. "rag-agent"
- rw.template.lang: "python" | "typescript"
- rw.template.version: semantic version from template release (e.g. "0.3.1")
- rw.template.install_id: UUID v4 generated on init (stored locally in .redwood/template.json)
- rw.template.channel: "cli" | "github" (set by scaffolder; github = user cloned/copied)

Optional tags (allowed but not required for v1 KPIs):
- rw.template.deployment: "local" | "docker" | "kubernetes" | "fly" | "render" (bounded set)
- rw.template.vectorstore: "local" | "hosted" | "none" (bounded set)

Rules
- install_id must be random (UUID v4) and never derived from user/device identifiers.
- Do not include repo name, file paths, hostname, email, org name, customer_id, IP address, prompt text, retrieved chunks, or tool output.
- Values must be from bounded enumerations where possible. template.version is the only semi-unbounded field; OK for event analytics, NOT for metrics cardinality.

Where tags are emitted
1) API request tagging (primary)
Templates must attach the tags to inference requests via a Redwood-supported mechanism.
Implementation guidance (v1):
- Prefer a single allow-listed header carrying encoded key/value pairs (validated at gateway)
  - Header name: "x-redwood-template-tags"
  - Format: semicolon-separated "k=v" pairs; keys restricted to the list above; values length-limited (<= 64 chars per value)
- If header is blocked by a corporate proxy, templates must allow users to disable it via env var:
  - REDWOOD_TEMPLATE_TELEMETRY=off
- For users who disable headers, we still compute partial TTFS using first tagged API request if available; otherwise only CLI funnel metrics (if enabled)

2) CLI events (secondary)
CLI emits minimal events to Redwood analytics endpoint (opt-in). These events are useful for funnel drop-off analysis that the gateway can’t see.

CLI event schema (all fields optional except event_name + timestamp):
- event_name
- timestamp
- rw.template.name/lang/version/install_id/channel
- outcome: "success" | "failure" (for doctor/deploy)
- error_class (bounded; see below)

Event list (v1)
A) CLI events
1. template_init
- emitted when CLI scaffolds a project successfully
- includes: name/lang/version/install_id/channel

2. template_doctor_run
- emitted at start and end (two events or one with outcome)
- includes outcome and error_class if failure

3. template_deploy_attempt
- emitted when user runs deploy command (if we ship it in v1) OR runs guided deploy script

4. template_deploy_success

B) API-derived “activation” events (server-side)
These are derived by Analytics from tagged traffic; templates do not emit explicit “success” events.
5. template_first_tagged_request
- first time we see install_id on an API request

6. template_first_success
- first time we see a successful completion per install_id

Error taxonomy (bounded values)
Used ONLY for CLI outcomes + (optionally) template-local error reporting; not required for API-derived KPIs.
- auth_invalid_key
- auth_missing_key
- quota_rate_limited (429)
- quota_insufficient_balance
- network_timeout
- network_dns
- network_tls
- streaming_disconnect
- tool_schema_validation
- retrieval_empty
- retrieval_backend_error
- config_invalid
- otel_exporter_misconfigured
- unknown

Dashboard requirements (Console/Analytics)
1) Templates overview
- Active installs (7d)
- Activation rate (60m)
- Median TTFS (by template + lang)
- Top failure classes from CLI doctor (last 7d)

2) Funnel dashboard
init -> first_tagged_request -> first_success -> deploy_success (if available)
- drop-off at each step
- breakdown by lang and channel (cli vs github)

3) Operational correlation (link-out)
From a segment (template_name/lang) provide links to:
- template-tagged traffic filters in Console usage analytics
- SLO dashboard from observability-pack (latency, error rate, streaming disconnect rate)

Open questions / decisions
- Decision: make header-based tagging opt-in and documented due to known proxy header restrictions. Default remains ON for CLI-created projects, but README must include “turn off telemetry tags” option.
- Decision: do not use OTel as KPI source-of-truth (sampling + customer-controlled collectors make it unreliable for adoption metrics).

Acceptance criteria
- Written spec (this ticket) reviewed by DevEx + Observability + Privacy/Security.
- Analytics can compute TTFS and activation rate using:
  - CLI init events when available
  - API-derived first_success from tagged requests
- Cardinality guidelines documented and agreed (no freeform tags).
- Console/Analytics owners confirm dashboard fields and filtering requirements.

Links / related work
- PR: redwood-quickstarts #115 (template telemetry tags)
- PR: redwood monorepo #18421 (gateway allowlist for telemetry header)
- PR: redwood monorepo #18439 (Console filter for template-tagged traffic)
- Thread: #devex "template-telemetry-tagging-and-privacy" (opt-in + redaction)

Notes for implementers
- SDKs should expose a safe, explicit hook for passing template tags without requiring userland header mutation.
- Ensure request-id propagation: log fields must include Redwood request_id and install_id (install_id only if telemetry is enabled).
- Any telemetry endpoint for CLI must accept anonymous, unauthenticated events OR use API key with strict rate limits; do not require user identity.

2025-02-06 (Nikhil Sharma): Creating as P0 so we don’t ship templates without measurable activation. Need TTFS definition + tagging mechanism that won’t explode metric cardinality.
2025-02-10 (Logan Wright): Drafted initial event list. Strong recommendation: derive "first_success" server-side from tagged requests rather than trusting client-side events.
2025-02-12 (Allison Grant): +1 on bounded attributes. Please avoid template.version on metrics; OK for event analytics. Also do not attach install_id to OTel metrics (traces/logs OK).
2025-02-18 (Marcus Lin): Privacy review notes: install_id must be random; forbid repo name / hostname. Provide explicit opt-out env var and ensure redaction processors cover headers in logs.
2025-02-25 (Henry Cho): Ensure success criteria accounts for streaming completion; don’t count partial streams as success. Also want dashboard breakdown by language + channel.
2025-03-02 (Brian Murphy): Gateway can allowlist a single header with strict validation + max length; prefer one header over many to reduce proxy issues and simplify support.
2025-03-05 (Sergio Costa): Dashboards: funnel + TTFS + activation are straightforward once tags are in warehouse. Need stable tag keys and a clear mapping doc for Console filters.
2025-03-10 (Nikhil Sharma): Incorporating incident learnings: some corp proxies block unknown headers. Mark tagging as opt-in with documented disable flag; CLI still usable without it.
2025-03-13 (Logan Wright): Final spec agreed. Action items moved to ENG tickets for SDK hooks + request-id propagation; Console team confirmed filter requirements.

Title: Template adoption telemetry header rejected by some corporate proxies (HTTP 400/431) — request never reaches Redwood

Template adoption telemetry header rejected by some corporate proxies (HTTP 400/431) — request never reaches Redwood

Customer reports that requests from the RAG+Agent Quickstart template fail only when routed through their corporate proxy. Proxy rejects "unknown" request headers; as a result the HTTP request never reaches Redwood (no request-id, no gateway logs).

Issue summary
- When using the Quickstart template defaults (telemetry tagging enabled), requests include one or more template-origin telemetry headers.
- Northbridge’s corporate proxy rejects requests containing unapproved custom headers, returning HTTP 400/431 before the request leaves their network.
- Removing the custom header(s) makes requests succeed immediately.

Impact
- Blocks template evaluation behind corporate network controls.
- Customer perception: Redwood API is down/unreliable (but failures occur upstream of Redwood).
- Limits our ability to use header-based adoption telemetry in enterprise environments.

Environment
- Customer network: corporate proxy with strict header allowlist (exact vendor not disclosed)
- Client: Python quickstart template (internal beta branch per customer)
- Redwood: Hosted API, prod, us-east

Steps to reproduce (customer)
1) Run template behind corporate proxy (HTTPS interception disabled; standard outbound proxy).
2) Execute template endpoint that triggers LLM call.
3) Observe proxy error: request rejected due to custom header.
4) Manually remove telemetry header(s) and retry.
5) Request succeeds.

Expected
- Template should work behind common enterprise proxies with default configuration.
- Telemetry tagging should not break baseline API calls.

Actual
- Proxy rejects request when template telemetry headers are present. Request never reaches Redwood gateway.

Evidence / logs (sanitized)
- Customer proxy response (reported):
  - Status: 431 Request Header Fields Too Large (sometimes 400 Bad Request)
  - Error text: "Request rejected: header not allowed" / "Unknown header: X-Redwood-Template" (wording varies)
- Redwood side:
  - No corresponding gateway request logs for the timestamp window.
  - No request-id returned.

Investigation notes
- Correlated with internal Slack incident-adjacent thread about telemetry headers causing 4xx in some proxies (see #incidents reference shared by Support).
- This is not a Redwood API failure; it’s a compatibility issue with our telemetry mechanism.
- Header approach is convenient for downstream filtering but fragile with strict proxy/header policies.

Workaround (provided to customer)
- Disable template telemetry headers and rely on standard SDK headers only.
- Template-level change: make telemetry opt-in instead of opt-out.

Decision / resolution
- Decision (DevEx + PM + Gateway): make template-origin telemetry tagging opt-in.
  - Default templates will NOT send template telemetry headers unless explicitly enabled.
  - For customers who want to participate, provide a clear env var toggle and docs section (privacy + compatibility note).
- Gateway will continue to allow/validate a small set of telemetry headers (for opt-in users), but templates should not emit them by default.

Customer-facing guidance (final)
- Set template telemetry to disabled (default in upcoming template release). For current version, remove/disable the header injection.
- If customer later wants telemetry tagging for internal KPIs, coordinate with network/security to allowlist the header(s) or use a non-header mechanism (future enhancement).

Follow-ups
- DevEx: Update Python + TypeScript templates to make telemetry tagging opt-in and document proxy compatibility note.
- Docs: Add troubleshooting entry: "Corporate proxy rejects unknown headers" with fix steps.
- Telemetry/PM: Confirm KPIs still measurable for self-serve users; enterprise adoption metrics may be undercounted by design.

---
Comments / timeline

2025-03-06 09:18 (Priya Shah, Support)
Customer reports 400/431 from corporate proxy when running RAG template. Removing template telemetry header makes it work. Asking Eng whether we can avoid non-standard headers by default.

2025-03-06 10:02 (Owen Phillips, Support)
Confirmed no gateway logs for customer timestamps. Likely request never reaches Redwood. Requested sanitized proxy error message and the exact header name(s) being flagged.

2025-03-06 11:11 (Northbridge Financial)
Proxy blocks unknown headers. The header flagged is "X-Redwood-Template" (exact case may differ). When removed, calls succeed.

2025-03-06 12:30 (Brian Murphy, Eng - API Ergonomics)
If proxy blocks unknown headers, this will keep happening. We can whitelist on our gateway but can’t force customer proxy behavior. Recommendation: make templates not send these headers by default; keep as opt-in.

2025-03-07 09:05 (Monica Patel, DevEx)
Agree. Templates should be production-minded by default; telemetry must not be a footgun. We’ll change default to off and add an env var toggle.

2025-03-07 14:22 (Priya Shah, Support)
Shared workaround with customer: remove template telemetry header injection; continue with standard SDK. Customer unblocked.

2025-03-10 16:40 (Brian Murphy, Eng)
Noted related gateway work to validate/pass a small allowlist of telemetry headers for opt-in usage. Also aligning with DevEx on naming and keeping cardinality low.

2025-03-11 10:15 (Priya Shah, Support)
Closing as resolved: customer has workaround, and product decision made to ship opt-in telemetry in templates + docs update. Tracking template change in DevEx queue and will reference in release notes.

Resolution
- Workaround provided and verified by customer.
- Product decision: telemetry headers from templates will be opt-in going forward to avoid corporate proxy incompatibilities.

Support closure notes
- If customer wants adoption telemetry tagging later, advise them to allowlist the exact header(s) with their proxy/security team, or wait for future non-header tagging approach if shipped.
- If they still see 4xx with headers removed, reopen with request-id + timestamp + region so we can check gateway/serving logs.

Title: Adaptive burst anchoring and cross-plan soft-fallbacks PRD

Adaptive burst anchoring and cross-plan soft-fallbacks PRD

Goal: provide a predictable yet flexible burst model for customers who have spiky traffic patterns, while preventing surprise overage charges and reducing operational overhead for billing support. This PRD outlines an 'anchored burst' construct (a reservable baseline burst allowance tied to a plan) plus an automated cross-plan soft-fallback mechanism that re-routes excess short-term demand to linked fallback credit pools or cheaper model variants without immediate billing spikes. The feature should minimize manual plan changes, reduce support tickets from burst-related billing surprises, and keep high-priority routes available during transients.
We have frequent support escalations where customers experience sharp traffic spikes (cron jobs, product launches, marketing campaigns) and receive large overage invoices or are abruptly throttled. Current options (hard quotas, manual plan bumps, or one-off credits) either create billing unpredictability or manual toil. Existing billing artifacts cover many quota and tier behaviors, but none provide a first-class, automated burst fallback that preserves per-route SLAs while controlling cost exposure.
Introduce two cooperating mechanisms: 1) Anchored Burst Allowance: each plan includes an explicit 'burst anchor' (X token-minutes per billing window) that is consumption-exempt from immediate overage for short windows (configurable sliding window, default 10 minutes). Anchors are priced into plans as a stable delta. 2) Cross-Plan Soft-Fallbacks: customers can designate fallback pools (e.g., lower-cost sandbox plan, pooled enterprise reserve, or assigned burst credits) that are consumed when anchors are exhausted. Soft-fallbacks apply policy-controlled degradations: non-critical routes (analytics embeddings, background batch jobs) are routed to cheaper model variants or a throttled path; critical routes preserve latency by consuming fallback credits. Policy rules include prioritization, max fallback consumption per hour, and automatic notifications when fallback thresholds are hit. Billing behavior: anchor usage is not billed as overage; fallback consumption is billed at the fallback pool rate and included in the next invoice with clear line-item labeling. Admins can opt into auto-refill rules, alerts, and automatic conversion of heavy fallback use into a temporary reserved capacity offer.
- Plan schema changes to include 'burst_anchor' value and 'anchor_window' default.- Billing line item generation for anchor usage and fallback consumption.- Policy engine to evaluate route criticality and decide when to route to fallback.- UI in Console for admins to configure fallback pools, anchor sizing, and alerting thresholds.- API extensions for programmatic opt-in/opt-out of fallback and anchor overrides by account owners.
- Changes to underlying GPU autoscaling or Dedicated capacity scheduling beyond billing-visible routing decisions.- Automated cross-customer credit borrowing (not allowed for privacy/compliance). - Complex ML-driven predictive resizing in initial rollout (can be a future enhancement).
Phase 1 (Beta, billing sandbox): implement anchor usage tracking and a developer-facing sandbox fallback pool; enable per-tenant opt-in and logs-only mode for 4 weeks. Phase 2 (Controlled GA): enable billing line items for anchors and fallback consumption for a subset of production accounts and surface Console controls; collect metrics and feedback for 6 weeks. Phase 3 (Full GA): enable auto-refill and reserved capacity offers, add REST API endpoints for programmatic control, and publish docs and migration guides.
AC1: Anchors are included in plan metadata and surfaced in Console and Plan API for all affected plans.
AC2: Anchor consumption is tracked with per-tenant granularity and exported to billing pipeline as distinct line items (anchor-usage, fallback-usage).
AC3: Cross-plan fallback routing can be configured via Console and API; fallback routing decisions obey route-level criticality rules and do not change request semantics.
AC4: When anchor is exhausted, critical routes continue with fallback credits (if available) and non-critical routes are downgraded according to configured policies; no silent hard-throttling occurs without prior admin opt-in.
AC5: Billing math must be validated end-to-end: invoices reflect anchor pricing, fallback unit rates, and any auto-refill charges; sample invoices for 3 synthetic spike scenarios must match expected calculations.
AC6: Alerts (Console and email) are sent when anchor utilization reaches 70%, 90%, and when fallback consumption surpasses configured hourly limits.
AC7: Performance: fallback decisions add no more than 2ms median request overhead in the routing path for 99% of requests in test harness.
AC8: Documentation and migration guide published; support playbook created and validated with Support team for common customer questions and invoice disputes.
Create synthetic spike scenarios (small: 10x baseline for 15 min, medium: 50x for 5 min, large: 100x for 2 min) across three tenant profiles (startup, scale-up, enterprise). Validate routing behavior, fallback consumption, line-item generation, and SLA preservation for critical routes. Automate end-to-end tests in staging billing pipeline and run cost-reconciliation jobs against golden calculations.

fallback_credit_consume_rate
billing_line_item_discrepancy_count
support_ticket_rate_for_overage_invoices

2026-03-10 Asha Menon: Drafted PRD and shared with Pricing & Billing guild. Initial ask: reduce billing surprise for mid-market customers with variable traffic.
2026-03-11 Liam O'Connor: Added scope inclusions and exclusions; requested engineering effort estimate and feasibility review from ENG-Infra.
2026-03-12 Priya Desai (Support): Noted common dispute patterns; requested clear invoice line-items and a support playbook before GA.
2026-03-13 Ravi Patel (Security): Reviewed data residency constraints for cross-plan fallback; confirmed permitted if fallback pool is within same customer org. security_review_required flagged false for initial beta.
2026-03-14 Engineering sync: ENG leads suggested 2ms routing budget, recommended a logs-only beta to validate decision paths without billing risk.

Title: Intermittent heartbeat-only SSE frames then abrupt close; finalization event missing causing truncated responses after reconnect

Intermittent heartbeat-only SSE frames then abrupt close; finalization event missing causing truncated responses after reconnect

Issue summary:
Customer sees intermittent SSE streams that send several consecutive keepalive/heartbeat events containing no tokens, then the connection is closed without the terminal/finalization event. After the client reconnects and attempts resume, the last portion of the response is missing (partial choice / sentence truncated) and there is no 'done' / terminal marker in the resumed stream.

Impact:
End users see truncated assistant replies in production workflows (estimated ~2-4% of streaming requests for this customer). Feature is user-facing (chat UI) and causing increased support tickets from the customer’s product team.

Environment:
- Customer: AcmeHealth (dedicated contract)
- Region: prod us-east (customer's dedicated pool)
- SDK: js-client v2.1.4 (custom reconnect logic)
- Edge: Fastly CDN + company reverse proxy in front of Redwood API
- Affected model: redwood-13b-v1

Steps to reproduce (observed by customer):
1) Open SSE stream for chat generation (stream=true) from browser behind their CDN/proxy.
2) Allow an artificially induced brief blip on the connection (TCP/HTTP/idle close or proxy restart) or wait for natural short disconnect.
3) Client receives several heartbeat events (data payloads with only meta/sequence info, no 'choice' tokens).
4) Connection terminates shortly after with no explicit terminal-final event.
5) Client reconnects and resume logic requests offset; resumed stream contains a partial last choice and never includes the finalization event, leaving the end of the assistant response missing.

Observed behavior (example SSE fragment captured by customer):
----begin-sse----
event: heartbeat
data: {"seq": 1024, "lat_ms": 12}

event: heartbeat
data: {"seq": 1025, "lat_ms": 9}

[connection close from client side / proxy reset]
----end-sse----

In a separate capture (server-side) we see a final token payload immediately followed by a heartbeat in the same TCP segment, but the client sees only the heartbeat and treats the packet as keepalive. There is no explicit 'event: done' observed by the client.

Expected behavior:
Finalization event or terminal token should be reliably delivered so clients can render completed responses and resume logic can produce a consistent finalization. Heartbeats should never mask or be coalesced in a way that hides terminal events.

Attachments and diagnostics provided by customer:
- pcap with two reproductions (attached to ticket)
- browser console logs showing SSE events (trimmed)
- sample trace to Grafana: https://grafana.redwood.local/d/stream/trace-123

2026-03-13 09:21 - Customer (AcmeHealth): We're seeing a handful of our chat messages arrive truncated for end users. We capture the SSE stream and only see heartbeats before the socket closes. Can you advise?
2026-03-13 10:05 - Support (Priya Nair): Thanks for the report. Can you attach the raw SSE capture and confirm whether you're proxying through Fastly / a customer edge? Also please include JS SDK version and whether you use custom reconnect logic.
2026-03-13 10:40 - Customer: Attached pcap and console logs. We do use Fastly and our own nginx reverse proxy. SDK v2.1.4. We attempted a client-side workaround to wait for a stray chunk but results are inconsistent.
2026-03-13 14:12 - Support (Priya Nair): Raising to Serving Runtime and SRE for proxy-coalescing hypothesis. Linking this ticket to previous heartbeat/resume issues for context.
2026-03-14 08:30 - SRE (Liam Chen): Initial triage: observed edge logs where small final message + heartbeat are written in the same backend write and Fastly/nginx coalesced segments downstream. Reproduced a similar pattern in staging when we enabled small-write coalescing. Preparing a minimal repro and spike to validate mitigation options.
2026-03-14 11:05 - Engineering (Marco Rossi): Hypothesis: proxy (Fastly) or Nagle-like coalescing reorders or masks the final token when combined with heartbeat due to missing clear double-CRLF separation between SSE events at the edge. We'll test two mitigations: 1) force newline padding between server writes, 2) send explicit 'event: done' as an independent write with TCP_NODELAY ensured.
Edge SRE reproduced scenario in staging by toggling Fastly small-write coalescing; final token can end up inline with heartbeat packet.
Server-side logs show final token emitted; client-side capture sometimes does not observe it when proxy coalesces and strips trailing separators.
JS SDK reconnect logic currently treats any subsequent immediate heartbeat after resume as a keepalive and may discard trailing payloads if not delimited by an extra blank line.
No evidence of model-level truncation; token stream on the serving-runtime includes finalization event in internal logs.
Related to but distinct from SUP-4721: that ticket focused on truncated final chunk after SSE resume from client refresh; this one reproduces behind edge coalescing in steady-state traffic.
Customer workaround: increase heartbeat interval on their proxy to reduce collision probability (temporary).
Customer workaround: add a 100ms client-side grace period after reconnect to allow stray final chunks to arrive and be appended rather than discarded.
Support suggested: temporarily disable Fastly buffering / small-write coalescing for the affected service.
Engineering to instrument server to emit terminal 'event: done' as a dedicated write and ensure explicit "\n\n" separator is present; PR planned: serving-runtime#812.
SRE to test Fastly config changes (disable small-write coalescing) in a canary and measure reduction in reproductions.
Support to coordinate with customer on enabling workaround and collect one additional pcap after change for verification.
Target: patch deployed to staging by 2026-03-18, production rollout contingent on canary results.

Title: Postmortem: Controlled failover test regression (us-east → eu-west) – transient 5xx + tail latency

Postmortem: Controlled failover test regression (us-east → eu-west) – transient 5xx + tail latency

## Summary
On **2026-01-15**, during a **planned controlled regional failover test** (Hosted API and a limited Dedicated slice) from **us-east** to **eu-west**, we introduced a **customer-visible regression**. A sequence of noisy regional-impairment signals and insufficient rollback/anti-flap guardrails caused repeated routing policy changes (“flip/rollback”) and a transient overload condition in the target region.

**Customer impact:**
- **Hosted API:** elevated 5xx/timeouts and tail latency for a subset of routes while traffic re-converged.
- **Dedicated:** minimal direct impact due to scoped tenants, but some control-plane operations (drain workflow status) were delayed.
- **Streaming:** some clients experienced disconnects on redirect and did not recover cleanly without application-level retries.

**Why this postmortem exists:** This was an intentional test. The regression was not catastrophic, but it was **customer-visible** and exposed gaps in our automation safety model. The goal is to make sure controlled testing improves reliability without creating new incidents.

## Severity and scope
- **Incident type:** Planned test causing unplanned customer-visible regression
- **Severity:** SEV-2 (customer-visible errors for a limited subset; short duration; mitigated quickly)
- **Services impacted:** Hosted API (gateway + smart routing), failover automation controller, region health evaluation pipeline
- **Regions:** us-east (source), eu-west (target)

## Customer impact (what users experienced)
- Transient **HTTP 5xx** and **gateway timeouts** during the flip/rollback window.
- Elevated **p95/p99 latency** for successful requests during the same interval.
- Some **streaming sessions** dropped when redirected cross-region; a subset of clients did not resume streaming until they retried from the application.

Notes:
- We did not publish an external status page incident because this was a planned test with limited blast radius; however, **Support received inbound tickets** from customers who noticed errors during the window. Support response guidance was issued in-channel and via SUP-25310.

## Timeline (UTC)
> Times are approximate; see dashboard annotations and incident-bot thread for exact event markers.

- **16:55** – Pre-flight checks complete (SRE + Routing + Infra). Dry-run output reviewed; “go” granted.
- **17:00** – Controlled failover test begins. Routing policy automation enabled for the scoped routes/tenants.
- **17:02** – Region health aggregator reports degraded reachability for us-east based on synthetic probe failures.
- **17:03** – Failover controller recommends and executes a policy flip to prefer eu-west (within the scoped policy).
- **17:04–17:08** – eu-west sees request surge; latency rises. Gateway retries amplify load; some 5xx/timeouts observed.
- **17:06** – A second reachability signal changes state; controller interprets as recovery + triggers rollback logic sooner than expected.
- **17:07–17:10** – Flip/rollback oscillation observed (multiple policy updates within minutes). Error rate and p99 spike.
- **17:10** – On-call disables automation for the scoped policy; routing stabilized manually.
- **17:14** – Error rates return to baseline; latency recovers as retries subside.
- **17:25** – Post-test validation begins; Support notified with customer-facing explanation.
- **18:10** – Initial retro notes captured; action item tracker created.

## Detection and response
**Detection:**
- We detected the regression via:
  - SRE dashboards for failover signals (5xx burn + tail latency burn)
  - Routing policy flip counters (unexpected rate)
  - Support ping that a customer saw transient errors (correlated to test window)

**Response:**
- Disabled failover automation for the scoped policy (feature flag / controller disable).
- Reduced gateway retry pressure using existing runtime/gateway knobs (temporary tuning) while traffic re-stabilized.
- Confirmed eu-west capacity headroom and verified no persistent impairment.
- Coordinated comms with Support: acknowledged planned test, explained transient errors, offered retry guidance.

## Root cause
The regression was caused by **policy oscillation** (flip/rollback) triggered by **noisy reachability signals**, combined with insufficient guardrails that allowed multiple routing policy changes in a short period. The oscillation produced a traffic pattern that:
1) **increased cross-region redirects**, and
2) **amplified retries** at the gateway/client level,
leading to transient overload and elevated error rates in the target region.

Key technical drivers:
- **Reachability probes produced false positives** (brief, correlated failures) that were treated as authoritative without adequate corroboration.
- **Hold-down and anti-flap timers were too permissive** for the observed signal volatility.
- **Rollback semantics were correct per implementation**, but not aligned with our intended ADR-level behavior (we rolled back too quickly and re-triggered failover immediately).

## Contributing factors
### 1) Trigger noise and insufficient corroboration
- Reachability was treated as “high priority,” but we lacked a strict requirement for corroboration (e.g., simultaneous 5xx burn or control-plane health degradation) before acting.
- Probe failures were short-lived and likely influenced by transient provider/network behavior; the region health pipeline did not dampen enough.

### 2) Rollback gaps / anti-flap guardrails
- Policy flip rate limiting (per policy/per tenant) was not strict enough for production-like behavior.
- The controller was allowed to both:
  - fail over on a high-priority signal transition, and
  - roll back on early recovery indication,
  without a sufficiently long “stabilization” window.

### 3) Retry amplification during routing changes
- Gateway retry budgets and client retry behavior interacted poorly with redirects and timeouts.
- During oscillation, some requests were retried across regions, increasing load at the exact time the target region was receiving new traffic.

### 4) Observability gaps during the test
- We had dashboards, but lacked consistent **automation-driven annotations** (start/stop, flip, rollback, reason) visible across all relevant panels.
- Signal evaluation logs were not easily searchable by policy + decision id, slowing triage.

## What went well
- Blast radius controls worked: the test scope limited impact to a subset of routes/tenants.
- On-call and engineering coordination was fast; disabling automation stabilized the system quickly.
- The team captured decision points and signal state changes in real time, enabling clear follow-up.

## What didn’t go well
- The automation acted faster than our operational ability to confirm whether the impairment was real.
- We did not have a single “confidence score” view combining signal corroboration, dampening state, and decision rationale.
- Support was notified quickly, but we did not proactively message a small set of known sensitive accounts before running the test (we relied on the planned-test guidance rather than a targeted heads-up).

## Where we got lucky
- eu-west had enough headroom that the overload was short-lived.
- The oscillation stayed within a few minutes; a longer duration could have caused a larger SLO burn and broader customer impact.

## Immediate remediation (completed during/after the event)
- Disabled automation for the scoped policy upon observing oscillation.
- Manual stabilization of routing preference and verification of regional health.
- Support response guidance provided for inbound tickets about transient errors.

## Corrective and preventive actions (CPAs)
> This section is the contract: what we will change so a controlled test does not regress customer experience again.

### A. Trigger signal pipeline hardening
1) **Corroboration requirements**
   - Require at least one corroborating signal for reachability-based failover in production scopes (e.g., 5xx burn OR control-plane health OR sustained probe failure above threshold).
   - Owner: **Ravi Menon** (Routing policy)
   - Target: **2026-02-14**

2) **Dampening + hold-down tuning**
   - Increase minimum sustain time for reachability impairment and increase recovery hold-down.
   - Add jitter/TTL protections on health reads to avoid stampedes.
   - Owner: **Victor Alvarez** (Network) + **Jordan Lee** (Policy engine)
   - Target: **2026-02-21**

### B. Rollback/anti-flap guardrails
3) **Rate limiting for policy flips**
   - Enforce max flips per hour per policy and per tenant tier, with hard stop + paging if exceeded.
   - Owner: **Benji Okafor** (Guardrails)
   - Target: **2026-02-21**

4) **Rollback semantics aligned to ADR-043**
   - Ensure rollback cannot immediately re-open the same decision loop; require stable window before re-evaluating for failover.
   - Produce an auditable “decision id” for each state transition.
   - Owner: **Jordan Lee** (Policy engine) + **Ethan Park** (Control plane)
   - Target: **2026-03-01**

5) **Approval hooks for production game days**
   - Require on-call acknowledgment before executing an automated flip in production during controlled tests until we meet success criteria in two consecutive game days.
   - Owner: **Rafael Mendes** (SRE) + **Ethan Park** (Control plane)
   - Target: **2026-02-10**

### C. Retry/load-shedding behavior
6) **Gateway retry budget + redirect guidance**
   - Cap retries during active failover events; prefer fast-fail with standardized Retry-After for overload.
   - Update SDK/docs guidance for idempotent retries and streaming reconnect.
   - Owner: **Peter Holtz** (Gateway) + **Vikram Singh** (Data plane)
   - Target: **2026-03-08**

7) **Streaming reconnect hardening**
   - Ensure redirect responses carry enough info for safe client reconnection; improve idempotency guidance.
   - Owner: **Vikram Singh**
   - Target: **2026-02-28**

### D. Observability and auditing
8) **Automation-driven annotations**
   - Add consistent dashboard annotations for: test start/end, flip, rollback, reason, decision id, policy id.
   - Owner: **Allison Grant** + **Sergio Costa**
   - Target: **2026-02-14**

9) **Audit log retention + supportability**
   - Persist failover audit events (recommended/executed/rolled back) with searchable keys: tenant tier, route, policy id, decision id.
   - Owner: **Devon Price** (Tooling) + **Allison Grant** (Observability)
   - Target: **2026-03-01**

### E. Process changes for future controlled tests
10) **Go/no-go criteria update**
   - Add explicit “anti-flap guardrails enabled + validated in staging” to go/no-go checklist.
   - Owner: **Talia Benson** (Program) + **Tomáš Novák** (Runbooks)
   - Target: **2026-02-07**

11) **Customer comms targeting**
   - For production tests, proactively notify a small set of enterprise accounts with strict HA expectations if their traffic might be in scope, even when blast radius is limited.
   - Owner: **Dev Patel** (Support escalation) + **Lauren Bishop** (Dedicated PM)
   - Target: **2026-02-14**

## Success criteria (for declaring this class of regression “fixed”)
For two consecutive production game days with scoped blast radius:
- No more than **one** routing policy transition per policy (flip only; rollback only if explicitly invoked by on-call).
- No customer-visible 5xx increase above agreed threshold for scoped tenants.
- p99 latency in target region remains within defined tolerance band during convergence.
- Audit events and dashboard annotations allow reconstruction of the decision timeline within 10 minutes.

## Appendix A: Key lessons
- “Reachability > 5xx burn” is correct only if reachability is truly authoritative; without corroboration, it can be the noisiest signal.
- Rollback is not inherently safe; rollback without stabilization can create a control loop that is worse than staying failed over.
- Controlled tests must be treated like real incidents operationally: annotations, clear decision authority, and customer comms preparedness.

## Appendix B: Open questions
- Should we treat reachability as authoritative only when multiple independent vantage points fail, or when combined with provider status signals?
- For Hosted API streaming, do we want a first-class “resume token” pattern to reduce user impact during redirects?
- What is the right default DNS/traffic-steering posture for faster failover without amplifying transient network noise?

## Owner
- Primary owner for follow-through: **Rafael Mendes (SRE delivery lead)**
- Architecture owner: **Miles Thornton (Failover architecture lead)**

## Status
- This postmortem is complete. Action items are tracked in **ENG-2426** and linked sub-issues. Updates should be reflected here if any CPA materially changes scope or target dates.
