Title: KV + prompt explorations: microbench and eval notes

KV + prompt explorations: microbench and eval notes

Quick overview:

This is a scratchpad for a two-day microbench on KV-cache behaviour + prompt permutations against the 7B open model we onboarded last week. Goal: surface surprising latency/throughput tradeoffs when using small-group quantization and when prefix caching is enabled for short-chat workloads. Not polished — notes to self + TODOs.

Environment:
- model: open-7b-a1 (float16 baseline)
- infra: local dev rig (A100-40GB) + dedicated dev node (T4 pooled) for repeatability tests
- serving runtime: local build at commit b3f9d2c (kernel selection tweak for rotary attention)
- quantization tool: qconfig-v2 (per-channel symmetric, group size paramizable)

What I ran (high level):
1) Baseline float16, no caching, batch_size 1, seq_len 64 -> token latency ~ 48ms (p99 82ms)
2) 4-bit per-channel (g=128), no caching, batch_size 1 -> token latency ~ 29ms (p99 54ms), small quality drop on long-range completion (>120 tokens)
3) 4-bit + KV-prefix cache enabled (cache warm) -> token latency down to ~12ms steady-state (p99 18ms), initial token for new convo still 28ms due to cache warm-up
4) 8-bit + KV cache -> similar latency to 4-bit in steady-state but slightly higher memory footprint; perplexity on eval set ~+0.6 relative to f16
5) Group-size sweep (g=64,128,256) showed min latency at g=128; g=64 increased kernel call overhead (slower), g=256 increased quantization error on feedforward weights

Prompt/Chat experiments (short-turn chat workload):
- Prompt pattern A: system + short user prompt (10 tokens) -> good candidate for prefix caching. Observed that caching only prefix tokens (system+static context) gave 1.8-2.2x speedup vs no-cache.
- Prompt pattern B: long dynamic user context (~120 tokens) -> caching had less impact because KV cache dominated by dynamic prefix; still saw ~1.2x benefit in repeated-turn chats where earlier turns reused tokens.
- Prompt variations: using a light instruction template ("You are a helpful assistant.") vs heavy context (document paste) changed token distribution and therefore batch efficiency. Heavy contexts amplify KV memory pressure.

Quality checks (quick):
- Rouge-like sketch on 200 eval prompts: 4-bit g=128 retained ~97% of f16 ROUGE-L for short answers (<40 tokens). Degradation grows for >100 tokens.
- Behavioral glitches: occasional repetition when mixing cached prefix with dynamic system messages — hypothesis: cache invalidation rule bug when system message changes mid-session. Filed Linear RED-345.

Oddities / gotchas noticed:
- On T4 pooled nodes, the p99 latency for 4-bit quant jumped ~10ms compared to A100 for same config. Seems tied to kernel parallelism (fewer warps) and increased kernel-launch overhead. Follow-up: compare kernel launches per token for each device.
- When enabling streaming + KV cache, observed slightly out-of-order token emission for long sequences on dev build b3f9d2c — might be a scheduling race between batch flusher and cache writer. Add tracing around StreamFlusher.
- Memory reporting in console sometimes undercounts KV memory by ~200MB. Suspect accounting vs reserved-alignment rounding.

Commands / quick reproducibility notes:
- baseline run: ./bench/run_microbench --model open-7b-a1 --dtype fp16 --batch 1 --seq 64 --commit b3f9d2c
- 4-bit test: ./bench/run_microbench --model open-7b-a1 --quant 4 --gsize 128 --cache on
- collect traces: ./tools/collect_trace.sh --run-id $RUN_ID --include stream,kv,alloc

Immediate TODOs (ordered):
- [ ] Reproduce cache invalidation bug (RED-345) with minimal script (today) and attach trace (Riley to help)
- [ ] Add kernel-launch counters to the microbench harness (compare A100 vs T4)
- [ ] Try hybrid 4+8-bit profile: attention layers 4-bit, FFN 8-bit (quick patch) — see if quality/latency sweet spot exists
- [ ] Clean up prompt templates used in eval set and push small eval harness to repo (PR candidate)
- [ ] Add a per-request KV-size metric to Console traces to help correlate p99s to per-request cache size

Notes to self / ideas:
- Maybe try a tiny LRU window for dynamic tokens: keep last 64 dynamic tokens in a hot buffer, move older parts to cold storage — could reduce cache pressure for long documents with small returns.
- Consider exposing group-size tuning suggestions in Optimize UI: scan workload seq_len distribution, recommend gsize 64/128/256.

References / links:
- Linear RED-231 (KV rollout plan): https://linear.app/RED-231/optimize-kv-cache-rollout
- Kernel PR that touched rotary kernels: github.com/redwood-inference/kernels/pull/442

End of scratchpad. Will iterate and move useful bits to a proper RFC once reproducible artifacts and traces are attached.

Title: Cleanup stale test instances and grant access for infra-eco team (archived volumes)

Cleanup stale test instances and grant access for infra-eco team (archived volumes)

Overview:
We identified long-running/stale test instances (mostly ephemeral GPU VMs and a few reserved volumes) created during internal spike projects in Q4 2025 that were not claimed. They were incurring small but persistent costs and cluttering inventory.

Impact (updated after verification):
- Monthly spend was closer to ~$0.9k (down from initial ~$1.2k estimate) once we excluded a few instances already stopped.
- Inventory noise for infra capacity planning and autoscaler reports.
- Potential security surface (old SSH keys / stale service accounts) if left indefinitely.

Requested actions:
1) Confirm the attached candidate list and terminate instances flagged as STALE-ORPHAN after a 5 business day grace window (updated from 72h per infra manager guidance).
2) Snapshot and retain any volumes that appear to contain non-temporary data (owner label present). Copy snapshot logs to the archived-volumes bucket.
3) Create an infra-eco service account and grant Miguel Reyes (infra) and Priya Desai (cost-ops) read/write access to the archived bucket and tagging permissions for the affected project.
4) Add a short runbook entry describing verification steps and approval flow (link in ticket).

Steps used to locate instances:
- Cloud Console > Compute > Instances. Filter by label: "spike=true OR temp=true OR created_by=automation-test" and running > 30 days.
- See attached CSV for the pre-filtered candidate list used for the final pass.

Runbook notes (final):
- Notify owners via tag-owner email and #infra-ops broadcast; wait 5 business days.
- If no reply, snapshot volumes (if non-empty) to archived-volumes, tag snapshot with INT-7832 and timestamp.
- Terminate instances and record instance IDs + snapshot IDs in ticket comments.
- Update billing tags on the affected project resources to "archived" for cost tracking.

Retention / rollback (updated):
- Snapshots retained for 90 days (updated from 30 days per Storage lifecycle policy as of 2026-03-10).
- Restore from snapshot if unintended data loss occurs.

Notes and links:
- Related support thread: INT-7720 (previous cleanup run Feb 2026).
- Cost dashboard: https://internal-dashboard.redwood/costs/q4-2025 (internal link).
- Runbook (new location): https://confluence.redwood/runbooks/cloud/instance-volume-cleanup
- Please check ACLs before granting access; follow least-privilege principles.

Outcome summary:
- 14 stale instances terminated; 3 volumes snapshotted + archived.
- IAM access granted to infra-eco service account and named users; tagging permissions delegated via project-level custom role.
Aisha Patel (2026-03-01): Created ticket after cost review flagged these resources. Attached CSV exported from cloud console.
Miguel Reyes (2026-03-02): Starting owner discovery. Requesting approval on grace window + termination criteria.

Title: Policy defaults serializer and synthetic-profile prober for tenant econ/quant automation

Policy defaults serializer and synthetic-profile prober for tenant econ/quant automation

Motivation: We need a deterministic, auditable way to produce tenant-scoped default policies (batching, cache presize, quant tiers) that can be serialized, reviewed, and deployed across Dedicated and Private. Current heuristics are ad-hoc and encoded in multiple places; this PR introduces a policy defaults serializer and a synthetic-profile prober that generates deterministic example workloads so defaults can be validated in CI and by SRE.

Summary of changes: Introduces a small policy DSL and a serializer that emits canonical JSON policy bundles for tenants; implements a synthetic-profile prober that runs against the sampler and prefill subsystems to produce a compact profile used to pick batch/cache/quant defaults; provides a CLI (redwoodctl defaults serialize/probe) and a small REST endpoint for the policy service for on-demand probes; hooks into the defaults-as-code import pipeline so product can review generated bundles before applying.

What this enables: 1) deterministic defaults generation for tenant onboarding; 2) CI validation of defaults via synthetic-profile replay; 3) easier code review of default policies as serialized artifacts; 4) ability to snapshot and roll back defaults in the tenant defaults registry.

Compatibility and rollout: Backwards-compatible. The serializer produces bundles that match the existing policy schema; we added a v2 mime-type for the new compact profile artifacts but the previous pipeline still accepts them. Rollout plan: feature flagged behind feature/defaults-serializer; will enable for a small set of tenants and run for 48h before gradual enabling.

Testing: Unit tests for serializer and parser (coverage added for edge cases where workloads have heavy streaming tokens), integration tests that run the prober against a local prefiller/sampler mock, and an e2e smoke that verifies the imported bundle deploys to a dedicated tenant and returns the expected recommended batch/cache/quant selection.

Checklist: - [x] Policy DSL and serializer implementation - [x] Synthetic-profile prober + deterministic seed - [x] redwoodctl CLI commands + docs snippet - [x] REST probe endpoint gated by feature flag - [x] Unit/integration/e2e tests - [x] Migration/compatibility checks and release notes

Notes: This PR purposely keeps the prober lightweight (synthetic workloads, not full traffic replay) to avoid production load. The serializer includes metadata (probe seed, runtime heuristics, timestamp) for traceability. Future follow-ups will add exportable diffs and a UI reviewer in Console.

Title: ModelObservability console 403 after Okta SCIM group update — role claim missing

ModelObservability console 403 after Okta SCIM group update — role claim missing

Issue summary:
A handful of platform engineers (team: model-platform) report being able to authenticate with Okta SSO but receiving HTTP 403 when opening the ModelObservability console. The browser shows a successful SAML/SSO redirect, but the console surface returns an RBAC denial.

Impact:
- 6 engineers (including two oncall) cannot access ModelObservability dashboards for alert triage.
- Potentially blocking incident response and model metric investigations.
- Scope currently appears limited to the ModelObservability console; other internal consoles (console.redwood.com) unaffected.

Environment:
- prod: us-east region
- Okta-managed SCIM provisioning for groups -> internal RBAC sync
- Affected users are on the dedicated model-platform Okta group: model-observability-admins (recently renamed in Okta to model-observability-admins_v2)

Steps to reproduce:
1) User logs into console via Okta SSO. 2) Okta redirects back to console with SAML assertion. 3) Console auth service calls internal /auth/claims endpoint to map SSO assertion to RBAC roles. 4) Auth service returns 200 but roles list is empty -> console shows 403.

Observed logs/snippets:
- Okta Provisioning event (2026-03-11 02:14:03 UTC): SCIM PATCH /Groups model-observability-admins_v2 -> 200 OK.
- Auth service trace (2026-03-12 08:05:12 UTC): requestId=8f3a7b; token_sub=U12345; okta_groups=["model-observability-admins_v2"] ; mapped_roles=[]
- RBAC sync job log (2026-03-12 03:00:00 UTC): "WARN: group attribute 'role' missing for group model-observability-admins_v2; skipping role assignment"

Initial hypothesis and findings:
- Suspect Okta-to-SCIM attribute mapping for 'role' claim was dropped when group rename (suffix _v2) was created. The RBAC sync expects a custom 'roles' attribute on the Okta Group object, and that attribute is only populated for groups created before the recent migration.
- Identity service accepts Okta groups but only assigns roles when the group-level custom attribute 'roles' is present. New groups created via the Okta automation lack that attribute due to a mapping condition in the provisioning policy.

Temporary workaround applied:
- Manual grant: Support manually granted 'observability.admin' in RBAC for 6 affected users via admin console at 2026-03-12 09:30 UTC to restore access.

Next steps and proposed remediation:
- Identity team to update Okta provisioning policy to include the custom group attribute 'roles' for new groups. (PR suggested: identity#4123)
- Backfill roles for groups created since 2026-03-01 via a one-off SCIM PATCH job.
- Add a defensive check in auth service: if group name matches known admin patterns (model-observability-*) and no group-level roles attribute present, emit audit alert and fallback to conservative role mapping only for emergency access (requires change and internal review).
- Add monitoring alert (Alert ID: MON-obs-rbac-empty-groups) when group mapped_roles == [] for users in console environment.

Acceptance criteria for closure:
- Okta provisioning policy updated and verified to populate 'roles' attribute for newly created/renamed groups.
- Backfill job completed and verified for model-observability groups.
- Affected users can authenticate and see expected admin UI without manual grants.
- Postmortem note added to Confluence and runbook updated with temporary mitigation steps.

Title: eng-ml

eng-ml

Priya Rao: Heads-up — our eval runner is flaky on the quantized-v2 onboarding suite. CI reported a 0.04 drop in BLEU on one run, then back to baseline on rerun. stack: `evals/runner.py::run_all`
Mike Chen: Ugh. Did the job show differing lengths or just metric jitter?
Priya Rao: Metric jitter mostly. Same prompts, same seeds (we thought). Logs show `seed=42` passed but outputs diff across runs.
Alyssa Gomez: Common culprits: sampling params (temp/top_p), nondeterministic CUDA kernels, or RNG not propagated to all libs. Are we doing do_sample=True anywhere?
Jordan Li: We default to sampling with `temperature=0.8, top_p=0.9` for some evals. That will be nondet even with same seed if decode uses sampling across threads.
Priya Rao: The eval config for quantize tests uses the canonical config from onboarding.yaml — it sets `do_sample: true`. The weird bit is we see differences even when we change to `do_sample: false` for some runs.
Mike Chen: If `do_sample=false` but we still see nondet, then it's likely from floating point / kernel order or dropout/amp. Which runtime? cudnn, torch 2.x?
Priya Rao: Runner is on a K80 prod node for CI debug and on A100 infra for nightly. Torch 2.1 in both. Quantized model uses int8 kernels on A100 (faster) and fallback ops on K80.
Alyssa Gomez: A100 int8 kernels sometimes reorder operations; also make sure `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` and `torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True` are set during eval setup. But note that quantized kernels may not be covered by those flags.
Jordan Li: Another angle — are we resetting RNGs per example? We seed at process start, but token sampling can be parallel across batch dim so RNG streams differ per batch ordering. I usually do `generator = torch.Generator(device).manual_seed(seed + shard_id)` and pass explicit generator to sampling operations.
Priya Rao: Good point. Our runner calls `model.generate(...)` without explicit `generator=`.
Mike Chen: Patch suggestion: always pass an explicit generator built from root seed + example index. Also add a small harness for reproducibility: run the same eval N times (N=5) and compute median metric and std. Fail CI if std > threshold.
Alyssa Gomez: Agreed. Also: add a deterministic decode mode for evaluations where we want bit-for-bit repeatability. It would enforce `do_sample=False`, `temperature=0`, `top_k=1`, and `generator` usage. Name it `deterministic=True` in eval config.
Priya Rao: I can add `deterministic` flag to eval schema. What about GPU-level nondet from quant kernels?
Jordan Li: For that, record a golden artifact (reference outputs) from a chosen baseline environment (A100 with Intel RT kernels) and treat other runs as comparators. We can compute a stable similarity metric (e.g., chrF/BLEU diff tolerance) and allow small differences due to quantization. For CI gating of regressions, gate on median across 3 seeds run on the same hardware.
Mike Chen: For CI wiring: 1) run per-commit quick eval in cheap env with deterministic mode, 2) nightly multi-seed non-deterministic checks on target infra (A100) comparing to golden baseline, 3) on-failure, auto-run debug job with expanded logging.
Priya Rao: What expanded logging do we need? I propose: seed, generator states (torch.get_rng_state hex), torch.cuda.get_rng_state_all for GPUs, model version, quantization config, and full decode tokens.
Alyssa Gomez: Yes. Also log sampling params: temperature, top_p, top_k, do_sample, and beam params. And artifacts: outputs.jsonl per run.
Jordan Li: Small pragmatic items: 1) Add `--repeat N` CLI to runner that runs the same eval N times and writes `outputs_run_{i}.jsonl`. 2) Add a simple `compare_runs.py` that computes metric mean/std and hashes outputs.
Priya Rao: I'll open a PR with the deterministic flag + generator plumbing and a CI job change to run `--repeat 3` for onboarding suites.
Mike Chen: Can you also include an integration test that runs the same prompt through quantized model and FP model on the same seed and asserts that difference is within expected envelope? Store envelopes per-model in a small `golden_metrics` json.
Alyssa Gomez: We should also include a note in the onboarding checklist: "Run quantized bring-up with 3 seeds, record median metric, add noise tolerance label if quantization expected to shift baseline."
infra-bot: @Priya Rao created debug job `evals/repro-debug/1751234567` on ci-redwood (queued).
evals-ci: CI note: running `evals/onboarding --suite quantized-v2 --repeat 3 --deterministic false` on a100-1. Artifacts will be stored under s3://redwood-evals/tmp/1751234567/
Priya Rao: I'll monitor the job and attach outputs. If we still see nondet under deterministic mode, we'll escalate to runtime/eng-runtime for kernel-level investigation.
Mike Chen: Thanks — this should reduce random flakes and make regression alerts actionable. :thumbsup:

Title: CI Eval Determinism and Flake Mitigation

CI Eval Determinism and Flake Mitigation

## Summary
Our evaluation harness previously produced intermittent metric drops (e.g., ~0.04 BLEU on a single run) for the quantized-v2 onboarding suite that disappeared on rerun. This page documents the current (2026) standard for reducing nondeterminism, preventing CI flakes, and making regressions actionable.

The root causes we have observed include:
- Stochastic decoding (temperature/top_p sampling) without per-example RNG control.
- RNG state not consistently propagated to all relevant libraries/ops.
- GPU-level nondeterminism (kernel selection, atomic ordering), especially in quantized/int8 paths.
- Cross-hardware differences (e.g., A100 int8 kernels vs legacy fallback paths).

## What changed since the initial investigation
The original debugging thread identified sampling parameters and missing explicit generators as primary contributors. The current harness incorporates the same core ideas, with the following updates:
- We now treat deterministic decoding as the default for per-commit CI gates for onboarding suites.
- The determinism flag is implemented as `--deterministic` / `deterministic: true` in eval config, and it hard-enforces decoding parameters (see below).
- The runner always constructs and passes an explicit `torch.Generator` for generation, derived from a root seed plus a stable per-example index.
- CI gating moved from single-run metrics to median-of-repeats, and flakiness is measured explicitly.

## Definitions
### Deterministic (harness-level)
A run is considered deterministic (for CI purposes) if repeated executions on the same hardware + container image + model revision produce identical decoded token sequences for the same prompts.

Notes:
- Hardware drift (A100 vs K80) is not expected to be bitwise identical.
- Some quantized kernels may still be nondeterministic even when framework-level deterministic flags are enabled.

### Flake
A flake is a CI failure caused by nondeterministic variation rather than a real change in model/code.

## Recommended CI strategy (current)
### 1) Per-commit (PR) gate: deterministic quick eval
Purpose: prevent random sampling jitter from blocking merges.
- Environment: standardized runner image + target GPU class when available (A10 preferred for cost; A100 acceptable).
- Mode: `deterministic: true`
- Repeats: `--repeat 3`
- Decision rule: gate on the median metric across repeats; also fail if output hashes differ across repeats (for suites that require bitwise stability).

### 2) Nightly: multi-seed + tolerance-based comparison
Purpose: catch real regressions and quantify expected variance.
- Environment: target infra (A100 for quantized-v2)
- Mode: `deterministic: false` (sampling allowed when the eval is designed to measure sampled behavior)
- Seeds: 3 seeds (default: 13, 37, 101)
- Decision rule: compare against the golden baseline using metric tolerance thresholds; alert on sustained shifts (median across seeds).

### 3) On failure: auto-trigger repro debug job
Purpose: make investigations fast and data-rich.
- Auto-collect artifacts listed in the Logging and Artifacts section.
- Include a run summary that states whether variance is:
  - decode-level (different token sequences)
  - metric-only (same outputs but metric computation drift)
  - environment-level (hardware/container mismatch)

## Deterministic decoding mode (required behavior)
When `deterministic: true`, the harness MUST enforce:
- `do_sample = false`
- `temperature = 0.0`
- `top_k = 1`
- `top_p = 1.0`
- `num_beams = 1` (unless the suite explicitly tests beam search)
- Explicit generator passed into generation APIs
- Stable batching order (no data-loader shuffling; stable sort by example_id)

Rationale:
- Simply setting a global seed is insufficient when generation draws randomness in parallel or across different batch shapes.

## RNG handling (current standard)
### Root seed and per-example seeds
- The runner accepts a `--seed` root seed.
- For each example, derive a stable per-example seed:
  - `example_seed = root_seed + example_index`
- Construct a generator on the active device and pass it explicitly to generation.

Operational guidance:
- Ensure `example_index` is stable across runs (do not use worker-local indices unless they are globally consistent).
- If sharding is used, include `shard_id` in the seed derivation only if shard assignments are stable across runs.

### Framework flags
We enable deterministic flags when `deterministic: true`:
- `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)`
- `torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True`
- `torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False`

Caveat:
- Quantized/int8 kernels may not fully respect these flags. Treat the flags as best-effort rather than a guarantee.

## Hardware notes (quantized-v2)
- A100 int8 paths can differ from legacy GPU fallbacks.
- CI determinism requirements are scoped to a single target hardware class per suite.
- The quantized-v2 onboarding suite is pinned to A100 for nightly baselines.

## Metric gating rules
### Per-commit deterministic gate
- Compute metric per repeat.
- Report: median, min, max, and standard deviation.
- Fail conditions:
  - Any repeat differs in output token hash (for deterministic suites).
  - Std dev exceeds threshold (default threshold: 0.005 BLEU-equivalent; suite owners may override).

### Nightly tolerance-based gate
- Compare nightly medians to golden medians.
- Default tolerances (may be tuned per suite):
  - BLEU: 0.03 absolute
  - chrF: 0.02 absolute
  - Task accuracy: 0.5 percentage points absolute

## Logging and artifacts (required)
Each eval run must emit the following into the run artifact directory:
- `run_metadata.json`: model revision, container digest, GPU type, torch version, eval suite name, config snapshot
- RNG details:
  - root seed
  - per-example seed derivation scheme
  - `torch.get_rng_state()` (hex or base64)
  - `torch.cuda.get_rng_state_all()` (per device; hex or base64)
- Generation parameters:
  - do_sample, temperature, top_p, top_k, num_beams, max_new_tokens
- Outputs:
  - `outputs_run_{i}.jsonl` for each repeat
  - include decoded text and decoded token ids
- Summary:
  - `metrics_run_{i}.json`
  - `summary.json` with median/std and output hash comparisons

## Runner CLI (current)
Required runner options for reproducibility testing:
- `--repeat N` : runs the same suite N times with the same config and seed
- `--deterministic {true|false}` : enforces deterministic mode when true
- `--seed SEED` : sets the root seed

Example:
- `evals/onboarding --suite quantized-v2 --repeat 3 --deterministic true --seed 42`

## Troubleshooting playbook
If you see nondeterminism with `deterministic: true`:
1) Confirm the run is on the expected hardware class and container digest.
2) Confirm output hashes differ (decode nondeterminism) vs metrics differ (metric computation drift).
3) If decode nondeterminism:
   - verify generator is passed explicitly
   - verify stable ordering of examples and stable batch shape
   - check for any remaining sampling knobs being set by a suite override
4) If still nondeterministic on A100 quantized kernels:
   - capture artifacts and escalate to eng-serving-runtime for kernel-level investigation
   - consider switching the suite’s CI gate to tolerance-based comparison if bitwise repeatability is unattainable

## Ownership and change control
- Owner: Applied ML & Evals
- Any change to determinism semantics (`--deterministic` behavior, seed derivation, gating thresholds) requires review from Applied ML & Evals + Serving Runtime.

Title: Model-serving regression incident review standards

Model-serving regression incident review standards

Purpose:
This page defines the standards and minimal evidence set for incident reviews when an incident is determined to be a model-serving regression. A model-serving regression is any incident where a deployed model's outputs degrade in a way that: (a) violates customer-facing SLOs, (b) introduces a measurable quality regression on internal evaluation prompts, or (c) materially increases error-rate or downstream exception rates relative to the pinned baseline.

Scope:
- Applies to Redwood inference endpoints (hosted, dedicated, private) serving text generation, chat or embeddings.
- Covers both transient regressions (reproduceable under a traffic slice) and persistent regressions after a deploy/rollout.

Definitions:
- Regression: observable drop in model quality, increased hallucination, or divergence from expected distribution.
- Baseline: the pinned model version and evaluation snapshot used for rollout checks.
- Regression Incident: an SEV/priority event opened against model quality.

Detection signals (examples):
- SLO alerts: p99 latency increase is excluded here; primary signals for regressions are quality SLOs such as mean ROUGE drop, embedding similarity fall below threshold, or classification accuracy fall.
- Customer tickets describing consistent incorrect outputs across requests.
- Automated evaluation harness failing prompt-set thresholds (e.g., holdout prompts used by Redwood Optimize).
- Rise in downstream errors: e.g., parser exceptions, schema validation failures, function-calling mismatches.
- Canary telemetry: divergence between canary and baseline scoring statistics.

Minimum triage checklist (first 30–60 minutes):
1. Confirm the signal: reproduce a failed request against the pinned baseline model and the currently deployed model. Record inputs and outputs.
2. Tag incident type: "regression" and note whether it coincided with a deploy, model swap, quantization change, or infra event.
3. Capture immediate artifacts (see "Required artifacts").
4. If regression affects customers or SLAs, escalate to SEV process and notify customer-success.
5. Assign temporary owner (engineer familiar with model onboarding or runtime).

Required artifacts (collected before post-incident review):
| Artifact | Required? | Responsible team | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Reproduction inputs + outputs | yes | eng-serving-runtime | Must include request headers, model version id, route, and timestamp |
| Baseline outputs (pinned model) | yes | model-onboarding | Needed for diffing and delta metrics |
| Eval harness snapshot (pre-deploy) | yes | applied-ml | Attach failing prompt ids and metrics |
| Trace sample (end-to-end) | yes | eng-sre | Include trace id, spans around request transform, model call, and post-processing |
| GPU/host logs | yes | eng-infra | Kernel OOMs, CUDA errors, driver messages if present |
| KV / cache stats | no | eng-serving-runtime | Cache eviction/prefix-hit metrics for affected route |
| Canary -> prod comparison dashboard | yes | eng-platform | Time-series and histograms for scoring, latency, tokens-per-request |

Telemetry and metrics to gather:
- Output-difference metrics: token-level edit distance, embedding cosine drop, classification confusion matrix changes.
- Input distribution drift: tokenization length changes, new tokens rate, out-of-vocab ratio.
- Latency and concurrency patterns correlated with regression window.
- Memory/GPU pressure: allocation spikes, kernel errors, swap activity.
- Prefix/KV cache miss rate and cache eviction counts.
- Canary vs baseline percentile scoring (mean, p50/p90/p99).

Reproduction and replay procedure (step-by-step):
1. Create an isolated replay environment (recommended: test-cluster or ephemeral dedicated node pool) with the exact software stack (runtime binary, quantization flags, CUDA/cuDNN versions).
2. Replay a representative subset of traffic: start with 100 recorded failed requests, then expand to a 1% traffic sample.
3. Run baseline model and current model side-by-side; capture token-by-token outputs and logits when available.
4. If determinism is an issue, fix random seeds and disable non-deterministic kernels where feasible.
5. Log differences to a delta artifact and compute the automated regression score used by applied-ml (attach to postmortem).

Root cause classification (postmortem should pick one primary and list contributing causes):
- Model artifact regression: weights or tokenizer changed, unintended quantization, or wrong model artifact uploaded.
- Data / input distribution shift: upstream preprocessing change, new client behavior, or corrupt data.
- Serving/runtime change: new kernel selection, batching change, KV cache eviction policy update.
- Deployment/config error: wrong model pinned to route, rollout policy misconfiguration, or partial rollback.
- Infrastructure fault: silent IO errors, GPU ECC events, or network flaps causing partial responses.

Quick decision criteria and rollback guidance:
- If regression score > 5% relative to baseline on critical prompt-set and customer impact is SEV2 or higher, perform emergency rollback to pinned model version.
- If regression is limited to a narrow route or config, perform targeted traffic re-routing (canary holdback or route-level pin).
- Document any hotfixes applied in the incident timeline and ensure a follow-up permanent fix is scheduled.

Post-incident artifact checklist (for the review board):
- Incident timeline with timestamps aligned to deploys, config changes, infra events.
- Reproduction script and environment.yaml used for replay.
- Delta metrics and evaluation prompt failures (CSV of failing prompt ids).
- Root cause analysis and list of contributing factors.
- Action items with owners, target dates, and verification criteria.

SLO and error-budget linkage:
- Tag each regression incident with the SLO(s) affected and the amount of error-budget consumed (hours/days or percentage of error-budget).
- The review board will prioritize follow-ups based on combined severity and error-budget burn.

Communications templates (short):
- Customer-facing: "We identified a regression affecting [route]. We have rolled back to the previously pinned model version and are investigating. We will follow up with a timeline and root cause. ID: <INC-XXXX>."
- Internal Slack: "INC-XXXX: Model regression detected on route /v1/chat. Reproduced vs baseline. Rollback executed at 15:12 UTC. Primary owner: @eng-sre-oncall."

Long-term remediation guidance (examples):
- Add pre-deploy delta checks in CI: embedding-similarity gating, prompt-set smoke checks, and a ratchet that prevents rollout if critical prompts exceed threshold.
- Expand canary policy: require zero regression on holdout prompt sets for 24h at 10% traffic before full rollout.
- Improve observable baselines: store model fingerprints and distribution sketches with each release.

Postmortem review meeting agenda (60 minutes):
1. Read the incident summary (5m).
2. Timeline and reproduction demonstration (15m).
3. RCA and contributing factors (15m).
4. Action items and verification plan (15m).
5. Open questions and owner sign-off (10m).

Acceptance criteria for closure:
- All critical action items assigned with owners and target dates.
- Verification plan documented and reproducible.
- Customer communications completed and linked in the postmortem.
- If regression involved a model artifact, the release process is updated to include a new check and a follow-up audit is scheduled.

Ownership and escalation:
- Initial owner: eng-sre oncall for triage.
- Secondary owner: model-owner from applied-ml team for RCA and corrective releases.
- If the incident crosses customer boundaries or contractual SLAs, notify Customer Success and Legal within 2 hours.

Related resources and links:
- Model onboarding guide: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/model-onboarding/overview
- Regression evaluation harness: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness/README
- Canary dashboard: /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/canary-comparison-template

Notes and rationale:
This standard recognizes that model regressions require evidence-centered reviews that combine both classical SRE telemetry and ML evaluation artifacts. The goal is fast, auditable remediation with minimal customer impact, and a feedback loop that prevents similar regressions in future rollouts.

Document maintenance:
- Maintainers: eng-sre (primary), applied-ml (reviewer).
- Review cadence: annually or after any regression that consumes >10% of a major SLO's error-budget.

Title: SLO to Customer Impact Classifier and Remediation Workflow

SLO to Customer Impact Classifier and Remediation Workflow

Overview

This page defines a reproducible classifier that maps SLO signals to a customer-impact tier and a prescriptive remediation workflow. It is intended to: align SRE, Product, and Customer Success during SLO degradations; minimize time-to-customer-remediation; and create consistent inputs for post-incident reviews and error-budget decisions.

Audience
- On-call SREs
- SRE leads and managers
- Incident commanders (ICs)
- Customer Success (CS) and Support for high-impact incidents

Principles
1) Tie every SLO alert to an explicit customer-impact tier (1–4).
2) Automate low-friction routing and remediation for common degradations.
3) Escalate proactively for any Tier 1/2 customer impact.
4) Preserve evidence for postmortems and error-budget reconciliations.

Definitions
- SLO: Service Level Objective (e.g., request_latency_p95 <= 200ms).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO target over the defined rolling window.
- Customer-impact tier: a 1–4 classification used to route and prioritize incident response.

Customer-impact tiers (quick guide)
| Tier | User-visible symptoms | Business effect | Escalation urgency | Owner to notify |
|------|----------------------|-----------------|-------------------|----------------|
| 1 | Widespread request failures or complete service outage across regions | Severe revenue/customer retention impact | Immediate (page) | SRE lead + Product PM + CS Director |
| 2 | Large subset of customers impacted (major tenants) or major feature down | Significant business disruption for key customers | High (page + slack) | SRE oncall + Product owner + CS manager |
| 3 | Localized errors, degraded latency for non-critical endpoints | Minor customer annoyance, limited support tickets | Medium (slack alert) | On-call SRE + Feature owner |
| 4 | Minor latency increase or transient errors with no customer tickets | No immediate business impact | Low (ticket) | On-call SRE |

SLO catalog excerpt (example mapping)
| SLO name | Metric | Target | Error-budget window | Default customer-impact tier |
|----------|--------|--------|--------------------|--------------------------|
| request_latency_p95_public | request_latency_p95{route=~"/v1/.*"} | <= 200ms | 30d | 2 |
| api_error_rate_5m | sum(rate(api_errors[5m])) / sum(rate(api_requests[5m])) | <= 0.5% | 7d | 1 |
| embedding_throughput_tail | embedding_infer_latency_p99 | < 1.2s | 14d | 3 |
| console_ui_availability | synthetic_check(console_login) | 99.5% monthly | 30d | 3 |

Classification algorithm (operational)
1) Alert receives telemetry: detector alerts on SLI breach or error-budget burn (alerting config).
2) Metrics enrichment: pull impact signals (affected tenant count, region distribution, top N tenants by RPS, open support tickets matching pattern).
3) Heuristics engine evaluates the following scores (0–100): failure-scope, severity, customer-exposure.
4) Combined score maps to Tier: Score >= 80 -> Tier 1; 60–79 -> Tier 2; 30–59 -> Tier 3; < 30 -> Tier 4.
5) Attach classification to incident and follow the tiered remediation workflow below.

Heuristics inputs (examples)
- affected_tenant_ratio: percent of total tenant RPS impacted.
- p95_latency_delta: percent change vs baseline.
- p99_error_spike: absolute increase in error count at p99.
- active_cs_tickets: number of open tickets tagged /inference or /api.

Operational remediations by tier
Tier 1 (Immediate response)
- Page the SRE oncall and SRE lead.
- Open an incident in the incident-management system using template: tag=CUSTOMER_IMPACT_TIER_1.
- Run mitigation playbook: fallback-to-compatible-model-variant (see runbook link).
- If capacity-related: trigger immediate capacity burst policy (see CLI below).
- Notify CS and Product leadership within 15 minutes with templated Slack/Jira.

Tier 2 (High-priority)
- Notify on-call via high-severity Slack alert.
- Execute targeted throttles or tenant fair-share configuration.
- Begin canary rollback of recent model or config changes (if correlated).

Tier 3 (Operational handling)
- Create ticket and schedule on-call investigation within 30–60 minutes.
- Apply mitigations from the runbook: restart worker pool, clear KV cache, or disabled newly-deployed feature flag.

Tier 4 (Monitoring)
- Monitor metrics and let automated remediation run. If unresolved after SLA window (6 hours), escalate to Tier 3.

Sample alert rule (Prometheus-style YAML)
alert: HighAPIErrorRate
expr: |
  sum(rate(api_errors_total[5m])) / sum(rate(api_requests_total[5m])) > 0.005
for: 2m
labels:
  severity: page
  impact: "possible-customer-impact"
annotations:
  summary: "API error rate >0.5% over 5m"
  runbook: "https://confluence.internal/s/reliability/runbooks/api-error-rate-mitigation"

Enrichment query examples (pseudo-SQL / analytics)
- Tenants affected in last 10m: SELECT tenant_id, count(*) FROM requests WHERE status >= 500 AND timestamp > now() - interval '10 minutes' GROUP BY tenant_id ORDER BY count DESC LIMIT 50;
- Support ticket correlation: count tickets where created_at >= now()-10m AND tags IN ('api','inference')

Capacity escalation knobs (examples)
| Trigger | Condition | Automated action | Escalation threshold |
|---------|-----------|------------------|----------------------|
| headroom_exhausted | available_gpu_slots < 5% | trigger-burst-alloc --pool=shared-burst | immediate (Tier1) |
| model_warm_pool_empty | warm_pool_size < configured_min | scale-up warm pool by 2 nodes | Tier2 |
| p95_latency_spike | p95 > baseline*1.5 for 10m | enable-prefetch-kv-cache=true | Tier2 |

CLI examples
- Trigger burst capacity (operators only):
  rcmd infra capacity burst apply --pool shared-burst --reason "Tier1 SLO breach" --expires 30m
- Re-route traffic to fallback models:
  rcmd infra routing promote --from model-xyz-v2 --to model-xyz-v1 --weight 100

Communication templates
Slack template (Tier1)
- Channel: #incidents
- Message: :rotating_light: *Tier 1 SLO breach* — request_error_rate_5m at 1.2% impacting ~32% of tenants. IC: @oncall. Mitigation in progress: toggling fallback routing. Please notify CS lead @renee.zhao. Incident link: <INCIDENT_URL>

Jira template fields
- Priority: P0 for Tier1, P1 for Tier2, P2 for Tier3/4
- Components: runtime, routing, capacity, product-feature
- Labels: slo-breach, customer-impact-tier-<n>, automated-enrichment

Post-incident / Error-budget reconciliation
1) Add classification evidence (metrics, tenant list, tickets) to the incident story.
2) Compute error-budget consumption attributable to the incident window.
3) For Tier1/Tier2 incidents: schedule a joint SRE/Product/CS triage within 72 hours. The triage determines whether to take a governance action (e.g., customer credits, temporary throttle, emergency capacity commit).
4) Document remediation plan and assign owners with due dates.

Postmortem checklist (to include in incident review)
- Summary of classifier result and whether the initial tier matched customer reports.
- Timeline of detection -> mitigation -> recovery.
- Root cause and contributing factors including capacity and SLO misconfigurations.
- Action items (owner + due date) and follow-up on error-budget policy.
- Evidence attachments: metrics, logs, enrichment query results.

Automation and operational tooling notes
- The classifier runs in the telemetry enrichment pipeline (owner: telemetry-team). Inputs are Prometheus alerts, request traces, and support ticket API.
- All automated classification decisions must be auditable: store the computed scores and inputs in incident metadata.
- Use feature flags to disable automatic Tier upgrades in sensitive customer accounts.

Ownership and governance
- SLO owner: Each SLO must list a primary owner (SRE or Product) and a secondary owner. Owners are responsible for maintaining mapping in this catalog.
- Classification engine owner: telemetry-team@redwood.com.
- Incident review owner for Tier1/Tier2: SRE lead on rotation.

Runbook links (examples)
- API error mitigation: https://confluence.internal/s/reliability/runbooks/api-error-rate-mitigation
- Fallback routing: https://confluence.internal/s/reliability/runbooks/fallback-routing-and-rollbacks
- Capacity burst playbook: https://confluence.internal/s/reliability/runbooks/capacity-burst-and-burst-rollback

Change log
- 2026-01-15 — Initial draft published (Priya Natarajan).
- 2026-02-20 — Added capacity knobs and CLI examples (review: Liam O'Connor).
- 2026-03-01 — Finalized communication templates and post-incident checklist (review: Renee Zhao).

Appendix: sample incident evidence payload (JSON snippet)
{
  "incident_id": "INC-2026-0115-001",
  "slo": "api_error_rate_5m",
  "computed_scores": { "failure_scope": 78, "severity": 85, "customer_exposure": 60 },
  "mapped_tier": 1,
  "top_affected_tenants": ["tenant-acme", "tenant-vela"],
  "evidence_queries": ["tenant_impact_query_2026-01-15-10m"]
}

If you are an on-call SRE and this workflow appears to misclassify an incident, immediately create a ticket in the SRE backlog and tag the telemetry-owner for a review.

Contact
- Document owner: Priya Natarajan (pri@redwood.com)
- Telemetry owner: telemetry-team@redwood.com
- Incident management: incidents@redwood.com

- Very focused on 'EU-only' residency for core customer datasets; UK and Canada must be selectable regions per workload.

Title: Client Handoff + Triage Landing Pad — Prep & Actions

Client Handoff + Triage Landing Pad — Prep & Actions

Purpose / quick context:
- Short: Capture everything I need to run a first 60–90m war-room + clean handoff to SRE/PM/Engineering for critical client incident. This is a personal landing pad — not the official postmortem.

Immediate objectives for first 30 minutes:
- Stabilize communication: confirm channel (slack #client-<org>-incident) and phone bridge if requested.
- Pull latest state: incident JIRA (JIRA-5923), last deploys, error-rate graphs, recent rollouts.
- Decide initial response tier: Is this page-to-oncall? (yes if P1 production outage or data loss).

Key info to gather (fast):
- Who reported and when: inbound from CSM at 08:07 PST, escalated by customer SRE.
- Scope: affected endpoints (/api/v1/generate, /chat-stream), % of traffic impacted ~40% (from dashboards).
- Impact: generation failures and latency >10s for >5% of calls.
- Recent changes: canary deploy 2026-01-17 (model pin + kernel swap) — check commit abc123.

Stakeholders / contacts (order to ping):
- Customer success: Maya Li (primary), Jamal Ortiz (backup) — call first to confirm customer expectations.
- On-call SRE: Omar Patel — priority.
- Serving runtime lead: Priya Menon — technical lead for kernel/model swap rollbacks.
- PM (product): Lina Gomez — for customer comms / timelines.
- Legal/security: if data exposure suspected, loop in security@redwood.

Initial comms templates (copy/paste, personalize):
- To customer (short): "We’ve opened an incident and our on-call is actively investigating. Initial investigations show increased latency affecting ~40% of requests. We’ll provide an update within 30 minutes with next steps. — Rene/Redwood CS"
- Internal Triage post (slack): "INCIDENT: JIRA-5923 — Elevated error/latency on /api/v1/generate. On-call SRE @omar on it. First update in 30m. Key suspects: canary kernel swap (2026-01-17) or KV cache regression. Link to dash: <dashboard-url>"

Triage checklist (first 60 minutes) — check off as done:
- [ ] Confirm incident channel + email thread + phone bridge if requested
- [ ] Snapshot key dashboards (latency, errors, QPS) + time window 30m pre/post spike
- [ ] Collect recent deploys and rollouts (deploy tags, model versions, quantization changes)
- [ ] Ask on-call to run targeted smoke: curl /health, /api/v1/generate with short prompt
- [ ] Check KV cache hit rates and batching latency metrics
- [ ] Validate fallback routes (model-variant, region fallback) are healthy
- [ ] Decide whether to rollback canary or scale dedicated pool

Decision criteria (quick rules):
- Rollback canary if errors spike correlated with canary hosts and rate >5% and customer impact is P1.
- If latency only at tail and local to a region, consider routing around region before rollback.
- If model outputs corrupted (data integrity), escalate to security and consider immediate rollback & disable model.

Action items (assign during call) — populate owners & ETA here:
- Create incident timeline note (owner: Rene) — ETA 20m
- SRE: run kernel/host health checks + attach sample traces (owner: Omar) — ETA 15m
- Runtime lead: validate recent kernel selection & compare perf on canary hosts (owner: Priya) — ETA 30m
- CS: confirm customer tolerance window and preferred comm cadence (owner: Maya) — ETA 10m
- PM: draft customer update if rollback needed (owner: Lina) — ETA 25m

Communication cadence (first 3 hours):
- T+0: Incident opened + customer ack
- T+30: Short internal status update (what we know, next steps)
- T+60: Decision on rollback / mitigation + customer update if impacted
- Every 60m after until stable: status updates, then shift to postmortem planning

Handoff checklist (to SRE/eng for follow-through):
- [ ] Save concrete artifacts: logs, request IDs, sample latencies, core dumps if any
- [ ] Push any agreed rollback through release-engineering checklist (link: confluence://deploy/rollback-steps)
- [ ] Assign postmortem owner once stabilized (preferably non-oncall)

Notes to self / heuristics I've learned:
- Keep comms templated and short; customers want cadence more than details early on.
- Early rollbacks can reduce blast radius but sometimes mask root cause; prefer targeted routing if viable.
- Lean on canary host logs — kernel selection and quantized model ops are frequent culprits for tail latency.

Open questions to resolve in call:
- Is there any scheduled maintenance in infra for the affected region?
- Any customer-side config changes reported recently?
- Are we seeing correlated increase in KV cache misses across models?

After-action quick notes (post-call to fill in):
- What we did (timeline entries) — fill and attach artifacts
- Who was informed and when (customer + execs)
- Short list of follow-ups with owners and deadlines

Scratch area (things I might paste into the incident):
- "Investigations pointing to kernel swap on canary hosts; rolling back canary while preserving traffic to dedicated pool. Temporary mitigation: increase pool size + route 30% away from canary region."
- "Sample request IDs: req_44af, req_44b0, req_44d9 — added to JIRA as attachments."

-- end landing pad --

(If this turns into a long-running incident, migrate notes to shared confluence page and drop this file into customer folder for record.)

Title: Audit retention: role-aware filtered data dump

Audit retention: role-aware filtered data dump

Provide a secure, role-aware bulk dump capability for audit logs from the Console that supports CSV, JSON, and NDJSON outputs while respecting RBAC v2 filters, retention policies, and SSO-backed admin permissions. The goal is to let enterprise admins and compliance teams extract query-scoped audit slices (time-window, actor, resource, action, outcome) for offline analysis and e-discovery without exposing redacted fields to users who lack privileges. Must handle multi-GB exports via cursored incremental downloads, enforce rate and size limits, and produce manifest metadata (query, applied filters, snapshot_time, schema_version).
Admins with export permission can request a filtered dump from Console and receive a download link when ready
RBAC v2 filters are enforced server-side; results never include fields flagged as 'sensitive' unless requester has explicit allow-list role
Supports CSV, JSON, NDJSON formats; manifest with schema and applied filters included in export bundle
Large exports (>500MB) are produced as multipart blobs with cursored pagination and resumable downloads
All export requests are logged to an immutable audit stream (separate from the exported data) with requester identity from SSO/SAML
Exports respect tenant-level retention and cannot retrieve records older than retention cutoff unless super-admin override is used (and is itself audited)
Server-side query engine will apply RBAC v2 masking rules before serialization
Use cursor-based incremental listing (time+id cursor) to avoid deep OFFSET scans on BigTable/ClickHouse
Export worker will stream directly to pre-signed object storage to minimize memory; manifest JSON recorded in metadata store
Encryption-in-transit and at-rest required; generated download links expire after configurable TTL
Rate limit export initiation per org and throttle per concurrent worker to preserve runtime throughput
Decided against synchronous on-the-fly CSV generation for >100k rows to avoid blocking request threads; background worker + presigned link chosen
Chose cursor (time+id) approach over purely time-windowed pagination to ensure deterministic ordering during concurrent writes
Opted to implement NDJSON as default for JSON exports to simplify incremental parsing for downstream tooling
Will gate inclusion of 'request_payload' and 'response_content' fields behind a separate sensitive-data allow-list to reduce blast radius
Test with synthetic 50M-row dataset to validate cursor stability and worker memory bounds
Verify RBAC masking across combinations: org-admin, security-reader, billing-admin, auditor_role
Test resumable multipart downloads and resume after simulated network failure
Pen test for indirect disclosure via manifest metadata (avoid including raw user identifiers unless necessary)

2026-02-18 Tom Ortega (Eng): Spike completed — streaming to S3 with multipart upload works. Cursor format proposed: <ts>|<event_id>. Avoids offset costs.
2026-02-23 Security Review (note): RBAC must redact PII fields by default; allow-list for security/admin roles only. Legal requested a record of who used super-admin override.
2026-02-28 Design feedback (Sara Li): Console UX should surface estimated file size, retention cutoff, and a clear warning when sensitive fields will be included. Include a preview first 500 rows for CSV/JSON.
2026-03-03 Eng update (Tom): Implemented server-side masking layer and integrated RBAC v2 policy evaluation. Unit tests added for masked vs unmasked retrieval paths.
2026-03-06 PM note (Maya): Add telemetry events for export_created, export_completed, export_failed with tokenized requester id for SSO traceability.
2026-03-09 Ops (Jared): Added quota to prevent noisy exports during peak inference traffic; default concurrent exports per org = 2, adjustable via plan tier.

Title: Audit log export: role-aware filtered dump (2026)

Audit log export: role-aware filtered dump (2026)

## Overview
This document specifies the Console and API capability to export filtered slices of tenant audit logs as a bulk dump while enforcing RBAC v2, retention limits, and SSO-backed administrative permissions.

The primary use cases are compliance reporting, e-discovery preparation, and offline analytics. The design explicitly prevents disclosure of sensitive fields to users without the appropriate allow-list role.

## Scope
### In scope
- Role-aware bulk export for audit logs, initiated from Console (Admin) and backed by a server-side export worker.
- Query-scoped exports: time window, actor, resource, action, outcome.
- Field-level masking and omission using RBAC v2 policy evaluation.
- Export bundles include a manifest describing query, filters, snapshot time, and schema version.
- Support for multi-GB exports using cursor-based pagination and resumable multipart downloads.
- Export request auditing to an immutable audit stream separate from the exported data.

### Out of scope
- Real-time streaming feeds for customer SIEMs (handled by the Audit Streaming project).
- Interactive “preview rows” in Console (removed; see decision ADR-EXPORT-004 below).

## User experience (Console)
1. Admin navigates to: Console → Security → Audit Logs → Export.
2. Admin configures filters (time range required; other filters optional).
3. Console shows:
   - Estimated record count and approximate size (best-effort)
   - Retention cutoff date for the tenant
   - Whether any sensitive fields may be included (based on role)
4. Admin submits export request.
5. Console shows export status: queued → running → completed/failed.
6. On completion, Console provides a time-limited download link and checksum.

## Data security and access control
### Authentication and identity
- Requester identity is derived from SSO/SAML session (Console) or service token (API).
- The exported bundle records requester identity in the immutable audit stream (not inside the bundle manifest).

### Authorization model
RBAC v2 is enforced server-side for every exported row.

Permissions:
- audit.export.create: can initiate exports
- audit.export.read: can view export status and download links for exports they initiated
- audit.export.read_all: can view exports initiated by other admins within the same tenant
- audit.export.sensitive_fields: can receive fields classified as Sensitive (PII / payload bodies / tokens)

Field handling rules:
- Default: sensitive fields are omitted entirely (not present) rather than present-but-null.
- If audit.export.sensitive_fields is present, sensitive fields are included, subject to any additional policy constraints.

### Retention and legal holds
- Exports cannot retrieve records older than the tenant retention cutoff.
- The previous “super-admin retention override” is deprecated.
- New approach (2026-03 update): retrieval beyond standard retention requires an explicit Legal Hold, represented by a legal_hold_id, and is only allowed for tenants with Legal Hold enabled.
- All uses of legal_hold_id are logged to the immutable audit stream with ticket reference.

## Export formats
Supported formats (2026-03 update):
- NDJSON (recommended/default): line-delimited JSON objects
- CSV: RFC 4180-ish with quoted fields and stable column order

Not supported:
- “Pretty JSON array” export (removed due to memory pressure and poor incremental handling).

## Export bundle structure
Each export produces a bundle containing:
- data.ndjson OR data.csv (may be split into multiple parts)
- manifest.json
- checksums.txt

Multipart behavior:
- Exports larger than 1.0 GB are produced as multiple numbered parts (part-0001, part-0002, ...).
- Download is resumable using HTTP range requests.

## Manifest contents (manifest.json)
The manifest is designed to support downstream compliance workflows without leaking sensitive data.

Fields (conceptual):
- schema_version: string (e.g., "2026-03-18")
- snapshot_time: RFC3339 timestamp when the export job started reading
- tenant_id: internal tenant identifier
- requested_by: NOT included (identity is captured in immutable audit log)
- query: normalized filters (time window, actor/resource/action/outcome)
- applied_rbac_policy_hash: hash of effective RBAC v2 policy used for evaluation
- retention_cutoff: timestamp
- output_format: "ndjson" | "csv"
- part_count: integer
- total_records: integer (best-effort)
- warnings: array of strings (e.g., "Some fields omitted due to RBAC")

## Backend design
### High-level flow
1. Console calls Export API to create an export job.
2. API validates permissions, normalizes query, enforces retention/hold rules.
3. API writes an export job record and enqueues work.
4. Export worker reads audit events in deterministic order, applies RBAC masking/omission, and streams output to object storage.
5. Worker writes manifest + checksums and marks job complete.
6. API returns a presigned download URL (time-limited) when requested.

### Storage and encryption
- Data is streamed directly to object storage using multipart upload to avoid memory pressure.
- Encryption:
  - In transit: TLS
  - At rest: object storage server-side encryption (SSE) plus KMS key per environment
- Presigned download link TTL (2026-03 update): 4 hours default; configurable per plan tier (max 24 hours).

### Query and pagination
- Use cursor-based incremental listing to avoid deep OFFSET scans.
- Cursor format: <event_ts_ms>|<event_id>
- Ordering: (event_ts asc, event_id asc) to ensure deterministic traversal during concurrent writes.

### Masking and serialization
- RBAC v2 policy evaluation happens before serialization.
- Sensitive fields are dropped unless audit.export.sensitive_fields is granted.
- Additional gating (separate allow-list) applies to:
  - request_payload
  - response_content
  - ip_address (masked by default; last octet removed unless sensitive_fields granted)

## Limits and quotas
| Limit | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Max concurrent exports per org | 1 | 2026-03 update (was 2) to reduce peak load |
| Max export lookback | Retention cutoff | Extended lookback requires legal_hold_id |
| Max parts per export | 2,000 | Prevent runaway multipart bundles |
| Rate limit: create export | 5 / hour / org | Burst allowed up to 2 within 5 minutes |

## Telemetry and auditing
Telemetry events:
- audit_export_created
- audit_export_started
- audit_export_completed
- audit_export_failed

Notes:
- Telemetry includes tokenized requester ID (for correlation) and tenant ID.
- A separate immutable audit stream records:
  - requester identity (SSO subject or service token)
  - export job id
  - query summary (redacted)
  - whether sensitive fields were included
  - whether legal_hold_id was used and associated ticket reference

## Operational runbook (high level)
### Common failures
- Object storage multipart upload failures: retry with exponential backoff; ensure worker has sufficient egress.
- Policy evaluation timeouts: reduce batch size and ensure policy cache is warm.
- Retention violations: confirm tenant retention and whether Legal Hold is enabled.

### On-call checks
- Dashboard: audit-export-metrics (queue depth, completion latency, failures)
- Verify KMS permissions for export worker identity
- Confirm org-level concurrency gate is functioning

## Testing and QA
- Synthetic large dataset test: 50M rows for cursor stability and throughput.
- RBAC masking matrix: org-admin, security-reader, billing-admin, auditor_role.
- Resumable download test: interrupt mid-download and resume via range requests.
- Security review: ensure no indirect disclosure via manifest, filenames, or error messages.

## Key decisions and changes
- ADR-EXPORT-001: Background worker + presigned link chosen over synchronous generation.
- ADR-EXPORT-002: Cursor (time+id) chosen over offset-based pagination.
- ADR-EXPORT-003: NDJSON recommended for JSON-like exports to support streaming parsers.
- ADR-EXPORT-004 (2026-03 update): Removed “preview first 500 rows” from Console due to data leakage risk and inconsistent RBAC UX; replaced with size estimate + schema description.
- ADR-EXPORT-005 (2026-03 update): Deprecated super-admin retention override; replaced with Legal Hold workflow using legal_hold_id and mandatory audit trail.

## Ownership
Primary owner team: Security (Audit & Compliance).
Implementation team: Engineering (Security-Logging-Initiative).

## References
- Linear: ENG-78123 (implementation tracking)
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/4321
- Privacy matrix: https://drive.redwood.ai/attachments/audit-privacy-matrix.xlsx

Title: Sev1/Sev2 incident process (engineering oncall)

Sev1/Sev2 incident process (engineering oncall)

# Overview
This page defines Redwoods standard process for Sev1 and Sev2 production incidents. It includes the required roles, decision points, and required outputs.

# Severity definitions (summary)
- **Sev1:** Widespread customer impact (majority of traffic impacted) or critical functionality unavailable in 1+ regions.
- **Sev2:** Significant degradation (elevated latency or elevated 5xx) affecting a subset of customers/regions/routes.

# When to declare
Declare an incident if any of the following are true:
- sustained 5xx rate increase beyond alert thresholds
- sustained p95 latency increase beyond SLO thresholds
- widespread streaming disconnects
- repeated crash-loop or GPU OOM affecting availability

# Required roles
- **Incident Commander (IC):** owns coordination, decisions, approvals for mitigations
- **Operations Lead (Ops):** executes changes and keeps timeline updated
- **Comms Lead:** posts status updates, coordinates with Support/CS
- **Subject Matter Expert (SME):** runtime/platform expert doing deep investigation

# Mandatory steps
1. Create incident Slack channel in #incidents (or use incident-bot)
2. Assign roles (IC, Ops, Comms, SME)
3. Establish update cadence (default: 15 minutes internal, 30 minutes external if impacted)
4. Identify mitigation candidates (rollback, feature flag changes, traffic shifting)
5. If an emergency production change is required: follow EPC policy approvals and create EPC record

# Timeline requirements
The incident timeline must include:
- first detection + alert source
- mitigations attempted and exact deploy/config times
- impact changes observed after each mitigation
- customer comms times (status page + direct comms)

# Exit criteria
- error rates and latency have returned to baseline and remain stable for 30 minutes
- support queue is stabilizing (no new spike of related tickets)
- rollback plan documented if the mitigation is temporary

# After-action requirements
- Sev1: postmortem required
- Sev2: incident review required if customer-visible or if EPC executed
- Follow-up items must be tracked in Linear

Title: Office inventory + keycard audit + disposal request (storage shelves + access system cleanup)

Office inventory + keycard audit + disposal request (storage shelves + access system cleanup)

Request type: Internal support / facilities + security coordination

Background
Office moved desks last quarter; storage now contains untagged peripherals, old keycards, and leftover badge holders. This ticket consolidates the remaining cleanup work so we can reconcile inventory, tidy shared spaces, and reduce risk from stray credentials.

Scope / Goals
- Produce a concise inventory of unassigned equipment (monitors, keyboards, spare GPU boxes, dongles)
- Audit and deactivate lost/old keycards in the access system and return/re-enroll active ones
- Clean and label community storage shelves and identify disposal candidates for Facilities pickup

Updates vs earlier plan
- Security requested we export access logs for the last 12 months (not 18) for the initial cross-check; they will expand the window only if anomalies are found.
- Anything that could contain data-bearing media (NVMe/SSDs/USBs) must be separated into a "Security review" bin and cannot go directly to e-waste.
- Facilities asked that disposal candidates be grouped into: e-waste, donation, recycle, landfill, and "needs approval".

Acceptance criteria
- CSV inventory uploaded to Drive with columns: item_id, type, location, status, owner_hint, notes
- Keycards deactivated or reassigned; list of card IDs with current status documented (include reason: lost, terminated, replaced, active)
- Disposal list handed to Facilities with approval note and the category breakdown

Planned steps
1) Quick sweep team (1-2 eng volunteers + Facilities) to inventory storage (target: 1 day on-site)
2) Collate CSV + apply physical tags/labels to boxes/shelves (target: 0.5-1 day)
3) Keycard audit with Security (Omar to coordinate) (target: 1-2 days, mostly admin work)
4) Disposal / reallocation decisions + update asset tracker (target: 0.5-1 day)

Notes / investigation log (messy)
- Found box labeled "quantization-experiments-2019" that may contain an older NVMe; moved to Security review bin (do not e-waste yet).
- Some badge IDs show up in access logs in 2024 despite being physically in lost-and-found; need cross-check against HR termination list and replacement cards.
- Facilities prefers completion before holiday break; if we slip, we should at minimum complete the keycard deprovisioning and isolate data-bearing media.

Links / artifacts
- Initial scan (older): drive:/shared_drives/operations/office-inventory/initial-scan.csv

If any item is sensitive (hard drives, HSM parts, private compute media) escalate to Security and open a separate INT ticket with chain-of-custody notes.

2025-11-19 - Omar Singh (Assignee): Sweep completed. ~37 items logged, 6 marked for Security review (possible data-bearing). Draft disposal list prepared; waiting on Facilities approval for donation vs recycle for monitors with no asset tags. Starting keycard cross-check next.

Title: SLA-aware GPU memory reserve planner for weights, KV shards, and activations

SLA-aware GPU memory reserve planner for weights, KV shards, and activations

Goal: produce an SLA-aware GPU memory budgeting plan that explicitly divides per-GPU reserved capacity across model weights, KV cache shards, and activation working set, with measurable safety margins ('reserve' aka 'safety buffer') to avoid OOMs under tail-load bursts and prioritized latency SLOs. This ticket produces the modeling, a small synthetic and live benchmark matrix, and an ops-ready config templating approach so Dedicated and Private deployments can apply conservative defaults and optionally tighten for cost.
1) Baseline footprint estimation: for target model families (e.g., RWKV/GPT-style LLMs at 7B/13B/30B), capture three components per model: weights (quantized footprint), static KV shard overhead, and per-request activation working set (sequence-dependent).
2) Quantized weight allocation: assume production default quantization Q4_0 for weights unless flagged. Record both compressed on-disk size and decompressed inference memory (kernel temporary overhead). Example target: 7B -> weights 6.0 GB (q4), 13B -> 11.0 GB (q4).
3) KV cache sharding model: model KV is sharded across GPUs for multi-GPU placements and sharded-per-socket for single-GPU. Use formula KV_bytes = tokens_cached * hidden_size * 2 (float16) * head_count_adjustment. Recommend a conservative KV reservation of 1.15x observed steady-state to cover jitter and in-flight writes.
4) Activation working set: model attention and intermediate activations scale with beam/seq-length and batch. Model per-request activation estimate uses A = base_activation_per_token * max_seq_length * effective_batch. For burst safety use peak_batch = observed_p50*2 or configured burst limit, whichever larger.
5) Safety margin & reserve policy: two-tier reserve: critical_reserve (for SLA-protection) = max(8% of total GPU memory, 0.5 GB), op_reserve (for opportunistic headroom to absorb KV insert bursts) = 1.1x KV + 1.05x activation baseline. Critical_reserve must not be sacrificed by autoscaling decisions without explicit override.
6) Allocation order on GPU: immutable weights pinned first -> critical_reserve pinned second -> KV shards allocation -> activations buffer (dynamically grown with preemption signals to batching controller).
7) Runtime knobs to implement: per-model memory profile metadata, 'reserve_mode' (strict|optimistic), kv_reserved_ratio (default 0.15), activation_slack_pct (default 5%), and 'oom_preempt_threshold' to trigger graceful shedding/fallbacks.
8) Cost/control trade-off guidance: tighter reserves reduce idle headroom and improve utilization but increase OOM risk for tail bursts. Provide recommended presets: 'conservative' (default for enterprise), 'balanced' (for Dedicated with SLA 99.9%), 'aggressive' (for non-critical dev workloads).
A) Synthetic sweep: for each model size (7B/13B/30B) run matrix of batch sizes {1,2,4,8} and seq-lens {128,512,1024} to measure: peak GPU allocation, transient spikes, KV growth rate per second, and time-to-reclaim after request finishes.
B) Live traffic shadowing: route 5% of production traffic as shadow to a dedicated cluster with current 'conservative' reserve and record OOM events and latency tail (p95/p99/p999).
C) Fault-injection: artificially delay KV deallocation in the runtime to simulate slower GC and observe how much reserve is needed to avoid cascading OOMs.
D) Metrics to capture: 'gpu_mem_total', 'gpu_mem_free', 'weights_committed', 'kv_committed', 'activations_committed', 'oom_count', 'preemptions_triggered', and trace annotated with request_id and seq_len. Store benchmark traces in the perf-dashboard and attach links to results.
1) Implement metadata + reserve knobs in runtime (PR # to follow). Ship behind feature flag 'reserve-planner-v1'.
2) Canary: enable for a small Dedicated cluster (non-prod) with conservative preset. Run Synth sweep + 24h shadowing. Verify no OOM regressions and stable latency.
3) Gradual ramp: enable 'balanced' preset for selected tenants with alerting on any OOM or preemption. Iterate on ratios based on observed KV growth delta.
4) Docs: add 'GPU memory budgeting' page to Console docs and add default presets for Dedicated and Private install manifests.
5) Ops playbook: add runbook steps for when 'gpu_mem_free' falls below critical_reserve: scale policy, enable eviction, or fallback model variant.
A) Models 7B/13B/30B run all synthetic matrix without binary OOMs on target presets (conservative/balanced).
B) Shadowing shows <=1 OOM per 100k requests and latency tail increase <5% relative to baseline.
C) Dashboard widgets created with live breakdown by weights/KV/activations and automated alerts when free memory < critical_reserve.
D) Runtime exposes metadata and reserve knobs usable by Console for policy configuration.
2026-03-02 - Aisha: Kickoff meeting notes attached in Drive: https://drive.redwood.company/drive/folders/GB-memory-planner. Decided to prioritize 7B/13B first; 30B coverage next sprint.
2026-03-04 - Mateo: Initial memory model spreadsheet uploaded (sheets id: 1a2b3c). Early estimate shows KV can dominate at long seq lengths; need to validate with live traces.
2026-03-05 - Priya (SRE): Recommended adding 'oom_preempt_threshold' and an alert driven link to PagerDuty. Marked as high customer impact for Dedicated tenants.
2026-03-07 - Design review with DX: UX needs to show per-route memory pressure + per-model preset selection in Console. Creating a follow-up DES ticket to mock screens.
2026-03-09 - Mateo: Implemented simulation harness for KV growth (branch: feature/gpu-reserve-sim). Opening PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4123
2026-03-10 - Aisha: Ran synthetic sweep on a 4-GPU dev cluster; attached results summary in perf dashboard: https://perf.redwood.company/d/kv-buffer-sweep. Observed transient spikes that exceed naive 10% slack; increasing KV multiplier to 1.15x reduced reclaims.

Title: Daylight-saving boundary caused missing prorated free-tier credit for cross-region batch-embed job

Daylight-saving boundary caused missing prorated free-tier credit for cross-region batch-embed job

Issue summary:
Customer reports an unexpected negative provisional balance and missing prorated free-tier credit on their finalized invoice for a bulk embedding job that spanned the US DST transition. Impact:
- PixelFlow saw a -$84 provisional adjustment and autopay failed on 2026-03-09 invoice finalization.
- The batch embed ran across us-east and eu-west and the scheduler split work across hour boundaries that crossed the DST boundary for the org's billing tag.
Environment:
- prod, dedicated capacity, regions: us-east-1 (primary), eu-west-1 (fallback).
Steps to reproduce (as reported by customer):
1) Schedule a large batch-embed job that starts 2026-03-08 22:30 UTC and runs until 2026-03-09 02:15 UTC.
2) Job shards route between us-east and eu-west workers.
3) Observe invoice provisional lines and autopay failure on 2026-03-09.
Observed behavior:
- Prorated free-tier buffer credit was applied to the earlier hourly window but not to the window that shifted due to DST rules for the customer's org timezone tag.
- Postbacks from eu-west arrived with hour tags that did not align with the aggregator's UTC-windowing logic, producing a split-hour attribution and eventual negative provisional balance.
Expected behavior:
- Free-tier prorate should be applied consistently independent of DST transitions; hour windows used by postback aggregator and billing pipelines should align and be anchored in UTC to avoid double-split attribution.
Logs & evidence provided by customer:
- Customer provided job IDs: job-pixelflow-20260308-9, postback fingerprints for two shards, and a screenshot of the invoice line showing -$84 provisional adjustment.
- Packet captures and timestamps included in the customer attachment (sensitive) and uploaded to secure support artifact store.
2026-03-10 - Support (Aisha): Acknowledged receipt and escalated to Billing & SRE. Asked for job IDs and invoice PDF. Customer provided artifacts same day.
2026-03-11 - Billing (Marco): Initial hypothesis: postback aggregator windowing misaligned for tags using localized timezone. Pulling aggregator logs for the billing window 2026-03-09T00:00Z-2026-03-09T04:00Z.
2026-03-12 - SRE (Chen Li): Found that eu-west postbacks carried hour_tag=2026-03-09T01:00+01:00 while aggregator normalized tags to local org timezone, causing one shard to be double-split across adjacent hourly buckets.
2026-03-12 - Support (Aisha) -> Customer: Requested permission to view org's timezone tag mapping and asked if they ran any overlapping scheduled jobs. Customer confirmed no manual overlap; they use local timezone mapping in Console (Europe/Paris).
2026-03-13 - Billing (Marco): Applied provisional credit to offset negative balance while fix is implemented; awaiting confirmation that autopay can be retried. Noted follow-up actions scheduled.
Hypotheses:
- Postback aggregator used org-local timezone mapping for some regions and UTC anchoring for others after a recent deploy (scheduler PR-3065) causing window misalignment.
- DST boundary caused hour_tag normalization to produce different hour boundaries for eu-west (CET/CEST) vs aggregator UTC buckets.
Findings:
- Aggregator logs (job-pixelflow-20260308-9) show three postbacks with timestamps 2026-03-09T00:58:12+00:00, 2026-03-09T01:03:04+01:00, 2026-03-09T01:58:50+01:00. Aggregator normalized second and third to local offsets resulting in split attribution.
- Billing pipeline assumes hour windows are inclusive of UTC-based boundaries; mismatch introduced during rollout of build that added 'local-hour-tag' for console display, but postback pipeline unintentionally used it for aggregation.
- No evidence of duplicate tokens or retry storms. Token metering looks consistent with expected counts.
Related code references: PRs linked above; scheduler change that introduced local tagging: PR-3065 (rolled back in staging but partial migration to prod happened on 2026-03-07).
Applied a provisional invoice credit equal to the negative provisional line (-$84) to allow autopay to succeed. Recommended customers schedule large cross-region batch jobs entirely within a single UTC/hour window until fix deploy. Support toggled a temporary postback normalization flag for PixelFlow to force UTC windowing.
Temporary mitigation: provisional credit applied and postback normalization flag set for PixelFlow org to force UTC anchoring. Long-term fix: change aggregator to ignore localized hour tags for billing aggregation and use server-side UTC truncation of timestamps; regression test added for DST boundary jobs. Patch PR-4287 prepared to normalize postback timestamps to UTC at ingestion and PR-3120 updates scheduler tagging docs. Deployment targeted for 2026-03-18 with monitoring alert added.
Deploy PR-4287 to prod to normalize postbacks to UTC at ingestion (owner: Billing team) - target 2026-03-18
Add end-to-end regression test that simulates DST-transition spanning batch jobs (owner: QA) - target 2026-03-16
Audit recent canary rollouts for other orgs with local timezone tags and flag any with overlapping windows (owner: SRE) - target 2026-03-15
Document fallback for customers that require localized hour display vs billing UTC anchoring in Console docs (owner: Docs) - target 2026-03-22
2026-03-13 - Support: Notified PixelFlow that provisional credit has been applied and autopay retried successfully. Explainer: DST boundary caused split-hour attribution; long-term fix will ensure billing uses UTC anchoring and avoid similar cases. Customer asked for an audit of prior month runs; billing agreed to perform audit and provide results by 2026-03-17.
