Title: Interactive Latency Canvas — model/route timelines and streaming vs blocking decomposition

Interactive Latency Canvas — model/route timelines and streaming vs blocking decomposition

Background:
We need a single exploratory dashboard (the "Interactive Latency Canvas") that lets SREs, runtime and product owners compare latency distributions across models and routes with automatic separation between streaming vs blocking (non-streaming) IO modes. Existing dashboards are numerous but fragmented; this work consolidates cohorting, trace hooks, and enriched metrics into a unified surface that supports root-cause drills and runbook actions.

Goals:
- Surface p50/p95/p99 latency by model_version and route_name with a toggle for streaming vs blocking IO.
- Allow cohort-based comparisons (prompt length, open/closed loop, kv-cache hit/miss) and request-shape bucketing (short/medium/long).
- Overlay KV-cache hit-rate, batch-size distribution and 'stream-early-output' metric to explain downstream latency variance.
- Link directly to pre-sampled traces that include kernel selection, batch_id, and early-output anchors.
- Provide alerting recipes for streaming-mode regressions (spike in p95 or increase in chunk-latency).

Design & instrumentation changes required:
- Tracing: add trace attributes: model_version, route_name, io_mode (streaming|blocking), batch_id, kernel_variant, kv_cache_hit (true|false), response_first_chunk_ts. Update trace hook to capture first-chunk timestamp for streaming flows.
- Metrics: enrich latency timer metrics with tags: model_version, route_name, io_mode, prompt_len_bucket, kv_cache_hit. Emit histogram buckets suitable for p50/p95/p99 calculation.
- Logs: surface error_code and internal_fallback flags per request; forward to logs pipeline with same enrichment tags.
- Metrics/log pipeline: ensure enrichment occurs in the metrics agent before aggregation and that the metrics backend stores per-model/route series (avoid cardinality explosion by using prompt_len_bucket).

Dashboard components (interactive):
1) Top-line selector: model_version, route_name, time window, compare axis (left/right).
2) Latency skyline: stacked percentiles (p50/p95/p99) over time with shading for streaming vs blocking. Clicking a percentile drills to the cohort table.
3) Cohort panel: single-click cohorts by prompt_len_bucket, kv_cache_hit, request_shape, and client_region with sparklines.
4) Batch/Kernel overlay: histogram of batch sizes and kernel_variant frequency correlated to latency spikes.
5) Streaming chunk inspector: distribution of response_first_chunk_latency and subsequent chunk inter-arrival latencies.
6) Trace link column: sampled trace IDs with reason tags (high p99, kv miss, fallback).
7) SLO heatmap: per-model/route p95 breach frequency and recent incidents.

Acceptance criteria (definition of done):
- Dashboard deployed in staging with live data for at least 48 hours and accurate p50/p95/p99 breakdowns for streaming and blocking modes.
- Trace hooks emit the new attributes and the trace link opens to a trace that includes kernel_variant and response_first_chunk_ts.
- Metrics enrichment is in place for model_version and route_name without unbounded cardinality; queries for p50/p95/p99 are efficient (< 5s for 1h window).
- Cohort filters correctly subset series and re-compute percentiles; KV-cache overlay aligns with latency spikes.
- Alerting rule for streaming-mode p95 increase is added with paging policy and runbook link.
- PR and design doc reviewed by Observability and Runtime teams and QA runbook created.

Implementation notes / queries for reviewers:
- Suggest storing prompt_len_bucket at source (agent) with buckets: short(<64), medium(64-512), long(>512) to limit cardinality.
- For streaming traces we need to decide sampling policy: 1% baseline + 100% for requests with p99 > threshold. Does SRE approve temporary higher sampling during rollout?
- Consider pre-computing p95/p99 in metrics ingest layer for common model/route combinations to keep query latency low.

Rollout plan:
1) Instrumentation PRs (tracing + metrics agent) -> staging smoke test -> metric cardinality sanity run.
2) Dashboard initial UAT with Runtime/Observability -> tweak cohorts.
3) Enable in prod read-only for 1 week, then open edit and alerts.
4) Postmortem after 2 weeks to capture false positives and tuning.

Notes for follow-up tickets:
- Follow-up: add model-compare mode to overlay two models on same route (separate ticket).
- Follow-up: per-customer (org) breakdown for Dedicated customers with private metrics routing.

2026-03-10 Asha Patel: Created ticket and sketched initial panels. Added project and cycle.
2026-03-11 Liam Chen: Synced with Runtime team. Agreed to add response_first_chunk_ts to trace hooks. Runtime to own kernel_variant attribute.
2026-03-12 Design review: Sizing for dashboard tiles looks acceptable. Request to add batch-size histogram and allow log-linking to error traces.
2026-03-13 PR: github.com/redwood-inference/observability/pull/189 - adds metric tag enrichment and prompt_len_bucket. Needs load test signoff.
2026-03-13 QA: staging smoke tests running; awaiting metrics backend cardinality report (expected <10% series growth).
2026-03-13 Note: SRE recommended 2% sample + triggered full-sample for p99 breaches during rollout.
Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/OBS/Interactive+Latency+Canvas

Title: Interactive Latency Canvas — Design & Instrumentation Guide (Model/Route timelines + Streaming vs Blocking)

Interactive Latency Canvas — Design & Instrumentation Guide (Model/Route timelines + Streaming vs Blocking)

## Overview
The Interactive Latency Canvas is a single exploratory dashboard that allows SREs, Runtime, and product owners to compare latency distributions across **models** and **routes**, with an explicit decomposition between **streaming** and **blocking** (non-streaming) response modes.

This page is the implementation guide for:
- Required **metrics + trace attributes**
- Cardinality controls (what we will/won’t tag)
- Dashboard panel requirements
- Alerting recipes and validation steps

## Goals
1. Surface p50/p95/p99 latency by **model_version** and **route_name**, with a toggle for **io_mode = streaming|blocking**.
2. Enable cohort-based comparisons:
   - prompt length bucket (token-based)
   - request shape bucket (short/medium/long *completion length*)
   - KV-cache hit/miss
   - client_region
3. Provide explanatory overlays:
   - KV-cache hit rate
   - batch size distribution
   - stream “first token” latency
   - kernel variant selection frequency
4. Link directly to pre-sampled traces (high p99, KV-miss, fallback) for root-cause drilldown.
5. Provide alerting templates for **streaming regressions** (p95/p99) and **first-token latency** regressions.

## Non-goals (explicitly out of scope)
- Per-customer/org breakdown in the default dashboard (Dedicated customers may require private metrics routing).
- Unbounded per-request dimensions (prompt hash, request id, user id, etc.).

---

## Instrumentation Requirements
### Required dimensions (tags)
All latency and first-token timing metrics MUST include the following tags:
- `model_version` (string, e.g., `llama3.1-70b-instruct@2026-03-07`)
- `route_name` (string, e.g., `chat.completions`)
- `io_mode` (`streaming` | `blocking`)
- `prompt_len_bucket` (token-based buckets; see below)
- `kv_cache_hit` (`true` | `false` | `unknown`)

Recommended additional tags where available:
- `client_region` (coarse: `na`, `eu`, `apac`, `sa`, `unknown`)
- `request_shape` (coarse: `short`, `medium`, `long`, `unknown`)

### Prompt length buckets (UPDATED)
To reduce cardinality and align with token-based capacity planning, prompt length buckets are defined in **tokens** (not characters):
- `short`: `<128`
- `medium`: `128–1024`
- `long`: `>1024`

Rationale: earlier char-based buckets produced inconsistent cohorting across tokenizers and languages.

### Metrics (canonical names)
The following metric names are the standard expected by the dashboard queries. If a service uses alternate names, add a translation layer in the metrics agent.

**Latency histograms**
- `inference.request_latency_ms` (histogram)
  - Definition: end-to-end request latency from request acceptance to final response completion.
  - Tags: required tags above.

**Streaming first-token timing (UPDATED field name)**
- `inference.first_token_latency_ms` (histogram)
  - Definition: for streaming only, time from request acceptance to first token emitted.
  - Tags: required tags above.

**Chunk inter-arrival (optional, streaming only)**
- `inference.stream_chunk_gap_ms` (histogram)
  - Definition: time between consecutive chunks (or token batches) emitted.
  - Tags: `model_version`, `route_name`, `io_mode=streaming`, `prompt_len_bucket`.

**KV cache**
- `inference.kv_cache_hit_total` (counter)
- `inference.kv_cache_req_total` (counter)

**Batching**
- `inference.batch_size` (histogram)
  - Tag: `kernel_variant` is allowed on this metric only if the allowed set is enumerated and stable.

### Tracing attributes
Traces should contain the following attributes to support drilldown from the dashboard:
- `model_version`
- `route_name`
- `io_mode` (`streaming` | `blocking`)
- `batch_id` (string or int; may be absent if not batched)
- `kernel_variant` (string; constrained set)
- `kv_cache_hit` (`true`|`false`|`unknown`)
- `first_token_ts` (timestamp; streaming only) **(UPDATED: replaces `response_first_chunk_ts`)**
- `internal_fallback` (`true`|`false`)
- `error_code` (string; e.g., `timeout`, `oom`, `upstream_429`, `unknown`)

**Note:** For legacy compatibility, services may emit both `response_first_chunk_ts` and `first_token_ts` during migration. The dashboard assumes `first_token_ts` when present.

### Sampling policy (UPDATED)
During rollout, use a stable baseline plus triggered escalation:
- Baseline: **1%** trace sampling
- Triggered: **100% sampling** for 15 minutes when any of the following conditions are met per (model_version, route_name, io_mode):
  - p99 `inference.request_latency_ms` exceeds 2× the 7-day median, OR
  - p95 `inference.first_token_latency_ms` exceeds 1.5× the 7-day median (streaming only), OR
  - `error_code` rate exceeds 2%.

SRE guidance: avoid a fixed 2% baseline unless incident-driven; use triggered sampling to manage cost.

---

## Cardinality Controls (must-follow)
1. Do NOT tag metrics with:
   - raw prompt length (numeric)
   - request id / trace id
   - customer org id (default pipeline)
   - model prompt template id
2. `route_name` must be a low-cardinality identifier (canonical route), not full URL paths.
3. `kernel_variant` must not be attached to the main request latency histogram unless the number of variants is tightly bounded and reviewed.
4. Enrichment must happen in the **metrics agent before aggregation**, and dashboards must query using the standardized buckets.

Target guardrail: total series growth attributable to this work should be **<15%** in the primary metrics backend for Serving + Gateway.

---

## Dashboard Specification (Interactive Latency Canvas)
### 1) Top-line selector
Controls:
- model_version
- route_name
- time window
- io_mode toggle: streaming / blocking / both
- compare axis (A vs B) for cohorts or model versions

### 2) Latency skyline panel
- Chart: p50/p95/p99 over time
- Ability to overlay streaming vs blocking (stacked shading or side-by-side)
- Click-to-drill: selecting a time region filters downstream panels

### 3) Cohort panel
Single-click cohorts with sparklines:
- prompt_len_bucket
- kv_cache_hit
- request_shape
- client_region

### 4) Batch/Kernel overlay
- Batch size histogram overlaid with p95/p99 spikes
- Kernel variant frequency (top N) shown as a time series or stacked area

### 5) Streaming inspector
Streaming-only panels:
- `first_token_latency_ms` p50/p95/p99
- `stream_chunk_gap_ms` distribution (optional where available)

### 6) Trace links table
A table of sampled traces including “reason tags”:
- high p99
- kv miss
- fallback
- elevated first-token latency

### 7) SLO heatmap
Per model/route p95 breach frequency:
- windowed by 1h / 6h / 24h
- includes links to recent incident tickets and runbooks

---

## Alerting Recipes
### Streaming p95 regression (recommended)
Signal:
- Metric: `inference.request_latency_ms` p95 where `io_mode=streaming`
- Condition: p95 > **1.25×** 7-day median for **10 minutes**
- Group by: `model_version`, `route_name`

Routing:
- Page if `customer_impact=high` model/route list; otherwise create ticket.

Runbook link:
- confluence://eng-sre/Runbook+Streaming+Latency+Regression

### First-token latency regression (streaming)
- Metric: `inference.first_token_latency_ms` p95
- Condition: p95 > **1.5×** 7-day median for **10 minutes**
- Add diagnostic links to:
  - KV hit-rate
  - batch size histogram
  - kernel variant frequency

### Blocking mode tail regression
- Metric: `inference.request_latency_ms` p99 where `io_mode=blocking`
- Condition: p99 > **1.3×** 7-day median for **15 minutes**

---

## Validation Checklist (Definition of Done)
1. Dashboard deployed in **staging** with live data for at least **48 hours**.
2. Metrics present and queryable:
   - `inference.request_latency_ms` with tags: model_version, route_name, io_mode, prompt_len_bucket, kv_cache_hit
   - `inference.first_token_latency_ms` for streaming paths
3. Traces:
   - trace attributes include `kernel_variant` and `first_token_ts` (streaming)
   - dashboard trace link opens to a trace showing the required attributes
4. Cardinality and performance:
   - series growth <15% in the primary backend (or approved exception)
   - p50/p95/p99 queries return in **<3 seconds** for a 1-hour window in prod
5. Cohort filters correctly subset series and recompute percentiles.
6. At least one alerting rule is created for streaming p95 regression with paging policy + runbook.
7. QA checklist completed, including:
   - compare streaming vs blocking for the same model/route
   - validate first-token latency distributions match trace timing within ±5%

---

## Rollout Plan
1. Land instrumentation PRs (metrics agent + trace attributes) behind a feature flag.
2. Staging smoke tests + cardinality audit.
3. Enable in prod read-only dashboard for 1 week (no alerts), validate performance.
4. Enable alerts for the high-impact model/route allowlist.
5. Two-week follow-up review:
   - false positive rate
   - sampling costs
   - any required bucket tuning

---

## Appendix: Example metric emission (pseudo-code)

Title: Postmortem: SEV-2 Usage metrics lag impacted billing exports (2026-03-05)

Postmortem: SEV-2 Usage metrics lag impacted billing exports (2026-03-05)

A backlog in the usage metrics pipeline caused downstream billing exports to lag behind real-time token usage.
Billing exports for a subset of enterprise contracts were delayed by up to 6 hours. No incorrect invoices were sent, but several Finance Ops workflows were blocked.
02:10 UTC: Automated job for hourly billing exports reported staleness >60 minutes.
02:20 UTC: Data Platform on-call engaged; identified increasing Kafka consumer lag.
03:05 UTC: Root cause traced to a schema change increasing message size and triggering slower deserialization.
03:30 UTC: Increased consumer resources and rolled back the schema change.
05:40 UTC: Backlog began clearing; staleness dropping.
06:35 UTC: Pipeline caught up; exports resumed on schedule.
A usage event schema change added an uncompressed prompt preview field which increased message size and CPU cost for consumers. Autoscaling thresholds were based on QPS, not processing time, so the consumer group did not scale fast enough.
Automated staleness check on billing exports.
Rolled back the schema change, temporarily increased consumer resources, and replayed affected partitions to ensure completeness.
Staleness check prevented incorrect exports. Replay tooling worked as intended.
Schema review did not consider downstream CPU impact; autoscaling policy was not aligned with processing latency.
Add schema-change checklist requiring downstream throughput impact assessment (Data Platform; due 2026-03-25).
Update consumer autoscaling to include processing time / lag slope (Data Platform; due 2026-04-05).
Move prompt preview field behind a separate topic for debug-only sampling (Data Platform; due 2026-04-15).

Title: PRD (2025): Cohort-driven evaluation harness, graduated A/B gates, and staged failover for Optimize

PRD (2025): Cohort-driven evaluation harness, graduated A/B gates, and staged failover for Optimize

## Summary
This PRD defines a production-ready evaluation harness for Optimize that:
1) uses cohort-driven and sentinel prompt sampling,
2) gates A/B rollouts with statistical + business thresholds, and
3) implements a staged rollback/failover policy that escalates from automated throttles to cohort-level reverts to full rollback.

The goal is to reduce undetected regressions while keeping rollout velocity high for model and configuration updates.

## Background / Problem
We have recurring incidents where model/config rollouts pass coarse checks but produce regressions in specific customer cohorts or long-tail prompts. Current canaries are per-model and global; they miss cohort-specific quality regressions and provide coarse binary pass/fail decisions.

Optimize needs a more granular, actionable evaluation contract that ties observable signals to deterministic remediation steps and human-in-the-loop (HIL) triage when necessary.

## Goals
- Detect cohort-specific degradation with >90% recall for regressions causing >5% change in a business-impact metric.
- Prevent silent regressions via sentinel prompt detection and progressive gating across traffic slices.
- Reduce mean time to mitigation (MTTM) to under 20 minutes for high-severity regressions via deterministic rollback actions.
- Enable safe rapid rollouts with objective pass criteria at each stage.

## Non-goals
- Improve underlying model training processes (this is a serving/eval policy change).
- Replace manual post-deploy human QA for complex policy/regulatory cases.
- Provide full auto-rollback for noisy low-signal metrics without human review.

## Scope and Definitions
### Cohorts (v1 taxonomy)
Cohorts are deterministically assigned at request time using request metadata + customer/account attributes. The v1 taxonomy is:
- Persona: developer, analyst, support-agent
- Region: NA, EU, APAC
- Flow: latency-sensitive, long-context, tool-calling, regulatory
- Customer tier: top-enterprise, enterprise, growth, self-serve

### Blocked cohorts (require HIL approval to ramp beyond 5%)
Finalized list for v1:
- EU-regulated flows (all tiers)
- Top-10 enterprise customers (account list maintained by Customer Success; synced daily)

## Requirements
1) Sentinel prompt library
- Maintain a versioned library of sentinel prompts organized by cohort (persona/region/flow/tier).
- Include safety sentinels, reliability sentinels (tool-calling), and business-value sentinels (retention-sensitive / conversion proxies).

2) Cohort labeling and bucketing
- Deterministic bucketing at request time with a stable cohort key.
- Cohort labels must be available in evaluation events and rollout decisions.

3) Evaluation pipeline
- Compute per-cohort metrics in near-real-time with a maximum 3 minute lag (updated from 5 minutes based on SRE sizing and on-call usability).
- Support both online sampling (production traffic) and controlled replay (sentinel runs).

4) Graduated A/B gates in Console
- Gate rule configuration includes: minimum sample size, minimum detectable effect (MDE), alpha/beta, max allowed regression, and sustained-duration requirements.
- Default statistical method updated: sequential testing is the default for low-to-mid traffic cohorts; fixed-horizon remains available.

5) Staged rollback / failover engine
- Actions include: throttling new variant traffic, cohort-level divert to previous stable variant, full rollback.
- Each action is tied to explicit triggers and produces an auditable event in the release timeline.

6) Human-in-the-loop (HIL)
- HIL holds are required for blocked cohorts past 5% ramp.
- HIL is required for ambiguous composite detector states.
- Reviewer SLO: 30 minutes for P1 releases.

7) Surfacing and alerts
- Expose evaluation results and runbook links in Console release UI.
- Alert integration for Slack + PagerDuty with cohort breakdown and recommended action.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Sentinel library: >= 650 prompts covering at least 10 predefined cohorts, versioned and attributable (updated from 500/8 based on Evals team coverage plan).
- Per-cohort metrics computed and stored with <= 3 minute latency.
- Gate config defaults:
  - alpha = 0.05
  - beta = 0.2
  - sequential mode enabled by default for cohorts with < 50k daily requests
- Minimum sample size calculator present in UI and enforced for gate validity.
- Automated rollback triggers implemented (updated thresholds after SRE + Evals calibration in staging):
  - (a) Immediate throttle if any safety sentinel shows > 0.3% absolute regression sustained for 5 minutes.
  - (b) Automatic cohort-level divert to previous stable variant if composite quality score drops > 3% sustained for 10 minutes in that cohort.
  - (c) Full rollback if business KPI regression > 4% sustained for 10 minutes (updated from 5% for 5 minutes to reduce false negatives while avoiding brief KPI noise).
- Console includes a playbook link for each trigger with owner, checklist, and comms templates.
- End-to-end test harness can simulate cohorts and verify gating/rollback behavior in staging.

## Rollout Strategy
Phases and traffic slices (updated ramp plan to reduce step-size risk for large enterprise cohorts):
- Phase 0: Staging validation with synthetic traffic (2 weeks)
- Phase 1: Internal canary (0.5%) for 48 hours
- Phase 2: Beta customers (2%) for 72 hours
- Phase 3: Gradual ramp (10% for 24 hours, 25% for 24 hours, then 100% if gates pass)

Rules:
- Each phase requires passing cohort-specific gates.
- If any cohort fails a gate, apply automated action per remediation playbook and pause the release pending investigation.
- Blocked cohorts cannot ramp beyond 5% without explicit HIL approval in Console.

## Statistical Approach
### Defaults
- Binary signals (e.g., sentinel hit rate): two-sided proportion test.
- Continuous scores (e.g., composite quality): Welch’s t-test.
- Default alpha = 0.05, beta = 0.2.

### Sequential testing (default for low-to-mid traffic cohorts)
For cohorts with limited traffic, use sequential analysis with alpha spending (Pocock-style boundary) to allow earlier decisions while controlling Type I error.

### Sample size and MDE
Console enforces a minimum sample size requirement. The UI provides an MDE and n estimator and records the assumed baseline used for the calculation.

## Remediation Playbook
- Level 1 (Transient noise)
  - Auto-throttle new release traffic by 30% immediately.
  - If signals persist for 10 minutes, increase throttle to 50%.
  - Notify on-call; continue observation for 15 minutes.
- Level 2 (Cohort regression)
  - Divert failed cohort traffic to previous stable variant.
  - Create a P1 investigation ticket and open a dedicated War Room channel.
  - Require an explicit “resume” action with notes in Console.
- Level 3 (Business KPI impact)
  - Immediate full rollback of the release.
  - Notify via status page + account reps; schedule postmortem within 48 hours.
- Human-in-the-loop
  - For ambiguous composite detector states or blocked cohort ramps, move the release to HOLD.
  - Reviewers have a 30 minute SLO to approve/deny for P1 releases.

## Monitoring Signals
- Sentinel hit rate per cohort.
- Composite quality score per cohort (weighted accuracy proxy + hallucination penalty + latency penalty).
- Business KPIs: conversion rate, retention signal (as provided by customer integrations).
- Infrastructure: token cost variance, GPU latency P95, request error rate.
- Anomaly detectors: distribution drift (embedding distance) and abrupt change in output length.

## Console / UI Changes
- Release details page
  - Add a “Cohorts” tab: per-cohort metrics, sentinel breakdown, sample viewer.
  - Add a “Gates” panel: pass/fail status, confidence intervals, and sustained-duration progress.
- Gate configuration
  - Configure alpha/beta, fixed vs sequential mode, MDE, sustained-duration requirements, and mapped remediation actions.
- Notifications
  - Slack + PagerDuty wiring integrated into the release flow with cohort-aware routing.

## Data & Infra
- Storage for per-request metadata and evaluation events; retention updated to 180 days (from 90) to support quarter-over-quarter regressions and enterprise audit requests.
- Streaming pipeline to route sampled requests to evaluation workers (implementation depends on platform standard; initial deployment uses Kafka as in SRE sizing).
- Evaluation workers to run controlled prompts and compute metrics; require autoscaling profile and quotas.
- Dashboard endpoints and Console API to surface near-real-time cohort results.

## Timeline (updated)
- 2025-11-05: PRD created
- 2025-11-12: Design review & cohort taxonomy finalized
- 2025-11-20: API contract for gates approved
- 2025-11-28: Staging harness deployed
- 2025-12-06: Internal canary start
- 2025-12-12: Beta customers start (updated from earlier plan to allow extra staging burn-in)
- 2025-12-18: Target GA (updated from 2025-12-15 based on ramp plan and blocked cohort review bandwidth)

## Stakeholders
- Aisha Patel — PM (owner)
- Marco Li — Engineering (release engineering)
- Rina Gomez — Head of Evals
- Victor Chen — Console UX
- Sanjay Rao — SRE
- Priya Desai — Customer Success

## Open Questions
- What is the acceptable latency tradeoff for running sentinel prompts synchronously vs async for latency-sensitive flows?
- After-hours escalation owner for Level 2 cohort regressions (proposal: SRE primary with Evals secondary).
- Should Console surface raw model outputs for sampled requests, or only aggregated signals (compliance implications; default proposal: aggregated-only, with restricted break-glass access for on-call)?

## Change Log
- 2025-11-20: Initial PRD moved to in-review in Linear pending sign-off on alpha/beta defaults and blocked cohorts.
- 2025-12-03: Updated (a) evaluation lag target to <= 3 minutes, (b) sentinel library target to 650 prompts / 10 cohorts, (c) ramp steps to 0.5% -> 2% -> 10% -> 25% -> 100%, (d) rollback thresholds for safety and KPI signals, and (e) retention to 180 days.

Title: Cross-region SLO drift & traffic-shaping retrospective

Cross-region SLO drift & traffic-shaping retrospective

Summary: On 2026-03-09 between 22:14 UTC and 23:02 UTC we observed a cross-region degradation that caused a sustained SLO miss for the hosted text-generation API. Symptoms included elevated p99 latency (baseline ~320ms -> peak ~1.1s), a spike in 5xx error rate (~0.05% -> 2.6%), and customer-visible increased tail latency across EU and NA regions. The root of the event was a combination of a recent autoscaler config change, a traffic-shaping rollback in the control-plane route weights, and a circuit-breaker threshold that was too permissive, which delayed failover protective actions. This ticket is the postmortem and consolidated follow-up actions.
2026-03-09T22:14Z: Pager triggered by SRE for elevated error rate on /v1/generate in eu-west-1
2026-03-09T22:18Z: Incident commander confirmed p99 latency > 800ms and 5xx > 1%; traffic shifted from eu-west-1 to us-west-2 by smart-routing policy
2026-03-09T22:22Z: We observed queued requests and backpressure on the runtime pods in us-west-2; autoscaler had delayed scale-up due to recent change (minPool=3 -> 1 for short spikes)
2026-03-09T22:30Z: Circuit breaker for runtime instances did not trip until 22:37Z due to threshold misconfiguration (tripping at 10% error rate instead of 0.5%)
2026-03-09T22:38Z: Manual override set to reduce route weight to us-west-2 and re-enable EU-only traffic; emergency scale-up of dedicated pool initiated
2026-03-09T22:50Z: Traffic stabilizes but p99 remained elevated due to cached KV saturation; we enabled prefix-KV eviction and adjusted batch sizes
2026-03-09T23:02Z: Incident declared mitigated; post-incident monitoring in place until 2026-03-10T08:00Z
SLOs impacted: availability SLA for hosted-generation endpoint (target 99.95% 5xx rate) was missed for a 48-minute window. Approximately 4.3% of requests in EU and 2.1% in NA experienced >1s tail latency. Customer impact: several high-volume customers reported increased latency; no data loss or confidentiality concerns. Estimated revenue-impact window: 48 minutes; small subset of production traffic rerouted and saw degraded quality-of-service.
Multiple contributing changes aligned: (1) autoscaler configuration change deployed 2026-03-07 reduced min pool size to reduce cost; under cross-region failover this produced insufficient spare capacity for burst; (2) control-plane rollback of a traffic-weighting adjustment caused excess routing to a partially loaded region; (3) circuit-breaker parameterization was set conservatively high by a recent tuning PR (trips at 10% errors) delaying protective shedding; and (4) runtime KV cache experienced fragmentation under uneven load causing longer KV lookups and increased tail latencies. The immediate trigger was the traffic-weighting rollback + inadequate autoscaler floor which caused queueing and resource exhaustion in the target region.
Recent autoscaler change aimed at cost reduction (minPool=1) reduced headroom for failover
Control-plane route weights rollback during a separate deployment led to misrouted traffic

Title: Postmortem: Hosted API latency spike and model fallback activation (2025-02-11)

Postmortem: Hosted API latency spike and model fallback activation (2025-02-11)

h2. Summary
On 2025-02-11, the Hosted API experienced elevated p95 latency on /v1/chat/completions for ~23 minutes. Mitigation included activating an automatic model fallback policy to keep requests flowing while we reduced load on the primary model pool.

h2. Impact
* Customer-facing: increased latency, intermittent timeouts, elevated 5xx for some bursts.
* Affected product: Redwood API (Hosted).
* Affected tiers: primarily Free and Growth tiers on the default route.

h2. Timeline (UTC)
* 17:06: Alert fired: Chat latency p95 > 4.0s (threshold 2.0s) for 5 min.
* 17:11: On-call confirmed queueing on primary model pool (rw-llama-3.1-70b-instruct).
* 17:14: Mitigation: enabled *automatic model fallback* on the router policy for the default route.
* 17:16: Router began automatically rerouting overflow traffic to rw-llama-3.1-8b-instruct (fallback target) when saturation exceeded 85%.
* 17:22: Latency recovered; errors returned to baseline.
* 17:29: Fallback policy left on for 30 additional minutes to protect SLO.

h2. What we changed (Mitigation)
We activated a policy-based *auto-fallback* on the router:
* Primary: rw-llama-3.1-70b-instruct
* Fallback: rw-llama-3.1-8b-instruct
* Trigger: saturation > 85% OR queue wait > 250ms
* Scope: /v1/chat/completions, tier in {free, growth}

h2. Root cause
A mis-sized continuous batching configuration on the primary pool caused queueing to grow quickly under a bursty prompt distribution (longer-than-expected context lengths).

h2. Detection
Automated latency and queue-wait alerts fired correctly, but we lacked a dedicated alert for “fallback activated” to help confirm mitigation status.

h2. Action items
1) Add a first-class router metric + alert: fallback_activated_count by route/model. Owner: Eng Platform.
2) Update the on-call runbook to include the fallback policy toggle and rollback conditions. Owner: Eng SRE.
3) Re-tune batching defaults for rw-llama-3.1-70b-instruct on A100 pool. Owner: Serving Runtime.

h2. References
* Related page: Router policies and safe-mode toggles (internal)
* Incident ID: INC-2025-0211

Title: Postmortem: EU-West capacity shortage and region fallback (2025-03-03)

Postmortem: EU-West capacity shortage and region fallback (2025-03-03)

h2. Summary
On 2025-03-03, a GPU capacity shortfall in eu-west-1 impacted a subset of Hosted and Dedicated traffic pinned to that region. Mitigation required activating *automatic region fallback* (eu-west-1 -> us-east-1) for eligible routes until additional capacity was brought online.

h2. Impact
* Elevated p95 latency and increased 429/503 responses for region-pinned routes in eu-west-1.
* Customers: 7 Hosted orgs and 1 Dedicated tenant with optional cross-region allowance enabled.
* Duration: ~41 minutes of degraded performance; ~18 minutes of hard errors for the most constrained pool.

h2. Timeline (UTC)
* 09:42: Capacity alert: available_gpu_count < 5 in eu-west-1 pool rw-a100-eu-01.
* 09:48: Saturation exceeded 95% and queue wait climbed > 400ms.
* 09:51: Mitigation: enabled *region fallback* for "chat-default" and "embeddings-default" where customer policy allows cross-region.
* 09:54: Router began directing overflow to us-east-1 for eligible traffic.
* 10:03: Error rate dropped; latency partially recovered.
* 10:23: Added 8 GPUs to eu-west-1 pool; disabled region fallback after stabilization.

h2. Mitigation details
We toggled a router policy flag:
* Primary region: eu-west-1
* Fallback region: us-east-1
* Triggers: saturation > 90% OR 503 rate > 0.5%
* Eligibility: routes not marked "data_residency_strict"

h2. Root cause
A delayed GPU delivery + slow provisioning left the eu-west-1 pool below the forecasted headroom for a scheduled customer load test.

h2. What went well
* Region fallback prevented a full outage for eligible traffic.
* On-call followed the capacity runbook and coordinated with Infra quickly.

h2. What went poorly
* We lacked a clear customer-facing flag indicating whether cross-region fallback was enabled for a tenant.

h2. Action items
1) Add tenant-level UI indicator and API field for cross-region fallback eligibility. Owner: Eng Platform.
2) Improve capacity forecasting for scheduled load tests and Dedicated bursts. Owner: Eng SRE.
3) Add automated comms template for region fallback events. Owner: Incident Response.

h2. References
* Incident ID: INC-2025-0303

Title: Postmortem: Router policy regression triggered unintended model fallback (2025-04-19)

Postmortem: Router policy regression triggered unintended model fallback (2025-04-19)

h2. Summary
On 2025-04-19, a router policy change caused the system to activate *automatic model fallback* more aggressively than intended for several chat routes. While this reduced errors, it also introduced a quality regression for some customers because the fallback target had different instruction-following behavior.

h2. Impact
* Increased fallback usage on chat routes (primary -> smaller model) for ~52 minutes.
* Some customers reported degraded response quality and formatting differences.
* No prolonged outage; error rate remained below 1.0% due to fallback.

h2. Timeline (UTC)
* 20:05: Router policy v2025.04.19-1 deployed.
* 20:12: Metrics show a spike in fallback_activated_count on chat-default.
* 20:17: Support ticket indicates response quality changes.
* 20:26: On-call reverted router policy to previous version.
* 20:31: Fallback usage returns to baseline.
* 20:57: Follow-up: validate that quality guardrails did not alert because the canary prompts did not cover the affected format.

h2. Root cause
A boolean default in the policy compiler changed from "fail-open" to "fail-closed" for an optional constraint, causing the router to deem the primary model "ineligible" and immediately trigger fallback for certain request shapes.

h2. Mitigation
* Reverted policy deployment.
* Temporarily disabled auto-fallback for enterprise routes with strict quality requirements while we validated the policy fix.

h2. Action items
1) Add a routing policy unit test suite covering eligibility constraints and fallback triggers. Owner: Eng Platform.
2) Expand eval harness prompts to include structured output format checks for top customers. Owner: Applied ML.
3) Add a canary alert when fallback usage deviates > 3x baseline for any route. Owner: Eng SRE.

h2. References
* Incident ID: INC-2025-0419

Title: Epochal reserve reconciler and slip-window fairing for sustained-rate reservations

Epochal reserve reconciler and slip-window fairing for sustained-rate reservations

Motivation: we continue to see oscillatory scale behavior when tenants alternate between short bursts and sustained ramps. Existing fractional reservation logic allocates strictly at request-time which causes unfair short-term giveaway and noisy autoscaler decisions. This PR introduces an epochal reservation reconciler and a slip-window fairing algorithm that smooths commitments across short epochs and provides proportional sustained-rate guarantees while preserving burst headroom. Implementation summary: add a light-weight epoch coordinator that buckets tenant reservations into fixed-duration epochs (default 30s) and reconciles desired commit volumes at epoch boundaries; introduce a slip-window fairing function that computes per-tenant credit allocations using a time-decayed moving average and a small tolerance window to allow short-term overshoots; implement a hedging mechanism that preserves a small cross-epoch safety buffer to avoid mid-epoch eviction thrash. The reconciler lives in pkg/fleet/reconciler and exposes a new ReservationEpoch API (internal), while the allocator is plumbed into the existing credit pool via a new CreditAllocator interface. Telemetry: new metrics added - fleet_epoch_duration_seconds, tenant_epoch_committed_tokens, tenant_slip_window_utilization, reserve_reconcile_latency_ms. Migration/compat: falling back to legacy reservation path if epoch coordinator disabled. Rollout plan: staged canary to 5% of dedicated fleets for 48h, followed by progressive rollout with automated regression checks on P95 latency and failed allocations. Tests: unit tests for allocator math, integration test simulating mixed burst + sustained workloads, and a canary harness script. Operational notes: default epoch length tuned after synthetic traces; operators can adjust epoch_length and slip_window_decay via Redwood Console and fleet config.
Lena Rios (reviewer): What's the expected steady-state error between committed and observed throughput? We should document failure modes.
Aisha Khan (author): Expected steady-state error is bounded by slip_window_tolerance (default 5%). Added math and rationale to docs/ops/epochal-reservations.md and unit tests that assert bounds.
Marcus Chen (reviewer): How does this interact with tenant reserve preemption? Could hedging delay reclaim long enough to violate SLAs?
Aisha Khan (author): Hedging is sized as a small fraction (default 3% of epoch capacity) and only used when shortfalls are transient; added a safety circuit that forces reclaim if decline persists for 3 consecutive epochs. See allocator comments and tests.
Priya Patel (reviewer): CI integration looked flaky initially; confirm we won't regress autoscaler CPU overhead.
Aisha Khan (author): Optimized reconciliation loop to amortize allocations; CPU delta measured <1% for 1000-tenant synthetic run. Added benchmark and CI profile artifact link in PR description.
Lena Rios: Approving after docs and one small rename in allocator interface.
Marcus Chen: Approved
Introduce epochal reservation reconciler and slip-window fairing to improve sustained-rate guarantees and reduce autoscaler oscillation. Config knobs: epoch_length, slip_window_decay, slip_window_tolerance. Backward-compatible with legacy reservation path. Operators should monitor tenant_slip_window_utilization after rollout.
If allocations are unexpectedly failing after rollout, check metrics fleet_epoch_duration_seconds and tenant_epoch_committed_tokens for skew. To rollback: flip feature flag fleet.epochal_reservations.enabled=false and redeploy controller. Canary script is tools/canary/epochal_canary.sh.

Title: Audit log retention and access

Audit log retention and access

# Scope
This page defines how long Redwood retains audit logs and who can access them. Audit logs cover security-relevant events across Hosted API, Dedicated, and Redwood-managed control plane components that support Private deployments.

# Retention
- Hosted API: 365 days retention for audit logs.
- Dedicated: 365 days retention for audit logs.
- Private: 365 days retention for Redwood control-plane audit logs (actions taken in Redwood-managed components).
- Customer-owned Private audit logs: customer-configured; Redwood does not set or enforce retention for customer-side logging systems.

# Access controls
- Audit logs are accessible only to Security and SRE on a need-to-know basis via the Audit Explorer tool.
- Access is governed by least-privilege RBAC and requires SSO + MFA.
- Any export of audit logs for a customer request must be approved by Security and tracked via a support ticket.

# Customer requests
- Standard turnaround: 5 business days for audit log exports (unless contractually obligated otherwise).
- Deletion: audit logs are not deleted early except where required by law or contract; exceptions require Legal + Security approval and are documented in a support ticket.

Title: Hosted API model intake: third-party LLM onboarding request

Hosted API model intake: third-party LLM onboarding request

# Purpose
This page describes the *intake* process for launching a new third‑party LLM in the Redwood Hosted API model catalog. It defines what the requester must provide, who owns each step, and what artifacts are required before engineering work starts.

# When to use
Use this process for any new entry in the Hosted API model catalog, including:
- New upstream model families (e.g., Llama, Qwen, Mistral)
- New sizes or instruction variants
- New upstream releases that change tokenizer, weights, or license

# Roles
- Requester: typically Product or Solutions Engineering
- Intake owner: Applied ML Onboarding (Applied ML)
- Runtime owner: Serving Runtime
- Release owner: Release Engineering
- Security gate owner: Security & Compliance
- Docs owner: DevEx / Docs

# Intake ticket and required fields
Create a Linear ticket in *ENG* with label `model-onboarding` and include the following fields (copy/paste section):

## 1) Model identity
- Upstream model name and version tag
- Model type: `chat` | `completion` | `embeddings` | `rerank`
- Upstream repo / source URL
- Tokenizer type and expected special tokens

## 2) Intended catalog surface
- Proposed Redwood model ID (e.g., `rw/llama-3.1-70b-instruct`)
- Compatibility target: `redwood` native | OpenAI-compatible endpoint
- Any planned aliases (e.g., `rw/llama-3.1-70b`)

## 3) License and redistribution
- License name + link to full text
- Redistributable weights: yes/no/unclear
- Any use restrictions that must be enforced in ToS / UI (e.g., geo, user class)

## 4) Data and policy
- Safety/policy concerns (e.g., uncensored, adult content)
- Any known PII or training data controversies (link sources)

## 5) Target customers and workload
- Example customer workloads (prompt length distribution, expected max tokens)
- Regions required (US/EU/APAC)
- Any explicit SLO expectations (latency, availability, streaming)

# Intake gates (must all be satisfied to proceed)
1. **License pre-check** (Owner: Finance-Legal liaison + Security)
   - Outcome: `approved`, `approved w/ restrictions`, or `blocked`
   - Artifact: link to Security risk review page entry (see Security space)
2. **Baseline evaluation plan** (Owner: Applied ML)
   - Outcome: evaluation suites selected + success criteria
   - Artifact: eval plan comment in Linear + link to eval harness run(s)
3. **Feasibility / runtime fit** (Owner: Serving Runtime)
   - Confirm tokenizer handling, KV cache behavior, and kernel coverage
   - Artifact: short feasibility note + any required runtime flags

# Artifacts produced during intake (and where they live)
- Model intake summary: Linear ticket (single source of truth)
- Eval plan + results: Eval harness run links and Confluence (Applied ML and Evals)
- Performance benchmark results: Confluence Performance Standards page + attached benchmark run IDs
- Quantization plan/results: Confluence Quantization Profiles space
- Security risk review: Confluence Security & Compliance space
- Rollout plan and fallback: Confluence Eng Platform runbook
- Model registry change: GitHub PR in `redwood-model-registry`

# Definition of “ready for implementation”
A model is ready to move from intake to implementation when all of the following are true:
- License is approved (or approved with documented restrictions)
- Eval plan includes at least one internal prompt set and one public benchmark
- Runtime owner has stated no known blockers
- A rollout owner is named (release + platform)

# Related pages
- Eval gates for model launch (Applied ML and Evals)
- Hosted model performance bar (Architecture and Standards)
- Quant profile requirements for catalog (Applied ML and Evals)
- Third-party model risk review workflow (Security and Compliance)
- Hosted model rollout and fallback runbook (Eng Platform)

Title: Model launch evaluation gates (Hosted API catalog)

Model launch evaluation gates (Hosted API catalog)

# Overview
This page defines the required evaluation gates for launching a new model into the Hosted API model catalog. The goal is to ensure we can safely serve the model, meet product quality expectations, and detect regressions after launch.

# Ownership and signoff
- Gate owner (quality): Applied ML (Onboarding + Evals)
- Required signoff: Applied ML + Product (for model positioning)
- Optional signoff: Customer Success (if a launch is for a named account)

# Required evaluation suites
All Hosted API catalog launches must pass *all* suites below. Each suite must be run on the candidate model build (exact weights + tokenizer + runtime config) and logged in the eval harness.

## Suite A: Internal prompt set regression
- Source: `prompt-sets/hosted-api/core-regression`
- Metrics: win-rate vs current default in family; structured output adherence for required schemas
- Pass criteria:
  - Overall win-rate >= 50% vs baseline (no regression)
  - Any critical prompt tagged `p0` must not regress
- Artifact: eval harness run link + summary paragraph

## Suite B: Public benchmark sanity
- Source: curated public tasks (e.g., MMLU subset, GSM8K subset, HumanEval-lite)
- Purpose: catch obvious misconfigs, broken tokenizer, prompt formatting issues
- Pass criteria:
  - No single task drops > 5% absolute vs upstream reported numbers *after adjusting for our settings*
  - If upstream numbers are unavailable, compare vs adjacent model sizes in family and explain outliers
- Artifact: table of scores + notes

## Suite C: Safety and policy screening (lightweight)
- Source: policy prompts + refusal behavior checks
- Pass criteria:
  - No increase in disallowed content generation on policy set
  - Refusal templates must be compatible with Redwood policy layer
- Artifact: pass/fail summary + any required policy config notes

## Suite D: Tool/function calling compatibility (if applicable)
- Required when the model is marketed for tools/function calling
- Pass criteria:
  - JSON schema conformance >= 99% on tool-calling prompt set
- Artifact: schema validation report link

# Required documentation artifacts
A launch packet must include:
1. Eval harness run URLs for all required suites
2. A one-paragraph risk assessment (what could go wrong in prod)
3. A recommended default inference config (temperature/top_p/max_tokens defaults)
4. Known limitations (e.g., cannot do reliable tool calling; poor multilingual)

# Escalations and exceptions
- Exceptions must be approved by the Applied ML gate owner and recorded as a label `eval-exception` on the Linear ticket.
- If Suite A fails on any `p0` prompt, do not ship.

# Post-launch monitoring requirement
For the first 7 days after GA:
- Enable quality canary (1% traffic shadow to baseline, where possible)
- Watch `quality_regression_alerts` dashboard and error budget burn
- File a follow-up ticket if any metric crosses thresholds (see Platform runbook)

# Related pages
- Hosted API model intake
- Hosted model performance bar
- Hosted model rollout and fallback runbook

Hosted model performance bar (catalog launch requirements)

# Summary

# Scope
Applies to: chat/completions models offered in the Hosted API, including OpenAI-compatible routes.
Does not apply to: one-off customer private builds (see Private Deployments standards).

# Owners
- Standard owner: Serving Runtime
- Enforcement: Release Engineering + SRE

# Benchmark methodology (required)
Run the perf suite using the current `perf-canary` harness with:
- Hardware class: `H100-80GB` (default) and one secondary class (e.g., `L40S`) when we expect meaningful traffic
- Context sizes: 2k, 8k, 16k
- Workload: mix of prompt lengths matching the top-10 Hosted API routes
- Concurrency: 1, 8, 32
- Streaming: on (default)

Required artifacts:
- Benchmark run IDs (perf suite output)
- Raw logs attached to the Confluence page or linked from Drive
- Summary table (p50/p95 TTFT and tokens/sec)

# Minimum bar for launch
A model can launch if all of the following are true for the *candidate default config*:

## Latency
- TTFT p50 <= 1.2s (2k context)
- TTFT p95 <= 2.5s (2k context)
- TTFT p95 <= 4.0s (8k context)

## Throughput
- Sustained output tokens/sec per GPU >= family baseline minus 10%
- Continuous batching must remain enabled; if disabling is required, document why and get Runtime signoff

## Stability
- No crash loops under 32 concurrency soak test (30 minutes)
- Error rate <= 0.2% for 2k and 8k tests
- No memory growth trend over soak (KV cache leak check)

# Launch decision and signoff
Required signoffs (recorded as links/comments on the model intake Linear ticket):
- Serving Runtime: performance/stability signoff
- SRE: capacity + readiness signoff
- Release Engineering: rollout plan present (see Platform runbook)

# If the model fails the bar
- If TTFT is the only failure and a smaller default max_tokens solves it, you may propose adjusted defaults, but must re-run suites.
- If throughput is low, evaluate quantization profiles and kernel flags; do not ship a degraded model without a Product signoff and a documented note in docs.

# Related pages
- Model launch evaluation gates (Applied ML and Evals)
- Quant profile requirements for catalog (Applied ML and Evals)
- Hosted model rollout and fallback runbook (Eng Platform)

tanya.cs: Acme approves the hosted fallback for those endpoints and can temporarily pause a few high-parallel feeds. They asked us to prioritize stability over throughput.

alex.sre: Throttle rule deployed (gateway): new sessions for tenant AcmeCorp limited to 60 reqs/min per org. Observability: queue_length dropping from 312 -> 198 in next 3m.

jamie.runtime: Eviction ran: removed ~18 low-priority pods, freed 2 nodes worth. After burst nodes come up, we should have ~6 extra node-equivalents. Watch for KV cache warmup.

Title: Expose optimization config version pinning via Helm values + document rollback procedure

Expose optimization config version pinning via Helm values + document rollback procedure

Summary: This PR adds first-class Helm values to pin the active Optimization Config version for Redwood Private installs and documents an operator-friendly rollback flow (pin to prior version + apply). Motivation: In Hosted/Dedicated, the control plane manages versioning and rollback; for Private, operators need a deterministic way to (a) hold a known-good version during upgrades and (b) roll back quickly when an optimization change causes a latency/5xx regression. This change introduces an explicit chart-level mechanism to pass the pinned version to the control plane/runtime, making the procedure consistent with the Safe Apply + Rollback project. What’s included: (1) New values: optimize.optimizationConfig.versionPin (string, optional) and optimize.optimizationConfig.allowUnpinned (bool, default true). When versionPin is set, the deployment will request that version from the Optimization Config Service and treat it as the active version for the configured scope. (2) Templating: inject OPTIMIZATION_CONFIG_VERSION_PIN and OPTIMIZATION_CONFIG_ALLOW_UNPINNED into the control-plane and runtime components; add checksum annotations so updating values triggers rollouts. (3) Validation: fail chart rendering when versionPin is set but empty/whitespace; add a warning note in NOTES.txt when allowUnpinned=false and no pin is supplied. (4) Docs: add a dedicated “Rollback optimization config” section with a copy-paste example (helm upgrade --set optimize.optimizationConfig.versionPin=<prior_version>) and post-rollback verification steps (check rollout status, confirm config_version tag on metrics, confirm p95 recovery). Backwards compatibility: Existing installs that do not set versionPin behave as before (control plane uses the currently-promoted version / unpinned resolution). No changes to defaults that would impact current clusters. Testing: helm lint, helm template, and a minimal kind-based smoke deploy in CI to ensure env vars are present and rollouts happen on pin changes. Follow-ups: (a) In a separate PR we can add a small “pin status” panel to the Private operator docs to align with Console wording, (b) add a values.schema.json pattern restriction once we finalize the canonical version ID format (currently treated as opaque string).
Vivek Kulkarni: Can we make sure updating versionPin forces a rollout? We’ve been burned by config-only changes not triggering new pods. Bruno Silva: Added checksum annotation keyed off the rendered env var values; confirmed that helm upgrade changes ReplicaSet hash. Ethan Park: Naming question—can we avoid calling it “activeVersion” since runtime semantics treat it as a pin override rather than a promotion? Bruno Silva: Renamed to optimize.optimizationConfig.versionPin and updated docs to call it “pin”; promotion remains a control-plane concept. Kira Thompson: The rollback docs should include a clear verification checklist and mention where to look for the applied version. Bruno Silva: Added steps: kubectl describe pod env var, check metrics tag config_version, and validate p95/5xx stabilization window. Connor O'Brien: CI failed on the first run due to values.schema.json indentation; please rerun once fixed. Bruno Silva: Fixed schema formatting, re-ran CI, all green. Approvals: Vivek Kulkarni approved; Ethan Park approved; Kira Thompson approved; Connor O’Brien approved with note to reference GA checklist doc in follow-up.
Private (Helm): Operators can pin an Optimization Config version via values to support safe rollback and deterministic behavior during upgrades.
Docs: Added rollback procedure and verification checklist for optimization config changes.

Title: Change Management Policy for Model-Version and Runtime Changes

Change Management Policy for Model-Version and Runtime Changes

h1. Purpose
This policy defines the minimum change-management requirements for production changes that affect model versions, routing policies, serving runtime configuration, or customer-facing inference behavior.

h1. Scope
This applies to all production environments across:
* Hosted API
* Dedicated capacity
* Private deployments (VPC and on-prem)

Examples in-scope:
* Introducing a new model version behind an existing model alias
* Changing default routing/fallback policy
* Changing runtime settings that alter batching/caching/quantization
* Adjusting context-length limits or tool-calling behavior

Out of scope (but still recommended): documentation-only updates and non-production experiments in isolated sandboxes.

h1. Change classes
* Class 0 (Low risk): no customer traffic, no routing changes, no behavioral change (e.g., internal benchmarking).
* Class 1 (Moderate risk): canary to <= 5% traffic with immediate rollback.
* Class 2 (High risk): > 5% traffic impact, new default version, or changes to safety/tool calling/formatting behavior.
* Class 3 (Critical): global default changes, broad customer impact, or changes that can violate contracts/compliance commitments.

h1. Required artifacts (all classes 1–3)
A production rollout plan MUST include the following sections (link to template is mandatory):
1. Summary (what is changing, why now, customer impact)
2. Scope (which environments, regions, and customer tiers are included)
3. Success criteria and guardrails (explicit thresholds)
4. Monitoring plan (dashboards, alerts, owners)
5. Rollout steps (canary, ramp schedule, decision points)
6. Rollback and fallback rules (what happens automatically vs manually)
7. Customer communications plan (who, when, channels)
8. Approvals and change window

h1. Approvals
Approvals depend on class. Approvals MUST be recorded in the rollout plan under the “Approvals” section.

Required approvers by class:
* Class 1: Oncall Eng Manager for affected service OR Platform Eng TL
* Class 2: Platform Eng Manager + SRE oncall delegate + Product Manager for inference
* Class 3: VP Engineering (or delegate) + Security (if any policy/compliance implication) + Product (Director+)

Additional approval triggers (any class):
* Private deployments: Solutions Engineering lead + Private Deployments Eng TL
* SLA/contract impact: Customer Success Director
* Data residency/retention impact: Security & Compliance

h1. Change window
* Hosted + Dedicated: preferred Tue–Thu, 09:00–14:00 PT (unless explicitly approved).
* Private: must align with customer change window; document customer-specific windows in the plan.

h1. Pre-change checklist (minimum)
* Confirm rollout plan is published and linked from the change ticket.
* Confirm dashboards and alerts are configured and owned for the duration of the rollout.
* Confirm rollback path has been tested in staging or perf-canary.
* Confirm “blast radius” controls are available (traffic caps, customer allowlist/denylist, per-region routing controls).

h1. Post-change requirements
Within 48 hours of completing a model-version rollout:
* Add a short “rollout outcome” note to the plan (final ramp %, any issues, any follow-ups).
* File follow-up tasks for any threshold violations or customer escalations triggered during rollout.

h1. Record retention
Rollout plans and approval records are retained for 2 years (minimum).
