Title: Design Spec: Model Version Rollouts (Canonical Plan Template)

Design Spec: Model Version Rollouts (Canonical Plan Template)

h1. Overview
This page defines the canonical rollout plan template for introducing a new LLM model version behind an existing model name (alias) or introducing a new model endpoint that will receive production traffic. It is intended to be copied into a new rollout plan page per change.

h1. When this template is required
Use this template for any of the following:
* Changing the default version behind a model alias
* Introducing a new version that will receive >0% external customer traffic
* Changing routing policy or fallback behavior in a way that affects customer requests

h1. Rollout plan template (copy/paste)

h2. 1) Summary
* What is changing?
* Why now?
* Expected customer impact (best-case and worst-case)
* Who is on point during rollout (name + Slack channel)

h2. 2) Scope
* Environments: Hosted / Dedicated / Private
* Regions impacted
* Customer tiers or allowlists (if any)
* Request types: chat, completions, embeddings, rerank (as applicable)

h2. 3) Versioning and compatibility
* Model alias (if any)
* New version identifier (e.g., rw-llama-3-70b@2025-10-01)
* Backward compatibility notes (tool calling schema, output formatting, tokenization differences)
* Max context and max output token limits

h2. 4) Success criteria (must be explicit thresholds)
Define pass/fail thresholds for each category and the evaluation window. Minimum required categories:
* Reliability: 5xx rate, timeouts, admission rejects
* Latency: p50/p95 end-to-end and time-to-first-token for streaming
* Cost/efficiency: tokens/sec/GPU, cache hit rate, batch efficiency
* Quality: regression guardrail (eval set delta) and customer-reported issues

Include a table with thresholds (example):
||Metric||Window||Pass threshold||Fail threshold||Owner||
|p95 latency|30 min|<= +5% vs baseline|> +10% vs baseline|SRE oncall|
|5xx rate|30 min|<= +0.05% absolute|> +0.2% absolute|Platform oncall|
|Quality score (internal eval)|per run|>= baseline - 0.3|< baseline - 0.7|Applied ML|

h2. 5) Monitoring and dashboards
* Links to dashboards (by service/model/region)
* Alerts to enable (list)
* Trace/log queries for fast triage
* Who watches what at each ramp step

h2. 6) Rollout strategy
* Canary design: what % first, for how long, and what signals decide next step
* Ramp schedule (with timestamps)
* Controls: per-customer allowlist, per-region traffic caps, concurrency caps
* A/B test plan (if used): experiment id, assignment, evaluation criteria

h2. 7) Rollback and fallback
* Rollback trigger conditions (must map to thresholds)
* Rollback procedure reference (runbook link)
* Fallback policy (automatic): target version(s), ordering, and constraints
* What happens for in-flight requests and streaming responses

h2. 8) Customer communications
* Which customers must be notified (Dedicated/Private, contractually sensitive)
* Channel: email, support ticket, status page, in-product banner
* Timeline: before/at/after rollout
* Message content requirements: change summary, risk, opt-out/pinning path, support contact

h2. 9) Approvals
* Change class (per policy)
* Approvers and timestamps
* Approved change window

h2. 10) Post-rollout validation
* Final KPIs after full ramp
* Customer feedback summary
* Follow-up tasks and owners

h1. Notes
* The plan should be treated as the source of truth during an incident.
* If any section is not applicable, write N/A with a brief justification.

Title: Runbook: Canary, A/B, and Fallback for Model Version Rollouts

Runbook: Canary, A/B, and Fallback for Model Version Rollouts

h1. Purpose
This runbook describes the operational steps to roll out a new model version using Redwood Router policies, including canary ramps, A/B experiments, and automatic fallback rules.

h1. Preconditions (must be met before any ramp >0%)
* A published rollout plan exists and links the dashboards and thresholds.
* The new version is registered in the model registry and is READY_FOR_PROD.
* The following toggles are confirmed available for the target alias: per-region traffic split, per-customer allowlist, and an immediate revert mechanism.
* Oncall coverage: Platform + SRE are present for the first ramp step.

h1. Key concepts
* Model alias: customer-facing name (e.g., rw-chat-default).
* Version: immutable artifact id (e.g., rw-chat-default@2025-09-28).
* Policy: routing rules, including traffic splits and fallback ordering.
* Fallback chain: ordered list of compatible versions used when the primary version fails admission or violates health checks.

h1. Required configuration elements
Every rollout MUST explicitly define these elements in the Router policy record:
1. Primary version id
2. Fallback versions (ordered)
3. Health check gate for automatic fallback (HTTP 5xx + timeout + saturation)
4. Blast radius controls
   * max_traffic_percent (global)
   * per_region_caps (list of regions + caps)
   * allowlist_customers (optional)
5. Rollback target policy id (the prior known-good policy)

h1. Procedure: canary ramp (recommended default)
1. Create a new Router policy POLICY_NEW referencing the new version as primary and the old version as first fallback.
2. Set initial split to 0.5% (or smaller) and restrict to a customer allowlist when possible.
3. Enable the rollout_slo_guard alert bundle for the alias/region.
4. Observe for at least 30 minutes (or the window defined in the rollout plan).
5. If all pass thresholds are met, ramp to 5%, then 25%, then 50%, then 100% with explicit decision points at each step.
6. Record each decision (time, step, owner, rationale) in the rollout plan.

h1. Procedure: A/B experiment (optional)
Use A/B only when you need quality or customer outcomes comparisons that are not captured by baseline guardrails.

Steps:
1. Create experiment id in the Router: experiment=MODEL_VER_<date>.
2. Configure assignment (sticky by org_id) to avoid flipping user experience.
3. Set success metrics (quality proxy, customer engagement, or task completion).
4. Ensure safety regressions still trigger immediate rollback regardless of A/B results.

h1. Automatic fallback rules
Fallback is permitted only to versions marked compatible for the request type.

Required fallback triggers (minimum):
* Sustained elevated 5xx rate above fail threshold
* Sustained timeouts above fail threshold
* Admission rejects due to saturation above fail threshold

Operational note: fallback reduces errors but can mask quality regressions; quality guardrails must still be evaluated.

h1. Rollback procedure
Rollback means restoring the prior policy (POLICY_OLD) as the active policy for the alias.

Steps:
1. Set active policy to POLICY_OLD for all regions.
2. Disable traffic to the new version (set split to 0%).
3. Confirm metrics return to baseline within 15 minutes.
4. If metrics do not recover, escalate to runtime oncall (possible broader incident).

h1. Customer-impact communications
If rollback or fallback occurs after any customer traffic >5% or any Dedicated/Private customer is impacted, follow the comms guide and consider a status page update per the incident comms doc.

h1. References
* Change management policy
* Rollout SLO thresholds
* Model readiness requirements

Title: Cost Model API v1 — Performance Budget Worksheet (latency, caching, cardinality)

Cost Model API v1 — Performance Budget Worksheet (latency, caching, cardinality)

Owner: Thomas Baird (Perf/Cardinality)
Last review: 2026-02-18
Audience: Platform (Cost Model service), Console backend, Optimize backend, Telemetry/Analytics, SRE

Purpose
- Define the performance budget for Cost Model API v1 so Console (hot-path dashboards) and Optimize (what-if projections) have predictable latency and bounded responses.
- Translate “don’t explode cardinality” into concrete request bounds + caching rules + query patterns.
- Establish default timeouts and fallback behavior expectations for callers.

Scope (v1 endpoints)
- /v1/cost:estimate (single request estimate; used in request traces + inline views)
- /v1/cost:breakdown (aggregated breakdown for a time window; used for dashboard tables)
- /v1/cost:what_if (scenario projection; used by Optimize)

Non-goals
- This is not the billing system of record.
- This does not define pricing; only compute budgets and bounds.


A) Latency + availability targets (service-level)

Assumptions
- Cost Model API is called by internal services (Console, Optimize). Some calls are on a user-facing path.
- We must tolerate telemetry lag. When inputs are missing/stale, return partial results with explicit status flags (see “Degraded modes”).

Targets by endpoint (prod, steady state)

| Endpoint | Typical caller | Expected QPS (steady) | p50 target | p95 target | Hard timeout (server) | Caller timeout recommendation |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| estimate | Console trace drilldown, debugging tools | 150–400 | 25 ms | 80 ms | 200 ms | 250 ms |
| breakdown | Console dashboards | 30–80 | 120 ms | 450 ms | 1200 ms | 1500 ms |
| what_if | Optimize | 5–25 | 300 ms | 1200 ms | 2500 ms | 3000 ms |

Notes
- estimate must be “fast and boring”: memory-local computation + cached model/runtime parameters; no large fan-out.
- breakdown is allowed to hit pre-aggregated telemetry tables (or cached aggregates), but must have bounded result cardinality.
- what_if is explicitly slower; it may run multiple candidate computations but must still be bounded.

Availability / error budget (draft)
- Availability: 99.9% monthly for estimate + breakdown (internal).
- what_if: 99.5% monthly acceptable due to non-hot-path nature.


B) Compute budget + caching strategy

Key principle
- All endpoints must have a “cacheable core” keyed by stable inputs. Anything high-cardinality must be caller-provided or pre-aggregated upstream.

Caches in play
1) Model Catalog + runtime metadata cache (L1 in-process)
- Contents: model_id -> (arch, param_count_bucket, context_len, quant_profile_id defaults, kernel_path_id mapping), hardware_sku -> $/sec, throughput baselines
- TTL: 15 minutes
- Warmup: on deploy + periodic refresh
- Expected hit rate: > 99% after warm

2) Telemetry aggregate cache (L2 shared, e.g., redis/memcache) — for breakdown
- Key: (org_id, project_id?, env, model_id, route_id?, region, time_bucket, schema_version, group_by_set)
- TTL: 2–5 minutes for “today” buckets; 30–60 minutes for historical buckets
- Eviction: LRU; cap by per-tenant quota (to avoid a single org dominating)

3) What-if memoization (L1 + optional L2)
- Key: (org_id, base_workload_summary_hash, scenario_hash, schema_version)
- TTL: 10 minutes
- Guardrail: only memoize if the scenario passes “cheap to reuse” predicate (scenario is common and response size is small)

Cacheability rules (caller-visible)
- estimate responses include cache_status: HIT/MISS (internal header), and “inputs_resolved_at” timestamp.
- breakdown responses include “computed_from”: [cache, preagg_table, raw_rollup] and a “time_range_truncated” boolean.
- what_if responses include “confidence” and “assumption_profile_id” (not a cache signal, but used to interpret results).

Recommended caller behavior
- Console: for dashboards, prefer breakdown requests with (a) coarse time_bucket (>= 5m) and (b) small group_by sets.
- Optimize: batch what_if calls by workload_summary and dedupe scenarios client-side.


C) Cardinality constraints (hard bounds)

Why this exists
- We saw early prototypes produce “group_by everything” breakdowns that explode in both runtime and response size (and create unbounded cache keys).

Hard request bounds (enforced server-side)
- Max time range per request:
  - breakdown: 31 days (hard), 7 days recommended for interactive
  - estimate: single request only (no ranges)
  - what_if: max 24 hours of workload summary input (summarized, not raw)
- Max group_by dimensions per breakdown request: 3
- Max distinct groups returned: 200 (top-K + “other” bucket required)
- Max models per request: 10
- Max routes per request: 50 (but only if route_id is NOT in group_by)
- Max regions per request: 10
- Max quant_profile_ids per request: 5
- Max response size (serialized): 512 KB (reject or truncate with explicit “truncated” flag)

Allowed group_by dimensions (v1)
- org_id (implicit; never group_by)
- project_id (optional; not recommended unless customer is small)
- env (prod/staging)
- model_id
- route_id
- region
- deployment_mode (hosted/dedicated/private)
- quant_profile_id
- cache_status_bucket (HIT/MISS/PARTIAL; only if derived from rollups)

Explicitly disallowed as group_by (v1)
- request_id, user_id, api_key_id, prompt_hash, tool_name, function_name
- any free-form tag keys (e.g., “metadata.*”)
Reason: unbounded, high-entropy.

Top-K semantics
- When group cardinality > 200:
  - Return top 199 by total_cost, plus one “other” bucket.
  - Provide dropped_group_count.
  - Provide ordering metric (total_cost) and stable tie-breaking (lexicographic) for determinism.


D) Budget by computation stage (internal breakdown)

For estimate endpoint (target p95 <= 80 ms)
- Request validation + auth/tenancy: 5–10 ms
- Resolve model + hardware + pricing primitives (cached): 5–15 ms
- Compute prefill/decode token accounting + kv cache attribution: 10–25 ms
- Overhead allocation (simple rule): 5–15 ms
- Serialization: 2–8 ms

For breakdown endpoint (target p95 <= 450 ms)
- Auth + bounds validation: 10–20 ms
- Aggregate fetch (pre-aggregated telemetry): 60–250 ms
- Post-processing (top-K, other bucket, normalization): 30–120 ms
- Optional joins (model metadata for display names): 5–30 ms

For what_if endpoint (target p95 <= 1200 ms)
- Validate scenario + guardrails: 10–40 ms
- Workload summary normalization: 20–80 ms
- Scenario compute (batching/caching/quant deltas): 150–900 ms
- Confidence + assumption stamping: 10–60 ms


E) Degraded modes + fallback behavior

Degraded modes we expect
1) Telemetry lag / missing bucket
- behavior: return partial with status=PARTIAL_INPUTS and missing_ranges list (bounded to 20 entries)
- do NOT block waiting for telemetry catch-up

2) Cache backend unhealthy
- estimate: continue (L1 only); never depend on L2
- breakdown: fall back to direct pre-agg query path; tighten bounds (max groups 100) and set status=DEGRADED_CACHE
- what_if: continue; skip L2 memoization; tighten scenario max_candidates

3) Downstream model catalog slowdown
- behavior: use stale cache up to 60 minutes; stamp “metadata_stale=true”

Caller fallback expectations (important for Console)
- Console must have a feature-flagged fallback to existing (legacy) cost breakdown for 30 days post-launch.
- If Cost Model API p95 > 800 ms for breakdown over 10 min window, Console should reduce refresh frequency + use cached UI data.


F) Request shaping guidance (to prevent expensive patterns)

Console dashboard recommended query patterns
- Time bucket: 5m for last 24h; 1h for 7d; 1d for 31d
- group_by: model_id + route_id (avoid adding region unless the user explicitly filters)
- Always pass filters when available (model_id, route_id, region) rather than using group_by to discover everything.

Optimize what_if recommended patterns
- Provide workload summary, not raw request samples.
- Cap scenario count per request to 5.
- Prefer one scenario per call if you need low latency; batch scenarios if you accept p95 ~1.2s.


G) Open questions / decisions needed (as of 2026-02-18)
1) Do we need a separate “async breakdown job” endpoint for heavy dashboard loads?
- Proposed: not for v1; revisit if breakdown QPS > 150 sustained.

2) Should route_id be allowed in group_by by default?
- Console wants it; perf risk if customers have high route cardinality.
- Proposal: allow route_id group_by only when time_range <= 7d OR time_bucket >= 1h.

3) Response truncation semantics
- Decision needed: reject vs truncate.
- Proposal: truncate with “other” bucket, plus explicit flags. Reject only if response would exceed 2 MB.


H) Action items (next 2–3 weeks)
- [Ethan Park] Confirm endpoint timeouts + default server limits in cost-model service config. (ENG-4821)
- [Thomas Baird] Add request bounds + top-K enforcement to breakdown endpoint; include deterministic ordering tests. (ENG-4822)
- [Logan Wright] Ensure pre-aggregated telemetry tables support required group_by sets with bounded scan. (ENG-4823)
- [Chloe Martin] Update Console integration to use recommended time buckets + filters; avoid “group_by region” by default. (ENG-4825)
- [Rafael Mendes] Draft SLO + alert thresholds aligned with p95 targets and degraded-mode behavior. (ENG-4827)

Appendix: Quick checklist for PR reviews
- Does the change add a new group_by dimension? If yes, is it bounded and documented?
- Does the change increase response size risk? If yes, confirm truncation behavior + tests.
- Does the change add new cache keys? If yes, confirm key includes schema_version and has bounded cardinality.
- Does the change affect p95? If yes, include benchmark results (staging load test or microbench).

Title: stability-guard-ops-cadence-and-holdback-map-mar-2025

stability-guard-ops-cadence-and-holdback-map-mar-2025

Purpose:
This is a compact, operational playpad for a stability-first rollout. Focus: minimal holdback windows, granular SLO thresholds, and short-cadence observability checks so we can iterate quickly without sweeping rollbacks.

Scope:
- Applies to minor and medium feature rollouts (non-breaking model config changes, routing adjustments, autoscaling policy tweaks).
- Not intended for major infra migrations or schema-incompatible changes. Separate plan required.

High-level rollout calendar (2-week sprint cadence):
- Day -7: Feature branch merges gated by unit/integration green. Notify release-channel.
- Day -5: Canary build deployed to staging; full run of smoke + e2e subset (20m budget).
- Day -3: Canary -> canary-prod (1% traffic) for 4h with active monitoring.
- Day -2: Expand to 5% if no SLO regressions. Prepare holdback lanes.
- Day 0: Gradual ramp to 25% in 3 step increments (25% each 30m, 1h, 2h) then evaluate for full rollout.
- Day +1 to +3: Observability sweep and regression evaluation; decide final 100% cutover by Day +3.

Minimal holdback & safety lanes (practical heuristics):
- Holdback tiers: 1% (micro-canary), 5% (small), 25% (mid), 100% (full).
- Safety triggers (any of these -> immediate holdback rollback to previous routing):
  - 99th pct latency increase > 40% sustained for 5 minutes relative to baseline
  - Error rate (5xx or inference errors) > 0.8% absolute or 3x baseline for 3 minutes
  - Token cost per request increase > 30% (unplanned cost spike detection)
  - User-facing correctness regression alerts from eval-suite (automated prompt-set fail rate > 5%)
- If trigger fires: reduce to prior stable tier and open a P0 investigation channel.

Preflight checklist (must be green before Day -5):
- [ ] Merge completed and tagged (PR link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/719)
- [ ] CI green: unit + integration + model-smoke tests <= 45m
- [ ] Baseline telemetry snapshot captured (latency, error, cost) for last 72h
- [ ] Rollout config stored in release-configs repo with rollback marker
- [ ] On-call rotation assigned for release window (see shift roster below)
- [ ] Observability dashboards and alerting tuned for this release (dash link in linked_artifacts)

Smoke test matrix (quick guide):
- Latency: synthetic 95th/99th over short bursts (5m window) for peak path
- Stability: 10k sample requests through main route, assert < 0.2% unexpected errors
- Regression: run golden-prompts eval set (subset of 200 prompts) and compare to baseline metrics
- Resource: check GPU memory, host CPU drain, queue lengths during 5m ramp test

Rollback decision tree (fast-path):
- Operator sees alert -> immediate step-down to last stable tier -> post-step notification to #release-ops and #sre -> start triage -> if Hotfix, target patch branch and initiate micro-deploy.
- If root cause unknown and impact > P1, schedule mandatory pause and paging of infra, serving-runtime, and model teams.

Communication plan (short blurbs for channels):
- #release-ops: minute-by-minute status during canary windows; use status tags [canary], [holdback], [rollback]
- Incident bridge: use scheduled Zoom bridge only for P1; otherwise use Slack huddle + async doc (confluence link)
- Customer notice: Only if user-visible error > 5% or region SLA affected > 10% — draft template below.

Draft release notes (internal + external snippets):
- Internal (for SRE/Product):
  - "Opt-in routing policy change to reduce tail latency for small-model workloads. Targets non-legacy routes. Initial canary 1% on Mar 12 2025. Monitoring: latency p95/p99 and inference error rate."
- External (changelog blurb):
  - "Improved routing for small-context requests to reduce latency on chat integrations. No action required by customers; rollout will be gradual over next 72 hours."

Observability playbook (what to watch during each stage):
- Canary (1%): p50/p95/p99, errors, token-cost per request, queue length, host OOM signals. Checkpoint every 15m.
- Small (5%): Add golden-prompts regression job. Checkpoint every 30m.
- Mid (25%): Full traffic simulation for peak 10m window; validate tracing span volumes and tail latencies. Checkpoint every 60m.

Shift roster suggestion (Day-of):
- Release lead: Priya Rao (primary)
- SRE: Marcus Li (on-call)
- Serving-runtime SME: Elena Gonzalez (warm standby)
- Product liaison: Samir Desai (customer comms)
- Extra observer: Tasha Nguyen (telemetry tuning)

Post-release: 72h retro snapshot items
- Collect: telemetry diff, fail-rate heatmap, golden-prompts pass rate, cost delta report
- Owner assignments for regressions > 2%: triage owner + remediation plan within 48h
- Suggested retro agenda: 30m signal review, 30m root-cause deep dive (if needed), 30m action planning

Open questions / TODOs:
- Confirm whether token-cost thresholds should be absolute or relative for model family X (ask Research/Applied-ML).
- Decide whether to auto-rollback on cost spikes during low-traffic hours — flagged for architecture review.
- Add synthetic traffic job that mimics vector-search-heavy workloads to the staging smoke pipeline (INF-4242).

Appendix: quick copy-paste customer-facing incident template
- Subject: Temporary degradation to inference latency for some customers
- Body: "On Mar 12 we rolled a routing change intended to reduce tail latency. A small percentage of requests experienced higher latency; we paused the rollout at 25% and reverted to the prior routing. No data loss. We are continuing post-release analysis and will follow up with root cause and remediation timeline."

Notes to self (scratch):
- Keep the canary window visible on the team dashboard and pin the three key metrics at top.
- If we get a false positive from jitter in p99, consider smoothing windows to 3m median to avoid noisy rollbacks.
- Follow up with applied-ml on golden prompts selection size — 200 might be small for model families with high variance.

End of doc.

Title: Chat streaming truncated after transient pipeline reset for dedicated customer

Chat streaming truncated after transient pipeline reset for dedicated customer

Issue summary: Customer reports that SSE/WebSocket streaming responses abruptly truncate mid-sentence following short transient errors in the serving pipeline (worker restart / routing flip). Impact: customer chat sessions for multiple users end with partial output (last token(s) missing), leading to degraded UX and automated retry loops on their side. Environment: LexiVoice dedicated cluster in us-west-2, running dedicated pool rp-lexivoice-usw2 on redwood-rlhf-13b pinned version v2026-02-28. Observed intermittently starting 2026-03-10 18:12 UTC and reproducible for customer under bursty input patterns (20-30 concurrent long-form chats).
1) Use LexiVoice account credentials to send a streaming chat request to /v1/chat with stream=true and model=redwood-rlhf-13b (pinned).
2) Send a long prompt that triggers ~800-1200 token response (typical LexiVoice assistant reply),
3) Simulate burst concurrency: 20 simultaneous streaming requests from distinct client sockets,
4) While streams are in-flight, trigger a light worker restart or cause a routing update (in test: toggle an autoscaler event or redeploy a serving worker).
5) Observe that a subset (~5-12%) of client streams terminate with a final socket close before end-of-stream token; no explicit 5xx returned to client.
Streaming socket closes without final chunk and without explicit error payload. Client receives partial text and then a TCP FIN/WS close. On platform side, logs show a short-lived pipeline reset (worker SIGTERM and graceful restart) correlated with router reassignments. No 5xx spike on public API layer, but internal worker logs show 'inflight-request-evicted' and 'kv-cache-miss -> eviction' in proximity.
Streaming responses should continue to completion or, if interrupted, return a clear error frame (HTTP 5xx or SSE event) and ensure client can resume or receive a final summary chunk. Model fallback or worker restart should trigger graceful draining of in-flight streams rather than silent truncation.
2026-03-10T18:12:23Z router[router-23]: reassigning request id=aa3f... to worker w-772 due to capacity reshuffle
2026-03-10T18:12:23Z worker[w-771]: SIGTERM received, beginning graceful shutdown, inflight=7
2026-03-10T18:12:24Z worker[w-771]: kv-cache eviction triggered for model redwood-rlhf-13b shard=2
2026-03-10T18:12:24Z worker[w-772]: accepted request id=aa3f..., start-forwarding-kv-cache-mismatch
2026-03-10T18:12:24Z worker[w-771]: inflight-request-evicted id=aa3f..., closed-connection-without-error
2026-03-10T18:12:24Z api-gateway[gw-9]: downstream connection closed by peer for client c-984 (status unknown)
Initial triage: patterns point to graceful shutdown window not fully draining SSE/WS streams when a worker is restarted under load; router reassigns requests mid-generation rather than waiting for completion.
Hypothesis A: draining timeout on worker is too short under long-response workloads leading to abrupt close before remote worker can finish sending final chunks.
Hypothesis B: KV cache miss when reassigning a long-running request causes partial output to be lost when the new worker cannot reconstruct the current generation state quickly, leading to immediate connection termination.
Temporary reproduction in staging: forced SIGTERM with 5s drain results in ~40% of streams truncating; increasing drain to 30s eliminated truncation in staging tests but increased tail latency and backpressure on autoscaler.
Observation: api-gateway does not always surface a 502/503 to client when downstream closes mid-stream; need to verify gateway stream-forwarding behavior on abrupt downstream close.
LexiVoice (customer) - 2026-03-10 18:45 UTC: We're seeing our users get partial replies frequently this evening. No consistent error codes on our side; clients just receive truncated text. Please prioritize.
Support (Aisha) - 2026-03-10 19:00 UTC: Thanks — triaging now. Can you provide 3 sample request IDs and approximate timestamps? Also confirm whether you use exponential backoff retries client-side.
LexiVoice - 2026-03-10 19:07 UTC: Sample request IDs: aa3f4c2b, b9f2d001, c7a1e33e. We do a single immediate retry on client timeout; not exponential.
SRE (Ben) - 2026-03-10 20:10 UTC: Reproduced in staging by forcing worker restarts. Short-term mitigation: increasing worker graceful-drain to 30s reduced truncation rate to near 0 in staging. However, this impacted autoscaling responsiveness.
Eng (Carla) - 2026-03-11 09:12 UTC: Noted kv-cache rebuild on takeover is expensive for large-context requests; propose warm handoff where router waits for new worker to prefetch KV context before reassigning the stream. Filing platform design spike.
Support (Aisha) - 2026-03-12 08:22 UTC: Applied temporary config change to LexiVoice dedicated pool: increased drain timeout and enabled connection-close-propagation flag on gateway. Observing fewer truncations in last 12 hours.
1) Engineering to implement prefetch warm-handoff prototype (router waits for KV sync) — tracked in PR #889.
2) Adjust worker graceful-drain default to 20s for dedicated pools with long-response heuristics while we evaluate tail effects.
3) Modify api-gateway to translate downstream abrupt closes to explicit 5xx frames for streaming clients to make failure visible to customers.
4) Run a controlled canary on LexiVoice pool with warm-handoff enabled and monitor truncation rate and autoscaler behavior for 72 hours.
5) Postmortem and customer communication draft once canary completes.
In Progress: temporary mitigations applied (increased drain timeout, gateway close propagation). Engineering has a design spike and a PR prototype for warm-handoff. Tracking canary rollout and will follow up with permanent fix and postmortem.
Multiple LexiVoice production chat sessions experienced truncated streaming replies, impacting end-user experience and causing retries. Affects ~5-12% of long-form streaming requests under bursty concurrency in their dedicated pool.

Title: micro-eval gating scratchpad

micro-eval gating scratchpad

Purpose:
Quick personal notebook for an idea: introduce a lightweight, in-production micro-evaluation harness to gate model rollouts and fallbacks. Goal is to detect small but important regressions (hallucination rate, safety triggers, instruction-following) on a per-release basis without full-batch offline evals.

Motivation / problem:
- We push model variants frequently; current rollout relies mainly on perf metrics (p50/p95 latency, errors) and a small manual eval set.
- Subtle regressions in factuality and instruction compliance slip through until customers raise tickets.
- Running large eval suites for every commit is expensive and slow. Need fast signal that integrates into canaries.

High-level idea:
- Ship a micro-eval harness embedded in the Serving runtime that:
  - Samples a tiny, targeted set of checks per request stream (randomized, low rate).
  - Uses lightweight probes: short QA pairs, instruction-following prompts, and safety-pattern detectors.
  - Aggregates signals per model-version and per-route, computes rolling deltas vs baseline, and flags regressions to Rollout Controller.

User stories:
- As an SRE/ML engineer I want to see a daily micro-eval report per model so I can decide whether to pause a rollout.
- As a PM I want thresholds (relative drop in pass-rate) that trigger automated canary rollback so we avoid broad outages of correctness.
- As a privacy officer I want probes to never include customer data and remain synthetic/owned by Redwood.

Probe types (fast):
- Factual QA (1–2 sentence prompts with verifiable answers).
- Instruction compliance (e.g., "summarize in 2 bullets").
- Toxicity/safety heuristics (fast regex + small classifier).
- Structured extraction (schema conformance checks).

Architecture sketch:
- Probe generator: centrally managed corpus (small, tagged). Exposed via the control plane.
- Runtime hooks: sample X% of requests to attach a hidden probe in parallel (no latency impact on caller). Probe executes async and writes to micro-eval stream.
- Aggregator: lightweight service that computes pass-rate deltas, p-values, and simple drift metrics.
- Rollout integration: expose signals to Console + automatic gating policies (threshold-based or Bayesian).

Acceptance criteria / metrics:

Title: Gateway: whitelist + validate quickstart template telemetry headers

Gateway: whitelist + validate quickstart template telemetry headers

Context: DevEx quickstart templates need a reliable, low-cardinality way to tag traffic as template-generated so we can measure activation funnel and time-to-first-success without relying on parsing user-agent strings. Today the API gateway drops unknown `x-*` headers by default; templates adding a telemetry header would silently lose that tag. This PR introduces an explicit allowlist in the gateway for a small set of template telemetry headers and performs strict validation to prevent abuse, high-cardinality explosions, and accidental PII leakage.

What this does: Adds a `template telemetry` header allowlist and validator at the gateway edge. Allowed headers are normalized into a structured internal context object that can be consumed by downstream logging/metrics/analytics (follow-up PRs). Invalid values are rejected with a 400 (clear error message) to avoid partial/ambiguous telemetry.

Allowed headers (v1): `x-redwood-template-id` (e.g. `rag-agent`), `x-redwood-template-version` (semver like `0.3.1`), `x-redwood-template-lang` (`python`|`typescript`), `x-redwood-template-origin` (`cli`|`github`), `x-redwood-template-otel` (`enabled`|`disabled`).

Validation rules: values must match `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._-]{0,63}$` (lowercase enforced), max length 64, no whitespace, no commas/quotes/newlines. `x-redwood-template-version` is additionally checked as semver-like `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` with an optional `-prerelease` suffix. Any header not in the allowlist continues to be stripped by default.

Security/privacy notes: These headers are intended to be low-cardinality and non-user-content. This PR does not accept arbitrary key/value tagging. We do not log raw request headers; we only log the validated, normalized fields. Review requested from Security and Observability to confirm cardinality + redaction posture.

Operational notes: This is required for the Quickstart Templates KPI dashboard (PM-912). Follow-up work will plumb these fields into usage analytics (Console filter work) and template repos will keep sending these headers behind an opt-in flag to avoid issues with restrictive corporate proxies.

Testing: Added unit tests for allowlist behavior, validation failures, normalization, and a regression test that unknown headers are still dropped.

Added tests for rejection and documented examples. If we see unexpected cardinality we can also sample/drop downstream, but the intent is low-cardinality only.
